## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority or influence with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they did so.*

*The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the modest price, and above all this collection—unique, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library has gathered together six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works dealing with every age, place, language, and form.*

*Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.*

Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Book One: Genuine Homilies

[Note: To understand the arrangement that we followed in reprinting the homilies of the Venerable Bede, see volume I of this edition of Bede, or volume VX of Patrology, column 30, number 31, the historical notice written by Mabillon. — Editor.]

## Homily One: On the Feast of the Annunciation of Blessed Mary

[Column 0009A]

**Luke 1.** “At that time the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary,” etc.

The reading of the holy Gospel that we have heard today commends to us the beginning of our redemption, dearly beloved brothers. It tells how an angel was sent from God in heaven to the Virgin, in order to proclaim the Son of God’s new birth in the flesh, through which we may cast off our harmful old nature, be renewed, and be counted among the children of God. Therefore, if we wish to be worthy to attain the gifts of the salvation that was promised, let us carefully receive with attentive ears its beginnings.

[Column 0009B] “The angel Gabriel,” it says, “was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph.” Surely the beginning of humanity’s restoration was fittingly marked by an angel being sent from God to a virgin who was to be consecrated by divine childbirth, because the first cause of human ruin occurred when the serpent was sent by the devil to deceive the woman with the spirit of pride. Indeed, the devil himself came in the serpent, and after deceiving our first parents stripped the human race of the glory of immortality. Therefore, since death entered through a woman, life rightly returns through a woman. The one, seduced by the devil through the serpent, offered her husband a taste of death; the other, instructed by God through an angel, gave birth to the author of salvation for the world.

Therefore the angel Gabriel was sent by God. We rarely read that angels appearing to human beings are identified by name. Yet whenever this occurs, it occurs for the purpose of indicating, even through the name itself, what they have come to perform.

For Gabriel is said to mean “strength of God.” And rightly does he shine forth under such a name, because he bears witness to God who was about to be born in the flesh. Concerning him the Prophet says in the Psalm: “The Lord is strong and powerful, the Lord powerful in battle” (Psalm 24). That battle, surely, in which he was coming to conquer the powers of the air and to rescue the world from their tyranny.

[Column 0010A] “To a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin’s name was Mary.” What is said concerning the house of David pertains not only to Joseph but also to Mary. For the Law had commanded that each man should take a wife from his own tribe and family, as the Apostle also attests when writing to Timothy: “Remember that Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, is of the seed of David according to my Gospel” (2 Timothy 2).

Christ truly was born from the seed of David because his incorrupt mother derived her true origin from the stock of David. But as to why the Lord wished to be conceived and born not from an unbetrothed virgin but from a woman betrothed to a man, the Fathers offer many reasonable explanations. The chief among them is that she should not be condemned as guilty of fornication if she bore a son without having a husband. Another is that in the circumstances that naturally required domestic care, the woman who had given birth might be supported by the assistance of a husband.

Blessed Mary therefore needed to have a husband who would be the most reliable witness to her integrity and the most faithful guardian of the Lord and Savior born from her. He would also, according to the Law, bring offerings to the temple on behalf of the child and, when persecution threatened, carry him with his mother to Egypt and bring them back again. He would provide him with many other necessities demanded by the weakness of the humanity he had assumed.

[Column 0010C] It was not greatly harmful if someone temporarily believed that he was Joseph’s son, since after his ascension, when the Apostles preached and all believers openly confessed that he had been born from a virgin, it became clear that this was so.

Nor should we pass over the fact that the blessed Mother of God also received testimony through her distinguished merits in her very name. For it is interpreted as “star of the sea.” And she shone like an exceptional star amid the waves of the fleeting world through the grace of her singular privilege.

“And the angel entered to her and said, ‘Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.’”

This greeting is as unheard-of in ordinary human usage as it is appropriate to the dignity of blessed Mary. For she was truly full of grace, to whom divine generosity granted the privilege of being the first among women to offer God the most glorious gift of virginity. Therefore she rightly deserved to enjoy both an angelic appearance and an angelic address, since she strove to imitate the angelic life.

She was truly full of grace, to whom it was granted to give birth to Jesus Christ himself, through whom grace and truth came to be. And therefore the Lord was truly with her: first, he had lifted her from earthly things to desire heavenly things through the love of a new chastity; afterward, through the medium of human nature, he consecrated her with the entire fullness of divinity.

She was also truly blessed among women, since, without any precedent among womankind, she rejoiced in the honor of motherhood together with the beauty of virginity and, as befitted a virgin mother, gave birth to God the Son.

After she had been troubled, as human weakness is, both by the vision of the angel and by the unusual greeting, the same angel immediately encouraged her through repeated words not to be afraid. To drive away her fear, as he would with someone well known and familiar, he called her by her own name and carefully explained why he had called her full of grace.

[Column 0011A] “Do not be afraid, Mary,” he said, “for you have found grace with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a Son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High.”

The order of the words should be carefully noted and inserted all the more firmly into the heart, since it is plainly evident that the entire substance of our redemption lies in them. For he most explicitly proclaims the Lord Jesus—that is, our Savior—to be both the true Son of God the Father and the true Son of a human mother.

“Behold,” he says, “you will conceive in your womb and bear a Son.” Recognize that this is truly a human being who assumed the substance of flesh from the Virgin’s flesh.

“He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High.” Confess that he is also the true God from true God, the Son eternally coeternal with the eternal Father.

But when it is said in the future tense, “He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High,” no one should understand this to mean that the Lord Christ did not exist before the Virgin’s childbirth. Rather, let us understand it in this way: the power of divine majesty that the Son of God possessed eternally was received by this same human being, born in time, so that there might be one person of our Mediator and Redeemer in two natures.

“And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.” By the throne of David he means the kingdom of the Israelite people, which David in his own time governed with faithful devotion, while the Lord both commanded and assisted him.

Therefore the Lord gave our Redeemer the throne of David his father when he ordained that he should become incarnate from David’s lineage, so that the people whom David ruled by temporal authority he himself might raise by spiritual grace to an eternal kingdom, of which the Apostle says: “He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians 1).

[Column 0012A] This is why the same people, instructed by divine inspiration, when he was hastening to Jerusalem to suffer, joyfully sang his praises: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (John 12). And according to another Evangelist: “Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that comes” (Mark 11).

For the time had come when the king of the world, redeemed by his blood, was to be recognized—not only as the king of David’s house, but also as the king of the whole Church, indeed as the founder and ruler of all the ages.

Therefore, after the angel had said, “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father,” he rightly added immediately: “And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever.” By the house of Jacob he means the universal Church, which through faith and confession of Christ belongs to the inheritance of the patriarchs, whether in those who derive the origin of their flesh from the stock of the patriarchs or in those who, born in the flesh from other nations, have been reborn in Christ through the spiritual washing.

In this house he will reign forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end. He reigns in it in the present life when, dwelling in the hearts of the elect through their faith and love, he rules them and guides them by continual protection toward receiving the gifts of heavenly reward.

He will reign in the future when, after the condition of temporal exile has ended, he brings these same people into the dwelling of their heavenly homeland. There, continually instructed by the vision of his presence, they rejoice in doing nothing except devoting themselves to his praises.

[Column 0012C] “But Mary said to the angel, ‘How will this happen, since I do not know a man?’”

“How,” she says, “can it happen that I should conceive and bear a son, when I have resolved to complete my life in the chastity of virginity?”

She does not ask this as an unbeliever, wondering whether the angel’s words can be fulfilled. Rather, certain that what she was then hearing from the angel and had earlier read as spoken by the Prophet had to be fulfilled, she asks in what order it was to be accomplished. The Prophet who foretold that this would happen did not say how it could happen, but reserved that explanation for the angel.

[Column 0012D] “The angel answered and said to her, ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.’”

The Holy Spirit, coming upon the Virgin, displayed the efficacy of his divine power in her in two ways. He purified her mind, as far as human weakness permits, from every stain of vice, so that she might be worthy of a heavenly birth; and in her womb, by his operation alone, he created the holy and venerable body of our Redeemer. That is, without any intervention of a man, he formed sacred flesh from the Virgin’s flesh, untouched by defilement.

The one whom he first plainly called the Holy Spirit, he again named the power of the Most High, in accordance with what the Lord said when promising his disciples the coming of the same Spirit: “And I am sending the promise of my Father upon you; but you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24).

The power of the Most High overshadowed the blessed Mother of God because, when the Holy Spirit filled her heart, he tempered it against every heat of carnal desire, cleansed it from temporal longings, and consecrated both her mind and her body with heavenly gifts.

“Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God,” because what you will conceive through the sanctification of the Spirit will be holy when it is born.

The birth corresponds to the conception, so that you who conceive as a virgin contrary to the custom of human nature may give birth to the Son of God beyond the ordinary course of human experience. All human beings are conceived in iniquity and born in sins. But all who, by God’s gift, have been predestined to eternal life are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit.

Our Redeemer alone, having deigned to become incarnate for us, was born holy at once, because he was conceived without iniquity.

[Note: Codex A of the Bibliothèque de l’Arsenal in Paris adds: “The Son of God was born, because, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, he was conceived from the Virgin.”]

[Column 0013B] In the words, “The power of the Most High will overshadow you,” we may reasonably understand something deeper concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

We say that we are overshadowed when, under the burning midday sun, we place a tree or some other kind of shelter between ourselves and the sun, so that its heat or light may be made more bearable for us.

Our Redeemer is therefore not inappropriately represented by the sun’s light or heat: he illuminates us with the knowledge of truth and inflames us with love. Hence he himself says through the Prophet: “But for you who fear my name, the sun of justice will rise” (Malachi 4).

The blessed Virgin received the rays of this sun when she conceived the Lord. But that same sun—that is, the divinity of our Redeemer—covered itself with human nature as with a kind of shelter, by which means the Virgin’s womb was able to bear him. Thus the power of the Most High overshadowed her, while Christ’s divine power both filled her with its presence and veiled itself in the substance of our weakness so that it could be contained by her.

[Column 0013C] “And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age.”

He does not encourage her to faith as though she were unbelieving through examples. Rather, because she already believed well what she had heard, he recounts further miracles of heavenly providence, so that she who was to bear the Lord as a virgin might also recognize that the Lord’s forerunner would be born from an aged and long-barren parent.

Nor is it surprising, according to the historical account, that Elizabeth is called Mary’s kinswoman, although earlier one is said to have arisen from the house of David and the other from the daughters of Aaron.

For we read that Aaron himself, from the tribe of Judah—from which David also arose—took as his wife Elizabeth, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, who was leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness when the Israelites departed from Egypt.

Again, during the reigns of David’s descendants, we read that Jehoiada the high priest took a wife from the royal tribe, namely Jehosheba, daughter of King Jehoram. This is the Jehoiada whose son Zechariah, an equally holy man, was stoned between the temple and the altar, as the Lord himself also testifies in the Gospel when he mentions the blessed martyrs.

Thus the two tribes—the royal and the priestly—are shown always to have been joined to one another by kinship.

[Column 0014A] Such a union could also have arisen in more recent times, when women were given in marriage from one tribe to another. Thus it could plainly be established that the blessed Mother of God, who descended from the royal tribe, possessed kinship of lineage with the priestly tribe, a circumstance most perfectly suited to heavenly ministries [Codex A: “mysteries”].

For it was necessary that the Mediator of God and human beings, appearing in the world, should derive the origin of his flesh from both tribes, since in the humanity he assumed he was to possess both offices: that of priest and that of king.

His royal power, by which he grants his elect an everlasting kingdom, is attested by the present reading of the holy Gospel: “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

His pontifical dignity, in which he deigned to offer the sacrifice of his flesh for our redemption, is attested by the Prophet, who says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110).

Having received such great grace, let us see upon what height of humility blessed Mary continues to stand.

[Column 0014B] “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

She displays a great steadfastness of humility when, although chosen to be a mother, she calls herself the handmaid of her Creator.

The angelic oracle proclaims her blessed among women, and she is taught mysteries of our redemption still unknown to the other mortals. Yet she does not exalt herself individually because of the singular excellence of her greater merit. Rather, mindful in every respect of her condition and of God’s gracious favor, she humbly joins herself to the company of Christ’s maidservants and devoutly performs for Christ the service that is commanded.

“Let it be done to me,” she says according to your word: let it be done so that the Holy Spirit, coming upon me, may make me worthy of heavenly mysteries; let it be done so that in my womb the Son of God may assume the form of human substance and, for the redemption of the world, may proceed like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber.

Dearly beloved brothers, following her voice and mind according to our ability, let us remember that we are servants of Christ in all our acts and movements. Let us dedicate all the members of our body to his service and direct the entire attention of our mind toward fulfilling his will. Thus, having received his gifts, let us render thanks by living rightly, so that we may deserve to be worthy of receiving greater gifts.

[Column 0014D] Let us earnestly pray with the blessed Mother of God that it may be done to us according to his word—namely, the word by which he himself, explaining the reason for his incarnation, says: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3).

There is no doubt that he will graciously deign to hear us more quickly when we cry out to him from the depths, for whose sake, while we still did not know him, Jesus Christ our Lord himself deigned to descend into this deep valley of tears.

He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily Two: On the Feast of the Visitation of Blessed Mary

[Column 0015A]

**Luke 1.** “At that time Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah; and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth,” etc.

The reading of the holy Gospel that we have heard both proclaims to us the beginnings of our redemption, which we must always venerate, and commends to us the saving remedies of humility, which we must always imitate.

Because the human race had perished after being infected by the plague of pride, it was fitting that the earliest moments of the salvation then beginning should immediately display the medicine of humility by which it was to be healed.

And because death had entered the world through the rashness of a deceived woman, it was appropriate [alternative reading: “had been appropriate”] that, as a sign of returning life, devout women should anticipate one another in services of humility and piety.

Therefore the blessed Mother of God first shows us the road to the heights of the heavenly homeland: a road of humility, and one worthy of veneration no less for its example of devotion than for its example of chastity.

The glory of a virginal and undefiled body indicates what life is like in the heavenly city for which we sigh—a city where “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven”—and it also indicates the outstanding virtue of mind by which we must attain that city.

For, as we learned from the preceding reading of the holy Gospel, after she had been exalted through an angelic vision and greeting, and after she had learned that she was to be burdened with a heavenly childbirth, she did not in any way exalt herself because of the heavenly gifts, as though they came from herself.

Rather, in order to become increasingly suited to divine gifts, she fixed the step of her mind in the keeping of humility and replied to the archangel who announced the good news to her: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

[Column 0015C] As we heard in today’s reading, she took care to display to human beings the same humility that she had shown to the angel—and, what is a greater virtue, she showed it even to those beneath her.

For who does not know that a virgin consecrated to God holds a higher rank than a woman devoted to God? Who would doubt that the mother of the eternal King is rightly to be preferred to the mother of a soldier?

Nevertheless, mindful of the Scripture’s command, “The greater you are, humble yourself in everything” (Sirach 3), as soon as the angel who had spoken to her returned to heaven, she arose and climbed into the hill country. Carrying God in her womb, she sought the dwellings of God’s servants and requested their conversation.

[Column 0015D] It was fitting that she went into the hill country after the angel’s appearance. Having tasted the sweetness of the heavenly citizens, she moved by the steps of humility toward the heights of virtue.

She therefore entered the house of Zechariah and Elizabeth, whom she knew would give birth to the Lord’s servant and forerunner, and greeted her—not as someone doubtful of the oracle she had received, but as one who wished to rejoice with her over the gift that she had learned her fellow servant had received; not to confirm the angel’s word by the testimony of the woman, but so that a young virgin might diligently offer service to a woman advanced in age.

[Column 0016A] “When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.”

As blessed Mary opened her mouth to greet her, Elizabeth was immediately filled with the Holy Spirit, and John too was filled with the Spirit. Taught by one and the same Spirit, she recognized the woman who was greeting her, and honored her with the blessing due to the mother of her Lord; he understood that the Lord himself was being carried in the Virgin’s womb and, because his tongue was not yet able to speak, greeted him with a leaping heart.

Before he was born, he indicated by every means available to him how devoutly and willingly he would fulfill the office of his forerunner when the Lord came. The time had arrived for the angel’s statement to be fulfilled: “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1).

[Column 0016B] “Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and exclaimed with a loud voice.”

Rightly with a loud voice, because she recognized the great gifts of God; rightly with a loud voice, because she felt bodily present the one whom she knew to be present everywhere.

“Loud voice” should be understood not so much as a clamorous voice as a devout one. For she who burned with the fullness of the Holy Spirit could not praise the Lord with merely a modest devotion of voice. She bore in her womb the one than whom no one born of women would be greater [the Basel Edition reads *is*]; and she rejoiced that he had come who, conceived from the flesh of a virgin mother, would be called and would be the Son of the Most High.

“But she exclaimed and said, ‘Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.’”

She was not merely blessed among women, but was specially distinguished among blessed women by a greater blessing.

“Blessed is the fruit of your womb.” He too was not blessed in the general manner of the saints, but as the Apostle says: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9).

The Psalmist bears witness in mystical language to the birth of this fruit, saying: “For the Lord will give goodness, and our land will give its fruit” (Psalm 84).

The Lord gave goodness because he determined to free the human race from the guilt of transgression through his only-begotten Son. He gave goodness because he consecrated the temple of the Virgin’s womb for the Son’s entrance by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

And our land gave its fruit because the same virgin, whose body came from the earth, gave birth to a Son who was, in his divinity, equal to God the Father, but, in the truth of his flesh, consubstantial with her.

Isaiah also, looking toward the time of human redemption, says concerning this: “On that day the bud of the Lord will be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth will be exalted” (Isaiah 4).

The bud of the Lord was in magnificence and glory when the eternal Son of God, appearing in the flesh in time, shone brightly before the world through the greatness of heavenly virtues.

The fruit of the earth was exalted when the flesh that God had assumed from our nature as mortal was raised to the heavens, already made immortal by the power of the resurrection.

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.”

She is blessed beyond comparison because she received the glory of the divine bud and preserved the crown of integrity.

Blessed are you among women, through whose virginal childbirth the curse of the first mother was removed from those born of women.

Blessed is the fruit of her womb, through whom we received once for all the fruit of incorruption and of the heavenly inheritance that we had lost in Adam.

And truly and uniquely blessed is he who did not, in the manner of our race, receive the grace of blessing from the Lord after he was born, but came blessed to save the world, in the name of the Lord [the Basel Edition omits *who*].

“And from where has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

Oh, what humility in the mind of the prophetess! How true is the Lord’s statement: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66.)

As soon as she saw the Mother of the Lord who had come to her, she recognized her. But finding in herself no merit by which she might be worthy to be visited by such a guest, she said: “From where has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

For the same Spirit who had bestowed on her the gift of prophecy also granted her the gift of humility. Filled with the prophetic Spirit, she understood that the mother of the Savior had come to her; but, attentive through the spirit of humility, she recognized herself as less worthy of his coming.

“For behold, when the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy.”

Elizabeth understood, through the revelation of the same Spirit with whom she had been filled, what her infant’s leaping signified: namely, that the mother of the one whose forerunner and herald he was to become had come.

And how wondrous, how swift is the operation of the Holy Spirit! There is no delay in learning where the Holy Spirit is present as teacher. At the very moment when the voice of the woman greeting her arrived, the infant’s joy arose. While the voice reached the bodily ears, spiritual power entered the heart of the hearer and kindled not only the mother but also her child with love for the Lord who had come.

Therefore the mother of the Lord’s forerunner immediately took care to proclaim openly to those who were present and listening what she had learned secretly. For she adds:

“And blessed is she who believed, because what was said to her by the Lord will be fulfilled.”

Elizabeth learned this also through the Spirit: what words the angel had spoken to Mary, that Mary had immediately believed the angel’s message, and that what had been said would be completed without any doubt through the operation of divine power.

In a wondrous manner, when the same Spirit filled her, he instructed her in knowledge of the present, the past, and the future.

She showed that she had been taught about the present when, calling blessed Mary the mother of her Lord, she indicated that Mary was carrying the Redeemer of the human race in her womb. Therefore she also confessed that the fruit of her womb was uniquely blessed.

She signaled that she had received knowledge of the past when she revealed that the angel’s words to Mary and Mary’s assent in believing had become known to her.

Nor did she conceal that knowledge of the future had been granted to her when she disclosed that what had been said to Mary would be fulfilled by the Lord.

But, my brothers, who could say or adequately estimate what grace of the Spirit of God filled the Mother of God at that time, when such a great light of heavenly gift shone forth in the mother of the forerunner?

Let us listen to the words she spoke, if perhaps from them we may be able to recognize something of what she possessed within.

[Column 0018A] After Elizabeth’s reply, in which she proclaimed Mary blessed among women, called her the mother of her Lord, praised her as strong in faith, and indicated that she herself and her son had been filled with the Holy Spirit at Mary’s entrance, Mary could no longer remain silent about the gifts she had received.

When she found a suitable time, she disclosed through a devout confession of her lips what she had always carried in her heart.

As befitted virginal modesty, she had for some time concealed in silence the oracle divinely given to her [manuscript: “of divinity”]. She reverently guarded the secret of the heavenly mystery hidden in the innermost recesses of her heart, and waited until the giver of gifts himself should reveal, whenever he wished, what special gift he had granted her and what secret he had disclosed.

But when she saw that the same spiritual gifts bestowed upon her had been revealed through others by the Spirit, she herself immediately opened the treasure of heaven that she had kept in her heart.

She therefore said:

“My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.”

In these words she first confesses the gifts specially granted to her; then she enumerates the general benefits of God, through which he never ceases to provide eternally for the human race.

Her soul magnifies the Lord when she dedicates all the affections of her inner person to divine praises and service, and when, through observance of God’s commands, she continually demonstrates that she considers the power of his majesty.

Her spirit rejoices in God her Savior when she takes no pleasure in earthly things, when no abundance of perishable goods softens her, and no adversity breaks her, but when she delights only in the memory of him from whom eternal salvation is hoped—her Creator.

Although these words rightly apply to all the perfect, it was especially fitting for the blessed Mother of God to utter them. She burned with the spiritual love of the one in whose bodily conception she rejoiced, through the privilege of her singular merit.

She was rightly able to rejoice in Jesus—that is, in her Savior—with a joy special above that of the other saints, because she knew that the one whom she recognized as the perpetual author of salvation would himself be born in time from her flesh, so that in one and the same person he would truly be both her Son and her Lord.

Through the following words she also teaches how lowly she thought of herself and that whatever good merit she possessed she received through the generosity of heavenly grace. She says:

“Because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid; for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.”

She shows by her own judgment that she had been a humble handmaid of Christ, but declares that, through the regard of heavenly grace, she had suddenly been exalted and glorified to such an extent that her special blessedness would rightly be admired by the voice of all nations.

She added still further gifts of divine mercy, praising them with worthy thanksgiving:

Because he who is powerful has done great things for me, and holy is his name. Thus she attributes nothing to her own merits, referring the whole greatness of what has happened to her to him who, being essentially powerful and great, is accustomed to make his faithful strong and great from their smallness and weakness. Well did she add, “And holy is his name,” so that she might admonish her hearers—or rather instruct all to whom her words would come—to hasten to faith and to the invocation of that same name, so that they too might become participants in eternal holiness and true salvation, according to the prophetic saying: “And it shall be: everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel II). For this is the very name of which she previously said, “And my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior.” Hence she adds still more plainly:

And his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him. By “generation and generation” she means either both peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, or certainly all the nations throughout the world whom she foresaw would believe in Christ. For, as Peter says, “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X).

The Lord’s own saying harmonizes with these words of blessed Mary. He declared blessed not only the mother who was worthy to give him birth bodily, but also all who obeyed his commandments. When, in a certain place, he was teaching the people and working miracles, and everyone was marveling at his wisdom and powers, a woman from the crowd raised her voice and said to him: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you” (Luke XI). But he gladly received this testimony to the truth and immediately replied: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.” Thus that woman herself—or rather all who heard him—might be confident that they would be blessed if they were willing to obey the divine commandments.

It is as though he plainly said: Although she has a unique privilege of blessedness who, as a virgin, was worthy to carry the incarnate Son of God in her womb, to give him birth, and to nourish him, nevertheless those too will have the foremost place in that same life of perpetual blessedness who conceive his faith and love in a pure heart; who bear the constant remembrance of his commandments in their minds; and who diligently strive to nourish this remembrance in the minds of their neighbors through earnest exhortation.

But since the venerable Mother of God had taught that his mercy would assist all throughout the world who feared him, it remains for her also to indicate what the proud and those who despise the warnings of truth deserve.

“He has exercised power in his arm,” she says; “he has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart.” By “his arm” she signifies the dominion of his own power. For he does not need another’s assistance to act, since, as it is written, the power to do lies subject to him whenever he wills. This is said by way of distinction from our good works: we do not exercise power by the rights of our own freedom, but in God, as it is written elsewhere: “Their own arm did not save them, but your right hand, and your arm, and the light of your countenance” (Psalm XLIII).

He has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart, because pride is the beginning of every sin. On account of its deserts, the Lord cast the human race out of the stable dwelling of its heavenly homeland and scattered it far and wide throughout the exile of this pilgrimage. Yet for those who do not fear to persist in their sins, he has also reserved the more grievous punishment of future scattering.

He has brought down the powerful from their throne. He calls “powerful” the same people whom he had previously called “proud.” They are called proud because they raise themselves above the measure of their condition. They are called powerful, not because they are truly powerful, but because, trusting in their own strength, they decline to seek the help of their Creator.

Those, however, are truly powerful who know how to say with the Apostle: “We can do all things in him who strengthens us” (Philippians IV). Of such people it is written: “God does not reject the powerful, since he himself is powerful” (Job XXXVI).

He therefore brought down the powerful from their throne and exalted the humble, because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” Yet this may also rightly be understood to mean that sometimes those very people who, on account of their self-exaltation, had been cast down by the Lord return again, through his mercy, to the grace of humility, and thus, by the merit of devoted humility, are raised to glory. Thus Saul was cast down from the throne of legal instruction because of his pride, but soon, on account of his humble submission, he was raised up to proclaim the faith of Christ.

He has filled the hungry with good things, and he has sent the rich away empty. Those who now hunger perfectly for eternal things and do not cease striving to attain them with tireless persistence in righteous works will surely be satisfied when the glory of their Redeemer, which they desired, appears. But all who rejoice in preferring earthly riches to heavenly riches will then, at the time of the final separation, be sent away by the Lord empty of every blessedness; and therefore, together with the devil, they will be punished with everlasting misery.

We also see this fulfilled to no small degree in the present life: the humble are filled with the nourishment of heavenly goodness and enriched by the abundance of heavenly virtues; while those who either grow proud by boasting of earthly riches or exalt themselves on account of their wealth of good works, as though they possessed these things of themselves, become inwardly empty of the light of truth.

To each of these verses, which blessed Mary uttered concerning the differing condition of the proud and the humble, we should append what she said earlier, “from generation to generation,” since throughout the whole passing age the just and merciful Creator is accustomed both to resist the proud and to give grace to the humble. Therefore, after a general remembrance of divine mercy and justice, she turns the words of her confession to the particular dispensation of the new incarnation, by which he deigned to redeem the world, saying:

He has helped Israel his servant, remembering his mercy. “Israel” is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” By this name the whole assembly of redeemed humanity is signified, for whose sake God himself appeared visibly among human beings as man, so that they might be able to see God.

He helped Israel as a physician helps a sick person whom he intends to cure, as a king helps a people whom he intends to defend from the attacks of enemies—or rather, after striking down the enemy, to make them free and grant them to reign with him forever.

And rightly did she add, “his servant,” signifying one who is humble and obedient, because no one can attain the lot of redemption except through the virtue of humility. Hence the Lord also says: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVIII).

She also rightly added, “remembering his mercy,” because God’s assuming humanity in order to redeem it was not the result of human merit, but the gift of divine compassion. For what did we deserve after the guilt of transgression except the just anger of the Creator? Therefore, whoever among us is restored to salvation and eternal life must attribute this not to ourselves but to his grace, to whom it is said: “In wrath you will remember mercy” (Habakkuk III).

As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed forever. In recalling the fathers, blessed Mary rightly names Abraham specifically. Although many fathers and saints gave mystical testimony to the Lord’s incarnation, it was to them first that the mysteries of that incarnation and of our redemption were openly foretold. To him in particular it was said: “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis XII). No believer doubts that this concerns the Lord and Savior, who, in order to give us perpetual blessing, deigned to come to us from the stock of Abraham.

By Abraham’s seed she does not mean only those elect who were born bodily from Abraham’s descendants, but also us, who, gathered from the nations to Christ, are joined to those fathers by fellowship in faith, although we are far removed from them in the origin of our bodily lineage. We too are Abraham’s seed and children when we are reborn through the sacraments of our Redeemer, who assumed flesh from Abraham’s line.

We are Abraham’s children when we seek with vigilant attention to see him whose day Abraham rejoiced to see—and he saw it and rejoiced. Hence the Apostle says: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise.”

It is rightly added in conclusion, “forever,” because the aforementioned promise of heavenly inheritance will never be closed by any end. For even until the end of this age there will not be lacking those who, by believing in Christ, become Abraham’s seed; and the glory of future blessedness will remain everlasting for that seed.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since the Lord promises us an eternal reward, we must strive for its attainment with unwearied exertion of mind. For, in order to obtain the good that we desire to possess without end, we must labor to strive for it without interruption until we receive it.

Let us therefore turn over the words of the Gospel reading through frequent meditation, and let us always retain in our minds the examples of blessed Mary, the Mother of God, so that, being found humble in the sight of God and submissive also to our neighbors with the honor that is due, we may deserve to be exalted forever together with her.

Let us carefully strive not to be lifted up by the undeserved favor of those who praise us, since we see her maintain an unshaken steadfastness of humility amid words of true praise. If an immoderate desire for temporal things delights us, let us remember that our Judge sends the rich away empty. If temporal affliction happens to trouble the mind, let us reflect that he also exalts the humble.

Let us never despair of obtaining pardon for our offenses, because his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him. Let the more grievous guilt of refusing to repent steal upon no one amid the evils he has committed, because God resists the proud and, separating them from the lot of the blessed, scatters them according to the variety of their sins through various places of punishment.

By the Lord’s generosity it comes about that, if we always recall blessed Mary’s deeds and words, both the observance of chastity and works of virtue may always persevere in us. For an excellent and most salutary custom has also arisen in the holy Church: her hymn is sung daily by all during the psalmody of evening praise, so that this may both kindle the hearts of the faithful toward devotion through the more frequent remembrance of the Lord’s incarnation and strengthen them in firmness of virtue through the examples of his Mother, recalled again and again.

It was fitting that this should take place at evening, so that our mind, wearied during the day and occupied with various thoughts, might, when the time of rest arrived, gather itself back into the unity of its own reflection; and, having been salutarily admonished, might cleanse anew through nightly prayers and tears whatever superfluous or harmful thing it had contracted amid the day’s occupations.

But since we have prolonged our sermon, let us now turn to the Lord and ask his clemency, so that we may both honor the memory of blessed Mary with fitting offices and deserve to come with purer minds to celebrate the solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity. May he himself assist our desire to perform spiritual works and to receive heavenly gifts—he who willed his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, to become incarnate for us and to give the human race a pattern of life among human beings. With him God lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY III. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

### MARK XIV

At that time John was in the wilderness, baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.

As you heard, dearest brothers, from the reading of the holy Gospel, John, preceding the Lord’s preaching, was in the wilderness baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. Here we must carefully observe the distinction in the words, where it says that he was baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.

He himself baptized with a baptism of repentance for the confession and amendment of sins, and he preached the baptism of repentance that was to come in Christ for the remission of sins. In Christ’s baptism alone remission of sins is granted to us, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God” (Ephesians IV).

This is rightly called a baptism of repentance, because no one desires to be baptized in the fountain of life for any other reason than that he is sorry to be bound by the death of soul and body because of the first transgression.

But if we ask why John baptized, since sins could not be remitted through his baptism, the clear reason is evident. Since he was preserving the office of his forerunning—just as he was to be born, preach, and die before the Lord—so also he had to baptize before him. This was also so that, if he himself had first given baptism to human beings, the envious contention of the Pharisees and scribes might not attack the Lord’s dispensation.

But if they had wished to ask by what authority he baptized, they would immediately have heard: “John’s baptism—from where was it? From heaven or from human beings?” (Mark II). Since they did not dare deny that it was from heaven, they would also have been compelled to confess that the works of the one whom John proclaimed were performed from heaven.

Nevertheless, John’s baptism, although it did not remit sins, was not entirely fruitless for those who received it. For although it was not given for the remission of sins, it was given as a sign of faith and repentance, so that all who were initiated by it might remember that they ought to abstain from sins, devote themselves to almsgiving, believe in Christ, and, as soon as he appeared, hasten to his baptism, by which they would be cleansed for the remission of sins.

John gives his baptism in the wilderness and preaches Christ’s baptism; indeed, he spends his entire life from childhood in the wilderness. This happens so that the supreme teacher might establish by his example what he preached in words, and that he who urged his hearers to depart from sins through repentance might himself avoid the vices of sinners not only by purity of mind but also by the manner of his bodily life.

Figuratively, the wilderness in which John remained signifies the life of the saints, separated from the allurements of the world. Whether they live alone or amid crowds, they always despise the desires of the present age with the whole intention of their mind; they delight in cleaving to God alone in the hidden place of the heart and in placing their hope in him.

The Prophet desired to enter this solitude of mind, most beloved by God, with the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit, when he said: “Who will give me wings like a dove? I will fly away and rest” (Psalm LV). And, rejoicing that he had soon attained it with the Lord’s help, he adds, as though mocking the common entanglements of earthly desires: “Behold, I have gone far away by fleeing, and I remained in solitude” (ibid.).

Finally, after freeing the people from Egypt by the blood of the lamb and leading them through the Red Sea, the Lord first trained them in the wilderness for forty years and then brought them into the promised land. For the people of the faithful cannot immediately enter the joys of the heavenly homeland after baptism; they must first be exercised through long struggles of virtue and afterward be granted the perpetual rewards of heavenly blessedness.

The fruit of John’s preaching is next shown when it says:

And the whole region of Judea and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins. The literal sense is clear: those who were nearer or more learned were the first to receive the word of salvation in abundance.

But since “Judea” is interpreted as “confession,” and “Jerusalem” as “vision of peace,” we may understand mystically that those who have learned the confession of right faith and who have loved the vision of heavenly peace are designated by the names of the people of Judea and Jerusalem.

For it is chiefly such people who should be believed to have gone out into the wilderness to John at that time to receive baptism. Such people also now, when they hear the word of God, are clearly seen to leave their former manner of life and enter the solitude of spiritual life, following the example of faithful teachers.

Through the daily discipline of a new way of life, as though through a daily baptism in the Jordan, they are cleansed by the tears of their compunction from every contagion of creeping vices, according to him who says: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Psalm VI).

Thus the stream of the Jordan is rightly interpreted as “judgment,” because the more carefully the elect examine their conscience by scrutinizing it, the more abundant streams of tears they pour from the innermost fountain of the heart, so that, because they discover themselves to be less than perfect, they may wash away the filth of their weakness in the waters of repentance.

It follows:

And John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey. As regards the literal meaning of his clothing and food, the poverty appropriate to a solitary and herald of repentance is shown.

Figuratively, however, camel’s hair, from which sackcloth is made, expresses the repentance or continence by which he himself was exercised and instructed others. The leather belt, which is taken from a dead animal, signifies both that he had mortified his earthly members and that he taught his hearers to do the same.

For it is well established that the loins often signify lust. Therefore, in order to undertake this struggle and obtain the glory of chastity, the Lord commanded: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII). Whoever has thoroughly subdued the movements of sexual desire has certainly girded his loins with a leather belt.

The locusts, which fly energetically up from the earth but quickly return to the earth, together with the wild honey that he ate, indicate both the brevity and the sweetness of his preaching. He was gladly heard by the people when he preached, and, with the Lord’s coming, he very quickly brought his preaching and baptism to an end.

If anyone wishes to interpret John’s clothing or food as a figure of the Lord and Savior, considering it appropriate that the one whom he revealed by prophesying should also signify him by his manner of life, this interpretation may rightly be followed. It should then be understood that the camel’s hair, because sackcloth is made from it, signifies those who strive to wipe away their sins through repentance, fasting, and weeping; and that the leather belt, because it comes from a dead animal, signifies those who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.

And because it is written: “As many as were baptized in Christ, you have put on Christ” (Galatians III), when such people cleave to Christ with the steady intention of love, they are clothed, as it were, in camel’s hair and girded around the loins with a leather belt.

The locust, because of its brief flight, signifies the fickle mind of the Jewish people, which was carried up and down between the Lord and idols. Wild honey signifies the sweetness of natural understanding by which the uncultivated peoples of the nations were refreshed.

And when the Lord chooses people from both peoples and teaches them to pass into the unity of his body, which is the Church, he is fed, so to speak, with locusts and wild honey. For he converts many into members of himself both from the people that had sought heavenly things with an unstable intention and from the nation that had known only the taste of earthly philosophy.

After describing John’s location, ministry, clothing, and food, the form of his preaching is immediately added. For it follows:

And he preached, saying: One mightier than I is coming after me. One who baptizes for the confession of sins is certainly mighty; mightier is the one who baptizes for their remission. Mighty is the one who is worthy to possess the Holy Spirit; mightier is the one who is worthy to bestow him. Mighty is the one than whom no one born of women is greater; mightier is the one to whose feet all things have been subjected, who was made a little lower than the angels. Mighty is the one who first came to preach the kingdom of heaven; mightier is the one who alone could give it.

“Of whom,” he says, “I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the strap of his sandals” (Mark I). If he had confessed himself worthy only of that ministry, in which he would stoop to untie the strap of his sandals, it would certainly have been a sign of great devotion. But now, through the virtue of extraordinary humility, he testifies that he is not worthy even to perform that ministry properly.

If we attend to the mystery, the decree of the Law becomes clear. When a man did not wish to take a wife to whom he was bound by the right of kinship, but wished to allow another to take her, he was commanded, as a sign of this permission, to give the man who took her the sandal removed from his own foot.

And because the people rightly believed John, on account of his virtues, to be the Christ, they certainly believed him to be the bridegroom of the Church. But John himself, to show who he was, said: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John III).

He therefore does not allow himself to be believed the bridegroom, lest he lose the friendship of the bridegroom. This is what he testifies by saying that he is not worthy to untie his sandal.

Finally, when Moses and Joshua were appointed leaders of the Synagogue, they were commanded to remove their sandals, so that they might understand that the one who gave this command was to be regarded as the bridegroom—that is, the Lord of the Synagogue—and that they themselves, because they presided over that Synagogue, ought to be called and to be the bridegroom’s friends.

I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. The evangelist Matthew reports that John said: “I indeed baptize you with water for repentance” (Matthew III).

John therefore baptized with water so that all whom he could persuade to repent and believe in Christ might be separated by the sign of his baptism from the crowd of unbelievers and impenitent people. But lest they should think that this baptism was sufficient for salvation, and so fail to hasten instead to Christ’s baptism, he appropriately added: “But he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

He baptizes with the Holy Spirit who, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, forgives sins and, once sins have been forgiven, also grants the grace of that same Spirit.

The bestowal of spiritual gifts is also rightly called the baptism of the Spirit. The one who was about to ascend into heaven himself bears witness to this when he promises his disciples, saying: “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts I). He signified that on the tenth day after his ascension the Holy Spirit would come upon them in tongues of fire.

It is reasonably asked whether the Lord, who baptizes all the faithful with the Spirit, also baptized some with water. It should not be considered unworthy of so great a Majesty that he performed the ministry of baptism for some of his disciples, through whom he might propagate the gifts of baptism to his other members. He did not disdain to undertake that memorable service of washing his disciples’ feet.

But whether he baptized with water at that time through himself, or afterward through his servants, he alone baptizes with the Holy Spirit, for he grants the Spirit to us and works virtues in us.

Let us take care, my brothers, always to preserve his grace in us whole and undefiled: at all times devoting ourselves to good works, but especially now, when we are soon to celebrate the Nativity of our Lord and Savior. Let us watch more diligently than usual, so that whatever negligence we discover to have crept into us, we may hasten to wipe away, and whatever virtue we see to be lacking in us, we may strive to acquire more quickly.

Let us uproot the thickets of discord, insults, quarrels, murmuring, and every other vice, and plant within us love, joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, self-control, and the other marks of the fruit of the Spirit, so that on that day, with body cleansed and conscience pure, we may deserve to approach the Lord’s altar and share in his most holy sacramental mysteries. He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY IV. ON THE SECOND DAY OF THE FIRST WEEK OF ADVENT

### JOHN I

At that time John bears witness concerning the Lord and cries out, saying: “This was he of whom I said to you, ‘He who is to come after me has been placed before me, because he was before me.’”

The forerunner of our Redeemer, bearing witness concerning him, declares in a clear voice both the certainty of his humanity and the eternity of his divinity. For he cries out, saying—as your fraternity heard just now when the Gospel was read: “This was he of whom I said to you, ‘He who is to come after me has been placed before me, because he was before me.’”

In saying, “He who is to come after me,” he indicates the order of the human dispensation: he was born after John, and was also to preach after him, baptize after him, perform signs after him, and suffer death after him.

But when he adds, “He has been placed before me,” he designates the preeminence of that same humanity, which rightly had to be preferred to all other creatures. The expression “before me” does not refer to the order of time, but to the difference of dignity, according to what is written concerning the sons of Joseph when Jacob blessed them: “He set Ephraim before Manasseh” (Genesis XLVIII).

There he could rightly have said: “Manasseh, who came after me, has been placed before me”—that is, although he was born after me, he surpassed me in the power of the kingdom.

For this reason John says concerning the Lord: “He who is to come after me has been placed before me”—that is, he who is to come after me to preach surpasses me in the height of an everlasting kingdom and priesthood.

Why, however, the one who was to come after him would surpass him in dignity, he explains when he adds: “Because he was before me.” That is: because he was God eternal before the ages, therefore, although he was born later than I, he will precede me in the glory of his majesty even in the humanity he assumed.

After the evangelist had set forth the testimony that the Lord’s forerunner had borne concerning him, he immediately gives the testimony of his own assertion, which he had begun to offer him. For it follows:

And from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace. Above he had said that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I).

After confirming this also through the testimony of his forerunner, who said, “This was he of whom I said to you, ‘He who is to come after me has been placed before me, because he was before me’” (ibid.), he himself again continues what he had begun, saying: “And from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (ibid.).

The Lord was full of the Holy Spirit, full of grace and truth, because, as the Apostle says, “in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians II). From his fullness we have all received according to the measure of our capacity, because grace has been given to each of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.

Of the mediator between God and human beings alone, the man Jesus Christ, could it truly be said: “The spirit of the Lord will rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isaiah XI).

All the saints, however, do not receive the fullness of his Spirit, but receive from his fullness as much as he grants: “To one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians XII).

Therefore, since we have received from the fullness of our Creator not merely something but everything good that we possess, we must take the greatest care that no one heedlessly exalts himself over a good action or thought. Otherwise, if he remains ungrateful to the giver, he will lose the good that he received and rightly be struck by the apostolic rebuke: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians IV).

Hence the Apostle himself, because he could neither know nor do anything worthy unless he received it from Christ’s fullness, plainly testifies elsewhere: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians III). And in another place: “His grace toward me was not empty, but I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians XV).

He diligently impresses this same thought upon his hearers with humility. Hence the saying: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Philippians II).

When the evangelist had said that we had all received from Christ’s fullness, he immediately added: “Grace upon grace.” He therefore testifies that we have received a twofold grace: one in the present and another in the future. In the present, faith that works through love; in the future, eternal life.

Faith that works through love of God is the grace of God. For in order that we might believe, love, and do the good works that we know, we receive these things not through any preceding merits of our own, but through the generosity of him who says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John XV).

And that we receive eternal life on account of faith, love, and good works is also the grace of God, because, so that we may not turn aside from the good path, we always need him as our guide. To him it is said: “Lead me in your way, and I will walk in your truth” (Psalm LXXXVI)—as though it were plainly said: “Unless I enter the path of truth under your guidance, I cannot at all persevere in the way I have begun.”

So that we may not fail in good works, we must always rely on the help of him who says: “Without me you can do nothing.” Hence the Psalmist, signifying that the beginning of faith and good action is given to us by the Lord, rightly says: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Psalm LIX).

And, teaching that the good things we do are to be brought to completion with his assistance, he says again: “Your mercy will follow me all the days of my life” (Psalm XXIII).

To show that the reward of eternal life, which is given to good works, is freely bestowed on us, he says: “He crowns you with compassion and mercy” (Psalm CIII). He crowns us with compassion and mercy when, because of the good works that he himself mercifully grants us to perform, he repays us with the rewards of heavenly blessedness.

This is what it means for us to receive “grace upon grace”: for, in place of the grace of a good way of life that he has given and by which he himself preserves and assists us so that we may not fail, he will give the grace of blessed recompense, in which we shall sing his mercies forever.

Finally, the Apostle did not hesitate to call the reception of eternal life itself “grace.” Although he had first said that “the wages of sin is death,” he did not wish, in contrast, to say that the wages of righteousness is eternal life, but said: “The grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans VI).

This is not because eternal life is not justly given by a just Judge in return for good merits, but because the merits for which it is given were themselves first freely bestowed by the merciful Savior.

It follows:

For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. The law was indeed given through Moses, in which heavenly law determines what must be done and what must be avoided. But what the law commands is fulfilled only through the grace of Christ.

The law was able to display sin, teach righteousness, and show transgressors that they were guilty before it. But the grace of Christ, poured through the Spirit of love into the hearts of the faithful, makes it possible for what the law commands to be fulfilled.

Thus the commandment “You shall not covet” (Deuteronomy V) belongs to the law through Moses because it is commanded; but it becomes grace through Christ when what is commanded is fulfilled.

Truth came through Christ because the law possessed a shadow of future goods, not the very image of the realities. As the Apostle says elsewhere: “All these things happened to them in figure” (1 Corinthians X). But in place of the shadow, Christ brought the light of truth; in place of the figure of the law, he brought the very image of the realities signified, when, having given the grace of the Spirit, he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures.

The law was given through Moses when the people were commanded to be cleansed by the sprinkling of the blood of a lamb. The grace and truth that were figured in the law came through Jesus Christ when, having suffered on the cross, he washed us from our sins in his own blood.

The law was given through Moses because, instructing the people by saving commandments, it foretold that, if they observed them, they would enter the promised land and dwell in it forever; but that, if they did otherwise, they would be overthrown by their enemies.

Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ because, by giving the gift of his Spirit, he granted both that the law could be understood and observed spiritually and that those who observe it might be brought into the true blessedness of heavenly life, which the promised land signified.

What the sum of the grace and truth that came through Jesus Christ is, the evangelist makes clear by adding:

No one has ever seen God. The Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known. For no greater grace can be given to human beings, and no higher truth can be known by them, than that of which the only-begotten Son of God speaks to his faithful: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V); and of which, praying to the Father, he says: “Now this is eternal life, that they may know you, the true and only God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent” (John XVII).

Since this exceedingly blessed apprehension of grace and truth cannot take place during the life of this age, it is rightly said: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John IV)—that is, no one still enclosed in corruptible and mortal flesh can gaze upon the unbounded light of divinity. Hence the Apostle says more plainly: “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. VI). “No human being” means no one still weighed down by human condition and subject to decay through human conduct.

For this reason Moses, desiring to see in his very nature the God whom he saw in the angel, prayed: “If I have found favor in your sight, show me your glory” (Exod. XXXIII). He heard: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live” (ibid.). Nor should this assertion be thought contrary to the fact that patriarchs or prophets are sometimes said to have seen God. The Lord appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre. Jacob said: “I have seen the Lord face to face” (Gen. XXXII). Isaiah likewise said: “In the year when King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated upon a throne, lofty and exalted” (Isa. VI).

But in all such visions it must rightly be understood that holy people contemplated God not through the appearance of his own nature, but through certain images. Thus the saints saw God through a created medium—for example, fire, an angel, a cloud, or electrum—and yet John truly testifies that “no one has ever seen God” (1 John IV). Truly it is said to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII), because those still enclosed in the fragile vessel of flesh can see him through bounded images of things, but can in no way behold him through the unbounded light of his eternity.

The evangelist next explains by what means one must attain the vision of the unchanging and eternal light, saying: “The Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known” (John XIV). The Lord himself says something similar: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (Matt. XI). And elsewhere: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.”

Under his guidance we must come to the Father; through his teaching we must know the Father and the Son, and also the Holy Spirit, as one God and Lord. For he himself, having become human for our sake and speaking in human form, clearly revealed to us what we ought rightly to believe concerning the unity of the holy Trinity, how the faithful must hasten toward its contemplation, and by what actions it is to be attained. Clothing us in the sacraments of his incarnation and sanctifying us with the gifts of his Spirit, he helps us to reach it. After he has carried out the final judgment in human form, he will exalt us into the vision of divine majesty and wondrously recount to us the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom.

When he says, “who is in the bosom of the Father,” he signifies “who is in the Father’s secret.” The Father’s bosom is not to be conceived childishly in the likeness of the bosom we have in our garments; nor should God, who is not composed of human limbs, be thought to sit as we do. Rather, because our bosom is within us, Scripture, speaking in our customary manner, says that he is in the bosom of the Father, meaning that he always remains in the Father’s secret, to which human vision cannot reach.

The Only-Begotten Son will not make God known—that is, the glory of the holy and undivided Trinity, which is one God—only when, after the universal judgment, he leads all the elect together into the vision of his splendor. He also makes him known daily, when he begins to fulfill in each of the faithful, immediately after they have been released from the corruption of the flesh, what he promised: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV). “I will manifest myself,” he says, “to those who love me,” so that they who knew him mortal in his own condition may now see him equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit in his divine nature.

This, however, should be believed to occur with the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and other men of more rigorous and perfect life. One of them, conscious of his struggles, did not hesitate to testify of himself: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I). There are, however, many righteous people in the Church who, after the dissolution of the flesh, are immediately received into the blessed rest of paradise. In great joy, among great choirs of rejoicing, they await the time when, having received their bodies, they may come and appear before the face of God.

Others, although predestined to the lot of the elect because of their good works, must nevertheless be severely chastised after death because they departed from the body stained by certain evils. They are received into the flames of purgatorial fire and are cleansed from the filth of their vices by this lengthy purification either up to the day of judgment, or else, having first been released from their punishments through the prayers, almsgiving, fasts, tears, and offerings of the saving sacrifice made by faithful friends, they themselves reach the rest of the blessed.

To all of them, nevertheless, the Only-Begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father will make God known according to the measure of each one’s capacity, when at the time of the resurrection he gives the blessing to the one to whom he gave the law, so that, walking from the virtue of faith and hope toward the virtue of contemplation, they may see the God of gods in Zion—that is, in the unchanging mirror of truth. To him, through whose benefits and eternal gifts, be praise and thanksgiving throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY V. FOR THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

**MATTHEW I.** At that time, when Mary, the mother of Jesus, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.

Matthew the evangelist describes the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, by which the eternal Son of God, existing before the ages, appeared in time as the son of a human being, in brief speech but with complete truth. Having traced the generations of the fathers from Abraham to Joseph, Mary’s husband, and having shown that all had been begotten and had begotten according to the common order of human generation, he immediately explained, when about to speak of Christ himself, how far his generation differed from that of the others: namely, that the others were born through the customary union of male and female, whereas he was born through a virgin, since he was to enter the world as the Son of God. Indeed, it was altogether fitting that, when God wished to become human for the sake of human beings, he should be born from no mother other than a virgin; and that, when a virgin was to give birth, she should bring forth no son other than one who was God.

“When his mother Mary,” he says, “had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.” The evangelist Luke sufficiently explains the order of events and the city in which this conception took place. Since this is well known to your holiness, we must say briefly what Matthew writes, and first note that in the expression “before they came together,” the verb “to come together” does not indicate sexual intercourse, but the time of the marriage ceremony that ordinarily follows the betrothal, when the woman who had previously been betrothed begins to be a wife.

Thus, “before they came together” means before they duly celebrated the solemnities of the wedding, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. In fact, according to the order mentioned, they came together afterward, when Joseph, at the angel’s command, took his wife—but they did not have intercourse, since it follows: “And he did not know her.” It was none other than Joseph who found her to be with child; by marital liberty he already knew nearly everything about his future wife and therefore promptly detected her swelling womb with an inquisitive gaze. The text continues:

“But Joseph her husband, since he was a righteous man and did not wish to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly.” Seeing that his betrothed had conceived, although he knew well that she had been touched by no man, and being righteous and wishing to act justly in all things, Joseph considered it best neither to disclose this to others nor to take her as his wife.
