Instead, he would quietly alter his intention concerning the marriage and allow her to remain in the condition of a betrothed woman, as she was.

For he had read in Isaiah that a virgin from the house of David would conceive and bear the Lord. He also knew that Mary derived her lineage from that house, and therefore did not doubt that this prophecy might be fulfilled in her. But if he quietly dismissed her and did not take her as his wife, while she gave birth as a betrothed woman, very few indeed would think her a virgin rather than a prostitute.

Therefore Joseph’s intention is suddenly changed by a better plan: in order to preserve Mary’s reputation, he would take her as his wife after celebrating the wedding feast, but would guard her chastity forever. For the Lord preferred that some people should be ignorant of the manner of his birth rather than that he should disgrace the chastity of his mother. For the text continues:

“While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife. For what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he himself will save his people from their sins.”

These words teach at once the manner of the conception and the dignity of the birth: namely, that she conceived from the Holy Spirit and would bear Christ. Although the angel does not call him Christ in an explicit statement, he clearly signifies that he is Christ by explaining the etymology of the name Jesus and showing that he is the author of salvation and the Savior of the people, when he calls them his people. Through this Joseph learns what he had not known and removes his mind completely from touching the mother of God.

Nevertheless, by an arrangement demanded by just necessity, he is commanded to take her as his wife in name only: lest she be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress, and so that, when she fled to Egypt, she might have the companionship of a male who, with familiar care, would be a guardian of female weakness and a witness to her perpetual virginity. Catholic interpreters report other reasons why Joseph ought to have taken the mother of God as his wife; anyone who wishes will find them in their proper places.

The evangelist also supports the virgin birth with an example from prophetic speech, so that the miracle of such great majesty might be believed with greater certainty, since he not only proclaimed that it had happened but also recalled that it had been foretold by the prophet. For it is characteristic of this evangelist, Matthew, to confirm everything he narrates with prophetic testimonies as well. He wrote his Gospel especially for those who had believed from among the Jews but were nevertheless unable, although reborn in Christ, to be torn away from the ceremonies of the law. Therefore he labored to raise them from the carnal understanding of the law and the prophets to the spiritual understanding that concerns Christ, so that they might receive the mysteries of the Christian faith with greater security when they recognized that these were nothing other than what the prophets had foretold.

“Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a Son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is translated, “God with us” (Isa. VII). The name of the Savior, whom the prophet calls “God with us,” signifies both natures in his one person. He who was born before the ages from the Father as God became Emmanuel—that is, “God with us”—in the fullness of time, having been made in his mother’s womb. He did this because he graciously chose to receive the weakness of our nature into the unity of his own person, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”: wondrously beginning to be what we are without ceasing to be what he was, assuming our nature without losing what he himself was.

“Joseph rose from sleep and did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him. He took his wife, and he did not know her.” He took her in the name of wife for the reasons we have stated, and he did not know her in the conjugal act because of the mysteries he had learned.

If anyone wishes to oppose this interpretation of ours and maintain that the blessed mother of God was never taken by Joseph as his wife after the wedding had been celebrated, let him explain this passage of the holy Gospel more convincingly. Let him also show that among the Jews it was permitted for a man to unite himself carnally with his betrothed, and we will gladly yield to his sound interpretation—provided only that we do not believe that anything was done concerning the Lord’s mother that could bring her into disrepute in the public estimation.

As for what is added, “until she bore her firstborn son,” let no one understand it as though he knew her after the birth of the Son, as some perversely suppose. Your Fraternity should know that there were heretics who, because it is said, “He did not know her until she bore her son,” believed that Mary was known by Joseph after the Lord’s birth, and that from this union arose those whom Scripture calls the Lord’s brothers. They also used the designation “firstborn” as support for their error.

May God avert this blasphemy from the faith of all of us, and grant us to understand with Catholic devotion that the parents of our Savior were always glorious in inviolate virginity, and that those whom Scripture customarily calls the Lord’s brothers were not their children but their relatives. The evangelist did not concern himself with saying whether Joseph knew her after she had borne her Son because he considered that no one would regard this as doubtful.

Indeed, no one should doubt that righteous spouses, to whom it was granted by singular grace that the Son of God should be born while they remained in the chastity of virginity, could in no way thereafter violate the rights of chastity or defile God’s most holy temple with the seed of corruption.

It should also be noted that, contrary to the opinion of the heretics, “firstborn” does not refer only to those who are followed by other brothers, but, according to the authority of Scripture, to all who first open the womb, whether some brothers follow them or none.

Nevertheless, the Lord can be understood to be called “firstborn” for a special reason, in accordance with what John says about him in the Apocalypse: “the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Apoc. I). The Apostle Paul likewise says: “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII).

He is called “the firstborn of the dead” because, although he was incarnated after many brothers, he was the first of all to rise from the dead and opened for believers the way from death to heavenly life. He is the firstborn among many brothers because, “to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God.” He is rightly called their firstborn because in dignity he surpasses all the adopted children, even those who preceded the time of his incarnation by their birth.

They can indeed testify with John most truly that “he who comes after us was made before us”—that is, although he was born into the world after us, he is rightly called the firstborn of us all because of the merit of his power and kingdom.

He can also appropriately be called “firstborn” in his very divine birth, because before he generated any creature by making it, the eternal Father generated the Son, coeternal with himself; and before he generated any adopted children for himself by redeeming them through the word of truth, the eternal Father generated the Word, coeternal with himself. Hence the Word himself, the Son of God, namely Power and Wisdom, says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Ecclus. XXIV).

Thus Mary bore her firstborn Son—that is, a Son of her own substance. She bore him who, before every creature, had been born as God from God, and who, in the humanity in which he was created, surpassed every creature by right of precedence.

“And you shall call his name Jesus,” he says. In Hebrew, Jesus is called *Salutaris* or *Salvator* in Latin, “the Saving One” or “Savior.” The giving of this name is plainly and most certainly foretold by the prophets. Hence those verses sung with the great desire to see him:

“My soul shall rejoice in the Lord and delight in his salvation” (Ps. XXXV).

“My soul has failed in your salvation. But I will glory in the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII).

“I will rejoice in God my Jesus” (Hab. III).

And especially this: “Save me, O God, by your name” (Ps. LIII), as though he were saying: “Glorify the glory of your name, by which you are called Savior, in saving me.”

Thus Jesus is the name of the Son born from the virgin. As the angel explains, it signifies that he himself will save his people from their sins. Now the one who saves from sins will certainly also save from the corruptions of mind and body that came about because of sins.

“Christ,” however, is a title of priestly or royal dignity. For priests and kings under the law were called *Christi*—“anointed ones”—from *chrisma*, that is, the anointing with holy oil. They signified him who, appearing in the world as the true king and high priest, was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

From this anointing, that is, from this *chrisma*, he himself is called Christ; and those who share in the same anointing, that is, in spiritual grace, are called Christians. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who as Savior deign to save us from sins, as high priest reconcile us to God the Father, and as king grant us the eternal kingdom of his Father, live and reign as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY VI. AT DAWN ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

**LUKE II.** At that time the shepherds said to one another: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word that has come to pass, which the Lord has made and shown to us,” etc.

When the Lord and Savior was born in Bethlehem, as the sacred history of the Gospel testifies, an angel of the Lord appeared with great light to shepherds who were in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. He proclaimed that the Sun of righteousness had risen upon the world not only by the voice of heavenly speech but also through the splendor of divine light.

Nowhere in the entire sequence of the Old Testament do we find angels, who appeared so frequently to the fathers, appearing with light. This privilege was rightly reserved for the present time, when light has risen in darkness for the upright in heart, the merciful and righteous Lord.

But lest the authority of one angel should seem insufficient, immediately after one had taught the mystery of the new birth, a multitude of heavenly hosts appeared, singing glory to God and simultaneously proclaiming peace to human beings. This plainly demonstrated that through this birth human beings were to be converted to the peace of one faith, hope, and love, and to the glory of divine praise.

Mystically, these shepherds signify the teachers and rulers of faithful souls. The night over which they kept watch for their flock indicates the dangers of temptations, from which all who keep perfect watch do not cease to guard both themselves and their subjects.

And it is fitting that, when the Lord was born, the shepherds kept watch over their flock. For he was born who says: “I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John X). The time was also approaching when this supremely good shepherd, having sent shepherds into the world, would recall his sheep—wandering far and wide in scattered confusion—to the ever-green pastures of heavenly life. He enjoined their care upon the chief shepherd: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John XXI). Explaining this more clearly, he says: “Strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII).

“And it happened that, when the angels had departed from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another: ‘Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word that has come to pass, which the Lord has made and shown to us.’ And they came in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in a manger.”

Those shepherds hastened with joyful eagerness to see what they had heard; and because they sought him with burning love, they immediately deserved to find the Savior whom they sought. The shepherds of intellectual flocks—in fact, all the faithful—likewise showed by both their words and their deeds with what spiritual diligence Christ ought to be sought.

“Let us go,” they say, “as far as Bethlehem and see this word that has come to pass.”

Let us also go, dearly beloved brothers, by thought as far as the city of David, Bethlehem, and let us recall with love that in it the Word became flesh, celebrating his incarnation with worthy honors.

Let us go, casting aside carnal desires, with the whole desire of our minds as far as the heavenly Bethlehem—that is, the house of living bread, not made by human hands but eternal in the heavens—and let us recall with love that the Word became flesh. He ascended there in the flesh; there he sits at the right hand of God the Father. Let us follow him there with every effort of virtue, and let us take care through attentive discipline of heart and body that we may deserve to see him reigning on the Father’s throne, whom they saw crying in a manger.

“Let us see,” they say, “this word that has come to pass.”

What a straight and pure confession of holy faith: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”! This Word, born from the Father, was not made, because God is not a creature.

In that divine birth he could not be seen by human beings. But so that he could be seen, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” “Let us see,” they say, “this Word that has come to pass,” because before it came to pass we could not see it. The Lord made it incarnate and, through this, presented it to us in visible form.

“And they came in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in a manger.”

The shepherds came in haste and found God born as a human being, together with the ministers of that birth. Let us also hasten, my brothers—not by the steps of our feet but by progress in good works—to see the same glorified humanity, together with those ministers rewarded with the worthy recompense of their service. Let us hasten to see him shining in the divine majesty of the Father and of himself.

Let us hasten, I say. Such blessedness is not to be sought with laziness and sluggishness; rather, the footsteps of Christ must be followed eagerly. For he himself desires to help our course, stretching out his hand, and delights to hear us say: “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” Let us therefore follow more swiftly with the steps of virtue, so that we may deserve to attain him.

Let no one delay turning to the Lord; let no one put it off from day to day. In all things and above all things, let us pray to him to direct our steps according to his word, and let no injustice rule over us.

“When they saw, they understood the word that had been spoken to them about this child.”

Let us also, beloved brothers, hasten in the meantime to receive with devout faith and embrace with complete love what has been said to us about our Savior, true God and human being, so that in the future we may be able to grasp these things through the vision of perfect knowledge.

For this alone is the true life of the blessed—not only of human beings but also of angels: to behold perpetually the face of their Creator. The Psalmist ardently desired this, saying: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLII).

He showed that his desire could be satisfied by the vision of God alone, and not by any abundance of earthly things, when he said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVII). But because those who labor in works of virtue, not the idle and sluggish, are worthy of divine contemplation, he first carefully declared: “But I shall appear in your sight with righteousness.”

Thus, when the shepherds saw, they understood the word that had been spoken to them about Christ, because the vision of God is knowledge of him, and this is the only blessed life of the human being. The human being himself says and bears witness to this when, commending us to the Father, he says among other things: “Now this is eternal life, that they may know you to be the true and only God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII).

“And all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds had said to them.”

The shepherds did not conceal in silence the mysteries they had learned from God; they told them to everyone they could. For spiritual shepherds of the Church are appointed above all for this purpose: to preach the mysteries of the Word of God and to display to their hearers as marvelous the wonders they have learned in the Scriptures.

Not only shepherds, bishops, priests, and deacons, or even superiors of monasteries, are to be understood here. All the faithful who take care of even their small household are rightly called shepherds, insofar as they preside over that household with vigilant care.

And any one of you who is responsible for the daily governance of even one or two brothers ought to fulfill the office of a shepherd. For insofar as he is able, he is commanded to feed them with the nourishment of the word. Indeed, each one of you, brothers, who is believed to live as a private person also holds the office of a shepherd and feeds a spiritual flock, keeping the watches of the night over it, if he strives to gather around himself a multitude of good deeds and pure thoughts, govern them with righteous moderation, nourish them with the heavenly pastures of Scripture, and guard them with vigilant diligence against the ambushes of unclean spirits.

“But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.”

Mary, preserving the rights of virginal modesty, did not wish to disclose to anyone the secrets of Christ that she knew. Rather, she reverently awaited the time and manner in which he himself wished them to be disclosed. In silence of mouth, but with a watchful heart, she diligently examined these same secrets. This is what is meant by “pondering them in her heart.”

She compared what she saw happening with what she had read was to happen. She saw that she, descended from David’s line and living in Nazareth, had conceived the Son of God from the Holy Spirit. She had read in the prophet: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazarene shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. XI).

She had also read: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, from you shall come forth for me the one who will rule in Israel; his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” She saw that in Bethlehem she had borne the ruler of Israel, who had been born before the ages as eternal God from the Father.

She saw that, although a virgin, she had conceived and borne a Son and had called his name Jesus. She had read in the prophets: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII).

She had read: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger.” She saw the Lord lying in the manger, to which ox and donkey customarily came to be fed.

She remembered that the angel had said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who shall be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

She had read that the manner of his birth could not be known unless an angel revealed it, as Isaiah said: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII).

She had read: “And you, tower of the flock, misty one, daughter of Zion, to you shall it come, and the former power shall come, the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem” (Mic. IV).

She heard that the angelic powers, who are daughters of the heavenly city, had appeared to the shepherds in the place that since ancient times had been called the tower of the flock because of the gathering of animals. It is one mile east of Bethlehem, where even now the three memorials of those shepherds are shown in a church.

She knew that the Lord had then come in the flesh, he who has one eternal power with the Father and would give the kingdom to the Church, namely to the daughter of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Thus Mary compared what she had read would happen with what she knew had already happened—not bringing these things forth from her mouth, but keeping them enclosed in her heart.

“And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all that they had heard and seen, just as it had been told to them.”

Let us also, dearly beloved brothers, learn to return from contemplating the Lord’s dispensation, by which he graciously chose to help us, to give thanks continually for his benefits. If they, knowing only his birth, returned glorifying and praising God for all that they had heard and seen, how much more ought we, who have come to know the whole sequence of his incarnation, who have been instructed in his mysteries, to proclaim his glory and praise in all things—not only in word but also in deeds!

Let us never forget that God was born as a human being for this reason: so that by being reborn he might restore us to the image and likeness of his divinity. For this reason he was baptized with water: to make the streams of water fruitful for the cleansing of all our sins. For this reason he was tempted in the wilderness: so that by conquering the tempter he might also grant us the skill and strength to conquer. For this reason he died: to destroy the dominion of death. For this reason he rose again and ascended into heaven: to provide us with the hope and example of rising from the dead and reigning forever in the heavens.

For each of these things, returning to contemplate his most merciful dispensation, let us glorify and praise our God and Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY VII. ON THE DAY OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

**JOHN I.** In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, etc.

Since we have learned from the words of the holy evangelists—Matthew and Luke—that the temporal birth of the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, which occurred on this day, has been revealed, we are pleased also to examine the words of the blessed evangelist John concerning the eternity of the Word, that is, of his divinity, in which he always remains equal to the Father.

By the singular privilege of chastity, John deserved to grasp and disclose the mystery of that divinity more profoundly than the other authors of sacred Scripture. For he is not said to have reclined at the supper upon the breast of the Lord Jesus without reason; rather, this teaches symbolically that he drank more excellently than the others from the most holy spring of that breast the draught of heavenly wisdom.

Hence, in the figure of the four living creatures, he is appropriately compared to a flying eagle. The eagle is accustomed to fly higher than all birds and to fix its gaze more clearly than all living creatures upon the rays of the sun.

The other evangelists, as it were, walk on earth with the Lord. They sufficiently explain his temporal generation and temporal deeds, and say little about his divinity. But John, as it were, flies with the Lord toward heaven. Explaining very few of his temporal actions, he understood more sublimely by flying in mind and contemplated more clearly the eternal power of his divinity, through which all things were made, and handed this understanding on to us in writing.

Thus the other evangelists describe Christ as born in time, whereas John testifies that he already existed in the beginning, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.” The others recall that he suddenly appeared among human beings, whereas John declares that he had always been with God, saying: “And the Word was with God.” The others speak of him as a true human being; John confirms that he is true God, saying: “And the Word was God.”

The others show him dwelling among human beings in time as a human being; John shows him remaining with God in the beginning as God, saying: “This was in the beginning with God.” The others testify to the great works he performed as a human being; John shows that God the Father made every visible and invisible creature through him, saying: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

In a remarkable way, at the beginning of his Gospel the blessed John both deeply instills the faith of those who believe rightly in the divinity of the Savior and powerfully overcomes the faithlessness of heretics.

There were heretics who said: “If Christ was born, then there was a time when he did not exist.” John first refutes them with the opening words, when he says:

“In the beginning was the Word.”

He does not say, “In the beginning the Word began to exist,” but “In the beginning was the Word,” thereby showing that he did not originate in time but already existed at the origin of time, and therefore was born from the Father without any beginning in time. This accords with what he himself says in Proverbs: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning; from eternity I was established” (Prov. VIII).

There were also heretics who, denying that there were three persons of the holy Trinity, said: “The same God is Father when he wishes, Son when he wishes, and Holy Spirit when he wishes; nevertheless, he is one.” To destroy their error, John adds:

“And the Word was with God.”

For if one was with another, then clearly the Father and the Son are two, and not one. The same one is supposedly Father at one time, Son at another, and Holy Spirit at another—as though the nature of the divine substance were changeable, although the Apostle James says most plainly: “With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (James I).

There were also certain authors of an evil doctrine who confessed Christ to be merely human and did not believe him to be God at all. John next exposes—or, according to another reading, overthrows—them when he says:

“And the Word was God.”

There were others who believed him to be God, but thought that he became God from the time of the incarnation and was not born eternally from the Father before the ages. One of them is reported to have said: “I do not envy Christ for having been made God, since, if I wish, I too can become like him.” The evangelist refutes their wicked opinion when he says:

This was in the beginning with God. That is, this Word, which is God, did not begin in time, but in the beginning God was with God.

There were also enemies of the truth who did not deny that Christ already existed before the Virgin gave birth, but believed that he was not born God from the Father, rather made by the Father, and therefore lesser than the Father because he was a creature. The evangelic proclamation also condemns these people when it says:

“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” For if none of the creatures was made without him, it is plainly evident that he is not a creature, through whom every creature was made. And lest anyone, hearing that the creature was made through the Lord, should believe that his will was changeable—as though he had suddenly wished to make a creature which previously, from eternity, he had never made—the evangelist clearly teaches that although the creature was made in time, it had always been ordained in the Creator’s eternal wisdom when and what it would be created.

And this is what he says:

[Col. 0040B] “What was made, in him was life.” That is, whatever appeared as having been made in time, whether living or without life, all this existed in the spiritual conception of the Maker as though it had always lived and still lives. Not because what he created is coeternal with the Creator, but because the rationale of his will is coeternal with him; in that rationale, from eternity, he had and has what he would create and when, how he would govern what had been created so that it might endure, and to what end he would bring each thing he created.

It continues:

“And life was the light of human beings.” By this statement it is plainly taught that this vital rationale, through which all things have been ordered and are governed, illuminates not every creature, but only the rational creature, so that it may understand. Human beings, who were made in the image of God, can perceive wisdom; animals cannot. Yet any human being who is merely animal does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God. Therefore, after saying, “And life was the light of human beings,” he appropriately added this concerning those who, withdrawing far from the honor of human condition, are compared with senseless beasts and have become like them, and therefore are rightly deprived of the light of truth:

“And the light,” he says, “shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” Christ is the light of human beings, illuminating by the presence of his knowledge all human hearts that deserve to be enlightened. The darkness, however, consists of the foolish and wicked, whose blinded inner hearts the light of eternal wisdom plainly knows as they are, although they are entirely unable, through understanding, to grasp the rays of that same light. It is as though some blind person were surrounded by the sun’s radiance and yet could not see the sun itself, whose light floods over him.

Yet heavenly mercy did not entirely disregard such people. Rather, it applied to them the remedy of salvation by which they might come to see the light. For the invisible light itself, the very wisdom of God, clothed itself in flesh, in which it could be seen; appearing in human form and speaking with human beings, it would gradually purify them through faith and raise their hearts to knowledge of its divine vision.

A man of great merit was sent before him, by whose testimony all would be prepared to hear, as soon as it appeared, that very wisdom of God; to see the very Sun of righteousness, now covered by the cloud of the body—that is, to see and hear a man who was God, full of grace and truth.

“There was,” he says, “a man sent by God, whose name was John. He came for a testimony, to bear witness concerning the light, so that all might believe through him.” He does not say, “so that all might believe in him.” For “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jeremiah XVII). Rather, he says, “so that all might believe through him”—that is, so that through his testimony they might believe in the light which they did not yet know how to see: namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, who testifies concerning himself: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII).

It continues:

“He was not the light, but came to bear witness concerning the light.” “He was the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world.”

Holy people, indeed, are rightly called light, as the Lord says to them: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew V); and the apostle Paul says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V). Yet there is a great difference between the light that is illuminated and the light that illuminates; between those who, by participation in the true light, receive the capacity to shine, and the perpetual light itself, which is sufficient not only to shine in itself but also, by its presence, to illuminate whomever it touches.

Compared with this true light, not only any of the least of the elect, but even John himself—than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women—is asserted not to be light, so that Christ might plainly be shown not to be what he was thought to be. For John, as it is written, “was a burning and shining lamp” (John V): burning, that is, with faith and love; shining in word and deed.

To infuse sinners [Al., hearts] with the grace of light belongs solely to him of whom it is said:

“He was the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” Every human being, that is, who is illuminated either by natural ability or by divine wisdom. For just as no one can exist from himself, so no one can be wise from himself; rather, he is illuminated by him of whom it is written: “All wisdom is from the Lord God” (Ecclesiasticus II).

The evangelist then appropriately describes both his natures: the divine, by which he always remains wholly present everywhere; and the human, in which, born in time and enclosed in a particular place, he appeared. He says:

[Col. 0041D] “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came into his own, and his own did not receive him.”

He was in the world, and the world was made through him, because he was God, because he was wholly present everywhere, governing without effort by the presence of his majesty and sustaining without burden what he had made. And the world did not know him because “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”

Here the evangelist calls “the world” those who have been deceived by love of the world and, clinging to the creature, have turned away from knowing the majesty of their Creator.

“He came into his own,” because in the world which he made through his divinity he appeared, through his humanity, born into it. “He came into his own,” because he deigned to become incarnate in the Jewish nation, which he had joined to himself by special grace above all other nations.

Thus he was in the world, and he came into the world. He was in the world through his divinity; he came into the world through the incarnation. For coming and departing belong to humanity; remaining and existing belong to divinity. Since, therefore, while he was in the world through his divinity, the world did not know him, he deigned to come into the world through his humanity, so that in this way the world might know him. But let us see what follows:

“He came into his own, and his own did not receive him.” They did not recognize him creating and governing all things in the power of his divinity; they refused to receive him shining forth through miracles in the weakness of the flesh.

And what is more grievous, “his own did not receive him”—namely, human beings, whom he himself created. The Jews, whom he had specially chosen for himself as a people, to whom he had revealed the mystery of his knowledge, whom he had glorified through the wondrous deeds of their fathers, to whom he had given the teaching of his law, from whom he had promised that he would be incarnate, and among whom he showed himself incarnate as he had promised—those very people, for the most part, refused to receive him when he came.

They did not all refuse him, for otherwise no one would have been saved [Note: [Col. 0041] Cod. bibl. Arsen. Paris. adds: “and his incarnation would have been superfluous”]. But now many from both peoples received him through believing. Concerning them the evangelist next says:

“But to all who received him, he gave the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.”

Let us consider, dearest brothers, how great is the grace of our Redeemer, how great is the abundance of his sweetness. He was born the Only-Begotten from the Father, and he did not wish to remain alone. He descended to earth, where he might acquire brothers for himself to whom he could give the kingdom of his Father. He was born God from God, and he did not wish to remain only the Son of God; he also deigned to become the son of man—not losing what he was, but assuming what he was not—so that through this he might transfer human beings into the sons of God and make them coheirs of his glory, so that what he himself always possessed by nature they might begin to possess by grace.

Let us consider how great is the power of faith, by whose merit human beings are given the power to become children of God. Hence it is rightly written: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk II). The righteous person lives by faith—not that faith which is expressed only by confession of the lips, but that which works through love; otherwise, if faith does not have works, it is dead in itself.

Let no one despise himself; let no one despair of his salvation. Let us all run, each one of us run, so that we who were far away may deserve to be brought near through the blood of Christ.

Let us see what is said: “To all who received him, he gave the power to become children of God.” “To all,” he says, “who received him.” For God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him (Acts X).

The evangelist next indicates in what manner believers could become children of God, and how greatly this birth differs from bodily birth:

“Who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God.”

Our bodily birth as individuals originated from bloods—that is, from the nature [Al., seed] of male and female—from the embrace of marriage. Spiritual birth, however, is supplied by the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the Lord distinguishes from bodily birth when he says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III). “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the spirit is spirit.”

Yet, lest anyone doubt that human beings can become sons of God and coheirs of Christ, the evangelist provides an example: the Son of God himself deigned to become human and dwell among human beings, so that, by becoming a sharer in human weakness, he might grant human beings to become sharers in divine power.

[Col. 0043B] “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” This means: The Son of God became human and lived among human beings.

Scripture commonly uses the terms “soul” and “flesh” to signify the whole human being. “Soul,” for example, as it is written: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Genesis XLVI); “flesh,” again, as it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III). Neither souls without bodies can descend into Egypt, nor can flesh without a soul see anything; rather, in one passage the whole human being is signified by “soul,” and in the other by “flesh.”

Thus, in this passage, when it says, “The Word became flesh,” nothing else should be understood than if it had said, “God became human,” assuming flesh and a soul. Just as each of us is one human being consisting of flesh and soul, so from the time of the incarnation Christ is one person consisting of divinity, flesh [Al., the flesh], and soul: true God, existing from eternity to eternity as he was, assuming in time a true human being whom he had not possessed, into the unity of his person.

It continues:

“And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.”

Human beings could not see Christ’s glory before the incarnation; after the incarnation they saw it, observing his humanity shining with miracles and understanding the divinity hidden within. This was especially true of those who merited to contemplate his splendor, before his passion, when he was transfigured on the holy mountain, and a voice descended upon him from the magnificent glory: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew XVII).

After his passion, they saw the glory of his resurrection and ascension, and were wondrously refreshed by the gift of his Spirit. Through all these things they clearly understood that such glory belonged not to just any holy person, but only to that human being who, in his divinity, was the Only-Begotten from the Father.

What follows is:

“Full of grace and truth.”

The same human being, Christ Jesus, was full of grace. By a unique gift beyond all other mortals, he was granted that, from the moment he began to be conceived in the Virgin’s womb and began to become human, he was truly God. Therefore the same glorious ever-virgin Mary is rightly to be believed and confessed not only as the mother of the human Christ, but also as the Mother of God.

He was and is also full of truth—namely, through the very divinity of the Word, which deigned to assume that specially chosen human being with whom there would be one person of Christ. It did not, as the heretics claim, transform something of its divine substance into the making of human nature; rather, remaining itself with the Father, it assumed the whole nature of a true human being from the seed of David, which it did not previously possess.

Therefore, dearest brothers, as we commemorate today with annual devotion the human birth of our Redeemer, let us embrace both his divine and human nature not with annual devotion only, but always with unceasing love: his divine nature, through which we were created when we did not exist; his human nature, through which we were recreated when we were lost.

Indeed, the divine power of our Creator was capable of recreating us without assuming humanity. But the human weakness of that same Redeemer could not recreate us without the divinity that assumed it, dwelt within it, and worked through it.

And therefore “the Word became flesh,” that is, God became human and dwelt among us, so that by living among us in the human form familiar to us he might accommodate himself to us, instruct us by speaking to us, provide us with a way of life, fight on our behalf against the enemy, and destroy our death by dying and rising again.

Through his divinity, coeternal with the Father, he would inwardly give us life and raise us to divine things, grant us forgiveness of sins together with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and, after the perfection of good works, lead us not only to see the glory of his glorified humanity, but also show us the immutable essence of his divine majesty. In that majesty he lives and reigns with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY VIII. ON THE FEAST DAY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

JOHN XXI. At that time Jesus said to Peter, “Follow me.” Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following—the one who also reclined at supper upon his breast and said, “Lord, who is the one who will betray you?” etc.

The reading from the holy Gospel that has been read to us, my brothers, must be weighed in each of its words with all the greater attention because it overflows throughout with the great sweetness of heavenly grace.

For the most blessed evangelist and apostle John commends to us the privilege of the exceptional love by which he deserved to be honored by the Lord above the others. He commends the testimony of the Gospel account, which, grounded in divine truth, no believer is permitted to doubt. He commends the peaceful release of his flesh, which he received when the Lord visited him in a special manner.

But so that we may be able to consider the beginnings of this complete reading, let us briefly attend to what precedes. After the resurrection, the Lord appeared to seven disciples, among whom were Peter and John. When they had labored all night in fishing without success, he stood on the shore and filled their net with a great multitude of fish, then invited them, when they had come ashore, to breakfast. During the meal he asked Peter three times whether he loved him; and when Peter confessed his love three times, because he had denied him three times, he entrusted his sheep to him to feed three times.

Then he disclosed that, on behalf of those same sheep—that is, the faithful souls—he would proceed through pastoral care all the way to the martyrdom of the cross, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked wherever you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.”

By the stretching out of his hands he signified that Peter would be crowned with the martyrdom of the cross through death; by another’s girding him, that he would be bound by a persecutor; by being led where he did not wish, that in the weakness of human nature he would suffer the torments of passion against his will.

But lest the passion of the cross foretold by the Lord should perhaps seem burdensome to Peter, he immediately sought to lighten it by his own example, so that he might bear the torment of martyrdom more easily when he remembered that he would receive a sentence of death like that of his Redeemer.

After indicating by what death Peter would glorify God, the Lord immediately added what we heard at the beginning of this reading:

“And he says to him: ‘Follow me.’”

As though he were plainly saying: Since I myself was not afraid to undergo the punishment of the cross for your redemption, why are you afraid to suffer the cross for confessing my name? You will be glorified by a more glorious palm of martyrdom because, in earning it, you will follow the path of your teacher.

The evangelist does not then add what the Lord and the disciples did after these words. Nevertheless, he hints at it by what he says next: “Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following.”

It is clear that when he said to Peter, “Follow me”—that is, imitate me by suffering the cross—Peter rose from the place of the meal and began to depart. Peter himself also followed him in the movement of his feet, wishing to fulfill what he had heard: “Follow me.”

The disciple whom Jesus loved followed as well. For he did not think he should be prevented from following Christ, since he knew that Christ had embraced him with no lesser grace of love.

Nor is it unbelievable that both disciples followed the Lord’s footsteps physically because they had not yet understood what he signified when he commanded Peter to follow him.

Your fraternity knows who that disciple whom Jesus loved was: John himself, whose feast of birth we celebrate today. He wrote this Gospel, and therefore preferred to identify his own person by indications of circumstances rather than by his proper name.

Jesus loved him not as though he alone, to the exclusion of the others, were loved, but as one whom he loved more familiarly than the others and whom the special privilege of chastity had made worthy of greater love. He proves that he loves them all when, before his passion, he says to them: “As the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love” (John XV).

But he loves this one above all because, chosen by him as a virgin, he remained a virgin forever. For histories relate that he called him away from marriage when he wished to marry; and because he withdrew him from carnal pleasure, he endowed him with the greater sweetness of his own love.

Finally, as he was dying on the cross, he entrusted his mother to him, so that a virgin might care for a virgin, and when he himself had ascended into heaven after his death and resurrection, his mother would not lack a son whose chaste life would protect her through chaste service.

Blessed John provides another indication of his own person when he adds: “Who also reclined at supper upon his breast and said, ‘Lord, who is the one who will betray you?’”

The preceding passages of this Gospel show more fully how this occurred. At the supper which the Savior held with the disciples as his last before the passion, when he washed their feet and entrusted to them the mysteries of his body and blood to be celebrated, the disciple whom he loved reclined upon his breast.

When he had said to them, “Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me,” that disciple responded, signaling to Peter to ask him: “Lord, who is it?” The Lord said, “It is the one to whom I shall give the dipped bread” [Al., “But the Lord said, ‘It is the one …’].

The fact that this disciple reclined upon the breast of the Master was a sign not only of present love but also of a future mystery. For it was already being represented that the Gospel which this same disciple was to write would contain, more abundantly and more profoundly than the other pages of sacred Scripture, the mysteries of the divine majesty.

Since all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in the breast of Jesus, it is fitting that the one whom he endowed above the others with the singular gift of wisdom and knowledge should recline upon his breast.

We know that the other evangelists spoke at greater length about the miracles of our Savior and less about his divinity. John, however, writing very little about human actions, devoted himself rather to expounding the mysteries of the divine nature, plainly indicating how many streams of heavenly teaching he had drawn from the breast of Jesus to pour forth for us.

It continues:

“When Peter had seen him, he says to Jesus, ‘Lord, but what about this man?’”

Because blessed Peter had heard that he would glorify God through the passion of the cross, he also wished to know concerning his brother and fellow disciple by what death he would pass into everlasting life.

“Jesus says to him, ‘If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.’”

“I do not,” he says, “want him to be perfected through the passion of martyrdom, but rather to await the final day without the violence of a persecutor, when I myself, coming, will receive him into the dwelling of eternal blessedness.”

“And what is that to you? You must remember only that, by undergoing the gallows of the cross, you ought to follow my footsteps.”

At that time the brothers interpreted this response of the Lord as though John would never die. John himself took care to show that it was not to be understood in this way. After first saying that this saying had gone out among the brothers, “because that disciple would not die,” he carefully added: “Jesus did not say to him that he would not die, but, ‘If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?’”

Therefore it must not be thought that this disciple did not die in the flesh, since the Lord did not predict this concerning him, and the Psalmist says: “Who is the human being who lives and will not see death?” (Psalm LXXXVIII).

Rather, it should be understood that, while the other disciples of Christ were perfected through passion, he awaited in the peace of the Church the coming of his calling.

This is what the Lord says: “I want him to remain until I come”—not because he had not previously endured many labors and afflictions for the Lord, but because he completed his final old age in peace, since the churches of Christ throughout Asia, which he governed, had already been established far and wide.

In the Acts of the Apostles he is also found being flogged with the other apostles, when they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus.

Ecclesiastical history also relates that Domitian Caesar had him placed in a vessel of boiling oil; yet, protected by divine grace, he emerged as unharmed as he had been free from the corruption of carnal desire.

Not long afterward, the same ruler exiled him to the island of Patmos because of his unconquerable perseverance in preaching the Gospel. Although deprived there of human comfort, he deserved to be consoled by frequent revelations of divine vision and speech. Finally, while there, he wrote with his own hand the Apocalypse which the Lord revealed to him concerning the present and future state of the Church [Al., “which he wrote”].

Thus it is clear that the promise that he would remain until the Lord came does not mean that he would live in the world without the labor of struggle, but rather that he would pass from the world without the pain of passion.

As we find in the writings of the Fathers, when, worn down by long old age, he knew that the day of his departure was near, he summoned his disciples and, after giving them exhortations and celebrating Masses, bade them his final farewell. Then he descended into the excavated place of his burial, prayed, and was laid beside his fathers. He was found as free from the pain of death as he was free from the corruption of the flesh.

Thus the truthful [Al., “that truthful”] saying of the Savior was fulfilled: he had wanted John to remain until he himself came.

We can also understand mystically, in what the Lord foretold to Peter and John and what took place in them, the two lives by which the Church is exercised in the present: the active and the contemplative. The active life is the common way of life for the people of God. Only a very few, those who are higher in this respect, ascend to the contemplative life after the resurrection [Al., “perfection”] of pious action.

The active life is for the diligent servant of Christ to devote himself to righteous labors: first, to keep himself unstained by this world; to restrain the mind, hand, tongue, and other members of the body from every pollution of sin that assails him; and to subject himself continually to divine service.

Then he must also meet the needs of his neighbor according to his strength: giving food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the cold; receiving the needy and homeless into his house; visiting the sick; burying the dead; rescuing the helpless from the hand of one stronger than he; delivering the needy and poor from those who seize them; showing the way of truth to the one who has gone astray; devoting himself to the other services of fraternal love; and even contending for justice unto death [Al., “fighting to the end”].

The contemplative life, however, is when someone, instructed by long practice in good action, taught by the sweetness of prolonged prayer, and habituated to frequent compunction of tears, has learned to be free from all the affairs of the world and to direct the eye of his mind toward love alone.

He begins even in the present life ardently to desire and, by longing, to taste beforehand the joy of the everlasting blessedness that he will receive in the future; and at times, insofar as it is permitted to mortals, he soars upward in sublime contemplation in an ecstasy of mind.

This life of divine contemplation especially receives those who, after the long beginnings of monastic virtue, know how to live apart from human beings. Their minds are freer to meditate on heavenly things insofar as they are separated from earthly disturbances.

The active life, as we have said, is proposed generally not only to monks in a monastery but to the entire people of God.

Although both apostles, Peter and John, though living among human beings, are clearly known to have been perfect in both lives through the excellence of grace, nevertheless one life is signified through Peter and the other through John.

For when the Lord says to Peter, “You will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish,” he expresses the perfection of active conduct, which is accustomed to be tested by the fire of temptations. Hence elsewhere he speaks of it more plainly: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”

To this he appropriately adds: “Follow me,” since, in the words of Peter himself, Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps.

When he says concerning John, “I want him to remain until I come,” he indicates the state of contemplative virtue, which is not to be brought to an end by death, as the active life is, but is to be perfected by the Lord’s coming after death [Al., “beyond death”].

The active labor ends with death, to receive an eternal reward after death. For who gives bread to the hungry in that life where no one hungers? Who gives water to the thirsty where no one thirsts? Who buries the dead where the land of the living is? Who performs the other works of mercy where no one is found to be wretched?

Therefore no labor of action remains there; only the perpetual fruit of past action endures.

Contemplative happiness, however, which begins here, is perfected there without end, when the presence of the heavenly citizens and of the Lord himself will be seen not through a mirror and in an enigma, as now, but face to face.

Therefore the Lord rightly speaks of it under the figure of the disciple whom he loved and whom he made to recline upon his breast: “I want him to remain until I come.”

As though he plainly said: I do not want the taste of contemplative sweetness—which I especially love in my saints, who hope in the protection of my wings and are inebriated by the abundance of my house [Note: Cod. bibl. Arsen. Paris. adds: “and are given drink from the torrent of my pleasure”]—to be brought to an end, like the practice of laborious action, by the condition of death. Rather, after death, when I appear more sublimely and bring them into the sight of my majesty, I want it to be perfected.

It continues:

“This is that disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them. And we know that his testimony is true.”

Now blessed John plainly identifies his person by his office, whereas he avoids identifying it by name.

We must not pass over without attention what is said: “Who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them.” He bore witness by preaching the Word of God; he bore witness by writing; he bore witness again by teaching the same things he had written; and even now he bears witness by opening the Gospel he composed for the churches to read.

From the time of the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven until the final years of Domitian’s reign—approximately sixty-five years—he preached the Word of God without any aid of writing.

But when he was exiled by Domitian, who became the second persecutor of Christians after Nero, heretics broke into the Church like wolves into sheepfolds left without a shepherd: Marcion, Cerinthus, Hebion, and the other Antichrists, who denied that Christ existed before Mary, stained the simplicity of evangelical faith with perverse teaching.

When, after Domitian’s death, John returned to Ephesus with the permission of the pious ruler Nerva, nearly all the bishops of Asia at that time, together with embassies from many churches, compelled him to speak more profoundly about Christ’s divinity coeternal with the Father. For they thought that in the writings of the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—they had sufficient testimony concerning his humanity and the things he had done as a human being.

John replied that he would do this only if all of them, having proclaimed a fast, prayed together to the Lord that he might be able to write worthy things.

When this had been done, instructed by revelation and intoxicated with the grace of the Holy Spirit, he dispelled all the darkness of the heretics with the sudden light of revealed truth:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.”

Giving a similar form to the beginnings of his entire discourse [Al., “course”], he taught with the clearest assertion that our Lord Jesus Christ was truly human, truly made from a human being in time, and also truly God, truly born eternally from God the Father, truly existing always with the Father and with the Holy Spirit. Indeed, he laid open all the mysteries of divine truth and true divinity as far as no other mortal had been permitted to do.

This privilege was rightly preserved for the virgin: that he should proceed to investigate the mysteries of the incorruptible Word with a heart—and also a body—that was himself incorrupt.

John himself also took care to show that no one should doubt the truth of his words. After saying, “This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them,” he immediately added: “And we know that his testimony is true.”

Since, therefore, together with all the faithful, we know that his testimony is true, let us strive in every respect, by understanding what he taught with right faith and practicing it through right action, to attain the eternal gifts he promised—through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY IX. ON THE FEAST OF THE INNOCENTS

[Col. 0050A]

MATTHEW II. At that time an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: “Rise and take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you,” etc.

The sacred reading of the Gospel, dear brothers, has been recited to us concerning the precious death of Christ’s innocent martyrs; yet it signifies the precious death of all Christ’s martyrs. The fact that little children were killed signifies that one reaches the glory of martyrdom through the merit of humility, and that unless a person is converted and becomes like a little child, he cannot give his life for Christ.

The fact that they were killed in Bethlehem and throughout all its territory shows that persecution by the faithless will rage not only in Judea, from which the Church began, but also throughout all the territories of that same Church, wherever it has been spread across the world; and that the endurance of the godly will be crowned. Those killed at two years old indicate the perfect in doctrine and conduct; those younger proclaim with equal force the simple or uneducated who are nevertheless strong through the steadfastness of an unfeigned faith.

The fact that they were killed, while Christ, whom Herod sought, escaped alive, signifies that the bodies of the martyrs [Alternative: of the martyrs added] can indeed be killed by the wicked, but that Christ, for whom the whole persecution rages, can in no way be taken from them, whether living or slain. Rather, they truly testify that “whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord. Whether we live, therefore, or die, we are the Lord’s.”

The fact that, according to the prophecy of Jeremiah, “A voice was heard in Ramah”—that is, “in the high place”—“weeping and great mourning” (Jer. 31), plainly announces the grief of the holy Church, which laments the unjust death of its members—not, as enemies chatter, so that their cries should disappear into emptiness, but so that they may ascend to the throne of the heavenly Judge. And, like the blood of the protomartyr Abel, the blood of the other martyrs also cries from the earth to the Lord, in accordance with the saying of the wise man: “You will not despise the prayers of the orphan, nor the widow, if she pours out her speech of lament. Do not the widow’s tears descend upon her cheek, and does not her cry rise against the one who causes them to flow? For from her cheek they ascend to heaven, and the Lord who hears them will not take pleasure in them” (Ecclus. 35).

The fact that Rachel is said to have wept for her children and refused to be comforted because they were no more signifies that the Church does indeed weep over the removal of the saints from this world, but does not wish to be comforted in such a way that those who conquered the world by death should return to endure with her again the struggles of this world. They are plainly not to be recalled into the world, from whose troubles they have escaped once for all, to be crowned with Christ.

Rachel, whose name is said to mean either “sheep” or “seeing God,” figuratively represents the Church, whose entire attention is devoted to striving to deserve to see God. She is also the hundredth sheep whom the good Shepherd, leaving in heaven the ninety-nine sheep of the angelic powers, went to seek on earth; and, having found her, placed her upon his shoulders and thus carried her back to the flock.

According to the literal sense, however, the question arises how Rachel is said to have wept for her children, since the tribe of Judah, which possessed Bethlehem, arose not from Rachel but from her sister Leah. The answer is readily apparent: the children were slaughtered not only in Bethlehem but also throughout all its territory. The tribe of Benjamin, which arose from Rachel, was adjacent to the tribe of Judah. It should therefore rightly be believed that the exceedingly cruel slaughter also swept away many children of Benjamin’s stock, whom Rachel’s offspring bewailed with a voice raised on high.

The passage can also be understood in another way. Rachel was buried near Bethlehem, as the inscription on her monument, which remains to this day, testifies: it lies to the west of the city, beyond the road that leads to Hebron. Thus, in prophetic language, it is rightly said that she herself did what was being done in that place, since the place was distinguished by her body and her name.

The fact that the Lord himself, so that he would not be killed by Herod, was taken by his parents into Egypt signifies that the elect are often driven from their own dwellings by the wickedness of evil people, or even condemned to exile. At the same time, an example is given to the faithful, so that they may not hesitate, when necessity requires, to evade the rage of persecutors by fleeing, since they remember that their God and Lord did this.

Indeed, he who was later to command his own followers, “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another,” first did what he commanded by fleeing from a human being, as a human being on earth—the one whom, shortly before, a star from heaven had shown [Note: Cod. bibl. Arsen. Paris. adds: “to be worshiped as God”].

The fact that Herod died not long after the children were killed for the Lord, and that, at the angel’s warning, Joseph brought the Lord with his mother back to the land of Israel, signifies that all the persecutions which were to be stirred up against the Church would be avenged by the deaths of the persecutors themselves. Once those persecutors had been punished, peace would again be restored to the Church, and the saints who had lain hidden would return to their own places.

Herod also rages in the devil, and groans that the kingdom of his iniquity is being taken away from him in those who pass over to Christ. Thus, if he kills little children, he thinks that he is killing Jesus. He continually attempts this by trying to seize the Holy Spirit at the beginnings of those who are reborn and to extinguish a certain infancy of tender faith.

We may also understand Herod’s hatred, by which he wished to destroy Jesus, specifically of the persecutions that took place in Judea during the apostles’ time. When envy grew strong, nearly all the preachers of the Word were expelled from the province and scattered far and wide among the Gentiles to preach.

Thus it came about that the Gentiles, represented by Egypt, who had previously been darkened by sins, received the light of the Word. For this is what it means that the child Jesus and his mother were transferred through Joseph into Egypt: the faith in the Lord’s incarnation and fellowship with the Church were entrusted through holy teachers to the Gentiles.

The fact that they remained in Egypt until Herod’s death indicates figuratively that the faith of Christ would remain among the Gentiles until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved. Herod’s death signifies the end of the malicious purpose with which he now rages against the Church.

The slaughter of the little children signifies the death of those humble in spirit, whom the Jews killed after Christ had been driven away from them. But the fact that, after Herod’s death, he returns to the land of Israel [Alternative: “the Lord” added] announces the end of the world, when, with Enoch and Elijah preaching, the Jews will receive the faith of the truth after the flame of their present envy has been put to rest.

It is fitting that, when he leaves Judea, he is said to flee, and that this happens at night; but when he returns to it [Alternative: “in it” omitted], there is mention neither of flight nor of night. For those whom he once left as persecutors because of the darkness of their sins, he will at last revisit when they seek him because of the light of faith.

Although Herod had been condemned, Joseph feared going into Judea because of his son Archelaus, who held the capital there; at the angel’s warning he withdrew into Nazareth of Galilee. This signifies the final times of the present Church, when, because of the universal blindness of that people which now does not cease persecuting Christians as far as it is able, a fiercer persecution of Antichrist will arise among some.

Many will indeed be converted from unbelief through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, while the rest, moved by Antichrist, will fight against the faith with undivided purpose. The part of Judea in which Archelaus ruled therefore represents the faithless followers of Antichrist. Nazareth of Galilee, to which the Lord is transferred, represents that portion of the same people which at that time will receive the faith of Christ.

Accordingly, Galilee is rightly interpreted as “transmigration completed,” and Nazareth as “flower” or “young shoot.” For the more ardently the holy Church migrates from the things it sees on earth in its desire to attain the heavenly things, the more abundantly it flourishes and bears spiritual virtues.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since on today’s feast we venerate the firstfruits of the martyrs, let us diligently consider the eternal feast of the martyrs that is in heaven. By following their footsteps as far as we can, let us strive to become participants ourselves in that same heavenly festival, as the Apostle testifies: “If we are companions in suffering, we shall also be companions in consolation” [Alternative: “consolation” singular].

Let us not grieve so much over their death [Alternative: “unjust” added] as rejoice in their receiving the just crown. For while each of them was driven from this life through torments, Rachel in her mourning—that is, the holy Church, which laments [Alternative: “gave birth to”]—accompanied them with grief and tears. But once expelled from this world, the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, immediately received them into the other life with ministers of joy meeting them, and led them into the joy of their Lord, where they are to be crowned forever.

Thus John says: “They stood before the throne, and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands” (Rev. 7). They now stand crowned before the throne of God, who once lay before the thrones of earthly judges, worn down by punishments. They stand in the sight of the Lamb, never to be separated from contemplation of his glory, from whose love they could not be separated here even by punishment.

They shine in white robes and hold palms in their hands, because they possess rewards in their works: they receive, glorified through the resurrection, the bodies which, for the Lord’s sake, they endured to have torn apart by fire and beasts, consumed by scourges, dismembered through precipices, scraped by claws, and scattered through every kind of punishment [Alternative: “which they suffered to be torn apart…”].

“And they cried out,” he says, “with a loud voice, saying: Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Rev. 7). With a loud voice they sing salvation to God, recalling with great thanksgiving that they overcame the struggles of their afflictions not by their own strength but with his help.

Again, describing both their past struggles and their everlasting crowns, he says: “These are they who came out of the great tribulation, and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (ibid.). The martyrs washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb when, by pouring out their blood for Christ, they cleansed from every stain the members which, in the eyes of the foolish, seemed to be defiled by the filth of punishments. Moreover, they rendered them worthy of the blessed light of immortality; this is also what it means to have washed and whitened their robes in the blood of the Lamb.

“Therefore,” he says, “they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple.” This service is not burdensome but lovable and desirable: to stand continually in the praises of God. “Day and night” do not properly signify a succession of times, but figuratively signify perpetuity.

There will be no night there, but one day, better than thousands, in the courts of Christ. There Rachel does not weep for her children; rather, God wipes away every tear from their eyes. They raise a voice of joy and eternal salvation in the tents of the righteous to him who lives and reigns, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY X. ON THE FEAST OF THE LORD’S CIRCUMCISION

**Luke 2.** At that time, when the eight days had been completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus, and so forth.

The evangelist has contained the holy and venerable memory of the present feast in a few words, yet he has left it pregnant with no small power of heavenly mystery. Having set forth the Lord’s birth—whose joys the angels soon exalted in worthy praises, whose celebration the shepherds honored with devout visitation, and at which all who heard it then marveled—we too, according to our limited ability and as far as the Lord Christ granted us, have celebrated it with suitable solemnities of Masses and hymns. He then continued and said:

“And when the eight days were completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.” These are the venerable joys of today’s festival; this is the solemnity of the sacred day; these are the holy gifts of heavenly mercy. Commending them to the hearts of the faithful, the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. 4).

In the great dispensation of his mercy for the redemption of the human race, God the Father deemed it worthy to send not an angel, not an archangel, but his only-begotten Son. Since we cannot see him in the form of his divinity, he provided once more, through a great art of love, that the one who was made from a woman—that is, conceived from the substance of a mother’s flesh without the admixture of a man—should present himself to human eyes as a true human being. While remaining in divine power and substance, and in every respect what he was, he assumed the true weakness of mortal nature, which he did not possess.

And so that he might commend to us, by his supreme example, the virtue of obedience which we need, God sent his Son into the world “made under the law.” This was not because he himself owed anything to the law—for he alone is our teacher, our one lawgiver and judge—but so that by his compassion he might aid those placed under the law who could not bear the burdens of the law. Having rescued those who were under the law from servile condition, he might by his generosity restore them to the adoption of sons, which comes through grace.

Therefore he who appeared in the flesh entirely without any stain of pollution accepted the circumcision decreed by the law in his flesh. He who came in the likeness of sinful flesh, but not in sinful flesh, did not reject the remedy by which sinful flesh was accustomed to be cleansed. Likewise, he underwent the washing of baptism, by which he wished the people of the new grace to be cleansed from the filth of sins—not out of necessity, but for the sake of example.

Your Fraternity should know that circumcision in the law provided the same saving remedy against the wound of original sin that baptism now provides in the time of revealed grace. The difference was that they could not yet enter through the gate of the heavenly kingdom until he who gave the law came and bestowed the blessing. Thus God, the God of gods, might be seen in Zion; meanwhile, comforted after death by blessed rest in Abraham’s bosom, they would await with joyful hope their entrance into heavenly peace.

For he who now cries out solemnly and beneficially through his Gospel, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3), formerly cried out through his law: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised, that soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. 17). That is, he has violated the covenant of life commanded to humanity in paradise when Adam transgressed; in him all sinned. He shall perish from the assembly of the saints unless he is helped by a saving remedy.

Both purifications, therefore—the circumcision prescribed in the law and the baptism prescribed in the Gospel—were established by the grace that removes the first transgression.

And lest the gifts of heavenly regard be lacking to any age of the passing world, those also who from the beginning of the world until the time when circumcision was given, or after circumcision was given, pleased God from other nations, entrusted their own souls and those of their people to the Creator, whether through offerings of sacrifices or through the sole power of faith, and took care to be released from the bonds of the first guilt. “Without faith it is impossible to please God”; and, as it is written elsewhere, “The righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2).

But when the Son of God came in the flesh—he who took from Adam the nature of flesh alone, but no contagion of sin, and who, because he was conceived and born of a virgin through the power of the Holy Spirit [Alternative: “was” added], needed no gift of renewing grace—he nevertheless deigned to undergo both kinds of purification. He was circumcised by his parents on the eighth day after his birth and baptized by John in the thirtieth year of his age. Indeed, the Lord of the temple did not refuse to have the third saving offering presented for him. On the thirty-third day after his birth, with the Lord’s help, your Charity will hear and celebrate this mystery together.

The Lord, who needed none of these forms of purification, did not disdain to accept all of them, both legal and evangelical, so that he might teach at the proper time that the ordinances of the now-completed law were most beneficial, and show all the faithful that the remedies introduced by the coming Gospel were likewise to be undertaken. Moreover, the fact that on the same day of his circumcision he received the name Jesus was done in imitation of an ancient observance. We believe this observance was derived from the fact that the patriarch Abraham, who first received the sacrament of circumcision as a testimony to his great faith and to God’s promise to him, on the same day deserved, together with his wife, to be blessed through the enlargement of his and his wife’s names.

He who until then had been called Abram, “exalted father,” was thereafter called Abraham, that is, “father of many nations,” because God said: “I have made you the father of many nations.”
