This most faithful promise has now been fulfilled so broadly throughout the world that we too, called from the nations to devotion to that faith, rejoice to have him spiritually as our father. The Apostle also says to us: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3).

“And your wife Sarai,” he says, “you shall not call Sarai, but Sarah”—that is, not “my princess,” but “princess.” He plainly taught that she who had become a participant in and companion of such great faith should be called and understood not merely as the princess of her own household, but absolutely as “princess,” that is, the mother of all women who rightly believe.

Thus the blessed Apostle Peter, exhorting believing women from the nations to the virtues of humility, chastity, and modesty, remembers our same mother Sarah with fitting praise: “As Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord, whose daughters you are when you do good and do not fear any disturbance” (1 Pet. 3).

We have wished to remind your Love of these things, brothers, so that each of you may remember that, having received the faith of Christ, you too have deserved a share with the patriarchs in an exalted name—if, having received in Christ the purification derived from the name of Christ, namely holy baptism, you rejoice to have assumed this surname and strive to preserve it firm and undefiled to the end.

Thus you may rejoice that Isaiah’s prophecy has been fulfilled in you: “And he shall call his servants by another name” (Isa. 65), namely, by the Christian name, with which all Christ’s servants now delight to be marked. For no other name has been given under heaven to humanity by which it is necessary for them to be saved.

Therefore the prophet adds: “He who blesses himself on earth shall be blessed in the Lord. Amen” (Acts 4).

Elsewhere, addressing the Church that was also to be multiplied from the nations, he says of the same matter: “The nations shall see your righteous one, and all kings your glorious one; and you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 65).

But why the child who was born for us, the Son who was given for us, received the name Jesus—that is, the name “Savior”—requires not merely an explanation that we can readily understand, but careful and vigilant attention, so that we too may be saved through participation in that same name.

For we read, with the angel interpreting it: “He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1). We firmly believe and hope that the one who saves from sins does not fail also to save from the corruptions which occurred because of sins, and from death itself. The Psalmist testifies, saying: “He forgives all your iniquities; he heals all your diseases” (Ps. 103).

When all our iniquities have been completely forgiven, all our diseases will be healed, when, at the appearance of the glory of the resurrection, the last enemy—death—has been destroyed.

This is our true and complete circumcision: on the day of judgment, when we have all at once been stripped of every corruption of soul and flesh, then, after judgment has been completed, we enter the hall of the heavenly kingdom to behold forever the face of the Creator. This is typologically signified when circumcised children are brought to the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem with praises and an acceptable sacrificial offering.

For the one purified by true circumcision enters the temple of the Lord with gifts who, refined by the glory of the resurrection from every stain of mortality, enters the eternal joys of the heavenly city with the fruits of good works.

“You have broken my bonds,” he says; “to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise. I will fulfill my vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the sight of all his people, in your midst, Jerusalem” (Ps. 115).

That most desired time of entrance into heaven is indicated by the eighth day on which circumcision is celebrated. There are six ages of this world, distinguished by the most recognizable divisions of time. In them it is necessary to devote ourselves to labors for God and to work for a time in order to obtain eternal rest.

The seventh age is the age, not of those resting in this life but of those resting in the other life, until the time of the resurrection of souls. The eighth age is itself the blessed day of the resurrection, without any end of time. Then, when the glory of true circumcision shines forth in every way, the body that is subject to corruption will no longer burden the soul; the earthly dwelling will no longer weigh down the mind occupied with many thoughts. Rather, the body, now incorruptible, will bring joy to the soul, and the heavenly dwelling will raise up the whole person, who clings to the vision of his Creator.

The Prophet consequently explains the blessedness of that eternal day in the psalm mentioned above. He stirs his own soul and all the affections of his inner person to bless the Lord and remember all his rewards: “He redeems your life from destruction; he satisfies your desire with good things; he crowns you with mercy and compassion; your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, if we desire to reach the rewards of this most beautiful renewal, which is like the supreme circumcision, let us meanwhile take care to undergo the remedies of the first circumcision and renewal, which comes about through the daily practice of virtue.

“Let us put off, according to our former way of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error; let us be renewed in the spirit of our mind; and let us put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.”

Nor, when we hear of circumcision in one member of the body, should we think that it is sufficient for us merely to chastise that member. Rather, as the Apostle warns elsewhere: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every stain and defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (2 Cor. 7).

Let us reread the Acts of the Apostles and see the most blessed protomartyr Stephen thunder terribly against the Jews who were persecuting him and the Lord: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit.”

If those who resist the admonitions of the Holy Spirit are uncircumcised in heart and ears, then there is certainly a circumcision of hearts and ears. And if there is a circumcision of hearts and ears, there is also a circumcision of all the senses of our outward and inward person.

Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her, whoever has haughty eyes, has an uncircumcised sight. To such people the Voice of Truth says: “The one who is of God hears God’s words. For this reason you do not hear them, because you are not of God” (John 8).

They are uncircumcised in ears; uncircumcised in tongue and hands are those whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity—those who speak peace with their neighbor, while evil is in their hearts, and whose right hand is filled with gifts.

They are uncircumcised in taste whom the prophet rebukes, saying: “Woe to you who are mighty for drinking wine and strong men for mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5).

They are uncircumcised in smell and touch who are anointed with perfume and various fragrances, who pursue the embraces of a prostitute, sprinkling their bed with myrrh, aloe, and cinnamon.

They are uncircumcised in their steps, of whom the Psalmist says: “Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Ps. 11).

But those who guard their heart with all vigilance; who turn their eyes away so that they may not see vanity; who hedge their ears with thorns so that they may not hear a wicked tongue; who taste and see how sweet the Lord is, and how blessed are those who hope in him; who guard their ways so that they do not sin with their tongue; who, while breath remains in them and the Spirit of God is in their nostrils, do not speak iniquity with their lips, nor does their tongue meditate on falsehood; who lift their hands toward the commandments of God, which they love; who restrain their feet from every evil way so that they may keep God’s word—all these show that they have all their senses circumcised by the rock of spiritual practice.

For we read that circumcision was performed with stone knives. The rock, however, was Christ; through faith, hope, and love in him, the hearts of the righteous are purified not only in baptism but in every devout action.

This daily circumcision of ours, namely the continual cleansing of the heart, never ceases to celebrate the sacrament of the eighth day. For it is accustomed to sanctify us in imitation of the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day, the Sabbath—so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.

May God grant this, he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XI. ON THE FEAST OF THE THEOPHANY

**Matthew 3; Mark 1; Luke 3; John 1.** At that time Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him, and so forth.

The reading of the holy Gospel which we have just heard, brothers, gives us a great example of perfect humility both in the Lord and in the servant. In the Lord, because, although he is Lord, he not only deigned to be baptized by a human servant but also himself came to this servant to be baptized.

In the servant, because, although he knew that he had been appointed the Savior’s forerunner and baptizer, he nevertheless, mindful of his own weakness, humbly excused himself from the office entrusted to him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?”

But because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted,” the Lord, who appeared humble in human form in order to instruct humankind, was immediately shown by a voice descending upon him from the excellent glory to surpass human beings—indeed, angels and everything created: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” And that most faithful and humble servant, John, who preferred to be baptized by the Lord rather than to baptize the Lord [Alternative: “desired”], deserved both to baptize the Lord himself and, with the eyes of his mind opened, to see the Spirit descending upon him before all other mortals.

But since we have briefly previewed these matters, let us now explain everything at greater length, beginning with the sacred reading itself.

“Then,” he says, “Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.” The Son of God came to be baptized by a human being—not from anxious necessity to wash away any sin of his own, for he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth, but through a loving dispensation to wash away the contagion of all our sin, since we all offend in many ways, and if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.

The Creator of the waters came to be baptized in the waters themselves, so that he might intimate to us, who were conceived in iniquities and born in offenses, the mystery of the second birth celebrated through water and the Spirit, which we ought to desire.

He deigned to be washed in the waters of the Jordan, although he was clean from every stain, in order to sanctify the streams of water for the washing away of all the stains of our crimes.

But since we have learned from the Gospel reading about the Lord’s most humble dispensation, let us also examine with careful attention the servant’s most humble obedience. It follows:

“John was preventing him, saying: ‘I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?’” He was astonished that the one who had no guilt for baptism to cleanse should come to him to be baptized with water—indeed, the one who by his grace would remove all the guilt of the world from believers.

Accordingly, what John says here—“I ought to be baptized by you”—is rightly understood as the same thing that he is reported to have said when the Lord came to him, according to the Evangelist John: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

For we must all be baptized by the one who came into the world for this purpose: to take away the sins of the world. John himself ought to have been baptized by him—that is, cleansed from the contagion of original sin. Although “no one born of women” was greater than John [Alternative: “lesser than John”], nevertheless, as one born of a woman, he was not free from the blemish of guilt.

Therefore, together with all those born of women, he needed to be washed by the one who was born of a virgin and appeared as God in the flesh. Since it is written, “What is a human being, that he should be undefiled, and that one born of a woman should appear clean?” (Job 15), a human being, although holy but nevertheless born of a woman and therefore not free from the stain of guilt, rightly feared baptizing the Lord, whom he knew to have been born of a virgin and to possess absolutely no stain of guilt.

But because true humility is itself never without obedience as its companion, he humbly fulfilled the duty from which he had first recoiled. For it follows:

“Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Permit it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.’ Then he permitted him.” That is, only then did he release him, only then did he consent, only then did he allow himself to be baptized by him, when he understood that all righteousness had to be fulfilled in this order.

“Permit it now,” he says; “permit me now to be baptized by you in water, as I have commanded, and afterward you will be baptized by me in the Spirit, as you ask.”

“For thus it is fitting for us to set forth an example of fulfilling all righteousness,” so that the faithful may learn that no human being can exist as perfectly righteous without the water of baptism, and that the service of life-giving regeneration is necessary for all, even those who live innocently and justly. They will know that I, who was conceived and born through the work of the Holy Spirit [Alternative: “I am” added], underwent the second birth—or rather, consecrated the washing to myself.

No one of higher rank should therefore despise being baptized by my humble servants for the remission of sins, when he remembers that the Lord, who is accustomed to baptize in the Holy Spirit and forgive sins, subjected his head to be baptized in water by the hands of a servant.

It follows:

[Col. 0059D] Now when Jesus had been baptized, he immediately went up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.

This too belongs to the fulfillment of all righteousness: that, when the Lord had been baptized, the heavens were opened to him and the Spirit descended upon him. Through this, surely, our faith is confirmed: by the mystery of holy baptism, the entrance to our heavenly homeland is opened to us and the grace of the Holy Spirit is bestowed.

For should we believe that the heavenly mysteries were first opened to the Lord only then, when the true faith holds that he remained no less in the bosom of the Father and held his heavenly seat during the time when he lived among human beings than both afterward and before? Or did he receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit from the age of thirty, when he was baptized, although from his first conception he had always existed full of the Holy Spirit? [Al. omits *suae*, “of his age.”]

Therefore, dearest brothers, these mysteries were celebrated for us. Since the Lord dedicated the bath of baptism to us through the immersion of his most holy body, he also showed us that, after receiving baptism, heaven’s entrance is opened to us and the Holy Spirit is given.

There is also a fitting and profound contrast here. The first Adam, deceived by the unclean spirit through the serpent, lost the joys of the heavenly kingdom; the second Adam, glorified by the Holy Spirit through the dove, reopened the threshold of that same kingdom and extinguished the flashing flame by which the Cherub, its guardian, shut off the entrance to paradise after the first Adam had been expelled.

Today the second Adam showed that this flame had to be extinguished through the water of the bath of rebirth, so that at the place from which the first Adam, defeated by the enemy together with his wife, departed, the second Adam might return victorious over the enemy together with the holy Church, namely his bride. Indeed, the Father, the Prince of the age to come and the Prince of peace, bestowed on the redeemed greater gifts of immortal life—gifts which the father of the present age, the prince of discord, sold under sin and lost together with his offspring.

That most blessed life which Adam abandoned, although exalted by incomparable light and peace, and glorified by the frequent vision and conversation of God and the angels, was nevertheless situated in the earthly places of this world; its fruits, though obtained without labor, were still the food by which it was sustained. But the life which Christ grants is everlasting life in the citadel of heaven, nourished not by intermittent but by continual light of divine contemplation. [Al. omits *e*, “by.”]

The first blessed life of humanity was immortal in such a way that a person might not die in it, provided that he guarded himself cautiously against the seduction of sin. The second, however, will be immortal in such a way that a person cannot die in it, nor be tempted by any seduction of sin that assails him.

The reconciling Spirit appropriately appeared in a dove, a very simple bird, so that through the form of this creature he might show the gentleness of his own nature. For “the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit,” so that he might teach the one upon whom he descended to be gentle, mild, and destined to be a herald and minister to the world of heavenly mercy; and at the same time he might admonish all who were to be renewed by his grace to enter simple and pure in heart [Al. *misericordes*, “merciful”], according to what is written:

“Think of the Lord in goodness,  
and seek him in simplicity of heart.  
For wisdom will not enter a malicious soul,  
nor dwell in a body subjected to sins” (Wis. 1).

This is why Simon, who consented to remain in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, could have no share or portion in this Spirit. He was filled with that spirit which, appearing to human beings in the serpent, carefully taught their hearts because it itself was infected with the plague of malice and treachery.

But when the Spirit had descended upon the Lord, let us see what follows:

“And behold, a voice from heaven saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

The Son of God is baptized in a human being; the Spirit of God descends in a dove; God the Father is declared in a voice. Thus the holy and undivided Trinity is revealed in the mystery of baptism [Al. *in mysterio*, “in the mystery”]. Rightly so: he who was to command the ministers of his sacraments to teach all nations and baptize them [Al. *eas*, “them,” feminine] in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, first revealed personally in his own baptism that the entire Trinity was present.

What the Father’s voice says—“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”—it says in comparison with the earthly human being, in whom God the Creator in a certain sense indicates that he was displeased when that human being sinned, saying: “It repents me that I made humankind on the earth” (Gen. 6).

Repentance does not, of course, occur in God; but he speaks according to our manner, since we customarily feel remorse when we see our actions turned against our intention. He said that he repented of having made the human being on earth when he saw him, through sinning, degenerate [Al. *deviate*, “turn aside”] from the uprightness of his creation.

But in his only-begotten Son he was uniquely well pleased, because he knew that the human being whom he had assumed remained free from sin. In this voice of the Father, as in the other mysteries of the Lord’s baptism, the fulfillment of all righteousness is also declared.

For when the Spirit descended upon him, it was made known to human beings that the Son is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, so that through this people might learn that, by the grace of baptism and having received the Holy Spirit, they can be transferred from being children of the devil to being children of God [Al. adds *se*, “themselves”], as the Apostle teaches when he says to the faithful:

“You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8).

And the evangelist John says: “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1).

Having recalled these things about the baptism of our Savior, dearest brothers, insofar as he himself granted us understanding, let us return to ourselves [Al. *utique*, “certainly”]. Since we have heard of the humility and obedience both of the Baptist and of the baptized Lord, let us take care to preserve the baptism we have received through humble obedience, cleansing ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit and perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

Let us therefore humbly commend the mysteries to those who have not yet been initiated into them, so that they may undertake and preserve them; and all of us who have been advanced through the priestly order to administer those sacraments should humbly fulfill the office entrusted to us.

Let us all be diligent and watchful, so that we do not ourselves close by human enticements the door of our heavenly homeland that has been opened to us through divine mysteries.

For it is not without reason that the evangelist Luke records that the Lord prayed after his baptism, and that, when heaven had been opened, the Spirit and the Father’s voice came; nor is it without reason that, after being baptized—as the three concordant evangelists also testify—he immediately undertook a solitary fast of forty days. Rather, he plainly taught us and instructed us by his example that, after receiving the remission of sins in baptism, we should devote ourselves to vigils, fasts, prayers, and the other fruits of the Spirit, lest the unclean spirit, which had been expelled from our heart in baptism [Al. omits *in*, “in”], return while we are sluggish and insufficiently watchful, find us empty of spiritual riches, and crush us with a sevenfold plague, so that our last state becomes worse than our first.

Let us carefully beware lest we ourselves repeatedly kindle the fuel of our vices into a fire that will block our path to life. For the flaming sword—whatever it may be—that guards the gates of paradise has been extinguished for each and every believer [Al. *quibusque*, “each”] by the baptismal font, so that the person who had been driven away may return; but for unbelievers it remains forever immovable.

Yet for false believers [Al. *falso fidelibus*, “believers falsely so called”], who are called but not chosen, when they do not fear entangling themselves in crimes after baptism, that same fire is, as it were, rekindled after having been extinguished. Thus they do not deserve to enter the kingdom which they seek with a false and divided heart, with the serpent’s deceitful tooth rather than with the dove’s simple eye—a quality which the Lord shows that he greatly loves in his Church when he says in the Song of Songs:

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved;  
behold, you are beautiful;  
your eyes are like those of doves” (Song 1).

Therefore, since the form of the dove is set before us so that we may learn the simplicity pleasing to God, let us examine its nature more carefully, so that from each of its examples of innocence we may draw rules for a more reformed life.

The dove is entirely free from the malice of gall. Let us, then, also be free from the gall of malice, and let every bitterness, wrath, and indignation, together with all malice, be removed from us.

Thus [Al. omits *Ita*, “thus”], it harms no one with its beak or claws, nor does it seek even the smallest flies or worms with which nearly all the lesser birds feed themselves and their young. Let us see to it [Al. omits *nos*, “us”] that our teeth do not become weapons and arrows, lest, biting and devouring one another, we be consumed by one another.

Let us restrain our hands from robbery: “The one who stole must steal no longer. Rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one suffering need” [Col. 0062C]. For the dove too is often said to feed the young of others as though they were its own.

It feeds on the fruits and seed of the earth. Let us hear the Apostle: “It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine” (Rom. 14). And the apostle Peter says: “Supply virtue in your faith, knowledge in virtue, self-control in knowledge, endurance in self-control, godliness in endurance, and brotherly love in godliness” (2 Pet. 1).

Its song is a groan. Let us be miserable, mourn, and weep before the Lord who made us. Let our laughter be turned into mourning and our joy into sorrow. For blessed are those who mourn, because they will be comforted.

The dove is accustomed to sit upon the waters, so that, foreseeing in the water the shadow of the hawk that is about to seize it, it may avoid it. Let us also be pure, and let us diligently sit beside the streams of Scripture, cleansed by them, so that, taught by their mirrors, we may be able to recognize and avoid the snares of the ancient enemy.

For the Church, namely the bride of Christ, loves such people, and sings in praise of her beloved:

“His eyes are like doves,  
washed with milk  
and resting beside abundant streams” [Al. *amatoris*, “of her lover,” instead of *amoris*, “of love”].

The dove usually nests in the holes of a rock, in a cavity of a stone wall. The rock is Christ, whose hands were pierced by nails on the cross and whose side was pierced by a lance; from it blood and water immediately flowed—the mystery, namely, of our sanctification and cleansing.

His stone wall is the united strength of the saints; the cavity within that wall [Al. adds *macerie*, “of the wall”] is the bosom of paternal love. When the saints receive the more tender souls of the faithful in order to nurture them toward the perfection of faith, hope, and love, they open a place within themselves, as though for doves building their nests.

Let us therefore, while we are still weak in faith, humbly submit to these supports of the stronger. Let us always take care to be sanctified by these mysteries of the Lord’s passion.

For the Lord seeks such conduct from all of us; he desires to see each of our lives devoted to such pursuits, and he rejoices to hear his praises sung and proclaimed by such people. He says:

“Rise up, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the holes of the rock, in the cavity of the stone wall. Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” (Song 2).

These seven examples of virtue drawn from the nature of the dove will suffice. And perhaps rightly so, since the grace of the Holy Spirit, who descended in the dove, is sevenfold.

[Col. 0063B] Yet, among all that human ingenuity can discover about its nature for moral interpretation, one thing remains that sacred history relates concerning its mystical action.

When the Lord, as a figure of the future baptism, was cleansing the crimes of the original world with the waters of the flood, and, after the cleansing had been completed, wished Noah to learn what the condition of the earth was, he sent out a raven. The raven disdained to return to the ark, signifying those who, although washed by the water of baptism, nevertheless neglect to lay aside through more disciplined living the blackest garment of the old human being. And, lest they deserve to be renewed by the anointing of the Holy Spirit, they immediately depart from the innermost unity of Catholic peace and repose, pursuing external things—that is, the desires of the world.

After it he sent out a dove. But the dove came to him in the evening, carrying in its beak a branch of olive with green leaves.

You understand this, I believe, brothers, and with your understanding you anticipate what I am saying: the olive branch with green leaves signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, abundant in words of life. Concerning its fullness, resting upon Christ, the Psalm says:

“God, your God, has anointed you  
with the oil of gladness  
above your companions” (Ps. 44).

Concerning this gift, given to Christ’s companions, John says: “You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things” (1 John 2).

And the shadow of the truth sings in a most beautiful comparison. The bodily dove, washed by the waters of the flood, carried an olive branch into the ark; the Holy Spirit, in the form of a bodily dove, descended upon the Lord after he had been baptized in the water of the Jordan.

We too are members of Christ and of the Church. We are represented not only by the human beings who were in the ark with Noah, but also by the animals that the ark contained, and even by the very wood from which that ark was made. After receiving the bath of the water of rebirth, we are marked by the grace of the Holy Spirit through the anointing of sacred chrism. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who gave this grace, graciously preserve it undefiled within us. He lives and reigns forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XII. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

Luke 2. “At that time, when Jesus was twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast, and when the days had been completed and they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem,” etc.

The reading of the holy Gospel has been opened before us, dearest brothers, and there is no need for us to say anything by way of exposition. It describes the infancy and childhood of our Redeemer, in which he graciously became a participant in our humanity. It recalls the eternity of his divine majesty, in which he remained and always remains equal to the Father.

Thus, by recalling the humility of his incarnation, let us also take care to practice the remedy of true humility against all the wounds of sin, always remembering with devout hearts how much we ought to humble ourselves for divine love and for our salvation—we who are earth and ashes—if that supreme power did not refuse to humble itself for us, descending to assume the weakness of our frailty.

Likewise, having heard, believed, and confessed the divinity of the Lord our Savior, by which he remains consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, let us hope that through the mysteries of his humanity, with which we have been instructed, we may attain to the contemplation of that same divine glory. He faithfully promises this to his faithful servants, saying:

“The one who has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. The one who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14).

“I will reveal myself,” he says—that is, not as everyone can see me, and as unbelievers too can see and crucify me, but as the King of the ages in his beauty: only the pure eyes of the saints can see me in this way. I will show myself thus, in return for their love, to those who love me.

Let us therefore hope, as we have said, that through the mysteries of his humanity we can ascend to behold the form of his divinity—provided that we preserve those same mysteries undefiled, with the worthy honor of justice, holiness, and truth, as we received them; provided that we humbly follow the examples of his human conduct and the teaching which he administered to us through his humanity.

For whoever disdains to follow the footsteps of his humility, with what presumption does he hope to enter upon the joys of beholding his glory?

That the Lord went up to Jerusalem with his parents every year for Passover is plainly an indication of human humility. It belongs to human beings to assemble in order to offer God the vows of spiritual sacrifices and to reconcile their Creator to themselves through abundant prayers and tears.

Thus the Lord, born as a human being among human beings, did what God had commanded human beings to do through the angels. He himself kept the law which he had given, so that he might show us, who are merely human beings, that everything God commands must be observed.

Let us therefore follow the path of his human conduct if we delight to behold the glory of his divinity, if we desire to dwell in his eternal house in heaven all the days of our life, if we rejoice to see the delight of the Lord and to be protected by his holy temple (Ps. 26). And so that no breath of evil may ever strike us, let us remember to frequent the house of the present Church with the necessary offerings of pure prayers.

That he sat in the temple at the age of twelve in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them, is an indication of human humility, indeed an outstanding example of learning humility.

For the power of God, the eternal wisdom of God, speaks divinely:

“I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel,  
and I am present among the learned in thought.  
Counsel and equity are mine;  
prudence is mine; strength is mine.  
Through me kings reign,  
and legislators decree what is just.  
Blessed is the person who hears me,  
who watches daily at my gates  
and keeps watch at the posts of my doors” (Prov. 8).

Wisdom itself, clothed in humanity, graciously came to listen to human beings, so that it might set before human beings, however gifted in intellect, the necessary pattern of learning the word—lest those who refused to become disciples of truth should become teachers of error.

And rightly so: since he was a young man who would undertake the office of teaching, while still a little boy he listened to and questioned his elders, so that by their prudent administration he might restrain the audacity of those who, not only unlearned but also immature, rush to teach rather than submit themselves to learning.

Let us follow the path of his humanity if we delight in the dwelling-place of the divine vision, always remembering that commandment:

“Listen, my son, to your father’s discipline,  
and do not abandon your mother’s law,  
so that grace may be added to your head  
and a necklace to your neck” (Prov. 1).

Through hearing the father’s discipline and observing the mother’s law, grace is added to our head and a necklace to our neck. For the more earnestly someone listens to divine commandments, and the more diligently strives to observe what he has learned within the unity of mother Church, the more worthily he will now ascend to the honor of preaching, and the more sublimely, in the future, to the blessedness of reigning with Christ without end.

But lest anyone suppose that the Lord Savior approached, listened to, and questioned the teachers because of a need arising from ignorance, let us see what follows:

“All who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers, and when they saw him they were astonished.”

Because he was both truly human and truly God, to show that he was human he humbly listened to human teachers; and to prove that he was God, he answered those same speakers with sublimity.

When his mother sought him and said:

“Son, why have you treated us this way? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in sorrow.”

He answered:

“Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?”

This was an indication of the divine majesty, concerning which he says elsewhere: “Everything that the Father has is mine.” Therefore he most rightly testifies that the temple belongs no less to him than to the Father.

When he was found in the temple, he says: “I must be in the things that belong to my Father,” because, since their majesty and glory are one, their throne and house are also one. Not only the material house of God, which is customarily made for worshiping him for a time, but also the intellectual house, which is built for praising him eternally, is known to be common equally to the Father and the Son, indeed also to the Holy Spirit.

Finally, the same Son of God, who promises concerning himself and the Father to the one who loves him, “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14), says concerning the Spirit:

“I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever: the Spirit of truth, who will remain with you and will be in you” (ibid.).

Since the holy Trinity has one and indivisible divine nature, its dwelling in the hearts of the elect cannot be different. Therefore, when the Lord, sitting in the temple, says, “I must be in the things that belong to my Father,” he declares the power and glory that he shares eternally with God the Father.

But that, on returning to Nazareth, he was subject to his parents is an indication of human reality and at the same time an example of humility. He was subject to human beings in the nature in which he is less than the Father. Hence he himself says: “I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I” (John 14). In that nature he was also made a little lower than the angels.

But in the nature in which he and the Father are one, in which he does not go to the Father at a particular time but is always in the Father, all things were made through him, and he is before all things.

Greatly to be admired is the dispensation of his profound mercy: when he saw that his parents were not yet able to grasp the mystery of his divine majesty, he displayed to them the humility of human subjection, so that through this he might gradually instruct them toward recognition of his divinity.

For after he had said, “Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” and they did not understand the word that he had spoken to them, as the evangelist subsequently indicates:

“He went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them.”

He had revealed to his parents the mystery of his divine power, to his mother—that is, to the true mother of his flesh—and to the most chaste guardian of her chastity, who at that time, before the Gospel light had been spread, was considered and called by nearly everyone who could know them to be his husband by carnal union and his father by carnal responsibility.

To these, I say, he had declared: “I must be in the things that belong to my Father.” Since they could not ascend through understanding to the summit of so great a mystery, nor determine that he could remain in the things that truly belonged to his Father except by understanding what those things were, he himself descended with them to the lower level of their way of life and began to remain in the things that belonged to them. In a gracious dispensation he was subject to them until, as the instruction of humility progressed, they recognized that he was to be preferred to every creature.

Let us consider briefly, I beg you, what our pride does in relation to this. Certainly, when we realize that our simpler brothers cannot understand the mysteries of Scripture which we explain—mysteries that we ourselves did not know eternally but learned in time with the Lord’s help—we immediately become accustomed to swelling with pride. Despising them, we boast as though our learning were singular and exceedingly great, as though there were not many much more learned than we are.

And although we do not want to be despised by those who are more learned, we ourselves rejoice to despise, indeed even to mock, those less learned than we are. We do not take care to remember that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is open not merely to those who comprehend the mysteries of faith or the commandments of their Creator through meditation, but rather to those who put into practice what they have been able to learn.

Moreover, “for the one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin.” And as the Lord himself testifies: “From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required” (Luke 12).

Let knowledge not inflate us, then, but let love build us up instead. Let us follow the example of the Son of God appearing in human form. When he saw that those whom he saw were not yet capable of following him in learning sublime things, he subjected himself to them in gracious humility, so that, instructed by his example, their minds might become worthy of heavenly grace and capable of the heavenly mystery.

“And his mother,” he says, “kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.”

Everything that the Virgin Mother had learned to have been said or done concerning the Lord or by the Lord, she carefully retained in her heart and diligently committed it all to memory, so that when the time finally came for his incarnation to be preached or written, she could adequately explain everything to those who asked, just as it had happened.

Let us too, my brothers, imitate the Lord’s devout mother. By keeping all the words and deeds of our Lord and Savior fixed in our hearts, let us drive away, through meditation on them day and night, the assaults of untimely and harmful thoughts. Through frequent discussion of these things, let us also take care to discipline ourselves and our neighbors away from empty tales and the falsely sweet conversations of detraction, and to kindle us toward continual praise of God.

For if, dearest brothers, we desire to dwell in the blessedness of the future age in the house of the Lord and to praise him forever, we must also in this age carefully demonstrate what we seek in the future: namely, by frequently visiting the thresholds of the Church, and not only singing the praises of the Lord in it, but also showing everywhere under his dominion, in words and deeds alike, whatever contributes to the praise and glory of our Creator.

“And Jesus,” he says, “advanced in wisdom, age, and grace with God and human beings.”

This indicates the nature of his true humanity, in which he chose for a time to advance, although in his divinity he is the same, and his years do not fail.

According to human nature he advanced in wisdom—not by becoming wiser in time, since from the first hour of his conception he remained full of the spirit of wisdom, but by gradually revealing to others in time the same wisdom with which he was full.

According to human nature he advanced in age, because he passed from infancy to childhood and from childhood to youth according to the customary human order of growth.

According to human nature he advanced in grace—not by receiving, with the passage of time, something he did not possess, but by revealing the gift of grace which he possessed.

And rightly, when it had been said that Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace, there was added, “with God and human beings.” For as, with advancing age, he revealed to human beings the gifts of wisdom and grace that were inherent in him, so he always took care to stir them to the praise of God the Father, himself accomplishing what he commanded others to do:

“Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

Therefore he is said to advance not only in grace and wisdom with human beings, insofar as they were able to recognize his wisdom and grace, but also with God, insofar as they referred the wisdom and grace which they recognized in him to the praise and glory of God. To him, through whose eternal benefits and gifts, be praise and thanksgiving throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XIII. FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

John 2. “At that time a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there,” etc.

That our Lord and Savior, when invited to a wedding, graciously chose not only to come but also to perform there a miracle by which he would gladden the guests, rightly confirms the faith of believers even apart from the figures of heavenly mysteries, when understood according to the literal sense.

Moreover, it shows how damnable was the unbelief of Tatian, Marcian, and the others who disparage marriage. If there were any fault in an undefiled marriage bed and in weddings celebrated with the chastity proper to them, the Lord would never have wished to come to them or to consecrate them by the beginnings of his signs.

But now, because conjugal chastity is good, widowhood in continence is better, and virginal perfection is best, he chose to be born from the undefiled womb of the Virgin Mary in order to approve the choice of every degree while distinguishing the merit of each. Shortly after his birth he was blessed by the prophetic mouth of the widow Anna; as a young man he was invited by those celebrating a wedding and honored them with the presence of his power.

But let us now return to the higher joy of the heavenly figures. The Son of God came to a wedding in order to perform miracles on earth and to declare himself to be the one of whom the Psalmist had sung beforehand under the figure of the sun:

“He is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber;  
he rejoiced like a giant to run his course.  
His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18).

In another place he himself says concerning himself and his faithful:

“Can the children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Matt. 9).

For from the time when the incarnation of our Savior began to be promised to the patriarchs, it was always awaited by the many tears and mourning of the saints until he came. Likewise, from the time when he ascended to the Father after his resurrection, the hope of all the saints has depended upon his return.

Only during the time when he lived among human beings could they not weep and mourn, because they already possessed bodily with them the one whom they loved spiritually.

Christ, therefore, is the bridegroom; his bride is the Church; the children of the bridegroom, or of the wedding, are each of his individual faithful. The time of the wedding is that time when, through the mystery of the incarnation, he joined the holy Church to himself.

Therefore it was not by chance, but for the sake of a definite mystery, that he came to a wedding celebrated on earth according to the flesh—the one who descended from heaven to earth in order to unite the Church to himself in spiritual love. His bridal chamber was the womb of his incorrupt mother, in which God was joined to human nature, and from which he came forth like a bridegroom to join the Church to himself.

The first place of the wedding was in Judea, where the Son of God graciously became human, consecrated the Church through participation in his body, and confirmed it in faith through the pledge of his Spirit. But when the nations were called to faith, the desired joys of the same wedding reached to the ends of the earth.

Nor is it without a mystery that the wedding is reported to have taken place on the third day, after the events described in the preceding passage of the Gospel. This signifies that the Lord came to prepare the Church for himself in the third period of the world.

The first period of the world, before the law, shone forth through the example of the patriarchs; the second, under the law, through the writings of the prophets; the third, under grace, through the proclamations of the evangelists, like the light of the third day shining upon the world. In this period our Lord and Savior appeared, born in the flesh for the redemption of the human race.

The fact that the same wedding is said to have taken place at Cana of Galilee—that is, in the zeal of accomplished migration—also announces figuratively that those are especially worthy of Christ’s grace who know how to burn with zeal for devout dedication, to strive for greater spiritual gifts, and, by doing good, to migrate from vices to virtues and, by hoping for and loving them, from earthly things to eternal ones.

When the Lord was reclining at the wedding, the wine ran out, so that, when better wine had been made by him in a wondrous manner, the glory of God hidden in the human being might be revealed and the faith of those who believed in him might grow stronger.

If we seek the mystery, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, that unmixed sweetness of the legal meaning had gradually begun to fail because of the Pharisees’ carnal interpretation. He immediately transformed commandments that appeared carnal into spiritual teaching, and by the power of evangelical heavenly grace changed the entire surface of the legal letter. This is what it means to make wine from water.

But first let us carefully investigate what it means that, when the wine had run out, the mother of Jesus said to him:

“They have no wine.”

He answered:

“What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.”

He was not dishonoring his mother—he who commands us to honor father and mother—nor was he denying that she was his mother, from whose virginal flesh he did not disdain to take flesh, as the Apostle also testifies when he says: “He was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1).

How could he be from the seed of David according to the flesh if not from the body of Mary according to the flesh, since she descended from the seed of David?

But in saying, as he was about to perform a miracle, “What is there between me and you, woman?” he signifies that he did not temporally receive from his mother the beginning of the divinity by which the miracle was to be performed, but always possessed eternity from the Father.

“What is there between me and you,” he says, “woman?”—since the divinity which I have always had from the Father has nothing in common with your flesh, from which I assumed flesh.

“My hour has not yet come”: it is not yet time for me to demonstrate by dying the frailty of the humanity assumed from you. First I must reveal the power of eternal divinity by performing mighty works.

But the hour would come when he would show what he shared with his mother, when, as he was about to die on the cross, he took care to commend the virgin mother to the virgin disciple.

Suffering the weakness of the flesh, he piously entrusted the mother from whom he had received that flesh to the disciple whom he loved most. But when he was about to perform divine works, he pretended not to know her, as though she were unknown, because he recognized that she was not the source of his divine birth.

There were six stone water jars set there for the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures. Jars are vessels prepared to receive water; for in Greek, ὕδωρ means “water.” Water, however, signifies the knowledge of Holy Scripture, which habitually both washes its hearers clean from the filth of sins and gives them drink from the fountain of divine knowledge. The six vessels containing the water are the devoted hearts of the saints, whose perfection of life and faith has been set before the human race as an example of right living and believing throughout the six ages of this passing world—that is, up to the time of the Lord’s Passion.

And fittingly the vessels are made of stone, because the hearts of the righteous are strong, solidified, as it were, by faith in and love of that stone which Daniel saw cut from the mountain without hands, made into a great mountain, and filling the whole earth; concerning it Zechariah says: “In one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. III)—that is, in Christ resides the fullness of spiritual knowledge. The apostle Peter likewise recalls him, saying: “Coming to him, the living stone, you yourselves are built up upon him like living stones” (I Pet. II).

The jars are fittingly set there only for the purification of the Jews, because the law was given through Moses only to the Jewish people. But the grace and truth of the Gospel were brought through Jesus Christ [Col. 0070C] no less to the Gentiles than to the Jews. “Each holding,” he says, “two or three measures,” because the authors and ministers of Holy Scripture, the prophets, sometimes speak only of the Father and the Son, as in the passage: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII). For Christ is the power of God in wisdom. At other times they also make mention of the Holy Spirit, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. XXXII). Understand “the word of the Lord” and “the breath” as the Trinity, which is one God.

But as far as water differs from wine, so far does that meaning differ by which the Scriptures were understood before the Savior’s coming from the meaning that he himself, when he came, revealed to the apostles and left to their disciples to follow perpetually. Indeed, the Lord could have filled the empty jars with wine, since at the beginning of human creation he created all things from nothing; but he preferred to make wine from water, thereby teaching figuratively that he had come not to abolish or condemn the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfill them, and that through the grace of the Gospel he neither did nor taught anything other than what the legal and prophetic Scriptures had indicated that he would do and teach.

Let us therefore see, brothers, the six jars of the Scriptures filled with saving water; let us see that same water changed into the most delightful fragrance and taste of wine. In the first age of the world, Cain, envious of his brother, killed the righteous Abel; and for this reason Abel himself, blessed with the perpetual glory of martyrdom, received the praise of righteousness even in the Gospel and apostolic writings, while the impious fratricide paid the penalties of eternal condemnation. Whoever, hearing these things, fears being condemned with the impious and desires to be blessed with the righteous, casts away every source of hatred and envy and takes care to please God through the sacrifice of righteousness, modesty, innocence, and patience. Such a person finds in Scripture a vessel full of water, from which he may rejoice to be healthfully washed and given drink.

But if he understands Cain the murderer as the faithlessness of the Jews, Abel’s killing as the Passion of the Savior, and the earth that opened its mouth and received his blood from Cain’s hand as the Church, which received Christ’s blood, poured out by the Jews, as the mystery of her renewal, then surely he has found water changed into wine, because he understands the sayings of the sacred law in a more sacred sense.

At the beginning of the second age of the world, the earth was wiped out by the waters of the Flood because of the greatness of its sins, [Col. 0071B] but Noah alone, because of his righteousness, was saved with his household in the ark. Whoever, hearing of the terrible devastation of this calamity and the marvelous deliverance of the few, begins to live more correctly, desiring to be saved with the chosen and fearing to be destroyed with the reprobate, has certainly found a jar of water by which he may be cleansed or refreshed.

But when he begins to look more deeply, and understands the Church in the ark, Christ in Noah, the baptismal water that washes away sins in the water that destroyed the sinners, the various distinctions among the baptized in the human beings and animals contained in the ark, and the anointing of the Holy Spirit with which the baptized are imbued in the dove that brought an olive branch into the ark after the Flood, he marvels that wine has been made from water, because he sees that his own cleansing, sanctification, and justification were prophesied in the ancient history of the event.

In the third age of the world, God, testing Abraham’s obedience, commanded him to offer as a burnt offering his only son, whom he loved. Abraham does not delay in doing what is commanded, but a ram is sacrificed in place of the son; nevertheless, for the excellence of his obedience he himself is granted the inheritance of perpetual blessing. Behold, you have the third jar. On hearing how great the power of obedience is and with what reward it is repaid, you too strive to learn and possess obedience.

But if you understand the sacrifice of the only beloved son as a figure of his Passion—of him concerning whom the Father says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III)—then, because the divinity remained incapable of suffering while only the humanity underwent death and pain, the son is offered, as it were, but the ram is slaughtered. If you understand the blessing promised to Abraham as the gift fulfilled in you from the Gentiles who were to believe, then surely he has made wine from water for you, because he has opened the spiritual meaning, whose new fragrance intoxicates you.

At the beginning of the fourth age, David received the kingdom of the Israelite people for its salvation: humble, innocent, and gentle, he was an exile on behalf of the one whose unjust persecution had long afflicted him. Behold the fourth jar, filled with a saving spring. Whoever, hearing these things, begins to devote himself to humility and innocence and to drive pride and envy from his heart has found, as it were, a draught of the clearest water by which he may be refreshed.

But if he recognizes that Saul signifies the Jews persecuting, and David Christ and the Church, and that the Jews’ carnal as well as spiritual rule was destroyed because of their faithlessness, while the kingdom of Christ and the Church will remain forever, he will certainly perceive a cup of wine made from water. For he knows that he reads there about himself, his life and kingdom, and even the king himself, where previously he had read an ancient history as though it concerned others.

In the fifth age of the world, the sinful people, when Nebuchadnezzar had taken them captive, migrated to Babylon. But after seventy years, having repented and been corrected, they were brought back to their homeland by Jesus the great priest, where they rebuilt the house of God, which had been burned, and the holy city, which had been destroyed. Whoever reads or hears this, is seized by the fear of sinning and flees to the remedy of repentance, has been washed in the water of the purifying jar.

But if he has learned to understand Jerusalem and the temple of God as the Church of Christ, Babylon as the confusion of sins, Nebuchadnezzar as the devil, Jesus the great priest as Jesus Christ, the true and eternal high priest, and the seventy years as the fullness of good works bestowed through the gifts of the Holy Spirit—namely, on account of the Decalogue and the sevenfold grace of that same Spirit—and if he sees this happening daily, with some snatched from the Church by the devil through sinning and others reconciled through Christ by recovering and repenting through the grace of the Holy Spirit, then he possesses wine made from water. For, understanding that what is written concerns him, he immediately demands to be freed by Christ’s grace from whatever sin of captivity he discovers within himself, growing hot with a great ardor of compunction, as though with new wine.

At the beginning of the sixth age of the world, the Lord appeared in the flesh and, on the eighth day after his birth, was circumcised according to the law. Thirty-three days later he was brought to the temple, and legal offerings were presented for him. Considering these matters literally, we plainly learn with what diligence we must undertake the mysteries of the evangelical faith, since he himself, bringing the blessing of grace—the one who gave the law of the letter—willed first to be consecrated by the ancient rite of the ceremonies by which he consecrates all things divinely, and thus took care both to receive and to hand on the new sacraments of grace.

Behold the sixth jar, bringing a purer water than the others for washing away the contagion of sin and for drinking the joys of life. But if, in the circumcision of the eighth day, you understand baptism, which redeemed us from the death of sins as a sign of the Lord’s resurrection, and recognize in the bringing into the temple and the offering of the purifying sacrifice a figure of the faithful entering from the baptistery into the holy altar and being consecrated by the singular sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood, then you have certainly been given wine made from water—and indeed unmixed wine.

Moreover, if you interpret the day of circumcision as referring to the general resurrection of the human race, when mortal offspring will cease and all mortality will be changed into immortality, and if you understand the circumcised being brought into the temple with offerings as referring to the time when, after the resurrection and the completion of the universal judgment, the saints, now made incorruptible, will enter forever to contemplate the appearance of the divine majesty, bringing with them the offerings of good works, then surely you will see wine being made from water, [Col. 0073A] concerning whose maker you may rightly proclaim and say: “And how excellent is your cup that intoxicates!” (Ps. XXII).

Therefore the Lord did not wish to make wine for the joys of the wedding from nothing, but, commanding the six jars to be filled with water, miraculously changed this water into wine, because he bestowed the six ages of the world with the abundance of saving wisdom, which he himself, when he came, enriched with the power of a higher meaning. For what had previously tasted merely carnal to the carnal-minded, he disclosed as something to be understood spiritually.

Do you wish to hear, brothers, how he made wine from water? After his resurrection he appeared to two disciples walking along the road and went with them; beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. Do you wish again to hear how they were intoxicated with that same wine? [Col. 0073B] Later, recognizing who it was that was offering them the word of life to drink, they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us when he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV).

Jesus therefore says to the servants: “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them to the brim. What are signified by the servants who are commanded to do these things, if not Christ’s disciples, who filled the jars with water? Not that they themselves filled the past ages of the world with the legal and prophetic writings, but that they filled them by understanding them wisely and opening them faithfully, since the Scripture delivered through the prophets was both healthful for drinking the wisdom of heaven and useful for disciplining conduct. They filled them to the brim, [Col. 0073C] because they rightly understood that no age of the world had been without holy teachers who, whether by words, examples, or even writings, opened the way of life to mortals.

And he says to them: “Go now, draw some out, and take it to the master of the feast.” And they took it. The master of the feast is some learned interpreter of the law of that time, perhaps Nicodemus or Gamaliel, or Saul, who was then his disciple but is now Paul the apostle, teacher of the whole Church. And when the word of the Gospel, which lay hidden in the letter of the law and prophecy, is entrusted to such men, wine made from water is offered to the master of the feast to drink.

Accordingly, it is appropriately reported that, after calling the bridegroom, the master of the feast said:

“Every man first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then the inferior. But you have kept the good wine until now.”

For it belongs to teachers to recognize the difference between the law and the Gospel, between truth and shadow, and to bring forth, in place of all the ancient institutions and all the promises of an earthly kingdom, the new grace of evangelical faith and the everlasting gifts of the heavenly homeland.

This was the beginning of signs that Jesus performed at Cana of Galilee, and he manifested his glory. By this sign he manifested that he was himself the king of glory and therefore the Bridegroom of the Church, who came to the wedding as an ordinary human being, yet, as Lord of heaven and earth, changed the elements as he wished.

There is a beautiful correspondence among these events. At the beginning of the signs that, while still mortal, he was to show to mortals, he changed water into wine; and at the beginning of the signs that, having already been made immortal through the resurrection, he was to show to those pursuing only the studies of immortal life, he first steeped their carnal and, as it were, tasteless minds in the flavor of heavenly knowledge. For, while he was still standing on earth, he opened their understanding by the gift of his Spirit, so that they might understand the Scriptures; and afterward, sending that same Spirit from heaven, he poured into their hearts a greater ardor both of heavenly love and spiritual wisdom, granting them in addition knowledge of all languages, so that they might be able to offer to the whole world the grace of life they had received.

Let us therefore love with our whole mind these nuptials of Christ and the Church, dearest brothers—nuptials that were then prefigured in one city and are now celebrated throughout the whole world—and let us join ourselves to their heavenly joys through tireless devotion to good works. Since we have entered them, called by faith and clothed in the garment of love, let us take care to celebrate them, and before the day of the final judgment let us diligently examine and wash away the stains of both our actions and our thoughts. Otherwise, when the king who made the wedding for his son enters, if he sees that we do not have the wedding garment of love, he may cast us out, bind our feet and hands so that we can no longer do good, and send us into the outer darkness.

Let us cleanse, by faith, the strong vessels of our hearts according to the purification of the heavenly commandments; let us fill them with the water of saving knowledge by attending more frequently to sacred reading. Let us ask the Lord to warm the grace of knowledge that he has bestowed on us by the fervor of his love—lest it puff us up—and to turn it toward seeking what is above alone and wisely, so that, spiritually intoxicated, [Col. 0074C] we too may be able to sing with the Prophet: “You have given us to drink the wine of compunction” (Ps. LIX). Thus it comes about that, as we make good progress, Jesus may manifest his glory to us also, now in part, insofar as we are able to receive it, and in the future perfectly—the glory in which he lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XIV. FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY

JOHN I; MATTHEW III; MARK I; LUKE III. At that time John saw Jesus coming toward him and said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world,” etc.

John the Baptist and forerunner of the Lord Savior, whom he had long proclaimed to the peoples as one who would come, now, as you heard just now when the passage from the holy Gospel was read, immediately pointed him out with his finger as he came toward him, saying:

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” Behold the Lamb of God: behold the innocent one, free from every sin, who indeed has bone from Adam’s bones and flesh [Al.: “flesh”] from Adam’s flesh, but drew no stain of guilt from sinful flesh. Behold him who takes away the sins of the world: behold him who, appearing as the righteous among sinners, the gentle among the impious—that is, as a lamb among wolves—also possesses the power to justify sinners and the impious.

But how he takes away the sins of the world, and in what order he justifies the impious, the apostle Peter shows when he says: “You were not redeemed with corruptible things, silver or gold, from your empty way of life inherited from your fathers, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ” [Col. 0075A] (I Pet. I). And in the Apocalypse the apostle John, whose Gospel this is, says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. I).

He not only washed us from our sins in his blood when he gave his blood for us on the cross, or when each one of us was washed in the baptismal water through the mystery of his most holy Passion; rather, he takes away the sins of the world daily. He therefore washes us from our sins daily in his blood when the memory of that same blessed Passion is recalled at the altar, when the creation of bread and wine is transferred into the sacrament of his body and blood through the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit. Thus his body and blood are not poured out and sacrificed by the hands of unbelievers to their destruction, but are received by the mouths of the faithful for their salvation.

The paschal lamb in the law rightly displayed a figure of this (*hujus*; Al. *cujus*, “of whom”). Once, by liberating the people from Egyptian slavery, it used to sanctify that same people every year through its sacrifice, in remembrance of that deliverance, until he should come to whom such a sacrifice bore witness. Offered to the Father for us as a sacrifice and an odor of sweetness, he transferred the mystery of his Passion, through the offering of the lamb, into the creation of bread and wine, having become a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

It follows:

John bore witness concerning the Lord, saying: “This is he of whom I said: After me comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me.” “After me comes a man”: he was born into the world after me; he will begin to preach to the world after me, yet he was made before me. He surpasses me in the power of his majesty as much as the sun surpasses the morning star [Note: Col. 0075D, Al.: “as much as a judge [surpasses] a herald, as much as the sun,” etc.], although he appears later, because he was before me, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.” “After me comes a man”: understand the time of human birth, in which he is later than John. “Who was made before me”: contemplate the primacy of royal power, by which he presides even over the angels. “Because he was before me”: understand the eternity of divine majesty, by which he is equal to the Father. “After me comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me”: he came after me in humanity, and for that reason surpasses me in dignity, because he was before me in divinity.

[Col. 0075D] “And I did not know him,” he says. It is certain that John knew the Lord, since he was sent to bear witness to him and proclaimed that he would come as judge of all, saying: “His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. III). He testified that the Holy Spirit was to be given by him, saying: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit,” and he desired to be washed by him himself, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?”

How, then, does he say, “And I did not know him,” unless it is because he recognized more perfectly, when he was baptized, the one whom he had previously known? He knew him as the Savior and judge of the world, but he recognized more deeply the power of his majesty when the Holy Spirit descended upon him. For there is no doubt that blessed John, when he was granted to see the Holy Spirit, even under bodily appearance, and to hear the Father’s voice, even though it sounded bodily, gained greatly from this sight and hearing. With the eyes of his mind now opened, he received from God [Note: Col. 0075D, Al.: “received, so much so that,” etc.] a great measure of heavenly knowledge concerning the excellence of divine power, so that, in comparison with the understanding by which he then began to be enlightened, he seemed to himself to have previously been altogether ignorant of how great he was. Bearing careful witness to the Lord concerning whom he had been sent, he adds:

“But so that he might be manifested in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water.” This is plainly to say: “I did not come baptizing in water because I can take away the sins of the world by baptizing, but so that by baptizing and preaching I might manifest him to the people of Israel. He, baptizing in the Holy Spirit, is able to take away the sins not only of Israel but of the whole world, if they are willing to believe in him. For this reason I came baptizing in water [Al.: “repentance”], so that by baptizing I might prepare the way for him who would baptize for the forgiveness of sins.”

And John bore witness, saying: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him.” Fittingly the Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, so that the faithful might learn that they cannot be filled with his Spirit in any other way [Note: Col. 0076D, Al.: “that they can become his members in no other way, in no other way [be filled] with his …”] unless they are simple and unless they have true peace with their brothers, which the kisses of doves signify. Ravens also have kisses, but they tear, which the dove does not do at all: they signify those who speak peace with their neighbor while evil is in their hearts. But the nature of the dove, which is innocent of tearing, most fittingly corresponds to those innocent people who pursue peace with everyone and holiness, being anxious to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

And therefore, by descending in the form of a dove, the Spirit signifies not only its own innocence and simplicity, or that of the one upon whom it descended, but equally that of those who think well of him and seek him in simplicity of heart. Praising their unanimous devotion and gentleness, bestowed by spiritual grace, the Lord himself says: “My dove is one, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her” (Song VI). For he calls the Church’s mother and begetter the grace of the Spirit, under whose inspiration she received the ability to be rightly called a dove herself.

Finally, in the Hebrew language in which Holy Scripture was published, “spirit” is expressed as a feminine noun. For this reason the one Church is fittingly named Christ’s dove, chosen for her mother and begetter: for the fact that she is gathered from many nations into the unity of Christian faith, that she rejoices in dove-like peace with one another, and that she is blessed by the lot of election, she possesses not by her own merit but has received as a gift of spiritual grace.

“And I,” he says, “did not know him.” You should understand: “I did not know him so subtly [or perfectly] as I came to know the Spirit descending upon him.”

“But he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” The Lord baptizes in the Holy Spirit by forgiving sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Whether he himself first baptized some of his disciples with water, through whom the stream of baptism would flow to the other faithful, and baptized them also with the Spirit by releasing their sins and dispensing the Spirit’s gifts; or whether his faithful, invoking his name, baptize the chosen with water and anoint them with sacred chrism, he nevertheless himself baptizes them with the Holy Spirit, because no one except him can release the bonds of sins or bestow the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, when the evangelist John had said, “The Pharisees heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John,” he immediately added: “although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples”—plainly saying [Al.: “teaching”] that although Jesus’ disciples baptize with water in his name, he himself is nevertheless to be understood as baptizing more truly, since he forgives sins.

The Lord also baptizes in the Holy Spirit when, through the breathing of that same Spirit, he kindles the hearts of his faithful with the fervor of his own (*sui*; Al. *suae*) or fraternal love. For, he says, “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.” He baptizes in the Holy Spirit when, by working virtues, he gives each of the chosen a manifestation of the Spirit for the sake of what is beneficial [Al.: “for working”]. Concerning this baptism, as he was about to ascend into heaven, he said to the disciples: “But you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts I).

But we must consider more carefully that, when he had said, “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending,” he added, “and remaining upon him.” For the Spirit descends upon his saints. Yet, because as long as they are in the body they cannot be without sin, and cannot continually fix the eye of the mind upon contemplation of heavenly things, but often bend it toward the care of earthly existence, the Spirit undoubtedly comes into their hearts at some times and departs at others.

Hence it is said: “The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John III). The Spirit comes to the saints and departs from the saints, so that those who are not capable of always possessing it may, through its returning light, be refreshed by frequent illumination from time to time.

But in the sole mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, the Spirit truly remains perpetually, since it finds in him no stain of an impure thought from which it would recoil. It remained wholly in him not only from the time when John saw it descend upon him, but from the time when, beginning to become human, he was conceived through its ministry and work.

Therefore he possesses the power of giving the Spirit to human beings no less than the Father does, as he himself testifies when he says: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” (John XIV). And elsewhere he shows that he himself sends it, saying: “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John XVI). For the substance of the Father, the Son, and the same Holy Spirit is one in divinity, and their operation is inseparable.

The Son also testifies concerning the Spirit that it comes of its own accord wherever it wills and works by its own power whatever it wills, when he says—as I mentioned above—“The Spirit breathes where it wills.” “But all these things,” says the Apostle, “the one and same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII).
