For this reason the Spirit is shown descending upon him who was baptized, although it always remained in him: so that the Baptist himself might recognize more clearly the one whom he was to preach [Al.: “foretell”], and so that it might give believers the indication that they cannot receive the baptism of that Spirit unless they have first been baptized with water.

Meanwhile, it must be asked how the special sign by which the Son of God was recognized was that the Spirit descended upon him and remained upon him, since he himself also promises the same to the disciples, saying: “And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John XIV). And shortly afterward: “Because he will remain with you, and he will be in you.” If the Spirit remains with God’s chosen servants and will be in them, what is so extraordinary about it being asserted that the Spirit remains in the Son of God?

It must be noted that the Holy Spirit always remained in the Lord, whereas in holy human beings, as long as they bear a mortal body, it partly remains forever and partly withdraws in order to return. It remains with them so that they may persist in good works, love voluntary poverty, attain gentleness, mourn out of desire for eternity, hunger and thirst for righteousness, and embrace mercy, purity of heart, and the tranquility of peace; and so that, for the sake of observing righteousness, they may not fear suffering persecution, but may desire to devote themselves to almsgiving, prayers, fasts, and the other fruits of the Spirit.

It withdraws for a time so that they may not always have the power to heal the sick, raise the dead, [Note: [Col. 0077D] Al. adds: “cleanse lepers”] cast out demons, or even prophesy. It remains always so that they may possess the power by which they themselves live wondrously; it comes for a time so that, through signs of miracles, they may also shine before others as the kind of people they are inwardly.

“And I saw,” he says, “and bore witness that this is the Son of God.” Earlier he had said, “After me comes a man who was made before me”; now he bears witness, “This is the Son of God,” clearly designating the truth of both natures—namely, the human and the divine—in one and the same person of Christ.

Let Manichaeus be ashamed when he hears, “A man came”; let Photinus fall silent when he hears, “This is the Son of God.” Let the meek hear and rejoice, because a man came after John, stronger than John, who baptizes in the Holy Spirit, and because this is the Son of God.

For because through pride we human beings departed from God, the Son of God, through mercy, became human, so that the same one might correspond both to the Father through divinity and to us through humanity: through a humanity like ours, he might fight the enemy on our behalf; through a divinity consubstantial with the Father, he might worthily restore in us the image and likeness of God, which we lost by sinning; through the death of our frailty, he might destroy the one who held the power of death; and through the impassible power of his divinity, he might reconcile us to God the Father, with whom God lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XV. FOR THE PURIFICATION OF BLESSED MARY

LUKE II. At that time, when the days of Mary’s purification according to the law of Moses had been completed, they brought Jesus, etc.

The sacred reading of the Gospel designates the solemnity of today’s celebration, which we honor with due observances on the fortieth day after the Lord’s birth, as dedicated especially to the humility of that same Lord and Savior and likewise to that of his undefiled mother. It explains that those who owed nothing to the law nevertheless submitted themselves in every respect to the fulfillment of the legal decrees.

For, as we heard just now when the Gospel was read: “When the days of her purification had been completed” (that is, of his mother) “according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.”

The law commanded that a woman who had conceived and borne a son should be unclean for seven days, and on the eighth day should circumcise the boy [Al.: “infant”] and give him a name. Thereafter she was also to abstain for another thirty-three days from entering the temple and from the bed of her husband, until on the fortieth day after the birth she should bring her son with offerings to the temple of the Lord.

The firstborn of every male was to be called holy to the Lord, and therefore clean animals were to be offered to God, while unclean ones were to be exchanged for clean animals or killed; and [Al. adds: “every”] human firstborn was to be redeemed for five shekels of silver. But if a woman had borne a female child, she was commanded to be unclean for fourteen days and to remain excluded from entering the temple for another sixty-six days, until on the eightieth day after the birth—the day called her purification—she should come to sanctify herself and her offspring with offerings, and only then should she be free to return to her husband’s bed.

Let us consider more carefully, dearest brothers, the words of the law that we have set forth, and we shall see most plainly how the most blessed Mother of God and perpetual virgin Mary, together with the Son whom she bore, was entirely free from every subjection to the law.

For since the law decrees that a woman who has conceived and borne a child is unclean, and that for a long period she must be cleansed together with the offspring she has borne by the offering of victims, it is perfectly clear that it does not describe as unclean the woman who, a virgin, bore a son without receiving male seed, together with the Son who was born to her, nor teach that she needed to be cleansed by saving sacrifices.

But just as our Lord and Savior, who gave the law of divinity, appeared in human form and willed to be made under the law in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons, so also his blessed mother, who by a singular privilege was above the law, nevertheless did not refuse to submit to the legal ordinances, in order to display an example of humility:

“In proportion as you are great, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III).

And to offer, he says, “a sacrifice according to what is prescribed in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” This was the sacrifice of the poor. For the Lord commanded in the law that whoever was able should offer a lamb for his son or daughter, together with a turtledove or pigeon; but whoever could not afford to offer a lamb was to offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Thus the Lord, mindful of our salvation in every respect, not only deigned to become human although he was God, but also, although he was rich, to become poor for us, so that by his poverty, together with his humanity, he might grant us participation in the riches of his divinity.

[Col. 0080B] But it is worthwhile to consider briefly why these birds in particular are commanded to be offered as the Lord’s sacrifice. For the patriarch Abraham is also read to have offered them to the Lord as a burnt offering long before the law; and in many of the ceremonies of the law, whoever was to be purified was commanded to be purified through them. The dove therefore signifies simplicity, while the turtledove indicates chastity; for the dove is a lover of simplicity, and the turtledove of chastity, so that if it should accidentally lose its mate, it does not trouble to seek another thereafter. Hence the Lord says in the praises of the Church: “Your cheeks are beautiful, like those of a turtledove” (Song of Songs I). And again: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like those of doves.”

[Col. 0080C] He has cheeks like those of a turtledove [Variant: Latin omits *ut*, “as”] who keeps himself chaste and free from every plague of impurity; he has eyes like those of doves who, desiring to harm no one, regards even his enemies with a simple love. But since both of these birds are mentioned because they customarily utter a lament instead of a song, they signify the weeping of the saints in this world, of which the Lord speaks, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI). And again: “Blessed are those who mourn [Variant: those who weep], for they shall be comforted” (Matthew V).

Rightly, then, are the turtledove and the dove offered to the Lord as a sacrifice, because the simple and chaste conduct of the faithful is for him an acceptable sacrifice of righteousness; because whoever labors in his groaning, whoever washes his bed with tears each night, slaughters a sacrifice most acceptable to God [Variant: adds *prorsus*, “altogether”]. But when both birds, because of their habit of lamenting, signify the present griefs of the saints and their heavenly desires, they nevertheless differ in this respect: the turtledove is accustomed to lament alone, whereas the dove laments in a flock. Thus the one signifies the secret tears of prayers, while the other signifies the public assemblies of the Church.

[Col. 0080D] The child Jesus is rightly circumcised first, and then, after an interval of days, is brought to Jerusalem with the sacrifice, because he too, when already a young man, first trampled underfoot all corruption of the flesh by dying and rising again; and afterward, after an interval of days, he ascended to the joys of the heavenly city with that same flesh, now immortal, which he had made a sacrifice to God for our salvation. Each one of us is first cleansed from all sins by the water of baptism, as by a true circumcision; then, as the grace of the new light advances, he enters the holy altar to be consecrated by the saving sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood.

[Col. 0081A] Indeed, the singularly simple and chaste humanity of our Savior, which was offered to God the Father for us, can not inappropriately be expressed figuratively through the sacrifice of a dove or turtledove. Moreover, at the end of the world the whole Church will first, in the common resurrection, strip off all the stain of earthly mortality and corruption; thereafter, commended to the Lord through the sacrifices of good works, it will be transferred into the kingdom of the heavenly Jerusalem.

[Col. 0081B] But the fact that Simeon and Anna—a man and woman, evidently, of advanced age—receive the Lord, whom they see as small in body but understand to be great in divinity, plainly represents in a figure that synagogue of the Jewish people which, wearied by its long expectation of his incarnation, as soon as he arrived eagerly [Variant: *promptis*, “ready”] strove to exalt and magnify him, both by the arms of pious deeds and by the words of sincere faith, acclaiming him and saying: “Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior [Variant: *salutaris*, “saving”], and I have waited for you all the day” (Psalm XXIV).

It must also be said that both sexes rightly came to meet him with rejoicing, since he appeared as the redeemer of both. Indeed, my brothers, the words with which that same Simeon, prophesying about the Lord, addresses his mother must be heard with great fear:

“Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be contradicted. And your own soul a sword will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.” [Col. 0081C]

We hear with great longing that the Lord is said to have been appointed for the resurrection of many, because just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ; and because he himself says: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even though he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John XI). But what is said earlier sounds no less fearfully: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall.” For he is truly unfortunate who, having recognized the glory of the resurrection, falls into a worse state; who, having seen the light of truth, is blinded by heavier clouds of sins. Therefore we must take the greatest care always to remember to exercise in action the right things we have learned, lest what the apostle Peter says be spoken of us: “For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down to them.”

“[Col. 0081D] “And as a sign,” he says, “that will be contradicted.” Many of the Jews often contradicted the sign of the Lord’s cross outwardly; many of the Gentiles did so as well; and many false brothers, which is more grievous, follow it inwardly with the outward appearance of profession, but persecute themselves [Variant: Latin omits *se*, “themselves”] excessively through the truth of their wicked conduct, saying that they know God but denying him by their deeds.

[Col. 0082A] “And your own soul a sword will pierce.” He calls the effect [Variant: *affectum*, “feeling”] of the Lord’s passion and death on the cross a sword, and this sword pierced Mary’s soul, because she could not see him crucified and dying without bitter pain. Although, as God, she had no doubt at all that he would rise from the dead, nevertheless, as one born from her own flesh, she grieved fearfully that he was dying.

“So that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.” Before the Lord’s incarnation, the thoughts of many were veiled, and it was not openly apparent who burned with love for eternal things or who preferred temporal things in his mind to heavenly goods. But when the King of heaven was born on earth, immediately every devout person rejoiced, while Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. When he preached and performed miracles, all the crowds both feared and glorified the God of Israel; but the Pharisees and scribes attacked his saving words and deeds with rabid speech. When he suffered on the cross, the wicked were filled with foolish joy and the devout with righteous sorrow; but when he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, the joy of the former was changed into sorrow, and the sorrow of the latter into everlasting joy. Thus, in accordance with the prophecy of blessed Simeon, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, the thoughts of many hearts were revealed.

[Col. 0082B] This revelation of differing thoughts did not occur then only in Judea [Variant: *et non etiam nunc*, “and not even now”]; it must also be believed to occur now among us. For even now, when the Lord appears, the thoughts of many hearts are revealed: when the word of salvation is read or preached, some of the hearers listen willingly, rejoicing to accomplish in action what they have learned by hearing; others, growing weary of what they hear, strive not to carry it out but rather to oppose it by mocking it.

[Col. 0082C] Therefore, brothers, whenever we perceive that the word of heavenly teaching is suffering some opposition from harsh [Variant: our] hearers, we should imitate the sorrow of those hearts who, when God’s Word appeared in the flesh, held him everywhere with worthy grief and compassion. But whenever we see that the same word rises through love in the minds of faithful hearers and advances toward the glory of our Creator through good works, let us rejoice with those who, in blessed hope, looked upon Christ as risen from the dead and ascending into heaven.

Since we have learned that chaste, simple, and lamenting birds were customarily offered to the Lord—and that these signify the sobriety, simplicity, and compunction of heart which we must always offer to our Creator—it is necessary to consider carefully why it is not without reason that two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, are commanded to be offered, one of them for sin and the other as a burnt offering.

[Col. 0082D] There are two kinds of compunction by which the faithful sacrifice themselves to the Lord on the altar of the heart. For, as we have learned from the sayings of the Fathers, the soul that thirsts for God is first pierced by fear, and afterward by love. At first it afflicts itself with tears, because, as it recalls its evil deeds, it fears that it will suffer eternal punishment for them. This is to offer one turtledove or young pigeon for sins. But when the fear produced by prolonged anxiety and sorrow has been consumed, a certain security concerning the presumption of pardon is born, and the mind is inflamed with love for heavenly joys. One who previously wept lest he be led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom. This is to make a burnt offering of the other turtledove or young pigeon; for a burnt offering is so called because it is wholly burned.

[Col. 0083A] A person makes himself a burnt offering to the Lord when, having scorned all earthly things, he takes delight in burning with desire for heavenly blessedness alone and in seeking only this through mourning and tears. For the mind contemplates what the choirs of angels are, what the fellowship of the blessed spirits is, and what the majesty of the eternal vision of God is; and it mourns more deeply because it is absent [Variant: Latin omits *a*, “from”] from everlasting goods than it wept earlier when it feared eternal evils.

[Col. 0083B] May Jesus Christ our Lord, who mercifully forgives the sins of those who mourn and are afflicted on account of sin, and who refreshes with the light of his eternal vision those who burn with the whole intention of their minds for entry into heavenly life, graciously accept both sacrifices of our compunction—he who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XVI. IN LENT

**John V.** “There was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.”

Today’s reading from the holy Gospel presents us with two miracles of human healing: one invisibly performed through the ministry of an angel, the other visibly accomplished through the Lord’s presence. We must briefly explain the mysteries of both, lest an extended explanation prove burdensome to anyone alongside the length of the reading.

[Col. 0083C] The sheep-pool (*probatica piscina*), which was surrounded by five porticoes, is the Jewish people, fortified on every side by the guardianship of the law so that they should not sin. For it is rightly represented by the number five, since the law is written in the five books of Moses. And the people who in some respects used to preserve the purity of life, but in others were accustomed to be troubled by the temptations of unclean spirits, are rightly signified by the water of the pool, which at one time used to remain calm despite the winds and at another to be disturbed when they rushed upon it.

The same pool is rightly called *probatica* (“sheep-pool”). For *probaton* means “sheep” in Greek, because in that people there were those who knew how to say to the Lord: “We are your people and the sheep of your flock; we will confess you forever” (Psalm LXXVIII). In common usage, however, it is said to have been called *probatica*, that is, “the pool of sheep,” because the priests were accustomed to wash sacrifices in it.

The multitude of sick people lying in the porticoes mentioned signifies the crowds of those who, hearing the words of the law, grieved that they could not fulfill it by their own strength and therefore implored the help of the Lord’s grace with all the devotion of their souls. They were blind because they did not yet possess the perfect light of faith; lame because they were unable to fulfill by the steps of action the good things they knew; withered because, although they possessed some eye of knowledge, they lacked the richness of hope and love.

[Col. 0083D] Such people lay in the five porticoes, but they were healed only in the pool when the angel came, because through the law came the knowledge of sin, whereas the grace of forgiveness came only through Jesus Christ. The angel signifies him who, descending invisibly into the pool to suggest the power of healing, moved the water. For the angel of great counsel descended, clothed in flesh—that is, the messenger of the Father’s will—into the Jewish people, and moved sinners by his deeds and teaching, so that he himself might be killed, although by his bodily death he was capable not only of healing those who were spiritually sick but also of giving life to the dead.

[Col. 0084A] The movement of the water therefore signifies the Lord’s passion, which took place when the Jewish people was moved and stirred up. And because through that same passion believers were redeemed from the curse of the law, those who had hitherto lain sick in the porticoes were healed as they descended into the troubled water of the pool.

The letter of the law, which taught those who were ignorant what should be done and what avoided, yet did not help those who had been instructed to fulfill its decrees, held them, as it were, brought out of their former dwelling places of ignorance, within its porticoes, but did not heal the sick. The grace of the Gospel, however, which through faith and the mystery of the Lord’s passion heals all the sicknesses of our iniquities—those from which we could not be justified by the law of Moses—sends the sick, as though cast out of the porticoes of the law, into the troubled water of the pool so that they may be healed. For through the water of baptism it washes away the sins that the law had revealed, as the Apostle testifies: “Whoever has been baptized into Christ Jesus has been baptized into his death. We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans VI).

[Col. 0084B] It is rightly said that whoever first descended after the movement of the water became healthy from whatever sickness afflicted him, because there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. Whoever is instructed in the mysteries of Christ within Catholic unity becomes healthy from whatever sickness of sin afflicts him; but whoever separates himself from unity cannot attain the salvation that comes from the One.

[Col. 0084C] Having spoken about the first miracle of the Gospel reading that the Lord performed, let us now speak about the second that he performed, for your fraternity. In this second miracle also, one person is commended as healed—not because the omnipotent mercy of the Savior could not have healed all whom he found sick there, but so that he might teach that outside the unity of the Catholic faith no place of salvation is open to anyone.

[Col. 0084D] “There was a certain man there,” he says, “who had been in his infirmity for thirty-eight years.” This man, held by the infirmity of so many years, signifies any sinner weighed down by the enormity or multitude of his crimes; and the length of time during which he suffered corresponds to the guilt that he signifies. For he had been ill for thirty-eight years.

The number forty, which is formed by four times ten, is customarily understood in Scripture as the perfection of upright conduct. Whoever performs the works of perfect conduct fulfills the law’s Decalogue through the four books of the holy Gospel. From this perfection the man who is empty of love for God and neighbor falls short by two, since that love is commended equally by the writing of the law and of the Gospel.

[Col. 0085A] The Lord taught this mystically when he healed the sick man, saying: “Rise, take up your mat, and walk.” When he says “Rise,” shake off the sluggishness of the vices in which you have long lain, and raise yourself to the practice of the virtues by which you may be saved forever. “Take up your mat”: lovingly carry your neighbor, patiently bearing his weaknesses, just as he has long and patiently sustained you, still weighed down by the burden of temptations. “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians VI). And as he says elsewhere: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians IV).

[Col. 0085B] “Walk,” then: love God with your whole heart, your whole soul, and your whole strength. And so that you may deserve to reach his vision, advance daily by the steps of good works from virtue to virtue. Do not abandon the brother whom you lead by bearing with him, for love of the one toward whom you are journeying; nor, for love of your brother, turn away from the intention of upright progress while seeking the one with whom you desire to remain. Rather, so that you may be saved perfectly, “Rise, take up your mat, and walk”—that is, leave your former sins, assist your brothers in their needs, and in everything you do take care not to fix your mind upon this world, but hasten to see the face of your Redeemer. Rise by doing good; carry your mat by loving your neighbor; and walk by awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God.

But what remarkable madness possessed the unbelievers! When they ought to have believed and been spiritually healed by the unexpected healing of one who had long been sick, they instead took offense and brought accusations both against the man who had been saved and against the Savior: against the man who had been saved because he had carried his mat on the Sabbath; against the Savior because on the Sabbath he had commanded both that the man be saved and that he carry his mat—as though they themselves knew more about the Sabbath than did such great divine power.

[Col. 0085C] Therefore those Jews said to the man who had been healed: “It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your mat.” They foolishly defended the letter of the law, failing to understand the dispensation of the one who had once decreed the law’s commands through a servant but had now come himself to transform that same law by grace, so that what carnal people had long observed carnally according to the letter, spiritual people might henceforth recognize as spiritually observed.

On the carnal Sabbath, which was observed according to the letter, the people were commanded to abstain on the seventh day from every servile work. The spiritual Sabbath, however, is that in the light of spiritual grace—which is understood as sevenfold—we remain free from every disturbance of vices, not on one day only but every day. For if, according to the Lord’s saying, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin, it is clear that sins are rightly understood as servile works. From these we are commanded to walk free, as on the seventh day, through the reception of spiritual grace—not merely restraining ourselves from evil but also persisting in good deeds.

[Col. 0085D] The Lord also showed this figuratively in the present reading when he commanded the man who had been sick for thirty-eight years, on the Sabbath day, not only to rise but also to take up his mat and walk. He was signifying that those who waste away in the long sickness of vices, and who, being empty of love for God and neighbor, fall short by two of the perfect sum of virtues, can now rise from vices through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Once their sluggishness has been shaken off, they must hasten toward the vision of their Creator while carrying the burden of brotherly love.

[Col. 0086A] The fact that the man who had been healed recognizes Jesus not while he is still in the crowd but afterward in the temple instructs us mystically that, if we truly desire to recognize the grace of our Creator, to be strengthened in his love, and to reach his vision, we must carefully flee the crowd—not only of disturbing thoughts and evil passions, but also of wicked people who might obstruct the purpose of our sincerity, whether by displaying their bad example, mocking our good works, or even prohibiting them.

Let us diligently take refuge in the house of prayer, where, calling upon the Lord in secret freedom, we may give thanks for the benefits we have received from him and pray with humble devotion for those we are to receive. Indeed, let us take care to become the holy temple of God in which he deigns to come and make his dwelling, hearing the Apostle say: “Your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you” (1 Corinthians VI).

[Col. 0086B] Among these matters we must consider especially, my brothers, that when the Lord found in the temple the man whom he had healed, he said to him: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.” These words plainly show that he had been sick because of sins and could not be healed until those sins had been forgiven. The one who healed him outwardly from sickness also saved him inwardly from crime; therefore he carefully warned him not to incur a sentence of condemnation more severe by sinning again.

[Col. 0086C] This should not be understood as though everyone who is sick is sick because of sins. For bodily sickness is found in Scripture to be given for five reasons: to sinners, so that they may either be corrected through repentance or, if they do not deserve correction, so that it may become apparent even in this life how they are to be condemned by eternal death; to the righteous, so that they may either receive a greater reward for patience or, warned by their infirmities, preserve the merit of righteousness with greater humility.

To many, moreover, bodily sickness is sometimes given so that through their healing the glory either of the Lord and Savior or of his saints, or of both, may be more widely revealed. That sinners are afflicted with bodily illness in order to seek the health of the mind is attested by today’s reading, where the healed man who had been sick heard: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.” It is also attested by that passage in which, healing the paralytic, the Lord says: “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven.”

[Col. 0086D] That those who are entangled in more grievous crimes and do not deserve to attain forgiveness sometimes receive even in the present life the beginning of eternal condemnation is shown by the punishment of King Herod. Because of the guilt of blasphemy, he was consumed by worms before the eyes of the living and died, hastening after death to the place where his worm would not die and his fire would not be extinguished.

That the righteous are afflicted with bodily pains to increase the reward of their patience is indicated by the history of blessed Job. Although there was no one like him on earth, he overcame with remarkable steadfastness the bodily sufferings that the savage adversary could devise, not to wash away guilt but to increase merit.

[Col. 0087A] That the righteous are also struck with illness as a discipline to preserve humility is shown by the Apostle, who says: “And so that the greatness of the revelations might not exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan to strike me” (2 Corinthians XII). Hence again he says: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (ibid., 9).

That some often grow weak in order to reveal the glory of the Creator and his saints is shown by the Lord himself, who, when the disciples asked about the man born blind, said: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in him” (John IX). And concerning Lazarus, who was sick, he said to his sisters: “This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (John II).

[Col. 0087B] But since it is uncertain whether we are punished for the increase of good merits or for the diminishing of evils, we must take the greatest care that whenever we are struck by bodily suffering, we immediately return to examine the inner things of our mind, and cleanse by worthy penitential discipline whatever we discover that we have done within ourselves against the will of our Creator. Let us not seek healing for the body before we have recognized that we have reached the purity of the inner person, lest a hidden illness within obstruct the bodily cure applied outwardly.

Let us learn humbly to submit to the scourges of our merciful Creator, believing that we suffer less than we deserve, always mindful of that saying: “Blessed is the person who is corrected by the Lord” (Job V). And he himself says in the Apocalypse: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation III).

[Col. 0087C] But once the man who had long been sick had been healed inwardly and outwardly—freed both from the scourges of evident correction and from the sins that had deserved them—the Jews, themselves inwardly sick in an evil way, began to suffer even worse by persecuting Jesus because he had done these things on the Sabbath.

They persecuted him as though following both the authority of the law and the examples of divine action: for the Lord completed the creation of the world in six days and rested from all his works on the seventh, and he commanded the people to work for six days and rest on the seventh. They did not understand that the carnal decrees of the law were gradually to be transformed by spiritual interpretation when Christ appeared, who is not only the lawgiver but also the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

[Col. 0087D] Nor did they observe that the Creator, on the seventh day, ceased not from the work of governing the world and renewing created things annually—or rather, daily—but from instituting a new kind of creation. They also failed to recognize the great mystery of the Sabbath: either that the Lord himself, crucified on the sixth day and having worked our salvation in the midst of the earth—that is, in the flesh he had assumed—was to rest on the seventh day in the tomb until he rose on the eighth; or that the saints, after the six ages of this world in which they labor by doing good, receive the seventh rest of souls in the life to come, until on the eighth they are granted the reception of incorruptible bodies as well.

But let us hear what he himself, the author of both grace and the law, answers the unlearned defenders of the law, with what force of reason he breaks their stiff necks.

[Col. 0088A] “My Father,” he says, “is working until now, and I am working.” This was not said as though, while the Father had been working until then, he himself were beginning to work after the Father at that time. Rather, it means that, since the Father has always been working from the beginning of creation, he himself has always worked the same works together with him.

To understand that God the Father works not only during the first six days but until now, read what is said to the prophet: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah I). And in the Psalm: “He formed their hearts one by one” (Psalm XXXIII). And elsewhere: “He covers the heavens with clouds, prepares rain for the earth, and makes grass grow on the mountains” (Psalm CXLVII), and other passages of this kind.

It should be noted that he did not use verbs of past time, saying, “He covered, prepared, and produced,” but verbs of the present: “He covers, prepares, and produces,” in order to show that the Father works every day, no less on the Sabbath than on the other days.

[Col. 0088B] So that you may not doubt that the Son likewise works all things, recall the Psalmist’s words: “He spoke, and the dog-fly and gnats came. He spoke, and the locust and caterpillar came. He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood still” (Psalm CV). For if he spoke and they came to be, he certainly made them through the Word. The Word, moreover, is the Son of the Father, of whom John says: “All things were made through him” (John I).

Again, when the Psalmist referred not only the original creation of the world but also the daily governance of creation to the praise of the Creator, he said among other things: “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm CIV). But if we rightly confess Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God, and if God made and governs all things in wisdom, then it is plainly established that the Father works until now, and the Son works as well.

[Col. 0088C] Therefore he says: “My Father is working until now”—not, as you think, having worked only during the six preceding days, but working until now (John V), not by instituting a new kind of creation but by propagating what he created in the beginning so that it may not perish. And “I am working,” with “until now” understood, since I arrange, govern, and increase all these things.

It is as though he were saying openly: “Why do you envy me? Why do you blame me, blind legislators, for working the salvation of one man on the Sabbath in the form of a human being, when in the nature of divinity, together with God the Father, I am always quietly working the whole human race—indeed, the entire structure of the world and all things visible and invisible?”

[Col. 0088D] But they, being less capable of such a great and profound mystery, sought all the more to kill him because he not only violated the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God. They were especially distressed because, although they recognized him as truly human on account of the weakness of his flesh, he wished to be believed to be truly the Son of God—not adopted by grace, as were the other saints, to whom the Prophet says, “I said, you are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm LXXXII), but by nature equal in every respect to the Father.

He is the one of whom the Father himself speaks, in the presence of his sons—that is, the prophets, who were adopted as sons by grace: “He called upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation. And I will make him my firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth” (Psalm LXXXIX).

The Jews who killed Christ understood what the Arians, who confess Christ’s name, fail to understand in Christ’s statement, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V): that he proclaimed himself equal to God the Father, because those whose operation is one and the same must also have equal majesty.

[Col. 0089A] Yet the impiety of both groups tends toward one end. The first understood what the Lord was saying but denied that he spoke the truth; the second indeed admit that the Lord testified truly about himself, but refuse to follow and comprehend the meaning of truth in his words. To avoid their most dreadful end, dearly beloved brothers, we must believe that the words of our Savior are full of truth, strive to understand them correctly, and place all our hope of salvation in them.

Let us truly believe that he proclaimed himself equal to the Father in power, glory, eternity, and kingdom; and by doing good, let us strive to reach the vision of both as one. When Philip asked for this and said, “Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us” (John XIV), the Lord himself answered: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

[Col. 0089B] It should indeed be noted that the words “making himself equal to God” are spoken from the perspective of the Jews, who thought that the Lord Jesus was claiming to make himself what he was not, rather than truthfully declaring what he was. But we, brothers, who have been instructed in the mysteries and teaching of the Catholic faith, should believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ became equal to us in nature in his humanity, while in his divinity he always remained equal to the Father.

[Col. 0089C] He did not pretend, by either nature, to make himself what he was not; rather, by truthfully proclaiming what he was, he revealed himself in both natures. May he deign to lead us into the perpetual vision of the glory of his majesty, in which he lives and reigns, God, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XVII. AFTER THE EPIPHANY

**John I.** “At that time Jesus wanted to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip and said to him, ‘Follow me.’”

From the Gospel reading, dearly beloved brothers, we have heard of the gracious kindness of our Redeemer: he not only mercifully calls us to follow him, but also customarily receives those who come with favor and lovingly leads them onward to know the splendor of his divinity.

[Col. 0089D] We have heard the devoted faith, love, and works of the disciples. These three virtues of heavenly life constitute the whole perfection of the present Church, since without faith it is impossible to please God, and faith without works is idle; and no matter what virtues a person possesses or how far he has advanced in faith, if he does not have love, it profits him nothing.

For when Philip not only follows Jesus, who calls him, but also proclaims to Nathanael that he should follow him, this is certainly faith working through love: faith, because he did not delay to believe in Jesus, whom he recognized as the Christ; and the work of love, because he immediately revealed how much he loved the one whom he had recognized by following him, and also showed through his evangelizing how ardently he burned with love for his neighbor.

[Col. 0090A] His neighbor Nathanael likewise showed how much care and love he had for the teacher of truth. When called, he did not delay to come; he made known how much he could comprehend of his greatness through the perfection of faith; and at once he openly confessed him as the Son of God and King of Israel—that is, the Christ.

But since we have briefly anticipated these matters, it is worthwhile to begin again from the opening and examine the entire sequence of the Gospel reading more fully.

Jesus wanted to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.” It is already clear from what precedes from where Jesus wanted to go out into Galilee—namely, from Judea, where John was baptizing and bearing witness to him that he was the Lamb of God. He urged two of his disciples to follow him; one of them, Andrew, also brought his brother Peter to him.

According to the spiritual meaning, and as your Fraternity has already come to know through frequent exposition, it is clear what it means to follow the Lord. For the one follows the Lord who imitates him; the one follows the Lord who, insofar as human frailty permits, does not abandon the examples of humility that the Son of God displayed in human form; the one follows him who, by sharing in his sufferings, earnestly longs to attain a share in his resurrection and ascension.

But it is not without a definite reason of mystery that it is reported that, when Jesus was about to say to Philip, “Follow me,” he wanted to go out into Galilee. Galilee is said to mean “made migration,” signifying the progress of the faithful, by which they strive either to migrate from vices to the heights of virtues, or gradually to advance in those very virtues and daily rise from lesser things to greater ones, until, with the Lord’s help, they reach from this valley of tears the citadel of heavenly joy. [Col. 0090C] In the sense that the word suggests revelation, it signifies the blessedness of eternal life, for which they labor in the present. The Psalmist comprehended both interpretations of the name in a single verse when he said: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII).

This is the vision of which the Apostle says: “But we, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III). Therefore, when the Lord was about to call a disciple to follow him, he rightly wanted to go out into Galilee—that is, into “made migration” or “revelation”—so that, just as he himself, according to the Gospel, advanced in age, wisdom, and grace before God and human beings, and just as he suffered and rose again and thus entered into his glory, so also he might show that his followers must advance in virtues and, through passing sufferings, migrate to the gifts of eternal joys.

Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. We should not think that the Evangelist wished by chance and without mystical reason to identify the city from which Philip came, or to show that it belonged also to Andrew and Peter. Rather, he intended to indicate typologically, through the name of the city, what Philip was then in spirit, what he would become in his office, and what Peter and Andrew would likewise be.

For Bethsaida is said to mean “house of hunters,” and hunters indeed were those who heard the Lord say: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men” (Matt. IV). A hunter also was the one who, even before he was ordained by the Lord to the office of preaching, immediately showed by voluntarily preaching how intent he was on capturing souls for life. For he found Nathanael and said to him: “We have found the one of whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote, Jesus from Nazareth.”

Let us see how large a net of faith he casts around his discovered brother, woven with the spacious meshes of devoted preaching, since he wisely desires to capture him for eternal salvation. He says that they have found the one whom Moses and the prophets had marked out in their writings as the one who would come, so that all who follow may understand that he is the one whose coming all the writings of the ancients served to proclaim. Thus he names the one whose future name the prophetic oracles sang.

Habakkuk says, desiring to be saved by his grace: “But I will rejoice in the Lord; I will exult in God my Jesus” (Hab. III). Zechariah, mentioning the temptation in which he conquered the devil, also says: “And he showed me Jesus the great priest, and he was standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan was standing at his right hand to oppose him” (Zech. III). Likewise, the patriarch Jacob, greeting from afar and awaiting the mystery of his incarnation, says: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. XLVIII). For what is called in Hebrew *Jesus* is called in Latin *Salvific* or *Savior*.

The Psalmist, promising his eternal vision to the people of the faithful, says in the person of God the Father: “I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my Salvation” (Ps. XC). Simeon too, that venerable old man and prophet of the New Testament, when he received him, small in body but perceived in mind as great in divinity, gave thanks under the instruction of the same Spirit: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace, because my eyes have seen your Salvation” (Luke II).

He calls him the son of Joseph—not to assert that he was born from the union of man and woman, since he had learned from the prophets that he would be born of a virgin, but to teach that he had come from the house and family of David, from which Joseph was known to have originated, in accordance with the prophecies of the prophets. Nor is it surprising that Philip should call him the son of Joseph, whom he knew to be the husband of his undefiled mother, since that undefiled mother, ever a virgin, is also read to have spoken according to ordinary usage: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow” (Luke II).

He adds his homeland, Nazareth, in order to identify him as the one of whom they had read in the prophets: “He shall be called a Nazaraean.” It is therefore no wonder that Philip immediately sought to win Nathanael to agreement in believing and coming to Christ, presenting him from every side with such nets of truth: “We have found the one of whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote, Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth” (John I). Nor is it without reason that he is said to have come from Bethsaida—that is, from the house of hunters—since he is shown to have received an equal measure of care and grace for the hunt beloved by God. For it follows:

And Nathanael said to him: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?”

Nazareth is interpreted as “purity,” or “its flower,” or “separated.” Nathanael, therefore, assenting to Philip’s words as he preached to him, says: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” As though he were saying openly: “Can it happen that something of supreme grace should arise for us from a city bearing such a name?”

Or perhaps he means the Lord himself, Savior of the world, who is uniquely holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and who says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys”; and of whom the prophet says: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. II), and “a Nazaraean”—that is, a flower—“shall rise from his root.” Or perhaps he means some outstanding teacher who has been sent to preach to us the flower and purity of virtues.

We may also rightly understand this passage in the following way. When Philip said, “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth, of whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote,” Nathanael understood correctly, but wondered how Philip could say that Christ had come from Nazareth, since the prophets sang that he would come from the house of David and from the city of Bethlehem, where David had lived. Therefore, in amazement, he replied, “From Nazareth?” But immediately, recalling how well the name Nazareth also suited the mysteries of Christ, he cautiously assented to the preacher: “Can anything good come from it?” What follows can suit both interpretations:

Philip said to him: “Come and see.”

He urged him to come and see, so that, if anything doubtful regarding the preacher’s words still remained in his heart, the whole of it might be removed by the present sight and conversation with the one whom Philip was proclaiming. The devout hearer did not delay in diligently seeking and piously knocking for the light of truth that had been preached to him, so that he might deserve to persist until he received it. Therefore, the Lord, hastening to satisfy his desire with good things, rewards his salutary beginnings with provident praise, so as gradually to lead him both to seek and to grasp higher things.

For he saw him coming toward him and said of him: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.”

Here we must note that God, who knows hearts, in praising a human being confirms not that he existed without sin, but without deceit. For “there is no one righteous on earth who does good and does not sin.” Many, however, are read to have walked without deceit—that is, to have lived with a simple and pure heart. Indeed, all the faithful are taught to live in this manner, as Scripture says: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. I). The Lord himself also says: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X).

Such was Job, the model of patience, of whom it is written: “That man was simple and upright” (Job I). Such was the patriarch Jacob, of whom it is said: “Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents” (Gen. XXV). Because he deserved to see God through the purity of a simple conscience, he was also called Israel—that is, “a man seeing God.”

Such was this Nathanael, whom the Lord, because of the likeness of his blameless conduct, considered worthy both of the merits and of the name of that same patriarch: “Behold,” he said, “truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John I). Behold the one who truly derives his lineage from the patriarch who saw God, and in whom, like the patriarch himself, no duplicity of deceit is found.

O what a beautiful beginning for one coming to God and desiring to see him! “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). Here also, one desiring to see God is praised as pure in heart and as an Israelite—not by another, but by God himself, who searches the reins and hearts; that is, he is declared to be born from a man who sees God.

O how great a hope of salvation is opened in this statement of our Redeemer for us also, who have come to faith from the nations! If the true Israelite is the one who walks without deceit, then the Jews have already lost the name of Israelites, although they were born carnally from Israel—all those who, with deceitful hearts, have degenerated from the simplicity of their patriarch. We, on the other hand, have been adopted into the seed of the Israelites, although we possess the lineage of the flesh from other nations, because in faith in the truth and in purity of mind and body we follow the footsteps of Israel, according to the Apostle’s statement: “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites. Nor, because they are the seed of Abraham, are all his children; but ‘in Isaac shall your seed be called’” (Rom. IX). That is, those who are children of the flesh are not considered children of God; rather, those who are children of the promise are counted as the seed.

It follows:

Nathanael said to him: “How do you know me?”

Jesus answered and said to him: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”

Nathanael answered him and said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.”

Nathanael recognized that the Lord had seen and known what was taking place elsewhere—namely, how and where he had been called by Philip, although the Lord himself was not physically present there. Considering the insight of divine majesty, he immediately confessed him not only as Rabbi, that is, teacher, but also as the Son of God and King of Israel, that is, Christ.

It is pleasing to observe how wisely the servant’s confession responds to the Lord’s praise. The Lord truly established him as an Israelite—that is, as a man who could see God—because he had no deceit at all. Nathanael, for his part, devoutly confessed him not merely as a teacher who would give useful instructions, but also as the Son of God, who would bestow heavenly gifts, and as the King of Israel—that is, of the people who see God. Through this confession he also indicated that this one was his king and that he himself was a soldier of his kingdom.

The Lord’s statement that he had seen Nathanael under the fig tree before Philip called him may also be understood mystically concerning the election of spiritual Israel, that is, of the Christian people. The Lord mercifully saw this people before it saw him, before it had been called by his apostles to the grace of faith, while it was still hidden beneath the covering of pressing sin. The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and immaculate in his sight in love” (Eph. I).

At times the fig tree in Scripture signifies the sweetness of heavenly love. Thus it is written: “He who keeps the fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who is guardian of his Lord will be honored” (Prov. XXVII). But because our first parents, confounded by the guilt of transgression, made themselves loincloths from fig leaves, the fig tree may not inappropriately signify the poorly sweetened habit of sinning among the human race. Under this habit, the Lord sees Nathanael as one of his elect, still placed beneath the fig tree, though not yet recognizing the grace of his election and not yet seeing the Lord.

For the Lord knows those who are his. The name Nathanael also most fittingly applies to their salvation. Nathanael is interpreted as “gift of God,” and unless each person is called by God’s gift, no one ever escapes the guilt of the first transgression or the badly flattering shadows of sins that grow cold day by day; no one ever deserves to come to Christ to be saved. Thus the Apostle says: “By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II).

It follows:

Jesus answered and said to him: “Because I said to you, ‘I saw you under the fig tree,’ you believe. You will see greater things than these.”

What the greater thing is of which he speaks, he subsequently reveals by promising believers the future opening of the kingdom of heaven and the proclamation to the world of the twofold nature of his one person. This is truly a far more excellent mystery than the fact that he foresaw that we, still placed in the shadow of sin, would be illuminated by him. For it is greater that he has filled us, saved by his grace, with the knowledge of him; that he has opened for us the joys of heaven; and that he has scattered throughout the world preachers of his faith, than that before the ages he foreknew that we would be saved by the power of his majesty.

“Amen, amen,” he said, “I say to you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man.”

We already see the fulfillment of this promise. We have seen heaven opened, because after God, the man, penetrated heaven, we also recognize that the entrance into our heavenly homeland has been opened to us who believe in his name. We see the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man, because we know that holy preachers announce both the sublimity of Christ’s divinity and the weakness of his humanity.

The angels ascend above the Son of Man when teachers proclaim that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). The angels descend upon the Son of Man when those same teachers add: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Nor is it without reason that holy preachers are figuratively called angels. From angels comes the name *evangelists*, which is habitually applied to them, so that, just as the former are messengers, the latter too may be called bearers of good news because of the same supreme office of preaching.

It should also be noted that the Lord calls himself the Son of Man, while Nathanael proclaims him the Son of God. The same thing appears when, according to the other Evangelists, he himself asks the disciples who people say that he, the Son of Man, is, and Peter replies: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI).

It was indeed accomplished by a just ordering of providence that, when the two substances of the same Mediator, God and our Lord, were to be mentioned either by the Lord himself or by a human being, God the man should assert the weakness of the humanity he had assumed, while a pure human being should assert the power of the eternal divinity present in him: he should confess his own humility, and the other his exalted nature.

It should also be noted that the Lord, who calls blessed Nathanael truly an Israelite, recalls in this statement too—“You will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man” (John I)—the vision of the patriarch Jacob, who was called Israel through the blessing.

When Jacob wished to rest in a certain place, he placed a stone beneath his head and saw in a dream a ladder standing on the earth, whose top touched heaven; he also saw the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder and saying to him: “I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac.” Rising in the morning and giving due praise to the Lord with reverence, he took the stone, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil over it.

The Lord therefore makes mention of this passage and very clearly testifies that it was a figure of himself and of his faithful. The ladder is the Church, which has its birth from the earth but its manner of life in heaven. Upon it the angels ascend and descend when the Evangelists at one time announce to more advanced hearers the sublime mysteries of his divinity, and at another time proclaim to those still inexperienced the weakness of his humanity.

Or certainly they ascend when they themselves pass in mind to contemplate heavenly things. They descend when they instruct their hearers how they ought to live on earth.

The stone beneath Jacob’s head is the Lord. We ought to lean upon him with all our attention, all the more because it is certain to us that without him we can do nothing.

Jacob anointed the stone and set it up as a pillar, because the true Israelite understands that our Redeemer was anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions. From this anointing, that is, from *chrism*, Christ receives his name. Its mystery is the title of our redemption through the Incarnation.

And it is fitting that, when the stone is anointed on earth and set up as a pillar, the Lord is revealed in heaven. He is the one who appeared in time among human beings as a human being, while he remains eternal God with the Father. Having conquered death, he ascended above the heavens of heavens toward the east. He remains with us as the title of our salvation all the days until the consummation of the age, transferring to heaven the body he assumed from earth, yet by the presence of his divinity embracing earth and heaven alike.

Therefore, in explaining the ancient history to us, the Lord shows that Israel signifies the simplicity of the faithful people, of whom Nathanael was a member. In the stone upon which the angels ascended and descended, he reveals himself as signified, whose two natures spiritual teachers announce in turn.

For Israel anoints the stone with oil, as it were, when Nathanael confesses how God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and with power, saying: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel” (John I).

Now that the reading of the holy Gospel has been explained, my brothers, it is clear that it was not without the reason of a great mystery that it was foretold at its beginning that Jesus wanted to go out into Galilee, and that it was subsequently related how he himself called Philip, and how he received Nathanael, who had been called by Philip, and instructed him with the light of truth.

For Galilee, as we have said, is interpreted as “made transfiguration” or “revelation.” He is rightly said to have wanted to go out into Galilee when he deigned to reveal to the faithful the mysteries of his majesty. Toward their perfect knowledge, which alone is the blessed life of the human being, we shall then ascend more sublimely in proportion as we now strive more earnestly to migrate from earthly things to heavenly things and to advance through the degrees of virtue. May he help us—the one who is accustomed to make good desires ascend, advance, and receive their crown—Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVIII. ON THE SECOND SUNDAY OF LENT

**Matthew XVII, Mark IX, Luke IX.** At that time Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother and led them apart up a high mountain, and he was transfigured before them, etc.

[Col. 0096B] Since our Lord and Redeemer has determined to lead his chosen ones, through the labors of this life, into that future life of blessedness which knows no labor, he describes through his Gospel at one time the sweats of temporal struggles and at another the palm of eternal rewards. Thus, when they hear of the necessities of the contest, they may remember that they must by no means seek rest in this life; and when they hear again of the sweetness of future repayment, they may bear more lightly the passing evils that they hope will be rewarded with lasting blessings.

For when he had shortly before mentioned his own sufferings and those of his followers, he immediately added what we have now heard in the reading, saying:

“For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his works.”

Here he most appropriately [Al.: most clearly] indicates the day of the final judgment, when he will come in great power and majesty to judge the world—the one who once came in humility and lowliness to be judged by the world. Then, with judicial strictness, he will seek the perfection of works from those to whom, in the generosity of his mercy, he had previously granted the grace of his gifts. Repaying each according to his works, he will lead the chosen into the kingdom of his Father, but will cast the rejected, together with the devil, into everlasting fire.

And beautifully it is said that the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father. The Son of Man will come in the glory of God the Father because the one who, in human nature, is less than the Father is, in divinity, of one and the same glory with the Father: truly human, existing in every respect also as truly God.

What follows rightly brings joy to the devout and rightly terrifies the rebellious: “And then he will repay each according to his works.” Those who now do good and are unjustly afflicted by the pressures of evil eagerly await that time, when, through the just Judge, they will not only be freed from the injuries of the unjust but will also receive the reward of their justice and patience. Those who live badly and regard the Judge’s patience as negligence are justly struck, though late in repentance, by the sentence of eternal condemnation.

The Psalmist’s statement agrees with this Gospel saying: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C). He declares that he will sing mercy first and then judgment, because the Lord will strictly demand at his second coming what he graciously bestowed upon us at his first coming. But every perverse person who despises the mercy of the one who gives it rightly fears the judgment of the Lord who examines. Whoever remembers with gratitude that he has received the grace of mercy, however, joyfully awaits the ordeal of judgment and therefore sings mercy and judgment to his Judge in free melody.

But because the time of the universal judgment is uncertain to all, and the hour of each person’s departure is uncertain, and the present affliction could seem long to those who did not know when the promised rest would come, the compassionate Teacher wanted to foreshow the joys of the eternal promise to some of his disciples while they were still living on earth. In this way, both those who had seen it and all who could hear of it might bear present adversities more lightly, frequently recalling to mind the gift of future recompense that they were awaiting.

Hence it follows:

“Amen, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”

The disciples saw him coming in his kingdom because they saw him shining on the mountain in that splendor in which, after the judgment has been completed, he will be seen by all the saints in his kingdom. But what the still mortal and bodily eyes of the disciples could not endure, the whole Church of the saints, already made incorruptible through the resurrection, will then be powerful enough to behold. Of it is written: “His eyes will see the King in his beauty” (Isa. XXXIII).

And after six days Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain.

Desiring to show his glory to the disciples, the Lord leads them up a high mountain, to teach all who desire to see this glory that they must not lie in the lowest pleasures, serve carnal enticements, or cling to earthly desires. Rather, out of love for eternal things, they must always be raised toward what is above and, insofar as is possible for mortals, continually imitate the life of angelic purity, piety, peace, love, and justice, according to the one who said: “Our manner of life is in heaven, and from there we also await a Savior, Jesus Christ our Lord” (Phil. III).

Desiring to show the glory of his majesty, he leads the disciples up the mountain so that they—and all who thirst to see this glory—may learn that it must not be sought for themselves in the depths of this age, but in the kingdom of heavenly blessedness.

And when he said that he led them up a high mountain, he appropriately added “apart,” because even now the righteous, though pressed by the proximity of the wicked, are wholly separated from them in mind and in the intention of faith. In the future they will be led completely apart from them, when he hides them in the secret place of his face from the disturbance of human beings and protects them in his tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues.

That he displayed the splendor of his vision after six days from the time he promised it to the disciples signifies that the saints will receive the kingdom at the day of judgment, which the God who does not lie promised them before the times of the ages. The times of the ages consist of six periods; when these have been completed, they will hear him say: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

The six days of the promised vision of the Lord and the glory of the good may also signify the perfection [Al.: the perfecting] of works, without which no one is able to reach the contemplation of the majesty of his Creator, though everyone may perform something. Because the Lord formed the creation of all things in six days and rested from his works on the seventh, the six days rightly express the good works by which we ought to reach rest. And because whoever desires to see God and attain the glory of blessed resurrection must do the good he knows, the Savior rightly showed the glory of his kingdom, which he promised to the disciples, after six days.

It follows:

And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun; and his garments became white as snow.

The Lord was transfigured before the disciples. He both signifies the glory of his body, with which it was to be illuminated through the resurrection, and reveals how great a brightness the bodies of all the chosen will possess after the resurrection. For elsewhere he says of them: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII). Here, as an example of future glorification, his face shone like the sun.

This does not mean that the brightness and glory of the Lord and of his saints can be equal, since the Apostle also says of those same saints: “Star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV). Rather, because we know of nothing brighter than the sun, not only the Lord’s but also the saints’ glory in the resurrection is compared to the sight of the sun; for nothing brighter than the sun could be found to provide an example for human beings.

No one should think that the glorious majesty of the Lord’s body or the brightness of the saints’ bodies will be seen at the judgment by the rejected. They will see only the one whom they pierced, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. But when, after the judgment has been completed, the wicked have been removed so that they do not see the glory of God, the righteous will enter to contemplate eternally the glory of his kingdom, themselves also transfigured in the light of incorruption according to their measure. Hence the Apostle says: “He will reform the body of our lowliness, configured to the body of his glory” (Phil. III).

If anyone asks what the Lord’s garments, which became white as snow, signify typologically [Al.: what they may signify], we may rightly understand them to represent his holy Church. Of these Isaiah says: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX), and the Apostle says: “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

At the time of the resurrection they are cleansed from every stain of iniquity and from every darkness of mortality alike. Therefore the Evangelist Mark beautifully says of the Lord’s garments that they became exceedingly bright and white as snow, “such as no fuller on earth can make white” (Mark IX), because it is evident to everyone that no one can live on earth without corruption and sorrow. This is evident to all wise people, even if heretics contradict it. No one can live on earth without touching some sin.

But what no fuller—that is, no teacher of souls or distinguished purifier of his own body—can do on earth, the Lord will do in heaven, cleansing his Church, his garment, from every defilement of flesh and spirit, and further refreshing it with the eternal blessedness and light of flesh and spirit.

It follows:

And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.

What sort of appearance they had and what they said to him, Luke records more clearly: “Now Moses and Elijah were seen in majesty, and they were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem” (Luke IX).

Moses and Elijah, therefore, who spoke with the Lord on the mountain and spoke of his passion and resurrection, signify the oracles of the Law and the prophecy. These have been fulfilled in the Lord and are now evident to the learned, but will be revealed more clearly in the future to all the elect.

They are rightly said to have been seen in majesty, because then it will be seen more openly with what dignity of truth not only the meaning but also the wording of all the divine utterances has been expressed. Nevertheless, Moses and Elijah may rightly be understood as representing all those who will reign with the Lord.

In Moses, who died and was buried, are represented those who will be raised from death at the judgment. In Elijah, who has not yet paid the debt of death, are represented those who will be found alive in the flesh at the Judge’s coming. Both, caught up together in the clouds at the same moment, will go to meet the Lord in the air and, once the judgment has been completed, will be brought into eternal life.

The statement that Moses and Elijah were seen in majesty aptly applies to them: through the excellence of majesty, the distinguished gift with which they will be crowned is shown.

It is also fitting that they are said to have spoken of his departure, which he was to accomplish in Jerusalem. For the passion of the Redeemer becomes the single subject of praise for his faithful. The more they have deserved to be redeemed by his grace, the more they continually turn over in their devout hearts the remembrance of their restoration and testify to it in devout confession. [Note: [Col. 0099] Al.: “The more they remember that they could not be saved without his grace, the greater their remembrance of that same grace, etc.”]

But because the more anyone tastes the sweetness of heavenly life, the more he detests everything that pleased him in the lower things, Peter, having seen the majesty of the Lord and of his saints, rightly immediately forgot all earthly things that he had known. He desired to cling perpetually to the things alone that he had seen, saying:

Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.

Blessed Peter, as another Evangelist testifies, “did not know what he was saying” (Luke IX), in thinking that tabernacles should be made in the heavenly manner of life. In the glory of that heavenly life no houses will be necessary, where the light of divine contemplation makes everything peaceful and no breath of any adversity remains to be feared. The Apostle John bears witness to this when, describing the glory of that same heavenly city, he says among other things: “And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Rev. XXI).

Yet he knew well what he was saying when he said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here,” because it is truly the sole good of the human being to enter into the joy of his Lord and to stand eternally in contemplation of him. Hence no one should be thought ever to have possessed any true good if, by the demand of his guilt, it happens that he never sees the face of his Creator.

If blessed Peter, contemplating Christ’s glorified humanity, is affected by such joy that he does not wish to be separated from his sight in any way, what do we think, dearly beloved brothers, is the blessedness of those who have deserved to see the height of his divinity? And if he considered it the greatest good to see on the mountain the transfigured appearance of Christ the man with only two saints, namely Moses and Elijah, what speech could explain, what mind could comprehend, how great the joys of the righteous will be when they have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem, and to the company of many thousands of angels, and have seen God, the very maker and founder of that city, not through a mirror and in an enigma as now, but face to face?

Concerning this vision Peter himself says, speaking of the Lord to the faithful: “Though you do not now see him, you believe in him; and when you see him, you will exult with an inexpressible and glorified joy” (I Pet. I).

It follows:

While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and behold, a voice from the cloud saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” [Col. 0100C]

Because they were seeking to make shelters, they are admonished by the covering of the bright cloud that dwellings are not necessary in that habitation of heavenly life, where the Lord protects everything with the eternal overshadowing of his light. For he who, as the people journeyed through the wilderness, spread out a cloud for their protection for forty years, so that neither the sun by day nor the moon by night would burn them—how much more will he protect those dwelling in the tabernacle of the heavenly kingdom forever beneath the covering of his wings? For we know, as the Apostle teaches: “If our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, an eternal house not made by hands in the heavens” (II Cor. V).

But because they desired to behold the shining face of the Son of Man, the Father was present in the voice [Col. 0100D], teaching that he was his beloved Son, in whom he was well pleased, so that they might learn to yearn from the glory of his humanity, which they saw, toward contemplating the presence of his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father. And what the paternal voice says about the Son, “in whom I am well pleased,” is what the Son himself elsewhere testifies: “And he who sent me is with me; and he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John VIII).

And when it added, “Listen to him,” it indicated that he was the one about whom Moses had beforehand warned the same people to whom he gave the law: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him according to everything whatever he speaks to you” (Deut. XVIII). For he does not forbid Moses and Elijah—that is, the Law and the Prophets—to be heard; rather, he signifies that the hearing of the Son, who came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, must be preferred to all these, and he makes clear that the light of evangelical truth must be placed before all the types and enigmas of the Old Testament.
