And indeed, by a gracious dispensation, the faith of the disciples is strengthened, lest it waver when the Lord is crucified, since, as the moment of the cross approaches, his humanity too is shown to be destined to be exalted through the resurrection by heavenly light. And because the Son is coeternal with the Father in divinity, this is proved by the heavenly voice of that same Father, so that, when the hour of his passion came, they would grieve less over the one who was dying, remembering that after death he would soon be glorified in his humanity, while in his divinity he had always been glorified by God the Father. But the disciples, still as though carnal and [Alt.: add. “and”] of fragile substance, hearing the voice of God, were afraid and fell upon their faces. The Lord, however, as a teacher compassionate in every respect, consoles and raises them up by word and touch alike.

“And as they were coming down,” he says, “from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man rises from the dead.”

He commanded that the vision of his manifested majesty remain silent for a time, lest, if it were openly proclaimed among the people, either those same people might oppose the leaders and hinder the dispensation of his passion, thereby delaying the accomplishment of human salvation that was to come through his blood; or, at any rate, those who heard and believed the vision might be scandalized when they saw the disgrace of the cross. But after his passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven had been completed, it was more appropriately preached by the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, so that all who wished to be initiated into his sacraments might learn from those who saw it [Alt.: “had seen it”] might not only believe in the effect of the resurrection, but also to understand the manner of that resurrection; and so that they might likewise preach to everyone as something to be believed and loved the eternity of the divine birth that they had heard from the Father.

Now that the reading concerning the Lord’s Transfiguration has been expounded, let us return, dearest brothers, to our own conscience. If we delight in seeing the Lord’s glory, let us pass beyond carnal desires and ascend the mountain of virtues. If we wish to belong to the Lord’s exceedingly white garments, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, completing our sanctification in the fear of God [Col. 0101D]. If we desire to hear the voice of God the Father and to gaze upon the majesty of his consubstantial Son, let us diligently strive to avoid the perverse and useless words of mortals; let us strive to turn our eyes away from the empty spectacles of the deceiving world, so that, when the glory of our resurrection shines forth, we too may be worthy both to see and to proclaim the mighty works of our Creator, which now we cannot, by the gift of him who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, and so forth. Amen.

## HOMILY XIX. FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY OF LENT

[Col. 0102A]

MATTHEW XV, LUKE XIX, MARK VII. At that time Jesus departed and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders and cried out, saying to him: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely tormented by a demon,” and so forth.

In the reading of the holy Gospel that has just been read [Alt. adds: “to us”], dearest brothers, we heard of the woman’s great faith, patience, steadfastness, and humility. Her [Alt. adds: “therefore”] devotion of mind is all the more to be admired by which [Alt.: “in which”], although she was a Gentile and therefore completely separated from the teaching of the divine utterances, she was nevertheless not deprived of the virtues that those same utterances [Alt.: “which”] proclaim. For she possessed [Alt.: “possesses”] the great perfection of faith, and, imploring the Savior’s compassion, she said:

“Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” For when she calls that same Lord the Son of David, it is clearly evident that she believes him to be truly human and truly God. When she pleads for her daughter, she does not bring her with her, nor does she ask the Lord to come to her; it is therefore perfectly clear that she trusts he can give salvation by his word, without requiring any bodily presence. But [Alt.: add. “also”] in prostrating herself after many tears and worshiping him, saying, “Lord, help me,” she shows no uncertainty about his divine majesty, since she has learned that his power is to be worshiped as God’s.

She possesses no small virtue of patience. Although the Lord does not answer her first request with a word, she does not cease praying, but with still greater insistence [Alt.: “persisting in”] implores the help of his compassion that she had begun to seek. The Lord delays answering her—not because the merciful physician despises the prayers of the wretched, concerning whom it is most truthfully written, “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor” (Ps. IX)—but in order to demonstrate to us the woman’s perseverance, which we should always imitate. The more she appeared to be disregarded by the Lord, the more ardently she persisted in the prayers she had begun.

He delays answering so that he might also stir the compassionate hearts of his disciples—who, being human, were embarrassed by the woman’s public clamor as she followed them—to ask together with her. For he himself knew the proper measure of his mercy, who ordered all things “in measure and number and weight” [Col. 0102D] [Alt.: “orders”]. He delayed answering lest the Jews be given occasion to complain that he had preferred Gentiles to them in teaching or healing [Alt.: “had preferred”], and that they therefore [Alt.: “and therefore”] might justly refuse to accept her faith.

And this is what he says:

“I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel.” For he himself alone taught the Jews, while through his disciples he also called the Gentiles to the grace of faith. Concerning these he says elsewhere: “And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd” (John X). Hence, when he was about to heal in person one Gentile girl, he did not accomplish this until the mother’s incomparable faith had been tested before everyone.

That same mother also possesses the outstanding mark of steadfastness and humility [Col. 0103A]. Although compared by the Lord to dogs, she nevertheless does not cease from persistently praying, nor does she withdraw her mind from hope in his merciful gift. Gladly embracing the insult she has received, she not only does not deny that she resembles dogs, but even adds that she should be compared with little dogs. By a prudent argument she confirms the Lord’s statement, yet she does not cease because of the boldness of the petition she had begun.

For she confirms the Lord’s statement. When he says:

“It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs,”

she replies:

“Yes, Lord.”

That is: “It is truly as you assert; it is so. For it is not good to take the salvation appointed from heaven for the people of Israel [Alt.: “for the people”] and give it to the Gentiles.” But when she adds:

“For even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters” [Col. 0103B],

she very wisely demonstrates how great a humility and how much steadfastness she carries within her heart. She is indeed unworthy of the Lord’s complete teachings [Alt.: “of the Lord’s teaching in its fullness,” or “of the Lord’s doctrine”], with which the Jews were nourished as at a feast; but she judged that whatever small portion of grace might be imparted to her by the Lord could contribute to her salvation.

Therefore she deserved to hear from the compassionate Savior, who had delayed her prayer for a time not out of proud disdain but by a provident dispensation:

“O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

She truly possessed very great faith. Though she knew neither the ancient things of the prophets nor the recent miracles, commands, or promises of the Lord himself, and though she had been so often disregarded by the Lord, she nevertheless persevered in prayer. She does not cease to knock by asking the one whom she had learned to be the Savior merely through the report of his fame. For this reason she also obtains a great result from her petition: when the Lord says, “Let it be done for you as you wish,” her daughter is healed from that hour.

Rightly, then, this woman—Gentile by nature, but steadfast and believing in heart—signifies the faith and devotion of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which [Alt.: “whom”] the holy preachers expelled from Judaea instructed by word and by the mysteries of heavenly grace alike. Let us reread the preceding reading of the holy Gospel, and we shall find that, when the scribes and Pharisees came from Jerusalem, they assailed the Lord and his disciples with the gravest tumult of their faithlessness, and that he immediately left them after restraining them with a fitting rebuke.

“And departing from there, he withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon” [Col. 0103D].

Here it is plainly prefigured that after his passion and resurrection the Lord would withdraw, in his preachers, from the faithless hearts of the Jews and depart into the regions of foreign peoples. Tyre and Sidon, cities that belonged to the Gentiles, indicate monuments of Gentile teaching and life, in which fools place their trust. Thus the woman who credulously prays to the Lord is rightly said to have come out from those borders, because unless she had abandoned the empty dwelling places of her former way of life, she would never have come to Christ’s Church [Alt.: “to Christ”; “to the Church”]. Unless she had anathematized the doctrines of her ancient error, she could never have received—or known—the new grace of faith [Alt.: “could not have known”]. Hence blessed Paul, after having advanced in Judaism, later, when called, advanced in the Church of God beyond those of his own age.

The daughter possessed by a demon, for whom she pleads, is any soul in the Church that is enslaved more by the deceptions of evil spirits than by the commands of its Creator. For this soul the mother Church must earnestly intercede with the Lord, so that the one whom she herself cannot correct outwardly by admonishing, entreating, and rebuking, he may correct inwardly by inspiring, and, once turned away from the darkness of errors, lead—or awaken [Alt.: “arouse”]—to the knowledge of the true light.

Moreover, even if the Lord delays answering the first tears of the praying Church—that is, delays giving the erring the requested soundness of mind—we must not for this reason cease asking, seeking, and knocking, nor must we give way to despair of obtaining what we seek. Rather, we must persevere with such insistence, summon the Savior with such persistent cries, and seek the aid of his saints so earnestly amid the litanies, until they too plead with the Lord from heaven that the Church may be heard [Col. 0104B]. Thus, if a person does not turn his mind away from the purpose he has set, he will by no means be deprived of the fruit of his petition; whether he intercedes for his own weakness or for others, he will obtain the desired result.

For if any one of us has a conscience polluted by the filth of avarice, arrogance, vainglory, indignation, anger, envy, or the stain of other vices, he surely has a daughter severely tormented by a demon, for whose healing he should run humbly to the Lord. For he harbors a thought born from the heart, driven mad through the devil’s craft; and its correction must be demanded from the compassionate Creator with frequent, indeed continual, lamentation and prayers.

If someone has defiled good deeds that he performed by the plague of perjury, theft, blasphemy, slander, quarrelling, or even bodily impurity, or by other such evils, he has a daughter agitated by the fury of an unclean spirit. For the action that he had produced by laboring well he has foolishly destroyed by serving the devil’s deceits.

Therefore, when he recognizes his guilt, he must immediately flee to prayers and tears and seek help through the frequent intercession of the saints. As they plead for his salvation, let them say to the Lord: “We beseech you, Lord, compassionate and merciful, patient and of great mercy” (Ps. LXXXV): “Dismiss her, for she cries out after us.” Forgive her guilt and grant grace to the one who, bowed down with deepest affection, seeks our aid [Alt.: “who seeks the aid of the saints with deepest affection”] [Col. 0104D].

It is necessary that, humbled beneath the proper humility, he no longer judge himself worthy of the company of the Israelite sheep—that is, of pure souls—but rather consider himself comparable to a dog and unworthy of heavenly gifts. Nevertheless, he must not cease from the persistence of prayer out of despair; rather, with unwavering mind he must trust in the goodness of the supreme Giver. For he who was able to make a confessor from a thief, an apostle from a persecutor, an evangelist from a tax collector, and children of Abraham from stones, can also turn the most shameless dog into an Israelite sheep. To such a one may he fittingly grant, for the chastity bestowed upon him, the pastures of eternal life; that is, may he deign to make the sinner who has turned from his evil way righteous, and may he deservedly lead him, through good action, to the heavenly kingdom.

When the Lord sees such ardor of our faith and such persistent perseverance in prayer, he will at last have mercy and grant that it may also be done for us as we wish: namely, that, once the tumult of vicious thoughts has been driven out and the bonds of sins released, both a pure serenity of mind and the perfection of good work may be restored in us.

Meanwhile, it should be noted that this persistence in prayer deserves to be fruitful only if we meditate in our minds upon what we pray with our mouths, and our attention is not split by a different cry of the lips from that of our thoughts. For there are some who enter a church and recite a psalm or prayer at length, yet, directing their hearts elsewhere [Alt.: “while directing them elsewhere”], do not even remember what they are saying. They pray with their mouths, but wander outwardly in their minds, and deprive themselves of all the fruit of prayer [Alt.: “depriving themselves”]. No one can fail to perceive that this happens through the prompting of the ancient enemy. For he knows the usefulness of prayer and envies human beings the grace of obtaining what they ask. He sends upon them various images of frivolous thoughts, and sometimes even of shameful and harmful fantasies, by which he obstructs prayer, so that at times, prostrate in prayer, we endure such great and rushing waves of thoughts as we would not know how to endure even while lying flat on our backs in bed.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must take care to overcome the devil’s recognized malice; we must preserve our minds, as far as we can, from such clouds as the enemy loves to scatter—or [Alt.: “to clear them”]—and continually implore the protection of our compassionate defender, who is able to grant even unworthy sinners [Alt.: “suppliants”] the grace both to pray purely and to obtain perfectly.

The purity of prayer is greatly helped if, in every place and at every time, we restrain ourselves from illicit acts; if we always discipline both our hearing and our tongue away from idle conversations; if we accustom ourselves to walk in God’s law and to search his testimonies with our whole heart. For whatever we habitually do, say, or hear most often must necessarily return to the mind again and again, as to its familiar and proper dwelling. And just as swine habitually seek muddy wallows while doves seek clear streams, so impure thoughts disturb an unclean mind, while spiritual thoughts sanctify a chaste one [Col. 0105D].

Certainly, if, following the example of the Canaanite woman, we persevere and remain steadfast in prayer, the grace of our Creator will be present, correcting all our errors, sanctifying what is unclean, and calming what is turbulent. For he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity, if we cry out to him with an attentive voice of the mind—he who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XX. FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY OF LENT

[Col. 0106A]

JOHN VIII. At that time Jesus came to the Mount of Olives, and at dawn he came again into the temple; and all the people came to him, and, sitting, he taught them.

We ought to consider the present reading of the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, and remember it all the more attentively because it commends to us the greatest grace of our Creator. [Col. 0101A–C] For behold, as we heard, when a sinful woman was brought before him by wicked accusers, he commanded not that she be stoned according to the precept of the Law, but that the accusers first consider themselves and then pronounce judgment upon the one who had sinned, so that from reflection upon their own frailty they might recognize how they ought to have mercy upon others.

But because it is customary for the Scriptures sometimes to indicate what is about to be narrated by the situation of the time, sometimes by the situation of the place, and sometimes by both, the Evangelist, intending to relate the Redeemer’s mercy tempering the severity of the Law, first stated that Jesus went to the Mount of Olives and at dawn came again into the temple [Col. 0106B]. The Mount of Olives signifies the sublimity of the Lord’s kindness and mercy. In Greek, *oleos* means “mercy,” while an olive grove is called *oleon*; and the anointing of oil itself ordinarily brings relief to weary and suffering limbs. Moreover, the fact that oil surpasses other liquids in both virtue and purity, and that whatever liquid one pours over it, it immediately rises above and floats upon it, appropriately suggests the grace of heavenly mercy, concerning which it is written: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV).

The time of dawn likewise demonstrates the rising of that same grace, by which, once the shadow of the Law had been removed, the light of evangelical truth was to be revealed. Jesus therefore goes to the Mount of Olives to declare that the stronghold of mercy resides in him; he comes again at dawn into the temple to signify that this same mercy was to be disclosed and offered to the faithful with the beginning light of the New Testament—in other words, in his own temple.

“And all the people,” he says, “came to him, and, sitting, he taught them.” The Lord’s sitting indicates the humility of his incarnation, for which he deigned to have mercy upon us. Hence we are also commanded: “Rise after you have sat” (Ps. CXXVI), as though it were plainly said: “Do not hope to receive the reward of heavenly exaltation until you have chastised yourselves with true humility.”

It is rightly said that, while Jesus sat teaching, all the people came to him, because after he became near to human beings through the humility of his incarnation, his word was more willingly received by many. By many, I say, his word was received, for by more people it was contemptuously rejected in their arrogance and impiety. The meek heard, and rejoiced, magnifying the Lord with the Psalmist and exalting his name among themselves. The envious heard, and were undone, but were not pierced with compunction; they tested him and mocked him, and, mocking him, gnashed their teeth at him.

Finally, while testing him, they brought a woman caught in adultery and asked what he commanded should be done with her [Col. 0107A], since Moses had ordered that such a woman be stoned. If he too decided that she should be stoned, they would mock him as having forgotten the mercy he always taught; if he forbade her to be stoned, they would gnash their teeth at him and condemn him, supposedly with justification, as a supporter of crimes and an opponent of the Law.

But far be it that earthly folly should find something to say while heavenly wisdom should lack an answer. Far be it that blind justice should stand in the way of the sun of righteousness, lest it shine upon the world.

But Jesus, bending down, was writing with his finger on the earth. Through Jesus’ bending is expressed humility; through the finger, which is flexible by the joining of its joints, the subtlety of discernment is expressed; and through the earth the human heart is shown, which customarily produces the fruits of either good or evil actions [Col. 0107B].

When the Lord was asked to judge concerning the sinful woman, he does not immediately give judgment. Rather, he first bends down and writes with his finger on the earth, and only then, because he is insistently asked, gives judgment. In this he figuratively instructs us: when we observe any errors of our neighbors, we should not first judge them by reproving them before we have humbly returned to our own conscience, carefully inscribed it with the finger of discernment, and diligently determined what pleases and what displeases the Creator in it, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Brothers, even if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI).

But when they persisted in questioning him, he straightened up and said to them: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”

Because the scribes and Pharisees were setting traps for the Lord on every side, thinking that he would either be merciless in judgment or unjust, he foresaw their deceptions, passing through them as though through the threads of a spider’s web. He showed in every respect both the judgment of justice and the gentleness of compassion. In them was fulfilled what we said from the Psalmist: “They were undone, and they were not pierced with compunction” (Ps. XXXIV). They were undone, so that they could not entrap the Lord; but they were not pierced with compunction, so that they might follow him in the duties of love.

Do you wish to hear the moderation of mercy? “The one among you who is without sin.” Do you wish again to hear the justice of judgment? “Let him be the first to throw a stone at her.” If Moses, he says, commanded you to stone such a woman [Col. 0107D], see that he did not command sinners but righteous people to do this. First fulfill the justice of the Law yourselves, and then, with innocent hands and a pure heart, come together to stone the guilty woman. First fulfill the spiritual decrees of the Law—faith, mercy, and charity—and then turn to judging what is carnal.

After giving judgment, the Lord again bent down and wrote on the earth. According to the customary manner of human conduct, it can be understood that the Lord wished to bend down and write on the earth before the wicked tempters so that, directing his face elsewhere, he might give them free opportunity to leave. He foresaw that, struck by his answer, they would depart quickly rather than ask further questions.

Finally, hearing this, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders [Col. 0108A]. But figuratively he admonishes us through what he writes on the earth while bending down both before and after giving judgment: before we correct a sinful neighbor, and after we have rendered him the service of due correction, we should examine ourselves with a fitting investigation of humility, lest perhaps we be entangled either in the same crimes that we reprove in them or in other offenses of whatever kind.

It often happens, for example, that those who publicly judge a murderer do not perceive the worse evil of hatred by which they themselves are secretly consumed; those who accuse a fornicator fail to recognize the plague of pride by which they themselves are exalted over their chastity; those who condemn a drunkard do not see the poison of envy by which they themselves are eaten away.

What remedy, then, what salvation remains for us in such dangers, except that when we see another sinning we immediately bend down—that is, humbly consider how cast down we would be by the condition of our frailty if divine mercy did not sustain us? Let us write with our finger on the earth; that is, let us carefully weigh the matter and ask whether we can say with blessed Job: “My heart does not reproach me throughout all my life” (Job XXVII). And let us diligently remember that if our heart reproaches us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things.

We may also rightly understand that, since he was about to grant forgiveness to the sinful woman, the Lord wished to write with his finger on the earth in order to show that he himself was the one who had once written the Decalogue of the Law with his finger—that is, through the work of the Holy Spirit—on stone [Col. 0108C]. The Law was rightly written on stone, since it was given to tame the hard and stubborn hearts of the people. The Lord rightly wrote on the earth, since he was about to give the grace of forgiveness to the contrite and humble in heart, who could produce the fruit of salvation.

He rightly bends down and writes with his finger on the earth: once he had shown himself exalted on the mountain, writing with his finger on stone. For through the humility of the humanity he assumed, he poured the Spirit of grace into the fruitful hearts of the faithful. When he appeared exalted in the angel, he had once given harsh commandments to a harsh people. He rightly speaks words of mercy when bent down and writes on the earth, because what he promised through fellowship with human weakness, he bestows upon human beings as a gift of compassion through the power of his divinity.

“Straightening up,” he says, “Jesus said to her: ‘Woman, where are they who accused you? Has no one condemned you?’ She said: ‘No one, Lord.’”

No one dared condemn the sinful woman, because each had begun to see in himself what he recognized as more deserving of condemnation. But let us see with what gift of mercy he raises up the accused woman—he who had driven away the crowd of accusers by bringing forth the weight of justice.

It follows:

“But Jesus said: ‘Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on do not sin any more.’”

Here the saying of the Psalmist is fulfilled, who sings in praise of the Lord: “Go forth prosperously and reign, because of truth and gentleness and justice; and your right hand will lead you wonderfully” (Ps. XLIV).

He reigns because of truth, since by preaching the way of truth to the world he expands the glory of his kingdom among crowds of believers. He reigns because of gentleness and justice, since many submit themselves to his kingdom for this reason: they recognize him as gentle in freeing penitents from sin and just in condemning the obstinate for sin—gentle in granting the grace of faith and heavenly virtues, just in rendering an eternal reward for the struggle of faith and heavenly virtues.

His right hand led him wonderfully, because God dwelling in a human being showed him to be wonderful in everything he did and taught; and he always showed, with marvelous prudence, that he was directing the plots that his cunning enemies could devise.

“Neither will I condemn you,” he says. “Go, and from now on do not sin any more.” Because he is compassionate and gracious and loves justice, he forbids her to sin any more.

But because some might doubt whether Jesus, whom they knew to be truly human, could forgive sins, he himself deigns to demonstrate more openly that he possesses divine power. After repelling the wickedness of the tempters and releasing the sinful woman from guilt, he again speaks to them, saying:

“I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”

Here he plainly teaches not only by what authority he forgave the woman’s sins, but also what he figuratively expressed by going to the Mount of Olives, by coming again at dawn into the temple, and by writing with his finger on the earth: namely, that he is the stronghold of mercies and the God of all consolation, both the herald and giver of unfailing light [Col. 0109C], the Lawgiver and likewise the giver of grace.

“I am,” he says, “the light of the world.” As though he plainly said: “I am the true light that enlightens every human being coming into the world; I am the sun of justice that rises for those who fear God, even though I seem for a time to be covered by the cloud of flesh. For I am covered by the cloud of flesh not to be hidden from those seeking me, but to be moderated for the weak. Let them heal the eyes of their minds and purify their hearts through faith, so that they may be worthy to behold me myself: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’” (Matt. V).

“Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” Whoever now obeys my commands and examples will not fear the darkness of condemnation in the future, but will have the light of life, where he will never die at all [Col. 0109D].

Let us therefore follow, brothers, now by faith the light of justice that works through love, so that we may then be worthy to attain it in its visible form, which will both reward and increase the merit of love, as he himself testifies, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (John XIV).

Let us come with the whole intention of our minds to him who has his place on the invisible Mount of Olives. For “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions,” so that he may also deign to make us participants in that same anointing of his—that is, of spiritual grace. Yet we shall be worthy to obtain this only by loving justice and hating iniquity. For the psalm that speaks these words first said of him: “You have loved justice and hated iniquity” (Ps. XLIV), so that, by proclaiming the glory of the Head, it might show the members who could belong to him how they ought to live [Col. 0110A].

Let us remember that he came into the temple at dawn and, while teaching, released the sinful woman from guilt. Let us strive to be the temple of our Creator; let us strive, once the darkness of vices has been dispersed, to advance in the light of virtues, so that the Lord may also deign to visit our hearts, instruct us in heavenly disciplines, and immediately cleanse whatever he finds filthy in us—he who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages.

## HOMILY XXI. DURING LENT

[Col. 0110B]

JOHN VI, LUKE IX, MARK VI, MATTHEW XIX. At that time Jesus departed across the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a great multitude followed him, because they had seen the signs that he performed upon those who were sick, and so forth.

Those who rightly receive the signs and miracles of the Lord and Savior when they read or hear them do not attend so much to what they should marvel at outwardly in these events as to what they ought to do inwardly by their example and what they ought to discern as mystical in them.

Behold, as the Passover, the feast of the Jews, approached, the Lord raised up the multitude following him both by the word of salvation and by the work of healing. For, as another Evangelist writes, he spoke to them about the kingdom of God and healed those who needed care; and when this teaching and healing had been completed, he abundantly fed them from a small amount of food.

And so, dearest brothers, as the feast of the Passover of our redemption approaches, let us, following this example, join the company of our brothers and follow the Lord with our whole heart. Let us contemplate most carefully along what path of actions he entered, so that we may be worthy to follow his footsteps. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked.

Whatever ignorance we discover to be present in us and harmful, let us wipe away through frequent hearing of his word. Whatever vice of the tempter’s disease—that is, of spiritual illness—we sense ravaging us inwardly, let us ask to be cleansed by the gift of his customary compassion. But even if we see ourselves united to him through the sweetness of heavenly life, let us implore his grace, so that he may deign to satisfy us with the necessary gifts of compunction and of the other spiritual virtues [Col. 0110D]. Thus, at the time of his most holy resurrection, adorned suitably both inwardly and outwardly, we may receive the mysteries of our salvation with a pure body and heart alike.

But since we have briefly anticipated these matters, I am pleased to examine more carefully the entire sequence of the sacred reading and to disclose to your charity whatever mystical meaning we may be able to investigate in it.

Jesus crossed the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias.

First, according to the historical sense, it should be said that the Sea of Galilee, which is distinguished by many names according to the diversity of the surrounding regions, is called Tiberias only in those places where it displays Tiberias, a city said to be healthful because of its warm waters, on the western shore. For, with the Jordan flowing through it, it extends eighteen thousand paces in length and five in breadth.

Mystically, however, the sea signifies the turbid and swelling currents of this age. In them, all the wicked, taking unjust pleasure, like fish immersed in the depths, do not direct their minds toward the joys above. Hence this same sea is appropriately called Galilee—that is, “wheel”—because, in truth, the love [Alternative: toil] of the passing age throws hearts into a whirlpool and does not permit them to be raised toward the desires of everlasting life. Concerning these the Psalmist says: “The wicked walk in a circle” (Psalm XI).

But as Jesus departed across the Sea of Galilee, a very great multitude followed him, in order to receive from him the supreme gifts of teaching, healing, and nourishment. Before the Lord appeared in the flesh, only the Jewish people followed him by believing; but after, through the dispensation of his incarnation, he approached, trod upon, and crossed the waves of corruptible life, a very great multitude of believing nations immediately followed him, desiring to be spiritually instructed, healed, and satisfied, and praying with the Psalmist: “Lord, I have taken refuge in you; teach me to do your will”; and: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled” (Psalm I, II). And again, trusting that they would receive from him the nourishment of eternal life: “The Lord feeds me,” he says, “and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture there he has settled me” (Psalm XXIII).

As for the fact that Jesus went up onto the mountain and sat there with his disciples, but when the multitude came to him he descended and fed in the lower places those whom he had shortly before healed in the higher places [Alternative: fed in the higher places those whom he had shortly before healed in the lower places], let us not believe that this was done without purpose. Rather, it mystically signifies that the Lord distributes his teaching and charisms according to the capacity of those who receive them: to minds still weak and spiritually immature he entrusts simpler mysteries, but to those who are higher and more perfect in understanding he discloses the more secret mysteries of his majesty, suggests the narrower paths of devoted conduct, and promises the higher gifts of heavenly rewards.

Finally, when someone asked what he should do to possess eternal life, as though still situated below, he bestowed the common gifts of his generosity, saying: “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and your mother.” But when the man afterward sought greater things and desired, as it were, to climb the mountain of virtues, he said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”

The Lord displayed this discretion of moderation not only by himself while teaching in the flesh; even now he does not cease to display it through the ministers of his word. Thus, speaking of them under the person of a good servant, he testifies that they ought to give their fellow servants a measure of wheat at the proper time—that is, to offer the nourishment of the word suitably and in measured portions according to the capacity of their hearers.

That the Lord teaches, heals, and feeds the crowds as Passover approaches can be interpreted mystically in this way: Passover is called a “passing over,” and all whom the Lord restores through the inward sweetness of his gifts he prepares for a salutary passage, so that they may transcend the desires of the flesh through the elevation of the mind, and alike trample underfoot the weak desires of the world amid prosperity and adversity, through heavenly hope and love. Even if they cannot yet reach the things above in soul or body—for this is promised in the future—they should nevertheless despise as nothing, in comparison with eternal things, whatever they see carnal people embracing as though it were great. This is according to the example of the one who, seeing the kingdom “exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon,” passed beyond temporal things in contemplation and regarded as though it did not exist what he foresaw would soon be taken away.

The statement that Jesus lifted up his eyes and saw the multitude coming to him is an indication of divine mercy: toward all who seek to come to him [Alternative: who run toward him], the grace of heavenly mercy customarily comes to meet them. And, lest they be able to go astray while seeking, he is accustomed to open the light of his Spirit to those who seek.

That the eyes of Jesus mystically signify the gifts of his Spirit is attested by John in the Apocalypse. Speaking figuratively of him, he says: “And I saw a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Revelation V).

When the Lord tested Philip by saying, “Where shall we buy bread so that these people may eat?”, he did so with provident dispensation—not so that he might learn what he himself did not know, but so that Philip, when tested, might recognize the slowness of his faith, which he himself did not recognize in the presence of a teacher who knew it, and might be corrected by the miracle. For Philip ought not to have doubted in the presence of the Creator of all things, who brings bread forth from the earth and gladdens the human heart with wine, that loaves costing a few denarii could suffice for many thousands of people, so that each might receive enough and depart already satisfied.

The five loaves with which he satisfied the multitude are the five books of Moses. When they are disclosed through spiritual understanding and multiplied through a now richer sense, they daily refresh the hearts of faithful hearers. They are rightly reported to have been barley loaves, because of the more austere commands of the Law and the covering of the coarser letter, which concealed the inner marrow, as it were, of spiritual meaning [Alternative: which conceal it].

The two fish that he added appropriately signify the writings of the psalmists and the prophets. The one group, by singing, and the other, by speaking, narrated to their hearers the future mysteries of Christ and the Church. They are fittingly represented by aquatic creatures, since the people of the faithful could in no way live without the waters of baptism.

The boy who had the five loaves and two fish, yet did not distribute them himself to the hungry crowds but offered them to the Lord for distribution, is the Jewish people, childish in the literal sense. It kept the sayings of Scripture closed within itself; nevertheless, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, he received them and showed what usefulness and sweetness they contained. He disclosed how, through the manifold grace of the Spirit, those things that had seemed few and insignificant overflowed, and through his apostles and their successors he extended them as nourishment to all the nations.

Hence other evangelists rightly report that the Lord gave the loaves and fish to the disciples, while the disciples ministered them to the crowds. When the mystery [Alternative: ministry] of human salvation began to be proclaimed by the Lord, it was confirmed in us by those who had heard him. He broke and distributed the five loaves and two fish to his disciples when he opened their minds so that they might understand everything written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms. The disciples placed them before the crowds when, having gone forth, they preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.

The grass on which the crowd reclines and is refreshed signifies the desire of the flesh, which everyone who wishes to be satisfied with spiritual nourishment must trample and suppress. “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass.” Let him therefore recline upon the grass so that he may crush the flower of grass—that is, let him chastise his body and bring it into subjection, tame the pleasures of the flesh, and restrain the excesses of lust. Whoever desires to be refreshed by the sweetness of the living bread, whoever loves to be renewed by the banquets of heavenly grace lest he fail through the decay of what is earthly, must beware.

The five thousand men who ate [Note: Thus the Basil edition and the manuscripts] signify the perfection of those who are refreshed by the word of life. In Scripture, more perfect people are commonly represented by the name “men”; no effeminate softness corrupts them. The Apostle desires such people when he says: “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and be strong” (1 Corinthians XVI).

The number one thousand, beyond which no human computation increases, customarily indicates the fullness of the matters under discussion. By the number five, however, the five well-known senses of our body are expressed: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Those who strive in each of these to act and be strong [Alternative: to act manfully and be strong], living soberly, devoutly, and justly so that they may deserve to be refreshed by the sweetness of heavenly wisdom, are represented by the five thousand men whom the Lord satisfied with mystical food.

It must not be passed over that, when he was about to refresh the multitude, he gave thanks. He gave thanks in order both to teach us always to give thanks for the heavenly gifts we have received [Alternative: gifts received from heaven] and to indicate how much he rejoices over our progress and takes pleasure in our spiritual refreshment.

Do you wish to know, brothers, how much he rejoices with us over our salvation? The evangelist Luke tells that he gave his disciples authority to tread upon all the power of the enemy, and indicated that their names were written in heaven [Alternative: omits “were”]; immediately afterward he says: “In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.’” It is therefore clear that he rejoices with the salvation and life of the faithful: by giving thanks, he praises the Father because he has revealed to the humble in spirit the secrets he has hidden from the proud.

The fact that, after the multitude had been satisfied, he commanded the disciples to gather the fragments that remained so that they would not perish clearly signifies that there are many mysteries of the divine utterances which the understanding of the common people does not grasp, and some which the less educated cannot attain by themselves but can immediately understand once they have been explained by the more learned. Those who are able must therefore gather these things by diligent examination and cause them to reach their less advanced brethren by word or writing, lest the nourishment of the word perish through their negligence and be taken away from the peoples who know how to gather it by interpretation, with the Lord granting understanding.

“They gathered,” he says, “and filled twelve baskets with the fragments.” Since the fullness of every perfection is commonly represented by the number twelve, the whole chorus of spiritual teachers is rightly expressed by the twelve baskets full of fragments. They are commanded both to gather through meditation the obscure passages of Scripture that the crowds cannot grasp by themselves and to preserve in writing, for their own use and that of the crowds, what they have meditated upon and learned.

The apostles and evangelists did this, inserting into their works many mystical sayings of the Law and the Prophets together with their interpretations. Their successors, the teachers of the Church throughout the world, did the same, examining even entire books of both Testaments through more careful explanation. Although despised by human beings, these teachers are nevertheless made fruitful by the bread of heavenly grace.

For baskets are ordinarily used for servile work. Hence, concerning the people who once served in mud and bricks in Egypt, the Psalmist says: “His hands served with the basket” (Psalm LXXX).

When the people saw the sign he had performed, they said: “This truly is the prophet who is to come into the world.” They were right to call the Lord a great prophet, already destined to be the herald of great salvation. He himself also deigns to call himself a prophet when he says: “It is not fitting for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.”

Yet they were not progressing toward complete faith, because they did not know how to call him Lord as well. Thus, seeing the sign Jesus had performed, they said: “This truly is the prophet who is to come into the world.”

But let us, seeing with more certain knowledge of truth and faith the world that Jesus made and the signs with which he filled it, say: “This truly is the mediator between God and human beings, who fills the world with divinity; and the world was made through him. He came to his own to seek and save the human race that had perished, and to restore the world that he had made. With his faithful, through the presence of his divinity, he is in the world all the days until the consummation of the age. At the consummation of the age he will come into the world in his humanity, to repay each according to his works: casting the impious and sinners into eternal fire, but bringing the righteous into eternal life, in which he lives with the Father, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

## HOMILY XXII: ON THE SECOND FERIAL DAY OF LENT

### JOHN II

At that time Jesus went down to Capernaum, he himself, his mother, his brothers, and his disciples; and there they remained for not many days.

Some people are accustomed to be troubled by what is said at the beginning of this Gospel reading: that when the Lord went down to Capernaum, not only his mother and disciples but also his brothers followed him. Nor were there lacking heretics who thought that Joseph, the husband of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, had begotten by another wife those whom Scripture calls the Lord’s brothers. Others, with even greater impiety, thought that he had begotten them by Mary herself after the Lord’s birth.

But we, dearest brothers, must know and confess without any scruple of doubt that not only the blessed Mother of God but also the most blessed Joseph, the witness and guardian of her chastity, always remained entirely free from every conjugal act; and that those who were not her children but her relatives were called the Savior’s brothers and sisters, according to the usage customary in Scripture.

Thus Abraham speaks to Lot in this way: “Please, let there be no quarrel between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds; for we are brothers.” And Laban says to Jacob: “Because you are my brother, will you serve me for nothing?” (Genesis XXIX.) It is indeed established that Lot was the son of Abraham’s brother Haran, and that Jacob was the son of Rebecca, Laban’s sister; nevertheless, because of their kinship they were called brothers.

According to this rule, which, as I have said, is exceedingly common in the sacred Scriptures, the relatives of Mary or Joseph must likewise be understood to have been called the Lord’s brothers.

That Jesus went up to Jerusalem as Passover approached certainly gives us an example of how vigilantly we ought to submit to the Lord’s commands. Appearing in the weakness of human nature, he himself observed the decrees that he had established by divine authority. Lest servants think that they could escape scourges or receive rewards without frequent prayers and the sacrifices of good works, the Son of God himself went up among the servants to pray and offer sacrifice. Let us see what he found them doing when he came to Jerusalem and what he himself did there.

“And he found,” it says, “in the temple those selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and the money changers sitting. And when he had made something like a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple, the sheep and oxen as well; he poured out the money changers’ coins and overturned their tables.”

Oxen, sheep, and doves were bought so that they might be offered in the temple. The money changers sat at tables so that payment could readily be assessed between the buyers and sellers of sacrifices. It therefore seemed lawful to sell in the temple things that were bought in order to be offered to the Lord in that same temple. But the Lord himself, unwilling that any earthly commerce—or even commerce thought honorable—should be conducted in his house, drove out the unjust traders together with everything they were trading.

What then, my brothers, what do you think the Lord would do if he found people divided by quarrels, occupied with idle talk, dissolved in laughter, or entangled in any other crime? He saw people buying sacrifices to be offered to him in the temple and hastened to expel them.

We have said this for those who enter the church and not only neglect the purpose of praying but even increase the very things for which they ought to have prayed. Moreover, when they are reproved for such folly, they pursue their reprovers with insults, hatred, and even slander—adding sins to sins, and, as it were, weaving an exceedingly long rope by their heedless accumulation, without fearing that they will be condemned through the examination of the strict Judge.

Twice, indeed, we read in the Holy Gospel that the Lord came into the temple and drove out such traders: here, namely, in the third year before his passion, as we recognize from what follows in the Gospel, and in the year in which he suffered, when he came to Jerusalem seated on a donkey five days before Passover.

But everyone who thinks rightly understands that he does the same thing in the temple of the holy Church through his daily visitation. These things are therefore greatly to be feared, beloved, and to be dreaded with fitting terror. We must carefully take precautions lest, when he comes unexpectedly, he find in us something perverse for which we deserve to be scourged and driven from the church.

This must be observed especially in the church, which is specifically called a house of prayer, lest we do anything foolish and hear the Apostle say to us, as he said to the Corinthians: “Do you not have houses for carrying on or discussing worldly matters, or do you despise the church of God?” And lest we hear from the prophet, together with the Jews: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jeremiah XI).

Indeed, we ought to rejoice because in baptism we ourselves have become the temple of God, as the Apostle testifies: “For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Corinthians III). We ourselves are the city of the great King, of which it is sung: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm LXXXVII)—that is, the foundations of the Church rest upon the solidity of the faith of the apostles and prophets.

But it is exceedingly fearful that the Apostle preceded this by saying: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians III). And the just Judge himself says: “I will destroy from the city of the Lord those who work iniquity” (Psalm C).

We ought to rejoice because the solemnity of Passover is celebrated in us when we strive to pass from vices to virtues. Passover is called a passing over. We ought to rejoice because the Lord deigns to visit our breasts—that is, his own city—and because he deigns to illumine this Passover of our good action by the presence of his mercy.

But we must greatly fear lest he find us doing in his city something other than what he loves and, as a strict avenger, reveal himself to us as one whom we do not love; lest, finding in his temple money changers, or sellers of oxen, sheep, and doves, he condemn us.

Oxen signify the teaching of heavenly life, sheep the works of purity and devotion, and doves the gifts of the Holy Spirit, because a field is customarily cultivated by the strength of oxen. The field is the Lord’s heart, cultivated by heavenly teaching and rightly prepared to receive the seeds of God’s word.

Innocent sheep provide their wool to clothe human beings. The Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove.

They sell oxen who offer the word of the Gospel to their hearers not out of divine love but for the sake of earthly gain. The Apostle rebukes such people because they proclaimed Christ insincerely.

They sell sheep who perform works of devotion for the sake of human praise. Of such people the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matthew VI).

They sell doves who give the grace of the Spirit they have received not freely, as commanded, but for a reward. They grant the laying on of hands by which the Spirit is received not for monetary profit, perhaps, but for the favor of the crowd; they confer sacred orders not according to the merit of life but as a favor.

Those who exchange money in the temple are people who do not serve heavenly things deceptively but openly serve earthly matters in the Church, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ.

The Lord shows what reward awaits such fraudulent workers when, having made a whip from cords, he drove them all from the temple. Those who, interposed among the faithful, either deceptively perform good works or openly perform evil works are driven from the portion of the lot of the saints.

He also drove out the sheep and oxen, because he showed that the life and teaching of such people were alike rejected. The cords with which he scourged and expelled the wicked from the temple are the growths of evil actions, from which material for condemning the wicked is supplied to the strict Judge. Hence Isaiah also says: “Woe to those who drag iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isaiah V). And Solomon says in Proverbs: “The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is bound with the cords of his sins” (Proverbs V).

Whoever heaps sin upon sin, increasing the offenses for which he will be condemned more severely, gradually lengthens, as it were, the cords by which he will be bound and scourged.

He also poured out the coins of the money changers whom he expelled and overturned their tables, because at the end, when the wicked have been condemned, he will remove even the form of the things they loved, according to what is written: “The world passed away, and its desire.”

And he said to those who were selling doves: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.”

He commanded that the selling of doves be removed from the temple because whoever has received the grace of the Spirit freely ought to give it freely. Hence Simon Magus, who wished to buy this grace with money in order to sell it at a higher price, heard: “May your money be with you for destruction; you have no part or share in this matter.”

It must be noted that not only those who sell doves make the house of God a house of commerce by seeking money, praise, or even honor when conferring sacred orders. Those also do so who exercise the spiritual rank or grace in the Church that they received through the Lord’s generosity, not with a simple intention but for the sake of some human recompense. This is contrary to the words of the Apostle Peter: “Whoever speaks, let him speak as the words of God; whoever ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter IV).

Therefore, whoever is such, if he does not wish to be removed from the Church when the Lord comes, must remove these things from his actions, lest he make the house of God a house of commerce.

It must also not be passed over that Scripture carefully commends both natures of our Savior: the human, that is, and the divine. To understand that he is the true Son of God, let us hear what he himself says: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.” He plainly shows himself to be the Son of God the Father when he calls the temple of God his Father’s house.

Again, to recognize that he is the true Son of Man, let us recall that at the beginning of this reading he is said to have gone down to Capernaum and to have had a mother.

It follows:

His disciples remembered that it was written: “Zeal for your house has consumed me.”

Because of zeal for the Father’s house, the Savior drove the wicked from the temple. Let us also be zealous for the house of God, dearest brothers, and, as far as we are able, insist that nothing perverse be done in it.

If we see a brother who belongs to the house of God swollen with pride, accustomed to slander, enslaved to drunkenness, weakened by luxury, troubled by anger, or subject to any other vice, let us strive, insofar as our ability permits, to correct him and to set right what is polluted and perverse. If we cannot amend anything of this kind, let us nevertheless endure it with the sharpest anguish of heart.

And especially in the house of prayer itself, where the body of the Lord is consecrated and where the presence of angels is always believed to be present, let us use all our strength to ensure that nothing foolish is done and that nothing occurs which might hinder our prayer or that of our brothers.

It follows:

The Jews therefore answered and said to him: “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” Jesus answered and said to them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

The evangelist afterward explained which temple he meant: namely, the temple of his body, which they would destroy through the Passion, but which he himself would raise from death after three days.

Since they were asking the Lord for a sign as to why he had rightly driven the customary traders from the temple, he answered that he was most rightly expelling the wicked from the temple because that temple signified the temple of his body, in which there was absolutely no stain of sin. Nor was it without reason that he cleansed the figurative temple of crimes, since he who could raise the true temple of God from the dead by the power of his divine majesty could cleanse it.

The Jews therefore said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?”

They answered according to how they understood him. But, lest we too understand the Lord’s spiritual saying in a carnal manner, the evangelist subsequently explained which temple he was speaking about.

When they say that the temple was built in forty-six years, they indicate not its first but its second construction. Solomon first completed the temple in the height of his kingdom’s peace through seven years of very rapid work. After it had been destroyed by the Chaldeans, it began to be rebuilt seventy years later, at the command of Cyrus the Persian, when the captivity had been released. But the children of the exile, who were carrying out the work under the leaders Zerubbabel and Jeshua, were unable to complete it for forty-six years because of the opposition of the neighboring nations.

This number of years also corresponds most appropriately to the perfection of the Lord’s body. Writers on natural matters report that the form of the human body is perfected over this many days: during the first six days from conception it has the likeness of milk; during the following nine it is changed into blood; then during twelve it is solidified; during the remaining eighteen it is formed until all the limbs have attained their finished outlines; from that point onward, until the time of birth, it increases in size.

Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen make forty-five. If we add one—the very day on which the body, once differentiated into its limbs, begins to increase in growth—the total is likewise forty-six days in the building of the Lord’s body, just as we find forty-six years in the construction of the temple.

Since that man-made temple prefigured the Lord’s most holy flesh, which he took from the Virgin, as we learn from this passage; and since his body, which is the Church, and the body and soul of each of the faithful were likewise signified by it, as we find in many passages of Scripture, it is worthwhile to recall some features of the temple’s structure, so that your brotherhood may recognize how everything written about it applies to Christ and the Church.

The temple stood facing east, with its doorway toward the rising sun, which, as soon as it rose, poured its radiance over all its interior. The holy Church likewise directs the whole attention of the mind toward the grace of him of whom Zechariah says: “The dawn from on high has visited us, to illumine those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke I).

Always mindful of his promise, in which he says, “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm LXXX), the Church joyfully responds: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit, because I desired your commandments” (Psalm CXVIII). This means: “I opened the devotion of my heart and deserved to draw in the light of your Spirit, because I have learned to observe in the world no other thing than the keeping of your commandments.”

Outside, the temple appeared to be built of white stone; inside, the ceilings, walls, pavement, beams, doors, and whatever vessels there were were covered with beaten gold. The Church likewise displays outwardly to everyone the strength of perfected action; but only those who have learned to enter it by devout contemplation understand how greatly it excels inwardly in the virtues of souls and how brightly the light of charity shines in each of these.

The sheets of gold themselves were fastened to boards of cedar, fir, or olive wood; and it is well established that all these are excellent woods. The radiance of the Lord’s love is impressed upon the hearts of the faithful through remembrance of his most sacred Passion, which was completed on the precious wood of the cross, so that it may not slip away.

The temple itself was divided by a veil at the middle wall. The outer house was called the sanctuary, while the inner one, where the ark of the covenant had been placed, was called the holy of holies. The Church likewise partly makes its pilgrimage on earth, away from the Lord, and partly reigns with the Lord in heaven.

The middle wall is understood to be heaven itself; the ark of the covenant is the Lord, who alone, acquainted with the Father’s secrets, entered the inner regions of heaven.

The stairway leading into the upper and third chamber was made through the interior of the southern wall, as though by an invisible step, so that only the beginning of that same ascent appeared at the eastern corner of the wall, while only the one who climbed knew how far the ascent proceeded. Scripture recalls it in this way: “The entrance to the middle side chamber was on the right side of the house, and by a spiral stairway they went up into the middle chamber, and from the middle into the third” (1 Kings VI).

When the Lord had suffered on the cross, one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. This is the water of baptism by which we are washed, and this is the blood of the Lord’s chalice by which we are sanctified.

Through these holy mysteries of his side, we rightly ascend by invisible faith from the present life of the Church, which makes its pilgrimage on earth, into the life of heavenly blessedness, which the souls of the righteous enjoy after they have been freed from their bodies.

But from that life, after receiving their bodies in the resurrection, we pass onward, with the faith of the Lord’s Passion preceding us, to the heavenly glory of everlasting happiness. Concerning this glory Isaiah says: “In their land they shall possess double; everlasting joy shall be theirs” (Isaiah LXI)—that is, in the land of the living, which alone is the land of the saints, they will receive the eternal joys of both body and soul in blessedness.

The lower house therefore signifies the present conduct of the saints; the upper one, the rest of souls received after this life; and the highest, the glory of the resurrection, which will never be changed by any end.

The entrance of the middle side, situated on the right side of the house and opening the way to the upper places, is the faith in Christ’s Passion. His right side, pierced on the cross, poured forth for us the mysteries by which, once instructed, we may ascend to the joys of heavenly life.

The first structure of the temple was completed in seven years and as many months. In the eighth year, and in the eighth month from the beginning of its construction, the solemnity of its dedication followed.

Likewise, throughout the whole present age, which revolves through seven days, the Church does not cease to receive the spiritual growth of its members until the times of the future resurrection, when, with the peaceful King, it will enter the festival of its dedication.

Since the Lord rose on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the Sabbath—this number rightly also signifies the future joys of our resurrection.

Let it suffice to have recalled these few things concerning the temple’s construction from among many others, so that it may become clearer how everything shines with spiritual meaning.

But as we bring the sermon to an end, let us return to the Lord’s saying in which he tells the Jews who were seeking a sign: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II). Let us give thanks for his mercy, because the mystery of his Passion and resurrection from the dead, which he presented in an obscure saying to those who were testing him in disbelief, he has now revealed in clear light to us who believe in him.

And because the time is already near when we desire to celebrate annually both the destruction of that venerable temple, which was carried out by the faithless, and its resurrection, which he himself miraculously accomplished on the third day, as he promised, let us cleanse the temples of our bodies and hearts, so that the Spirit of God may deign to dwell in us.

According to the Apostle’s admonition, let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day, not in feasting and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and indecencies, not in quarrels and rivalry; but let us put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans XIII), who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God before all ages and throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIII: ON PALM SUNDAY

### MATTHEW XXI; MARK XI; LUKE XIX; JOHN XII

At that time, when Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, toward the Mount of Olives, he then sent two of his disciples, saying to them: “Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me,” etc.

The Mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who for the salvation of the human race had descended from heaven to earth in order to suffer, as the hour of his Passion drew near, wished to draw near to the place of his Passion, so that it might also become clear through this that he suffered not unwillingly but voluntarily. He wished to come on a donkey and to be called and praised as king by the crowds, so that through this too everyone instructed in the matter might recognize [agnosceret; Al.: cognosceret, “might know”] that he was the Christ whom ancient prophecy had marked out as coming in this way. He wished to come five days before Passover, as we learn from the Gospel of John, so that through this too he might show himself to be the immaculate Lamb who would take away the sins of the world.

For the paschal lamb, by whose sacrifice the people of Israel were freed from Egyptian servitude, was ordered to be sacrificed five days before Passover, that is, on the fourteenth day of the moon, toward evening. This signified the one who would redeem us by his blood: five days before Passover—that is, on this present day—he was brought into the temple of God amid the great joy and praise [Al.: ad laudationem, “for praise”] of the peoples who had preceded and would follow him, and he taught there daily. When the fifth day had been completed, after he had brought to completion the mysteries of the former Passover that had until then been observed and had thereafter entrusted to his disciples the mysteries of the new Passover to be observed, he went out onto the Mount of Olives, was seized by the Jews, and was crucified in the morning. On that very day he redeemed us from demonic domination, on the day on which that ancient people of the Hebrews cast off the yoke of Egyptian servitude through the sacrifice of a lamb.

Therefore the Lord, in the likeness of the paschal lamb, approached the place of his Passion five days before he was to begin suffering, so that he might reveal himself to be the one of whom Isaiah foretold:

> Like a sheep he will be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent and will not open his mouth (Isaiah 53).

And a little earlier:

> But he was wounded for our iniquities, and by his bruise we were healed.

Yet the envious hearts of the rulers preferred to persecute him in everything he providently did rather than believe in him; and, in their great misery, they sought to hand over the author of life to death rather than to be made alive by him.

But let us, avoiding the blindness of the unbelieving, follow instead the example of those who faithfully praised the Lord, and let us examine his mystical journey with a mystical interpretation, as is fitting. The she-donkey and her colt, upon which he sat when he came to Jerusalem, signify the simple hearts of both peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile peoples. Seated upon them, he leads them to the vision of heavenly peace, restraining each from harmful freedom by his authority. For *Jerusalem* is interpreted as “vision of peace.”

And it was fitting that, when the Lord had come to the Mount of Olives, he sent disciples to bring these animals, because we reach him not through our merits but solely through the generosity of his grace, as John bears witness when he says: “In this is love: not that we loved God, but that he first loved us” (1 John 4).

The Mount of Olives signifies the height of the Lord’s love, by which he graciously chose to illumine and save us—not only because the nature of oil serves light and provides relief from labor and pain, but also because the oil mixed with other substances ordinarily surpasses them all. And when the Apostle speaks of love, he says: “I will show you a still more excellent way” (1 Corinthians 12).

Accordingly, when the Lord came to the Mount of Olives, he ordered donkeys to be brought to him so that he might proceed to Jerusalem, figuratively signifying what he says openly elsewhere: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3).

He sent two disciples to bring the two animals, signifying that preachers were to be appointed for both peoples, namely those of the circumcision and those of the uncircumcision. Or certainly he sent two to warn that these same preachers should be perfected in both doctrine and conduct, lest the unlearned mingle words of error with the truth, or deny by perverse living what they had taught correctly.

“You will find,” he says, “a she-donkey tied, and a colt with her; untie them and bring them to me.” The other evangelists likewise testify that the colt had been tied. Both peoples were surrounded by the cords of sins and needed divine release: the one sinned by misusing the law it had received, the other by never receiving it. Hence the Apostle rightly says: “There is no distinction: for all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace.”

And beautifully, the other three evangelists, who wrote for the Gentiles, mention only the colt as having been brought to the Lord. But Matthew the evangelist, who wrote from among the Hebrews and in the Hebrew language, also mentions the she-donkey, so that, in a provident treatment of both matters, he might mystically teach that those whose salvation they sought through writing were represented as destined to be saved by the Lord [Al.: “as those who would be saved”].

“And if anyone,” he says, “says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them, and immediately he will let them go.” This is also commanded to teachers: if any adversity hinders them, if anyone prevents sinners from being loosed from the snares of the devil and brought to the Lord through confession of faith, they must nevertheless not cease preaching, but steadfastly make known that the Lord has need of such people for the building up of the Church. For however savage and monstrous the persecutor may be, he cannot obstruct the salvation of those whom the Lord knows to be his, those whom he has predestined to eternal life.

The testimony of the prophet is added to this event, so that it may be evident that the Lord fulfilled everything that had been written about him, while the Scribes and Pharisees, blinded by envy, were unable to understand what they themselves were reading:

> “Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, meek, sitting upon a she-donkey and a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.”

The daughter of Zion is the Church of the faithful, belonging to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all. At that time her portion among the people of Israel was not small, and she had a meek king, because he is accustomed to give heavenly kingdoms not to the harsh but to the meek, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11).

Of these the Psalmist says: “The meek shall possess the land, and shall delight in an abundance of peace” (Psalm 36). The meek king gives the land of peace to the meek—that is, to those humble in heart—whom the impious king of old, namely the devil, had once struck down in the land of war and tribulations with the wound of pride.

He is said to sit “upon a she-donkey and a colt, the foal of a beast of burden” (Isaiah 66), because he rests in the hearts of the humble and quiet, who tremble at his words; or of those who in the synagogue learned to bear the yoke of the law; or of those who, long unrestrained in Gentile freedom, were converted by the synagogue’s insistence to the grace of faith and truth.

The disciples brought the she-donkey and the colt, placed their garments upon them, and made the Lord sit upon them. The disciples’ garments are works of righteousness, as the Psalmist testifies: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” [justitiam; Al.: justitia] (Psalm 131).

The disciples cover with their garments the donkeys whom they find naked, and thus place the Lord upon them, when holy preachers find certain people empty of the habit of holiness and, through the examples of their virtues, train them to receive faith and love of their Creator. For the Lord did not wish to ride upon a naked she-donkey or a naked colt, because neither Jew nor Gentile, unless adorned with the words and deeds of the saints, can have the Lord as ruler; rather, sin reigns in his mortal body, so that he obeys its desires.

But the very great crowd spread their garments on the road. This great crowd signifies the innumerable army of martyrs who gave their bodies—the coverings, namely, of their souls—for the Lord, so that for the elect who followed they might make the path of right living smoother. Thus no one would hesitate to place the foot of good action in the peace where they saw that not a few had gone before them in the battle of martyrdom.

Others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. The branches of the trees are the examples of the Fathers who preceded us. Whoever sets forth, as an example of right belief or conduct, what a prophet, an apostle, or any other saint said or did, truly cuts branches from the trees with which he smooths the road for the donkey carrying the Lord, because he extracts sayings from the books of the saints through which he builds up the simple hearts of Christ, lest they go astray on the road of truth.

The crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying:

> “Hosanna to the Son of David!”

With one and the same voice of confession and praise, those who went before and those who followed exalt the Lord, because there is plainly one faith among those who were approved before the Lord’s incarnation and those who came afterward, although their mysteries differed according to the circumstances of the times. Peter bears witness when he says: “But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they also were” (Acts 15).

When they say, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” this is what is read in the Psalm: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Psalm 3). It is also what the choir of the saints resounds in the Apocalypse in the great devotion of its praise: “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Revelation 7).

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” “In the name of the Lord,” that is, in the name of God the Father, signifies what he himself says elsewhere to the unbelieving Jews: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him” (John 5).

Christ came in the name of God the Father because in everything he did and said he took care to glorify the Father and to proclaim to human beings that the Father should be glorified.
