Antichrist will come in his own name; although he is the most wicked of all human beings and filled with the devil as his companion, he will not [Al. omits non] disdain to call himself the Son of God, for “he opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped.”

The crowds take up this verse of praise from Psalm 117, which no one can doubt was sung about the Lord. Hence the same Psalm beautifully prefaces its words about him:

> “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.”

For Christ, whom the Jews rejected while constructing the decrees of their traditions, became a stronghold for both believing peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile peoples.

That Christ is called the cornerstone in the Psalm is certainly the same as what, in the Gospel, is praised by the voice of the crowds who went before and followed afterward. What is added in the continuation of their praise—“Hosanna,” that is, “salvation,” or “salvation in the highest”—clearly teaches that the Lord’s coming in the flesh is salvation not only for the human race on earth but also for the angels in heaven. For as we who have been redeemed are led to the realms above, their number, which had been diminished when Satan fell, is filled up.

Paul says here that all things in heaven and on earth are restored in Christ (Ephesians 1). Rightly, then, “Hosanna in the highest” is sung in his praise, since the whole economy of his incarnation was directed toward fulfilling the glory of the heavenly homeland.

Therefore, my brothers, it is necessary for us to strive toward the homeland promised to us with complete devotion of mind, always remembering that, although the road by which we enter is narrow, the dwelling to which we hasten is blessed. It is more fortunate to be led to the kingdom by a difficult road than to punishment by a pleasant and level one. It is more fortunate to earn everlasting joy through the temporary restraint of the flesh than to gain eternal vengeance through a brief period of indulgence.

Behold, with the Lord’s help, we have now completed a large part of the Lenten fast; each person’s conscience bears witness to this. For the more strictly one remembers having dedicated oneself to the Lord during these holy days, the more joyfully one awaits the season of the Lord’s holy resurrection. But if anyone’s conscience, not yet disciplined perfectly, still accuses him, there is no doubt that he awaits the arrival of so great a solemnity with fear and trembling.

Yet such a person must not despair of salvation, lest, overwhelmed by the number or enormity of his sins, he fall into the abyss of despair, according to Solomon’s saying: “When the wicked comes to the depths of evils, he despises them” (Proverbs 18). Rather, let him carefully consider that if the time of the annual festival in which we rejoice at the resurrection of our Creator affects the chaste with such joy and the impure with fear and confusion, then much more will the time of the strict judgment, when the general resurrection of all is celebrated, affect them: once the judge’s sentence has been heard, a clean conscience will make some rejoice by acquitting them, while a guilty conscience will accuse and condemn others forever.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, whoever, armed with the weapons of bodily restraint, began at the beginning of Lent [Al.: “of Lent itself”] to fight against the proud tempter must carefully see to it that he does not abandon what he has begun before the enemy is struck down and he is granted the ministries of the angels.

But whoever has not yet clothed himself in the armor of virtues should begin today; today, with those faithful crowds, let him take up the works of faith. Let him implore the mercy of the one who, coming in the name of the Father, brought blessing to the world [Al. adds: et, “and”], proclaiming “Hosanna in the highest,” and let him ask that he may be saved in the heavenly homeland.

Let him spread [sternat; Al.: sternet, “he will spread”] his garments on the road—that is, let him humble the members of his body in the present, so that God may exalt them in the future—remembering the saying of David: “The humbled bones shall rejoice.”

Let him cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road—that is, let him diligently recall the writings of the saints. These strengthen those who stand, lest they fall; exhort those who have fallen, lest they lie there longer; instruct those who rise again to exercise themselves in virtues; and lift those practiced in virtue to hope for rewards in heaven.

Thus [Al.: hisque, “and by these things”] let him fortify the steps of his conduct, lest they stumble against the stone of offense and the rock of scandal. In this way he too may follow, with the other faithful, the footsteps of his Redeemer and venerate with suitable purity of mind the mysteries of his Passion and Resurrection. Jesus Christ our Lord, who [qui; Al.: quae, “which”] has deigned to give these mysteries to all his elect—that is, to his members—as both a remedy for wounds and a pledge of heavenly joys, lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIV. FOR THE MONDAY AFTER PALM SUNDAY

**JOHN 12.** At that time, six days before Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus had died, whom Jesus raised, etc.

It is customary for prudent people to learn the virtue of prudence not only from those things they have rightly understood [Al.: ac prudenter, “and prudently”], but also from those that they have recognized as having been done or said wrongly: the former they imitate by following them, while the latter they avoid so as not to fall into them.

This is what reason compels us to do, dearly beloved brothers, in today’s reading from the holy Gospel: not only to learn, as an example of virtue, the devotion of Christ’s lovers, but also [Al. adds: et, “and”] to consider and, having considered it, quickly avoid the faithlessness of those who persecuted him.

We must follow the prudence of those women whom we know to have clung to the Lord with such faith and love. We must flee the folly of the chief priests and Pharisees, who sought to ensnare and kill the wisdom of God by plots. We must beware the madness of those who had gone up to Jerusalem to be sanctified for Passover but, forgetting sanctification, were planning the Savior’s death in the very house of prayer.

Passover was approaching, when everyone who had been sanctified and purified ought to come to eat the lamb. Yet those who had gone up to the temple to be sanctified were already descending more defiled by their conspiracy to shed blood.

Let us act diligently [Al.: “carefully”], because the time of our Passover is approaching. As it now comes [Al.: Ut, “that”], let us, having been sanctified, approach the Lord’s altar, not to eat the flesh of a lamb but to receive the holy mysteries of our Redeemer.

Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God. Let no one turn the house of prayer into a den of thieves. Let no one lay snares of death for the members of Christ. Let no one who still remains in death presume to approach to receive the mysteries of life; for whoever does not love remains in death.

Let us love Christ in himself; let us love him in his members. Let us seek the Lord, and our soul shall live. Let us seek him not as the wicked do, in order to kill him, but as the faithful do, in order to enjoy him forever.

“They were seeking Jesus,” he says, “and were speaking to one another while standing in the temple: ‘What do you think? Is he not coming to the feast?’” The Jews were seeking Jesus, but wrongly: they were seeking him so that, when he came to the feast, they might kill him.

But let us seek him standing in the temple of God, persevering together in prayer, and let us speak to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, asking him in thanksgiving that he may deign to come to our feast, illumine us by his presence, and himself sanctify us with his gifts.

The chief priests and Pharisees had given orders that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it so that they might seize him. Let us also give one another this command, my brothers: if anyone knows that a brother’s heart contains greater depths of mercy, greater humility, kindness, moderation, strength, or a more abundant supply of the other virtues—clear signs of Christ’s presence—let him immediately report where such a person is, so that we may faithfully hold fast, by imitation, to the footsteps of Christ found with him.

The Lord knew that the Jews had conspired to kill him, yet he did not flee the hands of those plotting against him. Confident of the glory of the Resurrection, he first came to Bethany, the town near Jerusalem where he had raised Lazarus from the dead, and then also to Jerusalem, where he himself would suffer and rise again from the dead.

He went to Jerusalem so that he might die there; he went to Bethany so that the raising of Lazarus might be more firmly impressed upon everyone’s memory, and so that the impious rulers might be increasingly confounded and proved without excuse—those who were not afraid to kill one who could raise the dead, and who, neither moved by the benefits of his raising nor terrified by the divine power of the one who raised him, did not withdraw their minds from an unjust killing.

And lest the inventors of false accusations should say that Lazarus had been raised only in appearance, a supper was held there for the Lord, and Lazarus himself was one of those reclining with him. Thus, when they saw or heard him alive, speaking, eating, and conversing familiarly with his companions, they might either recognize the power of the one who raised him and receive grace, or, if in hardened hearts they refused to yield to the truth, incur punishment.

Mystically, this supper of the Lord, at which Martha served and Lazarus reclined among the others, is the faith of the Church that works through love. Hence elsewhere the Lord says to his disciples concerning the peoples who would believe in him: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John 4). Explaining this, he added: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.”

At this supper Martha serves when each faithful soul offers the Lord the service of its devotion. Lazarus becomes one of those reclining with the Lord when those who have been raised to righteousness after the death of sins rejoice in the presence of the truth together with those who have remained in their righteousness; the penitent are nourished together with the innocent by the gifts of heavenly grace.

And fittingly this supper is celebrated in Bethany, which is a town on the side of the Mount of Olives and is interpreted as “house of obedience.” For the house of obedience is the Church, which faithfully obeys the Lord’s commands. It is also the city established upon the mountain of mercy, which can never be hidden. Built from the side of its Redeemer, it has been imbued with the water of cleansing and the blood of sanctification that flowed from his side when he died for it.

There, too, Lazarus’s other sister, Mary, as the continuation of the Gospel reading shows, in testimony to her great love, received a pound of precious ointment of genuine nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped his feet with her hair.

By this act she not only gives evidence of her own devotion but also represents the pious service of the other faithful souls toward God. First, however, it must be noted that, as we learn from the accounts of Matthew and Mark, Mary poured nard not only over the Lord’s feet but also over his head.

There can be no doubt that she is also the woman whom the evangelist Luke reports (Luke 7) to have once come to the Lord as a sinner with an alabaster jar of ointment. Standing behind him at his feet, she began to wet his feet with her tears; she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with ointment.

Thus the woman is the same, but there she humbly anointed only the Lord’s feet, and did so amid tears of repentance; here, amid the joys of righteous action, she did not hesitate both to anoint his feet and to rise to anoint his head as well.

There she signifies the beginnings of penitents; here, the righteousness of perfected souls. Hence there the quantity of the ointment is not stated, whereas here it is said to have been a pound. What, then, is signified by a pound of ointment if not the perfection of righteousness?

There the kind of ointment is left unmentioned; here it is indicated to have been genuine nard—that is, faithful, not adulterated with foreign substances, but precious—so that the chastity of perfect faith and action might be signified.

By the Lord’s head, which Mary anointed, the sublimity of his divinity is expressed; by his feet, the humility of his incarnation. We anoint his feet when we proclaim with due praise the mystery of the incarnation he assumed; we anoint his head when we venerate the excellence of his divinity with a worthy confession.

For what is signified by ointment if not the good fragrance of reputation? Paul bears witness when he says: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place” (2 Corinthians 2).

The Lord’s head may also [Al. adds: ipse, “himself”] rightly signify the mediator between God and human beings, who is the head of the Church; his feet may suitably be understood as its lowest members. Of these he will say at the end: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25).

We anoint the Lord’s head when we embrace the glory of his divinity [Al.: “and likewise of his humanity”] with the worthy sweetness of faith, hope, and charity, and when we enlarge the praise of his name by living well. We anoint the Lord’s feet when we refresh his poor with words of consolation, so that they may not despair in their afflictions. We wipe those same feet with our hair when we share with the needs of the poor what is superfluous to us. Thus what follows is fulfilled in us:

“And the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.” For, according to our measure, the world is filled [Al.: “will be filled”] with the reputation of the devotion by which we are proved to venerate and love God and our neighbor with a simple and pure heart.

Thus is fulfilled what the bride in the Song of Love boasts, saying: “While the king was at his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” Here it is openly shown what Mary did once, and figuratively what the whole Church and every perfected soul always does.

Then one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said: “Why was this ointment not sold [vendidit] for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” [Vulg.: veniit, “was sold”]

Woe to the impious betrayer! Woe to his accomplices in wickedness, who even now persecute Christ’s members and do not cease to envy in others the reputation for virtue that they themselves do not deserve to possess!

Indeed, we might have thought that Judas had spoken this out of concern for the poor, but the truthful witness exposes his mind:

“He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief; and, having the money box, he used to take away [exportabat] what was put into it” [Vulg.: portabat, “carried”].

Judas did not perish at the moment when, corrupted by money, he betrayed the Lord. Rather, he was already lost when he followed the Lord. He had the Lord’s money box and was accustomed not only to carry in it what was placed there for his ministry, but also to steal it.

Seeing that Judas’s heart was already stained with greed, and foreseeing that it would be stained by an even worse betrayal, the Lord entrusted to his care whatever he had in the purses and allowed him to do with it whatever he wished, so that either the honor conferred upon him or the memory of the money he had possessed might turn his mind away from selling the Lord.

But because the greedy person is always in need and the faithless never remembers benefits, the impious man proceeded from stealing the money he carried to betraying the Lord who had entrusted it to him.

Then Jesus said: “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.”

As though Judas had asked innocently, the Lord explained simply and gently what Mary’s service signified: namely, that he was about to die and would be anointed with spices for burial. Therefore Mary, although she greatly desired to reach the anointing of his dead body and would not be permitted to do so, was granted the opportunity to offer him while he was still alive a service that, after his death, she would be unable to perform because his swift Resurrection would precede her.

Hence Mark rightly testifies that the Lord said of her: “She has done what she could; she has anticipated anointing my body for burial” (Mark 14). This means plainly: “Because she will not be able to touch my dead body, she has done the only thing she could now do; she has anticipated honoring me with the service of burial while I am still alive.”

“For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.” Here too, with the restraint of great patience, the Lord does not accuse Judas of greed or say that he speaks of the money out of concern for the poor. Rather, he shows by reason that those who ministered to him from their resources while he lived among human beings were not to be blamed, since he himself would remain bodily with the Church for only a short time, whereas the poor, to whom alms could be given, would always be present in it.

Many of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. Curiosity, not love, brought them to Jesus.

But let us, dearly beloved brothers, reverse their example. If we know where Jesus is, where he makes his dwelling, where he finds Bethany—that is, the house of the obedient soul in which he may dwell—let us come there through contemplation, not merely because of the human being whom he raised from the death of the soul and granted spiritual life, but so that, by imitating that person’s good life, we may thereby deserve to reach the vision of Jesus.

For we know with certainty where Jesus is. He rose after his death and ascended into heaven; there he has his everlasting dwelling. This is the true Bethany, the heavenly city, which no one can enter unless obedient.

Let us therefore strive to come there through the inward affections of the heart [Note: [Col. 0129D] Al.: “Let us hasten there with all the powers of our soul”]. Let us sigh for the founder of that house; let us all ask, each one of us, that we may dwell in his house all the days of our life—not to see Lazarus there, whom he raised from the dead, but, raised ourselves from the dead together with Lazarus and the other saints, to behold the Lord’s will and to be protected by his holy temple.

The chief priests then decided to kill Lazarus also [Al. adds: et, “also”], because many of the Jews were leaving on his account and believing in Jesus.

O blind cunning of the blind—to wish to kill one who had been raised, as though the one who could raise the dead could not raise the slain! Indeed, he taught that he could do both: he raised Lazarus, who had died, and he raised himself after being killed.

But let us, brothers, abandoning the malice of the faithless, follow the devotion of the faithful. Let us depart from the company of the wicked; let us not sit in the council of vanity, nor enter with those who do evil. Let us believe in him who saves from death not only the body but also the soul, and let us preserve by our deeds what we believe, so that, believing, we may have eternal life in his name—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXV. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

[Col. 0130A]

**JOHN 13.** Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end. And supper being finished, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him, etc.

As the evangelist John was about to write about that memorable mystery of the Lord, in which, at Passover, before going to his Passion, he deigned to wash the feet of his disciples, he first took care to disclose what the very name of Passover signified mystically, beginning in this way:

“Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end.”

For *Passover* is interpreted as “passing over.” The name derives from the fact that the Lord passed through Egypt, striking down the firstborn of Egypt and liberating the children of Israel, and from the fact that the children of Israel themselves passed over that night from Egyptian servitude, so that they might come to the land of the inheritance and peace promised long ago.

Mystically, however, it signifies that at Passover the Lord would pass from this world to the Father, and that, following his example, the faithful, casting aside temporal desires and the servitude of vices, must pass through continual devotion to the virtues to the promise of the heavenly homeland.

John the evangelist beautifully indicates how Jesus passed from this world to the Father when he says: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end”—that is, he loved them so greatly that through this very love he brought his bodily life to an end for a time, about to pass immediately from death to life and from this world to the Father.

“For no one has greater love than this: that someone should lay down his life for his friends.” Hence rightly both Passovers—the legal and the evangelical—were consecrated by blood: the former by the blood of the paschal lamb, the latter by the blood of the one of whom the Apostle says: “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5).

The blood of the latter was poured out on the cross; that of the former was sprinkled, in the form of a cross, upon the middle of the threshold and upon the lintel, and upon the doorposts on either side.

And when supper had been made, he says, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God, he rises from supper and lays aside his garments [Col. 0130D]. In speaking of the supreme humility of the humanity he had assumed, he first recalls the eternity of his divine power, both to demonstrate that he himself was truly God and man, and to remind us of that commandment by which, the greater we are, the more we ought to humble ourselves in all things. For he was truly man, since as man he could touch and wash human feet, be betrayed by a man, and be crucified by men; he was truly God, to whom the Father had given all things into his hands, because he had come forth from God and had returned to God.

The Lord therefore knew that the devil had already put it into Judas’s heart to betray him; he knew that the Father had given all things into his hands—among these “all things,” both the betrayer himself and those to whom he was to be betrayed, and the death which he was about to undergo—so that he might do with all these whatever he willed, and by his power turn their evil into good [Col. 0131A]. He knew that through the humility of his incarnation he had come forth from God, and that through the victory of his resurrection he was to return to God, neither abandoning God when he came forth from him, nor abandoning us when he returned. He knew all these things, and yet, as a sign of his great compassion and an example of great humility for us, he rises from supper and lays aside his garments, washes the disciples’ feet, fulfilling the duty not of God the Lord but of a human servant, so that he might humbly wash even the feet of the one whose hands he knew would be insolently defiled in betraying him.

If, however, we are pleased to examine this most humble mystery of our Savior with deeper inquiry, this most sacred supper, at which the Lord reclined with his disciples, signifies the whole period during which he dwelt bodily in the Church [Col. 0131B]. During that time he fed all people far and wide with the food of his saving word and the sweetness of his miracles, while he himself was nourished by the faith and love of those who listened; for all whom he converted to the grace of truth he made, as it were, by their means, the increase of his body, which is the Church, after the manner of those who eat.

He rose from supper and laid aside his garments when, ceasing to dwell any longer among human beings in a temporal manner, he laid down upon the cross the members of the body he had assumed. He took a linen cloth and girded himself when, having received from the Father the command to suffer, he surrounded his members with it in the very exercise of his Passion. For the affliction of sufferings is commonly represented by linen, which is produced through manifold labor and torment [Col. 0131C]. And the Lord, laying aside his garments, is girded with linen to signify that he laid down the bodily form which he had assumed not without the pressure of pains, but after the long tribulation of the cross.

He poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and wipe them with the linen cloth with which he was girded when, having died on the cross, he poured water together with blood from his side upon the earth. By these he cleansed the works of believers, and he deigned not only to sanctify those works through the sacraments of his Passion, but also to strengthen them through the examples of that same Passion.

When, after beginning the washing of the feet, it is said, “Therefore he came to Simon Peter,” this should not be understood as though he came to him after coming to some others, but because he began with the one who was first among the apostles; and because he did not know the mystery, it was not without reason that he recoiled from such a ministry. It is also beyond doubt that any one of them would have done the same, had he not been restrained by that sentence which was spoken to Peter [Col. 0131D]:

“If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me.”

Here it is plainly shown that this washing of the feet signifies the spiritual purification of flesh and soul, without which no one can attain fellowship with Christ. Therefore, when Peter heard this, immediately seized by his customary fervor of divine love, he replied:

“Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.”

As though he were plainly saying: “Since, now that you have taught me, I understand that by washing my feet you signify that you cleanse my sins, I offer you not only my feet but also my hands and head to be washed; for I do not doubt that I commit many things not only in my walk but also in my actions, as well as by sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, which ought to be forgiven by you” [Col. 0132A]. But let us hear what the Lord replies to this fervent lover, and how he gradually draws him toward an understanding of the mystical washing.

“He who is washed,” he says, “does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.”

He plainly declares that the washing of the feet signified the remission of sins—not, however, that remission which is given once in baptism, but rather that by which the daily guilt of the faithful, without which no one lives in this life, is cleansed by his daily grace. For the feet with which we walk and touch the earth—and which therefore we cannot keep free from the contamination of dust as we can the rest of the body—signify the necessity of our earthly dwelling. To the extent that we are daily made sluggish and negligent by this necessity, to that extent even men of great stature and supreme conduct are recalled from the contemplation of heaven, which they love above all [Col. 0132B], so that “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I).

Therefore, “he who is washed does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean,” because the one who has been washed in the font of baptism for the remission of all sins does not need to be washed again—in fact, cannot be washed in the same manner—but only needs the daily contaminations of worldly conduct to be wiped away by the daily forgiveness of his Redeemer. He is clean in the whole body of his actions, except only for those things which, by the necessity of temporal care, have clung to the mind. Because of their daily defilement, and likewise their daily cleansing, we say every day in prayer: “And forgive us our debts [Col. 0132C], as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI; Luke XI).

But these words were spoken concerning the apostles and those like them: namely, “Blessed and undefiled are those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways” (Ps. CXIX). We, however, who often forget the fear of God and walk along the left-hand path, cannot be freed from the filth of our errors by that light and daily solemnity of prayer. Rather, a greater defilement must be cleansed by a greater exercise of prayers, vigils, fasts, tears, and almsgiving; by these the one who sits at the right hand of God, in the bodily form he assumed, daily intercedes for us, cleansing inwardly the footprints of our hearts.

After the Lord had washed the disciples’ feet, he took his garments [Col. 0132D], and when he had reclined again, he once more explained in words the ministry of the washing which he had performed for them shortly before, when they did not yet understand it. For after suffering on the cross he consecrated for us the bath of remission; he took again the now immortal members which he had laid down as mortal. And after appearing to the disciples following his resurrection and dwelling familiarly with them even while eating together for forty days, he explained to them the benefit of his Passion, whose outcome they had feared greatly until then because they did not know its mystical power (Acts I).

“If I, therefore,” he says, “the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.”

This sentence ought rightly to be understood both literally and mystically, and it ought to be fulfilled devotedly: literally, so that through charity we serve one another, not only by washing the feet of our brothers but also by assisting them in whatever needs they may have [Col. 0133A]; mystically, so that just as the Lord is accustomed to forgive the sins of those who repent, so we may hasten to forgive our brothers who sin against us (Matt. VI; Mark XI).

Just as he washed us from our sins by interceding for us with the Father, so we too, if we know that our brother has committed a sin not unto death, should ask that life be given to him who sins not unto death (1 John V). And as the apostle James exhorts: “Let us confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, that we may be saved” (James V). Just as he laid down his life for us, so we also, when the moment requires, should lay down our lives for our brothers (1 John III). It follows:

[Col. 0133B]

“Amen, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him.”

He said this because the Lord had washed the feet of his servants, and because he himself was the one who sent those whom he sent. *Apostle* is Greek; in Latin it is called *missus*, “one who is sent.” Thus he showed that the things which the exalted one did humbly must be done still more humbly by the humble and the weak. But he also intended to call spiritual understanding to mind in this passage: if he who committed no sin, “nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. II; Isa. LIII), intercedes for our excesses, how much more ought we to pray for one another. And if he forgives us, although we have nothing that we must forgive him, how much more ought we to forgive one another our debts [Col. 0134A]. The Apostle likewise commands this, saying: “Be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Eph. IV).

“If you know these things,” he says, “you will be blessed if you do them.”

This saving saying of our Savior must be considered greatly and diligently, because we shall be blessed if we know the heavenly commandments, provided that we follow in practice what we know. For the one who neglects to keep his known commandments cannot be blessed; and the one who disdains even to know them is excluded still farther from the lot of the blessed.

The Psalmist agrees with this. He weighs the hearts of mortals and sees that all alike love blessedness, but that few seek it where it is to be found. He himself plainly declared what the greatest blessedness of a human being in this life is [Col. 0134B], saying: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. CXIX). And lest it be thought by the inexperienced and uneducated that this way of the undefiled and blessed could be understood casually, he consequently added and said: “Blessed are those who search out his testimonies; they seek him with their whole heart.”

Therefore, dearly beloved, let us ask the mercy of him who commanded that his commandments be kept exceedingly, so that he himself may direct our ways to keep his ordinances, and that, after keeping his commandments, he himself may lead us into the blessedness of beholding him eternally: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK TWO. HOMILIES, ALSO GENUINE

[Col. 0133]

## HOMILY ONE. ON THE EVE OF EASTER

[Col. 0133C]

MATTHEW XXVIII. MARK XVI. LUKE XXIV. JOHN XX. “At that time, in the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawned toward the first day of the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and coming near, rolled back the stone and sat upon it,” etc.

The resurrection of our Lord and Savior, dearly beloved brothers, has consecrated for us the vigils of this most sacred night, as we have heard from the Gospel reading. Rightly, then, do we celebrate this night with vigils and hymns for love of him who, for love of us, willed to sleep unto death in it and to be raised from death; for, as the Apostle says: “He died for our sins and rose for our justification” (Rom. IV) [Col. 0133D]. He also indicated this by the very time at which he died on the cross and rose from the dead.

Around the ninth hour, when the day was already inclining toward evening and the sun’s ray, warmed by the midday heat, had grown mild, he completed the mystery of his most victorious Passion, plainly showing that, in order to remove the crimes through which we had fallen away from divine light and love into the death of this pilgrimage, he had undergone the punishment of the cross. He rose in the morning of the first day of the Sabbath, which is now called the Lord’s Day, plainly teaching that he would raise us from the death of the soul and lead us into the light of everlasting happiness [Col. 0134C].

He also took care to disclose to us another memorable mystery through the time of his Passion, burial, and resurrection. He was crucified on the sixth day, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose from the dead on the Lord’s Day, signifying that throughout the six ages of this world his elect must labor in good works amid the dangers of persecutions. In the life to come, as in an everlasting Sabbath, the rest of souls is to be hoped for; and on the day of judgment, as on the Lord’s Day, the reception of immortal bodies is likewise to be celebrated, in which thereafter souls may enjoy heavenly joy without end.

What is said in the Gospel reading—that the holy women came in the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawned toward the first day of the Sabbath, to see the tomb—is to be understood in this way: they began [Al., *coeperunt*, “began”] to come in the evening, but arrived [Al., *venerunt*, “arrived”] at the tomb in the morning, as it dawned toward the first day of the Sabbath [Col. 0134D]. That is, they prepared in the evening the spices with which they desired to anoint the Lord’s body, but in the morning they carried [Al., *detulerunt*, “carried”] to the tomb the spices prepared in the evening. Matthew presented this somewhat obscurely for the sake of brevity, but the other evangelists show more clearly in what order it happened.

After the Lord had been buried on the sixth day, the women returned from the tomb [Col. 0135A] and prepared spices and ointments for as long as it was permissible to work; on the Sabbath they kept silence according to the command, as Luke plainly indicates. But when the Sabbath had passed and, with evening’s arrival, the time for working had returned, they promptly bought the spices which they had prepared in insufficient quantity, as Mark relates, so that they might come and anoint him; and very early on the first day of the Sabbaths they came [Al., came] to the tomb.

It may be asked why the evangelist, describing the night of the Lord’s resurrection, says:

“In the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawned toward the first day of the Sabbath.”

The customary order of times has evening grow darker into night rather than grow light into day. But the evangelist, speaking mystically, sought to indicate how much dignity this most sacred night received [Col. 0135B] from the glory of conquered death [Al., had received], when he declared that its beginning—at which the women devoted to Christ began to keep vigil in his service—was already dawning into the following day.

For the Lord, the author and arranger of times, who rose in the final part of this night, made the whole night festive and shining with the light of that same resurrection. From the beginning of the world’s creation until then, the course of time had been distinguished in such a way that day preceded night, in accordance with the order of the first creation. On this night, however, through the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, the order of time was changed.

Because he rose from the dead at night, while on the following day he showed his disciples the effect of that resurrection and, sharing a meal with them, established the truth of its power while they both wondered and rejoiced, that night was most rightly joined to the light of the following day, as though the order of time had been established so that day would follow night [Col. 0135C]. Formerly night quite appropriately followed day, because humanity, having fallen through sin from the light of paradise, descended into the darkness and hardships of this world. Now day appropriately follows night, when through faith in the resurrection, by Christ’s gift, we are led back from the darkness of sin and the shadow of death to the light of life.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, since we have recognized that this special night is illumined [Col. 0135D] by the grace of the Lord’s resurrection, we too must take diligent care that no part of it grow dark in our heart, but that it all shine into day—both now, as we worthily keep its vigils with devoted praise, and afterward, when the vigils have been completed, as we await the paschal festivals of the Lord’s Day with a sober and pure conscience.

“Mary Magdalene came,” he says, “and the other Mary, to see the tomb.”

Two women of one name and of the same love and devotion, who came to visit the Lord’s tomb, signify the two peoples of the faithful, namely the Jewish and the Gentile peoples, who with one and undivided zeal desire to celebrate the Passion and resurrection of their Redeemer wherever his Church is spread throughout the world.

That there was a great earthquake when the Lord rose from the tomb, just as there had also been one when he died on the cross, signifies that earthly hearts, previously cast down and without heavenly hope, must be shaken by faith in his Passion and resurrection toward repentance; moved by a most salutary fear, they must be raised to everlasting life [Col. 0136A].

The angel came and fulfilled the service of ministry which he owed to the Lord. Since Christ is God and man, throughout the events of his humanity the ministries of the angels owed to God are never absent, as the detailed history of the holy Gospel proves abundantly.

He rolled back the stone not to open a door for the Lord as he came out, but to provide human beings with evidence of his already accomplished departure. The one who, while still mortal, could enter the world by being born from a closed virgin womb could, without any doubt, now made immortal, rise and come out of the world even though the tomb was closed.

Nor should we pass over the reason why the angel, the witness of the Lord’s resurrection, appeared sitting [Col. 0136B], when the one who announced the joy of his birth to the world is recorded as having stood beside the shepherds. Standing belongs to one who fights, but sitting [Al., *but* omitted] belongs to one who reigns. The angel who preached the Lord’s arrival in the world rightly appeared standing, signifying even by standing that the one whom he preached was coming to overthrow the ruler of the world. The herald of his resurrection is rightly remembered as sitting, so that by sitting he might also signify that, having overcome the author of death, he had already ascended to the seat of an everlasting kingdom.

Concerning this, appearing shortly afterward to the disciples, he himself says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). And the evangelist Mark says: “The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven [Col. 0136C] and sits [Al., sat] at the right hand of God” (Mark XVI).

He was sitting upon the stone that had been rolled away, by which the entrance of the tomb had been closed, to teach that by his power he had cast down and overcome the barriers of hell, so that all whom he found there belonging to him might be raised to the light and rest of paradise, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “You also, by the blood of the covenant, brought out the prisoners [Al. adds: *your prisoners*] from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. IX).

“His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.”

By his very appearance and countenance he signified that the one whose resurrection glory he announced would be both terrifying in condemning the reprobate and kind and gentle in comforting the elect. In lightning terror for fear is expressed; in snow, the soothing quality of whiteness [Col. 0136D].

As an indication of this divine discernment, the angel himself appears, frightening the impious guards of the tomb with fear [Al., frightened them], casting them to the ground like the dead, and restoring the most devout women who came to visit the same tomb with kindly consolation, strengthening them so that they would not be afraid. Moreover, in familiar speech he himself first says that he knows they are seeking Jesus, adds that he has already risen, and then, in a gracious and joyful ministry, commands them to announce the joy of his resurrection.

How happy were the women who, taught by an angelic oracle, deserved to announce to the world the triumph of the resurrection and to proclaim that the dominion of death—which Eve, deceived by the serpent’s speech, had contracted—had been overthrown. How much happier are the souls of men and women, all those who on the day of judgment, when the reprobate have been struck with fear and subjected to fitting punishment, deserve, aided by heavenly grace, to triumph over death and enter the joy of blessed resurrection [Col. 0137A].

As they were running to announce this to the disciples, Jesus met them and greeted them, showing that he comes to the aid of all who begin the way of virtue so that they may reach everlasting salvation [Al. omits *everlasting*].

“They came up,” he says, “and took hold of his feet.”

Let us see, brothers, in the Lord rising from the dead, the truth of our flesh; let us see the glory of the new incorruption. Earlier it was read that he rose while the tomb was closed; now it is read that the women took hold of his feet and worshiped him [Col. 0137B]. He rose through the closed entrance of the tomb and came out, to show that the body which had died enclosed in the tomb had already become immortal. He offered the soles of his feet to the women to hold, to indicate that he truly possessed flesh which could be touched by mortals [Al., “to show”].

“Go,” he says, “tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me.”

O marvelous compassion of the Savior, marvelous kindness! Those whom before the Passion he had been accustomed to call disciples, and sometimes even servants, he calls brothers after the resurrection, both to show that by rising he had again assumed the form of the same humanity which he had possessed before, and to raise them toward earning and hoping for the crown of immortality in his flesh, in which he already stood supreme [Col. 0137C].

That he foretold that the disciples would see him in Galilee—and, as the following passages of the holy Gospel declare, did indeed present himself there—mystically signifies both the truth of his resurrection and the progress of our spiritual life. For *Galilee* is interpreted as “made transmigration” or “passage.” It is fitting that he is seen by the disciples in Galilee, since he had already passed from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, and from punishment to glory, so that he might commend the victory of the resurrection not only by the showing of his body and the exhortation of his speech, but also by the name of the place in which he appeared and spoke.

We too are able to enjoy the joy of his resurrection at that time only if we now strive to pass from the corruption of vices to works of virtue. Therefore, my brothers, we must take the greatest care: since we have recognized the time of the resurrection of our Lord and Savior, since we celebrate its solemn rites, let us pass over through continual progress in good works toward contemplating his majesty. We do not know the time of our own resurrection, although we have no doubt that it will come, and therefore at all times—and especially on this sacred night—let us keep vigilant vigils in expectation of it [Col. 0137D].

Let us implore the mercy of him who humbly accepted death for us and soon afterward sublimely overcame it, that at the time of our resurrection he may grant us to pass from death to life. Let us ask him who is Christ, sacrificed as our Passover, to grant that we may worthily complete the solemn rites of paschal joy which we have begun and, through them, attain eternal joys.

Among these things [Col. 0138A] we should note that the solemnity of this most sacred night and of our redemption, which we celebrate, was long ago mystically signified among the ancient people of God. When that people had long been burdened by Egyptian servitude, and the Egyptians were unwilling to let them go forth into the free service of their Creator, the Lord finally commanded them, in celebrating the Passover, to sacrifice a lamb, roast and eat its flesh on this night, and with its blood, which was to be poured out upon the threshold, anoint both doorposts and the lintel of the houses. They were to remain prepared and watchful within, awaiting the hour of their redemption.

While they were doing this, behold, in the middle of this night the Lord came, struck down the firstborn of the Egyptians, freed his people from the burden of long servitude, and led them to the land of the homeland formerly promised to them [Col. 0138B]. He commanded them to celebrate this night every year, in memory of their salvation, by the sacrifice of the paschal lamb.

That redemption of the people prefigured our spiritual redemption, which was completed on this night when the Lord rose from the dead. Likewise, the Egyptians, the carnal oppressors of that people, signify the harsher weapons of spiritual wickedness by which the human race, subjected to it, was oppressed under impious condemnation.

But the spotless Lamb came and deigned to be sacrificed for us. He gave his blood as the price of our salvation; by accepting death for a time, he condemned the dominion of death forever. In a wondrous and desirable spectacle, the lamb innocently slain powerfully crushed the strength of the lion who had slain. The Lamb who takes away the sins of the world [Col. 0138C] crushed the lion who brought sin into the world. The Lamb who refreshes us with the food of his flesh and blood, so that we do not perish, kills the lion who prowls around us roaring and seeks whom he may destroy. The Lamb placed upon our foreheads the sign of his death, to strike down the weapons of the deadly enemy.

For this reason the blood of the legal lamb was commanded to be placed upon the threshold, the lintel, and both doorposts of the houses in which it was eaten: so that the fourfold division of the blood might express the fourfold standard of the Lord’s Passion, by which we, having been marked, are set free. It cast down the adversary of our liberty and peace, who lies in wait for us secretly like a lion in his lair.

Just as, therefore, on this night, when the lamb had been sacrificed in Egypt, the houses of the faithful had been marked with its blood and its flesh had been eaten, the Lord suddenly came and, punishing those who remained deprived of the heavenly mystery, redeemed the people whom he saw imbued with the saving sacraments [Col. 0138D], so likewise our Lord and Redeemer, after offering his body and blood as a sacrifice to the Father for us, overturned the power of the devil and weakened the boldness of his attendants, namely the unclean spirits.

He shattered the bars of hell, rescued the elect who, although held there, were kept in the bosom of tranquility, and, rising from the dead on this very night, led them back to the joys of the heavenly kingdom, fulfilling the prophecy which says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII) [Al., omits “all these things”]. He took away not only the righteous whom he found among the dead, but also those [Al., “them”] whom he knew still to be his while they remained in the flesh; and for us also, whom he foresaw would believe in him at the end of time, he secured the remedy of salvation through his death and resurrection [Col. 0139A].

Even before we were created, he consecrated for us the spiritual food of life by which we might be refreshed [Al., are refreshed]; he prepared the sign of victory by which we might be protected from the ambushes of our enemies; he opened the path of everlasting life for us to follow.

Therefore we too, rightly mindful on this night of our redemption, devote ourselves to vigils worthy of God, to prayers, and to hearing the divine readings which recount the gifts of grace given to us. We consecrate to the Lord, through the font of regeneration, the new people of adoption, withdrawn from spiritual Egypt; we celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass; and we sacrifice anew to God, for the advancement of our salvation, the most sacred body and precious blood of our Lamb, by which we have been redeemed from sins [Col. 0139B].

And because we rejoice in the mysteries both of the Lord’s resurrection and of our deliverance with an annual solemnity, let us strive, dearly beloved, to embrace these same mysteries with inward love of mind, to hold them always by living them, and to preserve them like clean animals, now to be ruminated by the speech of our mouths, now to be turned over in the innermost chambers of our hearts. Above all, let us take care to lead our lives through such actions that we may also deserve, rejoicing, to behold the outcome of our own resurrection.

Then, when the final trumpet calls the whole human race to the tribunal of the just Judge [Col. 0139C], as it awakens them, may he separate us from the lot of the reprobate. May the vigils by which we await his coming separate us from the punishment of those who neglect him, and, after they have been punished with a fitting retribution, may he himself lead us into the dwelling of heavenly peace which he promised before the ages—he who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY II. ON THE EVE OF EASTER

LUKE XXIV. JOHN XX. “At that time, Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples and said to them: ‘Peace be with you; it is I; do not be afraid,’” etc.

The Lord and our Redeemer gradually and progressively revealed the glory of his resurrection to the disciples, because the power of the miracle was so great that the frail hearts of mortals could not grasp it all at once [Col. 0139D]. Therefore, taking account of the weakness of those who were seeking him, he first showed to the women who came to the tomb, fervent in their love, and to the men, the stone rolled away and the linen cloths, with which his body had been wrapped, lying there after the body had been removed.

Then, when the women made more careful inquiry and were inwardly shaken by what they had found, he showed them the vision of angels, who made it clear by an assured revelation that he had risen. Thus, when the report of the accomplished resurrection had gone before, the Lord of powers and King of glory finally appeared and disclosed with what power he had conquered the death which he had tasted for a time.

Indeed, as far as we find in the sequence of the Gospel reading, on the very day on which he rose he was seen by human beings five times. First, he appeared to Mary Magdalene at the tomb [Col. 0140A], when, as she desired to embrace his feet [Al., “to clasp”], she was told: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John XX).

Then he appeared to the two women running from the tomb to announce to the disciples what they had learned from the angels concerning his complete resurrection. Of them it is written: “They came up, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him” (Matt. XXVIII).

On that same day, as evening approached, he appeared to two men going to the village of Emmaus [Al., Emmaus]. When they invited him to stay with them, they recognized him in the breaking of bread. He also appeared to Peter (Luke XXIV). Although the evangelist does not specify when or where this happened, he does not conceal that it happened, writing that after the two disciples mentioned above had recognized the Lord at Emmaus, they immediately returned to Jerusalem and found the Eleven gathered, together with those who were with them [Col. 0140B], saying: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.”

Then he adds: “And they recounted what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread.” Immediately he connects this with his fifth appearance, which we have just heard when the Gospel was read, beginning as follows:

“While they were speaking of these things, Jesus stood in their midst and said [Al., ‘said’]: ‘Peace be with you; it is I; do not be afraid.’”

Here we must first note and carefully commit to memory that, while the disciples were speaking about him, the Lord deigned to stand in their midst and reveal the presence of his appearance. This is what he elsewhere promised to all the faithful, saying: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII) [Col. 0140C].

To confirm the steadfastness of our faith, the divine compassion, which always acts invisibly, sometimes also willed to display itself through the presence of a bodily appearance. Although we lie far below the feet of the apostles, we too ought confidently to believe that his mercy does this for us: namely, that he is in our midst whenever we gather together in his name.

His name is Jesus, that is, “Savior.” And when we gather to speak about the attainment of everlasting salvation, it is plainly evident that we gather in the name of Jesus. Nor is it lawful to doubt that he is present with us when we discuss what he himself loves—and all the more truly present the more perfectly we retain in our hearts what we utter with our mouths.

Next, we should observe that when the Savior appears to the disciples, he immediately commands them the joys of peace, repeating, now that the glory of immortality has been celebrated, what he had carefully commended to them as a special pledge of salvation when he was going to his Passion and death, saying: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John XIV).

The angels also proclaimed the grace of this gift immediately after he was born, when they appeared to the shepherds, praising God and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II), because the whole dispensation of our Redeemer in the flesh is the reconciliation of the world [Col. 0140D]. For this purpose he was incarnate, for this purpose he suffered, and for this purpose he was raised from the dead: so that we, who through sin had incurred God’s anger, might be led back by his reconciliation to God’s peace.

Therefore he is rightly called by the prophet “Father of the age to come” and “Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX). And the Apostle, writing about him to those who had believed from among the Gentiles, says: “And coming, he preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near, for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Eph. II).

[Col. 0141A]

When the Lord appeared, the disciples were troubled and terrified and thought that they were seeing a spirit. They recognized that the one who had appeared was the Lord, but supposed that they saw him not in the substance of his body but in that of his spirit; that is, they did not think they were seeing his body—the body which they knew had died and been buried—already raised from death, but rather the spirit which, after leaving the body, he had commended into the hands of the Father, present before their eyes.

But the most compassionate Teacher took care to wipe away both their error and their fear, by which they had been struck at the sight of a new and unfamiliar vision, through the kind grace of consolation and instruction [Col. 0141B].

“What, then,” he said, “are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and feet, because I myself am he.” He does not command them to see and recognize his hands and feet rather than his face, which they knew equally well, without reason; rather, when they saw the marks of the nails by which he had been fastened to the cross, they were to understand that what they were seeing was not merely a body, but the very body of their Lord whom they knew to have been crucified. Hence John, appropriately recalling the Lord’s appearance, reports that he also showed the disciples his side, which had been wounded by the soldier, so that the more indications of his well-known passion and the death he had undergone they recognized, the more confidently they might rejoice in the already accomplished resurrection and the destruction of death. To make them entirely certain of the resurrection, he presented the body that he was showing them to be immortal not only for their eyes to behold but also for their hands to touch, saying:

“Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having them.”

Thus, when they were to proclaim the glory of the resurrection, they would also be able to show us without any uncertainty what sort of body the resurrected body was to be hoped for. Therefore the blessed apostle John, with great confidence, calls his hearers to follow the mysteries of the faith and truth that he had learned, saying: “What was from the beginning, what we heard and saw with our eyes, what we looked upon, and what our hands touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John II).

The Gentiles, however, commonly set traps of deception at this point for the simplicity of our faith, saying: “With what presumption do you trust that Christ, whom you worship, can restore your bodies from dust incorruptible, when he himself could not cover over the scars of his wounds, which he received on the cross, but, after his body was supposedly raised from the dead, did not conceal that the marks of death still remained upon it?”

We answer them that Christ, although he is almighty God, will raise our bodies—as he promised—from corruption to incorruption, from death to life, and from the dust of the earth to heavenly glory; and he restored to life his own body, which by dying he had laid aside, in whatever condition he willed. Although he could have shown it to his disciples with the marks of his passion removed, he nevertheless, for the sake of a wholly appropriate dispensation, preferred to preserve the signs of his passion in it.

First, plainly, so that the disciples who saw these things might clearly discern that what they were seeing was not a spirit without a body but a spiritual body, and might proclaim to the world a firm faith in his accomplished resurrection and a firm hope of the future resurrection of all human beings.

Second, so that our Lord and God Jesus Christ, who in his humility [Al., humanity] pleads with the Father for us, might, by displaying the scars of his wounds, perpetually demonstrate to him how greatly he labored for human salvation; and, in a marvelous and ineffable way, might unceasingly remind him who can never forget anything and is always ready to show mercy how fittingly he should have compassion on human beings, whose nature he shared, and for whose sake the Son of God himself became a participant in suffering and passion, fighting on their behalf and, by dying, overthrowing the dominion of death.

Third, so that all the elect, received into perpetual blessedness, might see in their God and Lord the signs of his passion and never cease giving thanks to him through whose death they know themselves to live. Thus what the prophet sings in the Psalms with the voice of the whole Church might come to pass: “I will sing of the mercies of the Lord forever” [Al., “of your mercies, O Lord”] (Psalm LXXXVIII).

Finally, so that even the reprobate might behold in the judgment the signs of that same passion, as it is written: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (John XIX), and understand that they are to be condemned with complete justice—not only those who impiously laid hands upon him, but also those who either scorn his mysteries, once received, as worthless, or have never cared to receive what was offered to them, or, with still greater impiety, strive to extinguish or corrupt by hatred and persecution those who have received them.

The faith of Christ’s resurrection does not deceive us, therefore, nor does the hope of our resurrection mislead us, because “God the Father both raised up the Lord and will raise us up by his power” (Romans VIII). And as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans VIII).

It is evident that this was said especially of the elect, since we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed; only those who are now governed by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit will then be lifted up by the greater grace of that same Spirit into the blessedness of eternal life [Al., “into eternal-life blessedness”].

The Lord, therefore, to confirm faith in the resurrection, presented himself alive to the disciples, brought words of exhortation, and displayed the traces of his passion not only for them to see but also for them to touch. But their hearts were still weak and unable to grasp the novelty of so great a power; they began rather to marvel with joy at what they saw than to believe what they were being taught. Yet the Lord, lest any uncertainty remain in their minds, also took food and ate before them, so that, if they did not believe their eyes or the touch of their fingers, they might at least recognize through the consumption of bodily nourishment that what had appeared was flesh.

In this matter, brothers [Al. adds “dearest”], the foolish heresy of the Cerinthians must be avoided, lest anyone, foolishly childish in his error, suppose either that the body of God’s Mediator and our Lord, raised from the dead, needed the support of food, or that our bodies after the resurrection will require nourishment by material foods in spiritual life and conduct—when contemplation of divine glory will not allow the children of the resurrection to hunger or thirst, or to suffer want in any other respect.

Thus the most ardent lover of that life, confident in his devotion and rejoicing in hope of God, says: “But I shall appear in your presence with righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm XVI). And Philip, burning with the same love, says: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV).

We must therefore think simply and piously that the Lord’s body, raised from death and already made immortal, had no necessity to eat, but did have the capacity to do so; and that, whenever the opportunity to prove its natural substance required it, it was nourished by food. That food, however, provided it with no aid toward satiety, as it does to mortal bodies, but was consumed by its spiritual power as water is immediately consumed when thrown into fire.

Likewise, we must believe that our bodies after the resurrection, endowed with heavenly glory, will possess the power to do whatever they wish and will be entirely ready to reach wherever they desire. But since no necessity or usefulness for eating can then arise from any source, the immortal age will in no way enjoy mortal foods. For the children of the resurrection, food and drink will be nothing other than life and salvation, joy, peace, and every good thing. This is surely what is sung in the Psalm: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” [Al., “for age after age”] (Psalm LXXXIII). And again: “The God of gods will be seen in Zion” (ibid.). Therefore the Apostle, writing [Al., “describing”] the mysteries of that age, says: “When God will be all in all” (1 Corinthians XV).

When the meal was finished, the Lord added further words of exhortation, saying:

“These are the words that I spoke to you when I was still with you”—that is, when I was still like you in mortal and suffering flesh—

“because it is necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled.”

The Master of truth removes every scruple concerning pretense and confirms everywhere the rights of truth. He is seen, touched, and nourished; words of exhortation are supplied one by one; and, lest his testimony alone be thought insufficient, the authority of Moses and the prophets, who foreshadowed his incarnation, passion, and resurrection in their writings, is also brought forward.

And lest they perhaps remain slow to understand the mystical meaning of these words, he also opened their minds so that they might understand them. By doing this, he allowed no remnant of their former uncertainty to remain in their minds; yet he did not cease to explain to them the reason for his passion and resurrection [Al., “then he did not cease”]. For it follows:

“And he said to them: ‘Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name to all nations.’”

It was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise from the dead because it was impossible for the world to be saved unless God became human: appearing in human form, he would teach human beings the things that are divine; and, accepting death as a human being, he would overcome it by divine power. Thus he would both kindle those who believe in him to undertake death with contempt and encourage them with the certainty of the resurrection and of perpetual life.

For by what more fitting example could human beings be raised to faith in sharing glory and earning immortal life than by recognizing that God himself had become a participant in their humanity and mortality? By what more effective arrangement could they be summoned to endure every adversity for the sake of their salvation than by learning that their Creator had endured, for their salvation [Al., “their own salvation”] [Al. adds “and”], countless kinds of insult from the impious and even the sentence of death itself? By what more suitable means could they receive hope of the resurrection than by remembering that they had been washed and sanctified by his mysteries and joined to his body—he who, having tasted death for their sake, would soon provide the example of rising from death?

“It was therefore necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day,” he says, “and for repentance and forgiveness [Al. adds “of sins”] to be preached in his name to all nations.”

This order was necessary: first Christ’s blood had to be poured out for the salvation of the world; then, after the heavenly gate of the kingdom had been opened to human beings through his resurrection and ascension [Al. omits “after”] [Al. adds “through which”]; and only then were those to be sent who would preach the word of life to all the nations throughout the world and administer the mysteries of the faith, through which they could be saved and attain the joys of their heavenly homeland. The Mediator of God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, cooperates in this; he lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY III: ON THE FRIDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

**MATTHEW XXVIII.** At that time the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him, and so forth.

The Gospel reading, dearest brothers, which we have just heard, shines with joy even according to its literal meaning, because in plain speech it describes both the triumph of our Redeemer and the gifts of our redemption. And if we wish to treat it more fully, we discover that a more pleasing fruit of spiritual meaning has been placed within the literal text. For the word of God, like spices, yields a greater fragrance of its inner power the more finely it is examined, as though ground and sifted.

It is plain and sweet for the devout to hear that:

“The disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them, and when they saw him, they worshiped him.”

But it is not without a mystery that the Lord appeared to the disciples after his resurrection in Galilee, or that he appeared on a mountain. He appeared on a mountain to signify that the body which, by being born, he had assumed from the common earth of the human race had, by rising again, already been lifted above all earthly things and clothed with heavenly power. He appeared on a mountain to admonish the faithful that, if they desire to see there the height of his resurrection, they should here strive to pass from lowly desires to heavenly longings.

The name Galilee is known through the frequent exposition of the Fathers to contain a salutary mystery. Yet it is not irrelevant to repeat more often in words what must always be retained in the mind. Galilee is said to mean “migration accomplished” or “revelation.” Both interpretations of the name, however, point toward a single end. For earlier we read that the angel said to the women: “Go, tell his disciples that he has risen, and behold, he will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him.” And now, as the evangelist relates, we have learned that:

“The disciples went to Galilee, and when they saw him, they worshiped him.”

What, then, does it mean that the Lord Jesus goes before the disciples into Galilee so that he may be seen by them, while they follow and, seeing him, worship him, unless it is that “Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Corinthians XV)? Those who belong to Christ follow him; they too, each in their own order, migrate from death to life, and there, seeing him, worship him, because as they contemplate him in the appearance of his divinity, they praise him without end.

This vision agrees with the fact that Galilee is also interpreted as “revelation.” Then, as the Apostle testifies, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, we are transformed into the same image—we who now reveal our way to him and follow his footsteps with sincere faith.

“And when they saw him,” he says, “they worshiped him; but some doubted.”

If we ask why those who saw the Lord and worshiped him doubted, no cause presents itself more readily than the one Luke mentions when he narrates that the Lord appeared to the disciples on the very day of his resurrection: “They were troubled and frightened and supposed that they were seeing a spirit” (Luke XXIV).

Thus they recognize the Lord when they see him, and because they had learned that he was God, they worship him with their faces turned toward the ground. Yet a not insignificant doubt remained in their minds, because they thought that they were seeing not the body in which he had suffered raised again, but only the spirit which, when his passion was finished, he had delivered up.

Therefore the gracious Master immediately strengthens in faith those who have already believed and summons those who have still doubted to the grace of faith, making clear to all to what magnificent glory the humanity assumed for human beings and given over to death had attained by rising again.

“All authority,” he says, “has been given to me in heaven and on earth.”

He does not say this of his divinity, coeternal with the Father, but of the humanity he assumed. By assuming it, he was made a little lower than the angels; and, by rising from the dead, he was crowned with glory and honor, established over the works of the Father’s hands, and all things were placed under his feet (Psalm VIII). Among these things, death itself—which appeared for a time to prevail over him—was also placed beneath his feet.

What the Psalmist says to the Father about the Lord rising from the dead—“You have subjected all things under his feet”—is plainly what the Lord himself, rising again, says to the disciples:

“All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.”

Indeed, even before he rose from death, the heavenly angelic powers knew that they themselves were rightly subject to the human being whom they saw to have been specially assumed by his Creator [Al. adds “themselves”]. But blind human beings on earth disdained to submit to one whom they knew to be clothed with the same mortality as themselves. They refused to understand that the power manifested in his miracles was divine, because they saw human weakness present in his sufferings.

For this reason the Mediator himself, God and human being, wishing to make known even to human beings on earth that all authority had been given to him in heaven and on earth—so that they too might have everlasting life in heaven with the angels—sent teachers who would preach the word of life to all the nations throughout the world.

**MATTHEW, LAST CHAPTER; MARK XVI.** “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.”

The order of preaching is entirely correct and must also be followed with the greatest care by the Church’s preachers today: first the hearer is to be taught, then imbued with the sacraments of faith, and then instructed more freely and thoroughly in due course to observe the Lord’s commandments. For no one who is uneducated and ignorant of the Christian faith can be washed by the sacraments of that faith; nor is it sufficient to be cleansed from sins by the bath of baptism if, after baptism, one does not strive to devote oneself to good works.

He therefore commands that the nations first be taught—that is, instructed in the knowledge of truth—and then baptized, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews XI), and “unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III).

Finally, he adds:

“Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.”

For, just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. What reward awaits a devout way of life, and what pledge of future blessedness remains even in the present for the faithful [Al., “for the faithful ones”], he indicates next, saying:

“And behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.”

It is pleasing to compare with this testimony what Mark says: “And indeed, after the Lord had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark XVI).

Because he is himself both God and human being, he was taken up into heaven in the humanity that he had assumed from the earth; in his divinity, by which he fills earth and heaven alike, he remains with the saints on earth. He remains with them all days, until the consummation of the age. From this it is understood that, until the end of the age, there will not be lacking in the world those who are worthy of the divine dwelling and indwelling.

Nor should we doubt that those who, while contending in this age, have deserved to have Christ dwell as a guest in their hearts will remain with Christ in the kingdom after the struggles of this age.

Meanwhile, it should be noted that the divine Majesty, present everywhere, is present to his elect in one way and to the reprobate in another. He is present to the reprobate with the incomprehensible power of nature by which he knows all things, the newest and the oldest, understands thoughts from afar, and foresees the ways of each person. He is present to the elect with the grace of devout protection, by which, through present gifts or chastisements, he specially trains them as children, like a father, and advances them through instruction toward possession of their future inheritance (Psalm CXXXVIII).

He is present to the elect, as it is written: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Psalm XXXIV). He is present to the reprobate, as was stated above: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (ibid.).

Therefore the wicked must always tremble in their evil deeds, since even their individual thoughts are open to the sight of the strict Judge. The good, however, must always rejoice in the practice of righteousness and in the things they suffer for righteousness, since for those who love God all things work together for good (Romans VIII); and, whatever tribulation they endure, his mercy is never absent from them. To him it is sung in the Psalm: “For to you the poor man has been abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan. Crush the arm of the sinner and the wicked” (Psalm IX).
