He not only promised us this presence of his mercy in words, but also designated it by evident signs when, after his resurrection, he appeared frequently to his disciples until the day on which he went up to heaven, strengthening their minds by admonishing and reproving them and by giving them the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Of these appearances, we find only ten recorded in the writings of the evangelists; but the Apostle teaches that there were more, saying: “He rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and was seen by Cephas, and after that by the eleven. Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once; then he was seen by James, then by all the apostles; and last of all, as to one untimely born, he was seen also by me” (1 Corinthians XV).

We do not know in what places or at what times the appearances he mentions took place. We know only that the appearance of the Lord which he affirms to have been his last occurred after the Lord’s ascension—either when the Lord addressed him from heaven and made a teacher of the Church out of a persecutor (Acts IX), or when he was caught up into paradise and the third heaven and heard words of mystery that a human being was not permitted to speak (1 Corinthians XII). And, as he says elsewhere, he learned by a revelation of Jesus Christ the mystery of the Gospel, which he had not received from a human being (Galatians I).

As we have said, the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles record ten appearances of the Lord after his resurrection; in these writings he is said to have appeared five times on the very day of his resurrection.

First, to Mary Magdalene, weeping at the tomb; second, to the same Mary and to another woman of the same name, as they were returning from the tomb to announce to the disciples what they had discovered there, when he appeared and met them; third, to Simon Peter; fourth, to Cleophas [Al., Cleopas] and his companion, with whom he himself walked to Emmaus and was recognized there in the breaking of the bread. They immediately returned to Jerusalem and found the disciples saying: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.” For it is not reported elsewhere in greater detail when he appeared to Simon.

Fifth, he appeared to them in the same place with the doors closed, when Thomas was absent [Al., “was away.”] Sixth, after eight days, when Thomas was with them. Seventh, to those fishing on the Sea of Tiberias. Eighth, on the mountain of Galilee, as we heard in today’s reading. Ninth, he appeared to the eleven while they were reclining, on the day when he ascended into heaven. Tenth, on that same day they saw him no longer standing on earth, but lifted into the air and going toward heaven, while angels said to them: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.” (Mark XVI; John XX; Matthew XXVIII; Luke XXIV; John XX; John XXI; Matthew XXVIII; Mark XVI; Acts I; Mark XVI.)

By this frequent manifestation of his bodily presence, therefore, the Lord wished to show, as we have said, that in every place he is divinely present to the desires of the good.

He appeared at the tomb to those who were mourning (Mark XVI; John XX); he will also be present to us when we are healthfully saddened by the remembrance of his absence. He met those returning from the tomb so that they might proclaim the joy of the resurrection once they had recognized it (Matthew XXVIII); he will also be present to us when we rejoice to announce faithfully to our neighbors the good things we have learned.

He appeared in the breaking of the bread to those who, thinking him a stranger, invited him to their lodging (Luke XXIV); he will also be present to us when we willingly spend whatever good we can on strangers and the poor. He will also be present to us in the breaking of the bread when, with a pure and simple conscience, we receive the sacraments of his body—that is, of the living bread [Al. omits “living”].

He appeared in secret to those speaking about his resurrection; he is also present to us when, by his gift, we do the same. He will always be present to us when, for a time free from external works, we gather to speak of his grace (John I).

He appeared when they were sitting inside with the doors closed out of fear of the Jews (John XX). He appeared when, with that fear diminished, they sought him with open steps at the summit of the mountain [Al., “the summit of the mountain”] (Acts I). He was once present to strengthen the Church by his Spirit when she was oppressed by unbelievers and was prevented from coming into public and expanding [Al., “was prevented from coming into public, and …”]. He is also present to her now, when, with royal authority inclined toward the faith, the terror of persecution has ceased, and all the grandeur of the world has been subjected to the footsteps of the apostles.

He appeared to those fishing (John XXI), and by appearing to them helped them with divine benefits; he will also be present to us when we attend to the necessities of temporal life with right intention and joins the support of his mercy to our righteous labors [Al., “joined”].

He appeared to those reclining at table (Mark XVI); he will also be present to us when, according to the Apostle’s admonitions, whether we eat or drink or do anything else, we do everything for the glory [Al., “glory”] of God (1 Corinthians X).

He appeared first in Judea (Acts I), then in Galilee, and afterward again in Judea on the day when he ascended into heaven. He was present with the Church when she was enclosed within the boundaries of Judea alone; he is present now, when, because the Jews were abandoned on account of their guilt of unbelief, she has migrated to the nations.

He will be present in the future when, before the end of the age, he returns to Judea; and, as the Apostle says, when the full number of the nations has entered, all Israel will be saved (Romans XI).

Finally, he appeared to them as he ascended into heaven (Acts I). He will also be present to us, so that we may deserve to follow him after death into heaven, if before death we take care to follow him to Bethany, from which he ascended—that is, into the house of obedience (Mark XVI).

For as he was about to ascend into heaven, he came to Bethany because, as the Apostle says, “He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross; therefore God also exalted him” (Philippians II). We too come there if we do what he commands and direct our attention to what he promised. “Be faithful,” he says, “unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation II).

By his gracious generosity it comes to pass that he who remains with us until the end of this life lifts us after this life to see with him the rewards of heavenly life. In that life he lives and reigns with the Father, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY IV [Note: Thes. Anecd. Marten., vol. V, homily 8]: WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

**LUKE XXIV.** At that time: On the first day of the week, very early in the morning, the women came to the tomb, carrying the spices they had prepared. They found the stone rolled away from the tomb, and when they entered they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.

The reading about the resurrection of our Lord and Savior has been set before us, brothers; there is no need to labor over exposition where the very familiar mysteries of our faith are repeated in the Gospel oracles. We need only briefly point out what we should do by imitating this reading.

“On the first day of the week,” he says, “very early in the morning, the women came to the tomb.”

The first day of the week is the day after the Sabbath, which we now customarily call the Lord’s Day out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection. Thus the second day of the week, the third day of the week, and the remaining days in order receive their names from their number in Holy Scripture.

The same thing is signified wherever “one of the Sabbaths” is read: it indicates one day—or, more precisely, the first day—after the Sabbaths, that is, after the days of rest.

The fact that the women came very early in the morning to the tomb to seek the Lord demonstrates their great devotion of love toward him. As soon as the shadow of night had departed and the opportunity to go was given by the appearance of light, they hastened eagerly to his service.

They also provide us with a typical example, so that, if we desire to find the Lord and to be strengthened by the presence of angels, we may cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light, walking honorably as in the day.

It is fitting for us to seek the Lord shining with the light of good works and also filled with the grace of spiritual prayers. Hence it is appropriately reported that the women who came to the tomb carried with them the spices they had prepared.

The spices are the words of our prayers, by which we commend the desires of our hearts to the Lord. The apostle John bears witness to this when, mystically describing the purest hearts of the saints, he says: “They had golden bowls full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints” (Revelation V). What are called *aromata* in Greek are called *odoramenta*, “perfumes” or “fragrant substances,” in Latin.

We therefore bring spices to the Lord’s tomb at dawn when, mindful of the passion and death he endured for us, we show the light of good actions outwardly to our neighbors and burn inwardly in our hearts with the sweetness of pure compunction. This ought to happen at every hour, but especially when we enter the church to pray and when we approach the altar to receive the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood.

For if the women sought the dead body of the Lord with such care, how much more ought we, who have learned that he rose from death, ascended into heaven, and is present everywhere by the power of his divine majesty, to stand before his presence with complete reverence and celebrate his mysteries?

It is rightly said: “Carrying the spices they had prepared.” To prepare beforehand the spices that we are to carry in the Lord’s service is to cleanse the heart before the time of prayer from unnecessary thoughts, so that at the very time of prayer we may know how to admit no impurity into the mind, think of none of the passing things of the world, and remember nothing except what we are praying for and the one to whom we are praying, according to the example of the one who says: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord” (Psalm CVII).

For whoever enters the churches to pray and, amid the words of supplication, neglects to drive from his mind the habitual excess of wandering thought brings with him, as though seeking God, spices that are insufficiently prepared.

The women found the stone rolled away from the tomb, and when they entered they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. It is well known from the historical account, as the evangelist Matthew relates, that an angel descended from heaven and rolled the stone away from the entrance of the tomb—not, indeed, to make a way for the Lord as he came out, but so that the opened and empty place of the tomb might disclose to human beings that he had risen.

Mystically, however, the rolling away of the stone signifies the revelation of the divine mysteries, which had formerly been enclosed and hidden by the letter of the Law. For the Law was written on stone. Indeed, for each of us also, when we have come to acknowledge the faith of the Lord’s passion and resurrection, the tomb of that Lord, which had been closed, has certainly been opened. We too enter the tomb, yet we do not find the Lord’s body, when, carefully recalling in our hearts the order of his incarnation and passion, we remember that he has risen from the dead and is no longer to be seen in mortal flesh.

But for Jews and pagans, who mock the death of our Redeemer even while they profess to believe in it, and utterly refuse to believe in his triumph of true resurrection, the tomb still remains, as it were, closed by the stone; they cannot enter, so as to see that the Lord’s body has been taken away by rising again and thereby come to their senses. For the hardness of their unbelief prevents them from perceiving that the dead one cannot be found on earth who, having destroyed the entrance of death, has already penetrated the heights of heaven.

We should also imitate what happened when the women, not finding the Lord’s body, were mentally dismayed. We must continually remember that we cannot find the body of our Lord on earth; and we must humble ourselves all the more because we are known to cry to him from the depths who dwells in heaven. We must be the more dismayed in spirit because we see that we still wander far from him in whose presence alone we can live blessedly. We must strive with every effort of virtue to deserve to be more fully estranged from the world and to be present with him.

As the women mourned over the removal of Jesus’ body, angels appeared to them, bringing them the remedies of consolation by revealing his resurrection. We should not doubt that the same thing is now invisibly done for us, whenever, salutarily afflicted by the length of our present dwelling abroad and by the absence of our Creator, we suddenly recall what the eternal joys of the citizens above are. When we remember that blessedness in which we too hope one day to be, we begin to bear more lightly the hardship of the exile we endure; and we trust that we too can follow our Redeemer to the place to which he ascended when he rose from the dead, we whom he deigned to redeem.

Nor is it hidden that angels are often invisibly present with the elect, either to defend them from the snares of the crafty enemy or to lift them up by a greater grace of heavenly longing, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Hebrews 1).

Yet we should believe that angelic spirits are especially present with us when we are particularly devoted to divine service—that is, when, having entered the church, we either lend our ears to the sacred readings, devote ourselves to psalmody, apply ourselves to prayer, or celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass. Hence the Apostle instructs women to have a veil over their heads in the church because of the angels. And the prophet says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you” (Psalm 137).

Nor may we doubt that where the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood are enacted, there is an assembly of the citizens above, who keep such diligent watch over the tomb in which that venerable body had been placed and from which it had departed by rising again.

[Note: Thus Chrysostom, *On the Priesthood*, book 6, chapter 4: “At that time the angels also stand beside the priest . . . and the place near the altar, in honor of him who is sacrificed, is full of choirs of angels.” See John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 199.]

Therefore, my brothers, we must diligently strive so that, whenever we enter the church either to render the duties owed to divine praise or to perform the solemn rites of the Mass, we may always remember the angelic presence and, with appropriate fear and reverence, complete the heavenly service, following the example of the women devoted to God, who are said to have been afraid when the angels appeared at the tomb and to have bowed their faces toward the ground.

It should also be noted what it means that in this reading the angels are said to have stood beside the women, whereas in the other evangelists they are remembered as sitting while addressing them.

To sit on a king’s throne is to stand at the altar of a high priest. Since, therefore, our Redeemer deigned to become for us both King and Priest—the Priest, namely, to cleanse us from sins by the sacrifice of his passion; the King, to grant us an everlasting kingdom—the angels appear sitting when they announce the glory of his resurrection, signifying that after conquering death he sought the throne of the heavenly kingdom. They also appear standing, to show that in the secret presence of the Father he intercedes for us as a high priest, according to what the Apostle says of him: “Who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Romans 8).

The angels said to the women: “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen.” This plainly means: Why do you seek in the tomb, which is properly the place of the dead, him who has already risen from the dead to life? “Remember how he spoke to you when he was still in Galilee, saying that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again” (Luke 24).

These words of the angels are clear and known to all the faithful, since without knowledge of them no one can be a believer. Yet there is something in them by which we ought together to admonish your brotherhood: in accordance with the angels’ command, let us remember often and turn over in attentive minds that the Son of God deigned to become the son of man so that he might make those who believe in him sons of God. He was delivered into the hands of sinful men so that he might separate us from fellowship with sinful men and at the same time free us from the power of wicked spirits. He was crucified and rose again on the third day so that he might grant us the strength to suffer for him, the hope of rising in him, and the gift of living with him.

We should always retain these mysteries of the Lord’s dispensation in our minds, and more attentively than usual when the mysteries of his most blessed passion are accomplished, when the death of our Savior—which he trampled down forever by the swift power of his resurrection—is renewed in mystical rites upon the altar.

Nor should we pass without examination over why our Lord and Redeemer wished to rise on the third day, that is, to rest in the tomb for two nights and one day. For on the sixth day of the week, on which he suffered, he was placed late in the tomb; in the morning of the first day of the week he rose.

Human nature was held subject to two deaths: of the soul, namely, and of the flesh. The death of the soul occurs when, because of its sin, it is abandoned by God, who is its life; the death of the body occurs when, by divine judgment, it is abandoned by the soul, which is its life. Just as the resurrection of the soul is to receive God into oneself after casting away the stain of sin, so the resurrection of the flesh is to receive the soul into oneself after the punishment of corruption has been removed.

We were therefore subject to these two deaths through our first parent, the ancestor of our race. But there came the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus: in mercy he took upon himself one death, and in justice he condemned both. For he died in the flesh alone and rose in the flesh alone, because he had never lost through sinning the life of his soul, which he would have recovered by repentance, so that he might both show by the example of his resurrection that the whole human race would rise from the death of the flesh at the judgment and make known, through the mystery of that same resurrection, that all the elect would be raised from the death of the soul before the judgment.

He therefore who by his single death destroyed our double death rightly lay in the tomb for two nights and one day between them, so that even the period of his burial might signify that by the light of his single death he would scatter the darkness of our double death.

The women returned from the tomb and announced to the apostles what they had seen there and what they had heard from the angels. This is recognized as an act of divine mercy, arranged so that the reproach of the first transgression might be removed from the female sex. For behold: the death which one woman, seduced by the devil, had brought upon the world, many women, instructed by angels, now proclaim to have been destroyed.

One woman, going forth, opened the way of death.

[Note: “It seems that *iter mortis aperuit*—‘opened the way of death’—should be read.”]

Many, going forth from their present exile, assert that the gate by which they are to return to their heavenly homeland has already been opened.

But because those who know only ordinary tombs are not unreasonably puzzled about how that tomb of the Lord could have been made large enough to contain so many people together with angels, we think it appropriate simply to explain to your charity what we have learned about it, according to the account of those who in our time visited Jerusalem and, on returning, left in writing what they had seen there.

[Note: Namely, of Arculf, a Gallic bishop, whose narratives and descriptions of the holy places were committed to writing by Adamnan, a Scottish abbot. His work has been published by Mabillon in the third Benedictine century of the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, part 1, p. 502, where a figure of the Lord’s tomb is represented. Bede himself abridged the same work in his little book *On the Holy Places*.]

The structure was round, cut out of rock, and of such height that a person standing in the middle could touch the roof with his hand.

[Note: Bede speaks almost exactly this way in *On the Holy Places*, chapter 2.]

It had an entrance on the east, against which the great stone mentioned by the Gospels had been placed. For those entering, on the right was the place specially prepared to receive the Lord’s body. It was seven feet long and three palms in height above the remaining floor. Unlike ordinary tombs, it was not open from above but had been made accessible along its entire southern side, so that the body could be placed there.

This is what the evangelist Mark means when he says that, entering the tomb, the women saw a young man sitting on the right: the angel who was sitting by the place of the Lord’s body was, for those entering, on the right, and he himself was also sitting to the right of that same burial place.

All these features were continuous and not separated from one another, since they had been cut out of one and the same rock. This, then, is what we understand to have been the original arrangement of the Lord’s tomb.

But now they report that a round church of remarkable workmanship stands there, divided by a triple wall. In its center is the tomb, and its exterior is covered with marble slabs up to the highest parts of the roof. The roof itself is covered with gold and bears a substantial golden cross. To the east of the church is the church of Golgotha, which, among its other ornaments appropriate to such a place, has a very large silver cross at the spot where the Lord deigned to be crucified for our salvation. Above it hangs a great *pharus*, that is, a bronze wheel with lamps, which crown the cross with the reverence due to it through the proper light.

Near this church, on its eastern side, is the Constantinian church, also called the Martyrium. There the cross of the Lord was found by Helena, the mother of Constantine, and for that reason he himself built a church there with magnificent and royal adornment.

Having explained these matters concerning the locations of the holy places as far as we have been able, let us contemplate the fulfillment of Isaiah’s prophecy, in which he foretold both the Lord’s burial and resurrection and our faith and salvation:

“On that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples, the nations will beseech him; and his tomb will be glorious” (Isaiah 11:10).

The root of Jesse is the Lord: according to his humanity he was born from the stock of Jesse, but according to his divinity he is the creator of Jesse himself. He stands as a sign for the peoples because he is the sign of salvation, consecrated by his passion, by which the peoples of believers are fortified against the malice of the crafty enemy.

“The nations will beseech him,” because he has called not only the Jews but also us, who are known to cry out to him from the ends of the earth, by the grace of his visitation.

“His tomb will be glorious,” because he has preserved as memorable, with the signs of an everlasting triumph, the place in which he overthrew the kingdom of death.

Therefore, beloved, let us turn our whole minds toward him and beseech him to free us from the snares of our enemies by the sign of his protection. May he grant us worthily to celebrate the mysteries of our redemption and to reach the joys of blessed resurrection: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY V. ON THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

### JOHN 16

“At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: ‘A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father,’ and so forth.”

We ought to receive with joyful hearing of heart the joyful promises of our Lord and Savior, most beloved brothers, and persevere with attentive devotion so that we may deserve to attain them. For what can rightly be heard with greater joy than that we can reach a joy which can never be taken away?

It should be noted, however, that the entire sequence of this Gospel reading applies to those who were present and heard it from the Lord; part of it also applies most appropriately to us, who came to faith after the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

When he therefore says:

“A little while and . . . to the Father,”

this applies particularly to those who adhered to his discipleship while he preached in the flesh and who, after the sorrow of his passion, deserved to be made joyful when they saw his resurrection and ascension.

For since he spoke these words on the night when he was betrayed, “a little while” meant the time of that same night and the following day, until the hour when they would begin not to see him. For on that night he was seized by the Jews, crucified on the following day, and, when evening had come, taken down from the cross and shut away from human sight within the enclosure of the tomb.

Again, “a little while” meant the time until they would see him. For he rose from the dead on the third day and appeared to them by many proofs for forty days.

But he adds the reason why it would be a little while before they saw him, and again a little while before they would see him, saying:

“Because I am going to the Father.”

It is as though he plainly said: “Therefore, after a little while I will be hidden from your sight within the enclosure of the tomb, and again after a little while I will appear to be seen by you, having destroyed the dominion of death, because the time has come for me, after completing the dispensation of the mortality I assumed with the triumph of the resurrection, to return to the Father.”

What he says may also be understood in another way:

“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.”

The little while during which they would not see him was the three days during which he was to rest in the tomb. Again, the little while during which they would see him was the forty days during which he appeared to them frequently after his passion, until the time of his ascension.

When he added:

“Because I am going to the Father,”

according to this interpretation he is referring particularly to what he had said before: “And again a little while, and you will see me.” It is as though he plainly said: “For this reason you will see me, risen from the dead, for a short time: I will not remain bodily on earth forever, but through the humanity I assumed I am now going to ascend into heaven.”

These words of the Lord, as we have said, apply particularly to those who were able to see his resurrection. But what he adds in explanation to those who were asking applies both to them and to the whole state of the Church:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

The lovers of Christ wept and lamented when they saw him seized by his enemies, bound, led before the council, condemned, scourged, mocked, and finally crucified, pierced with a lance, and buried.

The lovers of the world—whom the Lord calls “the world” because of their lowly thoughts—rejoiced when they condemned to the most shameful death the one whose very sight was burdensome to them.

The disciples were sorrowful when the Lord had been placed in death, but when they recognized his resurrection their sorrow was turned into joy. When they saw the power of his ascension, they were lifted up by still greater joy and praised and blessed the Lord, as the evangelist Luke testifies (Luke 24).

This saying of the Lord also applies to all the faithful, who strive to reach eternal joys through present tears and afflictions. They rightly weep, lament, and are sorrowful in the present, because they are not yet able to see the one they love. As long as they are in the body, they know that they are wandering from their homeland and kingdom; and they do not doubt that they must reach the crown through labors and struggles.

Their sorrow will be turned into joy when, their contest in this life completed, they receive the prize of eternal life, of which the Psalm says: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psalm 125).

While the faithful weep and are sorrowful, the world rejoices, because those who either hope that the joys of another life do not exist or despair of being able to reach them rightly possess whatever kind of joy they may have in the present.

This may also be understood particularly of the persecutors of the Christian faith, because when the martyrs were tortured and killed, they rejoiced that for a time they had prevailed. But shortly afterward, while the martyrs were crowned in secret, the persecutors themselves suffered eternal punishments both for their faithlessness and for their murder.

To them the prophet rightly says by divine rebuke: “Behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be ashamed. Behold, my servants shall exult in joy, but you shall cry out because of the sorrow of your heart, and because of the contrition of your spirit you shall howl” (Isaiah 63).

The text continues:

“A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come.”

He calls the holy Church a woman, both because of the fecundity of her good works and because she never ceases to beget spiritual children for God. Of her it is also said elsewhere: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened” (Matthew 13; Luke 13).

The woman received the leaven when the Church, by the Lord’s gift, obtained the power of heavenly love and faith. She hid it in three measures of flour until all was leavened when she ministered the word of life throughout the regions of Asia, Europe, and Africa, until all the ends of the earth burned with love for the kingdom of heaven.

He signified that he belonged to the members of this woman when, because some had departed from the purity of the faith, he said sorrowfully: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4).

Those who, inflamed by heavenly desires, proclaimed in praise of their Creator, “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived and were in labor, and we gave birth to the spirit” (Isaiah 26), testify that they belong to her members.

This woman has sorrow when she gives birth, because her hour has come. But when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her anguish because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.

For as long as the holy Church is devoted to the progress of spiritual virtues in the world, she never ceases to be tested by the temptations of the world. But when, having overcome the contest of labors, she reaches the palm of victory, she no longer remembers her earlier anguish because of the joy of the reward received: “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Romans 8).

“He does not remember his anguish,” he says, “because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.”

Just as a woman rejoices when a human being has been born into this world, so the Church is filled with worthy exultation when the people of the faithful are born into the future life. For that birth she labors and groans greatly, suffering in the present as though in labor.

No one should find it strange if one who has departed from this life is said to have been born. For just as someone is customarily said to be born when he comes forth from his mother’s womb and enters into the light of this world, so one who, released from the bonds of the flesh, is raised into eternal light can most rightly be called born.

Hence ecclesiastical custom has prevailed that we call the days of the blessed martyrs or confessors of Christ on which they passed from the world their “birthdays,” and that their solemn observances be called not funerals but birthdays.

The Lord continues, himself explaining the example he had proposed concerning the woman:

“So you also now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.”

This is easily understood of the disciples themselves, because they had sorrow when the Lord had suffered and been buried; but after the glory of the resurrection had been accomplished, they rejoiced when they saw the Lord.

No one took their joy from them because, even though afterward they suffered persecutions and tortures for Christ’s name, they bore every adversity willingly, inflamed by the hope of resurrection and of seeing him. Indeed, they considered it all joy when they fell into various trials.

Thus, after being beaten by the chief priests, as it is written, “they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5).

No one took their joy from them because by suffering such things for Christ they deserved to reign without end with Christ.

The whole Church also, through the labors and hardships of this life, strives toward the eternal rewards of heavenly joys, as the Apostle testifies: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14).

When he says:

“Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice,”

he says, “I will see you”: I will rescue you from your adversaries, crown you as victors, and prove that I have always seen you contending.

For when would he not see his own surrounded by the greatest afflictions, since he himself promised to remain with them all the days of the age? Yet when the faithful were dying amid torments, their torturers imagined that they lacked divine protection, saying: “Where is their God?” (Psalm 113).

Hence one of them, surrounded by afflictions, said: “See, O Lord, my affliction, because my enemy has risen up” (Psalm 78).

This plainly means: “Because the pursuing enemy lifts up the neck of pride against your humble servants, raise us up by your help, almighty Creator; prove that, after your enemies have been conquered and repelled, you have always seen our contests and that they have pleased you.”

The Lord therefore sees the elect after their sorrow when, having condemned their persecutor, he rewards their patience.

What he says may also be understood in this way: “Again I will see you,” as though he said, “I will appear again while you are seeing me.” In the same way he said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear the Lord” (Genesis 22), meaning: “Now I have made human beings know that you fear God,” although until then they did not know what had always been certain to me.

If, therefore, beloved, we are now affected by salutary sorrow; if, in accordance with the Apostle’s exhortation, we are “rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation” (Romans 12); if we mourn our own faults and the miseries of our neighbors with fitting lamentation, the Lord will see us again—that is, he will show himself to be seen by us in the future—just as he once deigned to see you and grant us recognition of the same faith.

He will see us in order to crown us, just as once he saw us in order to call us. He will see us, and our heart will rejoice, and no one will take our joy from us, because this is the true and only reward of those who are sorrowful according to God: to rejoice in his perpetual vision.

He himself most exaltedly promised this reward when he said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

The Psalmist ardently desired it when he said: “My soul thirsted for you, the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41).

The Apostle rejoices that he and those like him will receive it. Conscious of his contests, he confidently declares: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13).

May we also faithfully seek and truly grasp it, until he himself—the helper of those who contend and the rewarder of those who conquer—Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY VI. ON THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER HOLY EASTER

### JOHN 16

“At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: ‘I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, “Where are you going?” But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart,’ and so forth.”

As we have heard from the Gospel reading, most beloved brothers, our Lord and Redeemer, as the moment of his passion approached, revealed to his disciples both the glory of his ascension, by which he was to be glorified after his death and resurrection, and the coming of the Holy Spirit, by which they were to be enlightened. Thus, when the hour of that passion arrived, they would grieve less over his death, since they would not doubt that after death he was to be raised to heaven; and they would be less troubled by their desolation, since, although the Lord was departing, they would hope to be comforted by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“I am going,” he says, “to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’”

It is as though he plainly said: “By ascending I am returning to him who ordained that I become incarnate, and the glory of this ascension will be so great and manifest that none of you will need to ask where I am going, since all will see that I am going to heaven.”

When he had spoken well of his ascension, saying, “I am going to him who sent me,” he added, “And none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’”

Earlier, when he was speaking of his passion, saying, “Where I am going you cannot come,” Peter questioned him and said: “Lord, where are you going?” And he was answered: “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but afterward you will follow.”

For they were not yet able to understand or imitate the mystery of his passion and death; but as soon as they saw and understood the majesty of his ascension, they desired with all the wishes of their hearts to deserve to follow him.

“But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.”

The Lord himself knew what these words would produce in the hearts of the disciples: they would generate greater sorrow over his departure, by which he would leave them, than joy over his ascension, by which he would go to the Father.

Therefore, consoling them kindly, he added:

“But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away.”

It is expedient that the form of a servant be withdrawn from your sight, so that the love of his divinity may be more firmly fixed in your minds. It is expedient that I bring the form known to you into heaven, so that for this reason you may sigh toward it with greater desire, and that, with your hearts suspended toward things above, you may become capable of receiving the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you.”

He does not say this because, while he was present on earth, he could not himself give the Spirit to the disciples, since it is plainly written that after his resurrection he appeared to them, breathed on them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20).

But while he was present on earth and living among them bodily, they were unable to raise their minds to thirst for the gifts of heavenly grace. Once he had ascended to heaven, they likewise transferred all their desire there, in accordance with what they had heard elsewhere: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6).

Thus they had already become capable of the Spirit. They were no longer sorrowful over his death but rejoiced in the gift of his promise, as Luke testifies when he says: “And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven. And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God” (Luke 24).

It is clear, and requires no laborious explanation, why he calls the same Spirit the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter. The coming of the Spirit would console and refresh the hearts of the disciples, which his departure had made sorrowful.

Likewise, whenever individual believers mourn the commission of sin or labor under the common affliction of this age, the Spirit inspires hope of pardon and heavenly mercy and thus lifts the mind by enlightening it, freeing it from the anguish of sorrow.

Because the Spirit not only pours into the mind he fills the power of divine love inwardly, but also, after driving away bodily fear, grants it confidence to rebuke the wickedness of evil people outwardly, it is rightly added:

“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment.”

It is clear that the Son of God himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, when he was in the world, convicted the world—that is, the followers of the world—concerning the sin of their unbelief. He convicted it concerning righteousness, because they were unwilling to imitate the righteousness of the faithful; and concerning judgment, namely, because they followed the devil, who had already been judged and condemned.

But it is not without reason that he says the Spirit will do this when he comes. Through the Spirit’s inspiration the minds of the disciples were to be strengthened, so that they would not fear to rebuke the world, which raged against them.

The Lord therefore explained his meaning, adding:

“Concerning sin, indeed, because they do not believe in me.”

He set the sin of unbelief apart as a particular sin, because just as faith is the source of virtues, so persisting in unbelief is the foundation of vices. The Lord solemnly testifies to this when he says: “But whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3). By contrast, “the righteous lives by faith.”

“And concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me.”

The righteousness of the disciples of Christ was their confession that they believed the Lord, whom they saw as a true human being, also to be the true Son of God; and that, although they knew he had been taken bodily from them, they continually honored him with unwavering love.

The righteousness of the other faithful—that is, of those who did not see the Lord in the flesh—is this: they believe and love him in their hearts as true God and true man, although they have never seen him with bodily eyes.

By this righteousness of faith unbelievers are convicted: why, although they likewise heard the word of life, did they refuse to believe unto righteousness? The wickedness of evil people is shown to deserve condemnation not only by its own depravity but also by comparison with the righteous.

Hence it is written: “When virtue has been proved, it rebukes the foolish” (Wisdom 1).

The Holy Spirit therefore convicts the world concerning its sin, because it did not believe in Christ. He also convicts it concerning the righteousness of believers, because it refused to follow the example of those who knew that he had ascended to the Father and would no longer live bodily on earth, yet could not by any means be separated from his love.

This is what he says: “Because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me.” You will not see me after I have ascended as you are accustomed to see me now, surrounded by mortal and corruptible flesh; rather, you will see me coming in majesty for judgment and, after judgment has been completed, appearing to the saints in greater glory.

The text continues:

“And concerning judgment, because the prince of this world has been judged.”

He calls the devil the prince of the world because he rules those who, in perverse order, love the world rather than the Creator of the world.

He has been judged by the Lord, who said: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). He was judged by him when he himself cast out demons and gave the disciples power to tread upon every power of the enemy.

The world is therefore convicted concerning the judgment by which the devil was judged: people are warned by the example of the archangel condemned for pride, lest they presume to resist the will of God.

The Holy Spirit convicts the world concerning the judgment by which the prince of this world was judged when the apostle Jude, speaking in the Holy Spirit to correct the wickedness of human beings, recalled the punishment of the proud angels, saying: “The angels who did not preserve their own principality, but abandoned their dwelling, he has kept in everlasting chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day.”

The text continues:

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.”

It is certain that, when the Spirit came from above, the apostles obtained much greater knowledge of the truth than, while still carnal, they had hitherto been able to attain, and they were inflamed with a greater desire to contend for the truth.

Yet it should not be thought that anyone in this life can comprehend all truth, since this reward of our faith has been promised for the other life, as the Truth himself says: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

And elsewhere to the Jews: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth” (John 8).

Hence the Apostle, who was caught up to the third heaven and heard secret words which it was not permitted for a human being to speak, says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13).

What he says about the Spirit—“He will teach you all truth”—must therefore be understood as though he said: “He will spread love in your hearts. Taught inwardly by its instruction, you will advance from virtue to virtue and become worthy to reach the life in which the eternal brightness of supreme truth and true exaltedness—that is, the contemplation of your Creator—will appear to you.”

For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak. The Spirit does not speak from himself—that is, without communion with the Father and the Son; for the Spirit is neither divided nor separated from himself—but whatever he hears he will speak, namely, he will hear through unity of substance and the distinct property of knowledge. He does not speak from himself because he is not from himself. For the Father alone is not from another. The Son, moreover, was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. [Col. 0161C] The Spirit will hear from him from whom he proceeds, because he is not from himself but from him from whom he proceeds. From him comes his essence, and therefore from him also comes his knowledge. From him, then, comes hearing, which is nothing other than knowledge. And what he added was:

“And he will announce to you the things that are to come.” It is evident that countless believers, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, have foreknown and foretold future events. Yet because there are some who, filled with the grace of the Spirit, heal the sick, raise the dead, command demons, and shine forth with many virtues—who themselves lead an angelic life on earth—and nevertheless do not know, through a revelation of that same Spirit, what is to happen to them, the Lord’s saying can also be understood in this way: the Spirit, when he comes, announces to us the things that are to come when he recalls to our memory the joys of our [Col. 0161D] heavenly homeland, when, through the gift of his inspiration, he makes known to us the festivals of that city above. He announces what is to come when, drawing us away from delight in present things, he inflames us with desire for the kingdom promised in heaven.

“He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and announce it to you.” The Spirit glorified Christ because through him such great love was kindled in the hearts of the disciples that, casting aside carnal fear, they boldly proclaimed the reality of his resurrection, whereas from the time of his passion they had fled in fear. Hence it is written: “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with confidence” (Acts IV). The Spirit glorified Christ when holy [Col. 0162A] teachers, filled with spiritual grace, performed so many and such great miracles in Christ’s name that they converted the whole world to faith in Christ, and endured so many and such great struggles of suffering for Christ’s name, until they subjected even the proud necks of their persecutors to Christ’s most gentle yoke. The Spirit glorifies Christ when by his inspiration he kindles us to love the vision of Christ, and impresses upon the hearts of the faithful that he must be believed equal to the Father in divinity.

“For he will take from what is mine,” he says, “and announce it to you.” The Holy Spirit receives from the Father, from whom the Son also receives, since in this Trinity the Son is born from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The one who is born from no one and proceeds from no one is the Father alone. “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore [Col. 0162B] I said that he will take from what is mine and announce it to you.” He spoke of those things that pertain to the very divinity of the Father, in which the Son is equal to him by possessing everything that the Father has. For the Holy Spirit was not going to receive from the created order, which is subject to the Father and the Son, what he says—“He will take from what is mine”—but certainly from the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds and from whom the Son is born.

But since, with the Lord granting it, we have passed through the reading of the holy Gospel by expounding it as we followed in the footsteps of the Fathers, it remains for me, together with you, dearest brethren, to admonish your fraternity that we should always preserve its memory with attentive concentration, examine its sweetness with devoted heart, and frequently chew it over with a pure mouth. For what benefit is there in gathering to hear the word of God, and, once hearing is complete, immediately turning to empty [Col. 0162C] and worldly conversations or actions? Let us therefore recall, in accordance with what the same reading admonishes, that our Lord, having completed his passion, returned to the Father by whom he had been sent, without abandoning either the Father when he came to us or us when he returned. Let us follow his footsteps there with every effort of our minds, and, if we desire to reach him and deserve to enter the gate of his kingdom, let us carefully consider by what steps of conduct he walked while dwelling on earth. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked. Certainly he reached the crown of glory through the struggles of suffering; rightly, therefore, it is also made known to us that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. Hence the apostle Peter, beset by the fervor of temptations, consoled [Col. 0162D] certain brethren by saying: “Do not be afraid, as though something strange were happening, but rejoice as participants in Christ’s sufferings, so that you may also rejoice and exult at the revelation of his glory” (I Peter IV).

Let us call to mind that he both promised to send and did send the grace of the Spirit to his disciples; and let us take every precaution lest, through enticing thoughts, we grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom we have been sealed for the day of redemption. For it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom I). Therefore the Psalmist, when he burned with desire for this Spirit, first sought a lodging of a pure heart in which he might receive it, and only then sought the entrance of so great a guest. “Create a pure heart in me,” [Col. 0163A] he says, “O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm L). He prayed first that a pure heart might be created within him, and then that a right spirit might be renewed in his inmost being, because he surely knew that a right spirit cannot have a dwelling in a polluted heart.

Let us diligently retain in our hearts that the same Spirit convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment. Let us beware lest, by seeking what is below, we belong to the world, for the world will pass away, and its desire. Let us seek the things that are above; let us set our minds on the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Let our manner of life, with the Apostle, be in heaven; and, lest we be convicted of the sin of unbelief, let us practice by our actions what we believe, for faith without works is idle.

Lest we be judged more severely by comparison with the [Col. 0163B] righteous whom we refused to imitate, let us remember with attentive mind what the Lord says concerning those who despise his grace: “The queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Luke XI). Lest we be condemned together with the prince of this world, let us resist him, strong in faith, and he will flee from us. Let us speak truth in our heart and not practice deceit with our tongue, so that the Spirit of truth, spreading love more and more in our hearts, may lead us to the knowledge of all truth.

Let us ask, dearest brethren, for the grace of this Spirit in all our actions; let us ask for his help. Let each of us say to the Lord, and let us all say together: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a right land.” Thus it comes about that he who, coming upon the apostles, announced the things that were to come may also [Col. 0163C] disclose to our minds the joys of the life to come and kindly inflame us to seek them, with the cooperation of him who is accustomed both to promise this Spirit to his faithful and to give him: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VII. FOR THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER HOLY EASTER

**JOHN XVI.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name,” etc.

[Col. 0163D] It may trouble weak hearers how, at the beginning of this Gospel reading, the Savior promises the disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name,” he says, “he will give it to you,” since not only do people like us fail to receive many things that they seem to ask the Father in Christ’s name, but even the apostle Paul asked the Lord three times that Satan’s angel, by whom he was tormented, might depart from him, and was unable to obtain this. But the difficulty of this question has already been resolved by the ancient explanation of the Fathers, who rightly understood that only those ask in the Savior’s name who ask for the things that pertain to everlasting salvation. Therefore they say that the apostle did not ask in the Savior’s name that he might be free from the temptation which he had received for the preservation of humility, because, had he been deprived of it, [Col. 0164A] he could not have been saved. He himself affirms this when he says: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (II Corinthians XII).

Whenever, therefore, we ask and are not heard, it happens for one of these reasons. Either we ask for something contrary to the help of our salvation, and therefore the merciful Father denies us, as a benefit, what we foolishly ask—as is shown to have happened to the same apostle Paul, who, when he asked three times, received the answer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness”; or we ask for things that are indeed useful and that concern true salvation, but by living badly we ourselves turn the hearing of the just Judge away from us, falling under Solomon’s saying: “Whoever turns his ear away so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed”; or, while we pray for certain sinners that they may come to repentance, and although we ask beneficially and are worthy of being heard because of our own merit, [Col. 0164B] their perversity nevertheless prevents us from obtaining what we ask.

It also sometimes happens that we seek things that are entirely salutary, both with earnest prayers and with devoted actions, and yet do not immediately obtain what we ask; instead, the effect of our petition is deferred until the future, as when we daily ask the Father on bended knees, saying: “Your kingdom come,” although we will not receive that kingdom immediately after our prayer has ended, but at the appropriate time. It is clear that this is done by the loving providence of our Creator so that the delay may increase the desires of our devotion, and so that, advancing more and more through daily growth, they may finally receive more perfectly the joys they seek.

Among these things it should be noted that when we pray for sinners, even if we cannot obtain their [Col. 0164C] salvation, we are by no means deprived of the fruit of our prayer. For even if they are not worthy to be saved, we will nevertheless be rewarded for the love we show them. Thus in such a petition that promise of the Lord will be fulfilled for us, in which he says:

“If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you.” Observe that he does not simply say “he will give,” but says, “he will give it to you,” because, even if he does not give it to those for whom we ask, he will nevertheless restore to us the reward of our kindness when we mercifully intervene for the errors of others. It follows:

“Until now you have asked nothing in my name.” Until then they had not asked in the Savior’s name because, [Col. 0164D] while they embraced the Savior himself in visible presence, they had raised the gaze of their minds less toward the invisible gifts of salvation. Our weakness likewise does not ask the Father in the name of Jesus—that is, in the name of the Savior—when it asks for something contrary to the reason of its salvation. This does not mean that the apostles’ simplicity was held back from seeking eternal salvation by the bodily sight of their Savior; rather, it was hindered from contemplating the Lord’s will by the obstacle of its own desire.

But what, above all, should be asked, and what the Father has prepared without any doubt for those who persist faithfully in asking, the Lord makes clear by adding:

“Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full.” The order of the meaning is: “Ask so that your joy may be full, and you will receive.” By “full joy,” therefore, he means the blessedness of everlasting [Col. 0165A] peace. To say nothing of the joy of the reprobate, by which they earn eternal grief for themselves, the saints also have joy in the present from hope of heavenly goods when they are exercised by earthly adversities for the Lord’s sake. They have joy when, urged by brotherly love, they learn to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep. But the joy that is mingled with alternating weeping is not full joy. Joy becomes full where, with no one weeping, one is permitted to rejoice with those who rejoice alone.

Thus he says:

“Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full.” It is as though he were openly saying: “Ask the Father not for the fleeting joys of the world, which are always mixed with sorrow and subject to a definite end, but for that unique joy whose fullness is diminished by no disturbance whatsoever and whose eternity is dissolved by no [Col. 0165B] end. If you persevere in asking, without doubt you will receive what you ask.” Concerning the fullness of this joy Peter writes to the faithful: “Believing, you will rejoice with inexpressible and glorified joy, receiving as the outcome of your faith the salvation of your souls” (I Peter II).

To ask for such joy is not merely to demand entrance into the heavenly homeland with words, but also to struggle for its attainment through worthy conduct. For it is of no benefit to seek heavenly things by praying well if one does not cease to become entangled in what is low through living perversely.

“I have spoken these things to you in proverbs. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce the Father to you openly.” He means, of course, that hour when, [Col. 0165C] after completing his passion and resurrection, he was going to give them the grace of the Holy Spirit. Then, instructed inwardly in a spiritual manner and inflamed with spiritual love, the more perfectly they had grasped all that mortals were to understand concerning knowledge of the divinity, the more ardently they would take care to ask for and desire only what would help them earn its vision. For this is what he added:

“On that day you will ask in my name.” We can understand the hour he promises as the future life, in which he announces the Father openly—that is, openly displays the Father to the elect—when, as the Apostle says, “We shall see him face to face” (I Corinthians XIII). John also speaks of this announcement: “Beloved, we are now children of God, [Col. 0165D] and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

There the elect truly ask in Jesus’ name when they intercede for our weakness, so that we may reach the lot of their salvation, from which we still wander as strangers on earth amid the ambushes of our enemies. He most suitably promised the petition of the saints for that future day: “On that day,” he says, “you will ask in my name.” They ask on that day because their intercession for us is poured out not in the darkness of afflictions, as ours is at present, but in the light of everlasting peace and the glory of the blessed spirits.

The spirits of the elect who have been placed in that heavenly city can also be understood to ask in the Savior’s name for themselves, because they desire the time of the universal judgment and the resurrection of the [Col. 0166A] bodies in which they contended for the Lord to come. Hence John says: “I saw beneath God’s altar the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony they had” (Revelation VI). “And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?’” Immediately afterward it continues: “And a white robe was given to each of them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until their fellow servants and their brothers should be completed.”

The souls now possess single robes, since they enjoy only their own blessedness; then they will receive double robes, when, once the number of their brothers has been completed, they rejoice also in receiving immortal bodies.

“And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father concerning you.” [Col. 0166B] Because our Lord Jesus Christ is both God and human, he sometimes indicates the greatness of his divinity and sometimes the humility of his humanity in what he says. When he says that he will not ask the Father concerning the disciples, he says this because of the power of his divinity, consubstantial with the Father. In that nature, he does not himself customarily ask the Father, but gives with the Father what is asked.

But when he says to Peter, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII), and when John says of him, “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (I John II), this is said with reference to the dispensation of the humanity he assumed. When he displays its triumph before the eyes of the Father, he mercifully intervenes for our weakness.

What he says—“And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father concerning you”—can also, without impropriety, be understood in this way: he does not say that he will ask concerning the [Col. 0166C] present, but uses the future tense, “I will ask,” concerning the future time. Once the saints have been received into inward peace, there will no longer be any need for anything to be asked concerning them, because they have been endowed with such great blessedness that it cannot become greater.

“For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came forth from God.” This should not be understood as though the disciples’ love and faith preceded the love with which the Father loved them, and as though human merit came before the gifts of heavenly grace, since the Apostle says most clearly: “Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Romans XI). Rather, it should be understood in this way: the Father preceded them with free love, and by loving them raised them up to love and believe in the Son; and because they themselves preserved the love and faith [Col. 0166D] they had recognized toward the Son with devout and attentive hearts, they were rewarded with greater gifts of the Father’s love.

Nor should it be supposed that the Father can love or give the gifts of love without the Son and the Holy Spirit. Nor, again, should it be thought that the Son can be loved or believed without the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, when he says, “The Father himself loves you,” this must be understood to mean that, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, he loves those whom he judges worthy of love. And when he adds, “because you have loved me,” it must be understood in the same way: whoever rightly loves the Son loves him together with the Father and the Spirit of both, because those whose divine nature is inseparable possess one and the same gifts of virtue.

“I came forth from the Father and came into the world. Again I am leaving [Col. 0167A] the world and going to the Father.” He came forth from the Father and came into the world because he who was invisible with the Father in divinity appeared visibly to the world in humanity. He came forth from the Father because he appeared not in the form in which he is equal to the Father, but in the created nature he assumed, in which he appeared lesser. And he came into the world because, in the form of a servant that he had received, he also offered himself to be seen by those who loved this world.

Again he left the world and returned to the Father because he withdrew from the sight of those who loved the world what they had seen, and taught his own lovers to believe that he is equal to the Father. He left the world and returned to the Father because through his ascension he brought the humanity he had assumed to invisible things.

These words of the Lord are indeed mystical and, as he himself testifies, were spoken in proverbs. But the disciples to whom they were spoken were still so [Col. 0167B] carnal that they could not grasp their depth at all; they did not understand not only the hidden meaning of the words but even their own ignorance, thinking that what had been spoken simply and clearly—though to those who did not understand it was proverbial—was plain. Therefore they immediately replied:

“Behold, now you are speaking openly, and saying no proverb.” They thought, then, that he was speaking openly, although they had not yet been able to comprehend the mysteries of his words. But what follows—

“Now we know that you know all things, and that you have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God”—

clearly shows that, when the Lord spoke to them, he was chiefly discussing those things they were pleased to hear and wished to ask about; he anticipated these very matters and freely brought them [Col. 0167C] before them. Hence they rightly believe and confess that he knows all things as God and that, as God’s Son, he came forth from God.

To know the secrets of thoughts is an evident sign of divinity, as Solomon affirms when he supplicates God: “For you alone know the hearts of all the children of men” (I Kings VIII). Hence Jeremiah also says: “But you, Lord of hosts, who judge justly and test the kidneys and the heart” (Jeremiah XI). These things should not be recalled casually or carelessly. Rather, my brothers, we must watch attentively so that not only our words and actions but also the very secrets of our hearts may be made worthy of the divine gaze.

In the temple of our breast, let there be no flame of hatred, no rust of envy [Col. 0167D] reside; from it let no root of shameful or insulting speech arise; within it let no thought of a harmful deed take root. Let us remember the Lord’s threat, which says: “For I am coming to gather their works and thoughts” (Isaiah LXVI). After casting out the rubble of vices, let us prepare such a dwelling of our heart that he himself may deign to dwell in it, he who is its unavoidable inspector and judge.

We should know that there are three kinds of evil thoughts. One consists of thoughts that pollute the mind through deliberation and the intention to sin. Another consists of thoughts that disturb the mind through the pleasure of sin, yet do not draw it into consent to sin. The third consists of thoughts that pass through the mind by natural impulse but do not entice it to commit vices; [Col. 0168A] instead, they hinder it from the good things it ought to think about. Such is the case when we recall to memory images of things we know to have been done or said at some time without purpose. The frequent reconsideration of these images, like the troublesome persistence of flies, habitually circles around the eyes of the heart and disturbs its spiritual vision more than it blinds it.

Solomon urged that we be disciplined from all these kinds of evil thoughts when he says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it flows life” (Proverbs IV). Following his admonitions, let us act attentively. If we have sinned in our mind by consenting to commit some crime, let us quickly wipe it away through confession and worthy fruits of repentance. If we perceive that we are being tempted by the pleasure of sinning, let us drive away that harmful pleasure through frequent prayers and tears, [Col. 0168B] and through frequent and continual remembrance of everlasting bitterness. If we see that we are not sufficient by ourselves to repel it, let us seek the help of our brothers, so that what we could not accomplish by our own strength we may obtain through their counsel and intercession.

“For the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful”; and, as the same Apostle has already stated, “the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.” Because we cannot entirely free ourselves from superfluous thoughts, let us drive them away as far as we can by introducing good thoughts, especially through frequent meditation on the Scriptures, following the example of the Psalmist, who says: “How I have loved your law, O Lord; it is my meditation all day long” (Psalm CXVIII).

Let us ask heavenly clemency—which is truly [Col. 0168C] to ask in the Savior’s name—to grant both purity of heart and effectiveness in good works. Above all, let us recall with attentive mind that hour and desire it to come more quickly, when the Lord will no longer speak to us through the Scriptures but will announce the Father to us openly, with whom he lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VIII [Note: [Col. 0168D] New Thesaurus of Anecdotes, Martène, volume V, homily 9]. FOR THE GREATER LITANY

**LUKE XI.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks it will be opened,” etc.

Our Lord and Redeemer, desiring that we should attain the joys of the heavenly kingdom, both taught us to ask him for those same joys and promised that he would give them to us when we asked. “Ask,” he says, “and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” These words of our Lord, dearest brothers, must be weighed with the greatest care and with our whole heart, because he plainly testifies that the kingdom of heaven is to be given, found, and opened not to the idle and inactive, but to those who ask, seek, and knock.

The door of the kingdom must therefore be asked for by praying, sought by living rightly, and knocked upon by persevering. For it is not enough merely to ask in words, unless we also seek more diligently and learn how we ought to live so that we may be worthy to obtain what we ask. The one who bears witness to this is he who says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7).

It is of no benefit to have begun good things if each person does not strive to carry through to the end what he has begun well. Indeed, it would have been better not to know the way of righteousness than, after recognizing it, to turn back. Therefore, my brothers, we must ask with diligence, pray without ceasing, fall prostrate before the Lord, and weep before the Lord who made us. And, if we wish to deserve to be heard, let us carefully consider how he wants us to live and what he who made us has commanded us to do.

Let us seek the Lord and be strengthened; let us seek his face continually. And, so that we may deserve to find and behold him, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, because only a chaste body can be raised to heaven on the day of resurrection, and only a pure heart can behold the glory of the divine Majesty. Let us also strike the ears of our merciful Creator with an indefatigable longing for eternal blessedness, and let us not desist from what we have begun before, with him opening the way, we may deserve to be freed from this prison of death and enter the gate of the heavenly homeland.

Let no one flatter himself because of his innocence; let no one cease from prayer on account of his own deeds, as though he did not need the mercy of the just Judge. Rather, even when someone recognizes that he has done some good, because he does not know with what strictness it will be judged, let him tremblingly proclaim with the Prophet: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142). And with blessed Job: “If I wished to justify myself, my mouth would condemn me; if I showed myself innocent, he would prove me perverse” (Job 9).

Let him always remember that apostolic saying: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us” (1 John 1).

Nor, on the other hand, should anyone, considering the character or magnitude of his sins, withdraw his mind from seeking forgiveness through despair. Let no one, seeing the corruption of his wounds, allow the greatness of his illness to hold him back from seeking salvation. The fact that our Creator himself deigned to become our physician, himself to come to us in the flesh, himself to take upon himself our infirmities in order to heal them and our pains in order to remove them, should give us great confidence in obtaining healing.

He himself shed his blood for us and offered his death for our life. He himself more especially showed the remedies of repentance to sinners’ offenses, saying through his forerunner: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3). And shortly afterward: “Whoever has two tunics,” he says, “let him give to the one who has none; and whoever has food, let him do likewise” (Luke 3).

For our lighter, daily failings—without which this life cannot be lived—he himself granted the daily medicines of confession and mutual intercession, saying through the apostle James: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5). He himself urges us to ask in order to grant our requests; as a generous giver, he raises the minds of the needy so that they may ask him: “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks it will be opened.”

There is therefore no doubt that when we ask, we receive; when we seek, we find; and when we knock, it will be opened to us, because the Truth who made the promise could not deceive. But this must be observed with greater vigilance: not all who seem to pray before human beings are proved to ask, seek, or knock at the entrance of the heavenly kingdom in the sight of the eternal Judge. For the Prophet would not say, “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144), if he did not know that some call upon the Lord but not in truth.

Those call upon the Lord in truth who do not contradict by their lives what they say in prayer. Those call upon the Lord in truth who, when they are about to offer their prayers to him, first hasten to fulfill his commands; when they are going to say to him in prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6), they have fulfilled his commandment, which says: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins” (Mark 11).

Therefore the Prophet appropriately adds concerning such people: “He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayers, and he will save them” (Ps. 144). Those, then, call upon the Lord in truth who are shown to fear him.
