When they cry out, he will hear their prayers; when they sigh for him with devout affection, he brings their desires to completion; and when they have passed from this life, he will raise them to eternal salvation.

But, on the other hand, there are those who call upon God, but not in truth. Rebuking them, James says: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4). They ask wrongly who, persisting in sins, imprudently beg that those same sins—which they themselves do not forgive—may be forgiven them by the Lord. Such people he himself rejects through Isaiah, saying: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply your prayer, I will not hear, for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1).

Then, still giving them counsel, he shows by what prayer they could obtain what they sought, when he adds: “Wash yourselves, be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (ibid.).

They ask wrongly who refuse through obedience to hear the voice of the Lord commanding them to come, yet nonetheless beg him in his mercy to hear the voice of their supplications. Rejecting them, he says in the Gospel: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6). Concerning them Solomon also says in Proverbs: “Whoever turns his ear away so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28).

They ask wrongly because they devote themselves to lengthy prayers not with a view to the reward above, but, like the Pharisees, for the sake of human praise. Concerning them the witness and terrible Judge himself solemnly declares that they have received their reward.

They too ask wrongly who seek earthly goods in prayer more than heavenly ones; the Apostle specifically censures their prayers in the very passage we are discussing. For after saying, “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly,” he immediately adds, “so that you may spend it on your desires” (James 4).

Yet citizens of the heavenly homeland, while journeying on earth, are not forbidden to ask the Lord for peaceful times, bodily health, abundant crops, clear weather, and the other necessities of this life—provided that these things are not sought as ultimate ends, and that they are sought only so that, with sufficient provision for the present journey, they may proceed more freely toward the gifts to come.

But because there are people who seek temporal rest and prosperity from their Creator not so that they may obey him with more devoted minds, but so that they may indulge more abundantly in feasting and drunkenness and serve the desires and pleasures of their flesh more securely and freely, such people are rightly said to ask wrongly.

Since, then, all such requests do not deserve to be granted because they ask wrongly, let us, dearest brothers, strive both to ask well and to make ourselves worthy to obtain what we ask. This happens if we seek in prayer the things the Lord commanded, if we approach prayer as people such as he taught us to become, and if we remain attentive in prayer until we obtain what we seek.

If we wish to know what he wants us to ask, let us hear the Gospel saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6). To seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness is to desire the gifts of the heavenly homeland and continually to inquire by what merits of righteousness we should reach them, lest, should we happen to stray from the road that leads there, we be unable to arrive where we are striving to go.

If we carefully examine the words of our Lord and Savior by which he urges us to pray to God the Father, using the example of an earthly parent, we quickly recognize what righteousness is, especially the righteousness that opens the road for us to the heavenly kingdom. “Which of you,” he says, “asks a father for bread—will he give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?”

This comparison is clear and exceedingly easy for all who hear it to understand. If any mortal and frail human being, still burdened with sinful flesh, does not refuse to give his beloved children whatever good things he possesses, though they are earthly and fragile, how much more will the heavenly Father bestow upon those who ask him goods that do not fail in heaven—upon those endowed with his fear and love.

According to the typological interpretation, bread signifies love. Just as bread is the chief food, so that without it the table seems empty, so love is the chief virtue, and without it the other spiritual virtues cannot appear to be spiritual virtues. Indeed, whatever good is done is perfected in love. Hence the Apostle says: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, and if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, and if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that it may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13).

True charity is that by which we are commanded to love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. Nor should a perfect person bestow the benefit of love only upon neighbors and friends; he must also bestow it upon enemies, as the Lord says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you. Pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

In the fish, unfalsified faith is expressed. Just as a fish is born, lives, and is nourished beneath the covering of the waters, so faith in God—which seeks the joys of another life through the lamentation and weeping of the present life—is invisibly conceived in the heart, consecrated by the invisible grace of the Spirit through the water of baptism, nourished by the invisible aid of divine protection so that it may not fail, and, with invisible rewards in view, performs whatever good it can. It remembers the Apostle’s saying: “The things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4).

We can also say that the fish bears the type of faith in this respect: just as a fish is battered by the restless waves of the sea but is not destroyed, so firm faith, however greatly it may be assailed by the pressures of the hostile world, remains unshaken and even emerges more glorious from the struggle, aided by him who, when he had sent his disciples to preach the gifts of that same faith, said: “In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage: I have conquered the world” (John 16).

The egg, moreover, signifies the certainty of our hope. For in an egg the offspring is not yet seen, but the offspring of a future bird is awaited in hope. So the faithful do not yet behold in the present the glory of the heavenly homeland that they believe in, but await it in hope for the future. Hence the Apostle says: “If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8).

These, therefore, dearest brothers, are the good things that we should principally ask of God; this is the righteousness of the kingdom that we should seek above all: faith, hope, and charity. For it is written: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1); “Those who hope in the Lord will be surrounded by mercy” (Ps. 31); and “The fullness of the law is love” (Rom. 13). “For the whole law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Gal. 5). And again: “Love of neighbor does no evil” (1 Cor. 13).

We need not fear that, if with devout dedication we seek from the Lord the grace of love, if from our inmost heart we say, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11), he will allow our heart to be constricted by the hardness of hatred. For he indicates this hardness through the stone when he says: “Which of you, if his father asks for bread, will give him a stone?” (Luke 17.)

Nor need we fear that, if we pray for strength of faith against the temptations of the ancient enemy, saying with our whole heart, “Lord, increase our faith,” he will allow us to perish from the poisons of unbelief. The venom of unbelief, rightly expressed under the name of a serpent—for through that serpent it was spread over the human race—is meant when it is said: “Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?”

Nor should we fear that, if we ask the Lord for hope in heavenly goods, by which we may despise both the adversities and the prosperities of the present, he will turn away his hearing and allow us, through despair of the future, to look back—that is, to seek again the flourishing advantages of the passing age that we have abandoned. For the harmful alteration of a good purpose and the return to carnal desire are rightly compared to the venom of a scorpion, which is behind and which it carries in its tail, when it is said: “Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?”

Let us therefore ask these things of the Lord, brothers: that he grant us the nourishment of pure love, sincere faith, and certain hope; that he remove from us the hardness of hatred, the venom of unbelief, and the sting of despair, which is accustomed to draw us back toward transitory life. Then, without any doubt, we will receive what we ask.

For the Apostle John says with truthful voice that “whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us.” The Lord himself also gives us firm confidence that we shall obtain what we rightly ask, when he adds: “If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?”

He calls the disciples evil, although, judged by human standards, they were good, because no one in this life can be free from every fault, as Solomon testifies when he says: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. 7). Therefore, foreseeing that he would show greater remedies of repentance for the grave guilt of sinners, he teaches that the daily errors of the elect—errors that occur especially in word or thought—must be healed by the daily practice of prayer. Among other things, he commands them to pray in this way: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6).

Or he calls the disciples evil because, in comparison with divine goodness, every creature is proved to be evil, as the Lord says: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10). Nevertheless, it is understood that rational creation can become good through participation in that same divine goodness. Hence the Lord also bears witness in his gracious promise that “the Father from heaven will give the good Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke 11), clearly showing that those who are evil in themselves can be made good through the grace they receive from the Spirit.

He promises that the good Spirit will be given by the Father to those who ask, because whether we desire to attain faith, hope, love, or any other heavenly good, these are bestowed upon us only through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Thus the same Spirit is called in Isaiah the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord; elsewhere he is called the Spirit of love and peace, the Spirit of grace and prayer. For whatever good we truly possess and whatever good we do, we receive it through the generosity of this same Spirit.

Understanding this, the Prophet, when he sought purity of heart, said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God,” and immediately added: “Renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. 50). For unless the Lord’s right Spirit fills our inner being, there is no source within us from which a clean heart may arise.

When, desiring progress in good works, he said, “Lord, I have taken refuge in you; teach me to do your will” (Ps. 142), he immediately showed by what means this should be attained when he said: “Your good Spirit will lead me on a straight path.”

Following the footsteps of that Spirit, dearest brothers, according to the measure of our ability, let us ask God the Father to lead us by the grace of his Spirit into the way of right faith, which works through love. And, so that we may deserve to obtain what we desire, let us strive to live in such a way that we may not be unworthy of so great a Father. Rather, let us always preserve undefiled in body and mind the mystery of regeneration by which we were chosen as sons of God in baptism.

For it is certain that, if we follow the commands of the supreme Father, he will reward us with the inheritance of eternal blessing that he prepared for us before the ages, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with him lives and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

---

### Homily IX: On the Ascension of the Lord

**Luke 24.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled.”

As the Lord was about to ascend into heaven, he first took care to instruct his disciples carefully concerning the mystery of his faith, so that they might preach it to the world with all the greater certainty, having received it both from the mouth of Truth himself and knowing that it had long before been signified by the mouth of the prophets.

Appearing after the triumph of his resurrection, as we have just heard when the Gospel was read, he said: “These are the words that I spoke to you when I was with you”—that is, while I still bore a body like yours, corruptible and mortal—“that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled.”

He says that the mysteries which Moses, the prophets, and the psalmist proclaimed have been fulfilled in him. From this it is plainly evident that there is one Church in all its saints and one faith of all the elect—of those who came before and of those who followed his bodily coming. For just as we are saved through faith in his completed incarnation, passion, and resurrection, so they, believing with complete certainty in that same incarnation, passion, and resurrection yet to come, hoped to be saved through the same author of life.

This is well signified by the two men who carried a cluster of grapes from the promised land to the people waiting in the desert on a carrying-pole (Num. 13). The cluster placed upon the pole is the Lord exalted upon the cross, who says: “I am the true vine” (John 15). Elsewhere, offering the disciples the cup of wine, he says: “This is the cup of the new covenant in my blood, which will be poured out for you” (Luke 22). Concerning this the Church also says: “My beloved is a cluster of henna to me” (Song 1).

The two men carry the cluster on a pole to demonstrate to the people the fertility of the promised land, because the preachers of both Testaments—who, through the Lord’s revelation, learned of the glory of the heavenly homeland—do not cease to make known to the peoples the mystery of his passion. From this it may be inferred how great a reward he will give the faithful in heaven, since for their salvation he sent his only-begotten Son to suffer on earth.

The fact that the two men carrying the cluster were indeed able to carry it in the same way, but were not able to see it in the same way, signifies what the Savior himself said to the disciples, glorified by the grace of his vision: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. 13).

Or it signifies that the prophets and Moses knew and preached beforehand the one and same triumph of the Lord’s cross, but the prophets did so at times in figurative and veiled language, whereas the apostles and the successors of the apostles, with the light of the Gospel revealed, always preached it openly. Thus now the whole Christian people ought to know and confess the faith that at that time only a very few—the more perfect—knew, although even then the whole people bore the mysteries of that same faith typologically in the ceremonies of the Law.

Therefore it is said here that, after completing the mysteries of his incarnation, the Lord opened the minds of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures. He opened their minds so that they could openly understand what the prophets had spoken obscurely and hand it on to believers for understanding. He opened their minds so that they might understand that whatever he did or taught in the flesh, the prophets had foretold that he would do and teach.

And he said to them: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.”

The name of Christ was already known by the faith of the prophets and fathers long before his passion and resurrection, as we have said. Peter bears witness to this when, speaking about them, he says: “But through the grace of Jesus we believe that we shall be saved in the same way as they” (Acts 15).

After his passion and resurrection, and also after his ascension into heaven, faith in that same name was preached not only more broadly and openly to their descendants, namely the Jewish people, but was also revealed by the same heavenly mercy to foreign nations.

Therefore Christ had to come in the flesh, suffer, and rise again, because the human race could not otherwise be instructed for life, redeemed from death, or formed in the hope of resurrection than through his presence, passion, and resurrection.

It was fitting that the preaching of repentance and forgiveness of sins in the confession of Christ’s name should begin at Jerusalem. There the magnificence of his teaching and virtues, the triumph of his passion, and the joys of his resurrection and ascension had been accomplished; there, therefore, the first root of his faith was to be planted, and the first shoot of the rising Church—like a great vine—was to be set in the ground. From there, multiplying the seed of the word, it would extend the branches of its teaching throughout the breadth of the world, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy: “The law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he will judge the nations and rebuke many peoples” (Isa. 2).

It was also fitting that the preaching of repentance and forgiveness of sins, which was to be proclaimed to idolatrous nations polluted by various crimes, should begin at Jerusalem, so that no one, terrified by the magnitude of his offenses, would doubt that forgiveness could be obtained if he produced the worthy fruit of repentance, since it was established that forgiveness had even been granted to the people of Jerusalem, who had blasphemed and crucified the Son of God.

“But you,” he says, “are witnesses of these things. And I am sending upon you the promise of my Father.” By the promise of the Father he means the grace of the Holy Spirit, about whom he had spoken much to them in the Gospel of John before his passion. Among these sayings is the following: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me, and you also will bear witness” (John 15).

And in the Acts of the Apostles: “He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father, which,” he said, “you heard from my mouth: John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1).

The expectation of this promise is also introduced here when it is said:

“But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

He promises that power will come upon them from on high, because although they had the Holy Spirit beforehand, they received him more fully once he had ascended into heaven. Before his passion, by the power of the Holy Spirit they cast out many demons, healed many sick people, and preached the word of life as far as they were able. After he had risen from the dead, they were especially renewed by the grace of that same Spirit, when, as John writes, “he breathed on them and said to them: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them’” (John 20).

But they were clothed with his greater power from on high when, ten days after the Lord’s Assumption, they received him in tongues of fire and were so inflamed by him with the confidence of strength that no terrors of rulers could prevent them from speaking to all in the name of Jesus.

Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them.

Because our Redeemer appeared in the flesh to remove sins, take away the punishment of the first curse, and grant believers the inheritance of perpetual blessing, he rightly concluded all that he did in the world with words of blessing, showing that he himself is the one of whom it was said: “Indeed, he who gave the law will give blessing” (Ps. 81).

And fittingly he led those whom he was going to bless into Bethany, which is interpreted as “house of obedience,” because contempt and pride earn a curse, while obedience earns a blessing. The Lord himself, in order to restore to the world the grace of the blessing it had lost, became obedient to the Father unto death. The blessing of heavenly life is granted only to those who, in the holy Church, strive to obey the divine commandments.

Nor should it be passed over that Bethany is described as situated on the side of the Mount of Olives. Just as Bethany expresses the Church obedient to the Lord’s commands, so the Mount of Olives very appropriately expresses the person of our Redeemer. Appearing in the flesh, he surpasses all who are merely human in both the height of his dignity and the spiritual grace of his virtue. Hence it is sung of him in the Psalms: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44).

As the present reading of the holy Gospel also bears witness, he promised the gift of that same holy anointing to his companions—that is, to the faithful—and, as we know, not long afterward he sent what he had promised.

If anyone wishes to hear how the house of obedience—that is, the holy Church—was built on the side of that same Mount of Olives, let him read the Gospel of John, where, after his passion had been completed on the cross, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came forth.

These are the mysteries by which the Church is born and nourished in Christ: the water of baptism, by which she is washed from sins, and the blood of the Lord’s cup, by which she is strengthened in her gifts. Since she is also marked with the chrism of the Holy Spirit so that she may be perfected on the day of redemption, it is rightly called the Mount of Olives—the mountain on whose side the holy city is situated and on which the grace of blessing is given.

“And it happened,” he says, “while he blessed them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.”

It should be noted that, after blessing his disciples, the Savior ascended into heaven. We should also commit to memory that, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, while they were watching his ascent, angels appeared and said: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1).

We must labor with every effort so that, just as the Lord will descend to judge in the same form and substance of flesh in which he ascended, so he who departed while blessing the apostles may, when he returns, make us worthy of his blessing and place us among those standing at his right, to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25).

And they returned to Jerusalem with great joy, worshiping him, and they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God.

Always, and especially in this passage, dearest brothers, we ought to remember the saying of the Lord by which he glorified the disciples, as we reported shortly above: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Matt. 13).

Who could say, or who could worthily imagine, with what blessed compunction they lowered their eyes to the earth when they saw the very King of heaven whom they were worshiping, having conquered the mortality he had assumed, now returning to the throne of his Father’s glory? What sweet tears they shed, burning with such hope and joy, at the entrance of the heavenly homeland, when they saw that their God and Lord was already carrying there a portion of their nature!

Rightly, therefore, refreshed by such a spectacle, after they had worshiped in the place where his feet had stood, after they had watered with abundant tears the footprints he had most recently left—

> **[Note: Here Bede appears to be referring to these words of blessed Paulinus, bishop of Nola, in Letter 31 to Severus: “It is remarkable amid all this that, in the basilica of the Ascension . . . the sand preserves the imprint of the divine feet for veneration, so that it may truly be said: ‘We worship in the place where his feet stood.’”]**

—they immediately returned to Jerusalem, where they had been commanded to await the coming of the Holy Spirit. And, so that they might prove worthy of the heavenly promises, they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. For they knew with complete certainty that the Holy Spirit deigns to visit and inhabit only those hearts that he sees frequenting the place of prayer and devoted to divine praise and blessing.

Hence we read concerning them in the Acts of the Apostles: “They were all persevering with one accord in prayer” (Acts 1). This is an example of apostolic practice that we should carefully imitate: since we possess heavenly promises and are diligently commanded to beseech God in order to receive them, let us all gather for prayer, persevere in prayer, and pray to the Lord with united devotion.

There is no doubt that, when we pray in this way, our merciful Creator will deign to incline his hearing toward us and pour the grace of his Spirit also into our hearts. He will also make our eyes blessed—not as were the eyes of the apostles, who deserved to see the Lord dwelling in the world, teaching and performing miracles, rising again after the triumph of death, and returning to heaven, but as those of whom he says to the apostle Thomas: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20).

For all believers alike—whether those who preceded the times of his incarnation by being born earlier, whether those who saw him in the flesh, or whether we who believe after his ascension—share in that most merciful promise of his, in which he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. 5).

We have passed through these matters from the Gospel reading by explaining them as best we could [Col. 0178C]. But since in that same reading we heard that the disciples’ understanding was opened so that they might comprehend the Scriptures, I would like to recall something from the writings of the prophets, and to increase and season the joy of the evangelical solemnity with prophetic proclamations.

The Psalmist therefore speaks of this solemnity: “God has gone up with a shout of joy; the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Ps. XLVI). He went up with a shout of joy because, while the disciples rejoiced in the glory of his exaltation, he sought heaven. He went up also with the sound of a trumpet because, while the angels proclaimed his return to judge the living and the dead, he entered the seat of the heavenly kingdom.

But how did God ascend, since he is always present everywhere and, being unconfined by place, cannot change from one place to another? [Col. 0178D] The same Psalmist testifies elsewhere, saying: “He makes the cloud his ascent; he walks upon all the wings of the winds” (Ps. CIII). By “cloud” he means the substance of human frailty, which the Sun of righteousness assumed so that he could be carried by human beings. Hence Isaiah says: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud, and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be shaken before him” (Isa. XIX).

The Lord ascended upon a light cloud so that, entering Egypt, he might overthrow its idols, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I); because, free from every stain of iniquity, he assumed a body in which, entering the world, he would destroy the rite of idolatry [Col. 0179A] and reveal the true light of divinity to the black and darkened hearts of the gentiles.

Through the cloud of human nature, he who is not confined by place deigned to come from place to place. In this nature he who always remains impassible in his divinity willed to suffer mockeries, scourges, and even death. Through it, crowned with the power of the resurrection, he ascended into heaven—he who by the power of his divinity fills heaven and earth.

He raised this nature above the wings of the winds when, lifting what he had assumed from the earth not only above all the spaces of this air but also to the height of the ether, he placed it at the right hand of the Father’s majesty.

Amos likewise speaks of the glory of this assumed humanity: “He builds his ascent into heaven, and pours out his promise over the earth” (Amos IX). He built his ascent into heaven because he himself created for himself human flesh and a human soul in which he could enter heaven [Col. 0179B]. He poured out his promise over the earth because, having sent the Spirit from above, he filled all the ends of the earth with the grace of faith, as he had promised.

The Psalmist, foreseeing in the Spirit the coming of this promised grace and desiring its arrival more quickly, says: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” (Ps. LVI). Here he clearly signifies that, before our Redeemer, having assumed mortal flesh, destroyed the kingdom of death, God was known only in Judea: “His name was great in Israel.” But when, rising from the dead, the God-man penetrated the heights of heaven, the glory of his name was already proclaimed and believed throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0179C] The prophets proclaimed the mystery of the Lord’s ascension not only in words but also through their deeds. Enoch, the seventh from Adam, was taken from the world, and Elijah was raised into the aerial heaven; thus they bore witness to the Lord who was to ascend above the heavens.

Enoch, in that he was born as the seventh from Adam, represented the Lord, who was to be conceived and born not according to the customary order of mortal nature but through the power of the Holy Spirit. He represented the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the prophet describes as sevenfold and which was to rest uniquely upon him; he represented the one who would baptize in the Holy Spirit and give the gifts of that same Spirit to believers.

In that Enoch lived among human beings for 365 years before he was taken away—the number of days in the solar year—he signified the Lord’s future life in the flesh [Col. 0179D]. The Lord, when he was about to ascend into heaven, showed himself to be the one and only light of the world. “I am,” he said, “the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII).

Hence the Prophet mystically calls him the sun, because he has deigned to illuminate by the grace of faith and truth every region of the world, from the rising of the sun to its setting, and from the north to the south.

Moreover, the name Enoch, who was taken away, is interpreted as “Dedication.” This signifies the one who, rising from the dead, ascended into heaven and now deigns to give the pledge of his Spirit for the consecration of the hearts of the faithful, and in the future to lead the Church, perfected in every respect, into the joy of the resurrection and everlasting solemnity.

[Col. 0180A] Elijah, however, presented a figure of this feast of the Lord with a still greater miracle. When the time was approaching for him to be taken from the world, he came to the Jordan with his disciple Elisha and, wrapping his cloak, struck the waters with it. They were divided, and both crossed over on dry ground. Then he said to Elisha: “Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken away from you.” He replied: “I ask that your spirit may be doubled in me” (IV Kings II).

As they walked along and spoke, suddenly, as Scripture says, Elijah was carried away in a fiery chariot and ascended as if even to heaven. This addition—“as if even to heaven”—signifies that Elijah was not raised into heaven itself, as our Lord was, but only into the heights of the air, and that afterward he was invisibly brought to the joys of paradise.

Elisha then lifted up Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen from him. Coming to the Jordan [Col. 0180B], he struck the waters with it; after calling upon the God of Elijah, he divided them and crossed over.

Let your affection, my brothers, observe how harmoniously the figure corresponds to the truth. Elijah came to the Jordan, removed his cloak, struck the waters, and divided them. The Lord came to the river of death, into which the human race had been accustomed to be submerged; temporarily removing the garment of flesh that he had assumed, he struck death by dying and opened for us the way of life by rising again.

The Jordan rightly expresses the flow and decline of our mortality, because Jordan is called in Latin “Descent of theirs,” and because the river itself, flowing into the Dead Sea, loses its praiseworthy waters there [Note: These are the words of Pliny, Natural History, book V, chapter 15; consult him if you wish.].

Elijah crosses over the divided river on dry ground, and Elisha crosses as well, because the Savior, rising from the dead, also grants his faithful the hope of rising again [Col. 0180C].

After crossing the Jordan, Elijah gave Elisha the choice of asking for whatever he wished. Likewise, after completing the glory of the resurrection, the Lord impressed more fully upon the minds of the disciples what he had previously promised: “Whatever you ask in my name, I will do” (John XV).

Elisha asked that Elijah’s spirit might be doubled in him. Instructed by the Lord, the disciples desired to receive the promised grace of the Spirit, so that they might be sufficient to preach it not only to the one nation of the Jews, whom he himself had taught while present in the flesh, but also to all the nations throughout the world.

Was he not promising a double grace of his Spirit when he said: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John XIV)?

While Elijah and Elisha were speaking, fiery chariot and horses suddenly carried Elijah [Col. 0180D] as if even to heaven. These chariot and horses must certainly be understood as angelic powers, of which it is written: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. CXIII).

Elijah, being a mere human being, needed their assistance so that he could be lifted from the earth. The Lord, speaking with the apostles, was suddenly raised up before their eyes. He was not supported by angelic assistance, but he was accompanied by angelic service; and he was truly taken into heaven, with the angels themselves bearing witness to him, for they said to them: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven” (Acts I).

Raised into heaven, Elijah left Elisha the cloak with which he had been clothed. Ascending into heaven, the Lord left the disciples—and indeed the whole Church—the sacraments of the humanity he had assumed, by which they might be sanctified and warmed by the power of love [Col. 0181A].

Elisha took Elijah’s cloak and struck the waters of the Jordan with it. When he invoked the God of Elijah, the waters were divided, and he crossed over. The apostles received, and the Church established through them received, the sacraments of its Redeemer. Spiritually instructed, cleansed, and consecrated by them, the Church itself learned, after invoking the name of God the Father, to overcome the force of death and, disregarding its obstacle, to pass over into eternal life.

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, venerate with complete devotion this glory of the Lord’s ascension, which was first signified by the words and deeds of the prophets and afterward completed in our own Mediator. Let us also, so that we may deserve to follow his footsteps and ascend into heaven [Col. 0181B], meanwhile humble ourselves salutarily on earth, always remembering that, as Solomon says, “disgrace follows the proud, but glory follows the humble in spirit” (Prov. XXIX).

Behold, in the ascension of our Redeemer we have learned where all our attention should be directed. Behold, when the Mediator of God and humanity ascended into heaven, we recognized that the gate of the heavenly homeland had been opened to human beings.

Let us therefore hasten with every effort toward the everlasting happiness of that homeland. Since we cannot yet be there in body, let us always dwell there in desire and in mind. In accordance with the words of the outstanding preacher, “let us seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; let us set our minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth.”

Let us seek him and strengthen ourselves with the hope of finding him. Let us always seek his face, so that when he [Col. 0181C] who ascended in gentleness returns in terror, he may find us ready and may introduce us with himself into the celebrations of the heavenly city—Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY X. FOR THE SUNDAY AFTER THE LORD’S ASCENSION

**John XV.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me,” etc.

From many passages of the holy Gospel we find that, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, the disciples were less capable of understanding the mysteries of divine majesty [Col. 0181D] and less strong in enduring the adversities of human wickedness [Col. 0181D]. But when the Spirit came to them, together with an increase of divine knowledge they were also given steadfastness for overcoming human persecution.

Thus the Lord now says to them in his promise:

“When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness.”

First of all, it must be noted that the Lord testifies both that the Spirit of truth is to be sent by him and that the same Spirit proceeds from the Father [Col. 0182A]. This does not mean that the same Spirit proceeds from the Father in one way and is sent by the Son in another, or that he proceeds from the Father at a different time from that at which he is sent by the Son [Al. omits: “than when he is sent by the Son”]. Rather, the Son says that he is sent by him and proceeds from the Father in order to designate the Father as one person and himself as another, and also to declare, amid this distinction of persons, that his operation and will are one with the Father’s will and operation.

For when the grace of the same Spirit is given to human beings, the Spirit is certainly sent by the Father and sent by the Son; he proceeds from the Father and proceeds from the Son, because his sending is itself the procession by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son. He also comes of his own accord, because, just as he is coequal with the Father and the Son, so he has one will in common with the Father and the Son. “The Spirit blows where he wills” (John III). And, as the Apostle says after enumerating the heavenly gifts: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII).

When the Spirit came [Col. 0182B], he bore witness about the Lord, because, breathing upon the hearts of the disciples [Al. adds *pro Deo*, “for God”], he revealed to them with clear light everything that mortals needed to know about him: namely, that before the ages he was equal and consubstantial with the Father; that at the end of the ages he became consubstantial with us; that, born of a Virgin, he lived in the world without sin; that, when and by whatever death he willed, he departed from the world; that by truly rising again he destroyed death; that [Al. omits “that”] by ascending into heaven he raised up and established at the right hand of the Father’s glory the true flesh in which he had suffered and risen; that all the writings of the prophets bear witness to him; that confession of his name was to be proclaimed to the ends of the earth; and that the other mysteries of his faith were disclosed to the disciples through the testimony of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0182C].

These things were granted not only to them but also to all who believe in the Lord through their word: whatever they rightly understand has been granted by the gift of that same Spirit.

“Therefore,” he says, “he will bear witness about me, and you also will bear witness,” because what they had received through the Spirit’s inward teaching, they supplied to others by speaking outwardly, after casting off their former fear.

For that same Spirit both illumined their hearts with knowledge of the truth and raised them, by the summit of virtue, to teach what they knew. Hence Isaiah rightly calls him the Spirit both of fortitude and of knowledge (Isa. XI). He is the Spirit of knowledge because through him we recognize what we ought rightly to do or even to think. He is also the Spirit of fortitude because through him we receive the ability to carry out what we know to be good, so that no adversity may drive us away from the good we have begun [Col. 0182D].

“And you,” he says, “will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.”

For [Al.: “When”], when the grace of the Spirit was given, this too strengthened the disciples’ confidence: they had been with the Lord from the beginning and were therefore able to proclaim without any ambiguity what they had seen and heard in his presence.

Thus, when Peter wished to appoint another apostle in place of Judas, he took care to choose not a novice but one tested over time, saying: “Therefore it is necessary that one of these men who have gathered with us throughout all the time during which the Lord Jesus went in and out among us to become with us a witness of his resurrection” (Acts I).

For this reason, when preaching Christ to the gentiles, he himself confidently said: “God raised him on the third day and granted that he should become visible, not to all the people but to witnesses appointed beforehand by God—to us who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts X).

But because, as the merits of the elect increase, the envy of the ancient enemy usually increases at once, and because he tries to overwhelm the beginnings of piety either secretly through himself or openly through people subjected to his wickedness, the Lord rightly showed [Col. 0183B] that the persecution of those who would resist their preaching would arise alongside the confidence in preaching that he had promised to the disciples, when he added:

“I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized. They will expel you from the synagogues.”

The compassionate teacher took care to predict to the disciples the future conflicts with wicked people, so that these events, when they came, might offend them less, because adversities that can be foreseen are naturally endured more lightly. Evils that are inflicted upon an unprepared and unsuspecting mind often cast it more severely from its state of integrity.

Hence Solomon rightly admonishes, saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear of the Lord, and prepare your soul for temptation.”

The Savior not only warned the disciples that they would be expelled from the society of their fellow countrymen but also that they would suffer the dangers of death from them. For it follows:

“But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.”

The Jews thought they were offering service to God when they pursued the ministers [Col. 0183C] of the New Testament with hatred and death, because, as the Apostle bears witness concerning them, “they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X).

He also speaks about himself [Al. reads *se ipse*, “he himself”]: “I myself had thought that I ought to do many things against the name of Jesus the Nazarene, which I also did in Jerusalem” (Acts XXVI).

After foretelling the pressures imposed by their adversaries, therefore, he added, as if to console the disciples:

“But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.”

It is as though he were saying openly: “You will indeed suffer battles of tribulation from your fellow countrymen, but receive these things all the more patiently because they will be inflicted upon you not so much out of hatred for you as out of zeal for the divine law.”

Mindful of this admonition, blessed [Col. 0183D] Stephen the martyr, kneeling for those who were killing him, pleaded with devout voice, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts VII).

The zealots for the law therefore thought they were offering service to God when they brought death upon the heralds of grace. But they defend the law, which was given through a servant, in vain, since they refuse to accept the grace that the Son himself offers. They mistakenly think they are pleasing God the Father while striving to despise—or even to persecute and blaspheme—the Son of God.

Hence it is rightly added:

“And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father, nor me.”

Since the Son is in the Father and the Father is in the Son, and whoever sees the Son also sees the Father (John XIV), it is entirely clear that all who stubbornly resist faith in the Son are thereby shown not to know the Father [Col. 0184A].

Thus the same John, implying the truth of the divine unity, says: “Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father; whoever confesses the Son also has the Father” (I John II). And again: “Everyone who loves the one who begot also loves the one who was born from him” (I John V).

But because the disciples, who knew the Father and the Son well, were going to suffer many things for the defense and proclamation of this knowledge, the Lord adds by his provident warning:

But I have told you these things so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you. It must be considered very carefully what he says: “I told you”—I who am to die for your life and salvation, who am to redeem you with my blood, who am always to help you in tribulation, who am to grant you eternal rewards after tribulation. For it brings great relief to those engaged in the struggle, and supplies great grace of consolation, when they remember that the one who foretold the struggles themselves as future is also accustomed to help his soldiers so that they may not be overcome, and, lest they conquer in vain, to repay them with an immortal palm after the battles. The one who here warned that the hour of persecution [Al.: “the persecution of the wicked”] was coming soon afterward promises his faithful ones his help in that same persecution, saying: “In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage: I have conquered the world.” Elsewhere he promises the crown of life to those who contend lawfully, saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).

We have briefly passed through these matters from the Gospel reading, dearest brothers, by explaining them; now I wish to say something more subtle about the very solemnity of the Fiftieth Day, which we celebrate. Just as, when the Paschal solemnities were approaching, we observed Lent through the discipline of fasting, so, when those days have been completed, we celebrate the Fiftieth Day with festal devotion, not without a definite mystical purpose. Since holy Church, in some of her members, is still laboring on earth for eternal rest, while in others, every labor having ended, she already reigns with Christ in heaven, our fathers established these two suitable solemnities of religious observance in remembrance of both states of life: namely, Lent, the season of affliction and fasting, as the time of the Lord’s resurrection was already drawing near, and the Paschal rejoicing, so that through it they might more often recall to us that through labors and self-restraint, through vigils and prayers, and through the other things that the Apostle mentions (2 Corinthians 6)—the weapons of righteousness—we ought to attain the rewards of immortal life.

Moreover, they wished the Fiftieth Day to begin from the very day of the Lord’s resurrection and to be celebrated with rejoicing and divine praises rather than with fasts, so that through its yearly festivals we might be more sweetly reminded to kindle and keep fixed our desire for the festivals that are not yearly but perpetual, not earthly but heavenly. For true happiness is not to be sought, nor true solemnity found, in the time of this mortality but in the eternity of the incorruption to come, where, when all infirmities have ceased, life is wholly conducted in the vision and praise of God. In accordance with what the Prophet, rejoicing in God with both heart and flesh, said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83).

Therefore, during the days of the Fiftieth Day we customarily sing “Alleluia” more frequently and more festively, in memory of this our most peaceful and blessed activity. “Alleluia” is indeed a Hebrew expression, and it is translated into Latin as “Praise the Lord.” Accordingly, in the psalms, wherever we sing “Praise the Lord,” the Hebrews always sing *Alleluia* for this expression; and the evangelist John testifies in his Apocalypse (chapter 19) that he heard the heavenly hosts of powers singing it.

The venerable father Tobias, too, understanding from an angelic vision what the glory of the heavenly citizens and how great the splendor of that heavenly Jerusalem is, said in this mystical utterance: “All her streets will be paved with precious and pure stone, and through her lanes Alleluia will be sung” (Tobit 13). Very rightly and beautifully, then, a universal custom of holy Church has grown up: this hymn of divine praise is sung by all the faithful throughout the world in the Hebrew language, out of reverence for its first authority. This is done so that, through such harmony of devotion, the Church may be reminded that even now she ought to remain in one confession of faith and love of Christ, and that in the future she must hasten to that homeland where there is no diversity of minds and no discord of languages.

For just as once in Jerusalem the multitude of believers in the Lord had one heart and one soul, and all things were common to them, so in that vision of supreme peace the multitude of those who see God will have one heart and one soul—namely, in loving and praising him whose grace they will see has saved them. There, truly, all things will be common to all, because, as the Apostle says, “God will be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15).

As a type of that time and of our future rest in praise, the final psalms, which are sung especially in the Lord’s praise, are marked beforehand with the title “Alleluia.” For the seventh day was commanded by the Law to be called and observed as the Sabbath, that is, as rest. And appropriately the book of Psalms, after so many institutions of heavenly precepts, after so many mysteries of spiritual things have been sung, and after so many voices of salutary confession and most humble supplication have been uttered, always ends with titles of “Alleluia.” For whatever good we do in this life, whatever we utter with a rejoicing tongue in the service of our Redeemer, whatever we think out of desire for the eternal homeland—all these things are surely repaid to us with such a reward that in everlasting rest we may be worthy both to hear the voice of his praise, and, with the saints, to bless him, to proclaim the glory of his kingdom, and to speak of the power of his might.

For this reason, several teachers of the Church decreed that the singing of “Alleluia” should be interrupted during Lent, although the Church never ceases from divine praise; rather, his gifts are sung every day in other words that signify the same thing perfectly. This was done so that its renewed repetition might lend greater and more pleasing honor and splendor to the Paschal solemnities. They also wished especially to signify by this mystery that, during the pilgrimage of this exile, just as we know in part and prophesy in part, so also we praise the Lord in part, saying with the Prophet: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm 136).

But when we have been deemed worthy to enter our homeland—the land of the living—and the house of the heavenly kingdom once promised us by the Lord, then, just as we shall be able to behold him perfectly, so also we shall be able to praise him perfectly, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “And in his temple all will speak of glory” (Psalm 38). Hence he says elsewhere: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” By “the heavens” he calls the citizens of the heavenly homeland. Earthborn people can indeed declare the glory of God, but only the citizens of heaven are sufficient to proclaim it fully; the nearer they see it, the more certainly they can express it.

The first authority that established both these solemnities for us—the solemnity of Lent and that of the Fiftieth Day—was not that of just any human beings, but of the Lord himself and our Savior. Lent was established by his fasting in the desert for forty days and forty nights, and by his overcoming the tempter’s cunning and enjoying the ministry of angels. There he instructed us by his example that through the mortification of the flesh we must avoid the stratagems of our spiritual adversary and attain fellowship with the angels.

He showed us that we must preserve the joys of the Fiftieth Day by presenting himself alive to the disciples after the resurrection, with many proofs, for forty days—appearing to them, speaking of the kingdom of God, and eating with them—as we read in the Acts, because by the frequency of his visits he caused them to experience this time as joyful and festive. Even when he ascended into heaven, he did not at all take away from them the sweetness of his former presence; rather, he increased it with the promised gift of the Holy Spirit.

Finally, when he promised that they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit after not many days, and, blessing them, ascended and was carried into heaven on the fortieth day of his resurrection, they immediately returned to Jerusalem after worshiping him with great joy, and they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. By this joy, praise, and heavenly blessing—while they awaited the coming of the Holy Spirit until the fiftieth day, which the Greeks call *Pentecost*—they taught that the joy of this solemnity should be prolonged.

In the midst of these matters, dearest brothers, we must look more carefully at the fact that, during those forty days of living with the disciples, the Lord not only foreshadowed the joys of the age to come that we shall share with him, but also displayed toward us the ineffable affection of his loving-kindness. Although he had already laid aside the weakness of the body—indeed, although that weakness had already ended and had been changed through the power of the resurrection into heavenly glory—he nevertheless deigned still to take part in the disciples’ meal, so that he might have them as companions in heaven and might commend more vividly, through that intimacy, the commandments by which they would reach the kingdom of God.

For what does this conjunction of words mean, “Appearing to them and speaking about the kingdom of God, and eating with them,” except that it plainly shows that he joined their meal especially while he was speaking about the kingdom of God, so that, taking earthly food among them by which he demonstrated his heavenly body, he might bind them more closely with the bonds of his love and strengthen them by the memory of that time about which he had promised and foretold to them before his Passion: “And I appoint for you, just as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22)?

Therefore, rightly, on these sacred days we too devote ourselves to more abundant meals and heavenly hymns: out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection, in memory of the Lord eating together with his disciples, and [Note: [Col. 0187D] Al.: “of the Lord’s meal with the disciples, together.”] in hope of our future rest and immortal life. Nor do we bend the knee in prayer, according to custom, because the bending of the knees is certainly a sign of repentance and mourning. Our fathers also instituted that this be observed on all Sundays, on account of the mysteries both of the Lord’s resurrection and of our own.

The Fathers have discussed the mystery of the number fifty and of the number forty in many ways. But since we have prolonged our discourse, it is enough for us now to say briefly to your brotherhood that the ceremonies of fasting are rightly observed for a period of forty days, so that this may signify that throughout the whole time of this life we ought to labor for the attainment of eternal life. Four times ten makes forty, and the present life is appropriately represented by the number four, either because it is entirely varied by the four yearly seasons, or because the world itself in which we live subsists through four elements, namely fire, air, water, and earth.

The blessedness of the future life is not inappropriately expressed by the number ten. Hence the Lord declares that the laborers in the vineyard were paid a denarius. The laborers of the vineyard are the cultivators of holy Church. The denarius signifies the perfection of heavenly life, in which, contemplating the glory of God, namely, of the supreme King, we are transformed into the same image—not only because the coin bears the king’s image and inscription, but also because it consists of ten *oboli*, and ten is the perfect number; hence it received its name.

Rightly, then, we celebrate the annual fast by a period of forty days—that is, four times ten days—so that we may thereby be more particularly reminded that, as long as we live in the world, we must always labor for the adoption of heavenly rewards. Rightly also, by the number fifty of the days, we venerate in image [Al.: “and the image of”] the state of our future blessedness: by relaxing the fasts, singing “Alleluia,” and praying while standing, all of which are most fitting foreshadowings of perpetual rest, resurrection, and praise.

Seven times seven makes forty-nine. It is perfectly clear that rest is often signified by seven. But seven taken seven times signifies the perfection of that rest, which is never closed by any end and is stained by no corruption; when the day of universal judgment and resurrection arrives, it is perfected by the greater grace of the bodies received.

For when one unit is added to the seven weeks—that is, the very Lord’s Day of Pentecost, on which the primitive Church received the Holy Spirit—the number fifty is completed in full. This reveals the time of judgment and the resurrection of all, when the rest of the holy souls, which is now enjoyed in that life, will be doubled by the reception of immortal bodies, and the Apostle’s saying will be fulfilled: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also make your mortal bodies alive [Al.: ‘will give life to’] through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8).

Yet no one should think that it is done without a discerning and fitting mystical reason that, when the fiftieth day has been completed, we do not immediately bend the knee to worship, but continue during that week [Al.: omits “that week”] to implore the Lord while standing; and although we resume the fasts that had been interrupted, we nevertheless sound forth “Alleluia” every day. Since the grace of the Holy Spirit is sevenfold, the solemnity of his coming is rightly celebrated for seven days with the due praise of hymns and likewise with the celebration of Masses.

Since at Pentecost the Church throughout the whole world is accustomed always to gather new peoples to God through the water of regeneration, we rightly rejoice with them in their salvation and, until they are clothed in white robes and display the brightness of their purified mind through the splendor of their clothing, offer to God a hymn of devoted praise, in accordance with the command of that most loving Shepherd and Redeemer of ours, who says: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost” (Luke 15).

Rightly, then, we now pray while standing [Al.: ‘then also’], to signify their liberation: through the gift of the Holy Spirit they have been deemed worthy to be revived and raised from the death of the soul to life. By his gracious gift we also hope to be clothed with the immortality of the flesh on the last day and to be led to the joys of the blessed resurrection, in accordance with what we taught shortly before on the testimony of the Apostle.

As for the fact that, amid these observances, the discipline of fasting is resumed, we should believe that it was taken from the example of the apostles. Having received the Spirit, the more perfectly they enjoyed the new sweetness of heavenly goods, the more deeply they withdrew their minds from the memory of earthly delights. The time had already arrived of which the Lord foretold that the disciples could not fast while he was with them, but that, when he had been taken away, they would fast.

When the disciples of John asked him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” he said to them: “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.” Since, both before the Passion and after the Lord’s resurrection, they had been unable to mourn and fast because of the Lord’s presence, it is entirely clear that after his departure they subjected themselves to voluntary fasts.

For once they had been refreshed by receiving the Holy Spirit, they turned their minds completely away from the desire for food, just as from all other worldly enticements: rejoicing in nourishment for the soul rather than for the body, and devoting themselves to salutary prayers and tears in remembrance of the heavenly homeland. Finally, through Luke’s account we learn how sparingly those three thousand men who believed on the very day of Pentecost, when Peter preached, were content with food, and how sober and heavenly a life they led on earth.

“They were persevering,” he says, “in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread and in prayers” (Acts 2). And shortly afterward: “Every day they continued together in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, they received their food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God,” and other things of this kind.

We must diligently conform our life and conduct to their example, because it is the perfect teaching of life always to imitate the deeds of the primitive Church and to preserve to the end that pattern of spiritual building which clearly was set forth by the apostles themselves on the foundation of faith. Nor should we doubt that, if we now follow in their footsteps, we shall in the future attain their rewards [Al.: “their footsteps”].

Indeed, my brothers, even in the present we bear a most beautiful image of future blessedness, of which we have touched briefly on a few points. But we must live in such a way that what we celebrate outwardly in image we preserve with a truthful heart before the eyes of our inner judge. Let us, then, persevere in the teaching of the saints, so that, learning what they teach and practicing it in our works, we may devote ourselves to constant prayers; let us strive to be worthy of communion in the Lord’s bread; let us remain together in the church at the canonical hours; let us offer bread to our needy neighbor, or whatever consolation of piety we are able to provide [Al.: adds “with affection”]; and let us indulge the body with food in such a way that the memory of the living bread rather gladdens the inmost recesses of the mind. Let us preserve simplicity of heart in all things, which means doing good works with the sole intention of heavenly reward. And, as especially befits the present festivals, let us sound forth the hymn of divine praise together, with one voice and one mind.

For our praise becomes pleasing to our God only if we do not contradict in our works what we sing with our mouths; if, while uttering “Alleluia” with our lips, we keep our hearts pure from shameful and evil thoughts. Our praise will nevertheless be sweet to him if we delight not in things fleeting and base but in the Lord. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who through the Paschal sacraments has granted us such great and splendid pledges of his benefits, deign to bring this about. He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XI: ON THE VIGIL OF PENTECOST

**John 14.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you for ever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him,” and so forth.

Because today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the coming of the Holy Spirit, we ought to correspond to the solemnity that we celebrate. For only in this way do we celebrate worthily the joys of this festival [Al.: ‘of this great festival’]: if, with the Lord’s help, we render ourselves suitable for the Holy Spirit to come to us and deign to dwell within us. We are fit for the coming and illumination of the Holy Spirit only if our hearts are filled with divine love and our bodies are devoted to the Lord’s commandments. Therefore, at the beginning of this Gospel reading, the Savior [Al.: “the Truth”] says to the disciples:

“If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete.” *Paraclete* means “comforter” in translation. And the Holy Spirit is rightly called the Paraclete, because he lifts up and refreshes the hearts of the faithful with the desires of heavenly life, so that they may not fail amid the adversities of this age. Hence, as holy Church grew, it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “And the Church was built up, walking in the fear of the Lord, and was filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 9).

What he says, then—“If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete”—was fulfilled in the very disciples, whom there is no doubt truly loved him and truly obeyed his commandments [Al.: “who doubt that they truly loved him …”] on this day, when, as they were praying in the upper room, the Holy Spirit suddenly appeared to them in fiery tongues. He taught them in their mouths through the diversity of languages, and strengthened them in their hearts through the consolation of his love.

They had previously had a Paraclete as well: namely, the Lord himself, dwelling with them in the flesh. Through the sweetness of his miracles and the assistance of his preaching, they were accustomed to be raised up and strengthened so that they might not be scandalized by the persecution of unbelievers. But because, after the resurrection, he ascended into heaven and thus departed from them bodily—although the presence of his divine majesty was never absent from them—he rightly added concerning this Paraclete, that is, the Holy Spirit:

“To remain with you for ever.” For he remains for ever with the saints: in this life he continually illumines them inwardly and invisibly, and in the future he introduces them perpetually to contemplate the appearance of his majesty. We too, dearest brothers, if we love Christ perfectly, so that we prove the truth of that love by observance of his commandments [Al.: ‘by pure observance’], he too will ask the Father for us, and the Father will give us another Paraclete. He will ask the Father according to his humanity, while according to his divinity he will give with the Father.

For we must not suppose that before his Passion he asked for the Church but does not ask now after his ascension, since the Apostle says of him: “He is at the right hand of God, and he also intercedes for us” (Romans 8). We too have a Paraclete, our Lord Jesus Christ. Although we cannot see him bodily, we hold in the Gospels the things that he did and taught in the body. If we devote care to hearing, reading, discussing with one another, and preserving in heart and deed these things, it is certainly clear that we shall overcome the troubles of this age with the greatest ease, as though the Lord were continually dwelling with us and consoling us.

If, then, we love this Paraclete and keep his commandments, he will ask the Father, and the Father will give us another Paraclete—that is, he will mercifully pour the grace of his Spirit into our hearts. In the midst of the adversities of our present exile, this grace will gladden us with the expectation of the heavenly homeland, so that with the Prophet we may say: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your *paracleses*—that is, your consolations—have gladdened my soul, Lord” (Psalm 93).

“Another Paraclete,” he says, “he will give you, to remain with you for ever.” And he added:

“The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive.” He calls “the world” those who are devoted to the love of this world. Conversely, the saints who burn with heavenly desire are rightly called “heavens,” as the Psalmist says: “And the heavens will declare his righteousness to the people who will be born” (Psalm 21). This means: Those who are lofty in mind, voice, and action—the teachers—will declare his righteousness to the people who, by coming to faith, now desire to be born in him.

Whoever, then, seeks consolation outside in worldly things cannot be inwardly renewed by the gift of divine consolation. Whoever longs for the lowest pleasures cannot receive the Spirit of truth. For the Spirit of truth flees the heart that he sees subjected to vanity, and he refreshes with the light of his coming only those whom he sees carrying out the commandments of truth through love. Thus, when he had said, “whom the world cannot receive,” he immediately added:

“Because it does not see him or know him. But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” Unbelievers did indeed see the Lord and Savior in the flesh before the Passion, but only believers could know that he was the Son of God and that he was the Paraclete sent by God into the world. Unbelievers could neither see the Holy Spirit with their eyes nor know him in their minds, because he did not appear to the disciples clothed in humanity. Rather, he chose to come to them and remain with them in such a way that he consecrated for himself a most welcome dwelling in their very hearts.

This is what he says: “But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” He who remains invisibly with the elect in this life also invisibly bestows upon them the grace of knowing him.

“I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” It seemed to the faithful that, when the Lord died on the cross, he would leave the disciples orphans. But he did not leave them orphans: after his Passion he presented himself alive to them with many proofs, appearing to them for forty days [Al.: omits “appearing to them”], and ten days after his assumption—that is, on this very day—he bestowed upon them from heaven the gift of the Holy Spirit. No one who understands the nature, power, and operation of the holy Trinity to be inseparable doubts that Christ himself came to them.

Expounding this more fully, he declares how greatly their cause is distinguished from an unholy nation:

“A little while, and the world will no longer see me. But you will see me, because I live, and you will live.” Since he was saying these things as he was going to his Passion, the interval until the time when the Passion was completed was short; after that, the wicked would never be able to see him. For only the righteous, who had been saddened by his death, were deemed worthy to see the joy of the resurrection. But those who rejoiced when they saw his death could not rejoice when they saw his resurrection; they had only to be troubled and grieved when they heard of it, as was fitting.

“But you will see me,” he says, “because I live, and you will live.” He used “I live” in the present tense and “you will live” in the future, because he saw that his own resurrection was near. Thus he named as present the hour in which, once death had been destroyed, he would rise again to eternal life. But he knew that their life was to be deferred to the future: each of them had to struggle for entry into everlasting life until the time appointed for his death, and they had to await the resurrection of their bodies until the end of the age.

He says, then: “A little while, and the world will no longer see me; but you will see me, because I live, and you will live.” It is as though he plainly said: “A little while, and those who love the world will cease to see me as a mortal; but they cannot see me rising from the dead, because they do not know that life whose lovers alone are deemed worthy to behold the glory of my resurrection. But you will be able to see me after these things for this reason: because I live, raised from the dead, and you are worthy to be strengthened by the example of my resurrection, since you too will come to perpetual life and to the joys of the blessed resurrection.”

“On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you.” Even then the apostles knew that Christ was in the Father through the unity of indivisible divinity; they knew that they were in Christ through the acceptance of faith and his sacraments; they knew that Christ was in them through love and the observance of his commandments. For he himself said to them: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

The apostles had certainly been instructed by Christ in these matters even then, and now the whole Church of Christ knows them, having been instructed through the apostolic writings. But on that day when the righteous truly begin to live, they know these things far better—namely, on the day of the resurrection, when they know all that is to be known more perfectly, the nearer they behold without end the very source of knowledge.

There is no doubt that this also occurs before the time of the resurrection for certain more perfect saints, namely, for those who can say with the Apostle [Al.: “with Paul”], relying on their good works: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ, for to me to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Philippians 1).

The Lord seems to address all these things especially to the apostles. But lest we think that he promises the blessedness of divine knowledge only to them and not also to us, if we follow their examples, he added a general statement after these words and promised the same rewards of his vision and knowledge to all who love him, saying:

He who has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him.

Here it must be considered with the fullest attention that truly to love Christ is not to profess that love with the lips, but to keep by one’s deeds the commandments of Christ, which we have received by learning. Hence John also admonishes us, saying: “My little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and in truth” (II John 3).

We must embrace with complete joy [Al. omits *nobis*, “for us”] the fact that the reward of our true love will be one greater than which none can exist: namely, that we shall be loved by the Father and the Son, and that the glory of the Son of God will be revealed to us for perpetual contemplation. We must not doubt [Col. 0193B] that those to whom the glory of the Son will be revealed will likewise be permitted to behold the Father and the Holy Spirit, because where there is one divinity, there is also one and inseparable vision. For this reason he says: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14).

It should also be noted that, when he said with a verb referring to the present, “Whoever loves me,” he added what belongs to the future: “will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” The Son, together with the Father, loves his lovers even now; but now he loves them so that they may live rightly through faith working by love [Al. *ex fide*, “from faith”]. Then he will love them so that they may attain the vision of the truth, which they had tasted through faith and for which they had contended even unto death.

Nor is it without the added phrase that he says, “And I will manifest myself to him.” He will make himself manifest to all human beings, but will manifest his very self only to the elect. The reprobate too will see Christ at the judgment, but, as it is written, “they will look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19); only the eyes of the righteous will see the King in his beauty. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

Thus far, dearly beloved, we have spoken to your fraternity about the Gospel reading, explaining it insofar as the Lord granted. It now seems appropriate to say briefly something further about today’s solemnity [Al. *ordine*, “order”]. First of all, it must be known that this solemnity was consecrated not only by evangelical graces, but was also foreshadowed long ago by legal mysteries and, by the Lord’s command, observed every year with sacred ceremonies.

For on this day, as we know, when the disciples were assembled in the upper room, suddenly there came a sound from heaven, and the Holy Spirit, appearing in the form of fire, bestowed upon them knowledge of all languages. When this sound had been made, devout men who had gathered at Jerusalem from various nations for the sake of the paschal festival came together; they were astonished and amazed because each one heard them speaking in his own language of the mighty works of God.
