When the disciples explained that what they were seeing was the grace of the Holy Spirit, formerly promised through the voice of the prophets and then sent as Christ’s gift, about three thousand of them believed; and, having been baptized, they too received the gift of the Holy Spirit.

This is the annual celebration of this day; this is the festival of heavenly grace, ever pleasing. To impress its memory more firmly upon the hearts of the faithful [Col. 0194A], a most beautiful custom has arisen in the holy Church: every year the mysteries of baptism are celebrated on it, and, when believers have been washed in the saving font, a venerable temple is prepared for the Holy Spirit who comes upon them. Thus, in it, not only is the memory of an event of the past renewed, but a new coming of the Holy Spirit is also celebrated among the new sons of adoption.

Let your charity therefore attend, my brothers, to how the type and figure of the legal feast corresponds to our own festival. The children of Israel, liberated from Egyptian slavery through the sacrifice of the paschal lamb, went out into the desert in order to come to the promised land, and they reached Mount Sinai. The Lord descended upon the mountain in fire, accompanied by the sound of a trumpet, thunderclaps, and flashes of lightning, and on the fiftieth day after the Passover had been completed he set forth the Ten Commandments of the Law [Col. 0194B] for them in an audible voice. In memory of the law that had been given, he established that every year, on the same day, a new sacrifice from the produce of that year—namely, two loaves of firstfruits—should be brought to his altar.

What the sacrifice of the paschal lamb and the deliverance from Egyptian slavery signify is clear to all who read: for Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed, and he is the true Lamb who took away the sins of the world. By the price of his blood he redeemed us from slavery to sin; by the example of his resurrection he showed us the hope of life and everlasting freedom.

On the fiftieth day after the killing of the lamb the Law was given, with the Lord descending upon the mountain in fire; and likewise, on the fiftieth day after the resurrection of our Redeemer—which is today—the grace of the Holy Spirit was given to the disciples assembled in the upper room [Col. 0194C]. When visible fire appeared outwardly, it invisibly illumined their hearts with the light of knowledge and kindled them with the unquenchable ardor of charity.

The height of the upper room here, and the summit of the mountain there, signify the sublimity of heavenly commandments and gifts. Since no one still clinging to lowly desires can either obey divine commandments or prove worthy of heavenly gifts, all those who received the Spirit were placed in the upper room as a sign of greater perfection. There, to signify the weakness of their hearers’ hearts, the whole people stood below the mountain, while only a few elders climbed partway up it.

Moses alone ascended to its very summit, where the divine majesty shone forth in fire and darkness [Col. 0194D], because only the more perfect know how to grasp and keep the higher and innermost secrets of the Law. The carnal people, content with the surface of the letter, stood outside and below, as it were, listening to the heavenly word from a lower place. Now, however, since the grace of the Holy Spirit has been given more widely, the hearts of the faithful are lifted up to understand more sublimely and fulfill more perfectly the sayings of the holy Gospel.

There, amid flames of fire and flashing lightning, the crash of thunder also sounded, together with the blare of a trumpet; here, with the appearance of fiery tongues, a sound likewise came from heaven, as of a mighty wind. Yet, although at both bestowals—the giving of the Law and the giving of grace—a sound was heard outwardly, here, with the hearing of the sound, there was also the greater miracle of the power of the heavenly gift, which taught the disciples’ hearts inwardly without sound [Col. 0195A].

There, when the legal ordinances had been heard, the whole people responded with one voice, saying: “All the words that the Lord has spoken, we shall both hear and do” (Exodus 19). Here, having received the illumination of the Spirit, the assembly of the newly born Church spoke of the mighty works of God in the languages of all nations—certainly for the sake of distinction—for the observance of the Law had been given only to the one nation of the Jews, whereas the word of the Gospel was to be preached throughout the world to all nations, so that the proclamations of the Christian faith might be spoken in the languages of all peoples. Thus the prophecy was fulfilled which says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise; the Lord is exalted above all nations” (Psalm 112).

Nor has what was commanded in honor of the Law that had been received—namely, that every year a new sacrifice should be offered to the Lord God at Pentecost—ever ceased to be performed spiritually in our own festival, from the time when grace was received. The Church offers a new sacrifice in it when, on the Sabbath beginning the holy Pentecost, it consecrates a new people of adoption to the Lord through baptism, in a truly fitting rite, as we have also noted above. Thus not only is the memory of the former event renewed among Christian peoples, but a new sending of the Paraclete by the Father is also celebrated in the new offspring of the reborn.

The apostles themselves also offered a new sacrifice to the Lord in it immediately after receiving the gift of the Spirit, when, by evangelizing those who had gathered, they converted many to the faith. Having been reborn in the baptismal font and sanctified by the grace of the Spirit, these people were offered as living firstfruits of the New Testament for communion at the Lord’s altar [Col. 0195C].

It was fitting that two loaves of firstfruits from the new harvest should be commanded to be offered, because the Church gathers people from both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles, whom it consecrates into the new household of its Redeemer.

Among these matters, one must carefully observe that the number fifty was not employed in the giving either of the Law or of grace without a great mystery. For the one was given to the people on the fiftieth day after Passover on the mountain, and the other was sent to the disciples in the upper room. This number clearly signifies the perpetuity of future rest: in it the Ten Commandments of the Law are rightly entrusted, and in it the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to human beings, so that it might plainly be shown that all who, with the help of the Spirit’s grace, fulfill the commands of the divine Law are certainly heading toward true rest.

Because the fiftieth year was commanded in the Law to be called the Jubilee—that is, “releasing” or “changed”—during which the people were to rest from every labor, all debts were to be remitted, slaves were to return free, and the year itself was to surpass the others in solemn ceremonies and divine praises, this number rightly indicates that tranquility of supreme peace. Then, as the Apostle says, “when the last trumpet sounds, the dead will rise, and we shall be changed into glory” (I Corinthians 15). The labors and afflictions of this age will have ceased, the debts of all sins will have been remitted, and the entire people of the elect will rejoice eternally in the contemplation of the divine vision alone, when that desirable command of our Lord and Savior has been fulfilled: “Be still and see that I am God” [Col. 0196A].

Since this repose and vision of unchangeable Truth can be attained only through observance of the heavenly commandments and the gift of the Holy Spirit, it was right that both the Decalogue and the grace of that Spirit should be given in a number signifying rest.

Nor should it be passed over that the number fifty is suited to signify inward rest because it is completed by seven weeks and one day. For in the Law the people were commanded to work for six days and rest on the seventh; to plow and reap for six years and cease in the seventh, because the Lord also completed the adornment of the world in six days and ceased from his work on the seventh.

Through all these things we are mystically admonished that those who in this age—which consists of six ages—devote themselves to good works for the Lord are brought by the Lord into the future Sabbath, that is, into eternal rest. The fact that seven days or years are multiplied sevenfold signifies the abundant fullness of that same rest, in which the sublime reward is given to the elect, of which the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Corinthians 2).

Since he testifies that knowledge of this reward cannot enter the human heart—that is, the heart of one who still possesses merely human understanding—he subsequently reveals how it can be shown to those who love God: “But to us,” he says, “God has revealed it through his Spirit.” Through the Spirit, therefore, the greatness of the everlasting reward is revealed. For while he inflames the hearts he fills with an invisible desire, he makes manifest how splendid those same invisible goods are and how greatly they are to be preferred to all earthly things [Col. 0196C].

Hence the sevenfold grace of that same Spirit is fittingly described by the prophet, because through his inspiration one reaches rest, and in his full reception and vision one possesses true rest.

Moreover, that fiftieth day or year, which follows the seven weeks and was venerable with a solemnity greater than the others, indicates the time of the future resurrection. Then the rest now enjoyed by the souls of the elect will also be increased by the glory of the bodies they have received.

Here, my brothers, it must be carefully understood that the Holy Spirit grants the righteous not only perfect rest in the future, but also the greatest rest in the present, when he kindles their minds with heavenly fire of charity. The Apostle says: “Hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5) [Col. 0196D].

This is the true—indeed, the only—rest of souls in this life: to be filled with divine love; to despise both the prosperity and adversity of the world through hope of heavenly reward; to uproot earthly desires completely; to renounce worldly lusts; to rejoice in insults and persecutions inflicted for Christ; and to be able to say with the Apostle: “We glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God; and not only that, but we also glory in tribulations.”

For whoever trusts that he can find rest in the pleasures and abundance of worldly things is deceived. The world’s frequent disturbances, and its very end, prove that he has placed the foundation of his rest upon sand [Col. 0197A].

But whoever, breathed upon by the Holy Spirit, takes upon himself that most gentle yoke of the Lord’s love and learns from his example to be meek and humble in heart enjoys even now some image of future rest. Separated in his whole mind from the disturbance of worldly people, he rejoices in always remembering the face of his Creator and longs to reach the perfection of his contemplation, saying with the Apostle John: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (I John 3).

If we desire to attain the reward of this vision, dearly beloved brothers, it is necessary that, remembering this Gospel reading continually, we present ourselves free from the enticements of the world [Col. 0197B], so that we may be found worthy to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the world cannot receive.

Let us love Christ, and let us keep his commandments, which we have received, by beginning and persevering. It is a just recompense that, by loving him, we should deserve to be loved more greatly by the Father; and he himself will also deign in the future to grant the greater grace of his love. By loving us now, he gives us the ability to hope in him as believers; then, he will enable us to see him face to face. He will manifest himself to us in the glory that he possessed with the Father before the world existed, with whom he lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XII. ON THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST

[Col. 0197C]

**JOHN 3.** At that time there was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, etc.

As you have heard from the reading of the holy Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, a ruler of the Jews came to the Lord by night, wishing to learn more fully, in a private conversation with him, the mysteries of the faith, of which he had already received some rudimentary understanding through the open display of signs. Because he took care prudently to understand what he saw being done by him, he deserved to investigate subtly [Al. *sublimely*] what he was asking him.

“Rabbi,” he said, “we know that you have come from God as a teacher. For no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.”

Thus he confessed that Jesus had come from God to provide the world with heavenly instruction; he understood from the miracles that God was with him, but he did not yet recognize that he himself was God. Since he approached earnestly for instruction from the one whom he knew as a teacher of truth, he rightly advanced, fully taught, to the knowledge of his divinity. He rightly learned the mysteries of both his births, namely, the divine and the human, as well as of his passion and ascension. He also learned, when the Lord revealed it, the manner of the second generation, the entrance into the kingdom of heaven, and many other mysteries of evangelical teaching.

Jesus answered and said to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone has been born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

This statement shines all the more clearly for all the faithful [Col. 0198A], since it is evident that without its light they cannot be faithful. For who can obtain remission of sins without the bath of regeneration and enter the kingdom of heaven?

But Nicodemus, who came to the Lord by night, did not yet know how to grasp the mysteries of the light. The night in which he came signifies the very ignorance by which he was oppressed. For he had not yet been joined to the number of those concerning whom the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5). Rather, he still remained among those to whom Isaiah speaks: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you” (Isaiah 60).

Nicodemus answered: “How can a person be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time [Col. 0198B] and be born?”

Because he still remained ignorant of the second birth, but had already become concerned about his salvation, he necessarily asked whether the one birth he knew could be repeated, or in what manner regeneration could be accomplished, lest, remaining without it, he be unable to share in heavenly life.

It should be noted, however, that what he said about carnal birth must also be understood of spiritual generation: namely, that once it has been completed, it cannot in any way be repeated. For whether a heretic, a schismatic, or any criminal person baptizes in the confession of the Holy Trinity, the one who has thus been baptized cannot be rebaptized by good Catholics, lest the confession or invocation of so great a name appear to be annulled.

Because Nicodemus, concerned by the Lord’s first response, carefully inquires how it should be understood, he now deserves to learn more fully [Al. *planius instrui*, “to be instructed more plainly”] and to hear that the second birth is not carnal but spiritual.

Jesus therefore answered him: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Subsequently explaining the manner of this birth and distinguishing it completely from the carnal, he says:

“What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.”

The nature of the spirit is invisible, while that of the flesh is visible. Therefore carnal generation is visibly carried out through visible growth: the one who is born in the flesh advances through the stages of life, whereas spiritual regeneration is accomplished wholly invisibly [Col. 0198D].

The person being baptized is indeed seen to descend into the font, is seen to be immersed in the waters, and is seen to rise from the waters; but what the bath of regeneration has accomplished in him cannot be seen at all. Only the devotion of the faithful knows this: a sinner descends into the font, but rises purified; a child of death descends, but a child of resurrection rises; a child of transgression descends, but a child of reconciliation rises; a child of wrath descends, but a child of mercy rises; a child of the devil descends, but a child of God rises.

Only the Church, that mother who gives birth, knows these things. To the eyes of those who observe [Al. *insipientium*, “of the foolish”], however, he seems to come out of the font just as he entered it, and everything being done appears to be mere play. Hence at the end, when they see the glory of the saints, they will say, groaning in their torments: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an example of reproach” [Vulgate: “of insult”] (Wisdom 5). “How, then, have they been counted among the children of God?”

The Apostle John likewise says: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (I John 3).

“What is born of the Spirit is spirit,” because the one who is regenerated from water and the Spirit is invisibly changed into a new person and from being carnal becomes spiritual. For this reason he is rightly called not only spiritual but also spirit: just as the substance of spirit is invisible to our sight, so the one who is renewed by the grace of God becomes invisibly spiritual and a child of God, although visibly he appears to all as flesh and a son of man.

It follows:

“Do not marvel that I said to you, You must be born again. The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

“The Spirit breathes where it wills,” because he himself has power over the one whose heart he enlightens by the grace of his visitation. “And you hear his voice,” when, in your presence, someone who has been filled with the Holy Spirit speaks; “but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes,” because, even if the Spirit fills someone for a time in your presence, you cannot see how he entered that person or how he returned, since he is invisible by nature.

“So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” Through the Spirit acting invisibly, such a person begins to be what he was not, so that unbelievers do not know where he comes from or where he goes—that is, because he comes from the grace of regeneration into the adoption of the children of God and goes into the reception [Col. 0199C] of the kingdom of heaven.

When Nicodemus was still asking how these things could happen, the Lord adds, saying:

“You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things.”

He does not say this as though wishing to insult the one called a teacher because he is ignorant of the heavenly mysteries, but to call him to the way of humility, without which the gate of heaven cannot be found.

“If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?”

He called them earthly things, as we found in the preceding reading, when he spoke of the passion and resurrection of his body, which he had taken from the earth, saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). Yet they did not believe the word he spoke, and they could not even understand that he was speaking of any temple other than the temple of his body [Col. 0199D].

If, then, they did not grasp earthly things when they heard them, how much less were they capable of grasping heavenly things—that is, the mysteries of divine generation? Yet the Lord still adds instruction both concerning heavenly mysteries and concerning earthly things for the one whom he sees attending wisely and diligently to what he hears.

His ascent to everlasting life is heavenly; his elevation to temporal death is earthly. He therefore speaks of heavenly things:

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

Then he adds what concerns earthly things:

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so the Son of Man must be lifted up” [Col. 0200A].

It is rightly asked how the Son of Man is said either to have descended from heaven or to have been in heaven already, at the time when he was speaking these words on earth. The confession of the Catholic faith is well known: the Son of God descended from heaven, assumed the Son of Man in the Virgin’s womb, and, when the dispensation of his passion had been completed, raised him from the dead and took him into heaven.

The flesh of Christ, therefore, did not descend from heaven, nor was it in heaven before the time of the ascension. Why, then, is it said, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven,” unless it is because Christ is one person existing in two natures?

For this reason the Son of Man is rightly said both to have descended from heaven and to have been in heaven before the passion: what he could not possess in his own nature, he possessed in the Son of God by whom he was assumed. On account of this same one person of Christ, who existed from two natures, the Apostle says: “The Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts 20) [Col. 0200B].

God did not have blood in his own substance with which he could shed it for the Church; he had it in the man he assumed. Hence the Psalmist also says: “God has ascended amid jubilation” (Psalm 46). For how could God ascend except in the man he assumed, since in the majesty of his own nature he is always present everywhere?

It must also be asked how it was said, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven,” when all the elect truly trust that they will ascend into heaven, since the Lord promises them: “Where I am, there also my servant will be” (John 12).

The clearest reasoning resolves this question: the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is the head of all the elect. Likewise, all his elect are members of that same head, as the Apostle says: “He gave him as head over the whole Church” (Ephesians 1), and again: “You are the body of Christ, and members individually” (I Corinthians 12).

“No one, therefore, has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.” This means plainly: no one ascends into heaven except Christ in his body, which is the Church. He first ascended in himself, in the sight of the apostles, who were his pre-eminent members; from that time onward, ascending daily in his elect, he gathers himself into heaven [Col. 0200D].

Hence this very body, found amid the adversities of the present age, rejoices and says: “Now he has exalted my head above my enemies” (Psalm 26), as though it plainly said: He who raised Christ, my head, slain by the Jews, from the dead, and, frustrating all the plots of his enemies, lifted him into heaven—I hope that, rescuing me also from present dangers, he will join me to my head in the kingdom.

Since, therefore, no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, whoever desires to ascend into heaven must be joined to him who descended from heaven [Al. adds *de vera*, “from true”] by the unity of faith and love, clearly understanding that no one can ascend into heaven by any other way than through him who descended from heaven. Hence he himself says elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14) [Col. 0201A].

These things are said to Nicodemus and to all catechumens so that they may learn to be incorporated by rebirth into the members of the one through whom they can ascend into the kingdom of God.

And because the ascent or entrance into the kingdom of heaven cannot take place without faith and the sacraments of the Lord’s passion, it is rightly added:

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

With great skill in heavenly instruction, the Lord leads the teacher of the Mosaic Law into the spiritual meaning of that same Law. He recalls an event of ancient history and explains that it was made a figure of his passion and of human salvation.

The Book of Numbers relates that, weary in the wilderness from the length and labor of the journey, the people of Israel murmured against the Lord and Moses; therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among them. When many had been wounded and killed by them, and they cried out to Moses, who prayed for them, the Lord commanded him to make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign: “Anyone who has been bitten and looks upon it,” he said, “will live.” And so it happened [Col. 0201B].

The wounds inflicted by the fiery serpents are therefore the poisons and incitements of vices, which bring about the spiritual death of the soul they touch. It was fitting that the people who murmured against the Lord should be struck down by the bites of serpents, so that from the outward order of the scourge they might recognize how great a destruction they were suffering inwardly by their murmuring.

The lifting up of the bronze serpent, by looking upon which those who had been bitten were healed, is the passion of our Redeemer on the cross; by faith in it alone the kingdom of death and sin is overcome.

Sins are rightly represented by serpents, which drag both soul and body to destruction—not only because they are fiery, venomous, and cunning in bringing about death, but also because our first parents were persuaded to sin through a serpent and, by sinning, were changed from immortal into mortal beings.

The Lord is rightly signified by the bronze serpent, because he came in the likeness of sinful flesh. Just as the bronze serpent had an image resembling the fiery serpents but had absolutely none of the burning poison that harms in its own members—indeed, by its being lifted up it healed those who had been bitten by serpents—so, truly so, the Redeemer of the human race did not assume sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh. In it, by suffering the death of the cross, he freed those who believed in him from every sin and even from death itself [Col. 0201D].

“Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so,” he says, “the Son of Man must be lifted up.” Just as those who looked upon the bronze serpent that had been lifted up as a sign were healed for a time from the bodily death and wound inflicted by the serpents’ bites, so those who, by believing, confessing, and sincerely imitating, look upon the mystery of the Lord’s passion are saved forever from every death which they had contracted in soul and body alike by sinning.

Hence it is rightly added: “So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

The meaning of this statement is clear: whoever believes in Christ not only escapes the punishment of destruction but also receives eternal life. This is the difference between the figure and the reality: through the former, bodily life was prolonged; through the latter, life is bestowed that will remain without end.

Yet we must carefully ensure that what the understanding rightly perceives is completed by fitting conduct, so that the confession of our true faith may, through a devout and sober manner of life, deserve to attain the life promised to us.

But because these things are said about the Son of Man, who could be lifted up on the cross and suffer death, lest Nicodemus think that he was merely the Son of Man, from whom everlasting life was to be expected, the Lord took care also to disclose to him the mystery of his divinity and to show that the one and same Son was both Son of God and Son of Man, the Savior of the world.

For it follows: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3) [Col. 0202B].

It should therefore be noted that he repeats concerning the only-begotten Son of God the same words that he had previously spoken concerning the Son of Man lifted up on the cross: “So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

For our same Redeemer and Creator, existing as the Son of God before the ages, became the Son of Man at the end of the ages. He who had created us through the power of his divinity restored us, through the frailty of our humanity, so that we might enjoy the blessedness of everlasting life and receive again the life we had lost.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we must strive to repay divine benefits by loving with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength God the Father, who first loved us with so great a love that he did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all.

Let us love the Son himself, who, although he existed in the form of God, for the sake of our freedom and life took the form of a servant and became obedient to the Father [Al. omits *Patri*, “to the Father”] even unto death, and death on a cross. As the Apostle John says of him: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Revelation 1).

Let us love the Holy Spirit of that same Father and Son, by whose grace we have been reborn and by whose anointing we have been sealed on the day of redemption. He breathes where he wills, and wherever he breathes he immediately kindles the flame of that divine love.

Let us believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God and our Lord, and let us exalt his name with due praises among one another. To him belong glory, dominion, and power, etc.

## HOMILY XIII. ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

**LUKE 1.** In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a certain priest named Zechariah, etc.

Our Lord and Redeemer, who was to come in the flesh, sent before him many witnesses and messengers of his dispensation. Born at different times from different tribes of the Israelite people, they proclaimed beforehand, through prophecy, the mystery of the same incarnation, not with different faiths but with one and the same understanding in every respect.

The last of these, and, as it were, a boundary between the Law and the Gospel, between figure and truth, was John. The Lord bears witness to this when he says: “The Law and the prophets lasted until John; from that time the kingdom of God is proclaimed in the Gospel” (Matthew 11). For this reason he was also called more than a prophet: what the others had foretold from afar through prophecy alone, he both marked beforehand by prophecy as still to come and shortly afterward displayed by pointing him out as already present.

He is certainly said to have been born, through the grace of the divine dispensation, not only to righteous parents but to parents descended from the priestly line.

For he was a priest, as we heard from the Gospel reading, named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah; and he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, whose name was Elizabeth. Both, moreover, were righteous before God. He was begotten of righteous parents, so that he might give the precepts of righteousness to the people with greater confidence, since he himself had learned these things not as novelties, but had preserved them as received from his ancestors by hereditary right [Col. 0203B]. He was born of a priestly lineage, so that he might proclaim the imitation of the priesthood with greater authority, since it would be clear that he himself belonged to the priestly order.

For when our Redeemer appeared in the flesh, just as he deigned to become our king by granting us the heavenly kingdom, so also he became a high priest by offering himself to God on our behalf as a sacrifice of sweet fragrance. Hence it is written: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109; Genesis 14). Melchizedek, as we read, the priest of the Most High God, came long before the times of the priesthood of the Law, offering bread and wine to God. And therefore our Redeemer is said to be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, because, when the legal sacrifices had been removed, he instituted the same kind of sacrifice in the New Testament by offering the mystery of his body and blood [Col. 0203C].

Who, then, could more appropriately prophesy the transformation of the legal priesthood, that is, the substitution of the evangelical priesthood, than the son of a high priest according to the Law? Although he himself might also have seemed able to become a high priest according to the Law, he preferred—taught inwardly by the unchangeable reason of truth—to be the herald of the new priest rather than the successor and heir of the old. Instructed by the Spirit, he preferred to preach the mysteries of the New Testament to peoples called into the desert, rather than preside over those coming to the temple in the most glorious office of the old priesthood at that time.

He preferred the long thirst and hunger of solitude to the continual solemnities of sacrifices [Col. 0203D]; garments of camel hair and a leather belt to the robes of the priests woven with gold. Why, my brothers, did he do these things, unless so that the one who had rightly claimed for himself the authority to preach on account of more perfect righteousness might also show, by disregarding the order [Al.: “by disregard,” with *order* omitted] of his father’s high priesthood, that he was without doubt the herald and forerunner of a better priesthood?

If it pleases your Fraternity to hear who Abijah was, from whose division Zechariah is said to have derived his lineage, he was the high priest in the time of King David. For, at the Lord’s command through Moses, Aaron alone was first established as high priest under the Law. After his death, his son Eleazar assumed the priesthood. When Eleazar too had died, his son Phinehas became his successor in the priesthood, and so down to the time of David [Col. 0204A] there were, for approximately four hundred and seventy years, successive heirs of the high priesthood, one after another.

But David, burning with great religious zeal and desiring to build a temple for the Lord, while the Lord preferred that it be completed through his son Solomon, nevertheless diligently prepared everything that would pertain to the future construction and reverence of that same temple. Accordingly, he also appointed singers who would daily resound with psalms and melody at the time of sacrifice, raising the minds of the surrounding people to the remembrance and love of heavenly things, not only through the sublimity of the words spoken, but also through the sweetness of the sounds by which they were spoken.

Wishing that, as the worship and magnificence of the temple increased, the dignity both of that ministry and of the ministers’ assembly might also increase [Col. 0204B], he summoned the entire offspring of Aaron’s sons—both those descended from Eleazar and those descended from the line of Ithamar—and divided them into twenty-four groups. From these he selected one high priest for each group, and commanded the others in those groups, who held the lesser priestly office now called the presbyterate, to perform their duties. He made this provision so that whenever any high priest died, whoever was considered the best in his group might succeed him in the high priesthood.

He arranged these groups in such a way that each high priest, with the priests subject to him, would minister for eight days, that is, from Sabbath to Sabbath [Al.: omits “that is, from Sabbath to Sabbath”]. Although all were equal in priestly rank, only one among them, whoever appeared more worthy, was to have the name of high priest, distinguished by special reverence and authority [Col. 0204C]. The order in which these groups were to serve was determined by lot before King David and the heads of the priestly families and the Levites. In the distribution of these lots, Abijah—of whose division and lineage Zechariah was descended—is found to have been placed eighth.

And rightly the herald of the New Testament, in which the glory of the resurrection is declared to the world, was born in the place of the eighth lot. For our Lord rose from the dead on the first day of the week, which is the eighth day from the day of creation; and after the six ages of this world and the seventh age of the rest of souls, which is in the other life, an eighth age of perpetual resurrection is promised to us at the end.

[Col. 0204D] “Both were righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame.” It often happens that those who are already judged perfect by human estimation still possess some deficiency in the eyes of the inward Judge. Conversely, it can happen that certain people, by devoting themselves excessively to particular works of virtue, offend the eyes of their neighbors while seeking to please God without knowledge.

The parents of blessed John are declared free from both these faults. For after it had been said, “Both were righteous,” the words “before God” are immediately added; and after it had been said, “walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord,” the phrase “without blame” follows. It is as though Scripture openly said: “They conducted themselves so carefully in both their actions and their thoughts [Col. 0205A] that they pleased both the divine gaze inwardly and human judgment outwardly,” according to the Apostle’s saying: “We take care to do what is good not only before God but also before human beings” (2 Corinthians 8).

“And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.” It was divinely arranged that John should be born of a barren mother and of parents both advanced in age, so that even by the miracle of his birth it might be revealed that the man who was born would be one of great virtue. For when all wantonness of carnal desire had ceased, it was evident that no cause of pleasure had been involved in his conception, but only the spiritual grace of offspring had been intended.

Thus Isaac, the son of promise, who was made obedient to his father even unto death as a figure of our Redeemer, was born of aged parents and a mother who had long been barren [Col. 0205B]. Thus also the patriarchs Jacob and Joseph, Samson, the strongest of the leaders, and Samuel, outstanding among the prophets, were born of mothers long barren in body but always fruitful in virtues. By the miracle of their births, the dignity of those born might be recognized, and it might be shown that those who transcended the laws of human condition at the very beginning of life would later be exalted in their manner of living.

What follows is:

“It happened that, while Zechariah was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to offer incense, and he entered the temple of the Lord.”

It is clear to everyone that, when the week of his division—assigned to him from the division of Abijah—returned in its regular order, he entered the temple to minister [Col. 0205C]. But it may be obscure to some because Scripture seems to be silent about the time of year when these events took place. They should be informed that Scripture did not omit this either, but quietly indicates it by what it adds:

“And all the multitude of the people,” it says, “was praying outside at the hour of incense.”

There was only one solemnity each year during which, when the high priest entered the Holy of Holies to pray, no human being was permitted to remain inside the temple doors; rather, at the time of the offering, everyone was commanded to pray outside. This solemnity had been established in the seventh month after Passover [Al.: “of Passover”], on the tenth day of the month. That day was called the Day of Propitiation or Atonement, because, after victims had been offered as burnt offerings on the altar, blood was brought into the Holy of Holies for expiation. Not only was blood sprinkled there, but incense was also burned, which the present reading records Zechariah as having done.

The Lord therefore says to Moses concerning this solemnity: “In the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict your souls, and you shall do no work” (Leviticus 16). “The high priest shall make atonement for the sanctuary, the tent of testimony, and the altar, as well as for the priests and the whole people. This shall be a perpetual ordinance for you, that you may pray once a year for the children of Israel and for all their sins.” A little earlier, when teaching the rite of that same atonement, he says among other things: “Let no one be in the tabernacle when the high priest enters the sanctuary to pray for himself, for his household, and for the entire assembly of Israel, until he comes out” (ibid.) [Col. 0206A].

It would be lengthy to provide the scriptural testimonies concerning each ceremony of this day, and much more lengthy to explain adequately how each is now enacted spiritually in the Church. Therefore, I especially wish to impress upon the ears of your Fraternity how fittingly the time was chosen in which the birth of the Lord’s forerunner and his future virtue were announced.

The seventh month and its tenth day are dedicated to this most sacred oracle, because the one whose birth was being proclaimed was destined to preach both the completion of observance of the Law and the beginning of evangelical grace. His birth was revealed who would be the first of all to show that the Lord and Savior was both to come and was already present. Of him it is written: “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10) [Col. 0206B]. The fulfillment of the Law is rightly represented both by the number seven, because of the Sabbath, and by the number ten, because of the Decalogue.

This was the day of propitiation and atonement, on which the entire people were commanded to abstain from work and to humble and discipline themselves through prayer and abstinence. This corresponds closely to the life and preaching of blessed John. He himself, abstaining from worldly works, devoted his mind solely to heavenly pursuits and desires; and he taught the crowds who came to him to abstain from evil works, to be cleansed through repentance and faith, and to be consecrated to Christ, because the time of divine propitiation was already approaching, when the entrance to the heavenly kingdom would be open to all who devoutly sought it [Col. 0206C].

The fact that on this day the high priest was commanded to atone for the sanctuary, the tent of testimony, the altar, the priests, and the whole people reveals who this high priest is and what this atonement is. When he came to his baptism, John said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). This atonement was appointed to be celebrated once a year because, as the Apostle says, “Christ was offered once to take away the sins of many; he will appear a second time, without sin, to those who await him for salvation” (Hebrews 9).

The fact that, when the high priest entered the sanctuary to pray, no one was permitted to be in the tabernacle until he came out signifies the weakness of the holy Church, which at that time was not yet capable of suffering for the faith. This was revealed in the apostles themselves, who, when his Passion began, all abandoned him and fled [Col. 0206D].

The high priest came out after the atonement had been completed so that the others might also be given the opportunity to enter the tabernacle. This signifies that, after Christ had completed the sacrifice of his Passion, he appeared to his disciples; and, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been given, he strengthened their hearts to offer sacrifices to God not only through the devotion of works and prayer, but also through their own blood.

We have explained these matters concerning observance of the legal festival at greater length so that your Charity might recognize how fittingly the new proclamations of grace began in that festival, in which the work of that same grace and the redemption of the whole world were signified in so many ways.

“An angel appeared to Zechariah as he was praying, standing at the right side of the altar of incense” [Col. 0207A].

It should be noted that the angel bears witness to the grace he had come to proclaim not only by the power of the words he uttered [Al.: “which his voice uttered”], but also by the time and by the position of the place in which he appeared. He appeared at the time of the priestly offering in order to signify that the true and eternal high priest was to offer a true sacrifice for the salvation of the world. He stood beside the altar of incense to show that he had come as the herald of the New Testament.

There were two altars in the temple, signifying the two Testaments in the Church. The first was the altar of burnt offering, covered with bronze and placed before the doors of the temple for the offering of victims and sacrifices; it signifies the carnal worshipers of the Old Testament. Then there was the altar of incense, covered with gold and placed near the entrance of the Holy of Holies, established for burning incense [Col. 0207B]; it signifies the inward and more perfect grace of the New Testament and of its worshipers.

He also stood at the right side of this altar to show that he promised human beings not earthly and inferior things, but the joys of heavenly and eternal blessedness, which are customarily signified by the right hand. He promised these especially to those who, through purity of heart, become themselves a golden altar; who, through continual reflection, stand near the entrance of the heavenly kingdom; who kindle the perfumes of their prayers to God through the fire of love; and who can say with the Prophet: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140).

When he said to Zechariah:

“Your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son,”

it should not be supposed that the high priest, who had entered to pray for the people, suddenly changed his mind and began to pray for private concerns, especially for children—when, as an old and decrepit man, he had turned all hope away from having offspring to such an extent that he did not believe the angel’s promise that a son could be born to him [Col. 0207C].

Rather, this must be known with certainty: he was praying for the salvation of the people, whom he knew to be afflicted by the greatest sickness of sins and additionally oppressed under the rule of a foreign king. Thus, through the angelic oracle, he learned both that he had been heard by the Lord and by what order the salvation he sought would come. A son would be born to him who, as an outstanding prophet and teacher, would turn that same people toward the way of truth and the hope of obtaining salvation [Col. 0207D]; and immediately afterward the Savior himself would follow, granting them the gifts [Al.: “joys”] of the heavenly kingdom.

“And you shall call his name John,” he said, “and he will be a joy and an exultation to you, and many will rejoice at his birth.”

It is a sign of great praise and virtue whenever, in Scripture, names are imposed or changed for human beings by God. The forerunner of our Redeemer is rightly commanded to be called John. *John* means “the grace of the Lord” or “in whom there is grace,” because he both received, beyond the other saints, the special grace of this fore-running office and came to preach to the world a heavenly grace of entrance previously unheard of.

Therefore, since he was full of grace and proclaimed God’s grace to others, he rightly signified the proclamation of grace even in his own name [Col. 0208A]. And it is rightly foretold that many would rejoice at his birth, through whom the author of the world’s regeneration was revealed.

“For he will be great before the Lord.”

It should be noted that the same proclamation of praise is attributed to John by the angel as is attributed to his parents by the Evangelist. They were righteous before God, and he is said to be great before the Lord. But the Lord himself, who alone both bestowed and knew the power of his greatness, indicates how great he was before the Lord, saying: “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11).

The angel also subsequently explained his greatness before the Lord in many ways:

“He will drink neither wine nor strong drink,” he said, “and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb, and he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God” [Col. 0208B].

By asserting that he would abstain from wine and strong drink—that is, from everything capable of causing drunkenness—the angel plainly indicated that he would be free from all vices and worldly allurements, which usually turn the mind from its proper state [Al.: “overthrow it”]. By stating that he would be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb, he clearly showed that, once born into the world, he would be glorified by every fruit of virtue.

For what virtue could be lacking in one who lived and moved among human beings, when, although he was conceived as a human being in iniquities, his mother nevertheless bore him—in accordance with the grace of remission—in a manner contrary to the usual condition of humanity, not in the sins of transgression? There is no doubt that the Holy Spirit, who filled him, also absolved him from all sins [Col. 0208C]. It is established by the truthful judgment of the Fathers that the gift of the Holy Spirit is not bound by the Law.

Therefore, the one who consecrated Cornelius and his household by his grace before their reception of baptism certainly also poured out the gift of that same grace upon John not only before his circumcision but even before his birth. Thus, while he was still in the womb, he offered the Lord the service of his forerunning office; since he could not yet do so by speaking, he already offered it by rejoicing. For, as the following passage of the holy Gospel bears witness, when the blessed Mother of God entered and greeted Elizabeth, the infant in her womb leaped for joy.

By asserting that he would turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, the angel also clearly indicated how great he would be before the Lord [Col. 0208D], declaring that he would conduct his life in the best possible manner. For what way of life among human beings could be more exalted and more pleasing to God than that of those who discipline themselves away from vices [Al.: “renounce them”], subject their minds to the pursuit of virtues, and also strive by daily practice to turn others toward the grace of their Creator, continually increasing the joy of the heavenly homeland through the acquisition of faithful souls?

“And he himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah.”

John is said to go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah because, just as Elijah, in the great power of the spirit, will precede his second coming, so John, endowed with no lesser power of the spirit, preceded his first coming [Col. 0209A]. As the former will be the forerunner of the Judge, so the latter became the forerunner of the Redeemer.

John preceded the Lord not only in the order of his coming, but also in the similarity of his teaching, in the spirit and power of Elijah. For, just as the angel continues concerning John:

“To turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous,”

so the Lord, through a prophet, uttered a similar statement concerning the preaching of Elijah, saying: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes, to turn the hearts of the fathers toward their children, and the hearts of the children toward their fathers” (Malachi 4) [Col. 0209B].

The work of both, therefore, is one and the same: namely, by preaching, to pour into the minds of children the faith and understanding possessed by the fathers.

The fathers are called the righteous, the ancient saints, of whom the Savior says to his disciples: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it.” The children, however, are called the disobedient people of that age in which either Elijah will preach or John preached.

John turned the hearts of the fathers toward the children because he transferred to the children, by teaching them to believe and rejoice that Christ had come in the flesh, the wisdom possessed by the fathers who believed in Christ and desired his coming in the flesh. He turned the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous because he taught those whom he found without faith in Christ, and vainly boasting in the works of the Law, to believe in Christ, to submit themselves wholly to his grace, and to imitate the wisdom of the earlier righteous. They had diligently striven to fulfill the Law, yet had learned to hope for salvation in the grace of the Lord Jesus, not in the righteousness of their own works [Col. 0209C].

One of them says: “The righteous person lives by faith.” Hence it is openly added:

“To prepare for the Lord a perfected people.”

This is the most beautiful perfection of the Lord’s people, which John prepared by preaching in his own time and which the Lord himself now fulfills more widely throughout the world by granting it: when we, instructed by evangelical words and imbued with the mysteries, learn to possess the same faith and love that the fathers, taught by the precepts of the Law, are shown to have possessed.

This is the most perfect adornment of the holy Church: that we long for the same joys of heavenly peace into which they are known to have entered, and that, in order to deserve to enter them ourselves, we strive to exercise a heavenly life on earth. Following their example, we attribute none of the good things we do or receive to our own merits, but in all things look to the grace of our Creator.

We are taught this also by their testimonies: he is God; he made us, and not we ourselves—not merely so that we might be human beings, but so that we might be holy and blessed human beings. If we pursue the gifts of his grace with a pure and tireless heart, may he, according to the promises of those same fathers, graciously forgive all our iniquities; may he satisfy our desire with good things; and may he crown us with eternal life—not on account of works of righteousness that we could possess from ourselves, but through the compassion and mercy that he himself has given. He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever, etc.

# HOMILY XIV. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

**Luke 1.** “At that time, the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they congratulated her,” etc.

The birth of the Lord’s forerunner, as the most sacred history of the Gospel reading reveals, shines with the great splendor of many miracles. For it was fitting that the one greater than whom no one born of women has arisen should immediately at his birth shine with a radiance of virtues greater than that of the other saints.

Aged and long-infertile parents rejoice in the gift of their most noble offspring. The mouth and tongue of the father himself, whom unbelief had made mute, are opened to greet the herald of the new grace. Not only is the ability to bless God restored to him, but the power to prophesy about him is also increased. All the neighbors, stirred by the report of what had happened, are struck with wonder and fear; and the hearts of all who heard are prepared throughout the surrounding region for the coming of the new prophet.

Therefore the holy Church throughout the world, which regularly celebrates the victories of so many blessed martyrs by which they merited entry into the heavenly kingdom, customarily celebrates, after the Lord’s own, this birth alone. It should by no means be thought that this custom arose without evangelical authority. Rather, it should be carefully stored in the mind that, just as the angel appearing to the shepherds at the Lord’s birth said, “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord” [Col. 0210C], so also the angel who announced John’s birth to Zechariah said: “He will be a joy and an exultation to you, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great before the Lord.”

The births of both are therefore rightly celebrated with festive devotion. But in the birth of the one—as Christ the Lord, as the Savior of the world, as the Son of almighty God, as the Sun of righteousness—joy is announced to all the people. In the birth of the other—as the Lord’s forerunner, as the outstanding servant of God, as the burning and shining lamp—many are said to rejoice [Al.: adds “to be”].

This one is said to be great before the Lord; concerning the other the Prophet bears witness: “For the Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise, and of his greatness there will be no end” (Psalm 47) [Col. 0210D].

The former, avoiding the company of sinners, abstained from everything that could cause drunkenness [Al.: “could intoxicate”]; the latter, living among sinners, remained free from every sin. The one was filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb; in the other “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” He himself, by the gift of his Spirit, consecrated the virginal womb in which he was to assume flesh as a dwelling for himself [Al.: *qui* (“who”) for *quam* (“which”); the alternative gives the grammatical sense].

The one turned many of the children of Israel to the Lord by preaching in his own time; the other does not cease daily to turn many from all the nations throughout the world to his faith and love by illuminating them inwardly.

The one went before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, baptizing his people with water and teaching them to be perfected in order to receive him when he appeared [Col. 0211A]; the other succeeded him in the spirit and power of God the Father, baptizing his people with the Holy Spirit and fire and granting them perfection so that they might see the face of his Father.

When John was born, the neighbors and relatives congratulated his mother because the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her. When the Lord was born, the angelic spirits congratulated the Church because the time had come for mercy to be shown to her. They are her neighbors and relatives—citizens, that is, of the same heavenly homeland which she too awaits [Al.: “which they themselves await”]—and, by singing a hymn of glory to God, they were the first to announce from heaven what she would accomplish throughout the world.

The birth of the one who approached the Lord’s works with such powerful greatness is therefore rightly celebrated. The solemnity of his birth is rightly honored, since the sublimity of his life was such that whatever is more exalted than he is plainly beyond human nature.

For when the Lord had said that no one born of women was greater than he, he immediately added: “But the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he,” clearly referring to himself. Although he came later than John in human birth, he was superior to him in the summit of the heavenly kingdom.

Nor is it without mystery that John’s birth is recorded as having occurred when the days begin to grow shorter, while the Lord’s occurred when the days begin to grow longer [Al.: “begins”]. John himself reveals the secret of this difference. When the crowds, on account of the greatness of his virtues, believed Christ to be John, while some, because of the weakness of the flesh, thought the Lord to be not Christ but a prophet, he said: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

The Lord increased because throughout the whole world it became known to believers that the one who had been thought a prophet was Christ. John decreased and was diminished because the one who had been considered the Christ was shown to be not Christ himself but Christ’s herald.

Therefore, rightly, when John was born, the daylight began to diminish, since the fame of his divinity was destined to cease and his baptism was soon to come to an end [Al.: “his baptism was soon destined to come to an end”]. Likewise, rightly, when the Lord was born, the shortened day returned to an increase of light [Al.: “returned”], because he appeared who would open to all the nations the light of knowledge of himself, which Judea alone—and even there only partially—had previously possessed, and would spread the warmth of his love throughout the whole breadth of the world.

[Col. 0211D] It should also be noted that this same birth of blessed John bears a certain resemblance to the Lord’s coming and to the grace he came to preach. For it is very fitting that the one to whom all the earlier prophets and patriarchs bore witness—whether by being born, dying, living, or preaching—should be designated by his forerunner, who was more than a prophet, not only in his life and Passion but also in his very birth.

Why was John born of aged parents, unless because the birth that was soon to follow his was being signified—the birth of the one who, bringing forth the mysteries of the New Testament, would teach that the carnal observance of the Law and of the old priesthood was now to come to an end? For what grows old and ages is close to destruction.

Why was the Lord’s forerunner born of a mute father [Col. 0212A]—namely, the chief of the priests at that time—unless because, when the Lord appeared, the tongue of the old priesthood had already become largely mute concerning the teaching of spiritual understanding? The scribes and teachers of the Law cared only for and taught the keeping of the letter; indeed, in many places they corrupted even the letter itself through their traditions, as the Lord is repeatedly shown in the Gospel to have reproached them.

And why was he born of a mother long barren, unless because the Law, which had been commanded, with the help of the priestly office, to beget spiritual offspring for God, brought no one to perfection? For it could not open the gates of the heavenly kingdom to its worshipers.

But the author of the Law himself, having been made subject to the Law, removed from the Law the reproach of barrenness. He showed that it was to be understood spiritually, and taught that the grace of heavenly blessedness, which now shines most openly in the Gospel, had long ago been prefigured and, as it were, conceived within it.

“And it happened,” he says, “that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were calling him by the name of his father Zechariah. But his mother answered and said, ‘No; he shall be called John.’”

John is interpreted as “the grace of the Lord” or “in whom there is grace.” This name signifies both the whole grace of the evangelical dispensation that he preaches and, in particular, the Lord himself, through whom that grace was given to the world.

Those who decided that the child should be called by his father Zechariah’s name rather than John clearly represent those who, when the Lord was revealing the new gifts of grace, desired him instead to preach the customary decrees of the old priesthood [Col. 0212C].

Hence Zechariah is rightly interpreted as “remembering the Lord,” because he figuratively proclaims the remembrance of the ancient observance, which was indeed given by the Lord.

Those who had gathered therefore disputed over the name of the newborn prophet and tried to have him called Zechariah. His mother, however, by her words, and his father, by writing, asserted that he should rather be called John.

There were some who were less skilled in the heavenly mysteries and who, at the beginning of the Gospel’s radiance, decided that the carnal ordinances of the legal priesthood were still to be observed together with it. The very teaching of the Law concerning the reception of Christ’s grace confirms them—like Elizabeth confirming John’s name with a living voice—when the Lawgiver says: “Your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall listen to him just as you listened to me, according to everything that he will speak to you” (Deuteronomy 18) [Col. 0212D].

The legal priesthood itself, through the silent types of its ceremonies and, as it were, the mute forms of its written signs, bears witness to the same grace as it arises, like Zechariah. For nothing at all in the observances of the old priesthood should be believed to have been done or said that did not, if rightly understood, express the grace of the Gospel.

When, after John’s name had later been declared and confirmed, Zechariah’s mouth was opened and he spoke, blessing God, it is plainly evident that, once the grace of the New Testament had been made known through the apostles, many even from the priestly class obeyed the faith. Abandoning their harmful silence, they devoted themselves to confessing, praising, and proclaiming the gifts of their Redeemer.

And indeed, on the day of John’s circumcision, when he also received his name:

“Fear came upon all their neighbors, and throughout all the hill country of Judea all these things were being spoken of” [Col. 0213A].

At the time of the Lord’s resurrection, however, when the glory of his name became known to the world through the apostles after the Spirit had been sent from above, a most salutary fear immediately shook not only the hearts of the Jews, who were his neighbors either by the location of their land or by their knowledge of the Law, but also the hearts of the nations abroad, to the ends of the earth.

The fame of his power surpassed not only all the hill country of Judea but also every summit of the worldly kingdom and of worldly wisdom, so that everywhere people abandoned their former worship and way of life and flocked to receive the mysteries of his faith.

The day of circumcision rightly bears the image of the Lord’s resurrection [Al.: “circumcision”], because it too took place on the eighth day, that is, after the Sabbath. And just as circumcision used to absolve from the guilt of perpetual death, so the resurrection both displayed in our Author the perfect newness of immortal life and showed that it is to be hoped for in us [Col. 0213B].

The fact that, during these events, Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied simultaneously about our Redeemer and our redemption signifies mystically that many from the priestly lineage, who had long kept their mouths closed in confessing Christ, would later be filled with the power of the Holy Spirit through the reception of his faith, raised up by the gift of prophecy, and placed before the people in the office of pastoral teaching.

It should also be believed that, in the same reception of the Spirit and in Zechariah’s prophecy, this too was fittingly prefigured: the time was approaching [Col. 0213C] when it would be disclosed to believers that all the rites and ceremonies of the legal priesthood abounded inwardly in spiritual knowledge and prophetic mysteries. These bore witness either to the temporal dispensation or to the eternal divinity of the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, according to what he himself says when rebuking the hardness of the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also. For he wrote about me” (John 5).

But let us hear what Zechariah said while prophesying and blessing God.

Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people. In these words, it should certainly be noted that blessed Zacharias, by prophetic convention, narrated as already accomplished what he had foreseen in the Spirit as begun and soon to occur. For the Lord visited us by appearing in the flesh, as though those who had withdrawn far from him were being sought out and justified, since they were placed in sins. He visited us as a physician visits the sick; in order to heal the long-standing illness of our pride, he applied to us the new example of his humility. He accomplished the redemption of his people: having paid the price of his blood, he freed us, who had been sold under sin and consigned to the service of the ancient enemy. Therefore the Apostle kindly exhorts us, saying: “You were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6). He says “his people” not, of course, meaning the people whom he found to be his when he came, but those whom, by visiting and redeeming them, he made his own. Would you like to hear, my brothers, what sort of people he found them and what sort he made them? The conclusion of this song, which, because of both its familiarity and its length, we have thought it tedious to recite and explain in its entirety to your charity, plainly declares, saying:

“He visited us, the dawn from on high, to shine upon those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.”

He therefore found us sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death—that is, weighed down by the long blindness of sins and ignorance, and deceived and besieged by the fraud of the ancient enemy, surrounded by errors. For he himself is rightly called death and falsehood, just as, by contrast, the Lord is called truth and life. He brought us the true light of his knowledge; having driven away the darkness of errors, he opened before us the sure path to our heavenly homeland. He directed the steps of our works, so that by walking along the way of truth which he showed us, we might be able to enter the dwelling of everlasting peace which he promised. Since we therefore possess these gifts of heavenly goodness and these promises of eternal gifts, dearest brothers, let us too bless the Lord at all times, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people. Let his praise always be on our lips; let us always retain his memory and proclaim his mighty deeds to one another [Al. adds: “his mighty deeds”], he who called us out of darkness into his marvelous light. Let us continually implore his help, so that he himself may preserve in us the light of knowledge which he has bestowed and bring it to completion on the final day. And in order that we may be worthy to be heard when we pray, let us cast away from ourselves the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light. For when we supplicate in this way, we quickly receive what we desire, because the hand of pious action assists the words of divine prayer. And since today we celebrate the feast of the blessed Forerunner’s birth, we ought to seek as the helper of our prayer the one whom we have received as the herald of eternal salvation. Let us therefore ask him, through his intercession, to obtain for us that we may be worthy to reach the light, life, and truth—to Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom he bore witness—who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, etc.

## HOMILY XV. ON THE VIGIL OF THE BLESSED APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

**John 21.** At that time Jesus said to Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” etc.

The present reading from the holy Gospel commends to us the virtue of perfect love [Col. 0214D]. Perfect love is that by which we are commanded to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. Neither of these loves can be perfect without the other, because God cannot truly be loved without one’s neighbor, nor can one’s neighbor truly be loved without God. Therefore, when the Lord repeatedly asked Peter whether he loved him, and Peter answered that he loved him—as the Lord himself knew—he added each time, concluding in this way: “Feed my sheep,” or [Al. adds: “Feed”] “my lambs.” It was as though he were saying openly: “This alone is the true proof of an undivided love of God: if you earnestly undertake the diligent labor of caring for your brothers.” For whoever neglects to offer a brother the work of mercy that he is able to offer shows that he loves the Creator less than he ought, since he disregards his command in supporting his neighbor’s need.

Since this charity cannot at all be possessed without the grace of divine inspiration, the Lord silently intimates this in a certain way when, questioning Peter about it, he calls him “Simon, son of John,” a title by which he is named nowhere else. “Simon,” he says, “son of John, do you love me more than these?” Although this may simply be understood as a reference to his earthly parent, it is not inappropriate for someone to wish to understand mystically that by the name “John” the household of heavenly generation is indicated. The Apostle John bears witness to this when he exhorts us: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves is born of God and knows God” (1 John 4). Simon means “obedient,” while John is said to mean “the grace of God.” Therefore it is rightly the case that the first of the apostles, when questioned about his love, is called “Simon, son of John,” that is, “obedient to the grace of God” [Al.: Latin *gratia*, “by the grace,” for *gratiae*, “of the grace”], so that it might be clearly shown to all that the fact that he obeys the Lord’s commands with greater obedience than the others, and embraces him with more ardent charity, is not a matter of human merit but of divine gift. Hence the Apostle Paul, strengthened by the same grace, said: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

Whoever is shown to love the Lord more fervently than the others is therefore called the son of John, because the power of this love is received only through the grace of the Spirit. Yet he himself—it should be noted—gives testimony to his lover with such caution and circumspection that, when the Lord asked whether he loved him more than the others, he did not dare to answer, “You know that I love you more than these,” but replied in a restrained and simple voice: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.” This is plainly to say: “I know that I love you with an undivided heart, as you yourself know better; but how much the others love you is unknown to me, though everything is known to you.” The caution of this answer is certainly an instruction for our speech and thought alike, so that by his example we may learn to presume less upon the purity of our own conscience and to judge less rashly the hidden matters of our brothers’ consciences, especially in doubtful matters, and [Al. omits: “and”] matters whose intention or necessity we cannot discern.

For concerning the manifest faults of our brothers, we have not only the authority but also the command to judge them so that they may be corrected, as the Lord says: “If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him” (Matt. 18). But we are commanded to reserve their ambiguous actions—those which can be interpreted in either direction—for divine judgment. The Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts” (1 Cor. 4).

Peter himself restrained himself from answering more boldly in this interrogation by the Lord for the reason that he remembered having previously, when the Lord’s passion was imminent, attributed more steadfastness to himself than he possessed. He had promised that he was ready to go with him both into prison and into death, yet when danger came he was not even capable of confessing that he knew him or had ever been with him. Having therefore been instructed by that earlier danger, he was more cautious in speaking with the Lord, for he had learned well that the Lord knew the condition of the human conscience better than the conscience itself could in any way know it.

He dares define nothing at all concerning the hidden matters of his brother’s heart; but concerning the integrity of his own love, he gives the testimony not of himself alone but also of the Lord who questioned him, saying: “Lord, you know that I love you.” O how happy and pure the conscience that does not fear saying to its Creator, who knows all things naked and open to his eyes: “Lord, you know that I love you”! How chaste and holy the soul that does not doubt that its thoughts are open to the Lord, and that knows it thinks nothing other than what the Lord approves!

Hence, in the Apocalypse, the hearts of the saints are aptly compared with golden bowls, as John says: “And they each held harps and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.” The elect have golden harps because all their speech, and everything about their deeds that, as rumor spreads, resounds to the knowledge of their neighbors, appears radiant with the light of pure love. They also have golden bowls, which are vessels spread open in broad capacity, because the more truly they feel their hearts glowing only with the fire of that same love, the more widely they rejoice to open them to the divine gaze. Therefore it is rightly added: “Full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.” The golden bowls overflow with the fullness of incense when the hearts of the righteous, shining with charity, become known to their neighbors also through the reputation of their spiritual virtues.

And beautifully, John himself, who saw these things, added by way of interpretation: “Which are the prayers of the saints.” For the incense of the bowls is the prayers of the saints, because whatever those who serve God with a simple intention do or say fulfills the role of prayer for them, whenever it commends the devotion of their minds to the divine gaze. Nor could we otherwise fulfill [Al.: Latin *valemus*, “we are able,” for *valeamus*, “we may be able to fulfill”] the apostolic command that says, “Pray without ceasing,” unless, with the Lord’s gift, we so directed all our actions, words, thoughts, and even our silences that each of these things was tempered by regard for his fear and all were made beneficial to our everlasting salvation [Al. “clear”].
