In his provident mercy, the Lord asks Peter a third time whether he loves him, so that by this threefold confession he might loosen the bonds by which Peter had been bound through his three denials; and so that as often as, terrified by the Lord’s passion, he had denied knowing him, so often, restored by his resurrection, he might testify that he loved him with his whole heart. In his provident dispensation, after Peter had confessed his love three times, he likewise entrusted his sheep to him to feed three times, because it was fitting that as often as he had faltered in the shepherd’s faith, so often, with his faith renewed, he should be commanded to care for the members of that same shepherd.

What he says to him here—“Feed my sheep”—is certainly what he had said to him more explicitly before his passion: “But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22). To feed Christ’s sheep, therefore, is to strengthen those who believe in Christ so that they do not fall away from the faith, and to labor earnestly so that they may advance more and more in faith.

It should be observed more carefully, however, that this feeding of the Lord’s flock is to be carried out not with uniform but with manifold care. For the ruler must diligently see to it that earthly assistance is not lacking to his subjects; he must also provide them with examples of virtue together with the word of preaching. If he discovers anyone opposing either their spiritual or even their ordinary welfare, he must resist that person’s violence as far as he can. And when his subjects happen to go astray, he must, in the words of the Psalmist, “Let the righteous strike me in mercy and reprove me,” and must not soothe their hearts with the harmful oil of consent (Ps. 140). This too belongs to the office of a pious shepherd. For anyone who neglects to correct the faults of his subjects and, as far as he is able, to heal the wounds of sin in them—on what grounds does he presume to number himself among the shepherds of Christ’s sheep [Al. “of the sheep”]?

The shepherd must also hold firmly in his heart that he is to treat those over whom he presides not as his own, but as the flock of his Lord, according to what is said to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21). “My,” he says, “not yours. Know that my sheep have been entrusted to you, and remember that you are to govern them as mine if you love me perfectly, so that you seek in them my glory, my lordship, and my gains, not your own.” For there are some who feed Christ’s sheep not out of love for Christ, but for the sake of their own glory, domination, or profit.

Grieving over the multitude of such people, the Apostle Paul says to the Philippians: “I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be encouraged when I learn how things are with you. For I have no one so like-minded who will be sincerely concerned for you. For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2). Therefore, in the Gospel the Lord calls such men not shepherds but rather hirelings, saying that when the wolf comes, the hireling flees, because he is a hireling and has no concern for the sheep (John 10).

A clear and distinctive sign of a true shepherd—one whose care for the sheep is sincere—is that he is prepared not only to lack all the advantages of temporal life but also to lay down his very life for Christ’s flock. Thus, after he had entrusted his sheep to Peter to feed—that is, peoples to teach and govern—he immediately added, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (John 21).

By the stretching out of his hands he indicates the position of his limbs, by which he was to be attached to the cross; by another’s girding him he expresses the imposition of the bonds by which he was to be restrained by persecution [Al. “by the persecutor”]; and by being led where he did not wish he indicates the bitterness of death and passion, which his bodily weakness recoiled from, while the spiritual strength of his soul rejoiced to endure every adversity for the Lord. For he did not seek his own will, but the will of Christ, who sent him.

Having first entrusted the feeding of his sheep, the Lord then added to this first of shepherds the triumph of his own passion. “You will stretch out your hands,” he said, “and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” It was as though he were saying openly: “You will clearly prove how greatly you love me when, fighting for the life of my little ones, you reach death; and so that they may be saved both in body and in mind, you yourself will endure with steadfast courage of mind all the bodily torments that the adversary may wish to inflict.”

The evangelist himself subsequently indicates this when he says:

“Now he said this to signify by what death he would glorify God.”

Peter glorified God by his death when, through this evidence, he showed everyone how greatly God ought to be honored and loved, since, when given a choice, he preferred to undergo the torment of the cross rather than cease preaching the heavenly word. It should be noted that he glorified God not only by his death but also by his life and by the sufferings that preceded his death. He glorified God by his life because in everything he did he sought not his own will and praise but those of his Creator. He glorified him also by his sufferings, since no pressure from his persecutors could recall him from the services of heavenly love to which he had devoted himself.

But since, together with the memory of blessed Peter, we also celebrate today the feast of his fellow apostle Paul, let us see, dearest brothers, whether he too glorified God by his life, sufferings, or death. Indeed, he did glorify him. The evangelist Luke bears witness to this, for in the book of the Acts of the Apostles he devoted most of his account to describing Paul’s struggles and labors for Christ. Paul himself also bears witness to it, for he sprinkled the work of his writings, which he completed in fourteen Epistles, with what I might call the fragrance of Christ.

Whatever you read there either reveals the mysteries of faith, displays the fruits of good works, promises the joys of the heavenly kingdom, recounts what he himself endured while preaching amid tribulations [Al. “whatever”], reports what he received of divine consolation amid tribulations [Al. “whatever”], or intimates by a general exhortation that persecutions cannot be absent from all who wish to live devoutly in Christ.

His life bears witness to how greatly he glorified God. When he was in chains and approaching his passion, he set forth the example of his own work to Timothy in an Epistle, saying: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4). He showed by what death he would glorify God when he prefaced this with: “For I am already being poured out as a sacrifice, and the time of my departure is at hand.” O how precious in the sight of the Lord was the death of that saint, who knew clearly and had proclaimed in a free voice that to be killed for the Lord was nothing other than to be offered to God as a most pleasing and most pure sacrifice!

Paul therefore glorified God, and the other apostles glorified him as well, because they too loved Christ with pure hearts and cared for Christ’s sheep with sincere intention. What was said to Peter—“Feed my sheep”—was certainly said to them all. The other apostles were what Peter was, but primacy was given to Peter so that the unity of the Church might be commended. They are all shepherds, but one flock is shown: that flock was then fed by all the apostles in unanimous agreement and thereafter is fed by their successors with shared care. Many of these are proved to have glorified their Creator by death, and all by their life.

Not only those great lights of the Church, but also the remaining multitude of the elect glorifies God, each in his own time, either by living or by dying. We too, my brothers, must follow their footsteps in our own time, both by directing the order of our life according to the examples of the good and by persevering in the rectitude of life we have undertaken until death, so that, becoming their companions in conduct, we may also deserve to become companions in reward.

We shall accomplish this if, according to the tenor of this most sacred reading, we embrace our Redeemer with the affection due to him and keep watch with fraternal concern for the salvation of our neighbors. May he himself assist us, who both commands us to do these things and promises to reward them when done: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVI. ON THE FEAST OF THE BLESSED APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

**Matthew 16; Mark 8; Luke 9.** At that time Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi and questioned his disciples, saying: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” etc.

The reading from the holy Gospel which you have just heard, brothers, must be pondered with all the greater attention and retained continually without forgetfulness, since it clearly commends to us a great perfection of faith and equally demonstrates the great strength of that perfected faith against every temptation [Col. 0219C]. If we wish to know how one ought to believe in Christ, what could be clearer than Peter’s statement to him: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”? Again, if we are pleased to hear how powerful this faith is, what could be more explicit than the Lord’s statement concerning the Church that was to be built upon him: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it”? These matters, however, will be explained more fully in their proper places. Now, returning to the exposition of the Lord’s reading in order, let us first consider the place in which he is said to have been staying [Col. 0219D].

“Jesus,” he says, “came into the region of Caesarea Philippi.” As Luke attests (chap. 3), Philippus was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis. He therefore founded a city at the place where the Jordan rises at the foot of Mount Lebanon, which is the boundary of Judaea toward the north, and called it Caesarea Philippi, in memory of his own name and likewise in honor of Tiberius Caesar, under whom he ruled.

When Jesus came into that region, he questioned his disciples, saying: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” He does not inquire as though ignorant of the opinion about him held by the disciples or by outsiders, but asks the disciples what they think of him so that he may reward their confession of the right faith with a worthy recompense. For just as, when all were questioned generally, Peter answered as one for all, so what the Lord answered Peter, he answered in Peter to all.

He asks what the others think of him so that, after the opinions of those who were in error had first been stated, the disciples might be shown to have received the truth of their confession not from common opinion but from the mystery of the Lord’s own revelation. “Who,” he says, “do people say that the Son of Man is?” He aptly calls those who knew only how to speak about the Son of Man “people,” because they did not know the mysteries of his divinity. For those who know how to grasp the mysteries of his divinity are rightly said to be above human beings, as the Apostle testifies: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2; Isa. 64).

After prefacing these words about human beings—that is, about those who are wise only with a human heart, ear, and eye [Al. “of human beings” and “of the wise”]—he immediately added something about himself and those like him who had transcended the general knowledge of humanity: “But to us God has revealed them through his Spirit” (ibid.). The same is true here: when the Lord had asked the disciples whom people said he was, and they had first reported the various opinions of various people, he said to them:

“But you, who do you say that I am?”

It was as though he were separating them from the generality of human beings and indicating that they had become gods and, by adoption, sons of God, according to the Psalmist’s words: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81).

Simon Peter answered and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

He calls him the living God in distinction from false gods, whom the Gentiles, deceived by various errors, either fashioned for themselves from dead human beings or, in even greater madness, created from insensible matter for worship. Of such gods it is sung in the Psalm: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths and will not speak,” etc. (Ps. 115).

Let your charity note the remarkable distinction by which it came about that, when a statement concerning both natures of the same Lord and our Savior was to be made by the Lord himself and by his faithful disciple, the Lord himself professed the humility of the humanity he had assumed, while the disciple displayed the excellence of his divine eternity. The Lord spoke of himself concerning what is lesser; the disciple declared concerning the Lord what is greater. The Lord spoke of himself concerning what he became for us; the disciple declared concerning the Lord that he is the one who made us.

Thus, in the Gospel, the Lord customarily calls himself the Son of Man much more often than the Son of God, in order to remind us of the dispensation he undertook for us. But the more humbly we remember that for our exaltation he descended to the weakness of humanity, the more necessary it is for us reverently to honor the heights of his divinity. For if, amid the mysteries of his incarnation by which we were redeemed, we always recall with devout mind the power of his divinity by which we were created, then we too, together with Peter, shall be granted the reward of heavenly blessedness. Since Peter confessed him to be the Christ, the Son of the living God, let us see what follows:

But Jesus answered and said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah.”

It is therefore clear that after the true confession of Christ, the true rewards of blessedness remain. But let us attentively consider what sort and what magnitude of name this is by which he glorifies the perfect confessor of his name [Al. “what”], so that by truly confessing him we too may deserve to share in it.

“Blessed are you,” he says, “Simon Bar-Jonah.” *Bar-Jonah* is said in Syriac and means in Latin “son of a dove.” The Apostle Peter is rightly called the son of a dove, because the dove is a very simple animal, and he followed the Lord with prudent and devout simplicity, mindful of the command which he had received from the same teacher of simplicity and truth together with his fellow disciples: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10).

Or certainly, because the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, he is rightly called the son of a dove, since he is shown to have been filled with spiritual grace. The Lord fittingly rewards the one who loves and confesses him when he testifies that he is a son of the Holy Spirit, by whom he himself is affirmed to be the Son of the living God, although no believer doubts that this occurs in very different ways. Christ the Lord is the Son of God by nature; Peter, like the other elect, is a son of the Holy Spirit by grace. Christ is the Son of the living God because he was born from him; Peter is a son of the Holy Spirit because he was reborn from him.

Christ is the Son of God before the ages—for he is the power and wisdom of God, which says: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything, from the beginning” (Prov. 8). Peter is a son of the Holy Spirit from the time when, illuminated by him, he received the grace of divine knowledge. And because the will and operation of the Holy Trinity are one, when he had said, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah,” that is, “son of spiritual grace,” he immediately added:

“For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

The Father revealed this to the son of a dove because the grace of the Father and of the Holy Spirit is one, and likewise the grace of the Son, as can readily be proved by examples from sacred Scripture. The Apostle says of the Father: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Gal. 4). The Son himself says of the Holy Spirit: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15). The Apostle says of the Holy Spirit: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12). The Father therefore sends the Spirit, the Son sends the Spirit, and the Spirit himself breathes where he wills, because, as we have said, the will and operation of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one.

Thus it is appropriately said that the Father who is in heaven revealed to the son of a dove the mystery of faith which flesh and blood could not reveal to him. “Flesh and blood” are rightly understood as human beings puffed up with the wisdom of the flesh, ignorant of the simplicity of the dove, and therefore utterly estranged from the wisdom of the Spirit. Of such people it was said above that, not understanding Christ, some said he was John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets [Al. adds “him”]. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2).

It follows:

“And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

Peter, who had previously been called Simon, received from the Lord the name Peter because of the strength of his faith and the steadfastness of his confession. He adhered with firm and tenacious mind to the one of whom it is written: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). Upon this rock—that is, upon the Lord and Savior, who granted his faithful knower, lover, and confessor a share in his own name, so that he might be called Peter from *petra*, “rock”—the Church is built [Al. omits Latin *supra quam*, “upon which”]. For it is only through faith and love of Christ, through receiving Christ’s sacraments, and through observing Christ’s commandments that one reaches the lot of the elect and eternal life, as the Apostle testifies: “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3).

“And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

The gates of hell are wicked teachings, which, by leading the unwary astray, drag them to hell. The gates of hell are also the torments and flatteries of persecutors, which, by frightening or softening the weak, open for them an entrance to eternal death by drawing them away from the stability of faith. The perverse works and foolish conversations of believers [Al. “unbelievers”] are also certainly gates of hell, insofar as they show their supporters or followers the path of destruction. For “faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself” (James 2); and “bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15).

There are therefore many gates of hell, but none of them prevails against the Church founded upon the rock, because whoever has received the faith of Christ with the innermost love of his heart easily despises whatever danger brought upon him from outside may assail him. But whoever, corrupted either in deed or through denial, betrays the faith of believers must be thought not to have built, with the Lord’s assistance, the house of his confession upon the rock, but, according to the parable in another passage (Matt. 7), to have placed it without a foundation upon sand—that is, to have appeared to follow Christ not with a simple and true intention, but to have assumed the Christian name for some earthly and fragile reason.

It follows:

“And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

Because he confessed the King of heaven with greater devotion than the others, he was deservedly granted the keys of the heavenly kingdom before the others, so that it might be clear to all that no one could enter the kingdom of heaven without that confession and faith. By the keys of the kingdom of heaven he names the knowledge and power of discerning by which he ought to receive the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy from the kingdom. Therefore he immediately adds:

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

Although this power of loosing and binding appears to have been given by the Lord to Peter alone, it must nevertheless be known without any doubt that it is also given to the other apostles, as he himself bears witness. After the triumph of his passion and resurrection, appearing to them, he breathed upon them and said to them [Al. “to all”]: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20).

Even now, moreover, the same office is entrusted throughout the whole Church to bishops and presbyters, so that, once they have learned the cases of sinners, they may mercifully absolve all whom they see to be humble and truly penitent from the fear of eternal death, while those whom they know to persist in the sins they have committed they may declare to be bound over to everlasting punishments. Hence elsewhere the Lord commands concerning a brother who has been rebuked once, twice, and a third time but has not repented, saying: “But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (Matt. 18). And lest anyone think it a small matter to be condemned by the judgment of the Church, he immediately added in a terrifying manner: “Amen, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

Authority to bind and loose is therefore granted to the whole Church of the elect, according to the measure of faults or repentance. But blessed Peter, who confessed Christ with true faith and followed him with true love, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the primacy of judicial power in a special way, so that all believers throughout the world might understand that whoever separates himself in any way from the unity of that faith or fellowship can neither be loosed from the bonds of sins nor enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must devote our whole attention both to learning the mysteries of the faith he taught and to displaying works appropriate to that faith. We must with complete vigilance avoid the manifold and subtle snares of the gates of hell, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may deserve to be rescued from them and to enter the gates of the daughter of Zion—that is, the joys of the heavenly city—in order to proclaim his praises.

Nor should we think that salvation is assured for us merely because we equal the crowds of the negligent or of any unlearned people in faith or conduct, when the sacred writings prescribe one rule both for believing and for living. Whenever examples of those who go astray are presented to us, let us immediately turn away the eyes of our mind so that they do not see vanity, and let us diligently search our hearts to discover what truth itself decrees. Let us follow the example of blessed Peter, who, rejecting the sects of those who went astray, brought forth with an unwavering confession of his mouth the mystery of the true faith which he had learned and preserved it with unconquerable care of heart.

We have learned here about the confidence of his confession; elsewhere he himself bears witness to the power of a single love for Christ. When some of his disciples were leaving him, and he said to the Twelve, “Do you also wish to go away?” Peter answered him, saying: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have known and believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God” (John 6).

If, therefore, my brothers, we earnestly strive to imitate his example according to our measure, we too shall be able both to be called blessed with him and to be blessed. The name of Simon—that is, “obedient to Christ”—will also suit us; and because of the simplicity of our unfabricated faith and the grace received from the Lord, we shall be called sons of virtues, sons of a dove. Rejoicing in the spiritual progress of our souls, he himself will say: “How beautiful you are, my beloved! How beautiful you are! Your eyes are like doves” (Song 4).

Thus it comes about that, as we build upon the rock of faith gold, silver, and precious stones—that is, perfect works of virtue—no fire of tribulations causes us harm, and no storms of temptations prevail against us. Rather, tested by adversities, may we receive the crown of life which he himself promised us before the ages, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BENEDICT, BISHOP

**Matthew 19; Luke 18; Mark 10.** At that time Simon Peter said to Jesus: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?” etc.

Hearing from the Lord that a rich man would enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty, and knowing that he and his fellow disciples had altogether spurned the delights of the deceiving world, Peter wished to learn what reward he and the other despisers of the world ought to hope for in return for their greater virtue of mind. And answering the Lord, he said:

“Behold, we have left everything and followed you.”

Here we must carefully observe that he glories not only in having left everything, but also in following the Lord. For it is plainly foolish—according to Plato, Diogenes, and certain other philosophers—to trample underfoot the riches of this life, yet not to do so in order to attain eternal life, but in order to pursue the empty praise of mortals; foolish to undertake present labors of one’s own accord, without hope of future rest and peace. But that person is perfect who, going away, sells everything he has and gives it to the poor, and then comes and follows Christ. For he will have an unfailing treasure in heaven. Therefore, when Peter rightly asked, Jesus said to such people:

“Amen, I say to you: you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

In this life, laboring for his name, he taught them to hope for a reward in the next—in the regeneration, that is, when we shall have been regenerated by rising into immortal life, we who had been born mortally into a transitory life. It is wholly just that those who here neglected the glory of human exaltation for Christ should there, glorified by Christ as judges, sit uniquely beside him, glorified as judges over human conduct; and that those who could not by any means be drawn away from following his footsteps should, by following him, arrive at the summit of judicial power.

Let no one suppose that only the twelve apostles will then judge, because Matthias was chosen in place of the traitorous Judas, just as not only twelve tribes of Israel are to be judged. Otherwise the tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth, would depart without judgment; and Paul, who is the thirteenth apostle because Matthias was chosen in place of the traitorous Judas, would be deprived of the lot of judging, although he himself says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more worldly matters?” (1 Cor. VI).

For it must be understood that all who, following the example of the apostles, have left everything of their own and followed Christ will come with him as judges, just as the whole human race will be judged. Since the number twelve often signifies universality in Scripture, the twelve apostolic thrones indicate the total number of those who judge, and the twelve tribes of Israel the totality of those who are to be judged.

Hence it must be noted that there will be two orders of the elect at the judgment. One consists of those who judge with the Lord, whom he mentions here: those who left everything and followed him. The other consists of those who are judged by the Lord—those who did not indeed leave all their possessions alike, but nevertheless took care to give daily alms from what they possessed to Christ’s poor. Thus they will hear at the judgment:

“Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. XXV),

and the rest—of which the Lord also speaks above in this reading, when a certain ruler asked what good he should do in order to possess eternal life [Al.: “what he might have perpetually”]:

“If you wish,” he said, “to enter into life, keep the commandments. You shall not commit murder; you shall not steal [Al.: “you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal”]; you shall not give false testimony; or, honor your father and mother, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” [Col. 0225C] (Matt. XIX).

Therefore, whoever keeps the Lord’s commandments enters into eternal life. But whoever not only keeps the commandments, but also follows the Lord’s counsel—which he gave concerning the contempt of the world’s riches and pleasures—not only will himself receive life, but will also judge the lives of others with the Lord. Thus, as we have said, there will be two orders of the good at the judgment.

We also learn from the Lord’s account that there will be two orders of the reprobate there. One consists of those who, having been initiated into the mysteries of the Christian faith, refuse to practice the works of faith. To them he testifies at the judgment [Al. adds: “it must be said”]:

“Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,”

and the rest (Matt. [Col. 0225D] XXV).

The second consists of those who either never received the faith and mysteries of Christ, or abandoned the faith they had received through apostasy. Of them he says:

“But whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John III).

Since they were unwilling even to honor Christ in word, they do not deserve to hear even his words by which they might be convicted at the judgment. They come to judgment only so that, together with the sinners who are judged, they may be sent into eternal condemnation.

But after recalling these matters briefly, and with due fear and trembling, let us rather turn our hearing toward the most joyful promises of our Lord and Savior. Let us see what great grace and kindness he promises his followers—not only the rewards of eternal life, but also extraordinary gifts in the present life [Col. 0226A].

“And everyone,” he says, “who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”

For whoever has renounced earthly affections or possessions for discipleship to Christ will find, in proportion as he progresses in love for him, more people who receive him with inward affection and rejoice to support him from their own resources: namely, people who share his profession and way of life, who delight in receiving into their houses and fields one who has become poor for Christ, and in refreshing him with a devotion of charity far greater than that shown by a wife, parent, brother, or natural child. When he says “a hundredfold,” this does not indicate the number of those who love and serve the faithful in Christ, but the universality and perfection with which they serve one another through charity.

Of this we ourselves, dearly beloved brothers, have often experienced an example, when, departing somewhere because of necessity, we found all the dwellings of the monasteries open to us as though they were our own, and saw everyone inclined to serve us with the most sincere devotion. Above all, in our blessed father Benedict, whose venerable day of assumption we commemorate today with due solemnity, we see the whole course of this reading fulfilled most perfectly.

For he left everything and followed Christ when, rejecting what he had acquired or was able to acquire in the royal monastery, and though noble by birth, he hastened as a pilgrim to the thresholds of the blessed apostles [Al. adds: “to Rome”]. Since the faith and ecclesiastical organization among the English people were still in their infancy, he wished rather to take there the perfect form of life where, through the chief apostles of Christ, the eminent head of the whole Church stands forth.

There, therefore, he was instructed in Christ; in those regions he was tonsured; there he was imbued with monastic institutions. There he would have spent the whole of his life if the apostolic authority of the lord pope had not forbidden it [Al.: “had not forbidden”], commanding him to return to his homeland in order to lead Archbishop Theodore, of holy memory, into Britain. Nor was it long afterward that even the kings of the world, having learned of his zeal for virtue, took care to give him a place for building a monastery—not one taken from some lesser person, but one granted from their own possessions [Col. 0226D].

When he had received it, he immediately established it most perfectly, inwardly and outwardly, according to regular discipline. He did not formulate rules for us according to his own capacity, but proposed for himself and his people the most certain statutes of ancient monasteries, which he had learned during his pilgrimage, for their observance.

Nor should it seem burdensome to any of you, brothers, if we speak of familiar matters. Rather, you should consider it pleasant, because we speak truthfully when we recount the spiritual deeds of our father, to whom the Lord, by a manifest miracle, fulfilled what he had promised to his faithful: “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.”

He left his relatives when he abandoned his homeland. But he received a hundredfold, because not only was he held in this land by all in deserved honor for his excellence in virtue, but he was also loved by all who were able to know him in Gaul and Italy, at Rome and on the islands of the sea. So greatly was he loved that the apostolic pope himself, for the advancement of this monastery—which he rejoiced to have recently founded—provided that John, its abbot and archcantor of the Roman Church, should be brought from Rome to Britain, as your charity well remembers. Through him the monastery received the canonical manner of singing and ministering according to the rite of the holy Roman and apostolic Church [Col. 0227B].

For Christ he left the houses and lands he had possessed, from whom he hoped to receive the ever-green field of paradise and a house not made with hands but eternal in the heavens. He left a wife and children—not a wife whom he had taken, nor children born from her flesh, but he scorned, for love of chastity, to take a wife and have children from her, preferring to belong to that hundred and forty-four thousand elect who sing a new song before the throne of God and the Lamb, which no one can sing except them:

“These are they who have not been defiled with women, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. XIV).

He received a hundredfold when many people not only in these places but also across the sea desired to receive him, as he traveled, into their houses and refresh him with the produce of their fields. Many matrons served him; men devoted to God, because of the excellence of his steadfast spirit, served him with an eagerness of love no less than that shown to their own spouses or parents.

He received a hundredfold of houses and lands when he obtained these places in which he could build monasteries. If he had dismissed a wife for Christ and received a hundredfold in this respect also, then surely the merit of charity among the self-restrained would be a hundredfold greater because of the fruit of the spirit than it once was among the wanton because of the desire of the flesh. He deserved to receive a hundredfold of spiritual children in place of the children whom he disdained to have carnally.

For, as has often been said, the number one hundred figuratively signifies perfection [Col. 0227D]. We are his children, whom the devout provider brought into this house of monastic devotion. We are his children if we hold to the path of virtue by imitating him. We are his children, whom he caused, though born carnally of different parents, to be gathered spiritually into one family of holy profession. We are his children if, through sluggishness, we do not turn away from the regular path that he taught.

For we remember, brothers—and those whom heavenly mercy gathered into our fellowship after his death learned through frequent hearing—that as long as he was sound in body, he never ceased laboring for the glory of God’s holy Church, and especially for the peace, honor, and tranquility of this monastery [Col. 0228A].

So often he crossed the sea, yet, as is the custom of some, he never returned empty-handed or without benefit. At one time he brought an abundance of books of the saints; at another, the venerable gift of relics of the blessed martyrs of Christ; at another, builders for the church that was to be constructed; at another, glaziers to adorn and secure its windows; at another, masters of singing and of ministering in the church throughout the whole year; at another, he brought a letter of privilege sent by the lord pope, by which our liberty might be protected from every external incursion; at another, he brought paintings of sacred histories, to be displayed not merely for the adornment of the church but also for the instruction of those who looked upon them—so that those who could not learn through reading letters might, by contemplating these images, learn the works of our Lord and Savior [Col. 0228B].

He devoted himself to laboring so much in these and similar matters so that the necessity of laboring in this way might not remain for us. He visited transmarine regions so often so that, abounding in all the nourishment of saving knowledge, we might be able to rest within the enclosure of the monastery and serve Christ in secure freedom.

Even when he was seized and more severely oppressed by bodily illness, he always found it pleasant, amid due thanksgiving to God, to speak and repeat what he had learned and taught concerning the observance of monastic rules; concerning ecclesiastical practices that he had seen throughout all the cities, and especially at Rome; and concerning the holy places that he remembered visiting in his youth.

Thus, exercised by long devotion to virtue and, in addition, refined by the long martyrdom of an enduring illness [Al.: “of an aged illness”], after the hundredfold gifts of present grace he passed into eternal life [Col. 0228C].

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, it is necessary that, as good sons and worthy of so great a father, we take care to preserve his examples and instructions in all things. Let no enticement of soul or flesh recall us from following the footsteps of so great a guide [Al.: “teacher”]. Thus may we, who have left carnal affections and earthly substance, and who have rejected taking wives and begetting children carnally through love of an angelic way of life, deserve, as the merit of spiritual virtues increases, both to receive a hundredfold in the present life through the fellowship of the saints and to possess eternal life in the age to come, by the gracious aid of our Redeemer, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVIII. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE

**MATTHEW XX; MARK X.** At that time the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached Jesus with her sons, worshiping and asking something of him, and so forth.

The Lord Jesus Christ, our Creator and Redeemer, desiring to heal the wounds of our pride, though he was himself in the form of God, took the form of a man and humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. He likewise warns us beforehand that, if we wish to climb to the summit of true exaltation, we must take up the path of humility. If we desire to see true life, he commanded us patiently to endure every adversity of the present age, even death itself.

He promised us gifts of glory, but first placed before us the struggles of battle. He said in promising:

“Your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High” (Luke VI);

but he foretold while commanding:

“Love your enemies, do good, and lend, hoping for nothing in return” [Al. adds: “and”].

Thus he promises rewards to the elect while also showing beforehand the merits worthy of rewards. He gives eternal life in such a way that he determines that it must be reached through the narrow gate and the constricted way. Hence he says:

“Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke XIII).

For no small struggle is required if anyone wishes to ascend to lofty heights. When we climb mountain peaks with so much exertion, how much effort must we make to deserve to have our way of life in heaven and to rest on the holy mountain of the Lord, of which the Psalmist sings [Col. 0229B]?

Hence also, in today’s reading of the holy Gospel, when the sons of Zebedee asked him for thrones in the kingdom, he immediately calls them back to drink his cup—that is, to imitate the struggle of his passion—so that they might remember that they ought to seek the heights of heavenly things only through the lowly and harsh things of earth.

“She approached him,” it says, “the mother of the sons of Zebedee with her sons, worshiping and asking something of him.”

He said to her:

“What do you want?”

She said to him:

“Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.”

No one should suppose that the mother asked this for her sons without their agreement and desire. Rather, let him understand that, by the unanimous counsel of them all, the disciples arranged to disclose their desire to him through the mother whom they knew to be especially beloved by the Lord [Col. 0229C].

Therefore, when the evangelist Mark reports this, he passes over the intervention of the mother and mentions only the disciples, whose desire of heart he knew:

“And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, approach him, saying: ‘Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.’ But he said to them: ‘What do you want me to do for you?’ And they said: ‘Grant us that one may sit at your right hand and the other at your left in your glory’” (Mark X).

Thus he asserts that only those approach the Lord and ask him whose will he sees to be more ardent in asking, and at whose urging he knows that their mother was prompted to make the request [Al.: “moved to make the request”]. It should be believed, however, that the chief cause that stirred either the maternal affection of the woman or the still-car­nal minds of the disciples to make this request was that they remembered the Lord’s saying:

“When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

They knew that the Lord loved them more particularly among the disciples; that they, together with blessed Peter, were often made privy to mysteries that the others did not know, as the frequent text of the holy Gospel indicates.

For this reason he also gives them, as he did Peter, a new name: just as the one formerly called Simon earned, through the strength [Al.: “strength”] and stability [Al.: “stability”] of faith, the name Peter, meaning one incapable of being overcome [Col. 0230A], so these were called Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder.” For they both heard, together with Peter, the voice of the Father over the Lord glorified on the mountain, and knew more of the secrets of the mysteries than the other disciples. And, most relevant to the matter, they felt that they clung to the Lord with an undivided heart and embraced him with the greatest love.

Therefore they did not doubt that it could happen that they themselves would sit nearer to him in his kingdom, especially since they saw John held in such love for the singular purity of his mind and body that he reclined upon his breast at the supper. But let us hear what the one who knows merits and distributes thrones answered them when they sought the dignity of those seats [Col. 0230B].

“Answering, Jesus said: ‘You do not know what you are asking.’”

For they did not know what they were asking, since they thought that someone would sit at Christ’s left hand in the kingdom of the heavenly homeland, whereas in the discernment of the final judgment all the elect are said to be placed at the right hand of the supreme King and Judge. That life has nothing sinister, that eternal happiness has nothing reprobate, and that everlasting peace admits nothing transitory.

Christ’s left hand, when understood in a good sense, signifies the present life of the holy Church. Hence it is written:

“Length of days is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and glory” (Prov. III).

The length of days in the right hand is the wisdom of our Redeemer, because in the homeland of the heavenly dwelling an unfailing light is granted to the elect, both angels and human beings. In his left hand are riches and glory, because in the exile of this pilgrimage we are refreshed by the riches of virtue and the glory of faith until we arrive at eternal things.

The Apostle says of this glory:

“We glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God; and not only that, but we also glory in tribulations” (Rom. V).

Of these riches he likewise says:

“In everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge” (1 Cor. I).

They did not know what they were asking, because they supposed that human judgment could determine in advance which seats each person would receive in the future and by what reward. Rather, they were asking the Lord to bring the confidence and glory of the hope they possessed firmly to its end by their good works, knowing that whatever good they did he would reward with an immeasurable recompense [Col. 0230D].

And indeed their devout simplicity is worthy of praise: in the confidence of a devoted mind they asked to sit near the Lord in his kingdom. But much more worthy of praise is the prudent humility of the one who, conscious [Al.: “conscious of”] of his own frailty, said:

“I chose to be rejected in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.”

They did not know what they were asking, because they sought from the Lord rather the exaltation of rewards than the perfection of works. But the heavenly teacher, indicating what must first be sought, recalls them to the way of labor by which they could reach the prize of recompense.

“Can you,” he said, “drink the cup that I am going to drink?” [Col. 0231A]

He calls his cup the bitterness of the passion that is frequently offered to the just through the harshness of unbelievers. Whoever humbly, patiently, and joyfully receives this for Christ will rightly reign sublimely with him. Since the sons of Zebedee desired to sit with him, he first admonishes them to follow the examples of his passion, and only then to desire the summit of majesty.

The Apostle teaches all the faithful to follow this order of life, saying:

“If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be together in the likeness of his resurrection” (Rom. VI).

“They say to him: ‘We can.’”

They were simply revealing to the Lord the disposition and devotion they possessed at that time, when they declared that they could drink his cup. Yet how great their weakness still was they later showed plainly, when the time came for the Lord himself to drink that same cup: they too fled with the other disciples, abandoning him [Al. adds: “him”].

But the same fear of drinking the cup did not long oppress their hearts. Rather, those who fled when the Lord was about to suffer quickly returned when he rose again. Because they had trembled when terrified by the storm of his passion [Al.: “because they had trembled”], they were strengthened [Al.: “corrected”] by the triumph of his radiant resurrection. Having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, they thereafter held a steadfast heart for drinking the Lord’s cup, because they began to be invincible in suffering and dying for him, fulfilling his promise in which he said that they would drink his cup [Col. 0231C]. For it follows:

“He said to them: ‘You will indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give, but it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.’”

He sits at the Savior’s right hand who rejoices in the vision of him in heavenly blessedness. He sits at the left hand who, in this pilgrimage of the holy Church, presides over it by priestly governance.

But we must examine more carefully how the truthful teacher says to the disciples who ask, “It is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father,” when elsewhere he himself says:

“All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. XI).

It is therefore clear that whatever gifts the Father gives or prepares for the faithful, the Son prepares or gives together with him. For the Lord again says of the Father:

“Whatever he does, the Son likewise does” (John V).

If, then, whatever the Father does the Son likewise does, how does the Son say, “It is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father,” unless it is because the same Son is both God and man? Therefore, throughout his Gospel he sometimes speaks with the voice of divine majesty, which is equal to the Father, and sometimes with the voice of the humanity he assumed, by which he became equal to us.

In this reading, because he was going to offer human beings an example of humility, he speaks especially from the nature of the humanity he assumed. At the beginning, when the mother came to him with her sons to make her request, he asked her what she wanted, questioning as a human being, as though ignorant of hidden things and unaware of the future—although in the eternity of divine power he knows all things before they happen [Col. 0232A].

And because she, in her prayers, gave precedence to the memory of his humanity rather than his divinity, asking for seats for her sons at his right and left—he who, in bodily appearance, had a right and left side, but who in divine majesty is not formed by any arrangement of limbs—it was fitting that he too, while the glory of his divinity remained silently impassible, should bring forward the memory of the passion he was to undertake in human form, and propose it to the disciples for imitation, confirming their devoted promise by his own testimony:

“You will indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”

It was as though he said openly:

“You will follow by suffering the passion that I undergo according to the flesh. But it is not mine, according to that human substance in which I suffer, to give you the gifts of heavenly things, which have been prepared by the Father for each of the worthy to receive. I prepare and give them together with him in divinity, because whatever he does, I likewise do through the unity of divine power.”

Since these same sons of Zebedee possessed a ready disposition for drinking the Lord’s cup, it is clear that they received, together with the other apostles, the dignity of the seats they sought. Yet they did not receive it in the arrangement they requested—one at his right in his kingdom and the other at his left. Rather, as we explained above, both first deserved to sit for a time at his left, and now both deserve to sit perpetually at his right [Col. 0232C].

They sat at Christ’s left when, by apostolic authority, they presided over the peoples of the faithful who had to be governed in this life—in that kingdom of which he himself says:

“The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII).

Now they sit at his right in that life which knows no death, as judges of the world with him. The Son himself, together with the Father, prepares both seats for them.

For the giving of gifts cannot be divided in those in whom the unity of nature always remains inseparable, as the same Son testifies when he says:

“I and the Father are one” (John X).

Nor should we pass over without reflection how the Lord said without distinction that the sons of Zebedee would drink his cup, since we know that one of them, James, ended his life by the shedding of his blood, while the other, John, rested in the peace of the Church.

For Luke openly testifies concerning James’s martyrdom:

“King Herod laid hands upon some of the Church to afflict them, and he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.”

Concerning his passion, ecclesiastical history (Eusebius II.9) also relates a memorable event:

“For,” it says, “the one who had brought him before the judge for martyrdom—James, that is—was himself moved and confessed that he was a Christian. They were both led together to execution. As they were being led along the road, he asked James to grant him forgiveness. After a brief deliberation, James said, ‘Peace be with you,’ and kissed him. And so both were beheaded together” [Col. 0233A].

As for John, faithful histories relate that, when he knew that the day of his departure had come upon him, he summoned his disciples at Ephesus. Having revealed Christ through many demonstrations of signs, he descended into the prepared place of his burial, and, after praying, was laid with his fathers, found as much a stranger to the pain of death as he was free from the corruption of the flesh.

How, then, is he said to have drunk the Lord’s cup, when it is clear that he did not depart from the body through the death of passion? It is because the same cup is drunk in two ways: first, when death inflicted by a persecutor is patiently received; second, when the mind is ready for suffering and one lives a life worthy of martyrdom.

John himself demonstrated how ready he was to drink the cup of death for the Lord when, together with the other apostles, as we read in the Acts, he endured prison and scourging with a joyful spirit; when he was exiled to the island of Patmos for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus; and when, as ecclesiastical history relates, he was sent by the emperor Domitian into a cauldron of boiling oil, from which, by the Lord’s favor, he emerged as safe and pure as he had been chaste in mind and life.

He was then sent into exile by the same ruler [Al.: “with the exile continuing”]. The more he seemed deprived of human consolation, the more abundantly he deserved to be consoled by the multitude of the citizens above. Thus he too is rightly understood to have drunk the Lord’s cup together with his brother James, who was killed by the sword, because the one who endured so much for the truth showed how ready he would have been to accept death itself, had it been offered [Col. 0233C].

But even we, dearly beloved brothers, although we suffer nothing of this kind—no chains, scourging, prisons, bodily punishments, or persecution by human beings for the sake of justice—can receive the cup of salvation and obtain the palm of martyrdom if we take care to chastise our body and subject it to service; if we grow accustomed to entreating the Lord in a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart; if we strive to receive with a peaceful mind the insults inflicted by our neighbor; if we love those who hate us and those who injure us, do good to them, and earnestly pray for their life and welfare; and if, together with the virtue of patience, we strive to adorn ourselves with the fruits of good works.

When we preserve such things, and, in the Apostle’s words, present our bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God, the Lord will grant that we may be rewarded with the common glory of those who gave their members over to death for Christ. For just as their death is precious in the sight of the Lord, so our life becomes precious. When the bonds of the flesh have been broken, we too will deserve to enter the courts of the heavenly city and, among the choirs of the blessed martyrs, offer hymns of thanksgiving to our Redeemer, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XIX. ON THE TWELFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0234A]

**MARK VII.** At that time, Jesus, departing from the borders of Tyre, came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the midst of the territory of the Decapolis. And the rest.

That deaf and mute man whom we have just heard was miraculously healed by the Lord when the Gospel was read; he represents the human race in those who deserve, by divine grace, to be freed from the error of diabolical deception.

For humanity became deaf to hearing the word of life after, swollen with pride, it heard the deadly words of the serpent against God. It became mute in praising the Creator from the moment it presumed to converse with its seducer. And rightly did it close its ears to hearing the Creator’s praise among the angels, since it had heedlessly opened them to hearing the same Creator’s condemnation in the enemy’s words. Rightly did it close its mouth to proclaiming the Creator’s praise with the angels, since, in its pride, it had filled that mouth with the transgression of forbidden food, as though it were improving the work of the same Creator.

And alas, what a miserable decline of the human race: what was born defective at the root began to spread much more defectively through the offspring of its branches. Thus, when the Lord came in the flesh, almost the whole world, apart from a few faithful people in Judea, wandered deaf and mute, without knowledge or confession of the truth [Col. 0234B].

But where sin abounded, grace abounded still more. For the Lord came to the Sea of Galilee, where he knew that the one whom he would heal was ill. Through the grace of his compassion he came to the swelling, turbulent, and unstable hearts of the nations, among which he knew there were those who belonged to his grace.

And rightly is he said to have come to the Sea of Galilee, in the midst of the territory of the Decapolis, to heal the sick man, because, having abandoned on account of its faithlessness the people who had received the commandments of the Decalogue, he came to the foreign nations so that, as John says, he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad [Col. 0234C].

“And they bring to him,” it says, “a deaf and mute man, and they beg him to lay his hand upon him.”

Since the deaf man could not recognize the Savior and the mute man could not ask, his friends bring him and plead with the Lord for his salvation. So, indeed, it is necessary for spiritual healing to take place: if someone cannot be brought to hear and confess the truth by human effort, he must be offered to the sight of divine compassion, and the aid of the heavenly hand must be sought for his healing.

Nor does the heavenly mercy of the physician delay, if the prayer of those who plead does not falter, nor their supplication fail. Hence it immediately continues:

Because Jesus took hold of the sick man, led him away from the crowd, put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue. He puts his fingers into the deaf man’s [another reading: “deaf men’s”] ears so that he may hear [another reading: “they may hear”], when through the gifts of spiritual grace he converts those who for a long time have not believed to hearing his word. Spitting, he touches the tongue of the mute man so that he may be able to speak, when through the ministry of preaching he grants the understanding of faith that he ought to confess.

For he himself teaches that the gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified by the Lord’s fingers, saying: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11); another Evangelist states this more clearly: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12). The Psalmist likewise says: “For I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Psalm 8) — that is, “I shall see the saints, suspended from earthly things not by the merit of their own virtue but by the gift of your Spirit, and made exalted by a heavenly way of life.”

The spittle of the Lord’s head and mouth is also the word of the Gospel, which, taken from the invisible mystery of his divinity, he graciously administered visibly to the world so that it might be healed.

It should certainly be noted that, before touching the sick man’s ears and tongue to heal them, the Lord took hold of him and led him away from the crowd. The first hope of salvation is to abandon the tumult and crowds of one’s accustomed vices, and thus humbly to bow one’s head in order to receive the gifts of health. Nor should anyone be thought capable of being saved while he clings to disordered conduct, delights in superfluous words, and does not fear being ravaged by turbulent thoughts [another reading adds *ut* (“so that”) after *devastari*, “being ravaged”; another reading omits “capable of being saved”].

But whoever, through the Lord’s mercy and help, has now changed the troubled life of his former conduct; whoever has conceived the inspiration of divine grace in his heart; whoever has learned through the word of heavenly teaching the confession of the true faith — it remains for him immediately to attain the desired joys of health. Hence, after the Lord separates the sick man from the crowd, after he puts his fingers into his ears, and after he touches his tongue with spittle, it follows at once [another reading omits “at once”]:

“He looked up to heaven, groaned, and said to him, ‘Ephpheta,’ which means ‘Be opened’; and immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed.”

And rightly, when about to heal the sick man, the Lord looks up to heaven and groans, to signify where we should hope for salvation, and with what devotion of compunction or tears it should be sought and requested. He looked up to heaven and groaned because he grieved that we, whom he created to possess heavenly things, had been cast down far into earthly things. He looked up to heaven and groaned so that he might indicate to us, who had departed from heavenly joys through earthly pleasures, that we must return to them through groans and sighs.

When he says “Ephpheta,” that is, “Be opened,” he speaks with reference to the ears that prolonged deafness had closed, but which his touch had now opened for hearing. Hence, I believe, the custom became widespread in the Church that priests, among the other beginnings of consecration, first touch with the saliva of their mouths the noses and ears of those whom they prepare to receive the sacraments of baptism, saying “Ephpheta.”

Through [another reading omits *per*, “through”] the saliva of his mouth they signify the taste by which those being initiated are to be introduced to heavenly wisdom; through the touching of the nostrils, they signify that, after casting away harmful pleasures, they should always embrace only the fragrance of Christ, concerning whom the Apostle says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place” (2 Corinthians 2). They should also remember that, following the example of blessed Job, “as long as breath remains in them, and the spirit of God is in their nostrils,” they must not speak iniquity with their lips or devise falsehood with their tongues.

Furthermore, through the touching of the ears, they are to abandon the hearing of an evil tongue, hear Christ’s words, and do them, like the prudent man who built his house upon the rock.

And each one of us, dearest brothers, who has rightly received Christ’s baptism has been consecrated in this order. All who will rightly receive the saving bath, whether in the coming Easter season or at some other time, are to be consecrated in this same order. Therefore it is very necessary that we fear defiling indiscriminately and profaning for nothing what the Lord in his mercy has deigned to wash and sanctify in us. But if any of us has fallen into the filth that stains us with wickedness, let us hasten to be cleansed again in the fountain of tears and repentance.

Let us renew the purity of our ears, which we know was divinely bestowed on us through the hearing of faith, taking care to avoid what the Apostle says when reproaching certain people: “They will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth, but they will turn to fables” (2 Timothy 4). Let us restrain from evil the tongue that has been sanctified by the confession of faith. Let us fear cursing human beings, who have been made in the image of God, with the very tongue [another reading omits Latin *in*, “in”] by which we bless God and the Father. For whoever thinks that he is religious without bridling his tongue — his religion is worthless.

For behold, it is said that his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke rightly. Since, therefore, at the time of our baptism we learned to speak rightly — believing with the heart unto righteousness, but making confession with the mouth unto salvation — we must take the greatest care not to turn after baptism toward unjust and harmful words.

For if, as the Judge himself testifies, people will give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word they have spoken, what do we think will happen to those who speak not only idle but criminal words; who do not fear serving impurity, boasting, blasphemy, and — what most delights wretched people — words of detraction; who utter lies, act as false witnesses, and sow discord among brothers?

It is not enough to chastise our ears and tongue from evil speech if we do not also, according to the Psalmist, incline our ear to the words [another reading: “word”] of God’s mouth; if our mouth does not speak wisdom and the meditation of our heart prudence. Moreover, since all the senses of our inner and outer person have been washed in baptism, we ought to keep them clean and always adorned with good works [another reading adds “moreover”].

But once the deaf and mute man had been healed, let us see what follows:

“And he commanded them,” he says, “not to tell anyone. But the more he commanded them, the more they proclaimed it, and the more abundantly they marveled, saying: ‘He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.’”

Why, dearest brothers, should we believe that these things happened? Is it really to be supposed that [another reading adds *non*, “not”] the only-begotten Son of God, while performing the sign, wanted it to remain hidden, and that it was disclosed to the crowds against his will — and that, if he had wished, he could not have concealed in silence the sign that he had been able to perform whenever he wished? Or perhaps he wished to give us an example, so that when we perform works of virtue we might altogether avoid the vice of boasting and human glory, lest our good action be deprived of the gift of heavenly reward through the empty approval of the crowd.

Yet we should know that, if our works are worthy of imitation, they can in no way remain hidden, but are disclosed for the benefit of fraternal correction by the dispensation of the one who says: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5). And elsewhere: “Whatever you have said in the darkness will be spoken in the light” (Luke 12).

And truly, the Lord’s command must be understood in every respect in this way. No one should suppose that it was said as though we ought to avoid the sight of our brothers when doing good, since the Lord says: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works” (Matthew 5). Rather, through the works that we display to our brothers, we should seek from them not praise but progress. For this is what follows: “And let them glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

Those who display good works with the intention that they alone should be praised, rather than that those who praise them should progress in goodness and that the Father who is in heaven should be glorified, are surely to be punished by that terrible rebuke which says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6).

This too must be said: if those who received the command to be silent cannot keep the Lord’s works of virtue silent, how much more ought we always to devote ourselves to proclaiming divine grace, since we are commanded to refresh one another daily with words and heavenly nourishment. The Apostle John says: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22). That is, whoever has conceived in his mind the grace of heavenly inspiration, whoever speaks a word of exhortation by which he can usefully strengthen his neighbor, must by no means hide in silence what he knows, but should immediately open himself to his brothers and share it with them.

For if we do not neglect to speak kindly to our neighbors of the good things we know, he will be present in whom “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Colossians 2), and what we now know only in part he will graciously disclose to us in the perfect light of truth: Jesus Christ our Lord, the only-begotten Son of the Father, who with him lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily XX: On the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist

Matthew 14; Mark 6; Luke 9. “At that time, Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus and said to his servants: ‘This is John the Baptist,’ etc.”

As we celebrate, dearest brothers, the birthday of blessed John, we ought not only to recall with devout reverence the steadfastness of his passion, but also to turn the wickedness of those by whom he suffered into weapons for our salvation. For we attend profitably to the sacred Scriptures when we set before ourselves for encouragement not only the virtues and rewards of the righteous, but also the vices and punishment of the reprobate.

We are taught this by the example of the Lord himself. In order to break the neck of human pride and impose upon us the lofty yoke of humility, he not only sets before us the pattern of his own humility for imitation, saying, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11), but also recalls for our warning the downfall of angelic pride, saying: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). Thus he may inflame us to the observance of the highest virtue [Latin *non solo*; another reading *non solum*, both “not only”] not only through the example of his divine goodness but also through that of demonic depravity.

Herod the tetrarch therefore heard the report about Jesus and said to his servants: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore miraculous powers are at work in him.”

He rightly understood that a dead human being could be restored to life and had a sound conception of the glory of the resurrection, since he perceived that after the resurrection the righteous would possess greater power than mortal weakness can comprehend [Latin *quos*; another reading *quam*, “than”]. But he miserably acted foolishly: what he could spontaneously believe concerning a mere human being, he refused on any grounds to believe concerning the God-man, despite so many miracles bearing witness to it and so many proclamations of the preachers agreeing with it.

Why was this so, dearest brothers, except that we may clearly understand that the miracle of the resurrection is not incredible, but that the minds of the wicked are hindered from the grace of believing by sins that stand in the way? Let us therefore give greater thanks to him who has deigned to open the light of truth to our hearts after removing the veil of error.

“For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother. For John had said to him: ‘It is not lawful for you to have her.’”

We see fulfilled in John what the angel had foretold about him to Zechariah before his birth: that he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. Both lived continent lives; both were rough in dress; both dwelt in solitude; both were heralds of truth; both suffered persecution from a king and queen on account of justice — Elijah from Ahab and Jezebel, John from Herod and Herodias.

Elijah, lest he be killed by the wicked, was carried up into heaven in a fiery chariot. John, lest he be overcome by the wicked, sought the heavenly kingdom in the perfect contest of martyrdom, carried there, assuredly, by the aid of the angels, concerning whom it is written: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is among them” (Psalm 68). And again: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm 103).

But perhaps someone asks who this Herod was, who his brother was, and who Herodias was, about whom this passage speaks.

This Herod, who both beheaded John and agreed with Pilate concerning the passion of our Redeemer, was the son of that Herod under whom the Lord was born. After the Lord’s birth, when that Herod had reigned for a short time, as the Gospel history testifies, his son Archelaus succeeded him in the kingdom. After possessing it for scarcely ten years, Archelaus was accused by the Jews of his arrogance (Matthew 2), expelled from the kingdom by Augustus, and condemned to perpetual exile.

Then Augustus, in order to diminish the power of the Jewish kingdom, divided the province into four parts and appointed four brothers of Archelaus to govern it. Each of them, from ruling a quarter, was called in Greek a tetrarch. One of these, Philip, took Herodias, the daughter of Aretas, king of the Arabs, as his wife. Aretas later took her away from him and gave her to Herod, because Herod himself possessed greater power and renown; and so public adultery was committed.

As wickedness is a cause of destruction for the faithless, so it is an opportunity for triumph for the most faithful herald of our redemption. By forbidding the crimes of an unjust king, John deserved to be punished by an unjust death, but after tasting death he received from the King of justice, to whom he bore witness, the just crown of eternal life.

John therefore said to him:

“It is not lawful for you to have her.”

“And wishing,” it says, “to kill him, he feared the people, because they regarded him as a prophet.”

It was not only the people but Herod himself who regarded John as a prophet, as the Evangelist Mark testifies, saying: “For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man, and he protected him. And when he heard him, he did many things, and he listened to him gladly” (Mark 6).

But the love of a woman prevailed and compelled him to lay hands upon the man whom he knew to be holy and just. Because he refused to restrain his lust, he slipped into the guilt of murder, and the lesser sin became the cause of a greater one. By the strict judgment of God, it happened to him that, because of his desire for the adulteress whom he knew ought to be detested, he shed the blood of the prophet whom he knew was pleasing to God.

For such is the dispensation of divine judgment concerning which it is said: “Let the one who does harm do harm still; and let the one who is filthy be filthy still” (Revelation 22). Conversely, what follows — “Let the holy be sanctified still” — is appropriately applied to the person of blessed John, who, already holy, was further sanctified as he reached the palm of martyrdom through the ministry of evangelizing.

“On Herod’s birthday, the daughter of Herodias danced in the midst and pleased Herod. Hence, with an oath, he promised to give her whatever she might ask of him.”

We have heard three crimes of the wicked together: the ill-omened celebration of a birthday, the wanton dancing of a girl, and the king’s rash oath. Each of these should instruct us not to do such things.

We ought not to recall the day of our birth through celebrations, nor devote any time to the allurements of the flesh. Rather, we ought to anticipate the day of our departure with tears, prayers, and frequent fasts. For this reason the wise man admonishes us, saying: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7).

Nor is it fitting for us to give the members that have already been consecrated to the Lord over to games and foolish movements. The Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6). “Taking the members of Christ, shall I make them members of a prostitute? By no means.” Elsewhere he also entreats us, by the mercy of God, to present our bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God.

How greatly we ought to avoid the rashness of swearing is taught both by the Lord himself in the Gospel (Matthew 5) and by James in his Epistle, saying: “Above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath. Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; No, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment” (James 5). It was under that judgment, clearly, that Herod fell, so that he either had to commit perjury or, in order to avoid perjury, perpetrate another crime.

But if it should happen that we have sworn something incautiously, and keeping it would clearly lead to a worse outcome, we should know that it must freely be changed by wiser counsel. It is better for us to commit perjury when necessity presses than, in order to avoid perjury, to turn aside into another and graver crime.

Thus David swore by the Lord to kill Nabal, a foolish and wicked man, and to destroy everything belonging to him. But at the first intercession of Abigail, a prudent woman, he immediately withdrew his threats, returned his sword to its sheath, and did not grieve that he had incurred any guilt through such perjury (1 Samuel 25).

Herod swore to give the dancing girl whatever she asked of him, and, lest he be called perjured by his dinner companions, polluted the very banquet with blood, making the prophet’s death the reward of a dance.

This moderation must be observed not only [another reading adds *autem*, “also”] in swearing but in everything we do: if we should happen to fall into some snare of the crafty enemy from which we cannot rise without some stain of sin, let us seek that means of escape in which we see that we will suffer the lesser danger.
