This is like those who, shut in by enemy walls and wishing to escape, realize that every approach to the gates is barred; they must choose a place for leaping down where, because the wall is lower, they will incur the least danger in falling.

It follows:

“But she, prompted by her mother, said: ‘Give me here on a dish the head of John the Baptist.’ And the king was grieved.”

The king’s grief is not acquittal but confession of crime. Such is the justice of the heavenly judgment: often the reprobate recognize and admit that they have gone astray, and feel definite remorse for their error, yet do not cease from error, so that by this very confession and repentance they bear witness against themselves.

They sin knowingly, since they refuse to be restrained from the sin they condemn; and they perish all the more justly because they neglect to avoid the pit of destruction that they were able to foresee [another reading: “that they neglected to avoid”].

Such was Herod’s grief, like the repentance of Pharaoh and Judas. Each of them, after unwillingly revealing his crimes under the accusation of conscience, increased them in his foolishness.

Thus, when Herod was asked for John’s head, he feigned grief in his expression, thereby condemning himself, making it clear to everyone that he knew the man he was about to put to death to be innocent and holy. But if we inspect the wicked heart more carefully, he was secretly glad that what was being requested was something he had already intended to do, if he could do it with an excuse. If Herodias’s head had been requested, there is no doubt that he would have refused to give it in genuine grief.

“But because of the oath and those who reclined with him, he ordered it to be given. He sent and beheaded John in the prison, and his head was brought on a dish.”

The king offered an unworthy spectacle for his birthday when, after summoning princes, tribunes, and the leaders of the people to a banquet, he brought out on a dish the head of the murdered man for them to watch.

And unworthy were the banqueters — or rather, worthy of their host — since none was found to forbid that a human being be punished amid the feast of those reclining at table; that a just man be punished by adulterers; that a judge be beheaded by criminals. This was especially so since the king, assuming the appearance of grief, protested that he was compelled to do this. It would have been an opportune moment for him to be recalled from his promised crime by the urging of his companions, if they had not recognized that he had deliberately arranged these circumstances, or rather if the same love of crime had not ensnared them also.

But the blessed forerunner of the Lord’s birth, preaching, and death displayed before the heavenly gaze the worthy virtue of his struggle. As Scripture says: “Though in the sight of human beings he suffered torments, his hope is full of immortality” (Wisdom 3).

We rightly celebrate the day of his birth again with festive solemnity: his own passion made it solemn for us and adorned it with the rose-colored splendor of his blood. We rightly venerate his memory with spiritual joy, since he sealed with the mark of martyrdom the testimony that he bore to the Lord.

For there is no doubt that blessed John endured prison and chains, and gave his life, for the testimony of our Redeemer whom he preceded [another reading adds *pro*, “for,” before *Domino*, “the Lord”]. His persecutor did not command him to deny Christ, but to keep silent about the truth; nevertheless, he died for Christ. Since Christ himself says, “I am the truth” (John 14), John certainly shed his blood for Christ because he shed it for the truth.

He had borne witness to the one who was to be born, preach, and baptize by first bearing witness through his own birth, preaching, and baptism. He also marked beforehand, by suffering first, the one who was to suffer.

Yet it was by a definite dispensation of heavenly providence that their passions were completed in different ways: our Redeemer was lifted upon the cross outside the city gate, with all the people present; his forerunner, while the officials and nobles of the people had gathered in a banquet house, was beheaded in the recesses of a prison by a single executioner.

It might indeed seem fitting that John, by being crucified, should prefigure the mystery of the Lord’s cross. But because that same John, bearing witness to the Lord, said, “He must increase, but I must decrease,” — that is, “The one whom you marvel to be a great prophet, Christ the Lord and true God, must be understood to be; but I, whom you suppose to be Christ, will be shown not to be Christ but Christ’s prophet” [another reading adds “and”] — the unequal quality of the two is indicated by the unequal manner of their passions. This was not determined by the power of executioners but provided by heavenly reason.

For since the same John again says: “The one who is from the earth is earthly and speaks from the earth; the one who comes from heaven is above all” (ibid.), the decrease of the one who is from the earth is signified by that beheading in prison and the removal of his head in darkness. The increase of the one who comes from heaven and is above all is openly proclaimed by that exaltation on the cross, which took place in the open air before the whole watching people.

When he was exalted on the cross, he held his head raised toward heaven and stretched his hands over the earth toward north and south, signifying even by the position of his body that he was Lord of heaven and that the whole earth and all the powers of the air were subject to his dominion. The lowest parts of the cross penetrated the hidden earth, signifying that the kingdom of the underworld had been pierced through and destroyed by his passion.

The Jews, Greeks, and Romans standing nearby read the title written on the cross, by which he was to be believed king, so that it might be evident that his rule would be extended among all nations.

The Apostle briefly encompasses all these things in one statement, saying: “He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

After John had been beheaded and his head brought on a dish, it follows:

“And it was given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. And his disciples came, took his body, and buried it.”

This too pertains to the decrease of the Lord’s forerunner: his body was given for burial without his head. For, as we find in ecclesiastical histories (Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII.10; Eusebius I.13), his body was buried in the city of Samaria, now called Sebaste, while his head was buried in Jerusalem. He was beheaded in a certain fortress of Arabia called Machaerus.

In these histories we also find that his most holy head was later revealed by him to two Eastern monks who had come to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. From there it was carried to Edessa [another reading: Emessa], a city of Phoenicia, where it was honored with the devotion due to the faithful.

As for his bones, in the course of time they were transferred from Samaria to Jerusalem and soon afterward sent to Alexandria. They are now preserved there in the church consecrated in honor of his name.

This is known to have happened by divine providence so that, when the relics of the blessed martyr were carried to several places, more miraculous signs might occur, and more people might be drawn through the memory of his teaching and life to faith in and love for the one whom he preached.

Among these matters we must carefully consider and commit more attentively to memory how almighty God permits his chosen and beloved servants, whom he has predestined to eternal life and kingdom, to be crushed in this life by the persecution of the wicked and consumed by so many and such great kinds of punishment and death. He does this so that, when we behold the passions of perfect men, we may grieve less over whatever adversities may happen to us and instead learn to consider it all joy when we fall into various temptations, remembering that “the Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives.”

For although the authoritative statement remains that “we all offend in many things,” who among us would dare say that blessed John sinned in action, word, dress, or food? The Gospel history praises the austerity of his clothing and the frugality of his food. Everything he said either bore witness to the truth or rebuked those who contradicted it; even those who did not love him revered his works of justice.

What room could sin have in his heart, which the coming of the Holy Spirit consecrated even before his birth? When could he have turned even slightly from the path of virtue by considering ordinary human society, since he spent his whole life from childhood onward in solitude?

And yet such a great man received the end of his present life after a long affliction of chains and the shedding of blood [another reading: “after the shedding of blood”]. He who proclaimed the freedom of heavenly peace was thrown into chains by the wicked; he who came to bear witness to the light was shut up in the darkness of a prison. He who merited from the very Light, who is Christ, the name of a burning and shining lamp — he than whom no one born of woman is greater — was beheaded at the request of the most disgraceful women.

He himself was baptized in his own blood, although he had been granted the privilege of baptizing the world’s Redeemer, hearing the Father’s voice over him, and seeing the grace of the Holy Spirit descend upon him.

But for such men it was not grievous; rather, it was easy and desirable to endure temporal torments for the truth, since they knew that these would be rewarded with everlasting joys. He regarded as desirable the death that inevitably threatened by the necessity of nature, so that he might receive it with the name of Christ confessed and with the palm of eternal life.

Hence the Apostle rightly says: “It has been granted to you by Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1). He calls it Christ’s gift that the elect suffer for him because, as he also says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come and will be revealed in us” (Romans 8).

When, therefore, we see such distinguished heirs of the heavenly kingdom suffering so greatly in the exile of this mortal life, what remains for us to do amid these things, dearest brothers, except to humble ourselves all the more before the merciful Creator and Redeemer, the more plainly we perceive that we can follow them neither in imitation of life nor in death?

Therefore, following the voice of the first shepherd, let us humble ourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt us at the time of visitation. Let us humble ourselves with John; let us fast and offer constant prayers; let us rejoice in being diminished before human beings; let us discipline ourselves, and let our spirit fail for a little while [another reading reads *spiritus, noster utique*, “our spirit, namely”] — that is, our carnal and proud spirit, which used to swell — so that we may be able to grow in the perfection of good action before him and to be exalted with him who deigned to come from heaven to earth, in order to raise us, who are from the earth, to heaven: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily XXI: On the Dedication of a Church

John 10. “At that time the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico,” etc.

We have heard from the Gospel reading, dearest brothers, that the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem. The Feast of Dedication was the solemn celebration of the dedication of the temple, which the people of God, following the ancient tradition of the Fathers, were accustomed to celebrate every year.

Following their example today according to the custom of the Christian world, we have endeavored to make the annual day of the dedication of our church solemn with divine praises and vigils. And we ought to celebrate this festival with the greater devotion because we have learned that it is especially pleasing to our Redeemer, so much so that on it he himself deigned to enter the temple, address the people, and disclose the mysteries of his divinity.

“The Feast of Dedication took place,” he says, “in Jerusalem, and it was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico.”

If, then, he wished to walk in the temple where the flesh and blood of brute animals were offered, how much more gladly will he visit our house of prayer, where the mysteries of his own flesh and blood are celebrated?

If he did not disdain to walk through the portico where a king who was once mortal and earthly, although most powerful and wise, used to stand for prayer, how much more does he desire to visit and illumine the innermost chambers of our hearts, provided that he perceives them to be Solomon’s portico — that is, provided that he finds them to possess his fear, which is the beginning of wisdom?

For we must not think that only the building to which we gather for prayer or the celebration of the mysteries is the Lord’s temple, and not also we ourselves who gather in the Lord’s name, who are and are called his temple to a much greater degree, since the Apostle plainly says: “You are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6), as God says: “I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them” (Leviticus 26).

If, then, we are God’s temple, let us carefully attend and strive through good works so that he himself may more often deign both to come into his temple and to make his dwelling there.

Let us beware the example of winter, lest, when the Lord comes, he find our hearts numb from the warmth of charity and therefore quickly turn away from and abandon them. For what reason did the Evangelist consider it relevant to mention the season of winter, except that through the harshness of winter winds he wished to signify the hardness of the Jews’ unbelief, and because the saying that he spoke aptly applied to many of those whom he then found in the temple: “Because iniquity has abounded [another reading: “will abound”], the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24)?

As he also openly declares in what follows, saying:

Therefore the Jews surrounded him and said: “How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly.” They did not say this because they were seeking the truth of faith, but because they were plotting against the one they questioned and constructing an accusation. For they believed that Christ—whom orthodox faith confesses to be true God and true man—would be merely a human being, and not also God. They remembered, to be sure, that the Lord had sworn to David concerning his humanity that one from the fruit of his womb would sit upon his throne; but they forgot that, concerning his divinity, he himself had sung through the same David: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Psalm 2).

They therefore believed that Christ would be born from David’s stock and would come as a king excelling all others. In this same madness their descendants have continued to err down to the present time, and will not cease until they receive the Antichrist in place of Christ. And if the Lord Jesus had answered that he was the Christ, they were considering handing him over to the governor’s authority for punishment, on the pretext that, resisting Augustus, he was unlawfully claiming imperial power for himself.

But he, concerned for our salvation—for whose sake these things had to be written—tempered his answer in such a way that he both closed the mouths of his accusers and openly disclosed to believers that he is the Christ. They were asking about Christ as man; he, however, openly expounds the mysteries of his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father.

Let us therefore surround him too, dearest brothers—not by attacking him with plots, as the Jews did, but by preparing for him, as his most faithful household, a peaceful dwelling within us, so that it may rightly be said of us: “The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle; God is in the midst of it, and it shall not be shaken” (Psalm 45). Let us ask him—not in their madness [an alternative text adds *qui dicunt*, “who say”], saying, “How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (for what could be more insane than their asking the Teacher of truth to take away their souls—the alternative *tollere quererentur* means “complaining that he was taking away their souls”—because he had not openly disclosed the secrets of his majesty to them in their unbelief and opposition)—but, as Scripture admonishes, seeking him by thinking of him in goodness and simplicity of heart [an alternative adds *in*: “and in simplicity of heart”]; for “he is found by those who do not tempt him, and he appears to those who have faith in him.”

Let us humbly say to him: “We have come to know that you are the Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with them in divinity, and that in time you became a sharer in our nature [literally, *nostrae substantiae participem*, ‘a participant in our substance’; an alternative adds *te*, ‘you,’ before this phrase]. Grant that what we meanwhile venerate in devout faith, we may contemplate in the future with complete vision.” For this is the one salvation and life of our soul: to behold your perpetual face, your light.

Nor should we doubt that he will hear us when we ask for what he himself commanded us to ask, and with attentive mind seek what he himself desires to give. For how could he be thought to deny devoutly supplicating servants the *bona*, “good things” [variant *dona*, “gifts”], that he did not refuse to reveal even to rebels beyond what they had asked? When they questioned him whether he was a man or the Christ, he did not conceal from them that he was not merely man, but also Christ God and the Son of God. For he answered them, saying:

“I speak to you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these bear witness concerning me. But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep.”

Thus, by testifying that he does his works in the name of the Father, he plainly indicates that he is to be believed to be the Son of God. But those people are held liable under a twofold charge: neither by the words he spoke nor by the deeds with which he confirmed the truth of his words could they be summoned to faith. And rightly they are said not to be of his sheep, because they were striving not to follow the good shepherd with the simplicity of sheep, but rather to persecute him with the savage fury of beasts.

But since there are some who preserve faith in words alone while concealing bestial hearts beneath the appearance of sheep, the shepherd himself next teaches what the life of his sheep is and what reward they receive:

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish.”

Whoever therefore desires to avoid eternal destruction and to see everlasting life must follow the voice of Christ—not only by hearing and believing, but also by living rightly.

When he says that he knows his sheep, he signifies that he chooses them and predestines them for the heavenly kingdom. Hence Solomon says: “The Lord knows the paths that are on the right” (Proverbs 4). Conversely, concerning the reprobate the Apostle says: “But whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14).

Beautifully, concerning those who would hear his voice and follow him, he says: “And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish” (Wisdom 3). The martyrs indeed appeared to the eyes of fools to die; they appeared to perish when, overcome by various kinds of punishment, they lost their mortal lives. But they did not perish forever, nor did they see death forever. Once released from the prison of the flesh, they immediately receive the rewards owed to their struggle. Concerning them it is further declared openly:

“No one shall snatch them from my hand.”

The wicked persecutors were indeed trying to snatch the devout confessors of Christ from his hand: either when they forced them by torture to deny the faith, so as to estrange their souls from Christ; or when, defeated by those who were dying, they nevertheless cast their lifeless bodies into the water to be dissolved or into the fire to be burned, as though they could thereby take away from Christ the power to raise them again.

But no one snatched them from the hand of him to whom, as he says elsewhere, “All things have been handed over by my Father” (Matthew 11). For he both helps those who struggle to conquer, crowns the victorious so that they may reign forever, and in due time will also restore immortal the flesh in which they struggled.

By these words he also rebuked the presumption of those who were preparing snares of death for themselves, plainly showing how foolishly they were plotting his destruction—he who could give immortal life, and from whose hand no one could snatch any of those whom he had foreknown before the ages to be his own.

But lest he appear, by speaking in this way, to be seeking his own glory, he refers all his power to the glory of the Father, adding:

“That which my Father has given me is greater than all.”

What the Father gave to the Mediator of God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, and what is greater than all, is this: that he is his only-begotten Son, in no respect unlike the one who begot him in nature, inferior in power, or later in time. This equality the Lord himself possessed in his divinity with the Father before the world existed; nor did he receive it in his humanity from the time of his incarnation [the variant *ipse* in place of *nec* gives: “he himself received it”].

“And no one can snatch from my Father’s hand.”

Above, concerning his sheep, he says: “No one shall snatch them from my hand.” Now he adds: “And no one can snatch from my Father’s hand.” He plainly gives us to understand that the hand—that is, the power—of the Son and of the Father is one and undifferentiated. Therefore Christ is to be believed to be not like others who were sanctified by grace in time, but the true Son of God who has always existed [*fore credendum*, “would be believed,” with the variant *esse credendum*, “is to be believed”].

He makes this still clearer in the following statement, saying:

“I and the Father are one.”

“One,” he says, “we are: one substance, one divinity, one eternity, perfect equality, no difference.”

With these words he explained not only the question then before the Jews, who were asking whether he was the Christ, but also showed how detestable would be the perfidy of the heretics whose future coming he foresaw.

Fotinus [variant spelling: *Photinus*] says: “Christ is only a man; he is not God.” But since Christ himself says, “I and the Father are one,” it is plainly evident that a mere human being cannot be substantially one with God the Father. And because Christ is the same as the Father, the heresy of Photinus, who prohibits him from being believed to be God, must be avoided.

Arius, however, says: “Christ was made by God; he was not born from God, and therefore he must be believed to be less than the Father.” Contradicting him, Christ himself says: “I and the Father are one.” For who could fail to see that no creature can naturally exist as one with the one who created all things? And because Christ is naturally one with the Father, the obstinacy of Arius must be condemned, since he asserts that Christ is a creature.

Moreover, Sabellius says: “We must not confess two persons, the Father and the Son; rather, the same one is Father when he wishes, Son when he wishes, and Holy Spirit when he wishes, though he is nevertheless one.”

The Son himself condemns him by the statement just mentioned. For it is clear that “I and the Father” could not be said of one person, nor would “we are” properly be said of one. Therefore, having rejected the error of Sabellius along with the others, we must follow the apostolic faith of blessed Peter, by which he confessed the Lord, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16).

We have passed through this Gospel reading by explaining it as the Lord granted us to do. But I would still like to discuss more fully with your fraternity the solemnity of the Encaenia, which the inhabitants of Jerusalem celebrated then and which we celebrate today.

First of all, this must be noted: the Encaenia that we learn from the Gospel reading to have taken place did not concern the first dedication of the temple, but the last. This can easily be inferred from the fact that it is reported to have occurred in winter.

The first dedication was carried out by Solomon in autumn; the middle one by Zerubbabel and Jesus the priest in spring; and the final one by Judas Maccabaeus in winter. At that time, it is recorded that a special decree was established whereby the same dedication would be recalled every year through solemn rites. We have just heard, when the Gospel was read, that this observance continued until the time of the Lord’s incarnation.

The reason for the second and third dedications was as follows. Solomon completed the temple that he built for the Lord God in seven years. In the eighth year—that is, on the tenth day of the seventh month, which we call October—he dedicated it amid the great glory of his kingdom. This day had already been established by the Law as a solemn day, so that on it the entire tabernacle was to be purified every year with greater sacrifices.

Finally, Zechariah, the father of blessed John the Baptist, while ministering at the altar during these same purifications, was instructed by the angel, who came to him, about the mystery of the Lord’s birth and the joy of human salvation.

But after four hundred and thirty years the Chaldeans burned this temple. They destroyed the city of Jerusalem and led the people of Israel captive into Babylon. After seventy years, when the Persians were ruling, the people were sent back to their homeland, and the temple was built again over forty-six years. On the third day of the twelfth month, which we call March, the work was brought to completion.

The most vigorous leaders of the people presided over this work, as we have said: Zerubbabel, of royal lineage, and Jesus the high priest. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah also assisted them and strengthened the heart of the people against the plots of their enemies, who were hindering the work.

Then, after approximately three hundred and fifty-six years, the most wicked king of the Greeks, Antiochus, captured Jerusalem by deceit and profaned the same temple with the filth of idols. He removed and broke up the golden altar of the Lord, the table of the bread of the Presence, the lampstand of light, and the other golden vessels of the temple that he was able to find. He also set up an image of Jupiter in the temple and forced the people by tortures to sacrifice to idols.

In that persecution many of the people were slaughtered for preserving the divine Law. Among them, that mother of seven sons, deservedly famous, earned for the Lord a most noble crown of martyrdom together with her children.

But Judas Maccabaeus, since he was of priestly descent (2 Maccabees 7), gathered an army of the righteous against the commanders of Antiochus, took up arms, and drove them out of Judaea (1 Maccabees 4). Thus he brought the most grievous persecution to an end. He cleansed the temple of the images of idols, made new altars and the other vessels and ornaments, placed them in the temple, and dedicated them together with the temple that he had purified and renewed.

He did this on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, which we call December, and it is beyond doubt that this belongs to winter. He also established the decree, as we said above, that every year the day of the Encaenia—that is, the festival of the temple’s renewal and dedication—should be celebrated with devout observance.

All these things, as the Apostle teaches, “happened as a figure of us” (1 Corinthians 10), and were certainly written for our sake; therefore we must examine them more carefully in a spiritual manner.

King Solomon, whose name is interpreted as “peaceful,” typologically represents our Redeemer, of whom Isaiah says: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (Isaiah 9).

The temple that he built is the catholic Church, which Christ gathers from believers throughout the world, as from living stones, into one bond of faith and charity.

The fact that the temple was built over seven years signifies that throughout the entire period of this age—which revolves through seven days—the holy structure of the Church never ceases to grow.

The fact that it was dedicated in the eighth year, and that the famous and greatest solemnity was celebrated by King Solomon for all the children of Israel when the dedication was complete, mystically signifies that, when the number of the elect has been completed at the end of the world, there will be a festival of the immortality long desired. Once the universal resurrection has been accomplished, all who belong to the kingdom of the most true peaceful King Solomon will immediately enter the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland with God.

[Note: Here the Basel edition ends, although I have not been certain whether Bede himself ended the homily at this point. Among the readings that I excerpted from manuscripts, the following fragment—from a tenth-century manuscript in the Bibliothèque de l’Arsenal in Paris—provides an appropriate conclusion to the homily on the dedication of the Church.

“For since our Lord wished to be raised from death on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh day of the Sabbath, the number eight rightly signifies also the future festival of our resurrection.

“The fact that the temple, burned by enemies, is rebuilt again through the Lord’s mercy, and that what was polluted by idolatries is cleansed anew through the aid of heavenly mercy, indicates the various events of the holy Church. At one time she is oppressed by the persecution of unbelievers; at another, restored to greater freedom from persecution, she serves the Lord in tranquil devotion. At one time, in certain of her members, she is endangered by the snares of the ancient enemy; at another, through the vigilant care of faithful teachers, she receives back those whom the enemy seemed for a time to have destroyed, now chastened through repentance.

“But the fact that the temple was built a second time over forty-six years refers especially to the signification of the Lord’s body, which he assumed from the Virgin. Concerning this he himself said to the Jews: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’ For when his body was destroyed through suffering, he himself raised it to life on the third day.

“For they say that the human body is formed in the differentiation of its members on the forty-sixth day after the beginning of conception. Therefore it did not happen by chance, but was arranged by divine providence, that the temple should be built over the number of years corresponding to the number of days in which the Lord’s body—represented by the temple—had to be perfected in the Virgin’s womb.

“The fact that it was decreed that the Encaenia should be celebrated every year plainly admonishes us always to keep in mind both the memory of the Lord’s resurrection, which we believe has already occurred, and of our own resurrection, which we hope is still to come. We should conduct ourselves in such a way that we may deserve to rise not for judgment but, as the Lord promised to those who have done good, for life.

“Nor should we pass over without examination the fact that, when Solomon had dedicated the temple and completed his prayers, fire descended from heaven and consumed the burnt offerings and sacrifices.

“For we are the burnt offerings and sacrifices of the true Solomon; all his elect are the burnt offerings and sacrifices of the supreme King. Concerning them the Apostle Peter says that Christ ‘died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might offer us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit’ (1 Peter 3).

“The heavenly fire is the fervor of extraordinary love by which the citizens of the heavenly homeland rejoice forever in burning with love both for one another in their blessedness and for the glory of their Creator, which they behold.

“Thus certain ranks of the heavenly powers, who, because of their singular proximity to their Creator, burn with incomparable love, are called by the special name seraphim—that is, ‘burning’ or ‘kindling.’

“Once the dedication of the temple was complete, fire descended from heaven and consumed the victims offered to the Lord. So, when the time of our resurrection has been completed, when the faithful servants have entered into the joy of their Lord, the fervor of true love with which the angelic powers are now inflamed will also absorb their minds when they see the form of their Redeemer.

“There is no doubt that even now many of the elect have been wholly absorbed in that heavenly city by this flame of love. But then this will certainly be fulfilled much more perfectly, when, having received their immortal flesh and having received into the same blessedness all their fellow servants and brothers whom they still see struggling on earth, they will no longer have any reason to turn the gaze of their thought outward, even for a moment. They will have God within them, rejoicing in his eternal vision, and they will have their neighbors with them, rejoicing with them in their eternal happiness.

“There the first and greatest commandment of the Lord will be perfectly fulfilled, toward whose fulfillment the righteous strive with all their strength in this life: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ For the more closely they behold the present face of the Lord, the more ardently they devote themselves wholly to his love. The more they recognize that all their neighbors are elect and beloved by God, and the more they perceive that their hearts are nourished by sincere love no less than their own, the more gladly they love them no less than themselves.

“But this too should be noted: after the dedication had been explained and the festival had followed, Scripture concluded in this way: ‘And Solomon dismissed the people, who departed to their tents, blessing the king and rejoicing with glad hearts over all the good things that the Lord had done for David his servant and for Israel his people.’

“For when the gift of resurrection has been completed, the Lord will dismiss his elect, rejoicing, into eternal tabernacles—not removing them any further from his presence, but admitting them from the danger of judgment, which, as we know from the Apostle’s teaching, will take place in the air, into the habitation of the heavenly homeland, so that each may receive the promised seat of the kingdom according to his merits.

“What is meant here by the people departing to their tents is surely what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘There are many dwelling places in my Father’s house.’

“It is rightly said that, blessing the king, they departed to their tents, because this is the one, most peaceful and blessed activity of the citizens above: to sing hymns of thanksgiving to their Creator. Hence it is written: ‘Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you.’ Hence the same prophet completed the final seven psalms with the sweetness of divine praise.

“Moreover, before the end of the Psalter he completed the eighth psalm by blessing the Lord for the victory of the battle in which he had struck down the giant. There he plainly indicates that all who here overcome the struggles of the wicked enemy will there, in true rest, sing the praise of their Redeemer and helper.

“‘Blessing the king,’ he says, ‘they departed to their tents, rejoicing with glad hearts over all the good things that the Lord had done for David his servant and for Israel his people.’

“Rejoicing in the good things they receive from the Lord, the righteous enter the tents of the heavenly dwelling places. For however burdensome and however long the labors of this age may have been, everything that ends in eternal blessedness surely seems brief and light.

“Therefore, dearest brothers, each of us must strive as much as he is able in the building of the house of God: exhorting, beseeching, reproving, and laboring himself through pious actions. Otherwise, if the heavenly King now sees someone idle in the work of his temple, he may make that person excluded at the time of the great dedication of his solemnity.

“Let us strive, through the mutual aid of charity, so that he may find us all glad of heart and tireless in the works he has commanded, and may lead us all into the rewards of perpetual vision that he has promised: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.” Gilles.]

# HOMILY XXII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MATTHEW THE APOSTLE

Matthew 9; Mark 2; Luke 5. At that time, as Jesus was passing by, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew, and said to him: “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him, etc.

We read, as the Apostle says: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace.” And again, commending the immeasurable greatness of the same grace, he says: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Romans 5). For the more grievous the sickness of sins that the Lord healed in his elect, the greater the power of his healing grace he displayed to all.

Therefore, in the Gospel reading we heard that the Lord suddenly took pity on Matthew, who was sitting at the tax office and absorbed in temporal concerns. He called him and made a righteous man from a tax collector, a disciple from a tax official. As the growth of that same grace progressed, he promoted him from the ordinary number of the disciples to the rank of apostle, and entrusted him with the ministry not only of preaching but also of writing the Gospel. Thus the one who had abandoned the care of earthly business began to be a dispenser of heavenly talents.

He arranged this through his heavenly providence so that no one would be held back from hoping for pardon by the enormity of his sins or the multitude of his crimes, when he saw this man released from such great worldly bonds and made so heavenly that, sharing a name with the angelic spirits, he was and was called an evangelist.

“He saw,” he says, “a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew, and said to him: Follow me.”

He saw him not so much with the gaze of the body as with the eyes of inward compassion. With the same eyes he deigned to look upon Peter when he denied him, so that Peter might recognize and mourn his guilt. With those eyes he looked upon his people, oppressed by Egyptian slavery, in order to rescue them, saying to Moses: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them” (Exodus 3).

He therefore saw the man and took pity on him—the man who, devoted only to human pursuits, had not yet proved worthy of an angelic name. He saw Matthew sitting at the tax office, evidently longing with a persistent mind for temporal profits. “Matthew,” he says, “by name.”

Matthew in Hebrew is said in Latin to mean “given.” This name plainly suits the man who received so great a gift of heavenly grace.

Nor should it be passed over that this same Matthew had two names, for he was also called Levi. This name too bears witness to the grace with which he was endowed. For it is interpreted as “added” or “taken up,” signifying that he was taken up by the Lord through election and added to the number of the apostolic rank.

But in this account of his election, Mark and Luke preferred to call him by that name, so as not to make their companion in the work of the Gospel publicly conspicuous because of his former way of life. When, however, they came to set out the catalogue of the twelve apostles, they suppressed the name Levi and openly called him Matthew.

Matthew himself, in accordance with what is written—that “the righteous person is the first accuser of himself; his friend comes and investigates him”—calls himself by his public name when he relates that he was called from the tax office. In the *decalogus*, “decalogue” [variant *catalogus*, “catalogue”], of the apostles he also identifies himself as a tax collector by adding that designation: “Thomas and Matthew the tax collector.” By this means he might offer greater confidence to tax collectors and sinners that salvation could be attained.

Paul too followed this method of teaching when he said: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I received mercy, so that in me, as the first, Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example to those who would believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1).

Jesus therefore saw the tax collector, and because he saw him with compassion and by choosing him, he said to him:

“Follow me.”

“Follow,” he said, meaning “imitate.” “Follow,” he said—not so much by the movement of the feet as by the practice of one’s way of life.

For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk as he walked. This means not pursuing earthly things, not seeking fleeting profits, fleeing honors, willingly embracing every contempt of the world for the sake of heavenly glory, benefiting everyone, loving, injuring no one, patiently enduring injuries inflicted upon oneself, and even asking the Lord to forgive those who inflict them; sometimes not seeking one’s own glory [*nonnunquam*, “sometimes”; variant *nunquam*, “never”], but always the glory of the Creator; and raising as many people as one can with oneself to love of heavenly things.

To conduct oneself in this way is to follow the footsteps of Christ.

“And rising,” he says, “he followed him.”

It is not surprising that the tax collector, at the first voice of the commanding Lord, abandoned the earthly profits with which he had been occupied and, neglecting his wealth, attached himself to the company of one whom he saw to possess nothing of worldly riches.

For the Lord who called him outwardly by his word also taught him inwardly, by an invisible prompting, to follow. He poured into his mind the light of spiritual grace, by which he understood that the one who was calling him away from temporal things on earth [*vocabat*, “was calling”; variant *vacabat*, “was free”] was able to give incorruptible treasures in heaven.

“Rising,” he says, “he followed him.” He rose in order to follow; he abandoned the fleeting things he was carrying on in order to attain eternal things, to which the Truth was inviting him. This is like the saying attributed to Ephesians 5 [variant attribution: *Isaiae*, “Isaiah”]: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.”

And it happened, as he was reclining at table in the house, that, behold, tax collectors and sinners came [an alternative adds *multi*, “many”] and reclined with Jesus and his disciples.

The conversion of one tax collector gave many tax collectors and sinners an example of repentance and forgiveness. For there is no doubt that they had ceased to be tax collectors and sinners, since they reclined with Jesus and his disciples; nor, if they had decided to persist in their sins, would they have dared to eat with the one who is without sin.

Tax collectors are called those who are either publicly defiled by crimes or entangled in public business, which can scarcely or not at all be administered without sin.

And in a very beautiful omen, the man who was destined to become an apostle and teacher of the nations, at his first conversion, leads after him a flock of sinners toward salvation. The work of evangelizing, which he would later complete as he advanced in the merit of his virtues, he begins already from the first beginnings of his faith.

For not only the person who instructs a brother by word, but also the person who converts someone to better things by example, performs the ministry of a teacher.

Finally, these same tax collectors did not recline with the Lord only at that time. Later as well, abandoning their worldly businesses, they rejoiced in following him in imitation of Matthew, as the evangelist Mark testifies when he says: “Many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples” (Mark 2). For there were many who also followed him.

It should be noted, however, that Luke, in relating these events, says that the Lord reclined with tax collectors in the house of Matthew himself, and that Matthew prepared a great banquet for him.

Insofar as this concerns the general judgment, Matthew rendered a fitting return for heavenly benefits: to the one from whom he hoped for eternal goods, he lent his temporal possessions and refreshed him with bodily food—the one whose gift had enabled him to taste spiritual sweetness.

But if we wish to investigate what happened in a deeper sense, he did not merely offer the Lord a bodily banquet in his earthly house. He prepared for him, through faith and love, a far more pleasing banquet in the house of his heart, as the Lord himself testifies when he says:

“Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Revelation 3). “If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me.”

The Lord stands at the door and knocks when he pours the memory of his will into our heart, either through the mouth of a human teacher or through his own inward inspiration.

When we hear his voice, we open the door to receive him whenever we willingly assent to his secret or open admonitions and devote ourselves to carrying out what we have learned must be done.

He enters so that he may dine with us and we with him, because through the grace of his love he dwells in the hearts of the elect. He continually refreshes them with the light of his presence, so that they may advance more and more toward heavenly desires; and he himself is nourished by their heavenly pursuits, as by most pleasing dishes.

The text continues:

“When the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples: ‘Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?’”

The Pharisees were held by a twofold error when they disparaged the Teacher of truth for receiving sinners [*detrahebant*, “disparaged”; variant *derogabant*, “detracted from”]. They considered themselves righteous, although through the arrogance of pride they had departed far from righteousness; and they accused as unrighteous those who, by repenting of their sins, were already drawing quite near to righteousness.

Blinded by envy of their brother’s salvation, they recalled that Matthew had been a tax collector and that many others who reclined with the Lord had been tax collectors and sinners. But they did not wish to remember that Matthew, as Luke writes, left behind everything he was engaged in and followed him.

The other tax collectors and sinners likewise reclined with him in the disposition of adhering to him thereafter. The Pharisees were therefore mistaken: they knew neither the hearts of others nor even their own.

But he who knows the secrets of the heart, who came to seek and save what was lost, strengthens in faith those whom he had already received as repentant, and calls those whom he still tolerates as proud and impious toward the grace of humility and compassion. For the text continues:

[Alternative addition: *At Jesus audiens ait*, “But Jesus, hearing this, said:”]

“It is not those who are well who need a physician, but those who are sick.”

By testifying that he had come as a physician for the sick, he increases the hope of obtaining health and life in those who, troubled by the sickness of their sins, had already begun to follow the teaching of the Savior and giver of life.

By saying that those who are well have no need of a physician, he rebukes the presumption of those who, relying upon their own righteousness, refused to seek the help of heavenly grace.

For who could be so righteous that he would not need divine assistance, when John—of whom no one born of women is greater—says openly of himself: “A human being cannot receive anything unless it has been given from heaven” (John 3)?

But when he adds:

Then go and learn what this means: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.” To those same Pharisees, swollen with false righteousness, he also presents a counsel of correction. For he admonishes them to seek for themselves the protection of heavenly mercy through works of mercy, and, without disregarding the needs of the poor, to trust that they can please the Lord by offering sacrifices. He set before them a testimony from the prophet, and commanded them to go and learn it: namely, to go away from the rashness of foolish condemnation and toward more diligent meditation on Holy Scripture, so that they who accused him of receiving sinners contrary to the decrees of Scripture might understand that they themselves had either failed to know what God’s commands were or, having known them, had not obeyed them. For those who persisted in daily offerings in the temple and showed no compassion toward sinners were plainly seeking sacrifice rather than mercy, contrary to the prophetic word.

But the Lord, who, as it is written, “went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil,” and who, whenever he entered the temple, devoted himself more to healing the sick by his word [Al., *there*], instructing the ignorant, rebuking the stubborn, or even driving them out, than to offering victims—clearly fulfilled the commands of the divine will of which the prophet had reminded them, carrying out the work of mercy rather than celebrating sacrifice. He did not disdain to give his critics an explanation of why he ate with publicans and sinners, so that in this way at least he might restrain them from their pointless grumbling and urge them to pursue the gifts of his compassion. “I have not come,” he said, “to call the righteous, but sinners.”

He therefore frequented the banquets of sinners in order that, by teaching, he might invite his adversaries to heavenly feasts. Yet someone may perhaps wonder how the Lord said that he had not come to the righteous but rather to call sinners, when it is clear to all readers that he also called many whom he found righteous according to the institutions of the Mosaic Law to the summit of evangelical perfection. For if he called sinners alone, and not also the righteous, Nathanael would never have become his companion in discipleship—Nathanael whom, when he first came to him, he judged worthy of such great praise that he said: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”

If he did not call the righteous, he would not have Peter and Andrew at the height of the apostolate; how fervently they burned with love of righteousness they showed when, at the testimony of the Forerunner, they rejoiced to see and hear the Lord at once. How, then, did he not come to call the righteous but sinners, unless it is because, as Luke says more explicitly in reporting these words, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5)?

The Lord calls all the elect to the kingdom of heaven, but he calls to repentance only those whom he finds entangled in more serious sins. Those whom he finds devoted to works of righteousness he does not call to repentance for their former way of life, but rather invites them to advance toward a more perfect life. He calls sinners so that they may be corrected through repentance; he calls the righteous so that they may be justified more and more.

This saying may also rightly be understood in the following way: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,” because he did not call those who, wishing to establish their own righteousness, were not subject to the righteousness of God, but rather those who, conscious of their weakness, are not ashamed to confess that “in many things we all offend.” If he calls some even from among those who are falsely righteous, once they have been corrected, to forgiveness, his saying will also be fulfilled in them: that he did not come to call the righteous but sinners—that is, not the proud but the humble; not those puffed up with their own righteousness, but those who with devoted minds submit to him who justifies the ungodly. When such people are converted, they too must plainly testify with sincere hearts that they are not righteous but sinners.

It is fitting, dearest brothers, to recall to what a height of righteousness the Lord brought Matthew, whom he chose from the business of tax collection in order to enlarge the hope of forgiveness for sinners. What kind of man he became is shown by the very number of the apostles into which he was incorporated. It is shown also by the Ethiopian people, whom he converted through preaching from the remotest ends of the earth to fellowship with the holy Church, and whom, washed in the baptismal font, he made beautiful from their dark complexion, because they had cast off the blackness of vices and adorned themselves with the beauty of virtues. It is shown by the Gospel itself, in which, by writing, he consecrated the beginning of the New Testament: by a special privilege, he was granted to be the first of all to describe as already accomplished the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, which all the prophets from ancient times had foretold as future, and to hand them on to believers to read.

He composed this Gospel, moreover, in the Hebrew language, for the building up of the faith of the primitive Church, which was gathered chiefly from the people of the Hebrews. But when the Church had spread throughout the world and Greeks and Barbarians were flowing into the unity of the same faith, the leaders of the faithful took care that it should also be translated into Greek and Latin speech. In the same way they soon rendered into Latin the Gospels of Mark, Luke, and John, which were subsequently published in Greek, so that all nations throughout the world might be able to read and understand them.

The prophet Ezekiel also testifies how brightly this same Matthew shone among the principal members of the holy Church, when, under the figure of four living creatures, he describes in fullest detail the remarkable virtues of all the Evangelists that he had learned through heavenly vision. The Apostle John, too, who was one of them and likewise instructed by spiritual vision, mentions these same Evangelists among the first mysteries of the Church.

Those who committed the deeds and words of our Redeemer to memory in writing were of such great dignity that they deserved commendation not only by prophetic but also by apostolic testimony. They were of such great dignity that Scripture of both Testaments rightly bore witness to them, and the citizens of heaven brought their glory to human remembrance—not only before their appearance but also after they had begun or completed their most holy work—and showed how highly they are regarded by God.

Ezekiel therefore related much about them, and the eminent John, one of them, related much as well. But since our discourse must now come to an end, it is sufficient at present to recall one testimony of John:

“And when the four living creatures gave glory and honor and blessing to him who sat upon the throne, who lives for ever and ever, the twenty-four elders fell down before him who sat upon the throne and worshiped him who lives for ever and ever, and cast their crowns before the throne.”

Whenever we recognize that the majesty of the eternal King is proclaimed in the holy books of the Gospels, we ought humbly to fall down before his mercy, entreat him with devout prayers, and attribute whatever good work we are able to possess not to our own merits but always to the grace of him who, seated upon the throne of the Father, lives and reigns as God with the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE

**John 1.** At that time, John was standing, and two of his disciples; and looking upon Jesus as he walked by, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God.” And the two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus. Then Jesus turned, and seeing them following him, said to them: “What do you seek?” They said to him: “Rabbi”—which, translated, means **Teacher**—“where do you live?” and so forth.

The sublimity of divine Scripture is so great that not only the words reported as spoken by the saints or by the Lord himself, but also the surrounding circumstances, which appear to have been set down simply, are filled with spiritual mysteries. Behold, dearest brothers: as the Evangelist narrates, we have heard that John was standing, as were two of his disciples, and that, looking upon Jesus as he walked by, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God.” We immediately understood—or rather, recalled to memory what was already known—why his Forerunner called Jesus the Lamb of God: namely, because he knew him to be uniquely innocent among mortals, that is, cleansed from every sin; and because he foresaw that he would redeem us by his blood, freely bestowing the gifts of his fleece, from which we might make a wedding garment for ourselves—that is, leaving us examples of how to live, by which we ought to be warmed in love.

This, then, is the testimony of the Lord’s Forerunner, whose meaning is readily apparent to the faithful when he pours the fuel of intimate love into the hearts of those who hear him. Yet it should not be thought that the Evangelist prefaced his account by saying, without a definite reason for the mystery, that John stood with his disciples while Jesus walked, and that he walked precisely where he might show John’s disciples, who were following him, the dwelling in which he lived. If the remaining details of this kind, which the succeeding passage of the Gospel recalls, are examined more closely, we shall find them overflowing with heavenly mysteries.

John was standing and looked upon Jesus because he had already fixed the step of his spirit upon a great summit of perfection, from which he rightly deserved to gaze upon the sublimity of the divine Majesty. He was standing because he had climbed that stronghold of virtues from which no violence of temptations could cast him down. His disciples also stood with him because they followed his teaching with steadfast hearts.

“And looking,” he says, “upon Jesus as he walked by, he said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God.’” Jesus’ walking signifies the dispensation of the incarnation, by which he deigned to come to us and offer us examples of how to live; his dwelling most suitably signifies the eternity of his divinity, in which he is always equal to the Father.

Thus John, looking upon Jesus as he walked by, says: “Behold the Lamb of God,” because, seeing him living among human beings and demonstrating the progress toward heavenly life by his deeds, he openly proclaimed in words that it was not John himself, as they supposed, but Jesus who had been sent by God the Father into the world for the redemption of the human race; it was he who would give believers the form of innocence and patience. Concerning him, the prophet, foretelling his coming in the flesh, said: “Like a sheep he will be led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, without a voice, so he will be silent” (Isaiah 53). And again: “He himself was wounded because of our sins, and by his bruise we were healed.”

“And the two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus.” When John testified that Jesus was the Lamb of God, two disciples followed him, desiring rather to receive from Jesus himself than from his Forerunner the word of grace by which they too might deserve to be counted among the Lambs of God. It was fitting that two disciples should be found to follow the Lord first, so that they might also mystically signify that all who would follow him perfectly must be devoted with a twofold love: burning both with love of their Redeemer and with love of their brothers.

“Then Jesus turned, and seeing them following him, said to them: ‘What do you seek?’” The Lord could not have been ignorant of what John’s disciples, who were following him, sought. But by turning toward those who followed him, by himself first asking what they sought, and by giving them confidence to ask whatever they wished [Al., *whatever they might ask*], he plainly revealed how much he delights in our good endeavors and how willingly he comes with help to those who begin the way of truth.

“They said to him: ‘Rabbi’”—which, translated, means **Teacher**—“where do you live?” They did not wish to enjoy the teaching of truth only in passing, but instead inquired about the dwelling in which he lived, so that both then they might be more freely instructed by his words in solitude and thereafter might visit him more often in order to be taught more fully. Therefore, when he saw that they were rightly asking, seeking, and knocking, he gladly opened to them the inner chamber of his mystery; introducing them to it, he enlightened them with the beginnings of evangelical truth that they desired. For it follows:

“He says to them: ‘Come and see.’” Immediately it is added: “They came and saw where he was staying, and they remained with him that day.”

If we wish to examine what the disciples suggest that we should do in a deeper sense, in that they came to the Lord who was walking by but immediately inquired where he lived, they plainly admonish us that whenever we recall to mind the passing of his incarnation, we should always ask him with watchful hearts to deign to show us the dwelling of his eternal habitation, which is with the Father, saying with Moses: “Lord, show us your glory” (Exodus 33).

But in commanding the disciples to come and see where he was staying, he clearly shows that we must undertake the pursuit of those virtues by which we may reach eternal joys. To come after Jesus so that we may see his dwelling is to persist in the good works that he demonstrated beforehand, and through daily progress in these works to attain the height of the divine vision.

“They came,” he says, “and saw where he was staying, and they remained with him that day; and it was about the tenth hour.”

Because the Law was given in ten commandments, perfection of the Law is often signified by the number ten. The disciples therefore rightly came at the tenth hour to see Jesus’ dwelling, because whoever desires to see God must humbly submit himself to God’s commandments; and whoever later longs to enjoy the light of divine contemplation must first, with the Lord’s help, fulfill the Decalogue of the Law through works of light, as though the sun were illuminating the ten hours of the day.

They, remaining with the Lord that day, awaited evening in the happiest contemplation of truth. But all the elect, after the perfection of good works and after fulfilling the commandments of God’s Law, will spend with him a perpetual day subject to no end—namely, the day that the prophet, desiring to see it, sang: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands.”

Now Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard John and followed him. He first found his brother Simon and said to him: “We have found the Messiah,” which is translated **Christ**. And he led him to Jesus.

Andrew proclaims to his brother Simon that the Lord whom he has found must also be followed, because this is truly to find the Lord: to burn with genuine love for him and also to take care for the salvation of one’s brother. For the one perfectly follows the guidance of his Creator who strives, as far as he is able, to have his neighbor accompany him as well.

“We have found the Messiah,” he says, “which is translated Christ.” Messiah is the same as Christ; but *Messiah* is Hebrew speech, *Christ* is Greek, and in Latin it is translated *anointed*. Hence *chrisma* in Greek is called *unctio*, “anointing,” in Latin.

Christ, that is, the Anointed One, is called Lord because, as Peter says, “God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10). Therefore the Psalmist also speaks in his praise: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

He calls us his companions because, in baptism, we too are anointed with visible chrism in order to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, and from Christ’s name we are called Christians. But he was anointed above his companions because, as John the Baptist testifies, God did not give him the Spirit by measure, but gave all things into his hand. Concerning his companions in this same anointing the Apostle says: “To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4).

In the Law, priests and kings were called *Christs*, as figures of that same true King and great High Priest, the Lord and Savior, in whose type they were also anointed with material oil. Not only were those people called *Christs*, but the faithful of our own time are rightly called Christians from Christ, and also *Christs* from the anointing of sacred chrism itself and from the grace of the Holy Spirit by which they are consecrated, as the prophet testifies when he says: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Habakkuk 3).

He went forth for the salvation of his people, to save his anointed ones [Al., *to save*], who for us human beings and for our salvation descended from heaven and was incarnate, so that, anointed and healed by spiritual grace, he might grant us participation in his holy name. It follows:

“Jesus looked upon him and said: ‘You are Simon, son of Joanna.’”

Jesus looked upon Simon not only with outward eyes but also with the inward gaze of divinity, in accordance with the saying of blessed Samuel: “Man looks at the face, but God looks upon the heart” (1 Samuel 16). He saw the simplicity of his heart; he saw the sublimity of his spirit, by virtue of which he was to be set before the whole Church. He saw that, when Andrew called him, he had hastened to him with ardent love. Therefore, when he came, he immediately addressed him in familiar speech: “You are Simon, son of John.”

It is no great thing for the Lord to name any man or his father, since he keeps the names of all the saints written in heaven. But, since he was about to give his disciple a name of higher merit and enrich him with a name fitting the prelate of the whole Church [Al., *give a name*], he first wished to show that the name he had received from his parents itself was not without a virtuous significance.

Thus Simon is called “obedient,” *Joanna* meaning “the grace of the Lord.” “You are Simon, son of Joanna”: you are an obedient son of the grace of God. And rightly is he reckoned by the name of obedience, for first, when Andrew invited him, he immediately took care to see the Lord; and afterward, when the Lord himself called him to discipleship, he did not delay to follow him together with the same Andrew, whom he called at the same time, leaving behind the nets by which he lived.

Hence the name Andrew also presents a true image of his mind. *Andrew* in Greek is called *virilis* in Latin, “manly” or “virile.” By willingly following the Lord, whether at John’s preaching or at the Lord’s own command, he showed that he belonged to the company of those who bravely disdain temporal things for love of eternal realities; those who, believing that they will see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, strive, with the Psalmist, to wait for the Lord until they receive them, to act manfully, and to strengthen their hearts.

That Simon was the son of Joanna, that is, of the grace of God, he plainly demonstrates, because whatever devoted obedience he offered to the Lord, whatever reward of eternal life he received from the Lord for his obedience, he received all this through the preceding grace of heavenly compassion, so that he might possess it.

Behold, dearest brothers, you have heard why the first of the Apostles was first called Simon and in what mystery he is the son of Joanna. It remains to examine what secret meaning is contained in the name by which the Savior called him anew.

“You,” he says, “shall be called Cephas,” which is translated **Peter**. We ought not to seek another interpretation for the name Peter, as though it were Hebrew or Syriac; rather, know for certain that what *Peter* signifies in Greek and Latin is signified by *Cephas* in Syriac, and that in both languages the name is derived from *petra*, “rock.”

He is called Peter because of the firmness of his faith; he is called Peter because of the unconquerable strength of his mind; he is called Peter because with undivided devotion he clung to that most solid rock of which the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

This is why that same rock—namely Christ—when he asked his disciples who they said he was, and Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16), immediately rewarded his pure confession with a fitting recompense according to the significance of both names; and he also disclosed what sacramental meaning the name Peter contained.

First he said concerning Simon: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Then he added concerning Peter: “And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church”: you are Peter, and upon this rock from which you received your name—that is, upon myself—I will build my Church; upon this perfection of faith that you have confessed I will build my Church. Whoever departs from the fellowship of this confession does not belong to the building of my Church, however great his deeds may appear to him.

Peter therefore received his name from the firm rock, namely Christ, whom he ardently loved. Christ is called the rock because he grants an impregnable refuge to those who flee to him, making those who hope in him secure and safe from the snares of the ancient enemy.

Nor should it be passed over that the Lord is also called the rock for this reason: because he supplies us with streams of spiritual gifts and purifies us through the sacred communion of his blood. This will be understood more easily and perhaps retained more agreeably if we recall what the rock was according to the historical account—the rock which the Apostle mystically explains as signifying Christ (1 Corinthians 10).

The people, released from Egyptian slavery, came through the Red Sea into the desert, where they traveled for forty years until they reached the promised land. When they were exhausted by hunger and thirst in the wilderness, they cried out to Moses. Then, when Moses prayed, the Lord, as it is written, rained manna upon them and gave them bread from heaven to eat. Again he commanded Moses to strike the rock with his staff. When he did so, water came forth, and the people drank. Hence it says [Al., *it is said*] in the Psalms: “For he struck the rock, and the waters flowed” (Psalm 77).

We, dearest brothers, are the people of God, because we escaped, freed from the yoke of Egyptian slavery through the Red Sea; because we received, through the water of baptism, remission of the sins that oppressed us; and because, amid the hardships of the present life, as though in the dryness of the desert, we await our promised entrance into the heavenly homeland.

In that wilderness we are endangered by thirst and weakened by spiritual hunger unless the gifts of our Redeemer strengthen us, unless the mysteries of his incarnation renew us [Al., *renew*]. He himself is the manna that refreshes us with heavenly nourishment, lest we fail on the journey of this world. He himself is the rock that intoxicates us with spiritual gifts, which, struck by the wood of the cross, poured forth for us a drink of life from his side.

Hence he says in the Gospel: “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst” (John 6).

In a sufficiently fitting order of figures, therefore, the people were first saved through the sea, and then came to the food of manna and to the rock of mystical drink, because first the water of regeneration washes us, and afterward leads us to participation in the sacred altar, where we share in the flesh and blood of our Redeemer.

I have wished to speak at greater length about the mystery of the spiritual rock, from which the first pastor of the Church received his name, in which the entire structure of the holy Church remains immovable and unshaken, and through which the Church itself is born and nourished. For things introduced through the antiquity of figures often cling more tightly, and sometimes more sweetly, to the hearts of hearers when they are finally clarified by a new spiritual explanation than things that are presented for belief or practice by simple narration alone, without any examples drawn from figures.

Let us take care, dearest brothers, always to cling to the protection of this rock, so that no adversity of passing things may frighten us away from the firmness of faith, and no seductive calm may tear us from it. Let us disregard temporal delights; in the present let the heavenly gifts of our Redeemer alone delight us, and amid the hardships of the world let the hope of seeing him alone console us.

Let us diligently recall the outstanding example of the prophet and king David. Although he possessed such abundance of royal power, honors, and riches, and could find no consolation for his soul, at last, with the gaze of his mind lifted toward heavenly desires, he remembered God and was delighted (Psalm 76).

In order that we may deserve to attain that same vision of him, let us strive to exclude from both our body and our mind the obstacles of vices that usually impede it. For one reaches him only by straight steps of good works, and his face is seen in purity only by those pure in heart. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

May Jesus Christ himself grant this to us—the God and Lord who deigned to promise it, and who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIV

**John 1.** At that time, Jesus wished to depart for Galilee, and he found Philip, and Jesus said to him: “Follow me.”

From the reading of the Gospel, dearest brothers, we have heard of the gracious kindness of our Redeemer: he has mercifully been accustomed not only to call us to follow him, but also graciously to receive those who come and lovingly to raise them to knowledge of the glory of his divinity.

We have heard of the disciples’ devoted faith, love, and action; in these three virtues of heavenly life the entire perfection of the present Church consists. For without faith it is impossible to please God, and faith without works is idle; and whatever virtues a person may possess, however much he may have advanced in faith, if he does not have love, it benefits him nothing.

When Philip not only follows Jesus who calls him but also proclaims to Nathanael that he should follow him, this is faith working through love: faith, because he did not delay to believe in Jesus, whom he recognized as the Christ; an act of love, because he immediately revealed how much he loved the one whom he had recognized by following him; and he demonstrated by evangelizing to him how ardently he burned with love for his neighbor.

His neighbor Nathanael likewise showed how much care and love he had for the teacher of truth. Called to him, he did not delay to come; he revealed how much of his greatness he grasped through the perfection of faith, immediately confessing openly that he was the Son of God and King of Israel, that is, the Christ.

But since we have briefly touched on these matters, let us return to the beginning and examine the entire sequence of the Gospel reading in greater detail.

“Jesus wished,” he says, “to depart for Galilee, and he found Philip, and said to him: ‘Follow me.’”

It is already clear from what precedes where Jesus wished to depart for Galilee: namely, from Judea, where John was baptizing and bearing witness that he was the Lamb of God. He urged two of his disciples to follow Jesus, and one of them, Andrew, also brought his brother Peter to him.

According to the spiritual meaning, and as your fraternity already knows from frequent exposition, it is clear what it means to follow the Lord. The one follows the Lord who imitates him; the one follows the Lord who, insofar as human weakness permits, does not abandon the examples of humility that the Son of God displayed in human form; the one follows him who, by sharing in his sufferings, earnestly longs to reach participation in his resurrection and ascension.

But it is not without a definite mystical reason that the account says that, when Jesus was about to say to Philip, “Follow me,” he wished to depart for Galilee. Galilee is said to mean “transmigration made,” signifying the progress of the faithful, by which they strive either to migrate from vices to the height of virtues or gradually to advance in the virtues themselves, daily ascending from lesser things to greater, until, with the Lord’s help, they pass from this valley of tears to the citadel of heavenly joy.

Insofar as the name signifies revelation, it indicates the blessedness of eternal life for which they labor in the present. The Psalmist comprehended both interpretations of the name in one verse, when he said: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Psalm 83).

This is the vision of which the Apostle says: “But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3).

It was therefore fitting that Jesus, about to call a disciple to follow him, wished to depart for Galilee—that is, for a completed transmigration or revelation—so that, just as he, according to the Gospel, advanced in age, wisdom, and grace before God and human beings, and, having suffered and risen, entered into his glory, so also he might show that his followers must advance in virtues and, through passing sufferings, migrate to the gifts of eternal joys.

“Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.”
