We should not suppose that the Evangelist wished by chance and without mystical reason to indicate the name of the city from which Philip came and to show that it also belonged to Andrew and Peter. Rather, through the name of the city he took care to signify what Philip then was in spirit, what he would be in office, and what Peter and Andrew would likewise be.

Bethsaida is said to mean “house of hunters,” and hunters certainly were those who heard the Lord say: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings” (Matthew 4). He too was a hunter who, even before he was appointed to the office of preaching by the Lord, immediately showed by freely preaching how intent he was on catching souls for life.

For he found Nathanael and said to him: “We have found Jesus, whom Moses wrote about in the Law, and the prophets, from Nazareth.” Let us see how he surrounds his brother whom he has found with the net of faith, woven with the capacious meshes of devoted preaching, since he wisely desires to catch him for eternal salvation.

He says that they have found the one whom Moses and the prophets marked out in their writings as the one who was to come, so that all who followed might understand that this is the one whose coming all the ancient writings served to proclaim. He names him whom the oracles of the prophets foretold as the future Christ.

Habakkuk, desiring to be saved by his grace, says: “But I will rejoice in the Lord; I will exult in God my Jesus” (Habakkuk 3). Zechariah too, mentioning the temptation in which he conquered the devil, says: “And he showed me Jesus the great priest, and he was standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan was standing at his right hand to oppose him” (Zechariah 3).

The patriarch Jacob, likewise, greeting from afar the mystery of his incarnation and awaiting it, says: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Genesis 48). For what is called *Jesus* in Hebrew is called *salutaris*, “saving,” or *Salvator*, “Savior,” in Latin.

The Psalmist also, promising the faithful people his eternal vision, says in the person of God the Father: “I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation” (Psalm 90).

Simeon, that venerable old man and prophet of the New Testament, when he received him, small in bodily form, into his hands but perceived him in his mind as great in divinity, gave thanks, instructed by the same Spirit, in these words: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2).

Philip calls him the son of Joseph—not to assert that he was born from the union of a man and a woman, for Philip had learned from the prophets that he would be born of a Virgin, but to show, according to the prophecies of the prophets, that he had come from the house and family of David, from which Philip knew Joseph to have descended.

Nor is it surprising if Philip calls him the son of Joseph, whom he knew as the husband of his undefiled mother, since the undefiled mother herself, always a Virgin, is read to have spoken in accordance with ordinary usage: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow” (Luke 2).

He adds that his homeland was Nazareth, to identify him as the one concerning whom they had read in the prophets: “For he shall be called a Nazaraean.”

It is therefore no wonder that Philip immediately sought to draw Nathanael to agreement in believing and coming to Christ, since he presented him with such great snares of truth from every side: “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth, whom Moses wrote about in the Law, and the prophets.”

Nor is it without reason that he is said to have come from Bethsaida, that is, from the house of hunters, since he is shown to have received from God an equally great care and grace for the hunt beloved by God. For it follows:

And Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Nazareth is interpreted as “purity,” or “its flower,” or “separated.” Nathanael therefore assented to the words of Philip, who was preaching to him: [Note: Bede understands these words, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” as spoken by Nathanael not only in an interrogative but also in an affirmative sense.] “From Nazareth,” he said, “something good can come.” As though he were plainly saying: “It may happen that from a city of such a name something of the highest grace may arise.” Or else, indeed, the Lord himself, the Savior of the world, who is uniquely holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and who says in the Song of Songs, “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II); and of whom the prophet says: “A shoot will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazaraean—that is, a flower—will ascend from his root” (Isa. XI). Or certainly some outstanding teacher who has been sent to preach to us the flower of virtues and the purity of holiness.

We may also rightly understand this passage in the following way: when Philip said, “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph of Nazareth, whom Moses wrote about in the Law, and the prophets,” Nathanael understood correctly, but was astonished at how he could say that Christ had come from Nazareth, when the prophets sang that he would come from the house of David and from the city of Bethlehem, where David had lived. Therefore, in his astonishment, he answered, “From Nazareth?” But immediately, recalling how greatly even the name Nazareth corresponded to the mysteries of Christ, he cautiously assented to the preacher: “Something good,” he said, “can come.” What follows can suit both interpretations:

And Philip says, “Come and see.” He urged him to come and see so that, if anything uncertain concerning the preacher’s words had remained in his heart, the sight of, and present conversation with, the one whom Philip was proclaiming might wipe it all away. The devout hearer did not delay, but diligently sought and piously knocked for the truth that had been preached to him, so that he might deserve to receive it by persevering. Therefore, the Lord, hastening to satisfy his desire with good things, immediately rewards his salutary beginnings with provident praise, so that he might gradually advance him both to seek and to grasp higher things.

For he saw him coming toward him and said of him, “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” Here we must note that God, who knows hearts, in praising the man confirms not that he was without sin, but that he was without deceit. For there is no just person on earth who does good and does not sin. Many, however, are said to have walked without deceit—that is, to have lived with a simple and pure heart. Indeed, all the faithful are taught to live in this manner, as Scripture says: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. I). And the Lord himself says: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X).

Such was Job, the model of patience, of whom it is written: “Now that man was simple and upright” (Job I). Such was the patriarch Jacob, of whom it is said: “Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents” (Gen. XXV). Because by the purity of his simple conscience he deserved to see God, he was also called Israel, that is, “a man seeing God.” Such was this Nathanael, whom the Lord, on account of the likeness of his blameless conduct, deemed worthy of the merits and name of that same patriarch: “Behold,” he said, “truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John I).

Behold the one who truly derives his lineage from the patriarch who saw God, in whom, as in that patriarch himself, no doubleness of deceit is found. O how beautiful a beginning for one coming to God and desiring to see him: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). And here, too, the one desiring to see God is praised as pure in heart and as an Israelite—not by another, but by God himself, who searches the kidneys and hearts; that is, he is declared to have been born from a man who saw God.

O how great a hope of salvation is opened in this saying of our Redeemer also for us, who have come from the nations to the faith! For if the true Israelite is the one who walks without deceit, the Jews have now lost the name of Israelites, although they were carnally born from Israel—those, namely, who by deceitful hearts have degenerated from the simplicity of their patriarch. We, on the other hand, have been adopted into the seed of the Israelites: although in the flesh we derive our lineage from other nations, in faith in the truth and in purity of mind and body we follow the example of Israel, according to the Apostle’s saying: “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites. Nor, because they are Abraham’s seed, are all his children; but, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called’” (Rom. IX, 6)—that is, not those who are children according to the flesh are counted as children of God, but those who are children of the promise are regarded as the seed. It follows:

Nathanael says to him, “From where do you know me?” Jesus answered and said to him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” Nathanael answered and said, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.”

Because Nathanael recognized that the Lord had seen and known things happening elsewhere—namely, how and where he had been called by Philip, although the Lord himself was not bodily present there—and because he considered the perception of the divine majesty, he immediately confessed him not only as Rabbi, that is, as teacher, but also as the Son of God and the King of Israel, that is, as Christ.

It is pleasing to observe how wisely the servant’s confession answers the Lord’s praise. The Lord had truly established Nathanael as an Israelite—that is, as a man capable of seeing God—because he possessed no deceit at all. Nathanael confessed him not merely as a teacher who would give useful commands, but also as the Son of God who would bestow heavenly gifts, and as the King of Israel, that is, of the people who see God through religious devotion. By this confession he also signifies that the Lord is his own King and that he himself is a soldier of the Lord’s kingdom.

The Lord’s saying—that he had seen Nathanael before Philip called him, when he was under the fig tree—may also be understood mystically concerning the election of spiritual Israel, that is, of the Christian people. The Lord mercifully deigned to see this people before it saw him, before it had been called to the grace of faith through his apostles, while it was still hidden beneath the covering of oppressive sin. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his presence in love” (Eph. I).

Indeed, the fig tree sometimes signifies in Scripture the sweetness of heavenly love. Hence it is written: “He who keeps the fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who is the keeper of his Lord will be honored” (Prov. XXVII). But because our first parents, ashamed by the guilt of transgression, made themselves coverings from fig leaves, the fig tree may not inappropriately signify the habit of sinning that has been made falsely sweet to the human race. While his elect are still placed beneath this habit, though they do not yet know the grace of their election, the Lord sees Nathanael as though he were established under the fig tree, not yet seeing himself.

For the Lord knows those who are his. The name Nathanael also most appropriately suits their salvation. Nathanael is interpreted as “gift of God,” and unless each person is called by the gift of God, he will never escape the guilt of the first transgression or the falsely flattering shadows of sins that grow cold day by day; nor will he ever deserve to come to Christ to be saved. Hence the Apostle says: “For by grace you have been saved through faith” (Eph. I). “And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast.” It follows:

[Col. 0266D] Jesus answered and said to him, “Because I said to you, ‘I saw you under the fig tree,’ you believe. You will see greater things than these.”

He himself subsequently explains what the greater thing is: he promises believers the future opening of the kingdom of heaven and the proclamation to the world of the twofold nature of his single person. This is truly a far more excellent mystery than the fact that he foresaw that we, still placed in the shadow of sin, would be enlightened by him. For it is greater that he fills us, once saved, with the knowledge of his grace; that he opens to us the joys of heaven; and that he scatters throughout the world preachers of his faith, than that before the ages he foreknew that we would be saved by the power of his majesty.

“Amen, amen,” he says, “I tell you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.”

We now see the fulfillment of this promise accomplished. For we have seen heaven opened, because after God, having become man, entered heaven, we recognize that the entrance to our heavenly homeland has also been opened to us who believe in his name.

We see the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man because we know that the holy preachers proclaim both the sublimity of Christ’s divinity and the lowliness of his humanity. The angels ascend upon the Son of Man when teachers preach that “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). The angels descend upon the Son of Man when those same teachers add that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Nor are the holy preachers called angels figuratively without reason. The name evangelists, customarily derived from angels, is granted to them so that, just as angels are messengers, they too may be called good messengers on account of the same lofty ministry of preaching.

It should also be noted that the Lord calls himself the Son of Man, while Nathanael proclaims him to be the Son of God. A similar example appears in the other evangelists, where the Lord himself asks his disciples whom people say the Son of Man is, and Peter replies: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI).

It was indeed carried out according to a just and well-ordered dispensation that, when the two substances of the same mediator, our God and Lord, had to be proclaimed either by the Lord himself or by a human being, the God-man should assert the weakness of the humanity he had assumed, while a mere human being should assert the power of the eternal divinity within him. He confessed his own humility; the other confessed his exalted nature.

It should also be noted that the Lord, who calls blessed Nathanael truly an Israelite, recalls in this saying—“You will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John I)—the vision of the patriarch Jacob, who was called Israel by blessing.

When Jacob wished to rest in a certain place and had placed a stone beneath his head, he saw in a dream a ladder standing upon the earth, with its top touching heaven. He also saw the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder, saying to him: “I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac.” Rising in the morning and rendering due praise to the Lord with reverent awe, he took the stone itself, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil over it.

The Lord therefore makes mention of this passage and most clearly testifies that it was a figure of himself and of his faithful. The ladder that Jacob saw is the Church, whose origin is from the earth but whose conduct is in heaven. Through it the angels ascend and descend when the evangelists at one time proclaim to perfect hearers the lofty mysteries of his divinity, and at another announce to those still immature the lowliness of his humanity. Or certainly they ascend when they themselves pass in mind to the contemplation of heavenly things; they descend when they instruct their hearers how they ought to live on earth.

The stone beneath Jacob’s head is the Lord. We must lean upon him with all our attention, all the more because it is certain to us that without him we can do nothing. Jacob anointed the stone and set it up as a pillar because the true Israelite understands that our Redeemer was anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions. From this anointing—that is, from chrism—Christ receives his name, and the mystery of his Incarnation is surely the title of our redemption.

And rightly, when the stone is anointed on earth and raised up as a pillar, the Lord is revealed in heaven, because he himself appeared in time among human beings as a human being, while he remains eternal God with the Father. Having conquered death, he ascended above the heavens of heavens toward the East; yet he remains with us as the pillar of our salvation all the days, until the consummation of the age. He transferred the body assumed from earth to heaven, while by the presence of his divinity he embraces earth and heaven alike.

Therefore, in explaining the ancient history for us, the Lord shows that Israel signifies the simplicity of the faithful people, of which Nathanael was a member. In the stone upon which the angels ascended and descended, he reveals that he himself was signified, whose two natures spiritual teachers proclaim in turn.

For Nathanael anoints the stone as Israel with oil when he confesses how God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and with power, saying: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel” (John I).

Now that the reading of the holy Gospel has been explained, my brothers, it is evident that it was not without reason, and because of a great mystery, that it was foretold at its beginning that Jesus wished to go out into Galilee, and that it was then related how he himself called Philip, or how he received Nathanael when Philip had called him, and instructed him with the light of truth.

For Galilee, as we have said, is interpreted as “transfiguration” or “revelation.” And he is rightly said to have wished to go out into Galilee when he deigned to reveal the sacraments of his majesty to the faithful. To the perfect knowledge of these mysteries—which is the only blessed life of human beings—we shall ascend then all the more sublimely the more earnestly we now strive to pass from earthly things to heavenly things and to advance through the stages of virtue. May he himself assist us, he who is accustomed to make good desires ascend, advance, and receive their crown: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: Thus the later codex ends: “Here ends the second book of homilies of Bede the presbyter, number 24.”]

## BOOK THREE. — SPURIOUS HOMILIES (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0267]

## HOMILY ONE. FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 0267D]

### LUKE XVI

“At that time Jesus spoke this parable to his disciples: ‘There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day,’” and so forth.

Almost no one doubts that purple is the color of royal dress, dyed from sea-shells. For when the shellfish are cut around with iron, they release tears of purple color with which wool is dyed. Byssus, moreover, is a kind of linen that is exceptionally white and very fine, which the Greeks call παπατήν (*papatēn*).

The Lord had previously instructed them to make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when we depart from this life, they may receive us into eternal dwellings; when the Pharisees heard this, they mocked him. But he supported what he had proposed with examples and showed that the rich man clothed in purple was tortured irredeemably in hell because he had neglected to make the poor Lazarus his friend, by whom he might have been received into the dwellings of life.

Some people think that the precepts of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New, but they are deceived by an unconsidered judgment. In the former, it is not stinginess but robbery that is punished; there, property unjustly taken is punished by fourfold restitution. Here, however, this rich man is reproved not for taking what belonged to another but for not giving what belonged to him. It is not said that he oppressed anyone by force, but that he exalted himself in the possessions he had received.

From this, then, and with the greatest care, we must infer what punishment awaits one who seizes what belongs to another, if the condemnation of hell strikes one who does not give what belongs to him.

There are also some who do not think that the wearing of delicate and costly clothing is a sin. But if it were not a fault, the word of God would never so carefully emphasize that the rich man who is tormented in hell had been clothed in fine linen and purple. No one seeks exceptional clothing except for empty glory—namely, so that he may appear more honorable than others.

We can better gather the nature of this fault from its opposite. If the rejection of cheap clothing were not a virtue, the evangelist would not have carefully said of John: “He was clothed in camel’s hair” (Matt. III; Mark I; Luke III; John I).

But we must carefully observe the order of the narrative in the mouth of Truth concerning the proud rich man and the humble poor man. For it says: “There was a certain rich man,” and immediately adds:

And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus.

Certainly, among the people, the names of the rich are usually better known than those of the poor. What, then, does it mean that the Lord, speaking of the poor man and the rich man, gives the poor man’s name but does not give the rich man’s name, unless that God knows and approves the humble, while he ignores the proud?

Thus, to certain people who are proud of the power of their miracles, he will say at the end: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke XIII; Matt. VII). On the other hand, to Moses it is said: “I know you by your name” (Exod. XXXIII).

Thus he says of the rich man, “A certain man”; but of the poor man, “A needy man named Lazarus.” As though he were plainly saying: “I know the humble poor man; I do not know the proud rich man. I possess the former as known through approval; I reject the latter as unknown through judgment.”

He lay at the rich man’s gate, full of sores, longing to be satisfied with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Moreover, the dogs came and licked his sores.

The beggar Lazarus, full of sores, lay before the rich man’s gate. By this circumstance the Lord fulfilled two judgments at once. The rich man might perhaps have had some excuse if the poor and diseased Lazarus had not lain before his gate; if he had been far away; if his poverty had not been an unwelcome sight to his eyes. Conversely, if the rich man had been far from the eyes of the ulcerated poor man, the poor man would have endured a lesser temptation in his spirit.

But by placing the needy and diseased man before the gate of the rich man, who overflowed with luxuries, the omnipotent God brought about two things through one and the same circumstance: by seeing the poor man, the unmerciful rich man incurred an accumulation of condemnation; and by seeing the rich man, the poor man, tested daily, was proved.

Poverty alone could have been enough for the poor man’s punishment, even if he had been healthy; and illness alone would have been enough, even if assistance had been available. But in order that the poor man might be tested more fully, both poverty and illness wasted him at once. In addition, he saw the rich man going out, supported by obedient throngs, while no one visited him in his sickness and poverty.

For no one came to visit him, as the dogs testify, since they willingly licked his wounds. Thus, through one circumstance, almighty God displayed two judgments: he permitted poor Lazarus to lie before the rich man’s gate so that the wicked rich man might increase the vengeance of his condemnation, and so that the tested poor man might grow toward his reward.

Now it happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell.

Abraham’s bosom is the repose of the blessed poor, whose is the kingdom of heaven, and to which they are received after this life. The burial in hell is the depth of punishment that devours the proud and the unmerciful after this life.

And lifting up his eyes while he was in torment, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom. And crying out, he said, “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am being tormented in this flame.”

O how subtle are the judgments of God! O how strictly the recompense of good and evil actions is carried out! It was said above that in this life Lazarus sought the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any. Now it is said of the rich man’s punishment that he desired water to drip into his mouth from the tip of Lazarus’s finger.

Thus the one who was unwilling to give even the smallest things from his table, placed in hell, was reduced to seeking even the smallest things. But we must carefully note why the rich man, placed in the fire, asks that his tongue be cooled.

It is the custom of sacred speech sometimes to say one thing while suggesting another through the same saying. Above, the Lord had described this proud rich man not as devoting himself to talkativeness, but as feasting excessively. He did not narrate that he sinned through talkativeness, but that he sinned through gluttony, together with arrogance and stinginess.

But because talkativeness commonly abounds at banquets, the one who is here said to have feasted badly is said to burn more severely in his tongue in hell. We must consider the following with very great fear:

And Abraham said to him, “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is being comforted, while you are being tormented.”

For when it says, “You received good things in your lifetime,” it indicates that this rich man possessed something good, because of which he received good things in this life. Again, when it says of Lazarus that he received evil things, it plainly shows that Lazarus also possessed some evil that needed to be purified.

But the fire of poverty purified Lazarus’s evils, while the happiness of passing life rewarded the rich man’s good things.

And in all these things a great chasm has been established between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to us.

In this matter we must carefully ask how it can be said, “Those who wish to cross to you cannot.” There is no doubt that those who are in hell desire to cross over to the lot of the blessed. But how is it said that those who have already been received into the lot of blessedness wish to cross over to those who are tormented in hell?

But just as the reprobate desire to cross over to the elect—that is, to depart from the affliction of their punishments—so it belongs to the just to cross over in spirit to those who are afflicted and placed in torment, through mercy, and to wish to free them.

Yet those who wish to cross from the seat of the blessed to those who are afflicted and placed in torment cannot, because although the souls of the just possess mercy according to the goodness of their nature, they are then so bound by their union with the justice of their Creator and by such uprightness that they are moved by no compassion toward the reprobate.

But after the hope of the burning rich man is taken away, his mind turns back to the relatives he had left behind. For punishment eventually teaches the mind of the reprobate, though uselessly, to love, so that even then they love their own spiritually—those whom, while they loved sins here, they did not love. Hence it now follows:

And he said, “I ask you, therefore, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment.”

Here we must note how many things are heaped upon the burning rich man for his punishment. For both knowledge and memory are preserved for his punishment. He recognizes Lazarus, whom he despised, and he remembers his brothers, whom he left behind.

His vengeance upon the poor man would not be complete if he did not recognize him in the recompense; nor would his punishment in the fire be complete if he did not fear for his own what he himself suffers. Thus, in order that sinners may be punished more severely in their torment, they both see the glory of those whom they despised and are tormented by the punishment of those whom they loved uselessly.

It should also be believed that, before the recompense of the final judgment, the unjust see certain just people in repose, so that when they see them rejoicing, they may be tormented not only by their own punishment but also by the goodness of those others. The just, however, always behold the unjust in torment, so that their joy may increase because they see the evil from which they mercifully escaped. They give greater thanks to their Deliverer the more clearly they see in others what they themselves might have suffered had they been neglected. For those who see the glory of their Creator see everything that takes place in creation.

And Abraham said to him, “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.”

But because he had despised the words, he thought that his own followers would be unable to hear them. Therefore the rich man replied:

“No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.”

To this he is immediately given the truthful answer:

“If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.”

For those who despise the words of the Law will fulfill the commands of the Redeemer, who rose from the dead, all the less readily because those commands are more subtle. It is plainly evident that those who refuse to fulfill the words of one person certainly refuse to believe in him.

But whom does this rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day, signify according to the allegory, except the Jewish people? Outwardly they possessed the observance of life; they used the delights of the Law they had received for splendor, not for usefulness.

And whom does Lazarus, full of sores, represent figuratively, except the Gentile people? When they turned to God, they were not ashamed to confess their sins, and thus they had a wound in their skin. For in a wound of the skin, poison is drawn from the inner organs and bursts out. What, then, is the confession of sins except a kind of rupture of wounds? For the poison of sin, which lay pestilentially hidden in the mind, is beneficially opened in confession.

But wounded Lazarus desired to be satisfied with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any, because that proud people despised admitting any Gentile to knowledge of the Law. Since it possessed the teaching of the Law not for charity but for arrogance, it swelled with pride over the riches it had received. And because words flowed from its knowledge, they fell from the table like crumbs.

On the other hand, dogs licked the wounds of the poor man who lay there. Sometimes, in sacred speech, preachers are understood by dogs. When a dog’s tongue licks a wound, it heals it. So also holy teachers, when they instruct us in the confession of our sin, touch the wound of the mind, as it were, with their tongue. And because by speaking they rescue us from sins, they bring us back to salvation as though by touching our wounds.

Hence Lazarus is rightly interpreted as “helped,” because they help him toward deliverance who heal his wounds through correction by the tongue.

It happened that both died: the rich man who had been clothed in purple and fine linen was buried in hell, while Lazarus was led by angels into Abraham’s bosom.

What does Abraham’s bosom signify except the hidden repose of the Father? Concerning this Truth says: “Many will come from the East and the West and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, but the sons of this kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matt. VIII; Luke XIII).

The one who is said to have been clothed in purple is rightly called a son of the kingdom. He lifts his eyes from afar to see Lazarus because, while unbelievers are below in the punishments of their condemnation, before the final day they look above them upon the faithful in repose. Yet they cannot in any way contemplate their joys afterward. What they see is far away because they cannot reach it by merit.

He is shown to burn more intensely in his tongue when he says: “Send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am being tormented in this flame.”

The unbelieving people held the words of the Law in their mouths, but refused to preserve them in their works. Therefore they will burn more intensely precisely where they show that they knew what they were unwilling to do.

He desires to be touched by the tip of the finger because, given over to eternal punishments, he wishes to share even in the slightest work of the just. He is answered that in this life he received good things because he regarded all his joy as passing happiness.

The just, too, may possess good things here and yet not receive them as recompense, because while they desire better things—that is, eternal things—and burn with holy desires, whatever good things may be present seem to them to be no good at all.

Among these matters we must also note that he is told, “Remember, son.” For Abraham calls him “son,” yet does not free him from torment, because the faithful forefathers of this unbelieving people, when they see that many have deviated from their faith, do not rescue them from torments through any compassion, although they recognize as their children those who are their descendants according to the flesh.

The rich man, placed in torment, says that he has five brothers because the same proud Jewish people, already condemned in large part, recognizes that its followers whom it left on earth are devoted to the five bodily senses. Thus, by the number five, he expresses the brothers he left behind, because, placed in hell, he laments that they do not rise to spiritual understanding.

He asks that Lazarus be sent to them, and he is told that they have Moses and the Prophets. But he says that they do not believe unless someone rises from the dead; and he is immediately answered: “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe him if someone rises from the dead.”

Truth certainly says concerning Moses: “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me” (John V). Therefore what is said through Abraham’s answer is fulfilled: the Lord rose from the dead, but because the Jewish people refused to believe Moses, it also disdained to believe in the one who rose from the dead. And because it refused to understand Moses’ words spiritually, it did not reach the one about whom Moses had spoken.

## HOMILY TWO. FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

### LUKE XIV; MATTHEW XXII

“At that time Jesus spoke this parable to his disciples: ‘A certain man made a great supper and invited many.’” And so forth.

Who is this man except the one of whom the prophet says: “And he is a man, and who knows him?” He made a great supper because he prepared for us the satisfaction of inward sweetness. He invites many, but few come, because sometimes those who are subject to him through faith contradict his eternal banquet by living badly.

And he sent his servant at the hour of supper to say to those who had been invited that they should come, because everything was now ready.

What is the hour of supper except the end of the world? We are in that hour, as Paul long ago bears witness, saying: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. X). If, therefore, it is already the hour of supper when we are called, we ought to make fewer excuses for God’s banquet, since we see that the end of the age has already drawn near.

This banquet of God is called not lunch but supper because after lunch supper remains, whereas after supper no meal remains. And because God’s eternal banquet will be prepared for us at the end, it was right that it should be called not lunch but supper.

But whom does this servant, sent by the master of the house to invite people, signify except the order of preachers? Everything is already prepared to remove our disgust, because, to wipe away the lukewarmness of our minds at God’s supper, the unique Lamb who took away the sins of the world has been slain for us.

And they all began together to make excuses.

God offers what ought to have been requested; unasked, he wishes to give what could scarcely have been hoped for. Though, when asked, he would deign to bestow them, he is despised when ready; he announces the delights of eternal refreshment, and yet all together make excuses.

Some say, however, “We do not wish to make excuses; we rejoice that we are both invited to and will reach that banquet of heavenly refreshment.” They speak truly, provided that they do not love earthly things more than heavenly things and are not more occupied with bodily matters than with spiritual ones.

Therefore the reason for the excuses is also added here, when it immediately continues:

The first said to him, “I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it; I ask you to consider me excused.”

What is signified by the farm except earthly possessions? He goes out to see the farm who thinks only about external things for the sake of possessions.

And another said, “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you to consider me excused.”

What do we understand by the five yoke of oxen except the five senses of the body? They too are rightly called yokes because each sense is doubled. Since these bodily senses cannot grasp inward things but know only what is external, and since they abandon what is within and touch what is outside, curiosity is rightly signified by them.

For curiosity is a serious fault. When it leads someone’s mind outward to investigate the life of another, it always hides his own inner life from him. For this reason, the same five yoke of oxen are said to be tested: the act of testing can sometimes belong to curiosity.

But it should be noted that both the one who excuses himself because of the farm and the one who excuses himself because he wishes to test the yoke of oxen mingle words of humility into their speech, saying:

“I ask you to consider me excused.”

For when he says “I ask,” yet refuses to come, humility sounds in his voice but pride appears in his action. And behold, every perverse person makes this judgment when he hears it, yet does not cease doing what he condemns.

When we say to someone acting perversely, “Turn back, follow God, abandon the world,” what are we doing except calling him to the Lord’s supper? But when he replies, “Pray for me, because I am a sinner; I cannot do this,” what else is he doing except asking and making excuses? By saying, “I am a sinner,” he suggests humility; but by adding, “I cannot turn back,” he displays pride.

And another said, “I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.”

What is understood by the wife except the pleasure of the flesh? For although marriage is good and was established by divine providence for the propagation of offspring, some people seek through it not the fruitfulness of children but the desires of pleasure. Therefore, by something just, something unjust may not inappropriately be signified.

The supreme master of the house therefore invites us to the supper of the eternal banquet. But while one person is occupied by earthly concern, another is consumed by an inquisitive concern for the conduct of others, and the mind of yet another is defiled by carnal pleasure. Thus each person who is full of disgust does not hurry to the banquet of eternal life.

And the servant returned and reported these things to his master. Then, enraged, the householder said to his servant: “Go out quickly into the streets [Col. 0273D] and alleys of the city, and bring in the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame.” Behold: the one who clings to earthly possessions more than is right refuses to come to the Lord’s supper; the one who toils at inquisitive pursuits disdains the provisions of life that have been prepared; the one who clings to carnal desires rejects the banquet of the spiritual feast. Since the proud therefore refuse to come, the poor are chosen. Why is this? Because, in Paul’s words, “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1).

The poor and the weak are those who, in their own judgment, consider themselves weak. For there are poor people who are, as it were, strong: even though placed in poverty, they grow proud. The blind are those who possess no light of understanding; the lame are those who do not have upright steps in their conduct. But when vices of character are signified by bodily disabilities, it is plainly evident that, just as those who were called but refused to come were sinners, so these too are sinners, who are invited and come. Yet proud sinners are rejected, while humble sinners are chosen.

[Col. 0274A] He therefore chooses those whom the world despises, because very often that very contempt brings a person back to himself. The poor and the weak, the blind and the lame, are called and come, because the weak and despised of this world generally hear God’s voice all the more quickly insofar as they have nothing in this world in which they may delight. But after the poor had been led to the supper, let us hear what the attendant adds:

“Master, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.” Many such people were gathered from Judaea for the Lord’s supper, but the multitude that believed from the people of Israel did not fill the place at the heavenly banquet. A considerable number of Jews have already entered, but room still remains in the kingdom, where the multitude of the nations is to be received. Hence the same servant is told:

“Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled.” When the Lord invites people from the alleys and streets to the supper, he evidently signifies that people who knew how to observe the Law within the life of the city. [Col. 0274B] But when he commands his guests to be gathered from the roads and hedges, he plainly seeks to gather a rustic people—that is, the Gentiles.

It should be noted that in this third invitation he does not say “Invite,” but “Compel them to enter.” For there are some who understand that good things ought to be done, but nevertheless cease to do them. As we said above, it often happens to such people that the adversity of this world strikes them amid their carnal desires. Often they waste away through prolonged illness, collapse under the pressure of injuries, or are afflicted by more serious losses. Then, reproaching themselves for their desires, they turn their hearts to the Lord. Those who, broken by the adversities of this world, return to the love of God and are corrected in their desires for the present life—what are they but compelled to enter?

But the sentence that immediately follows is exceedingly fearful. For he says:

“But I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper.” Behold, he calls through himself; [Col. 0274C] he calls through angels; he calls through the fathers; he calls through the prophets; he calls through the apostles; he calls through pastors; often he calls through miracles; often he calls through scourges; sometimes he calls through the prosperity of this world, sometimes through adversity. Let no one despise him, lest, while making excuses when called, he should be unable to enter when he wishes.

## HOMILY III. ON THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**Luke 15; Matthew 18.** At that time, tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him, and the Pharisees and scribes were murmuring, saying: “This man receives sinners and eats with them,” etc.

Because not only can a righteous person fall into sin through negligence, but a sinner can also repent through diligence, after it has been related [Col. 0274D] that salt which has lost its savor ought to be thrown outside, the company of penitents is immediately described as being admitted within. They drew near to hear the word of God and were received not only for conversation but also for eating together.

When the Pharisees saw this, they were disdainful, because true righteousness possesses compassion, whereas false righteousness possesses disdain—although the righteous too are accustomed to be rightly indignant toward sinners. Yet one thing is done in the pattern of pride, and another through zeal for discipline. But those who were ill—so ill that they did not know themselves to be ill, in order that they might recognize what they were—the heavenly physician cures with gentle remedies, presents a gracious example, and presses down the swelling of the wound in their hearts. For he says:

“Which of you, if he has a hundred sheep and loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost until he finds it?” Behold: by a marvelous dispensation of mercy, Truth offered a comparison in which a human being might recognize himself, yet which also applied especially to [Col. 0275A] the author of humanity. Because the number one hundred is perfect, he possessed a hundred sheep when he created the substance of angels and human beings.

But one sheep was lost when humanity, by sinning, abandoned the pastures of life. He left the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness because he left the highest choirs of angels in heaven. Why is heaven called a wilderness except because a wilderness means something abandoned or deserted? Humanity deserted heaven when it sinned. The ninety-nine sheep remained in the wilderness while the Lord sought the one on earth, because the number of rational creatures—namely, angels and human beings—which had been created to behold God, had been diminished by humanity’s loss; and, so that the complete number of sheep might be restored in heaven, the lost human being was sought on earth.

“And when he has found it, he places it on his shoulders, rejoicing.” He placed the sheep on his shoulders because, assuming human nature, he himself bore our sins.

[Col. 0275B] “And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.’” After finding the sheep, he returned home because our shepherd, having restored humanity, returned to the heavenly kingdom. There he found friends and neighbors—namely, those choirs of angels who are his friends because they continually preserve his will in their steadfastness. They are also his neighbors because they continually enjoy the brightness of his vision.

It should be noted that he does not say, “Rejoice with the sheep that has been found,” but “Rejoice with me,” because our life is his joy, and when we are brought back to heaven, we complete the celebration of his gladness.

“I tell you that there will be such joy in heaven over one sinner who repents as over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance.” There will be more joy in heaven over converted sinners than over righteous people who remain standing, because often those who know that they are oppressed by no [Col. 0275C] burden of sins do indeed stand on the path of righteousness and commit nothing unlawful, yet they do not yearn anxiously for the heavenly homeland. They permit themselves as much use of lawful things as they remember having committed no unlawful acts, and they often remain sluggish in practicing the more excellent virtues because they are very secure in having committed no more serious sins.

By contrast, those who remember having done certain unlawful things are sometimes pierced by their very grief, burn with love for God, and exercise themselves in great virtues. Thus there is greater joy in heaven over a sinner who has been converted than over a righteous person who remains standing, because even a commander in battle loves more the soldier who, after fleeing, returns and presses the enemy vigorously than the one who never turned his back and never did anything courageous.

Yet amid all this it must be understood that there are many righteous people whose lives contain such joy that no repentance of sinners can in any way be preferred to them. Many are conscious of no evil in themselves, yet they exert themselves in such ardent mortification as though they were burdened by every sin. They even reject everything lawful, gird themselves nobly for contempt of the world, [Col. 0275D] rejoice in lamentation, humble themselves in all things, and, just as some lament sins of action, so they lament sins of thought.

From this, then, it must be inferred how much joy a righteous person gives to God when he weeps humbly, if an unrighteous person produces joy in heaven when he condemns through repentance what he has done wrongly.

“Or what woman who has ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?” The one signified by the shepherd is also signified by the woman. For he is God himself, and he is also the Wisdom of God. Because an image is represented on a drachma, the woman lost the drachma when humanity, created in the image of God, withdrew through sin from the likeness of its Creator.

But the woman lights a lamp because the Wisdom of God appeared in humanity. A lamp is light in a clay vessel; [Col. 0276A] light in a clay vessel is divinity in flesh. Once the lamp has been lit, the woman overturns the house, because as soon as his divinity shone forth through the flesh, our entire conscience was shaken. The house is overturned when the human conscience is disturbed by reflection on its guilt. When the house has been overturned, the drachma is found, because when the human conscience is disturbed, the likeness of the Creator is restored in humanity.

“And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost.’” Who are these friends or neighbors except those heavenly powers already mentioned above? They are as close to the heavenly Wisdom as they are near to it through the grace of continual vision.

But we should consider why this woman is said to have had ten drachmas. The Lord created the natures of angels and human beings so that they might know him; and when he willed them to endure for eternity, he undoubtedly created them in his likeness. The woman had ten drachmas [Col. 0276B] because there are nine orders of angels; but, so that the number of the elect might be complete, humanity—the tenth—was created. Humanity did not perish even after its fault, because eternal Wisdom, shining through the flesh with miracles, restored it through the light of the clay vessel.

“So I tell you: there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” To repent is both to lament the evils one has committed and not to commit those that ought to be lamented. For whoever laments some sins while continuing to commit others either does not yet know how to repent or pretends to do so.

What good does it do if someone mourns the sins of sexual immorality while still panting in the heat of greed? Or what good does it do if someone now grieves the faults of anger while still wasting away in the flames of envy? But what we say is still insufficient: the person who laments sins must also take the greatest care not to commit what must be lamented.

For one who remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful things, so that by this [Col. 0276C] he may make satisfaction to his Creator; having committed what was forbidden, he ought to cut off from himself even what was permitted.

## HOMILY IV. ON THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**Luke 6.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned,” etc.

I think that in this passage nothing else is commanded us except that we interpret for the better those actions concerning which it is uncertain with what intention they are performed. For what is written—“You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7)—was said about manifest acts that cannot be done with a good intention, such as sexual immorality, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and anything of that kind, concerning which we are permitted [Col. 0276D] to judge.

But concerning kinds of food, since any human food can be taken without the fault of desire, with a good intention and a simple heart, the Apostle forbids those who ate meat and drank wine to be judged by those who abstained from such foods. “Let the one who eats,” he says, “not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. 14).

This also pertains to what he says elsewhere: “Do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of the heart” (1 Cor. 4). There are therefore certain indifferent actions whose intention we do not know, and which can be performed either well or badly. It is rash to judge such things, especially in order to condemn them. But the time will come when they will be judged, when the Lord brings to light the things hidden in darkness and discloses the purposes of the heart.

There are two matters in which we must avoid rash judgment when it is uncertain with what intention something has been done, or when it is uncertain what kind of person the one who now appears either bad or good will become.

[Col. 0277A] “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.” He commands us to forgive injuries and to give benefits, so that our sins may be forgiven and eternal life given to us. In this brief but excellent sentence he concludes by gathering together everything he had commanded at length concerning conduct toward enemies:

“They will give into your lap a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.” This resembles what he says elsewhere: “So that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). It is not the poor themselves, but Christ, who will repay those who practice almsgiving. Yet the reward is said to be given into their lap because they are to be provided with the opportunity to earn it: they show mercy to the needy, endure those who rage wickedly, support them through their beneficence, and sometimes draw them toward the faith itself by gentle grace.

“For with the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.” The Apostle too, encouraging the Corinthians to almsgiving, says among other things: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows with blessings will also reap [Col. 0277B] with blessings” (2 Cor. 9). This may also be understood of everything we do in thought, hand, and tongue, because, as he says, “you will repay each according to his works” (Ps. 61).

He also told them a parable: “Can a blind person lead a blind person? Will they not both fall into a pit?” The meaning of this sentence depends on what precedes, where he commands that alms be given and injuries forgiven.

“If anger against one who uses violence, or greed against one who asks, has blinded you, will you be able to cure the other person’s fault while your own mind is corrupted? Or will only the one who inflicted the injury be considered guilty, and not you as well, who did not know how to endure it?

“But if the other person’s wickedness finds you gentle and of tranquil heart, he will be moved to repentance, and you will be rewarded for your patience, because, with the eye of one who sees—that is, with a serene heart—you were concerned to lead a blind person toward the light.”

“A disciple is not above his teacher; but everyone, when perfected, [Col. 0277C] will be like his teacher.” If the teacher, who, as God, could have avenged his own injuries but preferred to make his persecutors gentler by enduring them, then his disciples, who are merely human beings, must necessarily follow the same rule of perfection.

“But why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, while you do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?” This too refers to what precedes, where he warned that a blind person cannot be led by a blind person—that is, that a sinner cannot be corrected by a sinner.

Many people, overtaken by pride, hatred, greed, avarice, or some other crime, judge these faults to be slight or nonexistent and sharply rebuke those whom they see disturbed by sudden anger, as though a speck had intruded and altered the eye of their mind from its usual state of purity. Forgetful of the Lord’s command—“Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned”—they prefer to blame and damn rather than to amend and correct.

“And how can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while you do not see the beam in your own eye?” You do this to your brother if, for example, [Col. 0277D] you criticize the anger with which he sinned while you yourself criticize him out of hatred. As much as there is between a speck and a beam, so much is there between anger and hatred.

Hatred is longstanding anger, as though through age itself it had acquired such magnitude that it rightly deserves to be called a beam. It can happen that, if you are angry with someone, you may wish him to be corrected; but if you hate someone, you cannot wish to correct him. Therefore it is said to be impossible for someone to remove the speck from his brother’s eye when he carries a beam in his own.

“Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” That is: first drive hatred away from yourself, and afterward you will be able to correct the person whom you love.

The kind of hypocrites—that is, pretenders—who undertake accusations of every vice out of hatred and envy, yet also wish to appear to be advisers, must truly be guarded against and avoided. Therefore we must watch carefully and devoutly: whenever necessity begins to require that we rebuke or reprove someone, we should first consider whether the vice is one we have never [Col. 0278A] had, or one from which we have already been freed.

If we have never had it, we should consider that we are human beings and could have had it. But if we have had it and still have it, the memory of our common weakness should touch us, so that mercy, not hatred, precedes the rebuke or reproof. Whether it proves useful for the correction of the person on whose account we act or for his corruption—for the outcome is uncertain—we should nevertheless remain secure in the simplicity of our own eye.

But if, upon examining ourselves, we find that we are guilty of the very vice present in the person whom we were preparing to rebuke, we should neither rebuke nor reprove him. Instead, we should groan with him and invite him not to obey us but to strive together with us.

Reproofs should therefore be used rarely and only under great necessity, yet in such a way that even in these matters we insist on serving not ourselves but God. For this is the goal: that we do nothing with a divided heart, removing from our eye the beam of envy, malice, or hypocrisy, [Col. 0278B] so that we may see to remove the speck from our brother’s eye.

## HOMILY V. ON THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**Luke 5.** At that time, when the crowds were pressing upon Jesus to hear the word of God, and he was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret, etc.

[Col. 0278C] They say that the lake of Gennesaret is the same as the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Galilee was named from the surrounding province; the Sea of Tiberias from the nearby city, which was formerly called Chinnereth but, after being restored by Herod the tetrarch in honor of Tiberius Caesar, was called Tiberias.

Moreover, Gennesaret derives its name from the nature of the lake itself, since it is said to stir up a breeze from itself through the rippling of its waters. In Greek it is called, as it were, “generating a breeze for itself.” For the water does not lie flat as in an ordinary pond, but is agitated by frequent breaths of wind; it is sweet to draw and suitable for drinking.

According to the usage of the Hebrew language, however, every gathering of waters, whether fresh or salt, is called a sea. This lake, through which the Jordan flows, extends one hundred and forty stadia in length and forty in width.

Since, then, the present lake or sea signifies the present age, the Lord stands beside the sea after, having overcome the mortality of passing life, he entered into the stability of perpetual rest in the flesh in which he suffered. The gathering of the crowds around him is a type of the nations converging in faith. Concerning them Isaiah says: “And all the nations shall flow to him, and many peoples shall go and say: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord’” (Isa. 2).

“And he saw two boats standing beside the lake.” The two boats placed beside the lake represent circumcision and uncircumcision. Jesus is rightly said to have seen them because the Lord knows his own in both peoples. By seeing—that is, by mercifully visiting—their hearts, he leads them from the waves of this world toward the tranquility of the future life, as toward the firmness of the shore.

[Col. 0278D] “But the fishermen had gone down and were washing their nets.” The fishermen are the teachers of the Church. They catch us in the net of faith, raise us from the depths into the light, and bring us, like fish to the shore, to the land of the living.

The utterances of preachers are like certain nets of fishermen: they hold those whom they have caught in the faith and do not let them go. Hence nets are so called, as it were, because they retain. But these nets are now cast out for a catch, now washed and folded, because not every time is suitable for teaching: sometimes the teacher must exercise his tongue, and sometimes he must attend to himself.

“Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat.” Simon’s boat is the primitive Church, concerning which Paul says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised also worked through me among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2). It is rightly called one because the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul [Col. 0279A] (Acts 4). From this boat he taught the crowds, because to this day he teaches the nations through the authority of the Church.

“When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: ‘Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.’” The fact that he first asked Simon to put the boat out a little from the land signifies that the word should be used moderately with the crowds: earthly matters should not be commanded to them, but neither should they be withdrawn so far from earthly matters into the depths of the mysteries that they understand nothing of them.

Alternatively, it may signify that the preaching should first be directed to the nearer regions and peoples, while what he says afterward to Peter—“Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch”—refers to the more distant nations to whom preaching later came.

“And Simon answered and said to him: ‘Master, we have labored all night and caught nothing, but at your word I will let down the net.’” “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126). Unless the Lord enlightens the hearts of those who hear, the teacher labors in the night. Unless the instruments of argument are let down in the word of heavenly grace, [Col. 0279B] the preacher casts the dart of his voice in vain. The faith of peoples comes not from the skill of composed speech but from the gift of the divine calling.

“And when they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. Their net was breaking.” The net was breaking because of the multitude of fish, since now, together with the elect, so many reprobate enter into the confession of faith that they even tear the Church itself apart through heresies. The net breaks, but the fish does not fall out, because the Lord preserves his own even amid the scandals of their persecutors.

“And they signaled to their companions who were in the other boat to come and help them.” The other boat, as we said above, is the Church from the Gentiles. It too, since one little boat is insufficient, is filled with elect fish, because the Lord knows those who are his, and the number of his elect is certain to him (2 Tim. 2).

Since he does not find as many in Judaea who will believe as he knows have been predestined to faith and eternal life, [Col. 0279C] he seeks another boat to receive his fish, as it were, and fills the hearts of the nations with the grace of faith.

The companion boat is rightly summoned when the net has broken, because Judas the betrayer was caught first, and Simon Magus, a most wicked fish, was caught first; Ananias and Sapphira deceitfully attempted to enter the net of faith first (Acts 5 and 8). Earlier, as John testifies, many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6); afterward Barnabas and Paul were set apart for the apostleship of the Gentiles (Acts 13).

“And they came and filled both boats, so that they were almost sinking.” The filling of these boats increases until the end of the age. But the fact that they sink when filled—that is, that they are pressed down into destruction—for they are not submerged, though they are endangered, is explained by the Apostle, who says: “In the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves,” etc. (2 Tim. 3).

For boats to sink means that people, through the perversity of their conduct, fall back into the world from which they had been lifted by faith. Peter himself, while still situated in weakness, demonstrates what such people are like in this [Col. 0279D] passage. Hence it follows:

“When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: ‘Depart from me, Lord, because I am a sinful man.’” Carnal people in the Church repel from themselves, in a certain sense, the governance of spiritual persons, in whom the person of Christ is especially prominent.

They do not say this with the voice of their tongue to the good ministers of God in order to drive them away. Rather, by the voice of their conduct and actions they urge them to withdraw, lest they be governed by good people. They do so all the more forcefully because they show them honor while nevertheless warning by their deeds that they should withdraw.

Peter’s falling at the Lord’s feet signified their honor, while his conduct was expressed in the words: “Depart from me, Lord, because I am a sinful man.” Yet because the Lord did not do this—for he did not withdraw from them but brought the boats, once drawn in, to the shore—it signifies that good and spiritual men ought not to have this desire: moved by the sins of the crowds, they should not abandon ecclesiastical office in order to live as though more safely and peacefully.

[Col. 0280A] And Jesus said to Simon: “Do not be afraid.” The Lord strengthens the fear of carnal people and raises up the spirits of the weak through consolation, so that no one may fear to begin the path of holiness, whether trembling at the consciousness of his own guilt or astonished at the innocence of others.

“And from now on you will be catching people.” This applies especially to Peter. The Lord explains to him what this catch of fish signifies: just as he now catches fish through nets, so at some time he will catch people through words. The entire order of this event shows what is done daily in the Church, whose type Peter himself represents.

“And having brought the boats to land, they left everything and followed him.” This may signify the end of time, when those who have clung to Christ will completely withdraw [Col. 0280B] from this sea.

It should be understood, however, that this is not the same account in which Matthew and Mark narrate that the Lord called two pairs of fishermen from the boats—first Peter and Andrew, and afterward the sons of Zebedee (Matt. 4; Mark 1). Luke does not now indicate that they were called by the Lord, but only that it was foretold to Peter that he would catch people.

This was not said as though he would never again catch fish, for we read that after the Lord’s resurrection they did fish. Hence it may be understood that they returned, as usual, to catching fish, so that what Matthew and Mark narrate would happen afterward, when he called them in pairs (John 21). At that time they followed him not after bringing the boats to land, as though they intended to return to their work, but in such a way as to follow him as one who was calling and commanding them to follow.

## HOMILY VI. ON THE SEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 0280C] **Mark 8; Matthew 15.** At that time, when there was a great crowd with Jesus and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples and said to them: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat,” etc.

In this passage we must consider the distinct operation of divinity and humanity in one and the same Redeemer of ours. The error of Eutyches, who dares to assert as dogma that there is only one operation in Christ, must be driven far from Christian territory.

For who does not see that the Lord’s compassion for the crowd, lest they should fail either from hunger or from the labor of a long journey, is an affection and compassion belonging to human weakness? But that he satisfied four thousand people with seven loaves and a few fish is the work of divine power.

Mystically, however, this miracle signifies that we cannot pass through the way of the present age unharmed unless the grace of our [Col. 0280D] Redeemer refreshes us with the nourishment of his word.

Typologically, the difference between this feeding and the feeding of the five loaves and two fish is that there the letter of the Old Testament was signified as being full of spiritual grace, while here the truth and grace of the New Testament is shown to be supplied to the faithful.

Both feedings, certainly, took place on a mountain, as the account of the other Evangelists makes clear, because Scripture rightly understood of both Testaments sets before us the height of heavenly precepts and rewards. Both proclaim with harmonious voice the height of Christ, who is the mountain of the house of the Lord, at the summit of the mountains (Matt. 1).

For whoever builds the city or house of the Lord—namely, the Church—upon him, raises it on high through good works and displays it openly to all the nations. He draws it away from lowly pleasures, refreshes it with the bread of heaven, and kindles it to desire heavenly sweetness by giving it the pledge of spiritual food.

“I have compassion,” he says, “on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will faint on the way.”

Matthew explains more fully why the crowd remained with the Lord for three days. He says: “And after ascending the mountain, he sat there. Great crowds came to him, having with them the mute, the blind, the lame, the weak, and many others; and they cast them at his feet, and he healed them” (Matt. 15).

The crowd therefore remains with the Lord for three days on account of the healing of its sick, [Col. 0281A] when all the elect, enlightened by faith in the Holy Trinity, persistently entreat the Lord on behalf of their own sins and those of their people—that is, the illnesses of their souls.

Again, the crowd remains with the Lord for three days when the multitude of the faithful, turning away through repentance from the sins it has committed, turns to the Lord in deed, speech, and thought.

The Lord does not wish to send them away fasting to their homes, lest they faint on the way, because converted sinners fail on the road of the present life if they are sent away in their own consciences without the nourishment of holy [Col. 0281B] teaching. Therefore, so that they may not grow weary on the journey of this pilgrimage, they must be fed with sacred instruction.

The gracious sentence that came from the mouth of Truth must be weighed with great care. It says:

“For some of them have come from far away.” There is someone who, having experienced no deceit and no carnal corruption, hastened to the service of almighty God. He did not come from far away because, through incorruption and innocence, he was near.

Another, stained by no impurity or disgrace but having experienced only marriage, turned to spiritual ministry. He too did not come from far away, because, having used a permitted union, he did not stray through unlawful acts.

Others return to repentance after sexual offenses; others after false testimony; others after committed thefts; others after inflicting injuries and acts of violence; others after committing murders. They turn to the service of almighty God. These plainly come to the Lord from far away. For the more someone has gone astray [Col. 0281C] in wicked conduct, the farther he has withdrawn from almighty God.

Let nourishment therefore be given even to those who come from far away, because the converted sinners must be offered the food of holy teaching, so that they may recover in God the strength they lost in their disgraceful acts.

Likewise, whatever Jews have believed in Christ came to him from nearby, because they had been taught about him through the writings of the Law and the prophets. Believers from the Gentiles, however, certainly came to Christ from far away, because they had received no advance warning of faith in him from the records of the sacred writings.

“And he asked them: ‘How many loaves do you have?’ They said: ‘Seven.’” Seven loaves are rightly placed in the mystery of the New Testament, in which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is more fully both revealed to all the faithful for belief and given to those who believe.

They are not reported to have been barley loaves, as were the five loaves by which five thousand people were satisfied, lest once again the vital nourishment of the soul should be hidden beneath bodily sacraments, as it was in the Law. For the kernel of barley is covered by an extremely tenacious husk.

[Col. 0281D] “And he commanded the crowd to sit down on the ground.” Earlier, at the feeding with five loaves, the crowd sat down on green grass. Now, where it is to be fed with seven loaves, it is commanded to sit down on the ground, because through the Scripture of the Law we are commanded to trample down and restrain the desires of the flesh. For “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40).

In the New Testament we are also commanded to abandon the earth itself and temporal possessions. Or certainly, because the mountain on which the crowd was fed with the Lord’s loaves signifies, as we said above, the height of our Redeemer, there the crowd is fed on grass, here on the ground.

There, the height of Christ is covered, on account of carnal people and earthly Jerusalem, by carnal hope and desire. Here, with every carnal desire removed, the guests of the New Testament are held by the foundation of enduring hope—as firm as the solidity of the mountain itself—with no grass placed between.

And taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke them and [Col. 0282A] gave them to his disciples to distribute; and they distributed them to the crowd. The Lord took the loaves and gave them to the disciples, so that they might distribute what they had received to the crowd: for, bestowing spiritual gifts of knowledge upon the apostles, he desired that through their ministry the nourishment of life should be distributed throughout the world to his Church. That he broke the loaves which he was to give to the disciples signifies the opening of the mysteries by which the world was to be nourished for everlasting salvation. For when the Lord himself says, “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Luke X), what else did he show than that the bread of life was to be opened to us through him, whose inner meaning we ourselves were unable to penetrate and behold? Concerning this the prophet, lamenting the pitiable hunger of certain people, said: “The children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lamentations IV). In other words: the unlearned sought the nourishment of the word of God, by which they might be refreshed and strengthened for virtuous action, but, with teachers lacking, there was no one to disclose to them the secrets of the Scriptures [Col. 0282B] and instruct them in the way of truth. Having received the loaves for breaking, the Lord gives thanks, both to show how greatly he himself rejoices in the salvation of the human race and to train us always to give thanks to God whenever, through the generosity of heavenly grace, we refresh either the body with earthly bread or the soul with heavenly nourishment.

And they had a few small fish, and he blessed these also and ordered them to be distributed. If the seven loaves signify the Scripture of the New Testament, in whose reading we find, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, inward banquets for the mind, whom should we understand by the small fish—which the Lord likewise blessed and ordered to be distributed to the crowd—except the saints of the period in which that Scripture was composed, or those whose faith, life, and sufferings that Scripture contains? Rescued from the turbulent waves of this age and consecrated by divine blessing, they have provided us with inward refreshment, so that we may not fail amid the passing course of this world, through the example of either their life or their death.

[Col. 0282C] And they ate and were satisfied. They eat of the Lord’s loaves and fish and are satisfied who, hearing the words of God and contemplating the examples set before them, hasten to be stirred and rise toward progress in a reformed life. To them the Psalmist’s saying aptly applies: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord; those who seek him shall live for ever and ever” (Psalm XXI). This plainly means: the humble will hear the word of God and do it, and they will attribute everything they do well not to their own praise but to that of the heavenly giver.
