Therefore, as those satisfied with the bread of life, they will deservedly attain the eternal life of the inner person. In contrast, the prophet reproaches sluggish hearers: “You have eaten, and have not been satisfied” (Haggai I). For they eat and are not satisfied who taste the bread of God’s word by hearing it, but, because they do not do what they hear, receive nothing of its inward sweetness—nothing by which their hearts may be strengthened—into the stomach of memory.

And they took up what remained of the fragments, seven baskets [Col. 0282D]. The apostles take up what remains after the crowd has been satisfied and fill seven baskets, because there are higher commands—or rather exhortations and counsels—of perfection which the general multitude of the faithful cannot reach by observing and fulfilling them. Their execution properly concerns those who, filled with a greater grace of the Holy Spirit, surpass the general conduct of God’s people in the sublimity of mind and deed. To such people it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have” (Matthew XIX). Thus the baskets in which the fragments of the Lord’s food were stored are appropriately said to have been seven, on account of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. Since baskets are usually woven from rushes and palm leaves, they are rightly used as a sign of the saints. For the rush commonly grows over water, while the palm adorns the hand of the victor. The elect are rightly compared to vessels of rushes when they set the root of their heart at the very source of life, lest it dry up through lack of love for eternity. They are likewise compared to things woven from palm leaves when they retain in a pure heart the unfailing remembrance [Col. 0283A] of eternal recompense. And appropriately the crowd, although it could not contain the remains of the Lord’s meal, is nevertheless said to have eaten and been satisfied: for there are some who, although they cannot leave all their possessions or fulfill what is said concerning virgins—“Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (Matthew XIX)—and other such commands, nevertheless hunger and thirst for righteousness and are satisfied when, by hearing the commandments of God’s law, they attain eternal life (Matthew V).

Now there were about four thousand who had eaten, and he dismissed them. “Four thousand” is appropriate, so that by this number also he might show that they had been fed with evangelical nourishment.

## HOMILY VII. FOR THE EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 0283B] **LUKE VI, MATTHEW VII.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. For there is no good tree that produces bad fruit,” and so forth.

Christ Jesus our Savior continues what he had begun concerning the hypocrite. “If,” he says, “you wish to have righteousness that is genuine and not feigned, take care to match in deeds what you display in words, so that, being a good tree, you may be adorned with good fruits.” For although the hypocrite pretends, he is not good who performs evil works; and although he reproves the innocent, the one who performs good works is not therefore evil.

For every tree is known by its fruit. The Apostle shows what sort of fruit distinguishes a good or bad tree, saying: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, contentions, rivalries, anger, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, which I declare to you, as I have declared before: those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians V). Almsgiving, prayer, and fasting, moreover, are indeed properly the fruit of the good, but sometimes they are also falsely practiced by the wicked, concerning whom the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matthew VI). And elsewhere: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew VII). Yet the sheep ought not therefore to hate their clothing, because wolves often conceal themselves in it: they display one thing in order to deceive and reveal another in order to plunder or kill those who cannot see the wolves beneath this sheep’s clothing. This, then, is not the fruit by which he urges us to recognize the tree, but the fruit mentioned above.

Nor do they gather figs from thorns, nor harvest grapes from a bramble. I think that the thorns and the bramble signify the cares of the world and the pricks of vices, concerning which it was said to the sinful man: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis III). The fig and the grape signify the sweetness of a renewed way of life, for which the Lord hungers in us, and the fervor of love that gladdens the human heart—concerning which, when the Gospel shone forth, the voice of the turtledove resounded far and wide throughout the land: “The fig tree has put forth its green figs, and the flowering vines have given their fragrance” (Song II). Figs are not gathered from thorns, nor grapes from a bramble, because a mind still weighed down by the habits of the old person can pretend, but cannot bear the fruit of the new person.

If someone should object and say that Moses also harvested grapes from a bramble when he received useful advice from his gentile kinsman (Exodus XVIII), and that those gathered figs from thorns to whom it was said concerning the Pharisees, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matthew XXIII), let him understand that, just as a fruitful vine sometimes lies enclosed within a hedge and, while bearing fruit, preserves the thorn—not its own—for human use, so the words or deeds of the wicked, whenever they benefit the good, are not themselves accomplished by the wicked; rather, this comes about through the providential purpose of heaven.

A good person brings forth good from the good treasure of the heart, and an evil person brings forth evil from the evil treasure. The treasure of the heart is the same as the root of the tree, and what comes forth from the heart is the same as the fruit of the tree. Whoever therefore possesses in his heart the treasure of patience and perfect love, pouring forth excellent fruits, loves his enemy, does good to the one who hates him, blesses the one who curses him, prays for the one who slanders him, does not resist the one who strikes or strips him, gives to everyone who asks, does not seek to recover what has been taken from him, does not desire to judge or condemn, corrects the one who errs patiently and lovingly, and does the other things that the Savior taught above (Luke VI). But whoever keeps a wicked treasure in his heart hates his friend, curses the one who loves him, curses the one who blesses him (Matthew V), and performs, in opposition to the good treasure, the other things condemned by the Lord’s word. So that no one might flatter himself uselessly on account of what follows:

[Col. 0284B] For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. As though not the fruit of the tree but its leaves—that is, words alone and not deeds—were being sought in either the true Christian or the hypocrite, the Lord appropriately adds:

“But why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” As though he were saying in other words: “Why do you boast that you put forth the leaves of right confession, when you display no fruits of good works?” Therefore the Apostle, about to separate what is precious from what is vile—that is, the good treasure from the evil, the good tree from the bad, the perfect disciple of a good teacher from the hypocrite, and the seeing guide from the blind—says: “I will come to you, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power” (I Corinthians IV). For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power.

By the expression “of the mouth,” therefore, the Lord indicates everything that we bring forth from the heart in deed, speech, or thought—things that are naked and open to his eyes even more than when spoken to human beings. It is also customary in Scripture to use words for realities. Thus the Psalmist says: “Say to my soul: I am your salvation” (Psalm XXXIV; Isaiah XXXIX; and II Kings [IV Kings] XX). And Hezekiah said: “There was no word that I did not show them.” Certainly he had revealed to the Chaldeans the secrets of realities, not of words. Likewise the Apostle says: “No one says, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Corinthians XII), meaning: no one perceives the Lord Jesus with understanding, and no one embraces him by the will, except through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## HOMILY VIII. FOR THE NINTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**LUKE XVI.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples this parable: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this steward was accused before him of having wasted his goods. And he called him and said to him: ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.’ But the steward said within himself: ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do, so that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses,’” and so forth.

In this steward whom the master expelled from his stewardship and praised because he had provided for his future, we must not take everything as something to imitate. We must neither defraud our Lord in any way in order to make alms from that fraud, nor may those from whom we wish to be received into eternal dwellings be understood as debtors of God and our Lord, since here they signify the just and holy who introduce into eternal dwellings those who have shared their earthly goods with the needy. Concerning these he also says: “If anyone gives one of them a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, he will not lose his reward” (Matthew X).

Yet these comparisons are also presented in the opposite direction, so that we may understand that if the master was able to praise the man to whom he was being defrauded, how much more must those please the Lord God who perform such works according to his command. Likewise, concerning the unjust judge who was importuned by a widow, he drew a comparison with God the Judge, to whom the unjust judge cannot be compared in any respect.

From the term “steward,” certainly, we learn that those who possess money should no longer be thought of as masters of their own property but rather as dispensers of another’s goods. If, following the example of this servant, they carefully foresee the time when their stewardship and accounting must end, they will readily be stripped both of delight in and love for all earthly things, and will take care to provide more for acquiring friends in the future than for gathering wealth in the present.

After anxiously considering many things within himself, he says: “What shall I do? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg.” Once the stewardship has been taken away, we cannot dig, because when this life has ended—in which alone it is permitted to work—we can no longer seek the fruit of a good way of life with the spade of devoted repentance. To beg is a matter of shame, namely, that worst kind of begging by which those foolish virgins are said to have begged. When the time of the wedding approached and the oil of virtues had failed, they said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matthew XXV). Solomon speaks of the same thing: “Because of the cold the lazy man would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him” (Proverbs XX).

Then, summoning each of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: “How much do you owe my master?” He replied: “A hundred measures of oil.” He said to him: “Take your bond, sit down quickly, and write fifty.” Then he said to another: “And how much do you owe?” He replied: “A hundred measures of wheat.” He said to him: “Take your document, and write eighty.”

A *cadus* is a Greek *amphora* containing three urns, while a *corus* contains thirty *modii*. As for the fact that he had the debtor write fifty in place of a hundred measures of oil, and eighty in place of a hundred measures of wheat, I think it signifies nothing other than that, in the Church of Christ, the righteousness of each person should abound beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees in matters performed similarly toward priests and Levites by a Jew. Thus, when they gave tenths, these should give halves, just as Zacchaeus gave not from his produce but from his actual possessions (Luke XIX); or else they should double the tithes, surpassing the expenditure of the Jews by giving two tenths.

Unless someone thinks the passage should be understood more simply: whoever alleviates the need of any poor person among the saints, whether from one-half or indeed from one-fifth—as twenty or fifty are portions of one hundred—will certainly be granted the reward of his mercy.

And the Lord praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently. For the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light. Let the wise of this age hear how highly divine equity has valued their wisdom, so that they may abandon foolish wisdom and learn the wise foolishness of God. He does not say that they are truly prudent, but that they are prudent in their generation, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent before yourselves” (Isaiah V).

By calling those who love eternal life “children of light,” he also condemns those who are wise enough to do evil but unable to do good as nothing other than children of darkness. The children of light and the children of this age are so called (Jeremiah IV), just as there are children of the kingdom and children of perdition. For each person is called the child of the one whose works he performs.

And I say to you: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.” He calls the money that we possess temporarily “the mammon of iniquity” because *mammon* is interpreted as “wealth.” Such wealth exists only for the wicked, who place in it the hope and abundance of their happiness. When the just possess these things, they are indeed money, but they are not wealth for them; their wealth is heavenly and spiritual. By spiritually supplying their need through these, and excluding the poverty of misery, they will be enriched with an abundance of blessedness.

If those who give alms make friends for themselves from unjust mammon, by whom they may be received into eternal dwellings, how much more ought those who distribute spiritual food—those who give their fellow servants nourishment at the proper time—to be raised up by the most certain hope of the highest reward?

Whoever is faithful in the least is faithful also in much; and whoever is unjust in what is little is unjust also in much. Some, ignorant of compassion and of the works of mercy owed to their neighbors, nevertheless consider themselves genuinely faithful on account of chastity, vigils, prolonged prayer, full faith, fasts, and the other virtues that the love of God usually produces. But the Judge himself bears witness that whoever is faithful in the least—that is, in sharing money with the poor—is faithful also in what is greater, namely, in that act by which he desires especially to cling to the Creator and become one spirit with him.

But whoever neglects to dispense properly the temporal things he possesses empties himself of the glory of eternal things, about which he is puffed up. “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (I John IV). And, as the same apostle says: “Whoever possesses the substance of the world and sees his brother in need, yet closes his compassion against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (John III).

If therefore you were not faithful in unjust mammon, who will entrust to you what is yours? It has already been explained above that unjust mammon signifies the wealth of the wicked. Referring to these, the Savior says elsewhere: “The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word” (Matthew XXIII). True riches signify either the joys of eternal life, concerning which it is written, “what are the riches of his inheritance among the saints,” or the abundance of spiritual virtues by which one reaches life. Of these Isaiah says: “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord is itself his treasure” (Isaiah XXXIII).

And if you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours? The resources of this age are alien to us—that is, they lie outside our nature. For we brought nothing into this world, and there is no doubt that we can take nothing away [Col. 0286C]. Our possession, however, is the kingdom of heaven; our life is Christ; our riches are the fruits of spiritual works (I Timothy VI), concerning which Solomon says: “The redemption of a man is his own riches” (Proverbs XIII).

He therefore accuses the Pharisees of fraud and greed: because they were not faithful with their possessions, preferring to hold privately the Creator’s common goods, they did not deserve to receive Christ. But that publican whom I mentioned shortly before, Zacchaeus, in order to acquire Christ, offered half of his possessions (Luke XIX).

## HOMILY IX. FOR THE TENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**LUKE XIX; MATTHEW XXIV; MARK XIII.** At that time, when Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem, seeing the city he wept over it, saying: “If you had known—even you, and indeed on this your day—the things that are for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will surround you and hem you in on every side,” and so forth.

Everyone who has read the history of the city’s destruction knows that, when the Lord wept, the overthrow of Jerusalem was being described—the overthrow carried out by the Roman emperors Vespasian and Titus. But we must first ask what is meant by the words:

“Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you had known—even you.’” The pious Redeemer wept over the ruin of the faithless city, which did not know that this ruin was coming upon it. The weeping Lord rightly says to it, “If you had known—even you,” with “you would have wept” understood: you who now rejoice because you do not know what is impending. Hence it follows:

“And indeed on this your day, the things that are for your peace.” Since it gave itself over to the pleasures of the flesh and did not foresee the evils to come, it possessed, on its own day, those things that could be for its peace. Why it possessed present blessings for its peace is made clear when it follows:

“But now they are hidden from your eyes.” For if the evils that threatened had not been hidden from the eyes of its heart, it would not have rejoiced in present prosperity. Its punishment, which—as I said—was impending from the Roman emperors, is immediately added:

“For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will surround you and hem you in on every side; they will cast you and your children who are within you to the ground.” What is added also testifies to the city’s subsequent removal: “They will not leave in you one stone upon another.” Since the city is now built in the place outside the gate where the Lord had been crucified, the former Jerusalem was utterly destroyed.

The fault for which the punishment of its destruction was inflicted is then added:

“Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” The Creator of all deigned to visit it through the mystery of the incarnation, but it did not remember his fear or love. Therefore, through the prophet’s rebuke of the human heart, the birds of heaven are brought forward as witnesses: “The kite in the sky knows its time; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork observe the time of their coming, but my people do not know the judgment of the Lord” (Jeremiah VIII).

And entering the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling and buying in it, saying to them: “It is written: ‘My house is a house of prayer.’” The one who had announced the evils to come and immediately entered the temple in order to drive out from it those who were selling and buying plainly made known that the people’s ruin arose chiefly from the guilt of the priests. In describing the destruction, yet striking the sellers and buyers in the temple, he showed through the very effect of his action from where the root of perdition emerged.

“But you have made it a den of robbers.” Those who sat in the temple to receive gifts would certainly seek injuries against those who did not give them; there was no doubt of this. The house of prayer had therefore been made a den of robbers, because they knew how to remain in the temple for this purpose: either to persecute bodily those who were unwilling to give gifts, or to kill spiritually those who did give them.

But because our Redeemer does not withhold the words of preaching even from the unworthy and ungrateful, after displaying the force of discipline by driving out the perverse, he immediately showed the gift of grace. For it follows:

“And he was teaching daily in the temple.”

We have passed briefly through these matters according to their historical meaning; now let us return to examine the same things in their moral sense.

“Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you had known—even you.’” He did this once when he announced that the city would perish; our Redeemer does not cease to do this daily through his chosen ones when he sees that some have passed from a good life to corrupt conduct. He mourns for those who do not know why they are mourned, because, in Solomon’s words, “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs II). If they had recognized the condemnation threatening them, they would have mourned themselves, with tears, for their sins.

“And indeed on this your day, the things that are for your peace.” The perverse soul has its own day here: it rejoices for a fleeting time, and the things that are present are for its peace. While it rejoices in temporal things, while it is lifted up by honors, while it dissolves in the will of the flesh, and while it is terrified by no fear of future punishment, it has peace on its own day, whereas on the day that is not its own it will experience the grievous downfall of its condemnation. For there it will be afflicted where the just will rejoice.

“But now they are hidden from your eyes.” The perverse soul, devoted to present things and dissolved in earthly pleasures, hides from itself the evils that follow, because it refuses to foresee the future things that would disturb its present joy. And while it abandons itself to the delight of the present life, what else does it do but go toward the fire with closed eyes?

“For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart.” Who are ever greater enemies of the human soul than evil spirits? They besiege it as it leaves the body, although, while it was set upon the love of the flesh, they had cherished it with deceptive pleasures. They surround it with a rampart when, bringing before the eyes of its mind the iniquities it committed, they hem it in and drag it into fellowship with their condemnation.

“And they will surround you and hem you in on every side.” Evil spirits hem the soul in on every side when they recall to it not only the iniquities of its deeds but also those of its speech and, beyond these, its thoughts, so that the soul which previously expanded itself through many sins may finally be constricted by them all in retribution.

“And they will cast you and your children who are within you to the ground.” Then the soul is cast down to the ground through knowledge of its guilt, and the flesh, which it believed to be its life, is forced to return to dust. Then its children fall in death, when the unlawful thoughts that now proceed from it are scattered in the final punishment of life, as it is written: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Psalm CXLV).

These harsh thoughts can also be understood through the symbolism of stones, for it follows:

“And they will not leave in you one stone upon another.” When a perverse mind adds a still more perverse thought to a perverse thought, what else does it do than place one stone upon another? But in a destroyed city no stone is left upon stone, because, when the soul is brought to its punishment, the entire structure of its thoughts is scattered.

“Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” Almighty God also customarily visits the perverse soul in many ways. He visits it continually through a commandment, sometimes through a scourge, and sometimes through a miracle, so that it may hear the truth that it did not know and, while it still remains proud and contemptuous, may either return, pierced by suffering, or, conquered by blessings, become ashamed of the evil it has done. But because it does not recognize the time of its visitation, at the end of life it is handed over to those enemies with whom it will be joined in fellowship of condemnation at the eternal judgment.

“And entering the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling in it and those who were buying.” Just as the temple of God is in a city, so the life of religious people is in the faithful community. Often some take on the religious habit, but when they obtain a place among the sacred orders, they turn the office of holy religion into a commerce in earthly business.

Those who sell in the temple are those who distribute for a reward what they are entitled to distribute by right. To sell justice is to preserve it in exchange for receiving a reward. Those who buy in the temple are those who, while unwilling to render to their neighbor what is just and while refusing to do what is owed by right, purchase sin by paying a reward to their patrons.

To them it is rightly said: “My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers.” For when perverse people occupy a place of religion, they kill there with the swords of their wickedness where they ought to have given life to their neighbors through the intercession of their prayer.

The temple and house of God is also the mind and conscience of the faithful. Whenever it brings forth perverse thoughts to injure a neighbor, robbers sit there as in a den, and they kill those who walk innocently when they drive the swords of injury into those who are guilty of nothing. The mind of the faithful is no longer a house of prayer but a den of robbers when, having abandoned the innocence and simplicity of holiness, it seeks to do what can harm its neighbors.

But because, through the sacred pages, we are continually instructed by the words of our Redeemer against all these perverse things, what is said to have happened is now still being enacted:

“And he was teaching daily in the temple.” For whenever he subtly instructs the minds of the faithful to avoid evils, Truth teaches daily in the temple.

The chief priests and scribes, and the leaders of the people, sought to destroy him, but they could not find what they should do to him. Whether because he taught daily in the temple, because he had driven the robbers from the temple, or because, coming as King and Lord, he had received the praise of a heavenly hymn from so great a crowd of believers [Col. 0289A], the envious leaders sought to destroy him.

For all the people hung upon his words as they listened to him. This can be understood in two ways: either, fearing an uprising of the people, they could not find what to do to Jesus, whom they had resolved to destroy; or they sought to destroy Jesus because, having neglected their teaching, they saw many people flocking to hear him.

Meanwhile, it is worth briefly observing how beautifully the legal shadow of Passover corresponds with our Passover, in which Christ was sacrificed, not only in its mystery but also in its timing. “On the tenth day,” it says, “of the first month, let each person take a lamb for the families of his household. According to this rite, you shall also take a kid, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month” (Exodus XII).

On the tenth day of the first month—that is, five days before Passover—as the evangelist John testifies, all the people going out to the Mount of Olives took the Lord from there (John XII). He is a lamb because he came to take away sins, and there is no sin in him (John I); he is a kid because he was accused of sin.

They brought the lamb into the house—the people who rejoicingly sang, “Blessed is he who comes, the King, in the name of the Lord” (Luke XIX); they brought the kid—the people who, out of hostility, said, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples” (ibid.).

The entire people who hung upon his words were the lamb; the leaders who desired to destroy him were the kid. Five days before Passover—that is, from the tenth day of the month until the fourteenth—they kept the lamb or kid that they were going to sacrifice. Although they already thirsted for his blood, no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.

Those who gladly listened to his words kept the lamb; those who lay in wait and sought to seize something from his mouth in order to accuse him kept the kid. But when the fourteenth day had been completed—that is, as evening approached—after he had handed over to the disciples the sacraments of his body and blood to be celebrated, and when those who were coming to seize and bind him arrived, what follows began to be fulfilled: “And the entire assembly of the children of Israel shall sacrifice him at evening” (Exodus XII). For standing beside the cross of Jesus were not only the wicked, who mocked his death, but also the holy, who mourned (John XIX).

## HOMILY X. FOR THE ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**LUKE XVIII.** At that time Jesus spoke this parable to certain people who trusted in themselves as righteous and despised others: “Two men went up into the temple to pray: one a Pharisee, the other a publican,” and so forth.

Because the Lord concluded the parable by which he taught that one should always pray and not grow weary by saying that, when the Judge came, faith would scarcely be found on earth, lest anyone perhaps flatter himself on the basis of a useless knowledge or even confession of faith, he immediately joined another parable and showed more carefully that God examines not the words of faith but its works. Among these works, humility is preeminent.

Thus earlier, when he compared faith to a tiny mustard seed, though kindled by contrition, he added by way of explanation: “When you have done everything that was commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants’” (Luke XVII). In contrast, the proud, although they do not do everything but only a little of what was commanded, immediately presume upon their righteousness, despise the weak, and therefore, as though empty of faith, are not heard when they pray.

Two men went up into the temple to pray: one a Pharisee and the other a publican. The publican, praying humbly, belongs among the members of that widow—namely, the Church—of whom it was said above: “But will God not avenge his chosen ones who cry to him?” (Luke XVIII). The Pharisee, however, boasting of his merits, belongs among those concerning whom the terrifying sentence is added at the conclusion: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?”

The Pharisee, standing, prayed this within himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this publican.”

There are four forms in which every swelling of the arrogant is displayed: when they think that they possess good from themselves; or, if they believe it was given to them from above, when they suppose that they received it on account of their own merits; or when they boast of possessing what they do not possess; or when, despising everyone else, they desire to appear uniquely to possess what they do possess.

The Pharisee is found to have suffered from this plague of boasting. He descended from the temple without justification because, attributing the merits of good works to himself as though they were uniquely his own, he placed himself above the praying publican.

“I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.”

The prophet Ezekiel writes concerning the living creatures shown to him in heaven: “And the whole body of the four of them was full of eyes, all around” (Ezek. 1). The bodies of the living creatures are described as full of eyes because the conduct of the saints is watchful on every side, eagerly providing for what is good and carefully avoiding what is evil. But we often attend to some matters while neglecting others; and wherever we are negligent, there, without doubt, we have no eye.

For behold, the Pharisee had an eye for displaying abstinence, for showing mercy, and for giving thanks to God, but he had no eye for guarding humility. And what benefit is there if almost the whole city is carefully guarded against the enemy’s ambushes, if one opening is left exposed through which the enemy may enter?

“But the publican, standing far off, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.”

What confidence of forgiveness this rightly gives to penitents: the publican, who fully recognized the guilt of his wickedness, wept and confessed; and though he came to the temple unjustified, he returned from the temple justified. Allegorically, the Pharisee is the Jewish people, which exalts its merits through the justifications of the Law; the publican, however, is the Gentile, who, placed far from God, confesses his sins. One of them, by growing proud, departed humbled; the other, by lamenting, merited to draw near and be exalted.

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” This can properly be understood both of the two peoples just mentioned and of every proud or humble person, just as we read elsewhere: “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. 15 and 16).

Therefore, from the words of the exalted Pharisee, through which he merited humiliation, we may in reverse take an example of the humility by which we are exalted. Just as he, considering both the vices of worse people and his own virtues, was lifted up to ruin, so may we, observing not only our own sluggishness but also the virtues of those who are better, humble ourselves toward glory, so that each of us may earnestly and submissively entreat within himself:

“Almighty God, have mercy on your suppliant, because I am not like the countless servants of yours who are exalted by contempt for the world, glorious through the merit of righteousness, angelic in the praise of chastity—or like the many who, after public sins, have merited through repentance to become devoted to you. Even if, by your gracious gift, I do anything good, I do not know with what intention I do it, or with what severity it is weighed by you.”

## HOMILY XI: ON THE TWELFTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**Mark 7.** At that time, Jesus, departing from the region of Tyre, came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, between the borders of the Decapolis, etc.

That deaf and mute man whom, as we have just heard when the Gospel was read, the Lord wondrously healed signifies the human race, in those who deserve to be freed by divine grace from the error of diabolical deception. Humanity became deaf to the hearing of the word of life after, in its pride, it heard the deadly words of the serpent against God; it became mute regarding the praise of the Creator from the moment it presumed to converse with the seducer.

And rightly did it close its ears to hearing the Creator’s praise among the angels—ears which, through the enemy’s words, it heedlessly opened to hear the same Creator’s condemnation. Rightly did it close its mouth to proclaiming the Creator’s praise with the angels—mouth which, as though to improve the Creator’s work, it proudly filled by transgressing through forbidden food.

And alas, what a miserable defect of the human race! What germinated as diseased at the root began to spread much more diseased through the branches of its offspring, so that, when the Lord came in the flesh, almost the whole world, except for a few faithful people from Judea, wandered deaf and mute, without knowledge or confession of the truth.

“But where sin increased, grace increased all the more” (Rom. 5). The Lord therefore came to the Sea of Galilee, where he knew that the one whom he would heal was afflicted. He came by the grace of his compassion to the swelling, troubled, and unstable hearts of the nations, among which he knew there were those who belonged to his grace.

And rightly is he said to have come between the borders of the Decapolis to the Sea of Galilee, where he would heal the sick man, because, having abandoned on account of unbelief the people who had received the commands of the Decalogue, he came to the foreign nations, so that, as John says, he might “gather into one the children of God who were scattered” (John 11).

“And they bring him,” he says, “a deaf man who could scarcely speak, and they beg him to lay his hand upon him.” Since the deaf man himself could neither recognize the Savior nor, being mute, ask him, his friends bring him and beseech the Lord for his health.

So indeed, so must it happen in spiritual healing: if someone cannot be turned by human effort to hear and confess the truth, he must be offered to the sight of divine compassion, and the help of the heavenly hand must be implored for his healing. The mercy of the heavenly physician does not delay when the earnestness of those praying does not falter and prayer does not fail. Hence it immediately continues:

“When Jesus took the sick man aside from the crowd, he put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue.” He puts his fingers into the deaf man’s ears so that he may hear when, through the gifts of spiritual grace, he turns those who have long been unbelieving toward hearing his word.

Spitting, he touches the mute man’s tongue so that he may speak, when through the ministry of preaching he grants the understanding of faith that he ought to confess. He himself teaches that the gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified by the Lord’s fingers, saying: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11). Another Evangelist states this more plainly: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12). The Psalmist likewise says: “For I shall see the heavens, the work of your fingers” (Ps. 8)—that is, I shall see the saints, raised above earthly things and made exalted in heavenly conduct, not by the merit of their own virtue but by the gift of your Spirit.

The spittle of the Lord’s head and mouth is also the word of the Gospel, which, taken from the invisible mystery of his divinity, he graciously bestowed visibly upon the world so that it might be healed.

It should certainly be noted that, before touching the sick man’s ears and tongue to heal them, the Lord took him aside and led him away from the crowd. The first hope of salvation is for anyone to abandon the tumult and crowds of habitual vices and thus humbly bow his head to receive the gifts of health.

No one should be thought capable of being saved so long as he clings to disordered behavior, delights in empty words, and does not fear being ravaged by turbulent thoughts. When, through the Lord’s mercy and help, a person has changed the troubled life of his former conduct, conceived the inspiration of divine grace in his heart, and learned through the word of heavenly teaching the confession of true faith, it remains for him immediately to attain the desired joys of health. Hence, after the Lord separates the sick man from the crowd, puts his fingers into his ears, and touches his tongue with spittle, it rightly continues:

“Looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him: Ephpheta,” which means “to open”; “and immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed.”

And rightly, when about to heal the sick man, the Lord looks up to heaven and groans, to signify where salvation must be hoped for and with what devotion of contrition or tears it must be sought and requested. He looks up to heaven and groans because he grieved that we, whom he created to possess heavenly things, had been cast down far into earthly things.

He looks up to heaven and groans so that he might show us who departed from heavenly joys through earthly pleasures that we must return to them through groans and sighs.

When he says “Ephpheta,” that is, “to open,” he speaks concerning the ears being healed, which prolonged deafness had closed, but which his touch had now opened for hearing. Hence, I believe that the custom became widespread in the Church whereby her priests, among the other beginnings of consecration, touch with the saliva of their mouths the noses and ears of those whom they are preparing to receive the sacraments of baptism, saying “Ephpheta.”

By the saliva of their mouths they signify the taste of the heavenly wisdom with which those being initiated are to be endowed; by the touching of the nostrils, they signify that, having rejected harmful pleasures, they should always embrace only the fragrance of Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2). They should also remember that, following the example of blessed Job, “as long as breath remains in them, and the spirit of God is in their nostrils,” they ought not to speak iniquity with their lips or devise falsehood with their tongue (Job 27).

By the touching of the ears, moreover, they are taught that, having abandoned the hearing of an evil tongue, they should hear Christ’s words and do them, like the prudent man who built his house upon the rock (Matt. 7).

And each one of us, dearest brothers, who has rightly received Christ’s baptism has been consecrated in this manner. All who are rightly to receive the saving bath, whether at the coming Easter season or at some other time, are to be consecrated in this same order.

Therefore it is very necessary that we fear contaminating and profaning without concern what the Lord has graciously deigned to wash and sanctify in us. But if any of us has fallen into the filth of wickedness that soils us, let us hasten to be cleansed again in the fountain of tears and repentance.

Let us renew the purity of our ears, which we know was divinely bestowed upon us through hearing faith, guarding against what the Apostle says in reproach to certain people: “They will turn away from hearing the truth and turn to myths” (2 Tim. 4).

Let us restrain from evil the tongue that was sanctified by the confession of faith. Let us fear using that very tongue with which we bless God and the Father to curse human beings, who were made in the image of God (Jas. 3). For whoever thinks he is religious but does not bridle his tongue—his religion is worthless (Jas. 1).

For behold, it is said that “his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke correctly.” Since, at the time of our baptism, we say that we speak correctly by believing in our heart for righteousness and making confession with our mouth for salvation (Rom. 10), we must take the greatest care not to turn after baptism toward unjust and harmful words.

If, as the Judge himself attests, “people will give an account for every idle word they speak on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12), what do we suppose will happen to those who speak not only idle words but criminal ones—those who do not fear serving impurity, boasting, blasphemy, and, worst of all, the words of detraction; those who utter lies, act as false witnesses, and sow discord among brothers (Prov. 6)?

It is not enough to purify our ears and tongue from evil speech if we do not also, according to the Psalmist, incline our ear to the word of God’s mouth; if our mouth does not speak wisdom and the meditation of our heart prudence (Ps. 77).

Indeed, we must preserve as clean and always further adorn with good works all the senses of our inner and outer person, all of which were washed in baptism.

But now that the deaf and mute man has been healed, let us see what follows:

“And he commanded them,” it says, “not to tell anyone. But the more he commanded them, the more they proclaimed it, and they were exceedingly astonished, saying: He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”

Why, dearest brothers, should we believe that this happened? Should we not suppose that the only-begotten Son of God, while performing the sign, wished it to remain hidden, yet that it was disclosed to the crowds against his will—and that, if he had wished, he could not have concealed in silence the sign which he was able to perform when he wished?

Or perhaps he wished to give us an example, so that when we perform works of virtue we may avoid entirely the vice of boasting and human praise, lest our good action be deprived of the gift of heavenly recompense through the empty favor of the crowd?

And yet we should know that, if our works are worthy of imitation, they can in no way remain hidden. For the sake of correcting our brothers, they are disclosed by the very one who orders all things, who says: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: “What you have said in the darkness will be spoken in the light” (Luke 12).

In every respect, then, the Lord’s command must be understood in this way. No one should think that it was said as though we ought to avoid the sight of our brothers when doing good, since the Lord says: “Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works” (Matt. 5). Rather, through the works we display to our brothers, we should seek not praise from them but their progress. For this is what follows: “And glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

Those who display good works with the intention that they alone should be praised, rather than that those who praise them should advance in goodness or that the Father who is in heaven should be glorified, are surely subject to that terrible rebuke with which it is said: “Truly, I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6).

This too must be said: if those who received the command to remain silent cannot keep the Lord’s virtues silent, how much more ought we always to devote ourselves to proclaiming divine grace, since we are commanded daily to refresh one another with words and heavenly nourishment. The Apostle John says: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22). That is, whoever has conceived in his mind the grace of heavenly inspiration, whoever speaks the word of exhortation by which he can usefully strengthen his neighbor, should by no means hide what he knows in silence. Rather, by immediately opening himself to his brothers, he should share it with them.

For if we do not neglect to speak kindly to our neighbors of the good things we know, he will be present in whom “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. 2); and what we now know in part, Jesus Christ, our Lord, the only-begotten Son of the Father, who lives and reigns with him in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages, will graciously disclose to us in the perfect light of truth.

## HOMILY XII: ON THE THIRTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**Luke 10; Matthew 15.** At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see,” etc.

Not the eyes of the scribes and Pharisees, who saw only the Lord’s body, but those blessed eyes that are able to recognize his mysteries, concerning which it is said: “And you have revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10). Blessed are the eyes of the little ones, to whom the Son deigns to reveal both himself and the Father.

“For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.” Abraham “rejoiced that he might see the day of Christ; he saw it and was glad” (John 8). Isaiah also (Isa. 6), Micah (1 Kings 22), and many other prophets saw the glory of the Lord, and for that reason they were called seers.

But all these, looking from afar and greeting the promises through a mirror and in an enigma, saw them. The Apostles, however, having the Lord present and dining with him, learning by asking him whatever they wished, had no need to be taught through angels or various forms of visions.

Those whom Luke calls many prophets and kings, Matthew more explicitly calls prophets and righteous people (Matt. 13). They are indeed great kings, because they learned not to succumb by consenting to the movements of their temptations, but to rule over them and prevail.

“And behold, a lawyer stood up, testing him and saying: Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” The lawyer who questioned the Lord, testing him about eternal life, seems, I think, to have taken the opportunity for testing from the Lord’s own words, where he says: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). But his very testing reveals how true that confession of the Lord is in which he speaks to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (ibid.).

“He said to him: What is written in the Law? How do you read it? He answered: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. 6).

In answering the lawyer, the Savior shows us the perfect path of heavenly life. To the man who first set forth the words of the Law concerning love of God and neighbor, he says:

“You have answered correctly; do this and you will live.” Then, after introducing the parable, he adds that the one who showed mercy to the wounded man was his neighbor: “Go, and you do likewise.” That is, remember that you must love and support your neighbor who is in need, with the zeal of such mercy. He makes it perfectly clear that the only love that leads to perpetual life is love displayed not merely in words but proved by the execution of a deed.

“But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: And who is my neighbor?” What madness of empty glory! The lawyer, seeking to gain the favor of the crowd so that he might boast of having answered wisely, first admits that he does not know the commandment of the Law—truly, according to the Savior’s judgment, wise and prudent in the Law.

But because he does not wish to humble himself with Christ’s little ones and desires to justify himself, he refuses to receive the blessed eyes of doves washed in the milk of innocence (Song 5), by which he might see Christ’s mysteries.

The Lord therefore so tempered his answer that he taught that everyone who showed mercy was a neighbor to anyone; yet the same parable also specifically designated the Son of God himself, who deigned to become our neighbor through his humanity.

Nor should we interpret the neighbor whom we are commanded to love as ourselves in such a way concerning Christ that we try to weaken or remove the moral principles of mutual brotherhood beneath the rules of allegory.

“Jesus looked at him and said: A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” This man is understood as Adam in the human race. Jerusalem is that heavenly city of peace; having fallen from its blessedness, he came into this mortal and wretched life, which Jericho—whose name means “moon”—aptly signifies, since it is always uncertain through varied struggles and errors of decline.

“And he fell among robbers.” Understand the robbers as the devil and his angels, into whom he fell because he was going down. For unless he had first become swollen with pride, he would not have fallen so easily when tempted from without. The saying is indeed entirely true: “Before destruction the heart is exalted” (Prov. 16).

“They also stripped him.” That is, they deprived him of the garment of the glory of immortality and innocence. This is the first robe with which, according to another parable, the profligate son is adorned when he returns through repentance (Luke 15), and which the first parents, having lost it, recognized that they were naked and put on tunics of animal skins belonging to mortal nature (Gen. 3).

“And after inflicting wounds, they departed, leaving him half dead.” The wounds are sins, by which, violating the integrity of human nature, they implanted in its exhausted inward parts, so to speak, a kind of seedbed for increasing death.

They departed not by ceasing in any way from their ambushes, but by concealing the deceits of those same ambushes. They left him half dead because they were able to strip him of the blessedness of immortal life but not to abolish the sense of reason.

Insofar as a human being can understand and know God, he is alive; but insofar as he wastes away through sins and fails in misery, he is dead, disfigured by a deadly wound.

“It happened that a certain priest was going down the same road, and when he saw him, he passed by. Likewise a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by.”

The priest and the Levite who passed by after seeing the wounded man signify the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament, where, through the decrees of the Law, the wounds of the world in its sickness could be shown but not healed. For, as the Apostle says, it was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of calves, lambs, and goats (Heb. 10).

“But a certain Samaritan, traveling along the road, came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with compassion.” The Samaritan, whose name means “guardian,” signifies the Lord. The Prophet rightly begs him, so that he may not fall among these robbers: “Guard me,” he says, “from the snare they have set for me and from the stumbling blocks of those who work iniquity” (Ps. 140).

For our sake, and for the sake of our salvation, descending from heaven, he undertook the journey of the present life and came near the one who was wasting away from the wounds inflicted upon him—that is, having been made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2), he became our neighbor by assuming our compassion and drew near through the consolation of mercy.

“And approaching, he bound his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.” He restrained the sins he found in human beings by reproving them, instilling hope of forgiveness in penitents and fear of punishment in sinners.

He binds the wounds when he commands: “Repent” (Matt. 3); he pours in oil when he adds: “For the kingdom of heaven is near” (ibid.); he also pours in wine when he says: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (ibid.).

“And placing him on his own animal, he brought him to an inn and took care of him.” His animal is the flesh in which he deigned to come to us. He placed the wounded man upon it because “he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Pet. 2). And, according to another parable, he placed the sheep that had strayed and been found upon his shoulders and brought it back to the flock (Luke 15).

Thus, being placed upon the animal means believing in Christ’s incarnation and being initiated into his mysteries, while at the same time being protected from the enemy’s attack. The inn is the present Church, where travelers are refreshed as they return from this pilgrimage to their eternal homeland.

And rightly did he bring the man who had been placed upon the animal to the inn, because no one who has not been baptized, no one who has not been joined to Christ’s body, will enter the Church.

“On the next day he took out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said: Take care of him.” The next day is after the Lord’s resurrection. Before that, indeed, through the grace of his Gospel he had enlightened those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1); but after the resurrection had been celebrated, the splendor of perpetual light shone forth more powerfully.

The two denarii are the two Testaments, in which the name and image of the eternal King are contained. “The end of the Law is Christ” (Rom. 10).

They were brought forth and given to the innkeeper on the next day because then he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). On the next day the innkeeper received the denarii, by whose price he was to care for the wounded man, because the Holy Spirit, coming upon them, taught the Apostles all truth (John 16), so that they would be able to devote themselves to instructing the nations and preaching the Gospel.

“And whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return.” The innkeeper spends beyond what he received in the two denarii when the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment” (1 Cor. 7). Likewise: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel, but we have not used this right,” so as not to burden anyone (1 Cor. 9).

When he returns, the Lord will repay the innkeeper what he promised, because, coming in judgment, the Lord says: “Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

“Which of these three, do you think, was a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” He said: “The one who showed mercy to him.”

According to the literal sense, the Lord’s judgment is clear: no one is more truly our neighbor than the one who shows mercy. The Samaritan, a resident of a foreign nation, became neighbor to the citizen of Jerusalem—not the priest or the Levite, who were of the same people, indeed born and raised in the same city, but the foreigner, because he showed greater mercy.

According to a more sacred understanding, since no one is more our neighbor than the one who healed our wounds, let us love him as the Lord our God; let us love him as our neighbor—for nothing is so near as the head is to its members; and let us also love the one who imitates Christ. For this is what follows:

“And Jesus said to him: Go, and you do likewise.” That is, to show truly that you love your neighbor as yourself, devotedly perform whatever you are able to do to relieve his bodily or spiritual need.

## HOMILY XIII: ON THE FOURTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 0296B]

**Luke 17.** At that time, as Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the midst of Samaria. And as he entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him, etc.

The lepers may not improperly be understood as those who, lacking knowledge of the true faith, profess various doctrines of error. They do not conceal their ignorance but bring it into the light as though it were the highest expertise and display the boasting of their speech.

Moreover, there is no false doctrine that does not mix in some truth. Thus, truth mingled disorderly with falsehood in a person’s single disputation or narrative, appearing like the coloring of a single body, signifies leprosy, which varies and stains human bodies with true and false patches of color.

Such people must be avoided by the Church, so that, if possible, standing farther away, they may call upon Christ with a loud cry. Hence it appropriately continues:

“They stood far off and raised their voices, saying: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” They rightly call Jesus “Master” in order to be saved. For by indicating that they had gone astray in his words, they humbly call him the Master who can save them; and when they return to knowledge of the Master, they immediately return to the form of salvation. For it follows:

“When he saw them, he said: Go, show yourselves to the priests. And it happened that, as they went, they were cleansed.”

The Lord is found to have sent none of those to whom he granted such bodily benefits to the priests except lepers. For the Jewish priesthood was a figure of the future royal priesthood that exists in the Church, by which all who belong to the body of Christ, the supreme and true chief priest, are consecrated.

And whoever, whether through heretical depravity, pagan superstition, Jewish unbelief, or even fraternal schism, has been deprived by the Lord’s grace of the variegated color of error must come to the Church and display the true color of faith that he has received.

The other vices, like disorders of health and, as it were, of the soul’s members and senses, the Lord himself heals and corrects inwardly through conscience and understanding.

Thus Paul, after hearing the Lord’s voice, “Why are you persecuting me?” and, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9), was nevertheless sent to Ananias, so that through the priesthood established in the Church he might receive the sacrament of the teaching of faith and his true color might be approved.

This was not because the Lord cannot do all things by himself—for who else performs these things even in the Church?—but so that the fellowship of the gathered faithful, by approving and sharing the doctrine of the true faith with one another in all that is spoken in words or signified in sacraments, might overlay everything with one appearance of true color.

Cornelius also, although an angel announced to him that his almsgiving had been accepted and his prayers heard, was nevertheless commanded to send for Peter on account of the unity of doctrine and the sacraments, as though it were said to him and his companions: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” For as they went, they were cleansed (Acts 10).

Peter had already come to them, but they had not yet received the sacrament of baptism and had not yet spiritually come to the priests; nevertheless, their cleansing was declared by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and the wonder of tongues.

“But one of them, when he saw that he was cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice, and fell on his face at his feet, giving him thanks.”

This one who returned glorifying God signifies the devoted humility of the one Church toward Christ. He rightly gave thanks by falling at the Lord’s feet.

For the person truly gives thanks to God who, repressing the thoughts of his own presumption, humbly sees how weak he is in himself; who attributes no virtue to himself; who recognizes that the good things he does come from the mercy of the Creator. Hence it rightly continues:

“And he was a Samaritan.” Samaritan, indeed, means “guardian.” This name most aptly signifies that people who, by giving thanks to the one from whom they received, attributes everything it has received to him, in a manner singing what is said in the Psalm:

“I will guard my strength toward you, for you, God, are my protector; my God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. 59).

He falls on his face because he is ashamed of the evils he remembers committing; for a person falls wherever he is put to shame. Hence Paul said, as though to certain people lying on their faces: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6).

In contrast, concerning the ascent of a horse—that is, concerning one who has been lifted up by the glory of this world—it is said: “May its rider fall backward” (Gen. 49). And again it is written concerning the Lord’s persecutors: “They went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18).

What does it mean that the elect fall on their face, while the reprobate fall backward, except that everyone who falls behind himself undoubtedly falls where he cannot see, whereas whoever falls before himself falls where he can see?

The wicked, because they fall among invisible things, are said to fall backward, since they collapse where they cannot now see what will follow them then. The righteous, however, because they voluntarily cast themselves down among visible things so that they may be raised among invisible things, fall as though upon their face, because, pierced by fear, they humble themselves while seeing.

“Jesus answered and said: Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” If one is added to nine, a certain representation of unity is completed. Such a combination is formed that the number cannot proceed farther unless it returns again to one, and this rule is preserved throughout the infinity of number.

The nine therefore need the one so that they may be joined together in a certain form of unity and become ten; but the one does not need them in order to preserve unity.

Therefore, just as the one who gave thanks was approved and praised as a sign of the one Church, so the nine who did not give thanks became reprobate and were excluded from the fellowship of unity. For this reason they will remain in the number nine like imperfect beings.

And rightly does the Savior inquire where they are, as though they were unknown: for God’s knowing is choosing, and his not knowing is rejecting.

“No one was found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner.” According to the bodily sense, it is easy to see that a person may not have leprosy and yet not have a good soul. But according to the meaning of this miracle, it troubles the observer to consider how the cleansed person can be called ungrateful.

Yet it is also easy to see that someone may acquire sound and true doctrine within the fellowship of the Church and discuss everything according to the Catholic rule, distinguishing the creature from the Creator, and thereby appear, through this variety of falsehoods, to have been freed from leprosy—yet still be ungrateful to God and to the Lord who cleansed him.

For, lifted up by pride, he does not prostrate himself in pious humility to give thanks. He becomes like those of whom the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1). By saying that they knew God, he shows that they had indeed been cleansed from leprosy; yet he immediately accuses them of ingratitude.

“And he said to him: Rise, go; your faith has saved you.” The one who devotedly fell before the Lord is commanded to rise and go. For the person who, subtly recognizing his weakness, lies humbly prostrate is commanded, through the consolation of the divine word, to rise to strong works and, as his merits increase daily, to advance freely toward greater perfection.

But if faith saved the man whom it inclined to give thanks to his Savior and cleanser, then unbelief destroyed those who neglected to give glory to God for the benefits they had received.

Therefore this reading is joined to the preceding one for this reason: there the parable determines that faith must be increased through humility; here the very events show more clearly that it is not merely the recognized understanding of faith but the enacted work of faith that saves the believer and gives glory to the Father who is in heaven. Amen.

## HOMILY XIV: ON THE FIFTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**Luke 16; Matthew 6.** At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: “No servant can serve two masters,” etc.

Because it is impossible to love transitory things and eternal things at the same time. If we love eternity, we possess all temporal things for use, not as objects of affection.

“For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and despise the other.” These words must be considered carefully. For he next explains who the two masters are, saying:

You cannot serve God and mammon. Let the miser hear this; let him hear who bears the name Christian, that one cannot serve mammon—that is, riches—and Christ at the same time. And yet he did not say, “Whoever has riches,” but, “Whoever serves riches.” For whoever is the servant of riches guards riches as a servant. But whoever has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes them as a master. Yet whoever serves mammon serves him who, because of his own perversity, has been placed over these earthly things and is called by the Lord “the prince of this world” (John XIV). Therefore, as is right, he will either hate the one or love the other: he will hate, that is, the devil, and love God. Or he will cling to one and despise the other: he will cling, that is, to the devil when he pursues temporal rewards as though they were his; but he will despise God—not, he says, hate him, but despise him, as those do who put his threats after their desires and flatter themselves into impunity because of his goodness. To such people Solomon says: “My son, do not add sin upon sin and say, ‘The mercy of God is great’” (Ecclesiasticus V).

But the Pharisees, who were avaricious, heard all these things and mocked him. The Lord was warning the scribes and Pharisees not to think arrogantly, not to presume upon their own righteousness, but both to receive repentant sinners and publicans and to redeem by almsgiving whatever sins might perhaps befall them. But they mocked the teacher of mercy, humility, and frugality especially for two reasons: either because he was commanding things that were less useful and that should never be done, as though he were a harmful teacher; or, certainly, because the things were useful but already practiced by them, so that his instruction seemed superfluous.

And he said to them: “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination before God.” They justify themselves before men who despise sinners as weak and desperate, while they themselves, as though perfect in every respect and free from every frailty, do not believe that they need the remedy of almsgiving. But he who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts (1 Corinthians IV) sees how rightly this height of harmful arrogance must be condemned.

## HOMILY XV. ON THE SIXTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 0299A]

**LUKE VII.** At that time, Jesus was going to a city called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd were going with him, and so forth.

Nain is a city of Galilee, two miles from Mount Tabor, toward the south, near Endor, which is a large village four miles from the same mountain, toward the south.

“And his disciples and a great crowd were going with him. When he drew near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother.” This dead man, who was carried outside the gate of the city while many looked on, signifies a man overcome by the deathly burial of crimes. Moreover, it signifies one who does not yet conceal the same death of the soul within the chamber of his heart, but exposes it to the knowledge of many through the indication of his speech or conduct, as though through the gates of his city.

He is rightly said to have been his mother’s only son, because, although the Church is one perfect and spotless virgin mother, gathered from many persons, each individual believer nevertheless rightly confesses himself to be a son of the universal Church. For every chosen person is a son when he is instructed in the faith, but a mother when he instructs others. Did he not act with a mother’s affection toward little ones when he said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians IV)?

The gate of the city through which the dead man was being carried out, I think, signifies one of the bodily senses. Whoever sows discord among brothers, whoever speaks iniquity on high (Proverbs VI; Psalm LXII), is carried out dead through the gate of the mouth. Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her (Matthew V) brings forth through the gate of the eyes the signs of his death. Whoever willingly opens his ear to idle tales, obscene songs, or detraction makes this the gate of death for his soul; and whoever does not guard the other senses makes them for himself entrances of death.

I beseech you, Lord Jesus, make all the gates of my city gates of righteousness [Col. 0299C], so that, entering through them, I may confess your name; and when your majesty, together with the heavenly ministers, visits it more frequently, may not the stench of a carried-out corpse meet you, but may salvation occupy its walls and praise its gates.

“And she was a widow, and a large crowd of the city was with her.” Every soul that remembers that it has been redeemed by the death of its bridegroom and lord recognizes that the Church is a widow. By divine providence, however, a large crowd followed the Lord, and a large crowd followed the widow, so that, having seen so great a miracle, many might become witnesses and many praisers of God.

“When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her: ‘Do not weep.’” “Stop,” he says, “weeping as though for one dead whom you will soon see rise again.” Here, mystically, the teaching of Novatian is confounded. Novatian, boasting arrogantly of his own purity, attempts to nullify the cleansing of humble penitents and denies that the true mother, the Church, who weeps over the spiritual extinction of her children, ought to be comforted by the hope of restored life. And the evangelist beautifully testifies that the Lord was first moved with compassion for the mother and then raised the son, so that in the one case he might set before us an example of piety to imitate, and in the other establish faith in a power to be marveled at.

“And he came near and touched the bier. And those who carried it stood still.” The bier on which the dead man is carried is the dangerously secure conscience of a despairing sinner. Those who carry him to be buried are either unclean desires, which drag a man into destruction, or the poisoned flatteries of flattering companions. By their favors they lift up sins and heap them higher, and by contempt they bury sinners beneath them as beneath a mound of earth. Of such people it is said elsewhere: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew VIII). The dead bury the dead when sinners, each like his companions, soothe others with harmful approval and, by piling up a mass of wicked flattery, crush them so that they may never at some point attain the hope of rising again.

Therefore, when the Lord touched the funeral bier, its bearers stood still, because the conscience, seized by fear of heavenly judgment and restraining both the frequent abundance of carnal pleasures and the crowd of those who praise unjustly, returns to itself and hastens to answer the Savior who calls it to life. Hence it rightly follows:

“And he said: ‘Young man, I say to you, arise.’ And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother.” The dead man sits up when the sinner comes back to life through inward compunction. He begins to speak when he shows the signs of restored life to all who had mourned his sin. He is returned to his mother when, by the decree of priestly judgment, he is joined again to the communion of the Church.

“Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: ‘A great prophet has arisen among us.’” The more hopeless the death of a soul that is recalled to life, the more people are corrected by the same example. Consider the prophet David; consider the apostle Peter. The higher the rank, the more grievous the fall; but the more grievous the fall, the more welcome is the mercy of the one who raises him. And the more welcome the Lord’s mercy appeared in them, the more certain the hope of salvation appeared to all penitents, so that all who hear may rightly say:

“Because God has visited his people.” Not merely by once incorporating his Word, but also by continually sending this into our hearts, so that we too may be raised up.

## HOMILY XVI. ON THE SEVENTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**LUKE XIV.** At that time, when Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him. And behold, there was a certain man with dropsy before him, and so forth.

The disease of dropsy takes its name from watery fluid: for in Greek, ὕδωρ means “water.” It is a subcutaneous fluid arising from a disorder of the bladder, accompanied by swelling inflation and foul breath. It is characteristic of the person with dropsy that the more he abounds in disordered fluid, the more greatly he thirsts. Thus he is rightly compared with the person weighed down by an overflowing stream of carnal pleasures; he is compared with the avaricious rich man, who, the more abundant he is in riches that he does not use well, the more ardently desires such things.

“And Jesus, answering, said to the lawyers and Pharisees: ‘Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?’ But they remained silent.” The statement that Jesus “answered” refers to what was said earlier: “And they were watching him.” For the Lord knows the thoughts of men (Psalm XCIII). They rightly remain silent when questioned, since they see that whatever they say will be turned against them. If it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, why are they watching to see whether the Savior will heal? If it is not lawful, why do they themselves heal animals on the Sabbath?

“But he took him, healed him, and dismissed him.” In a provident dispensation, the Lord heals the man with dropsy before the lawyers and Pharisees and then immediately argues against avarice, so that through the bodily illness of this man the illness of their hearts might be represented. Finally, after many exhortations in his discussion, it is added: “But the Pharisees, who were avaricious, heard all these things and mocked him” (Luke XVI). The more the man with dropsy drinks, the more he thirsts. So every avaricious person multiplies his thirst: when he has obtained what he desires, he pants more eagerly for other things.

“And answering them, he said: ‘Which of you, if his donkey or ox falls into a well, will not immediately pull it out on the Sabbath?’” Thus he convicts the Pharisees who were watching him and also condemns them for avarice. “If you,” he says, “hasten on the Sabbath to rescue a donkey, an ox, or any other animal that has fallen into a well, caring not for the animal but for your own avarice, how much more ought I to free a human being, who is far better than an animal?” He appropriately compared the man with dropsy to an animal that had fallen into a well, for the man was afflicted by fluid.

Likewise, he compared the woman whom he said had been bound for eighteen years, and whom he released from that bondage, to an animal that is untied in order to be led to water (Luke XIII). And he appropriately mentioned both an ox and a donkey in each place, because whether we understand them to signify the wise and the dull, or, as was said above, the two peoples, that is, the one whose neck the yoke of the law has worn down and the one whom any deceiver finds like a brute animal, resisting no reason, and drags into whatever error he wishes, the Savior, when he came, found all bound by Satan’s chain and all submerged in the lowest well of desire. For there is no distinction: all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans III).
