“And he was also telling a parable to those who had been invited, observing how they chose the first places at table, saying to them: ‘When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place.’” On the literal level, this admonition of the Savior is clear: it teaches that humility is praiseworthy not only before God but also among human beings. But since the evangelist does not call it a parable without reason, we should briefly consider what it also signifies mystically.

That the union of Christ and the Church is called a wedding is evident in many passages. One is: “Can the children of the wedding fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Mark II). Another is: “The kingdom of heaven has become like a man who made a wedding for his son and sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding” (Matthew XXII).

Whoever, then, comes to this wedding after being invited—that is, whoever is joined to the members of the Church by the grace of faith—should not recline in the first place, meaning that he should not exalt himself by boasting of his merits as though he were higher than the rest. Certainly, according to the parable in another passage (Matthew XXII), he should strive to appear clothed in a wedding garment, that is, radiant with the splendor of virtues; but he should adorn the very garment of his virtues with the ornament of devoted humility.

“Lest one more honorable than you be invited by him, and he who invited both you and him come and say to you, ‘Give this man your place,’ and then you begin with shame to take the lowest place.” The one who gives place to a more honorable person invited after him is the person who, having become overconfident through reliance on his long way of life, is surpassed by the swift progress of those who have followed him in Christ. He occupies the lowest place with shame when, recognizing better things in those who are higher, he humbles whatever he thought lofty in his own works, saying with the Prophet: “I am needy and in labors from my youth; I was exalted, but I have been humbled and put to shame” (Psalm LXXXVII).

“But when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place.” “The greater you are,” he says, “humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus III). The Psalmist also exults: “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word” (Psalm CXVIII), plainly indicating that he can be given life by the Lord if he himself thinks humbly of his virtues.

“So that when he who invited you comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’” When the Lord comes and finds someone humble, he will bless him by the name of friend and command him to ascend higher. “Whoever humbles himself like a little child, he is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVIII).

“Then you will have glory before those who recline with you.” Beautifully it says, “Then you will have glory,” so that you do not begin seeking now what is reserved for you at the end. For, as Solomon says, “The inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Proverbs XX).

This can also be understood as referring to the present life. The person who is found reclining in the lowest place is exalted when the Lord comes, because every day the Lord enters his wedding feast; every day he judges the character, places, and clothing of those at the banquet. Often, looking down on the proud, he grants the humble such great gifts of his Spirit that the assembly of those reclining together—that is, of those resting in faith—glorifies them with unanimous admiration, and, astonished, bursts forth in praise of its creator, saying: “But to me your friends have been honored exceedingly, O God; their dominion has been strengthened exceedingly” (Psalm CXXXVIII).

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” From this conclusion it is plainly clear that the Lord’s preceding speech is to be understood typologically. For not everyone who exalts himself before men will immediately be humbled, nor will everyone who humbles himself in the sight of men be exalted by them. On the contrary, sometimes a person who raises himself either to the summit of dignity or to any other honor he seeks does not cease to be exalted all the way to the end. Likewise, any humble and modest person may remain until the end of life in the modest condition with which he is content.

Therefore, because according to the judgment of Truth everyone who carelessly lifts himself up on account of his merits will be humbled by the Lord, and whoever prudently humbles himself because of his good works will be exalted by him, the preceding speech of the Redeemer—by which he forbids the seeking of the first places at weddings—plainly agrees with this same meaning.

“He was also saying to the one who had invited him: ‘When you give a luncheon or a dinner, do not invite your friends, or your brothers, or your relatives, or rich neighbors.’” He does not forbid brothers, friends, and the rich to hold banquets for one another as though this were a crime. Rather, just as with the other exchanges of human necessity, in which sinners lend to sinners so that they may receive equal returns, he shows that such conduct is of no value for earning the rewards of heavenly life. Finally, he adds:

“Lest they also invite you in return, and repayment be made to you.” He does not say, “and sin be made for you,” but, “and repayment be made to you.” This is like what he says elsewhere: “If you do good to those who do good to you” (Luke VI), “what thanks have you?” Here too he does not say, “It is sin for you,” but, “What thanks have you?” For even sinners do this.

Nevertheless, there are certain mutual banquets of brothers, friends, relatives, and rich neighbors that receive not only repayment in the present but also condemnation in the future. Indeed, they are counted by the Apostle among the works of darkness. “Let us walk honorably,” he says, “as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness” (Romans XIII). Revelries are luxurious banquets, celebrated either by the contributions of all or customarily provided in turn by companions, so that no one is ashamed to say or do anything dishonorable. For people gather for this purpose: that disgraceful things may be done there amid an abundance of wine and that various pleasures of lust may be stirred up.

“But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” He calls it the resurrection of the just because, although all rise again, it is not without reason given as though by its own particular name to those who do not doubt that they will be blessed in the future.

Therefore, whoever invites the poor to a feast will receive a reward in the future; whoever invites friends, brothers, and the rich receives his reward. But if he does this for God’s sake, following the example of the sons of blessed Job, as with the other duties of brotherly love, the one who commanded it himself rewards him. Whoever invites gluttons and the luxurious because of wantonness will be punished with eternal punishment in the future.

[Col. 0302D]

When one of those reclining together heard this, he said to him: “Blessed is he who will eat bread in the kingdom of God.” The bread eaten in the kingdom of God is not to be understood, according to Cerinthus, as bodily food, but as the one who said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever.” That is, if anyone is perfectly incorporated into me through the sacrament of my incarnation and is deemed worthy to enjoy the vision of my divine majesty, he will rejoice in the perpetual blessedness of immortal life.

## HOMILY XVII. ON THE EIGHTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**MARK XII; LUKE X AND XX; MATTHEW XXII.** At that time, one of the scribes came and asked Jesus what the first commandment was.

There were two heresies among the Jews, one of the Pharisees and the other of the Sadducees. The Pharisees preferred the righteousness of traditions and observances, which they call *deuterosis* [“a second teaching”], and hence they were called “separated” from the people. The Sadducees, whose name is interpreted as “just,” also claimed for themselves what they were not. While the former believed in and confidently awaited the resurrection of both body and soul and followed the teaching concerning angels and spirits, the Sadducees denied all these things, according to the Acts of the Apostles (Chapter XXIII).

“And one of the scribes came, who had heard them disputing, and, seeing that he had answered them well, asked him what the first of all the commandments was.” Jesus answered him that the first of all the commandments is: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy VI). This is the first commandment.

“The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” He calls this the first and greatest of all the commandments, meaning that before everything else each of us must place it deep in the heart as the one foundation of devotion. He demonstrated this more openly in his conclusion when he said:

“There is no other commandment greater than these.” The first and greatest of all the commandments is therefore knowledge and confession of the divine unity together with the execution of good works. Good works are perfected in love of God and neighbor. The Apostle briefly commends this when he says: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Galatians V).

“And the scribe said to him: ‘Well said, Teacher; you have spoken the truth, because there is one God and there is no other besides him; and to love him with all the heart, and with all the understanding, and with all the soul, and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.’”

This answer of the scribe shows that a serious question had often been debated among the scribes and Pharisees: what was the first or greatest commandment of the divine law? Some praised offerings and sacrifices, while others, with greater authority, preferred works of faith and love. For many of the Fathers before the law had pleased God through faith alone—which works through love—without any practice of victims and sacrifices, and they held the highest place with him. But no one was ever found to have pleased God through burnt offerings and sacrifices alone, without faith and love. This scribe declared that he too held this opinion.

“Jesus, seeing that he had answered wisely, said to him: ‘You are not far from the kingdom of God.’” He was not far from the kingdom of God because he proved to be a supporter of that judgment which belongs properly to the New Testament and to evangelical perfection.

It is therefore necessary to inquire more carefully how Matthew says (Chapter XXII) that this scribe, or doctor of the law, as Matthew calls him, tested the Lord by asking about the first or greatest commandment. According to this evangelist, the Lord declares that he is not far from the kingdom of God, although it is clear that those who seek wisdom by testing cannot find it and therefore cannot approach the gate of the heavenly kingdom, which is opened only to the wise. For Scripture says: “Seek him in simplicity of heart, because he is found by those who do not test him” (Wisdom I).

Unless perhaps we say that he did approach the Lord intending to test him, but, corrected when he heard the Lord’s answer, immediately returned to the grace of devotion; and that the one whom he had previously thought must be deceived by testing he later recognized as one whom he ought to embrace and follow. Or perhaps we should not understand his testing as evil, like that of an enemy wishing to deceive, but rather as cautious, like that of someone wishing to examine more fully what was unknown. For it is not without reason that it is written: “Whoever readily believes is light of heart and will suffer loss” (Ecclesiasticus XIX).

“And no one afterward dared to question him.” The Pharisees and Sadducees and the other leaders of the Jews were seeking an opportunity for slander and trying to find some word that could be exposed to ambush. Because they had been refuted in argument, they no longer questioned him but openly seized him and handed him over to Roman authority. From this we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but that they are difficult to quiet.

“And Jesus, answering, was teaching in the temple: ‘How do the scribes say that the Christ is the Son of David? For David himself says in the Holy Spirit: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet”’ (Psalm CX). ‘David himself calls him Lord; how then is he his son?’”

Jesus’ question benefits us even today against the Jews. Those who confess that Christ is to come also assert that he is a simple human being and a holy man from the lineage of David. Let us therefore ask them, instructed by the Lord: If he is merely a man and yet David’s son, how does David call him his Lord—not through an uncertain error or his own will, but in the Holy Spirit?

They are not reproved because they say that he is David’s son, but because they do not believe that he is the Son of God. For he is both Lord and son of David: he remained God before the ages, and appeared as David’s son by being born a human being at the end of time.

But the fact that his enemies are subjected to him by the Father signifies not the weakness of the Son but the unity of nature, by which one acts in the other. For the Son also subjects his enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father on earth.

## HOMILY XVIII. ON THE NINETEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**MARK II; MATTHEW IX; LUKE V.** At that time, Jesus entered Capernaum again after eight days, and it was reported that he was in the house. And many gathered, so that there was no room, not even at the door, and so forth.

The Lord, Savior of all, traverses everything with a saving step. Now in the desert, now in the city, now beside the sea, he offers the crowds the teaching of heaven and gifts of virtue; now he prays alone on the mountain; now he helps those laboring at sea so that they may not perish. Everywhere he bestows gifts of salvation, showing that every rank and condition belongs to his grace.

According to the mystical meaning, however, after performing a miracle in the city he withdraws into the desert, and there, when crowds gather to him, he receives them with gracious kindness, showing that he loves a quieter life, removed from the cares of the world, and that, because of his desire for it, he applies himself to healing bodies. Indeed, in human fashion, as though avoiding the crowds of those seeking him, he did not wish to enter the city openly.

But allegorically he was teaching that Truth does not display the open manifestation of itself to minds tumultuous with carnal passions. Rather, it pours forth the light of its gifts more generously upon all whom it sees to be separated from the allurements of temporal things. Yet because heavenly mercy does not abandon carnal people, but even grants them the grace of its visitation, through which they too may become spiritual, the Lord returns after the desert to the city. When many gather there, he speaks the word and, after healing the paralytic, gives many an opportunity for the inward healing that is found in faith.

But the fact that, while the Lord was teaching, so many gathered in the house that there was no room, not even at the door, signifies our salvation, since we came to faith from the Gentiles. While the Lord was preaching in Judea, we were not yet able to enter to hear him. Yet, although placed outside, he caused the words of his teaching to reach us, because he himself gathered us through the mouths of holy preachers and, although we were found outside the synagogue in which he preached, made us participants in his Gospel.

“And they came, bringing to him a paralytic who was carried by four men.” The healing of this paralytic signifies the salvation of a soul longing for Christ after a long period of carnal allurements and inactivity. First of all, it needs ministers to lift it up and bring it to Christ—that is, good teachers who offer the hope of healing and the help of intercession.

They are rightly said to have been four, either because the power and every word of all preachers are confirmed by the four books of the holy Gospel, or because there are four virtues by which the confidence of the mind is raised up to obtain health. Of these it is said in praise of eternal Wisdom: “For she teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life” (Wisdom VIII). Some call these virtues prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

“And when they could not bring him to him because of the crowd, they uncovered the roof where he was.” They desire to bring the paralytic to Christ, but the crowd intervenes and shuts them off on every side, because often a soul recovering from the sloth of the lower body and desiring to be renewed by the remedy of heavenly grace is held back by the obstacle of its former habit. Often, amid the sweetness of secret prayer and what seems a pleasant conversation with the Lord, a crowd of thoughts intervenes and prevents the mind from seeing Christ.

What should be done in such circumstances? Certainly one should not remain outside in the lowest places where the crowds are making tumult. Rather, one must climb onto the roof of the house in which Christ is teaching—that is, one must seek the sublimity of sacred Scripture and meditate day and night upon the law of the Lord with the Psalmist (Psalm I). “How does a young man correct his way?” “By guarding your words,” he says (Psalm CXVIII).

“And after opening it, they lowered the mat on which the paralytic was lying.” Once the roof has been opened, the sick man is lowered before Jesus, because through the mysteries of Scripture, when they have been opened, one arrives at knowledge of Christ—that is, one descends in the devotion of faith to his humility.

And according to the account of another evangelist (Luke V), Jesus’ house is rightly found to be covered with tiles. For beneath the contemptible covering of letters, if someone is present to open the divine things, the power of spiritual grace will be found. The uncovering of the tiles in Jesus’ house is therefore the opening, beneath the lowliness of the letter, of the spiritual meaning and the heavenly mysteries.

The fact that the sick man is lowered together with his mat signifies that Christ must be known by a person who is still established in this flesh.

“When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’” As the Lord was about to cure the man of paralysis, he first dissolved the bonds of his sins, to show that the man had been condemned to the loosening of his limbs because of the bonds of his faults, and that he could not be healed by the restoration of his limbs unless those sins were first released.

Thus, to the paralytic who had long waited in vain for the movement of the water beside the Sheep Pool, the Lord says after healing him: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John VI).

“Son,” he says, “your sins are forgiven.” O marvelous humility! He calls a despised and weak man, whose entire framework of limbs has been dissolved, “son”—a man whom the priests would not have deemed worthy to touch. Or he rightly calls him a son of God, because his sins are forgiven.

It is certainly worth observing how much the faith of each person is worth before God, since another’s faith was worth so much that the whole man was suddenly restored—that is, already saved outwardly and inwardly—and the faults of some were released through the merit of others.

“But some of the scribes were sitting there, reasoning in their hearts: ‘Why does he speak this way? He is blaspheming. Who can forgive sins except God alone?’” The scribes speak truly that no one can forgive sins except God, who also forgives through those to whom he has granted the power of forgiving. Thus Christ is proved truly to be God, because he can forgive sins as God. Yet they give true testimony concerning God while erring by denying the person of Christ.

The Jews therefore err: although they believe that Christ is God and can forgive sins, they do not believe that Jesus is the Christ. But the Arians err far more foolishly. Although, overcome by the words of the Gospel, they dare not deny that Jesus is the Christ and can forgive sins, nevertheless they do not fear denying that he is God.

But he desired to save the faithless and manifested himself to be God both through his knowledge of hidden things and through the power of his works. For it follows:

“Immediately, when Jesus perceived in his spirit that they were reasoning among themselves, he said to them: ‘Why are you reasoning these things in your hearts?’” He shows himself to be God, who can know the hidden things of the heart, and in a certain way says silently: “By the same majesty and power with which I see your thoughts, I can also forgive sins to human beings.”

From this you understand what the paralytic receives. “Which is easier to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your mat, and walk’?” There is a great difference between saying and doing. Whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven was known only to the one who forgave them. But “Rise and walk” could be confirmed both by the man who rose and by those who saw him rising.

Thus a bodily sign is performed so that a spiritual reality may be proved, although it is the same power to forgive the disorders of body and soul. We are also given to understand that many bodily weaknesses occur because of sins. Perhaps for this reason sins are forgiven first, so that, once the causes of weakness have been removed, health may be restored.

There are, in fact, five different causes for which we are afflicted in this life with bodily troubles.

Either we are burdened by the weakness of a righteous body in order to increase our merits through patience, as were the blessed fathers Job and Tobias and countless martyrs in both Testaments.

Or it is for the preservation of virtues already received, so that they may not perish when pride tempts us, as with the apostle Paul. To prevent him from being exalted by the greatness of his revelations, “a thorn of his flesh, an angel of Satan, was given him to buffet him” (2 Corinthians XI).

Or it is for understanding and correcting our sins, as when Maria, the sister of Aaron, was struck with leprosy in the wilderness because of words of rashness and pride (Numbers XII).

Or it is like the paralytic we are discussing, who could not be healed of his infirmity until his sins had first been forgiven.

Or it is for the glory of God who saves, whether through himself or through his servants, as with the man born blind in the Gospel (John IX). He himself did not sin, nor did his parents, but this happened “so that the works of God might be revealed in him.” Likewise Lazarus: his illness was not unto death but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God might be glorified through it (John XI).

Or it is for the beginning of eternal condemnation, which is proper to the reprobate, as with Antiochus and Herod. Both of them, in their own time, resisted God (2 Maccabees IX; Acts XII), and the misery of their present afflictions showed all people what torments they would suffer perpetually in Gehenna. To them the prophet’s words apply: “With a double crushing, crush them” (Jeremiah XVII).

Therefore, in all the adversities we suffer temporarily, we must give thanks to the Lord with humility and, conscious of our weakness, rejoice over the remedies bestowed upon us. We must return to our conscience, carefully examine both our works and our thoughts, and cleanse with fitting correction whatever we discover ourselves to have done wrong. Whatever we find to have perished in us through the fault of pride among the things we believed we had done rightly, we must also correct with humble satisfaction. For this is often the cause of our scourging.

But for the innocent and righteous to be scourged for the increase of their rewards is a special gift of perfect men. To be compelled by temporal blows toward eternal torments, however, is the punishment of the unrepentant reprobate.

So that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he said to the paralytic: “I say to you, rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” If, according to the Psalmist (Ps. 102), God is the one who has removed our iniquities from us as far as the east is from the west, and if the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, then he is both the same God and the Son of Man: thus Christ as man, through the power of his divinity, can forgive sins, and the same Christ as God can die for sinners through the weakness of his humanity.

Spiritually, to rise from one’s bed means to withdraw the soul from carnal desires, in which it lay sick. To take up the bed means to separate the flesh itself, restrained by the reins of self-control, from earthly pleasures through hope of heavenly rewards. To take up the bed and go home means to return to paradise. For this is our true home, the one that first received humanity, having been lost not by right but by deceit and finally restored by him who owed nothing to the deceitful enemy. Alternatively, the one who had been ill carries his bed home when the soul, having received forgiveness of sins, returns with its very body to the inward keeping of itself, lest after pardon it commit anything for which it may again justly be struck.

And immediately he rose, and after taking up his bed went away before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying: “We have never seen anything like this.” How wondrous is the power of divine might, where, with no intervening delay of time, swift healing accompanies the Savior’s command! Rightly, those who had been present, rejecting the darts of blasphemy, turn their astonished hearts to the praise of such great majesty.

## HOMILY XIX: ON THE TWENTY-THIRD SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**Matthew 22; Mark 12; Luke 20.** At that time, the Pharisees sent spies who pretended to be righteous, in order to trap Jesus in his speech and hand him over to the authority and power of the governor, etc.

As the chief priests and scribes sought to arrest the Lord, they feared the people; and therefore, since they could not accomplish through themselves what they wished, they tried to do it through the governor’s hands, so that they might appear themselves to be free from responsibility for his death. For recently, under Caesar Augustus, when the census was conducted throughout the whole world, Judea, having been subjected to the Romans, had become a tributary province. There was great sedition among the people: some said that taxes ought to be paid for the security and peace by which the Romans provided military protection for all. The Pharisees, however, who applauded themselves for their righteousness, were striving in the opposite direction, saying that God’s people, who paid tithes and gave the firstfruits and the other things written in the Law (Exod. 22; Deut. 12), ought not to be subject to human laws. The tinder of this sedition grew so strong that after the Lord’s Passion, when the Romans pressed them, they preferred to lose their country, nation, and kingdom, that noble Temple with its religion—in fact, the very light itself—rather than pay taxes. And they questioned him, saying:

“Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and that you do not accept a person’s status, but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful for us to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” This flattering and deceitful question provokes the respondent to fear God more than Caesar and to say that taxes ought not to be paid, so that the governor’s officials, who according to the other evangelists (Matt. 22; Mark 12) are said to have been present, might immediately seize him as a leader of sedition against the Romans.

But, considering their deceit, he said to them: “Why do you test me? Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it have?” Wisdom always acts wisely, so that those who test it may be refuted above all by their own words. “Show me,” he says, “a denarius.” This was a kind of coin reckoned as ten coins, and it bore Caesar’s image. Those who think that the Savior’s question indicates ignorance rather than condescension should learn from this passage that Jesus certainly could have known whose image was on the coin, but he asks in order to respond appropriately to their speech.

They answered, “Caesar’s.” And he said to them: “Then give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.” We should understand “Caesar” not as Augustus, but as Tiberius, his stepson, who had succeeded his stepfather and under whom the Lord also suffered. All the Roman kings, beginning with the first Gaius Caesar, who had seized imperial power, were called Caesars.

Moreover, when he says, “Give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar,” and to God what belongs to God, let us understand the coin, tribute, and money on the one hand, and tithes, firstfruits, offerings, and sacrifices on the other. Thus he himself pays tribute for himself and Peter, while giving to God what belongs to God by doing the Father’s will (Matt. 17).

Alternatively: “Give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.” Just as Caesar demands from you the impression of his image, so does God, so that, just as the coin is returned to Caesar, the soul—illumined and marked by the light of God’s countenance—may be returned to God. Hence the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4). This light is the whole of man, and the true good, perceived not by the eyes but by the mind. He said “marked upon us,” as a denarius is marked with the king’s image. For humanity was made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1), which it corrupted by sinning. Its good, therefore, is true and eternal if, through rebirth, it is marked again.

And they were unable to find fault with his statement before the people; and, amazed at his answers, they fell silent. They ought to have believed because of such great wisdom, but instead they marveled that their cunning plot had found no opening.

## HOMILY XX: ON THE TWENTY-FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

**Matthew 9; Mark 5; Luke 8.** At that time, when Jesus had crossed again by boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered around him. And one of the rulers of the synagogue, named Jairus, came; and when he saw him, he fell at his feet and earnestly begged him, etc.

In this reading, the ruler of the synagogue asks the Lord to save his daughter; but while the Lord is going to his house, a woman with an issue of blood anticipates him and seizes healing, and then the ruler’s daughter reaches the desired healing—or rather, she is recalled from death to life. The salvation of the human race is signified, a salvation arranged in this way when the Lord came in the flesh: first, certain people from Israel would come to faith; then the fullness of the Gentiles would enter; and thus all Israel would be saved (Rom. 11).

Who, then, is this ruler of the synagogue who comes to the Lord to plead for his daughter, if not Moses himself? Hence he is appropriately called Jairus, meaning “one who enlightens” or “enlightened.” Moses received the words of life in order to give them to us, and through them he enlightens others; he himself was enlightened by the Holy Spirit, so that he could write or teach life-giving admonitions.

When he saw Jesus, he fell at his feet, because, foreseeing in the spirit that the Lord would come in the flesh, he submitted with humble heart to his power. He understood that he would become man toward the end of the age, yet did not doubt that he existed as eternal God before every age. For if God is Christ’s head (1 Cor. 11), what should be understood as his feet more suitably than the humanity he assumed, by which he touched the earth of our mortality? And for the ruler of the synagogue to fall at Jesus’ feet means that the lawgiver, together with the whole succession of the fathers, recognizes and confesses that the Mediator of God and humanity far surpasses him in the glory of his dignity, confessing with the Apostle that “what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1).

And he earnestly begged him, saying: “My daughter is at the point of death. Come, lay your hands on her, so that she may be saved and live.” In Luke’s Gospel it is written: “For she was his only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying” (Luke 8).

The ruler of the synagogue’s daughter is therefore the synagogue itself, which, composed solely through the institution of the Law, was as though Moses’ only daughter. And she, at about the twelfth year of her age—that is, as the time of puberty approached—was dying. For, nobly educated by the prophets, once she had reached the age of understanding, once she ought to have begun to generate spiritual offspring for God, she was suddenly overwhelmed by the sickness of error and abandoned, in utter despair, the paths of spiritual life. Unless Christ came to her aid, she would have fallen utterly into a terrible death.

And he went with him, and a great crowd followed him and pressed upon him. As the Lord goes to heal the girl, he is pressed by the crowd, because, while giving the Jewish people saving admonitions by which he might raise up their conscience, sick with vices, he is burdened by the harmful custom of carnal peoples.

And a woman who had suffered from an issue of blood for twelve years, etc. The woman flowing with blood, but healed by the Lord, is the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Polluted by the inborn flow of carnal pleasures and already separated from the assembly of the faithful, while the Word of God was determined to save Judea, she seized for herself, with confident hope, the salvation already prepared and promised to others.

It should be noted that the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter is twelve years old, while this woman has been flowing with blood for twelve years—that is, the woman began to fall ill at the same time that the girl was born. Within almost one and the same age of this world, the synagogue began to be born in the patriarchs, while the nation of the foreign Gentiles began throughout the world to be defiled by the corruption of idolatry. The flow of blood may rightly be understood in two ways: both of the pollution of idolatry and of those actions produced by the pleasure of flesh and blood.

And she had suffered greatly from many physicians and had spent all she possessed, yet had gained nothing; rather, she was worse off. By the physicians understand either false theologians, or philosophers and teachers of secular laws, who, arguing very subtly about virtues and vices, promised that they were giving mortals useful principles for living and believing; or certainly understand the unclean spirits themselves, who, as though advising human beings, thrust themselves forward to be worshiped in place of God. The more the Gentiles expended the powers of their natural ingenuity in eagerly listening to these teachers, the less were they able to cleanse themselves from the filth of their iniquity. But when this woman learned that the Jewish people was ill and that the true physician had come from heaven, she too began both to hope for and to seek the remedy for her sickness.

When she heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. For she said: “If I touch his garment, I shall be saved.” And immediately the source of her blood was dried up.

The Church comes and touches the Lord when she approaches him through the truth of faith. She comes “behind,” either in accordance with what he himself says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12), and with the command elsewhere: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (2 Kings 13); or because, not seeing the Lord present in the flesh, she reaches the grace of faith and knowledge of him after the mysteries of his incarnation have been accomplished. Thus, by participation in his sacraments, she deserved to be saved from sins and, as though by touching his garments, dried up the source of her blood.

The source of blood is the origin of sin. Each person’s source of blood is the beginning of an unclean thought, from which every sin is born. But the Lord took care, through the words of the Gospel, not only to restrain evil works and words, but also to uproot the root of wicked thoughts, granting that both might be cleansed through the sacraments of the Gospel. It was as though he had placed in his garments the power to dry up the foul source.

And immediately Jesus, knowing in himself the power that had gone out from him, turned toward the crowd and said: “Who touched my garments?” He does not ask in order to be taught what he does not know, but so that the power he knew well—indeed, the power he himself had given—might be revealed in the woman, and so that, once the power of faith had been revealed and recognized, many might attain salvation.

And his disciples said to him: “You see the crowd pressing around you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” The crowd, accompanying him indiscriminately, presses upon him, but one believing woman touches the Lord, because the one who is burdened by various, disorderly heaps of heresies or by perverse conduct venerates him with the faithful heart of the Catholic Church alone. [Note: [Col. 0309D] The passage is corrupt.] For just as some see but do not see, and hear but do not hear, so also some touch but do not touch: they touch Christ not with a simple heart, but with a doubtful or pretended one. Hence he says to one who loved him but did not yet fully believe: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20), plainly indicating what it means truly to touch him: namely, to believe him equal to the Father.

And he looked around to see her who had done this. The Lord does not forget his children, nor does he cease to look upon those who hope in him; rather, he judges all who deserve to be saved worthy of his gaze and compassion. “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. 33).

But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. This shows what the Lord’s question was directed toward: namely, that, when the woman openly confessed the truth of her long illness, her sudden faith, the divine favor, and the healing granted to her, she herself might be more firmly confirmed in faith, and might provide an example of salvation and life to many.

Finally, the text continues:

But he said: “Daughter, your faith has saved you. Go in peace, and be healed of your affliction.” He calls her “daughter” because her faith has saved her. He did not say, “Your faith will save you,” but “has saved you.” By the very fact that you believed, you have already been saved.

While he was still speaking, people came to the ruler of the synagogue, saying: “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the Teacher any further?” After the woman had been healed of her issue of blood, the ruler’s daughter is immediately announced to have died. This signifies that while the Church, cleansed from the stain of vices and called “daughter” because of the merit of faith, was being healed, the synagogue was at once released into the mourning of both unbelief and envy: unbelief, because it refused to believe in Christ; envy, because it grieved that the Church believed.

For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “On the following Sabbath almost the whole city came together to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what was said by Paul, speaking abusively” (Acts 13).

And what the messengers said to the ruler of the synagogue—“Why trouble the Teacher any further?”—is still said by those who see the synagogue’s condition as so utterly abandoned that they do not believe it can be restored, and therefore do not think that one ought to pray for its resurrection. But what is impossible with human beings is possible with God (Mark 10); hence it appropriately follows:

But Jesus, hearing the words that had been spoken, said to the ruler of the synagogue: “Do not fear; only believe.” The ruler of the synagogue is understood as the assembly of teachers of the Law, concerning whom the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat” (Matt. 23). If he himself should wish to believe, the synagogue subject to him will also be saved.

And they come to the ruler of the synagogue’s house, and they see an uproar, and people weeping and wailing loudly. “Let all who hope in you rejoice; they shall exult forever, and you shall dwell in them” (Ps. 5). But because the synagogue lost this joy of the Lord’s indwelling through the merit of its unbelief, it lies as though dead among those who weep and wail. Nevertheless, heavenly mercy does not allow it to perish completely; rather, toward the end of the age it will restore its remnant, according to the election of grace, to salvation and life. Hence it appropriately continues:

And he entered and said to them: “Why are you troubled and weeping? The girl is not dead, but sleeping.” She was dead to human beings, who could not raise her; but to God she was sleeping. In God’s disposition, her soul lived after being received, while her flesh rested in expectation of resurrection. Hence Christian usage has established that the dead, whom we do not doubt will rise again, are called “sleeping,” as the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve as the others do who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4).

But also, in the allegorical sense, although “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18), nevertheless one whom the Lord foresees will be raised and come to eternal life may appropriately be said by us to have been dead, but to have fallen asleep for him.

And they mocked him. But he, having put everyone out, took the girl’s father and mother, etc. Because they preferred to mock the word of the one raising the girl rather than believe it, they are rightly excluded outside, as unworthy to see the power of the one raising her and the mystery of resurrection. Likewise, the crowd is put outside so that the girl may be raised, because if the intrusive multitude of worldly cares is not first expelled from the more secret places of the heart, the soul lying dead within will not rise. For while it scatters itself through innumerable thoughts of earthly desires, it cannot gather itself at all for self-examination.

And taking the girl’s hand, he said to her: “Tabitha, cumi,” which is translated: “Girl, I say to you, rise.” The diligent reader may ask why the truthful evangelist, explaining the Savior’s words, inserted the words “I say to you,” when in the Syriac expression he records there is nothing more than “Girl, rise.” Perhaps he thought this necessary in order to express the force of the Lord’s command, taking care to convey to his readers the speaker’s meaning rather than his exact words. It is also well known that evangelists and apostles, when they take testimonies from the Old Testament, are more concerned to set forth the prophetic meaning than the precise wording.

The Lord took the girl’s hand and raised her, because unless the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood, are first cleansed, their synagogue will not rise from death.

And immediately the girl rose and walked. Well does the text say that she rose and walked. For whoever has been touched by the hand of heavenly mercy, which intends to raise the dead in sins, ought not only to rise from the filth and lethargy of crimes, but also to advance at once in good works—namely, in the words of the Psalmist, walking without blemish and practicing righteousness (Ps. 14).

And they were overcome with great amazement. And he strictly commanded them that no one should know this, and ordered that she be given something to eat.

He commanded that the girl be given food as testimony to a true resurrection, lest unbelievers think that what appeared was not reality but a phantom. Likewise, if anyone rises from spiritual death, he must immediately be filled with heavenly bread and become a participant in the divine Word and the most holy altar.

According to the moral interpretation, those three dead whom the Savior raised bodily signify three kinds of resurrection of souls. Some, by consenting to an evil pleasure, bring death upon themselves through the hidden thought of sin alone. To signify that he gives life to such people, the Savior raised the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, who had not yet been carried outside but was dead in the house—as though she concealed a vice secretly in her heart.

Others not only consent to harmful pleasure, but also, by carrying out the very evil in which they delight, carry their dead person, as it were, beyond the gates. To show that he raises these if they repent, he raised the young son of the widow, carried outside the gates of the city, and restored him to his mother, because he restores a soul turning back from the darkness of sin to the unity of the Church.

Some, however, corrupt themselves not only by thinking or doing unlawful things, but also by burying themselves, as it were, in the very habit of sinning. Yet the Savior’s power and grace are no less effective in raising these, provided there are earnest thoughts watching over their salvation like sisters devoted to Christ. To signify this, he raised Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb and, as his sister testified, already stank (John 11), because notorious reputation commonly accompanies harmful acts.

It should be noted that the more grievous the death of the soul has become, the more fervently the penitent must strive if he is to deserve to rise. Lighter and daily errors can be cured by the remedy of lighter penitence. Wishing secretly to show this, the Lord raises the girl lying dead in a chamber with the easiest and briefest words: “Girl, rise.” Because she was so easily raised, he had even denied that she was dead.

But when the dead young man had been carried outside, he strengthens him with more words so that he may return to life, saying: “Young man, I say to you, rise.” But for the four-day-old dead man to escape the long barriers of the tomb and come forth, Jesus groaned in spirit, troubled himself, shed tears, groaned again, and cried out with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come outside.” And thus, at last, the one who had been regarded as beyond hope, shaking off the burden of darkness, is restored to life and light.

It should also be noted that because public wrongdoing requires a public remedy, while lesser sins can be erased by lighter and private penitence, the girl lying in the house rises before only a few witnesses, and those same witnesses are strictly commanded to tell no one. The young man is raised outside the gate, with a large crowd accompanying and watching. Lazarus, called forth from the tomb, became so widely known among the people that, because of the testimony of those who saw it, very large crowds went out to meet the Lord with palm branches; many Jews departed because of him and believed in Jesus.

But when the fourth dead man was announced by a disciple, the Lord heard him. Since, however, there were no living people to pray for his restoration, he said: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8)—that is, let evil people burden evil people with harmful praises; and since there is no righteous person present to rebuke them mercifully, let “the oil of the sinner fatten their heads” (Ps. 140).

## HOMILY XXI: ON THE EMBER-WEDNESDAY OF SEPTEMBER

**Mark 9; Matthew 17; Luke 9.** At that time, one of the crowd answered Jesus: “Teacher, I brought my son to you; he has a mute spirit,” etc.

In the preceding chapter of this holy Gospel it is related that, when the Lord came to his disciples, he saw a great crowd around them and the scribes disputing with them. Immediately, when all the people saw him, they were astonished and afraid, and they ran up and greeted him.

The difference between the minds of the scribes and of the crowd should be noted everywhere. The crowd was with the disciples, and the scribes were there as well; but when the Lord arrived, the whole crowd was immediately astonished, afraid, and ran to greet him. The scribes, however, are not said to have shown him any devotion, faith, humility, or reverence.

The evangelist does not say what the crowd or the scribes were disputing with the Lord’s disciples about. But, if I am not mistaken, it can appropriately be understood that the question concerned why, since they were the Savior’s disciples, they could not save the demoniac who had been placed among them. This may be inferred from the words that follow in the Gospel, where it says:

And he asked them: “What are you disputing about among yourselves?” One of the crowd answered: “Teacher, I brought my son to you; he has a mute spirit. Whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams, gnashes his teeth, and dries up. I told your disciples to cast it out, and they could not.”

It should be noted that circumstances always correspond to events. On the mountain the Lord prays, is transfigured, and reveals the secrets of his majesty to the disciples; descending to the lower places, he is met by the crowd and besieged by the weeping of the miserable. Above, he opens the mysteries of the kingdom to his disciples; below, he reproves the crowds for the sins of unbelief. Above, he discloses the Father’s voice to those who could follow him; below, he expels evil spirits from those who are afflicted.

Even now, according to the quality of their merits, he does not cease either to ascend for some or to descend for others. For those who are still carnal and beginners, he strengthens, teaches, and chastises them as though seeking the lowest places; but he glorifies the perfect, whose citizenship is in heaven, by lifting them higher, instructing them more freely about eternal things, and often teaching them what the crowds are not even able to hear.

Mark records that this demoniac, whom the Lord healed when he came down from the mountain, was deaf and mute, while Matthew says that he was epileptic (Matt. 17). He signifies those of whom it is written: “A fool is changed like the moon” (Sir. 27). Never remaining in the same condition, they change now to these vices, now to those, increasing and decreasing. They are mute because they do not confess the faith; deaf because they do not hear the word of truth in any way. They foam when they waste away in foolishness. It belongs to fools, the sick, and the dull to discharge froth from the mouth. They gnash their teeth when they blaze with the fury of anger. They dry up when they languish in sluggish idleness and, strengthened by no energetic pursuit of virtue, live weakly.

But when he says, “I told your disciples to cast it out, and they could not,” he subtly accuses the apostles, since the inability to heal sometimes refers not to the weakness of those healing but to the faith of those who are to be healed, as the Lord says: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (Matt. 9).

He answered them and said: “O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?” He does not say this because the gentle and meek one was overcome by weariness—he who did not open his mouth like a lamb before its shearer (Isa. 53) and did not burst into words of anger—but as though in the likeness of a physician. If a physician saw a sick person acting contrary to his instructions, he might say: “How long shall I come to your house? How long shall I waste the skill of my art, when I command one thing and you do another?”

Yet he was not angry with the man but with the vice, and through one man he reproved the Jews for unbelief, so that he immediately added:

“Bring him to me.” And they brought him, he says. And when he saw him, immediately the spirit convulsed him, and, thrown to the ground, he rolled about foaming.

When the boy is brought to the Lord, the spirit convulses and throws him down, because often, when we try to turn to the Lord after sins, we are attacked by the ancient enemy with greater and new forms of ambush. The cunning adversary does this either to inspire hatred of virtue or to avenge the injury of his expulsion. Hence—moving from the particular to the general—the holy Church’s beginnings were met with as many grievous struggles of persecution as the enemy grieved over the sudden loss of souls from his kingdom.

And he asked his father: “How long has this been happening to him?” He said: “From childhood. Frequently it has thrown him both into fire and into water, to destroy him.”

Let Julian be ashamed, since he dares to say that all human beings are born in the flesh without any stain of sin, entirely innocent, as Adam was when he was created. What did this boy possess that he should be tormented by a most savage demon from childhood, if he was held by no bond of original sin, when it is clear that he could not yet have committed any personal sin?

Let the Catholic confess that no one is born free from the guilt of the first transgression, and let him invoke the grace of God, by which he may be delivered from the body of death through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Let the learned scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven understand that in this demoniac healed by the Lord the salvation of all the faithful is signified: they come into the world under the guilt of original sin and can be saved only through the faith and grace of the one Redeemer, Jesus Christ.

The statement that the spirit frequently threw him into fire and water signifies the greatest crimes of human madness. Fire’s heat refers to the fervor of anger; water refers to the pleasures of the flesh, which commonly dissolve the mind through indulgence. Or certainly the demoniac is carried into the fire in which the hearts of adulterers have been inflamed, and into the waters that commonly extinguish charity.

“But if you can do anything, help us, taking pity on us.” Jesus said to him: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes.”

The Lord gives an answer appropriate to the petitioner. The man had said, “If you can do anything, help us”; and the Lord replies: “If you can believe, I can help you in my mercy,” because sincere faith deserves to obtain everything it asks for in a salutary manner.

The leper who faithfully cried out, “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,” received an answer appropriate to his faith: “I will; be cleansed” (Matt. 8).

And immediately the boy’s father cried out and said with tears: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.” No one suddenly becomes perfect; each person begins in a good way of life from small things in order to reach great ones. The beginnings of virtue are one thing, progress another, and mature advancement another.

For if faith itself were not led toward perfection by certain degrees, this man, when asked whether he believed, would not have answered: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.” If he believed, why did he speak of unbelief? But if he knew that he possessed unbelief, how did he believe? Because, through the hidden inspiration of grace, faith grows according to the degrees of one’s merits, the one who had not yet believed perfectly was, at one and the same time, both believing and unbelieving.

And when Jesus saw the crowd running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it: “Deaf and mute spirit, I command you: come out of him, and do not enter him again.” The Lord’s rebuke is the divine power of command. He did not rebuke the boy, who was suffering the violence, but the demon, which inflicted it. For whoever wishes to correct a sinner ought to drive out the vice by reproving and abhorring it, but restore the human being through love.

The Lord rightly, when he drives the unclean spirit from a person, commands at the same time that it should not enter him again. For a person is truly freed from demonic domination when he avoids returning through evil living to the sins from which he was once cleansed by repentance.

Crying out and violently convulsing him, it came out of him. As the unclean spirit was about to leave the man, it tore him and terrified the onlookers with a furious cry. For often, when the devil is driven from the heart, he generates more severe temptations in it than he had previously aroused when he possessed it undisturbed.

And he became like a dead man, so that many said that he was dead. But Jesus took him by the hand and raised him, and he stood up.

The impious enemy, compelled to flee, had thrown him down and made him appear dead; the merciful Savior raised him by the gentle touch of his right hand. Just as he showed himself truly to be God through the power of saving, so also he demonstrated through human touch that he truly possessed a bodily nature.

For the insane Manichaeus denies that Christ was truly clothed in flesh; but when Christ by his touch raised, cleansed, and illumined so many who were ill, he condemned that heresy before it was even born.

And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately: “Why could we not cast it out?” And he said to them: “This kind can come out by nothing except prayer and fasting.”

While teaching the apostles how the most wicked demon should be expelled, he instructed everyone in the way of life, so that we might know that the most serious temptations, whether from unclean spirits or from human beings, must be overcome by fasts and prayers, and that the Lord’s anger, when it has been kindled for vengeance upon our sins, can be appeased by this singular remedy.

Fasting in general means abstaining not only from food but from all carnal enticements; indeed, it means restraining oneself from every passion of vice. Likewise, prayer in general consists not only in the words by which we invoke divine mercy, but also in everything we do in obedient devotion and faith to the service of our Creator, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Always rejoice; pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5).

For how can anyone invoke God with words at every hour and moment without ceasing? We pray without ceasing when we do only those works that commend us to the devotion of our Creator. By such fasting and such prayer, with the Lord’s help, we shall conquer and repel all the ambushes of the ancient enemy.

## HOMILY XXII: ON THE EMBER-FRIDAY

**Luke 18.** At that time, Jesus told his disciples this parable: “There was a judge in a certain city who did not fear God and had no respect for anyone. There was also a widow in that city, and she kept coming to him, saying: ‘Vindicate me against my adversary.’ For a long time he refused. But afterward he said to himself: ‘Although I do not fear God and have no respect for anyone, nevertheless, because this widow is troublesome to me, I will vindicate her, lest she finally come and wear me out,’” etc.

The Lord presents parables either according to some likeness, as in the case of the man who had two sons, the elder near him in the field and the younger wasting himself in a distant land (Luke 15); or he proves something from the very unlikeness of the comparison, as in: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith?” (Matt. 6; Luke 12).

Thus the former type can be connected with the words, “As this is, so is that.” The latter type is expressed by: “If this, how much more that?” or, “If this, how much less that?” Sometimes these things are stated obscurely, and sometimes openly.

Here, therefore, the unjust judge has not been introduced on the basis of likeness. That unjust judge does not in any way allegorically represent God. Nevertheless, the Lord wished it to be inferred from him how much God, who is good and just, cares for those who entreat him: even an unjust human being cannot disregard those who press him with constant prayers, at least in order to avoid their persistence becoming burdensome. For this is what he means by: “Lest she finally come and batter me.”

The widow herself may represent the Church, which appears desolate until the Lord comes, although even now he secretly cares for her.

[Col. 0315B] But the Lord said: “Hear what the unjust judge says. And will not God avenge his elect, who cry to him day and night, and will he have patience with them? I tell you that he will quickly avenge them.” If anyone is troubled by the question why God’s elect pray to be avenged—something also said in John’s Apocalypse concerning the martyrs (Apoc. VI)—although we are most explicitly instructed to pray for our enemies and persecutors (Matt. V, VI; Luke VI), it must be understood that the vengeance of the righteous is that all the wicked perish. They perish in two ways: either through conversion to righteousness, or through the loss, by punishment, of the power by which they now act against the good, for as long as this is advantageous to the good or they possess some temporary strength. When the righteous desire this end to come, although they pray for their enemies, they are nevertheless not absurdly said to desire vengeance.

“Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on earth?” Although the almighty Creator is always prepared to avenge his elect who cry to him, on the day of judgment—something that must be held in trembling hearts—when that same Creator appears in the form of the Son of Man, there will be such a scarcity of the elect that the ruin of the whole world will need to be hastened not so much because of the cry of the faithful who are unjustly condemned as because of the apathy of those who are justly condemned. When the Lord says, as though doubtfully, “Do you suppose that he will find faith?” he is not doubting but reproving. For by a word of doubt unbelief is rebuked, not divinity made uncertain. We too sometimes use a word of doubt reproachfully about matters of which we are certain in our hearts. For example, if you were angry with your servant and said, “You despise me; perhaps I am your master”—the word “perhaps” would be reproachful, not doubtful. So too the Apostle says to certain people who despised him: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. VII). Whoever says “I think” appears to doubt; but he was reproving, not doubting. Thus the Lord also knows all things, through whom all things were made, and yet by seeming to doubt he reproves the hearts of unbelievers.

## HOMILY XXIII. ON THE SATURDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS IN SEPTEMBER

[Col. 0315D]

LUKE XIII, MATTHEW XXI, MARK XI. At that time Jesus was telling the crowds this parable: “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it, but found none,” etc.

This fig tree can indeed signify the nature of the human race, which was well planted—that is, created in the likeness of its author. But when God sought fruit from it for three years, it refused to give it, because before the Law, under the Law, and under grace it scorned to obey. Yet if you look back to what precedes, you will notice that, although it generally bears the type of all humanity, it especially represents the Synagogue. For immediately after that terrible and dreadful sentence, “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke XIII), he adds a parable about a barren tree destined to be uprooted, and plainly teaches [Col. 0316A] that those to whom he was speaking would be cut down like a fruitless fig tree if they did not repent. The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isa. V), as we learn from Isaiah’s song; and the Synagogue, established in that same house, is the fig tree in the vineyard. But the one who allowed his vineyard to be ravaged by passersby also ordered the fig tree to be cut down.

“And he came seeking fruit on it, but found none.” The very Lord who established the Synagogue through Moses appeared, born in the flesh; and teaching frequently in the Synagogue, he sought the fruit of faith but did not find it in the minds of the Pharisees.

“Then he said to the gardener: ‘Behold, it is three years since I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none.’” By the gardener the order of the apostles and teachers is signified, through whose prayers and admonitions constant care for God’s people is urged. For the Lord very often complained to them about the fruitless people of the Jews, because during the three years of his visitation—that is, in the enactments of the Law, in the prophetic testimonies, [Col. 0316B] and in the very grace of the resplendent Gospel—she had remained negligent.

“Cut it down, then. Why should it even occupy the ground?” The Jewish people were not cut down by the apostles, but by the Romans, and were expelled from the land of promise. Yet by saying, “Cut it down,” he proposed to it, by urging repentance, the impending disaster of its cutting down. By a just judgment it lost both land and kingdom, for whose sake it did not fear to persecute the citizens of heaven and to kill the very King of heaven and earth, saying through its chief priests and Pharisees: “If we let him go on, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John XI).

The crowd of the Jewish people may also be represented by the ground occupied by the barren fig tree. Crushed beneath the harmful shadow of its leaders, so that it could not receive the light of truth, and prevented by the example of their wickedness from being warmed by the sun of heavenly love, it fulfills what the Savior says elsewhere to the same people: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men. For you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter” [Col. 0316C] (Matt. XXIII).

“But he answered and said to him: ‘Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it.’” This is the voice of the apostles, who after the Lord’s Passion prayed most earnestly for the Jews, lest vengeance for the Lord’s cross be exacted from the impenitent. “Until I dig around it,” he says—that is, until I humble the root of its fruitless mind with the mattock of a two-edged denunciation, bringing before it both the pressures of the present and the terror of everlasting condemnation. Every ditch, of course, is at the bottom. And indeed rebuke, while showing the mind its own condition, humbles it.

“And I will put manure on it.” That is, I will bring back to its mind the evils it has committed as an abomination, and I will raise up the grace of compunction, as it were from the rottenness of manure.

“And if it bears fruit—otherwise, in the future you shall cut it down.” When he said, “And if it bears fruit,” he added nothing, but left the sentence suspended. But when he added, “Otherwise,” he immediately attached the judgment of future condemnation, saying, “In the future you shall cut it down,” because he saw that the Synagogue was much more inclined to deny God than to confess him. Hence elsewhere too, acting out the same figure in deeds that he presents here in words, he condemned the fruitless fig tree to eternal barrenness, showing that although the apostles might dig around it by rebuking it, and bring manure by reproaching it for its sins, it would nevertheless bear no fruit of repentance, but would be removed by the rigorous severity of the axe (Matt. XXI; Mark XI).

“Now he was teaching in their synagogue on the Sabbaths. And behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years.” After recounting the parable of the fig tree, the Lord is said to have taught in the synagogue, so that it might be indicated that the parable had no other object, but that this was the fruit he was seeking and failing to find on the fig tree: to lend the word to the Synagogue, and not have it received. Yet lest you suppose that it was to be completely uprooted because of the guilt of its barrenness, but should know that remnants were to be saved by the election of grace, [Col. 0317A] immediately there follows in the same place the healing of the primitive Church under the figure of a bent woman. She had rightly been bent for eighteen years, a number completed by six multiplied three times, because it shows that she who was languishing through weak works in the testimony of the Law, the prophetic oracle, and the revelation of grace was bent. For the number six, in which the creation of the world was completed, signifies the perfection of works. There are three periods, as I have said, of the Lord’s visitation; in them Judea, because she knew how to perform earthly rather than heavenly works, had been bent away from the uprightness of her mind, as though for eighteen years.

“And she was bent over and could not look upward at all.” Because, being earthly-minded and seeking things that are weak, she did not yet know how to think about heavenly things, hearing through the prophet: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. I). In opposition to her the Apostle says to the members of the Church: “Think about the things that are above, not the things that are on earth” (Col. III).

[Col. 0317B] “When Jesus saw her, he called her to him and said: ‘Woman, you are released from your infirmity.’ And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.” He saw her by predestining through grace, called her by enlightening through teaching, laid his hands on her by helping with spiritual gifts, and straightened her so that she might glorify God, advancing her to be firm in good works unto the end. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.”

“But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, answered and said to the crowd: ‘There are six days on which one ought to work; on those days, therefore, come and be healed, and not on the Sabbath’” (Exod. XXV). Jesus healed on the Sabbath, showing that the time had already come for the day to dawn according to the prophecy of the Song of Songs and for the shadows to be removed (Song II). But the ruler of the synagogue did not know either this or the much greater mystery that the Lord disclosed by healing on the Sabbath: namely, that after the six ages of this world he would give the perpetual joys of immortal life. As a figure of this, Moses commanded that the Sabbath be kept not from a good action but from servile—that is, harmful—action, prefiguring the time when our worldly works, but not religious acts, that is, acts of praising God, would cease. Thus the ruler of the synagogue both errs and misleads, because in the Sabbath the Law prohibited not healing a person but carrying burdens—that is, being weighed down by sins.

“But the Lord answered him and said: ‘Hypocrite, does not each one of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it to drink?’” He certainly accuses the rulers of the Synagogue of unbelief and rightly marks them with the name “hypocrites,” that is, pretenders. Although they wished to appear teachers of the people, they were not ashamed to put the healing of a human being after the care of livestock. But in a deeper sense, by the terms “ox” and “donkey” he signifies the Jew and the Greek. Of their calling it is written: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isa. I). Both, released from the bonds of sin, laid aside the thirst and heat of this world by drinking from the Lord’s fountain.

“And ought not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound—behold, for eighteen years—to be released from this bond on the Sabbath?” The daughter of Abraham is every faithful soul; the daughter of Abraham is the Church gathered from both peoples into the unity of faith. When the time of the Law and of the Lord’s resurrection had been fulfilled, she burst through the bonds of a long captivity by the grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit. For perhaps the mystery of the Sabbath and of the eighteen years can also appropriately be understood in this way. Mystically, therefore, to untie the ox or donkey from the manger and lead it to drink is the same as raising the daughter of Abraham from the bond of a harmful inclination: namely, freeing the Church, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, from the snares of sins through the water of baptism and raising her to hope for heavenly things.

It should certainly be noted that a most unspeakable heresy, on the basis of the Lord’s statement that the woman was bound by Satan, attempts to assert that the defects of human bodies belong not to God as their author but rather to the devil—as though, although the devil always desires to do harm, he could harm anyone unless he had received power from the Almighty. For what else is declared not only in the book of blessed Job—which this heresy, in its madness, rejects as belonging to a malignant ruler of the world, together with the other books of the Old Testament and with God himself, who gave them—but also in the Gospel, where the demons could not even enter the pigs unless he himself granted them permission (Mark V), as we have also taught above?

“And when he said these things, all his adversaries were ashamed, and all the people rejoiced in all the glorious things that were being done by him.” Those who are ashamed of the Savior’s words show that they rightly deserve comparison with the barren fig tree. Those who rejoice at his miracles declare that they belong to the daughter of Abraham who glorifies God for her restoration—that is, to the Church through the devotion of faith.

## HOMILY XXIV. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY OF ADVENT

[Col. 0318B]

LUKE XIX, MATTHEW XXI, MARK XI. At that time, when Jesus drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, to the mountain called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples, saying: “Go into the village opposite you. As you enter it, you will find a colt of a donkey tied, on which no one has ever sat; untie it and bring it. And if anyone asks you why you are untying it, say this to him: ‘Because the Lord needs it,’” etc.

Bethphage was a small village of priests on the Mount of Olives; Bethany too was a village or town on the slope of the same mountain, about fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, as the evangelist John makes clear. There Lazarus was raised from the dead, and the Church now built there points out his tomb. Bethphage is interpreted as “house of the mouth,” and Bethany as “house of obedience.” The Savior, as he was about to come to Jerusalem, exalted these places by the favor of his presence, because before his Passion he filled many people, through teaching, with the gifts of devout confession and spiritual obedience.

Beautifully, these towns are said to be situated on the Mount of Olives, that is, in the Lord himself, who refreshes us with the anointing of spiritual gifts and with the light of knowledge and devotion. Hence, when elsewhere he said, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden,” he immediately added, “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel” (Matt. V; Luke XI). For the same Mount of Olives—that is, the supreme distributor of spiritual gifts—which raises up its city so that it may stand prominent, also kindles it with the oil of gladness so that it may be able to shine.

And because he did not wish that same light to be placed under a bushel, he sent the disciples into the village opposite them—that is, he arranged to send teachers who, by preaching, would penetrate the unlearned and barbarous shores of the whole world, like the walls of a village set opposite them. Two are rightly sent, because of knowledge of the truth and purity of conduct, or because of the mystery of the twofold love—of God, namely, and of neighbor—to be preached throughout the whole world.

“Into it, as you enter, you will find a colt of a donkey tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. And if anyone asks you why you are untying it, say this to him: ‘Because the Lord needs it.’” Entering the world, the preachers found the people of the nations entangled in the bonds of unbelief. Everyone was bound by the cords of his sins—not only the nations but also the Jews, for “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III).

Hence in Matthew the donkey too is found tied together with the colt. The donkey, which was subject to the yoke and had been tamed to bear the yoke of the Law, signifies the Synagogue. The unruly and free colt of the donkey represents the people of the nations, on which no human being had ever sat—that is, no rational teacher had ever placed upon it the bridle of correction by which it might be compelled either to restrain its tongue from evil or to walk along the narrow way of life; no one had ever bestowed on it, through useful admonition, the garments of salvation by which it might be warmed spiritually. A human being would have sat upon it if someone using reason had corrected it by suppressing its foolishness.

Thus the two disciples sent to bring the animals to the Lord may appropriately be understood, following the example of the preceding parable, as the two orders of preachers: one sent to the nations, the other to the circumcision. It should also be noted that the three evangelists who wrote in Greek mention only the colt; but Matthew alone, who wrote his Gospel for the Hebrews in Hebrew speech, reports that the donkey too was untied and brought to the Lord, so that he might show that the salvation even of that Hebrew people, if it repented, was not to be despaired of. “Untie them,” he says, “and bring them” (Matt. XXI). “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (John XX).

“But those who had been sent went away and found the colt standing, just as he had told them.” Mark writes that the colt was found outside before the door, at the crossroads. The door himself is the one who says: “I am the door of the sheep. Whoever enters through me will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture” (John X). The pasture of life was lacking to this colt—that is, to the people of the nations—when it still stood tied outside this door at the crossroads. It was rightly at a crossroads, because it did not hold to one assured way of life and faith, but wandered along the many uncertain paths of sects. Of these the text appropriately continues:

“As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them: ‘Why are you untying the colt?’” It had many owners, since, being devoted not to one doctrine and superstition but dragged at the will of unclean spirits into various and diverse errors, the wretched creature proceeded wherever it was led toward mute idols (1 Cor. XII).
