Finally, in a customary vernacular usage of Scripture, what is unclean is called “common,” just as the voice from heaven says to Peter: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts X). For the one who is holy belongs to God alone and is not common with anyone; but the one who is a sinner and unclean belongs to many. “Many demons possess him,” and therefore he is called common.

“But they said: ‘Because the Lord needs it,’ and they led it to Jesus.” Those who had opposed the untying of the colt fell silent when they heard the Lord’s name, because the teachers of error, who resisted the teachers coming for the salvation of the nations, defended their darkness only until the power of the true possessor and Lord shone forth with miracles as witnesses. But once the power of the Lord’s faith appeared, the complaints of his adversaries yielded everywhere, and the free assembly of believers—carrying God in its heart—is brought to him.

“And throwing their garments upon the colt, they put Jesus on it.” The garments of the apostles may be understood either as the teaching of virtues, the exposition of the Scriptures, or certainly the varieties of ecclesiastical doctrines. With these they cover human hearts, previously naked and cold, so that they may become worthy for Christ to sit upon.

“And as he went, they spread their garments on the road.” While the donkey carries the Lord, the disciples spread their garments on the road. For, coming out from the covering of their own bodies, they prepare the way for the simpler servants of God by their own blood, so that they may proceed with unhindered steps of the mind toward Jerusalem, where Jesus leads them. Jesus goes toward Jerusalem while seated on the donkey when, governing the soul of each believer—his own beast, so to speak—he leads it to the vision of inward peace; or also when he presides universally over the holy Church and kindles her desire for heavenly peace.

Since according to the other evangelists not only the disciples but also many from the crowd spread their garments on the road, these may also signify those who, following the examples of the martyrs, tame their bodies through abstinence, preparing a road for the Lord into the mind, or offering good examples to those who follow.

“And when he was already approaching the descent of the Mount of Olives, all the crowds of those descending began rejoicing and praising God with a loud voice.” As the Lord descends from the Mount of Olives, the rejoicing and praising crowds themselves descend together with him. For when the author of mercy humbles himself willingly, those who greatly need mercy must imitate, as far as they can, the traces of his humility. We must, I say, look at how Jesus descends from the Mount of Olives—that is, how, although he was in the form of God, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II)—and we too must humble ourselves beneath his powerful hand, so that we may deserve to be exalted at the time of visitation.

“Because of all the mighty works they had seen, they said: ‘Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord.’” They had seen many of the Lord’s mighty works, but they were especially amazed by the recent raising of Lazarus from the dead, as the crowd that had been with him testified when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead (John XII). Indeed, the crowd also came out to meet him because they had heard that he had performed this sign.

It should be noted that this was not the first time the Savior had come from Galilee—that is, that he had gone to Jerusalem five days before Passover. Rather, in the preceding year, in the seventh month, he had come there for the feast of Tabernacles, as John records; and from then for six continuous months—that is, until the day of Passover on which he suffered—he was at times performing signs and teaching in Jerusalem, at times ascending the Mount of Olives, at times expelled from Judea and going beyond the Jordan, and at times staying with the disciples in the desert city called Ephraim. Yet during that period he never returned to Galilee (John VIII, X, XI).

Thus, for all the mighty works they had seen him perform over so long a time, the crowds praised God, saying:

“Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest.” “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord” should rather be understood so that “in the name of the Lord” means “in the name of God the Father,” although it can also be understood as “in his own name,” since he too is Lord. Hence elsewhere it is written: “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Gen. XIX).

But his own words guide our understanding better: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John V). Christ is the teacher of humility, who humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death (Phil. II). He therefore does not lose his divinity when he teaches us humility.

Christ is not King of Israel in order to demand tribute, arm an army with iron, or visibly defeat enemies, but he is King of Israel because he rules minds, provides for them eternally, and leads believers, hopeful and loving, into the kingdom of heaven. He is therefore the Son of God, equal to the Father, the Word through whom all things were made. That he willed to be called King of Israel is condescension, not promotion; a sign of mercy, not an increase of power. For he who was called King of the Jews on earth is Lord of the angels in heaven.

But because Christ, in the flesh, appeared as the propitiation of the whole world, of human beings and angels alike, heavenly and earthly things beautifully sing together in his praise in mutual harmony. At his birth, the ranks of heavenly powers praising God sang, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace”; and when he was about to triumph over the ruler of the world and soon return to heaven, mortals render back their tribute of praise: “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest.”

## HOMILY XXV. ON THE SECOND SUNDAY OF THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Col. 0320D]

LUKE XXI, MATTHEW XXIV, MARK XIII. At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on earth distress among nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves,” etc.

As the Lord declares in what follows, when the universal judgment appears, heaven and earth will pass away; and as we read in John’s Apocalypse, “the sea will be no more” (Apoc. XXI). It is therefore fitting that, as the judgment approaches, the roaring of the sea and the waves becomes confused, the inhabitants of the earth are afflicted as they press upon one another, and the great lights of heaven veil their troubled faces, their rays struck with a new terror.

Just as trees driven toward falling customarily give beforehand signs of their crashing and movement, so, as the end approaches, the elements tremble and sway as though afraid. Thus Matthew’s statement, “The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven” (Matt. XXIV), signifies the very presence of the judgment, when, as the glory of the true light appears, all the lights of the world are compared with darkness and shadows.

But when Luke says, “There will be signs in the sun, and moon, and stars,” he indicates the forerunners of the approaching judgment, as messengers announcing it. Among these is the prophet’s saying: “The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel II).

Likewise, what Luke says, “And on earth distress among nations” (Acts II), I think is the same as what Matthew says when describing the time of Antichrist: “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever shall be” (Matt. XXIV). But when Luke adds, “because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves,” he is the herald of what John saw among the other mutable things of the age: that the sea would exist [Col. 0321B].

“People fainting from fear and expectation of what will come upon the whole world, for the powers of heaven will be shaken.” I believe that this sentence signifies the very coming of the Judge. According to the parable in another passage (Matt. XXIX), all the virgins—that is, both the wise and the foolish—will then be awakened by an unusual cry and trim their lamps, that is, reckon up the works they have with them, for which they await with the greatest fear the outcome of the eternal judgment now at hand.

Until then, almost the whole world will act without any fear of the Judge, as the Apostle testifies: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. V). When fear and expectation of the strict examination therefore comes upon the whole world, many who seemed to flourish in this world will wither when they see themselves at the end without fruit. Then the faith that had flourished without works will wither when tested by the fire of the just Judge.

It is no wonder that human beings—that is, those earthly by nature or by understanding—are shaken before his judgment, since even the powers of heaven themselves, that is, the angelic powers, tremble at his sight, as blessed Job also testifies: “The pillars of heaven tremble and quake at his command” (Job XX). What, then, do the planks do when the pillars tremble? What does a little twig in the desert suffer when the cedar of paradise is shaken?

“And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.” They will see in power and majesty the one whom they refused to hear when he was placed in humility, so that they may then feel his power all the more severely because now they do not bend the neck of their hearts to his patience. But because these words were spoken against the reprobate, the discourse immediately turns to the consolation of the elect, for it continues:

“But when these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” When, he says, the blows of the world multiply, when the terror of judgment is revealed through the shaking of the powers, raise your heads—that is, gladden your hearts—because while the world, with which you are not friends, is coming to an end, the redemption you have sought is drawing near.

In sacred Scripture, “head” often signifies the mind, because just as the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind. To raise our heads, therefore, is to lift our minds toward the joys of our heavenly homeland. The Lord also makes clear by an apt comparison that the world ought to be trampled underfoot and despised. For he continues:

“And he told them a parable: ‘Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they are already producing fruit, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.’” He plainly teaches that just as the coming summer is recognized from the fruit of the trees, so the nearness of the kingdom of God is recognized from the ruin of the world.

These words clearly show that the fruit of the world is its ruin. For it grows in order to fall; it multiplies in order to consume with disasters whatever it has produced. The kingdom of God is rightly compared with summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow pass away, and the days of eternal life shine with the brightness of the everlasting sun. All this is confirmed with great certainty when the sentence is added:

“Amen, I say to you: this generation will not pass away until all things have taken place.” The Lord strongly commends what he declares in this way. His “Amen, I say to you” is, so to speak—if one may say so—an oath. For Amen means “true,” and yet it was not translated, although one could have said, “I tell you the truth.” Neither the Greek translator dared to do this, nor the Latin one. It remained untranslated so that it might possess the honor of being veiled in secrecy—not so that it would be denied, but so that, once laid bare, it would not become commonplace.

Therefore it is the Truth who says, “I tell you the truth,” and even if he did not say it, he could not possibly lie. Yet he commends and impresses the point upon us, awakens those who are somehow asleep, makes us attentive, and does not wish to be despised: “Amen,” he says, “I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all things have taken place” [Col. 0322B]. By “this generation” he either means the whole human race or specifically the Jews.

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” The heaven that will pass away must be understood not as the ethereal or starry heaven, but as the aerial heaven, from which the birds of heaven and the clouds of heaven receive their names. Peter bears witness to this when he says: “The heavens existed long ago and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed, flooded with water, perished. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been reserved by the same word for fire, kept for the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly people” (2 Pet. III).

He plainly teaches that it is not other heavens that will perish by fire than those that perished by water—that is, these empty and cloudy spaces of the windy air. For the water of the Flood, which rose only fifteen cubits above the mountain peaks (Gen. VII), should not be believed to have reached beyond the boundaries of the air and ether. But as far as the waters could reach, so surely, according to the foregoing statement of blessed Peter, the fire of judgment will also reach.

If heaven and earth will pass away, it may be asked how Ecclesiastes can say: “One generation comes, and the earth stands forever” (Eccles. I). The answer is clear: heaven and earth pass away with respect to the form they now possess, yet they continue without end in their essence. “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. VII). And the angel says to John: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Apoc. XXI). These are not other substances newly condensed, but these same things are renewed.

Heaven and earth, therefore, both will pass away and will remain: they will be cleansed by fire from the appearance they now possess, yet they will always be preserved in their own nature. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Ps. CI). They now announce this final change of theirs to us through the very alternations by which they continually serve our needs. The earth loses its appearance through winter’s dryness and becomes green again through spring’s moisture; the heaven is daily covered by the darkness of night and is renewed by the brightness of day. From this, then—from this—let every faithful person conclude that these things both perish and are restored through renewal, since they are constantly restored as though from decay.

## HOMILY XXVI. ON THE THIRD SUNDAY OF THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

LUKE VII, MATTHEW XI. At that time John summoned two of his disciples and sent them to the Lord, saying: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” etc.

I think that John’s disciples, provoked by envy, reported both Christ’s virtues and his miracles not with a simple heart. Elsewhere too they are reported to have complained to him in this way: “Rabbi, the one who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him.” John then answered them: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven,” etc. (John III). By this he plainly declares both that he is a mere human being and that Christ is the Son of God. But because envy remained and jealousy could not be driven out, observe what the excellent teacher did still for their correction.

“And John summoned two of his disciples and sent them to the Lord, saying: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’” He did this so that, at least through this opportunity, by seeing the signs he performed, they might believe in him and, questioning their teacher, might speak to themselves. Thus he did not say: “Are you the one who has come?” but: “Are you the one who is to come?” The sense is: “Tell me, since I am to be killed by Herod and descend to the underworld, whether I should also announce you to those below, as I announced you to those above; or whether it is unfitting for the Son of God to taste death, and you will send another for these mysteries.”

“In that same hour he healed many of their diseases and afflictions and evil spirits, and gave sight to many blind people.” John had asked through his disciples: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” Christ displays signs, not answering what he had been asked, but addressing the scandal of the messengers.

“Go,” he says, “and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and—something no less than these—the poor have the Gospel preached to them.” The poor may mean the poor in spirit, or certainly those poor in material possessions, so that in preaching there is no distinction between the noble and the lowly, or between the rich and the needy. These things prove the severity of the teacher and the truth of the instructor, since with him everyone who can be saved is equal.

“And blessed is whoever is not scandalized because of me.” He rebukes John’s messengers, who had not believed him to be the Christ, for the scandal of their unbelief; and he explains to John himself what he was asking: “With God are means of salvation, and with the Lord are escapes from death” (Ps. LXVII). In view of so many signs and such great works, no one could have been scandalized, but only filled with wonder. Yet the minds of unbelievers suffered a grave scandal in him when they saw him dying after so many miracles.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Blessed is whoever is not scandalized because of me,” except that he openly signifies the lowliness and humility of his death? It is as though he were saying plainly: “I indeed perform remarkable things, but I do not disdain to endure humiliation. Since by dying I follow you, people must take great care not to despise death in me while they venerate the signs.”

And when John’s messengers had departed, he began to speak about John to the crowds. Since the surrounding crowd did not understand the mystery of the question and thought that John was doubting about Christ, whom he himself had pointed out, he heaps upon that same John worthy praises, so that they might understand that John had asked not for himself but for his disciples.

“What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” This he introduced, evidently, not by asserting it but by denying it. For as soon as a breeze touches a reed, it bends to one side. And what is signified by the reed if not the carnal mind? As soon as it is touched by favor or disparagement, it inclines in whatever direction. For if a breeze of favor blows from human lips, it becomes cheerful, is lifted up, and bends itself entirely, as it were, toward approval; but if the wind of disparagement bursts forth from the same place from which the breeze of praise had come, it immediately inclines it, as though toward the opposite side, under the force of anger. But John was not a reed shaken by the wind: for neither did favor make him flattering, nor the anger of anyone make him harsh; neither did prosperity know how to raise him up, nor adversity how to bend him.

“But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are in costly clothing and luxury are in kings’ houses.” John is described as having been clothed in camel’s hair. “Those who flee,” he says, “from enduring hardships for God, but devote themselves solely to outward things and seek the softness and pleasure of the present life, serve not a heavenly but an earthly kingdom.” Let no one therefore suppose that sin is absent from luxury and devotion to clothing; for if this were not a fault, the Lord would in no way have praised John for the harshness of his clothing. Yet the statement that John was not dressed in soft clothing can also be understood figuratively. He was not clothed in soft things because he did not foster the life of sinners with flatteries, but rebuked it with the force of harsh denunciation, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III).

“But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.” The ministry of the prophets is to announce what is to come, not also to point it out. John, therefore, is more than a prophet: he announced by pointing out the one whom he had prophesied by running before him.

“This is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you’” (Mal. III). What is called *angelus* in Greek is called *nuntius*, “messenger,” in Latin. Therefore, rightly, the one who is sent to announce the heavenly Judge is called an angel, so that he may retain in his name the dignity which he fulfills by his work. The name is lofty, but his life is not inferior to the name. Moreover, all who are counted among the priesthood are called angels, as the prophet testifies when he says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II). Indeed, each of the faithful, insofar as he is capable and receives the grace of heavenly inspiration—if he recalls his neighbor from wickedness, if he takes care to exhort him to good works, if he announces eternal kingdom or punishment to one who has gone astray—when he offers words of holy proclamation, certainly becomes an angel.

## HOMILY XXVII. ON THE WEDNESDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS

**Luke I.** At that time, in the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary, and so forth.

Angels are designated by personal names for this reason: so that their names may also indicate what they are capable of accomplishing in their work. For in that holy city, which perfect knowledge of the vision of almighty God has established, they do not receive individual names because their persons could not otherwise be known; rather, when they come to us to perform some ministry, they also derive names among us from their ministries. Gabriel, therefore, is sent to the virgin Mary; his name means “strength of God.” He came to announce the one who deigned to appear in humility in order to overthrow the powers of the air. Of him the Psalmist says: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII). And again: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory.” Through the strength of God, therefore, he was to be announced who, the Lord of hosts and mighty in battle, was coming to war against the powers of the air.

Understand the sixth month as March, on whose twenty-fifth day our Lord is traditionally said both to have been conceived and to have suffered, just as he was born on the twenty-fifth day of December. If we believe that on the former day—as some think—the spring equinox occurs, or that on the latter the winter solstice occurs, then it certainly accords with the increase of light that he should be conceived or born who illuminates every human being coming into the world (John I). But if anyone should prove that before the time of the Lord’s birth and conception light either increases or overcomes darkness, we too say that John then evangelized the kingdom of heaven before his coming, and that even now preachers are commanded: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting sun” (Ps. LXI). Why John was conceived around the autumnal equinox and born around the summer solstice is taught by the one who speaks either in his own person or, as many think, in the person of the Old Testament: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John I).

“To a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin’s name was Mary.” For many reasons the Savior wished to be born not of an unmarried virgin but of a betrothed woman. First, evidently, so that through the descent of Joseph, whose relative Mary was, Mary’s own lineage might also be established. For it is not customary for Scripture to trace the genealogies of women. The statement that they were “of the house of David” may also be understood of both. Second, so that she might not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress, preferring that some should doubt her parentage rather than her modesty, and at the same time removing an opportunity for shameless women to say that the Savior’s mother had likewise been disgraced by false suspicions. Third, so that, when fleeing into Egypt and returning from there, she might have the comfort of a husband who would be both guardian and witness of her completely undefiled virginity. Fourth, so that her childbearing might not be exposed to the devil; for if he had known that Christ had been born of a virgin, he might perhaps have feared to deliver him to death as one superior to other human beings.

Mary means “star of the sea” in Hebrew, but “lady” in Syriac. And rightly so, because she was worthy to give birth both to the Lord of the whole world and to the everlasting light of the ages.

“And the angel entered to her and said: ‘Hail, full of grace. The Lord is with you, and blessed are you among women.’” She is rightly called “full of grace,” since she obtains a grace which no other woman had deserved: namely, to conceive and bear the very author of grace.

“When she heard this, she was troubled at his saying and considered what sort of greeting this might be.” Learn from the virgin her character; learn from the virgin her modesty; learn from the virgin the angelic oracle; learn from the virgin the mystery. It is characteristic of virgins to tremble and to be fearful at every entrance of a man, and to reverence every word spoken by a man. Let women learn to imitate her purpose of modesty. Alone in her inner chamber, where no man would see her and only the angel would find her, alone without a companion, alone without a witness, lest she be corrupted by any unworthy affection, she is greeted by the angel. Learn, virgin, to avoid wantonness in words. Mary herself was fearful even of the angel’s greeting. Yet, it says, she was considering what sort of greeting this was. And therefore she was modest, because she was afraid; prudent, because she marveled at a new form of blessing which had nowhere been read and nowhere previously encountered.

“And the angel said to her: ‘Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with God.’” When he saw her troubled by an unusual greeting, one reserved for her alone, he calls her by name, as though addressing an intimate acquaintance, and commands her not to fear. And because he had called her “full of grace,” he establishes and explains that same grace more fully, saying:

“Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus.” Jesus is interpreted as “savior” or “saving.” The angel explained the sacrament of this name when addressing Joseph: “For he himself,” he said, “will save his people from their sins” (Matt. XI). He did not say “the people of Israel,” but “his people”—that is, those called from uncircumcision and circumcision into the unity of faith, so that, gathered from different sides, they might become one shepherd and one flock (John X).

“He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.” It was also said of John that he would be great, but he was great as a human being, whereas this one is great as God. For John was “great before the Lord,” but of this one it says: “He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High.” The same, therefore, is the Son of the Most High who was conceived and born in the virgin’s womb. The same is the human being created in time from a mother who is God, born before time from the Father.

But if the same human being is God, let Nestorius cease to say that only a human being was born from the Virgin, and that he was received by the Word of God not into a unity of person but into an inseparable association. Otherwise he is shown to assert not one Christ, true God and human being, but two—which it is impious to say—and consequently to proclaim not a Trinity but a quaternity. The Catholic faith, however, just as it rightly confesses every human being to consist of flesh and soul, so rightly confesses the human being and the Word to be one Christ, in accordance with the words of the angels, which affirm that the throne of David his father is to be given to him. For when the angel declares that he has David himself as father, while also proclaiming him to be called the Son of the Most High, he clearly demonstrates one person of Christ in two natures.

He received the throne of David so that he might summon forever to the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world the nation to which David and his sons once provided the governance of a temporal kingdom.

“And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” Isaiah also says: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace. He will sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness” (Isa. IX). He did not say that this would occur through the acquisition of glory and earthly treasures, nor through victory over many nations and the destruction of proud cities, but through judgment and righteousness. Through these the kingdom of Christ is both multiplied and strengthened in each individual believer and throughout the Church spread across the world.

He calls the whole Church the house of Jacob: it was either born from a good root or, though it was a wild olive, was nevertheless grafted by the merit of faith into a good olive tree (Rom. XI). After the triumph of his Passion, the Savior addresses it, saying: “You who fear the Lord, praise him; all the seed of Jacob, glorify him” (Ps. XXI).

Jesus, the Son of the Most High, is not said in the words of future time to be destined to become great, to receive David’s scepter, and to reign in the house of Jacob because—as heretics think and, departing from the truth, foolishly imagine—Christ did not exist before Mary, but because the human being assumed into God was glorified with the glory which the Word of God had before the world existed with the Father. That is, the human being, full of grace and truth (John XVII), received the same name of Son and the same person of Christ together with God.

“But Mary said to the angel: ‘How will this happen, since I do not know a man?’” She reverently expressed the resolve of her mind: namely, that she had determined to lead a virginal life. Since she was the first among women to devote herself to so great a virtue, she rightly deserved to surpass other women by a unique blessedness. “How,” she says, “will this happen?” She does not say, “From where shall I know this?” but, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” She inquires about the order of the obedience to which she is to submit, not demanding a sign in which to believe.

For it was not fitting that the virgin chosen to bear God should be doubtful through distrust; rather, she was to be cautious through prudence, since a human being could not easily know a mystery that had remained hidden in God throughout the ages. Since she had read, “Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII), but had not read how this could happen, she rightly believed what she had read and asked the angel about what she had not found in the prophet.

“And the angel answered and said to her: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.’” “You will conceive,” he says, “not from the seed of a man whom you do not know, but through the work of the Holy Spirit, with whom you are filled. Conception will be in you; lust will not be. There will be no heat of desire where the Holy Spirit casts his shadow.”

Yet in the statement, “The power of the Most High will overshadow you,” the twofold nature of the incarnate Savior can also be signified. For a shadow is usually formed both by light and by a body. The one over whom it falls is refreshed sufficiently by the light or color of the sun, but the sun’s own heat, so that it may be endured, is tempered by the interposition of a light cloud or some other body.

Thus, because the blessed Virgin, being a pure human being, could not bodily receive the whole fullness of divinity, the power of the Most High overshadowed her: that is, the incorporeal light of divinity assumed in her a body of humanity. Concerning this the prophet beautifully says: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt” (Isa. XIX). This means: Behold, the Word of God, coeternal with the Father, light from light, born before the ages, will assume flesh at the end of the ages and a soul unburdened by any weight of sin, and will proceed into the world from the virgin’s womb like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber (Ps. XVIII).

“And therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.” To distinguish him from our holiness, Jesus, who was to be born uniquely holy, is declared holy. For although we are made holy, we are not born holy, because we are bound by the very condition of corruptible nature, so that each of us rightly says with the Prophet in lament: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. L). He alone is truly holy who, in order to overcome the condition of corruptible nature itself, was not conceived through the mingling of carnal intercourse.

“He will be called the Son of God.” What do you say here, Nestorian, who, while denying that blessed Mary is the mother of God, strive to attack the manifest truth? Behold, he said that God would come upon her and that the Son of God would be born. How, then, is the Son of God not God? Or how can the woman who gave birth to God not be *θεοτόκος*, that is, “God-bearer” or “mother of God”?

“And behold, Elizabeth your relative has herself conceived a son in her old age. And this is the sixth month for her who is called barren, because no word is impossible with God.” So that the Virgin would not distrust her ability to give birth, she receives the example of a barren old woman who was to bear a child, so that she might learn that everything is possible for God, even what appears contrary to the order of nature.

If anyone is troubled by the statement that Elizabeth was Mary’s relative, since Mary descended from the house of David while Elizabeth derived her origin from the daughters of Aaron, let him observe that their ancestors, by giving their children to one another in marriage, could have joined the two tribes. If this explanation should perhaps not satisfy someone who presses the objection contentiously, as though this could not have occurred because of the prohibition of the law, let him read Exodus, where it is written: “Aaron took as his wife Elizabeth, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab and Abihu and Eleazar and Ithamar” (Exod. VI). Let him see that, before the promulgation of the law, by heavenly providence the priestly lineage had already been joined to the royal lineage, so that the Lord Jesus Christ, who was to be a true king and priest according to the flesh, might also assume that flesh from both—namely, from the stock of David and of Aaron.

Hence in both these tribes the chrism was celebrated mystically according to the law, as a foreshadowing both of Christ’s name and of his generation. David himself, entering the house of God, received the holy bread and the sword as both king and priest, prefiguring the one who was to come from his seed, who would fight for our freedom by the right of a king and offer the bread of his flesh for our absolution.

“But Mary said: ‘Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.’” What devoted humility! She desires the angel’s promise to be fulfilled and calls herself, who is chosen to be a mother, a handmaid, openly indicating how little merit she claims for obeying the Lord’s commands. “Let it be done,” she says: let one conceived without a man’s seed be conceived in a virgin; let the holy one be born from the Holy Spirit in an intact body, born from a human mother without a human father; let him be called the Son of God.

## HOMILY XXVIII. ON THE FRIDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS

At that time, Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah, and entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And it happened that, when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and cried out with a loud voice and said: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And whence is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting came to my ears,” and so forth.

As soon as the Virgin had given her consent, the angel immediately returned to the heavenly realms, while she went into the hill country. She hastens to visit Elizabeth, not as one who doubts the oracle or is uncertain about the example, but joyful because of her desire and devout because of her duty. At the same time she provides a figurative example: every soul that has conceived the word of God in its mind should immediately ascend the lofty summits of virtue with the step of love, so that it may enter the city of Judah—that is, the citadel of confession and praise—and be able to remain there, as it were, for three months, until the perfection of faith, hope, and charity.

“And she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth.” Learn from the Virgin Mary humility, so that you may be both chaste in body and devoted in heart. The younger visits the elder; the virgin greets a wife. It is fitting that the more chaste the Virgin is, the more humble she should be, and that, showing deference to her elders, she should commend the appearance of chastity by the proclamation of humility.

In another sense, Mary comes to Elizabeth as the Lord comes to John: Mary, so that Elizabeth might be filled with the Holy Spirit; the Lord, so that John’s baptism might be consecrated. The humility of the greater is certainly the exaltation of the lesser. Thus it follows:

“And it happened that, when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.” Observe the distinction and the particular force of each word. Elizabeth first heard the voice, but John first felt the grace. She heard according to the order of nature; he leaped because of the mystery. She perceived Mary’s arrival; he perceived the Lord’s. The women speak of grace; the infants experience it inwardly. They begin the mystery of piety through maternal advances, and the mothers prophesy by the Spirit of their children through a twofold miracle. The infant leaped, and the mother was filled—not that the mother was filled before the son, but that, when the son was filled with the Holy Spirit, he also filled his mother.

“And she cried out with a loud voice and said: ‘Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.’” It should be noted that the prophecy previously uttered about Christ is fulfilled not only by the miracles of events but also by the precise wording. For this is the fruit that was promised to the patriarch David under oath: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Ps. CXXXI). At the same time, it should be observed that Mary is blessed by Elizabeth in the same words with which she was blessed by Gabriel, so that she might be shown to be worthy of reverence by angels and human beings and rightly preferred to all women.

“And whence is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” She does not ask as one ignorant of what she recognizes to be the work of the Holy Spirit: namely, that she has been greeted by the Lord’s mother for the advancement of her child. Rather, struck by the novelty of the miracle, she confesses that this is not the result of her own merit but of a divine gift.

“For behold, as the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb.” Elizabeth was ashamed of the burden of motherhood as long as she did not know the mystery of religion. But she who had hidden herself because she had conceived a son began to boast because she was giving birth to a prophet. She who had previously been ashamed now blesses; she who had previously doubted is strengthened. “For behold,” she says, “as the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb.” Therefore she cried out with a loud voice when she perceived the Lord’s arrival, because she believed the birth to be sacred. There was no cause for shame where the birth of a prophet supplied proof of a generation received in faith, not sought through pretence.

“And blessed is she who believed, because those things will be fulfilled which were spoken to her by the Lord.” You see that Mary did not doubt but believed, and therefore obtained the fruit of faith. “Blessed,” she says, “is she who believed.” Truly blessed is she who was superior to a priest: for when the priest had denied, the virgin corrected the error. Nor is it surprising that the Lord, intending to redeem the world, began his work with a mother, so that the one through whom salvation was prepared for everyone might herself be the first to drink the fruit of salvation from the pledge.

It should likewise be noted how much grace filled Elizabeth’s soul when Mary entered. Through the spirit of prophecy it illuminated her concerning the past, the present, and the future. By saying, “Blessed is she who believed,” she plainly indicates that, through the Spirit, she recognized the angel’s words spoken to Mary. Then, adding, “Those things will be fulfilled which were spoken to you by the Lord,” she foresaw what would also follow her in the future. By calling her “the mother of her Lord,” she understood that Mary carried the Redeemer of the human race in her womb.

“And Mary said: ‘My soul magnifies the Lord. And my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior.’” “The Lord,” she says, “has exalted me with so great and unheard-of a gift that it cannot be explained by any service of the tongue, but can scarcely be grasped even by the innermost affection of the heart. Therefore I offer all the powers of my soul in praises of thanksgiving; whatever I live, feel, and discern, I gladly devote to contemplating the greatness of him who has no end. For my spirit rejoices in the eternal divinity of the same Jesus—that is, of the Savior—while my flesh is pregnant with him through a temporal conception.” Similar is the Psalmist’s saying: “My soul has rejoiced in the Lord and delighted in his salvation” (Ps. XXXIV). For he too revered the Father and the Son with equal love.

“Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.” She rightly rejoices that the one whose humility is regarded is to be called blessed by all, just as, conversely, Eve—whose pride was despised and condemned—pines under the name of “Eve,” that is, “woe” or “calamity.” For it was fitting that, just as death entered the world through the pride of our first parent, so the entrance of life should again be opened through Mary’s humility.

“Because he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.” This looks back to the beginning of the hymn, where it was said: “My soul magnifies the Lord.” That soul to which the Lord deigns to do great things customarily magnifies him with worthy praises and can exhort those who share the same desire and purpose, saying: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together” (Ps. XXXIII). For whoever refuses, insofar as he is able, to magnify the Lord whom he has come to know and to hallow his name will be called least in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V).

His name is called holy because, by the height of his unique power, he transcends every creature and is separated by a great distance from all that he has made. This is better understood in the Greek expression, in which the very word used—*ἅγιον* (*hagion*)—signifies, as it were, being outside the earth. In imitation of him, we too are commanded, according to the measure of our ability, to separate ourselves from all who are not holy and not dedicated to God, as the Lord says: “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Lev. XI; 1 Pet. I). Whoever consecrates himself will rightly seem to be outside the earth and outside the world. For he too can say: “While walking upon the earth, we have our manner of life in heaven” (Phil. III).

“And his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him.” Turning from particular gifts to the general judgments of God, she describes the condition of the whole human race and explains in alternating verses what the proud and the humble deserve, what the children of Adam possess through free will, and what the children of God possess through grace. “Therefore,” she says, “the Mighty One has not done great things for me alone; in every nation and generation, whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.”

“He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the intention of their heart” (Acts X). “With his arm” signifies the Son of God himself. This does not mean that God the Father is defined by the shape of human flesh and that the Son clings to him like a bodily limb; rather, because all things were made through him, he is called the arm of the Lord. Just as your arm is the means by which you work, so the Word of God is called God’s arm, because he made the world through the Word (John I). Why does a human being extend an arm in order to accomplish something, unless it is because what he has said does not immediately come to be? But if he possessed such power that whatever he said came to be without any movement of his body, his word would be his arm. Therefore, when we hear that the Son of God is the arm of God the Father, let carnal custom not obstruct us; rather, insofar as he grants us the ability, let us contemplate the power and wisdom of God through which all things were made.

“He has brought down the powerful from their throne and has exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, and he has sent the rich away empty.” What was said, “with his arm,” and what was previously said, “from generation to generation,” must also be attached to these verses *ἀπὸ κοινοῦ*—that is, commonly or jointly—to each clause and verse, because throughout all the generations of the age the proud continue to perish and the humble to be exalted through the pious and just dispensation of divine power.

“He has received Israel, his servant, in remembrance of mercy.” He beautifully calls Israel the Lord’s servant, since Israel has been received by him for salvation: obedient and humble, in accordance with what Hosea says: “Because Israel was a child, and I loved him” (Hos. XI). For whoever refuses to humble himself cannot be saved, nor can he say with the Prophet: “For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the protector of my soul” (Ps. XXXIII). “Whoever humbles himself like a little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

“As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed forever.” He signifies not the carnal but the spiritual seed of Abraham: not merely those born from his flesh, but those who, whether in circumcision or in uncircumcision, followed the footsteps of his faith. For while still uncircumcised he believed, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. He then received circumcision as the seal of that same faith, so that through faith he might become the father of both peoples, as the Apostle fully discusses in his Letter to the Romans.

The coming of the Savior, therefore, was promised to Abraham and to his seed forever (Rom. IV)—that is, to the children of the promise, to whom it is said: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. III). It is fitting that the mothers should prophetically anticipate the birth both of the Lord and of John, so that, just as sin began with women, good things might also begin with women; and she who perished through the deception of one woman might receive life again through the eager proclamation of two women (Gen. III).

## HOMILY XXIX. ON THE SATURDAY OF THE FOUR EMBER DAYS

**Luke III.** In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judea; Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip his brother tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene. And the rest.

Herod, Philip, and Lysanias, who governed Judea together with the Roman prefect Pilate, were the sons of that Herod under whom the Lord was born. Among them Archelaus, their brother, also reigned for ten years; he was accused before Augustus by the Jews because of his intolerable savagery of character and perished in perpetual exile at Vienne.

In order to make the kingdom of Judea less powerful, that same Augustus arranged for it to be divided into tetrarchies. Pilate, moreover, was sent into Judea in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, assumed the administration of the nation, and remained there for ten continuous years, almost until the very end of Tiberius’ reign.

“Under the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness.” Both Annas and Caiaphas were chief priests when John began his preaching; but Annas administered during that year, while Caiaphas administered during the year in which the Lord ascended the cross. In between, three others had held the high priesthood, but the Evangelist mentions especially those who had the greatest bearing on the Lord’s Passion.

For at that time, while the legal commands were being set aside by force and ambition, the honor of the high priesthood was bestowed on no one because of the merit of his life or lineage; rather, by Roman authority the highest priesthood was granted now to one person and now to another. Josephus finally records the matter in these words:

“Valerius Gratus, having removed Annas from the priesthood, appointed Ishmael, son of Baffi, as high priest. But not long afterward, dismissing him also, he replaced him in the high priesthood with Eleazar, son of the high priest Ananias. After a year he likewise removed him from office and handed the high priesthood over to a certain Simon, son of Camythus. After he too had held the office for no more than the space of one year, Joseph, whose name was also Caiaphas, was appointed as his successor” (Book XIII, chap. 4).

Consequently, the entire period during which our Lord is described as having taught on earth is compressed within the span of four years. Within this period the four successions of high priests mentioned by Josephus are recorded, each having served scarcely a full year.

Since John came to preach the one who was to redeem some from Judea and many from the nations, the time of his preaching is indicated through the king of the nations and the rulers of the Jews. Since the Gentiles were to be gathered and Judea scattered because of the guilt of its unbelief, the very description of earthly rule also shows this: one ruler is described as presiding in the Roman state, while in the kingdom of Judea many ruled by its fourth part. For the voice of our Redeemer says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste” (Luke XI). It is therefore clear that Judea had reached the end of its kingdom, since it lay divided under so many rulers.

It is also appropriate that not only the kings but also the priests under whom these events occurred are identified. Since John the Baptist preached the one who would exist as both king and priest, the Evangelist Luke designated the time of his preaching by both kingship and priesthood.

“And he came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.” It is clear to all who read that John not only preached a baptism of repentance but also gave it to certain people; nevertheless, he could not give his baptism for the forgiveness of sins. The forgiveness of sins is granted to us only in the baptism of Christ.

It should therefore be noted what is meant by the statement, “preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins”: since he could not give the baptism that would release sins, he preached it. Just as he preceded the incarnate Word of the Father with the word of his preaching, so he preceded with his baptism the baptism of repentance by which sins are released, although his own baptism could not release sins.

“As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight’” (Isa. XL). When questioned about who he was, John the Baptist himself replied in the same words: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Luke III). He was called a voice by the prophet because he went before the Word; he cries in the wilderness because he announces the comfort of redemption to abandoned and desolate Judea (Isa. XL).

What he was to cry out is explained when it follows: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” Everyone who preaches the right faith and good works does nothing other than prepare a way for the Lord who comes to the hearts of his hearers. Thus the power of grace may penetrate and the light of truth illuminate, and he makes straight paths for God (ibid.) by forming clean thoughts in the mind through the word of good preaching.

“Every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill will be brought low.” What is signified here by the name “valleys” except the humble, and by “mountains and hills” except proud people? At the coming of the Redeemer, therefore, the valleys were filled, while the mountains and hills were brought low, because, in accordance with his saying, “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV; XVIII; Matt. XXIII). A filled valley rises, while a humbled mountain and hill decrease, because in the faith of the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, the Gentiles received the fullness of grace, while Judea lost through the error of its unbelief what had made it swell with pride.

“And crooked things will become straight, and rough ways will become smooth.” Crooked things become straight when the hearts of evil people, bent away through injustice, are directed toward the rule of justice. Rough ways are changed into smooth paths when harsh and angry minds, through the infusion of heavenly grace, return to the gentleness of meekness.

For when the word of truth is not received by an angry mind, the roughness of the road, as it were, repels the step of the traveler. But when an angry mind receives the word of correction or exhortation through the grace of meekness, the preacher finds a smooth path where previously, because of the roughness of the road, he could not proceed—that is, could not place the step of his preaching.

And all flesh shall see the salvation of God. Since “all flesh” means every human being, no one in this life was able to see the salvation of God, namely Christ (Isa. XL). To what, then, does the prophet direct the eye of prophecy in this statement, if not to the day of the final judgment? On that day, when the heavens have been opened, the angels are ministering, and the apostles are seated, Christ will appear on the seat of his majesty. All alike—the elect and the reprobate—will see him, so that the righteous may rejoice forever in the gift of their reward, while the unrighteous may groan eternally under the punishment of retribution (Matt. XIX; Luke XXII).

## HOMILY XXX. ON THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF THE LORD’S ADVENT

**John I; Luke III.** At that time the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John to ask him, “Who are you?” And he confessed and did not deny, etc.

While the people were supposing, and everyone was considering in his heart concerning John whether perhaps he himself might be the Christ, John answered, saying to all. How did he answer those who were forming this opinion about him and secretly thinking in their hearts that he was the Christ, unless because they were not merely thinking this but also—as another Evangelist makes clear—had sent priests and Levites to him to inquire whether he was the Christ (John I)? From this it is evident that the Jews were then thoroughly aware, according to the Scriptures, that the time of the Lord’s incarnation had arrived. Yet what astonishing blindness: what they readily believed about John, they refused to believe about the Savior, though he had been proved by such great signs and virtues and was himself attested by John.

“I indeed baptize you with water, but one mightier than I will come, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to loosen.” John baptizes not with the Spirit but with water, because, unable to release sins, he washes the bodies of those baptized with water but does not cleanse their minds through forgiveness. Why, then, does he baptize, when baptism does not remit sins? It was so that, preserving the order of his forerunning, he who had preceded the Lord who was to be born by being born himself might also precede him who was to baptize by baptizing; and he who had become Christ’s forerunner by preaching might also become his forerunner by baptizing, in imitation of the sacrament.

Among the ancients it was customary that, if someone did not wish to take as his wife a woman who was properly assigned to him, the man who came as bridegroom to her by right of kinship would loosen his sandal for him. What, then, did Christ appear among human beings to be, if not the bridegroom of the holy Church? John himself says of him: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). But because people thought that John was the Christ—a claim John denies—he rightly declares himself unworthy to loosen the strap of Christ’s sandal. It is as though he openly said: “I cannot uncover the Redeemer’s feet, because I do not presumptuously claim the name of bridegroom, which does not belong to me.”

Yet this may also be understood in another way. Who does not know that sandals are made from the skins of dead animals? The incarnate Lord, when he came, appeared as though shod: in his divinity he assumed the deadness of our corruption. But the human eye is not sufficient to penetrate the mystery of this incarnation. For it cannot in any way investigate how the Word becomes embodied; how the supreme, life-giving Spirit is conceived within the womb of a mother; or how he who has no beginning both exists and is conceived. The strap of the sandal, therefore, is the bond of the mystery. John cannot loosen the strap of his sandal because even he, who recognized the incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, is not sufficient to investigate its mystery.

“He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” This means both with the cleansing of sanctification and with the testing of tribulation. The same Holy Spirit may also be understood to be signified by the name “fire,” because he kindles through love and illuminates through the wisdom with which he fills hearts. Thus those to whom it was said, “John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts I), receive the same baptism of the Spirit in a vision of fire.

Some explain this as meaning that in the present we are baptized in the Spirit, and in the future in fire: just as now we are reborn of water and the Spirit for the remission of all sins, so then, before the final judgment, we shall be cleansed by the baptism of purgatorial fire from certain lesser sins that have clung to us as we depart this life. The Apostle says: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire; and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. If anyone’s work that he built upon the foundation remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. III).

Although this may also be understood of the fire of tribulation applied to us in this present life, if anyone takes it to refer to the fire of future purification, it must be carefully considered that he says the one who can be saved through fire is not the person who builds upon Christ’s foundation iron, bronze, or lead—that is, greater and harder sins, already insoluble at that time—but wood, hay, and straw, that is, the smallest and lightest sins, which the fire can easily consume. This, however, must be known: there, no one will obtain purification even from the smallest sins unless, while still living in this life, he has earned by good deeds the right to obtain it there.

“His winnowing-fan is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing-floor.” By the winnowing-fan—that is, the straw—is signified the discernment of just judgment; by the threshing-floor, the present Church, in which, unquestionably—and this is deeply grievous—many are called but few are chosen (Matt. XX). There are few grains destined to be received into the dwellings above, in comparison with the weeds that are to be handed over to everlasting flames (Matt. XIII).

The cleansing of this threshing-floor is now carried out individually, when a sinful person is either expelled from the Church through priestly correction for manifest sins or condemned after death by divine severity for hidden sins. It will be completed universally at the end, when the Son of Man will send his angels and they will gather from his kingdom all scandals and causes of sin (ibid.). The Lord therefore has the winnowing-fan in his hand—that is, he holds the distinction of judgment in his power—because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

“And he will gather the wheat into his granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.” The Lord likewise concluded the parable of the good seed into which the enemy sowed weeds by saying: “At the time of harvest I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my granary” (Matt. XIII). In this he plainly teaches that the impious and sinners are to be handed over to the fire of Gehenna, while the saints are to be crowned with heavenly glory.

There is, however, this difference between chaff and weeds: chaff arises from no seed other than that of wheat, although it degenerates from the nobility of a good root. Weeds, by contrast, differ not only in their fruit but are produced from an entirely different origin. The chaff represents those who are instructed in the mysteries of the same faith as the elect, but differ from their firm perfection either through the lightness of their works or through the emptiness of their faithlessness. The weeds represent those who do not even deign to hear the words of faith and are therefore separated from the lot of the good both in conduct and in profession.

Thus, in the field of this world, there is one fruit belonging to the elect and two fruits belonging to the reprobate. For everything the enemy sows is subject to the flames (ibid.); and, what is more serious, very much of what the good sower casts forth perishes—either snatched away by birds, dried up by the sun, choked by thorns, or turned into chaff. Only the wheat created from good soil and proved worthy by endurance will be stored in the granary of the elect’s heavenly life (Mark IV; Luke VIII).

Similarly, according to another parable, not only do the fish that evade the nets of apostolic faith remain hidden in the depths of sinful waters, but many who have been drawn with the good as far as the shore of final judgment deserve then, on account of their wickedness, to be sent into the outer darkness (Matt. XIII).

He calls the fire of Gehenna unquenchable in a twofold sense: because it can neither itself be extinguished forever nor ever extinguish those whom it torments, but will punish them with an immortal—as I may say—death. This distinguishes it from that most sacred fire by which, as he said above, Christ’s elect are to be baptized. Of this the Psalmist says: “You tested us by fire, as silver is tested by fire.” And shortly afterward: “We did not remain forever, but passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment. I will enter your house with burnt offerings” (Ps. LXV)—that is, after the anguish of our afflictions has been overcome, I shall enter the courts of your heavenly kingdom in thanksgiving. May the Son of almighty God the Father grant this to us. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXI. AT COCKCROW ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

**Luke II.** At that time a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered, etc.

From the Gospel reading, dearest brothers, we heard that, when the Redeemer of the world, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, was about to be born into the world, a decree went out from Caesar Augustus, who at that time held the summit of worldly rule, that the whole world should be registered. This should not be thought to have happened by chance but should be understood as arranged by the most certain dispensation of this same Redeemer.

For the Mediator between God and human beings, just as he divinely foreknew the mother whom he chose for himself, from whom he would be born in human form when he willed, so also chose the times of his birth as he willed. Indeed, he himself made them what he willed them to be—namely, times in which, once the storm of wars had been stilled, a new and extraordinary tranquility of peace might cover the whole world.

What greater proclamation of peace could there have been in this life than for the whole world to be registered by one man and enclosed under the coinage of a single census? He chose a virgin as his mother, because it was fitting that the Son of God should be born in the flesh only from an undefiled mother. He chose a time of supreme peace for his birth, because this was precisely the reason he came to be born in the world: to restore the human race to the gifts of heavenly peace.

For it is written: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II)—that is, the merciful Mediator and reconciler established one household of God from angels and human beings. Our Lord was born in times of peace [Al.: “therefore”], so that he might also show himself to be that very state of the age of which the prophet had said above: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace.”

For this reason the same prophet, after describing elsewhere in mystical language his incarnation and the mysteries of our redemption, saying, “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it will be raised above the hills, and all nations will flow to it,” also clearly indicated the tranquility of peace that would then come, adding: “They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning-hooks. Nation will not lift up sword against nation, nor will they train for war any longer.” Therefore, immediately afterward he added by way of exhortation: “House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.”

He therefore preceded his appearing in the flesh with times of peace. Then, appearing as the author of peace and the creator of the ages, he opened the gate of light first to the house of Jacob—that is, to the Israelite people—and afterward to all the nations flocking to him, and proclaimed the joys of eternal peace.

Nor should it be passed over that the earthly serenity [Al.: “of the earth”] of that same peace, when the heavenly King was born, not only bore witness to grace but also rendered service. It granted the preachers of his word the ability to travel throughout the world and to spread the grace of the Gospel wherever they wished. This could scarcely have happened if the whole world had not been governed under one empire.

The registration of the whole world itself, which is remembered as having been carried out by an earthly king, plainly signifies the work of the heavenly King. He appeared in the world for this purpose: to gather into the unity of his faith the elect from all the nations throughout the world and, as he himself promised, to write their names forever in heaven.

This also—that everyone went at Augustus’s decree to be registered, each to his own city—is something we must spiritually carry out in service to our King. Our city is the holy Church, which is partly still journeying away from the Lord on earth and partly already reigning with the Lord in heaven; after the end of this age, perfected, it will reign wholly with him forever.

We must all go to this city; no one should excuse himself from so health-giving a journey. We must all pay the due census to the newborn King—that is, both obey the divine commands now within the unity of the present Church and hasten toward entry into our heavenly homeland by an indefatigable course of good works.

In the declaration of the census, a denarius was given, bearing the weight of ten coins and containing Caesar’s image and name. We too must imitate this spiritually. We pay our King a denarius when we strive to fulfill the ten commandments of his law.

On this denarius, so to speak, we bear the name of the same King when, in all our actions, we remember that we are called Christians from Christ and take care to preserve the dignity of his name undefiled in us. We must also imprint his image on the same denarius through our good conduct—namely, the image he taught us, saying: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. XIX).

This is the image of God in whose likeness we were created in the first human being: namely, so that through participation in divine holiness we might be holy forever. Hence the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV). But because human beings lost this light of the divine countenance through sinning, it pleased God, by being born in the flesh, to assume the appearance of a human face, so that he might teach us that we must be reborn in the spirit. It pleased him to appear in the likeness of sinful flesh, without sin, so that he might cleanse us from every sin and restore in us the radiance of his image.

“But Joseph,” he says, “went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to register with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant.”

It is clear that divine providence arranged for each person to go to his own city and register there, so that, through this general decree, the parents of our Savior would happen to come from Nazareth to Bethlehem. Thus, in fulfillment of the prophets’ predictions, each city would be distinguished by the mysteries of his incarnation: one, namely, shining with the honor of his conception, the other with that of his birth.

The prophet Isaiah testifies that our Redeemer had to be conceived in Nazareth when he says: “A shoot will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazarene will rise from his root” (Isa. XI). “Nazarene” is interpreted as “flower” or “pure.” The incarnate Son of God could rightly be called by this name, because he assumed a human nature clean from every vice, and from him proceeded, for all who believe in him, the source and origin of spiritual fruits, by which he both showed examples of right and blessed living and bestowed gifts.

Thus a shoot went forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazarene rose from his root, because the undefiled virgin Mary arose from the stock of David, and from her flesh the Lord assumed, in the city of Nazareth, the reality of flesh without the pollution of flesh.

That he would be born in Bethlehem is likewise indicated by prophetic oracles, when it is said: “And you, Bethlehem Ephratha, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, from you will go forth for me the one who is to rule in Israel” (Matt. II). He is rightly said to have been born in Bethlehem not only because of the dignity of his royal lineage, since David was from there, but also because of the name itself, since Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread.”

For he himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI). Since he came down from heaven to earth for this reason—to give us the nourishment of heavenly life and satisfy us with the gift of eternal sweetness—it is rightly called “house of bread,” the place in which he is born.

There is also another reason arising from heavenly providence why our Lord was born not in the city in which he had been conceived but in another: namely, so that by this means the enemies lying in wait might more easily be avoided, whether they were aware of his birth or were serving it.

For he foresaw that Herod would immediately begin to persecute him after his birth and seek him for death. Therefore he willed that the mystery of his birth should be carried out in the city of David in such a way that his parents would have neither a house nor property there, but would arrive only as newcomers at the time of his birth, remain as guests, and, once that birth had been completed and the heavenly signs that were fitting to bear witness to him had been declared [Al.: “that they said”], withdraw with him into Egypt.

Thus it happened that Herod not only failed to find him while seeking him, but also had no opportunity to harass his relatives, since he could not discover who his parents were.

Nor should the supreme condescension of our Creator and Redeemer be passed over in silence. He willed not only to become incarnate for us but also to become incarnate at a time when, immediately after his birth, he would be entered in the census register.

He put on flesh so that he might clothe us with the power of the spirit. He descended from heaven to earth so that he might raise us from earth to heaven. He paid tribute to Caesar so that he might grant us the grace of perpetual freedom. The Son of God served an earthly king who did not know the service owed to God, so that through this he might also give us a pattern of humility, showing us how greatly we ought to serve one another through love, since he did not disdain to render service to one who was ignorant of true love.

Here too he demonstrated by his example what he would later teach through the words of the chief of the apostles: “Be subject, for the sake of God, to every human authority, whether to the king as supreme or to governors as sent by him” (Rom. XIII; 1 Pet. II).

“It happened,” he says, “that while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son.”

He calls the Lord “firstborn,” not because it should be believed that the blessed Mother of God bore other sons after him—for it is well known that she remained in perpetual chastity with her husband Joseph—but because he is rightly called firstborn in this respect: as John says, “But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God.” Among these children he rightly holds the primacy, since, before he was born in the flesh as the Son of God, he already existed, born without beginning.

He descended to earth, became a participant in our nature, and granted us a share in his grace, so that, as the Apostle says, “he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII).

“And she wrapped him in swaddling clothes,” he says, “and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.”

Here, dearest brothers, we must contemplate the great condescension of our Redeemer. Here each of us must say from the depths of our heart, with the prophet: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. CXV).

He whom we truly sing to be “the great Lord and greatly to be praised,” whose greatness has no end, was born little for us, so that by being reborn he might make us, who were little, great—that is, make us righteous from sinners.

He who sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven needed a place in an inn, so that he might grant us an abundance of blessed dwellings in his Father’s house.

He who clothed every creature—whether the invisible creatures in heaven or the visible ones in this world—with manifold adornments, who in his majesty is, as the Prophet says of him, “clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. CIII), was himself covered in the assumption of our weakness with small pieces of cloth, so that he might restore to us our first robe—that is, in his mercy bring us back to the grace of immortality, which we lost [Al.: “received”] in our first parent.

He through whom all things were made arranged for his hands and feet, indeed his entire body, which he had assumed, to be wrapped in swaddling clothes, so that he might make our hands ready for good works, direct our feet into the way of peace, and dedicate all the members of our body to divine service.

He whom heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain was enclosed in the narrowness of a small manger, so that he might grant us the spaciousness of heavenly thrones.

By a special grace of the sacrament, he chose a place for himself in the manger where animals customarily gathered to feed. For even then he indicated that he would feed all the faithful at the sacred table of the altar with the mysteries of his incarnation. He also showed that, while he habitually refreshes all who humbly serve him with the grace of inward sweetness, the following words of the prophet are fittingly spoken of them: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isa. I).

In the ox he signifies the Jewish people, which was accustomed to bear the yoke of the law and ruminate upon its words. In the donkey he portrays the people of the nations, which had always remained unclean in the filth of idolatry.

From both peoples many were converted to the grace of the Gospel. They came to know their owner, by whom they had been created, and sought to grow toward perpetual salvation through his heavenly nourishment.

We receive their firstfruits, consecrated to him, in those pastors who are rightly venerated: they were the first to deserve to see and proclaim his birth when the angel announced it; and in the magi who came from the East to his cradle with gifts and prayers, guided by a star. The former came to the Lord from the Jews, the latter from the nations.
