But concerning the magi, with the Lord whom they came to visit graciously assisting us, we shall hear more fully on the holy feast of the Epiphany. For now, let us examine what happened concerning the pastors, who came to him first and signify the faithful of the earlier people.

It follows:

“And there were shepherds in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them.”

It was very fittingly arranged by heavenly providence that, when the Lord was born, shepherds should keep watch in the vicinity of that city and, by watching, protect their flocks from the fear of the night.

For it was necessary that, when the great shepherd of sheep—that is, the nourisher of faithful souls—was born into the world, shepherds keeping watch over their flock should bear witness to his birth.

He is the one who says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life” (John X). It was also already destined that chosen shepherds throughout the whole world—that is, holy preachers—would be sent to gather peoples of believers into the Lord’s sheepfold, namely, the holy Church.

To their first, the blessed Peter, when he professed that he loved the Lord, the same Lord and chief of shepherds gave the command as proof of that love, saying: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI). For only the person who perfectly loves the Creator loves him who also bestows upon his neighbors the care of pure love.

“And behold,” he says, “an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone around them, and they were afraid with great fear.”

What does it mean that, when the angel appeared, the splendor of divine glory also surrounded them? Nowhere in the whole sequence of the Old Testament do we find this. Although angels appeared to prophets and righteous people innumerable times, nowhere do we read that human beings were surrounded by the radiance of divine light—unless this privilege was rightly reserved for the dignity of the present time.

For when the true light of the world was being born into the world, it was certainly fitting that the herald of his birth should also pour the novelty of heavenly light upon the bodily sight of human beings.

The Prophet speaks of his birth: “Light has risen in the darkness for the upright in heart” (Ps. CXII). And as though we were asking what the light was of which he spoke, he immediately adds: “The merciful, compassionate, and righteous Lord” (ibid.).

Therefore, when the merciful and righteous Creator and Redeemer of the human race deigned to illumine the world with the glory of a new birth, it was entirely fitting that the very region in which he was born should also be filled with the brilliance of the new light.

Let us therefore hear what the angel, appearing with glory, says to the shepherds:

“Do not be afraid. For behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people.”

Truly great joy: heavenly joy, eternal joy, joy disturbed by no intervening sadness, in which we are granted to rejoice with the citizens of the heavenly homeland alone.

“Which will be for all the people.” Not for all the people of the Jews, nor for all the people of the nations, but for all the people of believers, who from the Jews or from the nations throughout the world are gathered into one confession of Christ and are called Christians through participation in the same mysteries of Christ.

Of this people the Prophet says: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa. IX).

“For today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David.”

He rightly said, “Today he has been born.” He did not say, “This night,” because he appeared with heavenly light and proclaimed the birth of the day to those who were keeping the watches of the night—namely, the day of which the Psalmist sings: “Proclaim his salvation from day to day” (Ps. XCV).

The salvation of God—that is, the Lord Jesus—is “day from day,” because the one who appeared temporally as a human being in the city of David from a virgin mother was himself born before all ages—not locally, but as light from light, true God from true God.

Therefore, since the light of life has risen for us who dwell in the region of the shadow of death, the herald of his rising aptly says, “For today a Savior has been born for us,” so that, warned also by this word, we may always remember that the night of ancient blindness has passed and the day of eternal salvation has drawn near; that we should cast off the works of darkness and walk as children of light.

For, as the same Apostle says, the fruit of light consists in all righteousness, goodness, and holiness (Eph. V).

“And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger.”

We ought always to keep this sign of the Savior born in the flesh in our minds, so that we may learn to repay his benefits with gratitude by living well. For he willed to assume the condition of our weakness in such a way that he did not refuse even the general state of poverty.

The fact that he is an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes is an indication of the weakness he assumed; the fact that he is found lying not on a bed but in a manger is an indication of poverty.

Let us therefore sing the mercies of the Lord forever, because, so that we might live in blessedness forever, he did not refuse to become a companion of our lowliness and mortality.

While one angel was announcing the joy of the Lord’s birth, suddenly a multitude of the heavenly host appeared. They rendered the newborn Lord the service of their devotion and, now appearing on earth, celebrated with their customary hymn of praise the one whom they had always been accustomed to glorify in heaven.

Here the citizens of heaven also teach us, through their praise, how we ought to celebrate the joy of this most sacred solemnity and how many praises we ought to offer in word to the Word of God, who became flesh in it and dwelt among us (John I), so that he might raise us to the vision of his glory and grant us a share in grace and truth, since he is full of both.

They therefore praise God and say:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

They aptly proclaim glory to God and preach peace to human beings, because they know that the one whose birth they rejoice in is the Mediator between God and human beings—that is, true God and human being.

They sing glory to God in the highest because they rejoice that the time has now come when the world, having rejected gods made by human beings, would recognize its Creator, who is in heaven.

They wish peace to human beings because they understand that those whom, previously cast out from eternal happiness through the just consequence of sin, they had looked upon with contempt will now, through the Lord’s redemption, be with them in the joys of the same heavenly dwelling.

They announce peace to human beings whom they desire to have as companions in the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, in the perpetual vision of peace—in order also to admonish these human beings that they must reach their fellowship through the observance of peace.

And appropriately, when they say, “And on earth peace to human beings,” they add, “of good will,” because the angelic spirits hasten to have fellowship with those whose minds they observe to possess the purity of good will.

They rejoice to raise with themselves, after the dissolution of the flesh, to the contemplation of true peace those who, while dwelling in the flesh, they see bringing forth everything they do or say from the root of good will.

Such people, even if weakness or ignorance occasionally hinders them from completing the good action they desire, nevertheless have the integrity they hold in their hearts excused before the eyes of the inner Judge.

Good will consists in loving our Creator with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and loving our neighbors as ourselves; and in showing the power of this same love in ourselves through whatever signs of devoted action we can offer.

Since we ought to do this at every hour and moment, how much more should we do so when we celebrate the birth of our Lord and Savior either in the annual feast or by more frequent devotion and remembrance! In that birth we are especially taught by the angelic exhortation to offer him the gifts of good will. In it the citizens of the heavenly homeland promise our good will the fellowship of their peace. In it we too are accustomed to sing to God the same hymn with the angelic choir.

Let this solemnity, dearest brothers, therefore be shared by us all. Let this solemnity unite earthly beings with heavenly ones; indeed, let our entire manner of life be suited to the fellowship of the citizens above.

In the meantime, let us meditate on the life we desire to possess in our homeland. Let us also, insofar as we can, conform ourselves to that most pure life of the blessed spirits, with which we hope then to be joined in the inward purity of mutual love.

If we pursue in the present the gifts of divine praise in which we desire to be occupied in the future, let us learn to say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III), so that we may confidently add what follows: “From there also we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.”

For they await with joy the Savior coming to judgment who remember that, on earth, they have lived according to his heavenly will.

Our Creator and Savior also gives us, fragile and less perfect as we are, great hope of receiving salvation. Appearing in weakness for our strengthening, Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, soon promised, with one harmonious voice together with the heavenly host, the gifts of his eternal peace to our good will. He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXII. ON THE SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

**Luke II.** At that time Joseph and Mary, the mother of Jesus, were marveling at the things that were said about him, etc.

The Evangelist calls Joseph the Savior’s father, not because he was truly his father, as the Photinians held, but because, for the sake of preserving Mary’s reputation, he was regarded by everyone as his father.

The Evangelist had not forgotten that he had narrated that she conceived from the Holy Spirit and gave birth while remaining a virgin. Rather, expressing the opinion of the common people—which is the proper rule of historical narration—he calls Joseph Christ’s father.

He may also rightly be called Christ’s father in the sense in which he is rightly understood as Mary’s husband: without the mingling of flesh, through the bond of marriage itself, and much more closely joined than if he had been adopted from elsewhere.

Joseph was not thereby not to be called Christ’s father because no one had begotten him through intercourse, since a man is rightly called the father even of one whom he has adopted elsewhere, though he did not beget him from his own wife.

“And he said to Mary his mother: ‘Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed.’”

He is rightly appointed for resurrection, because he is light and the glory of the people of Israel, and because he says: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John XI).

How is he appointed for the fall, except because he is also “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Isa. VIII)—that is, a ruin for those who take offense at the word and do not believe? Of them he says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John XV).

He was appointed for the fall and resurrection of many not only in himself but also in those who preach him, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (1 Cor. II).

For the person who, when the Apostle preaches, follows the word he hears with love rises and is saved through a good fragrance; the person who pursues it with hatred falls and dies through that same good fragrance.

He is “a sign that will be opposed”: understand this as the faith of the Lord’s cross. Concerning it the Jews say to the Apostle Paul: “We know about this sect that it is everywhere opposed” (Acts XXVIII). And the Apostle himself says: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block and to the nations foolishness” (1 Cor. I).

And your own soul a sword will pierce. No history teaches that blessed Mary departed this life by the stroke of a sword, especially since it is not the soul but the body that is ordinarily killed by iron. It therefore remains to understand that sword of which it is said, “And a sword is in their lips” (Psalm 38), that is, that the sorrow of the Lord’s Passion pierced her soul. Although she did not doubt that Christ, as the Son of God, would die of his own free will and conquer death itself, nevertheless she could not see him crucified, born as he was from her own flesh, without experiencing sorrow. For the iron that is sung to have pierced Joseph’s soul is understood, better than anything else, as severe mental tribulation.

“So that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.” It was once uncertain which of the Jews would receive Christ’s grace, which they certainly knew was to come, and which would prefer to reject it. But when his birth was heard of, the thoughts of their hearts were immediately revealed: King Herod was troubled, “and all Jerusalem with him” (Matthew 2). The shepherds, with fear and joy, resounded praise to God and proclaimed to human beings the message of peace (Luke 2). When his teaching and power had become widely known, some flocked to him as a teacher of truth, while others fled from him as a deceiver. When the sign of his cross was erected, some, blaspheming against him as one justly condemned to death, mocked him; others, grieving bitterly as though the author of life were dying, mourned him.

Even to this day, and until the consummation of the present age, the sword of the most grievous tribulation does not cease to pierce the soul of the Church. She endures this when the sign of faith is opposed by the wicked; when, after hearing the word of God, she sees many rise again with Christ, but more—lamentably—fall away from belief; and when, with the thoughts of many hearts revealed, she observes that wherever the best seed of the Gospel has been sown, the weeds of vice either prevail beyond measure or—even more grievously—germinate and reign alone.

And there was Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She had advanced in years and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity. She was a widow until the age of eighty-four and did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and prayers night and day.

According to the historical account, Anna is shown to have been devoted in her conduct, venerable in age, and altogether worthy to bear witness to the incarnate Lord. According to the mystical interpretation, because she signifies the Church—which in the present age is widowed, as it were, by the death of her bridegroom and Lord—the number of her years of widowhood also signifies the period of the Church’s existence, during which, established in the body, she journeys away from the Lord. With great devotion she keeps watch at the threshold of the heavenly temple and awaits that daily coming of the Lord of which he says, “We will come and make our dwelling with him.”

Seven times twelve makes eighty-four. The number seven pertains to the course of this age, which revolves through seven days; twelve pertains to the perfection of apostolic teaching. Therefore, whether it is the universal Church or any faithful soul that strives to devote the whole of its life to apostolic institutions, it is praised as multiplying seven by twelve and serving the Lord through the symbolic eighty-four years. Likewise, the seven years during which she had remained with her husband most fittingly correspond to the time of the Lord’s incarnation. As I have said, the number seven ordinarily indicates the perfection of time; but there, because of the privilege of the Lord’s majesty—who, dwelling in the flesh, taught—the simple number seven years is expressed. Here, because of the summit of apostolic dignity, seven years are multiplied by twelve.

It accords well with the Church’s mysteries that Anna is interpreted as “grace,” and that she is the daughter of Phanuel, whose name means “the face of God,” while she sings with the Psalmist, “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4). She descended from the tribe of Asher—that is, “the blessed”—who among the twelve patriarchs is eighth in order of birth. It has often been emphasized that this number is sacred in the New Testament.

**[Col. 0341B]** And she herself, arriving at that hour, gave thanks to the Lord and spoke about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem.

Simeon prophesied; a married woman had prophesied; a virgin had prophesied. A widow, too, ought to prophesy, so that no profession or sex might be lacking. For this reason Anna is introduced with the support and conduct of widowhood such that she may rightly be believed to have been entirely worthy to announce that the Redeemer of all had come.

And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth.

At this point Luke omitted what he knew had been sufficiently explained by Matthew (Matthew 2): namely, that after these events the Lord was taken by his parents into Egypt, lest he be found and killed by Herod; and that, after Herod’s death, he finally returned to Galilee and began to live in his own city, Nazareth. For the evangelists often omit certain matters in such a way that, whether they have seen them mentioned by others or have foreseen in the Spirit that they would be mentioned by others, they seem, through the continuous sequence of their own narratives, to have omitted nothing. Nevertheless, when the attentive reader considers the Scripture of another evangelist, he can discover at what point those matters have been passed over.

**[Col. 0341C]** And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was in him.

The distinction in the words should be noted. The Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he was a child—that is, insofar as he had assumed the condition of human weakness—was to grow and become strong. But insofar as he was also the Word of God and eternal God, he neither needed to become strong nor could he increase. Thus he is rightly described as full of wisdom and grace (Colossians 2). He is full of wisdom because in him “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily”; and full of grace because great grace was granted to that same Mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, so that from the moment he began to become human, he was perfect both as man and as God. John writes something similar when he says that he was “full of grace and truth” (John 1), commending under the name of truth the same excellence of divinity that Luke commends under the name of wisdom.

**[Col. 0341D]** And his parents went every year to Jerusalem for the solemn feast of Passover.

You see that this evangelist is not compared without reason to a calf among the four living creatures (Ezekiel 1), since, like an animal appointed for sacrifice, he moves chiefly around the temple and Jerusalem in the course of his narrative. At the beginning he places a priest praying at the altar; he sets the multitude of the people in the temple courts; he soon sends Mary to Jerusalem after the Lord has been conceived; he brings her into the house of the high priest; there he reports the birth of John the Baptist; and immediately after the Lord’s birth he transfers him there with the offering. Each year he takes the same child there with his parents, and at twelve years of age he places him among the choirs of the teachers in the temple. There, among other things astonishing to the wise, he says, “I must be in the things that belong to my Father.” And at the end of his Gospel he concludes with the disciples praising God in the temple.

## HOMILY XXXIII. ON THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

**[Col. 0342A]**

**Luke 5; Mark 1; Matthew 8.** At that time, when Jesus was in one of the cities, behold, a man full of leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, saying, “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,” and so forth.

It is fitting that the place where the leper was cleansed is not explicitly identified, so that it might be shown that not merely one people of a particular city, but the peoples of all cities, were healed. And because the Lord says, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5), the man who was excluded by the law, presuming that he could be purified by the Lord’s power, judged that the grace capable of washing away the leper’s stain came not from the law but was above the law.

Yet just as the authority of power is revealed in the Lord, so the constancy of faith is revealed in the leper. He fell on his face, which expresses humility and shame, so that each person might be ashamed of the stains of his own life. **[Col. 0342B]** But shame did not restrain his confession: he displayed his wound and requested a remedy. His confession is itself full of devotion and faith: “If you will,” he said, “you can cleanse me.” He attributed power to the Lord’s will. He did not doubt the Lord’s will as though he distrusted his compassion; rather, conscious of his own filth, he did not presume.

And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying, “I will; be cleansed.” And immediately the leprosy departed from him.

There is nothing intermediate between God’s work and his command, because the work is contained in the command. Thus it is written, “He spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 148). You see, therefore, that there can be no doubt that God’s will is power. If his will is power, then those who assert one will necessarily assert one power. Accordingly, as one who possessed the power to heal and the authority to command, he did not refuse to provide testimony through his action. “I will,” he says, on account of Photinus; he commands, on account of Arius; he touches, on account of Mani. The law indeed forbids touching lepers; but the one who is Lord of the law does not obey the law—he makes the law. He did not touch him because he was unable to cleanse him without touching him, but to show that he was not subject to the law and did not fear contagion as human beings do. Since he could not be contaminated, the one who freed others caused the leprosy—whose custom was to contaminate the one who touched it—to flee at the Lord’s touch. At the same time, there was something remarkable in the fact that he healed him in the manner in which he had been entreated: “If you will, you can cleanse me.” “I will,” he said, “be cleansed.” You have the will, and you also have the affection of compassion.

And he commanded him to tell no one. Why was he commanded to tell no one, unless to teach that our benefactions should not be publicized but kept hidden? This means that we should abstain not only from monetary reward but also from the reward of gratitude.

“But go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them” (Leviticus 14).

He is commanded to show himself to the priest so that the priest might understand that he had been healed not according to the order of the law but by the grace of God, above the law. He is also commanded to offer a sacrifice so that the Lord might show that he had not abolished the law but fulfilled it: walking according to the law, yet above the law, he healed those whom the remedies of the law had not healed. And he rightly added, “as a testimony to them”—that is, if they should believe in God, if the leprosy of impiety should depart.

If anyone is troubled by the question of how the Lord appears to approve the Mosaic sacrifice, since the Church has not retained it, let him remember that the holy sacrifice of holies—which is his body—had not yet begun. For he had not yet offered his burnt offering in the Passion. The symbolic sacrifices ought not to be removed before that which they signified had been confirmed by the testimony of the apostles who preached and of the peoples who believed.

Because this man symbolically represents the human race weakened by sins, he is rightly described not merely as a leper but as full of leprosy: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3). They are to be cleansed from the variety of their former error by the outstretched hand of the Savior—that is, by the Word of God made flesh and touching human nature—and may thus hear with the apostles, “Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15). Those who for so long had been kept apart from the camps of God’s people as detestable may now at last be restored to the temple and offered to the priest, that priest to whom it is said, “You are a priest forever” (Psalm 109). They hear the Apostle say, “For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3). Let them offer for their cleansing what Moses commanded—that is, let them present their bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God (Romans 12).

Yet it is rightly asked what it means that the Lord commanded some things he had done to be concealed, although they could not be concealed even for an hour. Did the only-begotten Son, coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, wish to do something here that he was unable to accomplish? We should note instead that our Redeemer, through his mortal body, provided us with an example in everything he did. When he performed a miracle, he commanded that it be kept silent, yet it could not be kept silent, so that his elect, following the examples of his teaching, might indeed wish to remain hidden when they perform great works, but might be revealed against their will for the benefit of others. Thus it is a sign of great humility that they desire their works to be kept silent, and a sign of great exaltation that their works cannot be kept silent. The Lord therefore did not will something to happen and then prove unable to accomplish it; rather, through the instruction of his example, he showed what his members ought to desire and what happens to them even when they do not wish it.

## HOMILY XXXIV. ON THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

**[Col. 0343B]**

**Luke 8; Matthew 8; Mark 4.** At that time, it happened on one of the days that Jesus embarked in a boat, and his disciples with him, and so forth.

In this voyage the Lord graciously reveals the two natures of one and the same person: he who sleeps in the boat as a man restrains the fury of the sea as God by his word. Allegorically, the sea or lake that he wishes to cross with his own is understood as the dark and bitter turbulence of the present age. The boat into which they embark is best understood as the wood of the Lord’s Passion. By its benefit, the faithful, having crossed the waves of the world, attain the dwelling of their heavenly homeland, as though they had reached the security of a stable shore.

That the Savior himself embarks with his disciples in one boat, he explains elsewhere when, after announcing the mystery of his Passion and resurrection, he soon says to all: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9; Matthew 10; Mark 8).

And as they sailed, he fell asleep.

When the faithful trample upon the world, meditate in their hearts on the rest of the future kingdom, and, whether by the favorable breath of the Holy Spirit or by the labor of their own efforts, cast the treacherous things of the world behind them in rivalry with one another, the time of the Lord’s Passion suddenly arrives. Hence Mark rightly says that this occurred as night was approaching (Mark 4), so that the setting of the true Sun might be signified not only by the Lord’s sleep but also by the hour at which the light was declining.

And a storm of wind descended upon the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.

When the Lord had ascended the stern of the cross, on which he was to undergo the sleep of death, the waves of blaspheming persecutors, stirred up by demonic storms, rose against him. Yet it was not his own endurance that was disturbed; rather, the disciples’ weakness was shaken, trembling and endangered.

And they came and awakened him, saying, “Teacher, we are perishing.”

The disciples awaken the Lord so that, while he sleeps, they may not perish in the violence of the waves. They had seen his death and therefore sought his resurrection with the greatest longing, lest, if the sleep of his fleshly death continued too long, their minds should perish forever in spiritual death. Hence it rightly follows:

But he rose and rebuked the wind and the storm of the water; and it ceased, and there was calm.

He rebuked the wind as he rose because, by celebrating the resurrection, he overthrew the devil’s pride, destroying through death the one who held the power of death. Rising, he also caused the storm of the water to cease, because by rising from the tomb he shook the mad rage of the Jews, who had shouted with shaking heads, “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matthew 27; Mark 16; Luke 23).

Here, in the literal sense, it should be noted that all creatures perceive their Creator. Those to whom he gives orders and commands perceive the one who commands them—not through the error of heretics, who think that all things are living beings, but through the majesty of the Creator, to whom things that are insensible among us are sensible.

And he said to them, “Where is your faith?”

Those who were afraid in Christ’s presence are rightly reproved, since whoever clings to him cannot perish. Something similar occurred when, after the sleep of death, he appeared to the disciples and reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen (Mark 16). Likewise he said to them, “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” (Luke 24.) It is as though, using the metaphor of a boat, he were saying: Was it not necessary for Christ to sleep, while the waves swept back and forth over the boat in which he rested, and, once the swelling heaps of water had immediately been calmed, for him to reveal to all the power of his divinity?

And they were afraid and marveled, saying to one another, “Who, then, is this? For he commands even the winds and the sea, and they obey him.”

Matthew writes it this way: “The men marveled, saying, ‘What sort of man is this?’” and so forth (Matthew 8). It was therefore not the disciples but the sailors and the others who were in the boat who marveled. If, however, someone stubbornly insists that those who marveled were the disciples, we will rightly reply that they were called “men” because they did not yet know the Savior’s power.

We, too, each marked with the sign of the Lord’s cross, intend to leave the world; we also embark in the boat with Jesus and attempt to cross the lake. But although the one who guards Israel neither sleeps nor slumbers (Psalm 120), when we are often sailing, he seems to sleep amid the roaring of the waters—whenever, amid the repeated efforts of the virtues, whether through the assault of unclean spirits, wicked people, or the very force of our thoughts, the brightness of faith is darkened, the height of hope withers, and the flame of love grows cold.

Yet amid such storms we must run to that helmsman and diligently awaken him who does not serve the winds but commands them. Immediately he will restrain the storms, restore calm, and grant us the harbor of salvation.

In this connection, after briefly examining the changing fortunes of the apostolic voyage, it is pleasant to observe how its own hidden character benefits the good and how the mixture of the wicked disturbs them. For behold, beginning with the more perfect: after the solemn celebration of the Lord’s resurrection, seven chosen disciples embark in a boat to fish. Since they were not far from the land of perpetual rest—only about two hundred cubits away—that is, since they had applied as much mind to the world as the twofold commandment of love required, and since Peter had stripped himself of worldly business, they deserved to see the Lord already standing on the shore of mortality, to feast with him, and, when the morning of the heavenly light was mystically dawning, to receive their nets filled with a great number of fish, yet not torn, and to draw them out from the lowest waves of the world.

Elsewhere, as we read above, Peter, at the Lord’s command, lets down the nets for a catch and captures a very great multitude of fish (Luke 5). But because his spirit was still weak, so that he tremblingly said to Christ, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord,” the nets were then torn, and, if his companions had not helped, the boats too would have sunk beneath the water.

Again, in this passage, the disciples embark in the boat with the Lord and put out to sea. But because Judas was also present, and because the Lord is said to have slept in the stern, which was the helmsman’s seat, while the wind and sea raged outside, the boat was in danger. For although many merits of the disciples were sailing there, the treachery of the betrayer was still driving it; and those who were firm through their own merits were shaken by the faults of another.

Again, Paul, sailing with the brothers toward Jerusalem and hastening to celebrate Pentecost and the joys of the Holy Spirit there, travels the whole course with a favorable wind (Acts 20). But when he is sent from Jerusalem to Rome (Acts 27), because he is traveling with unbelievers, the sea rages, the winds oppose them, rain threatens, cold exhausts them, the stars are obscured, the land is denied them, wheat is thrown into the sea, and the ship’s equipment is cast overboard. Finally, the ship itself, driven onto the sands, breaks apart; the sailors, unable to recognize the land, swim toward it. Those who had entered the waves of the world weighed down by desires scarcely escape from that same hostile world naked, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “He himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3).

## HOMILY XXXV. ON THE SIXTIETH SUNDAY

**[Col. 0345B]**

**Luke 8; Matthew 13; Mark 4.** At that time, when a very large crowd had gathered and people were hurrying to Jesus from the cities, he spoke by way of a comparison: “The sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell beside the path, and it was trampled, and the birds of the sky ate it,” and so forth.

The Lord graciously chose to explain this parable himself so that he might make it known that he spoke figuratively and teach that the meanings of things should be sought even in those matters that he did not wish to explain personally. Since the Lord himself revealed that the seed is the word of God and that the different soils signify the differing hearts of hearers, we can understand the sower whom he left us to identify as none other than the Son of God. He went out to sow his seed because, leaving the bosom of the Father—which no creature could approach—he came into the world to bear witness to the truth (John 18; Matthew 13; Mark 4). Thus, appropriately, according to the other evangelists, when he was about to speak this parable he is said to have gone out from the house, approached the sea, and embarked in a boat: the position of his body itself was indicating what the progression of his speech conveyed.

And as he sowed, some fell beside the path, and it was trampled, and the birds of the sky ate it.

What the Lord explained should be received with devout faith; what he left unspoken for our understanding should be touched upon briefly. The seed that fell beside the path perished through a double injury: it was trampled by passersby and snatched away by birds. The path, therefore, is the heart worn down and dried out by the constant passage of evil thoughts, so that it is unable to receive and germinate the seed of the word. Thus whatever good seed comes near such a path is trampled by the movement of evil thoughts and seized by demons, who are called “birds of the sky,” either because they are heavenly and spiritual in nature or because they fly through the air.

And other seed fell upon the rock, and when it had grown, it withered because it had no moisture.

Here the rock rightly signifies a hard and untamed heart, penetrated by no plow of true faith. The moisture at the root of the seed is, according to another parable, the oil used to nourish the virgins’ lamps (Matthew 25): that is, love and perseverance in virtue.

And other seed fell on good soil and, when it had grown, produced fruit a hundredfold.

By fruit a hundredfold he means perfect fruit. The number ten is always understood as signifying perfection, because the keeping of the law is contained in the Ten Commandments. The active and contemplative life are joined together in the commandments of the Decalogue, because they command both love of God and love of neighbor. Love of God pertains to the contemplative life, while love of neighbor pertains to the active life.

The number ten, multiplied by itself, rises to one hundred. Hence a great perfection is rightly signified by one hundred, as it is said of the one who leaves earthly possessions for the Lord: “He will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew 19). Whoever for God’s name despises temporal and earthly things receives here the perfection of mind, so that he no longer desires what he has despised, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life. Thus good soil is made fruitful a hundredfold when a teachable heart is endowed with the perfection of spiritual virtues.

Saying these things, he cried out, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Whenever this brief admonition is inserted, whether in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, it shows that what is said is mystical and that we must seek it with greater attention.

His disciples asked him what this parable meant.

No one should suppose that the disciples asked the Savior about this immediately after the parable had ended. Rather, as Mark says, “When he was alone, those who were with him, together with the Twelve, asked him about the parable” (Mark 4).

And he said to them, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the others in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.”

Mark says it this way: “But for those who are outside, everything is given in parables.” Therefore, let us enter with Christ’s disciples into God’s sanctuary, so that we may understand the final realities of the mysteries of the kingdom of God. Those who draw near to his feet will receive his teaching, saying with the Psalmist, “Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118). Thus they rightly hear in parables and enigmas who, with the senses of their hearts closed, neither enter nor wish to know the truth, having forgotten the Lord’s command: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Those beside the path are those who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word from their hearts, lest they believe and be saved.

Mark writes about this seed as follows (chapter 4): “These are the ones beside the path where the word is sown; and when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes it away.” Matthew says: “Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it—the evil one comes and snatches it away” (Matthew 13). From this it is clearly taught that those sown beside the path are people who do not deign to receive the word they hear with any faith, any understanding, or even the slightest inducement of usefulness.

As for those on rocky ground and among thorns, as the Lord explains, they are people who approve the usefulness of the word once heard and taste the desire for it, but are prevented from reaching what they approve: the adversities of this life frighten them, while its prosperities flatter them. Against both kinds of loss the one who had received the seed sought to protect himself when he said, “With the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful” (2 Corinthians 6).

Know, then, that these three kinds of soil signify all who do not put the word into practice. The one who preserves the seed received is good soil. The Jews and the Gentiles, who do not even deserve to hear, are excepted from these categories.

As for what fell among thorns, these are those who have heard and, going along under the cares, riches, and pleasures of life, are choked and bear no fruit.

It is remarkable that the Lord interpreted the thorns as riches, since thorns wound while riches delight. Yet riches are thorns because, through the pricks of their thoughts, they tear the mind, and when they drag it as far as sin, they make it bleed as though from an inflicted wound. In this passage, as another evangelist testifies (Matthew 13), the Lord rightly calls them not simply riches but deceitful riches.

They are deceitful because they cannot remain with us for long. They are deceitful because they do not drive away the poverty of our minds. Only those riches are true that make us rich in virtues.

It should also be noted that, in explaining this, the Lord says that cares and pleasures choke. They choke because, through their intrusive thoughts, they strangle the throat of the mind; and when they do not allow a good desire to enter the heart, they kill the passage of life-giving breath, as it were. It should further be noted that he joins two things to riches: cares and pleasures. They oppress the mind through anxiety and relax it through abundance. In reality, by opposite means they make their possessors both afflicted and self-indulgent. But because pleasure cannot coexist with affliction, at one time they afflict their possessors through the anxiety of guarding their wealth, and at another they soften them into pleasures through abundance.

As for what fell on good soil, these are those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, retain it and bear fruit with perseverance.

As we said earlier, good soil is opposed to all three evil varieties of soil: it willingly receives the seed of the word and preserves what it receives patiently through adversity and prosperity until the season of fruit. In another sense, good soil bears fruit through perseverance because none of the good things we do have value if we do not patiently endure the evil of our neighbors. The higher a person progresses, the more severely he finds something to bear in this world. As our mind’s love for the present age diminishes, the adversity of that same age increases.

For this reason we see many people doing good and yet laboring under the heavy burden of tribulations. But, in accordance with the Lord’s word, they bear fruit through perseverance, because when they humbly receive the scourges, after the scourges they are exalted and received into rest.

According to Matthew it is said: “It bears fruit and produces, in one case a hundred, in another sixty, and in another thirty” (Matthew 13). The thirtyfold is referred to marriage. The joining of the fingers itself, embracing and binding them together like a gentle kiss, depicts the husband and wife. The sixtyfold refers to widows, because they are placed in hardship and tribulation; for this reason they are pressed down on the upper finger. And the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the allurements of pleasures once experienced, the greater the reward.

The hundredfold number—please, attentive reader, consider this carefully—is transferred from the left hand to the right. It is formed with the same fingers, but not the same hand, by which married women and widows are signified on the left hand; making a circle, it expresses the crown of virginity.

In another interpretation, the thirtieth fruit is produced by the word that builds faith in the Holy Trinity; the sixtieth by the word that teaches perfection of work, because there are six days in which one ought to work (Exodus 23); and the hundredfold by the word that proclaims the eternal life of the kingdom at the right hand.

## HOMILY XXXVI. ON THE FIFTIETH SUNDAY

**[Col. 0347B]**

**Luke 18; Matthew 20; Mark 10.** At that time, Jesus took the Twelve and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be accomplished. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.” But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said.

Now, when he was approaching Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road, begging, and so forth.

The Savior foresaw that his Passion would disturb the minds of the disciples, and long beforehand he foretold both the suffering of that Passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that when they saw him dying as had been foretold, they would not doubt that he would also rise. He also foresaw that certain heretics would arise in the Church who would say that Christ had taught things contrary to the law and the prophets, and that one God should be believed to belong to the Old Testament and another to the New. He therefore showed that the prophecies of the prophets were directed toward no other mystery than that of his own dispensation, which he temporarily assumed for our sake, so that his Passion is the fulfillment of prophecy and his subsequent glory its celebrated consummation.

He also most openly refutes the madness of the pagans, who mock his cross, when, as one who knew future events, he shows the time of his approaching Passion and, as one unafraid of death, goes to the place where he is to die.

And they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said.

In the Gospel according to John we read that, when the Lord said, “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12), the crowd answered and said, “We have heard from the law that the Christ remains forever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’?” Why, then, are the disciples unable to understand the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, so often repeated to them, while the Jews understand a single statement expressed so obscurely that the evangelist considers it worthy of explanation? For he writes, “He said this, signifying by what death he was going to die”; they immediately understand that the lifting up signifies the cross—unless it is because the disciples, who most desired to see his life, could not bear to hear of his death.

They knew him not only as an innocent man but also as the true God, and they thought that he could in no way die. Moreover, because they were accustomed to hearing him speak frequently in parables, whenever he said something about his Passion they believed that it should not be understood according to the sound of the words but, as love dictated, referred allegorically to something else.

The Jews, however, because they had conspired to kill him, understood whatever he said about his Passion or cross. For he was speaking of what they very much desired to happen and were striving to accomplish. Thus, in a marvelous and unprecedented way, the same mystery of the cross that was to be endured was concealed from the faithful by love but disclosed to the unbelieving by envy.

Now, when he was approaching Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road, begging. When he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was. They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by.

This blind man allegorically signifies the human race, which, expelled in its first parent from the joys of paradise and ignorant of the brightness of the heavenly light, suffers the darkness of its condemnation. But when Jesus is said to be approaching Jericho, the blind man is illumined.

Jericho is interpreted as “moon.” In sacred language the moon signifies the deficiency of the flesh, because, as it wanes at monthly intervals, it represents the defect of our mortality. Thus, when our Creator approaches Jericho, the blind man returns to the light: when Divinity assumes the deficiency of our flesh, the human race receives the light it had lost.

This blind man is rightly described as sitting beside the road and as begging. For Truth itself says, “I am the way” (John 14). Therefore, whoever does not know the brightness of eternal light is blind; but if he already believes in the Redeemer, he sits beside the way. If he believes but pretends not to ask for eternal light and ceases from prayer, the blind man indeed sits beside the way, but he does not beg. If he both believes and begs, then the blind man sits beside the way and begs.

And he cried out, saying, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.” Those who went ahead rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me.” What do those who go before Jesus as he comes signify, if not the crowds of carnal desires and the tumult of vices? [Col. 0348D] Before Jesus comes to our heart, they scatter our thoughts with their temptations and disturb the voices of our heart in prayer. Often, when we wish to turn back to God after committing sins, when we try to plead against those very vices that we have committed, the phantasms of the sins we have committed confront the heart, beat against the focus of our mind, confuse the spirit, and suppress the voice of our supplication. But the one whom the crowd rebukes into silence cries out more and more, because the more heavily we are oppressed by the tumult of carnal thoughts, the more fervently we ought to persist in prayer.

But Jesus, standing still, ordered him to be brought to him. Behold, he stands who had previously been passing by, because while we still endure crowds of phantasms in prayer, we sense Jesus as passing by to some extent. But when we persist in prayer with intensity, Jesus stands still and restores the light, because God is fixed in the heart and the lost light is restored.

And when he had drawn near, he asked him, saying: [Col. 0349A] “What do you want me to do for you?” He said, “Lord, that I may see.” Did the one who was able to restore light not know what the blind man wanted? He wished him to ask for what he already knew he would both ask and grant. For he persistently urges us to prayer, and yet says: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matt. VI). He therefore asks in order that the request may be made; he asks in order to stir the heart to prayer. Hence the blind man immediately adds: “Lord, that I may see.” Behold, the blind man seeks from the Lord not gold but light; he considers it of little importance to seek anything outside the light. For although a blind man may possess anything whatsoever, without light he cannot see what he possesses. Let us therefore imitate him whom we have heard was saved both in body and in mind. Let us seek from the Lord not false riches, not earthly gifts, not fleeting honors, but light: that light, namely, which we can see only with the angels, which has no beginning to initiate it and no end to confine it. The way to that light, certainly, is faith. Hence, rightly, after the blind man is immediately illuminated, [Col. 0349B] it is added:

And Jesus said to him: “See; your faith has saved you.” And immediately he saw, and followed him, glorifying God. He sees and follows who does the good that he understands; he sees but does not follow who indeed understands the good but refuses to do good works. For he follows Jesus who imitates him. Hence he says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John XXII). Let us therefore consider by what path he walks, so that we may be worthy to follow; and thus it comes about that not only does our own life advance toward God, but our very way of life also kindles others to the praise of God. Hence it is added there:

And when all the people saw it, they gave praise to God. The people gave praise to God not only for the gift of light they had obtained, but also for the merit of the faith by which it had been obtained. They gave praise to God because they saw that Jesus had mercifully and powerfully restored light to the one who asked, and because they recognized that the cry of steadfast faith, when it seeks rightly, can immediately obtain what it asks. Hence it should be noted that the Lord, appearing [Col. 0349C] in the flesh, confirmed by examples everything he taught in words. For he who commanded us: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V), himself, in all that he began to do and teach (Acts I), sought not his own glory from men but the glory of the Father.

# HOMILY XXXVII. ON ASH WEDNESDAY

**Luke XII, Matthew VI.** A reading from the holy Gospel according to Luke. At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there your heart will also be. Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands,” etc.

This command should not be understood as requiring the saints to keep no money in reserve, whether for their own use or to supply the needs of the poor, since the Lord himself, [Col. 0349D] although angels ministered to him, is nevertheless read to have had a purse for the instruction of his Church, preserving what the faithful offered and distributing it to the needs of his own and to other needy persons. Rather, the command is given so that one may not serve God for the sake of these things, nor abandon righteousness through fear of poverty.

“An unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys.” This may be understood simply to mean that money kept in reserve perishes, either because it is seized from the treasury by a thief or because, through its own fragility, it is spoiled in the treasury; but money given for Christ brings forth in heaven an everlasting fruit of mercy. Or certainly it may be understood in this way: if the treasure of a good work is stored up on account of some earthly advantage, it is easily corrupted and perishes; but if it is amassed solely with a heavenly intention, it cannot be stained outwardly by human favor or inwardly by the corruption of vainglory. The thief robs from outside; the moth tears apart within. The thief took away the riches of those of whom the Lord says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. VI). The moth corrupted the garments of those [Col. 0350A] whom the Psalmist rebukes, saying: “For God scatters the bones of those who please themselves” (Ps. LII). By “bones” he calls the strength of virtues.

“For where your treasure is, there your heart will also be.” This should be understood not only of money but also of all possessions. The god of the gluttonous is their belly. There, therefore, they have their heart where they have their treasure. The treasures of the lustful are feasts; of the wanton, amusements; of the lover, lust. Each person serves the one by whom he is conquered.

# HOMILY XXXVIII. ON THE THURSDAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY

**Luke VII, Matthew VIII.** At that time Jesus entered Capernaum. Now a certain centurion’s servant, etc.

When he had completed all his words in the hearing of the people, [Col. 0350B] Christ entered Capernaum. Here it should be understood that, after he had indeed completed all his words in the hearing of the people, Christ entered Capernaum—that is, he did not enter before he had finished these words—but it is not stated how much time elapsed between the completion of these discourses and his entering Capernaum. During that interval, the leper was cleansed, whom Matthew inserts in its proper place (Matt. VIII), while Luke anticipates him here.

Now a certain centurion’s servant was ill and close to death, and he was precious to him. Someone may ask this question either piously, in order to find an answer, or impiously, in order to criticize: why did the evangelist say that the servant, who was not dead but is subsequently reported to have been healed, was about to die? The brief answer is that he truly was about to die, had he not been restored to life by the faith of his master who pleaded and by the mercy of Christ who had compassion. So also King Hezekiah, according to a certain measure of human nature, was about to die when he heard from the words of the truthful prophet: “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live” (Isa. XXXVIII); yet, by the hidden judgment of divine providence, [Col. 0350C] which has ordered all things “by measure and number and weight” (Wis. XI), he was destined to gain fifteen more years of life through tears and prayers.

And when he had heard about Jesus, he sent to him the elders of the Jews, asking him to come and save his servant. By a dispensation from above it came about that the elders of the Jews were sent to the Lord, and that while they were present the sick man was healed, so that they would be without excuse if they did not believe while a Gentile believed. But it is asked how Luke’s account—that the centurion sent messengers—agrees with Matthew’s, which says that he himself approached the Lord. To those who inquire piously, it is readily apparent that Matthew, for the sake of brevity, said that he himself approached, since his desire and will were truly conveyed to the Lord even though others carried the message. Mystically, he also commends to us what is written: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII). Because the Lord praised the centurion’s faith, by which one truly approaches Jesus, so highly that he said, “I have not found such faith in Israel,” the prudent evangelist [Col. 0350D] preferred to say that he himself had approached Christ rather than those through whom he had sent his words. Luke, however, disclosed the whole sequence of events as it happened, so that from this we might be compelled to understand how the other evangelist said that he had approached, though he could not have lied. Just as the woman who suffered from a flow of blood (Mark V; Matt. IX; Luke VIII), although she touched the fringe of his garment, nevertheless touched the Lord more truly because she believed than did the crowds by whom she was pressed, so also the centurion approached the Lord all the more because he believed all the more.

“For he loves our nation, and he himself built the synagogue for us.” Those who report that the synagogue was built for him by the centurion clearly show that, just as we customarily call the Church both the assembly of the faithful and the place where they assemble, so they too were accustomed to call the synagogue not merely the gathering of the faithful but also the place where they gathered, as we explained above.

And Jesus went with them. Great [Col. 0351A] is the sublimity of the Lord, who was able to heal by a word alone; but no less is his humility, since he deigned to visit a sick servant. For, as one powerful, kind, and entreated to save, he set out; and midway through the journey, when entreated, he saved him by a word, lest anyone suppose that he went bodily because of weakness rather than as an example of humility. Elsewhere he refused to come to heal the ruler’s son, lest he appear to have honored riches (John IV); here, lest he appear to have despised a servile condition, he immediately agreed to go to the centurion’s servant.

And when he was now not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying: “Lord, do not trouble yourself. For I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Because of his conscience as a Gentile, he considered himself more burdened by the Lord’s condescension than helped by it, and he thought himself unable to receive Christ as a guest, since, although endowed with faith, he had not yet been instructed in the sacraments. But because divine grace knows how to give what our weakness does not presume to receive, and because another centurion, who, like this one, [Col. 0351B] prefigures the believing people from the Gentiles, received the gift of the Holy Spirit before he was baptized by the merit of his great faith and righteousness, this man too, although not yet catechized, merited both to have his faith praised by the Lord and to have his servant saved. Of him it is beautifully said allegorically that he had Jesus near his house, although he did not dare invite him under his roof, because “his salvation is near those who fear him” (Ps. LXXXIV). Whoever rightly uses the natural law, doing the good that he knows, thereby draws near to him who is truly good. But to those who have joined crimes to the error of paganism may be applied what the Lord says elsewhere to the crowds flocking to him: “For some of them have come from far away” (Mark VIII).

“For this reason I did not consider myself worthy even to come to you.” We too, who believe from among the Gentiles, cannot ourselves come to the Lord, whom we are now entirely unable to see in the flesh. But all who have recognized the sufferings of our servitude ought already to approach in faith the one seated at the right hand of the Father. [Col. 0351C] We ought already to send the elders of the Jews—that is, the highest men of the Church who went before us to the Lord—and by humbly entreating them to acquire patrons who, bearing witness that we love the Church and, insofar as it lies within us, take care to build it, may intercede with the Lord for our sins and those of our people.

“But say the word, and my servant will be healed.” Great is the centurion’s faith, by which he confesses that the work is accomplished by the word in Christ, and this is suited to the mysteries of our healing: although we knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer in that way.

“For I also am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me.” He says that he is a man subject to the authority of either a tribune or a governor, yet able to command those beneath him, so that it may be understood that he who is much more truly God and powerful over all possesses an innumerable army of angelic powers obedient to his commands.

[Col. 0351D] “And I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” He wishes to show that the Lord too can accomplish what he wills not only by the arrival of his body but also through the ministry of angels. For bodily illnesses and hostile powers, by which human beings are often reduced to weakness, had to be driven away by the word of the Lord and the ministry of angels. Another interpretation: the soldiers and servants who obey the centurion are natural powers, of which many who come to the Lord bring a considerable supply with them. Concerning these it is said in praise of the centurion Cornelius: “For he was a righteous man and feared God with all his household, giving many alms to the people and always praying to God” (Acts X).

When Jesus heard this, he marveled. He marveled because he saw that the centurion understood his majesty. But who had produced that faith or understanding in him except the very one who marveled at it? And if someone else had produced it, why would the one who knew beforehand marvel? It should [Col. 0352A] therefore be noted that when the Lord marvels at something, he signifies that it ought to be marvelous to us, who still need such instruction. For whenever such emotions are attributed to God, they are not signs of a disturbed spirit but of a teacher instructing.

And turning to the crowds that followed him, he said: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith even in Israel.” He is not speaking of all the patriarchs and prophets of former times but of the people of the present age. The centurion’s faith is placed before theirs because they were instructed by the teachings of the Law and the Prophets, whereas this man believed spontaneously, without anyone teaching him.

And those who had been sent returned to the house and found the servant who had been ill in good health. The faith of the Lord is proved, and the servant’s health is confirmed. The merit of a master can therefore benefit servants—not only through the merit of faith but also through the discipline of instruction. Matthew explains this more fully: when the Lord said to the centurion, “Go, and as you have believed, so let it be done for you,” the servant was healed [Col. 0352B] from that hour (Matt. VIII). But it is the custom of blessed Luke to abbreviate what he sees fully explained by the other evangelists, or even deliberately to pass it over; whereas what he finds omitted by them or only briefly touched upon, he more carefully clarifies. Mystically, as I have said, the centurion, whose faith is preferred to that of Israel, plainly represents the elect from the Gentiles. As though surrounded by a hundred soldiers, they are exalted by the perfection of spiritual virtues, and they ask from the Lord nothing earthly but only the joys of eternal salvation for themselves and their own. The number one hundred, which is transferred from the left to the right, is customarily used as a sign of heavenly life. Hence the ark of Noah was built over one hundred years (Gen. VI); Abraham, at the age of one hundred, received the son of promise (Gen. XVII); Isaac sowed and received a hundredfold in that same year (Gen. XXVI); the court of the tabernacle was one hundred cubits long (Exod. XXVII); and in the hundredth psalm mercy and judgment are sung to the Lord (Ps. C), along with other things of this kind. Men of such merit must therefore plead with the Lord for those who are still oppressed by the spirit of servitude [Col. 0352C] in fear, so that, as they are gradually raised to higher things, perfect love may cast out fear (1 John IV).

# HOMILY XXXIX. ON THE FRIDAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY

**Luke VI, Matthew V.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you,” etc.

Because above he had said what they might suffer from their enemies, he now shows how they themselves ought to act toward those same enemies. Many think it sufficient for virtue not to hate one’s enemies, failing to see that one is commanded to love them—something beyond what human nature can endure. Yet Moses, Samuel, and Stephen prayed for their enemies (Exod. XVII; 1 Kings XII; Acts VII), and David mourned for his dead enemies (2 Kings I). For the Lord would not command impossible things, but perfect ones: [Col. 0352D] “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. VI).

“Bless those who curse you; pray for those who slander you.” The Apostle also testifies that he and those like him have done this when he says: “We are cursed, and we bless; we are blasphemed, and we entreat” (1 Cor. IV). But here a question rightly arises: how is this command of the Lord not contradicted by the many imprecations against enemies found in the Prophets, which are considered curses, such as: “Let their table become a snare before them” (Ps. LXVIII), and the other things said there? The Apostle John also says: “If anyone knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life will be given to the one sinning not unto death. There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for that” (1 John V).

First, then, it should be observed that the prophets foretold through imprecation what would happen, not by the desire of one wishing it, but by the Spirit foreseeing it. They especially tend to prophesy future things in the form of one uttering an imprecation, just as they sang of things that were going to happen using the form [Col. 0353A] of the past tense. Second, in the Apostle’s words it should be understood that there are certain brothers for whom we are commanded to pray, since the Lord also commands us to pray for our persecutors (Matt. V; Luke VI). This question cannot be resolved unless we admit that some sins in brothers are more serious than the persecution of enemies.

“Brothers” signifies Christians, as can be proved by many testimonies of the divine Scriptures. I therefore think that the sin unto death occurs when, after acknowledging God, someone attacks the brotherhood through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and is inflamed by the fires of envy against that very grace by which he has been reconciled to God. The sin not unto death occurs when someone has not alienated love from a brother but, through some weakness of spirit, has failed to show the duties owed to the brotherhood.

For this reason the Lord also says on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII; Acts VII). They had not yet become [Col. 0353B] participants in the grace of the Holy Spirit or entered into the fellowship of the holy brotherhood. Blessed Stephen, too, prays for those by whom he is being stoned, because they had not yet believed in Christ and were not fighting against that common grace. The Apostle Paul, I think, therefore does not pray for Alexander (2 Tim. IV), because he was already a brother and had sinned unto death—that is, into envy—by attacking the brotherhood. For those who had not broken off love but had succumbed through fear, he prays that they may be forgiven. Thus he says: “Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works. You also avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words.” Then he adds for whom he prays, saying: “At my first defense no one stood by me, but everyone deserted me; may it not be counted against them.” This distinction between sins separates Judas, who betrayed, from Peter, who denied.

“If someone strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also.” He does not say, “Do not strike the one who strikes you,” although this too is a great commandment; [Col. 0353C] rather, he says, “Prepare yourself to be struck again.” Those especially understand that this pertains to mercy who, when those whom they love greatly—children or other beloved persons—are sick, serve them, or who serve little children or the mentally disturbed, from whom they often suffer much, and, when their health requires it, offer themselves to suffer even more until the weakness of age or illness passes. Since the Lord was instructing physicians of souls in caring for their neighbors, what else could he teach them except to endure with equanimity the weaknesses of those whose salvation they wished to promote? For every wickedness arises from weakness of spirit, since no one is more innocent than the one who is perfect in virtue.

Many know how to offer the other cheek, but do not know how to love the one by whom they are struck. Yet the Lord himself, who certainly first fulfilled the commandments he taught, did not offer his other cheek to the servant of the high priest who struck him; instead he said: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if I have [Col. 0353D] spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” (John XVIII). Nevertheless, his heart was not unprepared not only to be struck on the other cheek for the salvation of all but also to be crucified in his entire body.

“And from the one who takes away your garment, do not withhold your tunic either.” What is said about a garment and a tunic should be done not only in these matters but in everything that we call ours in some temporal right. For if this is commanded concerning necessities, how much more fitting is it to despise superfluities.

“Give to everyone who asks you.” He says, “To everyone who asks,” not “everything that everyone asks,” so that you give what you can give honestly and justly. What if someone asks for money because he is trying to oppress an innocent person? What if, finally, he asks for sexual immorality? But, not to pursue the many possibilities, which are innumerable, what must certainly be given is whatever, insofar as a human being can know or believe, harms neither you nor another person. And when you justly deny someone what he asks, your justice itself must be judged, so that you do not send him away empty-handed. Thus [Col. 0354A] you will give to everyone who asks you, although you will not always give what he asks. Sometimes you will give something better when you correct the one asking for something unjust.

“And from the one who takes away what is yours, do not demand it back.” He is speaking of clothing, a house, land, an animal, and generally all money. Whether this should also be understood of slaves is a major question, for a Christian ought not to possess a slave in the same way as a horse or silver. It may happen that a horse is worth more than a slave, and even more so that something made of gold or silver is worth more. But if that slave is educated or governed by you, his master, more rightly, honestly, and suitably for the worship of God than he could be by the one who wishes to take him away, I do not know whether anyone would dare say that he ought to be despised like a garment. For a human being ought to love another human being as himself, since the Lord of all commands him even to love his enemies.

“And as you wish people to do to you, do likewise [Col. 0354B] to them.” Because “love is patient and kind” (1 Cor. XIII), it not only endures the injuries of an enemy with the greatest fortitude but also most kindly anticipates the favor of a friend. Nature has taught everyone to love in return the one who loves; but only the teaching of Christ has instructed the perfect to compel the one who does not love to love through acts of kindness. When he commanded us first to do to others as we would wish to be done to us (Luke VI; Tob. IV; Matt. VII), he immediately confirmed the same meaning by explaining it more fully, saying:

“And if you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them,” etc. If even sinners, tax collectors, and Gentiles, guided by nature, know how to be kind toward those who love them, how much more should you, he says, whose higher profession requires a correspondingly richer care for virtue, embrace in the broad bosom of love even those who do not love you?

It therefore seems worth asking how it is that, when the Lord testifies that those who love only those who love them, those who do good to them in return, and those who lend to their friends not only do not possess perfect love but [Col. 0354C] are equated with sinners, that disciple who reclined on the Lord’s breast, having completed his Epistle concerning love of God and neighbor, nowhere instructed people to love their enemies but simply said: “If we love one another, God remains in us, and the love of God is perfected in us” (1 John IV).

If this troubles anyone, let him understand that John did not remain silent about love of enemies, but included them also under the name of brothers. He commanded that a brother be loved for the sake of love and that prayers be offered for them, so that they may not always remain enemies but may repent from the snares of the devil and be joined to us in a brotherly bond. Nor should it seem harsh when we say that those who do not yet believe can nevertheless be called brothers because of the hope that they will believe. For the same John is also read to call them children of God: “Jesus,” he says, “was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered” (John XI). As long as they are scattered, they are not yet children of God; but by gathering into one, they already become children.

# HOMILY XL. ON THE SATURDAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY

[Col. 0354D]

**Mark VI, Matthew XIV.** At that time, when evening had come, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and Jesus was alone on the land, etc.

The disciples’ labor in rowing and the contrary wind signify the various labors of the holy Church, which amid the waves of an opposing world and the blasts of unclean spirits strives to reach the rest of its heavenly homeland, as though a secure station on the shore. It is rightly said: “The boat was in the middle of the sea, and he alone was on the land,” because sometimes the Church has been not only afflicted but also defiled by such great pressures from the Gentiles that, if it were possible, the Church’s Redeemer might seem to have abandoned it altogether for a time.

Hence comes that cry of hers, caught amid the waves and storms of changing temptations and seeking the help of his protection with a groaning [Col. 0355A] shout: “Why, Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Why do you despise in times of need, in tribulation?” (Ps. IX). The Psalmist goes on to explain the voice of the enemy pursuing her, adding: “For he said in his heart, ‘God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so as not to see to the end.’” But he does not forget the prayer of the poor, nor does he turn his face away from those who hope in him. Rather, he helps those who struggle with their enemies to conquer and crowns the victors forever.

Hence here too it is plainly said: “He saw them laboring in rowing.” The Lord sees those laboring on the sea, although he himself is on the land. For even if he seems to delay for a time in bringing help to the afflicted, he nevertheless strengthens them through the regard of his mercy, lest they fail amid their tribulations; and at times, by manifest assistance, he also frees them after their adversities have been conquered, as though the masses of the waves had been trampled down and stilled. This too is subsequently indicated when it is said:

[Col. 0355B] “And around the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea.” Military stations and watches are divided into periods of three hours. When he therefore says that the Lord came to them in the fourth watch of the night, he shows that they had been in danger throughout the night and that help was offered at the end of the night.

They labored, then, throughout the whole dark night; but as dawn approached, and the morning star promised the rising of the sun and the day, the Lord came and, walking upon the swelling surface of the sea, subdued it. For when human frailty, burdened with pressures, considers the weakness of its powers, it sees nothing in itself but the darkness of distress and the heat of hostile forces engaged in conflict.
