But when it raises its mind toward the light of heavenly protection and the gifts of eternal recompense, it suddenly sees, as though amid the shadows of night, the rising of the morning star that announces the coming day.

The morning star is said to illuminate the night for three hours—that is, the whole morning watch. The Lord will come, bringing to those who have been delivered the full confidence of his protection after the dangers of temptation have been put to rest. [Col. 0355C] It follows:

“And he intended to pass them by.” But when they saw him walking on the sea, they thought it was a phantom and cried out. For they all saw him and were troubled.

Heretics still think that the Lord was a phantom and did not truly assume flesh from the Virgin. Theodore of Pharan, once a bishop, finally wrote that according to the flesh the Lord did not have bodily weight but walked upon the sea without weight or a body. Against this, the Catholic faith proclaims that he possessed both weight according to the flesh and bodily mass, and that with weight and bodily burden he walked upon the waters without his feet being submerged.

For Dionysius, an outstanding ecclesiastical writer, speaks in this way in his works *On the Divine Names*: “For we do not know how, by a law beyond the natural, he was formed from virginal blood, nor how, with feet not submerged, bearing bodily weight and material burden, he walked upon the fluid and [Col. 0355D] unstable substance.”

But how did the Lord intend to pass them by as though they were strangers, when he had come to free them from the danger of shipwreck? He did so in order that, after being troubled and afraid for a moment but immediately delivered, they might marvel more greatly at the miracle of their rescue and render greater thanks to their rescuer. For in the storms of sufferings inflicted by the faithless because of steadfastness in the faith, such providence is sometimes shown by God.

Often the heavenly mercy has seemed to abandon the faithful placed in tribulation in such a way that Jesus might appear to have wished to pass by the disciples laboring on the sea. Hence also comes that saying in the Psalmist concerning the Church laboring in the contest of martyrdom: “Why have you forgotten me? Why have you rejected me? And why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me? While all my bones are crushed,” etc. (Ps. XLI). But the enemies say, frightening them, “Where is their God?” as though threatening the apostles, exhausted by shipwreck. Their God himself says: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and the rivers [Col. 0356A] will not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not consume you” (Isa. XLIII). Hence here too it is rightly added:

“And immediately he spoke with them and said to them: ‘Take courage; it is I; do not be afraid.’ And he climbed up to them into the boat, and the wind ceased.” The first assistance given to those trembling and in danger is to drive away the fear inflicted upon their hearts; the second is to restrain the fury of the storms by the power of his presence. Nor is it surprising that when the Lord climbed into the boat the wind ceased. For in whatever heart God is present by the grace of his love, all the battles of vices and of the hostile world or of evil spirits are immediately compressed and stilled.

“And they were exceedingly astonished within themselves.” For they had not understood concerning the loaves; indeed, their heart was blinded. In the miracle of the loaves the Lord showed that he was the Creator of all things; by walking upon the waves he taught that he possessed a body free from all the [Col. 0356B] burden of sins; and by calming the winds and stilling the rage of the waves he demonstrated that he ruled the elements. But the disciples, still carnal, did not yet recognize that he was God. They were indeed astonished at the greatness of his powers, but they were not yet able to recognize in him the truth of divine majesty.

And when they had come out of the boat, they immediately recognized him. They ran through that whole region and began to carry on pallets those who were ill, wherever they heard that he was. They recognized him by report, not by his face—or else, because of the greatness of the signs he performed among the people, he was also known by his appearance to very many. And consider how great was the faith of the people of the land of Gennesaret: they were not content with the healing of those present but sent to the other surrounding towns, so that everyone might run to the physician.

And wherever he entered, into villages, country settlements, or cities, they placed the sick in the marketplaces and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. [Col. 0356C] And as many as touched him were saved.

Those who are ill do not touch the body of Jesus, nor his entire garment, but only its outer fringe; and whoever touches it will be healed. Understand the fringe of his garment as the least commandment: whoever transgresses it will be called least in the kingdom of heaven—or understand it as the assumption of flesh, through which we come to the Word of God and afterward enjoy his majesty (Matt. V).

# HOMILY XLI. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

**Luke IV, Matthew IV, Mark I.** At that time Jesus returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, etc.

Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days, and was tempted by the devil. Matthew and Mark indicate that these things happened immediately after the Lord’s baptism. [Col. 0356D] One of them, having described his baptism, immediately added: “Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matt. IV). The other says: “And immediately the Spirit drove him into the wilderness, and he was there forty days and forty nights, and was tempted by Satan” (Mark I).

But lest anyone doubt which spirit they meant when they said that he was led or driven into the wilderness, Luke deliberately first stated that Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan; then he added, “He was led by the Spirit into the wilderness,” so that no one might suppose that the unclean spirit had any power over him, who, full of the Holy Spirit, went wherever he wished and did whatever he wished. For below too, where he is expressly said to have been taken up or set by the devil, it is not the Savior’s weakness but the enemy’s pride that is condemned: the enemy considers the Savior’s will a necessity.

Jesus is therefore not led into the wilderness by the power of an evil spirit, but by the will of his own good spirit he enters the place of battle, certain [Col. 0357A] of victory, in order to overthrow his adversary. Here he likewise demonstrates to us the proper order of Christian conduct: after receiving the remission of sins in baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, we should gird ourselves more tightly against the new snares of our ancient enemy, withdraw from the world in mind, and learn to hunger, like the manna of the wilderness, only for the joys of eternal life.

[Cols. 0357B–0360C] And he ate nothing during those days; and when they were completed, he was hungry.

The forty-day fast has authority both in the earlier books, from the fasts of Moses and Elijah (Exod. XXXIV; 2 Kings XIX), and from the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days, demonstrating that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the Prophets. In the person of Moses, the Law is understood; in the person of Elijah, the prophets. He appeared gloriously among them on the mountain, so that it might become more evident what the Apostle says about him: “Bearing testimony from the Law and the Prophets” (Acts XXVIII).

At what time of year could the observance of Lent have been more appropriately established than adjacent and contiguous to the Lord’s Passion? For it signifies this laborious life, which requires self-restraint so that one may fast from friendship with the world itself. Alternatively, the Lord fasted when he was tempted before his death, while he still required food. But he ate and drank when he was glorified after the resurrection, no longer requiring food. In the former case he displayed our labor in himself; in the latter, his consolation in us, defining both by forty days.

By this number, the forty-day course of this age seems to be signified in those who are called by grace to him who did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. V). For there are ten commandments of the Law, the grace of Christ has already been spread throughout the world, and the world is divided into four parts; ten multiplied by four makes forty. For “the Lord gathered those who were redeemed from the regions, from the east and the west, from the north and from the sea” (Ps. CVI).

Thus, fasting for forty days before the death of his flesh, he seemed to cry out: “Abstain from the desires of this age” (1 Pet. II). Eating and drinking for forty days after the resurrection of his flesh, he seemed to cry out: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII; 1 Cor. IX). Fasting belongs to the tribulation of the contest, for the one who is in the arena abstains from everything; food belongs to the hope of peace, which will not be perfected until our body—whose redemption we await—has put on immortality. We glory in it not by possessing it yet, but are already nourished by hope.

The Apostle shows that we perform both at once when he says: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII)—as though the former belonged to food and the latter to fasting. For while we travel along the way of the Lord, we fast from the vanity of the present age and are refreshed by the promise of the future: here, we do not set our heart upon it; there, we nourish the heart above.

But the Lord’s hunger after the days of fasting had been completed—although nothing of the kind is written concerning Moses or Elijah when they fasted—occurred so that the fearful enemy would not flee from testing him whom he saw proclaimed by so many heavenly signs and also made equal to the most excellent men in abstinence. For God, humble man, became hungry so that the enemy would not recognize exalted man, God.

The devil said to him: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.”

The ancient enemy recognized that the Redeemer of the human race, his conqueror, had come into the world. Hence, through a possessed man, he also said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matt. VIII.) Yet when he first saw him subject to suffering and perceived that his humanity was capable of enduring mortal things, everything he had suspected concerning his divinity was thrown into doubt by the arrogance of his pride. Since he understood nothing except what was proud, when he saw him humble he doubted that he was God. Therefore he turned to the devices of temptation.

But the soul of our Redeemer was not disturbed by the necessity of temptation as we are, who are merely human and are often shaken when temptation breaks upon us. Although our enemy was permitted to take him up onto a high mountain, although he claimed that he would give him the kingdoms of the world, and although he showed him stones as though they could be turned into bread, he nevertheless could not shake the mind of the Mediator between God and human beings by temptation. He graciously consented to undergo all these things externally while his mind, inwardly cleaving to his divinity, remained unshaken. And even when he is said to have groaned in spirit when troubled (John XI), he himself divinely determined the extent to which he would be troubled in his humanity.

And Jesus answered him: “It is written (Deut. VIII): ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.’”

The Lord answered in this way because he had resolved to conquer the devil by humility, not by power. At the same time, we should observe that, unless the Lord had begun to fast, the devil would have had no opportunity to tempt him, according to the saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Eccles. II).

The Savior’s own answer also indicates that the one who was tempted was a human being: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” Therefore, if someone does not feed on the word of God, that person does not live.

Alternatively, while we remain placed in this life, our enemy strives all the more to overcome us the more he sees us rebelling against him. He neglects to strike those whom he feels he possesses by a settled right. Against us he is aroused more violently insofar as he is expelled from our heart as though from the legal possession of his own dwelling.

The Lord represented this in himself under a certain dispensation: he permitted the devil to tempt him only after baptism, so that he might indicate to us a sign of the conduct to come—that his members, after advancing toward God, would then endure more violent attacks of temptation.

And the devil led him away and showed him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in an instant of time.

When God as man is said to have been led by the devil, the mind recoils and human ears are terrified to hear it. Yet we know that these things are not incredible if we consider the other things that occurred in him. Certainly, the devil is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are members of this head. What, then, is surprising if he permitted himself to be led by him onto a mountain, when he even endured being crucified by the members of that head?

It is not therefore unworthy of our Redeemer that he wished to be tempted, since he had come to be killed. It was just that he should conquer our temptations by his own temptations, just as he had come to overcome our death by his death.

The fact that worldly and temporal things are shown “in an instant of time” is appropriate. This does not indicate so much the speed of the vision as the fragility of a power that passes away. In an instant all those things pass away, and often worldly honor has departed before it has arrived. For what can be enduring in the world, when the ages themselves are not enduring?

And he said to him: “I will give you all this power and their glory, because they have been handed over to me, and I give them to whomever I wish. Therefore, if you fall down and worship before me, all these things will be yours.”

Arrogant and proud, he says this boastfully—not because the devil has power in the whole world so that he can give all its kingdoms, since we know that many holy men have been made kings by God. “If,” he says, “falling down, you worship before me.” Therefore, the one who is about to worship the devil first falls down.

And Jesus answered and said to him: “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve’” (Deut. VI, X).

When the devil says to the Savior, “If, falling down, you worship me,” he hears in return that he himself ought rather to worship him as his Lord and God.

Someone may ask how it agrees that the command here is to serve the Lord alone with the Apostle’s statement: “Through charity serve one another” (Gal. V). The origin of the Greek language, from which Scripture was translated, readily resolves this question. In Greek, service is customarily designated in two ways and with different meanings. One term is *latreia* (λατρεία), and another is *douleia* (δουλεία).

“Dulia” means common service—that is, service rendered either to God, to a human being, or to any part of the natural order. From this the servant, *doulos* (δοῦλος), also receives his Greek name. “Latria,” however, is the service owed exclusively to the worship of the divinity and not to be shared with any creature. Hence those who offer idols the vows, prayers, and sacrifices that ought to have been offered to God alone are called idolaters.

We are therefore commanded to serve one another through charity—that is, in Greek, *douleuein* (δουλεύειν); and we are commanded to serve God alone—that is, in Greek, *latreuein* (λατρεύειν). Hence it is said, “You shall serve him alone,” which in Greek is *latreuseis* (λατρεύσεις). Again: “For we are the circumcision, serving the Spirit of God” (Phil. III), which in Greek is *latreuontes* (λατρεύοντες).

And he led him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple.

He whom gluttony or avarice could not overcome is now tempted by vainglory, in the hope that even the boastfulness of his victory might perhaps throw him down.

And he said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here.”

In every temptation the devil seeks to discover whether he is the Son of God; but the Lord so moderates his answer that he leaves him in uncertainty.

“Throw yourself down.” This is the devil’s voice, by which he always desires everyone to fall downward. “Throw yourself,” he says: he can persuade, but he cannot hurl down.

For it is written that he has commanded his angels concerning you, to preserve you, and that “they will lift you up in their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone” (Ps. XC).

We read this in the ninetieth Psalm. Yet there the prophecy concerns not Christ but a holy man. The devil therefore interprets the Scriptures badly. Certainly, if he truly knew that this had been written about the Savior, he ought to have said what follows against himself in the same Psalm: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample upon the lion and the dragon.” He speaks of the angels’ assistance as though addressing someone weak; of his own trampling he remains silent, like a deceiver.

And Jesus answered and said to him: “It has been said: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God’” (Deut. VI).

He breaks the devil’s false arrows from the Scriptures with the true shields of Scripture. It should also be noted that he brought forward the necessary testimonies only from Deuteronomy, in order to display the mysteries of the second Law.

“You shall not tempt,” he says, “the Lord your God.” He was being urged, as though he were a human being, to test by some sign how great he was—that is, how much power he had with God. This is done wrongly when it is done in that way. For sound doctrine requires that, whenever a human being has something to do, he should not tempt the Lord his God.

For even the Savior himself was able to protect his disciples, to whom he then said: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. X; John X). He first provided an example of this. Although he had the power to lay down his life and would not lay it down unless he wished, he nevertheless fled as an infant into Egypt, carried there by his parents (Matt. II). And he went up to the feast not openly but secretly (John VII), although at other times he spoke openly to the Jews while they were angry and listening with a most hostile disposition, yet unable to lay hands on him because his hour had not yet come (ibid.).

Thus, by teaching and reproving openly while preventing the fury of his enemies from having any power over him, he demonstrated God’s power; yet, by fleeing and hiding, he instructed human weakness, so that no one should dare to tempt God when there is something one can do to escape what ought to be avoided.

And when every temptation had been completed, the devil departed from him until a time.

You see that the devil himself is not persistent in his efforts and is accustomed to yield to true virtue. Although he does not cease to envy, he fears to press the attack, because he often shrinks from being defeated. Having heard the name of God, he departed, it says, “until the appointed time.” For afterward he came not to tempt but to fight openly.

Yet often, after the ancient enemy has inflicted upon our mind the contest of temptations, he withdraws from the contest for a time—not to bring an end to the malice he has inflicted, but so that, after making hearts secure through repose, he may suddenly return and break in more easily because he is unexpected.

It should be noted that, after setting forth only three deceits of the tempter, he says that every temptation had been completed, because these three embrace the origins and sources of all vices, as John testifies when he says: “For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life.”

In the Gospel parable, too, only three kinds of reprobate business exclude people from the banquet of eternal life. “The first,” he says, “says: ‘I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it.’ Another says: ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them.’ And another says: ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come’” (Luke XIV).

The desire for a wife, like gluttony, belongs to the desire of the flesh. The purchase of a farm, which is not free from avarice, looks toward the pride of life. The testing of five yoke of oxen—that is, curiosity about bodily things, which is vainglory—belongs to the desire of the eyes. For curiosity prevails especially through the eyes.

By these temptations the Lord is tested, as it were, face to face, because he is stronger. But we, when we too, having received baptism and the grace of the Spirit, approach the wilderness of virtues and undertake the forty-day fast—that is, when we resolve to abstain from worldly allurements throughout the whole period of our life—are attacked either by silent ambushes or sometimes even by the words of our neighbor.

When such a person says flatteringly, “You are a strong man; eat and drink, and remain as you are,” we must see to it that, without our knowing it, he does not offer us the poison of the ancient serpent. We must answer: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Deut. VIII).

But many, after conquering the desire of the flesh, are immediately attacked by avarice and sometimes even overcome by it, to such an extent that they are not afraid to worship the devil in exchange for offered gifts. When many praise their self-restraint, when even persons of higher rank honor them and give them gifts, it happens that the victors over pleasures are conquered by love of money. As their madness increases with time, they not only do not curse or rebuke the rich whom they recognize as filled with the demon through their open crimes; they even worship and admire them with bowed necks.

Hence the Apostle says that avarice is the service of idols (Col. III). If such people also triumph over avarice by the example of the Savior—worshiping the Lord their God and serving him alone for the sake of eternal joys—then the third garment, that of vainglory, will be present. It raises above their own strength those who have conquered the preceding vices, so that, assuming themselves placed as though at the summit of the virtues, they presume that they can no longer fall.

To tempt God with curious eyes is precisely this: for someone to glory in his own merits. Against this, increasing the faith of his disciples, he says: “When you have done everything that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke XVII).

And when elsewhere he commanded that we should not perform our righteousness before human beings, in defining this he added only fasting, almsgiving, and prayer (Matt. VI), opposing three weapons of defense to the enemy’s threefold weapon, so that desire of the flesh might be driven away by fasting, avarice by almsgiving, and boasting in one’s merits by prayers.

[Cols. 0360D–0363B]

## HOMILY XLII. ON THE THIRD DAY OF THE FIRST WEEK OF LENT

**MATTHEW XXI.** At that time, when Jesus had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, etc.

Christ, the Lord and God, author and restorer of the human race, had chosen beforehand with the Father, before the foundation of the world, when and where he would suffer for the salvation of humanity. When the fullness of this time had been completed and the Passion was now imminent, he wished to approach the place of his Passion, where he could be found by those through whom that Passion was to be carried out, lest he be thought to have fled from death. For he did not fear death; rather, by his power he commanded death. Thus the evangelist says:

For when Jesus had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying: “Who is this?”

At the Savior’s entrance the city was stirred, and the multitude of the people marveled, unaware of the power and might of the entering Lord. We read something similar concerning his ascension, when the angels saw him ascending in triumphal procession and carrying his already glorified flesh into heaven. In wonder they said: “Who is this King of glory?”

It should be noted, however, that, as another Evangelist says, six days before Passover the Lord came to Bethany, where he had raised Lazarus; and on the following day, sitting on a donkey while the crowds acclaimed divine praises, he entered Jerusalem. This had long before been mystically prefigured in the paschal lamb.

For it is written in the Law: “On the tenth day of the first month, each person shall take a lamb according to his families and houses, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening” (Exod. XII).

Therefore we should understand that, entering the city of Jerusalem on the tenth day of the first month—that is, five days before Passover—the Lord Jesus fulfilled this prophecy concerning the paschal lamb. While the council of the elders and rulers conspired against him, he awaited the hour when he would offer himself to God the Father as a sacrifice of pleasing fragrance for the salvation of the world.

But the people said: “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth.”

When the proud Jews asked who he was who was entering the city with such glory, the simple crowd confessed what it knew: “This,” it said, “is Jesus the prophet.”

They called him a prophet because they were in error and did not know what they were saying. They did not know to call him God or the Son of God, but their error was full of complete knowledge. For Moses had said concerning him: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall listen to him as to me.” And he himself says of himself: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII).

He must be understood as a prophet in such a way that he is the Lord of the prophets, just as he is King of kings and Lord of lords.

And Jesus entered the temple.

When the Lord entered the city, he first went to the temple, showing the pattern of religious conduct that we ought to follow. When we enter a town, a fortress, or any place where a house of prayer has been consecrated to God, we ought first to hasten there. After commending ourselves to God through devotion to prayer, we should then proceed to the business demanded by the necessities of fragile life.

And he began to drive out those who were selling and buying in it, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.

Among all the miracles that the Lord performed bodily in the world, this is the most outstanding and greatest. For, as blessed Jerome says, it was greater that one unarmed man drove many thousands of armed men from the temple than that he raised Lazarus, dead for four days, from the dead.

The radiance of divinity shone forth in the appearance of his humanity. Therefore, when they saw an extraordinary brightness shining in a human face, they turned their backs to the one striking them and did not dare resist.

And he said to them: “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer.’ But you have made it a den of thieves.”

That house of God had first been built by Solomon, and afterward by Joshua the priest and Zerubbabel—not because God dwells in temples made by human hands, but so that his name might be invoked there; so that there he might hear the prayers of the devout people, receive their vows, and accept their gifts and offerings.

But they had made it a den of thieves, because they sat in the temple for this purpose: either to punish bodily those who did not give gifts, or to kill spiritually those who did give them.

The precept of the Law was that all should assemble three times a year from the various parts of the kingdom of Judah at the most august and holy temple in the world: at Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Booths. The same Law commanded that they should not appear before the Lord empty-handed.

Often, however, those who came from distant regions did not have anything to offer in the Lord’s sacrifice, because they could not bring their livestock with them over the length of the journey. Therefore the priests kept the fattest animals required for sacrificial use and sold them to those who had none. After receiving the money, they accepted the animals back when they were bought again, thus plundering the simple people.

There were also some so poor that they lacked even the expenses and food necessary for the journey; they possessed neither sacrifices nor anything with which to buy them. For this reason the priests established money changers in the temple who would lend them money on this pretext.

But because the Law prohibited interest and they could not openly demand double payment from them, they devised another fraud: they accepted various kinds of gifts as interest, namely raisins and fruits of different kinds. What was not permitted in money, they demanded in goods purchased with money.

They called such men in their own language *collybists*, who gave *collubia*, that is, cheap little gifts, called in Greek *tragemata* (τραγήματα) and in Latin *bellaria*—dainties or sweetmeats.

Seeing such business and fraud being carried on in his Father’s house, as blessed John says, the Lord made a whip of cords and drove an innumerable multitude from the temple.

Let the priests of the Church take heed of this and beware lest they turn the house of God into a den of thieves. A thief is one who pursues profit from the sacred office and seeks an opportunity for business through the practice of holiness. They must therefore fear lest, just as those men were driven from the material temple, so they may be driven from the spiritual temple.

For every day the Lord enters the house of his Father, namely, the holy Church, and drives out those occupied with disgraceful profits. He regards sellers and buyers alike as guilty of one crime. Sellers are those who confer sacred orders for a reward; buyers are those who give money for justice and, having paid a price to their patrons, purchase sin.

It should also be noted that he is said to have overturned “the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.”

What else are the tables of the money changers to be understood as signifying except the altars, which through the avarice of wicked priests become tables of money changers? And what else are the seats of those selling doves to signify except the dignity of teaching in the Church, which, when it too turns toward profit, is brought to nothing?

What else are the doves to signify except the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove over the baptized Lord? And who are those who sell doves except those who bestow the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands for a price?

But the Lord overturns the seats of those selling doves because he destroys the priesthood of such men. For whoever sells the grace of the Holy Spirit, even if he appears to shine before human beings in a pontifical robe, has already been deprived of the priesthood before the eyes of God.

Hence the sacred canons anathematize the Simoniac heresy and command that those who seek payment for spiritual grace bestowed should be deprived of the priesthood.

Morally: just as the temple stands above the other buildings in a city, so does the life of religious people stand above the rest of the faithful. The temple of God is therefore the mind itself of the faithful, as the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you.”

If this faithful mind, having abandoned innocence, produces perverse thoughts to injure its neighbor, it surely becomes a den of thieves. It is no longer called a house of prayer but a hiding place of thieves, for it considers how it may harm its neighbor.

Therefore let there be no commerce in the house of our breast, no dealings of buyers and sellers, lest Jesus enter in anger and punish with the whip of severe judgment the accumulated filth of his dwelling.

And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.

After expelling the unworthy and profaners of the temple, he wonderfully healed the blind and the lame. Through this he gave his adversaries a judgment of his power and confirmed, by such testimony, the voice of the children who praised him and cried, “Hosanna in the highest.”

By his work he showed that they agreed with him in their voices; at the same time, those who saw such great power in Christ might be converted and believe. He gave sight to the blind before their eyes so that they might receive the light of faith; he made the lame walk so that they might cast off the lameness of their minds and begin to have better feet in right action.

When they saw the children crying in the temple, “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” they said:

“Do you hear what these are saying?”

They could not bear that the children should acclaim Christ with divine praises, praises appropriate to God alone. But the Lord so fortified his answer on every side and so carefully framed what he said that it was not exposed to the traps of his slanderers, nor did he reject the praises that were offered to him as though by erring children.

He did not answer what they wanted to hear: “The children speak well; they have a right understanding of me.” Nor did he say: “They are children; you ought to forgive their ignorance.” Instead, he answered: “Yes,” and thus confirmed their voices by the testimony of the Psalmist, saying: “Have you never read: ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?”

For God the Father perfected praise from the mouth of infants and nursing children because, through the simple and innocent, he bore witness to his Son. By this testimony he most clearly confounded his enemies, the Jews, his fiercest persecutors.

Then he left them and went out to Bethany, which is interpreted as “house of obedience.” This first signified that he was about to leave the synagogue and pass over to the house of obedience—that is, to the Church of the Gentiles.

We should also observe that he was so poor that he did not even have a hut, and so flattering to no one that, in so great and populous a city, no one received him. By day he preached in Jerusalem; in the evening he returned to Bethany, where his friend Lazarus lived with his sisters Martha and Mary.

Truly happy and greatly blessed are those who have been worthy to have the Lord as their guest, whose presence dispelled every sadness and provided all that was wholesome and joyful. But those too are supremely happy and most blessed who keep themselves so pure and free from every evil that the Lord deigns to dwell in them and remain with them.

Let us therefore seek this with diligent prayers and holy desires: that he may cleanse from us every vice and everything disgraceful, everything unworthy of his sight, and adorn us with the flowers of virtues, so that our Lord and Redeemer Jesus may deign to make the inner chambers of our heart a dwelling perfectly suited to him. He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Cols. 0363C–0364C]

## HOMILY XLIII. ON THE SAME DAY

**MARK XI; MATTHEW XXI; LUKE XIX; JOHN II.** At that time, when Jesus had entered the temple, he began to drive out those selling and buying in the temple.

What the Lord did figuratively by cursing the unfruitful fig tree, he soon demonstrated more openly by driving the wicked from the temple. The tree had not sinned because, when the Lord was hungry, it had no fruit, since its season had not yet arrived. But the priests had sinned: they conducted worldly business in the house of the Lord and had ceased to bear the fruit of devotion that they ought to have borne and that the Lord hungered for in them.

The Lord dried up the tree by his curse (Matt. XXI; Mark XI), so that people, seeing or hearing these things, might understand all the more clearly that they would be condemned by divine judgment if, without the fruit of works, they merely flattered themselves with the applause of religious speech, as though with the sound and covering of green leaves.

But because they did not understand, he consequently exercised upon them the severity of deserved retribution and drove the business of human affairs from that house in which only divine matters were to be conducted: sacrifices and prayers were to be offered to God, and the word of God was to be read, heard, and sung.

It should indeed be believed that he found in the temple only those things being bought and sold that were necessary for the service of the temple itself, in accordance with what we read elsewhere: when he entered the same temple, he found in it people selling and buying sheep, oxen, and doves (John II). For it must be believed that those who had come from far away purchased all these things from the local inhabitants only so that they could offer them in the house of the Lord.

If, then, the Lord did not want even those things sold in the temple that he wanted offered in the temple, because of the avarice or fraud that is characteristic of merchants, how severely do you think he would punish it if he found some people there occupied with laughter or idle talk, or enslaved to any other vice?

If the Lord does not allow temporal business to be conducted in his house when it could freely be conducted elsewhere, how much more do those things that are nowhere permissible deserve heavenly wrath when they are carried on in buildings consecrated to God?

Since the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove over the Lord, the charisms of the Holy Spirit are rightly signified by doves. Who, then, are those who sell doves in the temple today except those who in the Church receive a price for the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is given from heaven?

A dove is sold when the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is offered for a price. But our Redeemer overturns the seats of those selling doves because he destroys the priesthood of such merchants.

Hence the sacred canons condemn the Simoniac heresy and command that those who seek payment for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood. The seat of those selling doves is overturned because those who sell spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood either before human beings or before the eyes of God.

And he did not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the temple.

He speaks of the vessels that they brought in for the sake of trading. But far be it from us to think that the Lord drove sacred vessels from the temple or forbade them to be brought into the temple, where he offered an exemplary sign of his future judgment. Rather, he removes unclean and profane vessels from the temple and forbids them to be brought in again.

He does this when he not only drives all the reprobate from the Church and casts them out, but also restrains them with an eternal scourge so that they may not enter again to disturb the Church.

In the present life too, this is the true house of the Lord: the purification of the hearts of the faithful. Divine compunction should not only remove the sins that were present; the divine grace that perseveres in them should also help prevent those sins from returning.

And he taught, saying to them: “Is it not written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations’?” (Isa. LVI.)

“For all nations,” he says—not for the Jewish nation alone, nor in one place in the city of Jerusalem, but throughout the whole world; and not for bulls, goats, and rams, but for prayer.

“But you have made it a den of thieves” (Jer. VII).

Those who sat in the temple to receive gifts undoubtedly sought injuries from some who did not give them. The house of prayer had therefore become a den of thieves, because they knew how to stand in the temple for this purpose: either to persecute bodily those who did not give gifts, or to kill spiritually those who did.

The temple and house of God is also the mind and conscience of the faithful. Whenever it produces perverse thoughts to injure its neighbor, they sit there as in a den of thieves. They kill those proceeding simply when they drive their swords into people who are guilty of no offense.

The mind of the faithful is no longer a house of prayer but a den of thieves when, having abandoned innocence and the simplicity of holiness, it tries to do what may enable it to harm its neighbors.

[Col. 0364D]

## HOMILY XLIV. ON THE FOURTH DAY OF THE FIRST WEEK OF LENT

**MATTHEW XII; MARK VIII; LUKE XI.** At that time the Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus, saying: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” He answered them: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, etc.”

It is related above how the Lord had healed the demoniac who was blind and mute by a threefold miracle. But the scribes and Pharisees, who always clung to the Lord for the purpose of either denying his wonderful works or corrupting them by an evil interpretation, began, blaspheming, to say that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. When the Lord had argued at length against them, as the Evangelist now says, certain of the scribes answered, saying: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you” (Luke XI). Thus they demanded signs in the matter of the healing, as though what they had seen had not really happened. They also called him “Teacher” deceitfully, although their manifest wickedness opposed his teaching.

But what signs they requested, and from where, another Evangelist shows more clearly, saying: “We wish to see a sign from heaven” (Mark VIII). He therefore wanted him either, after the manner of Elijah, to command fire to descend from heaven, or even, in the likeness of Samuel, to make thunder roar, lightning flash, and rains pour down in the summertime (IV Kings I; I Samuel XII), as though the things the Lord had done had not come from heaven but were rather the works of Beelzebub. But those who slandered the things they had before their eyes and perceived to have been done without benefit either to themselves or to faith would have slandered those things much more, saying that these events had occurred not by Christ’s power but through various disturbances of the air. Perhaps they would even have said that the magicians had likewise performed many signs from heaven in Egypt (Exodus VII).

There are some who say that they asked the Lord for manna to rain from heaven (Exodus XVI), because, according to another Evangelist, they said: “What sign do you show us? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness” (John VI). But whether they asked for this or for that, they certainly did so with the intention of constructing a slander. Let us see, then, what the Lord answered them.

He answered and said to them: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign.” He very suitably calls the Jewish generation adulterous, because it had abandoned its lawful husband and, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy, had joined itself to many lovers (Ezekiel XVI).

“And,” he says, “a sign will not be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Jonah II). Because they had tested him by asking for a sign from heaven, the Lord answered that he would not give them a sign from heaven, which they were unworthy to receive, but one such as the shipwrecked Jonah received and gave after being swallowed by the whale and then delivered by God’s mercy. They did not deserve to receive a sign of divinity, but of humanity: of suffering, not of glorification. To his disciples, however, the Lord gave a sign from heaven, because he showed them the glory of his eternal divinity, first when he was transfigured on the mountain and afterward when he was lifted up by ascending into heaven.

“For just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.”

From this passage it is perfectly clear that the prophet Jonah bore a type of the Lord and Savior. For Jonah is interpreted as “dove” or “mourning”; and these names certainly suit the Redeemer, upon whom, after he was baptized, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove (Matthew III; Luke III; Mark I). And of him Isaiah says: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our pains” (Isaiah LIII).

Jonah was sent to preach to Nineveh, which is interpreted as “beautiful”; and the Savior was sent for the salvation of the nations, so that, once they had been converted to faith, he might prepare for himself the Church, cleanse it with his precious blood, and make it beautiful from its disgrace. The fish that swallowed Jonah in the sea signifies the death that the Lord endured in the world. Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights; so also Christ lay in the tomb for three days and the same number of nights. And just as Jonah did not remain in the belly of the whale but was cast out onto dry land, so the soul of our Savior was not abandoned in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption (Psalm XV); rather, through the glory of the resurrection, he was brought forth to the dry land of immortality.

By this example he declares, according to the literal sense, that the Jews, just as the Ninevites once had been, were subject to grave sins and, unless they repented, were near to destruction. Yet, just as time for repentance was given to the Ninevites, so it is still given to the Jews; nor should they despair if they wish to repent.

At this point a question of no little importance arises: why is the Lord said to have been in the heart of the earth three days and three nights, when, as the Gospel relates, he was crucified on the Preparation at the sixth hour and, about the ninth hour, bowing his head, gave up his spirit (Matthew XXVII; Luke XXIII; Mark XV; John XIX); rested in the tomb on the Sabbath; and rose from the dead very early on the first day of the Sabbath?

This must be understood synecdochically—*synecdochicōs*, that is, by the part standing for the whole. For if you count part of the Preparation together with the preceding night, during which he was seized, and likewise count the Sabbath together with its night, and then again the Lord’s night together with the same day at whose dawn he rose, you will certainly find a complete period of three days and three nights.

It must also be understood that our death will be twofold, namely, in soul and body. The Lord’s death, however, was single, because he did not admit sin, which is the death of the soul; and so his resurrection was also single. The Lord lay in the tomb for thirty-six hours: one day and two nights. The twelve hours of the day compared with the twenty-four hours of the two nights are onefold in relation to twofold; and the twelve daylight hours correspond to the single death of our Redeemer, while the twenty-four nighttime hours correspond to our twofold death.

Therefore, by a great mystery, he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our twofold death. Coming to us, who were in the death of flesh and spirit, he endured one death of his own—that is, death of the flesh—and released us from our two deaths; he joined his single death to our double one and subdued our double death.

“The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah” (Jonah III). The Ninevites will condemn the Jewish people, not by authority but by the comparison of a reformed life. They repented at Jonah’s preaching; because the Jews did not do so at the Lord’s preaching, they will rightly be condemned by comparison with the Ninevites.

“And behold, something greater than Jonah is here” (Luke XI)—that is, here in your midst; “here” is an adverb of place. Jonah preached for a few days, Christ for three and a half years. Jonah was sent to the Assyrians, who were barbarians and unbelievers; Christ was sent to the Jews, who ought to have been household members and the people of God. The one spoke to foreign nations, the other to his own citizens. Jonah preached only by his voice and displayed no signs. Christ, performing so many miracles everywhere, was not received; instead, he endured the slander that he acted by Beelzebub. Therefore, something greater than Jonah is here.

“The queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon.” The Scripture of the Book of Kings relates how the queen of Sheba, leaving behind both her nation and the dignity of her kingdom, came to Judaea through so many difficulties of travel because she wished to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and how she offered him many gifts but received even more in return (III Kings X; II Chronicles IX).

Therefore she will justly condemn the Jews in the judgment, because she sought from the ends of the earth one whom she knew to be renowned for the singular gift of wisdom. The Jews, however, had the Lord with them, who is the power and wisdom of the Father; yet they not only failed to listen to him but blasphemed him.

“The queen of the South,” he says, “will rise in the judgment with this generation.” From this passage it is evident that there will be one resurrection of the good and the wicked, since the chosen queen is said to rise with the reprobate.

[Col. 0366D] “And behold, something greater than Solomon is here.” That is, he who is incomparably superior to Solomon is now living among you.

Mystically, in the repenting Ninevites and in the chosen queen of the South, the faith of the Church is proclaimed and set above Israel. For holy Church is gathered from two parts: one consisting of those who have not sinned, the other of those who have ceased to sin.

“But when the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it.” This may indeed be understood simply as something the Lord added to show the distinction between his works and Satan’s, since he wishes to cleanse what has been polluted, whereas Satan seeks to contaminate with more serious filth those things that have been cleansed.

Nevertheless, it may also suitably be understood of any heretic or schismatic, or even of a false Catholic. The unclean spirit goes out from a person when, at baptism, the devil departs from a heretic or schismatic through the confession of the Catholic faith and the renunciation of worldly works. He travels through dry and waterless places—that is, around the hearts of the saints, which have been cleansed of the moisture of wandering thought. He seeks rest—that is, he investigates whether he can set the steps of his wickedness anywhere within them.

But he does not find it, because he cannot have a place in chaste and pure minds; he finds pleasant rest only in the hearts of the wicked. Hence the Lord also says to Job concerning the devil, under the figure of Leviathan: “Under the shade he sleeps in the secret place of the reed, in moist places” (Job IV), because he rests in dark and hypocritical consciences and delights in wanton and luxurious minds.

“Then he says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’” That is: “I will seek out the heretic whom I abandoned at baptism.” This little verse is greatly to be feared, lest perhaps the sin that we thought had been forgiven us should, through our negligence while we remain empty of good works, overwhelm us more grievously.

“And coming, he finds it swept with brooms and adorned”—or, according to another Evangelist, “swept with brooms, empty, and adorned.” For when the evil spirit comes to the house—that is, to such a person’s mind—he finds it swept with brooms, namely, washed from original sins by the grace of baptism; empty of good works; and adorned with pretended virtues.

“Then he goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering in, they dwell there.” The number seven is commonly taken in sacred discourse to signify universality, because the whole time of the world revolves through seven days. Through the seven other spirits more wicked than himself, therefore, the totality of all vices is signified.

Thus seven more wicked spirits enter because, whoever is seized after receiving the forgiveness of sins in baptism by heretical depravity or worldly desire, is made a servant of all vices. They are rightly called “more wicked spirits,” because although such a person is full of the seven capital vices, he nevertheless pretends to possess the virtues themselves.

“And the final state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Col. 0367C), because “it would have been better for them not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (II Peter II).

“So will it also be with this most wicked generation.” By these words it is plainly shown that this comparison especially concerns the Jews. “What,” he says, “I have narrated as customarily happening individually does not cease to happen generally in the Jewish generation.”

The unclean spirit went out from the Jews when, on Mount Sinai, receiving the law, they said: “Everything that the Lord our God has commanded, we will do, and we will be obedient” (Exodus XIX). He traveled through dry places, seeking rest, because, having been expelled by the Jews, he traveled through the solitudes of the nations, which were parched by the heat of vices and did not possess the richness of the Holy Spirit—a richness with which the Psalmist desired to be filled when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Psalm LXII).

When those nations later believed in the Lord, and he did not find a place in them, he said:

“I will return to my house from which I came.” That is: “I will possess the Jews whom I had previously abandoned.” And coming, he found it swept clean through circumcision, empty—that is, deserted by heavenly help—and without Christ as its guest, who says: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew XXIII); adorned with superstitious traditions and the hypocrisy of the Pharisees.

The devil returns to them because they were such; and, after the sevenfold fullness of all demons has been added, he inhabits his former house.

“And the final state of that person becomes worse than the first.” For the Jews who now daily blaspheme Christ in their synagogues are much worse than they once were when they worshiped idols in Egypt. It is indeed more serious not to receive him who has come than not to believe that he will come.

While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. While the Lord was occupied in the duty of preaching, his mother and brothers stood outside, seeking to speak with him; and someone announced this to him:

“Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, wishing to speak with you.” We should not think that this person simply reported it to the Lord, but that he deceitfully wished to test whether the Lord would place the affection of his relatives before the divine work. Therefore he very wisely pretends not to know his mother, in order to show that he recognizes and loves those who are near by kinship of spirit more than those who are near by kinship of flesh. Hence it follows:

“But he answered the one who told him and said: ‘Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?’” Yet the Lord did not reject the duty of filial affection, since through the law he commanded: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus XX). Rather, he places the service owed to God the Father before maternal affection. Hence elsewhere he says: “Whoever loves father and mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew X).

Nor does he despise his brothers; he teaches that the work of preaching must be preferred to kinship according to the flesh. Let no one be disturbed when he hears of “brothers,” because in the Gospel the Lord’s brothers are called his cousins—namely, the sons of his maternal aunt Mary, who is said to have been the mother of James the younger, Joseph, and Judas; these are called the Lord’s brothers in another Gospel (Mark VI).

Mystically, however, the Lord’s mother is understood as the synagogue according to the flesh, from which he was born; his brothers are the Jewish people. With the Savior inside, therefore, his mother and brothers stand outside, because, while the Jews were unwilling to believe in Christ and neglected to enter through faith into the one who had been sent for their salvation, the crowd of the nations entered first and now enjoys the Lord’s words and teaching.

Meanwhile they stand outside, lingering around an earthly understanding of the law and the observance of the letter; and, insofar as it depends on them, they force Christ to go outside to teach earthly things rather than entering themselves to learn spiritual ones.

“And stretching out his hands toward his disciples, he said: ‘Behold my mother and my brothers.’” He calls the apostles his mother and brothers because they fulfill the will of the Father, believing that he was sent by God the Father and attending to him with the readiest spirit.

He did not deny the mother from whom he had assumed flesh, as the Marcionites and Manichaeans rave, saying that he did not possess a true body but a phantom one. Rather, he preferred spiritual kinship to bodily consanguinity, in order also to teach us that, in God’s cause, we should recognize no one according to affection of the flesh. Hence he continues:

“Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”

It is not surprising that the Lord calls the one who does the will of his Father “brother” and “sister,” because of the two sexes that are gathered into faith. It is, however, most surprising and worthy of inquiry how such a person can also be called the Lord’s mother.

For after the resurrection he deigned to call his disciples brothers, saying: “Go, announce to my brothers” (Matthew XXVIII). Therefore, how someone becomes a brother by believing in him and fulfilling the Father’s will, and how he can also become a mother, must be investigated.

But it must be understood that just as someone becomes the Lord’s brother by believing in him, so he becomes his mother by preaching. For a person becomes, as it were, Christ’s mother when, through that person’s preaching, love for the Lord is generated in the mind of a neighbor.

Great is this condescension, immeasurable the goodness, indescribable the mercy: that you, who were not worthy to be called a servant, should be called the Lord’s brother. Since we cannot adequately comprehend this dignity, let us at least strive to venerate it worthily, and let us labor with every effort not to become degenerate through any foulness of vice and thereby be judged unworthy of so great a name.

Let us defend by our conduct what we are called by name, lest, failing to understand the honor of divine sonship, we be compared with senseless beasts and become like them (Psalm XLVIII). And that we may deserve to obtain what we speak, let us always ask that his help be present with us—he who, although he was the only Son of God, for our sake deigned to be the Son of Man, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLV. ON THE SATURDAY OF THE FIRST WEEK OF LENT

[Col. 0369A]

**MARK IX; MATTHEW XVII; LUKE IX.** At that time Jesus took Peter, James, and John and led them up a high mountain by themselves, alone, and he was transfigured before them, etc.

In Luke’s Gospel it is written as follows: “Now it came to pass about eight days after these words, that he took Peter, James, and John and went up onto the mountain to pray,” etc.

On the eighth day the Lord reveals to his disciples the promised glory of future blessedness, so that, by displaying the sweetness of heavenly life, he may refresh the hearts of all who are able to hear these things, and teach, by the number eight, that the true joy of the resurrection is to come at the appointed time.

For he himself also rose from the dead on the eighth day—that is, after the sixth day of the Sabbath, on which he ascended the cross, and the seventh day of the Sabbath, on which he rested in the tomb. And we, after the six ages of this world, during which we rejoice to suffer and labor for the Lord, and after the seventh Sabbath of souls, which is spent meanwhile in the other life, will certainly rise in the eighth age.

The fact that Matthew and Mark say that the Lord was transfigured after six days (Matthew XVII; Mark IX) does not conflict either in chronological order or in the reasoning of the mystery with Luke, who speaks of eight days. They mention only the intervening days, and therefore simply say that it happened after six days. Luke adds the first day, on which the Lord made this promise, and the last, on which he fulfilled his promise; for this reason he more cautiously says “about eight days.”

In the mystical interpretation, that passage indicates that after the six ages of the world the saints are to rest from all labor, while this one indicates, by the eighth time, that they are to rise. Hence the sixth Psalm is beautifully entitled “for the eighth,” beginning: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” For during the six ages in which it is permitted to work, we must devote ourselves to prayers, lest in the eighth time, the time of recompense, we be rebuked by the angry Judge.

The Lord himself also wished to teach us this in this passage by displaying the example of his prayer. According to Luke, it is said of him: “He went up onto the mountain to pray” (Luke IX).

He went up onto the mountain to pray and be transfigured in order to show that those who await the fruit of the resurrection and desire to see the King in his beauty (Isaiah XXXIII) must dwell in the heights of the mind and devote themselves to continual prayers.

He takes only three disciples with him, either because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew XX), or because those who now preserve with incorrupt mind the faith with which they have been instructed in the Holy Trinity will then deserve to rejoice in its eternal vision.

“And he was transfigured,” he says, “before them, and his garments became shining, exceedingly white like snow.” The transfigured Savior did not lose the substance of his true flesh but displayed the glory of the resurrection, whether future, his own, or ours. As he then appeared to the apostles, so he will appear after the judgment to all the elect.

For at the very time of judgment he will be seen by both the good and the wicked in the form of a servant, so that the impious may recognize the one they despised, the Jews the one they denied, the soldiers the one they crucified, and Pilate and Herod the one they judged, as Judge.

The Lord’s garments are rightly understood as his saints, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians III). These garments, while the Lord remained on earth, seemed despised and like those of others; but when he ascends the mountain they shine with a new brightness, because “we are now children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, however, that when he appears, we shall be like him. For we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

Hence it is suitably added concerning these same garments: “Such as no fuller on earth can make white.” For the fuller to be understood here is the one whom the penitent Psalmist beseeches: “Wash me more thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm L). He cannot give his faithful on earth the brightness that is preserved for them in heaven.

[Col. 0370A] “And Elijah appeared to them with Moses, and they were speaking with Jesus.” Moses and Elijah—one of whom we read was dead (Deuteronomy XXXIV), while the other was taken up into heaven (IV Kings II)—were seen in majesty with the Lord, signifying, as Luke writes, the future glory of all the saints in him. At the time of judgment, some will be found alive in the flesh, while others will be raised after having long ago tasted death, and together they will reign with him.

For the Apostle testifies: “The dead who are in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the air to meet the Lord, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thessalonians IV).

Alternatively, Moses and Elijah—that is, the lawgiver and the foremost of the prophets—appear and speak with the Lord who is coming in the flesh, to show that he is the one whom all the utterances of the law and the prophets promised.

They appear not in low places but on the mountain with him, because only those who transcend earthly desires in mind perceive the majesty of Holy Scripture, which has been fulfilled in the Lord.

Thus the children of Israel saw Moses, but were not worthy to follow him as he climbed into the mountains toward God; and when he returned to them, they saw him only with a veil (Exodus XXXIV). They knew Elijah, but Elisha alone, with the sons of the prophets, contemplated his triumph as he ascended (IV Kings II). Many of us read the words of Scripture here and there, but very few of the more perfect understand how lofty it shines in the mysteries of Christ.

“And Peter answered and said: ‘Rabbi, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tents, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.’ For he did not know what he was saying, since they were terrified by fear.”

O what great happiness would it be to be perpetually present amid the choirs of angels at the vision of the Deity, if merely the transfigured humanity of Christ and the company of two saints, seen for an instant, gave such delight that Peter wished to keep them from departing even by offering service.

Although, because of the astonishment of human frailty, he does not know what he is saying, he nevertheless reveals the affection implanted within him. He did not know what he was saying because he had forgotten that the Lord promised the kingdom of God to the saints not somewhere on earth but in heaven. Nor did he remember that he and his fellow apostles, still enclosed in mortal flesh, could not enter into the state of immortal life; in his mind he had forgotten that in the Father’s house, which is in heaven, a house made by human hands is unnecessary.

Even to this day, however, anyone is marked by ignorance who wishes to make three tents for the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels, although these cannot in any way be separated from one another, since they have one tent—that is, the Church of God.

“And a cloud came, overshadowing them.” He who sought a material tent received the shade of a cloud, so that he might learn that in the resurrection the saints are to be protected not by the covering of houses but by the glory of the Holy Spirit. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “The children of men will hope in the protection of your wings” (Psalm XXVI). And John says in his Apocalypse: “And I saw no temple in it. The Lord God almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Revelation XXI).

[Col. 0370D] “And a voice came from the cloud, saying: ‘This is my most beloved Son; listen to him.’” Because they had asked foolishly, they did not deserve a response from the Lord; but the Father answers on behalf of the Son, so that the Lord’s word might be fulfilled: “I do not bear witness concerning myself, but the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John VIII).

A voice from heaven is also heard—the voice of the Father speaking—to bear testimony concerning the Son and, once Peter’s error has been removed, to teach him the truth; indeed, through Peter, to teach the other apostles as well.

“This,” he says, “is my most beloved Son. For him the tent must be fixed; he must be obeyed. He is the Son; Moses and Elijah are servants. They too, together with you, ought to prepare a tent for the Lord in the innermost chambers of their hearts.”

This passage of the Gospel truly agrees with the words of Moses himself. Bearing witness to the Lord’s incarnation, he said: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him according to everything that he speaks to you. But every soul that does not listen to that prophet will be destroyed from among the people” (Deuteronomy XVIII; Acts III).

The one whom Moses foretold must be heard by every soul that wishes to be saved when he should come in the flesh—God the Father now shows to the disciples as the one who has come in the flesh and designates him as his Son by a heavenly voice.

And, as though introducing more clearly to them the faith of his coming, he says: “This man—this is the one whom this Moses repeatedly promised would be born into the world for you. According to Moses’ own command, listen to his words, and command all true lovers of truth to listen.”

It should also be noted that, just as when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan (Matthew III; Mark I), so when he was glorified on the mountain, the mystery of the whole Holy Trinity is revealed. For the glory of the Trinity, which we confess in faith at baptism, we will praise when we see it in the resurrection.

Nor is it without reason that the Holy Spirit appeared here in a luminous cloud, as another Evangelist recalls (Luke III), and there in a dove. For whoever now preserves with a simple heart the faith he has received will then contemplate in the clear light of vision what he believed, and will be protected forever by the very grace with which he is illumined.

“And immediately, looking around, they saw no one any longer except Jesus alone with them.” When the Son began to be designated, the servants immediately departed, lest the Father’s voice be thought to have been sent to them.

Alternatively: when the voice came concerning the Son, he was found alone, because when he reveals himself to the elect, “God will be all in all” (I Corinthians XV). Indeed, he himself, together with his own, will be one Christ in every respect: the head will shine together with the body. Because of this unity he said elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III).

“And as they were descending from the mountain, he commanded them not to tell anyone what they had seen, except when the Son of Man had risen from the dead.” The foretaste of the future kingdom and the glory of the triumphant one had been displayed on the mountain. He therefore did not wish this to be preached among the people, lest it be incredible because of the greatness of the event and lest, after so great a glory, the cross that followed should cause scandal in inexperienced minds.

## HOMILY XLVI. ON THE TUESDAY AFTER THE SUNDAY *REMINISCERE*

[Col. 0371D]

**LUKE XX; MATTHEW XXIII; MARK XII.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Beware of the scribes, who wish to walk in long robes, love greetings in the marketplace, the first seats in the synagogues, and the first places at banquets,” etc.

“To walk in long robes” signifies going out in public dressed in splendid garments. Among other things, that rich man who feasted splendidly every day is described as having sinned in this way.

It should be noted, however, that the Lord does not forbid those to whom such duties properly belong from being greeted in the marketplace or from sitting or reclining in the first places. Rather, he teaches the faithful to beware as reprobates of those who improperly love such things, whether they possess them or do not possess them, rebuking with just severity the disposition, not the rank.

Yet this too is not free from blame: that those who desire to be called teachers of the Synagogue from Moses’ chair should take part in those same lawsuits in the marketplace. For two reasons, certainly, we are commanded to beware of those who desire empty glory: lest we be led astray either by their pretence, thinking the things they do are good, or inflamed by rivalry, rejoicing in vain to be praised for the good things they pretend to do.

“Who devour widows’ houses while making a show of lengthy prayer; these will receive the greater condemnation.” He says not merely that they will receive condemnation but adds “greater,” thereby indicating that even those who pray standing in the corners so as to be seen by people (Matthew VI) deserve condemnation; but those who do such things at greater length, as though they were more religious, seeking not only human praise but also money, are to be punished with a more extensive condemnation.

For there are some who pretend to be righteous and to possess great merit before God and do not hesitate to accept money from any weak people troubled by the consciousness of their sins, as though they were to be their patrons in judgment. And while a hand extended in alms customarily assists the prayers of the poor, these men spend nights in prayer chiefly in order to take money from the poor.

To them that curse of Judas suitably applies: “When he is judged, let him go out condemned, and let his prayer become sin” (Psalm CVIII). He goes out condemned when he is judged, and he receives his prayer as sin who, now held in great esteem among human beings, then discovers in the divine examination that he is unable not only to intervene for others but even to have his own merits suffice for him. Indeed, he pays the penalties among the charges against him for the very prayers by which he deceived human judgment.

## HOMILY XLVII. ON THE FRIDAY AFTER THE LORD’S DAY

[Col. 0372B]

**LUKE XX.** At that time Jesus began to speak this parable to the people: “A man planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and himself went abroad for a long time,” etc.

While the Lord was teaching the people and preaching the Gospel, the chief priests and scribes, together with the elders, assembled and questioned him, testing by what authority he performed signs. Having overcome them by their own art, the Lord continued what he had begun. For, even while they were listening, he addressed the people—who heard his words more willingly—introducing a parable by which he both accused them of impiety and taught that the kingdom of God was to be transferred to the nations.

The man who planted the vineyard is therefore the one who, according to another parable, hired laborers for his vineyard (Matthew XX). For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isaiah V); the tenants are the same as the laborers who are said to have been hired to cultivate the vineyard at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours.

He himself went abroad, not by a change of place—for how could God be absent from anywhere, when he says: “I will fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah XXIII)? And elsewhere: “I am God who draws near, and not one who is far away,” says the Lord. But he is said to depart from the vineyard in order to leave the vinedressers free discretion to work.

The same idea appears when, through Isaiah, he says of the vineyard leased to tenants: “I waited for it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes” (Isaiah V).

“And at the proper time he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they might give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But they beat him and sent him away empty.”

He rightly says “the time of fruits,” not “of produce.” For no fruit came forth from the Jews; no produce of this vineyard was found, although it was sought frequently and earnestly.

The servant who was sent first is therefore understood as Moses, the lawgiver. For forty continuous years he sought from the tenants some fruit of the law that he had given, but they beat him and sent him away empty.

“They provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. Moses was troubled because of them, because they embittered his spirit” (Psalm CV).

He himself also openly declares in song what he thinks of the fruit of the vineyard, saying: “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall; their cluster is bitterness to them. The wine of dragons is their fury, and the venom of asps is incurable” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

“And he added another servant to send. But they also beat this one and treated him with insult, and sent him away empty.”

The other servant signifies David, the prophet and king, who was sent after Moses so that, after the legal decrees, he might rouse the tenants of the vineyard to the practice of good works through the melody of psalmody and the sweetness of the harp.

David himself, in order to lift the people’s heart toward heavenly things, established that the praises of the Lord should be sung continually with sweet melody in place of the slaughter of bodily victims.

But they also treated this man with insult and sent him away empty. For saying, “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (II Samuel XX), they exchanged both David’s kingdom for an ignoble lineage and religion for impiety.

Nevertheless, on behalf of this vineyard—which, transplanted from Egypt, covered the mountains of Palestine with its shade—he pleaded that it not be uprooted entirely: “Lord God of hosts, turn now; look from heaven, see, and visit this vineyard, and direct it, the vineyard that your right hand planted” (Psalm LXXIX).

There he also explains who the man is who planted this vineyard: namely, the Lord, the God of hosts.

And he added a third servant to send, and they wounded him too and threw him out. By the third servant understand the company of the prophets, who summoned the people through continual testimonies and foretold the evils that threatened this vineyard. But which prophet did they not persecute? “And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Just One” (Acts 7). These prophets also said much about the barrenness of this vineyard, but it is sufficient to cite the lament of one—Jeremiah: “I planted you as a choice vine, wholly a true seed. How then have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. 2). For the protection of this vineyard, lest—whether within it or on its behalf—a fragile, weak, and quickly perishing plant of sweetness should grow, we read that Naboth the Jezreelite was not merely wounded but also killed (3 Kings 21). Although we find no prophetic saying of his, nevertheless his prophetic deed prophesied in his own blood the many martyrs who were to come for this vineyard.
