These three ranks of servants can indeed be understood as encompassing the figure of all teachers under the Law, as the Lord plainly reveals elsewhere when he says: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke 24).

But the lord of the vineyard said, “What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps, when they see him, they will be ashamed.” The fact that the lord of the vineyard is said to speak doubtfully, and not in a deliberative manner, does not arise from ignorance. For what could the lord of the vineyard not know, since here he is understood to be God the Father? Rather, God is always said to doubt so that human freedom of will may be preserved.

When the tenants saw him, they considered among themselves, saying, “This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.” The Lord most clearly proves that the leaders of the Jews crucified the Son of God not through ignorance but through envy. For they understood that he was the one to whom it had been said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2). Therefore, as though consulting their own interests, they said: “Look, the whole world has gone after him; and if we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him” (John 12:19, 11). The Son’s inheritance, therefore, is the Church, given to him from all the nations. The Father did not leave it to him as an inheritance when dying; rather, he himself wondrously acquired it by his death, because by rising again he took possession of it. After killing him, the wicked tenants attempted to seize it, when the Jews, by crucifying him, tried to extinguish the faith that exists through him, to prefer their own righteousness, which is from the Law, and to implant it in the nations whom they sought to instruct.

And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. The heir of the vineyard is slaughtered outside the vineyard because Jesus suffered outside the gate “in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Heb. 13). Or he was thrown out of the vineyard and killed because he was first rejected by the hearts of unbelievers and then condemned to the cross. As a figure of this, Moses placed the altar of burnt offering, on which the blood of the victims was poured out, not inside the tabernacle but at its entrance (Exod. 40), mystically teaching that the altar of the Lord’s cross was likewise to be placed outside the gate of Jerusalem. Christ himself, the true sacrifice of the Father, was not to be received in the innermost heart by the house of the Jews, which he had approached in order to sanctify it; rather, outside it he was to be stained with his own blood.

But when Mark says, with the order changed, “They seized him, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard” (Mark 12), he indicates their obstinacy: even after the Lord had been crucified and raised from the dead, they refused to believe the apostles who preached him, but cast him away as though he were a worthless corpse. For, so far as lay in their power, they excluded him from their own borders and handed him over to be received by the nations.

What, then, will the lord of the vineyard do to them? “He will come and destroy these tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said to him, “God forbid!” They contradicted the Lord’s judgment because they recognized that it had been spoken against their own faithlessness. They understood the parable—not because they were already prepared by holiness to grasp its mysteries, but because they were inflamed by the fires of malice to do what was being described—and therefore, although the matters had been expressed in parables, they were ready to recognize them as things they had long meditated upon. Since the Jews denied that it would be right for the knowledge of the divine Law, which they themselves despised, to be transferred to the nations, observe what the Savior replies.

But he looked at them and said: “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?” (Ps. 117). How, he says, will this prophecy be fulfilled—which says that the stone rejected by the builders is to be placed as the cornerstone—unless Christ, rejected and killed by you, is to be preached to the nations who will believe? Thus, as the cornerstone, joining two peoples in himself, he may build from both peoples one city of the faithful and one temple for himself.

He calls the same teachers of the Synagogue whom he previously called tenants “builders,” because those who had been commanded to cultivate the people subject to them, as though it were a vineyard, so that it might bear the fruits of life, were themselves also commanded to construct and adorn them as a house worthy of God its inhabitant. Hence the Apostle, writing to the faithful, says: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. 3). But those who, as wicked farmers, denied the fruit of God’s vineyard also attempted, as wicked builders, to remove from the hearers of the Lord God the precious and chosen stone that was to be placed in the foundation at the corner—that is, to take away from their hearers the faith of Christ. Yet despite their unwillingness, that same stone made the head of the corner firm, because in his faith he joined together as many as he wished from both peoples.

“Everyone who falls upon that stone will be shattered; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.” It is one thing to offend Christ through evil works and another to deny him through impiety. Whoever is a sinner yet believes in him falls upon the stone and is shattered, but is not utterly crushed, for through wisdom he is preserved for salvation. But upon whomever it falls—that is, upon one into whom the stone itself rushes, who utterly denies Christ—it will fall and crush him, so that not even a potsherd will remain with which to draw a little water (Isa. 30).

Or he is speaking of those who fall upon him because they now despise him or subject him to insults. They therefore do not yet perish utterly, but are shattered so that they do not walk uprightly. But upon those over whom he falls, he will come from above in judgment with the punishment of destruction. Therefore he said, “It will crush them,” so that the impious may be like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth (Ps. 1).

At that hour the chief priests and scribes sought to lay hands on him, and they feared the people. For they understood that he had spoken this parable against them. The chief priests and scribes sought to kill the Lord as though he were lying against them, but in seeking to kill him they were proving that what he taught was true. For he is the heir whose unjust death he said would be avenged. Those wicked tenants were restrained from killing the Son of God for a short time by human fear, until his hour should come, but they could never be restrained by divine love.

In its moral sense, this is also entrusted to each of the faithful: when the mystery of baptism, to be put into practice through works, is committed to someone, it is as though a vineyard to cultivate is leased to him. One servant, then another and a third, are sent to receive fruit when the Law, psalmody, and prophecy are read, whose admonition he follows by doing good. But the servant who has been sent is driven out after being insulted or beaten when the word that has been heard is either despised or, worse, even blasphemed. The one who, so far as lies in him, tramples upon the Son of God and insults the Spirit of grace by whom he was sanctified also kills the heir who was sent. When the wicked cultivator has been destroyed, the vineyard is given to another, when the gift of grace that the proud despised is bestowed upon the humble.

This too—that the chief priests and scribes, seeking to lay hands on Jesus, are held back by fear of the people—happens daily in the Church. Whenever someone who is a brother only in name is ashamed or afraid to attack the unity of ecclesiastical faith and peace, which he does not love, because of the multitude of the good brothers living with him, the same thing takes place. Yet, as the Lord says of the most foolish of birds, the ostrich: “When the time comes, she will lift her wings high” (Job 39), so he will one day rejoice in persecuting the Church, as though he could hand the Lord over to the cross and make him a spectacle.

## HOMILY XLVIII. ON THE SATURDAY AFTER THE LORD’S DAY “REMEMBER”

### LUKE 15

At that time Jesus said this parable to his disciples: “A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the portion of the property that falls to me.’ And he divided the property between them,” and so forth.

When the scribes and Pharisees murmured because sinners were being received, the Savior set forth three parables in succession. In the first two, which have already been discussed, he indicated how much he and the angels rejoice over the salvation of the repentant; in the third, which follows, he not only demonstrates his own joy and that of his people but also reproves the murmuring of those who are envious.

The man who is said to have had two sons is understood to be God the Father, the father of two peoples and, as it were, the author and creator of two stocks of the human race. The elder son signifies those who remained in the worship of the one God; the younger signifies those who abandoned God in order to worship idols.

The portion of the property that falls to the younger son is the rational sense in the human being. To live, understand, remember, and excel with a lively intelligence is a substance of divine generosity. The younger son sought this from his father when, delighting in his own power, he wished to govern himself by free choice and to strip the Lord, his Creator, of what belonged to him. He divided the property between them by imparting to the faithful the protection of his grace, which they desired, but granting to unbelievers only the benefit of their natural intelligence, with which they were content.

And not many days later, after gathering everything together, the younger son departed into a distant country and there squandered his property by living luxuriously. He went far away, not by changing his location but by changing his mind. For the more anyone sins through evil works, the farther he withdraws from God’s grace. He says that this happened “not many days later,” when, after everything had been gathered, he departed into a distant country, because not long after the creation of the human race the soul chose, through free will, to carry with it a certain power, as it were, of its own nature and to abandon the one by whom it had been created, relying upon its own strength. It consumes those powers all the more quickly the more it abandons the one from whom they were given.

Thus he calls this a prodigal life, loving to pour itself out and to roam amid outward displays while becoming inwardly empty, since a person follows whatever proceeds from that life and abandons the one who is interior to him.

And after he had squandered everything, a severe famine arose in that country. Everything that he squandered signifies the adornments of nature that he consumed; the famine in the distant country signifies the lack of the words of truth through forgetfulness of the Creator. Of this it is said in the Prophets: “The Lord will send a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8).

And he began to be in need. So he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country. He rightly began to be in need, having abandoned the treasures of God’s wisdom and the height of heavenly riches. The one citizen of that country to whom he attached himself in his need is certainly the one who, through the perversity of his own desire, has been set over earthly lusts and is called by the Lord “the prince of this world” (John 14). Of him the Apostle says: “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (2 Cor. 4).

And he sent him into his estate to feed pigs. To be sent into an estate means to be subjected to desire for worldly possessions. In another parable, someone who disdained the spiritual banquets to which he had been invited said: “I have bought an estate, and I must go out and see it” (Luke 14). To feed pigs means to perform the things in which unclean spirits rejoice.

And he desired to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs were eating. The pods with which he fed the pigs are secular teachings that resound with barren sweetness. The praises of idols and stories about the gods of the nations are loudly proclaimed in them through varied language and song, and demons delight in them. When this man wished to be filled, he wanted to find in such things something solid and upright pertaining to the blessed life, but he could not. For this is what he says:

And no one gave him any. But when he came to himself—that is, when he turned his attention inward, into the interior of his conscience, away from the things outside that entice and deceive in vain—

he said: “How many hired servants of my father have an abundance of bread, while I am perishing here from hunger!” How could he know this, when he was in such forgetfulness of God as all idolaters were, unless this reflection belongs to one already recovering his senses, when the Gospel was being preached? The hired servants of his father therefore have an abundance of bread because those who strive to perform worthy deeds in view of the future reward are daily refreshed by the nourishment of heavenly grace.

But those perish from hunger who, placed outside the father’s house, desire to fill their belly with pods—that is, those who live without faith and seek the blessed life through the studies of empty philosophy. Just as bread, which strengthens the human heart (Ps. 103), is likened to the word of God, by which the mind is refreshed, so the pod—which is empty within, soft outside, and does not refresh the body but fills it, making it more a burden than a benefit—is rightly compared with secular wisdom, whose speech resounds with the applause of eloquence but is empty of useful power.

“I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.” How merciful and kindly a father he knew him to be, since, although offended by his son, the father did not disdain to hear himself called “father.” “I will arise,” he says, because I have recognized that I am lying down; “and I will go,” because I have gone far away, to my father, because under the prince of pigs I am wasting away in pitiable poverty. “I have sinned against heaven” signifies before the angelic spirits and holy souls in whom God’s dwelling is; “and before you” signifies in the innermost chamber of the conscience, into which the eyes of God alone could penetrate.

“And I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.” He does not presume at all to aspire to the affection of a son who does not doubt that everything belonging to the father is his; instead, he now desires the condition of a hired servant, prepared to serve for wages. Yet he testifies that even this he cannot merit except through his father’s favor. Where, then, are the Pelagians, who trust that they can be saved by their own virtue, against the clearest judgment of the truth, which says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15)?

And he arose and came to his father. To come to the father means to be established in the Church through faith, where the sinner can now make a lawful and fruitful confession.

[Col. 0376D] But while he was still far away—that is, before he understood God, although he was already seeking him piously—

his father saw him. The impious and proud are appropriately said not to be seen, as though they were not before the eyes. For only those who are loved are ordinarily said to be held before one’s eyes.

And he was moved with compassion, and he ran and fell upon his neck. The Father did not abandon the only-begotten Son, in whom he ran and descended even to our distant pilgrimage, because “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). The Lord himself also says: “The Father who dwells in me does his works” (John 14). What, then, does it mean to fall upon his neck except to bend down and humble his arm in an embrace? “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53)—namely, to our Lord Jesus Christ.

And he kissed him. To be consoled by the word of God’s grace in the hope of forgiveness of sins: this is to deserve the Father’s kiss of charity after returning from a long journey.

And the son said to him: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” Once established in the Church, he begins to confess his sins. He does not say everything that he had promised to say, but stops at: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” For he wants this to be accomplished through grace, which he confesses he is unworthy to receive through merits. He does not add what he had said in his earlier meditation: “Make me like one of your hired servants.” When he had no bread, he had wished even to be a hired servant; but after the father’s kiss, he now nobly disdains this. For he understands that there is no small difference between a son, a hired servant, and a slave.

A slave is one who, still through fear of Gehenna or of present laws, restrains himself from vices. A hired servant is one who, through hope and desire for the kingdom of heaven, strives to perform good deeds. A son is one who does so through affection for goodness itself and love of the virtues. In the consummation of these three virtues, the blessed Apostle sums up the whole of salvation when he says: “Now faith, hope, and charity remain—these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13).

Faith causes us to avoid the contagion of vices through fear of the future judgment and punishments. Hope, withdrawing our mind from present things, makes us despise all bodily pleasures in expectation of heavenly rewards. Charity, advancing within us through ardent love for the death of Christ and the fruit of spiritual virtues, makes us detest with complete hatred whatever is opposed to them.

Therefore, after this prodigal had come to himself and feared the punishments of dreadful hunger, he desired the condition of a hired servant, already thinking of wages, as though he had become a slave. But his father, running to meet him and not content to grant him lesser things, passed through both ranks without delay and restored him to his former dignity as a son. He no longer made him think of the wages of a hirer but of the inheritance of a parent.

[Col. 0377C] But the father said to his servants: “Quickly bring out the first robe and put it on him.” The first robe is the garment of innocence, which the well-created human being received but lost after being deceived, when, after the sin of transgression, he realized that he was naked and, having lost the glory of immortality, took on a leathern garment—that is, mortality. The servants who bring it out are the preachers of reconciliation. They bring out the first robe when they assert that mortal and earthly human beings are to be exalted so that they will become not only citizens of the angels but also heirs of God and coheirs with Christ (Rom. 8).

“And put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet.” The ring is either the seal of sincere faith, by which all promises are marked with a sure impression in the hearts of believers, or the pledge of those nuptials by which the Church is betrothed. The ring is rightly placed on the hand, so that faith may shine through works and works may be strengthened through faith.

The shoes on the feet signify the duty of evangelizing, so that the course of the mind, directed toward heavenly things, may be kept undefiled and clean from thoughts of earthly matters, and, strengthened by the examples of those who went before, may walk securely over serpents and scorpions. Thus the hands and feet—that is, the work and the course—are adorned: the work, so that we may live rightly; the course, so that we may hasten toward eternal joys. “For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. 13).

“And bring the fattened calf, and kill it.” The fattened calf is likewise the Lord himself, but according to the flesh. He is rightly called fattened because his flesh is so rich in spiritual virtue that it suffices for the salvation of the whole world, sending up to God a sweet odor—namely, the fragrance of sacrifice—and interceding for all. To bring the calf and kill it means to preach Christ and make known his death. For he is, as it were, freshly killed for each of us when we believe that he was killed; his flesh is eaten when the sacrament of his passion is received by the mouth for cleansing and contemplated in the heart for imitation.

“And let us eat and celebrate, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” Not only the son, who came to life and was found, but also the father and his servants feast, nourished by the flesh of the sacred calf that was killed for the son. For the Father’s food is our salvation, and the Father’s joy is the remission of our sins. This is true not only of the Father but also of the Son and the Holy Spirit: just as there is one will and one operation in the Godhead, so there is one delight of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Hence we read that blessed Abraham, receiving three angels as guests (Gen. 18), killed a tender and excellent calf and offered it to them to eat together with milk, bread, and butter. Whoever desires to refresh—that is, to gladden—the blessed Trinity through the services of right devotion must also celebrate the death of the only-begotten Son of God in the flesh, who is one person within that same Trinity, with the sincerity of a devout confession.

It should be noted that the first robe is provided first, then the ring, then the shoes, and only afterward is the calf sacrificed. For unless someone first puts on the hope of primordial immortality, unless he fortifies his works with the ring of faith, and unless he proclaims that faith by confessing it devoutly, he cannot participate in the heavenly sacraments.

And they began to feast. This banquet and celebration are now held throughout the world, as the Church has been extended and spread abroad. For that calf is both offered to the Father in the Lord’s body and blood and feeds the entire household.

His elder son was in the field. The elder son is the people of Israel. Although he did not go into a distant country, he is nevertheless said to have remained not at home but in the field, because this people neither abandoned the Creator so far as to worship idols nor penetrated into the interior meaning of the Law that it had received. Content merely with guarding the letter, it was accustomed both to perform and to hope for outward and earthly things, hearing through the prophet: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. 1).

And when he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. The son draws near to the house when that people, in whatever Israelites have understanding—for many such people existed and often still exist among them—rejecting the labor of servile works, considers from those same Scriptures the freedom of the Church. He hears music and dancing: namely, Spirit-filled voices preaching the Gospel in harmonious utterance. To them it was said: “I appeal to you, brothers, that you all say the same thing” (1 Cor. 1), with the soul and heart of those who live together united in praise of God.

And he called one of the servants and asked what these things were. And he told him. He calls one of the servants when he takes up one of the Prophets to read, and, seeking in it, asks in a certain way from where these celebrations are held in the Church, in which he does not see himself participating. The servant of the Father, the Prophet, answers him:

“Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe.” Your brother was at the ends of the earth, but for that reason there is greater rejoicing among those singing a new song to the Lord, because “his praise is from the ends of the earth” (Isa. 42). And for the sake of the one who was absent, the one to whom it was said, “May your burnt offering be made fat” (Ps. 19), has been killed.

But he became angry and was unwilling to enter. Therefore his father went out and began to plead with him. Even now he is angry and still unwilling to enter. When the fullness of the nations has entered, his father will go out at the appointed time so that all Israel also may be saved, since blindness has come upon part of it. This is like its absence in the field, until the fullness of the younger son—who had been established far away in the idolatry of the nations—returns and enters to eat the calf (Rom. 11). At some point there will be an open calling of the Jews into the salvation of the Gospel; he calls the manifestation of this calling the father’s going out to plead with the elder son.

But he answered and said to his father: “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your command.” The question arises how that people can be said never to have transgressed God’s command. The answer readily presents itself: he is not speaking of every commandment, but chiefly of the one most necessary commandment, by which they were ordered to worship no other God. Nor is this son understood to represent all Israelites, but those among them who never turned from the one God to idols.

Although, like someone situated in the field, this son desired earthly things, he desired these goods from the one God. This is also confirmed by his father’s own testimony when he says: “You are always with me.” He does not rebuke him as a liar; rather, by approving his perseverance with him, he invites him to enjoy a better and more delightful rejoicing.

“And you have never given me a young goat, so that I might feast with my friends.” A sinner is indeed usually signified by the name of a young goat, but let me not understand the Antichrist here. For it is entirely absurd to suppose that the one to whom it is said, “You are always with me,” wished this from the Father: that he should believe in the Antichrist. Nor is it permissible to understand this son as those Jews who will believe in the Antichrist. How could he feast upon that young goat if it were the Antichrist, since he would not believe in him? Or if feasting upon the slaughter of the young goat means rejoicing at the destruction of the Antichrist, how can the son whom the father receives say that this was not granted to him, when all the sons of God will rejoice at the condemnation of that adversary?

Clearly, then, he complains that the Lord himself has been denied to him for feasting, because he considers him a sinner. For when he is a young goat to that people—that is, when they regard him as a violator of the Sabbath and a profaner of the Law—he does not deserve to rejoice at his banquet. Thus, when he says, “You have never given me a young goat, so that I might feast with my friends,” the meaning is as though he were saying: “You have never given me for feasting the one who appeared to me as a young goat; by that very fact you did not grant him to me, because he appeared to me as a young goat.”

When he says, “with my friends,” this may be understood either as the leaders speaking with the people or as the people of Jerusalem speaking with the other peoples of Judea.

But after this son of yours, who has devoured his property with prostitutes, came, you killed the fattened calf for him. The prostitutes are the superstitions of the nations. To squander one’s property with them means, after abandoning the one marriage of the word of God, to commit fornication with the crowd of demons in the most shameful lust.

But he said to him: “Son, you are always with me, and everything that is mine is yours. But it was necessary to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”

When he says, “Everything that is mine is yours,” this should not be understood as though those things did not also belong to the brother, as if you were to suffer want in an earthly inheritance. How could everything belong to the elder son if the younger also has his share there? Everything belongs to the perfect, purified, and already immortal sons in such a way that each thing belongs to all and everything belongs to each. For just as desire possesses nothing without distress, so charity possesses nothing with distress.

When, therefore, we have attained that blessedness, the things above will be ours for living, equal things will be ours for sharing, and lower things will be ours for ruling.

If anyone is troubled by how Truth, praying to the Father, can say, “Everything that is mine is yours, and yours is mine” (John 17), which seems to sound much like what is said to this son—“Everything that is mine is yours”—let him know that everything belonging to the Father belongs to the only-begotten Son because he too is God and, born from the Father, is equal to the Father.

For when speaking of the Holy Spirit he also says: “Everything that the Father has is mine. Therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16). He was speaking of those things that belong to the Father’s own divinity, in all of which he is equal to the Father, since everything that the Father has belongs to him as well. For the Holy Spirit was not to receive from the creature subject to the Father and the Son what he says, “He will take from what is mine,” but certainly from the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds and from whom the Son was born.

Whether, then, you wish to refer these two sons to the two peoples, or—as some prefer—to any two human beings, namely, the penitent and the just, or one who seems just to himself, let the elder brother rejoice with him, because his younger brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.

## HOMILY XLIX. FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY OF LENT

**LUKE 11; MATTHEW 9; MARK 3.** At that time Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute, etc.

According to Matthew, this demoniac is related to have been not only mute but also blind, and he is said to have been healed by the Lord so that he both spoke and saw (Matthew 9). Thus three signs were accomplished at once in one man: the blind man sees, the mute man speaks, and the man possessed by a demon is set free. This was indeed done physically at that time, but it is also fulfilled daily in the conversion of believers: first the demon is expelled, then they behold the light of faith [Col. 0380B], and afterward their mouths, previously silent, are opened to the praises of God.

But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.” These words were uttered in slander not by some of the crowd, but by the Pharisees and scribes, as the other evangelists testify. For the crowds, who appeared less learned, always marveled at the Lord’s deeds. Those men, by contrast, labored either to deny the deeds or to pervert by a sinister interpretation what they could not deny, as though these were the works not of divinity but of an unclean spirit, namely Beelzebub, who is the god of Accaron (4 Kings 1). *Beel* itself is indeed Baal, while *zebub* is called “fly.” Nor, according to certain corrupt copies, should the letter *l* or *d* be read at the end of the name, but *b*. Beelzebub, therefore, is interpreted as “Baal of flies,” that is, “man of flies,” or “one who has flies,” evidently because of the filth of sacrificial blood. From the most foul rite or name of that god they called him the prince of demons.

And others, testing him, sought a sign from heaven. [Col. 0380C] They either wished fire to come from above in the manner of Elijah (ibid.), or, in the likeness of Samuel, for thunder to roar, lightning to flash, and rains to pour down in summertime (1 Kings 12), as though they could not slander those signs too and say that they had occurred through hidden and varying disturbances of the air. But you who slander what you see with your eyes, grasp with your hand, and perceive by its benefit—what would you do with those things that came from heaven? Surely you would answer that the magicians in Egypt also performed many signs from heaven (Exodus 7).

But when he saw their thoughts, he said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house.” He answered not their spoken words but their thoughts, so that even in this way they might be compelled to believe in the power of him who saw the secrets of the heart. Now if every kingdom divided against itself is desolated, then the kingdom of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is not divided. Without any contradiction, it is not destined to be desolated by any assault, but will remain in eternal stability. And if the kingdom of the holy and undivided Trinity remains undivided [Col. 0380D]—indeed, because it remains undivided—let the Arians cease to say that the Son is less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than the Son, because those whose kingdom is one also have one majesty.

“But if Satan too is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand, since you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub?” By saying this he wished it to be understood from their own confession that, by refusing to believe in him, they had chosen to be in the devil’s kingdom, which certainly could not stand if divided against itself. Let the Pharisees, therefore, choose whichever they wish: if Satan cannot cast out Satan, they could find nothing to say against the Lord; but if he can, they should all the more look to themselves and withdraw from his kingdom, which cannot stand divided against itself. And lest they suppose that the Lord Christ casts out demons through the prince of demons, let them attend to what follows and see through whom he casts them out:

“But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they themselves will be your judges.” [Col. 0381A] He said this, certainly, about his disciples, the sons of that people. The disciples of the Lord Jesus Christ were surely well aware that they had learned no evil arts from their good teacher by which they might cast out demons through the prince of demons. “Therefore,” he says, “they themselves will be your judges.” They themselves, he says—the ignoble and contemptible things of this world, in whom appears no contrived malice but the holy simplicity of my power—they themselves, my witnesses, will be your judges.

In another interpretation, by “sons of the Jews” he means the customary exorcists of that nation, who cast out demons by invocation. He confines them with a shrewd question so that they must confess this to be the work of the Holy Spirit. “But if,” he says, “the expulsion of demons by your sons is attributed to God and not to demons, why should the same work in me not have the same cause? Therefore they themselves will be your judges, not by authority but by comparison, while they assign the expulsion of demons to God, but you to Beelzebub, the prince of demons.”

*Source-boundary note: the supplied source ends here, in the middle of the continuing exposition.*
Moreover, if I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come [Col. 0381B] upon you. This is the finger which even the magicians acknowledge, they who performed signs against Moses and Aaron, saying, “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII), by which also the stone tablets were written on Mount Sinai (Deut. IX). Therefore the hand and arm of God is the Son, and his finger is the Holy Spirit; the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. Let not the inequality of the members scandalize you, since the unity of the body is being built up. Alternatively, the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God because of the distribution of gifts, by which particular gifts are given to each, whether to human beings or to angels. For in none of our members is division more apparent than in the fingers. But when he said, “The kingdom of God has come upon you,” he now calls the kingdom of God that by which the impious are condemned and separated from the faithful who are presently doing penance for their sins.

When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, what he possesses is at peace. He calls the devil “the strong man,” and his courtyard the world, which is placed in wickedness, [Col. 0381C] over which he possessed a badly pacified dominion until the Savior’s coming, because he rested without any opposition in the hearts of unbelievers. Hence elsewhere also he is called “the ruler of this world,” when the Lord says: “For the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV). And again: “Now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John XII). Concerning this expulsion also it is added here:

But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his armor in which he trusted, and distribute his spoils. He is plainly speaking about himself: not by a deceitful operation working in agreement with the devil, as they slanderously alleged, but as the victor by stronger power he would free human beings from the demon. The armor in which that supposedly strong one wickedly trusted consists of the malice of spiritual cunning and deceit; his spoils are the very people whom he deceived. Christ the victor distributes these, which is the distinction of one who triumphs, because, “leading captivity captive,” he gave gifts to human beings, appointing some as apostles, others as evangelists, these as prophets, and those as pastors and teachers (Ps. LXVII; Eph. IV).

[Col. 0381D] Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. Let no one suppose that this was said about heretics and schismatics, although it can also be understood in that way secondarily; rather, from what follows and from the wording of the discourse, it refers to the devil, and to the fact that the Savior’s works cannot be compared with the works of Beelzebub. The devil desires to hold human souls captive; the Lord desires to free them. The one preaches idols; the other, knowledge of the one God. The one drags people toward vices; the other recalls them to virtue. How, then, can those whose works are divided have harmony with one another?

When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through waterless places. Although it may be understood simply that the Lord added these words to distinguish his works from Satan’s—that he always cleanses what is polluted, whereas Satan hastens to defile what has been cleansed with more grievous filth—nevertheless, it can also suitably be understood of any heretic, or schismatic, or even wicked Catholic. At the [Col. 0382A] time of baptism, the unclean spirit that had previously dwelt in such a person is expelled when he professes the Catholic faith and renounces worldly conduct; afterward, it traverses waterless places—that is, it searches out the hearts of the faithful, which have been cleansed of the softness of fluid thought—to see whether, as the crafty ambusher, it might perhaps be able to plant there some foothold of its wickedness. But it is rightly said:

Seeking rest and finding none. For, fleeing chaste minds, the devil can find rest pleasing to him only in the heart of the wicked. Hence the Lord says of him: “Under the shade he sleeps in the secret place of the reed and in damp places” (Job IV). By “shade,” he signifies dark consciences; by “reed,” which is bright on the outside but hollow within, hypocrites; and by “damp places,” lascivious and soft-minded persons, into whom he insinuates himself.

He says: I will return to my house from which I came out. This verse is to be feared, not explained, lest the fault that we believed extinguished in us should, through [Col. 0382B] our negligence, overpower us while calling us back.

And when he comes, he finds it swept clean. That is, chastened by baptismal grace from the stain of sins, but not enriched by any labor of good works. Hence Matthew rightly says that he found this house empty, swept clean, and adorned (Matt. IX): cleansed from former vices through baptism; empty of good deeds through negligence; adorned with pretended virtues through hypocrisy.

Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there. By the seven evil spirits he signifies all vices. Whoever is seized after baptism either by heretical depravity or by worldly desire will immediately be thrown down into the depths of all vices. Hence those spirits are rightly called more wicked when they enter him, because he will possess not only the seven vices that are opposed to the seven spiritual virtues, but will also pretend through hypocrisy to possess the virtues themselves.

And the final condition of that person is worse than the first. [Col. 0382C] For it would have been better for him not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back (II Pet. II). We read that this was specifically fulfilled in Judas the betrayer (Matt. XXVI), Simon Magus (Acts VIII), and others of the same kind. But that this parable has a general application, the Savior himself explained according to Matthew, immediately adding after its conclusion: “So also will it be with this most wicked generation” (Matt. IX). That is, what I have narrated as customarily occurring in a particular individual will not cease to occur generally in the whole nation of this people.

For the unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the Law, and it walked through dry places seeking rest for itself: that is, having been expelled from the Jews, it wandered through the deserts of the nations. When these afterward believed in the Lord, not finding a place among the nations, it said: “I will return to my former house, from which I came out; I will take the Jews whom I had previously abandoned.” And when it came, it found it empty and swept clean. The temple of the Jews was empty, for it did not have Christ as its guest, who said: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII). Because, therefore, they did not have the protection of God and the angels, and were adorned with the superfluous observances of the Pharisees, the devil returned to them; adding to himself a sevenfold number of demons, he dwelt in the former house, and the latter condition of that people became worse than the former. For they are now possessed by a far greater number of demons, blaspheming Christ Jesus in their synagogues, than they had been possessed in Egypt before knowing the Law, because it is one thing not to believe in someone who is to come, and another not to receive one who has come. Understand the number seven added to the devil either with reference to the Sabbath or with reference to the number of the Holy Spirit, so that, just as in Isaiah seven spirits of virtues are said to have descended upon the rod from the root of Jesse and upon the flower that rises from the root (Isa. XI), so conversely the number of vices may be consecrated in the devil.

## HOMILY L. FOR THE SECOND FERIA AFTER THE SUNDAY OCULI

[Col. 0383A]

LUKE IV, MATTHEW XI, MARK VI, JOHN VI. At that time the Pharisees said to Jesus: “How many things we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in your native place,” and so forth.

The evangelist relates above that when the Lord had come to Nazareth and had performed the office of reader in the synagogue, and all had listened to him with attentive and earnest concentration, and everyone marveled at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth, the Pharisees and scribes began, out of envy, to say: “Is this not Joseph’s son?” What blindness of the Nazarenes: they recognize the one whom they know to be Christ in his words and deeds, yet despise him merely because they know his family. Nevertheless, their error is our salvation and the condemnation of heretics. For they perceived Jesus Christ so much according to his humanity that they called him the son of Joseph and, according to the other evangelists, the son of a carpenter or a carpenter himself. Among these matters, we must consider why Christ, appearing in the flesh, wished to be called the son of a carpenter—indeed, a carpenter himself. We must understand soundly that by this also he taught that he was, before the ages, the Son of the one who, as the maker of all things, created heaven and earth in the beginning (Gen. I). For although human things are not to be compared with divine things, the type is nevertheless complete, because the Father of Christ works with fire and spirit.

Hence his forerunner, speaking of him as the son of a carpenter, says: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke III). In the great house of this world he fashions vessels of different kinds; indeed, by softening the vessels of wrath with the fire of the Spirit, he transforms them into vessels of mercy (Rom. IX). Therefore Malachi, when he said in the person of the Father, “Behold, I will send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face. And immediately the ruler whom you seek will come to his holy temple” (Mal. III), added shortly afterward: “And he will sit refining and cleansing silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and like silver” (ibid.). But the Jews, ignorant of this mystery, [Col. 0383C] despise the works of divine power by contemplating carnal descent, as appears not only from what precedes in their case but also from the Lord’s words that follow:

And he said to them: Surely you will say to me this proverb: “Physician, heal yourself. How many things we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in your native place.” Their insane unbelief, though unknowingly, confesses a sound faith when it calls the Lord Christ a carpenter and a physician. For he is truly a carpenter, because all things were made through him (John I); and he is a physician, because all things in heaven and on earth have been restored through him (Eph. I). As he himself testifies: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke V).

And because we have said what instrument he uses for making, let us also say what kind of means he uses for healing. Passing by, he saw a man blind from birth; he spat on the ground and made clay from the spittle, spread it upon his eyes, and said to him: “Go, wash in [Col. 0383D] the pool of Siloam” (Matt. IX; John IX), which is interpreted as “sent.” He therefore went and washed, and came back seeing. Recognize, then, the method of the great medicine and rejoice, because through it you have been found worthy to be enlightened. The clay from the earth is Christ’s flesh; the spittle from his mouth is his divinity, because God is the head of Christ. The spittle mixed with clay enlightens us when we are baptized in the pool of Siloam, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory” (John I), which previously, because of the darkness that kept us away, we could not comprehend. Through Christ the carpenter you were created so that you might exist; through Christ the physician you were recreated so that, after your wounds, you might be healthy.

Although his fellow citizens mockingly urge him to heal himself—that is, to perform miracles in his native place—he is nevertheless not without reason excused by another evangelist (Mark VI), who says that he could not perform any miracle there, except that he healed a few sick people by laying his hands upon them. And he marveled because of their unbelief, lest perhaps anyone should think that affection for his native place ought to be less dear to us. He loved his fellow citizens, then, but they deprived themselves of his charity through envy.

[Col. 0384A] But he said: Amen, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his native place. The Scriptures call the Lord Christ a prophet, as Moses also does when he says: “God your Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers like me” (Deut. XVIII). Not only he, who is the head and Lord of the prophets, but also Elijah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets were held in lower esteem in their native places than in foreign cities. For it is almost natural that fellow citizens should always envy fellow citizens. They do not consider the present works of a man, but remember his fragile infancy, as though they themselves had not also passed through the same stages of life to reach maturity.

In truth I say to you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut up for three years and six months, when a great famine occurred throughout the whole land; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at [Col. 0384B] Sarepta of Sidon (III Kings XVII). He says: It is not contrary to the deeds of the prophets that I withdraw divine benefits from disdainful fellow citizens. For just as, when famine once pressed upon the whole land, no one in Judea was found worthy to offer Elijah hospitality, but a widow from a foreign nation was sought out, who on account of her faith deserved to be visited by so great a prophet; and just as, when there were many lepers there, only Naaman the Syrian, because he had sought healing devoutly, was found worthy to be cleansed by the prophet Elisha, so you too will be deprived of the heavenly gift for no other reason than envy and unbelief.

If you examine the deeds of the prophets in an allegorical sense as well, you will certainly find that the Lord marked the pride of the Jews’ unbelief in his native place, by which he was not received. By the name Capernaum, however, which is interpreted as “field of consolation,” he proclaimed the salvation of the nations, where greater signs are performed daily through the apostles and their successors, not so much in the healing of bodies as in the healing of souls.

Thus the widow to whom [Col. 0384C] Elijah was sent signifies the Church of the nations. Abandoned for a long time by her Creator, she nourished a people ignorant of the true faith, like a poor woman feeding a needy child with scant alms; that is, she taught the word of the fruit in part. Then prophetic speech arrived, which, while Israel’s fleece was dried up—as though the gate of heaven were closed—and it was suffering from famine in Judea, was nourished there and nourished others, both received by believers and itself refreshing believers.

Hence this same widow is rightly said to have lived at Sarepta of Sidon. For Sidon is interpreted as “useless hunting,” while Sarepta means “burning” or “narrowness of bread,” because “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V). Where care was spent on hunting, as it were, for acquiring superfluous things; where the burning of dreadful thirst and the former narrowness of spiritual bread prevailed; there, through the prophetic mouth, flour and oil are blessed—that is, the fruitfulness and gladness of charity, or the grace of the Lord’s body and the anointing of spiritual gifts, are made fertile through the unfailing gift of the heavenly word.

In her vessels, the oil of spiritual joy and the [Col. 0384D] flour of blessing and the flour of blessing have not ceased until now, while the other nations that do not believe suffer from a lack of divine bread and are devoted to useless hunting. And she herself most beautifully testifies that, before she dies, she wishes first to make a mystical bread for herself and says that she will gather two pieces of wood. By mentioning not merely wood but also the number of the pieces of wood, she expresses the sign of the cross, by which the bread of eternal life has been prepared for us.

And there were many lepers in Israel under the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian (IV Kings V). Since the historical account is well known, it is necessary to indicate briefly its mystery. This Naaman the Syrian, whose name is interpreted as “beauty,” signifies the people of the nations, once stained by the leprosy of unbelief and crimes, but cleansed through the sacrament of baptism from every foulness of mind and body. Instructed by the counsel of the captive girl—that is, by the grace of heavenly inspiration, which the nations seized because the Jews were unable to preserve it—he is encouraged to hope for salvation and commanded to wash seven times. For plainly only that kind of baptism which regenerates through the Holy Spirit saves.

Hence his flesh is recorded [Col. 0385A] to have appeared after the washing like the flesh of a little child, either because the grace of the mother gives all who are baptized in Christ one common infancy, or, more properly, because that child is to be understood of whom it is said: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us” (Isa. IX), to whose body the whole offspring of believers is united through baptism.

And so that you might know that all the sacraments of baptism were foreshadowed here—the renunciation of Satan and the profession of faith being commanded—Naaman denies that he will henceforth sacrifice to foreign gods and rejoices to serve the Lord alone in all things. He is also glad to take with him a portion of the holy earth, because those who have been baptized ought also to be strengthened by participation in the Lord’s body.

Naaman is therefore rightly preferred to the Jews, since, while water washes his body, faith washes his heart: that is, the people of the nations are preferred to the Jews, who are filthy with the leprosy of obstinacy. Likewise, the widow of Sarepta—that is, the Church, desiring to be refreshed by the wood of the cross—is restored, while the Jews perish from famine of the word, by the bread of the most holy body and the anointing of the life-giving Spirit.

[Col. 0385B] It is thus proved that the Lord denied the gifts of his power to his fellow citizens not because of his own inability but because of their envy. Finally, by this example he showed that the whole nation had been abandoned by him—not because it was not loved, but because it itself did not wish to be loved—while teachers were dispersed from it throughout the whole world for the salvation of the nations. But what the Lord testifies in word about the Jews, the Jews themselves testify by their deed about him. For it follows:

And all in the synagogue were filled with anger when they heard this, and they rose up and drove him outside the city. The sacrileges of the Jews, which the Lord had foretold long before through the prophet, saying, “Many repaid evil for good” (Ps. XXXIV), he teaches to have been fulfilled in the Gospel. While he himself spread benefits among the peoples, they inflicted injuries upon him. Nor is it surprising that they lost salvation, since they drove the Savior from their borders.

For the Lord is one who teaches by example and taught his apostles to become all things to all people. He neither rejects those who are willing nor binds those who are unwilling; he neither resists those who drive him out nor is absent from those who ask him. Thus elsewhere, when the Gerasenes could not bear his miracles, he left them as though they were weak and ungrateful (Matt. VIII; Mark V; Luke VIII).

Understand at the same time [Col. 0385C] that his bodily suffering was not imposed by necessity but was voluntary, and that he was not seized by the Jews but offered himself. For when he wishes, he is seized; when he wishes, he slips away; when he wishes, he is suspended; when he wishes, he is not held.

And they led him, he says, as far as the brow of the mountain upon which their city had been built, so that they might throw him down. But he, passing through the midst of them, went on. O inheritance of the disciples worse than their teacher! The devil tempts the Lord by word; the Jews by deed. He says, “Throw yourself down”; these attack him in order to throw him down.

Indeed, the Lord had ascended the brow of the mountain in order to be thrown down, but he descended through their midst when the minds of the raging crowd were suddenly changed or stupefied. He preferred still to heal them rather than destroy them, so that, seeing their wicked attempt frustrated, they might thereafter desist from seeking [Col. 0385D] his death.

For the hour of his passion had not yet come. It was to occur not on an ordinary Sabbath but on the Parasceve of Passover; nor had he yet approached the place of his passion, which was foreshadowed not in Nazareth but in Jerusalem by the blood of the sacrifices. Nor had he chosen this kind of death, since it had been proclaimed throughout the ages that he would be crucified. Therefore he did not wish to complete his life by being thrown down by the Nazarenes, stoned by the people of Jerusalem, killed by Herod among the children of Bethlehem, or by any other death, or any other, or any other.

For what judgment of royal power would stand out in such a death, by which the forehead of the faithful might be armed? Only the standard of the cross was awaited. Its form could be traced both by the swift movement of the right hand against the temptations of the wicked enemy, and, by that same figure, could be regarded as a type of singular monarchy, so that, as the Apostle says when explaining the triumph of the cross: “In the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. II).

For this is what the summit of the same cross signifies: its upper points extend toward heaven, its lower parts reach toward the underworld, and its arms cover the earth. See, then, the Savior’s clemency: moved neither by indignation, offended by no crime, and violated by no injury, he does not abandon Judea. Indeed, forgetful of the injury and mindful of mercy, he now by teaching, now by freeing, and now by healing, soothes the hearts of the people in faith.

## HOMILY LI. FOR THE THIRD FERIA AFTER THE SUNDAY OCULI

[Col. 0386A]

LUKE XVII, MATTHEW XVIII. At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.” And the apostles said to the Lord: “Increase our faith,” and so forth.

[Col. 0386B] We read something similar in Deuteronomy: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly rebuke him, lest you bear sin because of him” (Lev. XIX). He indicates by what order we can avoid scandals and escape perpetual woe: if we watch over ourselves so as not to injure anyone; if we correct the sinner out of zeal for justice; and if, toward the one who repents from the heart, we open the inward organs of mercy and compassion.

Here we must carefully observe that we are commanded not to forgive the sinner indiscriminately, but to forgive the one who does penance. First we are to rebuke the sinner mercifully, so that afterward there may be someone whom we can justly forgive. Therefore whoever sees his brother sinning and remains silent is no less a transgressor of the Lord’s command than the one who refuses to grant forgiveness to that same repentant person. For the one who said, “If he repents, forgive him,” first said, “If he sins, rebuke him.” Thus forgiveness is to be granted to a brother after rebuke, but specifically to one who turns away from error through repentance, so that forgiveness may be neither difficult nor indulgence too lax.

[Col. 0386C] Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying, “I repent,” forgive him. The number seven does not establish a limit for granting forgiveness; rather, it commands either that all sins be forgiven or that forgiveness be granted to the one who always repents. For it is customary for totality of any thing or period of time to be indicated by seven. Hence what is sung in the psalm, “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. CXVIII), means nothing other than: “His praise is always in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIII).

Elsewhere, when Peter asked how often he should forgive a brother who sinned against him—whether up to seven times—the Lord replied: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII), that is, four hundred and ninety times, so that he might forgive a sinning brother as many times in a day as that brother could not possibly sin.

Therefore, if a brother sins against you and repents, you have the power—in fact, the obligation—to forgive him, so that the Father who is in heaven may also forgive you when you repent and seek forgiveness. But if, after being rebuked, he neglects to turn back and [Col. 0386D] repent, observe what judgment the sentence of truth makes concerning this: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him,” and so forth, until it says: “But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (Matt. XVIII). And rightly so, because he has acted under the name of a believer according to the works of unbelievers.

In one way we are commanded to forgive a brother who asks forgiveness, and in another way an enemy who persecutes us. The brother is to be forgiven so that, having received remission of the sin by which he harmed us who were innocent, he may share with us in fellowship of charity. The enemy is to be forgiven so that, while he wishes us evil and does it if he can, we may always wish him good and do whatever we can for him.

For David could not extend to his persecutors, who were deprived of the remedy of repentance, the same kind of forgiveness that Joseph is rightly understood to have shown to his brothers, who had been chastened by salutary remorse (II Kings I; Gen. L).

## HOMILY LII. FOR THE FOURTH FERIA AFTER THE SUNDAY OCULI

[Col. 0387A]

MARK VII, MATTHEW XV. At that time the Pharisees and some scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around Jesus. And when they saw some of his disciples eating bread with common hands—that is, unwashed hands—they found fault, and so forth.

O what a confession of the Lord to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants!” (Matt. XI). The people of the land of Gennesaret, who seemed less learned, not only come themselves but also bring their sick—or rather, carry them—to the Lord, so that they may be found worthy at least to touch his fringe, through which they might be saved. And so they immediately obtain the desired reward of salvation.

But the Pharisees and scribes, who ought to have been teachers of the people, do not run to the Lord to hear the word or to seek healing, but merely to provoke disputes and conflicts of questions. They find fault with those whose hands were unwashed, although in their actions—which are performed through the hands or the other members of the body—they could find nothing of defiling [Col. 0387B] impurity. They ought rather to have condemned themselves, since, though they had hands washed with water, they carried consciences polluted by envy.

For the Pharisees and all the Jews, unless they wash their hands frequently, do not eat, holding to the tradition of the elders; and they do not eat after coming from the marketplace unless they have been baptized. It is a superstitious human tradition to wash repeatedly hands that have already been washed for eating bread, and not to eat after coming from the marketplace unless one has been baptized.

But necessary is the teaching of truth, which commands those who desire to share in the bread of life descending from heaven (John VI) to cleanse their works frequently with almsgiving, tears, and other fruits of [Col. 0387C] righteousness, so that with chaste heart and body they may be able to share in heavenly mysteries.

It is necessary that each person cleanse by persistent good thoughts and actions the defilements contracted from the cares of temporal affairs, if he wishes to enjoy the banquets of inward refreshment. But the Pharisees, taking the spiritual words of the prophets in a carnal sense—words by which they were commanded to correct their hearts and works, such as “Wash yourselves, be clean,” and “You shall be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. III, LII)—observed these commands only with regard to washing the body.

In vain, in vain do the Pharisees and all the Jews wash their hands and baptize themselves after coming from the marketplace, so long as they disdain to be washed in the Savior’s font. They observe the baptisms of vessels to no purpose, since they neglect to wash away the filth of their hearts and bodies. For it is certain that Moses and the prophets, whenever and for whatever reason they commanded the vessels of God’s people to be washed with water, purified with fire, or sanctified with oil, did not thereby command the cleansing of material things, but rather the correction and holiness of minds and deeds, and salvation for our souls.

And the Pharisees and scribes questioned him: Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with common hands? [Col. 0387D] What remarkable stupidity of the Pharisees and scribes! They accuse the Son of God because he does not observe human traditions and precepts. But the hands—that is, the works—must be washed, not bodily hands, certainly, but those of the soul, so that the word of God may be accomplished in them.

And he said to them: Well do you set aside the commandment of God in order to keep your own tradition. He refutes a false accusation with a true reply. When, he says, you neglect the Lord’s commandments because of human tradition, why do you think my disciples should be accused for disregarding the orders of the elders in order to observe God’s decrees?

For Moses said: “Honor your father and your mother; and whoever curses father or mother shall be put to death” (Exod. XX; Deut. V; Exod. XXI; Lev. XX). In the Scriptures, honor is understood not so much in greetings and the rendering of services as in almsgiving and the bestowal of gifts. “Honor,” says the Apostle, “widows who are truly widows” (I Tim. V). Here honor [Col. 0388A] means a gift. And elsewhere: “The presbyters are to be honored with double honor, especially those who labor in the word and teaching of the Lord” (ibid.).

Through this commandment we are also ordered not to muzzle the ox while it is threshing (Deut. XXV; I Cor. IX), so that the laborer may be worthy of his wage (Luke X). But you say: “If a man says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever gift from me might have benefited you is Corban,’ that is, a gift, you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother,” and so forth (Mark VII).

Considering the weakness, age, and poverty of parents, the Lord had commanded that children honor their parents even by supplying them with the necessities of life (Lev. XX; Deut. V). Wishing to overturn this exceedingly provident law of God, so that they might introduce impiety under the name of piety, the scribes and Pharisees taught wicked children that if anyone wished to vow to God, who is the true Father, the things that ought to be offered to his parents, the offering to the Lord should be preferred to gifts for the parents.

Alternatively, the parents themselves, shrinking from the things consecrated to God lest they incur the crime of sacrilege, were worn down by want. Thus it happened [Col. 0388B] that the children’s offering, under the pretext of the temple, passed into the profits of the priests and into their own use. This most wicked custom of the Pharisees arose from such an occasion. They had many people bound by debts and, unwilling to return what had been entrusted to them, assigned it to the priests, so that once the money had been collected it might serve the temple ministries and the priests’ needs.

This saying may also briefly have the following sense: “Whatever gift from me might have benefited you.” You compel, he says, sons to say to their parents: “Whatever gift I was about to offer to God, I am spending on your food, and it benefits you, father and mother.” Thus, fearing to accept what they saw dedicated to God, they would prefer to lead an impoverished life rather than eat from what had been consecrated.

And calling the crowd to him again, he said to them: Hear me, all of you, and understand. Nothing entering a person from outside can defile him; but the things that come forth from a person are what defile a person. [Col. 0388C] The word “common” is properly a scriptural term and is used in ordinary speech. The Jewish people, boasting that they were God’s portion, call “common” the foods used by all human beings—for example, pork, hares, and shellfish, and animals that do not divide the hoof or chew the cud, as well as fish without scales (Lev. XI; Deut. XIV). Hence it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: “What God has sanctified, you shall not call common” (Acts X).

“Common,” therefore, means what is open to other human beings and is regarded as though it were not part of God’s portion; thus it is called unclean. “Nothing,” he says, “entering a person from outside can defile him. But the things that come forth from a person are what defile a person.”

Let the prudent reader object and say: If what enters the mouth does not defile a person (I Cor. VIII), why do we not eat food sacrificed to idols? And the Apostle writes: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (I Cor. X). We must therefore understand that the foods themselves, as God’s creation, are clean in themselves, but that the invocation of idols and demons makes them unclean.

And when he had entered [Col. 0388D] the house away from the crowd, his disciples questioned him about the parable. And he said to them: Are you also without understanding? What had been plainly spoken and was clear to the hearing, the Apostles think was spoken as a parable; in an obvious matter they seek a mystical interpretation, and the Lord rebukes them for thinking that what he had spoken clearly was parabolic.

From this we perceive that a listener is defective if he wishes to understand obscurely what is clear or clearly what has been spoken obscurely. Do you not understand that everything entering a person from outside cannot defile him, because it does not enter his heart but his stomach and is expelled into the latrine, cleansing all foods?

Among heretics and perverse people, all the passages of the Gospels are full of stumbling blocks. From this little sentence some slander the Lord, saying that, ignorant of physical reasoning, he thinks that all foods go into the stomach and are digested in the latrine, when immediately after food is infused it is distributed through the limbs, veins, marrow, and nerves.

They point out [Col. 0389A] that many people who suffer continual vomiting from a weakness of the stomach immediately vomit after dinner or lunch what they have eaten, and yet remain well fleshed, because liquid food and drink are distributed through the limbs at the first contact. But people of this sort, while wishing to criticize another’s ignorance, display their own. For although the thinnest liquid and the most fluid food, once they have been cooked and digested in the veins and limbs, descend through the body’s hidden passages—which the Greeks call πόροι (*poroi*, “channels” or “passages”)—toward the lower parts and go into the latrine.

But he said that the things which come out of a person are what defile a person. For from within, from the heart of human beings, evil thoughts proceed: adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, greed, and so forth. “From the heart,” he says, “evil thoughts proceed.” Therefore the ruling faculty of the soul is not, as Plato maintains, in the brain, but, according to Christ, in the heart.

From this saying [Col. 0389B] those who think that thoughts are injected by the devil and do not wish them to arise from the will itself are also to be refuted. The devil can be an assistant and inciter of evil thoughts, but he cannot be their author. Yet if, always lying in ambush, he inflames the small spark of our thoughts with his fuel, we should not suppose that he also searches out the hidden things of the heart; rather, he infers what we are turning over within from the body’s appearance and gestures.

For example, if he often sees us looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded by the dart of love.

## HOMILY LIII. FOR THE THIRD FERIA AFTER PALM SUNDAY

MARK XIV, MATTHEW XXVI, LUKE XXII, JOHN XVIII. At that time it was Passover and Unleavened Bread, and after two days, and so forth.

Pascha, which in Hebrew is called *phase*, is named not from *passion*, as most suppose, but from *passing over*: for when the destroyer saw the blood on the [Col. 0389C] doorposts of the Israelites, he passed over and did not strike them; or because the Lord himself, offering aid to his people, passed above them (Exod. XII). Explaining the sacramental meaning of the word more sublimely, the evangelist John says: “Before the day of the Passover feast, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come, in order to pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII). He plainly declares that the day of this solemnity was mystically called “passing over” by the Law because the Lamb of God, who would take away the sins of the world, was on that day either himself to pass from this world, or to lead us by a saving passage from the slavery of Egypt.

According to the writing of the Old Testament, there is this distinction between Passover and Unleavened Bread: Passover is the name of the single day on which the lamb was killed in the evening, that is, on the fourteenth day of the first month. On the fifteenth day, when the people departed from Egypt, the feast of Unleavened Bread followed; [Col. 0389D] it was established as a solemnity lasting seven days, that is, until the evening of the twenty-first day of the same month (Exod. XII). Yet the evangelists commonly use “the day of Unleavened Bread” for Passover, and “Passover” for the days of Unleavened Bread. For Mark says: “It was Passover and Unleavened Bread after two days” (Mark XIV). Luke says: “The feast day of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover” (Luke XXII). Likewise John, when the matter took place on the first day of Unleavened Bread, that is, on the fifteenth day, says: “They themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover” (John XVIII).

They did this because they had been commanded both to celebrate the day of Passover with unleavened bread and, as though making a perpetual Passover, were commanded always to pass from this world. For one day, when the lamb had been sacrificed in the evening, is followed in due order by seven days of Unleavened Bread, because Christ Jesus, having once suffered for us in the fullness of time, commanded us to live in the flesh throughout the whole period of this age—which is reckoned by seven days—in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. V) [Col. 0390A], and always, with our eyes fixed upon it, to flee earthly desires as though they were the bonds of Egypt, and, as if withdrawing from worldly conduct, to undertake the secluded path of the virtues.

And the chief priests and scribes were seeking how they might seize and kill him by deceit. They were saying: “Not on the feast day, lest perhaps there be an uproar among the people.” Those who ought to have prepared the victims for the approaching Passover, smoothed the walls of the temple, swept the floors, cleansed the vessels, and purified themselves according to the rite of the Law so that they might become worthy to eat the lamb, instead gathered to deliberate how they might kill the Lord. As the plain statement shows, they were not fearing an uprising, but taking care lest he be snatched from their hands through the aid of the people.

And when he was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, and reclining at table. He who was about to suffer for the whole world and redeem all nations by his blood remains in Bethany, the house of obedience, which had once belonged to Simon the leper—not because he still remained leprous at that time, but because he had formerly been a leper and afterward [Col. 0390B] had been cleansed by the Savior, his former name remaining so that the power of the healer might be displayed. For in the catalogue of the apostles Matthew too is called “the tax collector” by his former vice and occupation, although he had certainly ceased to be a tax collector (Matt. X). Some wish to understand Simon the leper as that part of the people which believed in the Lord and was healed by him. Simon is also said to mean “obedient.”

A woman came with an alabaster vessel of costly spikenard ointment, and, breaking the alabaster, poured it over his head. This woman was Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, whom Jesus raised from the dead, as John expressly records (John XII). John also testifies that this occurred six days before Passover, on the day before Jesus came to Jerusalem seated on a donkey, amid palms and the praise of the crowds.

She was the same woman, and not another, who formerly, as Luke writes (Luke VII), while still a sinner, came and wet the Lord’s feet with the tears of repentance and anointed them with the ointment of devout confession. Because she loved greatly, she obtained from the merciful Judge forgiveness for many sins. [Col. 0390C] Now justified and made a familiar associate of the Lord, she poured holy oil not only on his feet, as that same John relates (John XII), but also on his head, as Matthew and Mark testify (Matt. XXV; Mark XIV).

Alabaster is a kind of white marble, marked with various spots, which is commonly hollowed out for ointment vessels, because it is said to preserve them especially well from spoilage. It is found around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria, whiter than elsewhere, but the finest is found in India. Nard is an aromatic shrub, said to have a heavy and thick root, though short, black, brittle, and highly fragrant despite its richness; or like a cypress, with a harsh flavor and a small, dense leaf whose tips spread into spikes. Therefore perfumers celebrate both the spikes and the leaves of nard for their twofold endowment.

This is why Mark says “costly spikenard ointment”: the ointment that Mary brought to the Lord was made not only from the root of nard, but, to make it more precious [Col. 0390D], its fragrance and power were enriched by the addition of its spikes and leaves. Naturalists state that nard is the principal ingredient in ointments; hence it was appropriately offered for anointing the Lord’s head and feet. There are indeed many kinds of it, but all are herbaceous except the Indian variety, which is more precious.

Mystically, this devotion of Mary serving the Lord signifies the faith and piety of the holy Church, which speaks in the Song of Love, saying: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song I).
