These words she fulfilled once, according to the literal sense, through Mary’s hands; and she does not cease to fulfill them spiritually every day in all her members, who rejoice that they are spread throughout the whole world and say: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place; for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. II).

[Col. 0391A] When the Church confesses with worthy reverence the power of his divine might, which he possesses together with the Father, and praises and proclaims it, she truly pours precious ointment over his head. But when with equal worthy reverence she regards the mysteries of the humanity he assumed, she pours over the Lord’s feet the ointment of genuine nard—that is, faithful and true nard—because by devout preaching she commends that nature of his by which he deigned to touch the earth, that is, to dwell among human beings, and venerates it with devoted service.

Some were indignant among themselves and said: “Why has this ointment been wasted? For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” Mark too speaks here, as Matthew does, by synecdoche (*synecdochicōs*), using the plural number for the singular. For John, speaking more distinctly, testifies that Judas said this (John XII), because of his greed, since he was a thief and, having the money box, carried away what was put into it.

It may also be understood that the other disciples either felt or said this, or were persuaded to think so when Judas said it, and that Matthew and Mark expressed the will of all [Col. 0391B] in their words. But Judas spoke for this reason, because he was a thief; the others, because of their concern for the poor. John, however, wished to mention only Judas, whose habit of stealing he believed should be disclosed on this occasion. What follows is:

“And they were angry with her.” I do not believe that this was said of the good apostles who loved Christ and were diligent in his service, but rather of that man, mentioned in the plural number, who was shown to have adhered faithfully neither to the Lord nor to his disciples and to have had no care for the poor.

But Jesus said: “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish, you can do good to them; but you will not always have me.” Another question arises: why did Jesus say to the disciples after the resurrection, “Behold, I am with you always, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII), while here he says, “You will not always have me”? [Col. 0391C] It seems to me that in this passage he is speaking of bodily presence, since after the resurrection he would not be with them in the same way as he was then, in all their companionship and familiarity. Remembering this, the Apostle says: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Cor. V).

“What she had, she did: she anticipated anointing my body for burial.” What you consider to be the wasting of the ointment is an act of burial. Nor is it surprising that she gave me the good fragrance of her faith, since I am about to pour out my blood for her.

“Amen, I say to you, wherever this Gospel is proclaimed throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” Observe his knowledge of future events: although he knew that he would suffer after a few days, he knew that his Gospel would be celebrated throughout the whole world.

It should also be noted that, just as Mary obtained glory throughout the world wherever the holy Church is spread because of the devout service she rendered to the Lord, so [Col. 0391D], conversely, the man who did not fear to disparage her service with reckless speech was branded far and wide with the stigma of treachery and deservedly became hateful to God and human beings alike. Yet the Lord, rewarding the good with worthy praise, passed over the future insults of the impious in silence.

And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went away to the chief priests to betray him to them. Unhappy Judas believed that he had suffered a loss from the pouring out of the ointment, and he wished to compensate for it by the price of his master. He no longer demanded a fixed sum, so that his betrayal might at least appear profitable; rather, as though handing over a worthless slave, he left the amount to the power of the buyers, whatever they wished to give.

When the text says, “He went away to the chief priests to betray him to them,” it shows that he had not been invited by the rulers, nor compelled by any necessity, but had acted from the deliberate choice of his own criminal mind.

When they heard this, they rejoiced and promised to give him money. And he was seeking how he might betray him at a convenient opportunity.

[Col. 0392A] Many people today shudder at Judas’s crime—that he sold the Lord, his master and his God, for money—as something monstrous and abominable, yet they do not guard against committing the same offense. For when they give false testimony against anyone in exchange for gifts, they plainly deny the truth for money and sell God for money. He himself said: “I am the truth” (John XIV).

When they stain a fellowship of brotherhood with the plague of discord, they betray the Lord, because “God is love” (1 John IV). Therefore those who despise the commands of love and truth betray God, who is love and truth—especially when they sin not through weakness or ignorance, but, like Judas, seek an opportunity to exchange truth for falsehood and virtue for crime when witnesses are absent.

And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover, the disciples said to him: “Where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?” He calls the first day of Unleavened Bread the fourteenth day of the first month, when [Col. 0392B], after leaven had been removed, they were accustomed to sacrifice the Passover—that is, to kill the lamb—in the evening (Exod. XII).

Explaining this, the Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. V). Although he was crucified on the following day, that is, on the fifteenth day, on this night, when the lamb was sacrificed, he both delivered to his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to be celebrated and, being seized and bound by the Jews, consecrated the beginning of that same sacrifice—that is, of his passion.

And he sends two of his disciples and says to them: “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you.” This is an indication of his foreknowing divinity, because, while speaking with his disciples, he knows what will happen elsewhere.

Appropriately, as the disciples prepare the Passover, a man carrying a jar—or, according to another evangelist, an amphora—of water meets them (Luke XXII), so that it may be shown that the mystery of this Passover was to be celebrated for the perfect cleansing of the whole world. Water signifies the bath of grace; the jar signifies the frailty of those through [Col. 0392C] whom that same grace was to be administered to the world. Hence they say: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. IV).

The disciples therefore prepare the Passover where a jar of water is brought in, signifying that the time has arrived when the blood of the type will be removed from the threshold and doorposts for the worshipers of the true Passover, and the baptism of the life-giving fountain will be consecrated for taking away the sins of the world.

“Follow him, and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house: ‘The Teacher says, Where is my dining room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’” The names both of the water-carrier and of the master of the house have deliberately been omitted, so that it may be indicated that an opportunity is granted to all who wish to celebrate the true Passover—that is, to be imbued with Christ’s sacraments and to receive him as a guest in the dwelling of their mind.

And he himself will show you a large upper room furnished; and there prepare for us, and so forth. The large upper room is the spiritual Law, which, leaving behind the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in a lofty [Col. 0392D] place. For whoever still observes the letter that kills, whoever understands nothing more in the lamb than an animal, makes a lesser Passover, because he has not yet learned to grasp the majesty of the spirit in the words of God.

But whoever has followed the water-carrier—that is, the herald of grace—into the house of the Church, transcends the surface of the letter through the illuminating Spirit and prepares a meal for Christ in the high chamber of the mind. He recognizes that all the mysteries of the Passover, as well as the other decrees of the Law, are mysteries belonging to Christ.

When evening came, he arrived with the twelve. And while they were reclining and eating, Jesus said: “Amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me, the one who is eating with me.” He had foretold his passion, and now foretells the betrayer, giving room for repentance, so that when the man realized that his thoughts and secret plans were known, he might repent of his deed.

Yet he does not identify him specifically, lest, being openly exposed, he become even more shameless. [Col. 0393A] He casts the crime into the number, so that the guilty man may repent.

They began to be distressed and to say to him one by one: “Surely it is not I?” The eleven apostles certainly knew that they were contemplating nothing of this kind against the Lord, but they trusted their master more than themselves. Fearing their own weakness, they sorrowfully asked about a sin of which they had no consciousness.

He said to them: “One of the twelve, who dips his hand with me into the bowl.” O wondrous power of the Lord! First he had said: “One of you will betray me.” The betrayer persists in evil; he is accused more clearly, and yet his name is still not specifically given.

While the others were grieving, withdrawing their hands, and preventing food from reaching their mouths, Judas, with the recklessness and shamelessness by which he was about to betray his master, also put his hand into the bowl with the master, so that audacity might counterfeit a good conscience.

And indeed the Son of Man goes as it is written concerning [Col. 0393B] him; but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man will be betrayed (Ps. XL). Corrected neither at the first nor at the second warning, he does not withdraw his foot from betrayal. Rather, the Lord’s patience nourishes his shamelessness, and he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath (Rom. III).

He foretells the punishment so that the announced penalties might correct the man whom shame had not overcome. And even today, and forever, woe to the man who approaches the Lord’s table with evil intent; who, with ambushes concealed in his mind and with a heart polluted by some crime, does not fear to participate in the most holy offerings of Christ’s mysteries.

Such a man too, in imitation of Judas, betrays the Son of Man—not indeed to sinful Jews, but nevertheless to sinful members, namely, his own, among whom he dares to profane that inestimable and inviolable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. He sells God who, neglecting fear and love of him, is shown to love and pursue earthly, fleeting, and even criminal things in his place.

[Col. 0393C] “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” He should not for this reason be thought to have existed before he was born, because no one could be well unless he had existed; rather, it is simply said that it is much better not to exist than to exist wickedly.

And while they were eating, Jesus took bread, and, blessing it, broke it and gave it to them, saying: “Take; this is my body.” When the solemnities of the old Passover, which were celebrated in remembrance of the ancient deliverance of God’s people from Egypt, had been completed, he passed to the new Passover, which he wished the Church to celebrate in remembrance of his redemption, substituting, as it were, for the flesh of the lamb the sacrament of his body and blood, and showing that he himself was that reality.

Concerning him the Lord swore, and will not repent: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). He himself breaks the bread that he gives to the disciples, to show that the breaking of his body would not occur without his own will and arrangement. As he says elsewhere, he had authority [Col. 0393D] to lay down his life and authority to take it up again (John X).

For the sake of the sacrament, he first blessed the bread before breaking it, because he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, filled with the grace of divine power the human nature that he had assumed and was about to suffer in. He blessed the bread and broke it because he deigned to subject the assumed human being to death in such a way as to demonstrate that the power of divine immortality truly dwelt in him, and therefore to teach that he would be raised from death all the more swiftly.

And having taken the cup and given thanks, he gave it to them, and they all drank from it. As he is said to have given thanks after taking the bread when his passion was approaching, so he gives thanks when he receives the scourges of another’s iniquity. Though he had done nothing deserving punishment, he humbly blesses in the midst of punishment, showing thereby what each person ought to do when suffering the scourge of his own fault, if he himself bears with equanimity the scourges due to another’s fault. Thus he shows what a subject should do when corrected, if one equal to the Father, placed beneath the scourge, gives thanks to the Father. [Col. 0394A]

And he said to them: “This is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many.” Since bread strengthens the body, while wine produces blood in the flesh, the former is mystically referred to the body of Christ and the latter to his blood.

But because Christ must remain in us and we in Christ, water is mixed with the wine of the Lord’s cup, for, as John testifies, the waters signify the peoples (Rev. XVII). It is permitted to offer neither water alone nor wine alone, just as one may not offer a grain of wheat alone without the addition and preparation of water to make bread. Otherwise such an offering would signify that the head ought to be separated from the members, and would falsely suggest either that Christ could suffer without the love of our redemption or that we could be saved and offered to the Father without his passion.

When he says, “This is my blood of the new covenant,” he distinguishes it from the old covenant, which was dedicated with the blood of goats and calves [Col. 0394B]. As the lawgiver said while sprinkling: “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you” (Lev. XVI; Exod. XXIV). For the earthly copies had to be cleansed with these things, but the heavenly realities with better sacrifices than these, as the Apostle explains throughout his Epistle to the Hebrews, distinguishing the Law from the Gospel with a most beautiful exposition and complete reasoning (Heb. IX).

“Amen, I say to you, I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” That the Synagogue is called the Lord’s vine or vineyard is attested throughout Scripture, and Isaiah states it more clearly in the song composed about it: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V).

From this vineyard the Lord had drunk for a long time, although many of its branches had been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine. For although many in that people strayed from the straight path of faith, throughout the whole period of the Law there were not lacking many whose devout thoughts and highest [Col. 0394C] virtues delighted God.

But when the Lord had suffered in the flesh and risen from the dead, the time had come for that legal and figurative observance to cease, and for the things performed according to the letter, transferred into a spiritual meaning, to be held more perfectly in the new covenant with the assistance of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, as he was going to his passion, the Lord said: “I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God,” as though he were plainly saying: “I will no longer delight in the carnal ceremonies of the Synagogue, in which even the sacred rites of this paschal lamb held the chief place. The time of my resurrection will come; that day will come when, placed in the kingdom of God—that is, exalted in the glory of immortal life—I will be filled with new joy with you from the salvation of that same people, regenerated by the fountain of spiritual grace.”

And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. This is what we read in the psalm: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek him [Col. 0394D] shall praise the Lord” (Ps. XXI).

The hymn may also be understood as the one that the Lord, according to John, sang while giving thanks to the Father. In it, with his eyes lifted upward, he prayed for himself, for the disciples, and for those who would believe through their words (John XVII).

Appropriately, after imbuing the disciples with the sacraments of his body and blood and commending them to the Father in a hymn of devout intercession, he leads them up to the Mount of Olives. This signifies typologically that through receiving his sacraments and through the aid of his intercession we ought to ascend to the higher gifts of the virtues and the charisms of the Holy Spirit, with which we are anointed in our hearts.

And Jesus said to them: “You will all be scandalized on this night.” He foretells what they will suffer so that, when they have suffered it, they may not despair of salvation but may be freed through repentance.

He significantly added: “You will be scandalized on this night,” because just as those who become drunk are drunk at night, so those who suffer scandal endure it at night and in darkness. Let us instead say: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (1 Thess. V; Rom. XIII).

[Col. 0395A] For it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” This is written in other words in the prophet Zechariah; unless I am mistaken, it is spoken by the prophet to God: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. XIII). The sixty-eighth psalm, which is sung entirely by the Lord, also agrees with this meaning: “For you struck, and they pursued” (Ps. LXVIII).

The good shepherd is struck so that he may lay down his life for his sheep, and from many flocks of error there may come to be one flock and one shepherd (John X).

But Peter said to him: “Even if all are scandalized, yet I will not be.” This was neither recklessness nor a lie, but the faith of the apostle Peter and his ardent affection for the Lord and Savior.

And Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you, today, on this very night, before the cock gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times.” Peter was making his promise from the ardor of faith [Col. 0395B], while the Savior, as God, knew what was to come.

Observe that Peter denies at night, and denies three times. After the cock crowed, and as the darkness diminished and the approaching light was announced, he turned and wept bitterly, washing away the defilement of his threefold denial with tears.

It should certainly not be thought contradictory that, while Mark says, “Before the cock gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times,” the other evangelists simply say, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” For Peter’s entire denial is a threefold denial. He remained in the same denial in his intention and purpose of lying until, reminded of what had been foretold to him, he was healed by bitter weeping and sorrow of heart.

If this entire denial—that is, the threefold denial—had begun after the first cockcrow, the three evangelists who say that the Lord foretold that Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed would appear to have spoken falsely. Again, if he had completed the whole threefold denial before the cock began to crow, Mark would be found to have reported unnecessarily, in the person of the Lord: “Amen, I say to you, tonight, before the cock gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times.”

But because that threefold denial began before the first cockcrow [Col. 0395C], those three evangelists considered not when Peter would complete it but how great it would be and when it would begin—namely, the threefold denial that could be understood as wholly present in his mind even before the first cockcrow.

Although the whole threefold denial began in the words of the denier before the first cockcrow and was completed before the second cockcrow, nevertheless, in the intention of his mind and in Peter’s fear, it had been conceived in its entirety before the first cockcrow.

It does not matter over what intervals of delay the three denials were announced by his voice, since his heart possessed the whole of them even before the first cockcrow. He had absorbed so great a fear that, when questioned, he could deny the Lord not only once but a second and a third time.

[Col. 0395D] Just as a woman has already committed adultery in her heart when she looks upon a woman in order to desire her (Matt. V), so, whenever Peter gave voice to the fear that he had conceived so violently in his mind that it could endure until the third denial of the Lord, the entire threefold denial must be assigned to the moment when a fear sufficient for the threefold denial seized him.

And they came to an estate called Gethsemane. The place of Gethsemane is still shown today, where the Lord prayed at the foot of the Mount of Olives; a church is now built above it. Gethsemane is interpreted as “the valley of the fruitful” or “of fatness.”

As has often been said, not only the words and deeds of our Savior but also the places and times in which he acts and speaks are filled with mystical figures. When the Lord prays on the mountain, he silently admonishes us that we ought to seek only lofty things in prayer and to plead for heavenly goods.

But when he prays in the valley—and in the valley of the fruitful or of fatness—he likewise signifies that humility must always be preserved in our prayers [Col. 0396A], together with the inward fatness of love. Thus no one who prays to God should dare to boast of his merits, after the example of the proud Pharisee; rather, with humble voice and mind, he should cry out: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII).

Nor should anyone whose heart is dry of love toward his neighbor bend his knee to obtain the favor of the Creator, like the man who, unwilling to forgive his brother the hundred denarii he owed him, vainly prayed the Lord to forgive him ten thousand talents (Matt. XVIII).

Nor should anyone whose breast is barren of love for the Creator seek in prayer merely temporal things rather than the vision of God, lest he be numbered among those of whom he himself says: “They have received their reward” (Matt. VI).

For what else is it to place one’s thought in lowly things than a certain dryness of mind? Those who, through holy desires, already feed upon heavenly things and the food of inward delight become fat, as it were, through richer nourishment. The psalmist desired to be nourished by this fatness when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” [Col. 0396B] (Ps. LXII).

As far as the dispensation of the Lord’s passion itself is concerned, it was fitting that the Lord, approaching death, prayed in the valley of fatness, because through the valley of humility and the fatness of charity he underwent death for us: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. II). And: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

And he took Peter, James, and John with him, and began to be afraid and distressed. And he said to them: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” Christ is afraid; while Peter is not afraid, Christ is afraid. Peter says: “I will lay down my life for you”; Christ says: “My soul is troubled.”

Both statements are true, and both are fully reasonable. The one who is lower does not fear, while the one who is higher bears the disposition of one who fears. The former, as a human being, does not know the power of death; the latter, as God established in a body, displays the frailty of the flesh [Col. 0396C], so that the impiety of those who deny the mystery of the Incarnation might be excluded.

Indeed, he said this, yet Manichaeus did not believe it; Valentinus denied it; Marcion judged it to be a phantom. He so fully conformed the human being whom he demonstrated by the truth of his body to the corresponding emotion that he said: “Yet not as I will, but as you will.”

He assumed my will; he assumed my sorrow. I confidently call it sorrow, because I proclaim the cross. The will that he called his own is mine, because as a human being he assumed my sorrow and, as a human being, said: “Not as I will, but as you will.”

My sorrow is one that no one else assumed in feeling. Therefore he sorrowed for me, who had nothing for which he himself should sorrow. The delight of eternal divinity having been set aside, he is affected by the weariness of my weakness.

“My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful unto death.” The Lord is not sorrowful because of death, since it was the condition and feeling of the body, not fear of death, that troubled him. For having assumed a body, he had to undergo everything belonging to the body: to hunger, thirst, be angry, and be sorrowful. Divinity, however, does not know change through these emotions.

[Col. 0396D] “Remain here and keep watch.” And when he had gone forward a little, he fell upon the ground. When he commands, “Remain here and keep watch,” he is not prohibiting sleep, whose time had not yet come because of the impending danger, but the sleep of unbelief and the sluggishness of the mind.

After giving them the command to remain and keep watch with him, he went forward a little, fell on his face, and displayed the humility of his mind through the posture of his flesh.

And he prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him, and said: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup away from me.” What was that voice but the sound of our weakness?

Many who are still weak are distressed by the death that lies ahead. Let them have a right heart and avoid death as far as they can; but if they cannot, let them say what the Lord himself said—not for his own sake, but for ours. What did he say? “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (John V).

[Col. 0397A] Here you have human will expressed. From this comes the right heart: “Yet not what I will, but what you will.” “I have not come,” he says, “to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

He called “his own will” the will that he had assumed temporally from the Virgin; but “the will of him who sent him” is the will that he signified as eternally possessed in common with the Father. He prays that the cup may pass, to show that he was truly human.

But remembering the reason for which he was sent, he fulfills the dispensation for which he was sent and cries out: “Yet not what I will, but what you will.” “If death dies without my dying according to the flesh, let this cup pass,” he says. But because this will not happen otherwise, he says: “Not what I will, but what you will.”

When, invoking the Father, he says “Abba, Father” by a twofold name, he shows that he is the God and Savior of both peoples, namely, the Jewish and the Gentile. *Abba* means the same as *Father*; but *Abba* is Hebrew, while *pater* is Greek and Latin.

Therefore, to teach that both peoples would believe in him [Col. 0397B] and that he should be invoked by both, he himself first invokes him in both languages. For he is the good shepherd who, by laying down his life for his sheep (John X), makes one sheepfold from the two flocks.

Thus he asks the Father’s help in the voice of both flocks, so that we, instructed by his example, whenever we sense adversity approaching, may invoke God the Father—we of the nations calling him “Father,” the Hebrews “Abba”—and seek heavenly protection with one devotion of faith and love.

Hence the distinguished teacher, receiving from the Lord the pattern of instruction, addresses his hearers in this way: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII; Gal. IV). *Abba* belongs to those who come from the people of Israel; “Father” to us who have come from the nations to the faith of Christ.

And coming, he found them sleeping and said to Peter: “Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not keep watch for one hour?” The man who had earlier said, “Even if all are scandalized, I will never be scandalized,” is now unable to overcome sleep because of the greatness of his sorrow.

[Col. 0397C] “Keep watch and pray, so that you may not enter into temptation.” It is impossible for the human soul not to be tempted. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Lead us not into temptation” (Matt. VI)—not rejecting temptation altogether, which we cannot endure, but asking for strength to withstand temptations.

Therefore here too he does not say, “Keep watch and pray so that you may not be tempted,” but “so that you may not enter into temptation”—that is, so that temptation may not finally overcome you and hold you in its snares.

For example, the martyr who shed his blood in confessing the Lord was tempted, but was not bound in the nets of temptation. The one who denies, however, falls into the snares of temptation.

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. This was said against the presumptuous, who think that whatever they believe, they can attain. Therefore, as much as we trust in the ardor of the mind, so much should we fear on account of the weakness of the flesh; nevertheless, according to the Apostle, “by the Spirit let us put to death the works of the flesh” (Rom. VIII).

[Col. 0397D] This passage also stands against the Eutychians, who say that in the Mediator between God and human beings, our Lord and Savior, there is one operation and that there was one will. For when he says, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” he shows two wills: namely, the human will, which belongs to the flesh, and the divine will, which belongs to the Godhead. The human will, because of the weakness of the flesh, refuses the Passion, whereas the divine will is supremely ready for it. For to fear in the Passion belongs to human frailty, but to accept the dispensation belongs to the divine will and power of the Passion.

And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. When he returned, he found them sleeping again. He alone prays for all, just as he alone suffers for everyone. The eyes of the apostles were growing weak and weighed down by the impending denial.

And he came a third time and said to them, “Sleep now and rest. It is enough; the hour has come. Behold, the Son of Man will be handed over [Col. 0398A] into the hands of sinners.” When he had said, “Sleep now and rest,” and added, “It is enough,” and then continued, “The hour has come; behold, the Son of Man will be handed over,” the meaning is evidently that, after saying to them, “Sleep and rest,” the Lord remained silent for a little while, so that what he had promised might take place, and then added, “Behold, the hour is near,” or, “The hour has come.” For this reason “It is enough” has been placed after those words: that is, “The rest you have now had is enough.” But because that intervening silence of the Lord has not itself been mentioned, it constrains the interpretation, so that another punctuation must be sought in those words.

“Rise, let us go. Behold, he who betrays me is near.” After he had prayed a third time and, through the repentance that followed, had obtained the correction of the apostles’ fear, he proceeds confidently toward his Passion and freely presents himself to be killed. He says to the disciples, “Rise, let us go. Behold, he who betrays me is near.” Let them not find us as though we were afraid and shrinking back; let us go willingly toward death, so that they may see the confidence and joy of those who are about to suffer.

Now his betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one whom I kiss is he; seize him and lead him away carefully.” And when he came, immediately approaching him he said, “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him. It was an impudent and criminal confidence to call his master “Rabbi” and to offer a kiss to the one whom he was betraying. Yet he still displayed something of a disciple’s modesty, since he did not openly hand him over to the persecutors, but did so through the sign of a kiss. The Lord received the betrayer’s kiss—not to teach us to pretend, but lest he appear to flee the betrayal—thereby also fulfilling that saying of David: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” (Ps. CXIX).

But one of those standing nearby drew a sword, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. Peter did this, as the evangelist John makes clear (John XVIII), with the same ardor of mind with which he had done the other things. For he knew [Col. 0398C] how Phinehas, by punishing the sacrilegious, had received the reward of righteousness and everlasting priesthood (Num. XXV). Luke adds that the Lord touched the servant’s ear and healed him (Luke XXII). The Lord therefore never forgets his mercy: he does not even allow his enemies to be wounded. They inflict death on the righteous man; he heals the wounds of his persecutors, mystically teaching that even those who, by consenting to his death, had contracted a wound of the soul could merit salvation if they produced worthy fruits of repentance.

And Jesus answered and said to them, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to seize me as though I were a robber? Every day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me.” It is foolish, he says, to seek with swords and clubs one who willingly hands himself over to your hands, and to investigate through a betrayer one who teaches daily in the temple, as though he were hiding at night and avoiding your eyes. But this is why you gather against me in darkness: because your power is in darkness [Col. 0398D].

Then his disciples abandoned him and all fled. The Lord’s saying was fulfilled, that all the disciples would be scandalized because of him on that very night. For although they fled when the crowd permitted it at the Lord’s request, as John writes (John XVIII), they nevertheless displayed the fear and timidity of their minds, since they were readier to seek the protection of flight than to show the confidence of suffering with Christ.

Now a certain young man followed him, clothed in a linen cloth over his naked body, and they seized him. But he, leaving the linen cloth behind, fled from them naked. When it says, “clothed in a linen cloth over his naked body,” the body is understood: that is, he had the linen cloth over a naked body, because he had no other garment than the linen cloth alone. The evangelist does not say who this young man was. Whoever he was, he proves that a greater love for the Lord remained in him than in the others, since, when they had already fled, he did not cease to follow him, bound by the bond of charity, until he himself was seized by the enemies [Col. 0399A], although he did not yet possess perfect charity, because, once he was seized, he was able to flee from the company of the Savior. For just as perfect charity casts out fear (I John IV), so fear, besieging the mind, demonstrates imperfect charity.

But we should observe more carefully that, in writing about this young man, the evangelist does not say, “He fled from the company of the Lord,” or, “He fled from following the Lord”; rather, he says, “Having cast off the linen cloth, he fled from them naked.” He fled from the enemies, whose presence and deeds he detested; he did not flee from the Lord, his Savior and teacher, whose love he kept fixed in his heart even while absent in body.

Nor does anything prevent us from understanding that this young man was John, the disciple especially loved by his teacher. The fact that he was still a young man at that time is indicated by the long life he afterward lived in the flesh. It could have happened that, having slipped from the hands of those who seized him, he soon returned after taking up his garment again and, in the uncertain light of night, mingled with the crowds leading Jesus, as though he were one of them [Col. 0399B], until he reached the high priest’s courtyard, where he was known, as he himself records in his Gospel (John XVIII).

Just as Peter, who washed away the guilt of his denial with repentant tears and utterly uprooted it by confessing his love for the Lord, displays the restoration of those who fall in martyrdom, so the other disciples, who anticipated the moment of arrest by fleeing, teach prudence in flight to those who feel themselves less capable of enduring punishments. For them it is much safer to seek the protection of hiding places than to expose themselves to the danger of combat.

Thus also this young man, who, having cast off the linen cloth, fled naked from the wicked, represents both their deed and their intention: those who, in order to become safer from the attacks of enemies, cast away whatever they seem to possess in this world and have learned to serve the Lord naked rather than, by clinging to worldly possessions, provide the adversaries with material for tempting them and turning them back from God. This accords with the example of blessed Joseph, who, leaving his cloak in the adulterous woman’s hands, leapt outside, preferring to serve God naked rather than, clothed in the desires of the world, serve the prostitute (Gen. XXXIX) [Col. 0399C].

And they led Jesus to the high priest. The high priest refers to Caiaphas, who, as the evangelist John writes, was high priest that year. Josephus bears corresponding witness concerning him (Antiquities, Book XVIII, chap. 4), saying that he had purchased the high-priesthood from the Roman ruler without possessing the requisite dignity. It is therefore not surprising if an unjust high priest judges unjustly.

Peter followed him from a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest. He rightly followed from a distance, since he was already about to deny him at close range. For he could not have denied him if he had clung closely to Christ. Yet in this he is especially worthy of our admiration: he did not abandon the Lord even when he was afraid. That he fears belongs to nature; that he follows belongs to devotion; that he denies belongs to sudden weakness; that he repents belongs to faith.

Alternatively, in the fact that Peter follows the same Lord from a distance toward his Passion, the Church was signified: the Church would indeed follow, that is, imitate, the Lord’s Passion, but in a greatly different manner. The Church suffers for itself, whereas he suffers for the Church [Col. 0399D].

And he was sitting with the attendants and warming himself at the fire. There is the fire of love, and there is also the fire of desire. Of the former it is said, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII). Of the latter: “All are adulterers; their hearts are like an oven” (Hos. VII). The former, descending upon the believers in the upper room of Zion, taught them to praise God in various languages (Acts II); the latter, kindled in the courtyard of Caiaphas by the prompting of the evil spirit, armed the harmful tongues of the faithless to deny and blaspheme the Lord.

For what the wicked council was doing inside the house of the high priest, that fire kindled materially outside in the courtyard amid the cold of night prefigured symbolically. Therefore, whoever extinguishes within himself a vicious and harmful fire can say with the Prophet to the Lord: “For I have become like a leather bottle in the frost; I have not forgotten your righteous judgments” (Ps. CXVIII) [Col. 0400A]. But those in whom troubled streams of vices have overwhelmed the flame of charity hear from the Lord: “Because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XIV).

With this cold numbing him for a time, the apostle Peter, as though by the coals of Caiaphas’s attendants, sought to warm himself, because he was seeking the comfort of temporal advantage through the companionship of the faithless. But shortly afterward, when the Lord looked upon him, he abandoned both the fire of the wicked in his body and infidelity in his heart. After the Lord’s resurrection, restored by the holy fire, he completely cleansed the lapse of his triple denial through a triple confession of love.

For when that memorable catch of fish had been completed, and he had come to the Lord with his fellow disciples, as soon as he saw the coals laid out, the fish placed upon them, and the bread, he kindled the secrets of his heart with the coals of love (John XXI).

And certain men rose and bore false witness against him, saying, “We heard him saying, ‘I will destroy this temple made with hands, and after three days I will build another not made with hands’” (John II). How are they false witnesses if they say what we read that the Lord said? A false witness is one who does not understand words in the sense in which they are spoken.

The Lord had spoken about the temple of his body, but they also slandered him in the very words themselves. By adding or changing a few words, they made their accusation seem just. The Savior had said, “Destroy this temple”; they changed it and said, “I will destroy this temple made with hands.” “You,” he said, “destroy it, not I,” because it is unlawful for them themselves to inflict death upon us [F.: *inferamus*, “for us to inflict death”]. Then they altered the statement: “And after three days I will build another not made with hands,” so that he might seem to have spoken specifically about the Jewish temple.

But to show that he had spoken of a living and breathing temple, the Lord said, “And I will raise it up in three days.” To build is one thing; to raise up is another.

And the high priest rose and came into the midst and questioned Jesus, saying, “Do you answer nothing to these charges [Col. 0400C] that they bring against you?” But he remained silent and answered nothing. Rash and impatient anger, finding no place for its slander, drove the high priest from his seat, so that he might demonstrate the madness of his mind through the movement of his body. The more Jesus remained silent before the false witnesses unworthy of an answer and before the impious priests, the more the high priest, overcome by fury, provoked him to answer, seeking an opportunity for accusation from any possible statement. Nevertheless Jesus remained silent, for, as God, he knew that whatever he answered would be twisted into slander.

Again the high priest questioned him and said to him, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” Jesus said to him, “I am.” In Matthew it is written that, when the high priest questioned him and adjured him to say whether he was the Christ, he answered, “You have said so” (Matt. XXVI). Mark gives, “I am,” in order to show that what Jesus says to him—“You have said so”—has the same force as if he had said, “I am.”

[Col. 0400D] “And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.” If, therefore, O Jew, pagan, and heretic, you regard contempt, weakness, and the cross in Christ as disgrace, see that through these things the Son of Man will sit at the right hand of God the Father, and that he who was born human from the Virgin’s womb will come in his majesty with the clouds of heaven.

For this reason the Apostle, after describing the humiliation of the cross, saying that “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross,” added and said: “Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II).

But the high priest, tearing his garments, said, “What further need have we of witnesses? You have heard the blasphemy.” The same fury that had driven him from the priestly seat now provoked him to tear his garments [Col. 0401A]. He tears his garments to show that the Jews have lost their priestly glory and possess an empty seat of the high priest.

It is also a custom of the Jews, whenever they hear something blasphemous and seemingly spoken against God, to tear their garments. We read that Paul and Barnabas did the same when they were honored as gods in Lycaonia (Acts XIV). Herod, however, because he did not give glory to God but consented to the people’s excessive praise, was immediately struck by an angel (Acts XII).

At a deeper, mystical level, it happened that, in the Lord’s Passion, the Jewish high priest himself tore his garments, while the Lord’s tunic could not be torn even by the soldiers who crucified him. This signified that the Jewish priesthood, because of the crimes of its priests, was to be torn apart and entirely removed from its state of integrity. But the solidity of the holy universal Church, which is accustomed to be called the garment of its Redeemer, could never be broken. Rather, even if Jews, Gentiles, heretics, or wicked Catholics despise the humility of the Lord and Savior, his chastity will nevertheless remain inviolate in those whom the lot of election finds until the consummation of the age [Col. 0401B].

And some began to spit upon him, to cover his face, to strike him with blows, and to say to him, “Prophesy.” And the attendants struck him with blows. Here the prophecy was fulfilled that says: “I gave my cheeks to those who struck me, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isa. L).

But he who was then struck with the blows of the Jews is also now struck by the blasphemies of false Christians; he who was then spat upon by the saliva of unbelievers is still dishonored and provoked by the insults of madmen who bear the name of believers.

They covered his face, not so that he might not see their crimes, but so that they themselves, as once they did to Moses (Exod. XXXIV), might hide from themselves the grace of knowing him. For if they believed Moses, perhaps they would also believe the Lord (John V). That veil remains upon their heart, unrevealed, to this day [Col. 0401C] (II Cor. III); but it has been removed for us who believe in Christ.

For it was not without reason that, at his death, the veil of the temple was torn in two, and that the mysteries of the holy of holies, which had remained hidden throughout the entire period of the Law and concealed from carnal Israel, were disclosed to the worshipers of the new covenant.

When they say to him, “Prophesy,” and, according to the other evangelists, “Prophesy—who is it that struck you?”, they say this as an insult to one who had wished to be regarded by the people as a prophet. But because he himself was ordering the dispensation, everything that he suffered took place for our sake, so that, as Peter urges (I Pet. IV), having armed ourselves with the same intention as Christ, who suffered in the flesh, we might be prepared to endure the insults of mockery for his name.

And while Peter was in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s servant girls came down. When she saw Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.” But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you are saying.”

What does it mean that a servant girl was the first to expose him, when men could certainly have recognized him more readily? Perhaps it was so that this sex too might appear to have sinned in bringing about the Lord’s death, and that this sex too might be redeemed through the Lord’s Passion. For this reason a woman first receives the mystery of the resurrection and guards its commands, in order to abolish the ancient error of transgression.

And he went out into the forecourt, and the rooster crowed. The other evangelists are silent about this crowing of the rooster, but they do not deny that it happened, just as some pass over many other things in silence that others relate.

Again, when the servant girl saw him, she began to say to those standing nearby, “This man is one of them.” But he denied it again. We should not believe that this was the same servant girl who had accused him earlier. Matthew says very plainly: “As he went out through the doorway, another saw him and said to those who were there,” and so forth.

From this denial of Peter we learn that Christ is denied not only by someone who says that he is not the Christ, but also by one who, although he is a Christian, denies that he is a Christian [Col. 0402A]. The Lord did not say to Peter, “You will deny my disciple,” but, “You will deny me.” Therefore he denied Christ himself when he denied that he was Christ’s disciple.

And after a little while those standing there again said to Peter, “Surely you are one of them. For you are also a Galilean.” This does not mean that the Galileans spoke a different language from the people of Jerusalem, since both were Hebrews, but that every province and region has its own peculiarities and cannot avoid its native manner of speech.

Thus, in the Acts of the Apostles, when those upon whom the Holy Spirit had rested were speaking in the languages of all nations, among the others who had come from different regions of the world, those who lived in Judea are also reported to have said: “Look, are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we each hear our own language in which we were born?” (Acts II).

And Peter, speaking to the brothers in Jerusalem, said: “It has become known to all who live in Jerusalem” (Acts I), so that that field was called in their language *Achaeldama*. Why “in their language,” unless the same name was pronounced differently by them—that is, by the people of Jerusalem—and differently by the Galileans? [Col. 0402B]

But he began to curse and swear, saying, “I do not know this man whom you are talking about.” And immediately the rooster crowed again. Scripture commonly signifies the mysteries of events by the condition of the times. Thus Peter, who denied at midnight, repented at the crowing of the rooster. After the Lord’s resurrection, in the light of day, he likewise professed three times that he loved the one whom he had denied three times (John XXI).

For what he had mistakenly forgotten in the darkness, he corrected by remembering the light that was already hoped for; and, having obtained the presence of that same true light, he completely restored everything that he had altered. I think this rooster should be understood as some teacher who awakens us when we lie fallen and rebukes us when we are drowsy, saying: “Awake, righteous people, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV).

And Peter remembered the word that Jesus had said to him: “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times,” and he began to weep. How harmful are the conversations of the wicked! Peter himself, among unbelievers, denied knowing even the man whom, among his fellow disciples, he had already confessed to be the Son of God.

Yet, while he remained in the courtyard of Caiaphas, he could not practice repentance. He went outside, as the other evangelists relate (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV; Luke XXII), so that, separated from the council of the impious, he might wash away the defilement of his fearful denial with free-flowing tears.

And immediately, in the morning, the chief priests, together with the elders and scribes and the entire council, held a council, bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate. He was led not only to Pilate but also to Herod, so that both might mock the Lord.

And observe the priests’ eagerness in evil. They stayed awake all night in order to commit murder, and they handed him over to Pilate bound. For they had this custom: whoever they had condemned to death, they handed over to the judge bound. Nevertheless, it should be noted that they did not bind him for the first time then. Rather, as John makes clear, they bound him immediately after seizing him at night in the garden [Col. 0402D], and thus brought him first to Annas.

And Pilate questioned him: “Are you the king of the Jews?” Since Pilate asks about no other charge except whether he is the king of the Jews, the Jews are convicted of impiety, because they could not find even a false accusation to bring against the Savior.

But he answered him, “You say so.” He answered in such a way that he spoke the truth while leaving no opening for his words to be turned into slander. Observe that he answered Pilate, who was passing sentence unwillingly, to some extent, but refused to answer the priests and rulers, judging them unworthy of his words.

But Pilate again questioned him, saying, “Do you answer nothing? See how many charges they bring against you.” But Jesus answered nothing further. The one who condemns Jesus is a pagan, but he lays the responsibility upon the Jewish people: “See how many charges they bring against you.” Jesus did not wish to answer anything further, lest, by clearing away the charge, he should be released by the governor and the benefit of the cross be postponed [Col. 0403A].

But the chief priests incited the crowd so that he would release Barabbas to them instead. Their petition, which they obtained with such effort, clings to the Jews to this day. For when they were given a choice, they chose a robber instead of Jesus, a murderer instead of the Savior, and a taker of life instead of the giver of life. They therefore deservedly lost salvation and life, and subjected themselves so completely to robberies and seditions that they lost both their homeland and kingdom, which they loved more than Christ, nor have they deserved to recover to this day the freedom—whether of soul or of body—that they sold.

But Pilate again answered and said to them, “What then do you want me to do with the king of the Jews?” They cried out again, “Crucify him.” But Pilate said to them, “What evil has he done?”

Pilate offered many opportunities for releasing the Savior. First, he set a robber beside the righteous man; then he asked, “What then do you want me to do with the king of the Jews?” When they answered, “Let him be crucified” [Col. 0403B], he did not immediately agree. Rather, following the prompting of his wife, who, as Matthew writes, had sent him a message: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man” (Matt. XXVII), he himself also answered, “What evil has he done?” By saying this, Pilate acquitted Jesus.

But they shouted even more loudly, “Crucify him,” so that what had been said in the twenty-first psalm might be fulfilled: “Many dogs surround me; the assembly of the wicked has besieged me”; and that saying of Jeremiah: “My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest; they raised their voice against me” (Jer. XXXII).

Isaiah also agrees with this judgment: “I waited for them to execute judgment, but they committed iniquity, not justice, but a cry” (Isa. V).

But Pilate, wishing to satisfy the people, released Barabbas to them and handed Jesus over, scourged, to be crucified. Jesus is to be understood as having been scourged by Pilate himself, and by no one else. For John writes plainly: “Again they all cried out, saying, ‘Not this man, but Barabbas.’ Now Barabbas was a robber. Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him” (John XIX).

After this he adds: “And the soldiers, weaving a crown of thorns, placed it on his head,” and the rest. He is believed to have done this, and to have handed him over to the soldiers to be mocked, so that, satisfied with his punishments and insults, the Jews would cease thirsting for his death.

This happened so that, because it was written, “Many are the scourges of sinners” (Ps. XXXI), we might, after he was scourged, be freed from blows, as Scripture says: “The scourge will not approach your dwelling” (Ps. XC).

But the soldiers led him into the courtyard of the praetorium, summoned the entire cohort, clothed him in purple, placed a crown of thorns upon him, and began to greet him: “Hail, king of the Jews.” Since the soldiers knew that he had been called king of the Jews and that the scribes and priests had brought against him the charge that he was claiming authority over the Israelite people, they did this in mockery: they stripped him of his former garments, clothed him in purple, the color worn by ancient kings [Col. 0403D], placed a crown of thorns upon him instead of a diadem, gave him a reed instead of a royal scepter, as Matthew writes (Matt. XXVII), and worshiped him as though he were a king.

We should understand all these things mystically. For just as Caiaphas said, “It is necessary that one man should die for all” (John XI), without knowing what he was saying, so also whatever these men did, although they acted with another intention, nevertheless bestowed mysteries upon us who believe.

It should be noted that, where Mark says, “And they clothed him in purple” (Mark XV), Matthew writes: “And stripping him, they wrapped him in a scarlet cloak” (Matt. XXVII). It is understood that what Matthew says—“They wrapped him in a scarlet cloak”—is what Mark expressed by saying, “They clothed him in purple.”

For that scarlet cloak was used by the mockers in place of royal purple. It was a kind of red purple, very similar to scarlet dye. It may also be that Mark mentioned the purple color that the cloak had, even though the cloak itself was scarlet [Col. 0404A].

Mystically, therefore, the purple in which the Lord was clothed signifies his own flesh, which he exposed to sufferings. Concerning it, the preceding prophecy had said: “Why then are your garments red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isa. LXIII).

In the crown that he wore, the acceptance of our sins is shown, for the sake of which he deigned to become mortal, in accordance with the testimony given to him by his precursor: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

For the Lord himself testifies that thorns are customarily placed as a sign of sins, when he said to the first-formed man after his fall into sin: “Your land will bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). This plainly means: “Your conscience will not cease producing for you the prickings and stings of vices.”

But according to Luke’s Gospel, the Lord is clothed in a white garment before Herod (Luke XXIII), whereas in the other evangelists he is said to have been mocked by Pilate’s soldiers in a scarlet or purple garment. When the two accounts are brought together, one expresses the innocence and chastity of the humanity he assumed, while the other expresses the truth of the Passion, through which he was to reach the glory of the immortal kingdom.

For just as purple imitates the color of the blood poured out for us, so it also signifies the royal garment of the kingdom into which he entered after the Passion and which he opened for us to enter. But since the Apostle said, “As many as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III), and Isaiah says to the Lord concerning all the elect, “You will clothe yourself with them as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX), the whole multitude of his elect—divided into venerable martyrs and the rest of the faithful—can most fittingly be signified by both garments of the Lord. He is clothed in white when he is surrounded by the pure confession of the righteous; he is clothed in purple or scarlet when he rejoices in the triumph of victorious martyrs [Col. 0404B].

And they struck his head with a reed, spat upon him, and, bending their knees, worshiped him. What the soldiers of Pilate did then, the heretics and pagans—soldiers, in truth, of the devil—do even now.

Because God is the head of Christ (I Cor. XI), they strike his head who deny that he is truly God. And because Scripture is commonly written with a reed, they strike Christ’s head as though with a reed when, contradicting his divinity, they attempt to confirm their error by the authority of sacred Scripture.

They spit in his face who, in the madness of an inwardly blind mind, reject his presence with words conceived to curse him and deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.

The soldiers worshiped him in mockery, as though he had falsely claimed to be God. But there are people today, displaying a more grievous madness, who worship him with firm faith as the true God, yet immediately despise his words as though they were fables through their perverse actions and place his promises of the kingdom far below temporal enticements.

And they lead him out to crucify him. And they compel a certain passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming from the countryside, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross.

This Simon appears to have been a person of considerable reputation at that time, since his sons too are identified by name as though they were already known to everyone. But we must take care lest anyone think there is a contradiction in the fact that John writes that the Lord himself carried his cross (John XIX), while the other evangelists report that this Simon of Cyrene carried it (Matt. XXVII; Mark XV; Luke XXIII).

For it was first carried by the Lord and afterward imposed upon Simon to carry, when they happened to encounter him as they were going out. This accords very fittingly with the order of the mystery, because he himself suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps (I Pet. II).

And because this Simon is said not to have been a man of Jerusalem but a Cyrenian—for Cyrene is a city of Libya, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles [Acts II]—the peoples of the Gentiles are rightly signified through him. Once strangers and foreigners to the covenants, they are now, through obedience, fellow citizens and members of God’s household (Eph. II), and, as it is said elsewhere, “heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII).

Accordingly, Simon is appropriately interpreted as “obedient,” and Cyrene as “heir.” Nor should it be passed over that this same Simon is reported to have come from the countryside. In Greek, “countryside” is called *pagos*. Hence we call “pagans” those whom we see as alien to the city of God and, as it were, lacking the civilized manner of life.

But Simon, coming out from the countryside, carries the cross after Jesus when the people of the nations, abandoning pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s Passion.

And they bring him to Golgotha, a place which is interpreted as “the place of the skull.” Outside the city gate are places where the heads of the condemned are cut off, and they took their name from skulls—that is, from those who had been beheaded.

The Lord was crucified there for this reason: so that, where previously there had been a field of the condemned, the standards of martyrdom might be erected. And just as he became a curse for us through the cross, and was scourged and crucified, so, for the salvation of all, he is crucified as though guilty among the guilty (Gal. III) [Col. 0405B].

And they gave him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he did not accept it. God speaks to Jerusalem: “I planted you as my true vineyard; how have you become a bitter vine of another kind?” (Jer. II; Isa. V). The bitter vine produced bitter wine, which the Lord Jesus was offered, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LVIII).

When it says, “And he did not accept it,” or, according to Matthew, “When he had tasted it, he would not drink” (Matt. XXVII), this indicates that he indeed tasted the bitterness of death for us, but rose again on the third day.

When Mark says, “He did not accept it,” this is understood to mean, “He did not accept it in order to drink it.” He tasted it, as Matthew testifies. Why, then, does Matthew say, “He would not drink,” while Mark says, “He did not accept it”? Mark has remained silent about the fact that he tasted it.

But what Mark calls “wine mixed with myrrh” should also be understood as what Matthew said was mixed with gall. For he used “gall” to signify bitterness, and wine mixed with myrrh is extremely bitter; although it is possible that the wine was made extremely bitter by both gall and myrrh [Col. 0405C].

And crucifying him, they divided his garments, casting lots over them to determine what each should take. John the Evangelist explains this more fully: namely, that the soldiers divided the other things into four parts, according to their number, but cast lots for the tunic, which was seamless, woven from above throughout (John XIX). The Lord’s four-part garment represented his four-part Church, spread throughout the whole world—which consists of four regions of the earth—and distributed equally, that is, harmoniously, among all those regions. But that tunic, assigned by lot, signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of charity. For if, according to the Apostle, charity both has the more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and is above all commandments (Ephesians III), then the garment by which it is signified is rightly said to have been woven from above. And what is commended by the casting of lots except the grace of God [Col. 0405D]? For thus it reaches all in one, when the lot is pleasing to everyone, because the grace of God likewise reaches all in unity. And when the lot is cast, the matter is yielded not to anyone’s person or merits, but to God’s hidden judgment.

And because, as the Apostle says, “our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be abolished, that we should no longer serve sin” (Romans VII), as long as our works are engaged in abolishing the body of sin, and as long as the outward man is being corrupted so that the inward man may be renewed day by day (II Corinthians IV), it is the time of the cross. These too are indeed good works, yet still laborious; their reward is rest. But for this reason it is said, “rejoicing in hope” (Romans XII), so that we may carry out our work amid labors with gladness, in expectation of the rest to come.

This gladness is signified by the breadth of the cross, in the transverse beam where the hands are fastened. By the hands we understand works; by the breadth, the gladness of the one who works, because sadness causes narrowness. By the height, to which the head is joined, we understand the expectation of reward from the height of God’s justice, who will render to each according to his works (Matthew XVI)—eternal life to those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption. Thus the length, by which the whole body is extended, likewise signifies perseverance; hence those who endure are called long-suffering. But the depth, which is fixed in the earth, prefigures the secret of the mystery. You remember, unless I am mistaken, that the Apostle’s words are explained in this representation of the cross, where he says: “Rooted and grounded in charity, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Ephesians III).

It was now the third hour, and they crucified him. Some think that the Lord was indeed crucified at the third hour, while darkness came from the sixth hour until the ninth, so that the three hours from his crucifixion until the darkness appeared are understood to have elapsed. This could certainly be understood quite correctly, unless John said [Col. 0406B] that, at about the sixth hour, Pilate sat upon the tribunal at the place called Lithostrotos (John XIX), in Hebrew Gabbatha. For it follows: “It was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour,” and he says to the Jews, “Behold your king,” and so forth.

If, then, at about the sixth hour, while Pilate was sitting upon the tribunal, he was handed over to the Jews to be crucified, how was he crucified at the third hour, as some have thought because they did not understand Mark’s words? Mark had already said: “Crucifying him, they divided his garments.” If, therefore, he intended to recall the time when this event occurred, it would have been sufficient to say, “It was the third hour.” Why did he add, “And they crucified him,” unless he wished, by recapitulating, to signify something that would be discovered when Scripture was read in those times when it was known throughout all the churches at what hour the Lord was hung upon the wood? Thus either an error in this matter could be corrected or a falsehood refuted.

But because he knew that the Lord was crucified by the soldiers, not by the Jews, he wished secretly to show that those who cried out for him to be crucified had crucified him more than those who, according to their office, rendered service to their ruler. It is therefore understood to have been the third hour when the Jews cried out that the Lord should be crucified. And it is most truthfully shown that they crucified him at the time when they cried out, especially since they did not wish to appear to have done this, and for that reason had handed him over to Pilate, as their words sufficiently indicate according to John. Thus what they most emphatically did not wish to appear to have done, Mark shows that they did at the third hour, most truthfully indicating that the Jews’ tongue was more the murderer of the Lord than the soldiers’ hands.

And there was an inscription of the charge against him: “The King of the Jews.” The inscription placed above his cross, on which was written “The King of the Jews,” showed that even by killing him they could not bring it about that they would not have him as king—the one who would repay them according to their deeds with the clearest and most exalted power. Hence it is sung in the Psalm: “Yet I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Psalm II). And fittingly, since he is both King and Priest, when he offered to the Father the excellent sacrifice of his flesh upon the altar of the cross, he also displayed by the inscription the dignity of kingship with which he was endowed, so that he might make known to all who wished to read—that is, to hear and believe—that through the cross’s instrument of execution he had not lost his dominion, but rather confirmed and strengthened it [Col. 0406D].

And they crucify with him two robbers, one at his right and the other at his left. The robbers who were crucified on either side of the Lord signify those who, under faith in and confession of Christ, undertake either the struggle of martyrdom or any discipline of stricter self-restraint. But whoever undertakes these things solely for eternal and heavenly glory is surely represented by the merit and faith of the robber on the right; whereas those who renounce the world either with a view to human praise or with any less worthy intention rightly imitate the mind and actions of the blasphemer and the robber on the left.

The Apostle speaks of either kind: “If I hand over my body so that I may burn, if I give all my possessions as food to the poor, if I appear to perform many other works of piety or to have received gifts of spiritual grace, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Corinthians XIII). Blessed, however, are those who leave what is theirs for the Lord and for the Gospel: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V; Luke VI).

Likewise, the chief priests, mocking him, said to one another with the scribes: “He saved others; he cannot save himself.” Even unwillingly, the scribes and priests confess that he saved others. Therefore your own sentence condemns you: for the one who saved others could certainly have saved himself, if he had wished.

“Christ, the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe.” A deceitful promise. What is greater: to come down alive from the cross, or to rise dead from the tomb? He rose, and you do not believe; therefore, even if he had come down from the cross, you likewise would not believe.

And those who were crucified with him reviled him. How did those who were crucified with him revile him? According to Luke’s testimony, one of them reviled him (Luke XXIII), while the other restrained him and believed in God. We must understand that Matthew and Mark, briefly touching upon this passage, used the plural number for the singular, just as in the Epistle to the Hebrews we read the plural expression, “They closed the mouths of lions” (Hebrews XI), although only Daniel is understood to be signified (Daniel VI). Likewise, “They were sawn apart” is said in the plural, although the tradition concerns Isaiah alone.

What, for example, is more commonplace than for someone to say, “The peasants insult me,” even if only one insults him? What Luke makes clear concerning one would be contradictory only if they had said that both robbers reviled the Lord, since one could not then be understood under the plural number. But when it is said “robbers,” or “those who were crucified with him,” and “both” is not added, this could be said not only if both had done it, but also because one had done it, since the customary manner of speech could signify him by the plural number.

According to Luke’s testimony, one robber blasphemes the Lord, saying, “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us”; but the other rebukes him with a fitting denunciation and entreats the Lord with faithful supplication, saying, “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” We see this same thing happening in the Church to this day, when true and false Christians alike, touched by the afflictions of the world: those who carry the mysteries of the Lord’s passion with a feigned disposition wish to be delivered by the Lord into the joys of the present life; but those who, with a sincere intention, glory with the Apostle in nothing except the cross of our Lord (Galatians VI), desire to be rescued from present hardships in such a way that they commend their spirit into the hands of its Creator and long to share with him in the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, rightly was the one who prayed to the Lord with doubtful faith utterly disregarded by the Lord and judged unworthy of any reply. But the prayers of the one who sought eternal salvation for himself the Lord soon deigned to receive with gracious hearing. For whoever, placed amid tribulations, seeks from the Lord only temporal consolations deprives himself alike of temporal and eternal joys. But those who truly sigh for the good things of their heavenly homeland arrive at them without any doubt, through Christ’s mercy [Col. 0407D].

And when the sixth hour had come, darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour. The clearest light of the world withdrew its rays, lest it see the Lord hanging there, or lest the impious, while blaspheming, enjoy its light. It should also be noted that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour—that is, when the sun was withdrawing from the center of the world—but at dawn, that is, when the sun had already risen, he celebrated the mysteries of his resurrection. By the timing he signified what he displayed through the accomplishment of his work, because he died for our sins and rose for our justification (Romans IV).

For when Adam sinned, it is written that he heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the breeze after noon (Genesis III). “After noon”: with the light of faith already declining; “toward the breeze”: with the fervor of charity growing cool. He was heard walking because he had withdrawn from the sinful human being. The order of reason—or rather, of divine mercy—therefore required that at the same hour when he had then closed the gate against Adam in his transgression, the Lord should now open the gate of paradise to the repentant robber; and at the hour when the first Adam, by sinning, had brought death into this world, the second Adam should at that same hour destroy death by dying (I Corinthians XV).

And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani,” which is translated, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” He used the beginning of the twenty-first Psalm; the words found in the middle of the verse, “Look upon me,” are superfluous. For in Hebrew it reads, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Do not be surprised at the humility of the words or the complaints of one forsaken when, knowing that he bears the form of a servant, you see the scandal of the cross. Just as hunger, thirst, and weariness were not proper to divinity but bodily sufferings, so also the words “Why have you forsaken me?” belonged properly to the bodily voice, since by nature the body ordinarily does not wish to be deprived of the life joined to it.

Although the Savior himself was saying this, he was properly displaying the weakness of the body while remaining the power and wisdom of God. As a human being, therefore, he speaks, carrying our own emotions: as a human being, he is troubled; as a human being, he weeps; as a human being, he is crucified.

And some of those standing nearby, hearing this, said: “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” Not all of them, but some—whom I think were Roman soldiers—who did not understand the proper character of the Hebrew speech, but, from his saying “Eli, Eli,” thought that Elijah had been invoked by him. If, however, you wish to understand that it was Jews who said this, then they too were acting according to their customary manner, calumniating the Lord in his weakness because he was imploring Elijah’s help [Col. 0408C].

But one ran and filled a sponge with vinegar, and, placing it around a reed, gave him a drink, saying: “Let be; let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.” John explains more fully why vinegar was given to the Lord as a drink, saying: “After this, Jesus, knowing that all things had now been accomplished, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, ‘I thirst.’ Now a vessel full of vinegar had been placed there. So they, putting a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop, offered it to his mouth” (John XIX).

He therefore saw that everything which had to happen had been accomplished before he received the vinegar and gave up his spirit. And so that this too might be fulfilled—“In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm LXVIII)—he said, “I thirst.” As though he were saying: “You have performed this service; give what you are.” For the Jews themselves were the vinegar, degenerate from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets, as though from a full vessel filled with the iniquity of this world, possessing hearts like a sponge, deceitful through hiding places that were, in a certain sense, cavernous and twisted [Col. 0408D].
