Because hyssop is a lowly herb and cleanses the breast, we appropriately understand the hyssop around which they placed the sponge full of vinegar as the humility of Christ himself, which they surrounded—and thought they had ensnared. Hence the Psalm says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Psalm L). For we are cleansed by Christ’s humility, because unless he had humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians II), his blood would certainly not have been poured out for the remission of sins, that is, for our cleansing.

By the reed on which the sponge was placed, Scripture is signified, since Scripture was being fulfilled by this event. Just as a language is called Greek, Latin, or any other language to signify the sound expressed by the tongue, so a letter written with a reed can be called a reed. But whereas we very commonly call the sounds of the human voice “languages,” to call Scripture a “reed” is less customary and therefore more richly figured mystically.

But Jesus, uttering a loud cry, gave up his spirit. What the Lord said with this loud voice Luke clearly indicates, saying: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; and, he says, having said this, he expired (Luke XXIII). But what John writes—that when Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, gave up his spirit (John XIX)—means that between the words “It is finished” and “And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit,” that loud cry was uttered, which John omitted but the other three evangelists recorded [Col. 0409A].

And the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. The veil of the temple is torn so that the ark of the covenant and all the mysteries of the law that had been covered might appear and pass over to the people of the nations. Earlier it had been said: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm LXXV). But now: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory,” he says, “over all the earth” (Psalm LVI). And earlier in the Gospel he said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matthew X); but after his passion: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations” (Matthew XXVIII).

But when the centurion who stood opposite him saw that he had expired while crying out in this way, he said: “Truly this man was the Son of God.” The evident cause of the centurion’s miracle is explained: seeing the Lord expire in this manner—that is, give up his spirit—he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God,” for no one has power to give up his spirit except the one who is the Creator of souls.

This too should be considered: the centurion, standing before the cross, confesses the true Son of God in the very scandal of the passion, while Arius proclaims a creature within the Church. Therefore, fittingly, the faith of the Church is represented by the centurion; when the veil of the heavenly mysteries was opened through the Lord’s death, the Church immediately affirmed Jesus, both truly a just human being and truly the Son of God, while the synagogue remained silent.

There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joseph, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him. He calls James “the younger,” James the son of Alphaeus, who was also called the brother of the Lord because he was the son of Mary, the Lord’s maternal aunt, whom John mentions in his Gospel, saying: “There stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Cleophas” (John XIX).

He appears to call her “Mary of Cleophas” either from her father or from her kinship. James was called “the younger” to distinguish him from James the elder, namely, the son of Zebedee, who was called and chosen by the Lord among the first apostles.

It was the custom of the Jews—and according to the ancient practice of the nations it was not counted as blameworthy—for women to provide their teachers with food and clothing from their own resources. Because this could cause scandal among the nations, Paul recalls that he rejected it: “Do we not have the power to lead about women who are sisters, as also the other Apostles do?” (Romans XV; I Corinthians IX). They ministered to the Lord from their own resources, so that he might reap their material things, while they reaped spiritual things. This was not because the Lord, the Creator of creatures, needed food, but so that he might show the pattern for teachers: that they ought to be content with food and clothing received from their disciples [Col. 0409D].

But let us see what sort of companions he had: Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons; Mary of James; the mother of Joseph, his maternal aunt; and the other women whom we read of in the remaining Gospels (Mark XVI; Luke VIII).

And when it had already become evening, since it was the Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a noble decurion, came. A decurion is so called because he belonged to the order of the curia and administered the duties of the curia; he was also commonly called a curial because he managed civic obligations. Arimathea itself is the city of Ramathaim, belonging to Elkanah and Samuel, in the region of Thamnitica, near Diospolis.

“Parasceve” is Greek; in Latin it is called “preparation.” By this name the Jews who lived among the Greeks called the sixth day of the week, because on that day they used to prepare what was necessary for the Sabbath rest, in accordance with what was once commanded concerning the manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much,” and so forth (Exodus XVI) [Col. 0410A].

Since, therefore, humanity was created on the sixth day and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh day the Creator rested from his work (Genesis II)—whence he also willed this day to be called Sabbath, that is, rest—it was fitting that the Savior, crucified on that same sixth day, should fulfill the hidden mystery of humanity’s restoration. Therefore, after receiving the vinegar, he said: “It is finished,” that is: “The whole work of the sixth day, which I undertook for the world’s restoration, has now been completed.”

But on the Sabbath, resting in the tomb, he awaited the coming of the resurrection, which was to take place on the eighth day. Here an example shines forth both of our devotion and of our blessed reward: in this sixth age of the world, we must suffer for the Lord and, as it were, be crucified to the world. But in the seventh age—that is, when one pays the debt of death—the bodies should remain in the tombs, while the souls remain with the Lord in hidden peace, and after good works they should rest, until at last, with the coming of the eighth age, the bodies themselves, glorified by the resurrection, receive with their souls entry into the incorruptibility of the eternal inheritance [Col. 0410B].

“Joseph of Arimathea came,” he says, “a noble decurion, who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God. And he boldly went in to Pilate and requested the body of Jesus.” This Joseph is praised as having been a man of great dignity in the world, but of greater merit before God. For it was fitting that the one who would bury the Lord’s body should be such a man: one who would be worthy of such a ministry through the justice of his merits, and who, through the nobility of secular power, would be able to obtain the means to perform it. For no unknown or insignificant person could approach the governor and obtain the body of the Crucified.

Joseph bought a linen cloth, and, taking him down, wrapped him in the linen cloth. The Lord’s simple burial condemns the extravagance of the rich, who cannot be without riches even in their tombs. But according to the spiritual understanding, we can take this to mean that the Lord’s body should be wrapped not in gold, gems, or silk, but in pure linen. It also signifies that the one who wraps Jesus in a clean linen cloth receives him with a pure mind.

From this the custom of the Church arose that the altar sacrifice should be celebrated not on silk or dyed cloth, but on earthly linen, just as the Lord’s body was buried in a clean linen cloth, according to what we read in the pontifical records was established by blessed Pope Sylvester.

And he placed him in a tomb that had been hewn from rock, and rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Those who in our time came from Jerusalem to Britain report concerning the Lord’s tomb that it was a round chamber hewn from the underlying rock, of such height that a person standing inside could scarcely touch the ceiling with an outstretched hand. It had an entrance on the eastern side, and that great stone was rolled against it and placed there.

In the northern part of this tomb was the sepulchre itself—that is, the place of the Lord’s body—made from the same rock. It was seven feet long and projected three palms above the rest of the pavement. This place, namely, was open not from above but entirely from the southern side, through which the body was brought in. The color of the same tomb and burial chamber is said to be a mixture of red and white [Col. 0410D].

But Mary Magdalene and Mary of Joseph were watching where he was placed. In Luke we read that all his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him (Luke XXIII). After these acquaintances of Jesus, once his body had been laid down, returned to their homes, only the women who loved him more closely followed the funeral and took care to see how he was placed, so that at the proper time they might offer him the service of their devotion.

Even to this day, holy women do the same on the day of the Preparation, that is, the day of preparation, when humble souls—who, the more conscious they are of their own weakness, burn with the greater love for the Savior—carefully follow the traces of his passion in this world, in which future rest is being prepared. And if they are perhaps able to imitate him, they examine with devout attentiveness in what order that same passion was completed.

# HOMILY LIV

[Col. 0411A]

## MATTHEW VIII

At that time, when Jesus had entered the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves; but he was sleeping. And his disciples approached and awakened him, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing,” and so forth.

When the Lord entered the boat, his disciples followed him—not weaklings, but firm and steadfast in faith, meek and devout, despising the world; not double-minded, but single-hearted. They followed him, therefore, not merely by tracing his steps, but rather by accompanying his holiness and pursuing his righteousness.

And behold, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. After he had displayed many great and wondrous things on land, he crossed over to the sea so that there too he might demonstrate still more excellent works, in order to show to everyone that he was Lord both of land and of sea [Col. 0411B]. He caused the sea to be troubled, stirred up the winds, and aroused the waves. Why? So that he might send the disciples into fear, that they might seek his help, and that he might manifest his power to those who asked.

That storm did not arise of itself, but obeyed the power of the one commanding—the one who brings forth the winds from his treasuries, who established the sand as the boundary of the sea. For he said to it: “Thus far you shall come and shall not pass beyond, but your waves shall be broken within yourself.” At his command and order, therefore, the storm arose upon the sea, for the reasons mentioned above.

A great storm arose, not a small one, so that a great work, not a small one, might be displayed. And the more violently the waves rushed upon the boat, the more fear disturbed the disciples, so that they might desire all the more intensely the Savior’s miraculous power to deliver them.

But the Lord was sleeping. O wondrous and astonishing reality! He who never sleeps is sleeping; he who governs heaven and earth is sleeping; he who neither sleeps nor slumbers is said to be sleeping. [Col. 0411C] He was sleeping in body, but awake in divinity; he was sleeping in body, but troubling the sea, raising up the waves, and terrifying the apostles, in order to display his power. He was sleeping in body, just as he sat tired and weary from his journey beside the well, showing that he truly bore a human body, which he had assumed in its corruptible condition. In that body he was sleeping, but in divinity he stirred up the sea and then again calmed it.

He therefore slept in body so that he might rouse the apostles and make them awaken. Above all, however, let us not sleep in mind, nor in understanding or judgment, but strive to keep watch at all times, to exult in the Lord, and to seek salvation from him. For he who was sleeping in body speaks that holy word: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs V, 2).

The disciples approached him and awakened him, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” They had been so terrified by fear and almost beside themselves that they rushed upon him and, rather than making their request modestly or gently, awakened him turbulently, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.”

O blessed ones, O true disciples of God! You have the Lord and Savior with you, and you fear danger. Life is with you, and you are anxious about death. Trembling before the one who troubles the sea, you awaken its Creator as though, while his body slept, he could not calm or quiet the waves.

But what do these most beloved disciples answer? “We are still little ones,” they say, “weak and not yet strong; therefore we fear, therefore we tremble. We have not yet seen the cross; the Lord’s passion and resurrection have not yet strengthened us; nor have we seen the ascension into heaven or the descent of the holy Spirit, the Paraclete, when he was sent. For this reason we waver in weakness; we bear the Lord’s rebuke for our small faith, and we gladly tolerate it and willingly endure it.”

Hence also now, when the Lord says: “Why are you troubled, you of little faith? Why do you have no strength? Why do you not maintain confidence and trust within yourselves? Even if death had rushed upon you, ought you not to have endured it with the greatest steadfastness?” Strength is necessary for everything that happens, for every danger or tribulation, even to the departure of the soul.

Likewise, strength of spirit must be maintained against pleasures, riches, and earthly honors, so that you may neither be lifted up, O human being, nor raised into pride; so that you may not despise your enemies, nor scorn the humble, nor forget the Lord, nor abandon the Creator, nor prove ungrateful.

If, then, strength is necessary in need and danger, so that you may endure everything manfully with faith, much more is strength necessary against pleasures and luxuries, as has been said, lest you fall into the devil’s trap. Why, then, are you troubled, you of little faith, if you have recognized that I am powerful upon the earth? Why do you not believe that I am also powerful upon the sea? If you have truly accepted that I am God, the Creator of all things, why do you not believe that I have in my power the things that were made by me? Why, then, did you doubt, you of little faith?

The one who believes little will be rebuked, and the one who believes nothing will be despised. Those weak in faith will be corrected; those wholly alien to faith will be punished. Such were the Jews and the pagans, and therefore they perished in their miseries. Such also are the heretics, and therefore they will be condemned on the day of judgment [Col. 0412B].

Then he rose and commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm arose. It was written: “And the Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a powerful man overcome by wine. And he struck all his enemies from behind” (Psalm LXXVII). Now, rising, he commands the winds and the sea as Creator, as their powerful Lord. Before the disciples he first commanded the winds and the sea, so that those who were coming might be strengthened in faith. The hidden power of his divinity commanded and rebuked it—or rather, ruled and calmed it—according to what someone said: “Power calmed the sea.”

He therefore commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm arose. From a great wind and a great storm, with the sea troubled and swelling, a great calm was produced. For it is fitting that this great one should do great and wondrous things. Therefore, having just before girded himself with great power, he magnificently troubled the depths of the sea; and now, again showing therein the magnificence of his power, he commanded a great calm to arise [Col. 0412C].

All this was done so that those who had been excessively troubled might be magnificently gladdened and rejoice. Through all these things the Lord gave us a figure and an image of instruction, so that in every disturbance and insult we might maintain patience, remain steadfast, and not abandon faith.

And if this whole world should seethe like the sea and rise up in fury; if all the winds and whirlwinds of demons should rage from every side; if, as we have said, every storm of the sea—that is, every principality and power of the world—should be stirred up; if they should foam or rage in the swelling of anger against the saints; and if they should still lift themselves up as far as heaven, like storms of the sea, maligning, stirring up plots and roars against any one of you—do not fear, do not be troubled, do not tremble, do not fail.

All of you who sail with the Lord in the boat of faith—all of you who, with the Lord, float above this wave-filled world in this most holy boat of the Church—even if the Lord himself is sleeping, awaiting your patience and endurance in a peaceful sleep, or enduring the repentance and conversion of the impious, approach him courageously, persisting in prayers, and say with the prophet: “Awake; why do you sleep, O Lord? Awake, and do not reject us forever” (Psalm XLIII). And again: “Awake, O Lord; help us and redeem us for the sake of your name” (Psalm XXVI).

And he himself, rising, rebukes the winds—these spirits of the air, the demons. For they stir up the storms of the sea; that is, they arouse the bitter and swollen waves of the rulers of this world, to send persecutions against all the saints and heap insults upon the faithful. The Lord rebukes and threatens them all, calms everything, and brings about a great calm around body and spirit, peace for the Church, and serenity for the world.

For how often have the counsels of unbelievers been stirred up against the true faith and the steadfast Church—at times those of pagans, at times those of heretics—just as the waves of the sea often rushed in, threatening and terrifying, while the rulers of this world thought that they could utterly destroy the children of the Church. But the Lord rose, rebuked the winds of the demons, made all the bold adversaries of the faith vanish, and gave his Church great peace and tranquility [Col. 0413A].

The men in the boat were amazed. Which men? Those, namely, who had this boat. Do not suppose that by the name “boat” the apostles are meant here. Nowhere do we find the Lord’s disciples called this, except through error; they are always called either apostles or disciples. Those men, then, were amazed—the men who walked with him, whose boat it was, who were crossing over in that same boat. They were amazed.

And it was worthy of wonder [Col. 0413B] that the sea, stirred up from its depths, was calmed; that its swelling waves were quieted; that the thirsting winds were restrained. They were amazed, saying: “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” They do not ask, “What sort of one is he to whom the sea and winds obey?” but say, “What sort of man is this?”—that is, how great, how strong, how powerful, how mighty! “What sort of man is this”—greater than Moses, more powerful than Elijah! Those two—one of whom, after striking the sea with a piece of wood, made it part with difficulty; the other, [lacuna] crossed the Jordan—this man, by a single word, commands those who have no words, and they obey him.

Those who have no hearing obey; those who lack reason and understanding bow before the one who commands; those who possess neither speech nor, as we have said, language obey him in the very substance in which they exist, move according to their nature, and serve his command—to the confusion of mortals and the condemnation of corruptible beings. He commands the sea [Col. 0413D], and it does not despise him; he speaks to the winds and storms, and at once they are restrained; he commands every creature, and none exceeds his command. Yet one class of human beings [Col. 0413C]—and that class which, made in the likeness of God, ought to be honored, to which speech and reason have been given—these alone resist him; these alone are disobedient; these alone despise him. Therefore these alone will be condemned in the judgment and punished by justice, as worse than many animals, or than those things in this world that are without spirit and soul.

Those men, then, were amazed because he had restrained the sea and the winds had been calmed. Let us also be amazed when the Lord displays his kindness and benevolence toward us; when he deigns to save us from dangers; when he frees us from disturbances; when he rescues us from pursuing enemies. Let us wonder, and, wondering, give thanks; let us obey grace; obeying, let us fear; fearing, let us love, so that by him we may become heirs of eternal Love.

They were amazed, saying, “What sort of man is this?” He appears as a human being, yet displays divine power; he is thought to be one of the fleshly, yet he performs great wonders above all fleshly things. He sleeps as a man, yet commands the sea and winds as God; he sits in a boat, yet bends every creature by his command wherever he wills—Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LV. ON THE BIRTHDAY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

### MATTHEW I

“The beginning of the holy Gospel according to Matthew: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham,” etc.

Blessed Matthew the Evangelist, dearly beloved, is not without reason described among the other heavenly living creatures with the face of a man (Ezek. I), because, beginning his Gospel far back among the ancient fathers, he set forth the genealogy of the Lord’s humanity more clearly than the others.

But it must be understood that all these names fully contain within themselves meanings of an allegorical and moral kind. Abraham is interpreted as “father of many nations”; Isaac [Col. 0414A], “joy”; Jacob, “supplanter”; Judah, “confession”; Pharez, “division”; Zarah, “rising”; Esron, “seeing an arrow”; Tamar, “palm.” Aram is understood as “chosen”; Aminadab, “spontaneous people”; Naasson, “a strong diviner”; Salmon, “perceptive.” Boaz means “strength in him”; Rahab, “broad”; Obed, “serving”; Ruth, “hastening.” Jesse means “burning”; David, “strong of hand,” or “desirable”; Solomon, “peaceful”; Uriah, “God is my light”; Bathsheba, “daughter of the oath.” Rehoboam means “breadth of the people”; Abijah, “the Lord is Father”; Asa, “taking away”; Jehoshaphat, “the Lord has judged.” Joram means “exalted”; Uzziah, “strong in the Lord”; Joatham, “perfect”; Ahaz, “grasping.” Hezekiah means “the strength of the Lord”; Manasseh, “forgetful”; Amon, “faithful”; Josiah, “the salvation of the Lord.” Jechoniah means “the preparation of the Lord”; Shealtiel, “my petition is God”; Zerubbabel, “this master”; Abiud, “this is my father.” Eliakim means “the resurrection of God”; Azor, “helped”; Zadok, “just”; Joachim, “my brother.” Eliud means “my God”; Eleazar, “God the helper”; Matthan, “gift”; Jacob [Col. 0414B], “supplanter.” Joseph means “added,” or “increased”; Mary, “illuminating,” or “star of the sea”; Jesus, “savior,” or “saving”; Christ, “anointed.”

Therefore, when Christ our Lord came into the world through these patriarchs, he allegorically performed in himself the office of them all, and in the interpretation of their names signified our salvation.

In Abraham he is the father of all believers, in whom, according to the Apostle, we all cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII). In Isaac he is the joy of all the faithful, concerning whom the angel said: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people” (Luke II). In Jacob he is the supplanter, because he himself disabled and crushed the devil, the destroyer of the human race, and plundered his vessels (Matt. XII; Luke XI). In Judah he is confession, because he himself said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI). In Pharez he is division, because he separates the sheep from the goats—that is, the good from the wicked, the elect from the rejected (Matt. XXV). In Zarah he is the rising, as it is written: “The rising from on high has visited us” (Luke I).

[Col. 0414C] In Tamar he is the palm of victory, as he himself said: “Take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John XVI). In Aram he is the chosen one, of whom the Father speaks: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my chosen one; I have placed my Spirit upon him” (Isa. XLIII). In Aminadab he is the spontaneous people, who voluntarily laid down his life in order to make us a people willing to serve him and acceptable to God (John X). In Naasson he is the diviner—that is, the strong prophet—when he says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, then he will sit to judge the world in righteousness” (Matt. XXV; Ps. XCV).

In Solomon he is the perceptive one—that is, the intellectual one—concerning whom it is written: “But he himself saw their thoughts” (Matt. IX). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings” (Ps. XCIII). And: “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. VII). In Boaz he is strength in himself, because he received strength from no one. Of him it is said: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII); and he himself says in the Gospel: “I will draw all things to myself” (John XII).

In Rahab the breadth [Col. 0414D] of his power is expressed: the whole world cannot contain him, and there will be no end to his kingdom (Dan. VII; Luke I). In Obed he is serving, because he did not come to be served but to serve, taking the form of a servant (Matt. XX). In Ruth he is hastening toward our salvation, for he hastens that all human beings should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II), saying in the Gospel: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. III).

In Jesse he is recognized as burning, as he says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII). And as John says: “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke III). In David he is the desirable one, because he was beautiful in form beyond the sons of men (Ps. XLIV). In the same person he is strong of hand, when, holding a whip of cords in his hand, he drove the crowd of sellers and buyers from the temple (Luke XIX; John II), or when he conquered the devil and crushed our accuser.

In Solomon he is peaceful, as he himself said: “I leave you peace [Col. 0415A]; my peace I give you” (John XIV). And the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II). In Bathsheba he is the son of the oath, concerning whom it is said: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever” (Ps. CIX). In Rehoboam he is the breadth of the people, when he says: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII).

In Abijah he is the Father, the Lord, who says: “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XXIII). In Asa he is the one who takes away, of whom John says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). In Jehoshaphat he is the judge, because he is the judge of the living and the dead (Acts X), as he himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

In Joram he is the exalted one, because he ascended above all the heavens in order to fulfill all things (Eph. IV). And as the Psalmist says: “The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory above the heavens” (Ps. CXII). In Uzziah he is strong in the Lord, because with a strong hand he liberated the captivity [Col. 0415B] of the human race and led it into the heights of heaven (Ps. LXVII; Eph. IV).

In Joatham he is perfect, as he says in the Gospel: “For it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. III). In Ahaz he is the one who grasps, who weighed the heavens with a span and enclosed the earth in a handful (Isa. XL). In Hezekiah he is the strength of the Lord, because, according to the Apostle, “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I).

In Manasseh he is forgetful of iniquity, as it is written: “On whatever day the sinner turns from his iniquity, I will not remember all his iniquities” (Ezek. XVIII). In Amon he is faithful, according to Paul, “so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God” (Heb. II), and according to John, “the faithful witness” (Rev. III). In Josiah he is the salvation of the Lord, because “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel II).

In Jechoniah he is the preparation of the Lord, who says: “If I go and prepare a place for you” (John XVI). In Shealtiel he is “my petition is God,” who says: “Holy Father, preserve those whom you have given me [Col. 0415C]” (John XVII). In Zerubbabel he is the teacher of publicans and sinners, so that he might call them back from the error of their way; and thus, as he himself says: “Do not be called teachers, because your one teacher is Christ” (Matt. XXIII).

In Abiud he is “my father,” because he is the Father and head of all believers (Rom. IV). In Eliakim he is the Lord’s resurrection, as he says: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me will not die forever, but I will raise him up on the last day” (John XI). In Azor he is the one who is helped, as he says: “The one who sent me is with me and has not left me alone” (John VIII). And again: “The works that I do I do not do from myself, but the Father who is with me performs the works” (John XIV).

In Zadok he is just, as it is written: “So that he himself may be just and justify those who are of the faith of Abraham” (Rom. III). In Joachim he is “my brother,” as he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. XII).

In Eliud he is “my God,” because he is God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages, who said on the cross: “Eli, Eli”—that is, “My God, my God” (Matt. XXVII; Ps. XXI). In Eleazar he is “God the helper,” because he is the helper in times of opportunity and in tribulation (Ps. IX), and the protector of all who hope in him (Ps. XVII). [Col. 0415D]

In Matthan he is the gift, because, ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings; and because through him God the Father freely bestowed all gifts (Ps. LXVII; Eph. IV). In Jacob, as we said above, he is the supplanter of the ancient enemy, who gave the faithful power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the strength of the enemy (Luke X).

In Joseph he is increased, to whom the Father gave the nations as his inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession (Ps. II); or he is the increase of eternal life, as he himself said: “I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly” (John X). In the holy and perpetual virgin Mary he is the star of the sea—that is, the light of the world—as he himself says: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII). And John says: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I).

In his proper name, Jesus, he is “saving,” or “savior” [Col. 0416A], as the angel declares when he says: “For he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I). He is likewise called Christ—that is, “anointed”—because God the Father anointed him in his humanity with the oil of gladness (Ps. XLIV), that is, with the anointing of the Holy Spirit, as eternal priest and king. Thus, through the fact that he is Savior, he would save from sins those called Christians after his name; through the fact that he is priest, he would reconcile them to God the Father; and through the fact that he is king, he would place them in the eternal kingdom.

These interpretations of the names are also known, in a moral sense, to pertain in many ways to our edification. Just as Christ everywhere carried out the cause of our salvation, so the names of the patriarchs signify our progress.

In Abraham, we are to become fathers of many virtues and, by right of inheritance, possess an increase of good things. In Isaac, we are to have joy in the Lord and not in the world, according to what he himself said: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). And [Col. 0416B], according to the Apostle: “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Phil. IV).

In Jacob, we are to be the supplanters of our vices and trample carnal desire beneath our feet, with living strength, from the power of the devil. In Judah, according to the Psalmist, we are to go before the face of the Lord in confession and confess his holy name (Ps. XCIV; Ps. CIII). In Pharez, we are to separate ourselves from the ungodly, withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly, and not share in his evil works (II Thess. III).

In Zarah, the true morning star is to arise in our hearts, and the sun of righteousness is to shine everywhere within us (Wis. V); and our light is to shine before human beings, so that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. V). In Esron, we are to be arrows of the Lord’s salvation (II Kings XIII), so that it may be said of us: “The arrows of the mighty are sharp” (Ps. CXIX).

In Tamar, with the palm of victory, we are to overcome the pageants of the devil and the desires of the world, for the sake of him who loved us (I John II). In Aram, we are to be “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation [Col. 0416C], a people for acquisition,” and announce the virtues of him who called us from darkness into his marvelous light (I Pet. II).

In Aminadab, we are to be the Lord’s willing people, for the building up of Christ’s body (Eph. IV). In Naasson, abandoning the divinations of the nations, we are to place our faith in the divine promises. In Salmon, we are to be found perceptive—that is, intellectual—of God’s truth, and doers of it, because it is not the hearers of the law but the doers who will be justified (Rom. II; Jas. I).

In Boaz, according to the Apostle, we are to be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, girding our loins with truth, putting on the breastplate of righteousness, taking up the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. IV). In Rahab, carefully observing the Lord’s exceedingly broad commandment (Ps. CXVIII), we are to love the Lord God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and embrace our neighbor as ourselves [Col. 0416D] (Matt. XXVI; Deut. VI).

In Obed, we are to serve the Lord through the spirit of fear and holy love (Ps. II), so that our service may be reasonable (Rom. XII) and our sacrifice acceptable (Dan. III). In Ruth, we are to hasten to enter that rest—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem—and, while we have time, do good to all (Gal. VI), because here we have no lasting city but seek the one that is to come (Heb. XIII).

In Jesse, we are to offer the incense of our prayers on the altar of our heart to the Lord in a contrite spirit, saying with the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, O Lord” (Ps. CXL). In David, fighting with strong hands against the spiritual Goliath (I Sam. XVII), we are to present our bodies as a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice to God and become a desirable temple for the Holy Spirit (Rom. XII).

In Solomon, as far as depends on us, we are to have peace with all human beings, attending to the Lord’s saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matt. V). In Bathsheba, we are to observe every oath [Col. 0417A], lest we fall through perjury into the devil’s snare (Matt. V; Jas. V).

In Uriah, God is to be our light: following him, we are not to walk in the darkness of death but have the light of life (John VIII). In Rehoboam, though dispersed far and wide throughout the world, we are to have unity of spirit in the bond of peace and charity, professing one God, one faith, and one baptism (Eph. IV), with a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (I Tim. I).

In Abijah, loving one another with brotherly charity (Rom. XII), we are to have one Father, the Lord in heaven, who voluntarily begot us by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of first fruits of his creation (Jas. I); and we are to possess the blessing as an inheritance and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God (Rom. V).

In Asa, we are to remove our members from the mud and dungheap of vices, so that they may not serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, but righteousness unto sanctification (Rom. VI), because God has not called us [Col. 0417B] to uncleanness but to sanctification (I Thess. IV).

In Jehoshaphat, we are to judge rightly without respect of persons, as it is written: “Judge rightly, sons of men” (Ps. LVII); and whatever we want people to do to us, we are to do to them (Matt. VII; Tob. IV), knowing likewise that with whatever measure we measure, it will be measured back to us (Mark IV; Matt. VII; Luke VI).

In Joram, having been made exalted or lifted up in the Lord, we are to seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; we are to think on the things that are above, not on those that are on earth (Col. III), because every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights (Jas. I).

In Uzziah, having been made strong in the Lord, in all our persecutions and tribulations that we endure, we are to take as our example the labor and patience of the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord Jesus. In Joatham, we are to be perfect, as our heavenly Father is perfect [Col. 0417C] (Matt. V), presenting ourselves as an example in all things (Tit. II) and teaching every human being in all wisdom, so that we may present every person perfect (Col. I).

In Ahaz, we are to grasp discipline, lest the Lord become angry and we perish from the righteous way (Ps. II), which is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). In Hezekiah, we are to stand firm in the Lord against our adversary, the devil, who prowls about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (I Pet. V); we are not to trust in our own strength but to praise the Lord’s strength with the prophet: “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” (Isa. XII).

In Manasseh, we are to be forgetful of our injuries and forgive [read: those] who act against us for the Lord’s name, lest we incur that curse: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI; Luke XI). In Ammon, we are to be faithful, rooted and founded in faith (Col. II), taking up in all things the shield of faith, with which we can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one (Eph. VI).

In Josiah [Col. 0417D], we are always to seek the salvation of the Lord and of our souls, lest we be blinded in unbelief, lest we stumble in the ways of his commandments, lest we become deaf to hearing the word of God, lest we die in sins, but so that we may always be saved by him who saves those who hope in him (Ps. XVI).

In Jechoniah, we are to be prepared for the Lord’s second coming, watching and praying, lest we enter into temptation (Matt. XXVI), but may deserve to enter with those whom he calls blessed: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, will find watching” (Luke XII).

In Shealtiel, our petition is always to be directed to God, so that our joy may be full (John XVI), not mixed with the sorrow of this age but everlasting in infinite blessedness; and this is to be in the Savior’s name, so that we may obtain what we ask.

In Zerubbabel, we are to be teachers of the truth, rejecting the teachings and confusions of heretics, and commending by our examples what we teach in words, lest the Lord say of us: [Col. 0418A] “Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take up my covenant in your mouth? You, however, hate discipline and have cast my words behind you” (Ps. XLIX).

In Abiud, God is to be our Father and we his children, possessing the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII). “And if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs with Christ” (ibid.).

In Eliakim, we are to rise from the tombs of vices to the height of virtues, from earthly things to heavenly things, from death to life, from Gaza to Galilee—that is, from hell to eternal migration—where the saints will go from strength to strength until the God of gods is seen in Zion (Ps. LXXXIII).

In Azor, helped by divine grace, we are patiently to endure everything that opposes us and praise the Lord our helper with the Psalmist: “The Lord is my helper and protector; in him my heart hoped, and I was helped” (Ps. XXVII).

In Zadok, we are to appear just before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances [Col. 0418B] of the Lord (Luke I), so that with the just we may deserve to hear the voice of him who says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

In Joachim, we are to deserve to be called brothers of Jesus Christ—not through kinship of the flesh but through the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which he poured abundantly upon us (Tit. III)—so that, doing his will and living soberly, justly, and piously in this age (Tit. II), we may in the future ascend to his Father and our Father, to his God and our God (John XX).

In Eliud, we are to have no God except the Lord Jesus Christ, before whom every knee bows and every tongue confesses (Phil. II); to him alone we are to offer a sacrifice of praise and fulfill our vows (Ps. XLIX), and him alone we are to adore, for he is to be worshiped in spirit and truth (John IV).

In Eleazar, we are to seek no helper except the Lord Jesus Christ, who is able to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand [Col. 0418C] (Eph. III); and whatever we do in word or deed, we are to do everything in the name of the Lord (Col. III), saying with the Prophet: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXXIII).

In Nathan, retaining the gift of heavenly grace—namely, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord—we are to possess discernment between good and evil, which is the mother of all virtues (Isa. XI).

In Jacob, we are to uproot from ourselves the weeds of vices and plant within us the spices of virtues, so that, like cinnamon and aromatic balsam, and like chosen myrrh, we may give forth fragrance (Ecclus. XXIV); and, planted in the house of the Lord, we may flourish forever before God (Ps. XCI).

In Joseph, adding virtue to virtue and sanctification to sanctification from day to day, we are to increase in merit and number, grow toward salvation in him, and ascend daily by the ladder erected into heaven, from step to step [Col. 0418D], until Christ is spiritually formed in us (Gal. IV).

In the holy and perpetual virgin Mary, whose name is interpreted as “star of the sea” or “illuminating,” we are to be illuminators of the world—that is, teachers of the holy Church—and cause the light of faith and the love of Christ to arise in the hearts of believers through the teaching of truth and examples of holiness, preparing a dwelling place for God.

In Jesus our Lord it is clearly declared that we should be able to be saviors of our souls. For whoever perseveres to the end in faith, hope, and charity; in vigils, fasts, and prayers; in chastity, sobriety, generosity in almsgiving, and love of God and neighbor; and whoever causes a sinner to turn from the error of his way, will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins (Jas. V).

In Christ, we are to be Christians in such a way that, as he walked, so we also may walk (I John II); and as he laid down his life for us, so we too may lay down our lives [Col. 0419A] for our brothers (I John III). And as he naturally bore within himself the interpretations of these names, so we too are to recall them spiritually in every active and contemplative life, as has been said.

For this reason Christ suffered, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps (I Pet. II), deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow him (Luke IX), as he leads us to eternal glory, which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and has not entered the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him. To him be honor, praise, and dominion through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LVI. ON THE VIGIL OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE MATTHEW

### LUKE V; MATTHEW IX; MARK II

“At that time Jesus saw a publican named Levi sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, ‘Follow me,’” etc.

Levi is the same person as Matthew, but Luke and Mark, out of modesty and respect for the Evangelist, did not wish to set down the name by which he was commonly known [Col. 0419B]. Matthew himself, however, in accordance with what is written, “The righteous person is his own accuser” (Prov. XVIII), names himself Matthew and publican at the beginning of his account, to show his readers that no convert ought to despair of salvation, since he himself was suddenly changed from a publican into an Apostle and from a tax collector into an Evangelist.

“And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.”

Understanding what it truly means to follow the Lord, Matthew follows him after leaving everything. For to follow means to imitate. Therefore, so that he might follow the poor Christ—not so much with his steps as with his affection [read: pursue]—he abandoned his possessions. [Col. 0419C] The man who had been accustomed to seize what belonged to others thereby gave us a perfect pattern of renunciation of the world. He left behind not only the profits of tax collection but also disregarded the danger that could come from the rulers of the age, since he had left the accounts of the taxes incomplete and unorganized. He was driven by so great a desire to follow the Lord that he reserved absolutely no regard or thought for this life. Therefore, with just reward, while diligently abandoning human affairs, he deserved to become the faithful steward of the Lord’s talents.

“And Levi made him a great banquet in his house.”

Whoever entertains Christ in the inner dwelling of his heart is nourished by the greatest delights of overflowing joys. Therefore the Lord gladly enters and reclines in the affection of the one who has believed. This is the spiritual banquet of good works, at which the rich people are in need and the poor feast.

“And there was a great crowd of publicans and others who were reclining with them.”

They saw that the publican had turned from sins to better things and had found a place of repentance; for that reason they too did not despair of salvation.

“And the Pharisees and their scribes murmured, saying to his disciples, ‘Why do you eat and drink with publicans and sinners?’”

While publicans banquet with the Lord [Col. 0419D], the Pharisees murmur and boast of fasting. Here the great difference between the law and grace is first made clear, because those who follow the law suffer the eternal hunger of a barren mind, whereas those who have received the word as nourishment in the depths of their souls, and have been refreshed by the abundance of the fountain, can neither hunger nor thirst.

Then the form of the future retribution is foreshadowed, when, while the elect feast with Christ, the unbelief of the proud will be tormented by fasting. To them it is said: “Publicans and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. XXI). What the election of Matthew signifies is the faith of the nations, which formerly longed for the profits of the world but now are diligently refreshed by devotion to the body of Christ. At the same time, the haughtiness of the Pharisees and the envy of the Jews are indicated, by which they are tormented at the salvation of the nations.

“And Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.’”

He reproves [Col. 0420A] the scribes and Pharisees, who, thinking themselves righteous, avoided the company of sinners. He calls himself a physician, who in a wondrous kind of healing was wounded for our iniquities, and by whose bruising we have been healed (Isa. LIII; I Pet. II).

He calls “the healthy” and “the righteous” those who, not knowing the righteousness of God and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. X); those who, relying on the law, do not seek the grace of the Gospel. But he calls “the sick” and “sinners” those who, overcome by awareness of their weakness and seeing that they cannot be justified through the law, submit themselves in repentance to the grace of Christ.

At the same time it is shown that the publicans did not come to Jesus while remaining in their former vices, as the scribes and Pharisees murmured, but after practicing repentance. Jesus himself also deigned to attend the banquets of sinners, so that he might have an occasion to teach and offer spiritual food to those who invited him. Finally, although he is often described as going to a banquet, nothing else is reported except what he did and taught there [Col. 0420B], so that the Lord’s humility in going to sinners and the power of his teaching in the conversion of the repentant might be displayed.

## HOMILY LVII. ON THE DAY OF THE ASSUMPTION OF MARY

### LUKE X

“At that time Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house,” etc.

These two sisters, beloved by the Lord, represent the two spiritual lives by which the holy Church is exercised in the present age. Martha represents the active life, through which we are joined to our neighbor in charity; Mary represents the contemplative life, through which we sigh in the love of God.

The active life consists in giving bread to the hungry; teaching the ignorant by the word of wisdom; correcting the one who has gone astray; recalling an arrogant neighbor to the way of humility; caring for the sick; distributing to each person what is suitable; and foreseeing how those entrusted to us may be able to endure [Col. 0420C].

The contemplative life, however, consists in retaining the love of God and neighbor with the whole mind, while resting from outward action and clinging solely to the desire for the Creator. Then one no longer wishes to do anything, but, trampling down every care, the spirit burns to see the face of its Creator. It already knows how to bear with sorrow the burden of corruptible flesh, and with all its desires longs to take part in those hymn-singing choirs of angels, to be mingled with the heavenly citizens, and to rejoice in the eternal incorruption before God.

“She sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his word. But Martha was busy with much serving.”

No one can doubt that these words correspond to the two lives. The perfection of the contemplative life is uniform: the mind, stripped of all earthly things, is united with Christ as far as human weakness permits. But how extensive the service of the active life is, the Teacher of the Nations makes clear (II Cor. XI, XII), recalling in his most celebrated words the labors he undertook for Christ [Col. 0420D] by land and sea and the dangers he endured. In the same passages, while commending the Lord’s visions and revelations, he indicates that he was no less perfected in the speculative virtue, which very few can imitate. Hence he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you” (II Cor. V).

“She stood and said: ‘Lord, is it no concern to you that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, therefore, to help me.’”

She speaks as the representatives of those who, still ignorant of divine contemplation, consider only the work of fraternal love that they have learned to be pleasing to God; therefore they insist that all who wish to be devoted to Christ must be assigned to this work. Martha is rightly described as standing, while Mary is described as sitting at the Lord’s feet, because the active life sweats through labor in the struggle, whereas the contemplative life, after the disturbances of vices have been calmed, already enjoys the desired repose of the mind in Christ.

“And the Lord answered and said to her: ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. But one thing is necessary.’”

Blessed David, defining this one thing as the only necessity for human beings, desires continually to cling to God, saying: “But for me [Col. 0421A], it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. LXXII). And elsewhere: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to see the will of the Lord and to visit his holy temple” (Ps. XXVI). There is therefore one and only one theory—that is, contemplation of God—to which all the merits of righteousness and every pursuit of virtue are rightly subordinated.

“Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.”

Behold, Martha’s part is not condemned, but Mary’s is praised. He does not say that Mary chose a good part, but the better one, so that Martha’s part too might be shown to be good. Why Mary’s part is better is added when he says: “It will not be taken away from her.”

For the active life comes to an end with the body. Who will offer bread to the hungry in the eternal homeland, where no one hungers? Who will give drink to the thirsty, where no one thirsts? Who will bury the dead, where no one dies? [Col. 0421B] With the present age, therefore, the active life is taken away; but the contemplative life begins here so that it may be perfected in the heavenly homeland. The fire of love that begins to burn here grows more fervent in love when it sees the one whom it loves. The contemplative life, therefore, is not taken away, because, when the light of the present age has been removed, it is perfected.

## HOMILY LVIII. ON THE COMMEMORATION OF THE DIVINE VIRGIN MARY, FROM THE GOSPEL: “A CERTAIN WOMAN LIFTING UP HER VOICE”

**LUKE XI.** At that time, when he was saying these things, a certain woman from the crowd, raising her voice, said to him: “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you,” etc.

This woman is shown to possess great devotion and faith. While the scribes and Pharisees were testing and blaspheming the Lord, she recognizes his incarnation with such sincerity above all others, and confesses it with such confidence, that she both confounds the slander of the rulers present and the faithlessness of future heretics. For just as at that time the Jews, by blaspheming the works of the Holy Spirit, denied the Son of God, true and consubstantial with the Father, so later heretics, by denying Mary to be ever-virgin, said that one ought not to confess that she, through the effective power of the Holy Spirit, supplied the material of his flesh to the only-begotten God who was to be born from human members, and that he was truly a son of man consubstantial with his mother.

But if the flesh of the Word of God, born according to the flesh, is declared foreign to the flesh of the Virgin mother, then without cause are the womb that bore him and the breasts that nursed him called blessed. For by what logic should he be believed to have been nourished by her milk if he is denied to have been conceived from her seed? Physicists establish that both fluids flow from the origin of one and the same source. Unless, perhaps, one should suppose that the virgin could provide the material of her flesh to the Son of God by nourishing him in the flesh, but could not do so by incarnation, as though that were a greater and more unusual miracle.

But the Apostle opposes this opinion, saying: “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Galatians IV). Nor should those be heard who think that one ought to read, “born from a woman, made under the law,” rather than “made from a woman,” because, having been conceived in the virginal womb, he drew his flesh not from nothing, nor from elsewhere, but from his mother’s flesh. Otherwise he would not truly be called the Son of Man, since he would have no origin from man.

Let us therefore also, in opposition to Eutyches, lift up our voice with the Catholic Church, whose type this woman represented; let us lift up our minds from the midst of the crowds, and say to the Savior: “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you.” Truly blessed is the mother who, as someone has said—Sedulius—

> gave birth—the mother in childbirth—to the King  
> who holds heaven and earth through the ages; whose  
> divine power, embracing all things in an eternal circuit,  
> and whose dominion remain without end; she who, in her blessed womb, possessed  
> a mother's joys together with the honour of virginity,  
> was seen neither to have one like herself before her nor to have a successor.

But he said: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.” The Savior fittingly assents to the woman’s testimony, affirming that not only she who was worthy to give bodily birth to the Word of God, but all who strive to conceive that same Word spiritually through the hearing of faith, and to give birth to it through the keeping of good works, either in their own heart or in the heart of their neighbors, and as it were to nourish it, are blessed.

For the same mother of God is blessed in one respect because she became the temporal minister of the Word’s incarnation; but she is much more blessed in that she remained forever the guardian of that same Word, whom she must always love. By this saying he secretly strikes the wise men of the Jews, who sought not to hear and keep the Word of God, but to deny and blaspheme it. Hence it is rightly said: “Blessed are those who hear the Word of God and keep it”; for, according to the statement of the Apostle James, it is not the hearers of the law who will be justified before God, but the doers of the law (James I). The psalmist also says of this: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times” (Psalm CV); for an everlasting reward will be repaid to them in glory, where, contemplating the face of God, they will sing praises to him forever—he who reigns and remains God in perfect Trinity and unity throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LIX. ON HOLY MARY THE VIRGIN

Today, dearly beloved brothers, we celebrate the feast of holy Mary, the Mother of God, who today has been taken from the world into heaven, so that she may pray to the Son for us; for the world would have been destroyed unless it were sustained through the prayers of holy Mary.

For we read that, after she herself ascended into heaven, she continually stands before God, pouring out prayer for our sins; she restrains the righteous so that they may not fall, strengthens sinners so that they may not perish, loves virgins if they remain in true virginity, and guards widows if they persevere in true widowhood.

We read what she did for a certain cleric who was born at Rome of noble family. His father and mother, brother and sister had died, and he alone remained. He possessed many honors and many estates, as well as a chapel near his house consecrated in honor of Blessed Mary, in which he daily sang all the Hours of holy Mary.

But his relatives began pressing him from every side to take a wife. He refused for a long time, but when they continued to urge him, he yielded to their wishes. They betrothed to him a bride from one of the better families of Rome. When the wedding day had been fixed, his relatives came with honor, and celebrated the wedding with joy, as was customary.

As they mounted their horses, the cleric remembered that blessed Mary had never abandoned him. He too mounted with the others, so that he might escort his wife with honor. When he had returned, they were singing with cymbals, harps, and other instruments. The cleric, remembering that he had not yet sung None of holy Mary, said to the soldiers: “Prepare the tables and whatever must be prepared according to the order of the wedding, and I will go to the church to sing None of holy Mary; afterward I will return to you.”

But they began to grieve, saying: “Do others who take a wife behave this way? Do they go to sing Matins?” When he opened the door of the church, he saw it filled with light and radiance, and blessed Mary seated before the altar. Struck with terror, he fell to the ground as though dead. She came to him, took his hand, and said:

“Do not be afraid. I am your friend, whom you have always loved and kept in your mind. But now you have abandoned me and taken another. Why have you done this? Am I not your friend? Am I not beautiful enough? Or are you seeking another who has greater beauty than I?”

And he, greatly afraid, replied: “Who are you, my Lady? I do not know you, but I see that you are beautiful and so dignified that there is no one like you in heaven. For the fragrance proceeding from you fills me, and I believe that I am in paradise.”

Mary replied: “I am blessed Mary, the mother of Christ. Until now you have served me; but why, having abandoned me, have you betrothed another? Do not abandon me for the sake of a mortal woman, whose existence lasts only a short time.”

After saying this, she vanished from his sight.

When he had said None, he returned to the palace where the soldiers were waiting for him. They pressed him to say why he had delayed so long. He replied: “Let any one of my relatives take my wife, for I have no other now except blessed Mary, whom I desire to serve day and night.”

When the bride heard this, she returned sadly and sorrowfully to her father’s house.

The cleric then went to blessed Pope Zephyrinus, who was pope at that time, and sought his advice about what he should do. The pope ordered him to give everything he possessed to the church in which he had seen the vision, to become a monk there, and to serve God and blessed Mary there all the days of his life—she who had freed him from the devil’s snare.

Now, brothers, let us always serve such a queen, who does not abandon those who hope in her. Since he loves and hears the prayers of the saints, how much more does he hear his mother as she prays for sinners? And while he himself was stretched out upon the cross, he entrusted her to blessed John the Evangelist, so that he might guard her day and night for as long as she remained in this world. Blessed John fulfilled what had been entrusted to him.

When the days and time approached in which the Lord wished to take her from this world, so that she might always stand near his face and pray for sinners, he called her, saying:

“Come to me, my beloved, my bride, my mother. It is time for me to exalt you above all the angels and archangels and the other powers who are in heaven, so that you may always be in my presence. On Sunday I will carry you into heaven.”

She came immediately and announced to John what the Lord had told her. Then blessed John said: “Let us pray together that our Lord, your Son, send us all the apostles, so that they may serve you.”

While they were praying, all the apostles, wherever they happened to be, were taken up and brought before the door where blessed Mary was. They remained with her until her Son took her into heaven. There she now stands in his presence, never ceasing to pray for sinners.

Let us therefore flee to her with our whole affection, so that through her prayers she may lead us to those joys where she remains forever with her Son.

## HOMILY LX. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW THE APOSTLE

**LUKE XXII.** At that time, a dispute arose among the disciples of Jesus about which of them seemed to be the greatest, etc.

Just as it is customary for the good always to seek in Scripture the examples of their forefathers, by which they may advance toward better things and, recognizing them, humble themselves concerning their own actions, so, conversely, the reprobate, if they happen to find anything blameworthy in the elect, are accustomed to embrace it most eagerly, as though they might thereby conceal their own wickedness or defend it as righteousness.

Therefore they read much more eagerly that a dispute arose among the disciples of Christ about which of them seemed to be the greatest than that the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul (Acts IV). They recall far more tenaciously that dissension arose between Barnabas and Paul, so that they departed from one another (Acts XV), than [supply: “the fact that”] Paul himself says: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal? Are you not human?” (1 Corinthians V).

It is as though the weakness of the saints were set before us for imitation, and not rather the fact that “they recovered from weakness and became strong in battle” (Hebrews XI)—especially in this passage, where the very cause of their dispute is unknown to us. For it is not credible that, in accordance with what is commanded elsewhere, “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke XIII), they competed by anticipating one another in honor (Romans XII).

But whatever the reason for their dispute, let us consider not what the disciples, who were still carnal, did, but what the spiritual Teacher commanded.

He said to them: “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But you are not to be so; rather, let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves.”

While the disciples were contending about precedence, the gracious Teacher did not rebuke the contention they had begun; instead, in a measured manner, he described the form of humility they should follow.

In attaining this form, however, the greater and those who precede others—that is, the teachers of the Church—need no little discernment, lest, like the kings of the nations, they rejoice in lording it over their subjects and in being lifted up by their empty praises. Rather, after the example of the eternal King, they should become as the younger and as servants to those whom they have been placed over in order to govern.

For it is necessary that, through humility, they be companions to those who act well, while through zeal for justice they stand firm against the vices of those who sin; thus they neither place themselves above the good in anything, nor, when the fault of the wicked requires it, fail immediately to recognize the authority of their precedence.

Lest the mind of a ruler be carried away by delight in his authority toward self-exaltation, it is rightly said through a certain wise man: “They have appointed you a leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus XXXII). Peter likewise says: “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock” (1 Peter V).

Yet sometimes a graver offense is committed if equality is maintained among the perverse more than discipline. Because Eli, overcome by false compassion, refused to strike his offending sons, he struck himself together with his sons with cruel condemnation before the strict Judge (1 Kings II).

Therefore it is necessary that toward his subjects a ruler display both the mother of compassion and the father of discipline. Amid these things, careful vigilance must ensure that neither strictness be harsh nor compassion lax.

For “who is greater, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as one who serves.”

To the words of his exhortation he adds examples, which John the Evangelist recalls more fully, writing among other things: “If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John XIII).

Yet by the word “serve” all that God did in the flesh can also be understood. For he signifies that he pours out even the sacrament of his own blood in order to serve us when he says: “The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew XX).

He also shows that this chief kind of service must be imitated by the greater ones in the Church, so that we may bestow upon our brothers not only the services of mercies, almsgiving, saving instruction, and spiritual example, but also, just as he laid down his life for us, learn to lay down our lives for one another (1 John III).

“But you are those who have remained with me in my temptations. And I appoint to you a kingdom, just as my Father appointed one to me.”

It is not the beginning of endurance but perseverance that receives the glory of the heavenly kingdom. For perseverance, which is also called constancy, is a certain strength and fortitude of mind, and, so to speak, the pillar of all virtues. When it stands upright and firm, nothing is more certain or safer for good conduct; but if, struck by some storm, it is thrown down, it does not fall alone, for all the goods of the mind collapse together.

Therefore, just as the Father appointed a kingdom for the Son, whom, having become obedient unto death, even death on a cross, he exalted and gave the name that is above every name (Philippians II), so the Son will lead those who remain with him in temptations into an eternal kingdom.

“For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be so in the likeness of his resurrection” (Romans VI).

The wretched Judas is excluded from the height of this promise. For before the Lord said these things, he must be believed to have gone out; he not only refused to remain with him in his temptations, but even helped those who caused his temptations.

Those also are excluded who, after hearing the words of the incomprehensible sacrament, went away and no longer walked with him (John VI). For those who depart from the Lord cannot be saved unless they return through repentance.

“That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.”

This table, set before all the saints for their enjoyment, is the heavenly glory of life. That food and drink are what is elsewhere described: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew V)—namely, by enjoying the joy of the true and unshaken good that they once desired and loved.

“And you shall sit upon thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

This is the transformation of the right hand of the Most High that the psalm sings about (Psalm LXXVI): those who now gladly serve their fellow servants in humility will then be nourished upon the Lord’s table with the food of eternal life; those who here remain with the Lord while unjustly judged amid temptations will there come with him as righteous judges over their tempters; and to the degree that they have been despised in this world with great humility, they will now, having received seats, increase to a greater height of authority. Amen.

## HOMILY LXI. ON HOLY EASTER DAY

**MARK XVI; MATTHEW XXVIII; LUKE XXIV; JOHN XX.** At that time, Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint Jesus, etc.

In the Gospel of Luke it is written that, returning from the tomb, they prepared spices and ointments, and on the Sabbath they kept silence according to the commandment. The commandment of the law was that Sabbath silence should be observed from evening until evening (Deuteronomy V). Therefore the devout women, after the Lord had been buried, occupied themselves in preparing the ointments for as long as work was permitted—that is, until sunset—as Luke writes (Luke XXIV).

Because they could not complete the task then on account of the pressure of time, they hastened, immediately after the Sabbath had passed—that is, after the sun had set, when permission to work had returned—to buy spices, as Mark reports, so that they might come in the morning and anoint his body. For on the evening of the Sabbath, with night already approaching, they could not reach the tomb.

“And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen.”

The first day of the week is the first day after the Sabbath, that is, after the days of rest; ecclesiastical custom now calls this day the Lord’s Day because of the resurrection of the Lord and Savior. It means the same thing when we read “on the first day of the week” or “on the first of the week”—that is, one day after the Sabbath, the day of rest observed on the Sabbaths.

The holy women who had followed the Lord came to the tomb with spices and, even after his death, devotedly performed an act of human service for him whom they had loved when he was coming. Therefore, if we believe in him who died and seek the Lord filled with the fragrance of virtues and with the reputation of good works, we too surely come with spices to his tomb.

That the women came to the tomb very early, when the sun had risen—that is, when the sky was already growing bright in the east, which does not happen except through the nearness of the rising sun—shows, according to the historical sense, the great fervor of love in seeking and finding the Lord. In the mystical sense, it gives us the example of offering to the Lord the fragrance of good works and the sweetness of prayers, with our face illuminated and the darkness of vices cast away.

“And they said to one another: ‘Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?’ And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away. For it was very large.”

How the stone was rolled away by an angel, Matthew explains sufficiently (Matthew XXVIII). But mystically the rolling away of the stone signifies the opening of Christ’s mysteries, which had been covered by the veil of the letter of the law. For the law was written on stone; when its covering was removed, the glory of the resurrection, the abolition of ancient death, and the hope of perpetual life began to be proclaimed throughout the whole world.

“And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished.”

Entering from the east into that round structure cut out of the rock, they saw an angel sitting on the southern side of the place where the body of Jesus had been laid; this was the right side. For since the body, lying on its back, had its head toward the west, it necessarily had its right side toward the south.

Matthew writes that the angel who rolled away the stone from the entrance of the tomb was first seen sitting upon the stone itself. He commanded them to enter the place where the Lord had been laid and to see that he had already risen from the dead (ibid.). Luke writes that, entering the tomb, they found two angels standing there (Luke XXIV).

Those women, therefore, see angels who came with spices, because those minds behold the citizens above who advance toward God with holy desires and virtues.

We should note what it means that the angel is seen sitting on the right. What is signified by the left except the present life? And what by the right except perpetual life? Hence it is written: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs VIII).

The Church of God has placed the left hand—that is, the prosperity of the present life—as though beneath its head, pressing it down with the intention of supreme love. But God’s right hand embraces her, because she is held wholly within his eternal blessedness.

Since, therefore, our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the present life, the angel who came to announce his perpetual life rightly sat on the right.

He appeared clothed in a white robe because he announced the joys of our festival. The whiteness of the garment proclaims the splendor of our festival. Should we say “our,” or “his”? To speak more truly, we should say both his and ours.

The resurrection of our Redeemer was our festival because it restored us to immortality, and it was the angels’ festival because, by restoring us to heavenly things, it filled their number. Thus, at his own festival and ours, the angel appeared in white garments, because through the Lord’s resurrection we are restored to the heights and the losses of the heavenly homeland are repaired.

But now let us hear the one who addresses the women as they come.

“Do not be afraid. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him.”

“Do not be afraid,” he says—as though he openly declared: Let those who do not love the coming of the citizens above be afraid; let those who, weighed down by carnal desires, despair of reaching their fellowship tremble. But why are you afraid, you who see your fellow citizens?

Matthew, describing the angel’s appearance, says: “His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow” (Matthew XXVIII). In lightning there is the terror of fear, while in snow there is the soothing quality of whiteness. Since almighty God is terrifying to sinners but gentle to the righteous, the angel who bears witness to his resurrection is rightly shown with both a lightning-like face and shining clothing, so that by his appearance he might terrify the reprobate and comfort the devout.

“You seek Jesus of Nazareth.”

In Latin speech, *Jesus* is interpreted as “saving,” that is, “Savior.” At that time, however, many could be called by this name—not substantially, but nominally. Therefore the place-name is added so that it may be made clear which Jesus is meant: “of Nazareth.” The cause is immediately supplied: “crucified,” and he adds: “He has risen; he is not here.”

“He is not here” is said with respect to the presence of his flesh, although he was nowhere absent with respect to the presence of his majesty.

“But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee.”

We must ask why, after naming the disciples, Peter is designated by name. But if the angel had not expressly named the one who had denied his Master, he would not have dared to come among the disciples. He is therefore called by name so that he would not despair because of his denial.

In this matter we should consider why almighty God permitted the one whom he had determined to place before the whole Church to fear the voice of a servant girl and to deny himself.
