We understand that this was done through a great dispensation of mercy, so that the one who was to become the shepherd of the Church might learn through his own fault how he ought to show mercy to others.

He first showed Peter his own weakness and then placed him over the others, so that through his own weakness he might learn how mercifully to endure the weaknesses of others.

It is fittingly said of our Redeemer:

“He is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you.”

Galilee is interpreted as “made migration.” For our Redeemer had already migrated from suffering to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, and from corruption to incorruption.

He is first seen by the disciples after the resurrection in Galilee because we will see the glory of his resurrection with joy if, in the present, we migrate from vices to the heights of virtues.

He who is announced in the tomb is shown in the place of migration, because the one recognized in the mortification of the flesh is seen in the migration of the mind—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## HOMILY LXII. ON EASTER MONDAY

**LUKE XXIV.** At that time, two of Jesus’ disciples were going to a village that was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus, and they were speaking with one another about all the things that had happened, etc.

A *stadium*, by which the Greeks, under the authority—as they say—of Hercules, measure distances along roads, is an eighth of a mile. Therefore sixty stadia signify seven thousand five hundred paces.

This distance of the journey appropriately corresponds to those who, certain about the Savior’s death and burial but uncertain about his resurrection, were walking. For who would doubt that the resurrection, which took place after the seventh day of the Sabbath, corresponds to the number eight?

The disciples, therefore, who walked along speaking about the Lord, completed the sixth mile of their journey because they were grieving that he had lived without blame until death, which he underwent on the sixth day of the week. They also completed the seventh, because they did not doubt that he had rested in the tomb. But they traveled only half of the eighth, because they did not yet fully believe in the glory of the resurrection that had already taken place.

Emmaus itself is the renowned city of Nicopolis in Palestine, which, after the conquest of Judea under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, was restored and changed both its status and its name.

“And it happened that, while they were talking and questioning one another, Jesus himself drew near and went with them.”

The Lord accompanies those who are speaking about him as he draws near, both to kindle belief in his resurrection within their minds and to show, through the presence of his hidden majesty, that he would always fulfill what he had promised: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them,” he said (Matthew XVIII).

“But their eyes were held, so that they did not recognize him. And he said to them: ‘What are these words that you are exchanging with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?’”

The Lord appeared to the disciples, but did not show them the appearance by which they would recognize him. Thus, outside, in the eyes of the body, the Lord did what was happening within them, in the eyes of the heart.

Within themselves they both loved and doubted; but outside, the Lord was present to them without showing them who he was. He manifested his presence to them as they spoke about him, but he concealed the appearance by which they could recognize him while they doubted about him.

“And one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering, said to him: ‘Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?’”

They thought he was a stranger because they did not recognize his face. Yet he truly was a stranger to them, since, having already attained the glory of the resurrection, he was far removed from the fragility of their nature. He was a stranger to them because, while they were still ignorant of his resurrection, he remained foreign to their faith.

“He said to them: ‘What things?’ And they said: ‘Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people.’”

They confess him to be a great prophet, but remain silent about the Son of God—either because they did not yet perfectly believe, or because they were concerned lest they fall into the hands of the Jews who were persecuting them. Since they did not know who the one was with whom they were speaking, they concealed what they believed to be true.

“And how the chief priests and our rulers handed him over to the condemnation of death and crucified him. But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

They walked sadly with good reason, because in a certain sense they were accusing themselves for having hoped for redemption in the one whom they had already seen dead and did not believe would rise again. Above all, they grieved that he had been killed without guilt, because they knew him to be innocent.

“And now, besides all this, today is the third day since these things happened. But certain women from among us also terrified us. They were at the tomb before dawn, and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had even seen a vision of angels who say that he is alive.”

They are said to have been terrified with good reason, because their minds, mourning the Lord’s body as not found, were able to derive more sadness from its absence than joy from the resurrection announced by the angels.

“And some of our companions went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but they did not find him.”

Since Luke earlier said that Peter ran to the tomb, and now reports that Cleopas said that some of them had gone to the tomb (Luke XXIV), it is understood that two went to the tomb. He mentioned Peter alone at first because Mary had announced the matter to him first.

“And he said to them: ‘O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?’ And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.”

At this point, we are confronted not with one reason for interpreting Scripture, but with a double necessity for humbling ourselves: we are neither instructed in the Scriptures as much as we ought to be, nor as attentive as we should be to fulfilling what we may have learned.

For if Moses and all the prophets spoke of Christ, and of his entering into his glory through the narrow way of suffering, how can those who, according to the measure of their strength, neither investigate how the Scriptures pertain to Christ nor desire to reach the glory they hope to possess with Christ through the sufferings of tribulation boast that they are Christians?

“And they drew near to the village to which they were going, and he pretended to go farther. But they compelled him, saying: ‘Stay with us, because it is toward evening and the day is now declining.’ And he entered with them.”

The simple Truth did nothing deceitful through duplicity. By saying that he pretended to go farther, Scripture shows that in his body he presented himself to the disciples as he was in their mind.

They had to be tested to see whether they could love him—even if they did not yet love him as God—at least as a stranger. But because those with whom the Truth walked could not be strangers to love, they invite him into their lodging as a stranger.

Why do we say that they invite him, when it is written there, “They compelled him”? From this example it is clearly gathered that strangers should not only be invited into lodging but also brought in.

“And it happened that, while he was reclining with them, he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him.”

They did not recognize him in the exposition of sacred Scripture, but they recognize him in the breaking of bread. They were not illuminated by hearing God’s commandments, but by doing them, because it is written: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Romans II).

Therefore, whoever wishes to understand what he has heard should hasten to fulfill in action whatever he has already been able to understand.

“And he vanished from their eyes. And they said to one another: ‘Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?’”

“I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

The Lord cast fire upon the earth when, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, he set the hearts of carnal people ablaze. The earth burns when the heart of a carnal person, previously cold in its own pleasures, abandons the desires of the present age and is kindled toward the love of God.

“Was not our heart burning within us,” they say, “while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?”

When the word is heard, the soul grows hot; the coldness of sluggishness withdraws; the mind becomes anxious with heavenly desire and alienated from earthly cravings. The true love that fills it torments it with tears. Yet while it is tormented by such ardor, it is nourished by the very torments it suffers. It delights to hear the heavenly commandments, and by each commandment with which it is instructed it is, as it were, inflamed by another torch.

“And rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem and found the Eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying: ‘The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.’”

There was already a report, made by the women and by Simon Peter, to whom he had already appeared, that Jesus had risen from the dead. The two disciples found these people speaking about it when they came to Jerusalem.

It is therefore possible that, out of fear, they had previously been unwilling to say on the road that they had heard he had risen, since the women had said only that angels had been seen. Not knowing with whom they were speaking, they could rightly have been anxious lest, by proclaiming Christ’s resurrection indiscriminately, they fall into the hands of the Jews.

Thus the Lord is understood to have appeared first of all the men to Peter, at least among all those whom the four Evangelists and the Apostle Paul mention. Paul says to the Corinthians concerning the Lord: “That he was buried, that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, and afterward to the Eleven” (1 Corinthians XV).

“And they recounted what had happened on the road, and how they had recognized him in the breaking of bread.”

Apart from the fact that, because of the state of their minds—which still did not know that Christ had to die and rise again—their eyes suffered something similar, not because the truth deceived them, but because they were unable to perceive the truth and thought something other than what was real, this also happened for the sake of a particular mystery.

It was done so that another likeness might be shown to them in him, and so that they would recognize him only in the breaking of bread. No one should think that he has recognized Christ if he is not a participant in his body—that is, in the Church, whose unity the Apostle commends in the sacrament of bread, saying: “Because there is one bread, we, though many, are one body.”

Thus, when he gave them the blessed bread, their eyes were opened and they recognized him. They were opened, of course, to the knowledge of him, once the obstacle by which they were prevented from recognizing him had been removed.

Nor is it inappropriate to understand that this obstacle in their eyes came from Satan, so that Jesus would not be recognized. Yet permission was given by Christ to continue until the sacrament of bread, so that, once they had shared in the unity of his body, the removal of the enemy’s obstacle might be understood, and Christ might be recognized—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## HOMILY LXIII. ON THE DAY OF THE LORD’S ASCENSION
**MARK 16.** At that time, finally, when the eleven disciples were reclining at table, Jesus appeared to them and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen, etc.

Why “finally,” as though they were not to see him thereafter? For that was indeed the final occasion on which the apostles saw the Lord on earth, when he ascended into heaven, which took place on the fortieth day after his resurrection. Was he then going to reproach them for not having believed those who had seen him risen, when they themselves had already seen him so many times after the resurrection? We should therefore understand that, after his many manifestations, during which he had been present to his disciples for forty days [Col. 0430A], he appeared also, finally, while the eleven were reclining at table—that is, on the fortieth day itself. And because he was already about to ascend from them into heaven, on that day he especially wished to reproach them for not having believed those who had seen him risen, before they themselves had seen him, since, after his ascension, when they preached the Gospel, the Gentiles who had not seen him would in any case believe.

After this reproach, Mark continues:

> And he said to them: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned.”

Since they were going to preach that whoever did not believe would be condemned—although such a person would not have believed precisely what he had not seen—were they not themselves the first to be rebuked, because before they had seen the Lord they had not believed those to whom the Lord had appeared? But what he said to them:

[Col. 0430B]

> “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature.”

Was the holy Gospel to be preached even to inanimate things or to brute animals, so that the disciples were told, “Preach to every creature”? Rather, by the name “every creature” every nation of the Gentiles may be designated. For earlier it had been said, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles”; but now it is said, “Preach to every creature,” so that the preaching rejected by Judea might then become an aid to us, when she had proudly rejected it as a testimony to her own condemnation.

> Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned.

Perhaps each person might say to himself: “I have already believed; I shall be saved.” He speaks truly, if he holds the faith by his works. For true faith is that which is not contradicted in conduct by what it says in words. Hence Paul says of certain false believers: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1). Hence John says: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments [Col. 0430C] is a liar” (1 John 2).

But when it is said, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned,” what shall we say here about infants, who because of their age are not yet able to believe? There is no question concerning adults. In the Church, therefore, infants believe in the Savior through others, just as through others they received those sins which are remitted to them in baptism.

> These signs, moreover, will accompany those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.

Is it because we do not perform these signs that we have no faith at all? But these were necessary at the beginning of the Church: for, so that it might grow toward faith, it had to be nourished by miracles. When we plant shrubs, we pour water over them for as long as it takes to see that they have become firmly established in the soil. But once they have taken root, the watering ceases. Hence Paul says: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” [Col. 0430D] (1 Corinthians 14).

Or do we not possess, in these signs and powers, matters that we ought still to consider more carefully? The holy Church performs spiritually every day what it then performed bodily through the apostles. For when her priests, through the grace of exorcism, lay hands upon believers and oppose the dwelling of evil spirits in their minds, what else are they doing but casting out demons? And when the faithful, who now abandon the worldly words of their former life and sound forth the holy mysteries, proclaim, as far as they can, the praises and power of their Creator, what else are they doing but speaking in new tongues?

When, through their good exhortations, they remove wickedness from the hearts of others, they pick up serpents. And when they hear poisonous suggestions but are in no way drawn into wicked action, what they drink is indeed deadly, but it does not harm them. When they see their neighbors weakened in good works and come to their aid with all their strength, strengthening by the example [Col. 0431A] of their conduct the lives of those who falter in their own actions, what else are they doing but laying hands upon the sick, so that they may be well?

These miracles are surely greater in proportion as they are more spiritual; they are greater in proportion as through them not bodies but souls are raised up.

And after the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. We must consider what Mark means when he says, “He sits at the right hand of God,” whereas Stephen says, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7). Why does Mark testify that he saw him sitting, while Stephen saw him standing?

But we know that sitting is the posture of one judging, while standing is that of one fighting or helping. Since, therefore, our Redeemer was taken up into heaven, now judges all things, and will come at the end as judge of all, Mark describes him as sitting after his ascension, because after the glory of his ascension he will be seen as judge at the end. Stephen, however, engaged in the struggle [Col. 0431B] of his suffering, saw him standing, because he had him as a helper: while Stephen overcame the unbelief of his persecutors on earth, Christ fought for him from heaven by his grace.

It follows:

> But they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.

What should be considered here, what should be commended to memory, except that obedience followed the command, and signs followed obedience? Among these matters it should be noted that, although Mark began his Gospel later than the others, he extended it in writing over a longer period. He records nothing about the birth of the Lord himself or of his forerunner, nothing about the infancy or childhood of either of them, and writes nothing at length about the Savior’s birth, except that at the beginning of his Gospel he calls him the Son of God. He began with the beginning of evangelical preaching, which took place through John, and by his narrative reached that time when the apostles spread the word of the same Gospel throughout the world by preaching it everywhere.

[Col. 0431C]

There remains, certainly, a considerable question: how the same evangelist could write that the angel said to the women, “Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you” (Mark 16), and yet did not report anywhere else in his Gospel that the Lord was seen there by the disciples.

Matthew, indeed, says that the disciples went away to Galilee (Matthew 28), and there saw and worshiped the Lord, and received from him the command to go, teach, and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Yet, when the writings of the other evangelists are examined (Luke 24), it is shown that he had already appeared to the disciples many times, especially on the very day of his resurrection, in Jerusalem and at the village of Emmaus.

Why, then, did he specifically say that he would go before them into Galilee and would there be seen by the disciples, when he was seen neither only there nor there first? Let us therefore see for what mystery Christ, according to Matthew and Mark, gave this command after rising: “I shall go before you into Galilee; there you [Col. 0431D] will see me.” Although this was fulfilled, it was fulfilled only after many other events, even though the command was expressed in such a way—without prejudice to necessity—that either this alone or this first might have been expected to occur.

There is no doubt, therefore, that since these words are not those of the evangelist narrating that something happened in this way, but of the angel speaking by the Lord’s command, and of the Lord himself, with the evangelist narrating that the angel and the Lord spoke in this way, the saying must be understood prophetically.

For “Galilee” is interpreted either as “transmigration” or as “revelation.” First, according to the meaning of “transmigration,” what else should we understand by, “He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you,” except that the grace of Christ was about to migrate from the people of Israel to the Gentiles? The apostles would in no way have been believed by those to whom they preached the Gospel unless the Lord himself had prepared the way for them in human hearts.

This is what we understand by, “He will go before you into Galilee.” But when, rejoicing, they marvel that, after difficulties have been broken through and overcome, a door has been opened for them in the Lord through the illumination of the faithful [Col. 0432A], this is understood by, “There you will see him”—that is, there you will find his members; there, in those who receive you, you will recognize his living body.

But according to the interpretation of “Galilee” as “revelation,” this is no longer to be understood in the form of a servant, but in that form in which he is equal to the Father, which he promised to those who love him through John, when he said: “I will love him and will show myself to him” (John 14).

This is not according to what they were already seeing, and which, after rising with his scars, he later showed not only to be seen but also to be touched. Rather, it is according to that ineffable light with which he enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1), according to which he shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend him.

He went before us there, and when he came to us he did not depart from there; and when he went before us there, he did not abandon us. That was the revelation, as it were, the true Galilee, when we shall be like him [Col. 0432B] and shall see him as he is (1 John 3).

It will also be the more blessed transmigration from this age into that eternity, if we embrace his commandments in such a way that we may deserve to be gathered at his right hand. For then the wicked will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25). From here they will migrate there, and there they will see him in a way that the ungodly do not see him. For the wicked will be taken away so that he may not see the glory of the Lord, and the ungodly will not see the light (Isaiah 26).

This is eternal life: that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent (John 17), as he is known in that eternity. Through the form of a servant he will lead his own there, so that, as free persons, they may contemplate him in the form of the Lord.

May Jesus Christ also grant this to us, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified as God through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXIV. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST BEFORE THE LATIN GATE

[Col. 0432C]

**MATTHEW 20; MARK 10.** At that time James and John, the sons of Zebedee, approached Jesus, saying: “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask,” etc.

Matthew writes that the mother of the sons of Zebedee asked the Lord on their behalf. But Mark, wishing to reveal their desire and intention to his readers, says nothing about the mother’s intervention and instead says that they themselves asked for what he knew had been requested through their mother at their urging. Accordingly, according to both evangelists, the Lord answered not the mother but them:

> “You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?”

But they said to him: “We can.”

Those who seek from the Lord a seat of glory that they had not yet deserved do not know what they are asking. They were already attracted by the summit of honor, but first they had to undertake the way of labor. They desired to reign exaltedly with Christ [Col. 0432D], but first they had to suffer humbly for Christ.

By the name of the cup or baptism he designates the passion of martyrdom, by which it was fitting that both he and they should be brought to completion. Hence elsewhere he speaks of his passion: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke 12). And as he approached that passion, he prayed, saying: “Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me” (ibid. 26).

> Jesus said to them: “You will indeed drink the cup that I drink, and you will be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized.”

The question arises how James and John, the sons of Zebedee, drank the cup of martyrdom, or how they were baptized with the Lord’s baptism, since Scripture reports that only the apostle James was beheaded by Herod (Acts 12), while John ended his life by a natural death.

But if we read the ecclesiastical histories, in which it is reported (Book 3, chapter 16) that he too was sent, on account of martyrdom, into a vessel of boiling oil, and from there, as an athlete of Christ, came forth to receive the crown [Col. 0433A], and was immediately banished into exile on the island of Patmos, we shall see that he did not lack martyrdom in spirit. John drank the cup of confession, which the three young men also drank in the fiery furnace (Daniel 3), even though the persecutor did not shed his blood.

But when he adds:

> “To sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give, but it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared,”

this should be understood as follows: The kingdom of heaven is not a matter of the giver but of the recipient. For there is no partiality with God (Acts 10); whoever presents himself as worthy of the kingdom of heaven will receive what has been prepared not for a person but for a way of life.

If, therefore, you are such as to attain the kingdom of heaven, which my Father prepared for those who triumph and conquer, you too will receive it.

Again: “It is not mine to give, but to those [Col. 0433B] for whom it has been prepared.” It is not mine to give to the proud—for such you still were. But if you wish to receive it, do not remain what you are. It has been prepared for others; become other than you are, and it has been prepared for you. What does “become other” mean? First humble yourselves, you who now wish to be exalted.

> And when the ten heard this, they began to be indignant at James and John.

The ten apostles were not indignant at the mother of the sons of Zebedee, nor did they attribute the boldness of the request to the woman, but to the sons, who, unaware of their own measure, had been inflamed by immoderate desire. To them the Lord had said: “You do not know what you are asking.”

> But Jesus called them and said to them: “You know that those who appear to rule the nations lord it over them, and their rulers exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you,” etc.

The humble and gentle Teacher neither rebukes the two who asked for immoderate things because of their desire, nor reproves the other ten for indignation and jealousy. Rather, he gives an example by which he teaches that the greater is the one who has been the lesser, and that the one who is servant of all becomes lord.

It was therefore pointless either for the former to have sought something immoderate or for the latter to grieve over the desire for superiority, since the summit [Col. 0433C] of the virtues is reached not through power but through humility.

Finally, he sets forth his own example, so that, if they paid little attention to his words, they might be ashamed before his works. He says:

> “For the Son of Man also did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many.”

Note that we have often said that the one who served is called the Son of Man, and that he gives his life as a redemption for many when he took the form of a servant in order to pour out his blood for the world. He did not say that he would give his life as a redemption for all, but for many—that is, for those who wished to believe.

## HOMILY LXV. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 0433D]

**LUKE 6; MATTHEW 7.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “A good tree does not produce bad fruit, nor does a bad tree produce good fruit. For every tree is known by its fruit. For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor gather grapes from a bramble,” etc.

Because, through the favor of God, dearly beloved brothers, we are celebrating the solemnity of the dedication of a church, we ought to conform ourselves to the solemnity we are honoring. Just as we have carefully adorned the walls of this church, increased the number of lamps, enlarged the number of readings, added the melody of psalms, and, according to custom, passed the night in joyful vigils, so also we should always adorn the inner chambers of our hearts with the necessary ornaments of good works.

May the flame of divine and fraternal love always increase in us; may the holy memory of heavenly commandments and the sweetness of angelic harmony always resound in the sanctuary of our breast. These are the fruits of a good tree; this is the good treasure of the heart; these are the foundations of the wise architect, which today’s reading of the holy Gospel commends to us, urging us to possess not merely the appearance but rather the power [Col. 0434A] of devotion.

The mystical history of the Old Testament also carefully intimates this to us, when Moses constructed the tabernacle, or Solomon the temple, for the Lord as a type of the holy Church. Each house is said to have been firmly founded: the tabernacle because it had walls joined together from boards set upon silver bases; the temple because it stood upon squared stones placed beneath it as a foundation [Alternative: “placed as a foundation”].

The wood was also imperishable. From it the whole tabernacle was made, and the temple was adorned within and shone with a roof above. Gold too, the finest from a good treasure, was brought forth. With it the walls of the tabernacle were clothed inside and out, and in the temple not only the walls but also the ceilings, beams, doors, doorposts, and pavements were covered.

Nearly all the vessels and furnishings of both houses were likewise of gold, and it was permitted that these be made only from the purest gold. The fruits of the trees that were offered in the house of the Lord were also commanded to be purest and most select: the vine, the olive, frankincense, myrrh, stacte (*stactis*), and other things of this kind [Col. 0434B].

All these things, understood spiritually, proclaim the true sincerity of our faith and conduct. For both houses, as we have said, prefigure the universal Church.

Let no one think it incongruous that there are two houses of the Lord made in mystery, since no believer doubts that the Church is one house of Christ. Two houses were built to signify the two peoples who were to come to the same faith—namely, the Jews and the Gentiles.

Thus, appropriately, the tabernacle was built in the wilderness by the Hebrew people alone, whereas the proselytes—that is, the newcomers from the Gentiles, as many as could then be found among the people of Israel—completed the construction of the temple with devoted faith.

The most powerful king of Tyre, whom Solomon hired, also helped most willingly by supplying craftsmen and wood. For before the Lord’s incarnation, God was known only in Judea. But after he was born and [Col. 0434C] suffered in the flesh there, was raised from the dead, and exalted above the heavens as God, the glory of his name immediately shone throughout the whole earth. The entire world hastened joyfully to build that house, having received from him the promise of heavenly gifts.

Let us therefore hear what our Creator and Redeemer himself says about the building of his house, which we are, in the reading of the holy Gospel that has just been recited.

> “A good tree does not produce bad fruit, nor does a bad tree produce good fruit.”

The wise King therefore seeks good trees and their good fruits for the construction or service of his temple. But what the end of a bad tree is, he teaches elsewhere in these words: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3).

By trees he means human beings; by fruits, their works. Do you wish to know which are the bad trees and which are the bad fruits? The Apostle teaches, saying:

> “The works of the flesh are evident: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these” [Col. 0434D] (Galatians 5).

Do you wish to hear whether trees that produce such fruits belong to the heavenly temple of the eternal King? The Apostle adds:

> “I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.”

He subsequently enumerates the fruits of the good tree, saying:

> “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, self-control.”

And elsewhere, giving instruction, he says:

> “Walk as children of light. For the fruit of light consists in every goodness, righteousness, and truth” (Ephesians 5).

These fruits, together with the trees from which they proceed, truly belong here to the house of faith and there to the dwelling of heavenly blessedness.

Finally, let us hear the good tree rejoicing in the abundance of good fruits:

> “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of my God [Col. 0435A] forever and ever” (Psalm 51).

The fruit of the olive is the shining work of mercy. Therefore, in the temple of eternity, the one who shines in the present house of God through the grace of mercy rightly hopes in God’s mercy.

Confidently trusting that he belongs to the temple of the great King, such a person rightly says elsewhere:

> “Your mercy [Alternative: his mercy] will follow me all the days of my life, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days” (Psalm 22).

But in contrast, let us see what fruits the bad tree bears, and let us avoid bearing such fruits ourselves. The prophet Jeremiah says:

> “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, who makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. He will be like a tamarisk in the wilderness” (Jeremiah 17).

A tamarisk is a fruitless and lowly tree, exceedingly bitter to the taste, utterly unworthy of human cultivation, and for that reason growing in the wilderness.

He is rightly compared with it who, turning away from divine fear and love, hopes for power or riches from human beings. [Col. 0435B] How far such a person must be judged to be excluded from the beauty of God’s house, the prophet makes clear by adding:

> “He will not see when good comes, but will dwell in the wilderness, in parched land, in a salt land and uninhabited” (ibid.).

Therefore, my brothers, let no one living wickedly in secret flatter himself with the favor of the crowd, as though he were good. Even if the leaves of his words are exceedingly beautiful, and if he produces the fragrant smell of a flower of fame, he is not a good tree if he produces bad fruits.

Nor should anyone who does what good he can with an upright heart despair of his salvation, because a bad tree is not one that produces good fruit.

> “For every tree is known by its fruit.”

This knowledge should be understood only of manifest vices or virtues, such as we mentioned above according to the Apostle’s teaching. For there are certain things whose motive is unknown to those close to us, and which may therefore be interpreted in either direction. But all ambiguous matters are more justly interpreted for the good by those who love what is good, so that the Apostle’s saying may be fulfilled:

> “Do not judge before the time” (1 Corinthians 4).

[Col. 0435C]

> “For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor gather grapes from a bramble.”

Thorns and brambles, trees filled with prickles, signify the hearts of those who are themselves defiled by the goads of luxury, envy, and desire, or who, because of the roughness of anger, detraction, hatred, pride, and bitterness, are unpleasant to their neighbors and, as it were, impossible to handle.

The fig signifies the sweet remembrance of the kingdom of heaven; the grape signifies the fragrance of love for the Lord. Therefore they do not gather figs from thorns or gather grapes from a bramble, because those who are still polluted by the prickles of vices are in no way able worthily to provide their neighbors with examples [Alternative: “an example”] or instruction in the virtues [Alternative: “the virtue of instruction”].

> “The good person brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings forth evil from the evil treasure of his heart.”

The treasure of the heart is the intention of the thought, from which the inner judge assesses the outcome of the work. [Col. 0435D] Hence it often happens that some perform lesser good works and receive a greater reward of heavenly grace, because of the intention of the heart by which they wished to accomplish greater good works if they could. Others, while displaying greater works of virtue, receive lesser rewards from the Lord because of the negligence of a lukewarm heart.

Finally, the deed of the widow who brought two coins to the temple is preferred by the searcher of hearts within to the countless gifts of the rich.

> “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

Human judgment is often deceived because it knows how to weigh the heart of another only from his mouth and deeds. The Lord, however, weighs the deed itself and our words [Alternative: “the words”] from the root of the heart. The mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart of the one who does not fail to know from what intention the words proceed.

This he then establishes, clearly showing that good speech without the testimony of works is entirely useless.

> “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?”

To call him Lord seems to be the good gift of the treasure and the good fruit of a good tree. For “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.” [Col. 0436A] But if the one who calls upon the Lord’s name contradicts the Lord’s commandments by living wickedly, it is plainly evident that what the tongue uttered did not come forth as good from the good treasure of the heart. Nor did the root of the fig produce such a fruit of confession; rather, it was a thorn—that is, a conscience made harsh by vices and burdened not with an abundance of love for the Lord—that brought it forth.

What the true distinction between good and bad fruits is, the Lord sets forth under another figure, adding:

> “Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them—I will show you what he is like. He is like a man building a house.”

This man building the house is the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who deigned to build and consecrate for himself a beloved holy house, namely the Church, in which he would dwell perpetually.

> “He dug deeply and laid the foundation upon rock.”

Because he strove to uproot completely from the hearts of his faithful whatever earthly [Col. 0436B] intention he found there, so that, once the ruins of former custom and superfluous thoughts had been removed, he himself might have in them a stable and unshaken dwelling.

He is the rock upon which he placed the foundation of this kind of house. For just as, in building a house, nothing is preferred to the rock upon which the foundation is laid, so the holy Church has her rock—namely Christ—indeed hidden within her heart. She places nothing before his faith and love, to such a degree that she does not hesitate to suffer death for them.

Because the chief of the Church clung most firmly to this rock [Alternative: “adhered to it”], he received his name from it when he heard:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16).

When the flood came, the river struck against that house but could not move it, because it had been founded upon rock. The explanation is clear: the Church has often been battered by afflictions, yet has not been overthrown. If some believers, [Col. 0436C] badly overcome, gave way, they did not in fact belong to this house; for if they had stood founded upon the rock of faith, and not rather upon the sand of unbelief or fickleness, they could never have been shaken at all.

It should be noted, however, that this flood of temptations attacks the Church in three ways. A person is either tempted after being drawn away and enticed by his own desire, or wearied by the wickedness of false brethren, or assailed by the more cunning plots of outsiders. The Lord elsewhere calls these temptations “the gates of hell,” and rightly so, because, if they prevail, they drag their victims into eternal destruction. “And upon this rock,” he says, “I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (ibid.).

Although, therefore, the devil’s gates assail Christ’s Church, they do not overthrow it; although the flood of unbelief rushes in, it does not destroy the house of faith. For the Church can truly say to her Helper: “When my heart was troubled, you lifted me up upon a rock.” She is not defeated by outsiders, because she overcomes the fury of persecuting unbelievers by suffering [Col. 0436D] with the crown of martyrdom; she is not corrupted by false brethren, because by right belief she refutes the doctrines of heretics, and by living soberly, justly, and devoutly avoids the vicious examples of certain Catholics; she is not blinded by the smoke of her own greed, because inwardly she burns only with the heat of the Lord’s charity.

To this man—that is, to our Redeemer—who joined the universal Church to himself through the invincible strength of his mind, the elect are each likened in their own measure, whenever they individually strive to accomplish in their own hearts what he does generally throughout the whole Church. For, as though digging deeply, they vigilantly examine their conscience; they carefully investigate whether anything sordid lies hidden within it; and with the diligent hand of discernment they empty out from the bottom of their hearts all hiding places of superfluous thoughts, so that they may prepare a firm and peaceful faith for that strongest Rock, namely, Christ. Thus, through his presence, they endure unconquered amid both the adversities and the flatteries of the world’s torrent.

With the Lord’s help, dearest brethren, [Col. 0437A] we have briefly traversed these matters in our exposition of the Gospel reading. But it seems fitting for the solemnity we are celebrating to recall something about the construction of the temple and to investigate how appropriately its adornment corresponds to the Church’s meaning.

Sacred Scripture therefore relates that Solomon commanded large stones and precious stones to be taken for the foundation of the temple and squared. The large and precious stones, placed in the foundation and bearing the whole weight of the temple imposed upon them, signify the outstanding teachers of the holy Church: large, indeed, in the excellence of their merits, and precious in the radiance of their signs. Hearing the word from the Lord himself, they brought forth by their preaching the entire structure of the growing Church.

Whenever foundations are mentioned in Scripture in the plural, they signify either holy preachers or the firm thoughts of the righteous. Hence the Psalmist says: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXI). But when “foundation” is placed in the singular, it most often [Col. 0437B] indicates the author of all good things, of whom the Apostle says: “For no one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III); and again, to believers: “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. II).

Upon this foundation, therefore, large and precious stones were placed to carry the whole temple, because through him the patriarchs and prophets first, and afterward the apostles, were instructed for the propagation of the Church throughout the world. The more closely they clung to his love, the more powerfully they supported their followers in the heavenly building. The king commanded these stones to be squared in order to signify that the teachers of the Church ought to be well ordered in conduct and immovable in mind. For just as a square stands firm whichever way it is turned, so the life of the perfect, carefully aligned with the rule of truth, knows no temptation’s force capable of throwing it from its stability.

The temple was built of Parian marble, which is a white [Col. 0437C] stone, to express the whiteness of ecclesiastical chastity. Of this the Lord says in the Song of Love: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song II).

It was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. The length of the temple therefore signifies the faith of the holy Church, by which she patiently endures the adversity of the wicked amid her good works; the width signifies charity, by which she expands inwardly through the depths of compassion; the height signifies hope, by which, because of the good works she performs through charity, she awaits the rewards of heavenly [Al.: *coelestis*, an alternative inflection] life.

It is fitting that its length was sixty cubits. For perfection in good works is customarily signified by the number six: the Lord completed the adornment [Al.: ornament] of the world in six days, and there are six ages of this world, in which the holy Church devotes herself [Al.: *insistit*, “persists”] to pious actions for the sake of eternal rest. It is fitting that the width was twenty cubits, because the commandment of charity is twofold, by which the Church is enlarged in tribulation, whenever each perfect person [Col. 0437D] is shown to love both the Creator with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength, and his neighbor as himself.

It is fitting that the height was thirty cubits, because the hope of all the elect prepares itself, as far as it can, through exercise and purification, for the vision of the holy Trinity. Thus six pertains to the long endurance of faith, three to the loftiness of hope, and two to the breadth of love. Through these three marks of virtue the whole state of the holy Church is understood to rejoice [Al.: to be perfected]. The multiplication of each of these by ten, which is a perfect number, figuratively announces a manifold increase of the same perfection.

It should also be noted that the thirty cubits of height did not reach to the highest roof of the temple, but only to the ceiling; afterward, another thirty cubits of height rose to the ceiling of the middle upper chamber. The third upper chamber, which remained above, had a height of sixty cubits. Thus the entire height of the building extended to one hundred and twenty cubits [Col. 0438A].

The first building therefore rises thirty cubits in height because the present Church is wholly suspended in eager longing to behold the appearance of the holy Trinity. The upper building likewise rises thirty cubits, because the souls of the perfect, released from their bodies, enjoy the present vision of that same blessed and undivided Trinity until the day of universal judgment. The highest building is sixty cubits high, twice thirty, because all the elect, raised from the dead, will rejoice in the contemplation of their Creator—who is one God in three persons—with the eternal immortality of spirit and flesh alike.

A middle wall of cedar boards, twenty cubits high, was made in the temple to divide the oracle—that is, the Holy of Holies—from the front part of the temple. The oracle was twenty cubits long and twenty cubits high. The temple itself, in front of the entrance to the oracle, measured forty cubits; in it were tables and lampstands of gold. There was also a golden altar [Col. 0438B] near the entrance of the tabernacle, so that, when incense was burned upon it, the rising vapor of smoke might open [Al.: cover] the oracle, where the ark of the covenant was, above which were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat.

The former building therefore signifies the condition of the present Church, while the inner part signifies entrance into heavenly life. Hence tables and lampstands were rightly made in the former, because in this life we need the light of the holy Scriptures and the nourishment of the heavenly sacraments. In the future, however, we will not need such aids, where, in the Psalmist’s words, those who appear with righteousness will be satisfied when the glory of Christ is revealed.

In this life also the hearts of the righteous, like a golden altar of incense, shine brilliantly through the purity of holiness. Filled with the spices of spiritual desires, they burn with the fire of constant love, and, as though placed [Al.: *posita*, an alternative inflection] near the entrance to heaven, they send forth [Col. 0438C] the sweetest vapor of their prayer toward the Holy of Holies above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.

The ark of the covenant, which was inside the veil, most aptly signifies him. In it was a golden urn containing manna, Aaron’s staff that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant. The ark itself signifies the nature of his humanity; the urn of manna, the fullness of his divinity; Aaron’s staff, the inviolable power of his priesthood; and the tablets of the covenant signify that he gave the law and will also give blessing to those who keep the law [Al.: “he is the one who gave the law and will also give blessing to those who keep the law”].

The temple was rightly forty cubits long in front of the entrance to the oracle, because in this present life we must be chastened by fasts and abstinence, so that we may deserve to arrive at the fullness of inward sweetness. Anyone who knows how to understand correctly the forty-day fast of Moses, Elijah, or the Lord himself recognizes that this number signifies the discipline of the present life.

The oracle itself, in which the ark was covered by the cherubim of glory, was twenty cubits long, wide, and high. As we have said, [Col. 0438D] this number signifies the perfection of the twofold love, because whatever is done for God during this pilgrimage is perfected wholly in that dwelling of the eternal homeland, where his magnificence is exalted by the continual praise of the blessed spirits, in the sole breadth of love.

There was also a portico twenty cubits long before the temple, equal to the temple’s width, and ten cubits wide. It had a doorway facing the temple doorway on the east. This portico signifies that people of the holy Church who preceded the time of the Lord’s incarnation nevertheless did not remain empty of faith in that same incarnation. The fact that the portico’s doorway stood opposite the temple doorway, toward the rising of the sun, signifies that the faith of the earlier people concerning Christ is the same as that of the later people, and that the hearts of all the faithful are illumined by the same light of the rising grace.

Hence it is fittingly related that in this same portico two bronze columns, of immense and wondrous workmanship, were set up near the temple doorway, with capitals [Col. 0439A] placed upon them, fashioned as though in the form of a lily.

The columns stand before the temple doorway because distinguished teachers preceded the coming of our Redeemer, who said, “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X). Of such teachers the Apostle says: “James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars,” who bore witness to that same coming (Gal. II). One stood on the right of the doorway and the other on the left, because they foretold the future incarnation of their Redeemer both to the people of Israel, who at that time were burning with divine faith and charity, and no less to the Gentiles, who, still situated as though toward the north, were languishing in the cold of unbelief. They proclaimed that the entrance of the same Redeemer would be opened to them.

The fact that the capitals of the columns were fashioned as though in the form of lilies signifies that the entire substance of their preaching resounded with the radiance of everlasting blessedness, and promised their hearers that they would behold his glory. He who existed as eternal God before the ages became man at the end of the ages, [Col. 0439B] so that, like a lily, he might have a golden color within and a white color without. For what is the redness of gold in whiteness except the splendor of divinity in man? This man he first showed glorious in virtues, and after death clothed him in the snowy radiance of incorruption.

Dearest brethren, we have been pleased to explain these few things from among many concerning the structure of the temple for the joy of our present feast, so that both the wondrous construction of the Lord’s earthly house might delight our hearing and these things [Al. adds: “these same things”], understood spiritually, might lift our minds more ardently toward love of the heavenly dwelling.

Let us therefore love with our whole heart, my brethren, the beauty of the eternal house that we have from God in heaven, and let us diligently strive to think about the place of his tabernacle of glory and to admonish one another concerning it. Above all, let us ask one thing of him and seek it with tireless devotion: that we may deserve to dwell in his house all the days of our life—that is, to be blessed with perpetual life and light.

He does not despise or scorn the prayers of the poor when [Col. 0439C] we pray for what he himself loves. Rather, Christ Jesus our Lord, hearing us mercifully, will grant that we may see his goodness in the land of the living. He lives and reigns forever [Al. adds: “with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”] [Col. 0439D]

## HOMILY LXVI. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

### LUKE XIX

At that time Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through it. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, who was a chief tax collector and was rich. He was seeking to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, since he was short in stature. Running ahead, he climbed a sycamore tree to see him, because he was going to pass that way, and so forth.

What is impossible with human beings is possible with God. For behold, the camel, laying down the burden of its hump, passes through the eye of a needle (Matt. X; Mark X)—that is, the rich man and the tax collector, abandoning the burden of riches and despising the proceeds of fraud, climbs through the narrow gate and along the constricted way that leads to life.

With marvelous devotion of faith, in order to see the Savior, he makes up by climbing the tree for what nature had denied him. Therefore, although he himself does not dare to ask, he rightly receives the blessing of the Lord’s welcome that he desired.

Mystically, however, Zacchaeus, whose name means “justified,” signifies the people from the Gentiles who believe. The more occupied they had been with worldly cares, the humbler they had become through the sins that weighed them down. Yet they were washed, sanctified, and justified [Col. 0440A] in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God (I Cor. VI). They were seeking to see the Savior as he entered Jericho, but they could not because of the crowd.

They desired to share in the grace of faith that the Savior brought to the world, but their ingrained habit of vice stood in the way and prevented them from reaching their desire. For that same crowd of harmful habit which earlier rebuked the blind man who cried out, telling him not to seek the light (Luke XVIII; Mark X), also delays the tax collector who looks upward, preventing him from seeing Jesus.

But just as the blind man overcame the voices of the crowd by crying out more and more loudly, so the short man must transcend the obstacle of the harmful crowd by seeking higher things, abandoning earthly concerns, and climbing the tree of the cross.

The sycamore is a tree whose leaves resemble those of the mulberry, but which surpasses it in height; hence it is called by the Latins “the lofty one.” It is called the “foolish fig.” The Lord’s cross likewise nourishes believers like a fig tree, but is mocked by unbelievers as foolish. “We preach Christ crucified,” for the Jews a stumbling block and for the Gentiles foolishness, but for those who are called, both Jews and Gentiles, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (I Cor. I).

Zacchaeus, short in stature, climbed this tree so that he might be raised up upon it, when every humble person conscious of his own weakness, [Col. 0440B] trusting in the Lord, proclaims: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). Having climbed the sycamore, he sees the Lord passing nearby, because through this praiseworthy foolishness he already directs himself toward the light of heavenly wisdom, seized by it—not yet solidly as it truly is, but as though in passing.

And when he came to the place, looking up, Jesus saw him. As the Savior passed through Jericho, he came to the place where Zacchaeus, running ahead, had climbed the sycamore. This happened because, having sent heralds of his word throughout the world—within whom he himself was both speaking and going—he came to the people of the nations, who, already exalted through faith in his passion, burned with desire to be blessed by recognizing the face of his divinity.

He looked up and saw him because he chose [Col. 0440C] the man who had been raised above earthly desires by the grace of faith and who surpassed the crowds of unbelievers. To see God means to choose or love him. Hence it is said: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII). We too hasten to turn our gaze away from what we detest and to look upon what we love.

Jesus therefore saw the one who was seeing him, because he chose the one who was choosing him and loved the one who loved him. The eminent teacher shows this very order of progress—that is, of reaching knowledge of divinity through faith in the Lord’s incarnation—as though by gazing upon Jesus’ face from the sycamore, when he says: “For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II).

Again, reproaching others, he says: “You have become people who need milk, not solid food” (Heb. V), calling the milk the weak things of the temporary dispensation, and solid food the lofty things of eternal Majesty.

And he said to him: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, because today I must remain in your house.” And he hurried down and received him joyfully.

At one time the Lord remained in the house of the chief Pharisee—that is, he taught in the synagogue of the Jews. But because they attacked him with their poisonous [Col. 0440D] tongues for not baptizing before the meal, for healing on the Sabbath, for receiving tax collectors and sinners, for arguing against greed, and for doing other things worthy of God, he grew weary of their crimes, departed from them, and fled, saying: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

Today, however, he must remain in the house of the short Zacchaeus—that is, he must rest, as the grace of the new light flashes forth, in the humble heart of believing nations. The command that Zacchaeus descend from the sycamore and thus prepare a dwelling for Christ in his house means what the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way. For although he died from weakness, he lives by the power of God” (II Cor. V).

And when they all saw it, they murmured, saying that he had gone in to a sinful man. It is clear that the Jews always hated the salvation of the nations. For it is written: “On the following Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted the things spoken by Paul” (Acts XIII).

And elsewhere even the faithful brethren disputed against the chief [Col. 0441A] of the apostles, saying: “Why did you enter men who are uncircumcised and eat with them?” (Acts XI).

But Zacchaeus stood and said to him: “Behold, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.”

While others were accusing the sinful man, Zacchaeus himself stood—that is, he persevered in the truth of the faith he had begun—and proved not only that he had been converted from sin, but also that he had taken his place among the perfect.

Since the Lord says, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX), anyone who lived innocently before his conversion can, after conversion, give everything to the poor. But whoever has taken anything by fraud must first restore it according to the law and then give to the poor whatever remains for him (Lev. VI). Thus he too, retaining nothing for himself, scatters all his possessions and gives to the poor; “his righteousness remains forever and ever” (Ps. CXI).

This is that wise foolishness whose fruit the tax collector [Col. 0441B] had gathered from the sycamore: to restore what had been taken, to abandon one’s own possessions, to despise visible things, to desire even to die for invisible things, to deny oneself, and to long to follow the footsteps of the Lord, who is not yet seen.

Jesus said to him: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.”

Zacchaeus is called a son of Abraham, not because he was born from Abraham’s lineage, but because he imitated Abraham’s faith. Just as Abraham, at the Lord’s command, abandoned his land, his kindred, and his father’s house for the hope of a future inheritance (Gen. XII), so Zacchaeus left his possessions to be distributed among the poor in order to acquire a treasure in heaven.

He says beautifully, “he too,” declaring that not only those who persevere in righteousness, but also those who repent of injustice, belong among the children of promise.

Alternatively: the salvation that once filled the house of the Jews has today shone upon the people of the nations, because that people too is a son of Abraham by believing in him. Of this the Apostle says: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s [Col. 0441C] offspring” (Gal. III). And elsewhere he says: “Abraham is the father of circumcision not only for those who are of the circumcision, but also for those who follow the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while still uncircumcised” (Rom. IV).

“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost.” This is what he says elsewhere: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX). The merciful Teacher does not disdain to explain his mysteries to the murmuring crowds. Indeed, he shows that the repentance of sinners must not be rejected, since the Son of God himself was sent to earth especially to seek this repentance.

To impress upon us the dispensation of his mercy, he very often calls himself the Son of Man, carefully commending to us what he kindly became for our sake.

## HOMILY LXVII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MICHAEL

[Col. 0441D]

### MARK IX; MATTHEW XVIII

At that time Jesus took a child, set him in the midst of them, and, when he had embraced him, said to them: “Whoever receives one of these children in my name receives me,” and so forth.

Seeing the thoughts of his disciples, the Lord seeks to heal their desire for glory through the contest of humility. He teaches that primacy must not be sought, first by a simple command concerning humility and then by the example of a child’s innocence.

When he says, “Whoever receives one of these children in my name receives me,” he either simply shows that Christ’s poor must be received, for his honor, by those who wish to be greater; or certainly he urges them to be little in wickedness, so that, like children in age, they may preserve simplicity without arrogance, charity without envy, and devotion without anger.

His embracing the child signifies that the humble are worthy of his embrace and love. When such people fulfill what he commanded—“Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI)—they may rightly [Col. 0442A] glory and say: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song II).

When he had said, “Whoever receives one of these children,” he fittingly added, “in my name,” so that those who follow the pattern of virtue that a child observes naturally might do so for Christ’s name, with the assistance of rational discipline.

But because he was teaching that he himself was received in children, as the head in his members, and lest this be thought to be only what appeared outwardly, he added:

“And whoever receives me does not receive me, but him who sent me” (Luke IX). He wished to be believed to be such and so great as the Father is. Indeed, he says, there is so little difference between me and him that whoever receives me receives him who sent me.

“And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone turned by a donkey were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.”

Although this may be a general statement against all who cause anyone to stumble, in accordance with the context it can also be understood as spoken against the apostles. While they were disputing among themselves about which of them was greater, they seemed to be contending with one another over rank (Luke XXII; Matt. XX). If they had persisted in this fault, they could have destroyed those whom they were calling to the faith by their scandal, when those people saw the apostles fighting among themselves for honor.

When he said, “It would be better for him if a millstone turned [Col. 0442B] by a donkey were hung around his neck,” he speaks according to the custom of the province, by which among the ancient Jews this was a punishment for greater crimes: the condemned were sunk into the depths with a stone bound to them. In truth, it is better to finish bodily life innocent, even under the most atrocious temporal punishment, than to earn eternal death of the soul by harming a brother.

The person who can be caused to stumble is rightly called little. Whoever is great, whatever he sees and whatever he suffers, does not depart from the faith; but the person who is little and small in spirit seeks opportunities [Col. 0442C] to be scandalized. Therefore, we must take particular care of those who are small in faith, lest they be offended by us, withdraw from the faith, and fall away from salvation.

It should also be noted that in a good work of ours the scandal of our neighbor must sometimes be avoided, but at other times disregarded as nothing. Insofar as we can avoid causing our neighbors to stumble without sin, we ought to do so. But if scandal arises from the truth, it is more useful to allow scandal to arise than to abandon the truth.

Likewise, by the millstone turned by a donkey the circuit and labor of secular life are expressed, and by the depth of the sea the final condemnation is signified. Therefore, whoever, having been led to the appearance of holiness, destroys others either by word or by example would have been better restrained unto death beneath an outwardly earthly way of life than to display sacred offices in such a way that others could imitate him in guilt. For if he fell alone, the punishment of hell would, in any event, torment him more tolerably.

[Col. 0442D] “And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire.”

Because he had taught above that we must not cause those who believe in him to stumble, he now consequently warns us how carefully we must avoid those who seek to cause us to stumble—that is, who strive to drive us toward the ruin of sin by their word or example.

He calls our hand a necessary friend, whose work and assistance we need every day. But if such a person wishes to injure us in the matter of the soul, he must be excluded from our fellowship, lest, if we wish to share in this life with one who is lost, we perish with him in the future.

Of this it is then said:

“Where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched” (Isa. LXVI). By the worm he signifies the corruption of Gehenna, just as by the fire he signifies its burning. Or by the worm he means the tardy remorse for crimes, which will never cease to bite [Col. 0443A] the conscience of those afflicted in their torments: the fire is the punishment raging outwardly, while the worm is the pain accusing inwardly.

“And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter eternal life lame than, having two feet, to be thrown into the Gehenna of unquenchable fire,” and so forth.

By the foot, as by the hand, he teaches that dear but incorrigible people must be separated from us, lest through the impurity of those whom we cannot correct we ourselves also be polluted and perish. He calls such people hands because of the necessary work they perform for us, and feet because of their ministry and movement, which are useful in our affairs.

“But if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than, having two eyes, to be thrown into the Gehenna of fire.”

The same people are signified by the eye that must be torn out because of scandal: carnally, they are our friends; spiritually, however, they are our adversaries. When we need their counsel and provision, but they seek to deceive us through wicked advice and turn us aside onto the path of error, we must completely [Col. 0443B] abandon their companionship.

“Scandal” is a Greek word, which we may render in Latin as “an obstacle,” or “a fall” and “a striking of the foot.” Some say that scandalum in Greek means “a scruple” in Latin. Therefore, a person causes his brother to stumble when by an improper word or deed he gives him an occasion for falling.

It may also be said simply: If someone seems so necessary to us that he is like a hand, foot, or eye—useful, attentive, and sharp in perception—but causes us to stumble and, through a discordance of conduct, draws us into Gehenna, then even so we ought not, at the risk of our souls, use or enjoy his temporal advantages.

## HOMILY LXVIII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT LUKE

### LUKE X

[Col. 0443C] At that time the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was going to come, and so forth.

Just as no one doubts that the twelve apostles simultaneously displayed and foreshadowed the pattern of bishops, so it must be understood that these seventy-two bore the figure of presbyters—that is, priests of the second order. Nevertheless, in the earliest times of the Church, as apostolic Scripture testifies, both groups were called presbyters and both were called bishops. One designation signifies maturity of wisdom, the other diligence in pastoral care (Titus I; I Tim. III).

The seventy-two are fittingly sent, either because the Gospel had to be preached to that many nations of the world, so that, just as the twelve tribes of Israel had been appointed, these too might be sent to instruct the foreign nations; or because by the very number of preachers it was indicated that the whole world was to be illumined through the Gospel of the supreme and undivided Trinity. Thus, as is established, the sun [Col. 0443D] pours the circuit of its light upon the world for seventy-two hours during its three-day course.

The Lord himself calls himself the day and his apostles the hours, saying: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble” (John XI). And in the Psalms it is rightly commanded: “Announce his salvation from day to day” (Ps. XCV)—that is, Light from Light, true God from true God.

In many passages of holy Scripture, moreover, the mystery of the Trinity is shown through three days, especially because the Lord rose from the dead on the third day. In the Old Testament also, when the people reached Mount Sinai, they received the law on the third day (Exod. XIX). Likewise, Joshua crossed the Jordan River, through which the grace of baptism was commended, on the third day after they had approached it (Josh. III).

“And he sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was going to come.” Because there are two commandments of charity—love of God and love of neighbor—and charity cannot exist between fewer than two (for no one is properly said to have charity toward himself, but by love he reaches outward toward another so that [Col. 0444A] charity may exist), the Lord sends the disciples two by two to preach. He thereby silently indicates that anyone who does not have charity toward another must not undertake the office of preaching at all.

It is rightly said beforehand that he sent them ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was going to come. For the Lord follows his preachers: preaching goes ahead, and then the Lord comes to the dwelling place of our mind. Words of exhortation run ahead, and through them truth is received in the mind.

And he said to them: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.”

The plentiful harvest signifies the multitude of peoples; the few laborers signify the scarcity of teachers. These are the laborers of whom the Psalmist speaks: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. Going forth they went and wept, carrying their seeds; but coming they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their [Col. 0444B] sheaves” (Ps. CXXV).

To speak more plainly, the plentiful harvest is the whole multitude of believers, and the few laborers are the apostles and their imitators who are sent to the harvest.

“Go; behold, I send you like lambs among wolves.” He calls the scribes and Pharisees wolves; they are the clerics of the Jews.

“Do not carry a purse, or a bag, or sandals, and greet no one along the way.”

A preacher must have such trust in God that, although he does not foresee the expenses of the present life, he nevertheless knows with complete certainty that these will not be lacking for him. Otherwise, while his mind is occupied with temporal matters, he will foresee eternal matters less carefully for others.

He is also forbidden to greet anyone along the way, in order to show with what haste he must travel the road of preaching. If anyone wishes to understand these words allegorically as well, money is enclosed in a purse; enclosed money signifies hidden wisdom. Whoever therefore possesses the word of wisdom but neglects to distribute it to his neighbor holds it as though it were money tied up in a purse. It is written [Col. 0444C]: “Hidden wisdom and hidden treasure—what benefit is there in either?” (Eccli. XX).

What else is signified by the bag except the works of the world? And what is signified here by sandals except examples of dead works? Whoever undertakes the office of preaching ought not to carry the burden of worldly affairs, lest, while this weighs down his shoulders, he fail to rise toward the preaching of heavenly things. Nor should he look upon examples of foolish works, lest he think to fortify his own works with something like dead skins.

Everyone who greets along the way greets because of the occasion of the journey, not from a desire to obtain that same salvation. Therefore, whoever preaches salvation to his hearers not out of love for the eternal homeland but from a desire for rewards greets, as it were, along the way, because he wishes salvation for his hearers from occasion rather than from intention.

Into whatever house you enter, first say: “Peace to this house.” And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon it; but if not, it will return to you. [Col. 0444D] The peace offered by the preacher’s mouth either rests in the house if a son of peace is in it, or returns to that same preacher, because either someone will be predestined to life and will follow the heavenly word he hears, or, if no one wishes to hear, the preacher himself will not be without fruit, since peace returns to him because the Lord recompenses him for the labor of his work. But observe: he who forbade the carrying of a purse and a bag nevertheless grants provisions and food from that very preaching, for he continues:

“Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have.” If our peace is received, it is fitting that we remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have, so that we may receive earthly support from those to whom we offer the rewards of the heavenly homeland. Hence Paul too, accepting these things as something small, says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (I Cor. IX; Rom. XV) And it should be noted that what follows is:

[Col. 0445A] “For the laborer is worthy of his wages.” Since the food that sustains us is already a wage for the work, the wage here begins from the labor of preaching, while there it is perfected through the vision of truth. In this matter we must consider that one work of ours is owed two wages: one on the way, the other in the homeland; one sustains us in our labor, the other rewards us in the resurrection.

“And into whatever city you enter, and they receive you, eat what is set before you,” and so forth. Having described the hospitality of different houses, he teaches what they should also do in cities: namely, to share in all things with the devout, but to be wholly separated from association with the impious.
