“And into whatever city you enter, and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say: ‘Even the dust that clings to us from your city we wipe off against you.’” This was either to testify to the earthly labor which they had undertaken for them in vain, or to show that they sought nothing earthly from them to such an extent that they would not even allow the dust of their land to cling to them. Alternatively: the feet of the disciples signify the very work and progress of preaching; the dust with which they are sprinkled signifies the lightness of earthly thought. Even the highest teachers cannot be free from this, when, out of concern for their hearers, they attend unceasingly to salutary cares and, as though traveling along the roads of the world, scarcely gather the dust of the earth upon a single heel. Those who receive the word turn the afflictions and cares of their teachers, which they endured for their sake, into an argument for their own humility. But those who reject the teaching turn the labors and dangers of their teachers, and the burden of their anxieties, into testimony for their own condemnation. This is the very dust which is to be wiped off upon the despisers of the Gospel, and from which the feet of the evangelists are commanded to be washed by good hearers—or rather, which the Savior himself is reported to have washed away (John XIII).

“But I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Sodom on that day than for that city.” The Sodomites, amid all the sins of flesh and soul with which they burned insatiably, were also inhospitable, as Ezekiel testifies; but no guests such as those found among the Jews—the prophets and the apostles—were found among them (Ezek. XVI). Lot was indeed just in sight and hearing, yet he is not reported to have taught anything or performed any signs there. Therefore, “to whom much has been given, from him much will be required,” and “the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (II Pet. II; Luke XII; Wis. VI).

“Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida.” Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, as well as Tiberias, which John names, are cities of Galilee situated on the shore of the lake of Gennesaret, formed by the flowing of the Jordan; it is also called by the evangelists the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias (John VI; Matt. IV). The Lord therefore mourns for the cities which, after so many miracles and mighty works, did not repent. Worse than the Gentiles, who violated only the natural law, they did not fear, after despising the written Law, also to trample upon the Son of God and to spurn grace ungratefully.

[Col. 0445D] “For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.” We see the Savior’s saying fulfilled today, since Chorazin and Bethsaida refused to believe while the Lord was present. Tyre and Sidon, however, had once been friends of David and Solomon (II Reg. V; III Reg. V), and afterward believed through the disciples who preached Christ. They received the faith with such devotion that, when the apostle Paul was departing from Tyre, all the citizens, with their wives and children, accompanied him outside the city; and, in a most beautiful spectacle, so great a multitude escorted their few guests—yet guests exceedingly dear to them because of Christ and the faith—all the way to the ships to bid them farewell (Acts XXI). But why the Gospel was not formerly preached to those who were able to believe, but rather to the Jews who refused to believe, is known to him whose every way is mercy and truth (Ps. [Col. 0446A] XXIV).

Certainly, when the Lord says, “sitting in sackcloth and ashes,” the sackcloth woven from goat hair signifies the harsh remembrance of the sin that wounds, with which the left side is to be clothed on the day of judgment; ashes signify consideration of death, through which the entire mass of the human race is to be reduced to dust. Sitting, moreover, designates the humiliation of one’s own conscience, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Rise up after you have sat down” (Ps. CXXVI). This means: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of visitation” (I Pet. V).

“And you, Capernaum, exalted to heaven, will be brought down to hell.” This sentence has a twofold meaning: either you will be brought down to hell because you resisted my preaching with the utmost pride; or because you were exalted to heaven through my hospitality, possessing such privilege through my signs and mighty works, and therefore you are punished with greater penalties because you nevertheless refused to believe these things. And lest anyone think that this rebuke applies only to those cities or persons who despised the Lord while seeing him in the flesh, and not to all who even today disregard the words of the Gospel, he accordingly added, saying:

“He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me.” Thus each person, in hearing or despising the preacher of the Gospel, might learn that he is hearing or despising not some insignificant persons, but the Lord and Savior—or rather, the Father himself. For it follows:

“But he who despises me despises him who sent me.” For undoubtedly the teacher is heard in the disciple, and the father is honored in the son. This may also be understood as follows: “He who despises you despises me. Whoever does not show mercy to one of my least brothers does not show it to me” (Matt. XXV), because I too assumed the form of a servant and the condition of a poor man for their sake. But whoever despises me, refusing to believe in God and trampling upon the Son of God, despises him who sent me, because “I and the Father are one” (John X).

“Now the seventy-two returned with joy, saying: [Col. 0446C] ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.’” They rightly confessed, rendering honor to the name of Christ; but because, in their still-weak faith, they rejoiced in their miracles, see what they hear:

“And he said to them: ‘I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning.’” “I see” does not mean only now; rather, “I was already watching” when he fell. By saying “like lightning,” he either signifies his precipitous fall from the heights above to the depths below, or that, having been cast down, he still transforms himself into an angel of light (II Cor. XI). Therefore, because he saw the disciples lifted up by the performance of signs, he frightens them by this example and recalls them to humility by reminding them of the one who first fell through pride (Isa. XIV), so that, remembering that he was cast out of heaven because of pride, they might recognize that they, born from the earth, would be humbled even more if they grew proud.

“Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you.” This means the power to cast out every kind of unclean spirit from possessed bodies. Yet it may also be taken quite literally. For Paul, when attacked by a viper, suffered no harm (Acts XXVIII); and John, as history relates, was not injured after drinking poison. I think, however, that serpents, which harm with their teeth, and scorpions, which harm with their tails, differ in this respect: serpents, raging openly, signify either men or demons; scorpions, lying in wait secretly, signify the same. Serpents present the poisons of evil persuasion to those who are beginning in virtue; scorpions strive to corrupt virtues that have already been brought to completion.

“Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you.” They are forbidden to rejoice in the subjection of spirits, since they are flesh, because casting out spirits, like performing other miracles, is sometimes not the merit of the one who acts, but is accomplished through the invocation of Christ’s name for the condemnation of those who invoke it, or granted for the benefit of those who see and hear, so that although people despise those who perform signs, they may nevertheless honor God, at whose invocation such great miracles are performed. Thus the sons of Sceva also appeared to cast out demons in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XIX); and Judas the apostle is reported to have performed many signs among the other apostles even though his heart was that of a traitor (Matt. X; Mark VI; Luke IX).

“But rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” If, he says, Satan through pride lost his place in heaven together with his companions, you ought to rejoice not in their humiliation but in your own exaltation, so that, from the place where they fell after being lifted up, you may ascend while remaining humble. This must not be understood childishly, as though God, to remedy forgetfulness, writes the good in heaven and the wicked on earth, when Jeremiah says: “All who forsake you shall be put to shame; those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. XVII). Rather, it should be understood salutarily: whether someone has performed heavenly or earthly works, he is, as it were, marked down by these letters and eternally fixed in God’s memory.

## HOMILY LXIX. ON THE SOLEMNITY OF ALL SAINTS

[Col. 0447B]

**Luke VI; Matthew V.** At that time Jesus, descending from the mountain with his disciples, stood in a level place, and a crowd of his disciples, and so forth.

When the Lord was choosing apostles, he went up into the mountains; but when he was going to teach the crowds, he returned to the level places, because the crowds are capable of seeing Christ only in humility. For this is the rule followed by the Apostle when he says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III). “For you were not yet able to receive it; indeed, not even now are you able.” But the apostles themselves, according to Matthew, as being more perfect, are said to have been taught both on the mountain and by the Savior’s open mouth (Matt. V). If anyone wishes to examine both evangelists more carefully, it may be understood that when he chose the twelve disciples on the mountain from among the larger number—whom he also called apostles, something Matthew omitted—he then delivered the discourse which Matthew inserted and Luke passed over, namely, the discourse on the mountain. Then, after he had descended, he delivered another similar discourse in a level place, which Matthew omits but Luke does not, and both discourses were brought to a conclusion in the same way.

“From all Judea and Jerusalem, and from the seacoast, and from Tyre and Sidon,” and so forth. I think that the multitude from the seacoast was not called so because of the nearby Sea of Galilee—for he would not have mentioned this in connection with a miracle—but because of the Great Sea, in which Tyre and Sidon could also be included. Yet because these are cities of the Gentiles, assigned to the Jews by lot but not possessed by them, since they were unable to drive out their inhabitants, they are deliberately mentioned by name so that the fame and power of the Savior might be made known: it summoned even foreign cities to receive healing and instruction.

Here it should be noted that although the Lord had compassion on Gentiles who came to him—and therefore, approving the faith of those who asked, he healed the centurion’s servant (Matt. VIII) and the daughter of the Canaanite woman (Matt. XV)—he is nevertheless not found to have entered their cities. He did this lest he provide an occasion for complaint to the Jews who sought grounds for accusation, reserving instead the perfect salvation of the Gentiles for the time of his passion and resurrection. When that time was approaching and the Gentiles were seeking to see him, he said: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII).

“And the whole crowd was seeking to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all.” Earlier, the leper was cleansed when the Lord touched him (Luke V); here, every member of the crowd who was able to touch him was healed by the power of his Spirit. The Savior’s touch, therefore, is the work of salvation: to touch him is to believe faithfully in him, while to be touched by him is to be strengthened by his gift.

Yet each person abounds in his own understanding. The crowds who come from far away to hear him are healed by the touch of the Lord as he descends into the plain. The disciples, already instructed in lesser matters, are led on the summit of the mountain to greater things; from among them those are chosen who are to behold him transfigured in secret on the mountain (Matt. XVII). One above all the others, as though he were to be inebriated from the fountain of sublime wisdom, reclines upon the breast of the Master (John XXI). Rarely anywhere will you find either crowds following the Lord to higher places or anyone weak being healed on the mountain. Rather, once the fever of lust has been extinguished and the light of knowledge kindled, each person gradually ascends to the summit of the virtues.

In the Old Testament also, Moses alone, together with Joshua, ascended the mountain of God, while he appointed Aaron and Hur to govern the people in the plain until they returned (Exod. XXIV). Aaron, whose name is interpreted as “mountain of strength,” signifies the singular excellence of the Lord’s incarnation; Hur, whose name means “fire,” signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit. For many of the little ones in the Church, although they cannot accompany their teachers in penetrating the mysteries of the highest divinity, can nevertheless be redeemed by the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation and marked by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

“And he, lifting up his eyes toward his disciples, said: ‘Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.’” Although he speaks generally to all, the Savior nevertheless raises his eyes more particularly toward the disciples, so that for those who receive the word with the attentive ear of the heart he may open more widely the light of inward savor. Matthew says something similar: “And when he had sat down, his disciples came to him; and opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit’” (Matt. V). To those for whom he opens his mouth while seated on the mountain, so that they may hear great things in a sublime manner, he directs his eyes while standing on the plain, so that they may plainly understand what they have heard.

“Blessed, therefore, are the poor”—not absolutely everyone, but only those who regard as nothing the whole summit of the present age, however lofty it may appear. They are rightly declared worthy of the gift of the heavenly kingdom, because they are shown to have been stripped of desire for human pleasure. King David declares the poverty he endured when he says: “But I am needy and poor” (Ps. LXIX). Elsewhere, scorning not only earthly things but even those above the heavens through the Lord, he says: “For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII). Immediately he makes clear where he fixed the anchor of his hope by adding: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (ibid.). Otherwise, some people, in the most wretched condition of poverty, lack both the joys of this age because of their want of possessions and the kingdom of God because of the wickedness of their merits.

“Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled.” Matthew explains what it means for the blessed to hunger and thirst: namely, for righteousness (Matt. V). He teaches us most plainly that we must never consider ourselves righteous enough, but must always love—or rather, burn with desire for—daily progress in righteousness. That perfect fullness cannot come in this age but only in the future, the Psalmist shows, aflame with desire for the things above, when he says: “But I shall appear in righteousness before your sight; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI).

It may also be taken simply: “Blessed are you who hunger now,” who chastise your bodies and subject them to servitude, who devote yourselves to the word in hunger and thirst; for then you will have the abundance of heavenly joys in which to delight.

“Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.” Those who weep over the loss not of temporal advantages but of spiritual virtues will be comforted with eternal blessedness. Here we are commanded to mourn not only our own sins but also those of our neighbor. If we love him as ourselves, we must consequently rejoice in his progress and grieve over his decline; indeed, we must not merely grieve but be inflamed even to tears. Thus Samuel and David mourn Saul’s sin and death (I Reg. XVI; II Reg. I); thus the Lord himself wept over the sinful city (Luke XIX); and, moved with compassion for the grieving sisters, he first wept in human pity for Lazarus, whom he was about to raise by his divine majesty (John XI), mystically signifying that those who are sunk in the death of sin must be mourned by their neighbors so that they may rise again.

[Col. 0449A] But when he promises that those who weep now will laugh, this must not be understood childishly. In keeping with Scripture’s manner of speaking, the name “laughter” should be understood to designate the exultation of the mind and a certain more joyful affection. Thus Sarah says: “God has made laughter for me” (Gen. XXI). And in Job it is said: “The mouth of the truthful will be filled with laughter” (Job VIII). By these expressions, as I have said, the inward joy of the soul is represented.

“Blessed will you be when people hate you, and when they exclude you and reproach you.” Whoever desires to endure weeping, hunger, and poverty for the riches of Christ’s inheritance in the saints, for the bread of eternal life, and for the hope of heavenly joys, is blessed. Much more blessed, however, is the one who is not afraid to preserve these virtues amid adversity. For however wickedly people may hate them, they cannot wound the heart beloved by Christ; though they exclude them and expel them from the synagogue, Christ finds and strengthens them; though they reproach the name of the crucified one, he raises them together with himself, after they have died with him, and makes them sit together in the heavenly places.

“And when they cast out your name as evil because of the Son of Man.” When he says “your name,” he means the name of Christians. As far as the Gentiles and Jews were concerned, this name was very often erased from memory and rejected by people, with no cause for hatred remaining except the Son of Man: namely, because believers wished to make the name of Christ their own title. Therefore the persecutors of the highest name are rightly branded by the name of “human beings.” “Blessed,” he says, “will you be when people hate you,” teaching them that they will be persecuted by human beings but blessed beyond the human condition.

“Rejoice on that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven.” This command can be fulfilled not by just anyone who suffers, but by one who suffers with regard solely to the heavenly reward, so that amid hatred in people’s hearts, insults on their tongues, and even the hands of persecutors, he may remain with an equal—or rather, an even more joyful—heart. Those like us are not capable of this, but those who went forth rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts V).

Whoever therefore endures many adversities on earth for Christ will receive many gifts from Christ in heaven. But consider how many verbal darts the false prophets endured from Elijah, who mocked them by saying: “Cry out with a louder voice, for he is a god; perhaps he is talking, or is at an inn, or on a journey, or at least he is sleeping, so that he may be awakened” (III Reg. XVIII)! What a slaughter those suffered who were killed all at once, eight hundred and fifty of them! Yet because Baal, not Christ, was at issue, they neither rejoiced when mocked nor earned the palm when killed, but rather eternal punishment.

“For they did the same things to the prophets as their fathers did.” He rightly encouraged them by this example, because those who speak the truth commonly suffer persecution. Nevertheless, the ancient prophets did not on that account withdraw through fear of persecution from preaching the truth.

It should certainly be noted that just as Matthew, through the eight beatitudes he sets forth, indicates the perfection of our hope, which is consecrated in the glory of the resurrection, so Luke embraces the four cardinal virtues. Blessed are the poor, who through temperance restrain themselves from the allurements of the world. Blessed are the hungry, who, reminded by their own hunger that the hungry deserve compassion, themselves show mercy through righteousness as far as they are able. That almsgiving is rightly called righteousness—the almsgiving by which we do not give our own things to Christ but return his own—the Psalmist testifies when he says: “He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Ps. CXI). For righteousness is that by which we give each person what is his, owing no one anything except that we love one another (Rom. XIII).

Blessed are those who, through prudence, discerning good from evil, know how to mourn what is passing away and yearn for eternal things. Blessed are those who, through the strength of faith, are able to endure every painful thing. Therefore, those who are not yet able to climb to the summit of perfected virtue must meanwhile be nurtured by the blessedness of general perfection, so that, progressing little by little from good things to better, while they gladly listen to the Lord standing on the plain, they may eventually ascend to him seated on the mountain.

For those whose hearts he is still laboring to tame and instruct he addresses as though standing—the posture of one who is working. But those whom he finds ready and already teachable through long exercise in spiritual study he addresses as the Savior, seated in the freedom and dignity of a teacher, revealing to them mysteries concerning heavenly things.

This difference among spiritual attainments is beautifully expressed through the figures found in the condition of the Israelite people. There, the whole populace, using garments of every kind, was commanded to make for itself blue fringes at the four corners of its cloaks; the priests were to have four garments, distinguished with an equal number of mystical colors in wondrous variety; and the high priests were to wear both the garments of the priests and four other kinds of clothing, in the same colors but with the more exalted grace of dignity, flashing with interwoven gold and marked with the name of the patriarchs and of the Lord himself (Num. XV). To explain or even merely set these forth one by one belongs to the labor of another work.

## HOMILY LXX. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY OF ALL SAINTS

[Col. 0450B]

Today, beloved, we celebrate the feast of all the saints in the single joy of one solemnity. Heaven rejoices in their fellowship; earth is glad through their patronage; the Church is crowned by their triumphs. Their confession is more glorious the stronger it was in suffering, because as the struggle increased, so too did the glory of those who fought, and the triumph of martyrdom is adorned by many kinds of suffering. Through more grievous torments, greater rewards were won.

The Catholic mother Church, spread far and wide throughout the entire world, learned in Christ Jesus her very head not to fear insults, crosses, and death. Strengthened more and more—not by resisting but by enduring—she inspired all whom penal imprisonment had enclosed in a glorious company, with an equal and similar ardor of virtue, to undertake the contest and seek triumphal glory.

O truly blessed mother [Col. 0450C] Church, whom the honor of divine favor so illuminates; whom the glorious blood of conquering martyrs adorns; whom the inviolate, radiant virginity of confession clothes! Her flowers lack neither roses nor lilies. Let each of the beloved now strive, so that they may receive the fullest dignity in both honors: crowns white with virginity or purple with suffering. In the heavenly camp, where peace and battle each have their flowers, the soldiers of Christ are crowned.

For God’s ineffable and boundless goodness also foresaw this: that he would not prolong the time of labor and combat, lest he make it lengthy or eternal, but brief and, so to speak, momentary. Thus in this brief and limited life there would be struggles and labors, but the crown and rewards of merit, which are eternal, would have no end. Labors would quickly come to an end, while the rewards of merit would endure without end, so that after the darkness of this life they would see the brightest light and receive a blessedness greater than all the bitterness of their sufferings. The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us.”

[Col. 0450D] With open arms the heavenly city receives those returning from battle; it goes out to meet them as they carry trophies from the enemy they have overthrown. Women come with the victorious men—women who have conquered both the world and their sex, and who have doubled the glory of their service. Virgins come with children, passing beyond their tender years through virtue. The rest of the faithful multitude also enters the royal hall of eternity: those who have observed with undisturbed peace the purity of faith, united with the disciplines of the heavenly commandments.

Come, then, brothers, let us now set out upon the journey of life; let us return to the heavenly city in which we are enrolled and appointed as citizens. We are not strangers, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, indeed heirs of God and coheirs with Christ. Fortitude will open the gates of this city for us, and confidence will provide a broad entrance.

Let us therefore consider the celebrated happiness of that city, insofar as it is possible to consider it; for no speech will suffice to comprehend it as it truly is. It is said of it somewhere that “pain, sorrow, and groaning will flee away there.”

What life is more blessed than that, where there is no fear of poverty and no weakness of illness? No one will be injured; no one will grow angry. No one envies; no desire burns there. No longing for honor strikes anyone, nor any ambition for power. There is no fear of the devil, no ambushes of demons, and the terror of Gehenna is far away. There is no death of body or soul, but a joyous life through the gift of immortality. There will be no discord anywhere, but all things will be harmonious and fitting, because there will be one concord among all the saints; peace and joy will contain everything.

All things are tranquil and quiet there, with perpetual splendor—not the splendor that exists now, but one far brighter, as it is also more blessed. For that city, as it is written, will not need the light of the sun; the almighty Lord will illumine it, and its lamp is the Lamb. There the saints will shine like stars through endless eternities, and like the brightness of the firmament, those who instruct many.

Therefore [Col. 0451B] there will be no night there, no darkness, no gathering of clouds, and no harshness of cold or heat. Instead there will be such a tempering of all things as eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and the human heart has not conceived—except the hearts of those who are found worthy to enjoy them, whose names are written in the book of life; those who have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb, who stand before the throne of God and serve him day and night.

There is no old age there, nor the misery of old age, since all attain to the perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age. Above all these things is fellowship with the companies of angels and archangels, with thrones and dominions, principalities and powers, and enjoyment of the companionship of all the heavenly and higher virtues. There one beholds the ranks of the saints sparkling like bright stars: patriarchs radiant with faith, prophets rejoicing in hope, apostles judging the world in the twelve tribes of Israel, martyrs shining with purple crowns of victory, and virgins wearing gleaming garlands.

[Col. 0451C] But no voice will suffice to speak of the King who sits in their midst. That glory, that beauty, that power, that splendor, that majesty escape every discourse and exceed every capacity of the human mind. It is beyond all the glory of the saints to attain his immeasurable vision and be illuminated by the radiance of his majesty.

Thus we ought daily to endure torments; thus we ought to tolerate Gehenna itself for a short time, so that we may see Christ coming in glory and be joined to the company of the saints. Was it not worth enduring everything that is grievous, so that we might share in so great a good and so great a glory?”

What will the glory of the righteous be, beloved brothers, how great the joy of the saints, when every face shines like the sun; when the Lord begins to enumerate his people, distinguished by their orders, into the kingdom of his Father; and when he restores to each according to his merits and works the rewards he promised—heavenly things in place of earthly, eternal things in place of temporal, great things in place of small? He will lead the saints into the vision of the Father’s glory and make them sit in the heavenly places, so that God may be all in all. He will bestow the eternity he promised to his lovers and the immortality for which he restored them through the vivification of his blood. He will bring them back again to paradise and open the kingdom of heaven through the faithfulness and truth of his promise.

Let these things cling firmly to our minds; let them be understood with full faith; let them be loved with all our hearts; let them be acquired through the greatness of works that never cease. The matter lies in the power of the one who acts, because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence.” This matter, O human being—that is, the heavenly kingdom—asks no price other than yourself. It is worth as much as you are. Give yourself, and you will have it.

Why are you troubled about the price? Christ gave himself to acquire you for God the Father. So give yourself, that you may be his kingdom; and do not let sin reign in your mortal body, but let the spirit reign for the acquisition of life.

To this palm of salutary works, then, let it be our delight to attain. Let us all willingly and eagerly contend in the contest of righteousness. Let us run while God and Christ look on, and, having already begun to be greater than the age and the world, let us not slow our course through any desire for the world.

If the final day finds us running prepared and swiftly in this contest of work, the Lord will never fail to reward our merits. He who will grant a purple crown in persecution for suffering will also, in peace, give a white crown to those who conquer for the merits of righteousness. For neither Abraham, Isaac, nor Jacob was killed, yet, honored for the merits of faith and righteousness, they deserved to be first among the patriarchs. Whoever is found faithful, righteous, and praiseworthy is gathered into their banquet.

We must remember that we ought to do not our own will but God’s, because whoever does his will remains forever, just as he himself remains forever. Therefore, beloved, with an undivided mind, firm faith, robust virtue, and perfect charity, let us be ready for every will of God, bravely preserving the Lord’s [Col. 0452B] commandments: innocence in simplicity; concord in charity; modesty in humility; diligence in administration; vigilance in helping those who labor; mercy in supporting the poor; constancy in defending the truth; and strictness in the severity of discipline, so that nothing may be lacking in us as an example of good deeds.

These are the footprints which all the saints, returning to their homeland, left for us, so that, clinging to their paths, we might follow them into joy. Let us also count paradise as our homeland with them. We have already begun to have the patriarchs as our parents. Why do we not hasten and run, so that we may see our homeland and greet our parents?

A great number of our beloved awaits us there; a crowded and abundant multitude of parents, brothers, and children longs for us—now secure concerning their own safety, but still anxious about ours. To come into their embrace and presence: what shared joy it will be for them and for us! What heavenly delight awaits us there in the fellowship of our fellow servants, who are waiting for us! What supreme and perpetual happiness!

There is the glorious choir of the apostles; there the distinguished company of rejoicing prophets; there the innumerable people of martyrs crowned for victory in their contests; there the most radiant crowd of virgins rejoices; there the fortitude of confessors is praised. Those also are counted among their reward who, keeping the Lord’s commandments, transferred their earthly possessions to heavenly treasures.

If we delight in coming to them, let us hasten with eager desire, so that we may soon be with them and soon come to Christ. Let us have him as the guide of this journey, the author of salvation, the prince of light, and the giver of joy, who lives and reigns with God the almighty Father and the Holy Spirit.

## HOMILY LXXI. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY OF ALL SAINTS.

We read in ecclesiastical histories that Saint Boniface, [Col. 0452D] who was fourth after blessed Gregory to hold the episcopate of the city of Rome, obtained by his prayers from the Emperor Phocas that the temple in Rome which had formerly been called the Pantheon be given to the Church of Christ, because it seemed to be, as it were, an image of all the gods. After removing all its impurity, he made it a church of the holy Mother of God and of all the martyrs of Christ, so that, once the multitude of demons had been expelled, the multitude of saints might there be kept in remembrance by the faithful; and that the whole populace, on the first day of November, as on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, might assemble at the church consecrated in honor of all the saints. There, after the solemnity of the Mass had been celebrated by the bishop of the apostolic see, and everything had been duly completed, each person would return home with joy.

Accordingly, from this custom of the holy Roman Church, as Christian devotion increased, it was decreed that in the churches of God built far and wide throughout the world, the honor and memory of all the saints should be observed on the day we have mentioned, [Col. 0453A] so that whatever human frailty, through ignorance, negligence, or preoccupation with worldly affairs, had performed less fully in the solemnity of the saints might be made good by this observance, so that, protected by their patronage, we might be able to reach the heavenly joys of the peoples.

The blessed Mother of God, and ever-virgin Mary—the temple of the Lord, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, virgin before childbirth, virgin in childbirth, virgin after childbirth—must in no way be believed to be absent from the solemnity of this present day, together with her virgins. By her example she urged the people of God to despise the perishing luxuries of the world, to withdraw from the enticements of mortal nature, and to preserve bodily chastity, together with the honor of virginity, within the hospitable chambers of the heart. She affirmed that this chastity is the queen of all virtues and the fruit of eternal salvation, and that it is also the companion of the angels. Thus an innumerable multitude of both sexes followed in her footsteps; [Col. 0453B] they preferred to attach themselves to the Bridegroom who is in heaven, in perpetual mind, action, conduct, and bearing, abandoning the bonds of marriage and rejecting the begetting of children. They persevered without ceasing in prayer; they devoted themselves to fasts; they loved sacred vigils; they pursued almsgiving; they revived the poor; they clothed the naked; they visited the sick; they rejoiced in tribulation; they endured words of slander and insult; they were humble in the advancement of their progress; and they gave thanks to God when temporal possessions were lost.

Devoting themselves to all these things and to their like, from desire for the heavenly kingdom and because of hope for eternal reward, with the most ardent love, continually and willingly, and thus persevering in love of God and of their neighbors, they rejoiced to bring their lives to an end for God alone.

O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor, or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid? How are all things from him, through him, and in him? To him be honor and glory [Col. 0453C] forever and ever. Amen. He has placed the heavenly kingdoms above, in a wondrous order, among the angelic spirits, for the praise, glory, and honor of his name and majesty forever.

We fear to speak at greater length about them, because God alone knows how or in what manner their invisible nature exists in its own purity, without contamination or diminution. Nevertheless, we have learned, on the testimony of sacred Scripture, that there are nine orders of angels, established to fulfill God’s judgments and ministries, whose principalities and powers are distinguished subtly and wondrously according to the will of the Almighty.

Some of them are sent to us into the world, coming to proclaim future things; others are appointed so that signs and miracles may more frequently be performed through them; others preside over subordinate angelic spirits and govern them by arranging them for the fulfillment of divine mysteries; others surpass the rest in wondrous power, because other hosts of angels have been subjected to them for obedience; others are filled with so much grace of Divinity that the Lord dwells in them and issues his judgments through them; others are filled with more perfect knowledge in proportion as they contemplate the brightness of God more nearly; while other [Col. 0453D] hosts of angels are so joined to God that no others stand between them and God, and they burn with love all the more intensely as they behold the brightness of his Divinity more subtly.

With such distinctions, as we have said, from the beginning of the life of the blessed spirits, the heavenly kingdoms above, wondrously established by God the Creator, continue forever.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we bring forward the memory of the ancient fathers who came before us—whom, as sacred Scripture demonstrates, we know existed before the Law and under the Law—only so that you may more easily understand how great and of what kind is the presence of this most sacred day, which is honorably established without end together with all those about whom we are speaking.

Now let us return to those whom the wave of baptism and the outpouring of Christ’s blood washed and purified, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, from the error of their ancestral sin and from the filth of ancient paganism, in the New Testament. [Col. 0454A] Blessed are their eyes, which were worthy to see Christ coming in the flesh.

Among those of such glorious vision was John the Baptist. Conceived through the announcement of the same angel by whom Christ’s conception was announced, he held the primacy at the beginning of preaching and baptism. He recognized Jesus, when he saw him taking away the sins of the world, and pointed him out with his finger. According to Christ’s testimony, no greater man had arisen among those born of women. Rightly, therefore, he is called the Lord’s forerunner, the herald of the Judge, and the prophet of the Most High. Before he had yet been born, he prophesied that Christ would come into the world, and by his glorious passion he went before him even as he descended to the underworld for the redemption of souls.

To this chosen athlete of God corresponds the number of the twelve apostles. Divine Providence chose them from all whom the world contained, beginning with the first mighty works of miracles, in order to lay the foundations of the new faith and raise up the still tender state of the Church, so that the sound of their preaching might go out into all the earth and their words proceed to the ends [Col. 0454B] of the world.

Clinging to the true vine—that is, to Christ—as branches, their fruit remains forever and does not wither. To them the Lord himself spoke, saying:

“You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

And again:

“I shall no longer call you servants, but friends, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.”

He promised that whatever they wished to bind on earth would be bound also in heaven, and whatever they loosed on earth would be loosed in heaven. And again, when he came to judge the world, he had foretold that they would sit upon twelve thrones and judge the world together with him.

This day, as we believe, is declared to be subject to such patrons. Subject to them is the triumphant name of the martyrs [Col. 0454C], who, through various kinds of torment, imitated Christ’s passion with hearts that did not shrink from suffering. Some were killed by the sword, others burned by flames, others beaten with scourges, others pierced with bars, others tortured upon the scaffold, others subjected to the perils of the sea, others flayed alive, others handed over to chains, others deprived of their tongues, others buried beneath stones, others afflicted by cold, others tormented by hunger. Still others, with their hands cut off or their other limbs severed, carried before the peoples, naked for the Lord’s name, the spectacle of insult.

These are the conquerors and friends of God. They despised the commands of wicked rulers, and now they are crowned and receive the palms of their labors; they were founded upon the firm rock, that is, Christ.

Concerning such people and their like, the Apostle, pierced in heart and sighing, says:

“Saints experienced mockeries and scourging, and moreover chains and prisons. They were stoned, they were cut apart, they were tested; they died by the killing of the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, in want, distress, and affliction—people of whom the world was not worthy,” and so forth.

And blessed Pope Gregory, [Col. 0454D] in his exposition of a certain Gospel, lamenting concerning such warriors, says:

“Behold, God’s chosen ones subdue the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command demons, and shine with virtues. They despise the present and proclaim the eternal homeland by their words and conduct; they love it even by dying, and reach it through torments. They can be killed, but they cannot be bent. Although they have suffered torments before men, their hope is full of immortality. Afflicted in few things, they will be well rewarded in many. ‘Thus God tested them and found them worthy of himself. As gold in the furnace he tested them, and as a sacrificial burnt offering he accepted them.’”

Now, then, we have heard of the struggles and victories of Christ’s martyrs. We believe that this day was sanctified by them precisely to the extent that they did not cease to labor through torments to sanctify it in themselves. We also believe that this day’s feast is not unknown to Christ’s priests and teachers, or to confessors, [Col. 0455A] who spiritually water the hearts of the faithful as though with heavenly rains, so that they may happily bring forth the unfading fruit of good works. They took care not merely to return the talents entrusted to them, but also to increase them without fraud and with interest. The good which they had learned through understanding by the grace of the Holy Spirit to be beneficial not only to themselves, they endeavored, according to the Apostle’s command, to implant in the minds of those subject to them by reproving, entreating, exhorting, and taking care of them.

Their mind is most luminous, while their hands are full of purity, because, as they celebrate the sacred mysteries of Christ’s body and blood at the table of the altar, they do not cease to offer in the inner chambers of their hearts a living and pleasing sacrifice to God—that is, themselves, without stain or admixture of evil work.

Although they did not experience the sword of persecutors, they are nevertheless not deprived of martyrdom, [Col. 0455B] since they are worthy of martyrdom before God by the merit of their life. Martyrdom is accomplished not only by the shedding of blood, but also by abstaining from sins and practicing God’s commandments.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us seek with the full attention of our minds the patronage of so many intercessors about whom we have spoken, so that, through the temporal feasts we celebrate, and through their merits interceding for us, we may be able to reach eternal things.

Everything celebrated as a temporal feast passes away. Therefore take care, you who attend these solemnities, lest you be separated from the eternal solemnity. What benefit is there in attending the feasts of human beings, if it should happen that you are absent from the feasts of angels?

Do not, then, weigh in yourselves the transitory things you possess; rather, consider what you are. Behold, the world that is loved is fleeing. These saints, whom we commemorate today, trampled upon the flourishing world through the contempt of their minds. At that time there was long life, continual health, abundance of possessions, fertility in offspring, and tranquility in lasting peace; yet, although the world flourished in itself, it had already withered in their hearts.

Behold, now the world has withered in itself, [Col. 0455C] and it still flourishes in our hearts. Everywhere there is desolation; from every side we are struck; from every side we are filled with bitterness; and yet, in our blindness, we love carnal desires and the very bitterness of the world. We follow what is fleeing; we cling to what is slipping; we slip together with the one who is falling, whom we hold while he falls.

Once the world drew us away from God; now, filled with such blows, the world itself is already sending us to the Lord. Consider, therefore, that the things which pass away in time are nothing, for the end of temporal things shows that nothing which can pass away has any substance. The collapse of things indicates that a passing thing was already nearly nothing when it seemed to stand.

Practice these things among yourselves, then; turn them over carefully in your minds. Although we are still held here in the weakness of the body, let us nevertheless strive with our whole heart toward those about whom we have spoken, so that afterward we may deserve to rejoice with them in the eternal age, through him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXII. ON THE HOLY DAY OF ONE APOSTLE

[Col. 0455D]

**LUKE IX; MATTHEW X; MARK III.** At that time, when Jesus had summoned the twelve apostles, he gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them to preach the kingdom of God and to heal the sick, and so forth.

Having first granted them the power of signs, he sent them to preach the kingdom of God, so that the greatness of the deeds might also bear witness to the greatness of the promises, and the displayed power might give faith, as it were, twice over, and so that they might do new things because they preached new things.

Thus now also, when the number of the faithful has increased, there are many within the holy Church who possess a life of virtue but do not possess signs of virtue, because a miracle is displayed outwardly to no purpose if that which should operate inwardly is lacking. For, according to the saying of the Teacher of the Gentiles, “Tongues are for a sign not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Corinthians XIV).

[Col. 0456A] And he said to them: “Take nothing for the journey, neither a staff, nor a bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics.”

It is customary to ask how Matthew and Luke could have recorded that the Lord told the disciples not even to carry a staff, when Mark says: “And he commanded them to take nothing for the journey except a staff only.”

This is resolved by understanding that the staff which, according to Mark, is to be carried is spoken of under one meaning, while the staff which, according to Matthew and Luke, is not to be carried is spoken of under another—just as “temptation” is understood in one sense where it is said, “God tempts no one” (James I), and in another where it is said, “The Lord your God tempts you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy XIII). The former is temptation to seduction; the latter is temptation for testing.

Both things, therefore, are to be accepted as having been said by the Lord to the apostles: both that they should not carry a staff and that they should carry no staff except one. For when, according to Matthew, he said to them, “Do not possess gold or silver,” and so forth (Matthew X), he immediately added: “For the laborer is worthy of his food.” From this he clearly showed [Col. 0456B] why he did not want them to possess or carry these things—not because they are unnecessary for sustaining this life, but because he was sending them in such a way as to show that these things were owed to them by those to whom they announced the Gospel as believers.

It is clear that the Lord did not command this as though evangelists ought not to live from any other source than from those to whom they proclaim the Gospel—for otherwise the Apostle acted against this command, since he supported himself by the labor of his hands, so as not to be burdensome to anyone (1 Thessalonians II). Rather, the Lord gave them authority by which they might know that these things were owed to them.

When something is commanded by the Lord, failure to do it is a fault of disobedience. When authority is given, however, anyone may choose not to use it and may, as it were, relinquish his own right.

Thus, when the Lord ordered what the Apostle says he ordered—namely, that those who announce the Gospel should live from the Gospel (1 Corinthians IX)—he was speaking to the apostles so that they might confidently possess or carry none of the necessities of this life, neither great nor small.

For this reason he said, [Col. 0456C] “Neither a staff,” showing that everything was owed by the faithful to his ministers, who demanded nothing superfluous. And by adding, “For the laborer is worthy of his food,” he fully disclosed and clarified the reason for all that he was saying.

He therefore signified this authority by the name of “staff” when he said, “They should take nothing for the journey except a staff only,” so that it might be understood that, through the authority received from the Lord—which is signified by the name of staff—even the things that are not carried will not be lacking.

The same is to be understood concerning two tunics: none of them should think that, besides the one he was wearing, he ought to carry another, anxious lest it should be needed, since through that authority he could receive one.

But when, according to Mark, he forbids them not merely to carry or possess two tunics, but more explicitly forbids them to wear two tunics, saying, “and not to be clothed in two tunics” (Mark III), what does he exhort them to do except to walk not in duplicity but in simplicity?

Alternatively, by two tunics it seems to me that he means a double garment—not that in the regions of Scythia, stiff with icy snow, anyone ought to be content with a single tunic, but that by “tunics” we should understand clothing, so that, while clothed in one garment, we should not keep another for ourselves out of fear of the future.

[Col. 0456D] “And into whatever house you enter, remain there, and do not depart from it.”

He gives a general command of steadfastness, so that they may observe the rights of hospitality, declaring it foreign to a preacher of the heavenly kingdom to run about from house to house and change the inviolable obligations of hospitality.

It is not without reason that, according to Matthew, the house into which the apostles enter is prescribed, so that there may be no opportunity to change their lodging and violate the obligations of hospitality.

“And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.”

Dust is shaken from the feet as a testimony to their labor: they had entered the city, and the apostolic preaching had reached the people there. Or the dust is shaken so that they may receive nothing from them—not even the necessities of food—because they rejected the Gospel.

[Col. 0457A] Allegorically, however, those who attend humbly to the word, if they are obscured by the stains of earthly levity like human beings, are cleansed through the traces of evangelical preaching which they receive. But those who, through unbelief, negligence, or even deliberate intention, despise it are judged to require avoidance of their company and flight from their synagogue. The dust of the feet must be shaken off, lest, carried away in the hands and compared with dust, it pollute the imprint of a pure mind.

But going out, they traveled through the villages, preaching the Gospel and healing everywhere.

Mark explains more fully what the apostles preached and how they healed. “They preached,” he says, “that they should do penance, and they anointed many sick people with oil, and healed them” (Mark VI).

James also says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James V).

Hence it is clear [Col. 0457B] that this custom of the holy Church was handed down by the apostles themselves: that the sick should be anointed with oil consecrated by pontifical blessing. They preached that people should do penance; and above he says, “He sent them to proclaim the kingdom of God.”

For they preached both things according to the example of John the Baptist and of the Savior himself: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew III). To draw near to the gates of the kingdom of heaven is to repent of those things by which each person had departed from it.

# HOMILY LXXIII. ON THE FEAST OF MARTYRS

**LUKE XII.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known. Therefore whatever you have said in the darkness will be spoken in the light, and what you have spoken in the ear in private rooms will be proclaimed upon the rooftops,” and so forth.

[Col. 0457C] Everything that the Lord had discussed earlier while reclining at the Pharisee’s table belongs to this leaven. Concerning it the Apostle also commands: “Let us therefore feast not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity” (1 Corinthians V).

For just as a little leaven corrupts the whole mass of flour into which it is put and immediately stains the entire dough with its flavor, so hypocrisy, once it has imbued the mind, will deprive it of the whole sincerity and truth of the virtues.

“Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known.”

How, then, does the hypocrisy of many remain hidden for a long time in the present age? Therefore this must be understood of the future time, when God will judge the hidden things of human beings.

For as one of blessed Job’s friends said most truly: “The praise of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite is like a moment. If his pride rises to heaven and his head touches the clouds, he will perish at the end like dung” (Job XX). “At the end,” he says, “he will perish”—the one who seemed to flourish at the beginning.

The meaning, therefore, is: Beware lest you imitate hypocrites, because surely a time will come when both your virtue will be revealed to all and their hypocrisy will be revealed.

But what follows—

[Col. 0457D] “For whatever you have said in the darkness will be spoken in the light, and what you have spoken in the ear in private rooms will be proclaimed upon the rooftops”—

can be appropriately understood not only of the future, when all the hidden things of hearts will be brought to light, but also of the present time. For what the apostles once spoke or suffered amid the darkness of pressures and the shadows of prisons is now publicly proclaimed throughout the world, the Church having been glorified, through the reading of their Acts.

The statement, “It will be proclaimed upon the rooftops,” is spoken according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where people commonly sit upon rooftops. Their roofs were not raised with peaks according to our custom, but were made level with a flat surface.

Hence the Law commanded [Col. 0458A] that whoever built a new house should place a wall around the roof (Deuteronomy XXII), lest innocent blood be shed there if someone slipped and fell headlong. In the construction of the Temple also we read: “He covered the house with cedar ceilings and built a floor over the whole house, five cubits high” (1 Kings VI).

Therefore it will be proclaimed upon the rooftops when it is openly spoken before all who hear:

“I say to you, my friends: Do not be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do.”

If persecutors of the saints have nothing more to do against them once their bodies have been killed, then they rage in senseless excess. They throw the dead bodies of martyrs to be torn apart by wild beasts and birds, or cause them to be scattered into the air, dissolved in the waters, or reduced to ashes by flames, although they can in no way resist the omnipotence of God, which can raise them and give them life again.

“But I will show you whom you should fear. Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna. Yes, I say to you, fear him.”

[Col. 0458B] There are two kinds of persecutors: one openly raging, the other flattering deceitfully and deceptively. The Savior wishes to fortify and instruct us against both. Above, he commands us to beware of the hypocrisy of the Pharisees; here, he commands us not to fear the slaughter of executioners, because after death neither the cruelty of the former nor the deception of the latter can endure. Rather, we must please the Lord, who always sees, and fear the Lord, who is always able either to punish or to deliver.

“Are not five sparrows sold for two asses? And not one of them will be forgotten before God.”

If, he says, God cannot forget the tiniest animals, the birds that fly through the air and are carried about everywhere, you who were made in the image of the Creator ought not to be afraid of those who kill the body. For he who governs irrational creatures does not cease to care for rational beings.

The dipondius for which five sparrows are sold—that is, the price at which they are sold—is a very small kind of weight composed of two asses.

[Col. 0458C] Perhaps someone asks how the Apostle can say, “Is God concerned with oxen?” (1 Corinthians IX), when an ox is certainly more valuable than a sparrow. But concern is one thing, and knowledge another.

Thus, when he subsequently says:

“But even the hairs of your head are all numbered,”

this is understood not as an act of counting but as a capacity for knowledge. God does not keep the anxious watch of one who counts, but for him who knows all things, all things are as though counted.

They are rightly said to be numbered, because we count the things we wish to preserve. Here he shows God’s immense providence toward human beings and signifies his ineffable affection: nothing belonging to us is hidden from God, and even our small and idle words do not escape his knowledge.

Those who deny the resurrection of the flesh ridicule the ecclesiastical understanding of this passage, as though we said that the earthly material itself—which becomes a corpse when the soul departs—must be restored in the resurrection in such a way that whatever has dissolved and been changed into the various forms and shapes of other things must return to the body from which it dissolved, and must necessarily return to the very bodily parts in which it formerly existed.

Otherwise, if what was removed by such frequent hair-cutting must return as hair, and what was so often cut away by trimming must return as fingernails, an ugly and indecent notion occurs to those who think about it—and for this reason do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh.

[Col. 0458D] But just as, if a statue made of some meltable metal were liquefied by fire, crushed into dust, or mixed into a mass, and an artisan wished to restore it from the quantity of that material, it would make no difference for its integrity which portion of the material was returned to which limb of the statue, provided that he recovered the whole substance from which it had been formed, so God, the wondrous and ineffable artisan, will restore our flesh from the whole substance of which it consisted, with wondrous and ineffable speed.

For its restoration it will make no difference whether hairs return to hairs and nails to nails, or whether whatever of them had perished is changed into flesh and recalled into other parts of the body. The providence of the artisan will ensure that nothing indecent occurs.

“Therefore do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows.”

[Col. 0459A] It should not be read, “You are more numerous,” which concerns comparison of number, but “You are worth more”—that is, you are of greater merit, dignity, and esteem before God than the countless bodies or kinds of sparrows that are counted.

“I say to you: Everyone who confesses me before men, the Son of Man will also confess before the angels of God. But whoever denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.”

He refers back to what was said above, where it was stated that every covered and hidden thing would be revealed, concluding that this revelation will take place not in some insignificant gathering, but in the presence of the heavenly city and of the eternal King and Judge.

And lest, from his statement that those who denied him would be denied, the condition of all deniers—that is, both those who deny deliberately and those who deny through weakness or [Col. 0459B] ignorance—be thought to be the same, he immediately added:

“Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.”

Whoever is scandalized by my flesh, thinking that I am merely a man, that I am the son of a craftsman and have brothers, James, Joseph, and Judas (Matthew XIII; Mark VI), and that I am a glutton and a drinker of wine (Matthew XI)—such an opinion, although it is not free from the guilt of error, nevertheless has forgiveness because of the usefulness of the body.

But whoever clearly understands the works of God, and, unable to deny their power, nevertheless, driven by envy, slanders them, saying that Christ, the Word of God, and the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub (Luke XI), will not be forgiven, neither in the present age nor in the future.

This is not because we deny that, if he is able to do penance, forgiveness can be granted to him by the one who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy II). Rather, because we believe in the Judge and giver of forgiveness—who says both that he always accepts repentance and that this blasphemy will never be forgiven—we believe that this blasphemer, because of the demands of his merits, will never reach forgiveness, nor even the fruits of worthy repentance.

[Col. 0459C] This accords with what the evangelist John wrote most truly concerning certain people blinded because of the merit of their blasphemy: “Therefore they could not believe” (John XII), because Isaiah again said: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” (Isaiah VI).

Some, indeed, wish to say that the one who speaks against or blasphemes the Holy Spirit is the person who, with an impenitent heart, resists the unity of the Church, where the forgiveness of sins takes place in the Holy Spirit. They say that the only refuge by which blasphemy may not be irremissible is to guard against an impenitent heart.

Their opinion seems by no means firm to many, because anyone who resists the unity of the Church with an impenitent heart—whether he is a Jew, a Gentile, or even a heretic—can certainly obtain forgiveness of sins in the Holy Spirit if he flees to the unity of the Church with a repentant heart.

[Col. 0459D] But they say: “As long as someone resists the Spirit of grace with an impenitent heart, he does not have forgiveness.”

Their opponents object that this condition applies to all crimes. For as long as someone practices fornication, idolatry, adultery, intercourse with males, theft, and other crimes, he does not have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God (1 Corinthians VI); but once these crimes have been renounced, he can be washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.

So also, they say, the impenitent person cannot have forgiveness as long as he possesses an impenitent heart; but as soon as he repents, he receives forgiveness. Impenitence is found to be no more bound to or more incapable of forgiveness than the other sins, since it remains, like the other crimes, until repentance, and is erased as soon as repentance has been performed.

[Col. 0460A] But blasphemy against the Holy Spirit alone—by which a person, like the devil and his angels, does not hesitate to attack the majesty of the Deity against his own conscience—does not have forgiveness forever, but is guilty of an eternal sin. The evangelist Mark explains this clearly: after setting down this testimony of the Lord, he added, “because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit’” (Mark III).

For neither those who believe that the Holy Spirit does not exist, nor those who believe that he exists but is not God, nor those who believe that he is indeed God but lesser than the Father and the Son, are held by this crime of irremissible blasphemy, because they act not from diabolical envy but from human ignorance.

Therefore the leaders of the Jews in particular, and all who are corrupted by the plague of similar envy and blaspheme the divine majesty, will perish without end.

# HOMILY LXXIV. ON THE FEAST OF MARTYRS

[Col. 0460B]

**LUKE XXI; MATTHEW X; MARK XIII.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “When you hear of wars and seditions, do not be terrified,” and so forth.

We must weigh the words of our Redeemer, through which he announces that we will suffer one thing inwardly and another outwardly. Wars pertain to enemies, while seditions pertain to citizens.

Both of these are known to have abounded sufficiently and more than sufficiently, from the time of the Lord’s passion, among the Jewish people, who chose a seditious robber in place of the Savior (Mark XV). With these events preceding, the apostles are warned not to be terrified and not to abandon Jerusalem and Judea. For the end would not come immediately; rather, it was to be deferred for forty years, after which would follow the desolation of the homeland and the final destruction of the city and Temple.

“Then he said to them: Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be great earthquakes in various places, and pestilences and famines.”

It is clear that these things literally occurred [Col. 0460C] before the end of the Temple’s desolation—that is, during the time of the Jewish revolt.

But “kingdom against kingdom,” the pestilence of those whose speech spreads like a cancer (2 Timothy II), famine in hearing the word of God, the shaking of the whole earth, and separation from the true faith can also be understood of heretics, who, fighting against one another, bring victory to the Church.

“And there will be terrors from heaven and great signs.”

Whoever reads Josephus’s History will find that these things too were completed at the same time.

“For, as he relates, a star resembling a sword hung over Jerusalem for an entire year and terrified the anxious citizens with an ominous portent. Likewise, armed chariots and horsemen were seen rushing through the air and imitating the behavior of combatants for forty days. Moreover, a heifer brought to the sacrifices gave birth to a lamb among the hands of those offering the sacrifice” (Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book VII, chapter 12).

The reason why these things deservedly happened is immediately added when it says:

“But before all these things they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, handing you over to synagogues and prisons, dragging you before kings and governors because of my name.”

This had been either the sole or the principal cause of destruction for the Jewish people: after killing the Lord and Savior, they also persecuted the heralds and confessors of his name with impious cruelty.

“But it will happen to you for a testimony.”

A testimony, clearly, of whom, if not of those who either inflict death by persecuting or fail to imitate the dead when they see them? The death of the righteous is a help to the good and a testimony against the wicked, so that the perverse perish without excuse from the very source from which the elect take an example in order to live.

[Col. 0460D] But when the hearts of the weak could be troubled by hearing so many terrors, consolation is added, and he immediately continues:

“Therefore settle it in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you will answer. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict.”

It is as though he were saying openly to his members in their weakness: “Do not be terrified; do not be afraid. You are approaching the contest, but I am the one who fights. You utter the words, but I am the one who speaks.”

You will be handed over by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends, and they will put some of you to death; and you will be hated by all because of my name. Evils inflicted by strangers cause lesser pain; but those torments that we suffer from people whose good will we had presumed upon rage more fiercely within us, because, along with bodily injury, the loss of affection also torments us. But because what is foretold about the affliction of death is harsh, consolation concerning the joy of resurrection is immediately added:

“And not a hair of your head will perish.” We know that cut flesh feels pain, whereas a cut hair does not. Thus he says to his martyrs: “Not a hair of your head will perish,” plainly saying: Why are you afraid that what causes pain when cut may perish, when even that which causes no pain when cut cannot perish in you?

Alternatively: Not a hair of the Lord’s disciples’ heads will perish, because not only the courageous deeds and words of the saints—of whom it is said, “The Lord guards all their bones” (Ps. XXXIII)—but also the fleeting, as it were, and exceedingly fine surface of the faithful’s thoughts, which issues from the hidden root of the heart like hair from the brain, will be preserved by the just Judge and rewarded with a worthy recompense. Hence the Prophet rightly demonstrates how acceptable to the Lord are even the merits of good thoughts: “And the remnants of their thoughts,” he says, “will keep festival for you” (Ps. LXXV).

For this reason, too, the Nazirite is commanded in the Law to grow his hair during the time of consecration (Num. VI; Judg. XIII), and it is reported that no razor ascended upon Samuel’s head (1 Sam. I). By contrast, a captive woman, so that she may be able to marry an Israelite man, and a leper, so that he may deserve to be admitted to communion with the Church, are commanded to shave all the hair of their bodies (Deut. XXI; Lev. XIV), because every thought of the wise that is good, pleasing, and perfect is saved forever, and its reward is with the Lord; but the root of the thoughts of fools and wicked people, as unworthy of God’s sight, must be cut away through repentance (Wis. V).

“And by your endurance you will possess your souls.” The possession of the soul is placed in the virtue of endurance because endurance is the root and guardian of all the virtues. Through endurance we possess our souls because, as we learn to rule ourselves, we begin to possess precisely what we are. For we have been wonderfully constituted so that reason possesses the soul, and the soul possesses the body; but the soul’s authority is excluded from possession of the body if the soul is not first possessed by reason. Thus the Lord showed endurance to be the guardian of your constitution, since through it he taught us to possess ourselves.

True endurance is to bear other people’s evils with equanimity and not to be moved by resentment even against the person who inflicts those evils. For one who bears the evil of a neighbor while silently grieving and waiting for the time of a deserved repayment does not display endurance but merely pretends to do so.

## HOMILY LXXV. FOR THE FEAST OF ONE MARTYR

**Luke IX; Matthew X; Mark VIII; John XII.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for me and the Gospel will save it,” etc.

He fittingly addressed this to everyone, because earlier he had dealt only with the disciples separately concerning matters relating to faith in the Lord’s birth or passion. We deny ourselves when we avoid what we were through our old condition and strive toward what we are called to be through the new. Let Truth therefore speak, let Truth say: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” For unless someone withdraws from himself, he does not draw near to the one who is above him; nor can he grasp what lies beyond him if he has not learned to put to death what he is.

But once someone has denied himself with respect to vices, he must seek the virtues in which he may grow. Hence it is immediately added:

“And let him take up his cross daily and follow me.” The cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the mind is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor. Let us consider how Paul took up his cross in both ways. He said: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Cor. XI). In his bodily affliction we have heard of the cross of the flesh; now let us hear of the cross of the mind in compassion for one’s neighbor. He says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burned?” (1 Cor. IX).

But in both ways of bearing the cross, we must note that we are commanded to take it up daily and, having taken it up, to follow the Lord.

“For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for me will save it.” This is said to the faithful as though one were saying to a farmer: If you preserve the grain, you lose it; if you sow it, you renew it. For who does not know that when grain is placed in the seedbed, it disappears from sight and perishes in the earth? Yet from the place where it rots in the dust, it grows green through renewal.

Since the holy Church has one time of persecution and another of peace, our Redeemer indicated these different times in his commandments. In a time of persecution, one’s life must be laid down; in a time of peace, earthly desires that are especially capable of ruling us must be broken. Hence it is now said:

“For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers the loss of himself?” When persecution from adversaries is absent, the heart must be guarded with much greater vigilance. In a time of peace, because it is permitted to live, it is also tempting to pursue worldly ambitions. Often we despise all passing things, yet we are still hindered by the habits of human respect, so that we cannot yet express in speech the uprightness that we preserve in our minds. But an appropriate remedy is added for this wound when the Lord says:

“For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty and that of the Father and of the holy angels.”

But now some people say to themselves: “We are not ashamed of the Lord or of his words, because we confess him openly.” To them I reply that in this Christian assembly there are some who confess Christ for no other reason than that they see everyone to be Christian. The spoken confession of faith is therefore not by itself sufficient as proof of faith when a general profession protects it from shame.

Yet each person should examine himself in order to prove whether he truly confesses Christ. Certainly, in a time of persecution the faithful could be ashamed, stripped of their possessions, cast down from their dignities, and afflicted with blows. In a time of peace, however, since these things are absent from our persecutions, there is another sphere in which we are revealed to ourselves. We are often afraid of being despised by our neighbors and disdainful of enduring verbal insults; if a quarrel should perhaps arise with a neighbor, we are ashamed to be the first to offer satisfaction. The carnal heart, while seeking the glory of this life, rejects humility.

“But I tell you truly: There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” In this passage the present Church is called the kingdom of God. Since some of the disciples were destined to live in the body long enough to see the Church of God established and raised up against the glory of this world, he now says by way of consoling promise: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.”

But when the Lord was giving so many commandments concerning the death they would have to undergo, why did he suddenly come to this promise? Surely it was because something concerning the present life also had to be promised to inexperienced disciples, so that they might be strengthened more firmly for the future.
