He promises them that they will see the kingdom of God on earth, so that through this the faithful may anticipate the kingdom in heaven.

If in this saying we wish to understand the kingdom of God as the future blessedness of heaven, then some of those standing there saw it on the mountain not many days later. They received, as it were, a swift taste of the contemplation of abiding joy, so that they might endure with greater restraint the adversities of the passing age. It is entirely fitting that he is said to testify that the saints taste death: bodily death is tasted by them in a preliminary way, while the life of the soul is held in possession.

## HOMILY LXXVI. FOR THE FEAST OF ONE MARTYR

**Luke XIV.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters—and even his own life—he cannot be my disciple,” etc.

It is worth asking how we are commanded to hate our parents and bodily relatives when we are also commanded to love our enemies. Certainly Truth says concerning a wife: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Mark X). And Paul says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church” (Col. II). Behold, the disciple commands that a wife be loved, while the Master says: “Whoever does not hate his wife cannot be my disciple.” Does the judge announce one thing while the herald proclaims another? Or can we both hate and love at the same time?

If we consider the force of the command, we can do both through discernment: we can love those joined to us by bodily kinship, whom we recognize as close to us, while hating and avoiding them insofar as we suffer them as adversaries on the way of God. To demonstrate that this hatred toward relatives does not arise from lack of affection but from charity, the Lord immediately added: “And even his own life.”

We hate our life rightly when we do not obey its carnal desires, when we break its appetite and resist its pleasures. Thus, when it is rejected, it is loved as though through hatred. In the same way, we must show discernment in our hatred of our relatives: we should love in them what they are, but hate what opposes us in them on the way of God.

Truth shows how this hatred of the soul ought to be expressed when it adds:

“And whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.” The cross takes its name from torment. We bear the Lord’s cross in two ways: either we afflict the flesh through abstinence, or, through compassion for our neighbor, we regard that person’s need as our own. One who experiences pain over another’s need carries the cross in the mind.

It must be understood, however, that some practice abstinence from the flesh not for God but for empty glory; and many show compassion to their neighbor not spiritually but carnally, favoring him not toward virtue but, as though out of pity, toward his sins. Such people appear indeed to carry the cross, but they do not follow the Lord.

Thus Truth rightly says: “Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.” To carry the cross and go after the Lord is to practice either abstinence from the flesh or compassion for one’s neighbor out of devotion to an eternal purpose. Whoever practices these things for a temporal purpose carries the cross but refuses to go after the Lord.

Since lofty commandments had been given, a comparison concerning the construction of something lofty is immediately added:

“For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost necessary to complete it?” Everything we do must be preceded by the preparation required for its accomplishment. Behold, according to the word of Truth, one who builds a tower first prepares the cost of the building. Therefore, if we wish to construct the tower of humility, we must first prepare ourselves for the adversities of this age.

The difference between an earthly and a heavenly building is that an earthly building is constructed by gathering expenses, whereas a heavenly building is constructed by distributing them. We spend for the former if we gather possessions we do not have; we spend for the latter if we also abandon what we possess. We must consider what is said:

“Lest, after he has laid the foundation and is unable to finish it, all who see it begin to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was unable to finish.’” For, in Paul’s words, “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Cor. IV).

In everything we do we must consider our hidden adversaries, who always watch our deeds and always rejoice at our failure. The Prophet, looking upon them, says: “My God, in you I trust; I shall not be ashamed, and let not my enemies mock me” (Ps. XXIV). If, while intent upon good works, we do not watch carefully against wicked spirits, we suffer as mockers those whom we have as persuaders toward evil.

But since a comparison concerning the construction of a building has been given, a likeness is now added, moving from the lesser to the greater, so that greater matters may be assessed from small ones. For it follows:

“Or what king, going to engage another king in war, does not first sit down and consider whether he is able, with ten thousand, to meet the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, sending a delegation, he asks for the terms of peace.”

A king comes against a king on equal terms for battle; yet if he judges himself unable to prevail, he sends a delegation and asks for peace. With what tears, then, ought we to hope for pardon, since in that fearful examination we do not come to judgment on equal terms with our King, for our condition, weakness, and cause all show us to be inferior?

But perhaps we have already cut away the sins of evil deeds and avoided every outward wrong. Are we then sufficient to give an account of our thoughts? The one who comes against us with twice the army against our single force examines us both in deed and in thought, while we are scarcely prepared in deed alone. Therefore, while he is still far away, let us send a delegation and ask for the terms of peace.

He is said to be far away because he is not yet seen present in judgment. Let us send our tears as a delegation; let us send works of mercy; let us sacrifice victims of reconciliation upon his altar. This is our delegation, which appeases the coming King.

“Thus, every one of you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.” In this conclusion the Lord most clearly teaches what it means to build a tower or to make peace with a stronger king: namely, to be his disciple.

To prepare the cost for completing the tower and to send a delegation to obtain peace means nothing other than renouncing all that we possess. Among these things we must understand both the love of our neighbors, mentioned earlier, and our very life, which some think is named here with reference to this temporal life. We must possess that life temporarily in such a way that it does not hinder us from eternal life, should someone threaten to take it away.

There is, to be sure, a difference between renouncing everything and abandoning everything. It belongs to the few who are perfect to abandon everything, set aside the concerns of the world, and cling solely to eternal desires. But it belongs to all the faithful to renounce all that they possess—that is, to hold worldly things in such a way that they are not held by them in the world; to have temporal possessions for use and eternal things as objects of desire; and to conduct themselves amid earthly things while directing their whole mind toward heavenly things.

## HOMILY LXXVII. FOR THE FIRST FEAST OF CONFESSORS

**Luke XI; Matthew V; Mark IV.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light,” etc.

The Lord speaks these words about himself, showing that, although he had earlier said that no sign would be given to this wicked generation except the sign of Jonah, nevertheless the brightness of his light was not to be hidden from the faithful. He himself lights the lamp, filling the clay vessel of human nature with the flame of his divinity. He did not wish this lamp to be hidden from believers or placed under a bushel—that is, enclosed within the measure of the Law or confined within the boundaries of the single Jewish nation.

“But on a lampstand,” he says, “so that those who enter may see the light.” By the lampstand he means the Church, upon which he placed the lamp, because he fastened the faith of his incarnation upon our foreheads, so that those who wish to enter the Church faithfully may plainly behold the light of truth. By this saying he also condemns the leaders of the Jews, who, seeking outward signs, refused to enter through the open door of the light by believing.

Finally, he commands them to remember to cleanse and discipline not only their deeds but also their thoughts and the very intentions of their hearts. For it follows:

“The lamp of your body is your eye.” By the body he means deeds that appear openly to everyone; by the eye he means the intention of the mind through which a person acts, and by whose merit those same deeds are discerned as works of light or of darkness, as he explains next:

“If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, your body also will be full of darkness.” If, he says, you strive to do what you can with a pure and upright intention, the works you perform are certainly works of light, even if they appear to possess some imperfection before human beings. For “all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose as saints” (Rom. VIII). But if the intention that precedes an action is perverse, every work that follows is wicked, even if it appears upright.

“See therefore that the light that is in you is not darkness.” That is, weigh carefully, with diligent discernment, whether the very intention of the heart—which is the light of the soul—is not darkened by the obscurity of vices. As it is commanded elsewhere: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV).

“If therefore your whole body is full of light, having no part of darkness, it will be wholly luminous, and it will illuminate you like a lamp with its brightness.” By our whole body he means all our deeds, because the Apostle also calls certain deeds that he condemns and commands us to put to death our members, saying: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, and such things” (Col. III).

If, therefore, you have done a good deed with a good intention, having no part of dark thought in your conscience, then even if one of your neighbors should happen to be harmed by your good action—for example, if he received money from you when he was in need and asking for it, and then did or suffered some evil, or if, through a word of exhortation by which you intended to correct someone who was in error, you perhaps caused him to fall into a more harmful error—you nevertheless, because of your simple and luminous heart, will be granted the grace of light both here and in the future.

## HOMILY LXXVIII. FOR THE SECOND FEAST OF CONFESSORS

**Luke XII; Matthew XXIV; Mark XV.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning,” etc.

Since the Lord had shown that many people were either wholly subject to the world or served the Lord with an eye to worldly advantage, he fittingly and briefly teaches his own to gird their loins, because of continence from love of worldly things, and to keep their lamps burning, so that they may do this with a true end and right intention.

We gird our loins in one way when through continence we restrain the lust of the flesh; we hold burning lamps in our hands when through good works we display examples of light to our neighbors. Our Redeemer cannot possibly be pleased with one without the other: either a person who does good has not yet abandoned the defilements of lust, or a person who excels in chastity has not yet exercised himself through good works.

But even when both are practiced, it remains necessary for each person to strive toward the heavenly homeland in hope. He must not restrain himself from vices merely for the sake of worldly respectability, but must place his entire hope in the coming of his Redeemer. Hence it is immediately added:

“And you must be like people waiting for their lord, when he returns from the wedding.” The Lord went to the wedding because, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he joined to himself, as a new man, the heavenly multitude of angels. He returns when he is revealed to us in judgment. It is rightly added concerning the servants who are waiting:

“So that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.” He comes when he hastens to judgment; he knocks when, through the troubles of illness, he indicates that death is near. We open to him immediately if we receive him with love.

One does not wish to open to the judge who knocks if one trembles to leave the body and fears to see the judge whom one remembers having despised. But one who is secure in hope and conduct opens immediately to the one who knocks, because he gladly endures the judge; and when he recognizes that the time of approaching death is near, he rejoices in the glory of his reward. Hence it follows:

“Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching.” The person watches who keeps the eyes of the mind open to the sight of true light. The person watches who preserves through action what he believes. The person watches who drives away from himself the darkness of sluggishness and negligence.

For this reason Paul says: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. XV). Again he says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. XIII). But let us hear what the coming Lord bestows upon the watching servants:

“Amen, I tell you: he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them.” “He will gird himself” means that he prepares himself for recompense; “he will make them recline” means that he will refresh them with eternal rest. For our reclining is our resting in the kingdom. Hence the Lord says again: “They will come and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Matt. VIII).

The Lord ministers while passing by because he satisfies us with the illumination of his light. “Passing by” is said because he returns from judgment to the kingdom. Or certainly, the Lord passes by us after judgment because he raises us from the form of his humanity to the contemplation of his divinity. His passing by is his leading us into the vision of his brightness: we see him whom we behold in his humanity at the judgment also, after judgment, in his divinity.

“And if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants.” The first watch is the earliest period, namely childhood. The second is adolescence or youth, which sacred Scripture treats as one period when it says: “Rejoice, young man, in your adolescence” (Eccles. XI). The third is understood as old age.

Therefore, whoever was unwilling to watch in the first watch should at least guard the second, so that whoever neglected to turn from his wickedness in childhood may at least awaken to the ways of life in youth. And whoever was unwilling to watch in the second watch should not lose the remedies of the third watch, so that whoever did not awaken to the ways of life in youth may at least repent in old age.

To shake off the sluggishness of our minds, outward dangers are also introduced by way of comparison, so that through them the mind may be aroused to guard itself. For it is said:

“Know this: if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.” From this preceding comparison an exhortation is also added:

“And you must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour when you do not expect him.”

The thief breaks into the house without the master’s knowledge because, while the spirit sleeps, neglecting its own guardianship, sudden death comes and bursts into the dwelling of our flesh. When death finds the one whom it finds as master of the house sleeping, it kills him, because when the spirit does not foresee the coming losses, death snatches him away to punishment unaware.

He would resist the thief if he were watching, because by anticipating the coming of the Judge who secretly seizes the soul, he would meet him through repentance and would not perish unrepentant. Our Lord wished the final hour to be unknown to us for this reason: so that it might always be feared, and so that, since we cannot foresee it, we might prepare for it without interruption.

Peter said to him: “Lord, are you telling this parable to us or to everyone?” In the preceding parable the Lord had warned of two things: that he would come suddenly and that they ought to await him prepared. But it is not readily apparent whether Peter asked about one of these or both when he said, “Are you telling it to us or to everyone?”—or whom he understood to be included with himself and his companions.

When he says “us” and “everyone,” he should perhaps be understood to mean no others than either the apostles and those like the apostles, together with the rest of the faithful, or those who, dying individually, willingly or unwillingly receive the arrival of their Judge every day, as well as those who will be found alive in the flesh when the universal judgment comes.

It would indeed be surprising if blessed Peter doubted either that all who desire to live soberly, justly, and devoutly, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God (Tit. II), who wills all people to be saved (1 Tim. II), must do so, or that judgment—unexpected for individuals and for all, for the great and the small, for the faithful and the unfaithful—would take place.

It remains, therefore, to understand that, since these matters were already well known, Peter considered it more worthwhile to ask about what he perhaps did not know: namely, whether those lofty principles of heavenly life—which commanded them to sell their possessions, make purses that would not grow old, store up treasure in heaven, watch with girded loins and burning lamps, and await the Lord—belonged only to the apostles and those like them, or also to all who are to be saved. That this was the meaning of his question is made clear, if I am not mistaken, by the Lord’s own reply.

The Lord said: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise steward whom his master will appoint over his household?” In answering the question, the Savior first teaches that judgment awaits everyone and that each person will receive rewards or punishments according to the merit of his deeds and the capacity of his understanding. Then, concerning what Peter had chiefly asked, he shows that the grace of the virtues which he brought to the world must be pursued by each person to the extent of his ability.

“I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII).

The phrase “Who, then, do you think?” indicates the difficulty, not the impossibility, of accomplishing virtue. Thus the Psalmist says: “Who is wise and will observe these things?” (Ps. CVI). He does not mean no one, but someone rare. Elsewhere the same expression refers not to what is difficult but to what is impossible: “God, who is like you?”—that is, no one. “For you alone are Most High over all the earth” (Ps. LXXXII).

“So that he may give them their measure of wheat at the proper time.” The measure of wheat expresses the manner of teaching. Lofty matters ought to be concealed from many hearers and disclosed to only a few, lest something beyond a narrow heart’s capacity be given to it and spill outside. For this reason Moses, coming forth from God’s secret presence, veils his shining face before the people, because he does not reveal the innermost mysteries of brightness to the crowds (Exod. XXXIV).

The speech of teachers must therefore be shaped according to the quality of their hearers, so that it may suit each person individually and yet never depart from the art of common edification.

“Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, finds doing so. Truly I tell you, he will set him over all that he possesses.” The difference in merit between good hearers and good teachers is matched by a difference in rewards. When the Lord comes and finds the former watching, he will make them recline and, passing by, minister to them. But when he finds the latter faithfully and wisely distributing the nourishment of the word to the household entrusted to them, he will set them over all that he possesses—that is, over all the joys of the heavenly kingdom—not so that they alone may possess the Lord, but so that they may enjoy eternal possession of those joys more abundantly than the other saints.

“For those who are learned will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars forever and ever” (Dan. XII). The Apostle also says: “Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching” (1 Tim. V).

“But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My lord delays his coming,’ and begins to beat the boys and maidservants, and to eat and drink and become drunk…” Just as the entire order of how good rulers should live and be rewarded is taught through one faithful steward, so in this most wicked servant the evil work of all bad rulers, which must likewise be condemned, and their eternal condemnation are described. Neglecting fear of the Lord, they not only devote themselves to luxury but also provoke those subject to them through insults.

Figuratively, however, “beating the boys and maidservants” may be understood as corrupting the hearts of the weak, who are not yet made firm in faith, hope, and charity, by displaying an example of wicked action or speech. “Eating, drinking, and becoming drunk” means being occupied with every crime and with the allurements of the age that bewilder the mind and cause it to go astray.

Notice, moreover, that among the vices attributed to the wicked servant is his belief that his lord’s return would be delayed. It is not, however, counted among the virtues of the good servant that he expected his lord to come quickly; rather, his virtue consists only in giving his fellow servants their measure of wheat at the proper time, according to the lord’s command, whenever he might come—that is, in showing them either the rule of divine speech or the example of his own conduct.

Indeed, we read of certain good servants whom the Apostle rebuked because, trembling and anxious, they believed that the day of the Lord was imminent, whereas he had promised that it would come unexpectedly (2 Thess. II). It is therefore proved to be best—although we may greatly desire, if permitted, to know when the one desired by all nations will come (Haggai II)—that we should calmly accept our inability to know what we are not permitted to know, and simply remain prepared, whether his coming is near or far away, as an example of a good servant, and love his arrival.

“The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and he will cut him in two and appoint his portion with the unfaithful.” He will cut him in two not by severing him with a sword but by separating him from the fellowship of the faithful and joining him to those who never belonged to the faith. For one who does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever, as the Apostle says (1 Tim. V).

“But that servant who knew his master’s will and did not prepare himself or act according to his will will be beaten with many blows.” Many people, misunderstanding this saying, do not want to know what they should do and imagine that they will be beaten less if they do not know what they ought to have done. But it is one thing not to know and another to refuse to know. One does not know who wishes to understand but cannot; however, one who turns away from the voice of truth in order not to know is judged not ignorant but contemptuous.

“But the one who did not know and did things worthy of blows will be beaten with few. Everyone to whom much has been given, from him much will be required; and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, more will be demanded.”

Why, after saying, “To whom much has been given,” did he add, “And to the one to whom much has been entrusted”? The divine judgments are understood. Unless perhaps by this he wished to indicate both orders among the faithful, namely, rulers and subjects, because much is often given even to private individuals, to whom both knowledge of the Lord’s will and the ability to carry out what they know are granted.

Much is entrusted to the one who, together with his own salvation, is charged with feeding the Lord’s flock. Thus “the mighty will suffer mighty torments,” and “a harsher punishment awaits the stronger” (Wis. VI): that is, if those who have been granted greater grace abandon it, greater vengeance follows.

The mildest punishment of all will be that of those who, apart from the sin they inherited from Adam, added no further sin. Among the others who added sins, each person’s condemnation there will be more bearable in proportion to the lesser iniquity he had here.

## HOMILY LXXIX. FOR THE THIRD FEAST OF CONFESSORS

**Mark X; Matthew XIX; Luke XVIII.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “It is easier for a camel, with its enormous body, to pass through the narrow opening of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God,” etc.

If it is easier for a camel, enormous in its huge limbs, to penetrate the narrow opening of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God, then no rich person will enter the kingdom of God. How, then, did Matthew the Evangelist, Zacchaeus, and Joseph enter it (Luke V; Luke XIX; Matt. XXVII), or how did the many rich people of the Old Testament enter the kingdom of God, unless it was because, inspired by the Lord, they learned either to regard riches as nothing or to abandon them wholeheartedly?

Did David place his confidence in the riches of his kingdom, when he sings of himself: “For I am solitary and poor” (Ps. XXIV)? And he urges others: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI). I believe he did not dare to say, “Do not accept them.” Is it believable that Abraham preferred his possessions to the Lord, for whose sake he did not hesitate to strike down his only heir (Gen. XXII)?

In a deeper sense, however, it is easier for Christ to suffer for those who love the world than for those who love the world to be converted to Christ. For by the name of the camel he wished himself to be understood, since in voluntary humility he bore the burdens of our weakness. Where is this more clearly understood than in the words written of him: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III)?

By the needle he signifies pricks, and by the pricks the pains he endured in his passion. The opening of the needle therefore signifies the narrowness of the passion through which he deigned, as it were, to mend—that is, to restore—the torn garments of our nature,so that, reformed for the better after our fall, we might rejoice in accordance with the Apostle’s testimony: “For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

They were all the more astonished, saying to one another: “Who, then, can be saved?” Why does this response fit, since incomparably more poor people could be saved than rich people who have been lost? It is because they understood that all who love riches, even if they are unable to acquire them, are to be counted among the rich.

And Jesus, looking at them, said: “With human beings it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.” This should not be understood to mean that the greedy and proud—who are signified by the name of that rich man—will enter the kingdom of heaven along with their greed and pride [Col. 0469D]. Rather, it is possible for God, through his word—as we see has happened and continues daily to happen—to convert them from desire for temporal things to love of eternal things, and from destructive pride to most salutary humility.

Peter began to say to him: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.” Great was Peter’s confidence. He was a fisherman; he had not been rich. He sought his food by his hands and his craft, and yet he speaks confidently: “We have left everything.” And because it is not enough merely to leave something, he adds what is perfect: “And we have followed you.” We have done what you commanded; what reward, then, will you give us?

Jesus answered and said: “Amen, I say to you, there is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or lands, for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this present time: houses, and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life.”

[Col. 0470A] Some people, taking this saying as their opportunity, teach the Jewish fable of a thousand years after the resurrection of the just: that everything we have left for God’s sake will be restored to us with manifold interest, and that eternal life will additionally be given. Foolish people do not see that, although the promise may be worthy with respect to the other things, in the case of wives, according to the other Evangelists, it appears shameful to receive a hundredfold—especially since the Lord also testifies that there will be no marrying in the resurrection (Matt. XXII), and insists that those things which have been left are to be received for his sake in this present time, with persecutions. Yet those Chiliasts affirm that these persecutions, as well as all other contrary things, will be entirely absent during their thousand years.

The meaning, therefore, is this: Whoever leaves carnal things for the sake of Christ’s Gospel will receive spiritual goods, which, in comparison and according to their worth, will be as though a hundredfold number were compared with a small number. For from brothers and companions in his chosen way, who are joined to him by a spiritual bond, he will receive a much more gracious love even in this life. Read in the Acts of the Apostles that [Col. 0470B] the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul, and that everything was held in common among them; nor was there anyone needy among those who had left their possessions for the Lord (Acts IV). Of these the Apostle also says: “As having nothing, and possessing everything” (II Cor. VI).

This statement—“He will receive a hundredfold now in this present time: houses, and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions”—can certainly be understood more profoundly through symbolism. For the number one hundred, transferred from the left hand to the right, although by the bending of the fingers it seems to retain the same figure that the number ten had possessed on the left, nevertheless greatly surpasses it in magnitude. For all who despise temporal things for the sake of the kingdom of God taste, even in this life full of persecutions, the joy of that same kingdom with certain faith; and, in expectation of the heavenly homeland—which is rightly signified by the right hand—they likewise enjoy the most sincere love of all the elect.

[Col. 0470C] But because many do not complete the pursuit of virtue with the same intention of devotion with which they begin it—either growing lukewarm after receiving the love of virtue, or falling back entirely into the mire of crimes after relapsing—there follows immediately a terrifying sentence.

“Many who are first will be last, and the last first.” Consider Judas, changed from an apostle into an apostate, and say that many who are first will be last (John VI; Luke XXIII). Consider the thief, made a confessor on the cross, rejoicing with Christ in paradise on the very day on which he was crucified for his own sins; and say that the last will be first. Moreover, every day we see many people living in the lay condition who excel in the great merits of their lives, while others, fervent in spiritual devotion from their earliest years, at the end grow weary as idleness makes them sluggish, and in inert folly complete in the flesh what they had begun in the spirit.

## HOMILY LXXX. FOURTH HOMILY FOR THE FEAST OF CONFESSORS

**Mark XIII; Matthew XXIV; Luke XII.** At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “See, watch, and pray; for you do not know when the time will be,” etc. [Col. 0470D]

The Lord clearly shows why he said: “But concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, nor the Father”: it is not expedient for the apostles to know, so that, kept in uncertainty by their suspended expectation, they may always believe that the one whom they do not know when he will come is about to come. He did not say, “Because we do not know at what hour the Lord will come,” but, “You do not know.” And, having first given the example of the master of a household, he teaches more clearly why he conceals the day of the consummation, saying:

“Watch, therefore, for you do not know when the master of the house will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning; lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping.”

The man who went abroad and left his house is undoubtedly Christ, who, after the resurrection, ascended victoriously to the Father and left the Church bodily; yet he has never deprived her of the protection of his divine presence, remaining with her all days until the consummation of the age. [Col. 0471A] The proper place of the flesh is the earth, which was, as it were, led into a foreign land when, through our Redeemer, it was raised to heaven. He gave his servants authority over each task, because, by the grace of the Holy Spirit granted to his faithful, he gave them the ability to serve through good works. He also commanded the doorkeeper to watch, because he orders the shepherds and spiritual rulers to care for the Church entrusted to them with vigilant diligence.

“What I say to you I say to all: Watch.” It is not only the apostles and their successors, namely the rulers of the Church, who are commanded to watch; we are all commanded to watch. We are individually ordered to guard continually the doors of our hearts, lest the ancient enemy break in by suggesting evil. We must diligently take care that, when the Lord comes, he does not find us sleeping. For each person will render an account to God on his own behalf.

He watches who keeps the eyes of his mind open to the sight of the true light [Col. 0471B]; he watches who preserves through his works what he believes; he watches who drives away from himself the darkness of sluggishness and negligence. Hence Paul says: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV). Again he says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. XIII).

## HOMILY LXXXI. FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT ANDREW

**Mark I; Matthew IV; Luke V.** At that time, as Jesus was passing beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew his brother casting nets into the sea, etc.

These were the first called to follow the Lord. Fishermen and uneducated men are sent to preach, so that the faith of believers might not be thought to rest on human eloquence and learning rather than on the power of God.

It may be asked how he called two fishermen from their boats—first Peter and Andrew, and then, going a little farther, the other two, the sons of Zebedee—as Matthew and Mark relate, when Luke says that both their boats were filled by that great catch of fish, and mentions [Col. 0471C] Peter’s companions, James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were called to help because they could not draw out the nets full of fish. He also says that they were astonished at the great multitude of fish that had been caught, and that Jesus said only to Peter: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching human beings” (Luke V), while they nevertheless followed him after bringing their boats to land.

It must therefore be understood, according to what Luke indicates, that this happened first, and that at that time they were not called by the Lord, but only that it was foretold to Peter that he would catch human beings. This was not said as though he would never again catch fish, for we read that after the Lord’s resurrection they went fishing (John XXI). It was therefore said that he would henceforth catch human beings; it was not said that he would no longer catch fish.

Thus, according to Luke, they may be understood to have returned to fishing as usual, so that afterward what Matthew and Mark relate might occur: when he called them two by two and commanded them to follow him—[Col. 0471D] first Peter and Andrew, and then the other two sons of Zebedee. At that time they followed him not after bringing their boats to land, as though intending to return, but as people following one who was calling and commanding them to follow.

## HOMILY LXXXII. FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT NICHOLAS

**Luke XIX.** At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable: “A certain nobleman went into a distant [Col. 0472A] country to receive a kingdom for himself and return,” etc.

Since the disciples did not understand what was being said about the Lord’s passion and resurrection, which were to be accomplished at Jerusalem, supposing that the kingdom of God was immediately about to appear, he illuminates their ignorance by showing that he would first spread the faith of his kingdom throughout the whole world, and that thus, at the end of the world, he would come as judge of all ages and as King.

He therefore said: “A certain nobleman went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and return.” That nobleman is the one to whom the blind man above cried: “Son of David, have mercy on me.” And when he was coming to Jerusalem, they sang: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. XXI; Mark XI; Luke XIX; John XII), “the King of Israel.”

The distant country is the Church from the Gentiles. Concerning that same nobleman, who says, “I have been appointed King by him,” the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II). This inheritance and possession is called a distant country for two reasons: either because it cries to the Lord from the ends of the earth (Ps. LX), or because salvation is far from sinners (Ps. CXVIII). Although God is present everywhere, the true God is nevertheless far from the understanding of those who worship idols. But those who were far off have been brought near in the blood of Christ (Eph. II).

“Having called his servants, he gave them ten minas.” The number ten pertains to the Law because of the Decalogue. The master of the household therefore calls ten servants because he chose [Col. 0472B] disciples instructed in the written Law. He gives them ten minas because he reveals that the words of the Law are to be understood spiritually. For after his passion and resurrection he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV).

A mina, which the Greeks call *mna* (μνᾶ), is weighed at one hundred drachmas. And the whole discourse of Scripture, because it suggests the perfection of heavenly life, shines as though with the weight of the number one hundred.

And he said to them: “Trade until I come.” That is: “Offer to the peoples the words of the Law and the Prophets, examined through mystical interpretation, and receive from them the confession of faith and uprightness of conduct.” In accordance with this, the Psalmist commands his hearers, saying: “Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine” (Ps. LXXX). That is, receive the praise of preaching in the intention of the heart, and apply devotion in action through the chastisement of the flesh. For a tambourine is a skin stretched over wood; the skin stretched over wood is our flesh, afflicted in imitation of the Lord’s cross.

[Col. 0472C] “But his citizens hated him and sent an embassy after him, saying: ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’” By “citizens” he means the impious Jews, concerning whom he declares elsewhere: “Now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John XV). They not only hated him while he was present, even to the death of the cross, but also after his resurrection they stirred up persecution against the apostles and rejected the preaching of the heavenly kingdom (Acts IV).

“And it happened that he returned after receiving the kingdom.” This signifies the time when he will come in the most manifest and exalted glory, though he had appeared to them in humility when he said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII).

“And he commanded the servants to be called, to whom he had given the money, so that he might know how much each had gained by trading.” “So that he might know,” he says—not that anything is hidden from him, to whom it was most truly said, “Lord, you know all things” (John XXI), but “that he might know” means “that he might make all know.” For then the works and thoughts of all will be openly displayed to everyone. [Col. 0472D] Thus in Deuteronomy: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. XIII)—that is, to make it known.

No one should suppose that only those to whom the grace of preaching was given will then be summoned to judgment, and not also those to whom preaching was addressed. They themselves are the money which the good servants acquired by trading. Indeed, he will also show that those to whom preaching was never given will be present there for condemnation, concerning whom we shall speak below.

“The first came, saying: ‘Lord, your mina has acquired ten minas.’” The first servant is the order of teachers sent to the circumcision. He received one mina to trade with because he was sent to preach one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God. But this same mina acquired ten minas because by teaching he joined to himself the people established under the Law.

“And he said to him: ‘Well done, good servant. Because you have been faithful in a little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’” [Col. 0473A] The servant is faithful in a little because he does not adulterate the word of God, but speaks as from God, before God, in Christ. Whatever gifts we receive in the present are very few and little in comparison with those of the future, because “we know in part, and we prophesy in part”; but when the perfect comes, “what is in part will be done away” (I Cor. IV; II Cor. II; I Cor. XIII).

The ten cities are souls coming through the word of the Law to the grace of the Gospel. It is rightly then that the one who has worthily lent them the money of God’s word is set over them in glory. Hence a distinguished trader, addressing the cities over which he presided—that is, the souls whom he had received to govern—says: “What is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before the Lord Jesus?” (I Thess. II).

“Another came, saying: ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’” This servant is the company of those sent to evangelize the uncircumcision. To him, going out to preach, the Lord had given one mina—that is, the one and the same [Col. 0473B] faith entrusted also to the circumcision. But this mina made five minas because he converted the Gentiles, previously enslaved to the senses of the body, to the grace of evangelical faith.

“And he said to him: ‘And you, be over five cities.’” That is: “Shine forth as great and exalted on account of the faith and conversion of the souls whom you had instructed.” Of these Isaiah speaks mystically: “On that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan” (Isa. XIX).

For the five cities in the land of Egypt are the five bodily senses that we use in this world: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her; whoever turns his ears away so as not to hear the poor; whoever becomes drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery; whoever rejoices in crowning himself with roses before they wither; whoever has hands full of blood and a right hand filled with gifts (Matt. V; Tob. IV; Wis. II; Eph. V)—the five cities of such a person speak the language of Egypt. That is, all his senses perform the works of darkness. For Egypt signifies “darkness.” [Col. 0473C]

But whoever stops his ears so as not to hear of blood and closes his eyes so as not to see evil (Isa. XXXIII); whoever tastes and sees how sweet the Lord is; whoever chastises his body and subjects it to servitude (Ps. XXV and XXXIII); whoever can say with Christ’s Apostle, “We are a good fragrance to God” (II Cor. II)—the cities of such a person speak a changed language, which is interpreted as “Canaan.” Whoever changes these cities by teaching them from darkness deserves rightly to be placed over five cities, because he is honored not only for his own progress but also for the progress of his hearers, whom he has called to the light.

“Another came, saying: ‘Lord, behold your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief. For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man: you take up what you did not lay down, and reap what you did not sow.’”

The servant who, having been commanded to trade, laid the money received from his master in a handkerchief shows those who are capable of preaching but, when the Lord commands it through the Church, refuse either to undertake the ministry of preaching or to carry out worthily what they have undertaken. [Col. 0473D] To tie money in a handkerchief is to hide the gifts received in the inactivity of sluggish torpor.

There are people who flatter themselves with this perverse reasoning, saying: “It is enough for each person to render an account of himself. Why is it necessary to preach to others, so that each person may also be compelled to render an account for them, when even those to whom the Law was not given and who did not sleep after hearing the Gospel are inexcusable before the Lord, because through creation they could recognize the Creator?” (Rom. I).

This is like reaping where he did not sow: that is, holding even those guilty of impiety to whom the word of the Law or of the Gospel was not given. Avoiding this supposed danger of judgment, they rest in sluggish weakness from the ministry of the word. This is what it means to tie up in a handkerchief what they have received.

He says to him: “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant.” He is called a wicked servant because he is both lazy and idle in carrying out his business, and insolent and proud in accusing his master’s judgment.

“You knew, then, that I am a harsh man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow. Why, then, did you not put my money on the table?” [Col. 0474A] What he had thought he was saying as an excuse is turned into his own guilt. “If,” he says, “you knew me to be harsh and cruel, pursuing what was not mine and reaping where I had not sown, why did such a thought not instill fear in you, so that you would know that I would seek my own more diligently, and would put my money—or silver—on the table?”

For the Greek word *argyrion* (ἀργυρίῳ) signifies both. “The sayings of the Lord,” he says, “are pure sayings, silver tested by fire” (Ps. XI). Therefore the money and silver are the preaching of the Gospel and the divine word, which ought to have been put on the table—that is, made known to the ready and prepared hearts of the faithful.

To that table, namely, the mind of the hearers, no money other than the Lord’s is to be brought, so that every word of the teacher may follow the meaning of Scripture (I Pet. IV). For what the Lord means by saying that not any money but his own is to be lent out by the money-changers, [Col. 0474B] the Apostle explains when he says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God.”

“And when I came, I would certainly have collected it with interest.” Whoever receives the money of the word from a teacher and purchases it by believing must repay it with interest through action, so that he may carry out in deed what he learned by hearing. For in interest even money that was not given is received back. Or certainly, the one who pays interest on the loan of the word received does so when, from what he hears, he also strives to understand other things that he has not yet learned from the preacher’s mouth.

“And he said to those standing by: ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to him who has ten minas.’ And they said to him: ‘Lord, he has ten minas.’” He rightly loses the grace bestowed on him because he neglected to communicate it by preaching to others, so that it may be increased in the one who labored with it. In accordance with this it is said to the angel of the church of Ephesus: “I will remove your lampstand from its place unless you repent” (Rev. II).

And when Saul lost the royal anointing through pride, which David gained through obedience, Scripture says: “The Spirit of [Col. 0474C] the Lord departed from Saul and was directed into David from that day onward” (I Sam. XVI), and so forth.

That the mina taken from the wicked servant was commanded to be given to the one who had ten minas, as I think, mystically indicates that, when the fullness of the Gentiles enters, all Israel will be saved, and that then the abundance of spiritual grace—which we now exercise lukewarmly—will be bestowed upon the teachers of that people (Rom. XI).

“But I say to you that to everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.” This sentence refers to what precedes, teaching that the one who has does not have—namely, does not use what he possesses—can also lose God’s gift, while it is increased in the one who, possessing it, does have it, that is, uses it well.

Since such an exchange of graces usually takes place in this life, it should be noted that the judgment of the returning Lord is even now celebrated in part, but then will be fulfilled universally. For he returns daily after receiving the kingdom from the Father, because he continually observes the condition of the Church as she journeys on earth. [Col. 0474D] Daily, among the great number of faithful servants, he lends his money to one who will trade with it; in another he examines the measure of completed work; he bestows on the one who labors faithfully and wisely the gift of greater grace, while he deprives the other, who pursues soft laziness and pleasure-laden leisure, of what he had given.

But when the universal judgment has been revealed—a thing terrifying even to say—many who seemed capable of teaching will, because of the guilt of their negligence, be counted among the unlearned. Other, simpler brothers, however, utterly ignorant of the elements of learning, will nevertheless, on account of their outstanding devotion of life, receive the highest rewards among the apostolic teachers. “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. X).

“Nevertheless, bring here those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, and kill them before me.” This signifies that on the day of judgment the impiety of the Jews, or of all the reprobate who refused to be converted to Christ, will be punished.

Through the two faithful servants are signified the teachers of both [Col. 0475A] peoples; through the ten and five minas, the believing peoples; through the wicked servant, evil Catholics; through the enemies who refused to have him reign over them, the impiety of those who preferred either never to hear the word of faith or to corrupt it by misinterpreting it; and through the harvesting of the field that was not sown, the examination of even those who had no opportunity to hear the word of God. These five persons express every kind of human being who will be present on the day of judgment.

## HOMILY LXXXIII. FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT STEPHEN, THE PROTOMARTYR

**Luke XIII; Matthew XXIII.** At that time Jesus was saying to the crowds of Jews and to the chief priests: “Behold, I send prophets and wise men to you. Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you,” etc.

By “Jerusalem” he does not mean the stones and buildings of the city, but its inhabitants. He laments it with a father’s affection, [Col. 0475B] just as we read elsewhere that, when he saw it, he wept (Luke XIX). In saying, “How often I wanted to gather your children,” he testifies that all the earlier prophets had been sent by him.

We also read in the song of Deuteronomy the likeness of a bird gathering its nestlings beneath its wings: “As an eagle protects its nest and desires to spread its wings over its young, he received them and carried them upon his wings” (Deut. XXXII). And beautifully, the one who had called Herod, plotting his death, a fox (Luke XIII), compares himself to a bird. For the deceitful fox never ceases to set snares for birds.

“Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” He now calls the same city that he had called his nest the house of the Jews. Not unjustly deprived of the Lord’s help, it is left to its own power, because it not only refused to be protected by the wings of that omnipotent bird whom Matthew calls a hen (Matt. XXIII), but also handed over Christ—the same bird who wished to protect it—[Col. 0475C] to the foxes, that is, to Herod and Pilate, to be crucified.

Soon afterward it was itself given as prey to those same foxes, namely, to the kings of the earth. For after the Lord had been killed, the Romans came and, as though plundering an empty nest, took away their place, nation, and kingdom.

“But I say to you, you will not see me until the time comes when you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’” The crowds did indeed say this to the Lord as he came to Jerusalem. But since Luke does not say where the Lord departed from there, so that he would not come except at the time when this would already be said—for he continues on his journey until he comes to Jerusalem—this plainly compels us to understand it mystically, that is, of the coming in which he will come in glory, especially since Matthew testifies that the Lord said this after the crowds had sung praises to him.

Alternatively, what he says means this: “Unless you repent and confess that I am the one of whom the prophets sang, the Son of the omnipotent [Col. 0475D] Father, you will not see my face.” The Jews have been given a time for repentance. Let them confess him blessed who comes in the name of the Lord, and they will behold the face of Christ.

## HOMILY LXXXIV. FOR THE FEAST OF THE CHAIR OF SAINT PETER

**Mark VIII; Matthew XVI; Luke IX.** At that time Jesus and his disciples went out into the villages of Caesarea Philippi, etc.

This Philip was the brother of Herod, whom we mentioned above, tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis. In honor of Tiberius Caesar he called Caesarea Philippi—which is now called Paneas—by that name. It is in the province of Phoenicia. He imitated his father Herod, who, in honor of Augustus Caesar, called Caesarea by that name; it had previously been called the Tower of Strato. He also built, across the Jordan, the city of Libyas, naming it after his daughter.

This is the location of Caesarea Philippi, where the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon [Col. 0476A]. It has two springs, one called Jor and the other Dan; when mingled together, they produce the name Jordan.

And on the way he questioned his disciples, saying: “Who do people say that I am?” They answered him, saying: “Some say John the Baptist; others Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.”

The Lord, intending to test the faith of the disciples, first asks the opinion of the people, lest their confession should seem to have been confirmed not by an examination of the truth but by popular opinion, and lest they appear to believe what they had discovered rather than, like Herod, to hesitate over what they had heard.

Hence, according to Matthew, when Peter confessed him to be Christ, he says: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matt. XVI)—that is, human teaching did not instruct you in the truth of faith. It is also fitting that those who give different opinions about the Lord are designated by the name “people.” For those who faithfully and devoutly recognize the truth of his power deserve to be called not human beings but gods. The Lord shows that the apostles were such in his second question [Col. 0476B]. For it follows:

“Then he says to them: ‘But who do you say that I am?’” Pay attention, prudent reader, to the fact that from what follows and from the wording of the discourse, the apostles are called not human beings but gods. Having said, “Who do people say that I am?” he adds, “But who do you say that I am?” To those who, because they are human beings, form human opinions, he says: “You who are gods, who do you think that I am?”

Peter answered and said: “You are the Christ.” Although the other apostles knew this, Peter nevertheless answered before the others. He embraced everything, expressing both the nature and the name in which the fullness of virtues resides.

And now, rather than raising questions about the generation of God, when Paul indicated that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ—and him crucified (I Cor. II)—and Peter thought that nothing more needed to be confessed than Christ the Son of God, we investigate when and how he was born, and how great he is, by contemplating human weakness.

The end of my faith [Col. 0476C], therefore, is Christ; the end of my faith is the Son of God. I am not permitted to know the sequence of his generation, yet I am not permitted to be ignorant of the faith of his generation.

And he sternly warned them not to tell anyone about him. And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders and by the chief priests, etc.

For this reason he did not wish to be preached before his passion and resurrection, so that, after the sacrament of his blood had been completed, he might more appropriately say to the apostles: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

It would not have been beneficial for him to be publicly preached and his majesty proclaimed among the peoples when shortly afterward they would see him scourged and crucified, suffering many things at the hands of the elders, the scribes, and the chief priests. It should also be noted that he calls the one who must suffer many things, be killed, and rise again “the Son of Man,” because, while Christ suffered in the flesh, his divinity remained incapable of suffering.

And Peter took him and began to rebuke him. Matthew explains more fully how he rebuked him [Col. 0476D], saying: “And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: ‘Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you’” (Matt. XVI).

We have often said that Peter possessed the greatest ardor and love for the Lord and Savior. After his confession, in which he had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” and after the Savior’s reward, when he had heard, according to Matthew, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven,” he suddenly hears from the Lord that he must go to Jerusalem, and there suffer many things at the hands of the elders, the scribes, and the chief priests, be killed, and rise again on the third day.

He does not want his confession to be destroyed, nor does he think it possible for the Son of God to be killed. He takes him into his own affection, or leads him aside privately, lest he appear to rebuke his teacher in the presence of his fellow disciples. He began to rebuke him out of loving affection, and wished to say: “Far be it from you, Lord”; or, as it is better given in Greek: “Be gracious to yourself, Lord; this shall not [Col. 0477A] happen”—that is, “It cannot happen, and my ears cannot accept that the Son of God is to be killed.”

But he turned and, seeing his disciples, rebuked Peter, saying: “Get behind me, Satan.” Satan is interpreted as “adversary” or “opponent.” “Because,” he says, “you speak contrary to my will, you must be called an adversary.”

Many think that it was not Peter who was rebuked, but the opposing spirit who suggested that he say these things to the apostle. But to me, the apostolic error, arising from a feeling of devotion, will never appear to be an incentive of the devil.

“Get behind me, Satan” is said to the devil; “Get behind me” is what Peter hears. “Get behind me”—that is, “Follow my judgment.” For “you do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings.” It is my will and the will of the Father, whose will I came to do (John VI), that I should die for the salvation of human beings. But you, considering only your own will, do not want the grain of wheat to fall into the earth so that it may bear much fruit (John XII).

## HOMILY LXXXV. FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT WIGBERTH

[Col. 0477B]

Praise and rejoice in the Lord, beloved brothers, who have gathered with devoted minds for the solemn feast of Saint Wigberth, and praise the Lord Jesus Christ with the most devoted praises in many ways. He never abandons those who hope in him, but mercifully provides us, established in this most wretched prison of the world, with praiseworthy patrons to intercede for us, so that, instructed through them in the Christian religion and satisfied with heavenly fare, we may now be able to possess hope of heavenly rewards, if we follow them there in heart and deed.

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the holy Creator of all, created all the saints, and no one ever becomes holy through himself without God’s generous providence. Therefore, as we read in the sacred Scriptures, from Abel the protomartyr until now he has glorified his saints and elect with saving miracles in this world—those who were not captured by worldly enticements, but who, with every effort of mind and body, thinking rightly and restraining themselves from every iniquity, resisted diabolical suggestions most effectively. Therefore, through the overflowing grace of God, they are companions and heirs of the angelic seats in heaven, where they can desire nothing further, but enjoy without satiety the vision of the Lord Jesus Christ and the fellowship of the heavenly citizens.

And therefore, dearest brothers, let us take up for ourselves, with divine assistance, the weapons and examples of those who, by the imaginable help of God, conquered transient kingdoms through faith, practiced justice, and obtained the promises. And just as the Lord Jesus Christ foretold with a truthful voice in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

The outstanding preacher Paul also gave this warning, saying: “We do not have here a lasting city in this muddy world, but we seek the one that is to come through good works.” Therefore, you who hold the purest faith of the apostles ought in all things, with an alert and tireless mind, to strive to imitate them as much as you are able. For, as we read in the sacred pages, the apostles were inflamed with such love for Christ that they could not in any way be torn away from him by tortures or threats of kings, nor even by the persecutions of unbelievers. Rather, persevering together in firm faith, deed, and undissoluble charity, they continued until, called from this world by God, they deserved to ascend to the heavenly realms.

What should we say about virgins? Human intelligence is not sufficient to write or imitate anything worthy of them, given the frailty of the flesh. They had one faith, immutable love, and one charity. They possessed virginity of the flesh, an untouched body, and virginity of the soul, an incorrupt faith. And because they were adorned with devout pursuits in the Lord Christ, they received in heaven the palms and crowns of virtues as worthy rewards.

What, moreover, should be said about the martyrs, who, in rags and despised garments, gave their earthly bodies over to torments, so that they might deserve to possess God, the ruler of all, and reign eternally with him? They rejected the flower-bearing blossoms of this world together with its deceitful cares, by which foolish people are mocked through their own fabrications, and they loved the Lord Christ with all their strength. For this reason he reigns in the heavenly chambers with the confessors—for one of whose company this servant of God is—and with all the saints.

We read in the divine histories that all these people ascended to heaven by different tribulations from the road of this world. Something from the most holy life of all of them is to be imitated by us, insofar as human frailty permits, because we too were made in the image of God, as they were. Therefore we ought to return our undefiled images to God enthroned on high, as he says elsewhere: “Let the image of Caesar be returned to Caesar, and the image of God to God.” Even if, in comparison with them, we do not have a life radiant with holiness, nevertheless, with the Lord’s help, we must not fall into the dangerous condition of despair, because all the ways of the Lord are distinguished by mercy and truth at their end.

Indeed, the kind and ineffable will of the Almighty discerns nothing except what most justly accords with it. None of the saints mentioned above was so learned that he did not need the greatest mercy. For the increase of divine gifts is never sufficient for anyone to such an extent that nothing further remains for a mind armed with divine assistance to desire to understand and accomplish.

Therefore, no one should despair because of the greatness of his sins, as he says elsewhere: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.” Nevertheless, the remedies of conversion to the Lord must plainly be hastened, lest the time of correction and amendment be lost through delay and negligence, since the final day is known to none of us.

Therefore let us lend the ears of our hearts to Paul’s truthful sentences, where he says: “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light, so that we may walk honorably as in the day.” None of the works of our Lord Jesus Christ is without mercy. For he provides a human being with both forgiveness and chastisement, and mercifully supplies temporal severity, lest he justly inflict eternal punishment.

Therefore let no one grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose the most delightful place in his homeland. Accordingly, whoever seeks God with a good will seeks the one in whom is the highest of all goods, who contains within himself every good thing in perfection [F.: “contains”]. He seeks nothing else except everlasting joy in heaven.

Let us therefore seek the Lord, as this blessed servant of God did, and for this reason he is honored before God and human beings. Let us seek him with the weapons by which we can find him: by loving God and loving our neighbor, by giving alms, by frequenting the church in continual prayers, and, with the Lord’s gift, always resisting the weapons of the devil. For mortal life has run through various circumstances like the circuit of the world.

No one possesses secure joys in this life. From the beginning of the world until now many have gone astray through ignorance, because amid so many turbulent and deceptive things it is difficult to know and love God. For this reason let us do as the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him.”

Seek, therefore, the good that is without end, and persist once you have found it, because true blessedness must necessarily be established in the highest God, and no one can contradict this. It is not permitted for a human being either to comprehend by intelligence or to explain in speech all the mechanisms of God’s work. A time will come when we shall grasp in the reality of things what we now enact in appearance.

We have touched on these matters briefly and in passing. For the rest, what is more fortunate or more salutary than to serve God, who governs the world with such great reins, desires all human beings to be saved, and to come to knowledge of the truth? Thus, when the universal day arrives, may we all, joyful for our good works and protected by God’s assistance, deserve to receive eternal blessedness together with his saints.

## HOMILY LXXXVI. ON THE SECOND FEAST DAY OF SAINT WIGBERTH

Something still remains to be said briefly about blessed Wigberth, who shone in this world through such great benefits and among all Christ’s faithful that, deservedly, the entire Christian people rejoices with the highest veneration in his solemn feast—especially we who place our confidence in his patronage with God, both here and in the future.

Indeed, we believe that in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ he is able to obtain everything for which he asks him with pious and devoted prayers, since he has made so many miracles famous in the presence of the people, as you have often heard, for his praise.

You see, therefore, dearest brothers, how great a glory it is for the human race to follow God with a devoted mind. He never abandons those who hope in him amid tribulations, but honorably exalts in eternal joys in heaven all who, for love of him, despise the flourishing world, just as the Truth itself testifies, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”

The apostle Paul also spoke of those who love God: “What eye has not seen, nor the bodily ear heard, nor has entered the human heart—these things God has prepared for those who love him.”

This holy man Wigberth was, as sacred report tells us, distinguished by every dignity: joyful in heart for the love of God, always well ordered in conduct, and vigorous in every work of God. His hidden way of life in vigils and prayers, and also in fasts, in holiness of life, and in the display of signs, is made known to us.

His constant labor showed his charity, which he endured daily for Christ’s name. Throughout all the days of his life he always advanced in the work of God, pleasing almighty God through his outstanding deeds and acceptable to all the people.

From childhood he gave everything he was able to possess to works of mercy with lavish hands, so that, himself needy, he might follow Christ, who became poor for us. For who could be so eloquent in speech as to explain one by one, in continual words, all the wonders and benefits that God works through him?

He did not think about tomorrow, but, always trusting in God’s clemency according to the Gospel, he fed all who came to him with eternal fare. He despised no one in his distress, but always refreshed the sorrowful with divine consolation, supported by fraternal love. He strove to benefit everyone for God’s sake, being raised in mind and body toward higher things.

He was a guest and a poor man in the world. Although he was nourished by earthly necessities, he always occupied himself with heavenly things with all his strength. Therefore he is crowned eternally with the most just Lord and with all the inhabitants of heaven, where he can never be deprived of joys, since Christ himself is his joy.

Accordingly, insofar as we can with the assistance of divine grace, let us strive to imitate him with all our strength, so that, even if we cannot acquire such rewards in heaven, at least we may not be deprived of some refreshment there.

We therefore possess the weapons of justice, as this servant of God possessed them: loving God, loving our neighbor without hypocrisy, and maintaining charity and peace with everyone. For it is a mark of Christian perfection to be peaceful with one’s enemies—out of hope for their correction, not through agreement with their wickedness—and to show humility and patience in heart and deed. For the evil spirit, proud, led the first human being into death through pride, whereas Christ, humble, restored the obedient human being to life.

Let us be lovers of mercy and Christian religion, compassionate and united in good work, firmly preserving concord, which is the guardian of virtues, as it says elsewhere: “Therefore beware, men, lest there be a discordant judgment in your minds. Let one love join together what we believe; let one and the same zeal establish what we live and understand.”

Nothing firm is dissociable, and nothing among human beings is pleasing to God without peace; nor is the most magnificent gift pleasing at the altar without it.

Likewise, armed with divine assistance, let us flee the weapons of the devil—that is, pride. For all vices have power in evil deeds, but pride alone must be guarded against in perfect and upright deeds, because without doubt God breaks every proud person, and God always resists the proud.

Afterward, with all effort and desire, we must avoid drunkenness, which is the root of all mortal beings’ inclination to sin. Let us flee anger, which very often, through irritation, falls into its own grief. With God’s help, let us drive luxury and avarice from ourselves like poison. Luxury, seducing through evil counsel and condemning through the taste of honey, leads to uncorrectable punishments.

Nothing in the present age devastates the entire human race so miserably as avarice. Let us therefore reject hatred and envy from our hearts, because it is wholly unfitting for a Christian to hate the image of God. Nevertheless, in the wicked we utterly hate wickedness, while loving the creature.

With the help of divine gifts, let us also flee discord and fraud, since nothing good can exist where fraud and discord reign.

But I think it would be too long to discuss these matters. With the Lord’s help, we omit the evil sirens that accustom human minds to disease rather than freeing them. We hold fast to those virtues in which alone there are health and eternal happiness.

Therefore, dearest brothers, know that the rich of this world are in the greatest poverty because they do not possess the wealth of justice and truth. But those who faithfully serve the Lord enthroned on high discover goods that can in no way perish. The goods of the present age are small in comparison with future goods.

A person may be forced to abandon temporal goods, but he never loses eternal ones except through negligence and carelessness. Therefore, you who have been marked with the triumphant sign of Christ, and who, with the Lord’s help, wish to overcome this precarious life—for it contains nothing but seductions and assaults—always love in conduct and deeds what Christ, the true lover, already possesses.

For lovers of the world burn with concern over losses and with desire for pestilential profits. The world is entirely full of bitterness and downfall, and its false joys flow away.

Draw near to God through good works, and he will draw near to you. Seek him not falsely but truly, and you will find him.

Let no one, I beg you, doubt in faith, hesitate concerning the abundance of forgiveness, or question the efficacy of a devout petition. For the more confidently and kindly we entreat God, the sooner we may deserve to be heard.

Faith abounds in every good thing, as the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “Everyone who asks with faith receives; whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.” And again: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.”

We therefore have many examples of our fathers in the divine books; we also have before our eyes the most certain example of this holy man whose feast we celebrate today. With fervent faith, for the love of God, he abandoned his homeland, his family, and his worldly friends; he despised earthly things together with their pompous praises, so that he might seek heavenly things.

With the Lord’s support, let us also despise the world and love our Creator together with his commandments, so that through the good things we do in the present we may be able to reach the eternal joys of blessedness, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, three and one by the Father’s power, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXVII. ON THE FEAST DAY OF THE HOLY VIRGIN SCHOLASTICA

At that time Jesus said this parable to his disciples: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls,” and so forth.

The reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, which your charity has just heard, has revealed a great heavenly mystery to human minds, showing us that the very one who is God, the Creator of all, is also the Redeemer of our salvation.

For, often giving instructions in virtue to the disciples who followed him from the crowds in parables, he sometimes gave teachings in concealed sayings to disciples followed by the crowds, as the prophet says: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning of the world.” He showed that he himself is the true wisdom of the Father, through whom all created things endure, as Solomon says: “I will dwell in the highest places, and my throne is in the pillar of cloud.”

For, wishing to reveal how greatly he had loved the human race through his mercy, for whose sake he emptied himself of the glory of his divinity and did not disdain to assume the form of our condition, he took human likeness in many figurative ways, as he himself says:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls.”

We ought first to ask with humble prayer that he who does not deny the boldness to speak, and who promises, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it,” may himself, loosening the bonds of our mind, grant an increase of his grace for speaking.

First, then, we must inquire who this merchant is, so great that, desiring to buy nothing except good pearls, he assumed for himself the appearance of a heavenly merchant.

Who is he? Who could he truly be except Christ, the Son of God? Although he is immutable God, he did not disdain to assume the form of our servitude, as the prophet says: “He was seen on earth and lived among human beings. And we saw him without appearance or beauty; he bore our sins.”

He who is God before the ages became a merchant for us at the end of the ages, so that he who had created all things well, seeing them lost for human use, might provide no other perfect restoration for us except through his own transaction.
