How greatly he grieved over the loss of the first human being, who had lost the joys of paradise, is clearly shown by the reconciliation of our life itself. He did not accomplish it with gold extracted from the veins of the earth—which Arabia sends and India supplies, and which thieves dig up and steal—but, laying down his immaculate soul for us, he destroyed the bond of our death.

He emptied the appearance of his glory through such great humiliations that he not only calls himself the Son of Man, although he is wholly God, but also, as the Psalmist says, declares: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of human beings and the outcast of the people.”

Therefore he wished his divine nature to be compared not only with sensible but also with insensible creatures. At one time he wished to be called the sun of justice, at another the angel of the covenant, at another the bridegroom coming forth from the bridal chamber, at another the good shepherd, at another the voiceless sheep, at another the innocent lamb, at another the lion from the tribe of Judah, and also the true vine, the light of the world, the cornerstone, as well as the worm and the door. And, in order to reconcile us to God the Father, he also became a merchant.

O Lord, who would dare to say this unless you had said it—you who are never deceived, who are true truth, who are perfect wisdom, in whom there can be nothing except the highest good—that the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant, when that kingdom is without the fault of avarice, whereas the merchant here always conducts business for ambitious profit?

As Solomon says: “‘Bad, bad,’ says every buyer; but when he has gone away, then he boasts.” And rejecting this, the Psalmist says: “Because I did not know commerce, I will enter into the powers of the Lord.”

The custom of merchants is to go around marketplaces, deceive unwary traders, trick the simple with oaths, buy more cheaply, sell more dearly, overthrow many through various deceptions, and—and what is worse, as Wisdom says—“rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things.”

And there is also the Psalmist’s statement: “Surely the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the scales, so that they may deceive, each through his own vanity.”

Let us see what follows.

> Seeking good pearls.

Truly, here is the good merchant of the kingdom of heaven. For what could previously have been doubtful has now become certain to the mind. If he were not seeking good pearls, he would not be the merchant of the kingdom of heaven, where no one is found except the good, where no one enters who gives his money at interest or accepts gifts against the innocent.

We must also examine which kingdom of heaven the Lord meant, since the expression can be understood in two ways.

There is one kingdom of heaven of which the Psalmist says: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth he gave to the sons of men.” And again: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet.” This kingdom can be obtained by anyone who produces the fruits of its righteousness, doing violence to it from the days of John the Baptist.

There is another kingdom which, holding the type of the holy Church, retains the good and the wicked together in one charity: the just, so that it may send them perfected to Christ; the unjust, so that through the patience of mercy it may recall them to salvation.

Certainly, in this kingdom there are ten virgins, five wise and five foolish. The wise have oil in their lamps—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—while the foolish, because they do not have it, seek to buy what belongs to others. The wise enter into joy with the bridegroom; the others, shut out from the door, know neither the hour nor the day of their salvation.

Of this kingdom the Gospel says: “He sends his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals.” In this kingdom Noah also, remaining in the ark—which is the holy Church—feeds clean and unclean animals.

It continues:

> And finding one precious pearl, he gave all that he had and bought it.

Behold, the one who was seeking many bought one, as the Gospel says: “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

He also bought one that was precious—the one, I say, of which he says in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, my perfect one, and there is no blemish in her.”

Behold, the pearl in the Gospel becomes a dove in the Song, and what is precious there becomes perfect here. For the holy Church is a pearl through the mother of good works, as the Lord says: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

And she is a dove through the nature of simplicity, as the Lord says: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.”

Truly, for her sake Christ deigned to give all that was his—that is, his soul and blood—and thus to buy her.

This is the holy Church on earth; this is the holy Jerusalem in heaven, adorned with every precious stone. On her gates the names of the apostles and pearls shine, and throughout all her streets “Alleluia” is sung by everyone.

She does not seek the sun through windows, the sun that shines during the hours of day so that it may make the grain’s ears white and paint the fields all over with various flowers, now hastening to it, to the citadel, now holding the western shadows [Note: At [Col. 0481] perhaps read: “and now it hastens [EOAM ACCURRIT, uncertain] to the citadel,” so that the sun’s rising may be set opposite its setting. EDITOR].

Nor is she that Jerusalem over which the Lord wept when he saw it, whose everlasting ruins he foretold, and which the tyrant devastated and whose lofty walls he cast down to the earth. Rather, she is the one that is truly the vision of peace, of which the Psalmist says: “This is my rest forever and ever; here I will dwell, because I have chosen her.”

For her light is no longer that of the sun just mentioned, but of the one who knows no setting. There, God and the Lamb are both splendor and temple.

But it is worthy to explore something deeper in these matters. For what could be truer than that this pearl is the one so pleasing in beauty and brilliance that everything is given up in comparison with her?

Perhaps she is the enclosed garden, the sealed fountain, the closed door, which the prophet, looking upon, says: “This door will be closed, and it will not be opened, and no man will pass through it, because the Lord God has entered through it, and it will remain closed.”

Or perhaps she is the one of whom the Psalmist says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed all around with variety.”

And why is this? Because: “The King desired your beauty,” for there is no blemish in you.

Truly, this is the queen, wholly beautiful and immaculate. Therefore the Lord chose her as his inheritance, and did not disdain to take flesh from her.

Let us see what follows:

> The queen stands at the right hand, because the Lord knows the ways that are at the right hand. In a garment of gold, clothed all around with variety.

This variety is the adornment of queens, by which she surpasses all through diversity of works—not through color or thread, which the Seres send from abroad, but through the activity of virtuous deeds that shines forth. She is not painted with artificial colors or depicted with dyed saffron, but is varied with sacred figures.

When we behold Abel’s offering, Abraham’s faithful obedience, Isaac’s sacrifice, Jacob’s pillar anointed with oil, Joseph’s being sold, Lot’s hospitality, Melchizedek’s sacrifice, David’s sackcloth bed, Zacchaeus’s tithes, the furnace of the three youths, as well as the prophecies of the prophets, the red color of the blood of the apostles and martyrs, the blush of virginal purity, and the teachings of salvation of confessors—what else shines in these things except variety?

Paul glitters with this variety when he says: “Who will separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger?” And again: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck,” and so forth.

And Peter says: “We must obey God rather than human beings.”

Through this variety of eternal works, all the saints shine like the sun in the kingdom of God the Father.

Having briefly introduced these matters, dearest brothers, since we are celebrating the birthday of blessed Scholastica, I wish to bring into this little work something about the merits of her life from the life of the most blessed Benedict, so that the greatness of her sanctity may not be concealed in silence.

But first let us send prayers to almighty God, who made all things in wisdom, so that he may deign to grant what he has deigned to promise: “Let the thirsty one come and drink,” and, “From his belly will flow living waters.” Thus may we continue what has been begun worthily, so that it may contribute to the honor of so great a feast and provide increase to your charity.

His sister Scholastica, dedicated to the almighty Lord from the very time of her infancy, was accustomed to come to him once a year.

First, let us investigate the power of so great a name, so that the discourse may proceed with its own beauty. Scholastica is derived from *schola*, which is the nurse of wisdom. From it all teaching of wisdom arises; from it the standard of all virtues grows; and through it the whole virtue of the soul becomes eager to learn good and evil, so that it may run along the straight path of salvation.

Thus it may despise the perishing things of the world, desire heavenly things that always endure, and avoid mistaking good for evil, evil for good, darkness for light, light for darkness, bitter for sweet, or sweet for bitter. It may also discern which virtue belongs to the spirit and which to the flesh, lest, doing everything indiscriminately, it hope to choose good where the entire rule is wickedness.

As the saying goes: “Whoever is not a disciple of truth will be a teacher of error.”

But let us see what kind of brother this Benedict can be to so great a sister, her equal in every respect—not only in name but also in deed, not only on earth but also in heaven.

She did not become a scholastic in the school of philosophers, but in the school of Christ. Fleeing the world’s mockeries from infancy, she fitted herself for a heavenly bridegroom. He, however, from the time of his boyhood, seeing at Rome the precipices of vices and the pursuits of worldly letters, with an old man’s heart withdrew the foot he had set at the threshold of the world.

How happy the land of Nursia, which sends forth such pupils! The golden realms of Canopus send forth tyrants; you send to Christ offspring worthy of heaven.

O happy womb of so great a mother, which gave such offspring to the world—offspring of blessing and wisdom! Truly, this is that fertile soil which, having received seed, produced in one place a hundredfold fruit and in another sixtyfold.

But why did you, holy sister, come only once a year? Perhaps you feared the length of the journey because of your tender feet? Or were you preparing a gift to bring? Or perhaps the good brother made you fruitful only once a year through the dew of heavenly speech, so that the meadows of the mind, once moistened, would be sufficient for growth in salvation?

Or did you have in mind Solomon’s saying: “Restrain your foot from your neighbor’s house, lest perhaps, being sated, he hate you”? And also this: “You have found honey, my son; eat what is sufficient for you, lest, when you are satisfied, you vomit it up.”

Let all sisters act in this way: let them not frequent their brothers’ thresholds with hurried steps; let them not seek carnal kisses; let them not utter foolish stories. Let them not bring merely a gift that a woven fabric displays or a skilled hand adorns; not perfumes, not cakes of various flavors. Instead, together with Scholastica, seek the sacred school of your brother Benedict, so that, satisfied more with heavenly food than with an earthly gift, you may be able to return to your homes.

It continues:

> To meet her, the man of God would go down not far outside the gate, on the monastery’s estate.

How holy, how modest, how discreet was this approach! So that the fragile sex might not be wearied, the brother came out to meet her, lest perhaps the labor of the journey break the devotion of her mind.

Or did he regard it as unlawful that a female foot should tread upon the threshold of so great a monastery? Or perhaps the merciful father avoided the barking of worldly people, who, like dogs, ravage the good conduct of monks and believe in them what they themselves do not refuse to practice through their wicked deeds?

And if it would have been unlawful to expect this of so great a father, with puffed-out throats the younger disciples would have curled their laughter. Therefore the beneficent father went down not onto the possessions of worldly people, but onto his own property.

It continues:

> One day she came as usual, and her venerable brother went down to her with his disciples.

He came as usual because he approached out of a good habit of mind and with an unfeigned faith. How holy was this approach, how holy this arrival, how devout this journey! This journey ran more through love of mind toward Christ than through the movement of feet toward a brother—indeed, toward Christ the brother.

For he himself says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother.”

But with what devotion she ran, the Psalmist says: “As the deer longs for the fountains of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.”

But why the Psalmist metaphorically introduced the deer, so that the soul might run toward God as a deer runs toward a fountain, does not remain without mysteries. Does only the deer, and not the dove, the turtledove, and the sparrow, seek the fountain?

But the deer returns to the stream of the fountain in one way, and the dove in another. The former descends through the running of its feet; the latter through airy flight. The deer, frequently pursued by hunters’ skill and wearied, runs to the water; the dove, however, approaches by its accustomed path without fatigue.

If we wish to consider this mystically, the invisible soul has the form of a visible animal. One, through a course of fatigue, proceeds here to an earthly fountain; the other to a heavenly fountain. The former, wearied by the voices of dogs, the latter, pursued by evil spirits, runs to that fountain which is the living fountain, the well of the house of Jacob, from which a vein of leaping water boils up into eternal life.

Certainly, so great a sister came to her brother with such faith. For the sick person goes to the physician in one way, the healthy in another: the healthy person in order to visit the healthy; the healthy person in order to care for the sick.

A thirsty person also hastens to the fountain in one way, and one drunk with wine in another. The former goes so that, after drinking, he may refresh his mind; the latter so that, no longer thirsty, he may proceed on the right path.

This sister, seeing both graces in so great a brother, came with an intelligent step and without weariness: first, so that, being healthy, she might visit the healthy; afterward, so that she might heal one sick not in body but in mind through instruction in salvation. For not even the stars are clean in God’s sight, and, according to the Apostle, neither is an infant of one day.

It continues:

> They spent the entire day in the praises of God and sacred conversations, and when the darkness of night was already pressing upon them, they took food together.

Blessed is such a meeting of relatives, with the Lord’s command before their eyes: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be added to you.”

Blessed are such dishes, where the bread of angels is set out before human food, and where the mind is refreshed before the stomach. Here food is stored that can please the heavenly table; there remains the nourishment that bodily indigestion casts out.

And blessed is the conversation that is extended throughout the whole day in divine praise, in which sacred proclamations are exchanged from the first rising of the light until sunset.

It continues:

> While they were still sitting at the table, and the hour grew later as the sacred conversations continued, the same holy woman, his sister, asked him, saying: “I beg you, do not leave me this night, so that until morning we may speak of something concerning the joys of heavenly life.”

They sit at the table and take food; with one tooth of charity they chew the bread, and they conduct sacred conversations as though there were one mouth with which they might break both earthly and heavenly bread.

For while the stomach was full of food, the mind was still hungry for the word of salvation. Therefore, as though famished, she asks that the most delightful heavenly discourse [the printed text is uncertain] might satisfy her mind with divine nourishment until daylight—so that the one who had been a teacher in the light of day might also become, amid the darkness, a teacher of the household (doctor herilis).

It continues.

To him she replied, “What is this? What are you saying, brother? I cannot possibly remain outside my cell.”

Behold, the brother questions his sister, the master his disciple, the holy man the holy woman, as though he did not know what his sister had said. But this inquiry is more the speech of one becoming angry than of one asking a question, [Col. 0485B] since the Father had clearly heard what his sister was requesting. It was as though he were saying: “What you are asking is not right: that I should remain outside my cell in an unusual manner, something I absolutely cannot do.”

O lover of holiness, why do you deny your sister what you provide even to strangers? But let religious devotion do this, not the cause of sorrow. You know the Lord’s command: “Whoever loves father, or mother, or brother, or sister more than me is not worthy of me.” And so you return to your accustomed place of prayer, where you are accustomed to cling more to God than to your sister.

But with bold speech we say: “Is God not here, where your good sister is seeking the mysteries of God, since he himself says, ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst’?” Behold, she is not asking to see you for a long time, as parents do, but is requesting the space of a single night, so that you may offer sacred conversation. How harshly you attend, holy brother, to your sister’s prayers, on account of your sacred religious observance.

She rightly asks that she may receive from you; you likewise, that you may return. She acts in faith, and you in faith; she out of love for God, and you likewise as she. She asks that you may spend the hours of the night in preaching with your sister; you ask that you may offer the customary praises to the Lord with the brothers. But which of the two acted better, the following statement shows.

The sky was so clear that no cloud appeared in the air. Truly, no cloud could have been present where there was the true light that illumines every person coming into this world. The account continues.

When the holy woman had heard her brother’s words of refusal, she placed her hands, with the fingers interlaced, upon the table and bowed her head into her hands, intending to entreat the almighty Lord.

Tell us, blessed virgin: what school taught you, that you propose an opinion against your teacher? Does he not say, “Every disciple will be perfect if he is like his teacher”? And in the Gospel he says, “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing”; yet you join both hands together. And he says, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat”; yet you immerse it correctly on both sides. He places the sheep on his right; do you also place them on the left?

The Psalmist places things here on the right, saying, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’”; and again, “The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me.” And in the Song: “Your right hand, O Lord, has been glorified in strength,” and so forth. Yet you, disregarding these things, not only clasp your hands but even interlace your fingers?

The Lord says in the Gospel: “But when you pray, enter your room and, having shut the door, pray to your Father”; yet, seated at supper, you pour forth prayers and tears before human eyes.

But how worthy of praise are your deeds, O holiest of women! What are you doing in a private chamber, when you perform such things beneath the open sky? For this reason your right and left sides are one: you attend to the work of him who has no left side, as he says, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” And in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.” And in the Psalm: “Your hands made me and fashioned me.” And in the Song: “My hands dripped with myrrh.”

By this authority, how beautifully your hands remain clasped, [Col. 0486A] upon which you rested your head and poured forth, weeping, a rain from heaven. But what head is this? The Apostle says, “The head of a woman is man, and the head of man is God.” And whose man is meant, if not the one of whom the prophet says, “Behold a man whose name is the Rising [Oriens]”?

Behold, he who, for the salvation of all, bowed his head on the cross and gave up his spirit, has now bowed his head upon your palms, so that the mystery of his secret purpose, which you were seeking in your mind, might flow to you from the stars. You performed such a miracle merely by interlacing your fingers; what would you have done if you had extended your palms in prayer?

When she lifted her head from the table, such a force of lightning and thunder, and such a downpour of rain, broke forth that neither the venerable Benedict nor the brothers who were with him could move a foot beyond the threshold of the place where they were seated.

How new these miracles were to the world, how worthy of proclamation to all generations: where there had been no shadow of a cloud, the whole air thundered with clamor, and dense peals of thunder resounded where there had been no shaking of the wind. For one fountain of tears watered the table, [Col. 0486B] while the ether watered the fields with rain.

Let holy charity now stand firm; let the brother’s feet remain immobile. What the sister requests, let the brother’s love not deny. Willingly or unwillingly, remain through the night, Father, in sacred conversation. Behold, she fulfills the Lord’s command: she asks in order to receive, seeks in order to find, knocks in order that it may be opened to her.

Let her herself say what she is asking: “That we may speak until morning about something of the joys of heavenly life.” For this reason you came down to meet her, so that you might bring forth these gifts: complete what you have begun. For the reward does not appear at the beginning, but at the end of good works. Therefore the Lord poured rain from above, so that you would not deny the river of preaching. Truly, she is not asking for a perishable gift, but seeking the gain of the heavenly kingdom. The account continues.

The holy woman, bowing her head into her hands, had poured rivers of tears upon the table, through which she drew the clear sky toward rain. The deluge followed her prayer without delay. But such was the correspondence between the prayer and the downpour that, as she lifted her head from the table, thunder already sounded, so that the lifting of her head and the falling of the rain occurred at one and the same moment.

How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart, and how kindly disposed to the soul that seeks him! Behold, he who searches minds and sees the hearts of all, who says through the Psalmist, “He will call upon me, and I will answer him; I am with him in tribulation,” did not delay. He did not require many prayers, but in the blink of an eye and at the very instant of the heart he granted the gift to the one who asked.

For when she lifted her head from her hands, prayer and downpour corresponded with one another. Rejoice and be glad, holiest of men, for behold, you hold what you wished; behold, you have what you always sought. Behold, you see remarkable miracles, attested by heaven and earth. Truly, if you had not denied what you desired, these signs would not have arisen before human eyes, signs that sacred reading will proclaim throughout the whole world.

Behold, Scholastica’s name now flashes forth in the praise of her virtues. Behold, the holy people rejoice together over her miracles. Behold, the branch that you cultivated bears the fruit of signs. The account continues.

Then the man of God, amid flashes of lightning, peals of thunder, and the deluge of the mighty [Col. 0486D] rain, seeing that he could not return to the monastery, began to complain in distress, saying, “May almighty God forgive you, sister. What have you done?”

Why do you ask, man of God, what your sister has done? Do you not see what she has done? Do you not see the drops of rain? Do you not hear the crashing roars of the heavens? Do you not feel the miracles flashing, the signs flowing, the foundations of the house trembling—and yet you say, “What have you done?”

Did she do this? Rather, your holy refusal did it. If you had not refused, the miracle would not have occurred. Christ brought this about, the lover of piety. When the Canaanite woman asked him, he delayed hearing her prayers in order to make her faith sharper, so that when she sought crumbs like a little dog, the children’s bread might be given to her.

But although she came then as a stranger from the borders, she was no longer a stranger to fellowship with Christ. This woman, however, dedicated to Christ from the cradle, deserved to hear, together with the glorious virgin Mary, “She has chosen the better part.”

And why, Father, do you say in distress, “May almighty God forgive you, sister. What have you done?” O man of God, the minds of human beings are open to you; for you the air pours forth coins; for you dry jars flow with oil; for you the depths of the lake bring iron up from below; the underworld itself gives back a soul. And now, as though distressed and ignorant, you say, “What have you done?”

O blessed Father, if it is permissible to say so, how much more just it would have been to say, “May almighty God forgive me, because I do not heed your good prayers,” than to say, “May almighty God forgive you; what have you done?” This is the saying of Solomon: “Reprove the wise, and he will love you.” The account continues.

She replied to him: “Behold, I asked you, and you were unwilling to hear me; I asked my Lord, and he helped me.”

The unstated meaning is: “I asked you as a brother, but you were unwilling to hear me as your sister. I hoped that you would have in mind a mother’s tenderness, the pains of childbirth, nursing breasts, a nurse’s cradle, the midwife’s baths, and the swaddling bands with which you once nourished my infancy. But you were unwilling to hear me, and you were hastening instead to the brothers whom only the charity of Christ makes your kindred—men whom you do not even know from what boundary the world sends to your cradle.

“Therefore I asked my Lord, and he heard me. You did not consider that one father joined our limbs together; you did not see that we shared one dwelling within the confines of the womb. Therefore I ran to that Father who gave us our souls, who granted earthly things and did not deny heavenly ones.

“Now then, if you can, go out, leave me, and return to the monastery. For ‘now’ refers to the present time: now, when almighty God has closed your roads; now, when he has denied you access to depart; now, if you can, leave me and return to the monastery.

“And why, Father, do you weary yourself? Is this not the monastery, where you are—the one who is head of all monasteries and teacher of all monks—since it is not a place that sanctifies a person, but a person who sanctifies a place? Remain now, most holy Father, unwillingly, so that the sun of another day may provide you with a way to go.”

The account continues. Unable to go outside the shelter, he who had not wished to remain willingly in that place remained unwillingly. How many holy men you resemble, man of God, who unwillingly performed good deeds! Jacob unwillingly fled from his brother, and afterward returned with many possessions. Joseph likewise went unwillingly to the position in which he would become teacher of God’s people. Daniel went to the Babylonian citadel, so that he might become foremost among all the wise. Saul unwillingly became Paul, so that he might become the preacher to the nations.

Therefore, holy man, let your charity not rest from standing unwillingly, so that it may offer lessons of Christ’s salvation. The account continues.

And so it happened that they spent the entire night awake and nourished one another through sacred conversations about spiritual life, each taking a turn in speaking. Behold, new spiritual joys now arise, because the one who had earlier refused has now become a giver of heavenly things; and those who had previously been divided from concord now nourish one another through sacred conversation.

How great are your wonders, almighty God! For all things that you willed, you made good, and there is no one who can resist the power of your majesty. Therefore the heavens, the air, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them praise you, [Col. 0487D] because you continually renew your signs and wonders, so that the whole world may acknowledge you as its Redeemer.

Now, in your mercy, grant pious Father Benedict a path by which he may return to his cell. Restrain the aerial stream, remove the drops of rain, grant the sun of clear weather, so that he who came joyfully may depart rejoicing; so that his sister may likewise bid her brother farewell and return to her own place; so that, rejoicing and exulting together in your gift, they may be carried back to their own dwellings.

The account continues. I said that he wished to do something but was entirely unable to do it because, if we consider the mind of the venerable man, there is no doubt that he wished the same clear weather in which he had descended to remain. But contrary to his wish, through the power of almighty God he found a miracle arising from a woman’s breast.

Nor is it surprising that the woman, who had long desired to see her brother, prevailed over him at that moment. For since, according to John’s saying, “God is love,” she who loved more was able to do more, by a very just judgment.

These matters should not be discussed at length. For, according to the grammarians, charity is a middle category, since charity can exist both among the good and the wicked, and among robbers and devout people. Thus it is said: “Perfect charity drives out fear.” Certainly, if the charity that drives out fear among the good is perfect, the imperfect kind is nevertheless believed to exist when it establishes an accord of wickedness among the evil and the proud.

Thus, in the Lord’s Passion, Pilate sent Jesus to Herod, and Jesus was sent back from Herod to Pilate. Herod and Pilate became friends on that very day, for previously they had been enemies of one another.

But this is perfect charity, which is God, and which here enabled one to do more than the other. Concerning it the Apostle says: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” The account continues.

When, on the following day, the same venerable woman had returned to her own cell, the man of God went back to the monastery. And behold, after he had remained in his cell for three days, raising his eyes into the air, he saw the soul of his sister departing from her body and entering the hidden regions of heaven in the form of a dove. [Col. 0488B]

How blessed are the eyes that can contemplate blessed souls, that can perceive spiritual things with bodily sight! These lights do not lie upon the foundation of the forehead, but shine within, at the windows of the heart. Concerning them it is said: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?”

Behold now, Father Benedict, this dove flies already to the windows of your heart, so that, passing through them, it may carry your sister’s soul to that heavenly gate. Thus she became the guide of so great a soul, she who once was the bird carrying the sign of peace back to the ark.

How happy is this bird, adorned with such mysteries, which was worthy even to bear the Holy Spirit above the Lord Christ! This bird, constant in royal service, gleaming on its back with accustomed silvered wings and gold, carries news to paradise. Of it the Song of Songs says: “Arise, my beloved, my bride, and come: my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow places of the wall.” The account continues.

Rejoicing with him over her great glory, he gave thanks to almighty God in hymns and praises, and announced her death to the brothers. For the holy Father announced to the brothers that he had been worthy to behold the hidden mystery with sacred sight. Rejoicing in such a desire fulfilled, he gave thanks to almighty God, because he saw her whom, three days earlier, he had drenched with the dew of heavenly speech ascending to the ethereal kingdoms in the form of a dove. The account continues.

He immediately sent them to carry her body to the monastery and place it in the tomb that he himself had prepared. When this had been done, it happened that, since their minds had always been one in the Lord, even burial did not separate their bodies.

Behold, brothers, the heavenly pearl once purchased by the merchant is fitted into heavenly ornaments. Now, feeding among the shining lilies, she follows the Lamb wherever he goes. Behold, she is placed by angels in the Lord’s paradise; behold, on earth she is placed by the hands of monks in her brother’s tomb, so that neither heaven’s gate nor earthly burial might separate the gift bestowed by one mother; and those whose mind had always been one in Christ might have one tomb for their bodies.

Behold, your losses have been repaired, O paradise. Behold, the virgin formed by God’s hand, whom the poisonous enemy stole from your place, now returns to the heights of heaven; now she recognizes the palm of her creator; now, because she had been conquered, she treads victoriously upon the neck of the evil enemy.

Speak, speak, minister of hell; speak, soldier of Tartarus; speak, race of Orcus filled with every poison through fraud. What did God’s most holy creature do to you? What harm did the well-formed woman do to you? For what reason did you, as adviser, thrust yourself forward so that she would eat what was not yours?

Speak, poisonous thief. Because you could not seize a share of God’s kingdom, you wished to seize God’s creature through the serpent. Indeed, such a Lord sends such a servant. You are the slippery serpent, he the twisted serpent; you are full of every grief, he of every poison; you give counsel of death, he hisses through his organs and dispenses counsel of death.

Could you not find another animal in God’s paradise that would agree with your wishes, other than the serpent? Truly, you could not. You were more cunning than the holy angels; he was more cunning than all living creatures. You were created good in heaven but willingly became evil; he was created good in paradise but, through you, was made guilty.

The virgin of God, God’s creature, God’s woman, was created good; through you and the serpent, by tasting what was forbidden, she was made a sinner. What did this profit you, mad one? You heaped upon yourself everlasting fires; he will eat earth all his days. You are bound with fiery chains; he is slain in the wrath of all, beaten upon the heels, and scourged with blows.

Woe, woe to you both in every respect! Behold, the woman has been restored through Christ’s blood. In place of the loss of the earthly paradise, she now holds the heights of heaven from which you fell headlong. Your gall has been changed into the sweetness of honey, your wicked fraud into *in reparatione* (“in the restoration”; F. *reparationem*, “into the restoration”) of *omnium salutem* (“the salvation of all”; F. *salutis*, “of salvation”).

Your throat’s jaw has been pierced, so that you bite no one and devour no one unless God wills it. And if you devour someone, suffocated by God’s mercy, you will cast him out with blood, and God will draw him from your entrails.

Rejoice now, virgin of God, raised to such triumphant heights. Exult, most holy Father Benedict, holiest of fathers, sweetest teacher of teachers, because, your holy works completed, you rejoice together above the kingdoms of heaven.

Intercede for those entrusted to you; plead for us who are afflicted; pray for our sins; ask Christ not only for the monks entrusted to you, but also for your handmaids, so that every age, every sex, and every order that submits its neck to your commands may despise the world that is passing away, desire eternal joys, seek the blessed kingdoms, and receive prosperity for soul and body.

May they suffer no disturbance from any demonic fraud; may they be afflicted by no attacks of the wicked; may they be destroyed by no calamities. Well done, blessed Father: favor those who pray; incline your ears to the prayers of your servants; grant forgiveness to those who ask; grant gifts to those who seek; spare sinners.

For you are shepherds, while we are sheep. Hear the bleating of your sheep; draw me after you, so that we may come to you, and there find the true pastures where there are true and everlasting joys.

Return to God the talents accumulated from us; carry back with interest the entrusted gifts of your teachings. Join me, an unworthy presumptuous author of this work, to your holy servants, so that, together with the whole flock entrusted to you, we may attain the rewards of life, and so that God may say to you:

“Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter, with all those entrusted to you, into the joy of your Lord”—through him who has deigned to promise worthy joys to his servants, who lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXXXVIII. ON SIMON AND JUDE

Simon and Jude, the apostles of the Lord, entered the region of Persia by the will of God. There they found two magicians, Zaroen and Arfaxat, who had fled from the presence of the apostle Matthew in Ethiopia and were no longer able to speak because of the apostles’ power.

Then Varradas, commander of the Badinomi, came before them and made them consult their own priests, so that they might predict the outcome of the war. One of them said, “I cannot speak.”

The apostles said, “We permit them to speak, so that you may recognize the lies of your priests.”

They came and announced to the king that he should go to war and would be defeated. But while they were keeping watch over him, the apostles said that on the following day, at the third hour, the messengers he had sent would bring him gifts, and that he would establish peace. And so it happened.

The priests had done evil against the apostles, producing serpents through enchantment. The apostles took the serpents into their cloaks and threw them against the priests. The serpents began to eat them, and the priests began to howl like wolves.

The king said to the apostles, “Allow them to kill them.”

They replied, “We were not sent to kill, but to give life.”

And they said to the serpents, “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, take away the poison that you are pouring forth, and return to your own places.” And they did so.

They remained there for six months, and six thousand people were baptized by them, excluding children and women—and the king first of all. They ordained as bishop Abidas, who had come with them. Crowds followed him eagerly, and more than two hundred men themselves received martyrdom. Their feast of martyrdom is celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, and they live in eternal rest.

## HOMILY LXXXIX

The prophet Ezekiel saw a certain tree possessing four roots extending around the four regions of the world. It had three branches that penetrated heaven, and there were seven leaves upon it. In its midst were the sun and the moon, and twelve stars.

By the four roots we understand the four evangelists. For just as the four roots extended around the four regions of the world, so the preaching of the four evangelists was extended. Hence David says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” and so forth.

By the three branches we understand faith in the Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. By the seven leaves we understand the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Hence David says elsewhere: “And its leaf shall not fall.”

By the sun placed in the middle we understand our Lord Jesus Christ, who is called the Sun of Justice. By the moon we understand the holy Church. Just as the moon waxes and wanes, so the holy Church grows in good virtues and diminishes by losing them.

By the twelve stars the twelve apostles are signified. Just as the moon and the stars receive their brightness from the sun, so the Church and the apostles receive light from Christ and the grace of the Holy Spirit.

By the tree we understand Mary, the mother of the Lord, concerning whom it is said: “A branch shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root.” Just as the sun was placed in the middle of the tree, so Christ was placed in the middle of the Virgin’s womb.

And just as the sun rises in the east, sets in the west, and circles the globe of the earth, so our Lord Jesus Christ wished to be born in the womb of a virgin. And because he is the Lord, he himself is the true Sun of Justice and the true light, as John says: “He is the true light that illumines every person coming into this world.”

Let us beseech him to deign to illumine our hearts and abolish the darkness of vices, so that, with him as our guide, we may be able to reach our heavenly homeland.

## HOMILY XC. ON SAINT BARTHOLOMEW

When blessed Bartholomew came to India, he entered a temple where there was a demon named Astaroth and began to remain there as though he were a pilgrim.

The people of that land said of this demon that he healed all the sick. Then many came from distant regions, and all sought him so that he might heal them. But by the power of Saint Bartholomew he remained mute.

The people went to that city where there was another demon and asked him whether he knew why Astaroth could not speak. He said to them:

“From the hour when the apostle Bartholomew entered there, your god has been so bound with fiery chains that he has been unable to speak or sigh.” [Col. 0490D]

They asked who this Bartholomew was. The demon Berith replied:

“He is a friend of almighty God, and for that reason he has come to this province to destroy all empty idols.”

They all replied and said to him, “Tell us a sign by which we may recognize him.”

The demon answered:

“He has black hair, his flesh is fair, his eyes are large, his nostrils are even and straight, his ears are covered by the hair of his head, and he has a long beard with a few gray hairs. His body is of even stature, neither very tall nor very short. He is dressed in a white cloak and has purple gems each year. For twenty-six years his garments have never grown old. By day he prays a hundred times, and by night just as often. His voice is like a trumpet. Angels of God walk with him and do not allow him to become tired or hungry. By night and by day he remains joyful in God; he foresees everything, speaks in every language, and understands.”

When the people returned, they found him preaching and recognized him. Then a certain man full of a demon came, crying out, and said:

“Apostle of God, Bartholomew, your prayers are burning me!”

The Apostle said, “Be silent, devil, and come out of him.” And immediately the demon came out.

Finally, the king ordered him to be beheaded. Then innumerable people from twelve cities came—people who had believed in God through him—and carried his body with hymns and every honor. They built for him a basilica of extraordinary size and placed his body in it.

On the thirtieth day after his burial, the king was seized by a demon. He came to the tomb of Saint Bartholomew, together with many priests filled with demons; they confessed the apostle of God, and thus they died.

Great fear came upon all the unbelievers, and everyone believed and was baptized by the priests whom Saint Bartholomew had ordained. Through a revelation of the apostle, while the whole people cried out, the entire clergy ordained the king as bishop.

The king Apollonius was ordained bishop, and he began to perform many signs in the name of the Lord and of Saint Bartholomew. He remained in the episcopate for twenty years and departed to the Lord through the intercession of Saint Bartholomew. May God receive us likewise, he who lives and reigns. 

## HOMILY XCI. ON SAINT LAWRENCE
Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. We ought to love greatly our Lord Jesus Christ, who calls us through the Holy Spirit and says that we should come to him and hear his teaching. For he will teach us how to fear and love the Lord; and he does not call us men or servants, but his children, because he cannot call us by a sweeter name than “children,” just as you have now heard at the beginning of this sermon, where the Holy Spirit says through the mouth of David: “O children, come and listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.” And the Holy Spirit rightly says that he will first teach us fear, just as he himself says elsewhere in the Psalm: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” [Col. 0491C]. Nor is any wisdom of value to a person who does not know how to fear and love God.

But because the devil deceives human beings in three ways, and by three arts makes them commit every sin, the Lord has commanded us to possess three virtues by which we may destroy the devil’s arts. You ought now to know what those three arts of the devil are by which he deceives people: thinking evil, speaking evil, and doing evil. No sin, whatever its nature, can be committed without these three arts. For in the case of sins that are not found in a person’s mind, no priest can absolve him unless he himself confesses them and names them.

Let us now hear of the three virtues that the Lord commanded us to possess against the devil’s three arts, as the apostle Paul indicates when he says: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity.” Every person ought to have faith and place his hope in God, because the person who does not place his hope in God is worse than one who worships idols. For we find it written: “To despair of God’s mercy is a greater sin than to sacrifice to idols.” But once he has faith and hope in God, he must possess charity, which is the greatest virtue of all, as the apostle Paul says: “But the greatest of these is charity”; and elsewhere the apostle John says: “God is charity,” and so forth.

Charity, however, is divided into two parts: love of God and love of one’s neighbor. These three virtues were possessed perfectly by that precious martyr, Saint Lawrence, whose feast we celebrate today.

We find in the reading that Saint Lawrence was the deacon of a certain bishop, a very holy man named Sixtus. Saint Sixtus loved him so greatly that he never celebrated Mass without Saint Lawrence. Lawrence guarded the treasures of the Church and was Sixtus’s chief attendant.

At that time Decius Caesar, who was a pagan and emperor at Rome, ordered his officials to seize Saint Sixtus and bring him before him. When Saint Sixtus had been brought before the emperor and refused to worship the idols as the emperor commanded him, the emperor ordered him to be thrown into prison at once, until the following day.

But Saint Lawrence, who followed his master, saw him being taken to prison and wanted to go with him. He said: “Where are you going without your son, Father? Where are you hastening, holy priest, without your deacon?” Sixtus replied: “I am not abandoning you, my son, nor leaving you behind; but it is God’s will that you endure greater sufferings for the faith of God. Now I command you: go and take the treasures of the Church that I entrusted to you, and give them to the poor, because in three days you will follow me.”

Saint Lawrence immediately thought that, if he spent and gave the treasures to the poor before that night had passed, his master would afterward permit him to accompany him to martyrdom. Therefore he quickly took the Church’s treasures, went out of the city, and climbed the mountain called the Caelian, to the house of a good Christian woman who had been a widow for thirty-two years. Her name was Cyriaca. There Saint Lawrence found many hidden Christians [Col. 0492B]. He washed all their feet, kissed them, and gave each of them some of the Church’s treasures.

That widow Cyriaca suffered from a serious illness of the head. She begged Saint Lawrence to deign to touch her head with his hand and pray to the Lord for her. Saint Lawrence did not allow himself to be asked at length [the text reads *rogare*, apparently corrupt], but, full of mercy, placed his hand upon her head, and God healed her through love of Saint Lawrence.

Afterward Saint Lawrence left that place and went to another, where he found many hidden Christians. He washed their feet and kissed them. There was also a certain blind man named Cercentius, whom Saint Lawrence restored to sight through the power of God. Before leaving, he gave all the Christians some of the Church’s treasures. He did nothing else except seek out the poor and distribute the Church’s treasures that he had carried with him.

In the morning he encountered Saint Sixtus, whom the emperor’s officials were leading to be beheaded. He said to Saint Sixtus: “Do not abandon me, holy Father, for I have already spent the treasures that you gave me.” Saint Sixtus could not answer him, because he was bound and the emperor’s officials were leading him to execution, together with two priests, Fidelissimus and Agapitus.

Then the emperor’s soldiers bound Saint Lawrence and led him to the emperor, saying that he possessed the treasures of his master, who had just been beheaded. For this reason they seized him and brought him before the emperor. The emperor ordered him to return the treasures that he had hidden. Saint Lawrence did not answer him. The emperor, angered by this, told his prefect Valerian to guard him until he had questioned him.

Valerian took him and handed him over for custody to one of his own estate managers, who guarded all those whom the emperor or Valerian, his prefect, ordered to be seized. That estate manager was called Hippolytus.

When Saint Lawrence was placed in Hippolytus’s custody, he found among the other prisoners a man named Lucillus, who was not a Christian. Lucillus had wept so much in prison that he had become blind. He begged Saint Lawrence to restore his sight through the power of God. Saint Lawrence promised him that, if he believed in God and were baptized, he would restore his sight to him at that very hour.

Lucillus said that he had always desired to be baptized. Saint Lawrence immediately instructed him, blessed the water, and baptized him in the name of the Holy Trinity. Afterward God restored his sight. Saint Lawrence did the same for all the blind people of the city.

Saint Hippolytus, who guarded him, saw Saint Lawrence performing such miracles and came to him, asking him to return the treasures for which he had been captured. Saint Lawrence answered him: “O Hippolytus, if you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, I will show you the treasures and promise you eternal life.”

Hippolytus replied: “If you do what you promise, I will truly believe in the Lord your God, Jesus Christ.” He was baptized by blessed Lawrence and was immediately illumined by the Holy Spirit, so that he saw holy souls rejoicing in heaven before God. At this sight he rejoiced and begged Saint Lawrence to baptize his entire household. Saint Lawrence baptized there in Hippolytus’s house twenty-nine men and women [Col. 0493A].

Then Hippolytus told blessed Lawrence that the emperor wanted to see him. Lawrence replied: “Let us go, for glory is being prepared for you and me.” When they were both before the prefect Valerian, Valerian told blessed Lawrence to hand over the treasures before he took him to the emperor.

Saint Lawrence asked him to grant him two or three days’ delay, after which he would hand over the treasures. Valerian granted him three days, on condition that he remain constantly in Hippolytus’s custody; for he did not know that Hippolytus was a Christian.

Hippolytus then took Saint Lawrence to his own house, and Valerian informed the emperor that Saint Lawrence had promised to return the treasures on the third day. During those three days Saint Lawrence did nothing except seek out the poor, the blind, the lame, and the lepers, and gather them together in Hippolytus’s house.

On the third day he went to the emperor’s palace with all the poor and with Hippolytus. He made the poor remain outside, while he himself entered the palace to the emperor and Valerian. When the emperor saw him, he asked where the treasures were that he had said he would return that day.

Blessed Lawrence told him to go outside, and he sent all the poor whom he had gathered before the palace. Then he said to the emperor: “These are the treasures of the Church of God, and from such people as you see, the glory of God has been perfected, just as he himself says in the Gospel: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.’”

The emperor told Valerian that Saint Lawrence had done this as a mockery, and ordered him to bring the most savage instruments of torture with which Lawrence could be tormented. And so it was done.

Then the emperor said to Lawrence: “Proud Lawrence, now worship our gods, whom we have worshiped. If you do not, I shall spend all these tortures upon you this very night, and you shall die an evil death.” Lawrence replied that he would neither sacrifice nor worship anyone except the living and true God, whom he had always worshiped.

The emperor, now still more enraged, ordered him to be stripped and severely flogged with small whips whose ends had knobs. After he had been beaten, the emperor ordered him to be placed upon an instrument of torture called a *catasta*, where all his limbs were stretched out so that he could not move.

But by God’s will a worthy soldier named Romanus, one of the emperor’s household, saw an angel in the form of a most beautiful young man standing beside Saint Lawrence. The angel healed all his wounds and wiped him with a cloth. Romanus said: “I see a most beautiful young man before you. Make haste to baptize me.” He brought a basin of water and set it before Saint Lawrence’s feet. After he had been baptized, he cried out before everyone: “I am a Christian.”

When the emperor heard this, he became extremely angry and ordered Romanus to be beheaded. Thus Romanus became a martyr [Col. 0493D].

After this the emperor ordered an iron bed in the shape of a grating to be brought, such as people use for roasting fish. He ordered blessed Lawrence to be stretched out upon it and coals to be placed beneath it. After Saint Lawrence had been roasted on one side, he said to the emperor: “This side is roasted; turn me over and eat.”

After he had said this, the angels received his soul and carried it into heaven. The emperor left his body upon the grating and went away utterly confounded. The Christians who were in the city came, lifted him from the grating, and buried him in a tomb.

We have heard how blessed Lawrence endured martyrdom for the love of Christ. But this benefits us nothing if we do not take from it an example of good living. Therefore the Apostle says: “If we are sharers in sufferings, we shall also be sharers in consolations.” Let us therefore pray to God that, through the intercession of Saint Lawrence, he may grant us to imitate this martyr in such a way that we may deserve to possess eternal life with him, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

## HOMILY XCII. ON SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST

Today, dearly beloved brothers, we celebrate the feast of Saint John the Evangelist—not the day on which he was born into the world, but the day on which he left the world.

He is the brother of blessed James, whose body rests in Spain. He is the son of Zebedee, who for God’s sake left his father at sea and followed Christ. The mother of Saint John the Evangelist was related to the blessed Virgin Mary. At the wedding feast the Lord made wine from water and sanctified the marriage; he called John away from the wedding, and John himself left his wife and followed him. For this reason Jesus loved him more than all the disciples: he drew him away from the love of a woman, and John remained chaste.

Afterward, on the night when he was betrayed, blessed John reclined upon the Lord’s breast and saw heavenly secrets, which he later wrote down and called the Apocalypse [Col. 0494B].

After he had ascended into heaven, blessed John preached at Ephesus. When King Domitian, an enemy of the truth, heard this, he went against John and had him brought to Rome in chains. Since he could not separate him from Christ, he placed him in a vessel full of boiling oil. But blessed John, signing himself with the sign of the cross, emerged unharmed and joyful.

When Domitian saw this, he had John’s hands bound behind his back and, with great humiliation, had him dragged into exile on the island of Patmos. But by God’s will Domitian was killed that same year, and Saint John returned from exile. While he was there, he raised the widow Drusiana from the dead.

When Aristodemus heard this, he was indignant and said to blessed John: “If you want me to believe in your God, I will give you poison to drink. If, after drinking it, you are not dead, I shall believe. But first I will give it to two robbers, so that when you see them dead you will be more afraid and abandon your unbelief.”

When they had died before him, blessed John took the cup containing the poison, armed himself with the sign of the cross, and drank everything that was in the cup. After drinking it, he remained unharmed. He raised the robbers who had died, and Aristodemus himself believed in Jesus Christ [Col. 0494C].

Later, when blessed John was ninety-eight years old, the Lord Jesus Christ came to him with his disciples and said: “It is time, dear friend, for you to sit at table with your brothers. You shall come to me on the Lord’s day.”

Then blessed John summoned the Christians who were there, both clergy and laity. He celebrated the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood and gave it to them, asking them to remain in the faith that they had professed. After doing this, he entered the church that he himself had built and taught everyone throughout the night to remain steadfast in the faith.

When dawn approached, he ordered a pit to be made beside the altar and entered it. Suddenly a light came from heaven, and the Lord descended with a multitude of angels. He took John alive and carried him into heaven. Thus he stands before God in prayer for us.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, if we want blessed John to pray for us, and if we want to share in his joy, we must prepare ourselves for his feast with complete humility and with the other virtues. We must also leave Zebedee in the boat—that is, the devil in this world—and walk after God, as blessed John did, so that, just as he did not taste death, we too may, through his holy prayer, possess eternal life. Amen.

## HOMILY XCIII. ON THE DISCOVERY OF THE HOLY CROSS

We ought to know how the holy cross was discovered.

In the time of Constantine there was a serpent that devoured many Romans and beasts. Constantine came and killed the serpent, but from the serpent’s poison he became a leper. His people began to seek physicians who could heal him.

At last a certain physician came and said that he could heal him. There was therefore great rejoicing among the Romans. The physician said to Constantine: “Find a large vessel, gather all the children, kill them, and bathe yourself in their blood; then you will be healed.”

And so it was done. All the children were gathered before the king’s palace. The king came out and saw the children with their mothers weeping. He said: “It is better that I perish than that so many people perish with their children.” And so it was done.

The women prayed to God to grant Constantine health, and the women’s prayer was heard.

One night blessed Peter and Paul came to Constantine and said to him while he slept: “O Constantine, seek out Saint Silvester, for he will cleanse you.”

When morning came, Constantine told his mother what Peter and Paul had said to him. When the queen heard this, she rejoiced, sought out Saint Silvester, and told him that her son wished to see him.

When Saint Silvester heard this, he took a staff and went to Constantine. Constantine said to him: “O holy Silvester, blessed by God, through whom God will display his power in me today, heal me.”

Silvester replied: “If you believe in the Son of the Virgin, you will receive health.” Constantine answered: “I love the love of God above all things.”

Then Saint Silvester ordered water to be brought and baptized him in it. Constantine was healed.

After this Constantine said to Saint Silvester: “What do you want me to give you?” Saint Silvester replied: “I ask nothing else except the bodies of the holy apostles.”

When Constantine heard this, he removed the bodies of the apostles from the well and immediately placed them in the finest location, with great joy and honor.

Afterward he summoned his soldiers and said that he wished to cross the sea and give Saint Peter everything he possessed on this side. And so it was done. He crossed the sea and founded Constantinople. Then the Saracens gathered and came to fight him.

When Constantine heard this, he became very afraid. But an angel of the Lord came to him by night and said: “Do not be afraid, because when you enter the battle, you will see the sign of the cross in heaven. You shall make it upon your spear; then enter the battle without fear, and you will have victory.”

And so it was done, and he killed many Saracens.

When this was accomplished, he sent his mother Helena to Jerusalem to seek the Lord’s cross. When she entered Jerusalem, she summoned all the Jews and demanded the cross. They said that they did not know where it was.

But she said: “By the God who made me, unless you return it, I shall kill you all.”

When they heard this, they asked for a delay, and she granted it until the following day. The Jews asked one another whether anyone knew where it was.

At last one named Judas said: “I heard my father say that his ancestor had told him where the Jews had placed it.”

Afterward they told the queen what Judas had said. The queen detained Judas and bound him until Judas himself prayed to God, and God revealed to him where the holy cross was.

They dug up the ground and found three crosses. They did not know which was the Lord’s cross. But when a dead man was placed upon the cross of the thieves, he did not move. When he was placed for the third time upon the Lord’s cross, he came back to life. Thus the holy cross was discovered [Col. 0495D].

After this they dug in the same place and found the nails with which they had pierced the Lord’s hands and feet. Helena gave one of them to Constantine, who placed it in his horse’s bridle. After this he was never defeated in battle.

Later she baptized Judas, giving him the name Quiracus, and appointed him bishop of Jerusalem. Through him the Lord deigned to perform many miracles.

## HOMILY XCIV. ON SAINTS PETER AND PAUL

Happily, throughout all the world’s regions, the most sacred feast of the apostles Peter and Paul shines forth joyfully. Christ consecrated them with his life-giving blood and appointed them princes of the Churches.

Dearly beloved brothers, we read that the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul is proclaimed throughout the four parts of the world—that is, from East to West and from North to South—because God appointed these apostles princes of the whole world and teachers of the Churches. One of them, Saint Paul, was beheaded today; the other, Saint Peter, was crucified [Col. 0496A].

“These are the two olive trees before the Lord,” and so forth. This means that the apostles who consecrated this day for themselves by their blood are flourishing before God and sweet-smelling like two beautiful olive trees. They are compared with olive trees because oil is made from olives, and oil signifies charity and mercy in the holy Church—virtues with which these men were filled.

Therefore Scripture says that these two become olive trees before God, as well as two splendid lights and two shining lampstands. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “You are the light of the world.” And Saint Augustine says: “God stripped the world of deep darkness; the light of apostolic teaching rose.”

These apostles loose and bind the bonds of our apostles. Scripture says that, just as a person sent to prison is bound, so the sinner is bound by the devil’s chains and led to hell.

The Lord gave these apostles the power to bind and to loose. If we show them our chains and confess our sins to priests, they then absolve us from our sins. Thus it is written: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained.”

But he gave the keys of paradise to Peter alone, because no one will enter paradise if he has scorned to keep the law that Peter taught.

Lest we become weary, let us leave this subject and speak of Saint Paul and Peter.

In their time there was a wicked man at Rome named Simon Magus. He had become a Christian through the apostles’ prayers, but afterward the devil entered his heart and made him consider how he might buy from the apostles the power by which he could perform miracles as they did.

When Saint Peter heard this, he replied that the power they possessed came from God; no human being could buy or sell it; and those who thought they could purchase it had become accursed and separated from God.

This curse first came upon Simon Magus and upon those who sell and buy the honor of the holy Church.

On another day Simon Magus rejected Christianity, worshiped an idol, and became an apostate—that is, one who had been turned back. This enemy of God possessed such power from the devil that through his incantations he did whatever he wished.

Indeed, the emperor loved him so much that he said Simon protected Rome from every evil, and he did nothing without his advice.

One day Simon Magus and Peter disputed before the emperor about many matters, and Simon was defeated in everything. When he saw that he could not overcome Peter, he became angry and told the emperor that Peter was opposing him. He said that he would no longer remain on earth but would ascend into heaven in full view of all the people.

When the emperor heard this, he promised Simon that, if he ascended, he would kill the apostles at that very hour.

Simon was pleased by this statement and told Peter that he would ascend into heaven the following day.

That night the Christian men and women who were in the city came to the holy man, begging him to leave the city secretly for the love of God and flee elsewhere. They did not want him to die so soon, although they knew that he was willing to die for God. They had no other shepherd or such counselor.

Saint Peter left the city secretly by himself, out of love for them, not out of fear. When he reached the gate, he encountered the Lord and said: “Lord, where are you going?”

“I am going to be crucified again.”

The Lord said this because the Jews had crucified him once before, but now he was coming to Rome to be crucified a second time with Peter. For whatever suffering Peter endured on the cross, Jesus Christ endured the same.

When Peter heard this, he understood that the Lord was not speaking about himself, but was saying it because Peter had left Rome, wishing to flee to a place where the Lord could not find him. Therefore Peter returned to the city and told the Christians how he had encountered Christ at the gate.

When the Christians heard this, they praised God for his miracles and no longer urged Peter to leave, because they understood that it was God’s will that he should be martyred [Col. 0497A].

The next day the emperor ordered Peter, Paul, and all the people of the city to come before him and see how Simon Magus would ascend into heaven and descend unharmed.

When they had gathered, Paul said to Peter: “Lord and master, who was chosen before me, whom God loves more and has appointed master of human beings, I fall prostrate and pray to God; but you, standing, when you see Simon flying, command the demons who hold him not to hold him any longer.”

Thus Saint Peter stood while Paul lay prostrate at his feet in prayer. Simon climbed a tall tower in full view of all the people, performed his incantations there, tied two wings to his legs and two to his arms, and began to fly.

Saint Peter knew that the higher Simon rose, the farther he would fall. Therefore he allowed him to ascend well into the air. When Simon was high above, Peter said to Paul: “Brother, lift your eyes and look.”

When Paul saw that Simon was able to do what he had promised, he was afraid and begged Peter to command the demons, through the power of God, to release him.

Peter then commanded them. The demons, compelled by the command, released Simon, and he fell to the ground and burst apart in the middle.

Then Saint Paul and all who saw it praised God, who had performed so great a miracle through love for blessed Peter.

When the emperor saw that Simon was dead, he was enraged and ordered Peter and Paul to be bound, Paul to be beheaded, and Peter to be crucified.

As Peter was being led to the cross, the entire people cried out that the whole city would perish if Peter died. But Peter urged them to be silent and not disturb his passion, because the Lord’s glory had been prepared for him.

When he reached the cross, he asked the executioners not to crucify him as the Jews had crucified the Lord, but to turn his feet upward and his head downward: “For it is not fitting that I, a sinner and a servant, should be crucified in the likeness of the one who made the whole world from nothing” [Col. 0497C].

They did as he requested.

Blessed Peter, stretched out upon the cross, prayed to God and said:

“Lord Jesus Christ, I now give you thanks, for you are the shepherd of all Christian souls. The sheep that you entrusted to me—that is, the souls—I commend to you and return to you, so that you may protect them from every evil, lest the devil harm them. May they have a share with me in your glory, in which you live and reign without end.”

All who stood near the cross and heard this prayer, which Peter offered for the living and the dead, answered: “Amen.”

After the prayer he gave up his spirit. Holy angels carried the soul of Saint Peter before God into heaven, singing: “Glory to God in the highest,” and so forth.

A certain disciple of Saint Peter, Marcellus, took the apostle’s body and washed it with an ointment such that it could never decay. Afterward he placed it in a tomb.

But the whole people of Rome took counsel together to kill Nero, because he had killed these two apostles, the friends of God.

When the emperor learned this, he left Rome out of fear and fled to the islands. There he died of hunger and cold, and was eaten by wolves and lions. His soul was carried to hell by the devils whom he had served.

You have heard, brothers, what sufferings the apostles endured for God. But their solemnity, which is celebrated today, benefits us little if we do not take from them an example of the Lord’s manner of living [F.: *Domino*, “for the Lord”].

Therefore Scripture says: “It profits nothing to attend the feasts of human beings if one is absent from the feasts of the angels.” That is, it does no good to celebrate a feast among human beings in this world if we cannot celebrate a feast in heaven with the angels who praise God day and night.

Therefore, since we are not such as to be able to praise God worthily, let us cleanse ourselves from vices and pray to God that, through his mercy and through the prayers of the apostles Peter and Paul, he may grant us to live in this world in such a way that, when our souls leave our bodies, they may come to that glory, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

## HOMILY XCV. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“The kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared,” and so forth.

The kindness of our Lord appeared when he came to redeem the world by assuming humanity. This happened like dew or rain: just as wool receives dew or rain and gives it forth without suffering any corruption, so the virgin Mary received Christ within herself and brought him forth while preserving the integrity of her virginity.

Hence it is said: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece and like a drop that falls upon the earth.” And elsewhere: “Let the earth be opened”—that is, the Virgin Mary—“and let it bring forth the Savior”—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ.

She was a virgin before giving birth, in giving birth, and after giving birth, like good earth that produces an ear of grain.

There are four parts in an ear of grain: the chaff, the stalk, the awn, and the grain. These are aptly represented in Christ. The chaff in Christ was his capacity for suffering, that is, his mortality. The stalk is the integrity of his human flesh. The awn is his most holy soul. The grain signifies the purity of his divinity. Just as the outer human being is made from grain, so through divinity Christ, the spiritual human being, is nourished.

Today, dearly beloved brothers, the Nativity of this Christ is celebrated, so that through its mystery and through worthy participation in him we may be freed from the devil’s power.

It should be noted that three Masses are celebrated today: the first at night, the second at dawn, and the third in full daylight. These three Masses are celebrated because of the three periods that existed in this world: the first period before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace.

The first Mass is sung for those who lived in the first period, in the dark night, in complete darkness of the world and without knowledge of God. The second is sung at dawn for those who lived in the second period, who through the Law that was given and through the prophets possessed knowledge of God, but not full knowledge. The third is sung in full daylight for those who live in the new age, to whom full knowledge of God has been granted [Col. 0498C].

Alternatively, the three Masses are celebrated because of the three virtues: hope, faith, and charity.

May he who reigns with the Father and the Son throughout all ages of ages deign to grant us his grace, so that we may celebrate this feast worthily. Amen.

## HOMILY XCVI. ON THE CHAINS OF SAINT PETER

It should be noted, dearly beloved brothers, why the feast of Saint Peter of the Chains is celebrated, namely, on the Kalends of August. This is what some people assert.

A Roman commander named Quirinus had a daughter with a goiter named Balbina. That commander had blessed Pope Alexander confined in prison because of his confession of the Christian faith.

The girl frequently went to the prison where blessed Alexander was held in chains. Every day she kissed the chains in which he was bound, hoping to recover her health.

Blessed Alexander said to her: “My daughter, do not kiss these chains. Instead, seek the chains with which blessed Peter was bound by Herod in Jerusalem, and kiss them; then you will receive your health.”

When the girl heard this, she told her father what she had heard from the aforementioned pope. When the girl’s father heard it, he sent messengers to Jerusalem to search out the prison where the apostle had been bound and to bring the chains back with them.

And so it was done. When the girl mentioned above kissed the chains that had been brought back, she immediately recovered her health.

Thus blessed Alexander, leaving the prison, established the celebration of this feast on the Kalends of August in honor of Saint Peter. In Peter’s name he built a church called Avincula, in which his chains were kissed by the devout people.

It is fitting that, through the generosity of the Lord, many gifts of healing are granted to our infirmities through blessed Peter, the apostle and prince of the apostles.

## HOMILY XCVII. ON THE GREATER LITANY

[Col. 0499A]

Fraternally beloved, it is fitting that you hear for what reason the litanies of supplication were instituted. In the time of the emperor Maurice, Saint Gregory was archdeacon at Rome, and Pelagius was pope. At that time there were such great rains that all the rivers overflowed their banks, so that the Tiber rose above the walls of Rome. The waters, having overflowed in this way, carried away whatever serpents and scorpions there were in the forests, and a great serpent, shaped like a beam, came down the Tiber, which all the Romans saw.

But after the rivers began to dry up, from the heat of the sun a great stench arose from the corpses of the serpents, so that whoever sensed the odor of the poison immediately died. There was a great mortality in the city of Rome, so that when evening came and the master went to sleep with his wife, children, and entire household, in the morning almost all were carried away for burial. Moreover, fiery arrows descended from heaven, struck people, and they died immediately. First Pelagius the pope was struck and died; afterward many thousands died such a death. Everywhere there was grief and mourning, because every day and hour the Romans did nothing but bury the dead.

They chose Gregory to be pope and sent him to Constantinople so that he might obtain the emperor’s assent. Meanwhile, while they were awaiting the emperor’s command and the mortality in the city was great, he summoned all the Roman people and told them to do penance for their evil deeds and to invoke God’s mercy. He established seven litanies, so that all might go together to Saint Peter.

The first litany was for all the clergy; the second, for abbots and monks; the third, for nuns; the fourth, for widows; the fifth, for married people; the sixth, for all children; the seventh, for women. And so, according to Gregory’s command, they came to [read: Saint] Peter, and all, crying out, said: “Kyrie eleison, Saint Peter, pray,” and so forth. Suddenly seventy fell dead in the church. Then the mortality ceased, and on that day they fasted on bread and water. He commanded the whole Church to observe this day, saying: “Whoever celebrates this day will not die a sudden death in that year.”

After a long time there was a great mortality in the city of Vienne. The bishop of the city was a holy and good man named Mamercus.
