While he was making a baptistery on the vigil of Easter, fire suddenly descended from heaven and burned the church and half the city. On one side there was a mortality among human beings; on the other, a fire that burned all the villages and fortresses. Lions and wolves also entered the streets and devoured people.

Then Saint Mamercus instituted three days of rogations, so that all the people might ask God for help and mercy, and that he might protect them from sudden death. Let us also pray to all the saints that they may intercede for us with God, so that he may deign to grant us remission of our sins and guard our bodies and souls, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XCVIII. TO THE PEOPLE.

A human being, born of a woman, lives for a short time; and while he lives, he endures many miseries, loving the body more than the soul. But the soul cannot die. When it leaves the body, the body quickly dies; and before it leaves the body, it endures great terror, because it sees Saint Michael before it, waiting for it, and because of the wretched hosts it fears to depart.

Woe to those souls whom the devil receives and binds beneath a noose, because they cannot escape from his snare, not even through almsgiving and the prayers of the faithful.

We read about Saint Macarius that one day, while he was walking, he came to a deserted place in a Jewish cemetery and found the head of a dead Jew. After he touched it with his staff, he said, “Why do you trouble me?” Saint Macarius replied: “Tell me, where are the souls of the Jews?” The head answered:

“There is a pit of marvelous depth, as great as the distance from earth to heaven. In the pit there is water colder than all cold, and fire hotter than every fire, and an intolerable stench, hunger and thirst, serpents; and amid these torments we and many souls of Christians stand and are tortured.”

Saint Macarius said: “Tell me whether you have any rest.” The head replied: “Whenever you or another such good person says Mass for the dead, for as long as the Mass lasts, for that long we are in rest.”

After this Macarius departed weeping, praying for the souls. And, dearly beloved, let us pray to our Lord Jesus Christ for the souls of all the faithful departed, with Masses and psalms, prayers, fasts, and almsgiving, so that through his mercy he may forgive them all their sins and grant them eternal life. And while we live, let us strive to do such things and thus obey his command, so that after this life we may deserve to enter the gates of paradise—a gift that Jesus Christ may deign to grant us.

## HOMILY XCIX. ON ASH WEDNESDAY.

Today, dearly beloved brothers, we enter into battle against the devil, and throughout the whole of Lent we must conquer him. For this reason today we place ashes upon our heads.

In ancient times, when soldiers had to go to war, they fed their horses light foods for seven days, so that they might run more swiftly. At the end of the seven days they placed ashes upon their heads, so that almighty God might give them victory. And we, dearly beloved brothers, should feed our bodies light foods during these days, so that we may be swift against the ancient enemy and so that God may give us victory over our adversary.

This is also understood in another figure: we must remember that we were made from dust and shall return to dust, just as God said to the first human being: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” Everything that is transitory for us ought to become worthless in our eyes, because the world and its desire will pass away. The apostle James teaches us this, saying: “Brothers, do not love the world, because whoever loves it does not have charity in him.”

There is another reason why we carry ashes today. The Father came from heaven to the prophet Jonah and said to him: “Go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it that, unless it abandons the idols it worships, it will be submerged at the end of forty days.”

Jonah answered: “My Lord, I do not know the city.” And Jonah fled from the presence of the Lord. Coming to the sea, he boarded a ship with sailors who intended to cross to another province. While they were sailing, a great storm arose at sea, and the ship began to founder. The sailors cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah. They threw him into the sea, and a sea monster swallowed him and carried him in its belly for three days and three nights, until it came to Nineveh and vomited him out there.

When he emerged from the fish’s mouth, he did not know where he was, and he had lost all his hair because of the fish’s heat. He asked the people what land it was, and they said that it was Nineveh. When Jonah saw God’s will, he entered the city and preached, saying: “At the end of forty days Nineveh will be overthrown.”

After the king heard Jonah’s words, he was struck with fear, rose from his throne, cast off his royal garment, clothed himself in sackcloth, covered himself with ashes, and ordered a fast throughout the entire city, so that neither people nor animals might taste food for three days. God saw that they had turned from their evil way and had mercy on his people.

And we, brothers, who have been deeply sunk in the abyss because of our sins, sprinkle ourselves with ashes today, so that God may see our humility, forgive our sins, and have mercy on us, just as he had mercy on Nineveh.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, today strive to vomit out your sins, and do not return to your vomit like a dog which, when it is full, vomits up carrion flesh and then eats it again. Let us fight with the devil during these forty days, so that on the day of the resurrection we may deserve to have eternal life with the Lord.

## HOMILY C

Sunday is a chosen day, on which the angels rejoice. We must ask who first requested that souls should have rest in hell; and the answer is that the apostle Paul and the archangel Michael asked the Lord when they came out of hell, because the Lord wished Paul to see the punishments of hell.

He saw wooden and fiery gates, and sinners tortured upon those trees: some hung by their feet, some by their hands, some by their hair, some by their necks, some by their tongues, and some by their arms. Again he saw a furnace of fire burning with seven flames, and many were punished in it. Seven plagues were around the furnace: first, snow; second, ice; third, fire; fourth, blood; fifth, serpents; sixth, lightning; seventh, stench.

Into that furnace were placed the souls of sinners who had not done penance in this world. There they are tortured, and each receives according to his works. Some weep, some howl, some groan, some burn and desire to have rest but do not find it, because souls will never die.

We must fear that place where there is everlasting pain, where there is groaning, where there is sorrow without joy, where tears abound because of the torture of souls, and where a fiery wheel turns a thousand times. On that day, at each turn, a thousand souls are burned by the angel of Tartarus.

Afterward he saw a horrible river in which many demonic beasts were like fish in the midst of the sea; they devour the souls of sinners. Above that river there is a bridge by which righteous souls cross without hesitation, while sinful souls cross according to their merit.

There Paul saw many souls of sinners submerged: some up to the knees, others up to the navel, others up to the lips, and others up to the eyebrows. They are tortured there every day without end.

Paul wept and, sighing, asked who those were who were submerged to the knees. The angel said: “These are those who slander others in their speech.” Those submerged to the navel, he said, “are fornicators and adulterers who have not returned to penance.” Those submerged to the lips “are those who enter the church but do not hear the word of the Lord.” Those submerged to the eyebrows “are those who rejoice in the misfortune of their neighbor.”

Weeping, Paul said: “Woe to those for whom such punishments are prepared!”

He saw another dark place filled with men and women eating their own tongues. The angel said to him: “These are moneylenders who receive interest and are not merciful; therefore they are in this punishment.”

He saw another place in which there were black girls wearing black garments, clothed in rags, sulfur, and fire, with dragons, serpents, and vipers around their necks. Four angels rebuked them; they had fiery horns and went around them saying: “Acknowledge that you have done evil.”

Paul asked who they were, and the angel said: “These are those who did not preserve chastity until marriage, those who defiled themselves with their relatives, and those who killed their infants, giving them as food to beasts.”

After this he saw men and women upon camels, with many fruits before them, but they could not take any of them. The angel said to Paul: “These are those who break their fast before the appointed time.”

In another place he saw an old man among four devils, weeping. Paul asked who he was, and the angel said: “He is the negligent man who does not keep God’s law. He was avaricious, deceitful, and proud; therefore he will endure countless punishments until the day of judgment.”

Paul wept, and the angel said to him: “Paul, why do you weep over the human race? You will see still greater punishments.” He showed him a sealed pit with seven doors and said to him: “Stand farther away, so that you may endure the stench.” He opened the mouth of the pit, and a great stench arose, surpassing all the punishments.

The angel said to him: “Those who are cast into this pit will never be converted in the sight of God.” Paul said to him: “Who are those who are cast into it?” He replied: “Those who do not believe that Christ, the Son of God, came in the flesh, and those who are not baptized and do not receive communion in the body of Christ.”

He saw in another place men and women whom worms and serpents were eating. Soul lay upon soul, like sheep in a sheepfold. The depth of that place was as great as the height of the heavens above the earth. He heard the groaning of those who sighed like a great thunderclap.

After this he saw, between heaven and earth, the soul of a sinner howling among seven devils. They led it out of the body on that day, and the angels cried out against it, saying: “Woe to you, wretched soul! What have you done on earth? You despised God’s commandments and did no good works; therefore you will be placed in the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

After this, in a single moment, the angels led a soul from the body to heaven. It heard the voice of thousands of angels rejoicing over it and saying: “O most happy and blessed soul, rejoice today, because you have done God’s will!”

They lifted it before God, because he had chosen its good works. Afterward Saint Michael placed it in paradise, where the saints were. They cried out with great joy to the righteous soul, and such a cry arose that it seemed heaven and earth were moved.

The sinners who were in the punishments cried out, saying: “Have mercy on us, Michael, and you, dearest Paul, beloved of God, intercede for us with God.”

The angel said: “Now weep, and we shall weep with you, and the angels with us, that perhaps God may have mercy and grant some relief.”

When those who were in the punishments heard this, they cried out in a loud voice, together with the archangel Michael, Paul, and thousands upon thousands of angels. The sound of their voices was heard in the fourth heaven, saying: “Have mercy, Christ, Son of Man!”

Paul saw heaven being moved and the Son of God descending from heaven, wearing a diadem upon his head. Again those who were in hell cried out with one voice, saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of the Most High!”

The voice of the Son was heard from above, saying to them:

“I was crucified for you, pierced with a lance, fastened with nails, given gall and vinegar to drink, and died for you, so that you might live. But you were liars, avaricious, envious, proud, and evildoers. You did no good and accepted no penance; you were unrighteous throughout your entire life.”

After this Michael, Paul, and thousands upon thousands of angels prostrated themselves, praying to the Son of God that all who were in hell might have rest.

The Lord said: “Because of Michael and Paul and my angels, and especially because of my resurrection, I grant you rest from the ninth hour of Saturday until the first hour of Monday.”

The gatekeeper of hell, called Cerberus, raised his head above all those who were in hell and was greatly saddened. Then all those who were in the punishments rejoiced and cried out with one voice: “We bless you, Son of David, who have granted us mercy! For the remedy of one day and night benefits us more than the whole span of our life that we spent on earth.”

The angel said: “Whoever observes Sunday will have a share with the angels of God.”

Paul asked the angel how many punishments there were in hell. The angel said: “There are one hundred and forty-four thousand punishments. Even if there were one hundred eloquent men from the beginning of the world, and each had four iron tongues, they could not number the other punishments of hell.”

But we, dearly beloved brothers, hearing of such great torments in hell, let us turn to our Lord, so that with his angels we may be able to reign.

## HOMILY CI. ON THE REVELATION OF SAINT MICHAEL.

Since God wished angels to be honored on earth by human beings, he first displayed this occasion, as we read.

There is a certain city in Apulia called Sipontus. In it there was a certain rich man named Garganus, who had many herds of cattle and flocks of sheep on a nearby mountain called Garganus.

There was an exceedingly proud bull. When the other oxen returned home, it alone remained wandering on the mountain. One day the Lord was angry because, while the others were returning, it did not return home. Garganus seized a bow and arrows, wishing to kill it; but by God’s will the sharp arrow turned back and wounded the man by whom it had been shot.

When Garganus saw this, he was very afraid and wished to approach more closely. He went to his bishop and told him everything that had happened. Then the prudent bishop instituted a three-day fast for the people, and they prayed that the Lord might show them what had happened and what it signified that Garganus had been wounded by his own weapon.

On the third night the archangel Michael appeared to the bishop and said to him: “Know that this has happened by God’s will. I am Michael, prince of the heavenly host, and I have consecrated to myself the place beside which the bull was standing, so that Christians may invoke help there and experience it.

“Therefore go, you and all the people, to the cave beside which the bull was standing. Enter it, and you will see an altar, and upon the altar a red pallium. There offer your prayers, remember me, and I will help you.”

When the bishop heard this, he rejoiced greatly. In the morning he ascended Mount Garganus with the people and entered the cave, just as the angel had said.

This was the first reason that the angels’ memory was established on earth. From that time until the present there have been churches and festivals in their honor, to the praise of God, who lives, and so forth.

## HOMILY CII. FOR ANY DAY.

The gracious and merciful Lord urges us through the prophet to contrition of heart and penance, saying: “Turn back to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning, because I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live.”

And again: “Do not delay turning to the Lord; do not put it off from day to day, because you do not know what the coming day will bring. Why do you delay turning to the Lord? Surely, to the danger of your soul, because death does not delay. If it finds you delaying, it will lead you to torments, because you, a sinner, put off turning and do not fear death, lest it suddenly snatch away your day of conversion.”

Do people not die suddenly? If it is good to abandon sins and turn to God, do it quickly. God has promised forgiveness of sins; he has not promised that you will live. Therefore let each person turn to God quickly, and let the wicked immediately abandon his way. When the final day comes, delay will perish and condemnation will remain. If you do not wish to perish, return to God and you will live.

Do not despair of forgiveness of sins, nor think about a long life. Turn, therefore, to penance. “Tomorrow,” you say, “I will turn.” Why not today? You say: “What harm is there if I say it tomorrow?” What harm is there if you say it today? Perhaps you will say: “My life will be long.” I reply: If life is long, let it be good; if it is short, let it too be good. You do not want a long and bad meal, yet you want a long and bad life. You buy an estate and desire a good one. You wish to marry and seek a good wife. You want your children to be born good. You buy excellent shoes and do not want bad ones, yet you want a bad life!

What benefit is your life to you, when you alone wish it to be bad, so that among all your good things you may be bad? Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day.

These are God’s words, not mine. You did not hear them from me; I hear them with you from the Lord. Perhaps you reply: “Tomorrow I will turn.” O raven’s voice! Who gave you this security? He promised that he would grant pardon; he did not promise you tomorrow for delay.

The raven did not return to the ark; the dove returned. If you wish to do penance then, when you cannot, your sins will have abandoned you, but you will not have abandoned them. He is sufficiently alien from faith who waits for a time to do penance.

We must fear that, while he hopes for mercy, he may fall into judgment. Whoever neglects the time given to him pours out prayers to God in vain. Let each person hasten to God while he can, because while he can, prayer will have power; when he wishes to delay, he will no longer be able.

Watch, Christian, under God’s mercy; fight with the devil, because you have Christ’s weapons with you. The God who commands you to fight desires to give you paradise if you fight well. There are your riches; there you will see Christ and the angels, and righteous people shining like the sun. There there is no night, hunger, thirst, or any pain.

What do you want, Christian man, when you do not amend yourself? Do you not know how many and what kinds of punishments are prepared in hell? There are weeping and gnashing of teeth; there are flame, lice, and frogs, and worms that do not die. The fire that is there is not extinguished. There are darkness and evils; there is no light and no consolation. There is a stench that no one can endure.

Consider more carefully the tombs of the proud dead and recognize that nothing remains in them except weeping, stench, and worms’ excrement. O man, look intently upon the tombs and say: “Woe to me, a wretched sinner!”

While this man lived in the world, he followed lust and fornication and did no penance. Of that wretched man nothing remains except bitter stench, and he is tortured with the wicked. “Woe to the wretched sinner! I fear that the same may happen to me.”

Then the dead man cried out from the tomb: “Look and acknowledge my dust, and abandon your evil desire, lest you be tortured with me in hell. What you are, I was; what I am, you will be.”

O man, abandon perjury, lust, murder, theft, avarice, and the other sins, which it would take too long to enumerate, so that you may not be tortured in hell but may have glory with God the Father, and so forth.

## HOMILY CIII. FOR ANY DAY.

Dearly beloved brothers, it is time to pass from evil to good, from darkness to light, from this utterly faithless world to everlasting joys, so that that day may not overtake us on which our Lord Jesus Christ will come to lay the inhabited world desolate and consign sinners to eternal torments—those who did not wish to do penance for the sins they committed.

There is a great crime in lying, as Solomon says: “The mouth that lies kills the soul.” The anger of man does not accomplish God’s justice, nor does greed. Hence the Apostle says: “The desire for possessions is the root of all evils.” And there is pride, through which that apostate angel fell, who, as we read in the prophecy, despised the beginning of God’s ways. Lucifer, who rose in the morning, fell.

Pride must be avoided, for it was powerful enough to deceive angels; how much more will it be able to deceive human beings! Envy also must be feared by us, through which the devil deceived the first human being, as it is written: “Through envy Christ was crucified.” Therefore whoever envies his neighbor crucifies Christ.

See that you always await the Judge’s coming in fear and vigilance, lest he find us unprepared, because the Apostle says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.” Woe to those whom he finds sleeping in sins!

Then, as we read in the Gospel, all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate the sheep, as a shepherd separates his sheep from the goats. He will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left.

Then the King will say to those at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth. There there will be no pain or sorrow. No voice will be heard there except charity, peace, and everlasting joy with all God’s elect; no good thing will be lacking.

Then the righteous will answer, saying: “Lord, why have you prepared such great glory and such great good things for us?” He will answer: “Because of mercy, faith, devotion, truth,” and so forth. “Lord, when did you see these good things in us?” The Lord will answer: “Amen, I say to you, whatever you did for one of the least of my brothers, you did for me; and whatever you did in secret, I will repay openly to you.”

Then the King will say to those at his left hand: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” There there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth and tears of the eyes; there death is desired but not granted; there worms do not die and the fire is not extinguished; there is no joy but sorrow, no rest but punishment, and no sound but groaning.

Then they too will answer, saying: “Lord, why have you prepared such great punishments for us?” The Lord will say: “Because of your iniquity and wickedness.”

Therefore, brothers, I ask you: those who are engaged in good works should persevere in every good work; those who are evil should correct themselves quickly, before sudden death finds them. While we have time, let us do good to everyone and cease doing evil, so that we may be able to attain eternal life.

## HOMILY CIV. FOR ANY DAY.

“Mercy and truth have met one another,” and so forth.

There was a certain head of a household, a powerful King, who had four daughters. One was called Mercy, another Truth, the third Justice, and the fourth Peace. Concerning them it was said: “Mercy and Truth,” and so forth.

He also had a very wise son, whom no one could equal in all wisdom. He also had a certain servant, whom he had exalted and enriched with great honor, since he had made him in his own image and likeness, without any preceding merit.

Now the Lord, as is the custom of such wise lords, wisely wished to know and test the servant’s character and whether he was faithful toward him. He gave him a light command, saying: “If you keep this command, you will be honored with greater honor; if you do not, you will die the worst of deaths.”

The servant, having received his lord’s command, immediately transgressed it. What more need be said? Why should I delay you with words instead of tears? Afterward, however, the transgression did not occur [as printed; the sense is problematic], but the proud, harsh, abusive, and puffed-up servant sought the cause of the transgression and turned all the blame back upon his lord. For when he said, “The woman whom you gave me as a companion—she deceived me,” he placed all the blame upon the Creator.

The lord was offended not so much by the transgression of the command as by the insult inflicted upon him. He summoned four exceedingly savage torturers, commanding one to imprison him, another to behead him alive, a third to cut his throat, and a fourth to devour him with cruel punishment.

Later, when the opportunity arises, I shall explain these four torturers by their proper names. These torturers, intent upon their cruelty, seized the wretched man and began to afflict him with every punishment.

When one of the king’s daughters, namely Mercy, heard of the servant’s punishments, she ran swiftly to the prison. Looking in and seeing the servant delivered over to the torturers and afflicted with punishments, she could not fail to have pity, because it is proper to mercy to show mercy.

She tore her garments, clapped her hands, loosened her hair over her neck, and, howling and crying out, ran back to her father. Kneeling before his feet, she began to say in a simple and mournful voice:

“Alas, dearest Father! Am I not your daughter Mercy, and are you not called merciful? If you are merciful, have mercy on your servant; and if you do not have mercy on your servant, you will not be merciful. If you are not merciful, you will not have me, Mercy.”

While she was arguing in this way before her father, her sister Truth arrived and asked her father why Mercy was weeping. Her father said to her: “Your sister Mercy wishes me to have pity on that proud transgressor upon whom I have imposed a punishment.”

When Truth heard this, she became exceedingly angry and, glaring at her father with harsh eyes, said:

“Am I not your daughter Truth? Are you not said to be truthful? Is it not true that you imposed a punishment upon him and promised torments through death? If you are truthful, you will pursue what is true; if you do not pursue what is true, you will not be truthful; if you are not truthful, you will not have me, Truth.”

Behold, Mercy and Truth have met one another.

The third sister, Justice, had heard these disputes, contentions, quarrels, and arguments. Summoned by their cries, she began to ask Truth about the matter. Truth, who could say nothing except what was true, said:

“Our sister Mercy, if she ought to be called a sister, since she does not agree with us, wishes our father to have mercy on that proud transgressor.”

Then Justice, turning with an inflated face and an unexpected grief in her heart, said to her father:

“Am I not your daughter Justice? Are you not called just? If you are just, you will exercise justice upon the transgressor; if you do not exercise justice, you will not be just; if you are not just, you will not have me, Justice, as your daughter.”

Behold, Truth and Justice are on either side, while Mercy alone remains wet with tears [printed: “madentes,” apparently corrupt].

The last of the heavenly beings, Astraea, left the earth—namely, Peace fled to a distant region. For where there is dispute and contention, there is no peace; and the greater the contention, the greater the absence of peace.

With peace lost and the three daughters placed in serious disagreement, he found it extremely difficult to decide what he should do and to which side he should more safely yield. If he yielded to Mercy, he would offend Truth and Justice; if he yielded to Truth and Justice, he would not have Mercy as a daughter. Yet it was necessary for him to be merciful, just, peaceful, and truthful.

Thus counsel was needed. The father therefore summoned his very wise son and consulted him about the matter. The son said to him:

“Commit this matter to me to pursue, Father, and I will take vengeance upon the transgressor for you and restore your four daughters to you, peace having been brought back.”

His father said to him: “Great are the things you promise, if deeds follow words. If you make your deeds match your words, I will do what you advise.”

Having received the royal command, the son took his sister Mercy with him. Leaping over mountains and crossing hills, he came to the prison. Looking through the windows and gazing through the bars, he saw the servant imprisoned, deprived of the present life and devoured; from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no soundness in him.

He saw him with his throat cut, because through him death entered the world. He saw him devoured, because once a human being dies, he is given as food to worms.

And since the opportunity has now arisen, hear the names of the four torturers.

The first, who imprisoned him, is the prison of exile from the present life, concerning which it is said: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged.”

The second, who beheaded him, is the misery of the world, which afflicts us all with punishments and miseries.

The third, who cut his throat, is death, which strangles and kills us all.

The fourth, who devoured him, is the worm, because, as I said, once a human being dies, worms take him up to consume him.

These four torturers—the prison of this exile, the misery of the world, death, and the worm—exact the punishments of the first transgressor from the first human being to the last, throughout the whole succession of generations.

The prison holds us, that is, the misery of the world, which brings every evil upon us. Death cuts our throats; the worm gnaws us.

When the son saw his servant delivered over to these four torturers, he could not fail to have pity, because he had Mercy as his companion. Leaping into the prison of death, he conquered death; having bound the strong man, he seized his goods and distributed the spoils. With abundant booty he ascended on high, led captivity captive, gave gifts to human beings, and restored the servant to his homeland with doubled honor, clothed in the robe of immortality.

When Mercy saw this, she had no cause for complaint, because she saw the servant return clothed in the robe of immortality and with doubled honor. Truth found no grounds for complaint, because the father had proved truthful. The servant had now paid all the punishments.

Justice likewise had nothing more to complain of, because justice had been carried out upon the transgressor. Thus the one who had perished was found again.

When Peace saw her sisters reconciled, she returned and made peace among them. Behold, Mercy and Truth have met one another; Justice and Peace have kissed.

Thus, through the mediator of human beings and angels, humanity was made peaceful and reconciled, and the hundredth sheep was brought back to God’s fold. May Jesus Christ lead us to that fold, to whom belong honor and glory forever. Amen.

## HOMILY CV. ON PALM SUNDAY.

When Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then he sent two disciples, etc. As the moment of his Passion began, Christ came to Jerusalem on account of Adam, who had gone down from Jerusalem to Jericho and had fallen among thieves. After wounds had been inflicted on him, he was left half-dead, stripped of his gratuitous gifts, and wounded in his natural faculties; he was healed by the Samaritan. Adam fell from Jerusalem to Jericho—that is, from immortality into mortality—when, through Eve’s suggestion and the forbidden fruit, he was stripped of his gratuitous gifts, that is, of the virtues of the soul, and wounded in his natural faculties, that is, in mind and reason. Adam sold us through the appetite, but he could not restore us. Therefore, on Adam’s account, the Samaritan—that is, Christ—came to Jerusalem, [Col. 0507B] wishing to restore us. The earthly thing that had fallen from his hand. This is the one who roasted himself in the furnace of his Passion: having become the living bread, he is the bread of angels.

Today Christ entered Jerusalem through the golden gates, and the children of the Hebrews came out to meet him. Some threw branches onto the road, others their garments. Likewise, the faithful today ought to come into Jerusalem through the golden gates, and ought to carry branches and cast their garments onto the road. Those enter through the golden gates who discipline their bodily senses with the sword of circumcision, lest, while grasping what is permitted, they seize what is forbidden. The eyes must be circumcised, lest they see vanity; the hands must be circumcised, lest the hands do anything by which God or one’s neighbor might be offended; and so with the other members. The flesh itself must be circumcised, since it wages war against the soul.

The faithful ought to carry branches, that is, good works, because through good works mercy goes before judgment. The works of mercy are to clothe the naked, welcome strangers, recall those who have gone astray, visit the sick, console the elderly, gather little children together, [Col. 0507C] and bury the dead, as is found in Tobit; as that saying of the Gospel testifies: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34), and so forth.

Beloved, you ought to cast your garments onto the road, that is, to mortify the flesh, because “the one who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.” You ought to take something away from your stomach and give it to the poor; thus your fasting will be properly ordered. If you do these things today, you are in Jerusalem; but if you persist in sin, you are in Jericho. Yet, that we may reach Jerusalem, let us entreat the Lord for Jerusalem, which is built from living stones. May he grant this to us who lives and reigns, God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY 106. ON THE THIRTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

## Luke 10; Matthew 15

At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see,” etc.

[Col. 0507D] Not the eyes of the scribes and Pharisees, who saw only the Lord’s body, but those blessed eyes that are able to recognize his mysteries, concerning which it is said: “And you have revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10). Blessed are the eyes of the little ones, to whom the Son deigns to reveal both himself and the Father.

“For I say to you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” Abraham rejoiced that he might see Christ’s day; he saw it and rejoiced. Isaiah also, Micah, and many other prophets saw the glory of the Lord, and for that reason they were called seers. Yet all these, looking from afar and greeting it, saw through a mirror and in a mystery. The Apostles, however, having the Lord present with them, dining with him, and learning by asking him whatever they wished to know, had no need to be taught through angels or through various kinds of visions. Those whom Luke calls “many prophets and kings,” Matthew more clearly calls them “prophets [Col. 0508A] and righteous men.” They themselves are great kings, because they knew how not to yield and succumb to the impulses of their temptations, but to rule over them and prevail.

And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him, and said: “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” The lawyer who questioned the Lord, testing him about eternal life, took, I think, the opportunity for his test from the Lord’s own words, where he says: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). But by this very testing of his he shows how true was that confession of the Lord when he speaks to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.”

But he said to him: “What is written in the law? How do you read it?” He answered: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” In answering the lawyer, the Savior shows us the perfect path of heavenly life. To him, who first set before him the law’s teaching about love of God and neighbor, [Col. 0508B] he says:

“You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.” Then, after introducing the parable, when he answered that the one who showed mercy to the wounded man had been his neighbor, he added: “Go, and do likewise”—that is, remember to love and support your neighbor who needs such devoted mercy. He makes it perfectly clear that love alone is mercy, and that it must not be displayed merely in words, but proved by the execution of works, if it is to lead to everlasting life.

But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: “And who is my neighbor?” What madness of empty glory! The lawyer, seeking the favor of the crowd so that he might boast of having answered wisely, first admits that he does not know the commandment of the law—truly, according to the Savior’s judgment, wise and prudent in the law. Yet because he does not wish to humble himself with Christ’s little ones, but desires to justify himself, he refuses to receive the blessed eyes of doves washed with the milk of innocence, with which he could see Christ’s mysteries. Therefore the Lord tempered his answer in such a way [Col. 0508C] as to teach that everyone who shows mercy is a neighbor to anyone; and yet this same parable specifically designated the Son of God himself, who deigned to become our neighbor through his humanity. Nor should we interpret “neighbor,” whom we are commanded to love as ourselves, solely as referring to Christ, in such a way that we attempt, under the rules of allegory, to diminish or remove the moral institutions of mutual brotherhood.

Then Jesus, looking up, said: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” This man is understood to be Adam in the human race. Jerusalem, that heavenly city of peace, signifies the blessedness from which he fell into this mortal and wretched life. It is well represented by Jericho, which is interpreted as “moon,” since it is always uncertain through various struggles and errors of decline.

“And he fell among thieves.” Understand the devil and his angels as the thieves. Because he was going down toward them, he fell among them; [Col. 0508D] for unless he had first become swollen with pride inwardly, he would not have fallen so easily when tempted outwardly. For that saying is very true: “Before destruction the heart of a man is exalted” (Prov. 16).

“Who also stripped him.” They deprived him, that is, of the garment of immortal glory and innocence. This is the first robe with which, according to another parable, the prodigal son is clothed when he returns through repentance; and when the first-formed humans had lost it, they realized that they were naked and clothed themselves in tunics of mortal nature made of skins.

“And after inflicting wounds, they departed, leaving him half-dead.” The wounds are sins. By violating the integrity of human nature, they implanted, so to speak, a kind of seed of increasing death in its weary inward parts. They departed, not by ceasing their ambushes in any way, but by concealing the deceptions of those same ambushes. They left him half-dead because they were able to strip him of the blessedness of immortal life, but not to abolish the faculty of reason. Insofar as a human being can understand and know God, [Col. 0509A] he is alive; but insofar as he wastes away through sins, fails through misery, and is disfigured by a deadly wound, he is dead.

It happened that a certain priest was going down the same road, and, seeing him, passed by. Likewise a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by. The priest and the Levite who passed by after seeing the wounded man signify the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament, where, through the decrees of the law, the wounds of the sick world could be displayed but not healed, because, as the Apostle says (Heb. 10), it was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of calves, lambs, and goats.

“But a certain Samaritan, while traveling, came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with compassion.” The Samaritan, whose name means “guardian,” signifies the Lord. The Prophet rightly entreats him lest he fall among these thieves: “Guard me,” he says, “from the snare they have laid for me and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity” (Ps. 140). Descending from heaven for us human beings and [Col. 0509B] for our salvation, he undertook the journey of this present life and came near the man who was wasting away from the wounds inflicted upon him—that is, having been made in the likeness of human beings and found in human form, he became our neighbor through sharing in our compassion and became near through the bestowal of mercy.

“And coming near, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.” The sins that he found in human beings he restrained by rebuking them, instilling hope of pardon in penitents and fear of punishment in sinners. He binds the wounds when he commands: “Repent.” He pours in oil when he adds: “For the kingdom of heaven is near.” He also pours in wine when he says: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3).

“And placing him on his own beast, he brought him to an inn and took care of him.” His beast is his flesh, in which he deigned to come to us. He placed the wounded man upon it because he himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood [Col. 0509C]; and, according to another parable, he placed the sheep that had gone astray upon his shoulders and carried it back to the flock. Therefore, to be placed upon the beast means to believe in Christ’s incarnation, to be initiated into his mysteries, and at the same time to be protected from the attacks of enemies.

The inn is the present Church, where travelers are refreshed as they return from this pilgrimage to their eternal homeland. And he rightly brought the man placed upon the beast to the inn, because no one enters the Church unless baptized and united to the body of Christ.

“And the next day he brought out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said: ‘Take care of him.’” The next day is after the Lord’s resurrection. Before this, indeed, he had illuminated by the grace of his Gospel those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death; but after the resurrection had been celebrated, the splendor of perpetual light shone forth more powerfully. The two denarii are the two Testaments, in which the name and image of the eternal King are contained. For Christ is the end of the law. These were brought out on the next day and given to the innkeeper, because then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. [Col. 0509D] On the next day the innkeeper received the denarii, with whose value he was to heal the wounded man, because, when the Holy Spirit came, he taught the Apostles all truth, so that they might be capable of devoting themselves to instructing the nations and preaching the Gospel.

“And whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return.” The innkeeper spends more than he received in the two denarii when the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice” (1 Cor. 7). And again: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel; but we have not made use of this authority, lest we burden anyone” (1 Cor. 9). When he returns, the Lord will repay the debtor what he promised, for at his coming in judgment the Lord says: “Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many [Col. 0510A] things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

“Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbor to the man who fell among thieves?” He said: “The one who showed mercy to him.” According to the literal sense, the Lord’s judgment is clear: no one is more truly our neighbor than the one who shows mercy. For the citizen of Jerusalem found that not a priest or a Levite of the same nation—indeed, not one born and raised in the same city—but a resident of a foreign nation became his neighbor because he showed greater mercy.

In a more sacred understanding, since no one is more truly a neighbor than the one who healed our wounds, let us love him as the Lord our God; let us love him as our neighbor—for nothing is so near as the head is to its members—and let us also love the one who imitates Christ. For this is what follows:

“And Jesus said to him: ‘Go, and do likewise.’” That is, in order to show that you truly love your neighbor as yourself, devotedly perform whatever you are able to do to assist him in his bodily or spiritual need. [Col. 0510B]

[Note: [Col. 0509D] We have taken the three homilies that follow from the *Anecdota litteraria* of Amadusius. They were first published from a thirteenth-century manuscript in the library [Col. 0510D] of the Casinensian congregation at Florence by Pietro Aloysio Galletti, Roman abbot of Fonte Vivo, in the territory of Parma.]

# HOMILY 107

## Luke 15

At that time, Jesus told his disciples this parable: “A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father: ‘Father, give me the portion of the substance that falls to me,’ and he divided the substance among them,” etc.

Beloved brothers, you have heard in the Gospel reading the parable of the two sons. But this man, who is said to have had two sons, is understood to be God the Father, the begetter and creator of two peoples. The elder son signifies those who remain in the worship of the one God; the younger those who deserted the Lord for the worship of idols.

“And the younger of them said to his father: ‘Father, give me the portion of the substance that falls to me.’ And he divided the substance among them.” What substance does this evangelical father divide among his spiritual son except [Col. 0510C] prudence, understanding, and also freedom of choice, which are true and lasting riches for the one who uses them well?

God the Father divides this substance among his sons because, in their first birth, reason is given equally to all who are born; but in their subsequent way of life each person is found to possess more or less of this substance. Those who neglect it through evil will abandon it within themselves, while those who love it preserve the natural good of reason. One person, mindful and understanding that what he had received came from the Lord his Creator, believing that these things belong to God the Father as they are, guards them as paternal possessions. Another, however, supposing that these things come from himself and belong to him, abuses them as though he had the freedom to distribute his own property, and soon, when his resources have been squandered, is deprived of them. Hence it follows:

“And not many days afterward, the younger son gathered everything together and went away to a distant country, and there he squandered his substance by living luxuriously.” By adding “distant,” he expressed not a change of place but an estrangement of mind, because the more anyone sins in wicked [Col. 0510D] conduct, the farther he withdraws from God’s grace. Thus the one who forgets God his Creator is truly said to be a wanderer from God, because evil conduct in worldly desire makes a person not only a stranger but also alien to God, just as those who make themselves strangers are exiled from the heavenly kingdom by the lusts of the flesh and the desires of this world.

Knowing that through this pilgrimage of great ignorance we had been strangers, blessed Paul says: “You who were once far from God through unbelief and your evil conduct have now been brought near in the blood of Christ, having been rescued from the destruction of eternal death” (Eph. 2). Do not again become distant from the Lord by clinging to earthly desires. Since you are still near through your confession of the true faith, persevere in [Col. 0511A] the encouragement of good works, adhering to him in your will at all times, because he himself is going to give the portion of his inheritance—that is, the joys of eternal life—to all who call upon him in truth, that is, to those who strive to keep themselves in accordance with his will.

It follows: “And after he had squandered everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. And he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him to his farm to feed swine. And he desired to fill his stomach with the pods that the swine were eating, and no one gave him any.”

After someone forgets the commands of his Lord because of his sins and does not serve his will, he is deprived of spiritual riches—that is, of prudence and understanding—and consumes all the adornments of the soul. He is said to feed swine, that is, to nourish filthy and unclean thoughts in his soul and desire useless food that benefits the body nothing—in other words, to fulfill carnal desires. This is the seduction and corruption of life, which contributes no virtue to the soul, [Col. 0511B] but utterly deprives the soul of all good and destroys it. By these things the demons are always eager to deceive and seduce the souls of the faithful.

Such a person is therefore rightly said to be in need, because he is deprived of the fruit and merits of every good work. Concerning him it is added: “But coming to himself, he said: ‘I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.’”

Who, then, is this son who, by sinning in a distant country, was separated from God, but at last, moved by repentance, returns to his father in confession? He is the Christian who had destroyed himself through lust and luxury and separated himself from God, had polluted himself through shameful deeds and utter filthiness, and had fed swine—that is, had enslaved himself to the service of demons. When, moved by God’s prompting and mercy, he recognizes that he is deprived of every good and surrounded on every side by a lack of good works, he returns to the father’s forgiveness. Before the angels of God in heaven and the saints of God, he confesses that he has sinned and is [Col. 0511C] guilty, and implores mercy so that he may receive pardon for his sins.

Therefore, beloved brothers, let us turn to the Lord our God and repent of our past sins. We must not be deterred by any despair, since we see this parable specifically applied to the person of the penitent, as the Lord himself more clearly declares, saying: “I tell you, so there will be joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15).

The Lord therefore gave penitents a way of escape and appointed those who turn from their evil deeds to their former goodness to the portion of the righteous. Therefore, beloved, if any one of us has been stained by the thought of grave crimes, if anyone has been polluted by the plague of filthy desires, let him disclose the secret of his iniquity to the merciful God and open the covering of his inward transgression. Everything we do is known to God. Even if the tongue does not speak it, the conscience cannot conceal it. Everything that is closed is open to him, and whatever seems shut away in our thoughts [Col. 0511D] is open to his eyes.

Since, then, he knows everything, he does not seek confession out of ignorance, but, out of mercy, desires it to be confessed rather than discovered. Recognizing this, dearest ones, let each person establish a serene state through the duties of confession and set his case in order, accusing himself. Let him pronounce sentence briefly against himself, so that he may avoid the anger of Christ the Judge; for whoever wishes to have him as a merciful judge should himself exercise judgment upon himself.

Everything that we fear will become pardonable if this fullness of justice is found in you. Behold, the Lord awaits the offering of our confession. Although human conscience is known to the divine eyes, he wishes the penitent to offer him, through tears, the sacrifice of confession concerning the very sin in which he stands.

Repentance, I say, is what embraces diverse duties in a single act. On the one hand, it makes the penitent’s confession public; on the other, it does not deny his guilt, by which it excuses the crime. On the one hand, it confronts the sinner with his own sins; on the other, it displays forgiveness to the one who confesses. [Col. 0512A]

O magnificent treasure of divine goodness! O singular institution of the most merciful Judge! When one who confesses before the judge of this world is immediately directed to punishment, one who confesses before the Lord proceeds at once to pardon. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY 108

## John 2

At that time: “The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. And he found in the temple those selling sheep, oxen, and doves, and the money-changers sitting; and when he had made something like a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple,” etc.

Beloved brothers, we must consider the present reading of the holy Gospel with attentive concentration. As the Passover of the Jews approached, the Lord went up to Jerusalem, plainly giving us an example of how vigilantly in spirit we ought to submit to the Lord’s commands, since the Son of God himself observed the decrees that he established by the authority of his divinity.

Lest people think [Col. 0512B] that they could escape punishments or attain eternal joys without frequent sacrifices of prayer and good works, the Son of God himself went up to Jerusalem to pray, to worship, and to offer sacrifice. Let us hear what he did when he came to Jerusalem: “And he found in the temple those selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and the money-changers sitting; and when he had made something like a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple.”

Among all the signs that Jesus performed, this appears to be the greatest: one man—and at that time himself despised, so worthless in the eyes of the Jews that they later crucified him—could, while their rulers looked on, hear his profits being destroyed and, with the blow of a single whip, drive out such a multitude and do things that an immense army could not have done. For a fiery radiance shone from his eyes, and the majesty of his divinity illuminated his face; therefore the rulers did not dare lay hands upon him.

It seemed lawful to sell in the temple things that were bought for the purpose of offering them to the Lord in [Col. 0512C] that same temple. But the Lord himself, unwilling that anything belonging to earthly commerce should take place in his house, drove everything out and expelled the sellers themselves.

What, then, do we think the Lord will do, my brothers, if he should find people quarreling, wasting their time in idle talk, or occupied with any crime, since he saw in the temple those buying the victims offered to him and hastened to cast them out? All these things were said and done for the sake of those who enter the church not merely negligently, with no intention of praying, but who even increase the very things for which they ought to pray, pursuing others with vices, hatred, and slander, adding sins to sins and not fearing condemnation in the judgment of the strict Judge.

Therefore, dearest ones, these things are greatly to be feared, to be dreaded with proper fear, and to be guarded against with diligent care, lest the Lord come when we least expect it and find something perverse in us for which we deserve to be scourged and driven from the church. Above all, in the church, which is especially the house of prayer, we must fear lest he find us doing something other [Col. 0512D] than what he loves, and lest he show himself to us as a stern exactor, such as we do not wish him to be.

Let him not find us in his temple as money-changers—that is, serving earthly things and the desires of this world and entangled in them. Let him not find us, placed among the saints, doing anything there for the sake of the world’s empty glory. Let him not condemn us when he finds us pretending to do good while openly doing evil. Let him not find us selling oxen—that is, offering the word of preaching, which we bestow, not out of divine love but with a view to eternal profit. Let him not find us selling sheep, as we said above, practicing works out of desire for human praise, concerning which the Lord says elsewhere that “they have received their reward” (Matt. 6). Let him not condemn us when he finds us selling doves—that is, when we bestow the grace of the Holy Spirit that we have received, not freely, as commanded, but for a price; or when we confer the laying on of hands or someone’s ordination, through which the Holy Spirit is received, if not for monetary profit, then nevertheless for the favor of the crowd.

It must be noted [Col. 0513A] that the sellers of doves who make the house of God a house of commerce are not only those who seek payment when they bestow sacred orders. They also include those who exercise the rank or spiritual grace in the Church that they receive from the Lord’s generosity, not with a simple intention but for the sake of some human recompense.

Therefore, whoever is of this kind, if he does not wish to be removed from the church when the Lord comes, should remove these things from his conduct, lest he make the house of God a house of commerce, for which he will feel a just punishment in the future.

It follows: “But his disciples remembered that it was written: ‘The zeal of your house has consumed me.’” Moved by zeal for the Father’s house, the Savior drove the impious from the temple. Let us also be zealous for the house of God, beloved brothers, and, insofar as we can, resist anything evil being done in it.

If we see a brother who belongs to the house of God swollen with pride, accustomed to slander, enslaved to drunkenness, overthrown by luxury, troubled by anger, or subjected to any vice, let us strive, insofar as our ability permits, to rebuke what is polluted [Col. 0513B] and correct what is perverse. If we cannot amend such things, let us nevertheless endure them only with the sharpest grief of heart. Above all, in that house of prayer where the Lord’s body is consecrated and where we do not doubt that the presence of the holy angels is always present, let us drive away with all our strength anything improper or anything that might hinder our own prayer or that of our brother.

It follows: “Then the Jews answered and said to him: ‘What sign do you show us, since you do these things?’ Jesus answered and said to them: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’”

The Evangelist later explained which temple he meant: the temple of his body, which they destroyed in death when they crucified him, but which he himself raised from the dead on the third day. Since they were asking the Lord for a sign as to why he was casting the customary commerce out of the temple, he answered that the impious were secretly expelled from the temple because that temple signified the temple of his body, in which there was no stain of sin. Nor was it without reason that he cleansed the stone temple of crimes, since by the power of his divine majesty he could raise from death the temple of his body, which was truly the temple of God, after it had been put to death by human beings. [Col. 0513C]

Since the time is now near when we desire to celebrate with annual solemnity both the dissolution of that venerable temple, which was carried out by the faithless Jews, and its raising, which he himself wondrously accomplished on the third day as he had promised, let us cleanse the temples of our bodies and hearts, so that the Spirit of God may deign to dwell in our hearts.

And in accordance with the Apostle’s admonition, having cast aside the works of darkness, let us put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in feasting and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and impurity, not in quarrelsomeness and rivalry; but “put on the Lord Jesus Christ,” who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God before all ages and forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY 109

[Col. 0513D] Luke 11. At that time, Jesus was casting out a demon; the man was mute, and the crowds marveled, etc.

We have heard and believe that the works of our Lord Jesus Christ were performed among the people of the Jews, but let us examine the miracles that were now being read. “Jesus was casting out a demon,” says the Evangelist, “and it was mute. When he had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled.”

This mute and blind man signifies unbelievers and all malicious people, who do not wish to see for imitation the Lord’s commandments, even when they are carried out in works, nor to hear them with the ear of the heart so as to understand them. Bound in their tongues by the bonds of unbelief and envy, they refuse to speak and proclaim to others the commandments of God that they themselves have heard. Or those who worship mute and deaf idols are blind and mute, as the Psalmist says: “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (Ps. 113).

Therefore three signs were performed together in this one man: the blind man is enlightened, the mute man speaks, and the one possessed by a demon is freed. This did indeed happen bodily at that time, but it also happens daily [Col. 0514A] in the holy Church, when someone is converted from unbelief to faith through holy preachers. After the devil, whom he previously served, has been expelled and renounced, he returns to the light of faith and comes to the knowledge of the heavenly Creator. Then he does not cease to bring forth God’s praise continually from himself and strives, as far as he can, to announce to others the word of truth and the joys of eternal salvation.

But some said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.” The Pharisees and all the unbelieving and perverse were slandering the works of God. To them the Lord says elsewhere: “Woe to you who shut the kingdom of heaven, for you yourselves do not enter, and you do not permit others to enter because of your envy” (Matt. 23).

It follows: “And others, testing him, sought a sign from heaven.” But he, seeing their thoughts, said: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house.” No one knows human thoughts except God alone. Therefore, because the Jews refused to believe in the Lord Jesus, let us love him [Col. 0514B] and fear him in faith, because all things were made through him; he knows the thoughts and hearts of all, and he will repay each according to his works.

For this reason he answered not the Jews’ words but their thoughts, so that even in this way they might be compelled by his power, since they had said within themselves that he cast out demons by Beelzebul—that is, by the power of the prince of demons—and not by the power of God. He showed that his kingdom is undivided, since he reigns everywhere and his kingdom will have no end.

He therefore showed that he had come into this world to destroy the devil’s kingdom, to open the gates of the heavenly kingdom to all who believe and wish to enter through works of righteousness, and to disclose the joys of eternal salvation to those who place their hope in him. It became clear that those who placed their hope in the devil rather than in the Lord’s mercy were separated from the company of the blessed and expelled from the joy of eternal life.

It is therefore a grave crime to believe that the works of God are demonic powers. Therefore, beloved, do not listen to the devil the deceiver. Rather, adhering to God’s will, [Col. 0514C] place your hope in him, and he will direct you in every good thing.

In all your distresses and tribulations, in every pressure that may befall you in this world, seek mercy and forgiveness from the Lord God Almighty. Seek his mercy with right faith; love him with sincere charity, believing that whatever tribulation or distress has occurred has occurred chiefly because of our sins.

Confess your sins to God, to his priests, and to holy men in the Church; do penance for everything you have done; wash the filth of your souls from yourselves through almsgiving; cry out to the Lord with a pure heart, sincere faith, and perfect charity; always place your hope in his mercy, believing that whatever you ask of him with right and sincere faith, you will receive.

He is immediately ready, in his mercy, to grant all who call upon him in truth forgiveness and everlasting refreshment at his table. Do not be led astray by the empty errors of demons; [Col. 0514D] despise the devil’s schemes with your whole heart.

For if once, twice, or perhaps three or four times you utterly reject, with all your mind and all your faith, the wickedness that the devil attempts to instill in you through temptation, and if you strive always to remain vigilant with the same caution, God will deign to drive the devil away from troubling you in such a way that he will never be able to deceive you by his cunning.

Therefore do not be led astray, brothers. Seek help nowhere except from Christ our Lord. Do not depart from him or seek remedies from empty and useless incantation-makers or from diabolical omens. For whenever we are scourged by the Lord through some necessity, distress, tribulation, or bodily illness, we call upon him for rest and everlasting remedy. And how do we wish to reach him if we do not patiently and humbly endure the scourges that come from him?

Therefore let us patiently endure the instruction of our heavenly Father, so that we may deserve to reach the homeland of the eternal kingdom. Beloved, we say these things [Col. 0515A] so that none of you, when he is ill or suffers some other pressure or tribulation, may seek or desire help or remedies anywhere except from the Lord, because he alone is the true physician of our souls. Therefore let us turn with all our heart and mind toward his mercy, [Col. 0516A] and in every distress let us always rely upon his assistance. For he himself strikes and heals wounds; he infects, and he himself brings everlasting health. To him be honor and glory through immortal ages forever and ever. Amen.

# THE SECOND SECTION OF THE VENERABLE BEDE’S EXHORTATORY WORKS, CONTAINING ASCETICAL WRITINGS

[Col. 0515B]

# BOOKLET OF PRAYERS

(*Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, Martene) (C, S)

[Col. 0515]

# PRELIMINARY NOTICE
[Col. 0515B] It is pleasing to append to the Homilies of the Venerable Bede a little book of prayers composed by him, which we recovered from an old Corbie manuscript written eight hundred years ago and therefore dating very nearly from the author’s own time. It consists chiefly of verses from the Book of Psalms, which the author excerpted from St. Jerome’s version according to the Hebrew truth; in that version the holy doctor distinguished the verses themselves by cola and commas, and we have conscientiously retained this feature as observed by Bede. From this book we can gather what in particular was the manner of prayer among our fathers, who derived the principal source of their prayers from the Book of Psalms. Some perhaps will regard these matters as insignificant; yet nothing should be considered trivial in great men, among whom even the slightest things carry great weight. Moreover, the scribe of the manuscript had placed Bede’s preface at the end of the book, and we have restored it to its proper place.

## Preface

We are thoroughly instructed by an angelic admonition always to bless the God of heaven and to recount his wonders attentively, as Raphael concluded his discourse to Tobit and his household: “Bless the God of heaven,” he says, “and confess him before all the living” (Tobit 12:6). And shortly afterward: “But you, bless God and recount all his wonders” (ibid. 12:20). And the Psalmist says: “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders” (Psalm 9:2). And again: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33:2). And again: “Recounting the praises of the Lord, his powers, and his wonders which he has done” (Psalm 77:4). Likewise: “Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples. Confess and invoke his name. Declare his works among the nations. Sing and make music to him; recount all his wonders. Remember his wonders which he has done” (Psalm 9:12). Therefore I would become guilty if I ceased to confess the Lord and recount his wonders.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] Here he alludes to the ten lepers restored to health by Christ, of whom only one, giving thanks, pleased God, while the other nine, ungrateful for the benefit, displeased him. [Col. 0516D]]

For through the conduct of one, the nine displeased God. I shall undertake, according to my abilities, to touch upon a few matters from among many, modest matters from among the greatest, and some portion of innumerable miracles in metrical verse, relying, of course, upon the authority of the holy Fathers, who composed many metrical praises of God. From the verdant meadows of those radiant men—Hilary of Poitiers, and also the presbyters Sedulius and Juvencus, as well as Arator, subdeacon of the Roman Church, and Aldhelm and Prosper—I have gathered meadow-born, paradise-like herbs with carefully arranged flowers, inserting here and there, according to my ability and as occasion required, a few little blossoms of my own weakness, and have woven this very small flowering garland.

## Here begins the little book of prayers of the Venerable Bede

[Col. 0515]

[Col. 0515D] Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,

nor stood in the way of sinners,

nor sat in the seat of scoffers;

but his delight was in the law of the Lord,

and in his law he will meditate day and night.

And he will be like a tree planted

beside streams of water, which will yield

its fruit in its season;

and its leaf will not fall,

and everything he does will prosper.

Now therefore, kings, understand;

be instructed, judges of the earth.

Serve the Lord in fear,

[Col. 0516D] and exult before him with trembling.

Worship purely, lest he become angry

and you perish from the way.

Have mercy on me and hear my prayer.

Give ear, O Lord, to my words.

Understand my murmuring, my King

and my God, for to you I pray.

O Lord, lead me in your justice because of

those who lie in wait for me. Make straight

my way before your face.

O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,

nor correct me in your wrath.

Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak;

[Col. 0517A] heal me, O Lord, for my bones

are troubled.

And my soul is greatly troubled;

and you, O Lord—how long?

Turn back, O Lord; rescue my soul

for the sake of your mercy.

O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me

from all who persecute me, and deliver me.

Lest he seize my soul like a lion and

tear it apart, with no one to rescue me.

O Lord, our Ruler, how great is

your name throughout all the earth!

I will rejoice and be glad in you;

I will sing to your name, O Most High.

How long will my enemy be exalted

[Col. 0517B] over me? Turn and hear me,

O Lord my God.

Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever

fall asleep in death,

lest my enemy say,

“I have prevailed against him.”

Jacob will exult and Israel will rejoice;

but God glorifies those who fear the Lord.

Guard me, O Lord God, for I have hoped in you,

saying to God, “You are my God; apart from you

I have no good.”

Guard me like the apple within the eye;

in the shadow of your wings protect me.

But I, in righteousness, shall see your face.

[Col. 0517C] I will love you, O Lord, my strength

and my redeemer.

Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord,

and spare your servant from those of others.

But we shall remember the name of the Lord

our God.

Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength;

we shall sing and make music

to your mighty deeds.

But you, O Lord, do not be far from me, my strength;

hasten to my aid.

Rescue my soul from the sword.

Save me from the lion’s mouth.

And kindness and mercy shall follow me

all the days of my life.

[Col. 0517D] And I shall receive blessing from the Lord.

To you, O Lord, I shall lift up my soul.

Show me your ways, O Lord,

and teach me your paths.

Lead me, O Lord, in your truth

and teach me, for you are God,

my Savior.

Do not remember the sins of my youth

or my transgressions.

According to your great mercy,

remember me.

For the sake of your name,

[Col. 0518A] pardon my iniquity,

for it is great.

Look upon me and have mercy on me.

Bring me out of my distress.

See my humiliation

and my labor, and bear

all my sins.

Guard my soul, redeem me,

and have mercy on me.

The Lord is my light and my salvation;

whom shall I fear?

Hear, O Lord, the voice of one calling upon you;

have mercy on me

and hear me.

Do not hide your face

[Col. 0518B] from me; do not turn away in anger

from your servant.

You have been my help;

do not abandon me or forsake me,

O God my Savior.

Show me your way, O Lord.

Lead me on a straight path,

because of those who lie in wait for me.

Do not hand me over, O Lord,

to the souls of those who afflict me.

But I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord

in the land of the living.

Hear, O Lord, my supplication,

when I cry out to you.

Do not hand me over with sinners

[Col. 0518C] and with those who practice iniquity.

God is my strength and my shield.

Worship the Lord in holy splendor.

Hear, O Lord, and have mercy on me.

O Lord, be my helper, so that my glory may praise you

and not be silent.

O Lord my God, forever I will confess you.

In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me not be put to shame forever;

in your righteousness save me.

Incline your ear to me; quickly

hear me.

For you are my strength. Into your hands

I commend my spirit. In your hand

are my times.

Deliver me from the hand of my enemies

[Col. 0518D] and from those who persecute me.

Show your face upon your servant.

Blessed is the one whose iniquity is forgiven

and whose sin is covered.

I make my sin known to you,

and I do not hide my iniquity.

You are my protection.

You will guard me from the enemy.

Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him,

and upon those who await his mercy.

Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us,

as we have hoped in you.

I will bless the Lord at all times;

his praise shall always be in my mouth.

[Col. 0519A] Magnify the Lord with me,

and let us exalt his name together.

I sought the Lord, and he heard me,

and from all my distress

he delivered me.

Taste and see that the Lord is good.

Blessed is the man who hopes in him.

Fear the Lord, all you his saints,

for there is no want for those who fear him.

But those who seek the Lord

shall lack no good thing.

The Lord guards all their bones;

not one of them shall be broken.

The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants.

Judge, O Lord, those who oppose me;

[Col. 0519B] fight against those who fight me.

Take up shield and spear,

and rise to my help.

Say to my soul, “I am your salvation.”

But my soul shall exult in the Lord;

it shall rejoice in your salvation.

I will confess you in the great assembly,

and my tongue shall meditate upon your righteousness;

all day long, upon your praise.

O God, in heaven is your mercy.

How precious is your mercy, O God!

For with you is the fountain of life,

and in your light we shall see light.

Extend your mercy to those who know you,

and your righteousness to the upright in heart.

[Col. 0519C] Let not the foot of pride come against me,

nor the hand of the ungodly move me.

For I was young, and I did not see

the righteous man forsaken.

For the Lord loves judgment

and will not abandon his saints.

They are guarded forever,

and the Lord will help them.

O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,

nor correct me in your wrath.

For I was waiting for you, O Lord; you will hear me,

O Lord my God, because I followed what is good.

Do not abandon me, O Lord my God;

do not be far from me.

Hasten to my aid, O Lord,

[Col. 0519D] God of my salvation.

You are my expectation. Deliver me from all my iniquities. Do not make me

a reproach to the fool. Take away from me

your blows.

With expectation I awaited the Lord, and he inclined toward me

and heard my cry.

O Lord, hasten to help me; let those who seek you

rejoice and be glad in you.

You are my help and my salvation,

O my God, do not delay.

I said, “O Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul,

for I have sinned against you.”

But you, O Lord, have mercy on me.

[Col. 0520A] As a plot of ground prepared for the irrigation of waters, so my soul is prepared for you, O God.

Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause

from an unholy nation; from a deceitful

and unjust man save me.

For you are my strength; why

have you cast me away?

Rise up, help us, and redeem us

for the sake of your mercy.

Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.

Therefore the peoples shall confess you

forever and ever.

Our God, our hope and strength,

you have proved a powerful help in tribulations.

[Col. 0520B] The great King over all the earth.

Sing to our God, sing; sing to our King,

sing.

For he is our God forever and ever.

He will be our light upon the mountain.

Nevertheless God will redeem my soul

from the hand of the underworld, when you take me.

The mighty Lord God has spoken: “It is not because of

sacrifices that I will rebuke you; your burnt offerings are always before me.

I will not take a calf from your house,

nor goats from your flocks.

For all the animals of the forests are mine.

I know all the birds of the mountains,

and the whole expanse of the field is with me.

[Col. 0520C] If I were hungry, I would not tell you,

for the world and its fullness are mine.

Sacrifice praise to God,

and fulfill your vows to the Most High.

And call upon me in the day of tribulation;

I will deliver you, and you will glorify me.

Whoever sacrifices confession glorifies me,

and to whoever walks in an ordered way

I will show my salvation.”

Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great

mercy.

According to the multitude of your mercies

blot out my iniquities.

Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity,

and cleanse me from my sin,

[Col. 0520D] and blot out all my iniquities.

Create in me a clean heart, O God,

and renew a steadfast spirit within me.

Do not cast me away from your presence,

and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.

Restore to me the joy of your Jesus,

and strengthen me with a powerful Spirit.

Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God,

God of my salvation,

and my tongue shall praise your righteousness.

O Lord, open my lips,

and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.

A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit;

a contrite and humbled heart, O God,

you will not despise.

The mercy of God endures all day.

[Col. 0521A] But I, like a flourishing olive tree in the house of God,

have hoped in the mercy of God forever.

Jacob shall exult and Israel shall rejoice.

O God, save me by your name,

and vindicate me by your strength.

O God, hear my prayer,

and do not despise my supplication;

attend to me,

and hear me.

But I shall place my trust in you

on whatever day I am terrified.

I shall trust in you.

I will not fear what flesh can do to me;

this I know, because you are my God.

Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me,

for my soul has trusted in you.

And in the shadow of your wings I hope

[Col. 0521B] until the snares pass away.

I will call upon God Most High,

upon God my avenger.

He will send from heaven and save me—

truly, God who judges on earth.
