Deliver me from my enemies, O my God,

and protect me from those who resist me.

I will reserve my strength for you,

for you are God, my lifter-up;

the mercy of my God will go before me.

For you have become my strength

and my refuge in the day of my tribulation.

To you I shall sing,

for you are God my helper,

my strength, my God, my mercy.

Give us help in tribulation,

[Col. 0521C] for vain is salvation from man.

In God we shall act valiantly,

and he himself will trample those who afflict us.

Hear, O God, my praise.

From the ends of the earth I shall cry to you,

when my heart is sorrowful.

When the mighty man rises against me,

you were my guide, my hope,

a most strongly fortified tower against judgment.

I shall dwell continually in your tabernacle;

I shall hope in the protection of your wings.

For you, O God, have heard my prayer;

you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.

Mercy and truth will preserve you.

For my expectation is from him. He is

[Col. 0521D] my strength and my salvation,

my protector; I will not fear.

O God, you are my strength; from the light I will rise

to you, my soul (thus).

My flesh has longed for you.

Thus I appeared to you in the holy place,

to see your strength and your glory.

Your mercy is better than life;

my lips shall praise you.

Thus I shall bless you throughout my life.

In your name I shall lift up my hands,

for you have been my help;

in the shadow of your wings

I shall praise you.

Hear, O God, the voice of one speaking.

From the fear of the enemy

[Col. 0522A] preserve my life.

Hear us, O God our Savior,

hope of all the ends of the earth.

Let all the earth worship you,

and sing to you;

let it sing to your name.

Bless our God, peoples,

and make the voice of his praise heard.

He has set my soul in life.

Blessed is the Lord,

who has not taken away my prayer

nor his mercy from me.

May God have mercy on us

and bless us.

May he make his face shine upon us.

May God bless us.

Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered,

and let those who hate him flee from his face.

[Col. 0522B] But let the righteous rejoice;

let them exult in the presence of God

and delight in gladness.

Hear, O Lord, for your mercy is good;

according to the multitude of your mercies

look upon me.

And do not hide your face from your servant,

for I am afflicted; quickly hear me.

Draw near to my soul and redeem it;

because of my enemies, deliver me.

Your salvation, O God, has received me.

O God, to deliver me and to help me,

hasten.

Let all who seek you

rejoice and be glad in you.

But I am needy and poor;

[Col. 0522C] hasten for me.

You are my help and my savior;

O Lord, do not delay.

In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me not be put to shame

forever. In your righteousness rescue me

and deliver me.

Incline your ear to me and save me.

My God, save me from the hand of the ungodly,

from the hand of the unjust and harmful man,

for you are my expectation, O Lord.

O God, do not be far from me;

O my God, hasten to my help.

Your name shall endure forever;

your name shall continue beyond the sun.

But for me, it is good to draw near to God.

[Col. 0522D] I have placed my hope in the Lord God.

But God is my King from the beginning.

Do not hand over the soul instructed by your law

to beasts; do not forget forever the life of your poor.

But I shall proclaim forever;

I shall sing to the God of Jacob.

When God rises to judge,

to save all the meek of the earth.

With my voice I cried to the Lord;

with my voice to God, and he heard me.

In the day of my tribulation I sought God.

But he, being merciful, will pardon iniquity

and will not destroy.

[Col. 0523A] Do not remember our former iniquities;

let your mercies quickly come to meet us,

for we have been greatly weakened.

Help us, O God, our Jesus,

for the glory of your name;

deliver us,

and pardon our sins

for the sake of your name.

Stir up your strength and come

to save us.

O Lord of hosts, restore us,

and show your face,

and we shall be saved.

Praise God, our strength.

Judge for the poor and the orphan;

render justice to the needy

and the impoverished.

Save the needy,

and deliver the poor

[Col. 0523B] from the hand of the ungodly.

O God, do not be silent;

do not keep silence or remain quiet,

O God,

and let them know that your name is

the Lord our God.

You alone are Most High over all the earth.

O Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer.

O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man

who trusts in you.

Restore us, O God, our Jesus,

and set aside your anger against us;

do not be angry with us forever.

Show us, O Lord, your mercy,

and grant us your salvation.

Incline your ear, O Lord,

and hear me,

for I am needy and poor.

Have mercy on me, O Lord,

for I shall cry to you

[Col. 0523C] all day long;

gladden the soul of your servant,

for to you I lift up my soul.

Hear, O Lord, my voice,

and attend to the voice

of my supplications.

In the day of tribulation

I shall call upon you,

for you will hear me.

Teach me, O Lord, your way,

and I shall walk in your truth.

Make my heart single,

so that it may fear your name forever.

But you, O Lord, are merciful and gracious;

look upon me and have mercy on me.

Give strength to your servant,

and save the son of your handmaid.

Give me a sign of goodness,

so that those who hate me may see it

[Col. 0523D] and be confounded.

For you, O Lord, have helped me

and comforted me.

And all my springs shall sing,

as in choirs, in you.

Let my prayer come before you;

incline your ear to my praise.

But I cried to you, O Lord,

and in the morning my prayer

will come before you.

The heavens shall confess your wonders,

O Lord.

Mercy and truth shall go before your face.

Let your work appear to your servants,

and your glory to their children.

[Col. 0524A] And let the beauty of the Lord our God be upon us,

and establish the work

of our hands.

For you are my hope, O Lord,

because you have gladdened me, O Lord,

by your work.

Your testimonies have become exceedingly faithful.

Your mercy, O Lord, sustained me.

Come, let us worship and bow down;

let us kneel before the face of the Lord,

our Maker;

for he is the Lord our God.

Glory and beauty are before his face.

You who love the Lord, hate evil.

The Lord guards the souls of his saints.

From the hand of the ungodly he will rescue them.

He remembered his mercy.

[Col. 0524B] Exalt the Lord our God.

Serve the Lord with gladness.

Enter before him with praise.

Know that the Lord himself is God.

He made us, and we are his.

I shall sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.

I shall sing praise and be instructed

in the perfect way;

when will you come to me?

O Lord, hear my prayer,

and let my cry come to you.

Do not hide your face from me

in the day of my tribulation;

incline your ear to me.

On whatever day I call upon you,

quickly hear me.

[Col. 0524C] Bless the Lord, O my soul,

and all that is within me,

his holy name.

Bless the Lord, O my soul,

and do not forget all his rewards.

He who is merciful to all your iniquities

and heals all your illnesses;

he who redeems your life from corruption

and crowns you with mercy

and compassion.

Bless the Lord, O my soul.

O Lord my God,

you have been greatly magnified.

May the glory of the Lord endure forever.

The Lord will rejoice in his works.

Seek the Lord and his strength.

Seek his face always.

[Col. 0524D] Remember the wonders he has done.

Blessed are those who keep judgment

and practice righteousness at all times.

Save us, O Lord our God,

so that we may confess your holy name

and sing praises to you.

Blessed is the Lord God of Israel.

Confess to the Lord, for he is good,

for his mercy endures forever.

Let them confess to the Lord his mercies,

and his wonders to the children of men.

For he has satisfied the empty soul,

and filled the hungry soul with good things.

Give us help in tribulation.

[Col. 0525A] For vain is salvation from man.

In God we shall be strong,

and he himself will overcome our enemies.

But you, O Lord, deal with me

for the sake of your name,

for your mercy is good.

Deliver me, for I am needy and poor.

Help me, O Lord my God;

save me according to

your mercy.

Rule in the midst of your enemies.

I will confess to the Lord with my whole heart.

Glory and beauty are his work;

the work of his hands is truth and judgment.

Blessed is the man who fears the Lord,

who greatly delights in his commandments.

[Col. 0525B] May the name of the Lord be blessed,

from this time forth and forever.

Not to us, O Lord, not to us,

but to your name give glory,

because of your mercy and truth.

I beseech you, O Lord, save my soul,

and I shall invoke the name of the Lord.

Precious in the sight of the Lord

is the death of his saints.

And the truth of the Lord endures forever.

You are my Lord God;

I will not fear what man can do to me.

The Lord is my helper,

and I shall look down upon those who hate me.

[Col. 0525C] It is better to hope in the Lord

than to hope in princes.

I will confess to you, O Lord,

for you have heard me

and become my salvation.

I will confess to you with uprightness of heart

when I have learned the judgments of your justice.

Do not let me stray from your commandments.

Open my eyes,

and I shall see wonders in your law.

Take the way of falsehood away from me,

and grant me your law.

Incline my heart to your testimonies,

and not to greed.

Let your mercies come to me, O Lord,

and your salvation according to your word.

[Col. 0525D] This is my consolation in my affliction,

for your word has given me life.

Your mercy has been completed.

Teach me your precepts.

Before I heard, I was ignorant.

Good and beneficent one,

teach me your precepts.

May your mercy, I beseech you,

be my consolation,

as you have spoken to your servant.

According to your mercy give me life,

and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth.

Had your law not been my meditation,

I might perhaps have perished in my affliction.

How sweet is your word to my throat,

sweeter than honey to my mouth!

[Col. 0526A] May the free offerings of my mouth please you, O Lord.

And according to your judgments teach me.

Strengthen me according to your word,

and I shall live.

Help me, and I shall be saved.

Deal with your servant according to your mercy,

and teach me your precepts.

Look upon me and have mercy on me,

and teach me your precepts.

You are righteous, O Lord,

and your judgment is right.

Hear my voice according to your mercy;

according to your judgment give me life.

See my affliction and rescue me.

According to your mercy give me life.

There is abundant peace for those who love your law,

and there is no stumbling-block for them.

[Col. 0526B] Let my praise come before you, O Lord;

according to your word teach me.

Let my supplication come before your face;

according to your word deliver me.

O Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips

and from a deceitful tongue.

I lifted my eyes to the mountains:

from where will help come to me?

May it go well with those who love you.

Have mercy on us, O Lord;

have mercy on us.

Our help is in the name of the Lord,

who made heaven and earth.

Deal well, O Lord, with those who are good

and upright in heart.

Restore, O Lord, our captivity,

like a stream in the south.

[Col. 0526C] Unless the Lord guards the city,

those who guard it watch in vain.

Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord,

who walks in his ways.

The blessing of the Lord is upon us.

O Lord, hear my prayer.

Let your ears be attentive

to the prayer of your servant.

O Lord, my heart is not exalted,

nor are my eyes lifted up.

This is my rest forever.

For there the Lord commanded blessing

and life forevermore.

You who stand in the house of the Lord,

praise the Lord,

for the Lord is good.

[Col. 0526D] Confess to the God of heaven,

for his mercy endures forever.

Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.

I will confess to you, O Lord,

with my whole heart.

O Lord, your mercy endures forever.

Do not abandon the works of your hands.

If I ascend into heaven, you are there;

if I lie in the underworld, you are present.

Rescue me, O Lord, from the evil man;

save me from unjust men.

Hear the voice of my crying to you.

Let my prayer be directed like incense

in your sight.

Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth.

[Col. 0527A] Guard the poverty of my lips.

Bring my soul out of prison,

so that it may confess your name.

O Lord, hear my prayer.

Hear me in your righteousness,

and do not enter into judgment

with your servant.

For no living person will be justified

in your sight.

Make me hear your mercy.

In you I trust.

Make known to me the way in which I walk,

for to you I have lifted my soul.

Deliver me from my enemies, O Lord;

I have taken refuge in you.

Teach me to do your will,

for you are my God.

[Col. 0527B] Your good Spirit will lead me

into a level land.

For the sake of your name, O Lord,

you will give me life in your righteousness.

For I am your servant.

Blessed is the Lord, my strong one,

my mercy and my strength,

my helper and my savior.

Every day I will bless you.

I will praise your name forever and continually.

My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord,

and all flesh shall bless his holy name

forever and continually.

Praise the Lord, O my soul.

I will praise the Lord

during my life.

[Col. 0527C] I will sing to the Lord as long as I exist.

Praise the Lord, for it is good.

May the Lord be pleased with those who fear him

and await his mercy.

He will send his Word

and dissolve it.

Praise the Lord from the heavens;

praise him in the heights.

Praise him, all his angels;

praise him, all his hosts.

Praise him, sun and moon;

praise him, all stars and light.

Praise him, heavens of heavens,

and let the waters above the heavens

praise the name of the Lord.

For he commanded,

and they were created.

Praise the Lord, kings of the earth

and all peoples,

princes and all judges of the earth.

[Col. 0527D] Young men and virgins,

old men with children,

let them praise the name of the Lord.

For his name alone is exalted.

His glory is in heaven and on earth.

And he has exalted the horn of his people.

Praise is due to all his saints.

Sing to the Lord a new song;

his praise is in the assembly of the saints.

He has exalted the meek in Jesus.

The saints shall exult in glory;

they shall praise him in their chambers.

The exaltations of God are in their throats.

Let everything that breathes praise the Lord.

## A Song of Ascents

[Col. 0528A]

I cried out to the Lord

when I was afflicted,

and the Lord heard

his servant very quickly.

I lifted my eyes

at once to the former mountains,

from which there will be

help from the Most High,

from the Lord.

I rejoiced in all

that the Lord said to me:

“We shall go to the house of the Lord,”

in which we shall always remain.

[Col. 0528B] To you I lifted my eyes,

O my inner God,

who are at heaven’s summit,

with the angelic host.

If the Most High,

the Lord, had not been among us,

let Israel say:

“We were weaker than all.”

Those who trust in the Lord,

the greatest Ruler,

are like Mount Zion,

which forever is not moved by anything.

When the Lord immediately

restored the captivity

of Zion,

we were greatly comforted

in everything.

Unless the Lord had built

and preserved us,

the work of all

who build houses would be vain.

[Col. 0528C] Blessed are the children of men

who fear their Lord,

and who walk in the narrow way

with steadfast faith.

They often attacked me,

but my enemies could not prevail;

they ceased at once,

while the Lord strengthened me.

From the depths I humbly

and faithfully cried out

[Col. 0528D] to you, God of victory,

eternal Father of glory.

My heart was not exalted

within me by pride,

nor was I inwardly

lofty in my thoughts.

Remember me, O Lord,

God from heaven’s summit,

before whom stand

thousands upon thousands of ministers.

Behold how good and sublime,

and how truly delightful it is,

for brothers to live together

and sit in the highest life.

[Col. 0529A] Behold now all the servants

standing in the house of the Lord:

bless the Lord,

the God of all days.

I beseech the Father of power

and Prince of knowledge,

that through these three times five steps

I may be able to ascend the heavens,

and through the ethereal regions

be carried to places of refreshment,

so that I may deserve

to possess excellent rewards.

## Three Prayers of the Venerable Bede

### First Prayer

[Col. 0529B] Deliverer of souls, Redeemer of the world, Jesus Christ, eternal God, immortal King: I, a sinner, beseech your immeasurable clemency, that through your great mercy and through the singing of the psalms which I, an unworthy sinner, have chanted, you may deliver my soul from sin. Turn my heart away from all evil, wicked, and treacherous thoughts; free my body from the slavery of sin; drive carnal desire far from me; rescue me from every hindrance of Satan and his visible and invisible servants, your faithless enemies who seek my soul. Guard me from these and from every evil, O Savior of the world, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit live, reign, and rule, God, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

### Second Prayer

[Col. 0529C] Lord God almighty, open my heart, and enlighten it by the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that I may ask for those things that are pleasing to your will. Direct my thoughts and senses toward meditating upon and considering how, through worthy conduct and actions, I may deserve the eternal joys of heavenly life. Order my actions according to your commandments, so that I may strive continually to fulfill them in practice and thereby also receive everlasting rewards.

### Third Prayer, after the Catholic Faith

“Whoever wishes to be saved…”

Lord our God, we believe in you, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For Truth would not have said, “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” unless you were Trinity; nor would you have commanded us, Lord God, to be baptized in the name of one who is not the Lord God. Nor would the divine voice have said, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord,” unless you were Trinity in such a way that you were one Lord God, and unless you yourself were God the Father, and the Son were your Word, Jesus Christ himself, and the Holy Spirit your gift. We would not read in the writings of Truth: “God sent his Son.” Nor would you, Only-Begotten, say of the Holy Spirit whom the Father sends in my name, “and whom I shall send to you from the Father.” Directing my intention according to this rule of faith, I turn toward the highest origin of things, the most perfect beauty, and the most blessed delight.

# APPENDIX. ASCETICAL WORKS REGARDED AS DOUBTFUL.

[Col. 0531]

## A BOOKLET ON DUTIES, EXCERPTED FROM THE SAYINGS OF CERTAIN FATHERS. (G,S)*

## ON THE LORD’S DAY

[Col. 0531C]

The apostles decreed that the Lord’s day should be honored with religious solemnity because on it our Redeemer rose again. It is therefore called the Lord’s day so that on it, abstaining from earthly works and the enticements of the world, we may serve only the divine worship, giving this day its honor and reverence because of the hope of our resurrection, which we have in it. For just as the Lord Jesus Christ himself, our Savior, rose from the dead on the third day, so we also hope to rise again at the end of the age.

For this reason we pray standing on the Lord’s day, which is a sign of the future resurrection. The whole Church does this—the Church found on pilgrimage in mortality—awaiting at the end of the age what was prefigured in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the firstborn from the dead.

On the preceding Sabbath the former people were to celebrate bodily rest, so that it might be a figure of repose; hence Sabbath is interpreted as “rest.” But the Lord’s day was revealed not to the Jews but to Christians through the Lord’s resurrection, and from that event it began to have its own festival. It is the first day, which is found after the seventh as the eighth. Hence in Ecclesiastes, by reference to the significance of the two Testaments, it is called seventh for the one and eighth for the other.

At first, therefore, only the Sabbath was handed down for observance, because previously there was the rest of the dead, but there was no resurrection. He who, having risen from the dead, will now die no more—death will no longer rule over him. But after such a resurrection had taken place in the Lord’s body, so that it might go before the Church in its Head—what the body of the Church hoped for at the end—the Lord’s day, the eighth day which is also the first, succeeded in its festivity.

It is clear that this day too is solemn in the sacred Scriptures. For it is the first day of the world: on it the elements of the world were formed, on it the angels were created, and on it also the Lord rose from the dead; on it the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the apostles. On that same day manna was first given from heaven in the wilderness.

For the Lord says: “For six days manna is gathered, but on the sixth day you shall gather twice as much.” The sixth day is the Day of Preparation, which is placed before the Sabbath. The Sabbath is the seventh day, and it is followed by the Lord’s day, on which manna first came from heaven. Let the Jews therefore understand that even then our Lord’s day was preferred to the Jewish Sabbath; even then it was shown that God’s grace descended upon them on none of their Sabbaths, but upon our holy Lord’s day, on which the Lord first rained it down.

## ON SEPTUAGESIMA, SEXAGESIMA, QUINQUAGESIMA, AND QUADRAGESIMA

[Col. 0532D]

According to the headings of the sacramentary and antiphonary, Septuagesima is reckoned nine weeks before Easter, ending with the seventh Sabbath. The people of God were held captive in Babylon for seventy years; when these had been completed, they returned to Jerusalem. The number seventy recalls to our memory the whole period of the present age, during which we are strangers to the heavenly Jerusalem.

Therefore the author of the Office placed Septuagesima in our observances, so that during this period, by abstaining from pleasures, we might show in our manner of life how those ought to live throughout the whole period of the age who, after baptism, separate themselves from the heavenly Jerusalem through sins. For who does not see that, just as the people returned from captivity after seventy years, so, after the periods have passed that run their course according to the sevenfold number of days, we too must return from our pilgrimage in this age to that same Jerusalem of God?

Accordingly, during that period we do not sing Alleluia among us, nor “Glory to God in the highest,” because these are heavenly songs. The Psalm says: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” Some spend the first week of Septuagesima without any change in the newly adopted manner of life, except for the change concerning Alleluia, and in certain places concerning the dalmatics, as well as the omission of “Glory to God in the highest.” The Greeks sanctify the following week, that is, Sexagesima, by their fast.

Our clergy, on the authority of Pope Telesphorus, observe the next period, that is, Quinquagesima. He established a fast of seven weeks before Easter. The director of our Office requires a more extensive change than we carry out through the establishment of his Office. For he intimated the fast itself in the first prayer of the Mass, saying: “So that we who are justly afflicted for our sins….” Here he speaks of affliction. In the Introit also he says: “The groans of death surrounded me, the pains of hell.” Because of these pains we cannot rejoice and be secure, but must prepare ourselves for battle, as the Apostle says: “Everyone who contends in the contest abstains from everything.”

Ambrose says: “The same discipline teaches that all things are to be avoided when they know that one person is to be crowned; how much more must this be observed by those to whom the whole of salvation has been promised!”

The Apostle teaches from what we who are going to battle must abstain when he says: “Fornication and every impurity or greed must not even be named among you.”

Pope Telesphorus, the ninth after the blessed apostle Peter in the Roman see, established that abstinence should be observed for seven weeks, as many still do. At that time it pleased them to call this period Quinquagesima for two reasons: either because, in the sequence, the number fifty stands after forty, or because from that point there are fifty days until the holy Resurrection. If one subtracts the eight Sundays, on which fasting may not be observed, forty-two days remain.

Among some people, these two days—the fifth and seventh days of the week, that is, Thursday and Saturday—which exceed the number forty, are included in the fast; among others they are counted as days of refreshment because of the Lord’s Supper and the holy Sabbath.

Later Pope Melchiades, an African by nationality and the thirty-fourth after Saint Peter, established that no one should presume to fast on the first or fifth day of the week. On the first, because of the Lord’s resurrection; on the fifth, because on that day the Lord dined with his disciples and on it ascended into heaven.

Then it pleased the faithful to consecrate eight weeks to fasting and to call the first Sunday Sexagesima—not because of a number of sixty days, but because of the usage of our speech: just as the fiftieth is joined to the fortieth, so the sixtieth is joined to the fiftieth, and the seventieth to the sixtieth.

From Sexagesima to Easter there are eight weeks. If from each one the first and fifth days of the week are subtracted from abstinence, as Melchiades established, and Easter day itself is also subtracted, only forty days of abstinence remain, in imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Septuagesima is said to be observed by the faithful so that they may both render tithes of their days to God and nevertheless be able to relax the fast on the first and fifth days of the week and on the Sabbath. From Septuagesima to Easter there are nine weeks, which make sixty-four days. If from each week you subtract the three days mentioned above, then until the holy Easter day you fast thirty-six days as a tithe of the year.

The one who established the Sabbath as a day of honor did not do so because of legal commandments, but because the Lord rested in the tomb on that day.

Augustine, in the fifteenth book of *The City of God*: “The names in which events are narrated ought also to be thought to signify something; but for the sake of those things that signify something, those that signify nothing are added as well. The field is not plowed only with the share; rather, for this to be done, the other parts of the plow are also necessary. Nor are only the strings on citharas fitted for song; rather, in order that they may be fitted, the other parts are present as well, and so forth.”

## ANOTHER VERSION

Why is it called Septuagesima, when from that day until Easter there are no more than sixty-four days? It is customary in the divine Scriptures that, whenever a number has passed beyond a decade so as to reach the third unit of the next [decade], it is not reckoned with the preceding decade but with the one toward which it tends. Read the book of Genesis in the genealogy of the sons of Noah.

## ANOTHER VERSION

[Col. 0534B]

Why is it called Septuagesima, when from that day until Easter there are not seventy days but sixty-four? Septuagesima extends to the Sabbath before the octave of Easter, when those who are baptized at the Easter vigil lay aside their white garments. At that time they ought to be confirmed by the bishop and receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. Since the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are described, those who are to receive this sacrament rightly celebrate Septuagesima beforehand.

For what the number seven signifies by itself, the same thing it signifies when multiplied by ten. Sexagesima extends to mid-Easter, that is, to the Wednesday of Easter week. Quinquagesima extends to Easter day itself; Quadragesima to the day of the Lord’s Supper.

Count, therefore, the number of days that are in abstinence from Septuagesima to Quadragesima, and you will find three times six, that is, eighteen days, excluding Sundays. If you divide this number by a double proportion, you will find six in one part and twelve in the other. Six is to twelve in a simple ratio, and twelve to six is a double ratio.

Likewise, between the Lord’s Supper and Easter day there are two days, and between Easter and mid-Easter, which is Wednesday, there are two days—the point toward which Sexagesima extends. From that day to the Sabbath, when Septuagesima arrives, there are similarly two days, making six in all. For four is double two, while two is the simple number.

The preceding numbers, therefore, which occur in the period of abstinence, signify that our double death was destroyed by Christ’s single death. We were subject to death in both soul and body, but Christ by his bodily death excluded death from both soul and body.

These days, which we celebrate with joy and gladness in the Lord’s resurrection, signify the resurrection that Christ bestowed in its double form through his single resurrection. For just as he died in body alone, so he rose in body alone; but he first raises us in soul by forgiving sins, and in the future he will also raise our bodies.

## ON THE FAST OF QUADRAGESIMA

[Col. 0534D]

According to the sacred Scriptures, there are four seasons of fasting in which we must entreat the Lord through abstinence and penitential lamentation. Although it is fitting to pray and abstain on every day, during these seasons we ought to devote ourselves more fully to fasting and penitence.

The first fast is that of Quadragesima. It derives from the ancient books, from the fasts of Moses and Elijah, and from the Gospel, since the Lord fasted for the same number of days, showing that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the Prophets. In the person of Moses, the Law is understood; in the person of Elijah, the Prophets. Between them Christ appeared gloriously on the mountain, so that what the apostle Paul says in the third chapter of Romans might stand out more clearly concerning him: “Bearing witness from the Law and the Prophets.”

In what part of the year, then, could the observance of Quadragesima be more suitably kept than adjacent and contiguous to the Lord’s Passion, since it signifies this laborious life? This life also requires restraint, so that we may fast from the enticements of the world itself, living on manna alone—that is, on heavenly and spiritual commandments.

This life is represented by the number forty for the following reason: ten is the perfection of our blessedness. The creature is represented by seven, which was present to the Creator; in this the unity of the Trinity is proclaimed throughout the temporal world. And because the world is outlined by the four winds, composed of the four elements, and nourished by the food of the four seasons, ten multiplied by four is completed in forty. By this number it is shown that we must abstain and fast from every pleasure of the seasons and live chastely and continently.

There is also another sacramental mystery expressed, on account of which the same fasts are celebrated for forty days. For in the Mosaic Law it was generally commanded to the whole people that tithes and firstfruits be offered to the Lord God.

[Col. 0535B] Thus, while we are admonished by this teaching to refer the beginnings of our desires and the completion of our works to God’s grace, in the reckoning of Quadragesima the total of these legal tithes is nevertheless fulfilled. The entire period of the year is tithed by the number thirty-six. For when the Sundays are subtracted from Quadragesima, on which the fasts are relaxed, we come together to the Church on these days as though for the tithes of the whole year, offering the activity of our works to God as a sacrifice of jubilation.

As our Cassian says, those who are perfect are not bound by the laws of this Quadragesima, nor are they content with subjection to this small canon. The leaders of the Churches established it especially for those who are entangled throughout the whole year in pleasures and secular business, so that, constrained by this kind of legal necessity, they would at least on these days be forced to be free for the Lord and dedicate to him as tithes the days of their life, which they had been about to devour entirely as though they were fruits.

## AGAIN, ON THE FAST OF QUADRAGESIMA

[Col. 0535C]

For an appropriate reason the teachers of the Church established that the season of Quadragesima should be observed before the Lord’s Passion, so that we might understand that the affliction of the present life produces future immortality.

To confirm this, the Lord himself, who fasted for forty days before his Passion, also spent forty days with his disciples after the resurrection, completing both periods with the number forty, so that he might show that the present life is a time of affliction and the future a time of joy.

When he fasted for forty days before the Passion, he seemed to cry out: “Unless you repent, you will die in your sins.” And Peter says: “Abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul.”

But when he remained with the disciples after the resurrection, making their hearts glad, he seemed to promise that unspeakable joy of which he says elsewhere: “I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.” And again: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

He fasted not only for forty days but also for forty nights, so that whether prosperity flatters us—represented by the days—or adversity terrifies us—represented by the nights—the Christian spirit may remain steadfast, as did the one who said: “By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet known.”

## THE MEANING OF EASTER

The sacrament of Easter, which is now most clearly celebrated as a mystery of our Savior, was first enacted figuratively in the Old Testament, when the people of God celebrated Passover in Egypt after the lamb had been slain.

Its figure was completed in reality in Christ, who was led like a sheep to be sacrificed. When our doorposts were smeared with his blood—that is, when our foreheads were marked with the sign of the cross—we are freed from the destruction of this age as from the captivity of Egypt.

We celebrate the day of his paschal resurrection not only because he rose from the dead on that day, but also because of the other sacraments signified through it. For in him who, as the Apostle says, “died for our sins and rose for our justification,” a certain passage from death to life was consecrated in the Lord’s Passion and resurrection.

Indeed, the very word *Pascha* is not Greek but Hebrew. Nor is it derived from the Passion, as though from the Greek word *paschein*, “to suffer,” but from the Hebrew word for “passing over,” from which it is called *Pascha*. The Evangelist especially made this clear when the Lord was celebrating Passover with his disciples: “When Jesus saw,” he says, “that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father.”

This passage from mortal life to another, immortal life—that is, from death to life—is proclaimed in the Lord’s Passion and resurrection.

This passage is now enacted by us through faith, which is given to us for the forgiveness of sins, when through baptism we are buried with Christ, as though passing from the dead from worse things to better, from bodily things to spiritual things, from the conduct of this life to the hope of the glory of the future resurrection.

Because of the beginning of this new life, to which we pass, and because of the new man whom we are commanded to put on and the old man whom we are commanded to put off, purging out the old leaven so that we may be a new lump, “for Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” the first month among the months of the year was assigned to this celebration. For it is called the month of new things.

Since now the third period has appeared in the entire course of the world’s age, the Lord’s resurrection is three days long. The first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. In this third period the sacrament that had previously been hidden in prophetic mystery has now been revealed.

The reason the annual day of Easter does not return on the same day of the year is the Lord’s day and the fourteenth day of the moon.

## II. ON EASTER

Easter, therefore, is called not from the Passion, as some think, but from passing over. From the time when the Lord, passing through Egypt, struck down the firstborn of the Egyptians and freed the children of Israel, Easter was commanded to be celebrated. In Hebrew it is *phase*; in Latin, “passing over.”

It is called “passing over” first because on that day the Lord passed over Egypt, devastating the Egyptians and freeing the Israelite people. Second, because on that day the destroyer passed through the kingdom of Egypt and killed its firstborn. Third, because in this festival our Redeemer passed from this world to the Father, as John more fully makes clear when he says: “Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father….”

How it was first commanded to be celebrated can be found in Exodus, chapter 37. According to the text of the Old Testament, there is this distinction between Passover and Unleavened Bread: Passover is the name given only to the day on which the lamb was killed in the evening, namely, the fourteenth day of the first month. The fifteenth day of the moon, when the departure from Egypt took place, was followed by the festival of Unleavened Bread, which was established as a solemnity for seven days—that is, until the evening of the twenty-first day of the same month.

## III. ON EASTER

The annual Easter is the anniversary of Easter. For example: last year Easter was on the seventh day before the Ides of April, and in the present year Easter is on the same Kalends—that is, on the seventh day before the Ides of April—the date on which it occurred in the preceding year. Easter is discussed in this way alone because it is unique, the solemnity of solemnities.

## ON THE GREATER LITANY

[Col. 0537A]

Roman custom inserts one day, namely, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, which it calls the day of the Greater Litany, not a fast. In Greek, *litania* means “supplication” or “petition” in Latin; hence the name Rogations.

A serene mind, free from evil intention, can pray to God even while eating moderately. At that time, namely, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, enemies are accustomed to stir up wars against neighboring kingdoms. I think this was prudently provided for, either because at that time everything is in a kind of growth: the crops are sprouting, the fruits of the trees are emerging from blossom, the vineyards and olive trees are bursting forth, and the animals are grazing the fields. Since these things are necessary for our use, we must ask that they be preserved by the Lord.

The three days of Rogations, which are celebrated before the Lord’s Ascension according to the custom of the Gallican Church, were instituted by Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, because of the invasion of harmful [Col. 0537B] beasts, which at that time were grievously afflicting the people of God. This custom is observed among us to this day with the greatest devotion on account of various calamities.

## ON PENTECOST

The origin and cause of the feast of Pentecost must be recalled at somewhat greater length. The day of Pentecost began from the time when the voice of God was heard thundering from above on Mount Sinai and the Law was given to Moses.

In the New Testament, Pentecost began when Christ brought about the coming of the Holy Spirit whom he had promised. He said that the Spirit would not come unless he himself ascended into heaven.

Finally, when Christ had entered the gate of heaven, after ten days had passed, the place suddenly trembled while the apostles were praying. The Holy Spirit descended upon them, and they were inflamed so that they spoke the mighty works of God in the languages of all nations.

The coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven upon the apostles, poured out in a diversity of languages, transmitted the solemnity to later generations. For this reason Pentecost is celebrated and the day itself is held in distinction.

This feast of the Gospel corresponds to the feast of the Law. There, after the lamb had been sacrificed, the Law written by the finger of God was given to Moses after fifty days had passed. Here, after Christ had been killed—Christ who was led like a sheep to be sacrificed—the true Passover is celebrated, and after fifty days have passed the Holy Spirit is given. He is the finger of God, bestowed upon the 120 disciples, constituted according to the number of the Mosaic age.

This feast also contains another sacramental meaning. It is composed of seven weeks. The weeks of days produce the same Pentecost, in which the forgiveness of sin takes place through the Holy Spirit. The weeks of years, however, produce the fiftieth year, which among the Hebrews is called the Jubilee. In that year likewise there is release for the land, freedom for slaves, and restoration of possessions that had been purchased for a price.

Seven multiplied by seven produces the number fifty, with the addition of one, which the authority of the elders teaches was taken in anticipation of the age to come. For this number is always both the eighth and the first; indeed, it is always one, and that one is every day.

It is necessary for the most sabbatical (*sabbatissimum*, sic) people of God’s souls to gather there and to be completed in the place where a portion is given to those who are eight, as a certain interpreter wisely explained Solomon’s words.

For this reason, throughout all the fifty days after the Lord’s resurrection, abstinence being relaxed, the days are celebrated in pure joy, because of the figure of the future resurrection, where there will no longer be labor but rest and gladness.

For this reason knees are not bent on these days, since, as a certain wise man says: “The bending of the knees is a sign of repentance and mourning.” Hence throughout those days we observe the same solemnity that we observe on the Lord’s day, concerning which our elders handed down that neither fasting should be undertaken nor knees bent, out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection.

## ON THE FAST OF PENTECOST

[Col. 0538A]

The second fast is begun, according to the canons, on the day after Pentecost, in accordance with what Moses also says: “You shall make for yourselves seven weeks from the beginning of the month of barley.”

Many complete this fast on the authority of the Gospel after the Lord’s Ascension, understanding historically that saying of the Lord in which he says: “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.”

During the forty days after the resurrection, while he is subsequently read to have lived with the disciples, they ought neither to fast nor to mourn, because we are in a time of joy. But after that period has been completed, when Christ flew up into heaven and withdrew his bodily presence, then a fast must be proclaimed, so that through humility of heart and abstinence of the flesh we may deserve to receive from heaven the promised Holy Spirit.

## ON THE FAST OF THE SEVENTH MONTH

[Col. 0538B]

The third fast is the one observed by the Jews after the feast of Tabernacles, which the Church celebrates on the tenth day of the month of September. This was first established in the Law by the Lord, who said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying: The tenth day of the seventh month shall be called the day of atonement. It shall be holy for you, and you shall humble your souls in fasting. Every soul that does not humble itself on that day of fasting shall be cut off from its people; and every soul that performs work on that day of fasting, that soul shall perish from its people.”

The book of Ezra records that the ancients used this fast. “After the children of Israel had returned,” it says, “to Jerusalem, they celebrated there the feast of Tabernacles with great joy. Afterward they assembled in fasting, in sackcloth, with dust upon them, and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. They rose to stand, and read four times a day in the book of the Law of the Lord their God, and four times [Col. 0538C] they confessed and worshiped the Lord their God.”

In this seventh month the sun, according to the reckoning, begins to make the day shorter and the night longer—that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, when the equinox occurs. Therefore a fast is observed in this month, because the waning of the sun and the increase of night show that our life declines as death approaches; and this death is attended by the judgment of God and the resurrection.

## ON THE FAST OF THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER

The fourth fast is that of the Kalends of November. Its beginning or institution by divine authority is shown by the testimony of the prophet Jeremiah, when the Lord said to him: “Take the scroll of the book and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah and against every nation, if perhaps each one may turn back from his evil way, and I may be merciful toward their iniquity.”

Jeremiah therefore called Baruch, the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the Lord that he had spoken to him in the scroll of the book. And Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying: “Go in and read from the scroll that you have written from my mouth the words of the Lord in the hearing of the people, in the house of the Lord, on the day of the fast of the Law, if perhaps their prayer may fall before the Lord and each one may return from his evil way, because great is the anger and indignation that the Lord has spoken against this people.”

And Baruch, the son of Neriah, did according to everything that the prophet Jeremiah had commanded him, reading from the scroll the words of the Lord in the house of God. It happened in the ninth month that they proclaimed a fast in the presence of all the people in Jerusalem.

On the authority of this divine Scripture, therefore, the Church adopted the custom and celebrates a universal fast according to this observance.

## ON THE FASTS OF THE FOUR SEASONS, ON WEDNESDAY

There are four seasons of the year: spring, summer, [Col. 0539A] autumn, and winter. These seasons customarily call us back from the love of charity by their consummations [the reading is obscure]. During them we ought to fast, even if one of them occurs within Pentecost, when the sevenfold feast of the Spirit is celebrated, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “The days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.”

Augustine says of these fasts: “Although no ordination takes place, it is nevertheless necessary for our religion to celebrate the fasts of the four seasons.”

Pope Leo says of the same fast in his *Homilies*: “So that the fast may be celebrated at the conferral of sacred orders, as the custom of the primitive Church has established.” As in the passage: “While they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work,” and so forth. “Then, after fasting and praying and laying hands upon them, they sent them away.”

On this day, that is, Wednesday, two readings are read, because those who proceed to sacred orders ought to be admonished to have knowledge of the Law and the Prophets. For in the fourth age the Law and prophecy flourished, and in that same age David, most skilled in warfare—whose name is interpreted as “strong-handed”—overthrew Goliath, that is, pride, by humility.

Against this Goliath, that is, the devil, those who are advanced to sacred orders must fight in humility. On Thursday there is no Office or Mass; therefore you should sing the Office of Pentecost Sunday.

## ON THE KALENDS OF JANUARY

These Kalends, according to the madness of the pagans, ought to be called things to be avoided rather than Kalends. At that time, when judges ruled the children of Israel—that is, before Samson—there was a certain pagan prince in Italy named Janus, after whom the month of January was later named.

Uneducated people who did not know God feared this Janus as though he were a king and began to worship him as a god. They fashioned two faces for him because of the East and the West, and also called him four-faced, namely, Janus the double, because of the four directions, or the four elements and the four seasons.

But in doing this they created a monster rather than a god. Therefore Numa, after Romulus, made the first month of the year the month of a two-headed god, looking toward the end of the past year and the beginnings of the future year; and it was called January because it is the boundary and doorway of the year.

Thus uneducated people, worshiping it as though it were a god, consecrated that day to many obscenities. Some changed themselves into monstrous forms and transformed themselves into the appearance of wild beasts. Others adopted feminine gestures and feminized their masculine faces. And not without reason do those who have taken on a woman’s appearance lack masculine strength.

Some were polluted by fanatical omens and made a din by dancing and stamping their feet with the applause of dancers. Some observed omens so carefully that they would give neither fire from their house nor any other benefit to anyone who asked for it.

They also received diabolical gifts from others and handed them on to others themselves. They even kept little tables prepared throughout the night, filled with food, believing that the Kalends of January could provide such things for the entire year.

Because the whole world was filled with these and other miseries, the universal Church established a public fast on this day, so that the Author of life might put an end to these calamities.

But because, by the Lord’s generosity, these things are regarded as worthless by the faithful, although some slight imitations of them may, God forbid, still lurk among savage people, they must nevertheless be prohibited and driven out with every effort.

Nothing new should be presumed on these Kalends, but only what is done on the other Kalends of the months, except that the Lord’s octave is celebrated with exceptional worship, as stated above.

Nor should the following be left unmentioned: when these diabolical superstitions were once being practiced at Rome, a certain holy man named Almachius said: “Today is the octave day of the Lord’s day. Stop these superstitions of idols and these polluted sacrifices.” At the command of Alypius, prefect of the city, he was killed for this reason.

## ON THE THREE-DAY FASTS

The practice of fasting for three days is taken from the example of the Ninevites. After condemning their former vices, they devoted themselves entirely for three days to fasting and penitence, and, covered in sackcloth, they moved God to mercy.

## ON THE FASTS OF VARIOUS DAYS AND SEASONS
Source/review notes: The transmitted goat-blood and iron riddle remains difficult and is marked accordingly.

Besides these appointed seasons of fasting, some fast every Friday because of the Lord’s Passion. Many also regard Saturday as consecrated to fasting, because on that day Christ lay in the tomb—namely, so that the Jews might not be granted the satisfaction of rejoicing over what Christ removed by dying. [Col. 0540C] On Sunday, however, one must always refresh oneself, so that we may proclaim Christ’s Resurrection and our joy, especially since the apostolic faith observes this rule. After Easter and until Pentecost, although ecclesiastical tradition has relaxed the strictness of abstinence at the midday meal, nevertheless, if any monks or clerics wish to fast, they are not to be forbidden; for Antony, Paul, and the other ancient fathers are also said to have abstained in the desert during these days, and not to have ended their abstinence except on Sunday. Who, indeed, would not praise frugality or proclaim fasting? For fasting is a holy thing, a heavenly work, the gate of the kingdom, and an image of the future. Whoever practices it in holiness is joined to God, separated from the world, and made spiritual. Through it vices are overthrown, the flesh humbled, and the devil’s temptations conquered.

[Col. 0539]

# EXCERPTS OF THE FATHERS, COLLECTIONS, FLOWERS FROM VARIOUS SOURCES, QUESTIONS, AND PARABLES (C, G, S)

[Col. 0539D] Tell me, please, what woman is that who offers her breasts to countless children and, the more she is suckled, the more abundantly she overflows? That woman is Wisdom. Tell me where the human soul is when people sleep. In three places: either in the heart, or in the blood, or in the brain. Tell me who first fashioned a letter. Mercury the Giant. What first proceeded from God? The Word: “Let there be light.” Who were born and did not die? Enoch and Elijah. Tell me who first offered a holocaust to God. Abel, a lamb. Tell me who was first a mother? Mary, Aaron’s sister—or who was the first widow? Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. Tell me who first devised the plough. Ham, Noah’s son—or who planted a vineyard? That same Noah, who was also the first to become drunk. Tell me who was the first priest in the Old Testament [Col. 0540D]. Melchizedek; in the New? Peter and James, the Lord’s brother. Who was the first deacon? Stephen. Tell me who are the sons who avenged their father in their mother’s womb. The sons of the viper. Tell me what land the sun and wind did not see except for one hour of the day, neither before nor afterward. The land through which the people of Israel passed in the Red Sea. Tell me who first prophesied. Adam, when he said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”

Every person who is placed in sorrow should remember that saying, “Nothing in excess.” I saw a son eating with his mother, whose skin hung on the wall. I sit upon a horse not yet born, whose mother I hold in my hand. I seek a barbarian whom I cannot find. In the northern part of the city, where the water touches [Col. 0541A] the wall, lift up a square stone; there you will find the barbarian.

Tell me what is that thing which, when it increases, will become smaller, and, when it diminishes, gains increase. No one harms the Church more than the person who has the name and reputation of holiness. The more one is trusted, the more is demanded from him. The powerful suffer powerful torments, as it is said through the prophet: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld.” There are four keys: wisdom, or skill in reading; persistence in asking questions; respect for the teacher; contempt for possessions. Tell me how many years Adam, the first parent, lived. Nine hundred and thirty. Who are the three friends and enemies without which no one can live? Fire, water, and iron.

It is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting, for in the former the end of all human beings is recalled, and the living person considers what he will be. It is better to be rebuked by a wise person than to be deceived by the flattery of fools. Whatever your hand can do, perform it diligently [Col. 0541B], because there is neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld, where you are hastening. A patient person is better than a strong man, and whoever rules his spirit is better than one who captures cities. Both the one who justifies the wicked and the one who condemns the righteous are abominable before the Lord. As an open city without a circuit of walls is, so is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking. The lazy man says, “A lioness is on the road, a lion on the paths.” As a door turns on its hinge, so the lazy man turns in his bed. The lazy man hides his hands beneath his armpit and labors if he turns them toward his mouth. There are three things that cannot be satisfied, and a fourth that never says, “Enough”: the underworld, the mouth of the womb, and the earth. Water is not satisfied with water; but fire never says, “Enough.” For small but countless drops of rain fill the lofty depths of rivers. The inexperienced, just as they do not know how to speak, cannot keep silent. A habit confirmed by long practice is avoided only with great effort. It is very difficult indeed to meditate on new things in the Old Testament [Col. 0541C]. If you do not sell what you love, you will not buy what you desire; for gold often gleams in a cheap purse. Let every person be quick to hear and slow to speak. The sand of the sea, drops of rain, the days of the age, the height of heaven, the multitude of stars, the depth of the earth and the bottom of the abyss, and the hairs of the head, whether of the human population or of animals—these are to be numbered by God alone. The soul is ordered in three ways: by good thought, right speech, and the work of justice. Paul planted, Apollos watered, and the Lord gave the increase. Have Christ in your hearts and his sign on your foreheads. We have many enemies who hasten to impede our course. Always arm yourselves with the sign of Christ’s cross, because this is what the demons fear and flee, terrified by the sign of our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.

The Magi are those who gave gifts to the Lord. The first is said to have been Melchior, an old and gray-haired man, with a long beard and long hair, wearing a hyacinth-colored tunic, a milenus cloak [uncertain textile term], and hyacinth-colored and white shoes of mixed workmanship; [Col. 0541D] he was clothed with a headdress of varied composition. He offered gold to the Lord the king. The second, named Caspar, was a beardless, ruddy youth, dressed in a milenica tunic [uncertain textile term], a red cloak, and hyacinth-colored shoes; with frankincense, an offering worthy, as it were, of God, he honored God. The third, dark-complexioned and fully bearded, named Balthasar, wore a red tunic with varied white coloring and yellowish shoes; through myrrh he professed that the Son of Man would die. All their garments are Syrian. For it belongs to the pure to touch pure things, and to the holy to recognize holy things. Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor a body enslaved to sins.

What is evil? The corruption of good. What is death? The absence of life. For the life of the flesh is the soul, and the life of the soul is the Lord. God despises anyone who rejoices in another’s misfortunes, for God established this order: that the earth should serve the body, the body the soul, the soul the mind, and the mind [Col. 0542A] should serve God. There are fifty-five books of the Old Testament, but twenty-seven of the New. There is a certain bird in the regions of India, near the rising of the sun, having twenty wings; when its voice is heard, all are lulled into sleep and slumber. Its voice can be heard for a thousand paces. The name of this great bird is Goballus. There is also a stone in the Ocean Sea of such wondrous beauty that at times it appears and at times is covered by sand. When this bird has produced a very beautiful and melodious little bird, and sees the stone shining in the sea on a clear day, it is seized by desire for it and flies to seize it. While it is still spreading its wings, the stone is covered with sand. There is also a very large whale in the sea which, when it sees Goballus flying toward the stone, immediately rushes to its nest, seizes the little birds, and devours them. Goballus, returning in great heat to its nest and thinking that it would find some consolation for its labor, finds the nest empty and cries out seven times, so that it not only pours forth enormous tears, but all who hear it are unable to restrain themselves from weeping. [Col. 0542B] Then it plunges itself into the depths and dies.

And you, human being, are Goballus, possessing an exceedingly beautiful nature that produces lovely wisdom. The stone in the sea is the love of riches, which leads a person astray; abandoning wisdom, he flies to gather riches. The whale in the sea is folly, which takes away wisdom together with riches. Folly is born, and the person loses wisdom, loses riches, and is carried away by an unhappy death. Hence Gelflidius says: “Wisdom is better than gold, counsel more precious than silver, and more splendid than every precious stone; but discipline surpasses every gem-studded garment.” Wisdom, which bursts forth from the clearest vein of the golden fountain, is found more precious than every gem, every variety of pearl, and all treasures; it leads its followers to the palace of the heavenly paradise. It is better to live for one hour with the wise than to drink wine with fools.

God established three principal dwelling places: heaven, [Col. 0542C] earth, and the underworld; and in these three, three principal things. In heaven he established peace and eternity; on earth, faith, repentance, and the remission of sins; in the underworld, fear, eternal punishment, and no remission. Heaven and the underworld will be filled from the earth, which is placed between them. There are three remedies: baptism, repentance, and martyrdom. In evil deeds, humble shame is better than proud boasting in good deeds. Faith opens understanding; unbelief closes it. As night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly iniquity does not darken those who cling faithfully to the firmament of Holy Scripture.

Tell me the names of the two thieves who were crucified together with Jesus. Matha and Joca. Matha believed; Joca denied life and chose death. Tell me the name of the rich man who speaks to Abraham from the depths of the underworld. I tell you: it is Tantalus. Tell me the name of the soldier who pierced the side of our Lord Jesus Christ. I tell you: he was called Legorrius. Tell me [Col. 0542D] how many Fathers there are in this age. I tell you, three: the heavenly Father, the earthly father, and the father in teaching. Tell me how many senses a human being has. I tell you, ten: sight, hearing, taste, touch, smell, flavor, love, trembling, change, and speech. Tell me how many lives are attributed to the saints. Three: the present life, the life in good works, and the future eternal life. Tell me how many deaths are reckoned to sinners. Death in sin, the separation of soul and body, and the death of punishment. Tell me how many kinds of baptism there are. Three: the first baptism is that by which the filth of sins is washed away through the bath of regeneration; the second is that by which a person is baptized in his own blood through martyrdom; the third is the baptism of tears. Tell me what is that thing which filled heaven and the whole earth, breaks forests and branches, and shakes all foundations, but cannot be seen with the eyes or touched with the hands. Tell me the three victories of fire. The first victory is that in which the Holy Spirit appeared [Col. 0543A]; the second, that which lifted up Elijah; the third, that which burns sinners and the earth on the day of judgment. Tell me the three victories of wind. The first victory inflates but is not seen; the second sanctified the world after the Flood; the third will not be burned on the day of judgment. Tell me whether heaven is higher than earth. The earth is higher: Elijah and Enoch are in heaven. Many are rejected among human beings but chosen by God. Better is the person who is diminished in understanding and is in the fear of God than one who abounds in understanding and transgresses the law. The sinner rules in this age, but the righteous in the kingdom of God. There are some who are accustomed to examine the affairs of others while neglecting their own; they do not look at themselves in their most wretched conduct. Tell me what the first question was: whether in the body, or in the spirit, or in what place. In the crafty suggestion of the serpent to the woman, when it said in paradise: “Why did God command you not to eat from this tree?” Wisdom can proceed without eloquence; folly without eloquence [Col. 0543B] destroys many. Tell me from where day flees before night, where night runs, and where each of them rests. Day rests in the sun, and night in the cloud. Tell me where God sat when he created heaven and earth. Upon the wings of the winds. When a horse falls, beneath which are four feet, how much more can a human being, who speaks with one tongue, fall and be unable to repeat his own statement after he has fallen. It is very disgraceful to seek to learn at the moment when one ought to unravel a question. “You were small, Rome, when you raised me, but you will be smaller when you cast me down. As long as the Colossus stands, Rome also stands; when the Colossus falls, Rome too will fall; when Rome falls, the world too will fall.” What are you standing for, what are you amazed at, British ox? “I stand and am amazed; I seek a goad with which to prick the Gallic ox.” I bind my thoughts with a stylus, lest they escape through forgetfulness; I investigate as though I had not been reckoned, because the tongue slips from memory. Three unhappy people are read of in the law: the one who knows and does not teach; the one who teaches and does not practice; and the one who does not know and does not ask. A king is made in three ways [Col. 0543C]: because he breaks his enemies, because he arms his army, and because he exacts tribute. My soul hates a proud poor man, a deceitful rich man, and a foolish old man. Even the unskilled can criticize and slander.

Smooth at the top, but I am not smooth at the bottom;

I turn both ways with a different hand and perform a different service:

One part reverses whatever the other part has done.

I have tears, but there is no cause of grief.

There is a road to heaven, but heavy air hinders me.

And the one who begot me is not himself born without me.

Multicolored, fleeing heaven, I leave the earth behind:

I have no place on earth, nor in any region of the poles:

No exile now fears anything so cruel:

Yet with dripping drops I shall make the world grow green with leaves.

[Col. 0543D] Sixty queens, eighty concubines, and young women without number. Rise up, North Wind, and come, South Wind; blow upon my garden, and let its spices flow. The whisperer and the two-tongued person are cursed by God, for they will greatly disturb those who possess peace. The true one who lives and reigns on the summit, powerful among the people, gracious on the earth, gentle in the world, is great everywhere. There is no comparison with a faithful friend. A friend is sought for a long time, scarcely found faithful, and difficult to preserve.

How many are the rivers of paradise? Four: Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates; milk, honey, wine, and oil. How many are the waters of the world? Two: salt and water. Where is memory? In the sense. Where is the sense? In the brain. To whom sense is not given, neither is a brain given. Tell me three days [or “ways”?] that cannot be investigated. The Law in Moses’ womb, John in Elizabeth’s womb, and Christ in Mary’s womb. What stone is more beautiful and harder than the sun? The stone rejected by the builders—that is, Christ.

There are four errors of reading: the divine canon, in which the future life is narrated and proclaimed; history, in which [Col. 0544A] the deeds of events are narrated; number, in which future signs and divine solemnities are understood; and grammar, in which knowledge of words is understood. Behold how much the justice of a king is worth in this age: it is plainly evident to those who observe it. The peace of the people is the protection of the fatherland; the immunity of the populace, the king’s defense; care for the sick, the joy of human beings; temperate weather, the calm of the sea; the fertility of the earth, the consolation of the poor; the inheritance of children, hope of future blessedness for themselves. For what could be more foolish than for the mind to strive to hasten toward perfection when the whole condition of the body, worn out by old age, is hastening toward destruction? While the eyes grow dim, the ear hears with difficulty, the hair falls out, the face changes to pallor, fallen teeth diminish in number, the skin dries, the breath smells unpleasantly, the chest is suffocated, the cough cackles, the knees tremble, and swelling inflates the ankles and feet—and the inner person, who does not grow old, is weighed down by all these things: all these signs quickly declare that the house of the body is about to collapse. [Col. 0544B] What remains, then, except that, as the decline of this life approaches, one should think of nothing else than how to gain prosperous entry into the future life? Frequent reading and daily meditation are accustomed to labor more than bodily work. There are two prophets, one of whom prophesied after death and the other before birth: Samuel and John.

What is it that my mother gave birth to me, and soon was herself born from me? Tell me what person was not born, died, and after death was baptized in his mother’s womb. It is Adam. What man died twice and was born once? Lazarus, whom Jesus raised. Who was born twice and died twice? What human being died without being buried and without having the corruption of flesh? How many sons did Adam have? Thirty sons and thirty daughters. Alternatively: according to what others say, the number of Adam’s sons was sixty-two, and the number of his daughters fifty-three. How many years did Abraham live? One hundred and eighty-five. Who first raised a dead person? Elijah. Where did he raise him? At Galgata. [Col. 0544C] How many kinds of winged birds are there? Thirty-seven. How many kinds of serpents are there? Thirty-six. Who was first made prince? Ninus, son of Belus. What was the first city? Nineveh. Who built it? Ninus. Who was first made emperor? Saul. How many provinces are there? One hundred and thirty. How many languages? Seventy-two.

Consider, please, the order of miserable human life: you were created from earth, you tread upon earth, you will go into earth, from earth you will rise again, you will be tested in fire, and you will await eternal judgment; after these things you will possess either punishment or a kingdom. No one knows which of the two he will possess. There are two kinds of almsgiving: one, to extend a morsel to the hungry; the other, to supply instruction to the ignorant. The dwellings in the kingdom of heaven differ according to the merits of individuals, for diversity of works produces diversity of rewards. A wise man does not think that he dies but that he departs; nor that he leaves friends but that he changes them. Whoever desires to be a teacher [Col. 0544D] must first be a disciple. Philosophy is a certain love and pursuit of wisdom, which is the source and nurse of every art and discipline. Solomon rightly says: “Do not give your honor to strangers and your years to the cruel, lest strangers be filled with your strength and your labors be in another’s house, and you groan at the end, when you have consumed your flesh and body.” The lamp of the Lord is the human breath, which searches out all the secrets of the belly. Whoever offers sacrifice from the substance of a poor person is like one who slaughters his son in the sight of his father. Human judgment is corrupted in many ways: by love, hatred, and fear; the integrity of judges is often violated by greed, and mercy is turned aside contrary to the rule of justice.

Tell me, what is gold? The slave of death. What is silver? A place of envy. What is iron? An instrument of every craft. Who are those who are sick while healthy? Those who attend to other people’s affairs. Tell me by what means a weary person [Col. 0545A] does not become weary. By making a profit. Tell me what is longest. Hope, or thought. What do a king and a wretched person have in common? Being born and dying. What is best and worst? The word. What is pleasing to some and displeasing to others? Life. Not all are bishops. Consider Peter, but also consider Judas; look to Stephen and Nicolaus. Ἀνατολή, δύσις, ἄρκτος, μεσημβρία: east, west, north, south.

It is the labor of the craftsman to fashion deceptive forms;

You, almighty one, can create living things.

For many the world is dead, but they are not dead to the world.

They love the good things of the age, but do not attain them at all.

Empty in both respects are those who lose the future and do not acquire the present.

Know that in the last days perilous times will come. There will be people who love themselves, seeking not the glory of God but their own. A person reserves anger for another person and seeks healing from God, yet has no mercy on a fellow human being like himself. [Col. 0545B] If he has no mercy, who will plead for his offenses?

Tell me, in how many ways is everything that is said said? Four: either good well, or evil badly; or good badly, or evil well. In six days God fashioned the creation of things. On the first day he made light; on the second, the firmament of heaven; on the third, the appearance of the sea and earth; on the fourth, the stars of heaven; on the fifth, fish and birds; on the sixth, beasts and cattle; finally, in his own likeness, the first human being, Adam. Why was the human being made last? Because he is of greater honor. Once everything had been ordered and well arranged, the human being had to be formed in the manner of a bridegroom. There are six things which the Lord hates, and the seventh his soul detests: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising wicked thoughts, feet swift to run into evil, a false witness uttering lies, and one who sows discord among brothers. The apostles of Christ, preachers of the faith and teachers of the nations, received their proper lots for preaching in various [Col. 0545C] places throughout the world. Peter received Rome; Andrew, Achaea; James, Spain; Thomas, India; John, Asia; Matthew, Macedonia; Philip, Gaul; Bartholomew, Lycaonia; Simon the Zealot, Egypt; Matthias, Judea; and James, the Lord’s brother, Jerusalem. No particular lot was assigned to Paul with the other apostles, because he was chosen as teacher and preacher among all nations.

There are eight principal vices that trouble the human race: first gluttony, second fornication, third greed, fourth anger, fifth sorrow, sixth listlessness—that is, idleness or weariness of heart—seventh vainglory, and eighth pride. Do not abandon an old friend, for a new one will not be like him. Avarice in old age is like a monster. What are the three mute things that teach wisdom in the human heart? The mind, the eye, and the letter. There are twelve abuses in this age: a wise person without works, an old person without religion, [Col. 0545D] a young person without obedience, a rich person without almsgiving, a woman without chastity, a household [or “master”?] without virtue, a contentious Christian, a proud poor man, an unjust king, a negligent bishop, a populace without discipline, and a people without law. Through these things the justice of God is supported. There are seven things not found in this world: life without death, youth without old age, light without darkness, joy without sorrow, peace without discord, will without injury, and a kingdom without change. These seven, however, are found in the kingdom of heaven. Do not be sluggish and lazy, but work with your hands, so that you may have something to give to the needy and the poor; for as much is demanded from you as has been entrusted to you.

It is asked at what hour the Lord rose, since he had been in death for forty hours. According to Augustine it is described thus: From the day on which the Lord was crucified, four hours remained; twelve hours of the night of Saturday, twelve hours of Saturday itself, and twelve hours of the night [Col. 0546A] of Sunday; but he was in the tomb for thirty hours. There are four principal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. The angels were created before every creature of the world, and the devil was formed before the whole creation of the angels, as it is written: “He himself is the beginning of the ways of God.” Walk well, and may God be on your journey, and his angel accompany you. Tell me how many grades or distinctions of things there are. Six: nonliving things, living things, irrational things, rational things, mortal things, and immortal things. Last of all, above everything, is God. But just as all these things increase by degrees, so they surpass one another in the quality of their nature: a tree is superior to a stone, an animal to a tree, a human being to an animal, an angel to a human being, and God is placed above the angels. Envy always follows virtues. Lightning strikes the highest mountains. Nor is this surprising among human beings, since the Lord himself was crucified through the zeal and envy of the Pharisees. Only misery is free from envy, because no one envies the miserable. Whoever refuses to confer upon another what he does not lose by giving does not wash away the stain of envy from himself [Col. 0546B]. Service produces friends; truth produces hatred.

To what should bad priests be compared, except to baptismal water, which washes away the sins of the baptized, sends others to the heavenly kingdoms, and itself descends into a sewer? Whoever stops his ears to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard. A friendship that can end was never true. In this world the human soul is like a ship ascending against the force of a river’s current; it is not permitted to remain in one place, because it slips down to the depths unless it is admitted to the heights. It is a greater fault to sin openly than secretly: for the person who acts and teaches is guilty in two ways. Of such people Isaiah says: “They proclaimed their sins like Sodom.” What is worse than a house in which a woman holds authority over her husband? I saw a son nourished among four springs: if he was alive, he shattered mountains; if he was dead, he bound the living. I saw a two-footed creature sitting upon a three-footed one; the two-footed one fell, and the three-footed one collapsed. [Col. 0546C] I saw a son not born but raised up from three persons and nourished until he was called alive. I saw a dead person sitting upon a living person, and through the dead person’s laughter the living person died. I saw a weeping and murmuring virgin; her paths are the paths of life. I saw a woman with six eyes, sixty fingers, three tongues, and one speaking mouth.

I have six eyes, and with as many ears I take in everything at once;

I carry six fingers ten times over, sixty upon my body;

Of these, behold, four are driven away, ten from the flesh,

Yet I seem to retain only five times four.
