What you want to remain silent, tell no one; for from whom else do you demand silence that you have not imposed upon yourself? Whoever wishes to dedicate his body to continence should not presume to live with women. Frequent sight of women softens the mind, dulls the sense, and does not allow a man to be wise. Who will find a wise woman? For it is the custom of women [Col. 0546D] not to love anyone from a distance; whoever wishes to reconcile himself with women must be near them. A wise man rejects every woman, but a fool desires her and is miserably deceived by her. Beware, my little sons, of the appearance of women, through which death enters, and of no small destruction. For love is strong as death, and it is compared to fire. Love bears all things. Perfect love casts out fear. Love is born from the fear of the Lord, as the Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, and if I know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains; and if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.” Although someone may be a virgin in body and spirit, if he sins with his hands, eyes, ears, or tongue, how can he be called holy in body? For it is not enough for you to be idle from evil if you are idle from good. [Col. 0547A] Do not look upon a woman’s face, lest her appearance cause you to stumble. “Has anyone bound fire in his bosom without his garments being burned? Or can he walk upon coals without the soles of his feet being scorched?” Solomon said this about intimacy with women. Avarice must be despised, for it procures unjust profits for us in order to make us its own; we would belong to ourselves if it did not belong to us. Avarice, I say, must be despised, for like fire, the more it receives, the more it seeks. The miser is like the underworld, because the underworld never says, “Enough”; so the miser is never satisfied with gold. If a priest is ignorant of preaching, what voice will a mute herald give? Do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think with sobriety. Therefore, if you have secular lawsuits, appoint those who are contemptible in the Church to judge them, so that those whom spiritual gifts do not adorn may serve earthly administrations. If anyone is overtaken [Col. 0547B] in some offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.

Admonish your friend in secret and praise him openly. A fraudulent friend is quickly revealed through adversity; for in prosperity friendship is uncertain. Often friendship is cultivated through pretense, so that the person who could not deceive openly may deceive fraudulently. Certainly, no force excludes friendship, and no time abolishes it: wherever time may turn, it remains firm. Few are those who remain dear to the end. For many are turned away from love either by the adversity of circumstances or by some dispute in their dealings; often, too, the character of certain people changes through honor. Those whom they formerly held fastened to them by love, after they reach the summit of honor, they disdain to have as friends. Remember what was said: “It is better to preserve well-tested friends than frequently to seek unknown ones and lose those who are known.” If a fool remains silent, he will be thought wise. Let another person’s mouth praise you, not your own. [Col. 0547C] Every lazy person is a prophet. Do not say to your friend, “Go, and return tomorrow I will give to you,” when you are able to give enough now. Whoever wants to withdraw from his friend seeks excuses. The mouth of the righteous is a vein of life. Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, and the rod of discipline will drive it away. Membranes are dyed purple, gold shines; books are clothed with letters and jewels, and their Christ will die before the doors. Whoever loves wine does not curse the cups; whoever loves kernels does not curse the husks; whoever loves crops does not curse the oxen; whoever loves milk does not curse the cows; whoever loves God should not reject his neighbor; and whoever loves knowledge should not shun grammar, without which no one can be learned or wise.

For what reason is it written: “On that great day of tribulation no one will be delivered except Noah, Daniel, and Job”? In these three holy men, three classes of people seem to be signified who are promised deliverance from dangers on the day of tribulation. In Noah, the rulers of the Church are prefigured; in Daniel, the saints who pursue continence; in Job, married people who love [Col. 0547D] justice.

Adam lived fifteen years in paradise, Eve fourteen; others say seven, without a wife, for forty days. On the sixth day Adam ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, in the fifteenth year of his age. There are three vessels of languages: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. For these three languages were consecrated in the title of Christ’s cross. The first is Hebrew, because of the law; the second Greek, because of the wisdom of the Greeks; the third Latin, because of the Roman empire. Therefore these three languages hold primacy among all languages, for it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.” On the first day he made seven things: namely, unformed matter, angels, light, the higher heavens, earth, water, and air. On the second day, the firmament alone. On the third day, four things: seas, seeds, sowings, and plants. On the fourth day, three things: the sun, moon, and stars. On the fifth day, three things: the fish of the waters, reptiles, and flying creatures. On the sixth day, four things: [Col. 0548A] beasts, cattle, reptiles of the earth, and the human being. And all twenty-two generations were made in six days; there are twenty-two generations from Adam to Jacob, from whose seed all the nations of Israel are born; and there are twenty-two books of the Old Testament up to Esther; and there are twenty-two letters of the alphabet, by which the teaching of the divine law is constituted.

I bring great powers from small forces:

I open closed houses and again open those that stand open:

I guard the house for its master, but in turn I am guarded by him.

There is a house on earth, bright, which resounds with a voice:

The house itself echoes while the guest is silent, but the guest does not sound:

Yet both run together, the guest and the house as one.

Once I was a wave, and I believe I shall soon become what I was;

Now joined to the hard chains of the rigid sky:

I cannot endure being trodden upon, nor being held uncovered.

No one can see me, nor seize me in his hands;

I quickly spread the sharp crackle of my voice throughout the world;

With thunderous powers I am able to shatter oak trees.

[Col. 0548B] For I strike the upper heavens and traverse the fields.

Believe me, no thing remains without me as its ruler;

No light will see my forehead and face,

Who does not know that the vault of heaven revolves under my dominion,

The heights of the pole, the sun’s radiance, and the moon’s courses.

Behold, I do not fear the dangers of hard iron,

Nor the burning heat of flames; but through the blood of a goat

The hard force of its rigidity is softened by the blood of a tamed goat [the wording is corrupt or uncertain].

Thus blood overcomes what the iron mass fears.

Moses was the first to baptize—in the cloud and in the sea, and in type and figure. For the sea had the form of baptism, the cloud that of the Holy Spirit, and the manna that of the bread of life. For Christ baptized in the Holy Spirit.

I saw a guest standing on one foot, his body made of earth, his blood of beer.

Always remember that the woman cast the inhabitant of paradise out of his possession.

The mind has three daughters: Faith, Hope, and Charity.

From Adam to Christ the demons were unaware of these three things: that Christ would be born of a virgin, suffer on the cross, be buried in the earth, and descend to the underworld.

In three places in the Gospel the Lord is read to have become angry and inflicted bodily harm. The first time, he sent the whole herd into the sea; the second time, he cursed the fig tree; the third time, he drove the sellers and buyers out of the temple.

Who first said “Alleluia,” or in what place, or for what reason was it said? It was said between Tabor and Hermon. The prophet David said, “Alleluia,” that is, “Praise of God.”

Augustine said: “Alle, the age [*saeculum*]—save me; lu, make me; ia, O Lord.” [The reading *salvum?* is uncertain.]

Jerome said: “Alle, praise; lu, give; ia, the Lord.”

Gregory: “Alle, the Father; lu, the Son; ia, the Holy Spirit.”

Ambrose said: “Alle, light; lu, life; ia, the salvation of the Most High God.”

Sobriety preserves memory, sharpens perception, purifies the mind, directs the face, restores modesty, moderates vices, gives shape to the gaze; it smooths the ears, lightens the brain, gives expression to the tongue, unfolds speech, nourishes the marrow, strengthens the blood, cares for the veins, tightens the sinews, despises lust, refreshes sleep, prolongs old age, [Col. 0548D] manifests the mystery, and establishes the human being firmly.

Drunkenness is the first weakness: it envelops memory, empties perception, neglects the mind, confounds understanding, arouses lust, entangles the tongue, hinders speech, corrupts the blood, dulls the sight, disturbs the veins, blocks hearing, weakens the sinews, overturns perception, loosens the entrails, burdens the brain, weakens memory, removes strength, demands sleep, impedes menstruation, blocks the mind, stains the body, pollutes a person through its own vice, and leaves him without honor.

All the tribulations of this life are compared with passing waters, because if some tribulation comes upon us in this life, it does not remain but quickly passes.

True praise is uttered to the Lord by the mouth of one who prays,

if what flows from the voice has the inmost heart within it.

[Col. 0549A] To judge rashly the hidden things of another’s heart is a sin.

The inmost things of the mind will shine forth from the appearance of one’s works,

and what spirit inwardly nourishes the human mind.

For the saints always have something left in which they may grow,

while the glory of the perfect is a beginning.

All who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer insults from the impious and from those unlike themselves, and must displease them. All vices have force only in evil deeds; pride alone must be guarded against even in rightly performed deeds. For the good person is neither exalted by temporal goods nor broken by evils:

But the lover of earth and briefly flowering grass,

whether he lacks what he desires or enjoys it, is wretched.

Great is the sin of immoderate love of possessing,

and of desiring more than suffices for life.

For there is no praise in despising what you are not worthy to attain; and Ecclesiastes commands us to give a seventh part and an eighth part: that is, to believe both Testaments. Call no one blessed before death. This is because as long as we live, we are in combat; and as long as we are in combat, there is no victory.

For everyone who produces nothing fruitful for God

will, as a barren trunk, be made equal to firewood that has been burned.

The righteous will flourish like a palm tree:

they always have leaves, and, like the cedar of Lebanon,

they are to be multiplied and will touch the stars with their crown.

For there are some who cannot correct their own errors and attempt to rebuke others. Just as one who does not speak cannot lie, so one who does not wish to swear cannot commit perjury. It is not contrary to God’s commandment to swear; but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury. Through these kindling materials, as through certain steps, every sin grows together. For thought of evil produces delight; delight, consent; consent, action; action, habit; habit, necessity. While each person is anticipated by divine illumination, he is immediately assailed by the troubles of shameful thoughts. Those who are conscious of no offenses, or of only rare ones, are either never or rarely wearied by nocturnal terrors. For whatever is lofty ought to be concealed from many hearers and opened only with difficulty to a few. What is possessed with great love is lost with great pain; but we grieve less when deprived of what we love less because we possess it less. When someone receives a particular gift, let him not desire more than he has deserved, lest, while he attempts to seize the function of another member, he lose what he has deserved. Do not provide for the flesh in its desires; therefore, whatever is forbidden to be done in desires is, without doubt, permitted in necessity. But when the tongues of those who disparage cannot be corrected, they must be patiently endured in every respect. Often, when we complain about the lives of our neighbors, we try to change our place and choose the seclusion of a more remote life, plainly unaware [Col. 0549D] that if the spirit is absent, place does not help. Neighbors must therefore be endured everywhere, because Abel cannot come to be when Cain’s wickedness does not exercise him. You see that Sacred Scripture often speaks of eternal things which are ordinarily understood as referring to the present. It is called a Testament because it was written and sealed with suitable witnesses appointed on both sides. If sins are such as remove a person from the altar like one who is dead, penance must first be performed, and only then may this saving medicine be received. For whoever ceases to sin should not cease to communicate. Married people, however, should abstain from intercourse for many days and devote themselves to prayer, and only then approach the body of Christ. For at the radiance of morning light the Lord and Savior rose from the underworld, when the light began to rise for the faithful—a light that had set for sinners when Christ died; indeed, at that time the hope of the future resurrection is believed by all.

It is greatly necessary that the righteous person in this life be both tempted by vices and scourged with a whip, so that, while he is assailed by vices, he may not become proud of his virtues. The righteous must indeed be tempted, but by the temptation of affliction, not by the temptation of lust.

“To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom in the same Spirit.” For there are some who, through the gift of grace, understand even those things which they have not heard expounded by teachers: these, plainly, have received the word of wisdom. And there are some who cannot understand by themselves what they have heard, but retain what they have read in expositions and attain the knowledge they have learned. With what, then, are these filled, if not with the word of knowledge?

Just as God foreknew that a human being would sin, so he also foreknew how he would restore him through his grace—though he might have recovered himself by his own will.

“For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” He was joined to the Almighty insofar as he had united himself to him in love, since he considered Christ alone to be life for him and death to be gain.

The mysteries of divine power, which cannot be comprehended, are not to be scrutinized when they are not understood, but to be revered by faith.

Tell me, then, if you know: the circuits of heaven, the hinges of the earth, the abysses of the waters—where do they end, and where are they suspended? We know that it was made from nothing and hangs upon nothing. But if there is something that is called “nothing,” then nothing is no longer nothing; if this is nothing, nowhere does the mass of the world hang, nor is there a place where what has been created to exist can be. How, then, is that nowhere which we know exists?

Consider, then, if you are able, how the Red Sea was divided by a rod; how water flowed from the hardness of a rock when the rod struck it; how Aaron’s dry rod blossomed; how the virgin who came from his line conceived; how she remained a virgin even in childbirth; how a man dead four days was raised at a command and came out of the tomb with hands and feet bound, whom the Lord afterward commanded his disciples to release; how the same Redeemer, rising in true flesh and bones, entered to his disciples through closed doors.

For this reason the Law also commands two altars to be made in the tabernacle: one outside and the other inside; one in the courtyard and the other before the ark; one covered with bronze and the other clothed in gold. Yet on the golden altar flesh is burned, and on the golden altar spices are also set alight.

Why is this, dearest brothers—that what is burned outside consists both of flesh and of spices? We see these two things every day: they are two kinds of compunction, when some still weep through fear, while others already afflict themselves with lamentation through love.

All those spiritual fathers believed that there is a Trinity in God, although the Fathers never spoke openly about that same Trinity. For Isaiah heard those angelic hosts in heaven crying, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth.” To show the Trinity of Persons, “holy” is said three times; but to show that the Trinity is one substance, it does not say “of the Lords of Sabaoth,” but “Lord of Sabaoth.”

David likewise, holding the same view, says: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us.” Though he had named the Lord three times, to show that this one is one, he added: “And may all the ends of the earth fear him.” Paul also speaks, saying: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.” “From him,” namely, from the Father; “through him,” through the Son; “in him,” in the Holy Spirit. Since he had named “him” three times, he added, “To him be glory forever and ever.” For by not saying “to them” but “to him,” while saying “him” three times, he distinguished the Persons; and by adding “to him be glory,” he did not divide the substance.

“I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been instructed, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me.”

Is it some kind of skill to be brought low and to abound, to be filled and to hunger, to abound and to suffer want, so that such a great preacher indicates that he regards these things as something great? It is indeed a skill, and a wondrous knowledge of discipline, which must be learned with the whole effort of our heart. For whoever is not broken by his poverty, is not drawn away from giving thanks, and is not inflamed by desire for temporal things knows how to be brought low; for in this passage the Apostle calls “being brought low” suffering want. For immediately he adds the contrary: “I know how to abound.” Whoever is not exalted by the things he has received, does not twist them toward the use of empty glory, does not possess alone what he receives but mercifully divides it among the needy; whoever uses the food he has received not for filling his belly but for restoring strength, and gives the flesh no more than necessity permits—knows how to abound.

He knows how to be filled who tolerates the lack of food without complaint; and he who does not, under the compulsion of hunger, do something by which the soul incurs the snare of sin knows how to hunger. Therefore, whoever is lifted up by no pride in abundance and provoked by no greed in necessity knows how to abound and knows how to suffer want. Since he immediately added, “I can do all things,” lest we think these words express exaltation, he added, “in him who strengthens me.”

The number ten, multiplied by itself, rises to one hundred. Hence one hundred rightly signifies great perfection, as it is said of the elect: “Everyone who leaves house or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”

For no holy person abandons earthly things so that he may be able to possess more of them in this world; for whoever does not leave the earth through earthly striving but desires it—and whoever leaves one wife—is not going to receive a hundred wives. Rather, perfection is signified by the number one hundred, after eternal life is also promised: someone despises temporal and earthly things for God’s name, and here receives perfection of mind, so that he no longer desires what he despises, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life.

Thus he receives a hundred times what he gave who, receiving the spirit of perfection, has no need of earthly things, even if he does not possess them. For that person is poor who lacks what he does not have; but whoever, though not having something, does not desire to have it is rich. Poverty is a lack of mind, not a quantity of possessions; for one who is well reconciled to poverty is not poor.

Sickness of soul—that is, the weakness of sins—is harmful. Concerning it the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not burning?” But that weakness of the flesh is useful, the same Apostle confirms, saying: “When I am weak, then I am strong.”

The zeal of contentious people struggles not for truth but for the desire for praise.

Nearly all the virtues of the body change in the elderly; as wisdom alone increases, the rest diminish.

Matthew is honey, Mark milk, Luke wine, John oil, and the Church paradise. Matthew plows, Mark sows, Luke waters, and John gives growth. Matthew is a human being, Mark a lion, Luke a calf, and John an eagle. “There are many dwelling places in my Father’s house,” according to the diversity of labors. Matthew was in Judea, Mark in Rome, Luke in India, and John in Asia.

Just as it is impossible for a hunter to slaughter an animal across a mountain, so it is impossible for the devil to slaughter the souls of the saints through many prayers.

No one can redeem you after your death if you yourself do not wish to redeem yourself. Let the unlearned say nothing else.

The work of writing is not laborious: three fingers write, while the whole body labors.

## On the Twelve Stones

Chrysolite: this stone is concealed by light and day, so that at night it is fiery, but by day pale.

Sapphire: it resembles gemstones but is not six-angled. It is found in the Red Sea; when struck by the sun’s rays, it emits a burning brilliance from itself.

Sardius: a stone purple in color, which, as they say, serpents fear because of its brilliance.

Asbestos: it is dyed by the sun itself with a blood-red color, and they say that once kindled it cannot be extinguished.

Hyacinth: they say that it perceives breezes and the clearing of storms.

Carbuncle: red in color, beloved by the eyes; from a distance it breathes out a radiance, but nearby it is not seen.

Cerdamios: it has a brilliance under the open sky, but in a house it is blue in color.

Chrysoprase: drawing from gold and purple as though a mixed light, it is beloved by eagles.

Beryl: it is covered with a golden cloud and has six angles; they say that it burns the person holding it in his hand.

Emerald: they say that it possesses the power of a purple color resembling hyacinth, and they believe that lunar movements are stirred up from it.

Sardonyx: it is an inexpensive stone, black in color, nourished by deep waters.

Agate: a gleaming stone with golden drops, resistant to scorpions; when placed inside the mouth, it calms thirst.

## On the Luminaries of the Church

Do you now wish, my brother Desiderius, that I should tell you clearly a few things about writers who were able to bring forth for us, toward the spiritual splendor of contemplation, much concerning the obscurities which impede understanding because of the carnal mind—just as if I were speaking about the luminaries of the firmament that shine throughout the whole world?

But I fear that the judgment spoken against Susanna, daughter of Helcias, by the unjust judgment of the presbyters may be fulfilled in me: “Distress is upon me from every side”; and I likewise am in distress. For if I wish to rebuke any one of these men, I shall stir up adversaries and hostilities against myself everywhere; but if I do not do what you have asked, you will never find it. Yet it seems better to condemn the will of one person than to pass over or despise the council of many. For each one deserved to be praised carefully in the Holy Scriptures; but I shall touch all of them gently and lightly, with complete affection, so that I may fulfill both obligations peacefully.

Augustine, the flying bishop, like an eagle over the peaks of the mountains, not considering what happens at the mountain roots, declares in clear speech many things about the spaces of heaven, the positions of the earth, and the circuit of the waters. For one who wishes to climb a fruitful tree hastens gradually toward the higher branches and there to pluck the larger fruits; he leaves the nearer branches to little ones. We, however, are little, weak, and lesser; if we are able to gather the lower things, we are doing well.

[Col. 0552C] Hilary, bishop of the Romans, the light-bearer of the churches, which are both a lamp and a precious stone to which mortals ascend, speaks of everything in beautiful speech and with a golden mouth. Even if some things may have fallen beside the road, nevertheless a great harvest has arisen from him in the Scriptures.

Origen Adamantius, thinking of higher and greater things, and finding his own talent insufficient, connects one thing to another. When he had considered these things with excessive fervor of mind, he loaded himself with greater burdens; and when he could not proceed in this way, he was rolled down there in a great fall, and his fall was equal to his doctrine. Through certain foolish seductions he led many from the straight road onto another road, and his poison, like the ringing voices of Sirens, was able to harm through many songs: better than all in good things, worse in evil ones. For some of his teachings are beautiful and useful, while others have been sown beside the road. Nevertheless, many other, most evil disciples of his seem to have published many poisonous things under his name.

Eusebius of Caesarea, the key of the Scriptures and guardian of the New Testament, is praised by the Greeks as much greater in composition. Three outstanding works truly testify to this in his writings: the Canons of the Four Gospels; the ten books of Ecclesiastical History, which recount and preserve the New Testament; and the chronicle, that is, the summary of times. We have never found anything that could repeat all his traces in every respect.

Heliodorus, like a father looking into a very large house through a small opening, attempting to see what doors were closed, and having no key, was scarcely able to bring a few things into the light; but what he was able to relate, he related faithfully.

Ambrose, brother of the deep places, carried away on a wing and swift through the air, seems, as long as he enters the depths, to seize fruit from on high; and all his judgments are firm pillars of faith, the Church, and every virtue.

Dardanus, also taking up many questions through the cleverness of his mind, and not breaking a nut without reaching the kernel, confidently speaks many impossible things in the Scriptures.

Paulinus thought it proper to become a teacher, though he had not previously been a disciple, and believed that fruit could arise without a root; he attempted to do this. Therefore his writings need neither a writer nor paper.

Pelagius is “speech among the faithful” [sic]. Concerning him, a grave cause involving the arrangement of words has also been announced to me throughout almost the whole world, so that all the churches might shun him like a wolf from the forest. He laid a golden color over black poison and mixed a sweet spring with the bitterness of the first honey of wickedness.

Jovinianus, with a cheerful face but harsh heart, gave many drink from a very sweet beverage mixed with gall, composing and presenting contrary opinions to Christians as an occasion for hatred; and he also continually afflicts and harasses Jerome, who was especially laborious in all things, with endless questions.

Julius Africanus, whose trace all the southern and eastern peoples diligently and unanimously investigate in the weeks of Daniel, constructed the whole span of times with complete expertise and stern language; and no contradiction has ever been brought forth throughout the world against anything that was written by him.

Famonius, blamed by many for his harsh judgment, vigorously attempted everything difficult in its kind; and just as one cannot at one moment navigate the waves of the sea, or at one moment swim against the force of a torrent, so everything he wrote could not stand against the Holy Scriptures. Thus they are, as it were, a shadow beside a person.

## On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit

The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit enumerated by Isaiah:

The spirit of wisdom, which was with Adam, who first prophesied and named every creature that is beneath heaven.

The spirit of understanding, which was with Noah, who understood that he should do what was good until he deserved to hear the word of the Lord: “Make an ark of wood.”

The spirit of counsel, which was with Abraham, who did nothing except according to the counsel the Lord gave: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I will show you.”

The spirit of fortitude, which was with Isaac, who endured the injuries of the nations among whom he dwelt, knowing what had been said to Abraham: “I will give you this land.”

The spirit of knowledge, which was with Jacob, to whom God appeared in a vision in the place called Bethel when he was with Laban; and he appeared to him when he returned from Laban and God met with him, after which he was called Israel.

The spirit of piety, which was with Moses, who said: “If you do not forgive this people this sin, erase me from your book, which you have written.”

The spirit of fear, which was with David, who said, “Let it not happen to me that I should lay my hand upon the Lord’s Anointed,” when he was pursuing Saul.

## On the Seven Orders

[Col. 0553D]

*Cleros* means “lot,” that is, “portion.” Hence someone is called a cleric because he is the Lord’s portion, or because the Lord is his portion.

Our head signifies the mind. The hair signifies thoughts. The upper part of the head, when shaved, signifies the mind contemplating the Lord. We shave the upper part when we cut temporal thought away from the soul; we make the lower part even in a crown when, while necessarily thinking about temporal things, we arrange them harmoniously with the crown. Let the hair not grow over the eyes or ears—that is, let temporal thoughts not impede the hearing or sight of the mind. We should not be overly concerned to seek the custom of actors; rather, we can derive customs from the crown.

In the Old Testament, doorkeepers guarded the doors of the temple, receiving the healthy and expelling the sick. Now in the Church they receive the faithful and expel the unfaithful.

In the Old Testament, readers taught the people openly and distinctly the words of the Law; now readers are those who treat spiritual matters of conduct.

The exorcist, that is, the adjurer, in the Old Testament had the power to lay hands upon a person and drive out a demon; now he ought to drive vices from the soul through prayer.

Acolytes and candle-bearers prepared the light in the Old Testament; now in the Church they ought to prepare the light of truth for the minds of the faithful.

Subdeacons, just as in the Old Testament, so now receive the offerings from the presbyters in the house of the Lord, and offer the vessels of the Lord’s body and blood to the deacons. The deacon places them upon the altar and receives them from there.

In the Old Testament the Levites kept watch, guarding everything that pertained to the worship of the tabernacle and serving in the ministry. In the New Testament they provided everything necessary for the multitude that had one heart and one soul. Therefore, now, while guarding the ministry entrusted to them, they arrange upon the Lord’s table whatever is necessary for the heavenly banquet and mark it with the hand. The hands and the distinctions of the fingers signify the distinct works of the Holy Spirit.

These orders began with Aaron himself: those who were then priests are now called presbyters; those who were then chief priests are now called bishops. Presbyters share many things with bishops, but differ in a few.

The bishop has a staff so that he may govern his subjects and support the weak; he has a ring so that he may not disclose the sacraments of God to everyone.

The first garment is the linen ephod, which is interpreted as “shoulder garment.” It signifies the guarding of speech and the purity of good works, according to which each person ought to be ordained for the ministry of God, so that the sincerity of his heart and faith may be proved through them.

The second is the linen tunic, called in Greek *poderis* and in Latin *talaris*, because it descends to the ankles. Josephus calls it *byssina*. It consists of byssus and linen and signifies continence. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Be faithful unto death.”

The third is the girdle, so that the tunic itself may not fall loose and impede one’s steps. This plainly signifies the vigilance necessary for a priest, lest chastity, signified by the tunic, become slack and, exposed to the wind of pride and the cold of iniquity, impede the course of good works and finally become degraded by the stains of desire.

The fourth is the *mappula*, that is, the *amapha*, which, as its name indicates, was provided for wiping the hands. The priest ought to hold the *mappula* in his hands, so that voluntary action may agree with correction of the mind and the office piously bestowed by divine gift may be worthily exercised. It is also called a napkin, with which sweat and every bodily excess are wiped away; it is to be carried on the left side. It signifies the concern of worldly thought, by which in this life we extinguish pleasures, weariness, and other excesses of the mind.

The fifth is the *orarium*, which some call the stole; it is something granted. The *orarium* also properly suits prayers, being a fitting garment for the office. For it openly covers both the priest’s neck and breast, so that whatever he brings forth with his mouth may be animated by his spirit and attend to the reasoning of the highest order, and, singing psalms, sing with spirit and mind, because “the heart of the wise instructs his mouth,” so that he does not speak rashly.

The sixth is the dalmatic, named from the province of Greece called Dalmatia. It has two bands at the back and two at the front, because the Old and New Testaments shine with love of God and neighbor. To be immaculate belongs to one’s duty toward the Lord; to visit one’s brother pertains to one’s neighbor.

It has thirty fringes at the back and forty at the front. Each of the lines on either side has fifteen, because the line of charity produces fifteen branches from itself in the Old and New Testaments, in prosperity and adversity: charity is from God, is patient, is kind, does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not inflated, is not ambitious, does not seek what is not its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth; it believes all things, suffers all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

The left side has fringes because the active life is anxious and troubled about many things. The right has none; the contemplative life is tranquil.

The breadth of the sleeves signifies a generous dispenser of the Gospel. At times the deacon reads the Gospel wearing the *casula*, so that he may approach the Gospel unimpeded or prepare the Lord’s table. The *casula* is open on the right side, from which the arm emerges, because the author of the Gospel, whom the deacon ought to imitate, was pierced with a lance in his right side.

The seventh is what they call the *casula*; the Greeks call it the *planeta*, because it is the highest of all the garments and, by its protection, covers the others. We may therefore understand this garment as charity, concerning which the Apostle says, after listing the garments of the virtues: “Above all these things, have charity, which is the bond of perfection.”

Similarly, the *casula* signifies works of righteousness, as in: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.” The *suppar* is at the back, between the shoulders and before the breast. Behind the shoulders it signifies the burden of good work, where there is a double garment, because good works ought to be displayed outwardly in such a way that inwardly, before God, they are whole in the breast. It is double because in them there ought to be both teaching for human beings and truth inwardly. The two doubled garments ought to be joined, because ministry is performed well when good work and true teaching agree.

Let priests also clothe their feet with sandals, as granted by evangelical authority. In this footwear the foot is neither covered nor bare against the earth, signifying that the Gospel should neither be concealed nor rely upon earthly advantages. The Gospel ought partly to be covered and partly to be made manifest, so that the faithful may find instruction and those who despise it may not find material for blasphemy.

## On the Fifteen Signs

Jerome found in the annals of the Hebrews fifteen signs, occurring during the fifteen days before the day of judgment.

On the first day the sea will raise itself forty cubits high above the heights of the mountains and will be like a wall; the rivers will do likewise.

On the second day they will descend to the lowest depths, so that their summits can scarcely be seen.

On the third day they will be at their original level, as they were from the beginning.

On the fourth day the fish and all the sea monsters will gather upon the waters and will utter cries and groans, whose meaning no one knows except God.

On the fifth day the waters themselves will burn from their rising to their setting.

On the sixth day all grasses and trees will give forth bloody dew.

On the seventh day all buildings will be destroyed.

On the eighth day the rocks will wage war against one another; each will divide into three parts, and each part will collide with another.

On the ninth day there will be an earthquake such as there has not been since the beginning of the world.

On the tenth day all hills and valleys will be turned into a plain, and the earth will be level.

On the eleventh day people will come out of their caves and run about like madmen, and one will not be able to answer another.

On the twelfth day the stars and signs will fall from heaven.

On the thirteenth day the bones of the dead will be gathered together and will rise up as far as the tomb.

On the fourteenth day all people will die, so that they may rise together with the dead.

On the fifteenth day the earth will burn down to the deepest reaches of hell, and afterward will come the day of judgment.

## On the Lord’s Cross

The Lord’s cross was made from four woods, called cypress, cedar, pine, and boxwood. But boxwood was not part of the cross, except that a board of that wood was placed above Christ’s forehead, on which the Jews wrote the inscription: “This is the King of the Jews.”

Cypress was in the ground up to the board; cedar was across it; pine was above.

There are seven grades in which Christ served.

He was a doorkeeper when he destroyed the gates of hell and bound the devil.

He was a reader when he opened the book of the prophet Isaiah, in which he found: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor.”

He was an exorcist when he drove seven demons out of Mary Magdalene.

He was an acolyte, and so forth.

He was a subdeacon when he washed the feet of his disciples.

He was a deacon when he made wine from water.

He was a presbyter when he broke bread for his disciples, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.”

## On the Seven Sins

These are the sins of Adam, which are also original sins.

The first sin was pride, because he loved it in his own power more than he loved God.

The second was sacrilege, because he did not believe God.

The third was murder, because by sinning he killed himself.

The fourth was spiritual fornication, because he corrupted the integrity of his mind.

The fifth was theft, because he touched the forbidden food.

The sixth was greed, because he desired more than he ought.

The seventh was gluttony, because he ate the forbidden fruit.

These are also the seven punishments:

the first, the cursing of his earth;

the second, expulsion from paradise;

the third, his arrival upon a worthless earth;

the fourth, the death of his son;

the fifth, labor;

the sixth, bodily death;

the seventh, his descent into hell.

And because he sinned seven times, he received seven punishments.

These are the seven sins of Cain. Concerning Cain’s seven sins, others hold various opinions. They assert that the first sin was that he did not divide correctly; the second, that he envied his brother; the third, that he said, “Let us go outside”; the fourth, that he killed him; the fifth, that he insolently denied it, saying, “I do not know”; the sixth, that he condemned himself, saying, “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve forgiveness”; the seventh, that even after being condemned he did not perform penance.

There are six ages of the world:

the first, from Adam to Noah;

the second, from Noah to Abraham;

the third, from Abraham to Moses;

the fourth, from Moses to David;

the fifth, from David to John the Baptist and the coming of the Lord;

the sixth, from the resurrection of the Lord to the end of the age.

Thus the elders hand down that the world had been reckoned by Almighty God at six thousand years.

There are six ages of a human being.

The first, infancy, lasts seven years.

The second, childhood, lasts another seven years.

The third, adolescence, lasts fourteen years.

The fourth, youth, lasts twenty-one years.

The fifth, old age, lasts twenty-eight years.

The sixth is called late old age, the final age, or decrepitude; it has no fixed number of years.

## On the Four Orders
The columns supporting the hall fell, and therefore the hall was buried beneath them. Our Lord Jesus Christ made one hall, that is, the world; and he made this hall from four things, namely, the four elements, which are fire, air, earth, and water. In this hall he made four corners, that is, the four parts of the world: East, South, West, and North.

To support this hall, the Lord appointed four columns, which supported that hall, namely, the four orders of human beings: those who pray, defenders, merchants, and laborers. The Lord appointed those who pray in the world for this purpose: that they might pray for the other orders, shine upon them through the night—for they are in the darkness of ignorance, that is, in sin—and bring them back to the light by showing them a good example and giving good preaching. But they neither live well nor teach; rather, by their evil example they kill the people of God. Of them it is said: “The stars did not shine,” and therefore they fell from heaven; and thus this column fell.

He appointed defenders, that is, soldiers, so that they might defend the other three orders. But when they ought to have defended them, they became robbers, living by robbery; from this they clothe themselves, and from this they suppose that they perform almsgiving, though it profits them nothing. Of them it is said: “Their days were consumed in vanity, and their years in haste.” Therefore the wrath of God rose against them, and thus this column fell.

He appointed merchants so that they might protect the other three orders from want: so that from Eastern abundance they might replenish Western poverty, and conversely, from Southern abundance they might replenish Northern poverty. But they mock the people, because through fraud and perjury they earn everything they possess. Of them it is said: “Those who trust in their strength and glory in the multitude of their riches shall all be placed in hell, and there death shall devour them.” And thus this column fell.

He appointed laborers so that the other three orders might be fed by their labor. These do indeed perform well what they were appointed to do, as it is said in the psalm: “The labors of your hands,” and so forth; those who eat of them are blessed. But although they could live justly in this way, by their own labor and sweat, and feed the people of God from it, thereby supporting the hall so that it would not fall altogether, and thus reach the kingdom of God, they fall by going astray. For first they take away from their Lord Jesus Christ, from the Father, and from his mother the Church their due rights, tithes, and firstfruits. It is astonishing how they dare to ask bread from him whose own they take away, when it is said: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

Again, they envy their neighbors their honors, fields, and vineyards; and, if they can, they remove one boundary marker from him or move the boundary. Thus this column falls, and thus nearly the whole world has perished, unless he comes to its aid who created it.

Brothers, since we cannot accomplish this ourselves, let us also beseech the King, our Lord Jesus Christ, that he who made the world may rule us and the world, so that we may be able to reach the kingdoms of heaven, with the help of him who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## ON RECEIVING THE EUCHARIST

In the Miracles of Pope Boniface we read that on the Lord’s Day he celebrated Mass. After Mass he blessed the bread, and while he was giving Communion to the people, a Jewish boy came, entered the church, took bread from the hand of Saint Boniface, and ate it. Immediately he began to burn and cry out: “Saint Boniface, hasten to baptize me, for the bread that I have received unworthily is condemning me.” The cry reached the Jews.

By the judgment of the Jews his father came, filled a house with wood and thorns, kindled a fire, and threw his son inside. The boy began to walk unharmed through the midst of the flames, but his mother, looking on, could not see her son through the flames. When she began with a great cry to call upon Saint Mary to heal her son, the Jews threw her into the middle of the fire.

When blessed Boniface heard this, he came dressed as though for Mass, entered the fire with many Christians, and brought the boy and his mother out unharmed. Let us beseech God to grant that we may receive his body in such a way that we may merit eternal life, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

## HYMNS FOR THE DAY OF JUDGMENT

“I inquired of the prophets concerning that day of judgment, whether it would be far off or near; they gave me these signs: On the dreadful day.”

God made the martyrs blessed, giving them his own Passion, so that they might suffer for him and intercede for us: on the dreadful day.

When dissolution and great tribulation come, intercessions will cease, and there will be an end: on the dreadful day.

God will appear from the south; he will come in terror to lay the world waste and repay vengeance: on the dreadful day.

The sun and moon will be extinguished, the stars will fall to earth, heaven will move from its place and be folded like a book: on the dreadful day.

The foundations of the earth will collapse with great wrath; the mountains will melt, the earth will dry up together, and the sea will become dry: on the dreadful day.

Christ will appear in glory; he will sit upon the throne to judge his people, to whom he himself gave the law: on the dreadful day.

He will fulfill what he said; the angel will sound the trumpet, and in the twinkling of an eye they will hear the voice: on the dreadful day.

There the wicked servant will stand, awaiting the coming of his lord; at the hour when he does not expect it, his deeds will be examined: on the dreadful day.

The slander of the proud and the plunder of the wicked will then meet there with the tears of the wretched: on the dreadful day.

Books are brought forth in the midst, and there will be a record; our sins, gathered from the beginning, are recited by the angels: on the dreadful day.

Wretched me—what shall I do, or what shall I answer? I shall hear with my own ears what is hidden from me: on the dreadful day.

No person is accepted on account of status; sacrifices will cease. The rich who have gathered sins will not redeem themselves: on the dreadful day.

O what mighty kings, whom nations obeyed! There they will stand before the throne, groaning with great weeping: on the dreadful day.

The exalted princes will gasp there from the heat; there will be no one to make wind for them or wipe away their sweat: on the dreadful day.

How bitter is that day of which the Prophet speaks—very swift and dreadful, terrifying to sinners: on the dreadful day.

Hell lies open, swift, dark, and horrible; it will open its exceedingly insatiable jaws: on the dreadful day.

Let there always be concern, as our God warns us; let our hearts not be weighed down with gluttony and wine: on the dreadful day.

Let such torments be prepared as our mind cannot desire; but the place itself reveals what will be there, where weeping will be in vain: on the dreadful day.

The only-begotten Son will judge the world; those who do not confess Christ will perish at the end: on the dreadful day.

**Χριστοῦ**—“of Christ”: so that his words may be fulfilled and his commandments carried out; those days will be shortened and will be like a single hour: on the dreadful day.

**Υιὲϊ**—“O Son”: those will be the days when the Lord comes to earth. God, deliver us from that eternal punishment: on the dreadful day.

With the devil instigating her through the serpent, Eve sinned. God, deliver us from that eternal wrath: on the dreadful day.

Bold is the young man while his restless flesh burns; boldly you act, wickedly defiling your limbs. Pay attention, human being, for you are dust and will return to dust.

Brief is the time, young man; consider that you will die. The final day comes, and you will lose your fairest flower. Pay attention, human being.

By consenting to your flesh, you deceive your soul; when you bend toward evil lust, you remain deceived. Pay attention, human being.

Your teeth gnash, your lips grow harsh, and your tongue produces evil; your life trembles. Pay attention, human being.

Lifting your eyes to see vanity, your wretched mind is bent, and you raise your limbs toward evil. Pay attention, human being.

You formed an evil plan and gave great offense, because you followed swelling pride too far into lust. Pay attention, human being.

You seek glory among the people, you love human praise, and you do not desire to please God, who looks upon you from heaven. Pay attention, human being.

You presumed to receive passing honor, but greater punishment follows the one to whom greater things are entrusted. Pay attention, human being.

You always look upon the earth and always think about the earth; yet here you will leave everything because of which you walk proudly. Pay attention, human being.

The flesh has dragged you into the pit; take care lest you perish miserably. Hasten to correct yourself before the end comes. Pay attention, human being.

Mourn now, while there is time, lest you groan at the judgment, where groaning is of no avail and there is no intercession. Pay attention, human being.

Labor bravely now, while you are in this body; amend your vice, lest you groan forever. Pay attention, human being.

Let greed not break you, nor frailty bend you; and do not participate any longer with the devil. Pay attention, human being.

O, if only you understood from the heart what the commandments of the law are—that the adulterer, for example, should be subjected to stoning. Pay attention, human being.

Through the Savior great redemption has come again, so that everything committed may be forgiven through repentance. Pay attention, human being.

Why do you not wish, young man, to return to the Lord? Ask his mercy, that he may grant forgiveness. Pay attention, human being.

Break the hardness of your heart and the wickedness of your mind; return to the Lord before the end comes. Pay attention, human being.

Christ receives repentance and grants forgiveness from that true soul which mortifies its flesh. Pay attention, human being.

Terrible Christ comes to judge the world, and he himself will repay each according to his work. Pay attention, human being.

The day of judgment will come; there will be stern judgment, where the father does not help the son, nor the son defend the father. Pay attention, human being.

**Χριστὸς**—“Christ”—comes with the angels, and he himself will repay each person according to his works. Pay attention, human being.

**Υἱὸς**—“the Son”—obtains grace and wipes away the stains of sin; humility and charity lead to heaven, to the homeland. Pay attention, human being.

He has good and excellent zeal who loves God and his neighbor; he will rejoice for ages and be glad forever. Pay attention, human being, for you were made from earth and will return to earth.

[Col. 0559]

## SIX FORMULAS OF PRAYER (G)

### FIRST PRAYER

[Col. 0559B]

Let us specially beseech Christ, the Ruler of the world, the King born of a virgin, and the Lord, together with the apostles. May the apostle Peter open for me the door of life, and Paul, preacher to the nations, bring me into heaven. May Andrew grant me strength before the tribunal of Christ. May James, having prostrated the darkened host, entrust me to the bosoms of the angels. May John, with grace, give me drink from the breast of the Almighty. May Philip bring me, adorned with lamps and rejoicing, to the King. May Thomas sing to me forever, amid the praises of instruments, of triumphal merits. May Bartholomew commend me in honey-sweet words where the Lover of Angels delights the hosts with himself. May James son of Alphaeus return to me a golden crown, shining with various flowers of gems in radiant light. May Simon the Zealot grant me holy necklaces, from which the angelic height will be seen by all in wonder. May Judas carry me, with voices confessing, to ineffable endurance, where the divine Trinity is adored with threefold voices: all together, with one mouth, they praise the Lord, the Father, the Son, and the Spirit.

### PRAYER II

O Jesus of Nazareth, son of Mary, I am guilty before you, the King of kings, whose kingdom is without end. My God and Lord, I am guilty before you of death; be patient with me now, you who are strong and powerful. I adjure the true Lord, ever one and threefold, that I may be able to visit Saint Martin. I now ask the King of kings, who is divine light, that I may be able to visit Saint Martin. Christ, God of gods, whose divinity is wondrous, make me come sound to mourn beside Saint Martin. Direct my path clearly, O Jesus of Nazareth, so that I may be able to lament my sins there in purity. My help in shipwreck will be the aid of Martin, Christ’s wondrous soldier. I desire to visit you; make me come to you, O my Saint Martin, who are of such great virtue.

O Saint Martin, now intercede, I beg you, for me who suffer, oppressed by the foul stain of sins. O my holy Martin, intercede for me now, lest the blazing locks of everlasting punishment touch me. O my holy Martin, beloved by the heavenly hosts, do not let me share in punishment; help me. O Saint Martin, help me, that at the end of life I may enjoy everlasting bread. Glory to you, Father, who are brother and mother.

### PRAYER III

Ruling Lord, almighty God, who are one Trinity—the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, with the Holy Spirit—who are always in all things, who were before all things and will be through all things, blessed God forever: I commend my soul into the hands of your power, that you may guard it by days and nights, hours and moments. Have mercy on me, God of the angels. Guide me, King of archangels; guard me through the prayers of the patriarchs, through the merits of the prophets, through the intercessions of the apostles, through the victories of the martyrs, and through the faith of the confessors who pleased you from the beginning of the world.

May Saint Abel pray for me, he who was the first crowned through martyrdom. May Saint Enoch pray for me, who walked with God and was taken away from the world. May Saint Noah pray for me, whom the Lord preserved in the flood because of his righteousness. May faithful Abraham, who first believed God and whose faith was reckoned as righteousness, plead for me. May Saint Isaac intercede for me, who was obedient to the Father unto death, as a model of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was offered to God the Father for the salvation of the world. May blessed Jacob ask for me, who saw the angels of God coming to his aid. May Saint Moses pray for me, with whom the Lord spoke face to face. May Saint David assist me, whom you chose according to your heart, Lord. May the holy prophet Elijah pray for me, whom you chose to be taken up to heaven in a fiery chariot. May Saint Elisha pray for me, who raised a dead man after death. May Saint Isaiah pray for me, whose lips were cleansed by heavenly fire. May blessed Jeremiah be present for me, whom you sanctified in his mother’s womb. May Saint Ezekiel pray for me, who saw wondrous visions of God. May the chosen Daniel, beloved of God, pray for me, who solved the king’s dream and interpreted it, and was twice delivered from the lions’ den; and the three youths were delivered from the fire; and the twelve prophets: Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Habakkuk, Jonah, Nahum, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, and Ezra. I invoke all these for my aid.

May all the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ assist me: Peter and Paul, John and Andrew; the three Jameses; Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew; Barnabas and Matthias; and all your martyrs. Drive from me, Lord, the desire for gluttony, and give me the virtue of abstinence. Flee from me, spirit of fornication, and give me the love of charity. Extinguish greed, and give me voluntary poverty. Restrain my anger, and kindle in me great gentleness and love of God and neighbor. Cut away from me, Lord, worldly sorrow, and increase spiritual joy in me. Drive from me boasting of mind, and grant me compunction of heart. Lessen my pride, and perfect true humility in me.

I am unworthy and an unhappy man. Who will deliver me from the body of this death of sin, except the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ? For I am a sinner, my offenses are innumerable, and I am not worthy to be called your servant. Awaken weeping in me; soften my hard, stony heart; and kindle in me the fire of your fear. For I am dead ashes. Deliver my soul from all the snares of the enemy and preserve me in your will. Teach me to do your will, for you are my God. To you be honor and glory, forever, etc.

### PRAYER IV

My God and my Father, my King and my protector, cleanse me from my sins and wash me from my iniquity, Lord, and save me; for I have committed many sins before you and am not worthy to be called your servant because of my iniquities, which are without number.

Forgive me, Lord, my debts, for I beseech you with every diligence and with the innermost love of my heart. I beg you, Lord, pour true love into my heart and heavenly love into my understanding; and let your mercies overshadow me, Lord God. Recall the struggle to my memory, so that I may merit to see in the heavenly kingdom, where the Father reigns with the Son and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

### PRAYER V

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: Gabriel, be my breastplate; Michael, be my belt; Raphael, be my shield; Uriel, be my protector; Rumiel, be my defender; Paniel, be my healing. And all saints and martyrs, I beseech you to help me before the just Judge, so that they may forgive me my sins on the day of judgment, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

I pray and beseech you to deem me worthy to have a place in your prayers, so that no enemy or adversary may be able to harm me. I have sinned, Lord, before you and before your angels. Show your mercy toward your servant. To you, Lord, belongs justice; to you, Lord, belongs mercy. Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed, for you are my salvation; and may my prayer come to your holy temple. To you be honor and glory, forever and ever. Amen.

### PRAYER VI

Open for me, who knock, the door of life. Let the prince of darkness not confront me, let the foot of pride not come against me, and let a strange hand not touch me apart from you. Rather, receive me according to your word and lead me to the banquet of your feasts, where all your friends feast with you. You are Christ, the Son of the living God, who live and reign with your Father forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0561]

## ON THE SEVEN WORDS OF CHRIST ON THE CROSS (G, S)*

### PRAYER

[Col. 0561B]

Blessed forever and beyond be the sweet name of our Lord God Jesus Christ and of his most sweet virgin mother Mary. Amen.

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who, hanging upon the cross at the end of your life, spoke seven words, so that we might always keep those most holy words in memory: I ask you, through the power of those seven words, to spare and forgive me whatever I have sinned and committed through the seven deadly sins or those proceeding from them, namely pride, avarice, lust, envy, anger, gluttony, and sloth.

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, just as you said, “Father, forgive those crucifying me,” make me, out of love for you, forgive all who do evil to me. And just as you said to your mother, “Woman, behold your son,” and then said to your disciple, “Behold your mother,” make your love and true charity unite me with your mother.

And just as you said to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise,” make me live in such a way that at the hour of death you may say to me, “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

And just as you said, “Eli, Eli, lamma sabachtani”—that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—make me say at every time of my distress and tribulation, “My Father and Lord, have mercy on me, a sinner; rule me, my King and my God, who redeemed me with your own blood.”

And just as you said, “I thirst,” namely for the salvation of the holy souls who were in limbo awaiting your coming, make me always thirst to love you, the fountain of living water, the fountain of eternal light, and desire you with my whole heart.

And just as you said, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,” make me, at the hour of my death, able freely and perfectly to say to you, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” Receive me as I come to you, since you have not appointed a fixed time for my life.

And just as you said, “It is finished,” signifying that the sufferings you had endured for us miserable sinners were now ending, grant that at the departure of my soul I may hear that sweetest voice of yours: “Come, my beloved soul, for I have now arranged to bring your hardships to an end. Come, that with my saints and elect you may ascend into my kingdom to feast, rejoice, and dwell forever and ever.” Amen.

[Col. 0561]

## A LITTLE BOOK ON MEDITATING UPON THE PASSION OF CHRIST THROUGH THE SEVEN HOURS OF THE DAY

### PREFACE

[Col. 0561C]

“Seven times a day I have praised you.” You asked me to show you some manner of meditating on the Passion of God according to the seven hours of the day, because, as you said, above all things you desired to be able to keep frequent remembrance of him who wished to suffer so much for you.

Therefore, with love for him and with his help, I have written, as briefly and as well as I could, what you most devoutly requested—not explaining everything, but touching upon many considerations which I have left for you to explain and complete. For a contemplative and spiritual soul draws much from little, whereas a simple and carnal soul expresses little from much.

Therefore know also that if you wish to advance in this knowledge, which is the noblest of all kinds of knowledge, you must abstain with great care from delicate food and excessive drink, and take only what is necessary from either [the printed form has *parcent*, corrected in the note to *parcum*]. You must also beware of much speaking, vain pleasure, and foolish amusement. For it is not fitting for one who wishes to feel Christ’s sorrow to occupy himself uselessly with playful words and matters and with empty joy.

To put it briefly, you must also abstain from temporal anxiety and carnal pleasure or consolation. You must think with great care that carnal consolation is incompatible with contemplation of the Lord’s Passion. It is also necessary that at times you think of these matters in your contemplation as though you were present at the time when he suffered. Conduct yourself in sorrow as though you had your Lord suffering before your eyes. Then the Lord himself will be present and will receive your prayers.

## MEDITATION AT COMPLINE

First, then, one must begin with Compline. Compline may be so called because in it the course of the day is completed. Likewise our Lord Jesus Christ, having completed the course of his preaching and having eaten supper with his disciples—you should frequently and devoutly think about that supper and about the most sacred gift of his body and blood given there—after that supper, which was celebrated so uniquely and gloriously, and after washing the disciples’ feet and delivering his discourse, went out with his disciples to the Mount of Olives, where he was to be captured and separated from his friends, when what the prophet had said had to be fulfilled: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.”

Second, here you will think about how the Lord said to his disciples, “Rise, let us go from here,” and you will answer him in spirit, “Lord, where shall we go?” And he himself will answer you in spirit: “We shall go to my Passion; we shall go to my anguish and to separation from you bodily in this world.” And: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” And you will answer: “I will go, Lord, and I also will go with you, and I will follow you both unto death and unto life. Lord Jesus, do not let me be separated from your side.”

Afterward think about how he said to his disciples: “Are you sleeping? Watch and pray that you do not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” And you will answer the Lord again: “Lord, who commanded us to watch and pray, give us grace to do this. For although we are willing in spirit, the flesh is weak, wholly sluggish, and wholly full of sleep, food, and drink; nor can it endure to watch perfectly with you for even one hour and to pray with you lest it fall into temptation.”

In this way you can entreat the Lord himself. Look also at how the disciples lay sleeping, and how he showed the manner of prayer by the posture of his body, by his devout words, and through the angel who appeared there. For it is said that he fell on his face upon the earth and prayed there, saying: “Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” And behold, an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him; and in his agony he prayed at greater length, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling down.

Note, therefore, all the words and the manner. You too must do this, namely, fall upon your face. Do not look backward, but keep before you and hold in your mind the things for which you are asking; do not speak while keeping your heart elsewhere. Let your will be present, and pray not lukewarmly but with great labor and sorrow, as God did. Pray not briefly but at length. Then you will immediately see how the angel will be present to help and strengthen you and present your prayer to God.

For the sake of an example for all of us, that angel appeared, strengthening the Lord. And one must pray not once but frequently, as he himself showed through his threefold prayer. Pray for the living, for sinners, for yourself, your friends, and those entrusted to you.

Consider, then, what that sorrow was when his most devoted disciples went away, when they had to be separated from their beloved master—how unwillingly, how devoutly, how weeping, uttering what voices, cries, and sighs, departing like orphans. Consider that as they went away they were saying: “O good master and gentle father, O kind Lord, why are we thus separated from you? O holy father, why do your sons flee from you? Where shall we go, Lord?” They could have said these and many similar things.

O how often they looked back, seeing how their Lord was bound and dragged away dishonored! O how often they threw themselves upon the ground and cried out to heaven! You can think, if his mother, the Lady, had been there, what she would have done. Say in your heart: “O my Lady, how can you not consider how your most beloved son is going? O Lady, how evil, how bitter tomorrow will be for you, when you hear and see so cruel a spectacle! O Lord Jesus, who can endure everything, may he not burst with grief when he thinks of you. O good master, innocent lamb, how you went among wolves, and the worst dogs bit you; yet you did not cry out, but went to death like an innocent lamb.”

For it is said that they placed a chain around your neck and bound your most holy hands; and, rushing upon you as though against a robber, withdrawing and striking you, they led you to Annas and afterward to Caiaphas, where the leaders of the Jews had gathered and were awaiting you.

You can also think well about how badly they received him and made him sit dishonorably, perhaps vilely upon the ground before them. And you will think about and see all these things in spirit.

Thus far concerning Compline, about which you will think much.

## MEDITATION AT MATINS

At the hour of Matins you will rise from your sleep, full of tears and worn out with sorrow because of what you considered after Compline. Then you will meditate and see in spirit how your Lord sat among his enemies, abandoned by his disciples and friends.

Behold, I believe you will say: “O Lord Jesus, how do you sit thus, so despised and dishonored? Where are your disciples and friends? O my only good, my singular joy and my counsel, what shall I do when I see you standing thus?”

You will also say to John, who was likewise present: “O John, how does the Lord and our master stand thus?” Think how Peter and John grieved when they saw these things. Think how the Lord Jesus said to the Jews, “Amen I say to you, you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of God.” Consider how then the high priest tore his garments, saying, “He has blasphemed!” and how almost all who stood around then rushed together upon your Lord Jesus.

Some struck his most serene face with their palms; others, with the back of the hand, struck his sweetest and honey-flowing mouth; others struck his most holy neck; others spat upon his kindest face; others plucked out his most holy beard; others dragged him by his venerable hair; and, as I think, they trampled your Lord and the Lord of angels between their feet, treating him brutally without reverence and without any pity.

And thus Jesus gave himself to each one for your sake. For since they were utterly cruel and without mercy, they inflicted upon him every evil and insult they could, some in order to please their superiors, who were exceedingly savage.

What will you do, then, if you see these things? Would you not throw yourself upon your Lord and say: “Stop now! Do not inflict such evil upon my Lord. Here I am; do it to me, but do not inflict such insults upon my Lord”? Then you would embrace your Lord and master on bended knees and willingly receive the blows upon yourself.

Think how the Jews go to sleep, while your beloved Lord is left bound. Afterward, when the leaders of the Jews are weary and have had their fill of wickedness, and the others go to sleep, the Lord is left bound with the guards, perhaps entirely apart in a corner of the house, afflicted by intense cold and weariness, since it was winter and the nights were especially long.

You, then, will go to him and sit at his feet, grieving and mourning. Then you will devoutly kiss his venerable hands and feet and those various bonds, and say: “O Lord, at least let your most holy head rest upon my shoulder, since I cannot free you.”

Then you will commend yourself to him most devoutly, as well as all your friends, and without doubt he will grant you whatever you ask and request of him. You will tell him that tomorrow you will announce it to his most worthy mother. Thus, at his most holy and blessed feet, or beside his most glorious breast, you will sleep and rest for a little while. Then you may sleep in such a condition, seeing your Lord.

## MEDITATION AT PRIME

At the hour of Prime, with a sorrowful and mournful heart, you will meditate on how, when morning came, the Jews gathered for their council, and your beloved Lord Jesus was brought there, greatly afflicted.

When they wish to lead him out of the house, saying, as I suppose: “Rise, rise, Jesus. What are you doing? Are you sleeping or not? For the leaders and priests command that you be brought to the council, where they are waiting for you with the people and intend to hand you over to Pilate.”

You will think that you are with him in these things and say: “Alas, my Lord! Alas, good master! For now they wish to hand you over to death. O Lord, how cruel and grievous are these rumors! O Lord, what a mournful sight your sweetest mother will see, what bitter tidings she will hear—she and all who love you! O Lord, what shall I, wretched man, do? Shall I go with you, Lord, or shall I go to announce it to my most worthy Lady, your mother, so that she may come to you?”

Afterward you will see how he enters, afflicted and bound. All look upon him and jeer at him: “O Jesus, here you are! If you were a prophet, why did you not foresee this?” Those accursed men could have said such things and many similar ones to him.

If, however, you wish to follow another path, think in this way: you will hear it said that Jesus is being held captive by the Jews. Then, coming, you will see him bound; you will fall before him, weeping and forming words expressing your sorrow.

Afterward you will hear false testimony against him there, and the high priest saying and asking: “Are you the Christ, the Son of the blessed God?” And you will hear the Lord answering most gently: “You have said it.”

And that word mentioned above—“From now on you will see the Son of Man,” and so forth—they regarded as blasphemy and, I suppose, acted as they had done before.

Consider also how afterward they led him to Pilate, with his hands bound behind his back or in front, and, as is said, with a chain around his neck. This chain was afterward displayed in Jerusalem to pilgrims as a great object of devotion; it was placed around their necks [the printed wording is grammatically uncertain]. For this reason the people gather at this hour to confess and praise the Lord, because he is the judge of the living and the dead—the judge whom the Jews, by condemning him at this hour, permitted to perish.

## MEDITATION AT TERCE
Source/review notes: Several penitential clauses are incomplete in the supplied text; their unstated objects or units remain explicitly unresolved where context does not determine them.

At the third hour, you will think, mournful and sorrowful, how you hear throughout all the streets of Jerusalem that your Lord is being held captive, and how they wish to crucify him. [Col. 0565B]

And when his sorrowful mother hears this, she is led by her elders with immeasurable lamentation, weeping, and mourning, as though dead, and comes to see her son so afflicted, so bound, so spat upon, deprived of every consolation and aid, abandoned by the disciples and by everyone, and not excusing himself in any way. Jesus himself sees her prostrate and lifeless on the ground, together with the sisters and others who had come with her. What sorrow do you think there was, I ask? Think, if you can, of such bitterness, if you possess a devout soul.

O good Jesus, O good Lord, everywhere and always your sorrow was multiplied. You counted the sorrow of your mother as your own. At last he is sent to Herod, and a great crowd gathers to follow him. O Lady, how did you go, or who helped you to go? Certainly you were an example of sorrow to all who love Christ. But you, dearest one, consider how gladly you would help and accompany her, so sad and sorrowful; and then see how Herod questioned him, while the Lord would not speak to him, but stood before him, bound like a gentle lamb. Consider how Herod mocked him [Col. 0565C] with his army and sent him back to Pilate.

Afterward consider how his most holy feet had been broken, because they had led him there and brought him back with the greatest haste. Do not suppose that he was shod, since neither he nor his disciples used footwear. Then consider how, after being brought back to Pilate, he is stripped and bound to a column, and how savagely he is scourged; how his most white side is reddened with his rosy blood; how a crown of thorns is placed upon his most reverend head, and his blood flows down his cheeks. Then he is wrapped in a red cloak, and a reed is placed in his hand for mockery and disgrace. Thus prepared, Pilate brings him out to the Jews, who had not cried out inside because of the feast; then those sons of the devil cried out: “Take him away, take him away; crucify him!”

All these things can rouse you to sorrow if you think of them attentively, at length, and frequently. Then you will cry out:

“O good Lord, how are you stripped, you who are accustomed to clothe the naked? How are you bound, you who free those bound by demons and those held by illnesses?” [Col. 0565D] And so think through each detail: how they bent their knees before him, struck his head with a reed, and said, “Hail, King of the Jews.”

O God the Father, how do you endure such disgrace, such insult being inflicted upon your beloved Son? If you are merciful to all who devoutly cry out to you, why do you appear so cruel toward my most beloved Lord, your Son? Why do you not allow your angels to help their Lord? Why do you wish him to suffer such torment at the hands of impious men?

O Lady, what were you doing when you saw this? What were you saying, I ask? Lady, reveal it to my soul—or rather, make me feel it, because I cannot feel it as I desire. Make me feel it for the love of your most beloved Son, my beloved Lady.

At last Pilate pronounced the most cruel sentence, that he should be crucified. Consider how greatly his friends cried out when they heard that sentence. Then they place the cross upon his shoulders, so that he may carry it. Certainly, dearest one, [Col. 0566A] you would do well to help your Lord and say: “Give me, I beg you, the cross of my Lord, and I will carry it.”
