O my Lady, I believe that you would gladly carry it if you could. O how sad, how sorrowful, how crying and weeping, the holy women went, supporting my Lady, his mother, who could not support herself. Turning to them, the Lord Jesus said:

“Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but over yourselves and over your children, for behold, the days are coming when they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed.’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us,’ for if they do these things [fiunt: “are done”] to green wood, what will happen to dry wood?””

Certainly, Lord Jesus, it is true: if you, the holy tree, the fruitful and blessed wood, suffer so much and are stripped of your branches, what will become of us wretches, who are dry wood fit for the fire?

## Meditation at the Sixth Hour

[Col. 0566B]

At the sixth hour you will think, sorrowfully and sadly, of all these things that I shall tell you. Consider how the shouting people came as far as Calvary; and there, with everyone looking on, he is stripped of his garments, with the greatest pain, because his undergarment clung tightly to him on account of the blood from the scourging. Then his body appeared, formed with such elegance, entirely covered in blood.

O most holy mother, what great sorrow was yours when you looked upon these things! Then, when the cross had been prepared, they said to him: “Ascend, Jesus, ascend.” O how willingly he ascended! O with what love he endured all these things for us! O what patience, what gentleness! O holy Lord and Father, how greatly you will delight in his obedience!

Thus, completely naked, he is raised up and stretched out upon the cross. But his most loving mother, filled with anguish, placed around him the veil that she had on her head and covered his private parts. O what sorrowful cries and wailings were heard there from his friends, and especially from his most sorrowful mother, when he was so cruelly [Col. 0566C] raised up, stretched out, and his entire sacred body distended and torn apart. Immediately, when the very large nails were driven in, blood began to pour out and flow down the cross to the ground.

Consider how he was exalted, as he had foretold: “The Son of Man must be lifted up,” and so forth. And as Moses, and so forth; and how those who were bitten by the serpent were healed by looking (sic): so against the bite and temptation of the devil there is no medicine so good as to look upon him who suffered for us upon the cross.

You will also see the Lord your God standing upon a lofty throne, prepared to judge; and for this reason he placed two men, one on either side: one is saved, the other condemned. You will also see Christ, who is the high priest of future blessings, offering with outstretched hands the pure offering—that is, his precious flesh—for us upon the altar, and so forth.

You will also see your teacher standing on high and preaching there, hanging upon the cross, seven words, which I briefly make known to you. Meditate upon them devoutly.

[Col. 0566D]

1. First he said for those crucifying him: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”—namely, good to me and evil to themselves. Truly it is so, because the one who does evil does not know how great a penalty he incurs for himself, nor how great a crown he prepares for another.

2. Second, he said to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” And truly, today and every day, this happens, because whoever devoutly and properly confesses his sins is immediately with the Lord in paradise through grace, and afterward will be there through glory; or he is in paradise, that is, in a certain rest and security of conscience.

3. Third, he commended his mother, deprived of consolation, sorrowful, and almost dying, to the disciple, and the disciple to his mother, saying: “Woman, behold your son.” Then he said to the disciple: “Behold your mother.”

In this commendation we understand not only John, but the whole Church of Christ, and every faithful soul, commended to the blessed Virgin, so that she may have us as sons to be loved and may seek our good with motherly affection; and so that we may have her [Col. 0567A] as our sweetest mother, always loving and honoring her after God. Therefore, just as the Lord’s Passion was necessary for salvation, so this commendation was necessary for our assistance; and for this reason we should confidently turn to her for every need and benefit.

4. Fourth he said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—to show the magnitude of his punishment. For he suffered so grievously as though he were not the Son of God but an enemy of God. The flesh of Christ appeared to have been so utterly forsaken that it received no relief or aid. Yet he himself willingly passed through this for our good, and endured it so that we too might sometimes suffer in such a way by his example and appear forsaken by God—whether when the Lord wishes to test us, or when we ourselves wish certain punishments to be inflicted upon us, so that we may be conformed to our Lord in punishment and thus be conformed to him in glory.

5. Fifth he said: “I thirst.” And they gave him a drink of vinegar [Col. 0567B] mixed with gall, as the prophet had foretold, saying: “They gave me gall for food; they gave me vinegar to drink.”

Behold what kind of supper was given to our Lord. It was already the hour of supper; but because of labor and pain he asked for nothing else as food or drink. You may judge literally that he was very thirsty, and that the sons of the devil gave him gall for food and vinegar for drink.

O wretched people that we are, what shall we do, since we wish to dine and drink in other ways and seek delicacies? Certainly, if a person lived for a thousand years and every day chewed bread and water, he could not adequately repay that supper in truth. Let the one who can understand, understand; for this is a hard saying for the carnal. Therefore they do not savor—that is, they do not follow with relish—the things that are of God, and they lose inward consolations.

6. Sixth he said: “It is finished”—that is, all my work which I ought to do in the world, and also every punishment and every struggle, have been completed and perfected. The time as well during which I ought to remain among human beings, for the honor of God the Father and the benefit of the faithful, has been fulfilled.

## Meditation at the Ninth Hour

At the ninth hour you will think, with a mournful and devout mind, if you possess a pious soul, how your most loving Lord, accepted above all for his graciousness, approached death. He begins to lower his eyes and grow pale, and begins to incline his head toward his mother, as though giving her a final “hail”—a hail of sorrow and complete desolation, which he could not express with mouth or word because of his overwhelming suffering and immeasurable pain [Col. 0568A]—and as though commending to her his body, so cruelly pierced and torn apart.

Having done this, he concluded by saying the final and seventh word: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” And saying this, he expired.

Note that after his death Christ also shed blood, so that he might make satisfaction for the punishment that man deserved after death, and also shorten that punishment through his blood.

Certainly you can well understand how, as he spoke the word, his mother saw him dying and herself left in the world in such pain and anguish. At last, if she was able to speak, she cried out and said:

“O sweetest Son, what is this wretched and most sorrowful woman to do, to whom you leave me, wretched, commended, my sweetest son?” [Col. 0568B] Remember me and all your household, whom you leave so desolate. Remember all who serve you, my son. Into your hands and into the hands of your Father I commend myself and your entire household.

“O holy Father God, O Father, into your hands I commend my son—indeed, my Lord—as far as I am able, though not as much as I ought, because I cannot. I am failing, and I desire to die before my son in your sight.”

Saying such things and unable to endure them, I think she fell upon her face to the ground.

Consider with what sorrow all his friends wept. Even those who had appeared to have nothing to do with him grieved greatly, such as the centurion and the others who had come to see. They beat their breasts and returned, saying: “Truly this was a righteous man,” and: “Truly this was the Son of God.”

After these seven words we can make our own exclamations: sometimes taking our Lord’s side against the Jews, sometimes suffering with our Lord, sometimes with his mother, and sometimes with ourselves in our misery. At the end of each of the words mentioned above, which he spoke upon the cross, we can make a prayer.

## Meditation at Vespers

At the evening hour you will come with devout steps and spiritual movements to take down the Lord from the [Col. 0568C] cross, to mourn for him with his blessed mother, to wash his most holy body, sprinkled with blood, with your tears, to anoint him with the ointments of prayer, to carry him in the arms of charitable and humble action, and to bury him with good spices, good conduct, good teachings and examples, lamentations and mournings.

You will cover him beneath the pavement of your conscience with love and devotion, and you will sit there beside him at the tomb of that same Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0567]

# On Remedies for Sins (G, S)*

## Preface

[Col. 0567C]

We have excerpted the very few remedies for sins that follow from the records of our predecessors. In all of them, however, we have used not the authority of a censor, but rather the advice of one who shares compassion, carefully admonishing every learned priest of Christ that, in everything noted here, he should diligently discern the sex, age, condition, status, and person of anyone wishing to do penance, as well as the penitent’s own heart; and according to these factors, he should judge each matter as seems appropriate to him.

For some must correct their errors by abstaining from food, others by bending their knees more frequently, or by standing in the form of a cross, or by doing something else of this kind that pertains to the purification of sins, while many must do all these things. All such matters must depend upon the examination of a discerning judge.

## Penitential for Souls

A remedy from the canons of the Catholic Fathers, excerpted by Archbishop Agbert.

That holy institution which was practiced in the days of our fathers never abandoned the right paths. They prescribed for penitents and mourners their sufferings as true medicines of salvation, because the diversity of faults produces a diversity of medicine for penitents—just as physicians of the body customarily prepare different medicines or potions against different illnesses, or as judges of secular cases use different judgments.

Accordingly, good and upright judges weigh and consider different judgments, examining how they may judge rightly between the wretched and the rich, between one case and another. How much more, then, O priests of God, must you weigh and consider different medicines for souls invisible to human beings, lest through a foolish physician the wounds of souls become worse, as the prophet says: “My scars have become foul and worse because of my foolishness.”

O foolish physician, do not deceive your own soul and that of the other, lest you receive a double, sevenfold, or thousandfold punishment. Hear Christ saying: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit.”

If you do not consider my judgment, another human being neither hears nor sees who will judge me. Do you not understand that God, the just and mighty judge, sees and hears, brings hidden things into the open, and repays according to [Col. 0569A] works?

And indeed there are some blind men, running like dogs toward the corpses of the dead, or like ravens in flight, who are carried into the priesthood. Blind to divine wisdom, they desire not the Lord but rather earthly honor. Gregory of Nazianzus said of such men:

“I fear this: that dogs are pursuing the pastoral office, especially when they have prepared no pastoral discipline within themselves.”

Ezekiel says: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who fed themselves and not the flock: they drank the milk, clothed themselves with their wool, and ate what was fat; but they did not bind up what was broken,” and so forth.

Ezekiel also says: “Woe to the priests who eat the sins of my people”—that is, taking their offerings for themselves and not praying for them. They consume the offerings and do not rebuke them. When they hear that people are about to die, they rejoice and prepare themselves for plunder, like ravens for the corpses of the dead.

Now, therefore, brothers, whoever wishes to receive priestly authority [Col. 0569B] should first consider God and prepare his weapons before the bishop’s hand touches his head: namely, the Psalter, the Lectionary, the Antiphonary, the Missal, the Baptismal Book, and the Martyrology; the cycle of the year for preaching, with good works, and the reckoning according to the cycle—that is, the law of priests. Afterward he should have his Penitential, which is arranged in this order according to the authority of the canons, so that he may investigate the distinctions of every case.

First, without these things right judgment cannot stand, because it is written: “In no matter should you appear undiscerning, but distinguish what, where, how long, when, and how you ought to do it.”

Therefore not everyone is to be weighed on the same scale, although they may be bound by one and the same fault. There must be discernment among each of them: between rich and poor; free and slave; infant, child, young man, adolescent, and old person; dull and knowledgeable; layperson, cleric, monk, bishop, priest, deacon, subdeacon, and lector; in an ecclesiastical rank or without one; married or unmarried; foreigner; virgin; woman; canoness or nun; disabled, sick, and healthy.

The holy apostles established places and times for the consideration of the condition of animals or human beings; for the continent or incontinent; for what is done willingly or by accident; in public or secretly; and for what is corrected by something like contrition, whether from necessity or voluntarily.

Then came the holy Fathers and Saint Pœnuphius. Then came the canons of the holy Fathers, and then others, such as Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and Theodore. From all their sayings and judgments we have faithfully written these things, so that all may be saved and not become fainthearted, because “the mighty will suffer mighty torments.”

Likewise, in Jesus son of Sirach: “In judging, be merciful to the weak as a father, and be in place of a husband to their mother.” Saint James also said: “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has not shown mercy; but mercy triumphs over judgment,” so that the same person may obtain it, as Saint Benedict says—that is, those who truly do penance in fasting and weeping, in almsgiving, in prayers, and do not do again what they have committed; and if they do it, nevertheless they do not persevere in it.

For God said: “You conceived evil; I forgave. You spoke evil; I forgave. You did evil; I forgave. To persevere in evil I do not forgive.” Therefore, do not forgive those who persevere in evil, but judge them with strict judgment according to the canons, so that others may have fear.

## On Fornication

If a young man sins with a virgin, let him do penance for one year. If it happened once and accidentally, let the penance be lightened, but nevertheless continue up to a full year.

If a young girl under twenty years of age commits the act, let her do three Lents and the prescribed fast days. If, because of this sin, they have been reduced to human servitude, let them do penance for forty days. If he merely strives but is not polluted, let him do penance for twenty days.

If a widow is violated, let her do penance for the whole year, with fasting days in the alternate year. If this continues until a child is conceived, let her do two full years and two further years more lightly. If they also kill the child, let them do three years and four other years more lightly.

If a monk sins with a laywoman, let him do penance for three years; let her do two years and the prescribed fast days. If a layman sins with a nun, let him do penance for two years and the prescribed fast days; let her do three years. If this continues until a child is conceived, let them do four years. If they also kill the child, let them do penance for seven years.

If an unmarried man violates another man’s wife, let him do penance for two years. If a married man sins with a virgin, likewise, but first he must abstain from his own wife; if she consented, otherwise an additional measure of penance is to be added.

If a married man sins with another man’s wife, let him do penance for three years. For the first of these years he must abstain from his own wife, with her consent.

If a married man sins with his own maidservant, let him do penance for one year, three Lents, and the prescribed fast days for the first three months, and abstain from his wife. If she suffered it unwillingly, let her do penance for forty days; if she consented, three Lents and the prescribed fast days.

If a young man sins with his sister, let him do penance for seven years. If with his mother, seven years, and for as long as he lives he must never be without continence.

For sodomy, seven years; if habitual, seven years. If a monk, seven years. If between the thighs, three Lents.

If a child is violated by force and suffers such things, let him do penance for forty days, or be chastised by psalms or continence.

If a woman fornicates by any contrivance, either with herself or with another woman, let her do penance for three years. If a nun does this with another nun by means of a device, let her do penance for seven years.

Whoever sins with an animal, one year; if he is a monk, two years.

If a layman repeatedly fornicates with a laywoman, let them do penance for three years. The more frequently or negligently they do so, the more time and severity should be added.

Whoever has long served fornication, perjury, theft, and other disgraceful acts, let him do penance for seven years.

If a mother imitates fornication with her young child, let her do two years and three Lents with the prescribed fast days.

If boys pollute one another with their hands, forty days; older persons, one hundred days. If boys soil themselves between the thighs, let them do penance for one hundred days; older persons, three Lents and the prescribed fast days.

If a small child is assaulted by an older boy, one week; if he consented, twenty days.

Whoever is polluted by an alluring embrace of a woman or by a kiss, let him do penance for thirty days. Whoever is polluted by her shameless touch upon the flesh, three months.

Let a boy who voluntarily pollutes himself do penance for thirty days.

A young man: forty days. Whoever is polluted through negligent obscene speech, let him do penance for seven days.

Whoever is unwillingly polluted through an assault of thought and nature should recite fifty psalms for four days and fast on Wednesday and Friday until None or Vespers.

Those who marry in a consecrated church, or whoever is polluted in a church through a dream, let them do penance for three days.

A married man must abstain for forty days before Easter and Christmas, and every Sunday, and on Wednesday and Friday from the time the conception is made known until after the child is born.

A man must abstain from his wife for three months. After giving birth, the wife must abstain from the church: thirty days if the child is a son, forty if a daughter.

During the time of menstrual blood, whoever has intercourse then shall do penance for thirty days; the following words are textually incomplete: “who, seven days.”

If anyone has intercourse with his wife from behind, let him do penance for forty days, because it is a Sodomite crime.

If a parent’s child dies unbaptized through negligence, let the parent do penance for one year and never be without some form of penance. If the priest responsible neglected to come when summoned, he shall be punished by the judgment of his bishop with condemnation of his soul.

Nevertheless, in every case, even laypeople, whenever they happen to find people about to die unbaptized, are to rescue their souls from the devil through baptism. That is, they should baptize them with plain blessed water in the name of the Lord, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. They should immerse them and pour water over them. Therefore those faithful who are able—and especially monks—ought to have knowledge of baptizing; and if they go farther away somewhere, they should always carry the Eucharist with them.

## On Killing

Whoever kills a monk or cleric should lay down his weapons and serve God, or do penance for seven years.

Whoever kills a layman out of hatred or desire to possess his inheritance, four years. Whoever does so in revenge for a brother, one year; and afterward two years, three Lents, and the prescribed fast days.

Whoever kills through sudden anger and quarrel, three years. Whoever kills accidentally, one year. Whoever kills in a public war, forty days. A slave who kills at his master’s command, forty days.

A free man who kills an innocent person at the command of his superior shall do penance for one year, followed by two years, three Lents, and the prescribed fast days.

Whoever, in a quarrel, makes a person disabled or disfigured by a blow must repay the medical expenses, compensation for the disfigurement, and the value of his work until he is healed, as well as do half a year of penance. If he has no means to repay these things, let him do a full year.

Whoever rises to strike a person, intending to kill him, let him do penance for two weeks. If he was a cleric, seven months. If he also wounded him, forty days; if a cleric, the whole year. He should also give the injured person money according to the degree of the wound, although the law does not prescribe it, so that the injured person may not cause scandal.

A woman who voluntarily loses her child before forty days shall do penance for one year. If after forty days, three years. If after the child has been born, she is like a murderer. Yet it makes a great difference whether a poor woman does this because of the difficulty of raising the child, or a fornicating woman does it to conceal her crime.

Whoever knowingly commits perjury, compelled by his master, shall do penance for three Lents and the prescribed fast days.

Whoever knowingly understands the force of an oath or perjury and commits perjury by the hand of a bishop or priest, or at an altar or consecrated cross, shall do penance for three years. If at an unconsecrated cross, one year. If by the hand of a layman, among the Greeks it counts for nothing.

Whoever leads an ignorant person into perjury, with harmful intent, and that person later recognizes his perjury, shall do penance for one year.

## On Unclean Meat

Whoever eats unclean meat or meat torn apart by beasts shall do penance for forty days. If compelled by the necessity of hunger, much more lightly.

If a mouse falls into a liquid, remove it and sprinkle that liquid with blessed water. If it is dead, the entire liquid must be discarded and not consumed by anyone, whether it is milk, beer, or anything of that kind.

But if the mouse or weasel dies after falling into the liquid, the liquid in which it died should be purified and sprinkled with holy water, and may be consumed if necessity requires.

If a bird defecates in any liquid, the dung should be removed, and the food should be cleansed with blessed water and consumed.

Whoever unknowingly swallows blood with saliva will not be harmed. Whoever is unknowingly polluted while eating is not harmed. But if he knows it, let him do penance according to the degree of the pollution.

## On Capital Crimes

Now, therefore, I shall explain the capital crimes according to the canons. The first are pride, envy, fornication, vainglory, long-lasting anger, worldly sorrow, avarice, and gluttony of the belly.

Augustine added sacrilege—that is, theft of sacred things, which is the greatest theft—or serving idols; that is, auguries and the rest.

Then come adultery, false testimony, theft, robbery, habitual drunkenness, and idolatry; the effeminate, sodomites, slanderers, and perjurers.

These, therefore, are the capital crimes. Saint Paul, Augustine, and other saints judged that generous almsgiving should be made for these, and that a long period of fasting should be maintained. That is, as others judge, for capital crimes—adultery, murder, perjury, fornication, and similar offenses—a layman should do penance for four years; a cleric, five; a subdeacon, six; a deacon, eight; a priest, ten; a bishop, twelve, if the offense was habitual.

## On Lesser Sins

That is, theft, false testimony, and similar offenses: laypeople should do penance for one year; clerics, two; subdeacons, three; deacons, four; priests, five; bishops, seven years.

Likewise, if sodomy was habitual, a bishop should do penance for fourteen years; a priest, twelve; a deacon, ten; a subdeacon, eight; a cleric, seven; a layman, five.

If a monk fornicates with a servant of God, let him do penance for four years. If with a girl, seven years.

Concerning parricides or fratricides, some prescribe seven years, others fourteen and seven.

## On Greed and Other Disgraceful Acts

Likewise, a greedy, avaricious, drunken, proud, envious, rapacious, or persistently angry person, a slanderer, or one guilty of similar offenses—which would take too long to enumerate—shall do penance for three years.

If a cleric fornicates with a quadruped, let him do penance for two years; a subdeacon, three; a deacon, five; a priest, seven; a bishop, ten years.

Whoever fornicates with his mother shall do penance for fifteen years. If with his daughter or sister, twelve years.

Whoever fornicates with his natural brother through carnal union must abstain from all flesh and do penance for fifteen years.

If a cleric practices hunting, let him do penance for one year; a deacon, two; a priest, three.

If a mother fornicates with her young son, let her abstain from flesh for three years and fast one day each week until Vespers.

If a priest, deacon, or monk marries, let him be deposed in the presence of the people. If he commits adultery with her and it becomes known publicly, let him be cast out of the Church and do penance among laypeople for as long as he lives.

Whoever abandons his wife for another husband shall do penance for seven years.

If a cleric commits murder and kills his neighbor, let him do penance for ten years. Let him be an exile and do penance for seven if it was motivated by hatred.

If a layman commits murder in rage and with premeditation, let him do penance for four, five, or seven years. If through a quarrel, four years.

Likewise, those who sacrifice to demons in great matters, if it is habitual, shall do penance for ten years; in lesser matters, one year. For auguries and divinations, five years.

Those who summon storms shall do penance for seven years, so that this order of penance may always be observed, beginning with one year and continuing thereafter for any sin.

That is: in each week, three days without wine, mead, or meat; let the penitent fast until Vespers and eat dry food; and for three Lents let him always eat dry food. Let him fast three days until None and three until Vespers.

On Sundays; for four days at Christmas; at Epiphany; from Easter until the White Days; at the Ascension of the Lord; at Pentecost; and on the feasts of Saint Michael, Saint Mary, Saint John the Baptist, the twelve apostles, Saint Martin, and the saint celebrated in that province [Col. 0572C], he should practice charity like his fellow clerics or laypeople.

Let everyone avoid drunkenness and the distension of the belly in all things. Let them do what the Apostle says: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.”

Then penance is worthy if this is fulfilled.

## On the Penance of Clerics

Likewise, the Apostolic Canon indicates that a bishop, priest, or deacon who is caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed, but not deprived of communion, because God does not judge twice for the same thing.

If a bishop commits fornication with a natural woman, let him do penance for twelve years; let him seek forgiveness from the Lord through many tears and almsgiving; after three or four years, more lightly.

If a priest sins with a girl who has not been dedicated by a monastic vow, let him do penance for three or four years, with three Lents and Wednesdays and Fridays always eating dry food.

If with a servant of God or with a male, more is to be added—that is, let him do penance for seven years, if it is habitual.

Likewise, deacons, if they are not monks, should do penance for two or three years.

So also a monk without ecclesiastical rank, if he sins with a girl, three years. If they are a deacon or monks, let them do penance for five or seven years.

Monks with ecclesiastical rank should do penance for seven years if without a vow. Monks with a girl, nine or ten years.

A cleric who fornicates without a monastic vow shall do penance for one year. If frequently, two years. If with a canoness, two years; if frequently, three.

If he fathers a child, he should do more penance—that is, four or five years; others say seven, and that he should become an exile.

So also a nun with laymen without ecclesiastical rank; if the clerics are canons, one year; if frequently, two. If in ecclesiastical rank, like a monk, three years.

Theodore said: “A monk committing fornication, and not finding [the object is unstated], shall do penance for one year and a half.”

Likewise, a monk who sins with a girl shall do penance for six years.

A layman who pollutes himself with a servant of God shall do penance for two years. If he fathers a child with her, three years.

If they are unmarried, three Lents. Some judge forty days—that is, the customary period.

Likewise, for sodomites, some prescribe ten years, namely for one who has done it frequently or is in ecclesiastical rank; some seven years; some a year for an effeminate person; some one hundred days for boys; for men, years; for boys, two years.

Whoever sins with an animal or beast shall do penance for ten years. Some prescribe seven, some three, some one, and some one hundred days for boys.

There ought to be discernment according to the kind of animal or human being, as we said above.

Likewise, if a bishop fornicates with a quadruped, let him do penance for eight years; if habitual, ten; a priest, five; a deacon, three; a cleric, two.

## On Oaths

Whoever takes an oath in a church, or on the Gospel, or on the relics of the saints, shall do penance for seven years. Others prescribe twelve years.

If by the hand of a bishop, priest, or deacon, or upon a consecrated cross, one year. Others judge three or four.

Upon an unconsecrated cross, one year, or seven months according to others.

Whoever is led astray in ignorance and later recognizes it shall do penance for one year, or three Lents, or forty days.

If anyone is compelled by any necessity, three Lents; others prescribe three [the unit is unstated], or one year, with some of it on bread and water, as others judge.

Likewise, perjurers: three years.

Whoever suspects the matter before the oath is administered and nevertheless swears by consent shall do penance for two years.

If anyone swears by the hand of a layman, among the Greeks it counts for nothing.

## On Women’s Abstinence

A woman should abstain from her husband when she has conceived, until she has given birth, and for forty days after childbirth.

Whoever has intercourse during these days shall do penance for ten, thirty, or twenty days.

Those who are married should abstain for three Lents, on Sunday night, on Saturday, on Wednesday and Tuesday, as prescribed, and for three nights before they receive communion.

Whoever has intercourse with his wife during Lent before Easter and refuses to abstain shall do penance for one year, or give his property’s value to the Church, or distribute it to the poor, or pay twenty-six solidi.

If he has intercourse through drunkenness or some other cause without it being habitual, let him do penance for forty days.

If a woman practices divinations or diabolical incantations, let her do penance for one year, or three Lents, or forty days, according to the character of the fault.

If a woman kills someone who imitates her evil practices—that is, by a potion or some other art—let her do penance for four years. If she is a poor woman, four years.

If a woman kills her own son by murder, let her do penance for eleven years.

If a man has intercourse with his wife from behind, let him do penance as with animals. That is, if it is habitual, let him do penance for three years.

But if in the meantime he marries and the practice is habitual, let him do penance for seven years.

## On Auguries or Divinations

[Col. 0573D] Auguries or lots—those practices called false observances of the saints—or observing divinations, or promising the future by examining any kind of writings, or making a vow to a tree or to any object except a church: if a cleric does this, let him be excommunicated from the Church; or let a cleric do penance for three years, and a layman for two years, or one year and six months.

If a woman places her son on a roof or in a furnace for the sake of curing fevers, let her do penance for five years. Do not perform such practices when the moon is eclipsed, trusting that you can defend yourselves from sacrilegious use by shouting and magic. For *caragios* and diviners who mutter incantations: laymen shall do penance for three days without beer, wine, or meat; others, twelve days.

If a faithful layman, out of wickedness, gets another drunk, let him do penance for forty days. If he vomits because of illness, he is without guilt.

## On Drunkenness

If through drunkenness or gluttony he vomits the Eucharist, let him do penance for forty days. A cleric, monk, or deacon, sixty; a priest, seventy; a bishop, one hundred and ten. If it is because of illness, seven days; otherwise, each person shall do four days on the day of sacrifice.

One man threw one psalter, another twice his psalter, into the fire on the day of sacrifice, or into a river: let him sing one hundred psalms. If dogs eat such vomit, one hundred days, if he knows of it; if he does not know, forty.

Those who become drunk against the Lord’s command—if they have made a vow of holiness, that is, if drunkenness changes their state of mind, their tongues stammer, their eyes are troubled, dizziness occurs, and abdominal distension and pain follow—shall do penance as follows: a cleric, four days; a monk, fourteen; a deacon, four weeks; a priest, four; a bishop, five; superiors, three days without wine and meat.

## On the Eucharist

If anyone loses the Eucharist through negligence, let him do penance for one year, or three Lents, or forty days. If the sacrifice falls to the ground through negligence, let him sing fifty psalms.

Whoever neglects the sacrifice so that worms are in it, and it has neither color nor taste, shall do penance for twenty, thirty, or forty days, and it shall be burned in the fire. Its ashes shall be hidden beneath the altar; if it falls all the way to the ground, let him do penance for one day.

If a star burns, or an altar falls, let him do penance for three days. Whoever loses a small portion in the church and does not find it shall do penance for twenty days, singing forty psalms each day.

Whoever loses his chrismal in the congregation and does not find it shall do penance for forty days, or three Lents. Whoever spills the chalice at the end of the solemnity shall do penance for thirty days.

## On Various Matters

Whoever loses a created object—incense, tablets or his writing tablet, blessed salt, newly consecrated bread, or anything similar—shall do penance for four days.

Whoever unknowingly eats carrion shall do penance for forty days. If knowingly, one hundred days. Whoever eats something adulterated, and is poor or dull-witted, shall do penance for four days. The healthy and the sick, if they know what they are eating, shall do penance for forty days. Those who do this repeatedly shall do penance for three Lents or one year.

Whoever eats or drinks something contaminated by a domestic animal—that is, by a dog or cat—and knows it, shall sing one hundred psalms or fast for one day.

If someone gives another a liquid in which a mouse or weasel is found dead, a layman shall do penance for four days; in monasteries, three hundred psalms shall be sung. Whoever later learns that he drank such a beverage shall sing a psalter.

If anyone unknowingly eats something half-cooked, let him do penance for three days, or sing a psalter. If knowingly, let him do penance for four days.

For a small theft, let him do penance for thirty days; for twenty-year-olds, [the penance is] twenty days; boys of ten years who commit some theft shall do penance for four days.

If anyone dips his hand into some food, and the hand is not suitable, he shall make amends with one hundred blows.

If a dead mouse or weasel is found in flour or in any dry food, or in porridge or coagulated milk, whatever remains around it shall be thrown out; [Col. 0574D] the remainder shall be eaten.

Moreover, whoever is able to fulfill what is written as an uncompromising penance, it is good. But whoever cannot, we give this counsel through the mercy of God:

First, for one day, on bread and water, let him sing fifty psalms while kneeling; or, without kneeling, seventy psalms, inside the church or in one place, in order. For one day, two hundred genuflections are equivalent; or one denarius is equivalent for a day; and three alms given to three poor people are equivalent. Some say that fifty blows or fifty psalms are equivalent for one day.

That is: in winter, autumn, and spring, one hundred blows or psalms; in summer, one hundred and fifty psalms or blows.

Likewise, for one month during which he must do penance on bread and water, let him sing 1,680 psalms, kneeling or without kneeling. Afterwards let him take food every day at the sixth hour, except that on Wednesday and Friday he shall fast until the ninth hour. Let him abstain from meat and wine, and take other food after singing the psalms.

In the second year the penance shall be lighter: from the Nativity of the Lord until Epiphany, and on those days mentioned above, which are not counted toward the penance.

Likewise, whoever cannot perform penance in the manner described above shall, in the first year, distribute twenty-three shillings as alms; for one year on bread and water, let him give twenty-two shillings as alms; and each week let him fast one day until the ninth hour and another until evening.

Three Lents: in the second year, twenty shillings; for three years, eighteen shillings, making sixty-four shillings.

Powerful men perform penance for criminal offenses as Zacchaeus says: “Lord, I give half of all my possessions to the poor; and if I have unjustly taken anything from anyone, I shall repay it fourfold; and I shall set slaves free and redeem captives.” From the day on which he ceases to sin, let him not cease to receive Communion, as the Apostle says: “Whoever sins through the body, makes amends through the body”—that is, through fasts, vigils, and prayers to the Lord.

Whoever has been converted after committing every evil—shedding blood, theft, fornication, lying, swearing, and all other evils—and afterward wishes to serve God to the end, shall do penance for three or two years, or according to the priest’s judgment.

[Col. 0575B] Nevertheless, he himself should consider the medicine of souls: how he may save his own soul and theirs by instructing and teaching sound doctrine. For whoever ministers well acquires for himself a good standing with him who is above all things, God, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## Likewise, on the Value of a Year or a Day

In the first year some prescribed four periods of three days, with one night intervening. Others say twelve such periods of three days—that is, some said one period of three days each month. Some prescribed four days by means of blows or by persevering in vigils; others prescribed it in this way, others in that.

The value of a day—that is, an *agape*—is food given to two or three poor people. Others prescribe an entire psalter; that is, in summer, and in winter, spring, or autumn, fifty psalms. Some prescribe twelve wounds or blows, more or fewer, according to the seasons.

Some prescribe another’s labor, or, by bending the knee, completing forty twice, forty three times, and one hundred and twenty six times; and ten are added, then twenty, then thirty, if there is no labor.

# Section Three of the Venerable Bede’s Paraenetic Works, Containing His Poems

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575]

# The Metrical Life of Saint Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*) (C)

## Prologue to John the Priest

[Col. 0575] To the most beloved John, priest and lord in the Lord of lords, Bede, servant of Christ, sends greetings.

It cannot be said, most beloved lord in Christ, how greatly I am bound to you by affection, and how gladly I would always enjoy your presence, if that were possible; nor how, even amid the hardships of the long journey you desire to undertake, I am continually pricked by the stimulus of remembering your holy sweetness.

Therefore, both as a memorial of my devotion and as a relief for your pilgrimage, I offer you the deeds of the blessed Bishop Cuthbert, which I recently published in verse. For without any doubt I trust that the companionship of so great a man will bring you great happiness. His gentle sweetness consoles the sorrowful; his fervent compunction awakens the sluggish heart; and his steadfast intercession protects the endangered.

You should know, however, that I have by no means been able to set forth all his deeds. Every day new miracles are performed through his relics, and ancient ones are newly reported by those who were able to know them. One of these is what I myself, as I have already told you, experienced when my tongue was healed while I was singing of his miracles.

If life remains, and heavenly will favors our purpose by granting its assent, I hope in another work to restore to memory some of the things I omitted. I ask you, when, under God’s protection, you reach the threshold of the blessed apostles, to remember to intercede for me.

## Chapter I. Prologue

[Col. 0575C]

The Lord has granted many lights to shine for their generations,

to illuminate the grim shadows of human night

with a divine flame from the summit of heaven.

And although Christ, himself born from God’s light,

is God, the highest Light,

he has rightly granted that the saints too should shine

as lamps of the Church. Under the guidance of that fire,

let love press upon their understanding and ardor burn in their speech.

He scattered throughout the world lamps of many branches,

so that the new light, poured forth as a torch of faith,

might fill every land beneath the heavens

with star-like virtues.

Rome, having marveled at the twin radiance of Peter and Paul,

rejoices in apostolic triumphs,

through which she will live forever.

[Col. 0576C] But John sows light through his words in Asia,

having drawn from the Lord’s breast the mysteries he pours forth.

Bartholomew flies triumphantly through the kingdoms of the East

and, glorious in arms, conquers the untamed Indians with his tongue.

You too, Mark, calming the furies of the Nile,

satisfy the thirsty fields with clouds of the Gospel.

Africa shines with Cyprian’s words and merits;

he urged her to despise her pleasures by shedding his blood.

Pictavis, greatly illumined by its teacher Hilary,

now dispels the darkness of the ages with true light.

Chrysostom, that John, illumines Constantinople

with the golden radiance of his splendid speech.

Nor is the lamp now content with the compass of the world:

shining, it is scattered beyond the seas.

And Britain, sharing in this light, has in our time

given birth to a venerable flash of lightning:

Cuthbert, living a golden life among the stars,

has taught the English by his own steps to climb the heights.

The honor of virtue has accompanied him

from the very threshold of life,

and heavenly glory attends him through evident signs.

Although I cannot recount all his deeds,

I would nevertheless prefer to touch upon the final traces of his works in verse,

through which the inner foundations of his holy mind may be revealed.

You, supreme Spirit, author of gifts, help me, I pray:

without you, your grace does not know how to speak worthily.

You who grant new utterances to tongues breathing flame,

grant gifts to the tongue that sings your gift of speech.

## Chapter II. How the Boy Cuthbert Was Warned by a Child about His Future Episcopate

[Col. 0577B] From his earliest age the life of this beloved servant of God

shines with heavenly light.

Christ calls him the bearer of a great office,

summoned by a special gift to true joys;

he teaches him to despise the splendid pageantry of the fierce world

and to establish his heart in heaven.

At last, through a gentle first instruction,

he directs him throughout the early years of life,

so that when he has matured he may bring him to the lofty stars.

By chance, while his slender youth was playing

on the wandering grass,

his noble character was likewise engaged in empty contests,

and through a light wrestling match the boy won the prizes.

But the Lord corrected his childish thoughts

through a fitting teacher.

For a tiny child from the tender flock

warned him, despite his uncertain strength,

not to trust in it,

nor to consume his brief years in premature luxury,

but to strengthen his steadfast mind through love of the Lord.

[Col. 0577C] But the boy, unwilling to accept the child’s sacred words, laughed at them,

scorning an infant of three years when he himself was eight.

He groaned and covered his face in bitter grief.

His grief dissolved into tears, and everyone in turn

tried anxiously to wipe away that one child’s weeping;

yet consolations could not alter it.

Cuthbert, with loving embrace, soothed him with kisses,

begging him to dry his cheeks and lay aside his grief.

He received from his troubled heart his justified complaints:

“Why, dear child, do you submit yourself to such empty and light play,

when the lofty God has consecrated you to heavenly honor,

appointing you over peoples for whom you will open

the courts of heaven?

Is it right for a nobleman to compete in the race with slaves,

or for a bishop of the people to be compared with their deeds?

Therefore abandon these trifles so unlike your proper acts,

and, devoted to God, join your sacred heart to him.”

Thus he spoke, and the gracious Spirit implanted

a mature understanding in the child’s heart,

to remain with him throughout his life.

Nor is it surprising that infants should reveal Christ’s mysteries,

or that the sacred breath should fill the breast of a nursing child,

since it makes an ass bray forth human speech.

## Chapter III. How He Became Lame from Pain in His Knee and Was Healed by an Angel

Meanwhile the little boy was struck by the sudden danger of illness

and guided his feeble steps with a staff.

One day, suffering and alone, he had placed

his weary limbs beneath the open sky, when suddenly

[Col. 0578A] there came a venerable rider in a snowy garment.

His bearing too was like that of a horseman,

and he greeted the reclining boy,

asking him to render him a service. The boy replied:

“I would now gladly attend to your service,

were my foot not weighed down by a dreadful fetter.

For look: my knee is swollen, and for a long time now

no treatment of physicians has for a long time been able to soften it

with hare-bones [Note: [Col. 0577D] That is, with hare-bones; for they say that hare bones cure diseases of the shins.].”

The visitor leapt from his horse and carefully felt the sick knee,

saying this: “Let a pot cook fine flour together with milk in boiling [lacuna],

and anoint this swelling with it while hot, so that it may be healed.”

Having said this, he mounted the horse on which he had come,

and returned home by that road. The prescribed medicine followed,

and the holy man recognized that a physician had come to him

from the throne of the heavenly Judge,

the fish who restored sight by the gall of Tobias.

*Textual note: the verse reads* Restituit visus piscis de felle Tobiae *(literally, “the fish restored sight by the gall of Tobias”); its unusual printed construction is retained.*

## Chapter IV. How, by Changing the Winds through Prayer, He Recalled Boats Drifting into the Ocean to the Shore

From this point, strengthened in heart by greater power,

he learned through prayer to strike the throne-bearing Thunderer.

There is a notable place above the mouth of the River Tyne,

already then flourishing with a distinguished community of monks.

While they were carrying wood across the back of the fierce current,

they were suddenly struck by the violence of the river and wind.

Five boats there were, all of which, borne along by the swift whirlpool,

slid headlong into the hollow waters of the ocean.

Already they had been snatched far from sight;

like a winged diver upon the waves,

the boat appeared as it moved across the blue waters.

The brotherhood went out and, bending their knees,

raised their prayers to heaven, asking for life and peace.

[Col. 0578C] But this victory was reserved for the chosen boy [Variant reading: *haec*, “these things”] [Note: [Col. 0578D] That is, chosen.],

who happened at that moment to be standing on the bank of the other shore.

An immense crowd and great company of people laughed,

for the good fortune of the righteous is grievous to the reprobate.

He said:

“Let us abandon these harmful joys, brothers,

and grieve with those whom mournful blows afflict.

Or rather, let us pray to the Lord,

who created the winds and waves,

that he may deign to grant them a saving journey.”

But the rustic crowd disagreed with this righteous advice.

He immediately pressed the fields with his knees and face.

The winds changed, and when the boats were thrown back upon the shore,

the crowd, ashamed at the sight of the divine power,

glorified God, who strengthens the prayers of his servants.

## Chapter V. How, While Staying with Shepherds, He Saw the Soul of Saint Bishop Aidan Carried to Heaven by Angels

[Col. 0578D] Meanwhile, while he was pasturing tender lambs

on pleasant hills, behold, during the nocturnal hymns

he saw fiery camps shining with starry companies

and carrying a holy soul through the heavens amid the joys of a radiant procession.

He said to his companions, whom sleep had overcome:

“Alas for us, wretched men, who are pressed by sluggish sleep

and are not worthy, while awake, to see heavenly deeds.

But I, fully awake, have in a brief moment perceived

great things of God [Note: [Col. 0578D] That is, ‘I saw.’].

The twin gates of Olympus are opened;

the blessed spirit is placed in the heavenly hall,

rejoicing as it is accompanied by angels.

It passes through the stars and now rejoices

to behold the King upon the highest throne.

I think that this was a bishop, or a leader of the consecrated people,

shining supreme in the citadel.

The fiery heaven receives him amid such choirs

and carries him to the lights of light.

Learn, shepherds, while vigilantly guarding your folds,

to beware the snares of night and the dark lions,

so that the sacred songs of angelic praise may be opened to you

and you may behold God, mighty in the citadel of Bethlehem.”

Remembering these things, he kindled astonishing praises

within his companion’s trembling heart.

That Aidan died at the time, praying joyfully

for the Lord’s heavenly dwelling.

## Chapter VI. How Aidan, Foretelling a Storm to Sailors, Gave Them Oil with Which It Might Be Calmed

The venerable deeds of this priest shine throughout the world,

and his teaching, worthy to be told in lasting remembrance, shines likewise.

It is enough to touch briefly upon one example.

A certain priest, ordered to cross the blue fords

of the wave-bearing sea, went humbly to the prophet’s oracle,

begging that he and his companions might be protected

by the holy man’s prayers.

The lofty bishop said to him:

“You are seeking the deep sea.

The north wind will rise against you with an adverse blast.

But remember promptly to calm the roaring wind and sonorous storms

with the chrism that I shall give you.”

Then, taking the oil of rich olive,

the sailors went out upon the sea.

With the sails spread like wings, the secure boat cut through the deep.

Suddenly a heavy winter storm arose;

the sea raged everywhere,

delaying the course begun by the ship as it was swept along.

At last, when a drop of the rich remedy had been introduced,

the wave, subdued, laid aside its fierce swelling

and opened a pleasant passage.

Thus a single power shines with twin rays:

the one who had earlier terrified them with gloomy words

now raises the grieving with ready consolation;

and he who foretells the future with prophetic mind

himself restrains the troubled elements by his commands.

## Chapter VII. How Cuthbert, Traveling, Found Food at His Horse’s Indication

Again Cuthbert, full of a heart chaste before God,

set out on a journey [Note: [Col. 0579D] Bede uses *itiner* and *iter* interchangeably here. Plautus (*Mercator*, act II, sc. 2), Lucretius (Book VI), Manilius (Book I), and other ancient writers noted by Vossius in his *Etymologicum* used the form likewise; see Nonius Marcellus, *On Changed Declension*.] and was enclosed by the rainy east wind.

A cloud, flying everywhere through the cold heavens,

covered the stars.

He turned aside beneath the roof of an old hut,

where a keeper had once sheltered livestock in a remote place,

and tied to the wall the horse on which he had come.

While he waited for the Lord to quiet the wet winds

and the holy man was consecrating the hour with divine praises,

he suddenly saw the horse tearing the thatched roof with its teeth.

Hay fell from the bundle of straw,

mixed with a splendid feast and given to the pious young man

as a supreme gift.

Such food as you once deserved when the grass was dried,

fiery prophet who climb the heavenly airs.

Thus the holy man, having been fed by a warm loaf

and heavenly meat, gives thanks.

When the storms had subsided,

he resumed his journey, rejoicing in the clear weather

with Christ accompanying him.

## Chapter VIII. How, Having Received an Angel as a Guest and Seeking to Offer Him Earthly Bread, He Was Deemed Worthy to Receive Heavenly Food in Return

[Col. 0580A] Seeking greater things from the monks of Ripon,

the holy man joined them in body, mind, dress, and deeds.

Soon he was appointed servant to the guests,

and, willingly subject to just service,

he joyfully deserved to behold the citizen of the lofty court

and to feed him.

This guest arrived in the midst of winter,

and, received according to the prophet’s humble custom,

had his suitable limbs washed [Note: [Col. 0580D] Perhaps, “limbs.”].

He gently warmed his feet,

leaning over them with the caress of his palms.

Supported by his arm, he asked that the guest deign to remain

until his limbs might be refreshed by joyful dishes,

lest cold, hunger, and snowy December blasts

should intensify the hardship of the long, freezing road

for one who had arrived chilled by the morning winds.

At last, invoking the kingdoms of the supreme Thunderer,

he persuaded the reluctant guest to stay

and drove away his hunger.

He departed, wishing to bring him warm bread,

since only a few fragments of the previous evening’s meal remained [Note: [Col. 0580D] Bede seems to have pronounced *sternae* for *hesternae*, as some pronounce *Spania* for *Hispania*.].

Returning to seek his guest, however,

he saw nowhere upon the snowy field

any trace of the traveler’s feet.

Entering the inner rooms, filled with a rosy fragrance,

he found—wondrous to relate!—three loaves shining there,

gleaming with bright whiteness.

Then Cuthbert, speaking with a frightened heart, said:

“Surely I see that a guest had descended from the heavenly court

and, light-winged, returned to his kindred stars.

He came to feed, not to be fed,

bringing dishes such as do not arise

from the produce of our harvest.

Lilies do not bloom so brightly,

nor does shining rose smell so sweetly.

Our honey, flowing with manna, is despised beside it.

Therefore these sacred gifts were not produced

by my furnace from baked substance;

rather, O paradise, your fruit has produced them.

Nor is it surprising that he rejected our rich food,

since he who enjoys the bread of life for ever

feeds upon it eternally.

For the man devoted to God in mind and joyful in speech,

who is accustomed to commemorate under the Lord’s praises

the sanctifying deeds of the fathers,

often also recounts his own deeds—

the triumphs he has achieved only with heaven as witness.”

## Chapter IX. How the Animals of the Sea, in Which He Had Prayed through the Night, Served Him on His Return, and How the Brother Who Saw This, Fainting from Fear, Was Revived by His Prayer

[Col. 0580D] Meanwhile, the young man went out to his customary nocturnal hymns.

A certain man followed him along the slow path,

trying to discern his uncertain footsteps.

They came to the sea.

Cuthbert, immersed in the waves up to his neck,

passed the night in song.

He came out of the sea and, kneeling on the shore,

stretched his two hands in supplication toward the stars.

Then, behold, two animals came from the depths of the sea

and lay down upon the golden sand before the prophet’s feet.

They warmed his cold feet with their fur [Note: [Col. 0580D] With their hair.]

and breath,

and dried the sea’s chill from the holy body.

Then, with humble nods, they asked to be blessed.

Complying with their request, he bestowed his blessing on these servants

by word and right hand,

and sent them back to their native waters.

At dawn he returned to the dwellings.

When his companion saw this,

struck with fear in his heart,

he drew half-dead breath while hiding in a bent-over cave.

But when the returning day drove away the shadows of night,

he came, sick, to the prophet,

fell at his knees,

and begged him to commend him to the Lord

with an abundant prayer,

because he had spent a grievous night beneath the burden of fear.

“Were you,” he said, “trying secretly to observe our journey

from your hiding place?

But your error will now be forgiven,

if you remain silent about what you have seen

until I depart from the world.”

He carried out the example of the supreme Master,

who, after sending light to the blind,

commands him to conceal the author of his restored health.

Then by prayer he drove away the illness

and released him from his fault.

Day by day, the highest grace of the Thunderer

stood forth as witness to the growth of his merits;

miracles opened his mind.

Already prophetic power from its starry height

was radiating his heart with a bright and brilliant breath.

## Chapter X. How, When Sailors Were Blocked by a Storm, He Foretold a Calm Sea on a Certain Day and Obtained Food through Prayer

Meanwhile he was carried toward the shores of the Picts,

but the closed sea delayed his return in harsh December.

Hunger, cold, and the dangers of the raging sea,

together with clouds, thunder, hail, and flashing heavens,

terrified the anxious sailors beneath the outer shore.

The holy day had come on which Christ,

born in the flesh, shone forth through signs

as the glory of heaven upon the earth.

He, being calm, spoke with gentle heart:

“Why, I ask, does such sluggishness hold our minds,

so that we do not cut through these savage bonds

with some effort?

You see how the earth grows white with the sea’s ridge;

the air pours down water, ice covers the sea,

night covers the heavens;

our hearts waste away with hunger,

and human assistance is lacking.

It remains, therefore, to strike God with suppliant prayers—

him who once opened the red thresholds of the sea,

who gave shelter in a cloud,

bread from a storm-cloud,

cups from a rock,

and by a guiding flame dispelled

the dreadful shadows of night.

This present day, whose gift has deserved such a benefaction,

is the day on which the magi, bearing four treasures,

look upon and worship the mortal, the King, and the God;

the day on which the Lord washes the world

in his own baptism,

opening the heavens, long closed to believers through the ages;

the day on which sweet wines blaze from the spring’s depths,

and water reddens in the cups through the Lord’s gift.

So too, I believe, our fortunes will return safely

under God’s guidance,

if trust strengthens the heart that implores him.”

When he had spoken, he settled his companions beneath the shore,

where he had been accustomed to pass the sleepless nights in prayer.

There he saw, as if cut apart, three pieces of a fish’s entrails.

He knelt and worshiped the Lord,

praising and enlarging the venerable gift of faith.

“Prophet,” he said, “enough remains for feasts for four days [Note: [Col. 0581D] That is, ‘there remains.’].

The Creator has made provision for us.

When these things have been done,

he will calm the sea and bring us back

by our native route to the sailor’s land.”

Then they carried the food to the hearth,

and, giving thanks, refreshed their bodies

for three days with the food supplied from heaven.

Its honeyed flavor bore witness that these were new gifts.

On the fourth day, when the cheerful south winds had ceased,

they crossed the sea and happily reached a safe harbor.

## Chapter XI. How, While Traveling, He Foretold That an Eagle Would Provide and That He Would Receive Food—and Then Received It

Afterward, having attained the rank and merit of a priest,

he went forth to renew the peoples with the streams of life.

Addressing his companion on the road—though he himself knew the future—Cuthbert said:

“Tell me, companion, where do you intend to obtain food?”

“I too,” the companion replied, “have this question in my uncertain heart.

We have brought no meal in our vessels;

there is no hospitable house;

we cannot complete the journey hungry and exhausted.”

The elder answered:

“If you learn to trust in the Lord,

he will provide food—

the one who ordered the ravens to feed the prophet.

Do you see the eagle cutting through the wandering winds?

The Almighty can satisfy us through this servant as well.”

As they continued the journey, they came to a river,

and saw the bird that had flown high beneath the red heavens

sitting on its marble bank.

The elder said:

“Do you see our servant above the waters?

Run, I ask, and bring what the Lord has sent.”

He brought back a fish.

He cut it in half;

with one part he drove away the hunger of the servant,

and with the other he strengthened their own hearts.

When they had completed the journey,

he opened for the peoples a path through the waters of salvation,

calling them into the realms of heaven.

## Chapter XII. How, While Preaching to the People, He Foreseeing the Sudden Arrival of the Devil’s Fire, Extinguished It When It Came

[Col. 0582C] At another time, while opening heavenly things to the earth,

he beautifully exposed the impious deceits of the serpent.

For suddenly he inserted such words into his sacred discourse:

“Whenever the mysteries of the kingdom are opened to you,

your heart should be attentive

and your understanding kindly disposed,

lest the wandering breath of the destructive serpent

harm you [*laudat* should perhaps be read *laedat*, ‘harm’].

For, perversely striving to overturn sacred efforts,

it rejoices if the faithful are disturbed

by even a small cloud,

so that the deceitful enemy may draw us away

from the sight and speech of the heavenly King,

as though he were a worthless servant.”

While these warnings were being given,

a devouring fire rose from empty fuel

and seized the neighboring houses without resistance.

Wherever the flames flew, the wind helped them,

and the crash rose to the stars.

[Col. 0582D] The people, deceived by the frightened apparition,

sprang up and hurried to bring water

against the fire-breathing roofs.

But the deception, unable to withstand the water poured upon it,

perished through its own insubstantiality,

and the spectacle returned beneath its native shadows;

the empty trickery hid itself in wandering caves.

The people, confused, returned home

and, prostrate, begged the prophet for pardon.

The proud men rejoiced to recognize themselves as frail—and to recognize the deceptions;

and the foreknowing power of the Holy Spirit extinguished

the weapons of the tyrant.

*Textual note: the syntax of* fragilesque superbi / se gaudent agnosse dolos *is compressed and permits uncertainty in how “frail,” “proud,” “themselves,” and “deceptions” are connected.*

## Chapter XIII. How He Extinguished by Prayer the Flames of a Certain Burning House

Moreover, when genuine fires with crackling flames

were once devouring the dry roofs of a house,

he confronted them with prayers,

turned back the winds and household fires,

and drove away the danger with his voice—

something that the strength of young men could not do.

Nor is it surprising that a fragile furnace yielded to the prophet,

who had been accustomed to turn back the fiery darts of Satan,

launched from his quivers,

against the heavenly shield of Christ.

## Chapter XIV. How He Cast a Demon from the Wife of a Certain Man Before He Himself Arrived

A man came to the great leader

and, trembling, repeated his entreaties in suppliant words.

His beloved wife lay at the threshold of death;

her limbs were already stiffening as sensation fled,

and only trembling life still burned beneath her gasping breast.

“Send,” he begged, “someone who now bears the mysteries of Christ,

that he may drive out the spirit before it leaves

her pale limbs.”

As he considered whom the prophet should send on this journey

(for at that time he was prior of the cell at Lindisfarne) [Note: [Col. 0583D] Thus Bede frequently uses *vatis* in the direct case, even where metrical necessity does not require it, as below in chapter 17.],

he learned by secret divine revelation

that this was not an ordinary kind of death,

but that the violence of a dark demon

was cruelly pressing upon her with dreadful torments.

He offered himself instead.

They set out, and suddenly the guide dissolved into tears.

He anxiously shuddered in his sorrowful heart as he approached,

fearing that, if he saw the woman beloved and long cherished by the prophet

oppressed by insane fury,

suspicion of her former life might arise

and an evil report damage her ancient reputation.

For she had been accustomed to attend diligently upon the prophet’s service

and to offer her eager ears to his teaching.

He relieved the man’s grim anxieties with pious consolation:

“Why do you grieve, melted by the silent fire of a hidden furnace,

and wash yourself with water as a mournful sign of your heart?

Do you think that I am approaching the house of my dear companion

and that she can be seized by the maddened coils of the serpent?

The enemy, accustomed to being conquered in repeated conflicts,

will now be overcome by the sword of victorious faith.

Rather, the woman will come to meet us

and receive these reins of a sound mind.”

His words came true.

They reached the house; the savage serpent fled.

The woman, restored, came to meet them,

took the reins with her right hand,

and asked the prophet to dismount and enter the house,

revealing new gifts of salvation:

at his arrival the water-snake (*hydrus*) had fled [Note: [Col. 0583D] *Hydrus*, “water-snake.”].

## Chapter XV. How, Having Contemplated the Life of a Hermit, He Lived among the Monks of Lindisfarne

[Col. 0583D] Lest he become deprived of heavenly and divine fame

through the fragile praise of admiring people,

he preferred to walk in hidden secrecy before God,

so that, with him as witness,

he might be protected, free from the breath of human praise.

At the same time, at the command of his own bishop,

he began to show the brothers a path

through the example of his virtue.

He joined the monks whom the bright island of Lindisfarne,

washed around by the returning waves of the blue sea,

enclosed.

In a short time, shining through many signs,

he raised innumerable sick people

by driving away their illnesses,

and drove the dark weapons of the enemy away

through the radiant trophy of the cross.

Although absent in body, yet present in heart,

he crushed the enemy

and cleansed Christ’s house of its foul inhabitant.

Why should I attempt to describe his inner life?

How gentle he was in speech,

how grave in conduct,

and how he sharpened his mind toward heaven

by kindling it with tears [Note: [Col. 0584D] Another reading: “raised it.”],

since outward beauty is an indicator of a pure heart!

## Chapter XVI. How He Made Himself a Dwelling on the Island of Farne after Driving Out the Demons

At last the elder sought Farne

and, having obtained the dwelling he desired,

energetically drove the dark inhabitants from their homeland.

Previously that island, horrible with phantom winds,

had kept human companionship away

through unseen terrors.

As soon as the Lord’s servant approached,

the terrible whirlwind, frightened by the cross,

fled through the empty air like a portion of smoke.

Holding that tranquil realm as the tyranny perished,

the holy man established a heavenly city

upon an earthly height,

and built humble dwellings beneath lofty walls.

From them he could gaze upon the starry summit

and, withdrawn, look safely upon the lofty King.

And so that the divine power of the holy man

might be evident in all things,

he fortified the walls with stones,

stones which scarcely two groups of three men

could carry upon their necks.

Yet he alone was able to carry them

and place them upon the walls,

with the hand of the supreme Thunderer accompanying him.

## Chapter XVII. How He Brought Water from Dry Ground through Prayer, Having Once Also Turned Water into Wine by Drinking

This place had lacked a spring,

but the holy man brought forth pleasant water

from the dry ground through unusual prayer.

Arising within the holy Cuthbert’s dwelling,

it still gives a sweet drink to all who drink from it.

Nor is it surprising that this servant of the Lord

could deserve such a thing,

since once, while slaking thirst with springing water,

he was able to turn the waters into unmixed nectar.

## Chapter XVIII. How He Drove Birds Away from the Harvest He Had Sown with His Own Hand

Wishing to obtain food by the work of his own hands,

he tried to break up the uncultivated soil with iron

and, as a sower, entrust the hope of the year

to the tilled clods.

While a rich crop was rising from the little seed,

the time of harvest came.

But suddenly swift birds attempted

to plunder the old man’s golden ears of grain.

He, calm, said to the savage marauders:

“Why do you touch the harvest with unlawful audacity,

the harvest that was not placed in the furrows

by your labor?

Has your poverty surpassed mine,

so that you rightly cast your curved sickle into this field?

If perhaps God commands you to persist in this plunder,

I do not forbid it.

But if not, remain within your own boundaries.”

He spoke, and at once the feathered crowd withdrew.

Never again did it dare to injure

the rights of the Lord’s soldier [Note: [Col. 0584D] Perhaps, “fields.”],

whom it rather loved as a unanimous friend

of its own kind, joined to him by the sweet bond of peace.

For he himself cared for them

as a shepherd cares for tender sheep.

## Chapter XIX. How the Ravens Cleansed through Prayer and a Gift the Wrong They Had Done to the Man of God

The ravens broke their pact beneath the charge of black guilt.

They broke into the house

and, tearing the reeds from the roof,

rejoiced to carry them away

to the nests of their own offspring.

The prophet warned them to cease.

But they rejected his counsel.

“What,” he said, “are you doing, tearing apart the dwelling of the brothers?

Go away,

and remain exiled from this land forever.”

He spoke, and they departed sadly.

After three days one of them came to the prophet,

falling at his feet,

its wings spread in mourning,

and begging for pardon and permission to return.

Having made peace, it returned

and revisited its companion.

At last both came joyfully,

bringing with them a fitting gift for their vow:

a piece of pork fat,

with whose grease the holy man might soften his shoes.

Afterward they built their shelter there

with harmless materials.

Why are you inflamed with savage pride

and an overbearing neck?

Look at the raven’s way

and lay aside your blind fury:

it cleanses its wrongdoing

through prayer, weeping, and a gift.

Do not be ashamed to take an example for life

from the heart of birds,

when Wisdom says: “Consider …”
paths
What the ants wear away, and learn prudent understanding.

## CHAPTER XX. How even the sea served his needs

What shall I say of the sea’s waters serving the just man, and of the elements offering obedience to those who, with devoted minds, submit themselves to heavenly commands?

For when he was constructing a cell suitable for his own use, whose foundations were to be supported on the side facing the sea, he asked the brothers who were present to bring timber appropriate for the work. They forgot, and returned without it; but the next tide of the sea brought the wood. And—wondrous to tell!—it set the timber down at the very threshold where he had intended to lay the foundations of the building. Thus the sea rebuked the forgetfulness of men and shook the sailors with the shame of its wave.

[Note: Alternatively, “basis” (“foundation”).]

## CHAPTER XXI. How, by giving admonitions of salvation to many who came to him, he exposed the fragile snares of the ancient enemy

Fame summoned many to seek the holy sayings of the prophet and to lend thirsty ears to his heavenly utterances, by which he might raise those wearied by various calamities of heart.

But he, gentle, renewing the sorrowful with sacred consolation, recalled to all the highest joys of heaven and the fleeting pleasures of the corruptible age, and how the malicious one stretches various snares wherever the mind slips miserably, naked of the Lord’s love. Yet, he said, let the weapons of faith pierce through his empty deceits without distinction.

“How often,” he said, “do they hurl me headlong from a lofty cliff of wickedness! How often do they roll rocks against my breast! Yet, believe me, I am injured by no blow of the enemy; nor has an impact harmed the soles of my feet, nor has even the slightest terror touched my heart.

“And do not be astonished as though these were the supreme heights of my life, because I trample beneath my heel the proud blandishments of deceptive luxury and, secretly, desire to be present with the Lord.

“The monk’s life is stricter: always subject to commands, it serves under the rule of devoted obedience. Watchfulness, hunger, prayers, and the labor of the hands—it gladly restrains all these at the will of the ruler, bowing down.

“Among those whose lives I have known through their highest stages, and who have gone before through the rays of prophetic wisdom, is Boisilus, the glory of the community of Mailros. I remember that once he disclosed to me his whole life, and what remained for me in the order of the age to come. Only one sentence of his remains—would that God, the judge of the world, never bring it to pass.”

[Note: “Only one remains.”]

The holy old man said this because, foreseeing the future, he had foretold with lofty speech that he himself would become a bishop.

## CHAPTER XXII. His prophecy concerning the life of King Ecgfrith and his own episcopate

While everyone rejoiced to see the holy prophet and to compose the disturbances of their hearts through his prayer, behold, among the others came the royal virgin—Elfled, below—who, as the perpetual bride of the King, herself a virgin and chaste mother, brings forth choirs beneath the joys of your paradisal kingdom. She asked the prophet to deem her worthy of strengthening through heavenly admonitions.

He consented, and, having crossed the sea’s waves, advanced in the boat. While he addressed her with friendly words, she suddenly, anxious with concern, asked him:

“Now it is clear from the radiance of your shining merit that your prophetic eyes are fixed upon future ages. Tell me, I adjure you by the kingdoms of the supreme Thunderer: what will be the duration of Ecgfrith’s rule?”

The prophet disclosed the truth in an unambiguous speech:

“You call a man’s reign long-lasting, although, however many years it may extend—if even a hundred—it will be closed within a brief hour, and the luxury of one year will be counted as nothing when black death spreads through his languishing limbs.”

She mourned and lamented the sad prophecy with tears, and said: “Tell me, I beg you, whom will he leave to govern the scepter of the kingdom, since he lacks both brother and son?”

The prophet answered her:

“Do you see how this sea spreads wandering realms far and wide? Perhaps the Lord preserves someone among them for himself, someone chosen to govern the reins of this kingdom, and so that Ecgfrith may be joined to you by the love of a brother.”

The supplicant virgin dared still to question the prophet:

“Often the hearts of men are divided by varied cares. One part [Note: The ancient witnesses have *pars* (“part”), correctly.] rejoices when a mortal has attained the summit of worldly pomp; another, desiring treasures that luxury consumes, lays down no end to its perpetual poverty.

“Although you despise the honor offered by the world and prefer to be buried in secret within humble caves, you are destined to attain the highest episcopal honor, than which our age possesses nothing more sacred.”

“I confess,” he replied, “that I am not worthy to undertake such heights. Yet the right hand of the Lord can be escaped by no hiding place of heaven, earth, or sea. If he commands me to bear so great a burden of office, I believe that he will soon release me; perhaps, after the course of two years has passed, I shall be set free and, joined once more to my companions, shall gladly return to my secret retreat. But you also, Aelfleda, must remember to keep our conversation hidden until I am released from the bonds and prison of the flesh.”

[Col. 0587A] Nor was there delay: the words of the truthful speaker were fulfilled in due order.
