Compelled by the commands, prayers, and tears of the Church, and himself with cheeks drenched in bitter grief, he was drawn from his sweet hiding place and placed in charge of ruling the people, so that the lamp might not remain hidden beneath a bushel but might spread the Lord’s high-crested radiance through the church.

He ruled the Church as bishop for two years and hastened joyfully to return to his former caves.

[Note: That is, “caves.”]

And so that the prophet’s words might be fulfilled in every detail, the sun completed a full year in its customary months while Ecgfrith fell beneath the hostile sword of the Picts, and his illegitimate brother succeeded to the honor of the kingdom. This was Aldfrith, below, who, although he had lived among the Scots as a resident in that land,

[Note: In place of “as an inhabitant on earth.”]

breathed heavenly wisdom in his great heart. For he had left the borders of his homeland and its pleasant fields so that, as an exile, he might diligently learn the Lord’s mysteries.

Now this man’s venerable offspring, clothed in Tyrian purple, rightly holds the scepters of his ancestral kingdom, already entrusted to him. Like a new Josiah, more mature in faith and spirit than in years, he rules our renowned realm.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How, in his episcopate, he did not abandon the monastic life

Having attained the dignity of the highest priesthood, Cuthbert shines in mind, hand, and speech, and protects the flocks entrusted to him through prayers and admonitions.

Rich toward the poor and poor toward himself, gentle toward the bitter, a monk amid crowds, he does not care to exchange either his accustomed clothing or the dry food of the desert.

He increases the miracles of the mind with the titles of his virtues—virtues which may be touched upon briefly with the lyric plectrum, lest a more elaborate verse produce weariness in the exhausted.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How he healed the earl’s wife through his priest with blessed water

The holy teacher, everywhere ministering heavenly gifts, crossed the earl’s fields. The earl’s wife, languishing under disease and approaching death, grieved him.

Through his priest’s service, he gave her the life-giving water, a blessed gift of the prophet, and removed her wasting illness. Immediately the woman, restored to health, offered him her service.

## CHAPTER XXV. How he cured a girl, anointed with chrism, of pain in her head and side

At another time a virgin, afflicted with pain in her side and exhausted by heaviness in her head, had long groaned in sickness. The bishop, having anointed her with sacred chrism, renewed her through the gifts of salvation.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How a sick man was healed by bread blessed by the man of God

The father of the household himself, weighed down by a grievous illness, summoned groups of friends to his final hour.

Many gathered. One of them happened to bring a loaf that the hand of the gracious teacher had once consecrated and given him, at his request, as a pious gift.

They dipped it in water for the sick man to drink. He received it, and immediately, beneath the healing draught, the illness withdrew; renewed health entered his relaxed limbs.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How, during a journey, he restored to life through prayer a young man who was about to die

While the watchful shepherd was inspecting the sheepfolds entrusted to him, behold, in the middle of the journey they carried in a bed a young man whose limbs were numb and who was drawing harsh breaths with difficulty. They asked that he help the wretched man.

He immediately drove everyone out, and, active in prayer, raised up the languishing limbs and restored the companion to his amazed comrades.

[Note: “Iteris” is used here for “itineris,” and correctly so, says Nonius Marcellus (*On Changed Declension*). Since the ancients used *iter* and *itiner* indiscriminately, as noted above, they formed *iteris* from *iter* and *itineris* from *itiner*.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. During a time of pestilence, he restored a dying boy healthy to his mother

At the time when dreadful pestilence was devastating the Britons, the holy man everywhere spread heavenly gifts of healing.

He saw a grieving mother carrying her dying son. Sharing in the sorrow of the half-dead child, he himself gave him kisses and addressed the anguished mother:

“Put away fear and tears. This boy will be healed, and your whole household will be spared death in this calamity.”

His words were followed by the healing of both the boy and the household.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That all his deeds cannot be enumerated

What shall I attempt to say—what verse could suffice to recount what cannot be fully told?

How often did he raise with a word the limbs of the weak, consumed by the wasting of illness? How many fevers did the sacred water restrain? How did poverty turn water from a spring into the joyful taste of wine?

How often did he drive away the terror of spirits through lonely places, when it confessed that it was accustomed to leave Cuthbert’s breast at his threats, and was forced beneath the fiery shadows of the abyss to suffer even in his absence?

And how could I attempt to grasp in number the miracles of the holy man, upon whom shone such honor of prophetic grace, and who now, with pure vision, traverses the heavenly ether?

## CHAPTER XXX. He saw in spirit, while absent, the death of Ecgfrith and of the soldier whose fate he had foretold

Meanwhile, while Ecgfrith was pressing against the kingdom of the Picts in battle, the watchful man clearly foresaw in his mind that the savage violence would end in a miserable conclusion.

He covered his face with tears, repeated frequent sighs, and trembled, now looking upon the fields, now upon the sky.

“Perhaps,” he said, “our soldier, his struggle completed, is receiving from the Lord, his judge, the end appointed for him.”

They asked him to describe the outcome of the battle more plainly. He, having recognized the uncertain dangers, concealed them in such words:

“See, my little sons, how a new terror disturbs the air. For the Lord’s hidden mysteries lie concealed, and no one is sufficient to grasp the traces of the King Most High.”

Not many days passed before dreadful rumor announced the impious slaughter of common people and nobles. It had occurred at the very hour which, grieving, the prophet had named, seeing from afar what he had previously foretold when the virgin asked him about the ruler’s future.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How the man of God foretold the death of the anchorite Hereberht and obtained from the Lord through prayer that he might accompany him

Then Hereberht came, bound to the prophet by a special love. Instructed by his admonitions, he lived a solitary life amid high and remote places, but desired to be strengthened by the accustomed sayings of the holy man. [Note: That is, “sayings.”]

While they watered their devoted hearts in turn with the heavenly food of the Word, Cuthbert joined these words:

“Now, beloved brother, it is fitting for us to spend this day in feasts and celebrations of speech, since the Father of all things joined us face to face as those eternally bound in heart, and granted that we should see one another before we are dissolved by the law of death.

“Therefore the path of heaven must now be sought with our lips. With our whole hearts we must now knock at the door of life, while it is permitted to kindle our hearts with mutual heavenly flames. For the approaching time of death presses upon me.”

When he heard the words of the venerable prophet, Hereberht fell down, entreated him, grieved, wept, and said:

“I beg you, do not abandon me; remember your dear companion. Do not enter alone through the golden gates of the shining kingdom while I remain shut beneath the prison of the flesh. You will enter the lofty realms of heaven more worthily with a companion. Therefore, suppliantly, ask the Thunderer that we who are held down on earth in the shadow of death may depart together to the shores of eternal light.”

Hereberht persisted in his prayers and prevailed upon his grieving companion to dry his cheeks and lay aside his weeping, saying that, through the Lord’s mercy, he had obtained what he had requested.

Why delay? Both departed from the world beneath the balance of a single day and were carried to the Lord’s palace.

But Hereberht, burning long in the furnace [of fever], at last sent his fire-refined spirit forth above the heavens. I believe that he was made purer by those flames so that he might equal his companion; and, ascending to the stars with joined steps, they enjoy a united reward forever.

## CHAPTER XXXII. He saw the soul of a man who died by falling from a tree carried to heaven

He had been seated at table and was feeding upon the food of Olympus, when suddenly he was separated from human fare. Fear shook his bones; his trembling right hand let go of the knife, and terror quivered through his astonished heart.

Aelfleda, who happened to be sitting beside him, asked what might have caused such a sudden trembling.

“An angelic company has come from heaven,” he replied, “and, taking with them one of your soldiers chosen from your ranks, has returned to the stars amid golden and melodious triumphs.”

She asked his name.

“Tomorrow,” he said, “when I offer the sacred rites at the altar, the name and the manner in which he has gone to the stars will be disclosed to you in due order.”

When he had sent a messenger rushing through all his people, she finally learned the matter the next morning. While the prophet was intent upon sacred vows and prayers, she reported at the altars that a certain man, while climbing the heights of a leafy wood to cut fodder for cattle from a tree’s crown, had fallen and surrendered his soul when his limbs were loosened; and that he had been taken from human affairs at the very time when the holy man had seen him carried away into the heavenly air.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. After two years of episcopacy, he resumed the solitary life

After he had diligently ruled the Church for two years by episcopal authority and watered its living meadows with the flowing word, he persisted in abandoning the burden of such great honor.

Shut away in the desert’s solitude, he preferred to be struck by Satan’s grim weapons rather than to seek the empty favor of an ignorant crowd.

The flattering praise of dependents generates idleness, whereas struggle completed through perseverance obtains everlasting crowns. He was especially moved by the prophetic utterances of the spirit, which rejoiced to warn him that the time of death was near, and he secretly desired to renew his gracious mind before, wearied by the wave-tossed cares of the age, he died.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. While ill on the island, he ordered that his body be placed there and also spoke of his posthumous glory

The beloved island soon restored him to its sacred walls. His holy limbs were gradually touched by immense pain. As the burning fever increased day by day in his bones, he came forth from his sweet retreat and sought frequently to strengthen the companioning community, which joyfully served the weary father, with persuasive words:

“Learn, my little sons, to break the restraints of the fragile age and now to store eternal treasures in your minds.

“Contempt and perishable honor hang in the balance upon a thread. Through this, pious hearts learn not at all to seek praise during fleeting time by their righteous merits, since no one can prevail either to know the hidden places of a closed heart or to repay deeds according to their worth.

“Rather, watching with pure vision for the gate of the kingdom that the renowned King will grant to those worthy of the heavenly court, they prefer to place their lights in olive-bearing vessels.

“You have already been astonished that I breathed the starry riches with my mind raised upward. But the hidden chambers of my heart are open to the Lord; once the weight of the flesh has been broken, I believe they will begin to reveal themselves through certain signs.

“But, I beg you, since death presses upon the threshold and knocks insistently, bury these limbs within these walls. Even if I am consumed by cold winds or swallowed by icy waters, I hope that I shall rise to meet Christ when he comes at the appointed moment.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. He says that in his final days he overcame more grievous struggles

While the old man repeated such things into the ears of his companions, he ordered them to return for a time.

[Note: Alternatively, “let them return.”]

They crossed the blue waters in their boat, drawing the company of the brothers with them. After they had been detained for five days by the raging waters, they finally returned and, with suppliant weeping, obtained permission to bury the body of their beloved father with them.

The prophet added these words:

“Whoever desires to ascend victoriously to the kingdom of the Most High must avoid shamefully yielding in a corrupted battle, lest, overcome in the final contest, he be deprived by the enemy of the crowns he has almost attained.

“He who strives through long labor to empty the faithful now strikes the final days with a greater blow.

“From the first flower of my youth the impious one has harassed me with frequent snares, but this battle of only five days surpasses all the deceits of the time that has passed.

“Yet, with Christ as leader, I easily checked his wicked weapons, although no small supply of food or drink was given me, and although, wasting away in that place, I could not move my limbs.

“You too, I beg, must preserve the lofty and perpetual laws which the heavenly rule of the Fathers has established for you. I myself was able to express them in a few words while I watered the seeds that the greatest leaders had planted.

“However violently the storm may rise in raging tempests, endure all things through faith. By force the court of the kingdom is sought.

“Founded upon the rock, do not yield to heavy rains. Despise the fury of the torrents and the savage north winds. Let the Father’s final judgment remain in your hearts.

“It is best for you to leave the borders of this homeland rather than turn your trembling minds away from the path which sacred Scripture has portrayed in its divine writings.

“And because this place buries the ashes of many who, in a blazing course, sought the golden stars, do not let favor or the wandering glory of empty praise tempt you. Those men rejoice in crowns according to their merits above the stars.

“Likewise, it is fitting for us to run the race with our feet and grasp the prize with our own hands.

“A man does not become venerable because of a place; rather, a place becomes venerable because of its holy people.

“And now, I beg you, admit me within the walls of my own city, for the time of the flesh is approaching when I must pay what I owe.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. How he healed his minister of dysentery

Struck with amazement by these words, they wept and entreated him, asking that he not hide his wounded limbs in secret places, but that he should, while holding the highest boundary between death and life, have the fire of his spirit refreshed by fraternal consolation.

At least, they asked that he receive his minister beneath the sacred roof, so that the diligent servant might care for his fragile limbs.

Moved by these pleas, he turned his gentle eyes toward them all and looked upon a brother burdened by a long illness, whose limbs had withered because his exhausted entrails were wasting away.

“If you wish,” he said, “let this man enter my dwelling and offer me the solace of love in my weariness under this affliction.”

The man who accompanied the prophet soon approached the sacred threshold. Unexpected health embraced the sick man; the illness was driven away, the diseases not having dared to penetrate beneath the lofty roof.

[Note: Supply “was.”]

Without delay the sick man who had entered departed healthy. Cuthbert sent the priest there worthily, so that, with him as witness, he might seek the stars, just as with him as witness he had governed his life.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Having received the viaticum, he gave up his spirit amid words of prayer

Now everything lay torpid beneath the sleeping night. While Farne pressed its darkness upon the watchmen, the island resounded with psalms wherever prayers rang out in measured melodies.

The prophet himself, already tasting the joys of his reward, spread his shadow joyfully beneath heavenly praises.

But when the flame-crested morning star arose blazing, behold, the holy bishop, seated before the altar, tasted the cup of life and fortified his upward journey with the blood of Christ. He raised his face toward the stars and his gracious hands, rejoicing, and entrusted his soul, intent upon joyful praises, to the heavenly stars.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How, in accordance with the prophecy of the psalm sung at his death, the Lindisfarne community was attacked but protected by the Lord’s help

The priest came out and sorrowfully announced the holy man’s death to his companions. At that time they happened to be singing this hymn in plaintive praise:

“Good Lord, repelling us, in anger you destroy us; in mercy you save us from the enemy. You shake the fields, and in your power stir up the crowds; you heal the terrified and offer your own the must that was formerly bitter. But with you as leader, the enemy’s battles rush on; you suppress the harmful weapons, so that the chosen may possess the light freely forever.”

Then, by a sign of fire, the Lindisfarne community learned that the hour which he had kept watch over all night from the lookout was the hour in which the prophet had entered the heavenly air.

At that very time, during the customary order of the night praises, they too were singing the same psalm with its wondrous melody and, in sorrowful rhythm, following the blows while singing the Lord’s holy gifts.

Nor did the ominous signs delay long. Soon, when the prophet’s honored limbs had been placed in a gracious tomb beneath the marble to the right of the altar, the North Wind, relying on its snowy weapons, beat the Lindisfarne roofs with such blasts on every side that that noble family tottered in the worn framework of its affairs.

They would have chosen to abandon the place rather than undergo the utmost danger. Nor did the anger last long: Eadbercht restored peace to the holy place when the storm had subsided and recalled the scattered sheep beneath the sacred fold.

As the prophetic psalm had foretold and resounded in lyric order, he restored the episcopal dignity and the honor of the people.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How, after eleven years, his body was found incorrupt

The holy heir, placed upon the Father’s conspicuous throne, had passed beyond the course of his eleventh year when it pleased them to lift the ashes from the blessed tomb and lay them before the community with careful art.

But the psalm sings that the death of the righteous is precious before God, and that he holds the cup which the mighty, protected by the King’s name, tremble to drink.

Again, as the mystical lyre resounds in its highest song:

“Nor will you permit your holy one, O Most High, to see corruption,”

you reveal the golden heights of flowing life. Divine miracles shine in human limbs, and the power of the Lord, which glows in the high places, is rightly bestowed as a gift upon his faithful servants.

The untouched limbs were brought forth from the sacred tomb, free from any such grievous stain of corruption. They were not hard or stiff, nor weighed down by cruel death; rather, as though their breasts were receiving peaceful sleep, the entire body appeared flexible in every joint.

Nor was the exceptional beauty of the garment less evident: it remained uncorrupted, having covered the holy limbs. They decided to divide it in the middle, and the holy limbs retained one half. The other half was preserved as a token of a memorable sign.

[Note: Alternatively, “they retain.”]

## CHAPTER XL. How, when they placed the body of Bishop Eadberht in the tomb of the man of God, they set his sarcophagus above it

After Eadberht had extolled the miracles of events in worthy praises, I remembered in verse, as formerly, his distinguished deeds, recounting the acts of that excellent bishop.

Consumed by fevers, he sent forth his gentle breath to the stars and ascended bodily to his heavenly homeland.

Above him they placed the splendor of a lofty chest, enclosing the immortal glory of the gracious martyr, whose renown shines forth wondrously through heavenly signs.

The stains of disease flee, as does the impious rage of the black demon. The living presence assists, and, as before, it used to display the radiance of miracles; now likewise wondrous power is spread everywhere through the limbs of the dead.

## CHAPTER XLI. A demon-possessed boy was healed by water into which earth from his body had been infused

A certain man carried his son, whom the demon’s blind fury had cruelly tormented, forcing him to utter savage cries and consume his own limbs with bites. He brought the boy’s limbs to the sacred tombs of the holy men, asking for the desired healing; but they would not grant it, so that Cuthbert’s surpassing power might shine forth.

Then, terrified by the boy’s wailing and crying, a faithful person hastened to the aid of the beloved Father. He knew the hallowed earth upon which the water that had washed the sacred patron’s body had once been poured.

From a small piece of soil he seized great healing,

[Note: That is, “earth.”]

mixed it into liquid, and consecrated it with gracious words. He gave it to the boy to drink. Immediately the bitter shriek ceased, and without delay complete health returned.

He himself reverently praised the heavenly gifts and, with joyful steps in every place, proclaimed to all the venerable gift of Cuthbert.

## CHAPTER XLII. A sick man was healed by praying at his tomb

Another man, consumed by the fire of disease, was scarcely led by the hands of servants to the sacred tomb of the lofty martyr. He placed his knee down and entreated that the gracious voice of so great a patron might release him from his bonds.

He rose, strengthened by the gift of heavenly grace, and set free feet upon the ground for the healthy. Day by day he recovered the former gifts of health.

## CHAPTER XLIII. He healed a man’s failing eyes by touching them with his orarium

Even the garments that had shared the body of the holy man overflow with healing power as a participating gift.

For while pain and wandering darkness oppressed a certain man’s eyes, he received the *orarium* of the holy prophet and touched both his eyes with it, and immediately the grace of the venerable garment opened a path back to health.

## CHAPTER XLIV. A paralytic was healed by his footwear

Another man’s limbs had been rendered useless by a heavy burden and lay abandoned to their functions; futile medicine had increased his long-standing pains.

At last he wrapped around his sick feet the footwear that had clothed the sacred feet of the gracious martyr. Soon a sweet sleep softened the first darkness.

For the servant had put on the sacred gifts of lofty healing. When he had done so, his nerves were strengthened with inward power, and amid joyful dreams he moved with alternating steps, as fish play upon the shore of a deserted sea.

Awakening, he raised his restored limbs with a staff and began, standing, to recite the morning praises. His limbs strengthened with their former power, he praised divine aid and, now healthy, offered just thanks to the heavenly Thunderer for the gift.

## CHAPTER XLV. That the sick are healed by the covering of his wall

Nor is the sacred building emptied of the heavenly gift where the holy man, seeking the stars, left his lifeless body.

Even now it distributes its accustomed healing everywhere, and let the high offspring of David marvel at the roof of its temple, for its stones rival the heavens with their glittering gems and shine, crowned with golden figures.

But I marvel even more at the skin beneath the prophet’s humble roof, with which the holy man covered his fragile dwelling, lest rain or the piercing cold of the North Wind rush in everywhere and weary hearts burning with chaste prayers.

Nor does my judgment deceive me. For the work that Solomon had made with shining gold—alas!—the Chaldean flame covered with stony ruins.

But the curtains that Cuthbert’s sacred hand hung there, gifts distributed throughout the open world by Felgeldus, spread the remedies of an unbegotten gift farther abroad.

Steel becomes brighter and more precious than Libyan gold, and the shining skin surpasses eastern gems.

Here the third leader now guards the camp, an heir who will follow the blessed Father to the lofty kingdoms.

## CHAPTER XLVI. How Oedelwoldus, successor of the man of God, strove to conceal his miracles

Among these men, Oedilwald, not less diligent than his holy companions, ruled the sacred citadel with foresight. They say that he rarely wished to disclose his own virtues to anyone, nor the weapons by which, meeting the savage arrows of the bloodthirsty serpent, he had victoriously broken them.

For this reason that memorable saying remains long celebrated among the blessed, once carelessly allowed to fall from his lips.

While the holy man was watering a faithful ear with heavenly admonitions, he received these words from the companion’s heart:

“What, I beg, is the reason that the speech flowing so often from your mouth breaks and varies the frequent silence, and that forgetfulness sets limits amid your words?”

The pious hero answered him briefly:

“This is what you must hold forever, beloved love, in a fixed and mindful heart: unless each of the sheep diligently turns its ears entirely away from conversation, it cannot speak among the heavenly hosts or open its ears to the joyful harmonies of heaven.”

He had spoken, and, struck in his heart by trembling fear, the companion was overcome by sobs. Burning, he beat his chaste breast with his fists, and at last, groaning and drenched in tears after his sorrowful silence, burst into these words:

“I humbly beg you, by the scepters of the supreme Thunderer, to conceal these words from everyone until I return my dying limbs to the earth and walk upon the path of my fathers.”

Thus, although the holy man preferred to hide his greatest gifts in secret chambers, they were revealed through an heavenly witness.

But Cuthbert, often recalling the deeds of his predecessors, used briefly to add how Christ had also been his companion beneath the heavenly praise of his own struggle.

Thus the same spirit, through different gifts, purified two men, and, by a divided path through the heights of heaven, led both to one kingdom.

## CHAPTER XLVII. How the anchorite Felgeldus was cleansed there of a swelling of the face

Come, then: Felgeldus, the giver of the gracious gift, himself first received a demonstration of its healing power.

His face had previously been afflicted by a hideous swelling. While he lived alone, rough and secluded in a rigid cave, a broader flame rose from its inborn source, and burning lividity sprinkled his cheeks with spots.

When he was setting up a new roof for an old building, the certain hope of healing taught him joyfully to divide the curtain torn from the wall for the weary man.

As the first strap was being dipped in gracious water, to open a path through which the horned iron might pass, a playful drop sprang from the sacred stream, sprinkled the saint’s eyes, and touched his reddened face.

He quickly wiped away the water with his right hand and, astonished, marveled that the disease had disappeared and that the doors were already opening beneath a healthy brow, restored by healing.

And lest anyone think that I am reporting an error, I shall speak with God as witness, because a faithful priest, who had spoken the matter faithfully into the poet’s ear, was recounting these things.

“Behold,” he said, “you know that a bitter blemish (*labis*; variant *labes*) once oppressed my face; but now the grace of Christ has calmed the grievous blows through Cuthbert’s merits.

“Put out your hand, touch me, and test whether I speak the truth.”

For the closed eye could not see with its sharpness, and when the disease fled it had restored the former health.

The holy man perceived from heaven that he would be present in those circumstances.

## Prayer of the blessed priest Bede

These gifts of your supreme gift, Christ, giver of all good things, we have offered to you.

Tasting great joys through modest words, we have touched upon the lofty struggles of your saints.

We hope through those intercessors that you, who as a just judge crown the worthy in the heavenly sphere, may mercifully release to us, unworthy as we are, what is due.

The final rewards are sufficient in that palace of his dwelling, where your vision, Christ, will bless all things, remaining forever life, light, and salvation to the chaste.

## PASSION OF SAINT JUSTIN THE MARTYR

When Christ, our God, was born of the Virgin, an imperial decree rang throughout the world, ordering that the whole globe be registered.

For he had then appeared in the flesh who would register in heaven all the elect whom their profession of the sacred faith had commended.

Those who worthily observe that faith together with good works—which are like a certain census-tax pleasing to the Lord—are registered as citizens of the heavenly city.

Both sexes and every age furnish this census, as the army of many martyrs testifies: it consists not only of steadfast men but also of women.

Nor did only those mature in age undergo martyrdom; we also read that many suffered for Christ and the catholic faith while still in tender years.

Among them was the holy Justin, a little boy of nine years. How he passed through suffering to the Lord will be shown by the following text for those who wish to know.

While the cruel Diocletian, together with Maximian, held the monarchy of the Roman Empire,

[Note: This verse contains two excess feet.]

such a persecution was stirred up against Christians that every kind of punishment was inflicted wherever anyone happened to be seized who was bound by the title of this profession.

And lest anyone be able to hide in secret places, snares were arranged everywhere in this way, so that those going about would be compelled to submit to the law of idolatry.

They were not permitted to buy or sell anything. Nor were they allowed to draw water itself before they had offered incense to the detestable idols.

At that time there was a prefect in Gaul,

[Note: This verse contains two excess feet.]

faithless, savage, ruthless, hating the name of Christ and raging against Christians. His name was Riciovarus.

When the princes mentioned above sent him to persecute the saints living in Gaul, he immediately became eager for the slaughter of the holy.

Entering a city called Basel, where the river Ara pours its course into the Rhine, he ordered many Christians there to be drowned.

Thus he issued an impious decree throughout every region, so that no Christian should be permitted to live; he determined that their lives should be taken away through torments.

At that time there lived in Auxerre a good and just man named Matthew, and he had two sons, Justinian and Justin.

Justinian had been born first in the flesh, but Justin surpassed him in the maturity of his character, putting on old age through an unstained life.

Completed in a short time, he fulfilled long ages, while the praise of his merits remains forever, because it is clear that his soul pleased God.

Before he was born, his elder brother Justinian, already mentioned, was captured by the enemy and carried far away from his father’s house.

But the blessed Justin, from early childhood, had unceasingly devoted his mind to divine matters, making daily progress through the grace of God.

When he excelled in the gifts of spiritual virtues, God granted him this first among other things: that he often possessed foreknowledge of future events.

Then, through a revelation from God, he was instructed about his brother’s servitude and about his master, who was called Lupus and lived at Amiens.

When this had been revealed to him by the Lord, he immediately took care to tell his father, urging him to undertake the journey for his brother’s redemption.

His father answered him as follows:

“O son,” he said, “I do not know what route leads there, and for this reason I confess that I do not know what we should do.”

Then the holy boy Justin was inflamed in spirit and immediately traveled throughout Auxerre, seeking whether a guide for their journey might be found.

But when the man they had sought could not be found, the blessed boy returned and announced this to his father, saying nevertheless that they must not cease from the journey.

“Let us go on, father,” he said, “with Christ as our companion. He will not permit us to be cheated of our desire, which we hold in mind concerning the redemption of my brother.

“And with Christ going before us on the road we must cross, nothing opposes us and nothing will stand against us; we shall walk unharmed and return safely.”

To these words of his son the father replied:

“I might perhaps endure such a long journey, dearest son, since I rely upon my strength.

“But because you are a child, I fear that you may be unable to bear it. Perhaps the tenderness of your body may be harmed, and exhaustion may make you fail.”

The holy Justin answered and said to his father:

A servant, he said, I am of Christ, in whom you should know, father, that I trust and to whom I always commend myself.

Let us therefore go, worshiping in his name,

committing the whole outcome of the journey to him,

and whatever pleases him thereafter, let that be pleasing to us.

His son’s encouragements persuaded the father,

and, taking with him the things necessary for the journey,

they soon began to set out from Auxerre.

When the day had begun to decline toward evening,

they were received as guests in the fortress of Milidona,

and rested there during the course of that night.

At the castle gate a certain poor man met them,

who both limped as he walked and lacked sight,

[Col. 0597D] whom grim hunger and nakedness alike afflicted.

As soon as Justin’s presence became known to him,

he begged him to give him alms,

by which he might revive his life, almost wrested from him by hunger.

Then the blessed boy suggested to his father

that food should be given to the famished man,

and, obtaining provisions from his father, relieved his hunger.

But he himself stripped off his own tunic

and took care also to cover the man’s nakedness,

thus offering the needy a double assistance.

Then his father, somewhat angered against him,

began to rebuke him for having done this,

and called so pious an act a waste.

“Do not,” said Saint Justinus, “call this a waste,

[Col. 0598A] for it is on account of this that blessedness is promised us,

as the Holy Spirit says through David the psalmist:

‘Blessed is the one who considers the needy and the poor;

how God delivers him on the evil day.’

Nor is he compelled to fear an evil report.

The evil day for the wicked is the day of judgment,

when they are condemned by God to eternal destruction,

to burn in everlasting fire together with the devil.

Those fear an evil report whose judgment hears

the terrifying voice from Christ’s tribunal:

‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into everlasting fire.’

But on that evil day, on which the ungodly are condemned,

the one who gives alms deserves to be delivered,

so that the evil report may not terrify him.

Rather, the mouth of the Judge Christ will say to him

[Col. 0598B] that he should enter the kingdom of God,

because of the alms which he himself bestowed on Christ’s least brothers.

You see, father,” he said, “with how great a good we shall be recompensed,

when we assist the poor from what we possess.

Therefore do not ask what was given to the beggar.”

Thus they rested by night at Milidona.

At daybreak they immediately hastened their journey,

and, with Christ guiding them, came to Paris,

where a man named Hippolytus received them.

They disclosed to him the whole reason for which they had come,

namely, that they were seeking their captive brother.

Accordingly Hippolytus proved very kind to them,

and, after refreshing them, dismissed them in peace,

so that with God’s help they might complete the journey they had begun.

Then, setting out, they reached the river Isère.

[Col. 0598C] When they had to cross it,

they could find no little boat there.

When the holy boy’s father was distressed by this,

the blessed Justinus, showing his troubled father

the sign divinely revealed to him, offered this prophecy:

“Although a vessel is not now at hand,

we must not be anxious about the journey,

because Christ has shown me a consolation.

A certain man with a boat is approaching us,

and his assistance will immediately be available to us,

so that we may cross this river before us.”

While the boy was still saying such things to his father,

behold, a sailor came with his little boat,

just as the saint had foretold in his prophetic spirit.

Then they approached the man who had come with the boat

[Col. 0598D] and asked to be helped across the river,

offering him the proper fare for the passage.

The sailor readily agreed to their request.

But when they wished to give him the fare they owed,

he accepted nothing, freely providing the service.

They then hurried on and came to Amiens,

and inquired for the house of their lord and brother Lupus.

As soon as they had found it, they offered him humble petitions.

The blessed Justinus first addressed him in these words:

“We have come to your mercy, Lupus,

so that you may return our captive brother to us free.

For we have learned that he lives under your authority.

To redeem him we have brought our little property,

[Col. 0599A] which we now offer as a gift for your favor.”

Then Lupus began to inquire who they were,

and learned that they were genuine worshipers of Christ

and that they lived at Auxerre.

“Our brother,” they said, “for whom we have come here

and whom we are trying to redeem from captivity,

is called Justinianus, and is one of your household.”

“I shall offer you hospitality,” said Lupus,

“and show you all the boys whom I have.

If your brother is here, let him be redeemed for a price.”

So, when they had entered Lupus’s house in the evening,

he showed them his twelve boys,

but among them the one they sought was not found.

The blessed Justinus, however, looking around,

[Col. 0599B] saw a boy standing apart from the others,

carrying a lighted lamp in his hands.

This was the brother of the glorious boy Justinus,

though he had been captured before the beginning of Justinus’s life;

he had never seen him before that time.

But the blessed Justinus, filled with the Holy Spirit,

recognized at once, without being taught by any human being,

this brother who until then had been unknown to him.

For when the mind of the saints clings to the Lord,

it is instructed by him concerning inward and hidden things

and is taught unknown matters by the prophetic Spirit.

The book recounting the Acts of the Apostles demonstrates this,

where we frequently read: “The Holy Spirit said”—

whether to Peter, or to Paul, or to any other disciple.

In this way, when Saint Justinus recognized his brother,

[Col. 0599C] he immediately disclosed this to Lupus, who held him:

“He is my brother,” he said, “the one carrying the lamp in his hand.

My father came to you to redeem him.

As you promised, now show us your kindness,

so that, accompanied by our brother, we may return home.”

When he heard this, his brother was struck with astonishment,

because he had never before seen him, yet had been recognized by him.

Those who were present marveled at this extraordinary event.

The faithful rejoiced, glad in the Lord,

and gave thanks to God for so great a miracle,

frequently repeating Christ’s name with praise.

At that same time there were there certain net-makers,

belonging to the judge mentioned above.

When they recognized that these men were Christians,

[Col. 0599D] they hastened to report this to their master,

in case he should wish to issue some order concerning them,

in accordance with the laws promulgated against Christians.

The judge immediately sent men to bring them in.

If they refused to follow, he ordered them to be shut in prison

until they could conveniently be brought before him.

Meanwhile Lupus, who had received them as guests,

roused them during the night

and urged them to leave before dawn.

“Late yesterday,” he said, “the prefect’s men came here.

As soon as they discovered that you were Christians,

they hurried away to report this to the prefect.

Take with you, then, the brother whom you sought.

I shall demand no price for his redemption.

Only flee quickly from the persecutors.”

When they had departed as he urged,

the men sent by the judge immediately arrived,

so that, if they could find them, they might arrest them.

When they did not find those whom they sought,

they returned to the prefect, who had sent them there,

and reported that they had already left the house.

Then the prefect quickly ordered four horsemen

to pursue them at the swiftest possible speed

and bring them immediately before his tribunal.

If they resisted in any way, he ordered them to be killed.

So, taking horses, they hastened in pursuit

of the place toward which the holy boy Justinus had gone with his companions.

There is an ancient place called Lupera.

As they approached it, the cruel executioners

sent by the prefect were not far away from them.

[Col. 0600B] Then Justinianus addressed Saint Justinus:

“You see that a suitable place is near where water may be drawn

and we may refresh ourselves with food.

If it pleases you, let us sit for a while, break bread,

and quench the burning of our thirst with a drink of water;

then we shall be better able to continue.”

The blessed Justinus, already foreseeing what was to come, replied:

“If you intend to taste anything there,

you must do so immediately.

For behold, the judge’s messengers are approaching,

and, if they can, they will bring us before the judge

and hand us over to him to undergo punishment.

Therefore, I beg you, hasten to refresh yourselves if you wish.

I shall stand watch and see whether anyone comes

to ambush us by order of the judge.

[Col. 0600C] If anyone should come upon us for this purpose,

I shall speak with him; but you enter

and hide yourselves in the hollow of this cave.”

The holy boy spoke in this prophetic manner,

and immediately his words were fulfilled,

the words he had foretold concerning the executioners sent against them.

For, while he was speaking, four men appeared,

whom the prefect had sent to arrest them

or, if they could not do so, to kill them.

When they saw them, the others hurried into the cave.

But the blessed Justinus stood fearlessly,

destined by Christ for the glory of martyrdom.

The judge’s officers approached him

and asked who he was, what profession he followed,

and who his companions were and where they were.

[Col. 0600D] He answered them in due order:

“I am called Justinus by name.

I joyfully profess that I am regarded as a Christian.

And because you are persecutors of this name,

I cannot betray my companions to you,

lest on my account they be subjected to various punishments.”

“Unless you quickly betray them to us,” they said,

know that you will now be killed by our sword,

both because you refuse this request of ours

and because you are a worshiper of Christ.”

Saint Justinus answered the executioners:

“The holy Gospel indeed promises us

that whoever loses his life for Christ

will truly preserve it for eternal life.

[Col. 0601A] Therefore I do not fear suffering for him,

preferring to die through love of him

rather than to live in offense against him.

But as for your command that I betray my companions,

the holy Gospel no less forbids this,

the Lord himself showing that he did not wish it to be done.

For when, during the Passion he endured for us,

he himself was compelled to betray his disciples,

he by no means wished to become their betrayer.

And when he was seized by the persecutors,

he commanded that the disciples be allowed to depart,

so that, as he had already said, he might not lose any of them.

Know, therefore, that I will do neither of these things—

[Col. 0601, note: A syllable is lacking for the meter. Perhaps read *neutrum hoc me facere*, “that I do neither of these things,” adding *hoc*, “this,” to the printed *neutrum me facere*.]

neither deny the holy name of Christ through fear of death

nor betray my companions contrary to the Gospel.”

At these words the messengers grew angry,

[Col. 0601B] and, encouraging one another, prepared the saint for death.

Their anger would not allow them to wait even a little.

At last one of them drew his sword

and cut off his head, while the others urged him on.

Thus the martyr ascended to heaven with glory and praise,

possessing a double reward in a twofold respect:

he had persevered in confessing Christ,

and he had loved his neighbors even unto death,

delighting in Christ’s sweet commandments,

for he commanded us to fear nothing from those

who kill this body woven with languid veins.

In this he was instructed by the holy apostle John,

who, just as Christ laid down his life for us,

says that we too ought to do this for our brothers.

Therefore, to show how great his glory was,

[Col. 0601C] the same venerable martyr, slain for the Lord,

was immediately manifested through a glorious miracle.

For after his most holy head had been cut off,

he took up his headless body in his hands

and stood motionless before his executioners.

The executioners, immediately stunned with terror

at this astonishing wonder, fled,

not daring to remain,

when they saw the saint perform so great a miracle.

His parents then came out from hiding places

and saw his holy body standing motionless,

and marveled that it carried its severed head in its hands.

They turned various thoughts over in their minds concerning his martyrdom:

nature urged them to rejoice in such glory bestowed upon him,

yet again urged them to weep for him.

Above all, they were anxious about where

the sacred little body should be buried,

and discussed the matter together.

[Col. 0601D] While they were doing this, amid their varied emotions,

the head of blessed Justinus, which he held in his hands,

began—wonderful to say—to address them plainly,

and to instruct them concerning the burial of his body:

“Go,” he said, “to the place called Lupera

and bury my little body there.

But bring this head of mine to my mother,

so that she may show it natural affection

and keep with her this pledge of my love.

If she is held by longing for me,

let her strive to follow me, placed in paradise,

[Col. 0602A] where the souls of the saints rest in happiness.”

Then, as the holy martyr Justinus had commanded,

they embalmed his body and buried it there,

where he himself had indicated the place by name.

They brought his head to his mother.

She received it joyfully, giving thanks to God,

because he had taken his innocent soul to himself.

“To you, Christ,” she said, “be honor, praise, and jubilation,

because you have deigned to receive this boy

and associate him with your blessed martyrs.

And you, blessed Justinus, my dearest son,

who have entered Christ’s kingdom with the palm of victory,

remember me there in your intercessions.”

As his mother prayed these words with tears,

a great light immediately shone over the dwelling

[Col. 0602B] in which his holy head had been placed.

This light illuminated everything all around,

so that those who were in the city marveled.

It was night when this miracle occurred.

In those days there ruled at Auxerre as bishop

a man who loved the Lord,

adorned with the gifts of divine graces.

When he saw the radiance sent from heaven,

he ordered three priests to go to Matthew’s house

and investigate carefully the wondrous event.

Matthew recounted everything to them in order:

how the affair concerning Saint Justinus had happened,

both his Passion and the burial of his body.

He also added the account of the head brought to his mother

and how, at the third hour of the night,

[Col. 0602C] a light from heaven had illuminated the entire house

in which it was kept.

The priests reported these things to their bishop,

who immediately ordered the whole clergy to assemble.

They gave thanks to the Almighty for the miracle.

At last the event was made known among the people.

Everyone hastened there joyfully and glorified the martyr—

or rather, the Lord, who had glorified him in such a wondrous way.

Meanwhile, at the command of the holy and devout bishop,

the sacred head was honorably placed in a coffin

and carried to the church with honor and hymns.

The bishop had prepared a place for it,

and there he arranged for it to be reverently deposited.

There the holy martyr grants many benefits.

For, to prove his power with God,

while worthy funeral rites were being celebrated for the sacred head,

[Col. 0602D] a girl who came blind returned seeing clearly.

She was sixteen years old

and came amid the rites being performed for the martyr.

“Help,” she said, “blessed martyr of Christ, help,

so that through your patronage,

with the Lord Christ granting it,

I may deserve to obtain the sight long denied me,

so that his name may be praised in your martyrdom.”

She spoke, and immediately, before all the people,

the light of her eyes was restored as she had asked.

She rejoiced and danced in celebration of the martyr.

Again the whole people joyfully multiplied their thanks,

praising the Savior Jesus Christ the Lord,

to whom be honor and power throughout eternal ages. Amen.

[Col. 0603]

# POETIC MARTYROLOGY (C, G, S)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0603A]

The year revolves through the twelvefold circuit of the months.

It runs through ten times five weeks,

together with two more,

and through three hundred, twice thirty, and five days.

It rejoices to stand divided into three columns—

namely, the Ides, the Nones, and the Kalends.

For all the months count four days up to the Nones,

except March and May, followed by

July and October; these alone are governed by six.

These are likewise shown to require seven [days in the reckoning] toward the Kalends,

and all alike have eight [days in the reckoning] toward the Ides,

while January, August, and December

run through nineteen [days in the reckoning] toward the Kalends.

These are likewise shown to require sixteen [days in the reckoning] toward the Kalends [the printed sequence is inconsistent].

But in contrast, June, April, September,

and November properly proceed with four Nones twice.

February alone quickly varies from all the others

with sixteen [days in the reckoning].

Thus the year revolves through twelve months,

running through Nones, Ides, and Kalends,

and through the feasts of the saints,

which are read as inscribed throughout the year

to be celebrated on appointed days.

## JANUARY

The first day of January is that on which the Lamb is circumcised.

The Theophany of Christ is celebrated on the eighth day before the Ides.

Paul, the first inhabitant of the desert, occupies the fourth day before the Ides.

Anthony occupies the sixteenth day before the Kalends.

Sebastian is reported to have occupied the thirteenth.

Agnes shines upon the world with her radiant merits on the twelfth.

Anastasius is commemorated on the eleventh through martyrdom.

The Conversion of Paul rightly rejoices on the eighth.

[Alternative omits this verse.]

## FEBRUARY

[Col. 0603C]

The first day of February is now the day on which Polycarp suffers.

On the fourth day before the Nones Christ was presented in the temple.

We celebrate Agatha’s feast on the day of the Nones,

and Valentinus on the sixteenth day before the Kalends.

Thus Juliana also adorns the fourteenth before the Kalends with honor.

[Alternative omits this verse.]

And Cephas is rightly said to have held the chair on the eighth,

while Matthias, by the strength of his merits, was allotted the sixth.

## MARCH

From here Gregory adorns the fourth day before the Ides of March,

the apostolic teacher, the light and star of the saints.

[One verse is missing.]

Patrick, the servant of the Lord, ascends to the palace.

Cuthbert occupies the thirteenth day before the Kalends,

after whom holy Benedict follows on the twelfth.

On the eighth, the Conception of Christ rightly rejoices.

## APRIL

[Col. 0604A]

Overcoming the executioners on the ninth day before the Kalends of May,

From there George flew aloft to the stars,

and Egbert, radiant with worthy praise for his virtues,

reverently ascended the star-bearing Olympus on the eighth.

On that day Bishop Wilfrid entered the blessed realm,

carried above the summits of heaven by an angelic company.

On the seventh, the Greater Litany shines throughout the world.

The blessed Dedication of the Church is to be celebrated on the fifth,

calling forth equal praise for the saints and Christ throughout the ages.

Wilfrid entered the heavenly palace on the third,

later in time, but second to none in the flowering of his character.

## MAY

James, the pious brother of the Lord, and Philip

are venerated with wondrous honor on the Kalends of May.

The holy bishop John flies to blessedness on the Nones.

The innocent Pancratius follows on the fourth day before the Ides.

Mark deserved to knock at the Kalends on the fifteenth.

## JUNE

On the Nones of June the world marvels that

the soul of the exalted Lantbert has been turned beyond the stars.

On the fourth day before the Ides he places Barnabas on equal terms [the opening *In quosvis*, “into whichever,” is irregular].

Gervasius suffers on the thirteenth day before the Kalends.

Protasius is summoned together with him into the everlasting kingdom.

And John the Baptist is honored on the eighth day before the Kalends.

The beautiful feast’s birthday is celebrated with a rejoicing crown.

Paul also exults gently through martyrdom, and John.

The teachers Peter and Paul are commemorated together on the third.

The world glorifies them as its greatest lights crowned with the palm.

## JULY

[Col. 0604C]

The Dedication of Martin shines on the fourth day before the Nones.

On the eighth day before the Kalends, July joyfully bears

James, the brother of John, to be venerated in the customary manner.

We celebrate Samson throughout the world on the fifth day before the Kalends.

Abdo and Sennes sanctify the third with reverent honor.

## AUGUST

The Maccabees are crowned at the beginning of the month of August.

The holy and blessed Xystus is commemorated on the eighth day before the Ides.

The victorious Laurence conquers his enemies on the twelfth.

The holy Mother of God, the Virgin,

is clearly said to approach the eighteenth day before the Kalends,

carried amid angelic choirs.

From there Timothy holds, in due order, the eleventh.

At the same time the martyr Symphorianus receives his lot.

The holy Bartholomew receives the eighth.

John the Baptist, having suffered on the fourth,

is honored.

## SEPTEMBER

[Col. 0605A]

The sixth day before the Ides of September was dedicated with honor,

on which the blessed Virgin Mary deserved to be born.

Cornelius consecrates the eighteenth day before the Kalends,

and Cyprianus likewise, in due order.

The undefiled Euphemia holds the sixteenth.

The gracious teacher Matthew occupies the eleventh.

Mauricius, the martyr, together with thousands, occupies the tenth.

Cosmas receives the fifth together with Damian.

The Dedication of Michael’s temple sanctifies the third.

And the good interpreter Jerome shines on the day before.

## OCTOBER

Bosa hopes to possess the sixth day before the Nones of October,

solemn days on earth, while he rejoices in the highest Olympus.

The two Ewaldi are honored by lot on the fifth.

Paulinus, the Master, rightly holds the sixth before the Ides.

Luke, the teacher, come to our aid on the fifteenth before the Kalends.

Let us offer vows on the fifth for Simon and Jude.

## NOVEMBER

[Col. 0606A]

November shines like a many-faceted jewel upon the brow,

resplendent with the honor of all the saints.

Martin ascends beyond the stars on the third day before the Ides.

Thecla completed her life on the fifteenth day before the Kalends.

Cecilia departed with praise on the tenth, meriting it.

We joyfully venerate Clement’s feast on the ninth.

Chrysogonus rejoices in the life-giving fields on the eighth.

Andrew is rightly venerated by the world on the day before.

## DECEMBER

Ignatius likewise on the thirteenth before the Kalends [printed *Ter decimas*, literally “three times the tenth,” apparently for *tredecimas*, “thirteenth”]; “of Dacian” (*Daciani*)—the construction is incomplete or corrupt.

Thomas began to ascend to heaven on the twelfth.

The Lord was born of a pure virgin on the eighth.

Stephen sought the blessed realm through martyrdom on the seventh.

On the sixth, the evangelist and writer John,

carried by angelic protection,

entered heaven.

The tender young Martyrs are struck down on the fifth.

We celebrate Silvester on the day before the Kalends,

to be venerated by the world.

[Col. 0605]

# THIRTEEN HYMNS (G, S)*

## HYMN I: On the Reckoning of Time

[Col. 0605B]

The solar year is contained in four seasons,

and afterward is completed by twelve months.

It runs through fifty-two weeks,

and through three hundred and sixty-five days.

But a fourth part of a night and day is excepted,

which is seen to remain in the series of the days.

After the completion of two pairs of years,

those calculating determined that a leap-day should be added.

Hence the years differ in their long extensions:

some become intercalary, others common.

For the short year, called common and lunar,

is always completed by only twelve months.

But the long year, which is altogether called intercalary,

is gathered from thirteen courses of the moon.

The entire cycle of the shorter year

is completed in three hundred and fifty-four days.

But the long lunar year, in its total number of days,

is contained in three hundred and eighty-four.

The short lunar year is exceeded by the solar year by eleven days in succession.

The intercalary year, however, appears

to exceed the solar year by nineteen days.

By this abundance of its continual increase,

the longer years make up for the deficiency of the shorter.

Then a period of nineteen years is established,

a fixed span in which the lunar reckoning is extended,

within which the moon’s courses are repeated in a subtle cycle:

twice a hundred, three tens, and five cycles.

Here and there, as the enduring reckoning requires,

it inserts a leap-day into the interval.

Within the period mentioned above it always has a space

in which the sun and moon possess an equal balance of parts.

The first portion of this cycle is called the preceding octad,

and afterward the latter portion is called the hendecad.

Eight earlier years are assigned to the octad;

the series of the remaining years belongs to the hendecad.

In this course the shorter years occur twelve times,

while the longer years are counted seven times.

When such a cycle of years is extended,

the cycle returns to the same course of the moon.

But the sequence of the sun does not return to the same point

until twenty-eight years have revolved.

When the sun’s period described above has been completed,

it reclines without any resistant friction.

Thus, alternating through these reciprocal courses,

the periods of the sun and moon vary in their seasons.

But after the years return to their first beginnings,

through a span of five hundred and thirty-two years,

the feasts of the Paschal days become manifest

through the conjunction of the heavenly lights in this cycle.

When this cycle has been extended through the turning of the years,

it returns, as I said, to the same beginning.

Many have written other cycles concerning the long and short Paschal reckonings,

varied in their interpretation.

For the sake of brevity I arrange to pass them over,

though their numerical science is known to us as well.

Glory to the King, to God alone,

who created the lofty heavens, the lands, and the seas,

through eternal ages. Amen.

## HYMN II: On the Celebration of the Four Seasons

The year runs its course through four fixed seasons.

The same threefold reckoning also unfolds the months.

Hence it is established that each season embraces three months,

which the ancient fathers instituted

for God to be celebrated by three days of fasting.

You asked me, dear friend, to explain their reasons.

Rather, I would wish you to seek such matters from others

who are able to set them forth in varied speech.

[Col. 0607A] For I have no abundance of speech,

nor do I know how to investigate this hidden meaning.

And even if we seem to chatter something correct,

we are mocked, scorned, spat upon, and torn apart.

Therefore I have decided to remain silent about such matters.

Nevertheless, the wisdom of the supreme Judge remains unknown to no one:

he will come in majesty to demand with profit

the entrusted talents of the word.

Those who return profits will enter the joys of the kingdom.

The idle servant will be handed over to outer darkness.

Remembering this, I fear concealing what the grace of the Almighty

bestows on many for their benefit.

Receive, therefore, what you have undertaken to learn,

and, so that it may be rightly spoken, pray diligently.

I said already that each season embraces three months,

and that three days are to be celebrated for each one.

When the excess of food and drink has been cut away,

therefore join three months to the same number of days,

so that one day corresponds to one month.

These days are not celebrated in the first or final month of the season,

but the middle month is devoted to them.

It joins what has passed to what follows,

so that it may complete the months placed around it

by linking them together.

Perhaps you also ask what the months and seasons are.

The ancient ordinance, which prescribes such observances,

calls the seasons spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

The fasts of March consecrate the mildness of spring,

and they shine, as though flourishing with flowers, on the sixth.

June cools the heat of summer with its water,

at once restraining the season’s impulses

and the impulses of the flesh.

With this fruit rather than its other ears of grain it grows white [the comparative wording is strained].

September enriches autumn with a similar and pleasant gift,

more delightful than the festival of Bacchus,

and, with the harvest already gathered,

teaches us to praise the giver.

The last month, taking its name from its number and from rain,

beautifies the winter season with the same garland.

Although it binds the fields with rigid frosts,

it is certainly believed to open the serene heavens

and urges earthborn people to accuse before Christ—the purified (*piatos*; its syntactic role is unclear).

This heaven, too, watered with joyful dew,

drips the Just One onto the fields from life-giving clouds.

And while the fields produce no fruit for beasts,

the living earth brings forth a saving *hichyn*—

[Col. 0607D, note: This word, *hichyn*, can neither be understood nor emended.]

And although we know that souls grow rich through these foods,

and that all these things are made for the sake of future life,

no one can traverse the hill he has begun

if provisions for the road and the cost of labor are lacking.

Yet these things must be sought from no one other than their Author.

He does not forbid us to ask him for them,

provided that we use these means

so that we may enjoy the true things in heaven.

Thus, by such means, let the welfare of souls first be sought,

and afterward the serious needs of the present life,

without which the human body cannot subsist.

Let those things, however, be sought

by which we are not hindered from attaining heavenly things.

And because these provisions come at fixed times,

the giver of them must also be praised at those same times,

although his praise must never be silenced.

[Col. 0608A] Spring is the beginning of the year,

and also the beginning of the world.

Spring thrusts the seeds of all crops from the fields,

clothes the woodland with foliage,

and adorns the earth with flowers.

Already the joyful vine’s buds swell upon the branch.

Then the herds seek the males again and crop the grass.

The Creator commanded these things to serve our needs.

Therefore let the servant’s devotion serve the Creator,

who gave these things to the fields

and will give eternal things among the stars.

Summer stirs up wars, and in summer nations are set in motion.

The Church’s devotion diligently asks that these be restrained,

so that we may enjoy tranquil peace,

and devote ourselves more freely to God with a secure mind.

Driving away all clouds and making the world serene,

summer cuts the meadows, stores the grain,

and bursts the granaries.

For these things it is right to offer the highest thanks to the Author.

[Col. 0608B] Autumn spreads peaceful grapes over the hills,

pleasant to the sight and sweet in taste and touch.

The presses distill a welcome liquid from them.

It gathers fruit from the tree and stores it throughout the cellars.

While the earth bears these things at the Almighty’s command,

let those forgetful of the Creator and of the age to come,

for whom no hope of heaven remains after these things,

fill their bellies with abundant drink and food,

regarding this portion as their highest gift.

Christians ought to hold frugal banquets,

and persist in continual vows and lavish prayers,

begging the gracious Father with humble petitions.

Let these things provide assistance for the journey,

not become its rewards.

Let him grant them only so long as their use requires,

but preserve in heaven those things

without which no one is blessed.

[Col. 0608C] At last, when the earth stiffens in winter’s cold,

exhausted of crops and no longer enduring the mattock,

there is no honor for the fields

and no beauty of flowers remains.

Winter, kindly in its torpor, invites one to the fire,

persuading leisure, luxury, drink, and food.

It is fitting to restrain these things with prayers and frugal nourishment,

and to chastise the allurements of the flesh

through the hunger of the belly.

I have spoken of fasts distinguished according to their seasons,

so that this holy observance may also be profitable

for our fleeting affairs

while we are bound by the tight fetter of the flesh.

Something still more sacred remains to be explained.

For the Church has the custom of consecrating ministers

in these same months and on these same days,

so that, purified through fasts pleasing to God,

they may worthily assume the duties of the sacred altar.

This custom, however, was not discovered by human skill.

The leaders and holy senate of the Church,

the apostolic assembly filled with the divine Spirit,

instituted it and thereafter transmitted it for observance.

Paul was once to be consecrated with apostolic honor.

Barnabas too, it is said, was chosen under such an auspice.

For truthful Scripture truly reports that they fasted first with prayers,

and thus were called to these duties;

and that a company of the devout, accompanying them with equal purpose,

sent these teachers into the world

after laying hands upon them.

The Holy Spirit, coming from his heavenly court,

filled those whom he found fasting and praying.

[Col. 0609A] Therefore the Church’s devoted faith desires

that he too should be present to her ministers in a similar manner [printed *fratione*; alternative *ratione*, “manner”].

Without this God, no one ministers worthily.

Nor is any victim pleasing to God

unless it has been consumed by such fire,

nor does it otherwise breathe a pleasing fragrance to him.

In so great a matter, the order of days,

shining with mystery and number,

is believed not to be idle.

How fittingly Christians discharge their fasts over three days—

they who confess the threefold and one God,

three in persons, one in divinity.

The order in such matters is no less sacred.

For the fourth, sixth, and seventh days

are reckoned in some respect as days on which sacred observances are to be performed.

The first two are called Wednesday and Friday,

while the name of Sabbath is borrowed from the ancient law.

The old age called these days those of Mercury and Venus,

venerating the portents of false gods,

and the father Saturn, whom it believed to be the father of the gods.

For on the fourth day the savage traitor of old,

having summoned a wicked crowd,

made a pact for himself,

so that he might betray Christ,

by which he made the unrighteous rejoice.

When the world rejoices, it is fitting for the faithful to grieve.

Conversely, when the faithful rejoice, the worldly must grieve.

On this devoted day let Christ’s assembly fast,

while the wicked band conspires in Christ’s blood.

Let these strive in prayers,

while those strive in deceit.

On the sixth day he created humanity

and restored the fallen human being,

the Maker overflowing everywhere with piety.

Nor would I deny that humanity perhaps sinned on that same day

and was driven from the seat of paradise.

Therefore, on the day when the desire for food

was punished by the death it deserved,

it is all the more fitting to restrain the desire for food.

On this day, too, the redeemed should mortify their earthly members,

the day on which they are made alive by the death of the Author.

When the seventh day requests chaste fasts with prayers,

on this day that sacred choir of the apostolic order of old,

mourning the unjust death of its pious Teacher,

extended its fast into the holy night,

awaiting the one who, as he had foretold, would rise again.

From this arose the Church’s salutary custom:

on each Sabbath the servants of Christ should fast

and await their King returning from the dead,

laden with the spoils of Acheron after his triumph over death.

Let what I have said about the sacred sequence of days suffice.

Now let us apply it to the ministers of the Church.

[Col. 0609D] It pleases me that those who approach the altar

are assigned these days by lot.

Six ages of this world proceed in a fixed order,

of which the fourth—the Law and the Prophets— [the sentence continues beyond this section].

### Textual notes to the preceding passages

- [Justinus, Col. 0597D] Alternative *praesagis* for *praesago*, both “prophetic”: the alternative changes the inflection of the adjective attached to *spiritu*, “spirit.”
- [Martyrology prologue, Col. 0603D] Alternative *tricentis*, “three hundred,” for *ter centenis*, “three times a hundred”; *divisus*, “divided” (nominative), for *divisis*, “divided” (ablative plural, agreeing with “columns”); *jam*, “now,” for *nam*, “for.” Another note cites *Octonis … flagitare Kal.*, “with eight … to require the Kalends,” and says an alternative omits these four verses. Other alternatives: *Nonae*, “the Nones” (nominative), for *Nonis* (ablative); *quaterni*, “four each” (nominative), for *quaternis* (ablative); *Julius*, “July,” for *Junius*, “June”; *Februas*, “February” (feminine accusative plural), for *Februus* (masculine nominative singular).
- [January, Col. 0603D] An alternative omits *et*, “and,” before Anastasius and reads *memoratur*, “is commemorated,” for *memorantur*, “are commemorated.” Another omits the verse concerning the Conversion of Paul.
- [February, Col. 0604D] *dierum*, “of days,” replaces *Nonarum*, “of the Nones”; *septenis*, “seven each,” replaces *bisseptenas*, “twice seven.” An alternative omits the verse concerning Cephas’s chair.
- [March, Col. 0604D] Alternative *quem … Benedictus*, “whom … Benedict,” at the words *quem sequitur Benedictus*, “whom Benedict follows.”
- [June, Col. 0604D] *Nonis mundo*, “on the Nones, to/in the world,” reverses the printed order *mundo Nonis*. Other alternatives: *sumis Thatberti* for *summi Lantberti*, “of exalted Lantbert” (the alternative name is Thatbert; *sumis* is an irregular form); *inque suis*, “and in his own,” for *in quosvis*, “into whichever”; *est Joannis*, “is John’s,” for *et Joannis*, “and John’s.”
- [July, Col. 0604D] An alternative omits the verse about Martin’s Dedication. Another omits *-que*, “and,” from *fratremque*, “and the brother.”
- [August, Col. 0604D] *coronati*, “crowned,” replaces *coronantur*, “are crowned.” An alternative omits the verses from *Atque simul martyr*, “and at the same time the martyr,” through *Bartholomaeus*, “Bartholomew.”
- [November, Col. 0605B] *rutilet*, “may glitter,” for *rutilat*, “glitters”; *meriti*, “of merit,” for *merito*, “deservedly/by merit”; *Octavi*, “of the eighth/of Octavius,” for *Octavis*, “on the eighth.”
- [December, Col. 0606B] *Silvestrem* for *Silvestrum*, two accusative forms of Silvester’s name; *Kalendis*, “on the Kalends,” for *colendum*, “to be venerated.”
- [Hymn II, Col. 0607D] Alternative *impediam*, “I may hinder,” for *impediamur*, “we may be hindered.” At Col. 0608D an alternative omits *et*, “and,” before the granaries; another reads *vetustus*, “old” (masculine adjective), for *venustas*, “beauty.” The *fratione/ratione* variant (Col. 0609D) is given at its passage above.

It is especially clear that they flourished, the knowledge of whom

Must always accompany the ministers of the altar.

The fathers intended this very thing to be signified.

For this reason, and for this purpose, the reading in the sacred rites is doubled

Every Wednesday throughout all the seasons.

In the sixth age God came to visit this world,

Made human, in whom the Law and the Prophets agree.

This is signified by the reading that is read on the sixth day;

[Col. 0610A] The seventh, since it has sixes, is entitled by twelves.

Because in the city of Rome, which is called the head of the world,

Peoples of many languages flow together in that city,

They read both in the Greek and in the Roman language.

Thus it is established that sixes become twelves,

Not in different meaning, but only in different sound.

On this day also the bishop’s blessing is conferred by his mouth;

The priest himself bears the form of Christ,

And an apostolic assembly of the same number stands in the readers,

Pouring out heavenly teachings in various languages.

The seventh day represents the divine Spirit,

For the prophet, by a name shared with Jesus, describes

The seven gifts of the Spirit itself.

Therefore Christ himself, blessing his ministers,

Marks their hearts with a spiritual gift.

[Col. 0610B] Yet why the gracious Spirit is signified by this number

the abstinence of my tongue cannot say.

Nevertheless, he himself is accustomed to loosen halting human tongues,

so that they may duly utter speech.

All created things praise him with their own voice;

therefore, if he deigns faithfully to disclose to me

how this calculation is fitted to him, I shall set it forth.

I pray that he himself guide the pen, the hand, and the speech,

so that our discourse may worthily set him forth.

Yet I see no division that partitions the gracious seven;

it remains undivided, because it rejects equal parts.

It also makes of one mind those whom the Spirit fills.

Or, because the ages run their course in seven days,

the Spirit is shown to fill with every kind of gift

[Col. 0610C] those whom he judges worthy of his majesty.

But let us at last return briefly to what we interrupted,

And say why the seventh day is chosen above all for so great a work,

Or what this number means.

We see that seven consists of four and three:

Four signifies the body, compacted from as many elements;

Three signifies the soul, cleansed in a threefold manner.

Thus the body joined to the soul forms the human being.

[Note: [Col. 0609D] Alternative reading: “joined.”]

Four and three, therefore, unite to make a human being,

But three things flowing from above sustain the four things below.

What comes from above powerfully gives life to earthly things,

Provided that this bond is properly fastened and holds together.

[Note: [Col. 0609D] Alternative reading: “if well.”]

And three joined to four make seven.

When the outward human being and the inward one agree amicably,

[Note: [Col. 0610D] Alternative reading: *cum jurat amicae*, “when he swears to a female friend.”]

And the mind, subdued by the plague of vices,

[Col. 0610D] Commands, while the body of clay obeys everything,

Then the minister offers acceptable libations to the Lord.

Three things may also represent the symbols of faith:

For we confess that we believe in three and one—

Three persons, but one in everlasting divinity.

Four, moreover, correspond to as many virtues,

By which the life of any faithful person is distinguished.

Four, therefore, remain as the things that must be done,

And exercise the worshiper in faith, lest he grow sluggish through idleness;

But three signify why he should do whatever he labors to do.

Thus four need three, and three are agreed to need four.

[Note: [Col. 0610D] Alternative reading: “are agreed.”]

[Col. 0611A] Without faith, indeed, no one can ever please God,

Nor does anyone please him who confesses him with bare speech:

For faith is dead if action does not accompany it.

But let the three be rightly joined to the related four;

Let gracious faith agree with works, and works with faith,

So that afterward, brought into a beautiful structure,

They may produce rest for seven ages to come.

For the seventh day is called the rest of the Creator.

The sacred ministers must always desire this;

They must always sigh for it through their actions and faith,

Admonished always by the sacred key of numbers.

The minister must also possess the apostolic teaching

and not be ignorant of what is designated by this same number.

For when its parts are multiplied in alternate order,

it signifies the summit of the twelvefold apostolic honor:

[Col. 0611B] whether you say four times three or three times four,

by a different route you enter the same path.

Thus the seventh completes twelve through its own parts,

and deservedly so, in the manner in which the apostolic order

first and preeminently brought the seven gifts into the world.

[Note: the variant *quomodo*, “how,” replaces *modo*, “in the manner,” in this last construction.]

Therefore the day chosen for carrying out such great things

Urges ministers to show themselves worthy,

With the doctrine of faith together with spiritual endowment.

The weary Muse hastens to break off her unending course,

But a few matters hold back the reluctant poet;

The Sabbaths’ still-not-to-be-despised leisure delays us,

And compels us to explain such important reasons:

Why may we not consecrate these things on other days?

For a new error has recently arisen and spread in our region,

And I am compelled to answer it:

[Col. 0611C] Our bishops attempt to celebrate these solemn rites

on the day on which Christ rose again from Avernus.

Even if no reason could be given for the practice,

the authoritative antiquity of the fathers ought to have been sufficient:

it is clear that they always assigned these duties to the Sabbath

and likewise to the evening.
