For they judged this hour of the day fitting

for the priest to handle the sacred victim in these rites,

at the time when that same victim was slain upon the altar of the cross.

Because these sacred rites require their ministers to be fasting,

they must not be celebrated on the day on which Life came to life again.

For ecclesiastical custom forbids fasting on that day,

since it declares it shameful for the redeemed to mourn

when their Redeemer rises after conquering their death.

[Col. 0611D] Since these rites therefore require fasting in the evening,

and since it is forbidden for any Christian to fast on that day,

another day must be sought for them.

None seems more suitable to me than the preceding Sabbath:

on it, I judge, the servants should be watchful and sober,

purified also by abundant generosity,

awaiting Christ victorious from the contest

and preparing ministers worthy to meet him.

Nor should we overlook the fact that the seventh day

Is rightly devoted to these sacred rites according to ancient custom,

For the same number corresponds to as many steps.

[Col. 0612A] There are seven steps, then, which are consecrated on this day;

Since it would take too long to explain them, we shall give only their names,

Avoiding the tedium of lengthy exposition:

The doorkeeper, the reader, the exorcist, and the acolyte,

The subdeacon, the levite, and the priest himself.

We say that the bishop is not bound by this law;

For he ought to be consecrated on a festive day,

Especially on that day on which Christ rose joyfully,

Since he seems to bear the person of Christ in the Church.

It is therefore more fitting that he be exalted on the day

On which this man is raised to office,

Rather than on the day on which that exalted one returns from death.

Thus this man now relieves the Church’s grief,

Just as that one then removed the apostles’ fear;

And as he, rising, gladdened his friends,

[Col. 0612B] So let this man now console the pupils entrusted to him.

For it is established that when a bishop departs from this life,

The members must necessarily grieve at the departure of their head.

But when he is restored, summoned by divine appointment,

Behold, all rejoice eagerly, their sorrow laid aside,

As though they were receiving Christ rising from the dead.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Alternative reading: *qui propter*, “who because of.”]

Therefore whoever is placed in the seat of the deceased

Seems to us, for this reason, both another and the same.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Alternative reading: *et alter idem*, “and another, the same.”]

Nor should we think it without reason that the first and eighth day

rejoices in the bishop who has been appointed,

Who remains eighth in order but first in rank.

For he must climb the seven aforesaid steps

Before he can be raised to such primacy of honor.

Behold, the bishop also bears here a type of Jesus,

Not only because Jesus rose on this day,

[Col. 0612C] But because Christ rose on this day

So that it might be clear that he himself is both beginning and end.

[Note: [Col. 0612D] Alternative reading: *pareat*, “may obey,” for *pateat*, “may be clear.”]

From him all things flow, and to him all things return—

First and eighth, because he is both Creator and Blessed One.

For he created all things, and in the eighth age he will bless them.

I ask you, shepherds, to consider carefully

How great an honor Christ has placed upon you,

And with what burden of responsibility he has again laden

The honor that has been conferred upon you.

Be heads of the flock in such a way

That you may be members of the supreme Shepherd,

[Note: [Col. 0612D] Alternative reading: “shepherd.”]

So that, seeking from those entrusted to you not your own profit but his,

You may receive from him the pastures of life,

With the people committed to you following after.

Let anger not make you fierce, nor favor make you soft.

Those whom Christ calls joyfully, release from their bonds.

[Col. 0612D] Feed the Lord’s flock now with spiritual bread,

So that he may grant you to enjoy angelic bread.

Command by example more than by speech.

Then you will lead them along the straight path to the life to come,

If by deeds and words you urge them to seek it,

As the rooster first rouses itself with its own wings,

And then proclaims the rising of the coming dawn.

So let the bishop himself first carry out what he has ordered to be done;

Then I shall gladly hear him.

Fathers, I beg you, reject a gift from mouth or hand.

Frequent gifts blind even the wise.

[Col. 0613A] Avoid the destruction of Simon and the leprosy of Gehazi.

That crafty man thought the Holy Spirit could be bought for himself,

and, wretchedly valuing it more highly because he could sell it to many,

thought that what God offers freely was for sale.

Therefore the miserable man, plunged into the depths of the abyss,

Is thrust downward when he is hurled from the heights into hell.

In his madness he sought the stars with levity

And fell into Tartarus, unable to land on his feet,

Because he had wrongly sought the high heavens on wings he had joined together.

Another man also attempted to weave a similar fraud:

He accepted the salvation granted by the Lord’s abundant mercy,

while, in the sickness through which he himself had deserved to be healed,

he greedily sought to sell it for a price.

The wretch is punished together with all his posterity.

Fathers, continually beware of these examples, which must be feared;

[Col. 0613B] Consider carefully upon whom you impose sacred duties,

Lest, taking them away from the just, you confer them upon the wicked.

Often recall what the supreme Teacher commands his pupil:

He must not hastily lay hands on anyone not yet tested,

And so participate in wicked deeds.

In the same way, unless you have examined them through lengthy scrutiny,

Beware of entrusting the rights of the sacred ministry to them.

Do not be angry with me, venerable fathers, I beg you,

Because I presume to warn shepherds while I am a sickly sheep.

The Almighty often reveals hidden things to the younger;

The divine Spirit is constrained by no law.

A servant often gives useful counsel to his master.

Let what has been said in excess concerning the order of bishops

Suffice; at last let us return to what we interrupted.

We must say briefly what the reading means.

[Col. 0613C] This seventh day claims one thing for itself:

It has often been related that seven signifies rest.

But we suitably apply the sixes to the work,

For in this number the good Creator made all things.

These ages are divided into six periods,

In which rest is to be hoped for after continual labor.

Nor is the sequence of the books to be disregarded:

Four are read before consecration takes place;

The fifth is read at the very stage of ordination;

The sixth is the daily reading, which is recited according to customary practice.

With four sung verses the Psalmist instructed us

Always to bless the Thunderer with supreme praise:

Israel, the house of Aaron, the house of Levi,

And all who fear the Lord among the nations.

Israel signifies those called from the Hebrew people;

[Col. 0613D] The illustrious house of Aaron discloses the sacred bishops;

The broad house of Levi expresses the remaining ministers;

And “those who fear the Lord” names all the rest of the people.

Among them consists the whole faithful multitude,

Which the preceding reading properly signifies by four.

These readings also change through the four seasons of the year,

And are read in keeping with those same seasons.

The fifth is always recited unchanged and in the same order;

From this it is clear that it does not refer to a particular season.

This reading, therefore, especially concerns men who are to be consecrated,

Revealing the fierce flames of a burning furnace

In which the hostile enemy persisted in cruelly burning the righteous.

Yet the fervor of divine love is not extinguished in them;

From it no attachment to the world turns the devout away.

[Col. 0614A] And although the savage enemy presses them relentlessly,

With continual fires fed by the fuel of vices,

Those who are worthy of God and call upon him

Repel the fiery darts far away by his aid.

And even if he persuades them to bend their necks to false gods,

As the tyrant is now said to have done,

He can compel them to this in no way:

For no dreadful desire casts them prostrate before him,

Nor do they worship a coin carved with a flattering image.

To signify this, it is always customary for the faithful

to pray upright and standing in this prayer,

which is drawn from that reading and recited after it.

No one takes care to place his knees upon the ground,

whereas at the other readings, when the minister proclaims this,

they strive to pray to the Lord with knees bent,

their whole body prostrate to the ground and their heart likewise contrite.

[Col. 0614B] Thus it becomes clear how great is the difference between their prayers

[Col. 0614B] Thus it becomes clear how great is the difference between their prayers

And the prayers of those who fear false divinities:

Those are said to prostrate themselves, while these wish to stand.

But because the furnace is always mentioned in these readings,

It is worth drawing from it what we can;

Such frequent repetition should not be thought empty.

No one can properly approach the service of divine worship

Unless a terrible temptation has tested him.

This, not without reason, is signified by the flames of the furnace.

The page of sacred Scripture also bears witness to the same:

As a Samian vessel is tested by a burning furnace,

So bitter temptation purifies the righteous.

Those whom the Lord has chosen do not know how to succumb;

[Col. 0614C] For he himself adds strength to those who trust in him.

When they have become victors in the contest,

They are able to praise him after the lofty fires have been quenched,

And faithfully resound with a joyful hymn to God.

They can properly be assigned to the gracious ministries;

I judge that such great duties should not otherwise be entrusted to them

Unless they have been tested as though in a powerful furnace,

They learn through many labors to approach heavenly things,

So that they may be joined in the eternal heaven to the King

Whom they serve here with devoted heart,

And who said that his ministers would be with him in the heavenly citadel.

This is always indicated to them by the preceding mention of the furnace,

And then by the hymn that follows after the fires have been extinguished:

Here they fight well; there they sing in peace.

When all these matters concerning them have therefore been duly completed,

[Col. 0614D] Paul immediately receives them with a thunderbolt,

And, urging and threatening, declares what must be done afterward.

Rightly the Old Testament is read first, before the consecration;

then the New Testament is read after they have been admitted to the Lord's lot,

so that they may be admonished to renew their life and conduct

and, stripped of the old person, follow the new—

all who deserve to pass into the lot of God.

Nor is it without meaning that five readings of the Old Testament are read first

and a sixth from the New: five for those about to be consecrated,

and the sixth after they have been consecrated.

Five ages were pressed beneath darkness;

The sixth sprinkled the whole world with new light.

And all who, by the Lord’s mercy, are appointed to sacred

[Col. 0615A] Duties must drive away the darkness of inherited error

And necessarily strive to migrate into the new light.

Through five ages they served the Thunderer with servile fear,

By the law sent through a servant.

In the sixth we are now called children of the Almighty,

A royal race and a royal priesthood,

Members of the supreme Priest and King in all things.

Although all who confess God with harmonious mind and mouth

May share in this honor,

Especially, however, those who deserve to share in the Name and are themselves called priests.

Having driven away the old and servile fear,

Let these rejoice more in serving through the love of children.

And so let them know themselves to be priests most strictly,

Yet let empty pride not strike them from this position,

[Col. 0615B] And let them understand how weighty and humble these ministries must be.

The tract that follows, sung in a restrained melody,

Signifies that such a melody reveals a humble mind.

There are many examples, but one will suffice.

Lent always claims this chant for itself,

Since at no other time does the Christian people submit itself more

To the gracious Lord, by fasting and praying.

Afterward the Mass is celebrated in the customary manner,

When all these things agree in a beautiful order.

Anyone who judges that these rites should be celebrated on another day cannot withstand these arguments by fair judgment; how foolish he is is made plainly clear.

Carelessly neglecting the day established by the fathers,

Since no one else claims this office for himself,

And since it is not fitting, as the teacher Paul commands,

To tear away the decrees of the fathers who came before us,

[Col. 0615C] If an angel should come from lofty Olympus

And attempt to impose another doctrine upon you,

Trying to turn you from the [lacuna] path of faith which the Lord willed to spread through us throughout the world,

Drive him from your homes as a blasphemer.

The ancient Scripture makes this equally clear:

“Do not move the ancient boundaries of your fathers.”

When we ran out upon the swelling sea in a fragile boat,

Although it struck against rocks and was battered by storms,

At last it reaches the desired land of the shore.

Nor is it surprising that it has undergone many dangers,

[Col. 0615D] Since we plowed seas never before attempted by anyone.

For all whom Roman eloquence exalts

Rely upon a well-worn path from antiquity:

Maro cuts through the Scyllaean sea with Homer as his rower;

The Sabellian poet proceeds along Pindar’s path;

The lover of biting satire follows Lucilius;

The comic poet is guided by the outstanding master Menander.

But no guide preceded our Thalia.

For this reason she, wandering, struck against a rugged reef.

But, borne onward by God breathing through favorable Zephyrs,

At last the vessel enters port with full sail.

## HYMN III. On the various rules of the calendar

The Lord’s Advent is not to be celebrated in December

Neither after the third Nones nor before the fifth day before the Kalends;

[Col. 0616A] Nor may Easter be celebrated before the eleventh day before the April Kalends,

Nor after the seventh day before the May Kalends.

The Virgin gave signs of childbirth in the second year

Of that great cycle, which had revolved twice,

The cycle containing five hundred and thirty-two years.

The Virgin gave signs of childbirth in the second year

Of that angelic cycle that gives the paschal dates,

Which consists of nineteen years.

It was then the eighteenth year,

Nearly even in the lunar cycle according to the verse,

The ninth year of the solar cycle and a leap year.

At that time it was also the fourth indiction.

The sun and moon held forty-four epacts.

The lunar cycle was now intending to rise,

The cycle extending through nineteen years.

[Col. 0616B] The solar cycle begins on the Kalends of March,

The page called the field of the great cycle,

Composed from the two joined cycles of Phoebe and the Sun.

It takes four times seven years for its span,

Adds one hundred and thirty-three leap years,

And five hundred and thirty-two years altogether.

You will time two such fasts in as many months within as many seasons;

the months containing the fasts are September, March, June, and December.

March names its fast from Wednesday;

June from seven weeks counted twice.

September likewise has the same fixed terminus,

and the tenth day before the January Kalends marks it.

*Textual note: the compact lines beginning* Temporabis duo tot jejunia *are transmitted in difficult syntax; the four named fasting months and their printed termini are retained without conjectural normalization.*

The experts, by this method, assign to the solar year

A span of three hundred sixty-five days,

[Col. 0616C] From which you will make fifty-two weeks.

The first concurrent remains as the one excess;

Thus you will assign one to each year,

Being careful to go beyond the rule that lies in seven.

Two are added because of the fourth-year leap.

In every ordinary year the limit of Easter stands

At six, counting upward, less two—

For the lunar year is so much shorter than the solar year.

Nevertheless, the final year must be excepted,

Which by calculation contains twelve lunar leap-days.

In an embolismic year the limit of Easter stands

At the downward count of nineteen.

For the solar year is so much shorter than the lunar year.

The sun wishes to remain in each sign of the zodiac

For thirty days, ten hours, and a half;

[Col. 0616D] From this you complete three hundred and sixty days,

Since the sun traverses three times twelve signs.

From the remaining hours you make five days and ten hours,

For every day is made from twice twelve hours,

Since nature gives a complete day together with night.

But from half an hour you make a quarter;

One day is thereby added to the year,

Which March, inserted, repeats for you among the six Kalends.

The solar year surpasses the lunar year by the epacts,

Which in Greek are called *epactae*, “additions” in Latin.

These proceed continually in the paschal verses;

They have their beginning at the first point and their end at the lowest,

And must change on the Kalends of September.

An ordinary year consists of twelve months;

[Col. 0617A] An embolismic year of more than twelve.

For one month then grows from the epacts.

The zodiac is divided into twelve signs.

There are as many months corresponding to all the signs:

Phoebus traverses each sign in thirty days

And ten and a half hours gradually.

From this come three hundred sixty-five days,

which you must distribute among the twelve months.

From the remaining hours you make five days;

because these cannot be distributed, you must assign them to March.

Why to March rather than another month?

Because Romulus assigned it to Mars,

Establishing ten months with Mars as the first.

Why with Mars as the first?

Because he honored him as his father.

His successor Numa became the author of the two-month addition.

If you wish to calculate the number of a month, proceed as follows:

[Col. 0617B] Take the days of the month and add the number of the preceding month.

Divide the number by seven, assigning the remainder to it.

Why by seven? Because in this way the week must be maintained.

Add to it the days belonging to it, which are not derived from elsewhere.

If you wish to know what this number means,

Add together the concurrent numbers of the years,

So that you may calculate for yourself the weekdays on which each Kalends falls.

The result will be a number—seven, less than seven, or more.

If it is seven or less, call it the weekday; if more,

Subtract seven and assign the remainder to it.

Give these to September and March, to which you assigned them earlier.

Begin from this point, because the Egyptian people prescribe it.

If you wish to assign a number to a month, proceed as follows:

Take the days of the month and add the number of the preceding month.

After doing this, the month requires its own lunar age to be subtracted.

[Col. 0617C] Write the remainder beside the following month.

If you do not know the lunar age of each month, learn it:

In even months the moon is twenty-nine days old;

In odd months its age grows to thirty.

The order in this catalogue will indicate this to you.

If you wish to know what the number means,

Add to that number the epacts of the current year.

The total will be thirty, less than thirty, or more.

If the whole moon is less than thirty, that is its age; if more,

Subtract thirty from the remainder, and the age becomes clear.

Thus the other months correspond to one another in their hours:

January to December, and February to November;

March corresponds to October, and September to April.

May corresponds to August, June to July.

[Col. 0617D] Behold, you know what the present position of Phoebus is.

There are nevertheless two proper divisions of the day:

One is called nocturnal, the other diurnal.

For there are twenty-four hours in the day;

The twelvefold span of hours indicates the hour.

They have further divided the diurnal span into three parts: morning, midday, and the time near nightfall.

Just as the calendar of peoples differs, so does the beginning of the day.

The Chaldean thinks that it begins at the rising of Phoebus;

The Egyptian people thinks that it begins at the rising of night;

The Roman thinks that it begins at midnight.

From this it is customary for roosters to sing of the coming day.

The light that was first made began to precede the night, foretelling Adam’s happiness before his fall; though well formed, through guilt he fell beneath night.

[Col. 0618A] Now the light follows the night, conquering death on the cross,

Restoring to life the human being who endured darkness.

The order of the planets varies the sequence of the weekdays,

For poets thought it pleasing to call the days by the names of gods.

The third belonged to Mars; the fourth remained with Stilbon;

Then, assigning the fifth to Jupiter, they call it Jovian.

The sixth belonged to Venus, the last to the father of the gods.

They assigned these days to the gods, thinking that the universe consisted of them.

Jupiter supplied temperateness; Cyllenian Mercury, skill; the Sun, breath; Mars, blood; and the Moon, body or moisture; Venus herself, the fire of lust.

According to our custom, the days are called *feriae*.

We believe that *feria* was named from *fari*, “to speak,”

For formerly the first day bore this name:

It was lawful on it both to speak and to rest in divine matters,

Or because God is said to have made all things.

We make a week consist of seven days,

Though Egypt is accustomed to call such a period a span of years.

There are working days, feast days, and days of rest;

Moreover, days are called *fasti* and *nefasti*.

Some are feast days of human beings; others, for some reason, are working days.

[Col. 0618B] *Mensis* (“month”) is a Greek word, derived from the name of the moon,

because the text claims that *menes* means “moon” in Latin.

The four seasons of the year are divided in themselves,

Their names being spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

In spring the Sun would face Boreas,

Since this season tends to make the nights equal to the days.

It begins on the eighth Kalends of March,

Lasting ninety-one days.

When Boreas is warmed by the sun, summer immediately follows,

[Col. 0618C] Shortening the nocturnal periods as the diurnal periods expand.

June commands it to enter on the eighth Kalends,

Lasting ninety-one days.

Summer consists of fire, and spring also of dryness, as the source claims.

Autumn is accustomed to equal the nights to the days,

And seeks to arrive at the eighth Kalends of September,

Lasting ninety-three days.

Thus it always arises from cold and dryness.

Winter brings back cold, since the sun is almost absent, when the nocturnal periods are long and the diurnal ones short.

It begins on the eighth Kalends of the tenth month,

Containing nine times ten days.

It always arises from cold and dryness.

The year has an allegory for the Church in these matters:

[Col. 0618D] Winter signifies the Church’s hardships—

When there is a storm with ice, snow, and whirlwind.

Summer is the neglect of faith and Christ’s vengeance,

During which the teachings are dried up by aridity.

Spring is the renewal of faith after the force of snow and ice,

When we shall celebrate Easter for the slain Lamb.

When autumn comes, the fertile year produces its harvest,

Giving the Church of the saints to its reverent assemblies.

They call spring the season when all seeds grow green,

When the earth is clothed with vines in bud and with grasses.

Summer is the season when heat burns in all things.

We believe autumn is named from a storm,

When leaves fall and everything is seasonable.

Winter receives its name from one hemisphere,

Because the sun then customarily revolves through a shorter space.

[Col. 0619A] It is called *bruma*, either because it is brief

Or because it comes from food;

Hence *imbrumari* is used of becoming weary of eating.

The term *hibernum* is nevertheless applied to a part of the interval;

*vernum* is a compound formed as though one were to say *hibernum*.

Spring, summer, autumn, and winter each retain three months,

From which the seasons are divided according to the months.

Spring, summer, and winter become mature, lest they be premature;

Thus autumn is new, premature, and mature.

When autumn comes, sickness grows excessively everywhere,

For heat corrupts the air, and the opposing cold does likewise.

The gentiles, who had suffered no little harm from former blows,

Assigned various materials to Jupiter as the four seasons of the year—

Not four forms, but four vessels of silver, iron, glass, and lead.

This silver crater of Jupiter bears spring,

[Col. 0619B] The iron one carries Vulcan’s summer and fire.

The glass one holds Juno’s autumn and abundant breasts.

The lead vessel contains winter and Saturn’s destruction.

When darkness arises, night is the absence of the sun.

Philosophers say that night comes into being

Either because the weakening sun breathes out its declining fires,

Or because what is above is bent down into the earth.

Night took a fitting name because it obstructs sight.

The interval of the solstice is named from the sun’s standing still,

Because, when it stands, either nights or days increase.

The summer solstice occurs in Cancer, the winter solstice in Capricorn;

Thus there are two solstices and two equinoxes, when night and day have equal hours. Libra corresponds to autumn, Aries to spring.

[Col. 0619C] January is the first month, or is called by the name of Janus,

Who formerly, according to pagan custom, was the god of the year;

Or because you are a doorway through which the year comes and goes.

From him we now call the forehead by the same name.

February is Pluto, from whom the month February takes its name; this month was devoted to rites for the Manes.

March must have its name from Mars,

Or it is so called because it joins many things to the husband.

It was the beginning of the year and of the new months.

April is said to derive its name from the fact that it is “open,”

Since plants put forth their shoots and living creatures produce offspring.

The countryside, covered with snow; the sky, with cloud; the sea, freed from the whirlwind—

The countryside returns to farmers, the sky to astrologers, and the sea to sailors.

May is called May from Maia, the mother of Mercury.

These are the places assigned for inserting embolismic months.

September receives the second embolismic placement, and December the first;

[Col. 0619D] Sextilis receives the sixth, and November the fifth.

Each month allows its Nones to have four days.

The following compressed mnemonic is preserved line by line because several of its forms are corrupt or highly elliptical:

- *Martis trite diem Nonarum sume priorem* — “For the third of March, take the preceding day of the Nones.”
- *Ad bine ternas Martis cape septime Nonas* — “From there take the third Nones of March, seventh” [wording uncertain].
- *Prima necat Jani, nocet astans septima fini* — “The first strikes January; the adjacent seventh harms the end.”
- *Quarta necat Februi, nocet astans tertia fini* — “The fourth strikes February; the adjacent third harms the end.”
- *Mars, tua frons cuspis, prope finem quarta fit aspis* — “March, your beginning is a spear; near the end the fourth becomes an asp.”
- *Aprilis decimam, notat undecimam prope caudam* — “April marks the tenth, and near its tail the eleventh.”
- *Tertia mors Maii, sed septima proxima fini* — “The third is May's death, but the seventh is nearest the end.”
- *Junius in decimo ferit et quindenus ab imo* — “June strikes at the tenth and the fifteenth from the bottom.”
- *Alter ab undecimo nepa Juli, nonus ab illo* — “July's other scorpion is from the eleventh, the ninth from that one.”
- *Augusti primus ferit et de fine secundus* — “The first of August strikes, and the second from the end.”
- *Stat Septembris acus hinc tertius inde decenus* — “September's needle stands third from here, tenth from there.”
- *Octobris stat acus hinc tertius inde decenus* — “October's needle stands third from here, tenth from there.”
- [Col. 0620A] *Quinta necat capitis, sed tertia fine Novembris* — “The fifth strikes at November's beginning, but the third at its end.”
- *Frontis septenam notat ultimus ordo decenam* — “The last order marks the seventh at the beginning and the tenth.”

The ordering of December in a leap year is set out with four-day Nones, three, and twice eight Kalends. July likewise agrees with March and May; the eight of the rainy month occurs among the six-day Nones and the seven and ten of December. June, April, September, and December have four-day Nones, three times five and three Kalends. February has four-day Nones and twice eight Kalends. All the months agree in the October Ides. Thus two months contain thirty days, February alone twenty-eight, and every remaining month four times eight less one.

If you wish to know on which weekday each Kalends falls, combine these assigned weekday numbers with the concurrents:

- [Col. 0620B] January gives three to May; June gives six from here to February.
- September gives seven; the tenth gives [it] to September; March gives five to November.
- April and July preserve one; August takes four; October alone takes two.

If you carefully consider the lunar age at the Kalends, add these lunar numbers to the current epacts: September has five, and the “eighth rainy” month has five; the ninth has seven, and the tenth supplies the same. April gives ten to February; March gives three to January. May has eleven, June twelve, Sextilis twice seven, and July ten and three.

*Textual note: the mnemonic's unusual month names, case forms, and numerical syntax are retained; the supplied text does not support a uniquely reconstructed calendar table.*

Time, having the appearance of an age, is the motion of the world.

Constant in past, present, and future,

It is called time for this reason: because it regulates the universe.

Reason itself proves this, because the order of time is threefold,

[Col. 0620C] Standing by the command of nature, or by the Creator, or by command.

The sun and moon make their year under nature’s guidance.

The sun does so through three hundred sixty-five days,

Together with a quarter of one complete day.

The moon passes through that many days in ordinary years,

But if you add to this period six and five days,

It grows through nineteen embolismic years.

As custom has it, a month consists of twice three times five days.

Yet this custom is not usage but abuse,

Since neither the moon nor the sun follows such a course.

For the moon’s course, without considering its leap,

Is reported to be shorter than this span by twelve hours.

The sun’s delay is longer by ten and a half hours.

One must regard this as the work of either divine or human power.

By the Lord’s edict establishing the laws for Moses,

[Col. 0620D] The seventh year removes agricultural labor from the Jew,

The weight of mortal affairs requiring this command.

The Romans repeat their games after four years,

And February receives the same four-year cycle.

Time is found in atoms, moments, minutes,

parts, *ostenta*, points, quadrants, hours,

and in days, weeks, months, years,

lustrums, ages, and epochs alike.

“Atom” in our language means indivision.

There are five contexts in which an atom is customarily found:

sunlight, number, time, speech, and body.

An atom in sunlight means a speck of dust;

an atom in number is the monad, its beginning;

an atom in time is like the swift stroke of an eye;

[Col. 0621A] an atom in speech is each individual letter by itself;

an atom in a body is something to which scarcely any color belongs.

An atom of an *ostentum* must be taken as its complete portion;

it becomes three hundred, or twice two and twice forty.

An *ostentum* is one-sixtieth of an hour.

An hour is made of five points, ten minutes,

sixty *ostenta*, and one hundred parts;

it is made by four *moneta*, “that is, ten *serenta*,” in the source's wording.

A point consists of three particles and two minutes,

eight moments and twelve *ostenta* together.

Two half-parts make one minute,

making four moments and six *ostenta*.

Four *ostenta* are contained in one part;

two moments are two parts “from the lowest,” as the verse states.

A moment customarily yields one and a half *ostenta*.

[Col. 0621B] The sun gives an hour in five points, the moon in four.

*Textual note: the printed computistical equations contain compressed or corrupt forms, especially* moneta, serenta, *and* et ab imo. *They are transliterated rather than silently changed into modern units;* ostentum *is retained as the source's technical unit, not translated as “sign.”*

## HYMN IV. On all the works of God

First God established the globe of heaven

And the mass of earth,

But the abyss had covered the earth, hidden beneath shadows:

*Abyssus al* […] *texerat* [the source preserves only *al* before the lacuna].

Then, through the days corresponding

To the ages of passing time,

He adorned the world and the heavens,

And the whole structure of the universe.

On the first day the Creator of the world,

Driving away the darkness,

Illuminated with light

The world still hidden beneath the waters.

[Col. 0621C] With the joys of blessed light

He filled the inhabitants of the world.

Then, in the first age, the Most High Creator of the world

Was placed among the blue heavens.

On the second day, the greatest globe of God’s sky

Was established, and the flowing waters

Were divided on either side.

At the first moment of the second age,

The mystical ark,

With the waters running together from either side,

Was placed among the blue heavens.

On the third day of the shining age,

The deep abyss, flowing beneath the heavens,

Sank down into its depths,

[Col. 0621D] And the green dry land appeared.

The chosen offspring of Abraham,

From the waves of the faithless,

Bloomed and flourished in the third age,

On the third day of the shining age.

On the fourth day the radiance

Of the lofty stars shone,

To give the sky and the earth

The grace of light.

The Hebrew people, illustrious,

Shone under David’s kingdom,

Displaying the radiance of its deeds

In the fourth age, on the fourth day.

A new race is generated

[Col. 0622A] On the fifth day, born from the clear waters—

Those that swim and those that fly beneath the sky.

In the fifth age, while Judaea

Was paying the penalty in Chaldaea,

A new race is generated from the faithful,

From those formerly faithless.

On the sixth day the human being was created,

Bearing the image

Of God his Creator,

So that he might always live blessed.

The supreme Creator of all,

Through whom the human being was created,

The Son of God, in the sixth age,

On the sixth day created the human being.

[Col. 0622B] While Adam slept, a splendid woman was fashioned—bone from his bones, bringing forth flesh from flesh.

From Christ’s own flesh,  
and from the mystery of blood,  
the bride was now born splendidly  
upon the cross for the sleeping One.

After accomplishing sublime deeds, the Creator,  
resting on the seventh day,  
commands that it be called throughout the ages  
and that it be the Sabbath.

The seventh age of rest  
will be the age that follows this one,  
in which he sabbaths with his own,  
after accomplishing sublime deeds, the Creator.

The eighth remains, higher  
than all the other ages,  
when the dead will rise  
from the ancient mound of earth,  
and the righteous will behold  
the everlasting, lovely face of Christ.  
They will be radiant like angels  
in the heavenly citadel—  
the path to himself  
which he, going before us, showed,  
born of a virgin mother,  
God and Son of God.

For by destroying death through death,  
he subdued the sixth age [lacuna].  
But he rested on the Sabbath,  
buried in the heart of the earth;  
and by rising he opened  
the first day of the Sabbath,  
and, while his own rejoiced with him,  
he ascended to the throne of the Father.

And through the six ages  
of this world he commands us  
to conquer every power of death  
by bearing now our own cross.

After all the battles of the world  
have been defeated,  
freed from the bonds of the flesh,  
we shall enter the Sabbath  
of everlasting life.

One Sabbath will follow,  
to be closed by no limit,  
when the immortality of the flesh  
is restored to us forever.

Thus, possessing the twofold joy  
of flesh and spirit,  
we shall climb to the heavenly  
walls of the everlasting kingdom.

To which, we beg,  
holy Trinity, grant that we may come,  
and that throughout the ages  
we may know you as the one true God.

Glory, etc.

## HYMN V. On the Nativity of the Holy Innocents

Singing a hymn of the martyrs,  
let us speak of the Innocents,  
whom the earth lost in weeping,  
but whom heaven receives in joy.

Their angels behold  
the Father’s face forever,  
and praise his grace,  
singing a hymn of the martyrs.

The impious king slew them,  
but the merciful Creator gathers them,  
placing them with himself, blessed,  
in the light of the everlasting kingdom.

He who grants each of them  
a dwelling in the Father’s house  
gives them the heavenly abodes—  
the impious king slew them.

Herod’s anger struck  
the little ones of two years and under,  
and sprinkled the borders of Bethlehem  
with holy blood.

The innocent death  
of the faithful shone gloriously for Christ;  
the angels carried them to heaven—  
the little ones of two years and under.

A voice rang out in Ramah,  
the lamentation of deepest mourning;  
Rachel, drenched in tears,  
wept for her sons.

They rejoice in everlasting triumph,  
each of whom had conquered torments;  
their voice, mourning over the blows,  
rang out in Ramah.

Do not fear, little flock,  
the treacherous teeth of the lion;  
for the good Shepherd  
will give you heavenly pastures.

You who follow the white Lamb of God  
along the path of the world,  
do not fear the impious hands  
of the robber.

The Father will wipe away  
every tear from your faces.  
Death harms you no longer,  
once you have received the strongholds of life.

Those who sow in tears  
will reap in lasting joy;  
the Creator will wipe away  
the tears from the cheeks of the mourners.

O city exceedingly blessed,  
in which the Redeemer is born,  
and in which, for the newborn One,  
the first victims of the martyrs are proclaimed!

You are never called little  
among the thousands of cities,  
for from you a new leader has arisen—  
O city exceedingly blessed!

They stand before his throne,  
shining in radiant garments—  
those who had washed their robes  
in the red blood of the Lamb.

Those who had groaned for the kingdom  
of their homeland,  
now joyful, with praises to God,  
stand shining in radiant garments.

Glory, etc.

## HYMN VI. On the Ascension of the Lord

Let us sing a hymn of glory;  
let new hymns resound:  
Christ, by a new path,  
has ascended to the throne of the Father.

He passes in triumphal glory  
over the heights of heaven,  
he who had taken death upon himself,  
mocked by mortals.

For by his power  
he surveyed the dread gates of death  
and the blind shadows of the underworld,  
and bound the prince of death,  
together with all whom he knew  
to have been chosen as his own  
in deeds and in faith.  
He saved them all  
from the savage jaws of Avernus.

The Redeemer opened  
the joyful gate of life to all  
whom the bitter law of the body  
had deprived of pious life.

O wondrous splendor of creation!  
Wondrous is the Savior’s  
twofold power and grace,  
which destroys the kingdoms of death.

For by his spirit  
he led many back  
from the gates of the underworld,  
and by his own body  
he rescued many  
from the jaws of death.

So that the joys of Christ  
rising from the dead might resound,  
two choirs celebrate Easter:  
the new life of those who rejoice.

Two companies, following Christ,  
ascended through the air,  
and took their everlasting seats  
among the angels in heaven.

Therefore let us bear this day  
with harmonious praises,  
on which radiant Jesus, the Victor,  
seeks the gates of Olympus.

There, going before us in blessedness,  
he himself has prepared for us  
with the Father,  
the couches and many dwellings,  
the author of heaven.

There the whole company  
of the faithful who had gone before,  
from the beginning of the age,  
entered the royal court of heaven  
when Christ opened it.

In the wondrous triumph  
of the high-throned King  
were gathered together  
the heavenly hosts,  
the ranks seeking heaven.

Then the apostles, standing  
on the mystical mountain of chrism,  
together with his glorious virgin mother,  
beheld the glory of Jesus.

And, accompanying him  
as he sought the stars  
with joyful light and glad hearts  
through the breezes,  
they led on the King of the world.

The angels addressed them:

“Why do you stand gazing at the stars?”

“This is the Savior,” they said,  
“Jesus, noble in triumph.

“He has been taken up from you  
to the heavenly realms,  
and from there he will come  
at the end of the age  
as judge of all.”

They had said this, and without delay,  
joined to the blessed choirs,  
shining with the King of kings,  
they approached the gates of Olympus.

Then an angel’s voice was sent forth:

“Open the gates now,” he said,  
“and the everlasting  
Leader of peace and King of glory  
will enter.”

From within, a voice replied  
from the walls of the gracious city:

“Who is this King of glory  
who is to enter the gates of heaven?

“We are accustomed always  
to behold Christ in the heavenly realms,  
and together with the Father  
we rejoice in equal glory.”

But the herald of the great Judge replied:

“The Lord is powerful and strong,  
who in battle struck down  
the dark prince of the world,  
triumphing over him.

“Therefore be lifted up,  
everlasting gates of heaven;  
let the King of glory enter,  
of power and grace.”

Still amazed, the heavenly court  
of the citizens inquired:

“Who,” it said, “is the King of glory,  
this King so worthy of praise?”

Then the lordly trumpet answered:

“The Most High, the author of all,  
the source of virtues—  
he himself shines as  
the King of glory.”

At these words the King of glory,  
with his glorious host,  
entered the lofty kingdom of glory  
in heaven.

There he granted fitting dwellings  
to each of those  
whom he had led up  
from the depths of the underworld,  
according to their virtuous deeds.

And he himself, passing through  
all the shining heights of heaven,  
sat at the right hand of the Father,  
the coeternal Son.

From there he will come in glory  
to judge the living together with the dead  
according to their deeds,  
with a just and powerful judgment.

At that time, we beg you,  
Jesus, only Redeemer,  
gather us among your merciful servants  
in heaven.

Grant us to hasten there  
with constant devotion,  
where we believe you sit with the Father  
in the citadel of the kingdom.

There, filled with your Spirit  
in our hearts,  
show us the Father;  
that one vision is sufficient for us.

## HYMN VII. On the Nativity of Saint Agnes

The blessed day of the holy virgin  
has shone upon the ages;  
she, having conquered death,  
received the joys of everlasting life.

Agnes entered triumphantly  
the golden court of heaven,  
and, joined to the Lamb,  
rejoices in the sweet wedding.

Admitted among the chaste companies  
of virgins in the heavenly citadel,  
she sings a new song  
to God the Father  
and to the Son as one.

Now worthy of such a reward,  
she had rejected, for love of Christ,  
the fleeting prosperity of the world  
and the filthy pomp of the age.

Struck as well by the harsh darts  
of adversity,  
she persevered bravely in faith  
to which she had once vowed herself to Christ.

The fierce enemy took  
the girl’s outer garment from her limbs,  
but no one could take away  
the robe within her heart.

Christ also sends the virgin  
a robe from without,  
teaching that she is clothed within  
in the linen of truth.

Led into a house of disgrace,  
the martyr is freed from disgrace;  
indeed, from a place of prostitution  
it suddenly becomes a place of prayer.

The former hiding place of demons  
is illumined from heaven;  
the prince of death is driven away,  
and the minister of life is seen.

The upright approve the miracles  
and honor the martyr’s God;  
the mocker at the miracle is soon punished  
with a death he deserves.

The blessed martyr, raising him  
from the gates of the underworld,  
thus flies on ahead to the stars  
through the household shrines and iron gates.

There she beholds forever  
the glory of her Creator,  
and, as a citizen among the citizens  
of the heavenly homeland,  
she sings hymns.

Glory, etc.

## HYMN VIII. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

The exalted forerunner of the Light  
and herald of the Word is born.  
Rejoice, heart of the faithful,  
and receive the Light with joy.

His wondrous birth,  
which an angel made known  
to his parents already endowed  
with devout faith,

Gabriel himself gives him  
the exalted name John,  
and foretells his illustrious deeds.

While still a little child,  
held within his mother’s womb,  
he received the holy breath of grace,  
destined to be a witness to grace.

Not yet born, he already gave  
testimony to the Light,  
which he himself, once born,  
fulfilled in wondrous glory.

He brought many in Israel  
under the faith of Christ,  
and, teaching heavenly things,  
turned the hearts of fathers  
toward their children.

He came in the spirit  
of the prophet Elijah  
to prepare Christ’s path  
and open the way of salvation  
for the peoples.

Among the sons of women  
no prophet is greater than he;  
indeed, by wondrous deeds  
he shone forth as more than a prophet.

He preached and gave  
the baptism of repentance,  
and offered the crowds  
to the grace of Jesus  
to be illumined.

He baptized Jesus himself,  
who cleanses all things  
in the Holy Spirit,  
washing him in the stream  
of the Jordan’s deep waters.

Immediately after he was baptized,  
he saw the heavens opened.  
By his baptism  
he opens to us  
the royal court of heaven.

He saw the Spirit descend upon him  
in the form of a dove—  
the Spirit who knows no deceit  
and seeks simple hearts.

He also heard the Father’s voice:

“This is my beloved Son,”  
he said, “from eternity,  
in whom I have been well pleased.”

Taught by these oracles,  
the Baptist proclaims Jesus,  
the Son of God, born  
to cleanse the faithful  
in the Holy Spirit.

What more can our speech sing  
in praise of this herald?

Of him the Father’s voice,  
which once spoke concerning the Son,  
prophesied:

“Behold, I send an angel,”  
he said, “who will prepare your path  
and go before your face,  
ruddy like Lucifer, the morning star.”

## HYMN IX. On the Apostles Peter and Paul

Let us sing with fitting hymns  
the glory of the apostles;  
let us devote ourselves  
to yearly vows.  
Jesus, favor those who pray.

Simon Peter, Bar-Jonah,  
and the gracious teacher of the nations  
dedicated festive joys  
to the ages with their blood.

The hour of their departure  
joined together those seeking  
the gate of heaven—  
those whom one love  
had always joined  
while they remained in the world.

They drew the diverse nations,  
dissonant through long error,  
toward the grace of truth  
with harmonious words.

The holy prince of the Church  
beholds Jesus on the mountain  
and hears the Father’s voice  
from the fiery summit of shining heaven.

Paul, ascending the third heaven,  
uttered mysteries  
which no other person  
is permitted to disclose.

The steps of Cephas  
across the waters are aided  
by the right hand of Christ;  
Christ lifts his own up,  
lest the sea of the world  
swallow them.

Paul teaches that the dangers  
of this age are conquered  
by the faith of believers,  
already saving his companions,  
shipwrecked, from the waves.

Simon draws the faithful  
from the deepest waves of the world,  
bringing them to the homeland of light  
so that he may rescue  
the good fish.

Paul teaches that the righteous  
remain as inhabitants  
in the camps of this age,  
and that tents suitable  
for the camps must be woven.

As he passed by those weary  
with sickness, Simon’s shadow  
raised them up;  
it cleansed the contagion of leprosy  
and strengthened the lame  
for walking.

The exalted teacher of the nations,  
by his own handkerchiefs,  
powerfully drives away  
the dark spirits’ frenzies  
and every illness.

Night shuts both of them in prison,  
but with the full light of heaven  
they see the shadows and chains;  
they see the glory of Christ.

They raise bodies oppressed by death  
to the airs of light,  
and consign the treacherous enemies  
of the righteous  
to the darkness of the underworld.

They had washed their robes  
in the Lamb’s radiant blood;  
tasting the cup of death,  
they triumphed over the prince of death.

How greatly Peter desired  
to follow Christ’s footsteps!  
He did not fear coming to him  
by the harsh ladder of the cross.

Paul entered the everlasting kingdom  
through the sword’s royal path,  
for whoever fears God  
freely gives his head to the blade.

Thus the princes of the Church,  
thus the true lights of the world,  
through the noble triumph of death  
received the palm of glory.

Rome, blessed now,  
contains their distinguished trophies;  
the whole circuit of the world  
celebrates their crowns.

May our voice resound to you, God;  
may our hearts resound to you;  
may every age praise you,  
wondrous in your own servants.

Christ, we beg you:  
grant us, who sing their praises  
with rejoicing,  
to enjoy forever  
the sight of their radiant faces.

May our choir here resound  
through heaven with hymns  
and sweet praises of the apostles.

Benevolent One, gird us  
with a golden belt of chastity,  
so that, seeing you,  
we may devote ourselves  
to your praises forever.

## HYMN X. On the Passion of Saint John the Baptist

Gracious predecessor of grace,  
angel of truth,  
lamp of Christ,  
and evangelist of everlasting light.

The proclamations of prophecy  
which he had sung with voice, life,  
and deeds,  
he confirms by the sign  
of his holy death.

He had foretold by his birth  
the one who was to be born  
through the ages,  
and by his own baptism  
he had shown the one  
who would baptize.

By the foreshadowing of his own blood,  
the Baptist, a martyr, signifies  
the innocent death of Christ,  
through which life was restored  
to the world.

The savage tyrant  
shut him away in bonds and prison,  
but no bonds harm the man  
whom the gifts of the heart sustain.

He who beholds the glory of Christ  
and the gifts of the Spirit  
is frightened neither  
by the darkness of prison  
nor by bodily punishment.

He willingly offered  
his most holy head  
to be severed;  
yet the pious man did not lose his head,  
for Christ is his true head.

The gracious spirit rejoices  
to leave the herald’s limbs,  
so that, having completed  
the gifts begun  
in his holy precedence,

he may preach to the dead  
that Christ is coming—  
the one whom, while remaining  
in the body,  
he had shown to the living.

The underworld is astonished  
at the news of this deliverance;  
the choirs of the faithful rejoice,  
the fathers together with the peoples.

The righteous prophets and martyrs,  
and all who from the beginning  
had loved Christ with pure hearts  
and worshiped him by holy deeds,

all rejoice in John’s  
sweet words,  
and urgently ask Christ  
to come to his little servants.

Gracious forerunner, tell us:  
when do you think he will come?  
“Come down, Jesus,  
that coming which is near,  
and rescue us.”

At last the Redeemer appeared,  
gathering all into one;  
he took the pious from the underworld  
and placed them in the kingdoms of heaven.

Thus the excellent preacher,  
the great forerunner of Christ,  
after he had sung to those  
held in the body,  
and afterward to the dead,

with Christ leading into heaven  
all the choirs of the faithful,  
entered himself with the others  
into everlasting joys.

## HYMN XI. On the Nativity of the Holy Mother of God

Be present, Christ,  
to our voices;  
dwell within our minds;  
with your gracious right hand  
protect the choirs of singers.

You who were born of the Virgin  
for the sake of our salvation,  
give us pure hearts;  
give us chaste bodily limbs.

And you, blessed above all women,  
Virgin Mary,  
illustrious Mother of God,  
favor our praises.

Your chaste womb,  
consecrated to the Holy Spirit,  
carried the King of the world,  
arisen from David’s seed.

Blessed are your breasts,  
filled with the highest gift,  
which nourished on earth  
the unique glory of earth and heaven.

You who joyfully fulfilled  
the sacred rites of the Law  
at the lofty threshold of the temple,  
you carried in your sweet arms  
the Prince of the heavenly court.

Seeing the Magi  
behold the little one  
lying in your lap,  
they offer their prayers  
to the greatest King and God.

You who, bearing Christ,  
overthrow the sacred things of Memphite divinity,  
make foreigners behold the God  
whom his own homeland drives away.

You sorrowfully seek  
the joy of the world  
with Father Joseph,  
and, rejoicing, find him seated  
in the house of the Most High Father.

At your request, Christ,  
seated at the mystical wedding,  
transformed water  
into cups of red wine.

The sword of sorrow  
pierced your holy spirit  
when you saw the God  
born from your body  
dying.

From the height of the cross,  
the Author of heaven,  
thundering, commends you,  
the virgin, to the son of thunder,  
so that he may guard the Virgin.

You who now behold  
the glory of your Son and God  
with blessed light,  
after the dreadful bonds of death,  
the glory of the Resurrected One;

you who behold the light of heaven  
and his approach to the right hand  
of the Father,  
whom you had seen first  
approach the earth  
from the Father’s bosom;

exalted among the shining stars  
of the apostles,  
filled with the flame of the Holy Spirit,  
you sing praises.

Mother of Christ,  
may your intercession commend  
to God the praise  
which we offer as suppliants,  
singing to Christ.

Emmanuel, receive  
the hymns which we speak  
to the holy Virgin  
and the chaste Mother,  
and free your people.

## HYMN XII. On the Nativity of Saint Andrew

Now let us sing with joyful voices  
the solemn feast of Andrew,  
who adorns the glory of the apostolate  
with the triumph of his blood.

While he was casting a net  
for fish through the troubled seas,  
Christ called him, together with his brothers,  
to the kingdoms of heaven.

He sent him to the nations far and wide  
to proclaim the word of salvation  
and lift believing minds  
from the waves of the world.

Soon, as he illuminated  
the shores of Greece  
with the lamp of faith,  
radiant with Christ God,  
he drove away  
the shadows of error.

The Achaean leader attacks  
the Leader of light with weapons of darkness,  
but the soldier of God  
bravely repels the enemy’s assault.

He reveals the mysteries of the cross,  
which powerfully loosen  
the dreadful bonds of former death  
and bring life to the world.

He recounts the sacrifice of the Lamb,  
who frees us from the enemy,  
bestows life beyond heaven,  
and takes us with him  
into the everlasting kingdom.

Shut in a dark prison,  
the minister of light  
opens golden paths of peace  
to the stars for companies  
of the peoples.

Struck seven times with whips,  
he laughed at every torment;  
the seven gifts  
of the Holy Spirit  
had already filled him.

At last lifted onto the cross,  
he left the filthy earth  
and, blessed in his final steps,  
sought the gates of heaven.

The gracious city received him,  
our mother of all,  
and rejoiced in Christ’s martyr  
and greatest apostle.

The whole choir of the heavenly citizens  
rejoices with us,  
seeing the everlasting solemn feast  
of great Andrew now celebrated.

## HYMN XIII. To Be Sung at the Cross on the Same Feast

Hail, trophy of glory;  
hail, sacred sign of victory,  
through which God, by dying,  
redeemed the lost world.

O glorious cross,  
shining with radiant powers,  
which Christ himself  
consecrated with the limbs  
of his own body.

Once you oppressed  
the race of mortals  
with pale fear;  
but now you fill  
the hearts of the faithful  
with joyful love.

Behold, it is the sport of believers  
to enjoy your embraces.  
What great joys you bring forth!  
You open the gates of heaven.

After the sweet limbs of the Creator,  
you have become sweeter to us than honey  
and are preferred to all  
the honors of the world.

Now I rejoice to approach you;  
I embrace you with the arms of love;  
through you I climb  
to heavenly joys.

Thus receive me willingly,  
the gracious servant of him  
who redeemed me  
through your glory,  
the exalted teacher.

Thus speaks Andrew,  
seeing the horns of the cross  
raised upright;  
and, handing his garment  
to the soldier,  
he is lifted onto the tree of life.

Nor does he cease from the height  
of the cross to teach the crowd  
standing by,  
to reveal everlasting life with God  
and the kingdom of heaven.

Alarmed by their already fervent faith,  
the judge of the crowd  
promises to release him  
from the bonds of this dark death.

But Andrew, gazing upon  
the paths of heaven,  
the King of heaven,  
and the sweet company  
of citizens already numerous  
in the heavenly citadel, says:

“Good Jesus, my teacher, I beg you:  
from this cross let no one  
take me alive in the body,  
freed from my bonds,  
before you have taken up  
my spirit, torn from my flesh,  
and placed me within  
the walls of the homeland  
in which I serve.”

He said this, and a light  
sent forth from the heavenly seats  
surrounded the mighty martyr  
of Christ with flashing radiance.

Its splendor, brighter than the sun,  
remaining before him for a long time,  
teaches what palm  
and what glory  
will follow the cross.

Then, soon raised to heaven  
and returning,  
he carries with him  
the apostle’s spirit,  
released from the knots  
of the body.

There, victorious and blessed  
over the world,  
he joyfully sings forever  
with your faithful  
the songs of triumph, Jesus.

There, among the ranks  
of the blessed exalted ones,  
grant, Christ, a place  
to the little ones  
who sing hymns to you.

## HYMN ON THE DAY OF JUDGMENT (C)

Among the flower-bearing grasses  
of the fertile turf,  
while the branches resounded everywhere  
with the breath of the winds,  
I sat alone, sorrowful,  
beneath the shade of a leafy tree.

Suddenly, disturbed  
by bitter and mournful grief,  
I sang these lamenting songs  
with a saddened mind,

remembering, as I did,  
the crimes I had committed,  
the stains of life,  
the hateful time of death,  
the great day of judgment  
with its dreadful examination,  
and the everlasting anger  
of the stern Judge against the guilty.

And I remembered the whole human race,  
separated into distinct abodes:  
the joys of the saints  
and the punishments of the wicked.

Remembering these things with myself,  
I said in a quiet murmur:

“Now I beg you, now open  
the hot fountains of my veins,  
while I strike my guilty breast  
with my fists, or while I throw  
my limbs upon the ground  
and summon the pains I deserve.

“I beg you, fountains, do not at once spare  
the outpouring of tears,  
but cover my sorrowful face  
with salty drops.

“Reveal wickedness to Christ  
with a groaning voice,  
and let none of the heart’s sins remain hidden  
in its cave.”

“Let everything be brought into the light  
in plain words:  
the savage crimes of heart and tongue,  
of flesh as well.

“This alone is salvation for the soul,  
and certain hope for the sorrowful:  
to open wounds with tears  
to the heavenly physician,

“who is accustomed to heal  
the shattered and release the bound.

“He does not wish to break  
with his hand bruised reeds,  
nor to extinguish  
the lukewarm smoke of flax.”

“Did not the thief hanging on the cross  
give you an example  
of how much true confession  
can accomplish for sin?

“He had been impious in wicked deeds  
right up to the cross,  
but at the hour of death  
he cried out words of prayer  
and, by the mere speech of faith,  
earned salvation;  
with Christ he entered  
through the open gates of paradise.

“Why, I ask, do you delay, mind,  
to open yourself entirely  
to the physician?

“Or why are you silent, tongue,  
while you have time for forgiveness?

“The Almighty now hears you  
with open ears.  
That day will come when the Judge  
of the world arrives,  
and you will have to render  
an account of yourself.

“I advise you to anticipate  
the Judge’s anger now with tears.

“Why do you lie in filth,  
flesh full of sinful offenses?

“Why do you not cleanse your sins  
with abundant tears,  
and pray for yourself  
for the soothing remedies  
of a peaceful cure?

“While the grace of continual weeping is given,  
it is beneficial for you now  
to repent, and salutary to weep.

“The eternal Judge  
will be merciful to you,  
with you as your own accuser.”

“Nor does the heavenly God  
avenge the same crimes twice  
against anyone.

“Do not despise  
the definite times of forgiveness.

“Remember how great torments  
await the wicked,  
and how fearful is he,  
high-throned in the citadel of heaven:  
the Judge will come  
to return to everyone his due.

“What signs will suddenly precede him?  
The earth will tremble,  
the mountains will collapse,  
and the hills will melt.

“The sea will confuse minds  
with a terrible roar.

“The sky will be covered  
with darker and sadder shadows.

“The stars will fall,  
and Titan will grow dark  
at his fiery rising.

“The pale moon will not provide  
the lamp of night.

“Signs threatening death  
will come from heaven.

“Then suddenly the power above  
will come in motion,  
with angelic hosts  
surrounding the heavenly King.

“He will sit, shining,  
on a lofty throne high above.

“Before him we shall be swept,  
with crowds gathered from everywhere,  
so that each may receive judgment  
for his deeds.

“Remember that terror  
which will then strike  
the hearts of all  
before the tribunal  
with stunned cries.

“While countless angelic armies  
come together, accompanying  
the King of heaven,  
the angelic ranks will arrive  
in heavenly companies.

“And all human beings alike  
will be compelled to appear:

“Those who are, those who were,  
those who will be,  
and all who are yet to come.

“All the hidden things  
of everyone will be revealed to all.

“What the heart, tongue, and hand  
did in dark hiding places,  
and what anyone now blushes  
to know,  
will then be known by all alike  
in the open.

“Moreover, the air will be filled  
with consuming flames;  
fire, released from its restraints,  
will reign everywhere.

“And where the air now spreads  
its empty embrace,  
then fiery flame  
will fill it with fierce sound,  
hastening to avenge  
the savage causes of sin.

“Nor will the avenging fire  
then care to spare anyone,  
unless that person comes there  
washed clean of every stain.

“Then tribes and peoples  
will strike their guilty breasts  
with blows.”

“Both will stand there together,  
the poor and the powerful;  
the wretched and the rich  
will fear under the same dominion.

“A river vomiting fire  
will bitterly torment the wretched,  
and the worms of sin  
will gnaw the innermost parts  
of their hearts.

“No one present there  
will trust in his merits  
before the Judge.

“Rather, excessive terror  
will pass through every breast,  
and the impious crowd alike  
will stand stunned with dreadful fear.

“What will you do, flesh—  
what will you do at that weeping hour—  
you who now rejoice  
to serve miserable lust  
and drive yourself onward  
with the sharp goads  
of your luxury?

“Why will you not fear  
the fiery torments  
prepared long ago  
for wicked demons?”

“They surpass the senses  
of all and the words of every person;  
no voice is able  
to describe the wretched punishments.

“Black places of eternal Gehenna  
are full of fire,  
with icy cold mixed together  
with burning flames.

“Now the eyes weep  
with the excessive heat of the furnace;  
now again the teeth chatter  
with excessive cold.

“By these miserable turns  
the wretched are rolled forever  
through dark nights  
amid pitch-black gloom.

“There no voice sounds,  
except the hard weeping everywhere;  
no face is seen there  
except the faces of torturers.

“Nothing is felt there  
except cold and flames;  
stench fills the nostrils  
with immense corruption.

“The fire-vomiting mouth,  
also mourning,  
will be filled with fire,  
and worms will tear the bones  
with fiery teeth.

“Moreover, the breast  
is tormented by bitter cares:

“Why would luxuriant flesh,  
within so brief a span of time,  
have earned for itself  
everlasting punishments  
in a dark prison,  
where no spark of light  
shines for the wretched?

“Neither peace nor mercy,  
indeed no hope of rest,  
smiles upon those who weep;  
all consolations flee.

“No one will provide help  
in their bitter circumstances;  
no face of joy  
will ever be seen there.

“Only pain and groaning,  
chattering, terror,  
and dreadful fear;  
weariness, sadness,  
cruel indignation, and languor;

“wandering souls  
in a prison of blind flames.

“Then the sinful joys  
of this age will cease:

“Drunkenness, banquets, laughter,  
wantonness, jesting,  
dreadful desire, clinging luxury,  
criminal lust,

“idle sleep, heavy torpor,  
sluggish laziness,  
whatever pleasure of the flesh  
now entices  
and plunges the mind  
into the blind whirlpool of sin.

“Then it will plunge  
the wretched without end  
into blind flames.

“O exceedingly blessed,  
and blessed forever through the ages,  
is the one who successfully escapes  
those disasters of punishment  
and rejoices with the saints  
through all ages!

“Joined to Christ,  
he will possess the heavenly kingdoms.

“There no night steals away  
the splendor of pleasant light;  
no pain or groaning will come,  
no weary old age,

“no thirst, hunger, sleep,  
or any labor;

“no fever, disease, disaster,  
cold, or flames;

“weariness, sadness, care,  
torments, ruin;

“lightning, rainstorm, winter,  
thunder, snow, hail, storm;

“anguish, poverty, sorrow,  
death, accident, need.

“Rather, peace and mercy,  
goodness and abundance reign:

“joys, gladness, virtue, light,  
everlasting life,

“glory, praise, rest, honor,  
and sweet concord.

“Moreover, God himself  
provides every good thing  
for all.

“He is always present,  
sustains, fills, honors,  
glorifies, preserves, venerates,  
loves, and adorns everyone.

“He places them with the Most High  
and, joyful, in the heavenly seat,  
gives them everlasting rewards  
through heavenly gifts,

“among angelic companies  
and holy ranks,

“joined to the prophetic patriarchs  
and prophets,

“among apostolic citadels  
with rejoicing hearts,

“among camps shining  
with rose-colored triumphs,

“and at the same time among  
the white ranks blooming  
with virgin purity.

“The gracious Mother of God,  
the devout Virgin Mary,  
leads them through the blessed,  
shiningly adorned kingdoms  
of the Father,

“among the saints of the Church,  
among sons and fathers,  
and among the heavenly senate  
in heavenly peace.”

What, I ask, what hard thing  
is sown in this age,

so that it may be permitted me  
to dwell among those companies  
and always rejoice  
in the blessed seats of heaven?

May Christ’s dearest offspring  
protect you safe for me  
and make you blessed forever without end;  
and commend me to your Christ  
through your gracious prayers.

## Prayer to God

King God, on whom  
the structure of the immense world depends,

what I, wretched, implore of you  
through Christ, merciful and kind:

give me a watchful mind,  
King of kings who governs all;

give me, I beg, understanding;  
give me the honorable light of the mind.

Let me have a right faith,  
opposed to false sects;

let me have, above all,  
present correction of conduct.

May I be dear, humble, truthful,  
prudent with time;

silent concerning secrets,  
and cautious of the thunderbolt of the tongue.

Give me a faithful companion,  
give me an unchanging friend.

# APPENDIX

## Doubtful Poems (G, S)

### HYMN I. On the Twelve Signs of the Zodiac

First appears Aries, gliding  
with dim light;

next approaches Taurus,  
advancing with outstretched body;

then Gemini shines,  
casting fire from its two circles;

heat-bearing Cancer  
spreads its burning stars;

beneath it the fierce power  
of Leo crawls, shining;

Virgo follows it,  
gleaming with ruddy body.

Then the Claws [Libra]  
with their outstretched, bright radiance;

the great shining power  
of the Scorpion follows them;

then Sagittarius, powerful with the bow,  
holds the bent bow in his right hand;

after him Capricorn proceeds  
with horn-bearing light;

moist Aquarius shines  
with its broad circle;

then the scaly Pisces swim  
in their straight order.

### HYMN II. On the Ages of Life

Ninety-six years  
are the proper span which fills  
the life of aging men.

The talkative crow exceeds these  
by ninefold living;

the stag exceeds the crow’s ages  
by fourfold measure;

the Raven, brazen-footed,  
thrice conquers the stag;

and the recoverable Phoenix,  
the bird, multiplies him ninefold.

The Hamadryad nymphs,  
whose life is longest,  
surpass it tenfold  
in perpetual age.

This is the limit  
that confines the long-lived creatures;  
the rest of the secret age  
God, the arbiter, knows.

## DIONYSIUS ON THE YEARS (S)

The years of the Lord  
are marked in the present line,  
when the Lord, having taken pity  
on the world to remove its sins,  
advanced here as a human being,  
bearing the womb of nature.

### To Find the Indiction

Add three to the years of Christ  
for the regular indiction numbers,  
and divide by the number fifteen;  
then without delay you will see  
what its number is.

Christ the Lord was born  
in the fourth indiction.  
Therefore three are added  
for the indictions,  
to the number of Christ’s years  
from the number twelve.

### To Verify the Incarnation

Divide the series of indictions  
by fifteen;

then add to these  
the regular numbers ten and two;

let the indiction of the present year  
be added there as well.

### To Exhort the Reader

Reader, who strives  
to know the calculation  
with resolute mind,

let the series of the indictions  
stand deeply fixed in memory;

if these are absent,  
through negligence you will lose  
the years of Christ.

### To Find the Lunar Epacts

Divide the years of Christ  
by nineteen.

Extend whatever exceeds these  
by eleven;

dividing by thirty,  
you will find the epacts.

As above.

Subtract one  
from the nineteen-year cycle of Easter.

Multiply by eleven;  
divide by thirty;

you will immediately find  
the epact of that year.

### To Find the Solar Epacts

For the solar epacts,  
take the years of the Lord.

Add to these  
the fourth part of the years  
that have elapsed;

add four regular numbers,  
and divide by seven.

As above.

Always retain the ninth day  
before the Kalends of April,  
the feria which is established  
as the place of the concurrents;

the numbers by which the days increase  
grow by the number seven.

### What Degree the Solar Cycle Holds

Subtracting eight years  
for the solar cycle,

divide the remainder  
by twenty-eight;

you will rejoice to have found  
the solar cycle in this way.

### To Verify the Concurrent

Divide this solar cycle by four;

then add its fourth part to it;

dividing by seven,  
the concurrent is found.

### To Find the Lunar Cycle

If you wish to know  
which lunar cycle it is,

always subtract two years  
from the highest number;

divided by nineteen,  
it is found.

### To Find the Nineteen-Year Cycle

If you properly add one  
to the years of Christ  
and divide them  
by nineteen,

you will find  
the final nineteen-year cycle.

### The Place of the Epacts

The place of the epacts  
is clear, easy, and convenient:

it is set on the eleventh day  
before the Kalends of April,  
where the number of the moon  
is equal to the epact.

### Also Concerning the Fourteen Epacts

When the fourteenth epact  
is held in the cycle,

the law sanctioned by the fathers  
requires one to calculate  
the fourteenth moon  
on the eleventh day  
before the Kalends of April.

### When the Epacts Increase

For when the epacts increase  
to the number fifteen,

you will hold the fourteenth moon  
on the twelfth day before the Kalends  
and likewise on the Kalends of April,  
without doubt.

### On Fewer Epacts

When there are fewer epacts,  
according to the observed rule,

they continue increasing by days  
up to the fourteenth;

that itself will be  
the legal and legitimate one  
which you were seeking.

### On More Epacts

But if they are said  
to be more than fifteen,

advance by that number  
up to thirty.

Thus begin anew,  
up to the Paschal limit.

### The First Rule of the Month

Our Easter is to be kept  
according to the rule  
of the first month:

after the Christians have completed  
the fourteenth moon,  
it is observed on Sunday  
after the equinox has passed.

### The Difference Between Unleavened Bread and Easter

This is the difference  
between Unleavened Bread and Easter:

the day of Easter  
is to be observed on the fourteenth moon;

the seventh solemnity  
of Unleavened Bread follows.

### How It Varies Over Seven Days

The moon of Easter varies  
by the number seven,

on the day when Christ,  
the Savior of all, rose,

from which it rightly took  
the name “holy” and “Lord’s day.”

### On the Common Year

The common year,  
consisting of three hundred  
and fifty-four days,

contains twelve months,

with eleven days remaining  
from the course of the sun.

As above.

This number of eleven  
is now placed every year  
to seek the moon annually;

for the epacts receive their name  
from a Greek term.

### On the Embolism

The embolism, however,  
is made longer by nineteen days  
by exceeding the course of the sun,

having three hundred  
and eighty-four days.

### On the Ogdoad and Hendecad

There is also another division  
of the aforesaid cycle,

in which the Ogdoad  
and the Hendecad of years  
are sought.

Who is said to equalize the course of the sun and moon.

## Concerning the Moon of January

If you seek the moon on the Kalends of January,

always extend the lunar cycle by eleven;

add one to the regular number and divide by thirty.

## Likewise as Above

For the cycle is reckoned through the final three years:

do not add one regular number, as in the others,

because two must be inserted in these, with vigilant care.

[Col. 0639D] ## In Which Sign the Moon May Be

If perhaps you seek to know in which sign the moon may be,

multiply its age four times and combine it by portions;

then, dividing by thirty, you will find the signs.

## Likewise

There is a ready calculation in the middle or at the beginning:

however many portions it has in one sign,

add that many to all the following, or subtract them from all.

## How Long It Remains in a Sign

The moon is said to illuminate each sign

for two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour,

and, passing through them all in this way, returns to the same point.

## Concerning the Three Years That Are Not Observed

Moreover, the eighth, eleventh, and nineteenth

cannot preserve the general reckoning,

when an intercalary month is inserted into them.

[Col. 0640A] ## Concerning the Month of May

First, then, concerning the three years of which we spoke:

at the Kalends of May, according to the customary rule,

the twenty-eighth is then shown.

## Likewise

Because the intercalary month is inserted in March,

and one day is taken away from it,

it will remain at twenty-seven.

## Concerning the Month of July

Likewise, in the same manner, at the Kalends of July,

be content with twenty-nine out of thirty;

the excess causes the intercalary month to remain [at that number].

## Concerning the Intercalations of the Eleventh Year

In the eleventh year, in which on the day before

the Nones in December it customarily begins in the usual manner,

it then causes it to fall back, the order being changed in this way.

## Likewise

[Col. 0640B] For the lunar reckoning at the Kalends of March

usually counts the twenty-ninth.

The intercalary month occupies only the twenty-eighth.

## Concerning the Nineteenth Year

In the nineteenth year, which is the last of these,

because it is placed on the third day before the Nones of March,

it makes the Kalends of May bear this additional number.

## Concerning the Lunar Leap

Finally, on the thirtieth day of July,

the lunar leap is to be observed according to the general order,

which normally increases through nineteen years.

## From What the Leap Is Produced

Each hour, by adding one point per year,

this subtraction consists of a nineteenth part of a point.

Over nineteen years the subtraction of a day is produced.

## Likewise

[Col. 0640C] Eleven are always added for all the preceding years;

here the epacts are the number for increase in the twelfth.

When thirty is completed, it was decided that none should be stated.

## Likewise

On the twenty-ninth day, since the other one,

by its swiftness, compels this to be counted as the first,

it makes the day leap over; thus you begin with the Nones.

## To Test the Moon

If, then, you wish to know the moon at this or that time,

take the days of January from the beginning of the month,

and add the age of the moon at the Kalends of that month.

## Likewise

If you first divide by nine times fifty,

and nevertheless divide a second time by thirty,

you will easily find the true moon that you were seeking.

## To Test the Weekday

Likewise take the days of the year and divide by seven,

and remember how many exceed seven;

attach these to the weekday of the stated Kalends.

## Likewise

When you have gathered these together into one sum,

and divided it again into its parts by sevens,

you will find the reckoning you were seeking—the weekday.

## Concerning the Equinox

You must keep the spring equinox on the twenty-first

of March, because the rule of the Fathers

strongly urges that it be observed with careful calculation.

## Another Matter

Thus September too, with its number made equal,

because the two are proved to be years of one [reckoning],

keeps its autumnal equinox; “the other” preserves an equinox [the relationship is corrupt/elliptical in the printed text].

## Concerning the Reckoning of the Twelve Signs

Truly marvelous and savage is the madness of the pagans,

who transferred such diverse beasts into the heavens,

although hosts of angels are known to be with Olympus.
