They say that a bull shines among the stars—

the bull into which, as they fabulously assert, Jupiter was transformed,

and in that form carried Agenor’s daughter to Italy.

Christian faith possesses a memory of the signs:

first, the Lamb, who in splendid majesty in heaven

reigns alone with the Father through endless ages.

Therefore our bull must not be thought of as grim in face

or swollen in neck, though it has been given that noble name;

rather, it is a sweet, gentle, mild, and pleasant calf.

It is therefore the fattened calf that must be understood,

whose flesh, sacrificed on the gallows of the cross,

“bore these by its leg from the danger of death” (*hos crure suo tulit*); the referent of *hos* is not supplied by the text.

It does not cease to exhort us with diligent piety:

to plough away our vices by submitting to Christ’s yoke,

and to bring back the seeds of the divine commandments.

With what follows, it exhorts us through the two Testaments:

to trample down idolatry, to seek the Lord alone,

and to avoid greed, the incurable crab.

[Col. 0641B] Our Lion fell asleep so that he might conquer in death;

therefore he awoke so that we might be able to rise,

through whom we rightly deserved to be rescued from punishments.

This sixth sign properly follows that of the Virgin.

In the sixth age of the world the Son of God came;

he holds the scales of justice and is rightly called God.

[Col. 0642A] Whoever serves him with a pure heart

will now fear no longer, secure from the deadly poison;

with his foot he will be able to trample the scorpion.

Protected by the shield of faith, he will not fear the savage Archer,

deformed with horse’s legs;

he too will overcome the wicked devil.

Capricorn, deformed and despicable in appearance,

makes some insane, others sacrilegious,

murderers, madmen, and others adulterers.

But when all these have been converted and wept well,

the bright Water-Bearer customarily wipes from the forehead

the crimes committed willingly or at the instigation of demons.

The two fish that follow, born from one womb,

represent two peoples, called by grace,

washed in the water of baptism, believing in God alone.

Let the madness of those people cease now—

those who believe that there are mortal things in heaven;

let them reject empty things and believe what God’s Church teaches.

Little animals, great animals, and reptiles,

[Col. 0642B] weighed down by the burden of flesh, do not seek heavenly things,

but believe that souls perish together with this flesh.

Wherever the mediator of human beings and God has been,

we believe that the souls of the elect are also there;

infinite goodness has promised that it will give them this.

[Col. 0641]

# MANFRED’S POEMS (S)

## CONCERNING THE SOLAR YEAR

[Col. 0641B]

The solar year, often called the great year,

is the sun’s single circuit through the zodiac.

## Concerning the Sun’s Course

The course is completed in twenty-eight years.

## Concerning the Lunar Year

The lunar year is the moon’s circuit, which

[Col. 0641C] is sometimes common and sometimes intercalary.

## Concerning the Moon’s Course

But its course is completed in three and twice eight years.

From these two lights it is fitting for us

to draw our discussion and add a foundation to our calculations,

so that the arguments placed upon these foundations

may not be overturned by objections.

But first we wish to disclose something that presses upon us,

something that seems to us of great usefulness.

## CONCERNING THE FOUR SEASONS OF THE YEAR

Spring, summer, autumn, and winter are the four

seasons of the year, which become evident when divided

according to a definite number; contemplation has assigned three months to each.

### Concerning Spring

March, April, and May belong to spring.

### Concerning Summer

June, July, and August are present for summer.

[Col. 0641D] ### Concerning Autumn

October, September, and November belong to autumn.

### Concerning Winter

January, February, and December are winter’s months.

In the first of these, the unchanging God and King,

the Creator of the world, made the beginning of nature,

and fixed beginnings for all creatures.

He completed his work, which is written to have lasted six days,

and rested from it on the seventh light.

Therefore I am pleased to disclose more deeply the secrets of this arrangement

and afterward to hand on instruction to those born later.

## CONCERNING THE SEVEN DAYS AND THEIR NAMES

In the beginning of the world that Creator God

established seven cycles, which the sphere’s circle encloses;

he fashioned the individual stars according to fixed courses,

and philosophy marked them with their own names:

first with the name of Saturn, and second with that of Jupiter;

Mars runs beneath them, and Mercury is sixth.

The moon, indeed, runs through the smallest heaven as the seventh.

Each day received its name from these stars,

and this arrangement corresponds suitably to our work:

light together with its night consists of twenty-four hours,

and carries on its eternal course from the ether.

Now begin counting from Saturn at the summit;

after those, you will count the moon and its sphere.

Thus the reckoning will proceed in a circuit through them all.

The first number, after twice fourteen,

corresponds to it and takes its name.

### Concerning Sunday

Therefore the first day was called by the name of the sun.

### Concerning Friday

Now the true Sun, who redeemed us from death,

gives the second part the moon’s number as its name;

and thus each day received its name from the stars.

But now let us bend back and sing what we have set forth,

according to the subject and the duty of the pen.

On the fourth light God fashioned the two lights of the world.

### Concerning Mercury

And he added the other planets, stars, and all the constellations

in the firmament, whose course is unchanging,

and commanded them not to exceed their proper course.

This is the day on which Wisdom wrote

that the hours of night should be equal to those of day,

and by careful calculation learned the sun’s course.

The watchful year recognized its circuit:

three hundred and sixty days,

with five added and a quarter also included.

But a quarter of anything is its fourth part;

the remaining three are called by the name *dodrans*.

From this the days proceed and are reckoned;

we explain it clearly in our instruction, if you wish to know.

## CONCERNING THE COURSE OF THE SUN AND THE YEAR, AND THEIR SIGNS

The course of the stars, the moon, and the sun’s sphere

was first learned and written down by the Egyptian nymphs;

they handed on knowledge of this art to mortals,

and called the path of the sun by which the year is led

the zodiac, marking it with remarkable investigation.

That learned Macrobius explains it well,

and with sound judgment and commendable study teaches the labor involved.

Prudent, he divided it into twice six parts,

calling the parts signs and marking them according to their arrangement.

### Concerning Aries

The first part of heaven is called by the name Aries,

either because this animal especially burns before its horns,

as the sun, with the rays of its heat like horns,

begins to work upon the earth congealed by ice

and upon the rigor of winter, unlocking it for the seeds;

or because from this point Aries lies forward upon the right shoulder,

just as at this season the sun illuminates the right-hand part

of the zodiac. For there are two hemispheres of heaven.

The head of Aries belongs to the first,

and Libra to the second;

each circles through the space measured in equal portions,

and Aries lies down in the left-hand part.

### Concerning Taurus

They gave the name of Taurus to the second part,

because when the sun passes through these regions of heaven,

the crops turn white, and the work of bulls and oxen is now reaped with the sickle in the hotter fields.

### Concerning Gemini

They say that another sign is called Gemini.

The adulterer, in the form of a swan, deceived Leda;

[Col. 0643B] she bore from her womb a pair of twin brothers.

Castor loved his brother Pollux in turn.

The one was mortal, carrying death from his mother;

the other was immortal, free from death because of his father.

“Because he received a father from his brother’s death,

he shared in his brother’s death from life” (*Hic quoniam patrem de fratris morte recepit / Fraternae morti de vita participavit*); the causal and possessive relations are syntactically defective. Sharing turns, they became a constellation in the ether,

occupying a portion of heaven.

Thus, while the sun runs through this region,

plants and crops dry beneath the sun’s heat,

and what flourished with green foliage begins to die;

throughout summer they appear dry, as though dead.

This part of the world has a zone near the burned region.

### Concerning Cancer

They mark the sign that bears the name Cancer.

The meaning of Cancer is plainly evident:

it advances by moving backward, like a crab.

Thus, when the sun cannot pass beyond this part of heaven,

it seeks the lower regions after traversing the solstice,

beneath the fourth part of it, where it first completes its rising.

[Col. 0643C] It is not a fitting time to write for the *exsortes* (“those without a share/lot”); the referent is unresolved.

### Concerning Leo

They assigned the name of Leo to the fifth part.

This animal surpasses all others in the heat of its warmth.

Its limbs possess vigor and strength in the first part,

but degenerate and weaken in the latter.

Thus the sun burns more strongly than through the other signs

and spreads its strength over the panting earth.

Yet in the final parts of this sign

it tempers its heat, though only for the weaker things

placed upon the earth, which it leaves behind in its tracks.

### Concerning Virgo

The sixth sign bears the name Virgo in due season,

because the earth stands like a barren virgin woman

and produces no fruit beneath this star.

### Concerning Libra

The seventh part of the zodiac is called Libra,

displaying by its own name

that in this part of heaven night and day become equal.

### Concerning Scorpio

Scorpio bears the eighth name, and Sagittarius the ninth;

from this point they indicate rains and blows of hail.

### Concerning Capricorn

The tenth sign of the sphere is called Capricorn.

The goat always seeks high branches while feeding;

in the same way the returning sun seeks the heights,

makes the fourth part of the solstice, and sends the sun back.

### Concerning Aquarius

The eleventh sign is given the name Aquarius.

### Concerning Pisces

The twelfth is called by the name of fish,

because at this time the earth gives way to snow and water.

[Col. 0644A] ### Concerning the Leap Year

Thus, by contemplating these things, we understand the sun’s return.

By this method the year is shown to be formed:

the sun traverses each of these signs

in thirty days, five hours, and a half-hour.

You shall multiply all these together into one sum,

reducing from all the signs the hours and the half-hour.

You will find three hundred and sixty days.

The calculation adds five days to these,

and twice six half-hours remain in addition.

If you collect these hours, you will make six;

these joined together constitute a quarter,

the fourth part of a day.

It has been determined that this quarter is not counted for three years.

But in the fourth year four quarters complete one day

and establish it beneath the threshold of the year.

This entire year is called leap-year,

consisting of three hundred and sixty-six days.

## WHY IT IS CALLED BISSEXTUS, AND WHY IT WAS INVENTED

[Col. 0644B] If this were neglected, an error so great would arise

that the summer months would meet the winter months,

and, conversely, would exchange places with them.

That day, therefore, which seems to be so great an error,

is inserted and is rightly called *bissextus*,

because in the reckoning it is read as “twice the sixth day before the Kalends of March.”

The Romans called this the place of the concurrent numbers,

for whatever weekday is reckoned on that day,

the same number of concurrents is taken in the other year;

but in the leap year it is taken as an addition.

## CONCERNING THE NAMES OF THE MONTHS

Since the significance of the signs has now been made clear,

let us try to write about the names of the months.

When powerful Rome once flourished with the jewels of philosophy

and imposed its course upon the whole world,

it first divided the year into twelve parts

and then assigned suitable names to each part.

### Concerning March

March is called from males, and is named the first part,

because at that time Juno asks Jupiter,

and the earth asks for rain,

so that it may become pregnant and swell, fit to bear offspring.

### Concerning April

April is so called because nature is opened,

for flowers, fruits, and all grasses.

### Concerning May

May is called from the greater part of the elders.

### Concerning June

June, the fourth, was named from the younger men.

For the Romans had been divided into two groups according to custom:

the older part deliberated in the city,

while the strength of the young men directed military affairs.

Thus May and June received their names.

### Concerning July

July derives its name from the great Caesar.

### Concerning August

They gave the following month its name from Augustus.

## CONCERNING THE FOUR FINAL MONTHS

[Col. 0644D]

The other four thereafter took their names from their number.

### Concerning September and October

They were first called Quintilis and Sextilis.

### Concerning November and December

They also signify by number how far they are removed from the first month,

and by their number indicate the condition of the sky.

### Concerning January

January was named from Janus.

Ancient custom believed that Janus was the beginning of things,

and, admiring him, dedicated that month to him.

Therefore January is the head of the year.

### Concerning February

They give the final part the name February,

for the Latins say that *februare* means “to purify.”

Such a custom once prevailed among Roman citizens:

in the fifth year, when the census was brought to the city,

they purified the walls, temples, and shrines of the gods,

specifically under the light of the second day of this month,

so that they might cleanse the city from the excesses of sin,

and so that pardon and safety might be granted through these rites.

Thus we are accustomed to say “to perform a lustration” and “to purify.”

Thus too the term “five-year purifications” (*quinquennia lustra*) is often used.

But now it is necessary to proceed through inaccessible passes

and lighten the journey begun with varied speech.

## CONCERNING THE REGULAR NUMBERS OF THE WEEKDAYS AND KALENDS, AND THEIR ORIGIN

First, then, let us examine the regular numbers:

from where they proceed and what their origin is.

The first day of the world is described as having been that day

on which we read that the created light first shone;

that is, the first portion of the zodiac and of the Ram.

Beginning from that day, therefore, we shall count to the Kalends

of the month about which you seek information.

Then divide all the days that follow by seven,

since they can never exceed that number;

whatever exceeds it you shall retain as the regular number.

If it is less, let it likewise serve for the regular numbers.

If there are seven, add seven to all the months,

and subtract the place of the concurrents from the sum.

After reckoning the Kalends, *Veneris ad Marti* [the printed wording is corrupt, literally “of Venus to Mars”],

remember to assign the five that remain to it.

That day appeared to run as the first weekday,

while Phoebus had not yet set the year’s course in motion.

This was called the first concurrent because it was begun earlier;

for it runs joined to the whole year.

### Why They Are Called Concurrents

Now we add the origin from which the first concurrent proceeds

and explain to us what such a conjunction signifies.

They are plainly called concurrents for this reason:

they run together with the regular numbers throughout the year,

indicating which weekday will come on the Kalends.

This is accomplished by the rule of the sun’s course.

Take, then, the day on which the world first shone with light,

and count all the days together up to that point,

to the place where the seat of the concurrent is found.

### How the Regular Numbers Are Found: The First Concurrent

We also command that these be divided by seven alone.

The remainder marks the origin of the concurrents.

The rest that follows is discovered in this order:

as was done from this point, divide the second year.

These two run in the year that passes,

and you should add whatever remains to one.

The third and fourth are multiplied in the same way by the rest.

But in the fifth year, because it is a leap year,

the excesses that accumulate in this place remain together.

Two weekdays are counted in one at the stated place,

and the sixth retains the course previously mentioned, followed by the seventh.

Whatever exceeds seven, as the rule says,

after it has been removed, is rightly retained as the concurrent.

### How the Weekday Is Found from the Regular Number

When these concurrents are added to the preceding numbers,

they show which weekday will come on the Kalends.

If the number is seven, the seventh will be yours.

If it is less, count the entire weekday on the Kalends.

If it passes seven, remove seven from the number.

## FINDING THE WEEKDAY OF ANY DAY OF THE MONTH BY THE DAYS OF THE MONTH

If you wish to know the weekday for every day of a month,

take all the days of the preceding month,

but do not count that same day again.

Add the entire weekday of the Kalends to these.

If the result is seven, the seventh will be yours.

If the number is less, it will rightly remain yours.

If it exceeds seven, remove seven from the number.

Thus, what is held by this method is marked.

## CONCERNING THE REGULAR NUMBERS OF THE MOON AND THEIR ORIGIN

[Col. 0646A]

Since the sun’s circuit has been written in verse,

let us now assign, as far as possible, the moon’s movements.

But first let us disclose other regular numbers,

which are appended to these lunar months.

### Concerning the Epacts

The moon’s circuit is called the lunar year.

### Concerning the Discovery of the Null Epact

Its beginning, which is now held at September,

is found in the month, as the page of the ancients reveals.

The clever Egyptian astrologers first discovered it.

They carefully examined the secrets of the heavens,

and the Latins learned their science,

imitating them while admiring their school and arts.

After them, others who described these matters determined

the seat of the epacts to be the sixth day before the Kalends of September.

They report that the moon was created and fixed in heaven at this point,

when it gave no radiance to the earth.

[Col. 0646B] Because its age varied in the light by no number,

it could not fully be called the thirtieth.

Hence, knowing Phoebe to be without splendor,

they called that year “without epacts.”

But when it first poured light upon the earth,

shining with new brightness, it was rightly called the first.

And because it first illuminated the earth with light,

its counting was first begun on the fifth day before the Kalends.

Because this occurred on the fifth day before the Kalends of October,

whatever the moon then was, and on whatever Kalends,

the same number of regular numbers is written in these months.

This rule indeed runs through all the months.

### Concerning the Eleventh Epact

After this, learn the eleventh epact in the following year.

“The epact is complete” (*Epactam tota est*); Phoebe’s position has been marked,

and she shines for all in whatever numbered place is hers, “empty” (*inanis*) [the syntax is defective].

The same number of epacts always runs in those [positions].

## THAT THE EPACT AND THE REGULAR NUMBER MUST BE JOINED TO FIND THE MOON’S AGE

[Col. 0646C]

When the epacts are joined to these regular numbers,

they indicate on which day Phoebe will shine at the Kalends.

If their number comes out below thirty,

Phoebe remains complete;

but if it grows beyond that,

after those numbers have been removed, the complete moon will be present at the Kalends.

Whatever remains establishes the rule for all.

### How the Moon’s Age Is Found by the Days of the Month

But if you wish to know this throughout the whole month,

take the days of the month that precede the present day,

and whatever the moon was at the Kalends at that time,

add its number to the days that have passed.

If their number comes out below thirty,

Phoebe remains complete;

but if it grows beyond that, after those numbers have been removed,

the remaining number gives the complete moon.

Nevertheless, it is necessary to note this with vigilant attention:

if the twenty-ninth has been inscribed for the month,

subtract that much, and the remainder will reveal the moon’s age.

I shall also try to disclose in verse why this happens.

## CONCERNING THE LUNAR YEAR

[Col. 0646D]

The moon traverses each sign in two days,

six hours, and two-thirds of an hour.

Collect, then, the days from all the signs,

and together they amount to twenty-four.

You can add three days from the six-hour portions.

Now I shall explain what a *bessis* is by this method.

If you divide something into three equal parts,

each part is called a *triens*;

if one part is subtracted, the two remaining parts are called *besses*.

From these besses you will complete eight hours with six.

Thus by this reckoning Phoebe would traverse the whole zodiac

in a number of days and under the stated conditions,

but she does not pass beneath the sun in exactly the same interval.

For while she flies through the portions of the zodiac,

the sun nearly completes the whole sign.

The moon cannot rise or be called first

unless she has first been beneath her brother,

nor can she pass beyond him.

Therefore two days and the four hours mentioned above

must be added, during which interval she follows Phoebus.

She will pass beyond him and become first in the higher light.

This completes the lunar month in every respect.

We declare it to consist of twenty-nine days,

with twice six hours additionally set down,

for a day does not remain whole in these hours.

Because one month is then divided,

the second month will be filled out by the hours of the other.

This occurs especially when the first month is at the world’s hinge,

kindled at midday;

in the second month it occurs alternately at midnight.

Thus the whole course proceeds.

Let all these months be reduced to one sum,

and we acknowledge that the year consists of

three hundred and fifty-four days.

This is the year properly called lunar.

## THAT ONE EPACT IS FOUND FROM ANOTHER BY ADDING ELEVEN

[Col. 0647B]

Now contemplate this with attentive understanding,

and place what we give you, once disclosed, in your memory.

Here the series and origin of the epacts will become clear.

We have shown you two unequal years.

The lunar form is exceeded by eleven days,

because the lunar year is surpassed by the solar year.

Eleven epacts are therefore taken in the first order.

From this point add the number in every year

to the epacts belonging to the preceding years.

Whatever is less or more than thirty, according to custom,

you shall retain as the epact of the year that passes.

The final year contains the eighteenth epact;

when this is added to those preceding it, one is added—

the one that is always subtracted from the lunar year,

which philosophers call the lunar leap.

If God grants permission, we shall discuss it at length.

When you join these together, you will have thirty.

These are the epacts that run at the first hinge,

which retain the cycle that the Hebrews always maintain.

[Col. 0647C] If you join them to the regular numbers of the months,

you subtract them according to the number of the moon,

and count the moon as the regular numbers indicate,

at the Kalends of each month of the year.

Hence also comes the present practice of calling the epacts “null” (*nullae*).

## CONCERNING INTERCALARY AND COMMON YEARS

Now we decide that it is necessary here

to discuss intercalary and common years,

so that we may disclose more clearly the moon’s leap.

The page of the divine book testifies that the moon,

fixed in heaven, had a course beneath the sun.

Placed on the fourth weekday, she then began her course,

and on the day on which she first existed she did not first shine,

but only after nineteen years had passed.

This course of the moon is rightly called a cycle.

Then, as it first passes through the same orbit,

the first lunar month of the world crosses its starting point.

It brought the fourteenth day of the moon, with its light complete,

on the Nones of what is now the month of April.

As Memphis more suitably taught, you can see these things;

for their rule differs from the Hebrew cycle.

But because of Easter we describe these matters in various ways.

Thus the cycle is called by this name.

Through it common years and intercalary years are produced.

The two that precede are properly called common,

because they were closed with twelve months in the year.

But the third is called “increasing,”

because one month—that is, one lunar month—was added.

The following year took its beginning from that month,

which reveals the fourteenth lunar day,

after equal hours of night and day,

in which the Easter term is present from the first,

or occurs only at an equal time.

Thus that cycle always increases in this way,

except in the ogdoad, because it does not occur in the hendecad.

For the one that has preferred the common year

is more notable because it consists in the same cycle.

It is called the eighth, a name formed from the Greek.

The hendecad is so called because it is the eleventh after the ogdoad.

You will easily mark these according to their number.

Finally, there are seven intercalary years,

and ninety-one months are counted.

The common years, which the rule marks as twice six [twelve],

add one hundred and forty-four to the others [the grammatical relation is unclear].

Together, thirty and two hundred and five are joined: 235.

But now let us begin to explain what was promised

and disclose the moon’s leap through these months.

## CONCERNING THE MOON’S LEAP

After the circuit of the zodiac, when she was called first

and was kindled at the completion of the lunar month,

the moon had not yet completed twelve hours.

There remained for her the hours we mentioned:

twice two moments, a twelfth of a moment, and one atom,

the atom being suitably the indivisible part of time.

All these increase through the months,

so that one is diminished from the number of the lunar year.

Now let us prove by calculation at the end of the cycle

how one complete day grows from these.

Since there are two hundred and thirty-five months,

you will see that, according to the number of moments mentioned earlier,

there are four hundred and ninety-four.

And since we say that an hour consists of four points,

and individual points of ten moments,

divide the whole sum by forty.

You will find twenty-three hours and a half.

But if the other part of this hour is supplied,

the twelfth part of a thing, called an *uncia*,

the number twelve completes the moment.

Thus the two hundred and thirty-five months produce

five times two and nine moments,

and beneath them are seven atoms,

which must complete the months.

Forty-seven atoms together make an *uncia*.

Therefore, from the two hundred and thirty-five atoms,

the *unciae* increase; the printed numerical wording (*quinque decemque*) is materially uncertain.

If you join these equally to the seven prescribed above,

you will make a moment.

Another must be added to it,

by which the number will complete half an hour.

When that is joined to twenty-three and a half,

the complete day, consisting of twenty-four hours,

is formed.

This is regarded as the lunar leap.

In the nineteenth year of the cycle, when July

must always count at the third before the Kalends,

the August moon becomes its twentieth.

Here “having passed the thirtieth” is spoken of;

and the third before the Kalends of August is counted by right.

It is established by the reckoning of the second epact,

and from there keeps an unbroken course through all [the numerical sequence is difficult and is retained without reconstruction].

## HOW MANY HOURS THE MOON SHINES

But if you wish to know for how many hours Phoebe shines,

apply four points for the increase of light.

We know her from the first nights

until she becomes full at the fifteenth,

and she shines with sixty points.

Make an hour consist of five points,

and you will find at which point of the hour the moon shines.

From the fifteenth the number will be diminished,

until she loses her light and becomes the thirtieth.

Likewise, according to however many points the moon shines by hours,

you will find it;

but Phoebe shines not at all on the thirtieth,

subject to the greater light of the sun and robbed by it.

The Greeks call this hour [the Greek term is absent from the supplied text], and the Latins call it *coitus* (“coming together”), because the two run together in conjunction.

At that time a solar eclipse becomes apparent.

But from this matter a suitable poem will be written elsewhere.

## WHAT HE EARLIER DEFERRED CONCERNING THE STARS, HE NOW COMPLETES

Now it is necessary to recall certain things about the zodiac,

in which fixed signs vary time,

under which the planets vary their course through the seasons.

Thus the circle of the zodiac is inclined from the north,

so that its middle zone stretches toward the south.

It lies among the four zones, the one burned by the sun;

in its middle Aries and Libra reside.

These two signs are also placed in the middle of the world,

opposite and yielding to each other along a straight path.

They circle around the earth on every side, as though despairing,

and as though by a diameter divide the zodiac equally.

They behold one another from the opposite side,

and alternately fall and rise again.

For Libra remains down for a long time while Aries rises from the east;

then Aries sets, and Libra rises again from the east.

There are also two others, Cancer together with Capricorn.

Cancer is the highest of the signs, and Capricorn is the other.

These are the two tropics, which are called turning points,

because when the sun is placed in these signs it turns back.

These are also called the gates of the sun on either side,

because, while the sun runs through their fourth parts,

“its approach is closed and the end of the signs increases” [a literal but defective astronomical claim].

In them the summer and winter solstices occur.

For the twelfth [day] according to the established reckoning

produces the summer solstice in July and the winter solstice in January.

They call the sun’s solstice by the name of its station,

because it is as though the sun stands still at that time.

But when the highest or lowest part of the zodiac is touched

by Phoebus even by a single atom, it is reckoned by this name.

### Concerning the Rising and Setting of the Sun

With these four signs, three principal risings occur.

When the sun rises while traversing these same parts,

you seek the ones we marked earlier:

the southern rising occurs at Capricorn,

the northern at Cancer,

and the third, the middle one, is marked at Libra and the Ram.

The rest is evident, since the alternating signs disclose it.

From this you will be able to see everything clearly,

if you depict it in the form of a celestial sphere.

With nature showing the globe, you too will keep watch,

for you will see that heaven is encircled by five zones.

By their nature the force of cold and heat

is brought upon the earth and moderates the regions of the world.

You will also understand why the nights are shorter

during the summer suns and, conversely, are wintry.

By easy observation of the nights all things will be clear to you.

From this you will also distinguish the planets tending toward the east,

and how they move through the signs of the sphere.

No single interval of the oblique ether is present;

rather, they traverse the intervening spaces,

and are said to move only through the signs themselves.

But enough has been said about the zodiac.

Let us now disclose the eclipse of the sun and moon.

## CONCERNING THE ECLIPSE OF THE SUN AND MOON

The zodiac is a belt of twice six parts.

A “part” is the extent which the sun can encompass,

or the limit of the sun’s diameter in each direction [the definition is compressed and uncertain].

Only two middle parts are traversed by the moon throughout,

as she rises and again inclines toward the south.

If, then, with these two [parts] in the middle of the world,

the earth lies beneath them, the sun is below and the moon moves both above and below,

and Phoebe is placed beneath her brother on the thirtieth,

then, because the moon stands in the way,

the sun’s splendor and heat are withdrawn from us

who are placed only in the lower regions.

But if she deviates through the outer parts,

where the earth is not beneath her but stands at the outside,

she cannot conceal the sun’s lights from us.

That is why an eclipse rarely occurs in its proper order.

But a lunar eclipse occurs in another manner.

For although it always occurs at the full moon,

it is eclipsed only in a different manner.

For the moon has her own light,

but shines like a mirror when irradiated by the sun.

Although the earth is overcome by the great body of the sun

in eight parts, as careful investigation makes clear,

the moon, when full, is carried through those same parts;

through the sun’s appearance she is deprived of light

and moves grieving through the shadows over the earth’s losses.

Above or below, she is covered with a dark mantle.

But if she deviates through the outer parts,

she escapes the loss of the light she has received.

Thus Phoebe is not always deprived of light.

Astrologers call these “defective parts” of the scheme,

because there the eclipse of either body occurs.

## HOW FAR THE MOON IS ELONGATED FROM THE SUN EACH DAY

[Col. 0650A]

But if your mind perhaps wishes to add this to its labor,

so that you may truly know by how many portions the receding moon

is separated from the sun, or in which signs she lingers,

take again her age, whatever it may have been,

multiply it by four, and then multiply the number itself by three.

Whatever you discover, you will know to be the number of portions

by which she is separated from Phoebus;

at the same time she remains in the sign

to which he will come after that many days.

For these portions mean nothing other than this:

the sun’s progress through the several signs on each day.

If you wish to know the sign through which the moon travels on that same day,

you will add the number of portions stated above [the object of *addes* is outside the supplied boundary].

Determine how much remains for the sun himself to complete the sign,

the course through which he travels; and examine it with a capacious mind.

Then assign thirty parts to each sign,

and learn in which sign the moon herself is found in that same order,

if they cannot advance as far as the number alone,

or if, once the signs have been completed in order, something remains.

[Col. 0650B]

This usually happens in the first sign, and often in the second,

when Phoebe travels through the same sign as the sun.

Often it is the ninth, the twentieth, and the thirtieth day;

this also occurs in the sign through which the sun is traveling.

Philosophers call these days interlunia,

because they fall between the waning moon and the moon’s rebirth.

These, then, are the daytime calculations

which we have set before you; but now let us hasten to the annual reckoning.

## OF THE YEARS FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE WORLD

At the beginning of the world there are five thousand three hundred

and sixty-four years besides,

with one year preceding, without the concurrent numbers;

then the Virgin gave birth, and the Virgin brought forth salvation,

mother of the human race and of both man and God.

Blessed Virgin, deign to pour forth prayers to your offspring;

may the Spirit come to the mind, who breathes wherever he wills,

who proceeds from the Father, whom his Son sends,

so that he may guide me, drifting across the deep sea,

[Col. 0650C]

and may his hand bring my vessel’s sails back to shore.

Behold, I ask and seek; blinking, I knock at the doors,

trusting in whose help and protection alike,

that I may be able to establish that the world’s age is such.

From the writings of the divine books

I shall show that the watchful philosophers have reckoned,

from the world’s beginning,

a memorable span of years extending to the time

when the Savior’s incarnation took place:

the ancient page reveals more than five thousand years,

but we do not admit that there were more than five hundred beyond that;

what is more or less you will learn from this tradition.

That great cycle, which always revolves through the years

on a pivot of five hundred and thirty-two,

is said to be the concord of two cycles,

because the courses of the moon and sun agree within them,

only when they have been completed; before that they do not fully coincide.

Then days, months, hours, moons, and Kalends—

everything agrees, and afterward returns to its beginning.

If you multiply that cycle ten times,

you will truly find five thousand years,

[Col. 0650D]

together with a total of three hundred and twenty,

and forty-four is added to these years.

In the sequence of the cycle this is described as the second [year];

in this year Christ was born in holiness from the Virgin.

From this, therefore, you see that there are five thousand three hundred

and sixty-four years besides,

with one year preceding, without the concurrent numbers.

But you must not multiply the same number eleven times,

for what the page states then increases excessively,

and the indiction added above disturbs the calculation

and conflicts with the number and reckoning of the Gospel.

Therefore, through this cycle, which proceeds in its great sequence,

let us first find the cycle, epacts, and concurrents

that were present in the time of Christ,

so that the doctrine may not be disturbed in the years that follow.

### Of the Cycles

Three cycles remain in our written account.

The first is that which the Hebrews always remember;

its beginning is the first lunation of the world.

The second was the cycle of the epacts in September;

this too changes and varies through the months.

The third is called solar, from the sun;

for this reason they established its beginning at the Kalends of March.

The fourth is lunar and conveys no useful information;

its beginning is therefore at the Kalends of January, when the moon is new.

If, then, you wish to learn the first cycle—

which year of it passes in the time of Christ—

take the number that began from the world’s origin,

and divide its whole sum by nineteen.

Seven remain; therefore it was the seventh year.

Thus the cycle of the epacts remains to be found,

but you will find only the epacts that run in the time of Christ in another way:

the seven that remained you must extend by the number eleven.

Thus you see seventy-seven together;

it is proper to divide all of these by thirty,

and to write down the seventeen that remain:

[Col. 0651B]

these are the epacts that were running in the time of Christ.

The solar cycle, however, will be discovered differently.

Divide the larger number written above

carefully by twenty-eight,

but first omit the year without concurrent numbers,

for it is never counted in that total.

The division will produce the sixteenth year.

But the concurrents of that year you will determine as follows:

add to this same number its fourth part,

divide the sum by seven, and five remain.

Yet consider this carefully in your mind:

unless the remainder has been surpassed after the division is complete,

from the years lacking the exact quarter,

with one year omitted because it is a leap year,

the seventh concurrent began at the Kalends of March.

But if you wish to know which indiction is passing at that time,

the truth will easily become clear by this method.

Divide the stated number by groups of fifteen,

and you will find the tenth indiction passing in that year.

Long ago, when the Romans almost ruled

the peoples of the whole world

with power and authority,

they established a tax and imposed tribute,

so that each person would pay a census three times in five-year periods:

bronze in the first,

silver also in the second,

and likewise gold in the following lustrum.

Then, as though the first arrangement had been repeated from the beginning,

the sequence does not exceed the number that governed it;

after the fifteenth, the first indiction begins again.

## TO FIND THE SUM OF THE YEARS OF THE LORD

If you desire to know the total of the years of the Lord,

fix this calculation in your watchful mind.

Multiply the sum of the orders, which are sixty-nine,

by fifteen, and add five besides.

What remains from this order in the time of Christ

must be added to the indiction of the present time.

You should also mark this carefully in your attentive heart:

when the order now running has been completed

and the first indiction has again been taken up,

be sure to add one to the stated orders.

By adding it after each fifteen,

you will know that the reckoning always increases with these orders.

### To Find the Indiction

But if you wish to know which indiction is now passing,

divide the stated number by groups of fifteen.

Thus, under Christ, the first added number passes;

whatever increases beyond it remains the indiction of the year,

and you call it the fifteenth when nothing remains over.

Now it is the year one thousand and fifty,

and the tenth indiction is also passing at present.

The epact contained by the cycle runs in this year;

the first is under the eleventh, and the twelfth follows after it.

The order holds the second year of the solar cycle,

and the concurrent in this year is likewise the second,

for in the cycle’s order this is described as the second.

If, then, you wish to know the first cycle—

which year is now passing in our time—

take the number of the years of the Lord at this time,

and divide its entire sum by nineteen.

Yet take care to add seven to this number,

for the whole year had passed in the body of Christ.

Whatever remains will clearly show the year;

if nothing remains, that is the last year of the cycle.

If you desire to know which epacts are now running,

take what remains after they have been divided off at the same limit.

You must extend it by the number eleven,

and whatever the result may be, subtract thirty from it.

The excess that always remains then produces the epacts.

But if the number thirty remains below your result,

that same number is reckoned as the epact of the present year.

The final year, however, is not governed by this method;

another rule grants it no epacts,

but one is added to it on account of the lunar leap.

The solar cycle, however, will be discovered differently.

Divide the aforesaid number, which is written above,

carefully by twenty-eight,

and take care first to add thirteen to the number—

the year of the cycle that was running in Christ’s time.

whatever is increased is the whole year in the sequence.

The final year is the one that the division encloses.

### Concerning the Concurrents

If you wish to know the concurrents of the Lord by years,

it is proper to remove one from the total number—

the one that alone remained beyond the number seven.

For the seventh concurrent began under Christ;

after this, the first occurred in the following year,

from which we take the beginning of this number.

Once that has been removed, we do not ascend beyond seven.

This same number, together with its fourth part,

is divided by seven;

and, as usual, what remains is counted as the concurrent.

If nothing remains, the seventh is rightly marked.

## TO FIND THE LEAP YEAR

Whether a year is leap-year or is the fourth year from it

is never difficult to determine.

Divide the years of the Lord by four.

Whatever remains after the division shows how far the year is from the leap year.

If nothing remains, that year is a leap year.

## THAT ELEVEN EPACTS COINCIDED WITH THE TIME OF CHRIST’S DEATH

But now let the evidence suppress the earlier error,

and, from the statements of the sacred Gospels,

let the calculation be affirmed so that it is not mutilated:

we shall prove by certain reasoning that the time of Christ’s thirty-two years,

together with eleven epacts, was running at the time of his death,

and not another number.

We rely on what Luke reports, and it is true:

Christ was baptized after departing from the river,

and he was plainly beginning his thirtieth year,

for thirteen days of that thirtieth year had passed.

After his baptism he undertook the sacred fast,

and in that year chose disciples for himself.

Then another consecrated day shone forth in the year,

on which the Father’s voice glorified the baptized one.

At that time the wedding took place at Cana of Galilee,

and before his disciples he performed the beginning

and made manifest the glory of his signs.

In his Gospel John describes this Passover

and first records the miracles performed by Christ.

After many events he then adds a second Passover,

namely, the one that passed in another year.

He then again relates events memorable for all ages:

he brings forth the limbs of stinking Lazarus from the tomb,

and records the crowd that came out to meet Christ,

bearing branches and assigning praises to him.

Then Christ, as a servant, washed the disciples’ feet

on the day when the end of Passover was drawing near.

He was seized that night under the light of the full moon.

He was seized on the fourth, and crucified on the tenth in that [lunar period],

which descends on the fifteenth from the middle of the sky [the transmitted numerical wording is uncertain];

and that day is marked as the holy day of Christ’s crucifixion.

The angel here announces Christ himself as destined to come,

from the Father’s throne into the Virgin Mother’s womb,

to assume mortal form for the world’s sin.

On this cross, too, he laid aside that form when released from the cross.

On the third holy day he rose again, restored to life from death,

and by rising brought back immortal life.

And a like day again brought forth the mortal one from his mother’s womb,

and just as the seventeenth epact returns,

on which Christ, when born, descended into the Virgin’s womb,

so on this lunar day the seventeenth shone forth.

It shone also on the twenty-first Kalends of April [i.e. 12 March].

From this, therefore, you will be able to see clearly what has been accomplished:

he carries eleven epacts through the years.

Thus we rightly acknowledge that Christ’s life consisted

of thirty-two years and three months.

## OF THE END OF PASCHA

The limit of Pascha is the fourteenth day of the moon

that shines in the springtime, in the first month.

On this day the Lord commanded the Hebrews to celebrate Pascha.

Therefore, remembering this, they celebrate Pascha at that time,

and begin the festivals of the years on the following day.

We likewise await that same fourteenth day,

and, out of religious observance, postpone our own celebration

until the very day of the Lord’s Pascha,

which bears and possesses its name from this event,

and on which Christ’s resurrection brought salvation to all,

restoring those turned aside by hostile acts to their hearts

[the transmitted wording is uncertain].

This was not accomplished only then,

but also what will be fulfilled at the end.

In the sequence of time this day returns as the first and the eighth.

It is the first because we read that on it

the created light first shone.

It arose because it came after seven;

it was itself first because the same day preceded it.

In our Head there is resurrection; when the six ages

and the labors of this life have been completed,

the seventh rightly grants souls the light of rest.

We, who are his members, are worthy of his resurrection.

In the eighth age of the world it is to be accomplished,

when every dead person will hear the voice of the Head

and, death having been overcome, will rise from the tomb.

Therefore the limit itself is from the twelfth Kalends of April [i.e. 21 March]

to the fourteenth Kalends of May [i.e. 18 April];

it can be neither earlier nor later than this.

On whatever day this limit falls, the Lord’s Pascha is rightly celebrated on the following Lord’s Day,

and it can never be earlier than the fifteenth.

Nor can Phoebe, the moon, be later than the twenty-first.

## WHENCE THE LIMIT OF PASCHA PROCEEDS

But if you wish to know the day on which this limit occurs,

keep those verses carefully in mind.

The first of them begins from the Nones of April,

because on the Nones Phoebe first shone full.

That limit is marked at the beginnings of these verses;

their ends show the regular [cycles].

Join these, therefore, with the concurrents of the year,

and you will know the weekday, as we have written for you earlier,

on which the limit you seek becomes clear.

But if it slips from your mind which verse is in question,

just as I first taught you to recognize the cycle,

learn by the years which verse of the Lord is running.

I shall also teach you to find this verse by another method,

by which it may be discovered in the following way:

place the left thumb on the first division,

then count the others and all of them in turn,

and pass across the upper fingers of the hand

until you reach the place on the thumb where you began.

Whatever day occurs again in that same place

will mark the approaching limit;

by this you may recognize the future one.

Distinguish the successive upper [finger divisions] in the same way,

and by the positions alone determine where the limit returns.

You should circle the position with the added one and the third,

if you wish to learn their regular [cycles].

Place the first day of the world on the first weekday,

and count all the days from it

up to the place, weekday by weekday,

where the limit occurs for you.

Then, whatever weekday the limit is found to be,

add to it as many [units] as the regular cycles you seek.

[Col. 0654A]

From this you will be able to find the others by the Paschal [cycle].

Observe carefully how many days separate

that first Paschal limit of the world

from the tenth Kalends of February.

It will be useful to count the same number,

at whose evident end the limit occurs

which Septuagesima indicates.

At the end you will always mark the tenth moon;

this will belong to the month of February

and will close within it.

It is likewise useful to count to the Nones of February,

and to add the limit sought by Quadragesima.

Here you must count the second moon.

This will belong to the month of March

and will close within it.

If the year is a leap year,

and the limit falls beyond the leap day,

it will begin after the Nones.

There is another limit which the holy Rogations seek.

By the prescribed rule it is sought from the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

The twentieth moon also indicates it.

This will belong to the month of May

and will close within it.

But if Pentecost itself is sought,

it is rightly found from the second Nones of May.

The fourth moon also marks it at that time.

This will belong to the month of July

and will close within it.

But on whatever weekday that limit falls,

defer it to the following Day of the Lord,

from whom it receives its name

and on whom the resurrection took place.

## OF THE CONTROVERSY OF THE OCTAD AND OF THE INTERCALATION

Since a controversy arises concerning the first cycle—

although it occurs in three years, and often in certain others—

and the moon at the Kalends conflicts with the sequence of the epacts,

the intercalary lunation reveals it.

We shall clearly set out in the concluding poem

in which of these it occurs at the Nones, the Ides,

and the Kalends.

The eighth, the eleventh, and the final year contain it.

“Octad” (*ogdoas*) means “eighth” and is derived from the Greek name.

In this year the seventeenth epact returns,

and the moon begins on the second Nones of March.

The intercalary lunation begins after this on the thirtieth day before the Nones,

and properly ends on the second Nones of April.

But the lunation of April begins on the Nones of April,

and ends on the twenty-fifth day before the Nones of May.

At the Kalends of that month the moon is found

to be around the twenty-seventh according to the number of the epacts.

The lunation of May begins on the fourth Nones

and ends on the thirtieth Nones of June.

The moon takes its beginning in June on the third day,

and ends on the twenty-ninth day before the Kalends of July.

According to the number of the epacts it is established as the thirtieth,

and from there the rule keeps its course through all the months.

In the eleventh year it remains at the twentieth.

The epact and the intercalary lunation of the year

begin on the third Nones of January.

It closes on the thirtieth day before the Kalends of February;

its lunation begins on the fourth Nones.

On the sixth Nones of March its twenty-ninth day occurs,

but in a leap year this is counted as the thirtieth.

In this year the moon falls near the epacts at the Kalends of March,

and from there the rule keeps its accustomed course through all the months.

[Col. 0654D]

From this point the final, eighteenth year contains eighteen epacts in March,

and its lunation begins on the third Nones; 

in this year the intercalary lunation begins.

It ends, on its thirtieth day, on the third Nones of April.

But the April moon begins on the second Nones.

Beginning on the Nones of May,

its twenty-ninth day closes;

its twenty-ninth day occurs at the Kalends.

According to the number of the epacts the moon is clearly formed.

The lunation begins on the fifth Nones of May

and the thirtieth moon ends at the Kalends of June.

It begins on the fourth Nones of August

and likewise ends in that month on the twenty-ninth day.

When the thirtieth occurs contrary to the sequence of the epacts,

the leap is closed; this is proved by the calculation,

and one lunar day is subtracted from the year.

But the moon beginning at the Kalends of August

is counted there contrary to the sequence of the epacts;

from that point it resumes its course inviolate through all the months.

Thus Manfredus desires, and Plato commands, that we rest.

But now, holy Mary, gracious Virgin,

deign to lighten the ways of wickedness

and the labors of life.

From this point, brothers and companions,

offer worthy thanks.

On the feast day let us sing what is worthy of Mary;

let us speak her praise and render her glory:

“I have reached the harbor toward which my course was set.”

[Col. 0655A]

## CALCULATION BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

From the origin of the world, as one reads in Orosius,

there are five thousand one hundred and ninety-nine years

up to the birth of Christ.

From the founding of the world to the founding of the city

there are four thousand four hundred and forty-seven years.

From the founding of the city to the birth of Christ

there are seven hundred and fifty-two years.

Thus the total is five thousand one hundred and ninety-nine years.

From that point the years of the Lord are reckoned.

[Col. 0655B]

## OF THE CITY OF ROME

Rome, a city in Italy and once mistress of the whole world,

was so called from the name of its founder, Romulus.

Because of its exceptional power, many writers preferred to call it “the City,”

as though it alone were worthy of that name.

As Orosius records in his chronicle,

it was founded four thousand four hundred and forty-seven years later,

that is, in the seven hundred and fifty-second year

before the incarnation of the Lord.

[Col. 0656A]

Once you were built for noble patrons;

now, alas, Rome, subjected to slaves, you fall disastrously.

Your kings have abandoned you for so long,

and your name and honor have passed to the Greeks.

Constantinople flourishes and is called the new Rome;

ancient Rome, you fall in character and in walls.

Empire passes away, but pride has remained with you.

The worship of greed overwhelms you too greatly.

The common crowd, drawn from the farthest regions of the world—

slaves of slaves—are now your masters.

No noble ruler remains in you,

and your freeborn people cultivate the Pelasgian fields.

You cut down the living saints with a cruel death;

now you grieve to sell their dead limbs.

For unless the merit of Peter and Paul sheltered you,

poor Rome, you would long ago have ceased to exist.

## OF THE CITY OF THE TREVIRI

Semiramis of Nineveh, fortunate in such a husband,

possessed very many things, but added more to what her predecessors had possessed.

Not content with her own possessions, nor with the whole extent of the world,

she drove her stepson Trebeta from his ancestral kingdom.

As an exile he founded our distinguished city,

giving it the name Treveris out of love for its founder.

It is known from antiquity as the head of Europe.

I, his heroic son, set down these verses for my father’s funeral rites.

At whose funeral altar Mars stands with Jupiter,

there is peace, in harmonious accord beneath the stars.

[Col. 0655]

## EPIGRAM ON BLESSED JOHN AND HIS APOCALYPSE

[Col. 0655B]

While John is driven from the human world in exile,

and forbidden to behold the realms of the earthly sun,

the beloved of the Lord enters rejoicing into heaven’s court

and is glad to stand among the choirs of the high-throned King.

When here he turned his sacred eyes toward the inhabited world,

he saw ships traveling everywhere over the waves,

and Babel and Solima fighting with mingled armies;

from both sides, in turn, they took up weapons and flight.

[Col. 0655C]

But the white soldier follows the gentle Lamb,

that with his Leader he may receive the blessed kingdoms of heaven.

The scaly serpent, through the blind depths of Tartarus,

submerges his own companies in flames,

[Col. 0656B]

with pestilence and hunger.

While I wished to unfold what his appearance was,

what was the strategy or order of the battle,

what art, phalanx, victory, or weapons were involved,

I traversed the broad fields sown by the ancients

and plucked a few shoots from the sacred fields,

lest greater abundance produce disgust at the meal

or prevent me from preparing so great a banquet for a modest guest.

Therefore, if my dishes taste good to your lips,

give praise above the stars to God who reigns.

But if otherwise, still embracing friendly feelings,

correct what I sing and, I beg you, abrade it with pumice.

## FOURTH SECTION OF THE VENERABLE BEDE’S EXHORTATORY WORKS, CONTAINING HIS LETTERS

### [LETTERS (C, G, S)*]

## LETTER ONE, TO ABBOT ALBINUS

[Note: Albinus, the abbot to whom the venerable Bede addressed this letter, was his patron and assistant in writing the *History of the English*, as Bede testifies in the dedicatory letter to King Ceolwulf. This Albinus is a different person from Albinus Flaccus, or Alcuin, who lived almost a century later; he was, however, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Canterbury. Through Nothelm, a priest of the Church of London, he sent Bede small gifts and the materials that Bede needed in composing the *History of the English*. All this is established by Bede’s preface to Ceolwulf. Moreover, I obtained this letter from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz, and the religious man Dom Placidus Beuvillonius, then subprior of that place, sent it to me. In that codex the letter bears the following heading: “Here begins the preface of the priest to Abbot Alcuin.” This suggests that some scribes attached the preceding letter as a preface to Bede’s *History of the English*, believing that this Albinus was the same person as Alcuin. It will be useful to observe here that in the commonly circulated version of Bede’s letter to Wichred concerning the vernal equinox according to Anatolius, an example of the year 876 is added. On the strength of that example Baronius extended Bede’s lifetime beyond that year. But in the oldest copy of this letter, preserved in the library at Lobbes, the example does not appear; it was doubtless inserted by the copyist who was transcribing the letter in that year. (*Mabillon, Ancient Analecta*).]

(Giles, *Works of Bede*, vol. I.)

[Col. 0655D]

To the most desired and most reverend Father Albinus,

Bede, servant of Christ, sends greetings.

I received with the greatest gratitude the little gifts of your affection,

which you deigned to send through our venerable brother Nothelm the priest,

and especially the letters with which, now for the second time,

you have frequently assisted and instructed me

in the ecclesiastical history of our people,

which you had long ago urged me to write.

For this reason I rightly sent that same history to you for transcription

as soon as I was able to complete it.

I also sent you, as a form of repayment,

another volume which I learned that you partly desired,

namely, the work I recently published

on the structure of Solomon’s temple

and its allegorical interpretation.

And I earnestly beg you, most loving Father,

to remember to intercede diligently before the merciful Judge

for my weakness, together with the servants of Christ who are with you.

Also instruct those to whom you cause these same little works of ours to come

to do the same.

Farewell, ever most loving and excellent Father in Christ.

## LETTER TWO, TO BISHOP ECGBERCT

(Smith, *Historical Works of Bede*.)

To the most beloved and most reverend Bishop Ecgberct,

Bede, servant of Christ, sends greetings.

[Note: He became bishop of York in the year 732. This letter was written around the beginning of the year 734, in which Bede died.]

I remember that last year, when I stayed with you for several days

in your monastery for the sake of reading,

you said that this year also, when you came to the same place,

you wished to summon me to converse with you

(variant *accipere*: “receive me”) because of our common devotion to reading.

If this could, with God’s will, have been fulfilled,

there would have been no need to send these things in writing,

since I could have spoken face to face more freely

and suggested privately whatever I wished

(variant *velim*: “might wish”) or considered necessary.

But because, as you know, the condition of my body

which supervened prevented this from happening,

I nevertheless took care to do what I could

out of brotherly devotion toward your affection:

namely, I sent by letter what I could not accomplish

by coming in person and conversing with you.

And I beg you by the Lord not to suppose

that the words of this letter display the arrogance of pride,

but rather recognize them as a true service of humility and piety.

I therefore exhort your holiness, my dearest Bishop in Christ,

to remember to strengthen, by holy action and teaching

(the variant omits *et*, “and”), the sacred office

which the Author of offices

and the giver of spiritual gifts has deigned to entrust to you.

Neither of these virtues can properly be fulfilled without the other:

whether a person who lives well neglects the duty of teaching,

or a bishop who teaches correctly refuses to practice right action.

But whoever genuinely performs both

(variant *At qui*: “but he who”) will certainly await the coming of his Lord with joy,

hoping soon to hear:

“Well done, good and faithful servant;

because you have been faithful over a few things,

I will set you over many things.

Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25).

But if anyone—God forbid—having received the rank of bishop,

does not take care either to correct himself by living well

or to correct the people subject to him

by chastising or admonishing them,

the Gospel sentence clearly declares what will happen to him

when the Lord comes at an hour he does not expect:

“Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness;

there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid.).

Above all, I advise your holy fatherhood

to restrain yourself, in keeping with episcopal dignity,

from idle conversations, slander,

and the other contagions of an undisciplined tongue.

Occupy both tongue and mind with divine utterances

and meditation on the Scriptures,

especially by reading the letters of the blessed apostle Paul

to Timothy and Titus,

and also the words of the most holy Pope Gregory,

in which he discussed with great care both the life

and the vices of rulers,

whether in the book of the *Pastoral Rule*

or in his homilies on the Gospel.

Thus your speech may always be seasoned with the salt of wisdom,

may shine above ordinary conversation,

and may be more worthy of the divine hearing.

For just as it is improper for the sacred vessels of the altar

ever to be profaned for ordinary uses and base services,

so it is wholly perverse and pitiable

if one who has been ordained to consecrate

the Lord’s sacraments upon the altar

should now stand in service of the Lord

to celebrate those same sacraments,

but then, after leaving the church,

begin suddenly to speak or do frivolous things

with the very mouth and hands

with which he had just handled the sacred rites,

thereby offending the Lord.

For guarding the purity of tongue and conduct,

the companionship of those who serve Christ

with faithful devotion is of great help,

together with divine reading.

Thus, if my tongue should ever begin to become wanton,

or a sinful action begin to creep upon me,

I may at once be supported by the hand of faithful companions

and kept from falling.

Although it is very useful (variant *utilissimum*: “most useful”) for all God’s servants

to provide such protection for themselves,

how much more necessary is it for one who holds that rank,

since he must care not only for himself

but also devote himself to the salvation

of the Church entrusted to him,

according to the one who said:

“Besides those things that are external,

my daily burden is the care of all the churches.

Who is weak, and I am not weak?

Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?”

(2 Corinthians 12.)

I do not say this as though I knew you to act otherwise,

but because it has become widely reported concerning certain bishops

that they serve Christ in such a way

that they keep with them no men of religion or continence.

Rather, they keep those who are enslaved (variant *subjugantur*) to laughter, jokes, stories,

feasting, drunkenness, and the other attractions

of a more lax way of life (variant *remissioribus*, referring to the attractions),

and who feed their bellies daily with dishes

rather than nourish (variant *parent*: “provide for”) their minds with heavenly sacrifices.

If you find such bishops anywhere,

I ask you to correct them by your holy authority

and admonish them to have as witnesses of their daily and nightly conduct

men who are capable of benefiting the people

by actions worthy of God and suitable exhortation,

and of assisting the spiritual work of the bishops themselves.

Read the Acts of the Apostles,

and you will see, as the blessed Luke reports,

what kind of companions the apostles Paul and Barnabas had with them,

and what work they themselves performed wherever they came.

As soon as they entered cities or synagogues,

they took care to preach the word of God

and to spread it everywhere.

This, too, I earnestly desire you,

my beloved head, to fulfill wherever you can.

For you were chosen by the Lord for this office,

and consecrated for this purpose (variant repeats *implere. In hoc consecratus*, “to fulfill. For this you were consecrated”):

to proclaim the Gospel with great power

(variant *multa*: “great abundance”),

with the Lord Jesus Christ, the King of virtues,

providing you assistance.

You will rightly accomplish this

if, wherever you arrive,

you immediately gather the inhabitants of that place to you

and offer them a word of exhortation,

while, together with all who have come with you,

you show an example of living

as the leader of a heavenly army.

And because the territories belonging to the governance

of your diocese are more extensive

than you could traverse alone in every direction,

and because you could not preach the word of God

in every village and little field

even over the course of an entire year,

it is entirely necessary for you

to obtain many assistants in sacred work,

namely, to ordain priests

and to establish teachers

who will devote themselves in each village

to preaching the word of God,

to consecrating the heavenly mysteries,

and especially, whenever the opportunity arises,

to performing the offices of holy baptism.

In presenting this preaching to the people,

I think that above all else,

with every possible diligence,

you must take care to impress deeply upon the memory

of all who belong to your governance

the Catholic faith contained in the Apostles’ Creed

and the Lord’s Prayer,

which the Scripture of the holy Gospel teaches us.

It is certainly beyond doubt

that all who have learned the Latin language

through the practice of reading

have also learned these things well.

But make the uneducated—that is,

those who know only their own language—

say and diligently recite these very things

in their own language.

This must be done not only for laypeople,

that is, those who still live in the secular condition,

but also for clerics or monks

who lack knowledge of the Latin language.

In this way the whole assembly of the faithful

learns how it ought to be faithful

and with what firmness of belief

it must fortify and arm itself

against the battles of unclean spirits.

In this way the whole choir of those who supplicate God

(variant begins *Fit ut chorus*, “thus the choir”) learns what above all should be sought

from divine mercy.

For this reason I myself have often offered

to many uneducated priests

both of these things translated into the language of the English:

the Creed, namely,

and the Lord’s Prayer.

For the holy bishop Ambrose,

speaking about the faith,

also admonishes the faithful

always to recite the words of the Creed

in the morning hours

and to prepare themselves with it,

as with a spiritual antidote,

against the poisons of the devil

which he might cunningly set before them

during the day or night.

The Lord’s Prayer, too,

should be recited frequently (variant *cantari*: “sung”);

the very practice of constant prayer

and bending of the knees has taught us this.

If, then, your pastoral authority accomplishes these things

in governing and feeding Christ’s sheep,

as we suggest,

it cannot be said how great a heavenly reward

you will have prepared for yourself in the future

with the Shepherd of shepherds.

For the rarer you find examples

of this most sacred work among the bishops of our people,

the higher will be the rewards of singular merit

that you receive (variant omits *praemia*, “rewards”),

since by the frequent recitation of the Creed

and of the sacred Prayer

you will have kindled the people of God,

through fatherly piety and concern,

to understand, love, hope for, and believe in,

and to seek,

the heavenly gifts that are recited.

But, by contrast,

if you fulfill less diligently

the task entrusted to you by the Lord,

you will in the future receive your portion

with the wicked and lazy servant

for withholding your talent—

especially if you presume to seek and accept

temporal advantages from those

to whom you have shown yourself unwilling

to repay any gifts of heavenly benefit.

For when the Lord, sending his disciples to preach

(variant omits *discipulos*, “disciples”), had said:

“Go and preach, saying,

‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand’”

(Matthew 10),

he added shortly afterward (variant *adjunxit*: “joined/added”):

“Freely you have received;

freely give.

Do not possess gold or silver”

(ibid.).

If, then, he commanded them to preach the Gospel freely

and did not permit them to receive gold,

silver, or any temporal payment

from those to whom they preached,

what danger, I ask,

must threaten those who do the opposite?

Pay attention to what an exceedingly grave crime those men have committed who both diligently demand earthly profits from their hearers and strive to expend no labor whatsoever for their eternal salvation by preaching, exhorting, or rebuking [Al.: “strive”]. Weigh this carefully and with attentive concern, most beloved bishop. For we have heard—and it is commonly reported—that many estates and hamlets of our people are situated in inaccessible mountains and wooded wildernesses, where for many years no passing bishop has been seen who might have provided any ministry or heavenly grace there [Col. 0660D]; yet not one of their inhabitants can be exempt from rendering tribute to the bishop. Nor is it merely that such places lack a bishop who might confirm by the laying on of hands those who have been baptized; every teacher who might instruct them in either the truth of the faith or the discernment of good and evil action is also absent.

Thus it comes about that certain bishops not only do not evangelize freely [Al.: “not only do they evangelize freely”], or lay hands upon the faithful, but also—and this is more serious—having accepted money from their hearers, which the Lord forbade, they disdain to perform the work of the word that the Lord commanded them to perform. Yet the bishop Samuel, beloved of God, is read to have acted very differently, with the whole people bearing witness. “Having lived,” he says, “before you from my youth until this day, behold, I am here; speak concerning me before the Lord and before his Christ: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or anyone’s ass; whether I have falsely accused anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have accepted a gift from anyone’s hand—and I will despise it today and restore it to you.” And they said: “You have not falsely accused us, nor oppressed us, nor taken anything from anyone’s hand” (1 Samuel XII). By the merit of this innocence and justice he deserved to be numbered among the foremost leaders and priests of the people of God and to become worthy of heavenly hearing and address in his prayers, as the Psalmist says: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who invoke his name: they invoked the Lord, and he heard them; in the pillar of cloud he spoke to them” (Psalm XCVIII).

[Col. 0661B] But if we believe and confess that some benefit is conferred upon the faithful by the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, it follows conversely that this same benefit is absent from those to whom the laying on of hands has been denied. To whom does this deprivation of good pertain more than to the bishops themselves, who promise that they are the overseers of those to whom they either neglect or are unable to provide the spiritual service of oversight? The cause of this entire crime is nothing so much as avarice. Against it the Apostle, in whom Christ was speaking, declared: “The desire for money is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy VI, 10). And again: “The avaricious,” he says, “shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians VI, 10).

When, dictated by love of money, a bishop has taken into the name of his episcopate a greater part of the people than he could have traversed or visited by preaching throughout the entire year, it is plainly shown that he has contrived a highly destructive danger both for himself and for those over whom he has been placed under the false title of bishop.

I have briefly brought these matters to your attention, most beloved bishop, with regard to the calamity under which our people suffer most miserably. I earnestly beseech you to strive, as far as you are able, to restore to the proper rule of life the abuses that you see being carried on in the most perverse manner. For you have, as I believe, a most ready helper for so just a labor—namely, King Ceolwulf. Because of the religious devotion naturally implanted in him, he will immediately undertake with firm resolve to support whatever pertains to the rule of piety; and especially in those matters which you, as his most beloved kinsman, begin well, he will assist so that they may be completed [Al.: “he will take care to assist in completing them”].

I would therefore have you diligently admonish him to take care, in your days, to restore the ecclesiastical condition of our people to something better than it has hitherto been [Al.: “that you take care”]. In my view this can be accomplished by no other arrangement more effectively than by consecrating more bishops for our people and following the example of the lawgiver. When he could not alone sustain the disputes and burden of the Israelite people, he chose for himself, with divine counsel assisting him, and consecrated seventy elders, whose help and counsel [Al.: “care”; “assistance”] would enable him to bear more lightly the burden imposed upon him [Al.: “more freely”]. Who does not see how much better it is to divide so enormous a burden of ecclesiastical government among several persons, who may bear it more easily when it has been distributed, than for one person to be crushed beneath a load that he cannot carry?

For even the holy Pope Gregory, when he was discussing in letters sent to the blessed Archbishop Augustine the faith of our people, which still had to be brought into being and preserved in Christ [Note: [Col. 0661] See this letter of Gregory among his Works, *Patrology*, vol. LXXVII, col. 1200. EDIT.], decreed that twelve bishops should be ordained in it after its people had come to the faith [Al.: “after they came”]. Among them, the bishop of York, having received the pallium from the Apostolic See, was to be metropolitan.

I wish, therefore, that your holy fatherhood, with the protection and patronage of the most pious and God-beloved king mentioned above, would diligently strive to fulfill this number of bishops, so that, with teachers in abundance, the Church of Christ may be more perfectly instructed in those matters pertaining to the worship of sacred religion. Indeed, we know that through the negligence of preceding kings and through exceedingly foolish grants it has come about that a vacant place where a new episcopal see could be established cannot easily be found [Al.: “cannot easily find”].

For this reason I would consider it advantageous that, after a greater council has been held and both episcopal and royal consent obtained [Al.: “consent and decree”], some place belonging to the monasteries should be designated by decree as the site of an episcopal see. And lest an abbot or the monks should attempt to oppose or resist this decree, let them be given permission to choose from among their own number the man who is to be ordained bishop, and let him exercise episcopal care over the neighboring places belonging to the same diocese, together with the monastery itself [Col. 0662C].
