Or, if no one should be found in that monastery who ought to be ordained bishop, nevertheless let it depend upon their examination, in accordance with the canonical statutes, who from their diocese is to be ordained bishop.

If, with the Lord’s help, you accomplish this as we suggest, you will, as we think, very easily obtain this as well [Al.: omits “as well”]: that, in accordance with the decrees of the Apostolic See, the Church of York may have a metropolitan bishop. And if it should seem necessary that, for the purpose of assuming the episcopate, some monastery ought to be increased by additional lands and possessions, there are innumerable places, as we all know [Al.: “there are innumerable places, in the most foolish manner of expression, as we know”], entered under the designation of monasteries [Col. 0662D] but possessing nothing at all of monastic discipline. From these I would wish that, by synodical authority, some places should be transferred from luxury to chastity, from vanity to moderation [Al.: “truthfulness”], and from intemperance of belly and gluttony to self-restraint and purity of heart, and that they should be assigned as support for the episcopal see that is now to be established [Al.: “that ought now to establish”].

And because places of this kind are very numerous and extensive [Al.: “more numerous”]—places which, as the common saying goes, are useful neither to God nor to human beings, since neither is a regular life according to God maintained there, nor are they possessed by soldiers or secular officials who might defend our people from barbarians—if, in response to the needs of the times, someone establishes an episcopal see in those same places [Col. 0663A] [Al.: “if someone establishes an episcopal see there,”], he will be proved not to have incurred the guilt of transgression but rather to have performed an act of virtue.

For how can it be counted as sin if the unjust judgments of rulers are corrected by the right judgment of better rulers, and the lying writing of wicked scribes is erased and reduced to nothing by the considered decision of prudent priests? This is in accordance with the example of sacred history, which, in describing the times of the kings of Judah from David and Solomon to the last king, Zedekiah, indicates that some of them were religious but that more were reprobate. In alternating succession, the wicked sometimes condemned the deeds of the good who had preceded them, and at other times the just, as was right [Al.: “as was fitting,”] and with the Spirit of God assisting them, corrected through holy prophets and priests, with every diligence, the harmful deeds of the wicked who had gone before them [Col. 0663B]. This accords with the saying of blessed Isaiah, who commanded and said: “Loosen the bonds of violent exchanges. Release the broken for remission, and tear apart every unjust written obligation” (Isaiah LVIII).

Following this example, it is fitting that you too, together with the religious king, tear down the irreligious and unjust deeds and writings of former rulers of our people, and take care to provide for whatever is useful to our province, whether according to God or according to the world. Otherwise, in our times either, when religion has ceased, love and fear of the inner Inspector may be abandoned, or, when the supply of secular soldiery has grown scarce, there may be no one to defend our borders from barbarian attack.

For it is shameful to say that so many places, under the name of monasteries, have been taken into their possession by men who are wholly strangers to monastic life, as you yourselves know better, so that no place remains where the sons of nobles or of veteran soldiers may receive an estate. Consequently, remaining unmarried and without a wife after the age of puberty has passed, they continue without any purpose of self-restraint; and for this reason they either leave their native land, for which they ought to have served as soldiers, and depart overseas, or, with still greater crime and shamelessness, those who have no intention of chastity devote themselves to lust and fornication and do not abstain even from virgins consecrated to God.

Others, however, in an even graver outrage, although they are laymen and have been trained neither by practice in any regular life [Al.: “of regular life”] nor endowed with love for it, purchase with money given to kings territories for themselves under the pretext of constructing monasteries, in which they may indulge their lusts more freely. Moreover, by royal decrees they have these properties entered into their hereditary right, and they obtain confirmation of the very documents of their privileges—as though those documents were truly worthy of God—through the subscriptions of bishops, abbots, and secular authorities.

Thus, having usurped little estates or villages for themselves, and thereafter being free from both divine and human service, laymen, while commanding monks there, serve only their own desires. Indeed, they do not gather monks there, but instead gather anyone whom they find wandering about after being expelled for disobedience from genuine monasteries, or whom they themselves have been able to summon to monasteries; or, at any rate, those whom they can invite from among their own retainers to receive the tonsure, after promising them the obedience owed to monks.

With these deformed bands they fill the cells they have built, producing a highly disgraceful and unheard-of spectacle. The same men sometimes attend to the care of wives and the begetting of children, and sometimes, rising from their beds, deliberate earnestly about what ought to be done within the monastery walls. They even seek out lands for their wives to construct monasteries in the same foolish manner, as they themselves say; and although these women are likewise laypersons, with equal folly they allow themselves to be the superiors of Christ’s female servants [Al.: “male superiors”]. To them the common proverb aptly applies: “Although wasps can make honeycombs, they do not store honey in them; rather, they store poisons.”

For approximately thirty years [Note: [Col. 0663D] Aldfrid, king of the Northumbrians, died in the year 705. If one begins the calculation from that year, it will be found that this letter was written in the very year in which Bede died, namely 734. Thus this letter may be regarded as Bede’s swan song; it is therefore not surprising that it is absent from the Catalogue of Works written out by Bede himself.]—that is, ever since King Aldfrid was taken from human affairs—our province has been driven mad by that insane error, so that scarcely any prefect has existed from that time onward who did not acquire for himself a monastery of this kind during the days of his prefecture and likewise bind his wife to an equal guilt by purchasing her into the same crime [Al.: “had acquired”; “had bound”]. As the worst custom prevailed, the king’s ministers and servants also tried to do the same.

And so, by a perverse arrangement, innumerable men have been found who call themselves both abbots and prefects, or ministers or servants of the king [Al.: “both prefects and ministers”]. Although, as laymen, they may have been able to learn something of monastic life not by practicing it but by hearing about it, they are nevertheless wholly deprived of that person and profession whose duty it is to teach this life [Al.: “who ought to teach it”]. Such men, as you know, suddenly receive the tonsure according to their own pleasure and, by their own judgment, are made not monks but abbots out of laymen.

But since they are proved to possess neither knowledge nor zeal for the virtue mentioned above, what other curse from the Gospel is appropriate to them than this: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit” (Matthew XV)? This blindness could at some point be brought to an end, restrained by regular discipline, and expelled far from the boundaries of the holy Church by the authority of the bishops and of a synod, if the bishops themselves were not found rather to aid and support such crimes [Col. 0664D]. They not only fail to take care to invalidate such unjust decrees by just decrees, but rather, as we have said, strive to confirm them by their own subscriptions [Al.: “prescriptions”]. They do this under the prompting of the same love of money—*phylargyria*—that compelled the purchasers to buy such monasteries, confirming what was badly written.

I could still communicate many things to you in this letter about these and similar transgressors by whom our province is most miserably afflicted, if I did not know that you yourself are already thoroughly acquainted with them. For I did not write these things as though I were going to teach you with certainty what you had previously not known [Al.: omits “with certainty”], but to admonish you by friendly exhortation to correct, with as much diligence as you can, the errors that you knew perfectly well.

And now, again and again, I earnestly beg and implore you in the Lord to protect with vigilant care the flock entrusted to you from the wickedness of attacking wolves. Remember that you have been appointed not as a hireling but as a shepherd, who should demonstrate his love for the supreme Shepherd by diligently pasturing his sheep; and, for those same sheep, if circumstances demand it, be ready, with the blessed chief of the apostles, to lay down your life.

I earnestly beg you to take care lest, when that same chief of the apostles and the other leaders of faithful flocks offer Christ, on the day of judgment, the great fruit of their pastoral care, some portion of your sheep should deserve to be separated among the goats on the judge’s left and to go into eternal punishment with a curse. Rather, may you then deserve to be numbered among those of whom Isaiah says: “The least shall become a thousand” [Al.: “among a thousand”], “and the smallest a very strong nation” [Al.: “among a very strong nation”] (Isaiah LX).

It is your duty to examine most diligently what is rightly and what perversely done in each monastery of your diocese, so that neither an abbot ignorant of or contemptuous of the rules, nor an abbess of insufficient worth, may be placed over the governance of Christ’s male or female servants. Nor, again, should an undisciplined and rebellious crowd of hearers resist the foresight of spiritual teachers. This is especially important because, as the common report has it, you are accustomed to say that what is done in each monastery pertains not to the concern of kings or to the authority of any secular ruler, but solely to the investigation and examination of you bishops [Al.: “of you, the bishops”], unless someone in the monasteries is proved to have sinned against those rulers themselves.

It is, I say, your duty to ensure that in places consecrated to God the devil does not usurp a kingdom for himself; that discord does not claim the place of peace, quarrels the place of piety, drunkenness the place of sobriety, and fornication and murder the place of charity and chastity. Nor should there be found among those subject to you any of whom it may rightly be asked and said: “I saw the wicked buried; while they lived, they were in a holy place, and they were praised in the city as though for the works of the just” [Al.: “the good”] (Ecclesiastes VIII).

You must also take diligent care of those who still remain in the life of the people, so that, as we warned at the beginning of this letter, you remember to provide them with sufficient teachers of a saving way of life. Among other things, you should teach them what works especially please God; from what sins those who desire to please God ought to abstain; with what sincerity of heart they should believe in God; with what devotion they should beseech divine mercy in prayer; how frequently and carefully they must fortify themselves and all that belongs to them with the sign of the Lord’s cross against the continual snares of unclean spirits; and how salutary daily reception of the Lord’s body and blood is for every class of Christians [Col. 0666A], as you know is diligently practiced by the Church of Christ throughout Italy, Gaul, Africa, Greece, and the entire East.

This form of religion and God-devoted sanctification is so far removed from almost all the laypeople of our province, through the negligence of their teachers, as though it were nearly foreign to them, that those who appear to be more religious among them presume to communicate in the sacred mysteries only at Christmas, Epiphany, and Easter. Yet there are countless innocent people of the most chaste way of life—boys and girls, young men and virgins, old men and old women—who could communicate in the heavenly mysteries every Sunday, and also on the feast days of the holy apostles and martyrs, without any scruple of controversy, just as you yourself have seen done in the holy Roman and Apostolic Church. Married people too, if someone shows them the proper measure of self-restraint and commends to them the virtue of chastity, could and would willingly do the same.

I have tried briefly to set these matters down for you, most holy bishop, both out of regard for your affection and for the sake of the general good. I greatly desire, and greatly exhort you, to take care to draw our people away from their ancient errors and to strive to lead them back to a more certain and direct path of life. And if there are men of any rank or order who attempt to restrain or hinder the good beginnings you have made, nevertheless strive, mindful of heavenly reward, to carry the purpose of holy virtue through to a firm conclusion.

For I know that some will strongly oppose this exhortation of ours, especially those who recognize that they themselves are entangled in the crimes from which we forbid you. But you ought to remember the apostolic response: “It is necessary to obey God rather than human beings” (Acts V). For God’s command is: “Sell what you possess and give alms” (Luke XII). And: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV).

But it is the modern practice of certain people who profess to be God’s servants not only not to sell what they possess [Al.: omits “not only”], but also to purchase again what they do not possess [Al.: “to acquire once more what they have not possessed”]. With what face, then, does anyone dare, when about to enter the service of the Lord, either to retain what he had possessed in secular life [Al.: “those things which he had”], or, under the pretext of a holier life, to gather together the riches that he had not possessed? The most famous apostolic judgment declares that Ananias and Sapphira, when attempting this, were not corrected by any remedy of repentance or satisfaction, but were immediately punished by the condemnation of an avenging death.

They preferred, indeed, not to gather the property of others but improperly to retain their own. From this it is plainly evident how far the apostles’ minds stood from accepting the acquisition of money, since they served the Lord under this very rule: “Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke VI); and, conversely, they were instructed by the example of those assigned to the left-hand side: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (ibid.).

Or should we perhaps think that the Apostle was mistaken and wrote a falsehood when, warning us, he said: “Brothers, do not err”; and immediately added: “Neither the avaricious, nor the drunkards, nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians VI)? And again: “Know this, that every fornicator, or unclean person, or avaricious person, who is an idolater, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians V).

Since, therefore, the Apostle plainly calls avarice and rapacity idolatry, how can we think that those who either withdrew their hand from subscribing to an avaricious purchase, even when ordered by the king, or applied their hand to erasing useless documents and subscriptions, were in error? [Al.: “to scrape away”; “to correct”]

The rashness of fools—or rather, the pitiable misery of the blind—is certainly astonishing. Without any regard for heavenly fear, they are shown openly to cut apart and treat as worthless the things that the apostles and prophets wrote under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Yet, conversely, they fear to erase or correct what they themselves, or others like them, wrote under the prompting of avarice or lust, as though it were sacred and divinely protected.

In this, unless I am mistaken, they imitate the pagans, who, having despised the worship of God, venerate, fear, worship, adore, and implore as deities the things they themselves have imagined and fashioned from their own hearts. They are most deserving of that denunciation of the Lord by which he rebuked the Pharisees when they placed their own *deuteroses*—their traditions—above the law of God, saying: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?” (Matthew XV).

Even if they produce documents written in defense of their desires [Col. 0667C] and confirmed by the subscriptions of noble persons, never, I beg you, forget the Lord’s sanction, which says: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (ibid.).

And certainly I would like to learn from you, most holy bishop, when the Lord testifies and says: “Broad is the gate and spacious the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it; but narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matthew VII), what confidence you have concerning the life or eternal salvation of those who are known to walk throughout the whole of their lives through the broad gate and spacious way, and who take care not to resist or oppose, even in the smallest matters, their own pleasure of body or mind for the sake of heavenly reward.

Unless perhaps they should be thought capable of being absolved from their crimes by the alms that, amid their daily desires and luxuries, they appeared to give to the poor. Yet the very hand and conscience that offers a gift to God must be clean and free from sins. Or perhaps they hope that, through the mysteries of the most holy offering—mysteries of which they were unworthy while alive—they may, once dead, be redeemed through others.

Or does the sin of desire seem to them perhaps very small? Let me discuss it at somewhat greater length. It deprived Balaam, a man filled with the spirit of prophecy, of the company of the saints [Al.: “It deprived the man…”]; it polluted Achan with the communion of the ban and destroyed him; it stripped Saul of the insignia of the kingdom; it deprived Gehazi of the merits of prophecy and defiled him, together with his offspring, with the perpetual disease of leprosy. It cast Judas Iscariot down from the glory of the apostleship. It rendered Ananias and Sapphira, whom we mentioned above, unworthy of the fellowship of the monks and punished them even with bodily death. And, to ascend to earlier examples, it cast the angels down from heaven and expelled our first parents from the paradise of perpetual delight.

And if you wish to know, this is that three-headed dog of hell to which legend has given the name Cerberus [Al.: “has assigned”]. Against its rabid teeth the Apostle John warns us, saying: “Beloved, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but is from the world” (1 John II).

These remarks have been made briefly against the poison of avarice. If, however, we wished to treat drunkenness, feasting, lust, and other contagions of this kind by the same method, the length of the letter would be extended beyond all measure.

May the grace of the supreme Shepherd preserve you perpetually safe and sound for the saving pasturing of his sheep, most beloved bishop in Christ. Amen [Al.: “bishop. Written on the Nones of November, third indiction”].

[Note: [Col. 0667C] This Ecgberct was, as Malmesbury writes, *On the Kings*, I, 3, the brother of Eadberct, king of the Northumbrians. His father, Eata, had given him to a monastery in childhood. At a more advanced age he went to Rome with his brother Ecgred and received the rank of deacon; after his brother died there, he returned to his homeland. See Simeon of Durham, *On the Church of Durham*, II, 3. Writers disagree about the first year of his episcopate. In this confusion, the year 732, which the continuator of Bede’s *Epitome* selects, appeals to me most strongly; for it is established from Alcuin, a disciple of this Ecgberct, that he was bishop before Bede’s death, who undoubtedly died in 734. In the same poem, the same Alcuin, who was present at Ecgberct’s death and whom Ecgberct had ordained deacon shortly before his own death—as is clear from his Life in Mabillon, part I, fourth century—together with Simeon of Durham, *On the Deeds of the Kings of the English*, and Hoveden in the first part of his *Annals*, write that he governed the Church for thirty-four years. Since, by the common agreement of historians, he died in 766, he therefore assumed the episcopate in 732, when the younger Wilfrid laid down the burdens of pastoral care. He was the first bishop of York after Paulinus to receive the honor of the pallium: according to the Saxon Chronicle, Bede’s *Epitome*, and Simeon of Durham, this occurred in 735; according to Thomas Stubbs, in the following year. In that same year he consecrated Fridwald to Candida Casa and Fridberct to the Church of Hexham, from which, I do not know by whom, Acca had been expelled. Ecgberct was an armory of all the liberal arts and founded the most noble library at York. See Malmesbury, *On the Bishops*, III. He also wrote a *Dialogue on Ecclesiastical Institution*, a short work *On Priestly Law*, and a *Penitential Work* divided into four books. Some have mistakenly confused him with the man who studied in Ireland. According to the Saxon Chronicle, his day of death was 13 Kalends of December; according to Florence, 14 Kalends of the same month. In Ware’s edition this letter is said to have been written on the Nones of November, in the third indiction—that is, in 733—but this chronological note appears to have been added by a more recent hand. For it can be demonstrated that Bede died in 734, or at least on Ascension Day in 735, that is, before the time assumed here; and the Merton manuscript has no date whatsoever.] 

**LETTER III, AN APOLOGETIC LETTER TO PLEGWIN, because he was accused by certain persons of holding an incorrect view concerning the ages of the world.**

[From the edition of Giles, and the following letters.]

[Col. 0669A]

To Plegwin, my most beloved brother and honorable in the bowels of Christ, Bede sends greetings in Christ.

Two days ago, most loving brother, a messenger from your holiness came to me. He brought from you the happiest words of a peaceful greeting, but immediately mingled them with sadness by adding that you had heard me sung of among heretics over drinks by wanton peasants. I confess that I was horrified; turning pale, I asked what heresy I was accused of holding. He replied that I denied that the Lord and Savior had come in the flesh in the sixth age of the world.

I therefore began to inquire how this was being said: whether it meant that the Lord had not come in the flesh although it was the sixth age, or that, although the Lord had come in the flesh, the sixth age had not yet arrived, or certainly that the seventh age had already arrived—although, by clear reasoning, the sixth age could have begun only with his incarnation. I discovered that, whichever of these accusations was being made against me, in either case I was a participant in sound faith and ecclesiastical unity.

How could I, denying that Christ had come in the flesh, be a priest of Christ in the Church? Or how, believing the evangelical and apostolic writings, could I disbelieve that he was incarnated in the sixth age of the world, when the evangelist Matthew, in the same book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, distinguishes the four final ages by the well-known divisions of time marked by fourteen generations each?

The Apostle Peter, however, distinguishes the first two by this brief indication: asserting that the earth and heavens were destroyed by the Flood and that others had been set in their place, so that they may be called not so much two ages of the world as two worlds—if we did not fear the Valentinian heresy.

When, therefore, I examined myself repeatedly and saw that I was free of accusation, I began diligently to consider where this slander against me had arisen. At last I remembered that recently I had shown one of you my little work *On Times*, which I published five years ago. In it I had recorded the succession of years according to the Hebrew truth, where it is much shorter than in the Septuagint interpreters, so that by the coming of the Savior in the flesh not even five thousand years had been completed.

I urged him—for I confess that I did so out of brotherly love and regard for the truth—to learn to place his faith in the sacred Scripture translated for us after Christ by a Christian interpreter, rather than in Jewish interpretations or the ignorance of chroniclers. I pointed out that Eusebius, in his account of times, followed neither the Hebrew truth nor the edition of the Septuagint translators in every respect. I shall undertake to demonstrate the same thing here in writing.

But he—whoever he was—to whom I had offered these suggestions turned a service of brotherly love into hatred born of rivalry, and the heavenly Ruler, in a just recompense, changed for him the light of the truth that had been shown into the darkness of blind falsehood.

Therefore, beloved, do not think that, after the mark of heresy, I am seeking refuge in the evasive defense of denial rather than accepting the teacher of truth. Listen to what I wrote in the little book mentioned above, *On the Ages*.

After I had briefly treated, as far as I believed sufficient for myself and my readers, the moments and hours, the day, the night, the weeks and months, the year and matters pertaining to the year, the nineteen-year cycle and its accidents, the time had come to abbreviate something likewise concerning the ages. Accordingly, in the sixteenth chapter I made the following beginning:

“The periods of the world,” I said, “are distinguished into six ages. The first age, from Adam to Noah, contains ten generations and 1,656 years. It wholly perished in the Flood, just as forgetfulness is accustomed to engulf infancy.

“The second, from Noah to Abraham, likewise embraces ten generations, but 292 years. It was found in the tongue—that is, in the Hebrew language. For after infancy a human being begins to know how to speak in childhood, which also received its name from this fact, because he cannot yet speak—*fari*, that is, ‘to speak.’

“The third, from Abraham to David, contains fourteen generations and 942 years. And because a human being begins to be able to beget children at adolescence, Matthew took the beginning of the generations from Abraham, who was also appointed the father of the nations.

“The fourth, from David to the transmigration to Babylon, extends, according to Matthew, through fourteen generations and 473 years. From this age the times of the kings began; for youthful dignity is suited to kingship.

“The fifth, then, extends to the coming of the Savior in the flesh, likewise through fourteen generations, and stretches over 589 years. In this age, as though wearied by a grievous old age, the Hebrew people are shaken by increasingly frequent evils.

“The sixth age, which is now in progress, has no fixed sequence of generations or periods; but, like an age of decrepitude, it will be brought to an end by the death of the whole world.”

While recording these matters in the aforementioned little book *On the Ages of the World*, I immediately appended another chapter in which the course and order of the entire world might be disclosed, beginning as follows:

“The first age, therefore, contains, according to the Hebrews, 1,656 years; according to the Septuagint interpreters, 2,242. Adam, at the age of 130, begot Seth, who was born in place of Abel. Seth, at the age of 105, begot Enos, and so forth up to the Flood.”

Then I added:

“The second age contains, according to the Hebrews, 292 years; according to the Septuagint interpreters, 942 years, or, with Cainan added, 1,072. Shem, in the second year after the Flood, begot Arphaxad, from whom came the Chaldeans. Arphaxad, at the age of 35, begot Shelah. Here the Septuagint interpreters, whom the evangelist Luke followed, inserted Cainan, who, when he was 30 years old, begot Shelah.”

Likewise, concerning the third age:

“The third age,” I said, “contains 942 years.”

Again, when I came to the fourth age:

“The fourth age,” I said, “contains, according to the Hebrews, 472 years; the Septuagint interpreters add 12.”

When, therefore, in the course of the work I came to the birth of the Lord and Savior, I wrote as follows:

“Octavian reigned for 56 years. In his forty-second year the Lord was born, after 4,952 years had been completed from Adam, according to one reckoning, and 5,199 according to another.”

These are the matters which, in accordance with the testimony of sacred history, I have taken care to abridge briefly and simply for myself and my own people, at their request, as I believed and understood them—by no means contradicting so learned a chronographer, and one worthy of such great praise, except in those points in which he is not contrary to divine Scripture. When, in his book the *Hexapla* (Ἑξαπλοῦς), fearing Origen’s rod, he removed Cainan’s generation from the text, he equally diminished the authority of the Gospel of Luke and of the interpreters of the Septuagint, and erased 130 years from their translation. Yet, when he had corrected the genealogies according to the Hebrew books, he did not take equal care to correct the number of years according to those same books. In the total of his computation he exceeded their sequence [Col. 0671B] by 232 years, and thus, observing neither path, he proceeded by a route of his own choosing.

For in the first and second ages, there is this kind of discrepancy between our books—that is, those transferred from the Hebrew source—and the Greek codices. As Jerome, the interpreter of sacred history, reports in his books of *Hebrew Questions*, before the birth of the one whose birth is mentioned, the father is found among the Hebrews to have lived one hundred years less; but after that son has been born, that same father is found among the Greeks to have lived one hundred years less than among the Hebrews. Thus, in both places, the total of the numbers agrees. From this corruption of the Greek codices arises that most famous question concerning Methuselah, who is calculated to have lived fourteen years after the Flood, although it is certain that according to the Hebrew codices [Col. 0671C] he died in the very year of the Flood.

But if someone should say that the Hebrew books were later falsified by the Jews, and that, out of envy toward our authorities, they took the truth away from themselves, let him hear what Origen answered to this little question in the seventh [volume] of his explanations of Isaiah: the Lord and the Apostles, who rebuke the other crimes of the scribes and Pharisees, would never have remained silent about this crime, which was the greatest of all. Let him hear Josephus, the Jewish historian, who, writing in the first book of the *Antiquities* (Ἀρχαιότητος) against Apion the Grammarian, plainly and clearly demonstrated both that the smaller number of years is the true one and that holy Scripture had in no way been falsified by the Jewish people.

[Col. 0671D]

“For,” he says, “we do not possess countless volumes disagreeing with one another, but only twenty-two books, which contain the sequence of all times and are rightly believed to be divinely inspired. Of these, five are the books of Moses, containing the laws and the genealogy of human life and succession, extending down to the end of Moses himself; they comprise almost three thousand years.”

And shortly afterward:

“The facts themselves therefore demonstrate how reverently we use our Scriptures. For although so many ages have passed, no one has ever dared either to add anything, or to take anything away, or afterward to alter anything. Rather, all the people of our race have this faith implanted and, as it were, innate: to believe that these are the ordinances of God, to cling to them continually [Col. 0672A], and, if circumstances should demand it, willingly to lay down their lives for them.”

Let him hear blessed Jerome, who says that it was not the Hebrew but the Greek codices that had been falsified. When he was compelled to translate the *Books of Chronicles*, he introduced the work with the following complaint:

“If the pure edition of the Seventy Interpreters, as it was translated by them into Greek, had remained intact, you would be urging me in vain, most holy and learned Chromatius, bishop, to transfer the Hebrew volumes for you into the Latin language. For what had once occupied the ears of men and strengthened the faith of the newborn Church ought rightly to have been confirmed also by our silence. But now, since different copies are circulated according to the variety of regions, and that genuine and ancient translation has been corrupted and violated, [Col. 0672B] you suppose that it belongs to our judgment either to determine from the many what is true or to forge a new work within the old work,”

and other things of this kind, in which he develops the same meaning at greater length.

Blessed Bishop Augustine also agrees with this opinion. For when he did not wish to attribute the cause of this discrepancy either to the malice of the Jews or to the error or envy of the Seventy Interpreters—who themselves were also Jews, and whom he would not wish to accuse everywhere of falsification, since elsewhere he had filled the seventy cells with the one Spirit of divinity—he found the following explanation:

“It is therefore more credible that, when these things first began to be copied from Ptolemy’s library, something of this kind could have occurred in a single codex, namely the one first copied from it, from which the matter then spread more widely; and there, indeed, a copyist’s [Col. 0672C] error could have occurred.”

This is not absurd to suspect in the question concerning Methuselah’s lifetime.

And shortly afterward:

“For even now, where numbers do not serve to make something understood easily, or where nothing useful appears to be learned, they are copied negligently and corrected even more negligently. For who would think that it needed to be learned how many thousands of men each of the tribes of Israel might have possessed individually, since it is not thought to be of any use?”

And somewhat later:

“But however this may be understood, I would in no way doubt that it is right, when something different is found in the two codices, since both cannot be true in matters of historical fact, to give preference to the language from which the translation into the other language was made by interpreters.”

[Col. 0672D]

Read Book XV of *The City of God*:

> “For by no means should we listen to those who think that the years in those times were reckoned differently—that is, as being of such short duration that one of our years is believed to have contained ten of theirs,”

each being completed, evidently, by thirty-six days. They use as evidence the fact found among many historical writers that the Acarnanians had a year of six months, the Arcadians one of three months, and the Egyptians one of four months, and that they themselves sometimes even bounded their year by the course of the moon. But Scripture itself openly refutes such an interpretation.

For where the Hebrew text reads:

> “And Adam lived 130 years and begot Seth; and the days of Adam after he begot Seth were 800 years, and he begot sons and daughters; and all the time that Adam lived was [Col. 0673A] 930 years, and he died,”

the Seventy say:

> “And Adam lived 230 years and begot Seth; and his days after he begot Seth were 700 years, and he died. And all his days were 930 years,”

and so forth in this manner.

What then? Did they place shorter years in the first part of each verse, longer years in the middle, and equal years at the end? To do this would be an error, and even to suspect it would be foolishness.

Some wonder why that great and outstanding interpreter of holy Scripture, Jerome—of whom it was said, and rightly said:

> Jerome, most learned interpreter in many tongues,  
> Bethlehem celebrates you; the whole world resounds with you—

why, I say, he did not wish, when translating [Col. 0673B] the Book of Chronicles, to hand on to the Latins what he had learned from the Hebrews to be true.

Whoever is troubled by this should know that, as he himself stated in the same *Book of Times*, he either wished to be an interpreter or the founder of a new work. Perhaps he did not wish, where no pressing necessity existed, voluntarily to provoke against himself the madness of enraged men, and therefore left this particular task to posterity. Thus, in one passage, he says to the virgin Eustochium that he wishes to prepare the shuttles and the threads, but to leave to others the care of weaving.

Indeed, in translating divine Scripture, a work of such necessity, he was almost overwhelmed with stones by Latins and Hebrews alike: by the Hebrews, because the opportunity to mock Christians and bring accusations against them on the basis of faulty codices was taken away; by the Latins, [Col. 0673C] because new and unfamiliar things, even if better, were being forced upon them in place of the old and customary things.

Thus blessed Augustine also took care to insert the following in letters sent with the most affectionate friendship across so many stretches of sea and land:

> “I do not want you to labor over translating the canonical books into the Latin language, except in the manner in which you translated Job, so that, by means of signs, it may be apparent what differs between your interpretation and that of the Seventy, whose authority is extremely weighty.
>
> “Yet I cannot sufficiently wonder if something is found in the Hebrew copies which escaped the most skilled interpreters of that language. I say nothing here about the Seventy: concerning either their judgment or the greater harmony of their spirit than if they had been one man [Col. 0673D], I do not presume to offer a definite opinion in any direction, except that I consider their pre-eminent authority in this work to be indisputably due to them.
>
> “Those move me more who, when interpreting later, and holding more tenaciously—as is reported—the way and rules of Hebrew speech, not only failed to agree among themselves but also left many things behind to be brought out and published only much later. For if these things are obscure, it is believed that you too could be deceived in them; if they are clear, it is not believed that they could have been deceived in them.”

Meanwhile, concerning Times and Years, I admonish your simplicity, dearest brother, lest, deceived by popular opinion, you expect the present age to last for six thousand years [Col. 0674A]. Nor should you, in accordance with the book of some heretic—which, when I was a boy, I remember seeing copied in an ancient script—think that although the day and hour of judgment are unknown, the year can be foreknown by human beings, because the Lord said, “But of that day and hour no one knows,” and did not say, “of the year”; and because he said again, “It is not yours to know the times or the moments,” without adding “the years” there either.

This chronographer and heresiarch was endeavoring to establish that 5,500 years had passed before the Lord’s incarnation, and that from then until the day of judgment 500 years would nevertheless remain—of which more than 300 had already elapsed at the time when he was considering these matters. He accumulated the total of this number partly from Genesis and partly from the Book of Judges, while also assigning forty years twice each to Samuel and Saul [Col. 0674B].

He used as an argument the fact that the last laborers in the Lord’s vineyard worked for one hour, and that the apostle John said, “Little children, it is the last hour.” Since one hour in a day corresponds to 500 years in six thousand years, there ought to be 500 years in that one hour. And since evening comes after the twelve hours of the day, after twelve periods of 500 years have been completed—that is, after six thousand years—the eternal recompense of the just Judge would arise.

For this reason I grieve greatly, I confess, and, as far as I may—or even more than I should—usually become angry whenever I am asked by country people how many years remain of the final thousand years of the age. I in turn ask them where they know that the final thousand is now in progress, since the Lord in the Gospel does not testify that the time of his coming is near [Col. 0674C] or far away, but commands us always to keep our loins girded and our lamps burning, to watch and await him until he comes.

I observe that, when we are speaking to our brothers and, as the occasion arises, discuss the ages of the world, some of the simpler people suppose that we preach six thousand years. Nor have there been lacking those who thought that the present state of the world, which turns through seven days, would end after seven thousand years. The often-mentioned teacher Augustine clearly rebukes them for manifest rashness in his exposition of the sixth Psalm, saying among other things:

> “For if that day is to come after seven thousand years, every person can, by counting the years, assign its coming. Where then will be the statement that not even the Son knows this?”

This was said because human beings [Col. 0674D] do not learn this through the Son—not because he himself does not know it, according to the expression, “The Lord your God tests you, so that he may know,” that is, “so that he may make you know”; and, “Arise, Lord,” that is, “make us arise.”

When, therefore, the Son is said not to know this day, the meaning is not that he does not know it, but that he makes those to whom it is not expedient to know it ignorant of it—that is, he does not reveal it to them. What, then, does that rashness mean which, by counting the years, confidently expects the day of the Lord after seven thousand years?

These letters I send you, dearest brother, as pledges of my innocence and tokens of friendly affection, lest you suppose me wholly lacking in human or divine knowledge. Rather, in accordance with the Scriptures and the teachings [Col. 0675A] of the Fathers, I faithfully and catholically profess that the Lord and Savior assumed mortal flesh for us in the sixth age of the world, but that the course of the world has not been fixed for us by any definite number of years and is known in its entirety only to the knowledge of the Judge himself.

Even if someone says to me, “Behold, here is the Christ,” or, “Behold, there,” that is, that he will come to judgment at this or that time, I do not listen to him or follow him. For I know that, just as lightning flashing from heaven shines upon the things beneath heaven, so will the Son of Man be in his day.

You should also recognize the opinion by which the common people have arrived at six or seven thousand years, and the authority by which I support my own computation: namely, the Hebrew truth made known through Origen, published by Jerome, praised by Augustine, and confirmed by Josephus [Col. 0675B]. In such matters I find no one more learned than these men.

Nor is it surprising that the worthy Eusebius—although, through his remarkable skill in wisdom and speech, he could, as the saying goes, glue brass and iron together—was nevertheless unable to do what he had not learned, namely, to know the Hebrew language. Out of fear of it, as though rightly revering it, he did not fear to corrupt even what he himself knew, as we have shown above.

I earnestly ask you to deliver these letters of my defense to our religious and most learned brother David, so that he may read them before our venerable lord and father, namely Bishop Wilfrid. Since, in that man’s presence and hearing, I was previously attacked with insults so foolishly, let it now also appear, in his hearing [Col. 0675C] and judgment, how undeserving I was of having suffered those same insults.

I ask David above all to strive, following the example of the boy who shared his name, to drive away the fury of the evil spirit from his foolish brother by the encouragement of wholesome words, as though by the melody of sweet psalmody.

David could not accomplish this at that supper, at which a man drunk with wine tried to find fault with me—a man who ought instead to have made himself blameless by attending to reading—because David was not yet acquainted with the sense and purport of the words of mine that he was praising.

For it has truly been said:

> “If a serpent bites in silence, there is no advantage for the enchanter.”

Amen.

## EPISTLE IV, TO WICREDA: On the Celebration of Easter, or On the Vernal Equinox According to Anatolius

[Col. 0675D]

To the most reverend and most holy brother Wicreda, presbyter, Bede sends desirable salvation in the Lord.

I gladly received the letter of your kindness, most loving brother in Christ, and I hastened, ready to copy and send to you the chapters you requested, mindful of the familiarity and affection with which you received me when I arrived there.

I have also endeavored to explain at greater length in writing that deservedly famous question concerning ecclesiastical history, about which you asked me when I was present and to which I then answered briefly as best I could. It concerns the vernal equinox, which the most reverend Bishop Anatolius is said to have noted in the aforementioned book as occurring on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, whereas the other teachers of the Egyptians determine that it should rather be noted on the twelfth day before those same Kalends.

For Saint Proterius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, writing to the most blessed Pope Leo concerning Easter, says:

> “And it is indeed clearly known, according to the course of the sun, that the twenty-fifth day of the month Phamenoth—which is also the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—is the equinox. But it is not right to attach the beginning of the first month altogether to this equinox according to the course of the moon; otherwise the course of the moon ought in every respect to have agreed with the circle of the sun.”

Saint Cyril, bishop of the same Church, also says:

> “For the sun itself is enclosed every day over land and sea at the end of the day and is opened at the beginning of the day, and the sun completes the course of the entire year on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.”

Therefore, you are rightly troubled, as are the other learned men, by the question of how Anatolius, although he too is Egyptian by learning and birth, could write, seemingly contrary to the written teaching of the Egyptian doctors, that this same equinox customarily occurs on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

“For,” he says, “in the first year the beginning of the first month occurs when the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle occurs: according to the Egyptians, on the twenty-sixth day of the month Phamenoth; according to the Macedonians, on the twenty-second day of the month Distri; but according to the Romans, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. On that day the sun is found not only to have ascended into the first part, but also already to possess a quarter of it on that same day, that is, in the first of the twelve parts.”

This first part is the vernal equinox itself, and it is the beginning of the months, the head of the cycle, and the completion of the course of the stars called planets—that is, wanderers—as well as the end of the twelfth part and the terminus of the entire cycle.

But I believe that it can be demonstrated by a very simple argument that in this matter he is not contrary to the other teachers of Egypt and the East. The calculation of the quarter—which they call the leap day—causes the sun to reach the equinoctial point of its course in the zodiacal circle sometimes at its first rising, sometimes at noon, sometimes at sunset, and sometimes at midnight. Whenever the equinox occurs in the morning or at midday, it belongs to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; whenever it occurs in the evening or at midnight, it belongs to the eleventh day before those same Kalends.

For, without contradiction, every night, from the time when the Lord rose from the dead, is placed before the times of the following day, not added to those of the preceding day. Thus Anatolius wisely does not prohibit the celebration of Easter on the eleventh day, but before the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. For immediately after the words we have quoted, he adds:

> “And therefore we say that those who think Easter ought to be celebrated before the beginning of this new year commit no small offense.”

He therefore does not forbid Easter to be celebrated at the beginning in which he says the equinox occurs, but before this beginning of the new year. In the same book he carefully affirms, from the writings of both ancient and recent Fathers, that Easter cannot be celebrated before the passing of the equinox.

He himself was his own witness that, when writing, he marked not the first but the final times of the equinox—that is, those from which he knew that the celebration of Easter could begin. For when, in the second or third year after the leap year, Easter Sunday falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [Al.: occurs], it is plainly evident [Col. 0677A] that the time of Easter begins together with the equinox.

The parts of this ceremony are celebrated during the first night [Al.: the first part of the first night], although no one doubts that the equinox is completed in the middle of that night or even at its beginning, because indeed [*eo quod profecto*; alternative *eoque perfecto*, “and when it has been completed”], the hour of the Lord’s resurrection—which occurred at dawn—is rightly celebrated [Al.: the hour of the Lord’s resurrection, which occurred at dawn, is rightly celebrated].

And so that you may clearly observe that Anatolius specifically writes of the evening equinox [Al.: describes it], from which Easter can begin, and that he regularly refers it to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [Col. 0677B] [Al.: refers it], attend to what he records in what follows from the opinion of the ancient Fathers [Al.: appends]:

> “Since there are two equinoxes, of spring and autumn, separated by equal intervals, and since the solemnity of the fourteenth day of the first month has been established after evening, when the moon is found opposite the sun, as can also be demonstrated with the eyes, the sun is found to possess the portion of the vernal equinox, while the moon, conversely, possesses that of the autumnal equinox.”

What, then, is surprising if he says that the equinox occurs on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, when he declares that he is speaking of the hour at which, as the sun sets toward evening, the moon conversely raises its rising [Al.: the word “rising” is omitted]?

Here we must also observe [Col. 0677C] that he said that the equinoxes of spring and autumn are separated by equal intervals. From this we must conclude that we should reckon half a year from equinox to equinox and note the autumnal equinox on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October [Al.: the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October], separated from the vernal equinox by 182 days [Al.: the number “two” is omitted].

A review of the sundials also shows this to be entirely true, especially since he supports this most equal division of the year between the equinoxes with the words of the most ancient and learned teacher Aristobulus, who was one of the seventy illustrious interpreters of sacred Scripture.

As for what Anatolius likewise says—“On which day the sun is found not only to have ascended into the first part, but also already to possess a quarter [Col. 0677D] of it on that day [printed *quartam*; alternative *quadram*, both expressing a quarter], that is, in the first of the twelve parts”—he calls the twelve parts the twelve signs of the horoscope, each of which holds the sun for thirty days and a few additional hours.

Thus Maro also says of these same parts:

> Therefore the golden sun rules the sphere, measured out in fixed divisions,  
> through the twelve stars of the world.

The first of these portions, naturally, begins at the place of the vernal equinox [printed *a loci*, an irregular form; alternative *loco*, giving “from the place”]. [Al. adds: “Therefore Anatolius rightly adds below.”]

This first of the twelve portions is the vernal equinox because, clearly, the beginning of that same portion [after *partis*, “of the part,” an alternative adds *particula*, “a small part”]—namely, the place where the sun is first situated—contains the equinox itself. He therefore rightly says beforehand that on that day the sun not only ascended into the first portion but also already possessed a quarter in [Col. 0678A] it, because whenever, according to the calculation stated above, the equinoctial time falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, at that very moment the quarter of the day which annually tends to increase is recognized as having been naturally completed.

For when the equinox occurs on the twelfth day before those same Kalends, then on that very day and at that very equinoctial hour the same quarter is naturally completed. We add the word “naturally” because it is a human custom to insert that quarter at different times of the year, according to what pleased each people [*generi*, “race/kind”; alternative *genti*, “people/nation”]. But according to the natural order of reason, it is added at the completion of the solar cycle. Cyril marked this [printed *quam*, “which”; alternative *quod etiam*, “which also”] in the sentence that we quoted above [printed *quam ut*, “which, as”; alternative *et*, “and,” for *ut*], saying:

> “And the sun completes the course of the entire year on the twelfth [Col. 0678B] day before the Kalends of April.”

And lest anyone perhaps contend that, in this statement of Anatolius, we have been unable to understand what he himself meant, I shall briefly append what the most learned man Victor, bishop of the city of Capua, described concerning these same portions and the equinox [Al.: writes]:

> “The celestial circle,” he says, “through which the sun, moon, and stars called planets are carried by their own motion against the movement of the whole heaven, has been divided, by the judgment of wisdom, into twelve parts. When these have been completed in 365 days [that is, in the three hundred and sixty-fifth day], during which whole period the year is completed, when the sun has returned to the beginning of the first part of the aforesaid circle, the beginning of the year arises. This occurs from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April until the eleventh [Col. 0678C].
>
> “For it is often found to occur in the evening, sometimes at night, and sometimes on the very eleventh day before the Kalends of April [Al.: on the eleventh day before the Kalends]. Thus on the twenty-fifth or twenty-sixth day of the month of March according to the Alexandrians—that is, according to the Latins, on the twelfth or eleventh day before the Kalends of April—the beginning of the first month occurs according to the course of the sun.
>
> “But lest anyone wish to accuse us of inconsistency because, wavering as if amid uncertainty, we do not define the day of the first month with precision, let such a critic, or rather investigator, know that the most diligent and exceedingly subtle inquiry of the Egyptians teaches that from the seventh hour of the day the first hour of the following day begins. Thus, when it is the twenty-fifth day of the month of March, the twelfth [Al.: eleventh] day before the Kalends of April, if in the evening of that day the sun illuminates the extent of the first part, the twenty-sixth [Col. 0678D] day is already reckoned, according to the subtle Egyptian tradition, which is without doubt plausible.
>
> “And shortly afterward:
>
> “‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘if the moon is found to be fourteen days old, with the sun established in the first part of its circle [Al.: “The moon,” he says, “being fourteen days old—that is, full of light—with the sun established in the first part of its circle”], it is rightly assigned to the first month. But if the moon first shines forth in its fourteenth day [Al.: the word “moon” is omitted]—that is, in full light [Al.: adds “that is”]—before the sun has touched the aforesaid first part of its circle, it is found, or will be reckoned [the alternative omits only *reperitur vel*, “it is found, or”; *reputabitur*, “will be reckoned,” remains], to belong to the twelfth month. And [an alternative adds *ideo*, “therefore”] whenever this has occurred [*contigit*; alternative *contingit*, “occurs”], the solemnity of Easter is deferred until the next full moon, which necessarily occurs while the sun is still established in the first of the twelve parts of the circle.’”

[Col. 0679A]

I have wished to draw these words from blessed Victor so that the opinion of Saint Father Anatolius—which is obscure to many both in his own Paschal work and in ecclesiastical history—might be made clearer to you through Victor’s words.

Nor should this be passed over: there are some who maintain that Anatolius in this statement did not place the equinox on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April but on the eighth day before them. They say that Eusebius, when inserting this statement in his ecclesiastical history, changed one day for another, and that, although he saw that the rest had been expressed well and philosophically [Al.: saw it], he wished to correct with a single word what he perceived to have been stated less perfectly in it, lest the man whom he had undertaken [Al.: intended] to praise should plainly appear blameworthy if he inserted his unaltered words, exactly as he himself [Col. 0679B] had written them, into his histories.

But it would be astonishing if Eusebius, a writer so circumspect in speech and thought, could have been so eager for another’s praise that, inflamed by their writings [*scripturis deflagrans*; alternative *scripta deflorans*, “despoiling/culling their writings”], he fabricated that they had said things they had not said, and did not fear being accused once his readers had examined their complete little works and encountered in his authors what he had taken from them stated differently.

It would be astonishing if such an imposture escaped Victor, whose words we have quoted and who was likewise a man of outstanding learning. In another work, writing about Easter, he inserted this same statement of Anatolius concerning ecclesiastical history as something rightly praiseworthy and memorable, wherever he thought it appropriate, and he too wrote the eleventh rather than the eighth day before the Kalends of April [Col. 0679C].

It is also astonishing why Dionysius, surnamed the Short, a man outstanding in knowledge, should himself have sought Anatolius’s support from ecclesiastical history in his Paschal letters, if he knew that Anatolius’s words there had been falsified. Since Dionysius was also highly skilled in the Greek language, it could not have escaped him how these things had first been published.

For he says:

> “But since it cannot be established clearly from the writings of Moses where this month takes its beginning or where it ends, the aforesaid venerable 318 bishops, investigating more carefully the observance of ancient custom, handed down from Saint Moses and reported in the seventh book of ecclesiastical history [Al.: is reported], said that the new moon born between the eighth day before the Ides of March and the day of the Nones of April [Col. 0679D] should constitute the beginning of the first month, and that the fourteenth day of the moon should be sought with care between the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.”

It therefore seems likely that Eusebius faithfully inserted into his histories what he had found in the Greek authority. But Anatolius’s own little book was later corrupted in some Latin copies, through the fraud, evidently, of those who, ignorant of the true time of Easter, desired to defend their error by the authority of so great a Father.

But those who ask whether Eusebius corrected one statement, rather than others falsifying the whole little book of Anatolius, should consider how that book itself is written.

But what is surprising if they made a mistake concerning the eleventh [Al.: twenty-first] [Col. 0680A] moon, when they added three days before the equinox, during which they determine that Easter can be sacrificed? It is certain that this is altogether absurd to suppose [Al. adds: “even to be considered”].

They should be answered that Anatolius may have known many people [an alternative adds *eorum*, “of them”] who held this or that opinion concerning Easter, although their views have not come down to our knowledge. Conversely, one should ask them how the same little book can contain the following:

> “Therefore, in the first year, the beginning of the first month occurs at the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle: according to the Egyptians, on the twenty-seventh day [Al.: twenty-sixth] of the month Phamenoth; according to the Macedonians, on the twenty-second day [Col. 0680B] of the month Distri [Al.: the twenty-sixth day]; but according to the Romans, on the twenty-fifth day of the month of March [Al.: the twenty-sixth day of March], that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.”

Yet the twenty-sixth day of the Egyptian month Phamenoth and the twenty-second day of the Macedonian month Distri do not correspond to the eighth day before the Kalends of April, but to the ninth [Al.: eleventh] day before the Kalends of April.

Does it not appear most likely that the statement has been falsified, since the person who substituted the eighth day before the Kalends for the ninth [Al.: eleventh] day before the Kalends of April forgot also to change the position of the Egyptian or Greek months? But, allowing those matters which were less familiar to remain as they were [Al.: had been], he changed only what was visible to himself and to his own people.

As to which of these is more accurate, let those who read Anatolius in Greek [alternative *dicunt*, “say/speak,” for *legunt*, “read”; the alternative construction is unclear] decide.

But whether Eusebius changed this one statement [Al.: this statement alone], or someone else altered the entire little book from its original state [alternative *transfert*, “transfers,” for *mutaverit*, “may have changed”], it is established beyond any doubt—although he altered very many things [Al.: although a great multitude of the ancients confirms it]—that the equinox cannot occur [Col. 0680C] on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

This will be demonstrated both by observation of the sundials and by clear reasoning. For the rule of ecclesiastical observance [Al.: consecration] holds, approved both by the decrees of the earlier Fathers and more clearly by the Council of Nicaea, that Easter Sunday is to be sought from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April through the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

Likewise, the rule of catholic instruction commands that Easter not be celebrated before the passing of the vernal equinox. Therefore, whoever thinks that the equinox occurs on the eighth day before the Kalends of April must necessarily either say that it is permissible to celebrate Easter before the equinox, or deny that it is permissible to celebrate Easter before the seventh day before the Kalends [the alternative omits *dicat, a. a. VII Kal. d. p. c. lic.*, abbreviating “say, or [that] Easter is lawful to be celebrated before the seventh day before the Kalends”; the final *neget*, “deny,” remains].

He must also affirm either that the Easter which the Lord [Col. 0680D] celebrated with his disciples on the day before he suffered did not occur on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, or that it occurred before the equinox.

[Al. adds: “Farewell always in the Lord, dearest Father.”]

### Further details of the supplied alternative readings

These give the printed forms where English alone does not show the distinction.

- [Col. 0677A, occurrence of Easter] *occurrerit* / alternative *incurrerit*: both mean “has fallen/occurred.” For the ceremony’s first night, the alternative is abbreviated *prima n. e. parte celeb.*, “in the first … night … part … celebrated.” For the resurrection sentence, the alternative gives the order *resurr., q. d. f. e, rite c. h.*, placing “resurrection, which occurred at dawn” before “the hour is rightly celebrated.”
- [Col. 0677A–B] *scribat*, “writes,” / *describat*, “describes”; *respiciat* / *respicit*, “refers,” subjunctive / indicative; *annotat*, “records,” / *adnectat*, “appends.” After “there are two,” an alternative adds *inquit*, “he says.”
- [Col. 0677C] *dimidium anni* / *dimidiam anni partem*: “half a year” / “half the portion of a year”; *aequinoctiorum* / *aequinoctiarum*: masculine/neuter and feminine genitive-plural forms, both “of the equinoxes.”
- [Col. 0678B] *describebat*, “was describing,” / *scribat*, “writes/may write.”
- [Col. 0678C] *Kalendarum XI* / *XI Kal.* give the same date, the eleventh day before the Kalends, in reversed word order. At the following twenty-sixth day (Col. 0678D), the alternative repeats *XXVI*, “twenty-six”; no numeral difference is printed.
- [Col. 0678D, the fourteen-day moon] The alternative actually reads *Luna, inquit, XIV, hoc est, pleno lumine in prima parte sui circuli constituto*: “The moon, he says, [being] fourteen, that is, with full light established in the first part of its circle.” It does not expressly supply “the sun,” although the main text does; the alternative’s syntax is compressed. The later twelfth-month numeral is *XII* in both the main text and the cited alternative.
- [Col. 0679A–B] *videret* / *viderit*, “was seeing” / “has seen” (subjunctive forms); *proposuerat* / *disposuerat*, “had proposed” / “had planned”; *et ut* / *ut et*, “and as” / “as also.”
- [Col. 0679C] *venerabilis* / *venerabiles*, “venerable,” singular / plural, before the 318 bishops; *fertur* / *refertur*, “is said” / “is reported.”
- [Col. 0680A] *quaerunt* / *quaerant*, “they ask” / “let them ask”; *infalsasse* / *infalsare*, “to have falsified” / “to falsify.” After *certum*, “certain,” an alternative adds *est*, “is”; before *putari*, “to be thought,” another adds *etiam*, “even.”
- [Col. 0680B] *Martis* / *Martii*: alternative forms for “of March”; *fuerunt* / *fuerant*, “were” / “had been.”
- [Col. 0680C] *hanc* / *unam*, “this” / “one,” with “statement.” Before *in conspectione horologica*, “by observation of the sundials,” an alternative adds *et*, “also.” *observationis* / *consecrationis*, “of observance” / “of consecration.” The first *aut*, “either,” in the concluding alternative argument is replaced by *ut*, “that.”

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is thirty on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April; and in that same year the fourteenth moon falls on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, that is, on the Nones of April. Add this to thirty and take the regular numbers of April in the year in which the fourteenth moon enters April. But in the year in which the fourteenth moon falls in March, take thirty-six as the regular number of March. From the epacts you can readily determine whether the fourteenth moon occurs in March or in April. For if you have more than fifteen or fewer than five epacts, the fourteenth moon is calculated in April.

Therefore take thirty-five as the regular number in April, subtracting always the epacts of that year; what remains is the day of the fourteenth moon. For example, in the third year of the nineteen-year cycle there will be twenty-two epacts. Take twenty-two from thirty-five, and thirteen remain: the thirteenth day of April, that is, the Ides of April, is when the fourteenth moon occurs.

If, however, you seek the weekday of the fourteenth moon, add to the number that remains the concurrent number of that year. For example, for the thirteen that are present at present, the regular number in April is also seven. Add all these together and then divide by seven; what remains is the weekday of the fourteenth moon, and in this way you will arrive very easily at Sunday.

In March, however, take thirty-six as the regular number, and subtract the epacts of that year. For example, in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle there are eleven epacts; twenty-five remain: the fourteenth moon will be present on the twenty-fifth day of that month, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. If you seek the weekday of that same day, add to the prescribed number the concurrent number of that year, and add four as the regular number in March. Collect these also into one sum and divide by seven; what remains is the weekday of the fourteenth moon. If nothing remains, it is the seventh weekday.

Thus, if, after the epacts have been subtracted from thirty, anything remains, that remainder is the day of the month on which you will find the fourteenth moon. For example, in the year in which there are four epacts, take four from thirty-five and thirty-one remain. Take away thirty, and one remains. The fourteenth moon occurs on the first day of the month, that is, on the Kalends of April.

If, after the epacts have been subtracted, only fourteen remain from thirty, the fourteenth moon occurs on the fourteenth day of the month. This happens once in the nineteen-year cycle, when six epacts are assigned, and the fourteenth moon falls on the third day before the Kalends of April.

To instruct you by examples in finding the weekday on which the fourteenth moon occurs: take, for example, the present year of the Lord’s incarnation, 776. Take the epacts of this year, twenty-six; subtracting them from the regular number of April, thirty-five, nine remain. Behold, the fourteenth moon will be on the ninth day of the month, that is, on the fifth day before the Ides of April. Add also the concurrent number of the present year, namely one, to nine, making ten; add seven to this, making seventeen. Divide seventeen by seven: twice seven makes fourteen, and three remain. It will therefore be the third weekday when the fourteenth moon occurs:

- the fourteenth moon: Tuesday;
- the fifteenth: Wednesday;
- the sixteenth: Thursday;
- the seventeenth: Friday;
- the eighteenth: Saturday;
- the nineteenth: Sunday, which is the day of Easter, the fifth day before the Ides of April.

The fourteenth moon is on the fourth day before the Ides of April; the fifteenth on the third day before the Ides; the sixteenth on the day before the Ides; the seventeenth on the Ides; the eighteenth on the fourth day before the Kalends of May; and the nineteenth on the Kalends of May.

In the second year after this one, the seventh [epact], because it is more than five and less than fifteen, belongs to the fourteenth moon in March. You will find it as follows. Take the regular number of March, thirty-six; subtract seven from it, and twenty-nine remain. On the twenty-ninth of March, that is, the fourth day before the Kalends of April, the fourteenth moon occurs.

To find the weekday, take the same twenty-nine and add to it the concurrent number of that year, namely two, making thirty-one. Add also the regular number four, and the whole sum will be thirty-five. Divide by seven. Five times seven makes thirty-five, and nothing remains; therefore the fourteenth moon will be on the seventh weekday, the fourth day before the Kalends of April, and the fifteenth moon on the third day before the Kalends of April. That is the Sunday of Easter, in every year of the nineteen-year cycle.

By always subtracting the annual epacts according to this method from these regular numbers, you will find the fourteenth moon without error; and by adding the prescribed concurrent number to those regular numbers, you will also find the weekday of the fourteenth moon. Then, by calculating the weekdays that remain in that week and assigning the increasing age of the moon to each successive day, you will determine with complete certainty both the moon’s position and its age.

These arguments, beloved companion, with labor of my own,

I have written out for you; now say what gift you would give me

In return today, while weary I offer such things to you.

## Fragment: Appendix to the preceding letter

### Explanation of the three-quarters and half-ounce in divisions of the hours, by which writers calculate the course of lunar light

When the three-quarters and half-ounce of a single hour have always elapsed—that is, when the space of one hour is divided into twenty-four half-ounces, since there are that many half-ounces in a full pound—and when the twenty-four are again divided by four, namely into four groups of six, three times six is called a three-quarters, while once six is called a quarter. This is what is meant by “three-quarters of one hour,” namely, three parts and eighteen half-ounces.

But it is intended that one half-ounce of the six remaining half-ounces belonging to the quarter be added to the three-quarters, so that there are nineteen half-ounces, and the tide of the Ocean arrives later each day and withdraws later.

### On the ordering of the weekdays of Easter, by Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea, and the remaining bishops in synod

After the resurrection or ascension of the Lord and Savior, the Apostles were unable to establish any regulations concerning how they ought to observe Easter, because they had been scattered throughout the whole world and were occupied with preaching. But on whatever day the fourteenth moon fell in the month of March, they celebrated Easter.

After all the Apostles had passed from this world, the various provinces maintained different fasts. The Gauls always celebrated Easter on whatever day fell on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when Christ’s resurrection was proclaimed. In Italy, some fasted twenty days and others seven. The Easterners, following the example of the Apostles, as was said above, kept Easter on the fourteenth moon in the month of March.

When such observances were maintained in the various provinces, the priests were saddened, because those who rightly held one faith were divided in their fasts. Then Pope Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, sent an authoritative letter to Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, so that a regulation might be established there concerning how Easter should rightly be celebrated by all catholic churches, in the place where the Lord and Savior of the world had dwelt in the flesh.

Having received this authority, the aforesaid bishop summoned not only all the bishops of his own province but also those from different regions. When that multitude of priests had assembled, Bishop Theophilus produced the authority sent to him by Pope Victor and showed what task had been entrusted to him.

Then all the bishops said together: “Unless we first investigate how the world was made in the beginning, nothing can safely be ordained concerning the observance of Easter.”

The bishops therefore said: “What do we believe was made first in the world, unless it was the Lord’s Day?”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you say.”

The bishops replied: “According to the authority of Scripture, ‘There was evening and there was morning, the first day.’”

Then came the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh. On the seventh day God rested from all his works, and he called that day the Sabbath. Since the Sabbath therefore signifies the last day, what can be the first except the Lord’s Day?

Bishop Theophilus said: “You have proved concerning the Lord’s Day that it is the first day. What do you say about the season? Four seasons of the world are recognized: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Which season, then, was made first in the world?”

The bishops answered: “Spring.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you say.”

They replied: “It is written: ‘Let the earth bring forth grass, plants according to their kind, and fruit-bearing trees, producing their fruit.’ This is understood to have occurred in the season of spring.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “At what point do you believe the world’s beginning was: at the beginning of time, in the middle of time, or at the end?”

The bishops answered: “At the equinox on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you say.”

They replied: “It is written that God made the light, and God called the light day; he made the darkness, and he called the darkness night; and he divided equal parts between the light and the darkness.”

Theophilus said: “You have proved your case concerning the day and the season. What do you think about the moon? Was it consecrated by God while waxing and already full, or while diminished?”

The bishops answered: “Full.”

He said: “Prove what you say.”

They replied: “He made two great lights and placed them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth: the greater light for the beginning of the day and the lesser light for the beginning of the night. This could not have been otherwise unless the moon had been full.”

“Now, therefore, we have investigated how the world was made in the beginning: on the Lord’s Day, in springtime, at the equinox, which is the eighth day before the Kalends of April. At that time the full moon and the elements themselves rise again.”

Theophilus said: “Now, then, we must deal with the regulation of how we ought to keep Easter.”

The bishops said: “Can the Lord’s Day be passed over so that Easter is not celebrated on it, when it has been sanctified by so many and such great blessings?”

Theophilus said: “Tell me, then, by what and by how many blessings you assert that it was sanctified, so that we may write them down.”

The bishops said: “The first blessing bestowed upon it is that on it the darkness was removed and the light appeared.

“The second blessing is that on it the people were liberated from the land of Egypt, as from the darkness of sins, through the Red Sea, as through the font of baptism.

“The third blessing is that on the same day the heavenly food, manna, was given to human beings.

“The fourth blessing is that by which Moses commands the people: ‘Let the first and the last day be observed by you.’
