“The fifth blessing is expressed in Psalm 117: ‘They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns.’ Concerning the Lord’s resurrection it says: ‘This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it,’ as far as the horn of the altar.

“The sixth blessing is that on it the Lord rose again.

“You see, therefore, that the Lord’s Day, the day of the resurrection, can uniquely be kept as Easter.”

Theophilus said: “Concerning the season, God commanded Moses: ‘This month shall be for you the beginning of months; celebrate Easter in it.’ All thirty days, therefore, have been consecrated by the Lord.”

The bishops said: “We already gave the answer above: the beginning of the world is the equinox on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. From the eighth day before the Kalends of April up to the eighth day before the Kalends of May, we read that the days have been consecrated.”

Theophilus said: “Behold, is it not impious that the Lord’s Passion, a mystery of such great sacramental significance, should be excluded beyond the boundary? For the Lord suffered beginning on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the night on which he was handed over by the Jews, and rose again on the seventh day before the Kalends. How, then, can three days be excluded beyond the limit?”

All the bishops said: “By no reasoning should so great a mystery be excluded beyond the boundary. These three days must instead be brought within the limit, and it has been established that the boundary should be drawn back from below. Therefore, in that synod they decreed that Easter should be observed from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April up to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, and that no one may transgress the established limit, either before or afterward.”

The divine command concerning the moon must likewise be observed. Moses was commanded: “Let it be observed by you from the fourteenth moon up to the twenty-first.” It is therefore clear that these seven moons were likewise consecrated for observance at Easter.

When, then, the Lord’s Day falls within its proper boundary—from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May—and the moon is sanctified as the eighth among those, it seems to us that Easter should be celebrated.

Whatever the age of the paschal moon may be, if you subtract seven from it, the result will be the age of the moon at the beginning of Lent. For example, if the fifteenth moon is the paschal moon, take twelve from fifteen, and three remain [the preceding instruction to subtract seven is inconsistent with this example]. The moon is third at the beginning of Lent in the year when the fifteenth moon falls on the Sunday of Easter, and similarly in the other cases.

Remember that in a leap year the moon of February has thirty days, and that the moon of March also has thirty days, as it always does, lest the calculation of the paschal moon be disturbed.

## Letter V, to Acca: On the beginning of Genesis

To the most beloved and most reverend abbot Acca, Bede, the humblest of Christ’s servants, sends greetings.

Concerning the beginning of the book of Genesis, in which the creation of this world is described, many have said many things, and many have left behind memorials of their learning for posterity. Above all, so far as our limited ability has been able to learn, there are Basil of Caesarea, whom the interpreter Eustathius rendered from Greek into Latin; Ambrose of Milan; and Augustine, bishop of Hippo. From these, the first poured forth for readers the abundant streams of salutary teaching in nine books; the second, following in his footsteps, in six books; and the third in twelve books, and again in two others written specifically against the Manichaeans. In them the promise of Truth was fulfilled, when he said: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

Augustine also, in the books of his Confessions and in the books that he composed with exceptional skill against the adversary of the Law and the prophets, as well as in various other short works scattered here and there, preserved some recollection of that primordial creation together with an appropriate exposition.

But because these works are so abundant and so profound that scarcely anyone except the wealthy can acquire so many volumes, and scarcely anyone except the learned can investigate such depths, it pleased your holiness to entrust me with the task of selecting from all these works, as from the most delightful fields of a widely flowering paradise, whatever might seem sufficient for the needs of the weak.

Nor was I sluggish in carrying out what you deigned to command. Rather, as soon as I had examined the volumes of the Fathers, I gathered from them and arranged in two little books those things that could instruct a reader still inexperienced, so that, once educated by them, he might learn to ascend to the higher and more demanding reading of the great authors.

In this work I endeavored to set down throughout the thought of the Fathers mentioned above and of other equally catholic Fathers—sometimes in their own words, sometimes, for the sake of brevity, in my own; sometimes without naming them, sometimes with their names mentioned—as the requirements of the passages seemed to dictate.

I extended the work until Adam, expelled from the paradise of delight, entered the exile of temporal life. I also intend, if God wills, with the help of your intercession accompanying me, to write something about the subsequent sacred history, once I have first examined briefly the book of the holy prophet and priest Ezra. In that book, as the prophet and historian composed it, the mysteries of Christ and the Church are represented under the figure of the end of a long captivity, the restoration of the temple, the rebuilding of the holy city, the return to Jerusalem of the vessels that had been carried away, the rewriting of God’s law that had been burned, the correction of the people concerning foreign wives, and their conversion with one heart and soul to the service of God. With God’s favor, I shall make some of the mysteries I have mentioned clearer to the diligent.

Farewell always, most loving bishop, and remember us in the Lord.

## Letter VI, to the same Acca: On Solomon’s Temple

The chosen Vessel and teacher of the nations urges us to read the divine utterances, declaring with truthful voice that “whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.” In this passage he makes it perfectly clear that, in order to obtain hope of heavenly goods, we must possess patience and contemplate the consolation of the Scriptures.

Patience means that, when adversities arise, we should endure the blows inflicted—as though by a just judge and loving father—with a humble and submissive mind, whether we suffer them for the glory of virtue and the increase of our merits, if we are just and innocent, or for the correction of our conduct, if we are entangled in vices.

The consolation of the Scriptures means that by frequent meditation on them we should recall how much those supreme Fathers and distinguished lights of the Church endured in the present life amid dark affliction; how much glory they received in the future life, together with the divine reward of their devotion and patience; and how much unfailing praise and honor they left behind in this life among all the faithful. As Scripture says: “The memory of the just is with praises” (Prov. 10). And again: “The bodies of the saints were buried in peace, and their names will live for generation after generation” (Eccli. 44).

The apostle James also says: “Behold, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of Job’s endurance, and you have seen the end of the Lord” (Jas. 5).

He did not add “you have seen the end of the Lord” without reason to the mention of the afflictions of the just, because even he did not leave this life without punishment, although he lived here without sin. He who appeared in the world to heal the sick and raise the dead himself chose to return from the world through the weakness of death, in order to set before us an example of patience.

Thus, when the Psalmist had said, “Our God is the God of salvation” (Ps. 67), he immediately added, in wonder—or rather in astonishment: “And the exits of the Lord, of the Lord, are from death.”

Therefore, through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures, we have hope that we too will be comforted after the afflictions of our sufferings, provided that we have shown patience in tribulation and recalled to mind the deeds of those who have gone far before us in the merit of righteousness and have endured far greater struggles with adversity.

They often suffered persecution from the unrighteous because of the righteousness in which they excelled, so that, together with the practice of righteousness, they might receive the crown of unconquerable patience and leave behind for all who followed them the glorious traces of their perseverance.

We, however, are more often chastised by the mercy and providence of our Creator for our errors, so that, returning to our conscience through salutary remorse, we may carefully punish with cleansing tears what we have committed through deceptive allurements and negligence. Thus, with the Lord’s help, once corrected, we may become worthy to belong to the fellowship of those who were afflicted though innocent.

Here too, in the consolation of the Scriptures, we find that the Lord has blessed all who fear him, the small together with the great, and has declared that there are many dwellings in his Father’s house.

By the consolation of these dwellings, beloved among bishops, I do not doubt that you daily lighten the present anxieties of temporal affairs and are nobly encouraged to behold the goods of the Lord in the land of the living, since you abound not only in the pages of divine literature but also in the pious expositions of those writings that the venerable Scripture of the Fathers has left to us.

But because new things sometimes delight people more, I thought it appropriate to send your holiness for reading a little work that I recently composed allegorically on the structure of God’s temple, following in the footsteps of great interpreters.

When you attend to its reading and find there more of the mysteries of Christ and the Church implanted in the ancient pages, and perceive there greater gifts of God, either already given to us in the present or promised for the future, I believe that you will judge all perishable things, both adversity and prosperity, to be lighter and less worthy of concern. You will do so according to the example of blessed John, who, when the wicked emperor confined him within the narrow limits of a very small island, was immediately introduced by the pious Creator, through the Spirit, to contemplate the infinite mysteries of those heavenly dwellings.

Where he was thought by his deceived enemies to be deprived of the help and companionship of human friends, there he deserved to enjoy the sight and conversation of angelic friends. Taught by them, he learned all the more to despise the world’s allurements and bitterness the more sublimely he contemplated those things which, because of their greatness and eternity, are clearly either much more to be feared or much more to be loved.

Farewell always, beloved, and intercede for us.

## Letter VII, to Nothelm the presbyter: On the Thirty Questions

To his most beloved brother Nothelm, Bede sends greetings.

The matters from the book of Kings that you sent me to clarify, dearest brother, I immediately undertook to explain as far as I could, with the Lord’s help. I arranged them in the following manner: I gathered into this volume thirty of the questions, those that perhaps seemed more difficult, set out in brief chapters so that they could be found more easily.

The other names or words that you noted together, which could be solved more easily and briefly, I collected separately on other sheets and sent them at the same time to your fraternity.

I myself knew that many things in the same book were much more obscure than those that you judged should be asked of me. Yet I also knew that it often happens that someone who has already understood certain more obscure matters well—because he has found them sufficiently explained in the treatises of great authors—nevertheless remains uncertain and doubtful about some easier points. Those who were treating the deeper matters perhaps did not consider these worth asking about.

It also happens that not everything written by the Fathers can be possessed by everyone, and that readers remain ignorant of questions concerning the Scriptures—not because they have not been explained by teachers, but because the questions themselves are either unavailable or are not understood as questions by those who seek answers. This is evidently what has happened with many of the matters for which you both asked me for answers and received them.

In these answers, in which I tried to satisfy your requests by following the traces of the Fathers, I ask you, in return for the devotion owed to us, to remember to intercede for the health of our body and heart, together with the brothers who serve the Lord with you in those places.

And if you happen to find any of what I have written explained somewhere more suitably—as could very easily have happened—do not hesitate to send it to us promptly.

## Letter VIII, to Bishop Acca: On the exposition of the Gospel according to Mark

We have judged that, as we are about to write an exposition of the Gospel according to Mark, with the help of the Gospel’s own grace, we should first briefly indicate what occasion Mark had for writing the Gospel.

When the clear light of the true God had arisen for the city of Rome through the preaching of blessed Peter the Apostle, the word of truth so illuminated the minds of all by the pleasure of hearing it that those who listened to it daily were never satisfied.

Consequently, hearing alone was not sufficient for them. They earnestly begged Mark, his disciple, to commit to writing for their continual remembrance those things that Peter preached orally, so that at home and abroad they might persist in meditating on such teaching.

They did not cease their entreaties until they obtained what they had requested. When Peter discovered that, through the Holy Spirit, he had been deprived by a devout theft, he rejoiced. Considering their faith and devotion in this matter, he approved what had been done and handed the written work over to the churches to be read forever.

Clement describes these events in this way in the sixth book of his *Dispositions*. A similar testimony is given by the bishop of Hierapolis, Papias, who also says that Peter mentioned Mark in his first Epistle, which he wrote from the city of Rome, naming Rome figuratively as Babylon when he says: “The church that is elected in Babylon greets you, and so does Mark, my son.”

Having taken up the Gospel that he himself had produced, Mark went to Egypt. There, announcing Christ first at Alexandria, he established a church through such great teaching and self-control of life that he compelled all Christ’s followers to conform themselves to his example.

Finally, Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, seeing that the first church at Alexandria still retained Jewish practices, wrote a book about their way of life, as though in praise of his own people. Just as Luke relates that the believers in Jerusalem held everything in common, so Philo committed to memory what he observed taking place at Alexandria under Mark’s instruction.

They report that Mark was Israelite by nation and descended from a priestly lineage. After the Passion and resurrection of the Lord and Savior, he was instructed in the evangelical faith and its mysteries through the apostles’ preaching and became one of those about whom Luke writes: “A great many of the priests were obedient to the faith.”

Accordingly, since he had been trained in the ordinances of the Law, he set before the people whom he was calling to the faith an exemplary way of life in every respect. He also displayed the canonical observance of Easter, which was to be imitated by all the churches of Christ.

At the urging of your exhortation, beloved Acca, most honored among bishops, and of many other brothers, we shall undertake to write on this Gospel, placing here and there, as the Lord grants, especially those things that we have found in the examples of the venerable Fathers.

We shall also insert, where it seems appropriate, some of our own material modeled on their thought. I earnestly beg the reader that, if he considers these little works worthy of transcription, he preserve with careful writing the annotation of the names placed above in the margin, just as was done in the exposition of the Gospel of blessed Luke that, with the help of God’s grace, we composed many years ago.

May heavenly grace always protect your holiness as you pray for us. Above all, I beg in the Lord that all who may happen to read these writings deign to become intercessors with the merciful Judge for the frailties of my body and soul.

## Letter IX, to Acca: On the Gospel of Luke

To the most blessed and greatly desired Bishop Acca, Bede, the humble presbyter, sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

Truly marvelous, and marvelously true, is the saying of the outstanding teacher: “Love believes all things, hopes all things.” For, in letters sent to me, you say that you ask me to write something for you; yet while making your request, and before receiving any response accepting my agreement, you compose the mark of a preface for the little works you seek as though they had already been obtained and perfectly completed.

Before the foundation has been laid, before even the material has been brought, you send the keys with which the entrance should be secured, as though the building of so great a labor were already complete. Your friendly confidence presumes that a work which ought to be undertaken quickly should be entered upon quickly and completed still more quickly, making it shameful for me not to begin at once.

Certainly, nothing other than the unquestioning trust of mutual love produces this confidence, which—as was said—believes everything that can be done by a friend’s heart and hopes everything.

Therefore, as soon as I had read the pages of your most sweet holiness, I submitted myself to the labor of the work entrusted to me. To pass over the countless restraints of monastic service, I became at once my own dictator, notary, and copyist.

Gathering from here and there, as though they were the most distinguished and worthy craftsmen of such a great undertaking, the little works of the Fathers, I diligently examined what blessed Ambrose, what Augustine, what Gregory—most vigilant, in keeping with his name, and apostle of our people—what Jerome, interpreter of sacred history, and what the other Fathers had thought and said about the words of blessed Luke.

As you commanded, I immediately committed the material to sheets, sometimes in their very syllables and sometimes, for the sake of brevity, in my own words, as seemed appropriate.

Since it would have been laborious to insert their names individually and to indicate by name what had been said by each author, I thought it convenient to print the initial letters of their names from a distance in the margin and, by means of these, to indicate one by one where each of the Fathers’ material begins and where the discourse I have transferred ends. In all things I was concerned lest anyone say that I had stolen the sayings of my elders and composed them as though they were my own.

[Note: After examining many very old copies, we were unfortunately unable to find these signs in any of them. — Giles.]

I earnestly beg—and I adjure those who read this by the Lord—that if anyone should happen to judge these little works of ours, whatever their quality, worthy of transcription, they remember also to affix the aforementioned signs of the names, just as they find them in our copy. I have appended as well, wherever it seemed appropriate, certain things that—as I may put it in the words of Your Holiness—the Author of light disclosed to me, indications of my own labor. Although in meditating on divine law I am not able—as you yourself have written—to spend my days and nights in continual vigilance, I do not doubt that I have devoted no small amount of study to the Scriptures, and that I have been able to perceive—not only in this little work but in every reading whatsoever—only those things which the Author of light has deigned to disclose to me: that is, to discern them by judging rightly.

But as for your statement that some people wonder why, in the new interpretation of the Apocalypse, I assigned Matthew to the lion and Mark to the man, all those whom this troubles ought to have observed that I said this was not my own innovation, but was handed down in the ancient exposition of the Fathers. For I did not arrive at this opinion by myself; rather, I recalled that it had been expounded in this way by blessed Augustine, and I added briefly the grounds on which he made this assertion. It is not out of place, therefore, to set down his very words as well, showing what he thought about the evangelists and the living creatures symbolizing them. In this way our work may be protected from unjust criticism, and its argument strengthened by the authority of so great a teacher.

After first saying many beautiful and distinguished things about the evangelists in the first book of his *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, he continues among other matters as follows:

“Although each of them appears to have maintained a certain order of narration of his own, nevertheless none of them is found to have wished to write as though unaware of the preceding writer, or to have omitted things of which he was ignorant but which another is found to have written. Rather, as each was inspired, he added the appropriate cooperation of his own labor, without superfluity.

“Matthew, then, is understood to have undertaken the account of the Lord’s incarnation according to the royal line, and of many of his deeds and sayings according to the present life of human beings. Mark, following him like an attendant and abridger, appears to have done so. For with John alone he said nothing; with Luke alone, very little; with Matthew, however, very much, and almost as much as Matthew himself, often agreeing with him word for word, whether with him alone or with the others.

“Luke, on the other hand, appears to have been more concerned with the Lord’s priestly lineage and person. For in tracing the line back to David, he does not follow the royal genealogy, but proceeds through those who were not kings until he reaches Nathan, the son of David, who himself was not king. This is unlike Matthew, who descends through King Solomon and then follows the other kings in order, preserving in them—as we shall discuss later—a mystical number.

“The Lord Jesus Christ, one true king and one true priest, revealed that these two persons, separately commended by the Fathers, prefigured him: the one for ruling us, the other for cleansing us. A little later he says:

“‘According to his humanity, Christ became both king and priest. God gave him the throne of David his father, so that of his kingdom there might be no end, and so that Christ Jesus, the man, might be the mediator between God and human beings, interceding for us.’

“Luke did not have an abridger joined to him, as Mark was joined to Matthew; and this perhaps was not without some mystery, since kings are not accustomed to be without the service of attendants. Thus the one who undertook to narrate Christ in his royal person had attached to him, as it were, an attendant to follow his footsteps in a certain manner. But because the priest entered the Holy of Holies alone, Luke—whose concern was with Christ’s priesthood—did not have a companion following him who might, in some manner, abridge his narrative.

“Nevertheless, these three evangelists differed chiefly in their treatment of those things which Christ accomplished temporally through human flesh. John, however, principally contemplated the very divinity of the Lord, by which he is equal to the Father, and took particular care to commend it in his Gospel to the extent that he believed sufficient for human beings. Thus he is carried far above these three, so that you may see them, in a certain sense, moving about on earth with Christ the man, while he passed beyond the cloud that covers the whole earth and reached the clear heaven. There, with the sharpest and most steadfast vision of mind, he saw ‘in the beginning the Word of the Lord with God,’ through whom all things were made, and recognized that the Word himself became flesh in order to dwell among us.

“Again, a little later, he says:

“‘Hence it seems to me that those who interpreted the four creatures of the Apocalypse as signifying the four evangelists attended more plausibly to the matter who understood the lion in Matthew, the man in Mark, the calf in Luke, and the eagle in John, than those who assigned the man to Matthew, the eagle to Mark, and the lion to John. They wished to derive a conjecture from the beginnings of the books, rather than from the whole intention of the evangelists, which ought to have been examined more carefully.

“‘For it is much more fitting that the one who chiefly commended the royal person of Christ should be understood as signified by the lion. Thus also in the Apocalypse the lion is mentioned together with the royal tribe, where it is said: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered.” According to Matthew, the Magi are said to have come from the East to seek and worship the king who had appeared to them as having been born through the star; and King Herod himself feared the infant Christ as king, and, in order to kill him, slaughtered so many little children.

“‘No one has doubted that Luke is signified by the calf because of the priest’s principal sacrifice. For there the narrative begins with the priest Zechariah. There the kinship of Mary and Elizabeth is recalled. There the mysteries of the first priesthood are narrated as fulfilled in the infant Christ. And whatever other details may be carefully observed make it evident that Luke’s concern was with the person of the priest.

“‘Mark, however, who chose to narrate neither royal nor priestly lineage, nor kinship nor consecration, and yet is shown to have occupied himself with those things which Christ accomplished as a man, appears to signify only the figure of the man among those four creatures.

“‘These three creatures—the lion, the man, and the calf—walk upon the earth. Hence these three evangelists are chiefly occupied with the things Christ accomplished in the flesh and with the commands he gave to those bearing mortal flesh for the conduct of mortal life. But John, like an eagle, flies above the clouds of human weakness and gazes upon the light of unchangeable truth with the keenest and most steadfast eyes of the heart.’”

I have inserted in the preface of this letter a few of blessed Augustine’s testimonies, excerpted from many more, to repel the slander of complainers. As has been said, may they provide protection for our earlier work and set an honorable seal upon the present one. May the grace of heavenly assistance preserve Your Holy Paternity, who prays for us, and always strengthen you for the defense of his holy Church.

## LETTER X, TO ACCA

### On the Exposition of the Acts

To the most dearly desired and truly blessed lord in Christ, Acca, bishop, Bede sends perpetual salvation in the Lord.

I have received very frequent letters from Your Blessedness, in which you have deigned to admonish me not to allow the keenness of my mind to grow sluggish and fall asleep through idle leisure, but to devote myself daily, watchful and tireless, to meditating upon and examining the Scriptures. You also urged me, after the exposition of the Apocalypse of the holy evangelist John—which, at the request of our brother Eusebius, I completed in three books and immediately intended to have transcribed for you—to devote whatever labor I could to an explanation of the blessed evangelist Luke, following in the footsteps of the Fathers.

Because I have not yet been able to do this—frightened, on the one hand, by the immense size of the work and, on the other, hindered by the necessity of pressing affairs, which you know better than I do—nevertheless, lest the authority of your request be disregarded, I have done what I could in the meantime. I have sent you a little work on the Acts of the Apostles, which, having been composed only a few days ago, I had written on parchment and corrected as quickly as the time allowed, so that your most sacred wish might not be impeded. In it I have attempted, as far as I could, to clarify those matters that appeared either to have been accomplished mystically or to have been expressed obscurely.

In this little work I was assisted by many other writers of the Catholic faith, but especially by Arator, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church. He went through the whole book in order in heroic verse and interspersed several flowers of allegory in the same meter, giving me the opportunity either to gather other things from them or to explain the same things more plainly.

As blessed Jerome says, the Acts of the Apostles seem indeed to present a bare history and to weave the infancy of the nascent Church. But if we know that their author Luke was a physician—whose praise is in the Gospel—we likewise perceive that all his words are medicine for the sick soul. Of these matters we shall explain some according to the measure of our small ability.

First, we shall point out that the evangelist Luke, as has been said, was, according to the tradition of the ancient interpreters of the Church, highly skilled in the medical art and knew Greek letters better than Hebrew ones. Hence his speech, both in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, is more polished and bears the scent of secular eloquence, and he uses Greek testimonies more often than Hebrew ones.

From this arises something that greatly astonishes me. Because of the slowness of my understanding, I am struck with the greatest wonder and scarcely know how to investigate the reason why, when in the Hebrew truth ten generations are found from the Flood to Abraham, Luke himself—who, with the Holy Spirit guiding his pen, could not have written anything false—preferred to place eleven generations in the Gospel according to the Seventy Interpreters, adding Cainan.

In the preface to his Gospel he says that he seemed good to him to write carefully and in order, because many had undertaken to do so. We must understand him to mean those who possess great authority in the Church, because they were unable to accomplish what they had undertaken. But he not only carried his narrative as far as the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, thereby earning a place worthy of his labor among the four authoritative books of evangelical Scripture; he also wrote what was subsequently accomplished through the apostles—what he considered sufficient to build up the faith of readers or hearers—in such a way that his alone has been considered worthy of belief in the Church as an account of the Acts of the Apostles, while all those who dared to write the apostles’ deeds and sayings without the faith that was required have been rejected.

For Mark and Luke wrote at a time when their work could be approved not only by the Church of Christ but also by the apostles themselves, who were still living in the flesh. By the Lord’s will it was arranged that not only the apostles who had seen Christ’s deeds, but also the disciples who had learned them by hearing, should record Christ’s deeds and sayings, so that succeeding teachers of the Church might receive both the confidence and the authority to preach and write about what they had not seen.

Luke composed the Acts of the Apostles, and especially of blessed Paul, whose constant companion he was on his journeys, just as he himself had seen them. The whole course of this work, as far as we have been able to observe from the histories of others, covers twenty-eight years: six years of Tiberius Caesar, four of Gaius, and fourteen of Claudius. Under this emperor the apostle Peter came to Rome; in his fourth year there was a famine, and in his eighth year the Jews were expelled from Rome. Then come four years of Nero, during the last two of which blessed Paul remained in Rome under free custody. From this we understand that the book was composed in that same city.

To distinguish the same periods also by the kings of the Jews: the tetrarchs Herod, Philip, and Lysanias ruled for six years; Herod the king, also called Agrippa, who perished at Caesarea, for seven years; and Agrippa, his son, under whom Paul was sent to Rome, for fifteen years. From that time twelve years remain until the overthrow of Jerusalem.

I have set this out more distinctly so that, when you reread the history of this little book, you may clearly recognize what happened under each period.

I have also sent a brief explanation of the letter of the most blessed evangelist John. I excerpted most of it from the homilies of Saint Augustine, which are extended with the broadest sweetness, acting as a concise abridger. At the end I added several matters from my own labor. If you find anything useful in either work, ascribe it to God’s gifts. If anything is superfluous, have compassion on my weakness. May the almighty Lord preserve Your Blessedness, who intercedes for us, safe forever for the governance of the Church.

## LETTER XI

### Preface on the Revision of the Acts

We know that the outstanding teacher and bishop Augustine, when he was advanced in age, composed books of *Revisions* concerning certain little works that he had written as a young man. His purpose was to commit to written memorials and leave for posterity to read what he had learned over time, through repeated practice in reading and through the gift of heavenly generosity—not as one ashamed of his former ignorance, but rather as one rejoicing in his own progress.

We too have been pleased to imitate his diligence according to the measure of our ability. Thus, after the exposition of the Acts of the Apostles that we wrote several years ago, at the request of the venerable Bishop Acca, with all the skill we possessed, we shall now compose in the same volume a brief work of revision. Our principal aim is either to add what was said too briefly or to correct what appeared to have been said in a manner different from what was satisfactory.

In it we have also taken care briefly to mention certain passages that we saw placed differently, or with more or less material, in the Greek. Whether they were omitted or expressed differently through the negligence of the translator, or corrupted or left out through the carelessness of scribes, we have not yet been able to determine. For I do not dare to suspect that the Greek copy itself was falsified. Therefore I warn the reader to read these passages wherever we have included them as a matter of learning, but not to insert them into his own volume as though they were corrected readings—unless, perhaps, he finds that they were anciently translated in this manner in the Latin codex of his edition.

Jerome, too, explains many testimonies of the Old Testament according to the Hebrew truth; nevertheless, he did not wish either to translate these passages in such a form in our copies or to have us correct them. For example:

“I shall not look upon a human being any longer, nor upon an inhabitant; my generation has ceased”; and:

“His tomb shall be glorious”; and:

“From the ends of the earth we have heard praises”; and:

“Everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.”

He says that in Hebrew it is written: “He shall release seven acts of vengeance”; and: “From the wings of the earth”; and: “His rest shall be glorious”; and: “An inhabitant of quietness; my generation has been taken away.”

He wished the reader to know that these are found in this form among the Hebrews for the sake of learning alone, not for the purpose of correction—

## LETTER XII, TO EUSEBIUS

To his most beloved brother Eusebius, Bede sends greetings.

The Apocalypse of Saint John, in which God has deigned to reveal in words and figures the wars and internal fires of his Church, seems to me, brother Eusebius, to be divided into seven sections.

In the first, after an ample preface intended to strengthen the faith of the weak, and after enumerating the Lord’s sufferings and subsequent glories, the Church sees one like the Son of Man clothed accordingly. After recalling those things that have been or will be accomplished in particular in the seven Churches of Asia, he describes their struggles and palms of victory. In the sixth place he deliberately places the Jews who are to be added to the Church, and announces the future temptation of the whole world, promising that he himself will come soon. In the seventh he places lukewarm Laodicea: “For when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?”

In the second section, after describing the four creatures and the twenty-four elders in the seat of God, he sees the Lamb, when the seven seals of the sealed book have been opened, disclosing the future conflicts and triumphs of the Church. Here, in accordance with the custom of this book, he preserves the order up to the sixth number; then, passing over the seventh, he recapitulates and, as though following the order, brings two narratives to a conclusion with the seventh.

But this recapitulation itself must be understood according to its several locations. At one time he recapitulates from the beginning of the Passion; at another, from the middle of the period; at another, speaking only of the final distress itself or of what occurred not long before it. Nevertheless, he consistently observes this principle: he recapitulates from the sixth.

The third section, under the appearance of seven angels sounding trumpets, describes various events of the Church.

The fourth, under the figure of a woman in labor and a dragon pursuing her, discloses the labors and victories of the same Church and repays each army with worthy rewards. Here the words and deeds of the seven angels are also recalled, though not in the same manner as above. For with mystical skill he observes this number almost everywhere, while it is also characteristic of this same John, in the Gospels and Letters as well, to say nothing half-heartedly or briefly.

The fifth section pours out upon the earth, through seven angels, the seven final plagues.

The sixth concerns the condemnation of the great prostitute, that is, of the impious city.

The seventh shows the adornment of the Lamb’s bride, namely, holy Jerusalem descending from heaven from God.

I have also thought it worthwhile to recall briefly the seven rules of Tychonius, a man highly learned among his own people, by which those devoted to understanding the Scriptures are greatly assisted.

The first concerns the Lord and his body, when the transition is made from the head to the body or from the body to the head, while one does not depart from one and the same person. One person speaks, saying: “As to a bridegroom he placed a mitre upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with ornamentation.” Nevertheless, it must be understood which of these expressions applies to the head and which to the body—that is, which to Christ and which to the Church.

The second concerns the Lord’s divided body, or rather the Lord’s true and simulated body, as Saint Augustine preferred to call it. The Church says: “I am dark and beautiful.” But she said that she was both because of communion in the sacraments and because of the temporary mixture within one net of good and bad fish. For the tents of Kedar belong to Ishmael, because he will not be heir together with the son of the free woman.

The third concerns promises and the law; it may also be called, in another way, the rule concerning spirit and letter, or grace and commandment. To Saint Augustine this appears more a great question than a rule to be applied in resolving questions. For it is this very matter that the Pelagians, through failing to understand it, either made the basis of their heresy or increased it.

The fourth concerns species and genus. A species is a part, while a genus is the whole of which it is a part. Thus each city is part of an entire province, and each province is part of the whole world. Hence these terms have even entered common knowledge, so that the uneducated understand what has been established specifically and what generally in any imperial command.

The same occurs with human beings. For example, things said about Solomon exceed his own measure and become clear when they are referred instead to Christ and the Church, of which he is a part. Yet the species is not always exceeded. Often things are said that apply most clearly either to the species itself or perhaps only to it. But when Scripture passes from species to genus, as though it were still speaking about the species, the reader’s attention must remain vigilant.

He sets down the fifth rule, which he calls the rule concerning times. In my view, however, it may also be called the rule concerning numbers. He says that it operates through the figure of synecdoche or through legitimate numbers. Synecdoche is a figure in which the whole is expressed by a part or the part by the whole.

This manner of speech also resolves the question concerning Christ’s resurrection. The final part of the day on which he suffered cannot amount to one of the three days unless it is understood as the whole day, including the preceding night; nor can the night during the final part of which he rose amount to one of the three nights unless the entire day is understood, including the dawning of the Lord’s Day. Otherwise there cannot be three days and three nights during which he foretold that he would be in the heart of the earth.

By legitimate numbers he means those that divine Scripture commends in a particularly prominent way, such as seven, ten, and twelve. These generally signify either the totality of time or the perfection of some matter. Thus, “Seven times a day I have praised you” means nothing other than: “His praise is always in my mouth.”

The same values apply when these numbers are multiplied either by ten, as in seventy and seven hundred—so that Jeremiah’s seventy years can also be understood spiritually as the whole period during which the Church is among strangers—or by themselves, as ten times ten makes one hundred and twelve times twelve makes one hundred forty-four, the number by which the totality of the saints is signified in the Apocalypse.

Tychonius calls the sixth rule recapitulation. In Scripture certain matters are narrated as though they followed in temporal order or as though they were related in continuous sequence, while the narrative secretly returns to earlier matters that had been passed over.

For example, in Genesis we read: “These are the sons of Noah in their tribes and languages. From these the islands of the nations were divided upon the earth.” Immediately afterward: “Now the whole earth had one language and the same words.” This appears to be said as though, at the very time when they were dispersed, all had one language, whereas the narrative was instead secretly adding by recapitulation: “This is how the languages were divided.”

The seventh rule of the same author concerns the devil and his body. Sometimes something is said about the devil that must be recognized as applying not to him personally but to his body. Thus the Lord, explaining to blessed Job the frauds and powers of that enemy, says among other things: “Will he multiply prayers to you, or speak soft words to you?”

For the devil himself is nowhere read to repent, but his body, which will be condemned at the end, is to say: “Lord, Lord, open to us.”

Whoever examines these rules attentively will find that they operate not only in the Apocalypse—that is, in the revelation of the holy apostle John, which Tychonius himself both understood vigorously and expounded truthfully and with sufficient Catholic orthodoxy—except in those passages where, seeking to defend the schism of his own party, the Donatists, he laments the persecutions that they themselves suffered under the religious emperor Valentinian as heretics, when their churches and peoples, houses and possessions were handed over to Catholic control and their priests confined in exile; calling these martyrdoms, he boasts that they were foretold in the same Apocalypse—but also throughout all canonical Scripture, and especially the prophetic books.

In this work we too have followed the sense of that author. For the sake of brevity we omitted some matters that he placed externally, but we took care to add many more which appeared plain to him, as to a gifted man—and one who, as was said of him, blossomed like a rose among thorns—and not worthy of investigation, insofar as we could grasp them either through the teaching of masters, the memory of our reading, or even the capacity of our own understanding.

For we also have this instruction: that, having received the talents, we should return them to the Lord with interest.

When it had been decided to divide the work in question into three little books for the sake of revealing its meaning—for, as blessed Augustine says, somehow the reader’s attention is refreshed at the end of a book just as a traveler’s labor is refreshed by reaching an inn—we nevertheless thought that the same uninterrupted sequence of chapters should be preserved throughout, so that those seeking particular passages might find them more easily, according to the brief divisions that I had once placed at the head of the little book.

I judged that provision should be made for the sluggishness of our nation—that is, the English—which received the seed of the faith only recently, in the time of blessed Pope Gregory, and has cultivated it rather lukewarmly, especially as regards reading. I therefore resolved not only to clarify the meanings but also to condense the statements. For clear brevity is usually impressed upon the memory more deeply than prolonged disputation.

Farewell in Christ, most beloved brother, and deign always to remember your Bede.

## LETTER XIII, TO ACCA

### On the Allegorical Interpretation of the First Book of Samuel

“Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.” And elsewhere: “All these things happened to them in figure. They were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.”

The blessed apostle Peter too, recalling the times of the Lord’s incarnation, Passion, and subsequent glory, says among other things: “And all the prophets, from Samuel and afterward, who spoke, also announced these days.”

If everything was written for our correction, instruction, or consolation—not only Jeremiah and Isaiah and others like them, who marked future events in their words, but also Samuel, Jonah, and Ezra, together with those like them, who recorded things already past, whether their own deeds and sayings or those of others—then these men too indicate these days, namely, the days shining with the light of the new grace.

We must therefore apply ourselves with the greatest diligence and strive, each according to his ability, with the help of Christ’s grace, lest through our sluggishness or carelessness we pass by as though they were foreign to us those things that were written for our sake.

Let us attend carefully and vigilantly to the sense in which we may gain correction from them, the manner in which we may gain instruction, and the understanding through which we may gain consolation; and to the way in which all things speak of and announce these days. Let us imitate, according to the capacity of our small intellect, that learned scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven who brings forth new and old things from his treasure.

For if we care to bring forth from the treasure of the Scriptures only old things—that is, if, in Jewish fashion, we follow only the figures of the letter—what do we gain from the things we read or hear amid the correction demanded by daily sins, the consolation needed amid the increasing troubles of the world, and the spiritual instruction required amid the countless errors of this life?

When we open the book of blessed Samuel, for example, and find that Elkanah, one man, had two wives, what benefit is there for us—who, by the custom of ecclesiastical life, are resolved to remain far from a wife’s embrace and to live celibate—unless we also know how to draw from such sayings and others like them an allegorical sense that restores us inwardly through lively chastisement, instruction, and consolation?

Therefore, prompted by your frequent exhortation, most beloved and most desired Acca—of all the prelates dwelling on earth—and relying upon your prayers, I shall examine the writings of that mentioned prophet, who was then called “the Seer,” and shall commit to writing whatever spiritual and mystical meaning I may be able to perceive, through the gift of him who gave him the ability to see many spiritual things.

After whatever exposition of the sayings of blessed Luke in which he describes the evangelical deeds of the Lord himself and of his apostles, I shall also strive to prove that this most holy Nazarene of the Lord from his mother’s womb fulfilled in his writings the office of an evangelist no less than that of a historian. For he himself faithfully set forth all the mysteries of the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, in the figurative form of a true history, but with the fullest possible expression.

Finally, to say nothing of other matters, consider David’s lineage, his birthplace, his pastoral office, the redness and beauty of his appearance, the manner of his anointing, the distinction of his virtues, the weight of his tribulations, and the glory of the kingdom once promised to him. You will see how many mysteries of evangelical faith and truth have been gathered into each of these details.

But these matters will be explained more plainly in their proper place. For now, relying solely upon heavenly assistance and following the footsteps of the Fathers, I shall undertake the work assigned to me in order.

If, as I desire, my labor proves useful and beneficial to many, I hope that the Lord will grant me a great reward together with them. If not, nevertheless my diligence cannot prove fruitless, since it has not permitted me throughout so long a period to remain idle in this labor or to indulge my mind in useless things.

Come, then, let us see what the prophet Samuel, who spoke and announced these days, made the beginning of his speech and announcement. Proceeding in order, with the assistance of blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles, who taught in full how everything is to be fitted to these days, let us seek how each individual matter is to be fitted to them.

## LETTER XIV

### On the Encampments of the Children of Israel

To the most beloved lord in Christ, and the prelate always to be named with every honor, Acca, your faithful servant Bede sends greetings.

By sending me certain questions to solve, most beloved of prelates—questions that do not all have the same degree of difficulty—you compel me to turn aside for a little while from the exposition of blessed Samuel the prophet, which I had begun, in order to examine Moses and Isaiah.

Of these questions, the first, which concerns the history of past times, will perhaps become clear without difficulty, or else may remain hidden without great danger. The second, however, concerns the faith regarding future things; if it is understood otherwise than it should be, we must beware lest we fall into the pit of a most abominable heresy.

You ask, therefore, to which years, and to how many of them, the encampments of the children of Israel—forty-two in all, as they are counted in the final part of the Book of Numbers—should be assigned during that very long journey undertaken from Egypt to the promised land.

It is clear to all readers that, although the years of this journey are concluded at nearly the same number as the encampments, nevertheless the Israelites are by no means said to have spent a separate year in each camp.

Here, as I usually do in all matters, I readily tell Your Blessedness what I think: namely, that these same camps or encampments correspond to only three courses of years—the first, the second, and the fortieth from the departure out of Egypt.

The first of these years contains twelve encampments, clearly distinguished. The first encampment was entered on the twelfth day of the first month; the last, the wilderness of Sinai, was entered on the first day of the third month and was not left for eleven consecutive months, during which the tabernacle was constructed and the law taught.

Of these twelve encampments, the Book of Exodus names only nine explicitly; the remaining three it passes over without distinction under the name of the wilderness of Sin, which is said to lie between Elim and Sinai.

The second year comprises twenty-one encampments. In the historical narrative they are all indiscriminately included under the name of the wilderness of Paran; only the first, the second, and the last—that is, the Graves of Craving, Hazeroth, and Kadesh—are distinguished by their names. But in the catalogue of the encampments it is carefully shown both how many there were and by what names they were called.

The first encampment, namely the Graves of Craving, was entered on the twenty-second day of the second month of that same second year. For, as Scripture says, in the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, they broke camp from the wilderness of Sinai; “and the cloud,” it says, “rested in the wilderness of Paran.” They set out from the mountain of the Lord on a journey of three days, until they came to the place of encampment which, appropriately, received the name Graves of Craving because of the people’s desire for Egyptian meat. [Col. 0700A]

It is not stated on what day or in what month of that year the last of these encampments, Kadesh, was entered. Nevertheless, since it too was situated in the wilderness of Paran, it is not left unsaid that it was reached in that same year. For it is written:

> “And the people did not move from that place until Miriam had been recalled; and they set out from Hazeroth and pitched their tents in the wilderness of Paran. There the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Send men to inspect the land of Canaan.’”

To prevent anyone from supposing that this command was given and carried out at the encampment immediately following Hazeroth, but rather to understand that it was fulfilled at the last of those included under the name of the wilderness of Paran, let us consider what is written below: [Col. 0700B]

> “And the explorers returned from surveying the land after forty days, having traversed the whole region, and came to Moses and Aaron and to the entire assembly of the children of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, which is at Kadesh.”

Moses himself also says to the people in Deuteronomy:

> “And when you had come to Kadesh-barnea, I said to you: ‘You have come to the mountain of the Amorites, which the Lord our God is about to give us. See the land which the Lord your God is giving you; go up and take possession of it.’ And you all approached me and said: ‘Send men to inspect the land,’ and so forth.”

That they reached this same encampment in the second year after their departure from Egypt, although on account of the sin of their murmuring they deserved to turn back from it, wander for a long time through the wilderness, and fall everywhere, Moses testifies in what follows: [Col. 0700C]

> “So you remained at Kadesh-barnea for a long time. Then we set out from there and came into the wilderness that leads to the Red Sea, as the Lord had told me, and we went around Mount Seir for a long time.”

And below:

> “The time during which we travelled from Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the torrent Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation of fighting men had perished from the camp, as the Lord had sworn.”

Zered is not the name of an encampment—I mean one of those forty-two—but the name of a torrent. After crossing the thirty-eighth encampment, which is called Iye-abarim, they came to it, as we read in the book of Numbers. “And leaving it,” the text says, “they pitched their tents opposite Arnon, which is in the wilderness and extends along the borders of the Amorites.” That this happened in the fortieth year is hidden from us. [Col. 0700D]

That year—the fortieth and last—contains ten encampments along the very long route through the wilderness. The first of these was reached only after great hardship: the same Kadesh of the wilderness of Zin which, thirty-eight years earlier, as has been said, they had left behind when they turned back on account of their transgression.

Concerning it, Scripture says:

> “And the children of Israel and the whole congregation came into the wilderness of Zin in the first month, and the people stayed at Kadesh. Miriam died there and was buried there. And when the people lacked water, they gathered together against Moses and Aaron,”

and so forth, up to the passage:

> “This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarrelled with the Lord and he was sanctified among them.” [Col. 0701A]

It should be noted that Scripture places this same Kadesh both in the wilderness of Paran and in the wilderness of Zin. From this it may be inferred that, according to the customary usage of place-names, the part of the wilderness of Paran in which Kadesh lies was specifically called Zin.

This Zin, however, is not the same place as that through which they passed immediately after crossing the Red Sea, between Elim and Sinai, but is an entirely different place, written with different letters among the Hebrews.

The second encampment of that fortieth year was Mount Hor, where Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month. The last was the plain of Moab, beyond the Jordan opposite Jericho, where they remained, meditating on Deuteronomy, until, after Moses’ death, under the leadership of Joshua, they crossed the deep channel of the Jordan on dry ground on the first day of the tenth month.

Thus the encampments of the first year number twelve; those of the second, twenty-one; and, in the last year, Kadesh itself—which is the twenty-first—and nine others, making forty-two in all. [The transmitted enumeration is arithmetically difficult.] [Col. 0701B]

Here we must examine more carefully why the legislator, having written out the catalogue of three years with such painstaking care, preferred to pass over the remaining years in silence, so that places of encampment separated by so long a span of time—or rather of ages—are linked together in the continuous narrative as though they followed one another immediately:

> “And departing from Hebron they pitched their tents at Ezion-geber. From there they set out and came into the wilderness of Zin; this is Kadesh. Departing from Kadesh, they pitched their tents at Mount Hor.”

Yet the earlier passages, investigated more carefully, show that in the second year of their journey they came from Ezion-geber, and that, after the long detours of thirty-eight years, they finally left that same Kadesh and came to Mount Hor. This should not be understood as having been done and written in this manner without purpose, but for the sake of a great mystery. Subject to a more subtle treatment, I think it should be understood morally as follows. [Col. 0701C]

The sequence of the encampments by which those liberated from Egyptian slavery are brought forward to the promised land—as blessed Jerome explains more fully in the book he composed on this subject—is a lofty ascent of spiritual virtues. By these virtues the Church of Christ, and every faithful soul, hastens upward from this valley of tears toward the heights, in the hope of freedom, to the place appointed for it: namely, to behold the God of gods in Zion.

As long as we advance safely in good works, we proceed from virtue to virtue, travelling through the wilderness of this thirsty world as though through a series of camps and encampments, under God’s leadership, all upright and worthy of the sight of God. But whenever, through the intrusion of various vices, we stray from the path of truth on which we had begun, we cannot immediately ascend to the higher degrees of virtue. Instead, we must meanwhile return gradually, through repentance, from the lowest failures of our wretched mind to the higher things, until, having produced worthy fruits of repentance, we come back to that summit from which we fell. [Col. 0701D]

Then, for a time, we may again pursue the journey of virtue, having put off the old person with his deeds and put on the new person, who has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness. This is signified by the death and burial in the wilderness of the sinful fathers, together with the vigorous youth of those who were born and grew to maturity there—a youth worthy to enter the kingdom of the heavenly promise after overcoming the river of death.

So it comes about in the renewed youth of our good conduct, as eagles [the syntax is corrupt], that, despite the repeated attacks of evil spirits upon such great spiritual grace, we are able to establish firmly the camps of heavenly progress. These camps are pleasing not only to the divine gaze but also worthy of the writings and praise of spiritual fathers. [Col. 0702A]

This concludes what I have to say about your first question, dearest friend. Since it was clear to those who could see and had already been dealt with in the course of the historical narrative, I hastened to write back as soon as I had read the letters of Your Blessedness. As for the testimony of the Prophet which you likewise sent to be explained, if, by God’s permission, I am able to discern anything worth remembering, I shall take care not to conceal that from you for long.

May the holy and undivided Trinity preserve Your Blessedness, who prays for its Church, in safety.

## LETTER XV

### On what Isaiah says: “And they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited.”

[Col. 0702B]

To the most blessed lord, always revered with the deepest affection, the holy bishop Acca: Bede, the humblest of the servants of Christ, sends greetings.

Since, when replying hastily to your first proposal, I thought it more appropriate to consider the second—which seemed to me more obscure—at a more suitable time, I shall now explain it according to the ability of my small intellect, insofar as it may be stated and understood in a catholic manner and without danger to the faith.

You ask—and this is entirely worthy of inquiry, although I do not know whether it ought to be asked of people like me—how we should understand what Isaiah says, among other things, when writing about the day of judgment:

> “And it shall come to pass in that day that the Lord will visit the host of heaven in the heights and the kings of the earth who are upon the earth. And they shall be gathered together in the gathering of one bundle into the pit, and they shall be shut up there in prison; and after many days they shall be visited. And the moon shall blush, and the sun shall be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and is glorified in the sight of his elders.” [Col. 0702C]

You say that you were led to ask this by reading the third of our little books on Samuel. There, while interpreting the stone fixed in Goliath’s forehead as signifying the eternal punishment of the devil, his angels, and their companions—a punishment from which they will never be completely released—we recalled this passage. Yet we explained not how it should be understood, but how it should not be understood: namely, that those to whom it will be said at the final judgment, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire,” are not to be liberated after many days.

For the same prophet cannot contradict himself. Elsewhere he says:

> “And they shall see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me; their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.”

But if the question is how the passage should be understood, I openly confess to Your Holiness, my lord most beloved in Christ, that I do not dare say that I have understood what the prophet Isaiah meant or wished to be understood by this statement. Nevertheless, I do not refuse, at your command, to disclose what I myself think, as I believe, purely and in a catholic manner. [Col. 0702D]

First, I examined more carefully what blessed Jerome said in his beautiful work on this same prophet:

> “But what follows—‘And after many days they shall be visited’—seems to applaud my friends, who assign repentance to the devil and demons, saying that after many ages they will be visited by the Lord. But they should consider that divine Scripture does not say explicitly, ‘They shall be visited by the Lord,’ or ‘They shall be visited by angels,’ but simply, ‘They shall be visited.’ From this ambiguity of the verb, both remedy and correction may be understood: after the righteous have received their rewards, those condemned may be visited in everlasting punishments. Yet it must be known that human frailty cannot know God’s judgment, nor pass sentence concerning the magnitude and measure of punishments, which has been left to the Lord’s decision.”

By these words that most learned man both refutes the error of those who assert that, even after a long time, the devil, together with his angels and condemned human beings, will be rescued from the punishments of the completed final judgment, and demonstrates that the prophet’s words may be understood to mean that, after the righteous have received their eternal rewards at the judgment, the condemned wicked will be visited according to an order unknown to us in everlasting punishment. [Col. 0703A]

As for the possibility that they will receive some slight remedy—not, however, that they will be released from all torments—or that they will instead be subjected to an even harsher correction, whatever its nature, extent, or time of arrival may be, this is disclosed only to the knowledge of the eternal Judge.

Yet nowhere else in Scripture do we read anything that suggests such an alteration in the punishments of the wicked after the day of judgment. Some, taking as support for this interpretation a passage from the prophet Habakkuk, cite: “In wrath you will remember mercy.” This is ambiguous. Another matter, however, is perfectly clear: because of the wrath occasioned by human transgression, God expelled human beings from the joys of paradise into this valley of tears; nevertheless, he did not remove from them, as he did from the angels who fell from heaven, the hope of repentance. Indeed, he supplied them abundantly with the means of recovering salvation. [Col. 0703B]

The phrase “the mentioned spirit, going and not returning” [the source is syntactically corrupt] may be understood to mean that, whenever we sin, God—who is always tranquil in himself—appears to grow angry when he punishes us, yet remembers to show mercy immediately to those who repent worthily. The following sentence about the prophet’s prayer for the ignorant is corrupt: it appears to say that God, though angry for a time at the sinner, immediately had mercy on the one who prayed (*ignorantem peccanti ad oram irascens statim sit misertus oranti*). Similar is the Psalmist’s statement:

> “Will God forget to show mercy, or will he restrain his mercy in his anger?”

This and all similar statements, as well as:

> “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and I will add your blows sevenfold,”

and other passages of this kind, certainly apply to the state of this present age, in which the saints sing to the Lord of mercy and judgment. [Col. 0703C]

It is uncertain whether they also apply to the future age, in which the words of another psalm are fulfilled:

> “For you will repay each one according to his works.”

Since Scripture does not plainly speak of any such future change after the universal judgment, there are those [printed *est*, “is”; conjecture *sunt*, “are”] who think that the prophetic verse which says that the kings of the earth, shut up in the prison of the pit, will visit after many days [printed *visitaturos*, “about to visit”; conjecture *visitandos*, “to be visited”] is to be fulfilled not after the long period following the completion of the final judgment, but during the judgment itself.

They understand it in this way: people guilty of greater crimes, gathered into the pit of misery for many days before the judgment, will at the time of judgment be briefly called forth from the pit through the resurrection; then, once judgment has been completed, they will be shut up again in the same pit with the bodies they have received. [Col. 0703D]

The verses that follow will likewise be fulfilled at the time of this future visitation after many days—that is, at the time of the resurrection and the approaching judgment:

> “And the moon shall blush and the sun shall be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem.”

These things will occur on the day of judgment, when Christ will reveal both the glory of his kingdom to all and the blessedness of his vision to the saints.

Prophecy often speaks of this, and the Gospel does so more openly, when the Lord says:

> “But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give its light, and the stars of heaven shall fall, and the powers that are in heaven shall be shaken. And then they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory.” [Col. 0704A]

Nor should anyone think that the words, “And it shall come to pass in that day: the Lord shall visit,” contradict this interpretation, as though something that is known to be fulfilled many days before the judgment could not be said to occur “in that day.”

When Scripture speaks of the day of judgment, it often designates not only that day but also “that hour,” using those expressions to indicate the periods immediately preceding the judgment. Thus the apostle John, writing so long before the day of judgment, says:

> “Little children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that Antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have arisen. Hence we know that it is the last hour.”

The Lord himself, in the Gospel, after saying:

> “On the day when Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulfur from heaven and destroyed them all; so it will be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed,”

immediately added:

> “In that hour, let the one who is on the housetop, with his possessions in the house, not come down to take them; and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back.” [Col. 0704B]

Since he had first mentioned the day of revelation and then immediately added “that hour,” it might seem that no other hour could be intended than the hour in which that revelation would occur. Yet, after naming the hour, the Lord indicated not what would happen on the day of the revealed judgment itself, but what would have to be done before the day on which the judgment would be revealed.

For when the Lord rained fire and sulfur from heaven upon Sodom, no one had time to return in repentance for his sins, any more than he had time to advance further in them. Nor, once the Son of Man has been revealed, will anyone have either the opportunity or the will to reclaim the desires that, in ascending to higher things, he had left behind together with the world, or to abandon the fruits of spiritual virtues in whose practice he had until then been engaged. [Col. 0704C]

This is what is meant by descending to take the possessions left in the house, and by turning back perversely from one’s work in the field: the unexpected coming of the Judge will seize everyone and compel them only to fear and to consider the recompense for their works.

Thus the Apostle testifies that the last hour had already come at the very beginnings of the New Testament. And when the Lord, speaking about the day of judgment and the revelation of his coming, suddenly added what should be avoided in that hour and what the faithful should do—although it is clearly proved that these warnings do not concern the very moment of the coming judgment, but rather the times immediately approaching it—he was speaking of the period concerning which it had been promised:

> “The days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you: ‘Look here,’”

and shortly afterward:

> “And just as it happened in the days of Noah, so shall it be in the days of the Son of Man: they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage.” [Col. 0704D]

How much more, then, could the prophet, whose prophetic vision reached across so many ages of the New Testament and extended far ahead to observe the events of the final age, while speaking of the end of the world, insert alongside one another events which he saw as occurring not when the consummation had already arrived, but while it was still approaching?

It is therefore useful to examine more carefully the verses immediately preceding this prophetic passage about which the question is raised, and to explain how some pertain to the day of judgment and others to the times near the judgment. [Col. 0705A]

“Transgressing,” he says, “they have transgressed, and by the transgression of transgressors they have transgressed.”

Who does not see that these things occur before the day of judgment, when, as the Lord foretold:

> “Many will be scandalized, and they will betray one another and hate one another. And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. And because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold.”

Then he adds:

> “Fear and the pit and the snare are upon you, inhabitant of the earth. And it shall come to pass that whoever flees from the voice of fear will fall into the pit, and whoever escapes from the pit will be caught in the snare.”

It is clear that these things will come in the times when judgment is approaching, but has not yet appeared—namely, in the time of Antichrist. [Col. 0705B]

For when the Lord comes from heaven and all are raised in the twinkling of an eye, who will have empty time to flee from place to place or turn his mind toward various plans of escape? Such things belong only to the condition of this present life.

Thus, as I have said, these words more appropriately apply to the time of the final persecution: “fear,” and so forth. The prophet says that the inhabitant of the earth will be seized beforehand. This refers to the storm of the persecution mentioned above, concerning which the Lord, explaining the deeds of Antichrist to blessed Job, says:

> “Around his teeth is fear.”

And in the Gospel he says to the disciples:

> “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever shall be.”

This is the fear from which the prophet wished to be delivered when he said:

> “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.” [Col. 0705C]

It should be noted that he does not say, “from the sword of the enemy,” but “from fear of the enemy.” The brave martyr does not pray [printed *erat*, “was”; conjecture *orat*, “prays”] that the enemy might not kill him bodily, but that he might not fear the one who kills the body but cannot kill the soul; lest, by fearing him, he should offend the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.

This is plainly seen to have happened in the struggle of those who, unable to endure adverse punishments, denied eternal life. Concerning such people it is said:

> “And it shall come to pass that whoever flees from the voice of fear will fall into the pit.”

The one who flees from the voice of fear falls into the pit when, because of the threats or tortures of the persecutor, he abandons the constancy of faith and is not afraid to lose Christ. [Col. 0705D]

There were some who, compelled by the violence of torture, denied Christ more with their voice than with their mind. Having escaped from the hands of their torturers, they later returned to Christ through the help of fraternal compassion. They stood firm once more in confessing the one whom they had previously denied in fear, and completely erased their guilt of apostasy either through the long medicine of repentance or even by restoring the contest of martyrdom.

But those who fell during martyrdom, so that they would not have time to recover, return to repentance, and obtain the forgiveness they had sought, were immediately killed, while the enemy burned to slaughter their souls rather than their bodies. To them the prophet’s next words aptly apply:

> “And whoever escapes from the pit will be caught in the snare.”

Since we know that the ancient persecutors of the Church, the members of the devil, inflicted this kind of death upon Christian souls, who could doubt that it will be inflicted much more severely when Satan himself, the leader and source of every evil, raises his head from the abyss to persecute the Church? [Col. 0706A]

After predicting these things about the time immediately preceding the day of judgment, the prophet adds what, unless I am mistaken, may rightly be understood in two ways:

> “For the windows from on high are opened, and the foundations of the earth are shaken. The earth is utterly broken; the earth is thoroughly shattered; the earth is violently shaken; the earth is greatly agitated, like a drunkard.”

This may be understood as being said of the element of earth itself, which at the end of time will be completely shaken from its former condition. The word “earth” may also designate the people who dwell upon the earth. The shaking, breaking, shattering, commotion, and agitation of this rational earth, like that of a drunkard, may then be understood as that of which the Lord speaks in the Gospel.

After saying:

> “There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars,”

he adds:

> “And upon the earth there will be distress among nations,”

or else the distress of which he immediately says:

> “People will faint for fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world,”

while the sea and the waves roar. [Col. 0706B]

But when the prophet adds:

> “It shall be removed like a tent for one night; its iniquity shall weigh it down; it shall fall and shall not rise again,”

he refers specifically to the day of judgment, when the appearance of this world passes away and the human way of life that is now in it comes to an end.

After briefly interrupting his statement about the final day, he again turns his discourse to the events that precede that day’s terror—namely, to the destruction of Antichrist:
