> “And it shall come to pass in that day,” he says, “that the Lord will visit the host of heaven in the heights and the kings of the earth who are upon the earth. And they shall be gathered into one bundle in the pit, and they shall be shut up there in prison.”

God will visit the host of heaven in the heights when, after Antichrist has been killed, he has largely crushed the power of the unclean spirits. This force is rightly called the host of heaven either because it fell from heavenly places to the depths at the beginning, or because it dwells in the air, which Scripture often calls heaven, and stubbornly wages war against the human race. [Col. 0706C]

Thus the Apostle says:

> “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places.”

And the Lord, describing their future destruction through the prophet, says:

> “My sword is drunk in heaven.”

“In that day,” therefore—that is, in the period when fear, the pit, and the snare of that final tribulation will seize the inhabitant of the earth, when nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and the foundations of the earth will be shaken, while the earth itself, as its inhabitants attack one another, will be broken, shattered, shaken, and agitated like a drunkard—when its removal and ruin are approaching and already imminent, the Lord will visit the host of heaven in the heights by sending an angel from heaven.

Through divine power that angel will destroy the man of sin, the son of perdition, who is lifted up and exalted above everything called God or worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God. [Col. 0706D]

Blessed Pope Gregory understands this to be accomplished through the archangel Michael, on the basis of the Apocalypse of Saint John, where it is written:

> “And there was a battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon fought and his angels. And they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven.”

Thus the host of heaven will be visited when Antichrist is killed. For once he has been destroyed, the power of the evil spirits who had assisted him in displaying false signs will be weakened and rendered ineffective. Antichrist himself may also rightly be counted among the host of heaven because he presumes to exalt himself not only above all the angels but even above the whole height of the divine majesty.

The Lord will also visit the kings of the earth who are upon the earth—namely, the ministers of Antichrist and the supporters and collaborators in his deeds and frauds. These exercise an impious dominion over earthly and low-minded people, and there is no doubt that they will perish when the same fury of their tribulation comes to an end. History records that this happened to all who raged against the Church, the instigators of wars. [Col. 0707A]

It should be noted that the prophet does not say explicitly, “over all the kings of the earth,” any more than he says, “over the entire host of heaven.” Rather, he says without qualification: “The Lord will visit the host of heaven in the heights and the kings of the earth who are upon the earth.”

Hence these words may be understood not of the general overthrow of all wicked human beings and angels, but of the particular overthrow of certain evil human and angelic beings.

“And they shall be gathered into one bundle in the pit, and they shall be shut up there in prison.” This is said of their souls, whose bodies, when the Lord visits them, will be given over to death. Although they did not all leave their bodies at the same time, each in its own order they will all be gathered into the same bundle and shut up in the same prison of everlasting punishments.

This will occur according to the disposition of the strict Judge, so that those who attacked the Church with a like mind may together pay the penalty for their warfare against God. [Col. 0707B]

The teachers of the Church say that the same will happen to the other condemned: those who are equal in guilt will likewise be condemned to equal punishments. This is what the Lord says concerning the weeds:

> “Bind them in bundles to burn them”—

the avaricious with the avaricious, the lustful with the lustful, the perjurers with the perjurers, and all the other sinners with those who share their guilt, so that together they may be plunged into the eternal fires.

Therefore, when Antichrist has perished, his ministers of deception will be gathered into the prison of infernal punishments, and after many days they will be visited—namely, at the time of the resurrection of all, when their souls will be summoned briefly from the underworld for this purpose: once they have received their bodies, they will immediately, after judgment has been completed, return with the other sinners to the same punishments. [Col. 0707C]

No one should think that our interpretation—that Antichrist will be killed many days before the coming universal judgment—is contradicted by the Apostle’s statement about him:

> “Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming.”

By saying this, the Apostle signifies that the power of that devil will be crushed and brought to an end by such a great and terrible blow that no one could doubt that the presence of the Lord’s coming had appeared to destroy his pride. Scripture records something similar concerning Herod, who killed James and sent Peter to prison; ecclesiastical history records the same concerning other persecutors of Christians.

Alternatively, the Apostle says that the Lord will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming because, when Christ comes to judgment, death—the last enemy—will be destroyed, and together with the one who holds the power of death, namely the devil, the power of all his attendants will perish completely.

That the universal judgment will not come immediately after the extinction of that man of sin, the son of perdition, is testified by the prophet Daniel. In the final vision of his prophecy, while describing the deeds of that kingdom and including its duration within 1,290 days—that is, three and a half years—he suddenly adds: [Col. 0707D]

> “Blessed is the one who waits and reaches the 1,335 days.”

Blessed Jerome the presbyter explains this verse in these words:

> “Blessed is the one who, after Antichrist has been killed, waits for the forty-five days beyond the appointed number, during which the Lord and Savior will come in his majesty.”

Why there should be a silence of forty-five days after Antichrist’s death belongs to divine knowledge. Unless perhaps we should say that the delay of the saints’ kingdom is a test of their patience.

It should also be noted concerning the words, “And after many days they shall be visited,” that the expression “many days” more appropriately belongs to the times of this present age, which are multiplied by the alternating succession of days and nights, than to the future age. In that age the movement of the hours will cease: the Lord will be everlasting light for the saints, while the wicked, with hands and feet bound, will be sent into the outer darkness. [Col. 0708A]

Therefore we should rightly understand that those who are now held in the prison of infernal darkness will be visited after the many days of this passing age, at that hour when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Lord and come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.

At the time of this visitation, what follows will also occur:

> “And the moon shall blush and the sun shall be confounded.”

The Lord himself bears witness to this in the Gospel:

> “Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds.” [Col. 0708B]

But when the prophet, as though within the same sequence, adds at the conclusion:

> “When the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and is glorified in the sight of his elders,”

this will be fulfilled more fully after the ordeal of judgment has been completed, when the wicked have been removed so that they may not see the glory of God, and all the saints enter the dwelling of the heavenly city to contemplate forever the appearance of their Creator.

Here we should note that, just as the things mentioned in this passage appear to be future at the same time, although a clear explanation [printed *quaeratis*, “you may seek”; conjecture *quae ratio*, “which reasoning”] shows that they will occur separately, so earlier events are woven together as though they belonged equally to the single moment of the day of judgment, although some are certainly to be fulfilled while that day is approaching and others when it has already appeared. [Col. 0708C]

Which reader does not know that the reddening of the moon and the darkening of the sun will occur either before the day of judgment or on that very day? But the glorification of the Lord—not that by which he will appear in judgment to all, both righteous and wicked, but that by which he will be revealed only in the sight of his elders, that is, the elect—will rather be shown to them at the time when the wicked depart into eternal punishment and the saints into eternal life.

At that time—if it is permissible to speak of time in relation to what is eternal—the moon’s redness and the sun’s darkness will no longer obscure the radiance. Rather, as the same prophet says elsewhere:

> “The light shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the blow of his scourge.” [Col. 0708D]

Having explained this most perilous question, holy bishop, according to the measure of our ability, I repeat at the end what I said at the beginning: I have not dared [printed *non summe ausus*, with *summe*, “to the highest degree”; conjecture *sum*, “I am,” supplies the auxiliary in *non sum ausus*, “I have not dared”] to say that I understood what the prophet wished to mean by this passage.

I hope, however, by the gift of heavenly grace, that what I have written in discussing it is not inconsistent either with the text of the prophetic reading or with the reason of the catholic faith. Nor do I believe that I shall be fruitless for my reader in what I have written. Even if I did not know how to lead him into the sanctuary of the prophetic meaning, I have at least led him farther away from the plough of heretical deception, warning him not to interpret the prophet’s words wrongly and thereby believe that sinners once condemned for their crimes in the prison of hell will at some time be recalled to pardon by a divine visitation. [Col. 0709A]

Rather, let him diligently care for himself and his own, so that, cleansed from vices and adorned with good works, they may await the final day. There is no doubt that both the prophet now under discussion and all the teachers of the Church have taught this.

May heavenly grace always deign to aid Your Blessedness, who intercedes for us. [Col. 0709B]

## LETTER XVI

### On the Seven Canonical Epistles [Col. 0710A]

James, Peter, John, and Jude published seven Epistles, which ecclesiastical usage calls “Catholic,” that is, universal. The Epistle of James is placed first because he undertook the governance of the Church of Jerusalem. For in the catalogues of the apostles, Peter and John are ordinarily named first. Yet the fountain and source of evangelical preaching, beginning from Jerusalem, was spread throughout the world and over all peoples. The dignity of that see the apostle Paul also honored when he named him, saying: “James, Cephas, and John, who were regarded as pillars of the Church” [Col. 0710B]. Or, certainly, because he sent his Epistle to the twelve tribes of Israel, which were the first to believe, it rightly had to be placed first.

Peter’s Epistle was rightly placed second, because he wrote to the elect sojourners, who in Greek are called *proselytes* (προσήλυτοι), that is, to those who had been converted from paganism to Judaism and from Judaism to the grace of evangelical election. John’s Epistles were rightly placed third, because he wrote to those who believed from among the Gentiles, although they had belonged to neither of these groups by birth or profession. Indeed, many ecclesiastical writers—including Saint Athanasius, bishop of the Church of Alexandria—testify that his first Epistle was written to the Parthians.

Jude was rightly placed last, because, although he too was a great man, he was nevertheless inferior to the three apostles who preceded him [Col. 0710C]. Or because the Epistle of James was written first, then Peter’s, and after them John’s, they have retained to this day the order in which they were written. For it is established that blessed James completed his martyrdom in the thirtieth year after the Lord’s Passion; Peter suffered in the thirty-eighth year, that is, in the final year of Nero, and he himself wrote in his second Epistle: “I know that the laying aside of my tabernacle is near, just as our Lord Jesus Christ also revealed to me.” Hence it is evident that he wrote this Epistle when his passion was approaching, since James had departed to Christ long before.

Nor was it appropriate to separate Peter’s Epistles from one another, since he wrote them to the same Churches. Moreover, John wrote his Epistles and his Gospel together much later; after returning from exile following the Lord’s death [Col. 0710D], he found the Church, which had been disturbed in his absence by heretics—heretics whom he often strikes in his Epistles by calling them Antichrists.

# HISTORICAL WORKS OF THE VENERABLE BEDE THE ANGLE-SAXON, OR THE FOURTH PART OF ALL HIS WORKS

## FIRST SECTION.—HAGIOGRAPHICAL

# THE LIVES OF THE HOLY ABBOTS OF THE MONASTERIES AT WIRAMUTHA AND GIRVUM [Note: [Col. 0711] Learned men do not agree about the spelling of this and the other names; and, unless I am mistaken, this should be attributed to the pronunciation of the Anglo-Saxon language, which is especially uncertain. EDITOR.], BENEDICT, CEOLFRID, EASTERWIN, SIGFRID, AND HUAETBERCT, composed by Bede, a priest and monk of the same monastery.

[From Smith, *Historia ecclesiastica Anglorum*.]

[Col. 0711]

# MABILLON’S PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0711A] **1.** The Venerable Bede, in the *Epitome of English History*, where he compiled a list of his works, mentions the history of the abbots of his monastery in these words: “I wrote in two little books the history of the abbots of this monastery, in which I rejoice to serve the heavenly goodness: Benedict, Ceolfrid (add Sigfrid), and Haeberct.” Edward Maihew, a Westminster monk, published this history, torn into two fragments, in 1625 in his *English Benedictine Martyrology*: part of it in the second table of additions, and part under 25 September. Since James Ussher, knight, was unaware of that edition, he undertook another in 1664, printed at Dublin; Louis Billaine, a bookseller in Paris, revised it two years later. Here we reproduce that same history, containing the deeds of the aforesaid abbots, in continuous sequence, both because it seemed preferable to present the author’s complete work and because it was not possible to divide the narrative concerning the deeds of these same abbots. Whether Bede also composed a discourse on Saint Biscop will have to be investigated later.

**2.** No one is unaware of Bede’s authority. Yet here he deserves even greater credence because he writes about matters known and observed by himself. For he was “Bede, servant of God and priest of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter, which is at Wirimuth and Ingirvum”; he was “born in the territory of that same monastery, and when he was seven years old, he was entrusted to the care of his relatives to be educated by the most reverend abbot Benedict, and afterward by Ceolfrid; and from that time he spent the whole period of his life residing in that same monastery,” as he himself testifies in the passage cited.

**3.** The monastery of Saint Peter at the mouth of the river Wira—whence it was called Wiremuth—was situated approximately five miles from the monastery of Saint Paul, located on the river Tine in the territory of Girvum, commonly called Jarrow; hence the monastery of Saint Paul was called Girvum. Biscop founded both and wished them to be subject to the same abbot and the same institutions. This caused Bede and other authors sometimes to treat them as though they were one monastery. Bede lived at Girvum, which was later destroyed by the Danes once and again.

**4.** Different writers render the name and surname of Saint Benedict Biscop in different ways. The Venerable Bede calls him Biscop by surname, both in the history that follows and in *English History*, book IV, chapter 18, and book V, chapter 20. Florence of Worcester and more recent writers, however, commonly call him Benedict Biscop. Bede appears to use the surname as a second name, or as a name equivalent and interchangeable with a surname; we observe that it was sometimes used in this sense by medieval authors. Biscop therefore had two names; nevertheless, following customary usage, we shall everywhere call him Benedict Biscop.

**5.** Benedict is said to have written certain works: Pitseus lists one book of *Exhortations to Monks*, one book *On His Privilege*, one book *On the Celebration of the Feasts of the Whole Year* [Col. 0713A], and others about which there is no occasion to pronounce a judgment. Some attribute to him the book *On the Concordance of Rules*, which is known to have been written by another Benedict, the abbot of Aniane. Our Menard, in his preface *On the Authors of the Rules Cited in the Concordance*, suspects that the *Rule of the Master* was written by Benedict Biscop. Yet it seems rather to be attributed to a Gallic author; but that matter can be discussed elsewhere.

**6.** No mention of Saint Benedict Biscop is found in the ancient Martyrologies of Bede or of others. From this it might be questioned whether the homily circulated under Bede’s name concerning this saint is genuine or should be attributed to someone else. Whatever the case may be, it was certainly composed by a monk who had seen Biscop’s own disciples, as appears from the context; and therefore it is certain [Col. 0713B] that his feast was celebrated in ancient times. “Therefore his body,” says William, a monk of Malmesbury, in book IV of *The Bishops of England*, “Adelwold—bishop of Winchester, who died in the year 984—purchased at great cost and brought to Thorney, bringing a shining ray to the more obscure saints.” The monastery of Thorney, moreover, lay not far from the city of Ely in the county of Cambridge.

**7.** We discussed the rule established by Biscop in his monasteries in the preface to the first century of Benedictine studies, § 8. For Bede states in the following history that Biscop and Ceolfrid commended the rule of a certain great abbot to their disciples. In the monastery at Wiremuth there was also a church of the blessed Father Benedict, as appears below, book II, no. 19. Indeed, Albinus Flaccus Alcuin supplies us with excellent testimony on this matter in Letter 49, addressed to the brothers of the Church of Wiremuth and Girvum, in these words: “Observe with the utmost care the discipline of the regular life which the most holy Fathers, namely Benedict and Ceolfrid, established for you” [Col. 0714B]. But which rule was it? The same author explains shortly afterward: “The Rule of Saint Benedict should be expounded in the assembly of the brothers in their own language, so that it may be understood by everyone.” We believe that this will suffice for fair-minded readers.

[Col. 0713]

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF THE FIVE HOLY ABBOTS. (C, S)

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0713B] Biscop, a religious servant of Christ, surnamed [Note: [Col. 0713C] Benedict. He is also called Baducing by Fridegod, the author of the *Life of Saint Wilfrid* (Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, century III, part I, p. 173). SMITH.] Benedict, with heavenly grace inspiring him, built a monastery in honor of the most blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, beside the mouth of the river Wira toward the north [Note: [Col. 0713C] With the help of and grant of land from.], with the help of and land granted by Ecgfrid, the venerable and most devout king of that people. He diligently governed that same monastery for sixteen years, amid innumerable hardships of journeys and illnesses, with the same religious devotion with which he had built it.

To use the words of the blessed Pope Gregory, by which he glorifies the life of an abbot of the same name: “He was a man of venerable life, Benedict in grace and in name, bearing a mature heart from the very time of his boyhood, passing beyond his age in character [Note: [Col. 0713C] Surpassing.], and giving his mind to no pleasure. He was indeed born of the noble stock of the English people, but with no lesser nobility of mind he was always raised toward attaining the fellowship of the angels.

“Finally, when he was a servant [Note: [Col. 0713C] Oswiu’s.] of King Oswiu and, by the king’s gift, received a landed possession suitable to his rank, at about twenty-five years of age he despised perishable property so that he might acquire what is eternal. He rejected worldly military service with its corruptible reward so that he might serve the true King and merit an everlasting kingdom in the heavenly city. He left home, relatives, and country for Christ and for the Gospel, so that he might receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life. He refused to serve carnal marriage so that he might follow the Lamb, radiant with the glory of virginity, in the heavenly kingdoms. He declined to beget mortal children according to the flesh, having been predestined by Christ to raise children for him through spiritual instruction, children everlasting in heavenly life.

“After leaving his homeland, he went to Rome [Note: [Col. 0713C] He visited it. He had Wilfrid as his companion on the journey, as Bede testifies, V, 19. Wilfrid undertook that journey either while Honorius, archbishop of Canterbury, was still alive or certainly shortly after his death, according to the same passage and author, who places the death of Honorius in the year 653 from the Lord’s Incarnation in book III, chapter 20. Biscop began his second pilgrimage in the time of Pope Vitalian, whose pontificate must be reckoned to have begun in 658. Waraeus incorrectly reads, ‘in the time of the late Pope Vitalian, of blessed memory.’ MABILLON.], desiring to see in the body and to venerate bodily the places where the blessed apostles whose desire had always inflamed him rested.

“Soon after returning to his homeland, he did not cease to love, venerate, and preach to those whom he could the institutions of ecclesiastical life that he had seen, with greater devotion. At that time, Alchfrid, son of the aforesaid King Oswiu, himself also intending to come to Rome to adore the thresholds of the apostles, took him as his companion on that journey. When his father recalled him from the intention of the journey and made him remain in his homeland and kingdom, Biscop nevertheless, as a young man of good character, immediately completed the journey he had begun and returned to Rome [Col. 0715A] with the utmost haste [Note: [Col. 0715C] In the time of Pope Vitalian, of blessed memory.]. There, after absorbing no small amount of salutary knowledge, as before, and departing some months later, he went to the island of Lérins [Note: [Col. 0715D] Lérins. It is an island belonging to Gaul, also called the island of Saint Honoratus, where there was a famous monastery of monks. WARAEUS.]. There he entrusted himself to the company of the monks, received the tonsure, and, marked by the monk’s vow, observed the regular discipline with due care. Having been instructed there for two years in the suitable teaching of monastic conduct, he was once more overcome by love for blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and resolved to return to the city hallowed by his body [Note: [Col. 0715C] To revisit. [Note: [Col. 0715D] To retrace his steps. Near the end of 667, when Wighard died (III, 29; IV, 1). SMITH.].”

Not long afterward, when a merchant ship arrived, he fulfilled his desire. At that time Ecgberct, king of the people of Kent, had sent from Britain a man named Wighard, chosen for the office of bishop. He had been sufficiently instructed in every ecclesiastical discipline in Kent by the Roman disciples of Pope Gregory. The king wished him to be ordained bishop at Rome so that, possessing a bishop of his own people and language, he might be instructed more perfectly in the faith and its mysteries together with the peoples subject to him, insofar as he would receive these things not through an interpreter but through the tongue and hand of a man who shared his kinship and people [Note: [Col. 0715C] These matters, namely, not through an interpreter. [Note: [Col. 0715C] Of one known to him.].

“When this Wighard came to Rome with all the companions who had come with him, he died of an illness that broke out before he received the rank of bishop. But the apostolic pope, lest the religious mission of the faithful should lack its proper fruit because the envoys had died, took counsel and chose from among his own men someone to send as archbishop to Britain: Theodore, a man endowed alike with secular and ecclesiastical learning, and that in both languages, Greek and Latin. He gave him as companion and adviser the equally vigorous and prudent man Adrian, an abbot. And because he perceived that the venerable Benedict was a wise, capable, religious, and noble man, he entrusted to him the bishop whom he had ordained, together with all his companions. He ordered Benedict, abandoning the pilgrimage that he had undertaken for Christ, to return to his homeland for the sake of a higher benefit and to bring to him the teacher of truth whom he had diligently sought [Note: [Col. 0716C] Carefully.], so that he might serve him either while he was traveling there or while teaching there as interpreter and guide alike.

“He did as he had been ordered. They came to Kent and were received with great joy. Theodore ascended the episcopal see; Benedict took charge of the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter, to govern it; afterward the aforesaid Adrian became its abbot.”

When he had governed the monastery for two years, he undertook and successfully completed his third journey from Britain to Rome, with his customary good fortune [Note: [Col. 0715D] Third. This was indeed Benedict’s third Roman pilgrimage from Britain, but his fourth in total, since during his second departure from Britain he went to Rome twice before returning home. Therefore Bede’s next departure, which he calls his fourth from Britain, should be interpreted as his fifth absolutely. MABILLON. Benedict undertook this journey in 671. FLORENCE OF WORCESTER.], and brought back many books of every kind of divine learning, some purchased at a fixed price and others given by friends.

On his return, when he reached Vienne, he recovered the books that he had entrusted there to friends [Note: [Col. 0716C] The books that he had entrusted to himself—or, more probably, to friends.]. Entering Britain [Note: [Col. 0715D] He entered. In 672, for Coinwalch died that year. *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* and Florence of Worcester.], he thought he should present them to Coinwalch, king of the West Saxons, whose friendship he had previously enjoyed more than once and by whose favors he had been helped. But since Coinwalch had been carried off by a premature death at that very time, Benedict finally turned his steps toward the homeland, people, and soil in which he had been born, and went to Ecgfrid, king of the Trans-Humbrian region.

He recounted everything he had done since, as a young man, he had left his homeland; he did not conceal how passionately he burned with the desire for religion; he disclosed what ecclesiastical and monastic instruction he had learned at Rome and in the surrounding regions, how many divine books and how great a number of relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs of Christ he had brought back [Note: [Col. 0716C] He brought back.]. He found such favor with the king in intimate friendship that the king immediately granted him land belonging to seventy households and ordered him to build there a monastery for the first pastor of the Church.

This was done, as I also mentioned in the preface, beside the mouth of the river Wira toward the north, in the year 674 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second indiction, and in the fourth year of the reign of King Ecgfrid.

No more than a year had passed after the monastery was founded when Benedict crossed the Ocean and went to Gaul. He requested, received, and brought back masons who would build for him a stone church [Note: [Col. 0716D] A stone church. That is, a church with a stone roof, as William of Malmesbury explains, or with a vault; for long before this Bishop Paulinus, as Bede himself testifies in II, 16, had built in the city of Lincoln a church of excellent workmanship in stone. He had also done this earlier at York, according to chapter 12. Although at that time churches in Britain were often made of wood. Finan, bishop of the Mercians, as Bede testifies in book III, chapter 25, “built a church in the manner of the Scots, not of stone but entirely of hewn oak, and covered it with reeds. But Eadberht, bishop of that place, after removing the reeds, covered the whole of it—that is, the roof and walls—with sheets of lead.” This was also sometimes practiced in Gaul. See Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 72, and *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 101, and elsewhere. MABILLON.] according to the Roman manner that he had always loved.

He displayed such devotion in the work, out of love for blessed Peter in whose honor he was building, that within a year from the laying of the foundations, once the roof had been placed upon the walls, one might have seen the solemn celebrations of Mass being performed there [Note: [Col. 0717D] When the work was approaching completion.].

As the work was approaching completion, he sent envoys to Gaul to bring back makers of glass—craftsmen previously unknown in Britain—to glaze the windows of the church, its porticoes, and its dining halls [Note: [Col. 0717D] To adorn.]. This was done, and they came. They not only completed the work that had been requested but also taught the English people to know and practice this kind of craftsmanship: an art notably suited both to the lamps of the church and to vessels for many different uses.

Moreover, since he could not find at home all the things appropriate for the service of the altar and the church, the devout purchaser took care to have sacred vessels and vestments brought from overseas regions [Note: [Col. 0717D] Namely, vessels or vestments.].

And so that he might also bring from the Roman territories to his Church ornaments and defenses that could not even be found in Gaul, the diligent provider completed his fourth journey [Note: [Col. 0717D] Fourth. Florence of Worcester writes that Benedict undertook this pilgrimage in 676; but since we read that he was honorably received by Pope Agatho, who was not raised to the chair of Saint Peter before 678, I think this later year should rather be chosen. Bede discusses this journey at greater length in IV, 18. SMITH.] [Note: [Col. 0717D] That journey.] and returned enriched with a greater abundance of spiritual goods than before.

First, he brought back an immeasurable supply of books of every kind. Second, he brought an abundant treasury of relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs of Christ, destined to benefit many English churches. Third, he introduced into his monastery the order of singing, chanting psalms, and ministering in the Church according to the custom of Roman practice. For this purpose he requested and received from Pope Agatho John, the chief singer of the church of the blessed apostle Peter and abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0717D] John. Bede discusses this John and Pope Agatho’s privilege more fully in IV, 18. SMITH.], and brought him, a Roman, to Britain as the future teacher of the English in his monastery.

When John arrived there, he not only transmitted by word of mouth to those learning the ecclesiastical arts what he had learned at Rome, but also left a considerable amount committed to writing, which to this day is preserved in the library of that same monastery for the sake of remembrance.

Fourth, Benedict brought back a valuable gift: a letter of privilege from the venerable Pope Agatho, obtained with the permission, agreement, desire, and encouragement of King Ecgfrid, by which the monastery he had founded was to be made forever safe and free from every external incursion [Col. 0717D].

Fifth, he brought paintings of holy images [Col. 0718A] with which to adorn the church of the blessed apostle Peter that he had built [Note: [Col. 0718D] To adorn.]. Specifically, he brought an image of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, together with images of the twelve apostles, so that he might enclose the central vault of that same church with them, in a panel extending from wall to wall. He brought images of the Gospel narrative with which to decorate the southern wall of the church, and images of the visions of the Apocalypse of blessed John with which to adorn the northern wall likewise.

Thus, all who entered the church, even those unacquainted with letters, might see wherever they turned their eyes either the ever-lovable appearance of Christ and his saints, even though represented in images, or might recall with more vigilant minds the grace of the Lord’s Incarnation, or, as though they had the danger of the final judgment before their eyes, remember to examine themselves more strictly [Col. 0718B].

King Ecgfrid was greatly pleased by the virtue, industry, and religious devotion of the venerable Benedict. Since he saw that he had made a good and fruitful gift of the land he had granted him for building the monastery, he took care to enlarge it by granting an additional possession of forty households [Note: [Col. 0717D] Forty. Florence of Worcester also reads forty; hence Matthew of Westminster, a monk, should be corrected, since he has sixty households. By “households” Bede understands a hide or ploughland; and the men of ancient times reckoned a ploughland as a portion of land sufficient for the cultivation of one plough each year, as Waraeus noted. MABILLON.].

After a year, Benedict sent there nearly seventeen monks, appointing Ceolfrid as abbot and priest. With the advice and indeed the command of the aforesaid King Ecgfrid, he built the monastery of the blessed apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0718D] Of blessed Paul. Benedict began this monastery in 682, and Ceolfrid completed it in 684. This is attested by an old inscription once carved on the church wall, as follows: “The dedication of the church of Saint Paul, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifteenth year of King Ecgfrid, under Abbot Ceolfrid, founder of this church by God’s authority, in his fourth year.” Thus Waraeus and the *Monasticum Anglicanum*; the Bollandists, however, have the sixteenth year. MABILLON.].

He did so on the express condition that the peace and harmony of the two places, together with their perpetual familiarity and goodwill, should be preserved; so that, just as a body cannot be separated from the head through which it breathes, nor can a head without which the body does not live forget the body [Note: [Col. 0718D] So that neither.], no one should attempt by any effort to disturb these monasteries, joined together by the brotherly fellowship of the chief apostles [Note: [Col. 0718D] Bound together.].

Ceolfrid, whom Benedict appointed abbot here, had been his most vigorous assistant in every matter from the earliest beginnings of the first monastery. At the appropriate time he had also gone with him to Rome, both to learn what was necessary and to worship.

At that time Benedict also chose the priest Easterwin from the monastery of the blessed Peter and appointed him abbot over that same monastery, so that he might bear more lightly, through the assistance of his beloved fellow soldier, the labor that he could not bear alone.

Nor should it seem strange to anyone that one monastery had two abbots at the same time. The frequent journeys that Benedict undertook for the monastery’s benefit, his repeated departures across the Ocean and uncertain returns, caused this arrangement. Histories relate that the most blessed apostle Peter himself had established two bishops in succession under him to govern the Church when necessity demanded it [Note: [Col. 0719D] Two under him. Epiphanius mentions this occurrence, *Against Heresies*, 18. There are other examples of this kind in Eusebius Pamphilus. Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, had Alexander as his colleague in book VI, chapter 11; Theotecnus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, had Anatolius in book VII, chapter 32. In this seventh century Saint Sulpicius adopted Wlfolend as his coadjutor, and Saint Praejectus adopted Evodius. MABILLON.]. The great abbot Benedict himself, as blessed Pope Gregory writes about him, placed twelve abbots over his disciples as he judged useful—not to the detriment of charity, but rather for its increase.

The aforesaid man therefore assumed responsibility for governing the monastery in the ninth year after its foundation. He remained there until his death for four years: a noble man, but he turned the distinction of his nobility not into material for boasting and contempt of others, as some do, but toward the greater nobility of spirit that befits a servant of God [Col. 0719B].

For he was the cousin of his abbot Benedict. Yet such was the openness of mind possessed by both, and such their contempt for worldly nobility as a thing of no value, that when Easterwin entered the monastery he neither sought any special honor above the others on account of kinship or nobility, nor did Benedict think of offering him such honor. Rather, as a young man of good purpose, he gloried in observing the regular discipline in every respect on an equal footing with the brothers.

Indeed, although he had been a servant of King Ecgfrid, once he had abandoned secular affairs, laid aside his weapons, and taken up spiritual service, he remained so humble and so like the other brothers that he gladly and obediently took part with them in winnowing and threshing, milking sheep and calves, and in every task of the monastery—in the bakery, the garden, and the kitchen.

Even after he had been raised to the office and rank of abbot, he remained toward everyone with the same disposition as before, in accordance with the admonition of a certain wise man: “They have appointed you as ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them, gentle, approachable, and kind to all.”

Whenever he found it appropriate, he corrected those who sinned through regular discipline [Note: [Col. 0719C] Reprimanding them, but.], yet he was still more diligent in admonishing them through his innate habit of love, lest anyone should wish to sin and hide from himself beneath the cloud of his own unrest the clearest light of Easterwin’s face.

Often, when he went somewhere to attend to the monastery’s business, if he found brothers at work, he would immediately join them in the task: guiding the ploughshare by its handle, taming iron beneath the hammer, shaking a winnowing fan in his hand, or performing some similar work.

He was a young man strong in bodily vigor and pleasing in speech; he was cheerful in spirit, generous in kindness, and honorable in appearance. He always ate in the same house and the same food as the other brothers. He slept in the common place where he had slept before becoming abbot, so that even after he had fallen ill and already knew from certain signs that his death was near, he continued to rest for two days in the brothers’ dormitory.

For the remaining five days, until the hour of his departure, he stayed in a more secluded building. On one of those days he came out and sat under the open sky. Calling all the brothers to him, he gave them the kiss of peace according to the custom of a compassionate nature, while they wept and mourned the departure of so great a father and shepherd.

He died [Note: [Col. 0719C] On the day before the Nones. [Note: [Col. 0719D] On the Nones of March. Hence Saint Easterwin is entered on 7 March—*Nonis Martii*, says Henschenius—in a manuscript calendar of the abbey of Saint Maximin at Trier, and in the Benedictine Martyrology and the English Martyrology of Richard Whitford, printed in 1526, in these words: “In the monastery of Saint Paul” (one should read “Saint Peter,” for Easterwin governed not the monastery of Saint Paul at Girvum but that of Saint Peter at Wiremuth), “near the river Tine in England, the feast of Saint Easterwin, abbot there and a man of great perfection.” Florence of Worcester writes that the holy man was carried off by pestilence on the Nones of March in 685, and also records the translation of Easterwin’s relics by Hwaetberht. MABILLON.] on the Nones of March, during the night, while the brothers were occupied with the praise of the morning psalmody [Col. 0720B].

He was twenty-four years old when he entered the monastery; he lived there for twelve years; he served as a priest for seven years; and for four of those years he governed the monastery. Thus, leaving behind his earthly limbs and dying body, he sought the heavenly kingdoms.

But having briefly set out these matters about the life of the venerable Easterwin, let us return to the order of the narrative.

After Benedict had appointed Easterwin abbot of the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter, and Ceolfrid abbot of the monastery of the blessed Paul, not long afterward Benedict came hastening from Britain to Rome for the fifth time [Note: [Col. 0720D] Fifth. On this occasion he went to Rome, according to Florence of Worcester, in 684. SMITH.] [Note: [Col. 0720C] Fourth time.], and returned enriched, as always, with innumerable ecclesiastical gifts and benefits. He was furnished with a great abundance of sacred books, but no less than before with a gift of holy images.

For on that occasion also he brought paintings of the Lord’s history with which to encircle the entire church of the blessed Mother of God that he had built in the larger monastery. He also brought images, composed according to a thoroughly considered scheme, to adorn the monastery and church of the blessed apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0720C] “Of our Paul”; [Note: [Col. 0720D] Paul. See the book of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, *On the Virtues of Saint Felix*, book IX, where he explains why he painted the holy houses of Saint Felix in the likeness of living beings. MABILLON.], depicting the concord between the Old and New Testaments.

For example, in adjacent scenes, one above the other, he joined in painting Isaac carrying the wood on which he was to be sacrificed and the Lord likewise carrying the cross on which he was to suffer. Similarly, he compared the serpent lifted up by Moses in the wilderness with the Son of Man lifted up on the cross.

Among other things he brought two silk curtains of incomparable workmanship. Later, Benedict exchanged these with King Aldfrid and his counselors for land comprising three households south of the river Wira, near its mouth, since after his return he found Ecgfrid already dead [Note: [Col. 0721D] Before he returned.].

But amid the joyful things he brought back, he found sorrowful things at home: namely, the venerable priest Easterwin, whom he had appointed abbot before departing, and a considerable company of the brothers entrusted to him had already departed from this world, since the pestilence was raging everywhere.

Yet there was also consolation, because he learned that in Easterwin’s place a man equally reverend and gentle from that same monastery had immediately been appointed: Sigfrid, namely, a deacon, chosen by his brothers and by his co-abbot Ceolfrid. He was sufficiently instructed in knowledge of the Scriptures, adorned with excellent morals, and endowed with remarkable abstinence; but bodily infirmity did not greatly weaken him in guarding the virtues of his spirit; in preserving the innocence of his heart, he suffered from a harmful and incurable disease of the lungs [Note: [Col. 0721D] Weakened, but for preserving.].

Not long afterward Benedict himself also began to be afflicted and wearied by advancing illness. For, in order that the virtue of patience might prove so great a devotion as well, divine mercy struck both men down upon a bed by temporal sickness, so that, once illness had been overcome by death, it might refresh them with the perpetual repose of heavenly peace and light. For Sigfrid too, as we have said, chastened by a long affliction of his inward organs, reached his final day. And Benedict, gradually weakened by increasing illness over three years, was so dissolved by paralysis that he became completely half-dead in all his lower limbs, with only those upper members without which a human being cannot live preserved for the exercise of patience and virtue. In his suffering he always strove to give thanks to the Creator, always to devote himself to the praises of God and to fraternal exhortations.

Benedict frequently summoned to himself the brothers who came to visit him and strengthened them in keeping the rule he had established:

> “You must not suppose,” he said, “that, being ignorant in heart, I have produced from myself these decrees which I laid down for you. From the seventeen monasteries which, during the long journeys of my frequent travels, I found to be excellent, I learned all these things and entrusted them to you for wholesome observance.”

He ordered that the library which he had brought from Rome—most distinguished and extremely extensive—be carefully preserved intact as necessary for the instruction of the Church, and not be disfigured through negligence [or scattered here and there]. He also used to repeat this command diligently to the same men: no one should suppose that, in the election of an abbot, noble lineage was to be sought, rather than excellence of life and teaching.

> “And truly,” he said, “I tell you that, in comparison with two evils, it would be far more tolerable for me that this entire place in which I founded the monastery, if God should so judge, be reduced to perpetual desolation, than that my carnal brother—whom we know does not walk in the way of truth—should succeed me in governing it under the name of abbot. Therefore, brothers, take great care always never to seek a father for yourselves according to family descent, nor from outside or elsewhere. But, in accordance with what the rule of the great abbot Benedict once prescribes, and in accordance with what the decrees of our privilege contain, seek in the common assembly of your congregation, by common counsel, one who is judged more suitable and more worthy to fulfill such an office according to the merit of his life and the teaching of his wisdom. Whoever you elect, having recognized him as the best by unanimous charitable inquiry, ask the bishop whom you summon to have him confirmed as abbot by the customary blessing [to strengthen him]. For those who beget carnal children in the carnal order must necessarily seek carnal and earthly heirs for their carnal and earthly inheritance. But those who beget spiritual children for God by the spiritual seed of the word must have everything they do be spiritual. Among their spiritual children, let them esteem as the elder the one endowed with the greater grace of the Spirit, just as earthly parents commonly recognize as the first of their children the one whom they have brought forth first in birth and consider him preferable to the others in the distribution of their inheritance.”

[Note: “Benedict.” The great abbot Benedict, in chapter 64 of his Rule, prescribes that the abbot “be chosen for the merit of his life and the teaching of his wisdom, whom the entire harmonious congregation shall elect for itself according to the fear of God.” Ceolfrid also inculcates the same rule. Mabillon.]

Nor should this be passed over in silence: the venerable abbot Benedict, to relieve the weariness of the long night, which he spent sleepless beneath the burden of his infirmity, would summon a reader and order that either Job, the model of patience, or some other passage from Scripture by which the sick man might be consoled and, though bowed down in the lowest depths, might be raised more vigorously toward heavenly things, be read aloud before him. And because he could in no way rise to pray, nor easily lift his tongue or voice to complete the customary course of psalmody, the prudent man, prompted by the devotion of his heart, learned to call some of the brothers to himself at each hour of the day or night prayer. While they recited the customary psalms in two resonant choirs, he himself sang with them as far as he could, supplying through their assistance what he could not accomplish alone.

But when both abbots, exhausted by prolonged illness, saw that death was already near and that they were no longer fit to govern the monastery—for such was the weakness of the flesh that afflicted them, so that the power of Christ might be perfected in them—then, one day, when they desired to see and speak with one another before departing from this world, Sigfrid was carried on a bier to the chamber where Benedict too lay upon his own bed. There, when attendants had arranged them together in one place and placed both their heads upon the same pillow, the spectacle was moving to tears: they did not even have enough strength to bring their faces, set near one another, together for a kiss. Yet they completed this fraternal duty as well. Benedict, after taking counsel with him and with all the brothers, summoned Ceolfrid as abbot—the man whom he had appointed over the monastery of the blessed apostle Paul—one who was related to him not so much by ties of flesh as by fellowship in virtue. With everyone favoring the decision and judging it most useful, he appointed him Father over both monasteries. He considered it wholly beneficial for preserving the peace, unity, and harmony of the communities that they should have one father and ruler permanently. He frequently recalled the example of the kingdom of Israel, which had always remained unconquerable by foreign nations and inviolate so long as it was governed by leaders of its own people who were one and the same; but after, because of the sins that had preceded, it was divided from itself by hostile conflict, it perished for a time and was shaken from its stability and collapsed. He also continually warned that the evangelical saying should be remembered without interruption: every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0723]

[Col. 0723B]

Thus, two months having passed after these events, first the venerable and God-beloved abbot Sigfrid, having passed through the fire and waters of temporal tribulations, was led into the refreshment of everlasting rest. He entered the dwelling of the heavenly kingdom, rendering to the Lord, in the perpetual sacrifices of praise, the vows which he had promised with the careful distinction of pure lips.

[Note: “Entered.” That is, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, on which day he is commemorated in the Benedictine calendars; specifically in the year 689, four months before Benedict, who died in the following January.]

Then, after four further months had been added, Benedict, victor over vices and outstanding performer of virtues, was brought to his end, overcome by the weakness of the flesh. A night cold with winter winds descended; soon the holy day of everlasting happiness, serenity, and light was to arise for him [was being born]. The brothers gathered in the church and passed the shadows of the night sleepless in prayers and psalms. By the continuous melody of divine praise they consoled the burden of their father’s departure. Others did not leave the chamber in which the sick man, strong in spirit, awaited the departure from death and entrance into life. Throughout the night, a presbyter read the Gospel, as had customarily been done on other nights as well, for the relief of his suffering. When the hour of departure drew near, the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood was given to him as viaticum. Thus that holy soul, baked and purified in the flames of long and blessed scourings, left the muddy furnace of the flesh and flew free into the glory of heavenly blessedness.

The psalm which was then sung on his behalf also bears witness to his most victorious departure, which was in no way hindered or delayed by unclean spirits. For the brothers, having hastened to the church at the beginning of the night and singing through the Psalter in order, had reached, as they sang, the eighty-second psalm, which begins:

> “O God, who is like you?”

Its entire text resounds with the message that the enemies of Christ’s name, whether carnal or spiritual, always strive to destroy and scatter Christ’s Church and every faithful soul; but that they themselves, confused and disturbed, will perish forever, weakened by the Lord, to whom no one is like and who alone is Most High over all the earth. It was therefore rightly understood that heaven had arranged for such a psalm to be sung at the hour when the soul departed from the body—one which, with the Lord’s help, no enemy could overcome.

[Note: “Sixteenth.” Therefore the year was not 703, as Matthew of Westminster writes, but 690, since the monastery at Wearmouth was founded at the beginning of the year 674. Smith. This is confirmed by the death of Easterwin, reported above in section 8, which occurred in the twelfth year after the monastery’s foundation, namely in 685. It is also confirmed by the death of the abbot Ceolfrid, which Bede explicitly states below, in section 21, occurred on the seventh day before the Kalends of October in the year 716. Ceolfrid, having been placed over both monasteries as abbot six months before Biscop’s death, held the government for twenty-eight years, beginning—as section 15 shows—from the year 689. This calculation runs from July of the year 689 to October of the year 716. Mabillon.]

In the sixteenth year after he founded the monastery, the confessor rested in the Lord, on the day before the Ides of January, and was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter. He had always loved that apostle while living in the flesh, and through Peter, who opened the door of the heavenly kingdom for him, he entered; therefore after death he would not be far removed in body from Peter’s relics and altar.

[Note: “January.”]

As we have said, he ruled the monastery for sixteen years: the first eight by himself, without another abbot being appointed; and the remaining eight with the assistance of the venerable and holy men Easterwin, Sigfrid, and Ceolfrid, who supported him under the name, authority, and office of abbot—Easterwin for the first four years, Sigfrid for three, and Ceolfrid for one.

The third of these, Ceolfrid, was a man industrious in all things, keen in intellect, energetic in action, mature in spirit, and ardent in the zeal of religion. As we have mentioned above, with Benedict both commanding and assisting him, he founded, completed, and governed the monastery of the blessed apostle Paul for seven years. Thereafter he presided for twenty-eight years over both monasteries—or, more correctly, over one monastery situated in two places, that of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul—with diligent administration. Everything which his distinguished predecessor had begun as an excellent work of virtue, he took care to complete no less zealously.

Among the other necessities of the monastery which, during his long period of administration, he discovered had to be arranged, he also built several more chapels. He enlarged the vessels and furnishings of the altar and church of every kind. He doubled the libraries of both monasteries through no less industrious effort than that with which Abbot Benedict had begun them: in addition to the one old translation which Benedict had brought from Rome, Ceolfrid himself added three pandects of a new translation.

[Note: “Pandects of the new translation which from…” The note is incomplete as printed.]

When, in his old age, he returned to Rome, he took one of these with him, among other gifts, and left two for the two monasteries. He also acquired, for the monastery of the blessed apostle Paul, a tract of land of eight hides beside the river Fresca, in exchange for a book of cosmography of marvelous workmanship which Benedict had bought at Rome. Benedict, while he was still alive, had fixed the terms of this exchange with the same King Aldfrid, most learned in Scripture, but died before he could complete it. Later, under King Osred, Ceolfrid, adding a suitable price, received in exchange for this land a tract of twenty hides at a place called in the language of the inhabitants “at the villa of Sambuce,” because it appeared closer to the same monastery.

He sent monks to Rome in the time of Pope Sergius, of blessed memory, and received from him, for the protection of his monastery, a privilege modeled on that which Pope Agatho had given to Benedict. When it had been brought to Britain and made public before a synod, it was confirmed by the subscriptions of the bishops then present and of the magnificent King Aldfrid. It is likewise well known that the earlier privilege had publicly been confirmed in a synod by the king and bishops of its own time.

In Ceolfrid’s time, when Witmer—a veteran and religious servant of Christ who governed the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter and was learned in every kind of secular knowledge as well as in knowledge of Scripture—gave himself to that monastery, he donated to it, by right of perpetual possession, the ten hides of land which he had received from King Aldfrid at the place called the villa of Daldun.

But when Ceolfrid, after the many disciplines of regular observance which he had prudently imposed upon himself, just as his father Benedict had done, by the authority of his predecessors; after his incomparable diligence in prayer and psalmody, in which he never ceased to exercise himself daily; after his marvelous fervor in restraining the wicked and his gentleness in consoling the weak; after his extraordinary restraint in food and drink and his plainness of dress—when he saw that, now advanced in age and full of days, he could no longer, because of the impediment of extreme old age, prescribe to his subjects the proper form of spiritual discipline either by teaching or by example, he pondered the matter at length within himself. He decided that it would be more useful to instruct the brothers to choose for themselves, according to the statutes of their privilege and the rule of the holy abbot Benedict, one of their own number who would be more suitable as their father.

[Note: “To prescribe.”]

[Note: “Of the blessed.” Through the carelessness of scribes these words appear to have been omitted, as Mabillon conjectures: “he should proceed to the threshold of the blessed apostles.” Smith.]

He himself would proceed to the threshold of the blessed apostles, where he had been with Benedict as a young man, so that, before death, he might for a time be released from worldly cares and devote himself more freely to solitary repose; while they, having taken a younger abbot, might more perfectly, in accordance with the age of their master, preserve the institutions of the regular life.

Although all at first resisted, repeatedly falling to their knees amid tears and sobs and earnest appeals, what he desired was done. So great was his desire to depart that on the third day after he had disclosed the secret of his purpose to the brothers, he set out on his journey. For he feared what in fact occurred: that he might die before he could reach Rome. At the same time he wished to avoid having his plans delayed by friends or leading men, all of whom held him in honor, and to avoid receiving money from certain people to whom he could not repay it in due time. He always had this custom: if anyone offered him a gift, he would repay it either immediately or after an interval with something appropriate, and with no less gratitude.

After Mass had first been sung in the church of the blessed mother of God and ever-virgin Mary and in the church of the apostle Peter on the day before the Nones of June, a Thursday, and after those present had received Communion, preparations were immediately made for departure. Everyone gathered in the church of the blessed Peter. Ceolfrid, having burned incense and recited a prayer at the altar, gave peace to everyone while standing on the steps, holding the thurible in his hand. Then, while the weeping of all resounded during the litanies, they went out.

They entered the oratory of the blessed martyr Laurence, which lay in their path within the brothers’ dormitory. There he gave his final farewell, admonishing them to preserve mutual love and, according to the Gospel, to correct those who sinned. To anyone who might have offended him, he offered the favor of his forgiveness and reconciliation [wherever anything had been done]. He begged everyone to pray for him and to remain at peace with him if there were any whom he had rebuked more harshly than justice required.

They came to the shore. Again he gave everyone the kiss of peace amid tears; they knelt, he offered a prayer, and then he boarded the ship with his companions. The deacons of the church also boarded, carrying burning candles and a golden cross. He crossed the river, venerated the cross, mounted his horse, and departed, leaving in his monasteries nearly six hundred brothers.

[Note: “Wherever.”]

When he had departed with his companions, the brothers returned to the church and commended themselves and all they possessed to the Lord with tears and prayer. After a short interval, when the psalmody of the third hour had been completed, they all gathered again. They consulted about what ought to be done and decided that they must seek their Father from God more quickly by praying, singing psalms, and fasting. Through some of the monks of the blessed Paul who were present, as well as some of their own number, they announced their decision to their brothers. Those men agreed. The two communities became of one mind; all hearts were raised upward, and all voices were lifted to the Lord.

At last, on the third day, when the Lord’s Day of Pentecost arrived, all who were in the monastery of the blessed Peter gathered in council. A considerable number of the elders from the monastery of the blessed Paul were also present.

[Note: “Who were in the monastery of the blessed Paul.”]

There was one agreement and the same judgment on both sides. Thus Huaetberctus was chosen as abbot. From the earliest years of his boyhood he had been trained in that same monastery not only in the discipline of regular observance, but also in writing, singing, reading, and teaching, in which he had been exercised with no small diligence.

He had also hurried to Rome in the time of Pope Sergius, of blessed memory, and, remaining there for a considerable period, had learned, written down, and brought back whatever he judged necessary for himself.

[Note: “What was necessary for himself.”]

[Note: “He said, wrote down.”]

In addition, twelve years before this he had undertaken the office of presbyter. Having therefore been elected abbot by all the brothers of both aforesaid monasteries, he immediately took some of the brothers with him and came to Abbot Ceolfrid, who was waiting for a ship in which he might cross the Ocean.

[Note: “A ship which…”]

[Note: “Waiting for him…”]

They announced to him the one whom they had elected as abbot. “Thanks be to God,” he replied, confirming the election. He received from Ceolfrid a letter of recommendation to be delivered to Pope Gregory.

[Note: “Gregory.” That is, Gregory II. Smith.]

For the sake of preserving his memory, we have thought it appropriate to include in this work several verses:

> “To the Lord’s beloved in the Lord of lords, thrice most blessed Pope Gregory, Huaetberctus, your humble servant, abbot of the monastery of the most blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, in Saxony, sends perpetual health in the Lord.
>
> “I do not cease to give thanks to the administration of the heavenly judgment, together with the holy brothers who with me in these regions desire to bear the most sweet yoke of Christ in order to find rest for their souls, because it has pleased God to appoint you, so glorious a vessel of election in our times, to govern the whole Church. Through this, by means of the light of truth and faith with which you yourself are filled, he might abundantly sprinkle even the least of us with the radiance of his mercy.
>
> “We commend to your holy kindness, most beloved father and lord in Christ, the venerable gray hairs of our most beloved Father, namely Abbot Ceolfrid, our nourisher and protector in the spiritual freedom and peace of monastic repose.
>
> “First, we give thanks to the holy and undivided Trinity because he, although he departed from us not without our greatest pain, sighing, mourning, and procession of tears, nevertheless reached the holy joys of the repose he had long desired. Always remembering that he had visited, seen, and adored those places when he was young, he returned in devotion, even weary with old age, to the thresholds of the blessed apostles.
>
> “After more than forty years of long labors and continual cares, during which he governed monasteries by right of the abbatial office, summoned as though only recently to the way of heavenly life by an incomparable love of virtue, exhausted by extreme old age and already near death, he again begins to travel for Christ, so that, with greater freedom, the spiritual fire of burning compunction may consume the ancient thickets of worldly anxieties.
>
> “Moreover, we beseech your Paternity to complete toward him, through your diligent final act of piety, what we were not worthy to do: for we know with certainty that, although you possess his body, both you and we have in him, devoted to God, whether his spirit remains in the body or has been released from its bonds of flesh, a great intercessor and patron with the heavenly mercy for our offenses.”

And the rest, which follows in the letter.

When Huaetberctus returned home, Bishop Acca was summoned and confirmed him in the office of abbot by the customary blessing.

[Note: “In the office of abbot, by the blessing, he confirmed him.” Thus abbots were already being blessed by bishops at that time, as Benedict also testifies in Book I. Acca was bishop of Hexham from 714 to 740; Bede speaks of him with the highest honor in *Ecclesiastical History* V.21. Mabillon.]

Among the countless rights of the monastery which he recovered by youthful and penetrating diligence, he did one thing above all that was pleasing and gratifying to everyone: he took up the bones of Abbot Easterwin, which had been placed in the portico at the entrance of the church of the blessed apostle Peter, and also the bones of Abbot Sigfrid, once his teacher, which had been buried outside the sanctuary on the south side. He enclosed both sets in one reliquary, divided by a central partition, and placed them inside the same church beside the body of the blessed Father Benedict.

[Note: “Father Benedict.” Here Bede calls the great abbot Benedict his own Father; certainly not Benedict Biscop, since during Bede’s lifetime Biscop had no church consecrated to him, and nowhere in this history does Bede call him blessed. Indeed, in chapter 13 of Bede’s *Life of St Cuthbert*, he calls Benedict of Cassino “the most holy Father Benedict,” and in chapter 13 “the blessed Father Benedict,” and again in chapter 19. Mabillon.]

He did this on Sigfrid’s feast day, that is, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September. On that same day, by the marvelous providence of God, the venerable servant of Christ Witmer, whom we mentioned above, also departed, and in the place where the aforesaid abbots had previously been buried, he who had been their imitator was himself laid to rest.

As has been said, the servant of Christ Ceolfrid, traveling toward the thresholds of the blessed apostles, died before he reached them, struck by illness. Having arrived at Langres around the third hour of the day, he departed to the Lord at the tenth hour of that same day. The next day he was honorably buried in the church of the blessed Twin Martyrs. Not only the English by nationality, more than eighty in number, who had been in his company, but also the inhabitants of that place dissolved in tears and mourning because they had been deprived of the expected presence of so venerable an old man.

No one could easily restrain his tears on seeing that some of his companions, having lost their father, began the journey; some, changing the intention with which they had desired to go to Rome, were returning home instead, in order to announce that he had been buried; while others remained at the tomb of the deceased among people whose language they did not know, out of their unquenchable affection for their Father.

[Note: “Langres.” Today Langres, an episcopal see subject to the archbishopric of Lyon in Gaul.]

At the time of his death he was seventy-four years old. He had exercised the priestly rank for forty-seven years and administered the office of abbot for thirty-five—or rather forty-three years.

[Note: “Forty-three years.” This is correctly read in the English Benedictine Martyrology, from which the Paris edition of this History should be corrected, since it reads “three years.” Mabillon.]

[Note: “Three years.”]

For from the first time when Benedict began to establish his monastery in honor of the most blessed chief of the apostles, Ceolfrid had been his inseparable companion, co-worker, and teacher of regular and monastic discipline.

[Note: “Benedict.” Bishop Adilwald of Winchester, who died in 984, purchased his body at great cost and transferred it to Thorney. William of Malmesbury, *On the Bishops*, IV.]

So that neither age, illness, nor the journey should ever diminish his ancient rigor, from the day on which he departed from his monastery until the day on which he died—that is, from the day before the Nones of June until the seventh day before the Kalends of October, for 114 days—he took care to chant the Psalter in order twice each day, apart from the canonical hours of prayer. Even when illness brought him to the point that, unable to ride, he had to be carried in a horse-litter, he offered God daily the gift of the saving sacrifice after Mass had been sung, except on the one day when he was sailing across the Ocean and during the three days before his death.

He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, in the year 716 from the incarnation of the Lord, on a Friday, after the ninth hour, in the meadows of the aforementioned city. The next day he was buried one mile south of that city in the monastery of the Twins, while a considerable company stood by and sang psalms—both Englishmen who had arrived with him and inhabitants of the monastery and city.

[Note: “The seventh day before the Kalends of October.” His name is entered in the Benedictine calendars on that very day. In *Ecclesiastical History* V.22, Bede attributes to Ceolfrid the persuasion of the Picts concerning the Catholic Easter and the tonsure, and reports the elegant and lengthy letter which he wrote on this subject to King Naiton. “The remains of his bones,” writes William, monk of Malmesbury, in Book III, chapter 3, of *The Kings of England*, “were carried in later years to the monastery, namely Wearmouth, and then, during the time of the Danish devastation, to Glastonbury.” Mabillon.]

[Note: “The Twins.” That monastery is now a conventual priory of Canons Regular of the Order of St Augustine, one and a half French miles from the city of Langres. From there Ceolfrid’s bones were later brought to the monastery at Wearmouth and then, during the Danish devastation, to Glastonbury. Malmesbury, *On the Kings*, III.3.]

The martyrs called the Twins, whose monastery and church received his burial, are Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus. Born at one birth from the same mother and reborn in the same faith of the Church, they left to that place a worthy memorial of their martyrdom together with their grandmother Leonilla. May they also extend to us, unworthy as we are, and to our Father, the aid of their intercession and protection.

# PROSE LIFE OF SAINT CUTHBERT, BISHOP OF LINDISFARNE, BY THE VENERABLE BEDE, ALMOST HIS CONTEMPORARY

[Text from Smith, *The Ecclesiastical History of the English People*; notes from Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of St Benedict*, and Smith.]

[Col. 0729]

[Col. 0729D]

## MABILLON’S PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

### 1

We present two Lives of Saint Cuthbert, or Cuberht: one written by Bede in prose, the other in verse, as Bede himself testifies in the preface to each Life, in Book IV, chapter 28, of his *History*, and finally in the catalogue of his works. We prefer the prose Life, since it is more complete, more carefully composed, and better attested, although the metrical Life was written first.

[Note: The Life written in verse is found in the third part of Bede’s works, section three, column 575 of this volume.]

A third Life of Cuthbert was issued around the year 700 in four books by an anonymous monk of Lindisfarne, a contemporary of Cuthbert and certainly a weighty authority. The Bollandist associates first published it in their March volume. We shall extract only its distinctive points and refer to them in notes.

Besides these authors, Turgot—first prior of the monastery of Durham of the Order of St Benedict and later bishop of St Andrews in Scotland—related the deeds of Saint Cuthbert near the end of the eleventh century in his *History of Durham*. Shortly afterward Simeon, likewise a monk and teacher of Durham, divided that work into four books and chapters and published it under his own name. John Selden, however, in the preface to his edition of the *Ten Writers of English History*, vindicated it for its genuine author.

### 2

The memory of Saint Cuthbert is celebrated in the ancient Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Wandalbert, Ado, Hrabanus, and Notker. He illuminated not only the kingdom of Northumbria but the entire island of Britain, and indeed the whole Church, with his splendor. Alcuin refers to this in Epigram 178, where he sings as follows:

> Great Father also, bishop, shepherd, priest,
>
> Cuthbert, now the glory of your Church:
>
> How much he achieved through pious prayers granted by the Lord,
>
> There is no need for our little verses to tell;
>
> Since earlier the illustrious master Bede
>
> Set forth in heroic verse the recorded deeds of the Father.
>
> All Britain celebrates him with frequent praises
>
> And thinks to aid itself through pious prayers.

Hence his feast day was not only celebrated with great distinction in the churches of Britain from ancient times, but also in other kingdoms and provinces, especially in Gaul on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.

For in the Book of Sacraments written by order of Ratold, abbot of Corbie, before the year 980, there is a special office of Saint Cuthbert, with a proper preface and an episcopal blessing, which was customarily used only on the more solemn days. In the Collect, or first prayer, Saint Cuthbert is called a martyr:

> “Holy and glorious Cutberht, a marvelous and powerful martyr and anchorite, whose work the Lord rejoices in, an excellent intercessor and most powerful protector: in God, remember us always in the presence of the Lord; grant aid here and forever.”

Then follow the Prayer over the Offerings and the Preface, and finally the Blessing, which it is useful to record here:

> “Lord, God of all graces, deign to look upon all this people of yours, who serve you in divine worship in your honor; and whatever contributed to the blessedness of your holy martyr Cutberht on this day, may it contribute to this Church as an example. Amen.
>
> “Through his intercession, may there be in them right faith, an imitable form of chaste sobriety, hospitable charity, spiritual prudence, profound wisdom, a humble mind, and an exalted life. Amen.
>
> “So that, when they stand before you in the presence of the fearful day of judgment, they may hear from your mouth not a sentence of condemnation but the gentle sentence of absolution. May he himself deign to grant this, and so forth.”

In these passages the name “martyr” is used in the strict sense for a confessor.

### 3

As a young man, Cuthbert became a monk at the monastery of Mailros on the River Tweed—called Tinidim or Tuveda—in the kingdom of Bernicia, now a river in the border region, or March, of modern Scotland. This occurred in 651. He remained there until 664, serving for some time in the office of prior.

He later exercised that office on the island of Lindisfarne until 676, when he led the eremitical life on the Farne until the year of his election as bishop, 684.

Lindisfarne is called the Holy Island in English because of the habitation there of holy monks. As Bede says in Book III, chapter 3 of his *History*, with the tide advancing and receding, the sea surrounds it with waves twice each day, like an island, and twice, when the shore is laid bare, returns it to the mainland. Lindisfarne takes its name from the River Lindo, which lies opposite the coast of Northumbria and flows into the sea. According to Turgot in Book II, chapter 5, of his *History of Durham*, the river is two feet wide and can be seen only when the sea has withdrawn.

From there, seven miles toward the east-southeast, the island of Farne can be seen, enclosed by the very deep Ocean. Saint Cuthbert completed his final day on Farne; at Lindisfarne he obtained burial.

## 4. What Rule Cuthbert Followed

What rule Cuthbert followed must be investigated briefly. The Bollandist associates seem to suggest that the rule of Saint Columba, abbot of Iona, was then observed in the monasteries visited by Cuthbert; whether this is so, let the reader judge from the arguments that follow.

Columba, a Scottish abbot, followed the institutions of the Scots with regard to the tonsure and Easter. “This disagreement concerning the observance of Easter,” says Bede, Book III, chapter 25, “was patiently tolerated by everyone while Aidan was alive.
