But after Finan, who followed him, had died, when Colman succeeded him in the episcopate—he too having been sent from Scotland—a more serious controversy arose concerning the observance of Easter and also concerning other disciplines of ecclesiastical life.”

A synod was held in the monastery of Streaneshalch, over which Abbess Hilda then presided, in the year 664, according to the same author in the following chapter. When the conflict was over, Colman, seeing that his doctrine had been rejected and his sect despised, took with him those who wished to follow him—that is, those who refused to accept the Catholic Easter and the circular tonsure—and returned to Scotland, that is, Ireland.

For the brothers who preferred to remain in the Church of Lindisfarne after the Scots had departed, the most reverend and gentle Eata, who was abbot in the monastery called Mailros, was appointed as abbot. They say that Colman, when he was about to depart, requested and obtained this from King Oswiu, because Eata had been one of Aidan’s twelve boys whom, at the beginning of his episcopate, Aidan had received from the English nation to educate in Christ.

Eata bestowed on Cuthbert the tonsure and the monastic habit: the tonsure, I say, not the Scottish one, but Peter’s, in the form of the crown of thorns encircling Christ’s head, according to an anonymous Lindisfarne monk. The continuators of Bollandus suspect that the anonymous text has been interpolated at this point. Bede’s authority, cited above, seems to support the conjecture; from it, it would appear that Scottish practices were retained in the monasteries of Mailros and Lindisfarne until the year 664, when the synod was held.

Moreover, Cuthbert had received the tonsure at Mailros in 651. Yet Abbot Eata, although a disciple of Colman, could, as an Englishman, already have renounced Scottish customs and adopted the Roman observance. In any event, it is at least certain that after the synod just mentioned Cuthbert adhered to the Roman party and to the Benedictine Rule.

Certainly, as Bede testifies in chapter 39 of his prose Life, Cuthbert, when he was near death, is said to have warned his disciples that they should have no communion with those who departed from the unity of Catholic peace, whether by celebrating Easter at the wrong time or by living perversely.

And the Anonymous author says in Book III:

> “While living there”—that is, on the island of Farne—“according to Holy Scripture, he led a contemplative life amid active duties, and first established and composed for us a regular way of life, which to this day we observe together with the Rule of Benedict.”

The Anonymous author was writing while King Aldfrith was reigning peacefully, as appears from Book III, section 6; therefore he wrote before the year 705, when that king died. Thus, already before the year 700, the Rule of Saint Benedict was being observed by the monks of Lindisfarne—indeed, while Cuthbert himself was alive.

For those monks practiced the midday rest with Cuthbert as their superior, doubtless in accordance with the prescription of the Benedictine Rule in chapter 48: “After rising from the sixth hour, let them rest on their beds.” The office of prior, which Boisil and Cuthbert exercised under the abbot, also seems to have derived from the decree of the same Rule in chapter 65. One would not easily find a prior together with an abbot in the same monastery except in monasteries devoted to Benedictine institutions.

Finally, Wilfrid, an outstanding propagator of the Benedictine Rule, after defeating the Scots at the aforesaid synod and driving them from Northumbria by the force of truth—his opponents themselves agreeing—without doubt imposed the Rule of Saint Benedict on the monasteries abandoned by the Scots. Nevertheless, we do not doubt that certain decrees or statutes, in addition to the Rule of Saint Benedict, were prescribed for the monks of Lindisfarne.

## 5.

“In almost none of the churches,” says Turgottus in Book II, chapter 17, “which the blessed confessor, whether before, during, or after his flight, illumined by the presence of his sacred body, is there known to this day to be any permission for women to enter.” We shall note below, in chapter 10, the reason assigned by the author in that passage.

Thus, with both men and women consenting, he entirely prohibited female companionship, both for his own time and for all future times, and completely excluded women from entering his church. Accordingly, when a church had been built on the island of his episcopal see—called in the language of the natives Grenechiche, that is, “the green church,” because it stood on the level ground of a green field—he ordered women to gather there to hear Mass and the word of God, so that they might never approach more closely to the church in which he lived with the monks.

This custom is carefully observed to the present day, to such an extent that, unless fear of an enemy or the burning of the place compels it, women are not even permitted to enter the cemeteries of those churches where his body had rested for a time. These matters are to be treated more fully in chapter 8 and following of the *Miracles of Saint Cuthbert*, to be assigned to the fourth Benedictine century.

---

# [THE LIFE OF SAINT CUTHBERT (C)]

## Preface, to Eadfrith, Bishop of Lindisfarne

[Col. 0733B] To the holy and most blessed lord and father, Bishop Eadfrith [Note: [Col. 0733D] Edfrith.] [Note: [Col. 0733D] Eadfrith. He governed the Church of Lindisfarne from 698 to 720; and for the use of Saint Cuthbert he wrote that most celebrated manuscript of the Gospels, which is still preserved in the Cotton Library. He also restored the anciently dilapidated oratory of the hermitage at Farne during the time of Felgeld. Aldhelm, abbot of Malmesbury, wrote a letter to him, which is preserved in *Epistolae Hibernicae*, Sylloge no. 13. —Smith.] and to the entire congregation of brothers who serve Christ on the island of Lindisfarne, Bede [Note: [Col. 0733D] “Faithful fellow servant.”], your faithful fellow servant, sends greetings.

Since you, dearest brothers, ordered me [Note: [Col. 0733D] “That in the book.”] to place at the beginning of the book which I composed at your request concerning the life of our father, blessed in memory, Cuthbert, a preface according to custom, so that through it the desire of your will and the fraternal assent of our obedience might alike become clear to all readers, I thought it appropriate, at the beginning of the preface, both to recall for you, who know these things, and to make known to those who may read them in ignorance, that I presumed neither to write anything about so great a man without the most certain investigation of the events of his life, nor finally, after writing it, to give what I had written to certain persons for copying here and there without the most careful examination [Note: [Col. 0733D] “With subtle examination.”] of unquestionable witnesses. Rather, I first diligently investigated the beginning, progress, and conclusion of his most glorious conduct and life from those who had known him. I judged that their names, too, should be included at several points in the book as evidence of the truth known to them; only then did I begin to set hand to my tablets.

When the little work had been arranged, though still retained on tablets, I frequently presented what I had written for reading and immediate reconsideration to our most reverend brother, the presbyter Herefrith, whenever he came here, and to others who had lived longer with the man of God and knew his life very well. I carefully corrected some passages according to their judgment, as they seemed appropriate. Thus, after all the tortuous uncertainties had been completely removed, I took care to entrust to these parchment leaves a sure investigation of the truth, expressed in simple language, and to bring it also into the presence of your fraternity, so that, by the judgment of your authority, either [Note: [Col. 0733D] “False things might be corrected.”] the things written might be corrected as false, or approved as true.

When, with the Lord’s help [Note: [Col. 0733D] “With the Lord assisting.”], I had accomplished this, and the little book had been read for two days before the elders and teachers of your congregation, and each point had been most diligently weighed according to your examination, no statement at all was found that ought to be changed. Rather, by common agreement, everything written was judged [Note: [Col. 0734D] “Without any ambiguity.”] without any doubt to be suitable for reading and to be handed over for transcription to those who wished to pursue their religious studies.

Moreover, in our presence you added many other matters concerning the life and virtues of the blessed man, matters no less important than those we had written, discussing them together. They seemed wholly [Note: [Col. 0734D] “Worthy of remembrance.”] worthy of remembrance, if it were not clear that, once a work had been deliberated and completed, it would be inappropriate and unbecoming to insert or append new material.

I then thought that your blessedness’s crown [Note: [Col. 0734D] “Crown.” In former times bishops were addressed in this way. Consult Salmasius, in his book *On the Hair*, where he holds that by the word “crown” not the clerical crown, as they say, but episcopal dignity is expressed. —Mabillon.] should be reminded that, just as I did not delay in promptly fulfilling the duty of obedience which you deigned to command, so you too should not be reluctant to repay me with the reward of your intercession. When, as you reread this little book, the pious memory of our most holy father raises your minds more ardently toward the desires of the heavenly kingdom, remember also in your prayers my lowliness, and beseech divine mercy on my behalf, so that I may deserve both now to desire with a pure mind and in the future, in perfect blessedness, to behold the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.

And when I have died, deign to pray and celebrate Masses for the redemption of my soul [Note: [Col. 0734D] “As though for a familiar servant.”] as though I were your familiar servant and household slave, and to write my name among those of your congregation.

For you too, most holy bishop, still remember that you promised me this. As evidence of that future inscription, you instructed your religious brother Gudfrith, the sacristan [Note: [Col. 0735] Gudfrith. He later presided over the monastery of Lindisfarne with the authority of abbot; see V, 1. —Smith.], to place my name now also in the register of your holy congregation.

But let your holiness know that the life of that same father of ours, beloved of God, which I gave you in prose, somewhat shorter but nevertheless in the same order, I also published, at the request of certain of our brothers, in heroic verse composed long ago. If you are pleased to have these verses, you may receive a copy from me. In the preface to that work I promised that I would write elsewhere at greater length about his life and miracles; I am now hastening to fulfill that promise in the present little work, as the Lord grants [Note: [Col. 0735A] “As God wills.”].

While I pray for you, may the almighty Lord deign to keep your blessedness safe and unharmed, dearest brothers and my lords. Amen.

# SAINT CUTHBERT, BISHOP OF LINDISFARNE: BOOK ON HIS LIFE AND MIRACLES

## Chapter One — How the boy Cuthbert was warned by a child about the episcopate foretold for him

[Col. 0735B]

The prophet Jeremiah consecrates the beginning of our writing about the life of the blessed Cuthbert. Glorifying the state of anchoritic perfection, he says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he will sit alone and remain silent, because he will lift himself above himself.”

Set aflame by the sweetness of this goodness, the man of God Cuthbert, from the beginning of adolescence, subjected his neck to the yoke of monastic discipline [Note: [Col. 0735C] “Submitted.”]. Whenever opportunity allowed, he also adopted the anchoritic way of life. For no little time he took delight in sitting alone and, because of the sweetness of divine contemplation, remaining silent from human conversation.

But so that he might do these things at a more mature age, heavenly grace had already driven him gradually toward the way of truth from his earliest years [Note: [Col. 0735C] “Toward life.”]. [Note: [Col. 0735D] “Years.” Nothing is said here of Saint Cuthbert’s homeland or parents. We shall indicate his homeland below, in chapter 4; that his parents were of humble rank is sufficiently apparent from the shepherd’s service which, in the same place, the holy man is said to have performed. —Mabillon.] For until the eighth year of his life—the first year of childhood after infancy—he had known how to give his mind only to the games and frivolity of little boys. Thus the testimony once given about the blessed Samuel could then be applied to him: “Cuthbert did not yet know the Lord, nor had the word of the Lord yet been revealed to him.”

This was said as a proclamation of praise for his childhood [Col. 0736B], since when he grew older he would come to know the Lord perfectly and receive the Lord’s word through the revealed ear of his heart.

As we have said, he delighted in games and childish cries. As the order of his age required, he wished to join the gatherings of little boys and desired to play with those at play. Since he was agile by nature and sharp in intelligence, he often used to prevail over those competing with him in games, so that when the others were sometimes exhausted, he, still tireless, would cheerfully ask whether any of them wished to compete with him further [Note: [Col. 0736C] “If anyone wished to continue with him.”].

Whether they exercised themselves by jumping, running, wrestling, or any other movement of their limbs, he boasted that he had defeated all his peers and even some older boys. While he was little, he thought and reasoned as a little boy; but later, when he became a man, he completely put away the things that belonged to childhood.

Indeed, divine providence first deigned to restrain the pride of his boyish spirit with a teacher suited to him [Note: [Col. 0736C] “Worthy of him.”]. For the blessed-in-memory Bishop Trumwine [Note: [Col. 0735D] Trumwine. Consecrated bishop of the Picts in 681; he persuaded Saint Cuthbert to accept the episcopate, IV, 28. After Ecgfrith was defeated, the Picts expelled him from their territory, IV, 26. —Smith. —The Anonymous author, Book I: “First we relate what we learned from the testimony of many people to have happened in his earliest years. Among them was Bishop Tuma, holy in memory, who learned from Saint Cuthbert that God’s spiritual election had been predestined; and there was also Elias, a priest of our Church.” The Benedictine calendars list Saint Trumwine, bishop of the Southern Picts, on the fifth day before the Ides of February. Bollandus, however, places his eulogy on the following day and assigns his death to about the year 700. Concerning the discovery of Saint Trumwine’s relics, see William of Malmesbury, Book III *On the Bishops of the English*. He is also mentioned below, chapter 24, and in Bede, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 26. —Mabillon.] used to report that Cuthbert himself had told him the following.

One day, when a considerable crowd of boys was engaged in its customary wrestling in a certain field, Cuthbert himself was among them. As is usual with the frivolity of players, many of them were twisting their limbs in various ways contrary to the proper condition of nature. Suddenly one of the little boys, about three years old, as it seemed, ran up to Cuthbert and, with something like the firmness of an old man, began to urge him not to indulge in games and idleness, but rather to subject both mind and limbs to stability.

When Cuthbert disregarded the warning, the child fell to the ground, lamenting and wetting his face with tears. The others ran up to console him, but he continued to weep. They asked what sudden thing had happened and why he was afflicted by such great lamentation.

At last he cried out to Cuthbert, who was consoling him:

> “Why, most holy Bishop and Priest Cuthbert, are you doing things contrary both to your nature and to your rank? It is not fitting for you to play among little children, since the Lord has consecrated you as a teacher of virtue even for those older than yourself.”

Hearing this, the boy of good character received the words with fixed attention. Gently caressing the sorrowful child with loving kindness, he immediately abandoned the vanity of play, returned home, and from that time onward began to be more stable in mind and more mature in spirit. It was plainly the Spirit who taught his inmost heart inwardly, the same Spirit who had sounded in his ears outwardly through the child’s mouth.

No one should wonder that, by the Lord’s action, a child’s frivolity could be restrained by means of a child. For, in order to restrain the prophet’s folly [Note: [Col. 0737D] “Folly by the mouth.”], the Lord caused rational words to come forth, when he wished, from the mouth of a dumb beast of burden; and in his praise it is truly said: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise.”

## Chapter II — How he became lame because of a painful knee and was healed by an angel acting as physician [Note: [Col. 0737D] “Healed without delay by a physician.”]

[Col. 0737C]

But because “to everyone who has, more will be given,” that is, because the abundance of virtues will be granted by a heavenly gift to one who possesses the purpose and love of virtue, the boy of the Lord, Cuthbert, deserved to be strengthened even by the sight and speech of an angel, since he carefully retained in his heart the exhortations he had received through a human being [Note: [Col. 0737D] “Which he received through a human being.”].

For suddenly he was seized by a sharp pain in the knee, and it began to swell greatly, so that, with the tendons contracted behind the knee, he first carried his foot raised from the ground, walking with a limp; then, as the affliction grew worse, he lost all ability to walk.

One day, after attendants had carried him outside and he was lying in the open air, he suddenly saw a horseman approaching from a distance. The man was dressed in white garments and was honorable in appearance, and the horse on which he rode was of incomparable beauty [Note: [Col. 0737D] “Which he was riding.”].

When the rider arrived and greeted him with gentle words, he added, as if joking, a question as to whether Cuthbert wished to offer any service to such a guest.

Cuthbert replied:

> “I would already be most eager to devote myself to your service, if I were not, because of my sins, held fast by the fetter of this illness. For a long time now I have been oppressed by the affliction of a swollen knee, and no skill of any physician can heal me.”

The rider dismounted and examined the ailing knee carefully.

> “Cook wheat flour in milk,” he said, “and with this warm preparation anoint the swelling; you will be healed.”

After saying this, he mounted his horse and departed. Cuthbert obeyed the command and was healed after a few days. He recognized that the one who had given him this advice had been an angel, sent by the one who once deigned to send the archangel Raphael to heal Tobit’s eyes.

If anyone thinks it incredible that an angel appeared on a horse, let him read the history of the Maccabees, in which angels are said to have arrived on horses both for the defense of Judas Maccabaeus and for the defense of the Temple itself.

## Chapter III — How, by changing the winds through prayer, he recalled to shore rafts that had drifted out into the ocean

[Col. 0738B]

From that time onward, the boy devoted to the Lord, as he later used to attest to his familiar friends, often deserved to be defended by angelic assistance when he prayed to the Lord amid the troubles surrounding him. Moreover, when he prayed with kindly compassion for others who were in danger, he was heard by the one who habitually hears the poor man when he cries out and rescues him from all his tribulations [Note: [Col. 0737D] “With that benevolent compassion.”].

There is a monastery situated not far south of the mouth of the River Tyne [Note: [Col. 0737D] Tyne. The Tyne meant here is the river of modern Scotland in the province of Lothian, beside which the celebrated monastery of Tyningham was situated; it is not the River Tyne of modern Northumbria. —Smith.], which at that time was flourishing with a noble company of men, but now, as the condition of things commonly changes with time, with a distinguished community of virgins serving Christ.

The servants of Christ were transporting by rafts, from a distance along the bed of the aforesaid river, timber suitable for the needs of the monastery. When they had come opposite the monastery in the course of their journey and were attempting to draw the rafts onto the land [Note: [Col. 0738D] “They reached it.”], suddenly an untimely wind rose from the west [Note: [Col. 0738D] “Unseasonable.”], seized the rafts, and began to drag them away from the mouth of the river.

When the brothers in the monastery saw this, they sent little boats onto the river and tried to assist those laboring on the rafts [Note: [Col. 0738D] “Sending boats onto the river.”]. But, overcome by the force of the river and the violence of the winds, they were entirely unable to do so [Note: [Col. 0738D] “They were unable.”]. Having therefore despaired of human assistance, they fled to divine help.

They left the monastery and, gathering at the nearest barrier as the rafts drifted into the ocean [Note: [Col. 0738D] “At the nearest bank”], bent their knees and implored the Lord on behalf of those whom they saw about to plunge into such extreme danger of death.

But by divine providence the prayers of those who had been praying for a long time were delayed, so that the power of Cuthbert’s prayer might be revealed.

A considerable crowd of ordinary people was standing on the opposite bank of the river, and Cuthbert himself was among them. When they watched with the sorrowful monks as the rafts were carried farther out to sea, they appeared almost like five small birds [Note: [Col. 0739D] “For five rafts with their occupants were visible.”]—for indeed five rafts appeared to be sitting upon the waves. The crowd began to mock the way of life of the monks, as though they deserved to suffer such things because, scorning the common laws of mortals, they were establishing new and unknown rules of living.

Cuthbert forbade the mockers’ insults:

> “What are you doing, brothers,” he said, “cursing those whom you see already being dragged to death? Would it not be better and more humane to pray to the Lord for their safety than to rejoice in their dangers?”

But those rustic people, angry in both mind and speech against him, replied:

> “Let no human being pray for them, and let God have mercy on none of them—men who have taken the ancient observances away from men, and no one knows how the new ones ought to be observed.””

After receiving this answer, Cuthbert himself knelt to pray to the Lord and bowed his head to the ground. Immediately the force of the winds turned back, brought the intact rafts and those joyfully hauling them onto the shore, and set them down in a suitable place beside the monastery.

When the rustics saw this, they were ashamed of their unbelief. They proclaimed the faith of the venerable Cuthbert, now worthy of praise, and thereafter never ceased to proclaim it. A most trustworthy brother of our monastery, from whom I learned this account, used to relate that he himself had often heard these things from one of those rustic men—a man of simple nature and entirely incapable of pretense—in the presence of many others.

## Chapter IV — How, while he was with shepherds, he saw the soul of Saint Aidan carried to heaven by angels

When the grace of Christ, which guides the life of the faithful, wished its servant to undertake the virtue of a stricter purpose and to earn the glory of a higher reward, it happened that he was tending the flocks entrusted to him in remote mountains [Note: [Col. 0740D] “In the mountains.” That is, beside the River Leader, as Simeon of Durham writes, p. 2. This river of Scotland is today called the Lauder and flows into the Tweed. Hence understand that Cuthbert was born in the eastern region of modern Scotland. —Smith.].

One night, while his companions were sleeping and he himself, as usual, remained constantly awake in prayer, he suddenly saw a light poured out from heaven interrupt the darkness in the middle of the long night. In that light he saw choirs of heavenly hosts come down to earth and, without delay, take with them a soul of exceptional charity [Note: [Col. 0740D] “Carrying it away with them”] and return to the heavenly homeland.

The youth beloved of God was deeply moved by this vision, and immediately gave praise and thanks to God, in order to undertake the grace of spiritual discipline and to earn the happiness of everlasting life among glorious men. He also urged his companions to praise the Lord with fraternal exhortation:

> “Wretched men that we are,” he said, “devoted to sleep and idleness, we are not worthy always to see the light of Christ’s ever-watchful servants. Yet here I was, keeping vigil in prayer for only a short part of the night, and I saw such great marvels of God. The gate of heaven was opened, and the spirit of some holy man was led there in an angelic company. Now, blessed forever, he beholds the glory of the heavenly dwelling and Christ, its king, while we remain here amid the lowest darkness. Indeed, I think that he was either some holy bishop or an outstanding man from among the faithful. I saw him borne into heaven in the splendor of such great light and by so many choirs of angels leading him.”

By these words the man of God Cuthbert greatly kindled the hearts of the shepherds toward reverence and the praise of God. When morning came, he recognized that Aidan, bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne and certainly a man of great virtue, had departed from the body and sought the heavenly kingdoms at the very time when he had seen the vision. He immediately entrusted the sheep he was tending to their owners and resolved to seek the monastery [Note: [Col. 0739D] “Immediately.” That is, in the year 651, when Bishop Aidan died; Cuthbert went to the monastery, III, 14. But it is more difficult to determine in what year Saint Cuthbert was born; perhaps around the time when Aidan came to the English to be ordained bishop, namely about the year 635, III, 3. —Smith. “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 651,” says Simeon, or rather Turgottus, in Book I of the *History of Durham*, chapter 3, “when Bishop Aidan passed to the heavenly realms, that most holy young man entered the monastery of Mailros, intending to serve Christ alone, and was received by the most reverend Abbot Eata.” Mailros, moreover, is said to be a place in modern Scotland, situated on the bank of the River Tindi, commonly called the Teude, according to Bede, *History*, Book IV, chapter 27. —Mabillon.].

## Chapter V — How, while traveling, he received food through the Lord’s provision

While he was already carefully considering in his heart the beginning of a new and more abstinent life, heavenly grace came to strengthen his mind more firmly in its purpose and to teach him by clear signs that, for those who seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, the things needed for bodily sustenance are added through the benefit of the divine promise.

One day, as he was traveling alone, he turned aside at the third hour to a village which he happened to find at some distance. He entered the house of a devout married woman, wishing to rest there briefly, and taking care to ask for food more for the animal on which he rode [Note: [Col. 0740D] “On which he was riding.”] than for himself; for it was the beginning of winter.

The woman received him kindly and earnestly asked whether she might prepare a meal and refresh him. The man of God refused:

> “I cannot eat yet,” he said, “because today is a day of fasting.”

For it was Friday, on which most of the faithful, out of reverence for the Lord’s Passion, customarily prolonged their fast until the ninth hour [Note: [Col. 0740D] “Hour.” Bede, in Book III of the *History*, chapter 5, attributes this as a point of praise to Saint Aidan, the bishop of Lindisfarne mentioned above: “Following his example, at that time religious men and women everywhere made it their custom throughout the year, except during the relaxation of the Easter Pentecost, to prolong their fast until the ninth hour on the fourth and sixth days of the week.” —Mabillon.].

The woman, devoted to the practice of hospitality, persisted in her request.

> “Look,” she said, “along the road by which you are traveling you will find neither a village nor any human dwelling. A long journey still remains, and it cannot be completed before sunset. Therefore, I beg you, take some food before you leave, lest you be forced to endure or even postpone your fast throughout the entire day.”

Although the woman pleaded at length, he overcame her insistence through his love of religious observance and spent the day fasting until evening.

When evening was already approaching and he saw that he could not complete the journey he had undertaken that day, and that there were no human dwellings nearby where he could stay, he suddenly saw, beside some shepherds’ huts, the temporary shelters that had been poorly erected in summer and now stood abandoned.

He entered one of them in order to spend the night, tied the horse on which he had arrived to the wall, and placed before it a bundle of hay which the wind had torn from the roof. He himself began to spend the hour in prayer.

Suddenly, while he was singing psalms [Note: [Col. 0741D] “While chanting psalms.”], he saw the horse, raising its head upward, biting at the roof and pulling down with its mouth a cloth which, wrapped among the falling hay, also came down. Wishing to discover more certainly what it was, he approached after finishing his prayer and found half a loaf of warm bread and some meat wrapped in the cloth—enough to provide him with one meal.

Giving praise, he sang:

> “I give thanks to God, who has deigned to provide a supper both for me, fasting for love of him [read: *eius*, “of him”], and for my companion.””

He therefore divided the piece of bread he had found, gave half of it to the horse, and reserved the rest for his own food. From that day onward he became more ready to fast, since he understood that, in the wilderness, food had been provided for him by the gift of the one who once fed the solitary Elijah for a long time by means of birds, since no human being was present to minister to him.

His eyes are upon those who fear him and hope in his mercy, to rescue their souls from death and feed them in famine.

A religious presbyter of our monastery situated at the mouth of the River Wear, named Ingwald [Note: [Col. 0741D] “Of the presbyter.”], who now, through the grace of a long old age, contemplates heavenly things with a pure heart rather than earthly things with bodily eyes, declared that he had heard this from Cuthbert himself, who was already then a bishop.

The Anonymous author, briefly summarizing the miracles, adds the following at the end of Book I:

> “I omit how, when he was sitting in a camp with an army against the enemy, although he had only a small allowance, he nevertheless lived abundantly throughout the entire period, divinely nourished, just as Daniel and the three boys, not content with royal food, were marvelously fattened on servile and very scanty fare. Nor do I pass over how he saw the soul of a prefect, at the time of his death, carried up to heaven.”

These matters Bede omits. —Mabillon.

## Chapter VI [Note: [Col. 0742D] “What testimony he gave him … how he …”] — What testimony the holy man Boisil prophetically gave Cuthbert in spirit when he came to the monastery

Meanwhile, the venerable servant of the Lord, having abandoned the affairs of the world, hastened to undertake monastic discipline. A heavenly vision had stirred him to desire the joys of eternal blessedness, and heavenly banquets had invited him to endure hunger and thirst for the Lord for a time.

He knew that the Church of Lindisfarne possessed many holy men whose teaching and example could instruct him, but, having been forewarned by the fame of Boisil’s lofty virtues, he preferred to go to Mailros [Note: [Col. 0742D] Mailros. Concerning this monastery, see IV, 27. —Smith.].

It happened by chance that, when he had arrived there with his horse and dismounted, and was about to enter the church to pray, he gave both the horse and the spear he had held in his hand to a servant. For he had not yet laid aside his secular clothing. Boisil himself, standing before the doors of the monastery, saw him first.

Foreseeing in spirit what sort of man Cuthbert would become in his way of life, Boisil said only this to those standing nearby:

> “Behold the servant of God,”

imitating the one who, seeing Nathanael coming to him [Note: [Col. 0742D] “Nathanael unwillingly.”], said:

> “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” [Note: [Col. 0742D] “A true Israelite.”].

So the devout and veteran servant of God, the presbyter Sigfrid [Note: [Col. 0742D] This Sigfrid must be distinguished from Sigfrid, abbot of Wearmouth and Jarrow, who is known from the *History of the Abbots of Wearmouth and Jarrow*, published below, to have died in 689. —Smith.], used to testify. He was among those standing beside Boisil when he said these things. At that time he was a young man in the monastery itself, still being instructed in the first beginnings of monastic life. Now, in our monastery—that is, the monastery of Jarrow—he is living as a man perfected in Christ and, amid the afflicted sighs of his final illness, joyfully longs for entry into the other life.

Boisil said no more. When Cuthbert soon came to him, he received him kindly. After Cuthbert explained the reason for his journey—namely, that he had preferred the monastery to the world—Boisil kept him with him in kindness [Note: [Col. 0742D] “He kindly retained him for himself.”]. For he was the prior of that monastery.

And a few days later, when Eata, a man of blessed memory—then priest and abbot of that monastery, and afterward of the Church of Lindisfarne, as well as bishop of that same place—arrived, he told him about Cuthbert and explained that he possessed a mind inclined toward a good purpose. He prevailed upon him to accept the tonsure and be joined to the company of the brethren.

[Note: With the help of the Lord, he had received the tonsure in the form of Peter’s tonsure, like a crown of thorns encircling Christ’s head, says the Anonymous author at the beginning of Book II. Certainly, the Northumbrians had accepted Catholic Easter and the Roman tonsure in the year 664, as Bede testifies in Book III, chapter 25; indeed, the monks of Ripon had accepted them earlier. Hence, when close to death, Cuthbert warned his disciples to avoid schismatics. Mabillon.]

[Note: And having entered.]

When he entered the monastery, he immediately took care to observe the same rule of life as the other brothers, or even to surpass them in the pursuits of stricter discipline. He was especially diligent in reading, working, keeping vigil, and praying. Like the example of the once exceedingly strong Nazarite Samson, he carefully abstained from everything that could intoxicate; but he was unable to undertake such strict abstinence from food, lest he become less capable of the necessary tasks. For he was strong in body, sound in his powers, and fit for every kind of labor he wished to undertake.

## CHAPTER VII. How, when he received an angel as a guest, he deserved to be rewarded by him with heavenly food while seeking to provide earthly bread.

When, after some years, King Alchfrith wished, for the redemption of his soul, to give Eata the abbot a certain place in his kingdom, called Inhyrpum, in order that a monastery might be built there—

[Note: Eata … Eata.]

[Note: To give. Before the year 660. Smith.]

[Note: In-Hrype. According to Camden, Rippa, in Saxon Hrippum, was situated between the River Ure and the boundary of the northern and western divisions of Yorkshire, and the small River Skell. Bede speaks of it more than once in his History. In Book III, chapter 25, he says that King Alchfrith gave Wilfrid a monastery of forty households at the place called In-Hrippum, which shortly before he had given into the possession of those who followed the Scots. Wilfrid is said to have lived there for three years and finally to have been buried there, in Book V, chapter 20. Mabillon.]

—the same abbot took some of the brothers with him, among them Cuthbert, founded there the monastery that had been requested, and instructed them in the discipline of the rule according to the practices by which they had previously been formed at Mailros.

There the servant of the Lord, Cuthbert, being appointed to the duty of receiving guests, is said, as an opportunity to prove his devotion, to have received an angel as his guest.

[Note: For, going out.]

Early in the morning, therefore, he went from the inner buildings of the monastery to the guesthouse and found there a certain young man sitting. Thinking him to be a human being, he immediately received him in the customary manner of hospitality. He gave him water for washing his hands, himself washed his feet, wiped them with a linen cloth, and humbly placed them in his lap to warm them with his hands. He then asked him to wait until the third hour of the day so that he might be refreshed with food, lest, if he departed fasting, he should become weary from hunger as well as from the winter cold. For he thought that the man, exhausted both by a night journey and by blasts of snow, had turned aside at dawn in order to rest.

The man refused, replying that he would soon depart, because the lodging to which he was hurrying was farther away. But Cuthbert, entreating him at length and with great persistence, finally compelled him to remain by adding an adjuration in the divine name. As soon as, after the prayers of the third hour had been completed, the time for eating arrived, he set the table and offered food to be eaten. “I beg you, brother,” he said, “refresh yourself while I go back to bring hot bread; for I hope that it has now been baked.”

[Note: Third hour. Was it therefore forbidden at that time to take food before the third hour? Certainly, the Council of Carthage, chapter 12, prohibits banquets before the third hour; see Burchard, Book II, chapter 165. Mabillon.]

[Note: The loaves are baked. But …]

When he returned, he did not find the guest whom he had left eating. He examined his footprints to see where he had gone, but nowhere could he see any. Fresh snow had covered the ground, which would very easily have revealed the traveler’s path and shown where he had turned aside.

[Note: He went.]

[Note: But fresh snow … had covered it; fresh snow.]

Astonished, therefore, the man of God, and pondering what had happened, replaced the table in the room. As soon as he entered, he encountered a fragrance of marvelous sweetness. Looking around to discover the source of such extraordinary fragrance, he saw three hot loaves placed beside one another, of unusual whiteness and excellence.

Afraid, he said to himself: “I perceive that the one whom I received was an angel of God. He came to feed, not to be fed. Behold, he has brought loaves such as the earth cannot produce. They surpass lilies in whiteness, roses in fragrance, and honey in taste. Hence it is clear that they did not arise from the dense soil but were brought from the paradise of delight. Nor is it surprising that he refused to eat human food on earth, since in heaven he enjoys the bread of eternal life.”

[Note: Of eternal life.]

Thus the man of God, moved by the power of the miracle that had been displayed, devoted himself thereafter with even greater care to works of virtue. As his virtues increased, so too did heavenly grace. From that time onward he often deserved to see and speak with angels; and when he was hungry, he also deserved to be refreshed with special foods prepared for him by the Lord.

[Note: By a special gift from the Lord.]

Because he was affable and cheerful in character, he often recounted to those present, as examples for living, the deeds of the fathers who had gone before. He would also humbly insert what gift of the spirit heavenly goodness had bestowed upon him. At times he tried to do this indirectly, almost under the guise of another person. Yet those who heard him understood that he was speaking about himself, following the example of the Teacher of the Gentiles,

[Note: Who sometimes speaks under a pretext.]

who sometimes openly recounts his own virtues and sometimes speaks under the pretext of another person,

[Note: He speaks, saying.]

saying: “I know a man in Christ, fourteen years ago caught up to the third heaven.”

[Note: Heaven, and the rest of that passage.]

## CHAPTER VIII. How Boisil, after Cuthbert had been healed of an illness, foretold what was going to happen to him.

Meanwhile, because the condition of the whole world is fragile and changeable, as is its customary course, a sudden storm arose. The aforementioned abbot Eata was expelled, together with Cuthbert and the other brothers whom he had brought with him; the monastery he had founded was given to other monks to inhabit.

[Note: He was expelled. On this expulsion, see III, 25, and V, 20. Thus Saint Cuthbert still observed the Easter of the Scots and retained their tonsure. They yielded and gave place to Wilfrid because they refused to change their own, that is, the Scottish, custom, III, 25; V, 19. Hence Mabillon, in his preliminary observations on the Life of Saint Cuthbert in the *Acta Benedictina*, second section, p. 878, seems to have been mistaken when he asserted that Saint Cuthbert received not the Scottish tonsure but Peter’s; conversely, the continuators of Bollandus rightly suspect that the text of the Anonymous author who wrote the Life of Saint Cuthbert has been interpolated at that point. Smith.]

Nor did that athlete of Christ, because of the change of places, change his mind from the purpose of heavenly service that he had once undertaken. Rather, most diligently, as he had previously been accustomed to do, he listened equally to the words and observed the actions of the blessed Boisil.

At that time, as Herefrith, his close associate, formerly priest and abbot of the monastery of Lindisfarne, testifies that Cuthbert himself used to relate, he was seized by the pestilence from which at that time very many people throughout Britain were dying far and wide. The brothers of that monastery spent the entire night in vigilant prayer for his life and health. For they all considered his continued bodily presence necessary to them, as he was a holy man.

When one of them reported this to him in the morning—for they had done it without his knowledge—he immediately replied: “Why, then, am I lying here? For it must not be thought that God has disregarded the prayers of so many such men. Give me my staff and shoes.”

[Note: For it must not be doubted.]

At once he rose and began to test his walking, leaning on a staff. As his strength increased day by day, he did indeed regain his health. But because the swelling that had appeared in his thigh gradually subsided from the surface of the body and slipped into the inner organs, he continued to feel some intestinal pain for almost the whole remainder of his life—so that, in accordance with the Apostle, strength might be perfected in weakness.

When the servant of the Lord, Boisil, saw that he had recovered from his illness, he said: “You see, brother, that you have been freed from the affliction from which you were suffering, and I tell you that you will not be troubled by it again, nor will you die of it. At the same time I warn you: since death is close at hand for me, do not fail to learn something from me while I am able to teach. I have no more than seven days in which the health of my body and the power of my tongue will be available to me for teaching.”

[Note: Boisil. On him, see IV, 27, and V, 9. Id.]

Cuthbert replied, with no hesitation about the truth of his words: “What, I ask, would be best for me to read, something that I could nevertheless complete in one week?”

He answered: “The evangelist John.”

“I have a book,” he continued, “containing seven quires, which, with the Lord’s help, we can read through one quire each day, discussing between ourselves as much as is necessary.”

[Note: In the final chapter of the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Cuthbert*, this codex is said to be kept in the church of Durham. Mabillon.]

[Note: Quires.]

[Note: One each.]

And so it happened as he had said. They were able to complete the reading so quickly because they dealt in it only with the simplicity of the faith that works through love, not with the depths of theological questions.

When the reading had been completed after seven days, the man of God, Boisil, seized by the illness already mentioned, reached the final day. He passed through it with great rejoicing and entered the joys of perpetual light.

[Note: He reached it. Boisil died shortly after Eata and his companions left the monastery of Ripon, an event occurring about the year 661 according to Matthew of Westminster. See also the note on the time when this monastery was granted to Wilfrid, V, 19. Mabillon, in his second century, and the continuators of Bollandus, under 20 March, wrongly say that Boisil died in 664. For in chapter 9 Saint Cuthbert is said to have assumed Boisil’s office as prior of Mailros and to have held it for several years; but he could not have held it for several years if he had assumed it in 664, since in that very year Eata, who then governed the same monastery as abbot, made him prior of Lindisfarne. See chapter 16, III, 26, Florence of Worcester, Simeon of Durham, p. 3, and IV, 27. Smith.]

[Note: With great …]

[Note: To joy.]

[Note: Around the year 664, specifically on the fifth day before the Ides of September, on which day he is celebrated in the Benedictine calendars. Bede also discusses him in Book IV, chapter 27 of his History, where he places the monastery of Mailros on the bank of the River Tweed, on the borders of England and Scotland. Some remains of that monastery, which later passed to the Cistercians, still survive, as David Camerarius testifies. Mabillon.]

They say that during those seven days he disclosed to Cuthbert everything that remained destined to happen to him; for, as I have said, he was a prophetic man of extraordinary holiness. Finally, three years before the arrival of Eata, he foretold to his abbot that the previously mentioned pestilence would come, and he did not conceal from him that he himself would be taken away by it. But he truthfully warned his own abbot that he would not die of that disease, but rather of the illness that physicians call dysentery, as the outcome of events later showed.

He also intimated to Cuthbert, among other things, that he was to be ordained a bishop. Therefore, afterward, when Cuthbert was living in the retreat of the hermit’s life, he did not wish to tell anyone that Boisil had foretold he would become a bishop. Nevertheless, when brothers occasionally visited him, he used to protest with great sorrow:

“For even if it could happen that I might hide, having a very small dwelling, in a cave, where the waves of the swelling Ocean, surging around me on every side, might shut me away both from the sight and from the knowledge of all mortals, even there I do not consider myself free from the snares of the deceitful world. There too I fear that, for whatever reason, love of money might tempt me and carry me away.”

[Note: Inconsiderately.]

## CHAPTER IX. How diligently Cuthbert devoted himself to the ministry of the word.

After the death of the priest beloved by God, the aforementioned Boisil, Cuthbert assumed the office of prior. For several years he exercised it with the spiritual diligence befitting a holy man. He not only offered the monastery itself instruction and example in regular life,

[Note: Not only. Nearly the whole chapter is transcribed in IV, 27. Smith.]

but also strove to turn the surrounding population, far and wide, from a life of foolish custom toward love of the joys of heaven.

For many profaned the faith they possessed through wicked deeds. Some, even during the time of the plague, neglected the sacrament of the faith with which they had been imbued and ran to the wandering remedies of idolatry,

[Note: Idolatry. Thus writers of the Middle Ages spelled the word, although *idololatriae* should be restored. Mabillon.]

as though they could restrain the scourge sent by God the Creator through incantations, amulets,

[Note: Amulets. *Alligaturae* are certain charms for warding off diseases, hung around the neck or tied around other parts of the body. See further in Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under “Ligaturae.” Smith.]

or any other secrets of demonic art.

To correct the error of both groups, he often went out from the monastery. At times he rode a horse, but more often he walked on foot, visiting the surrounding villages and preaching the way of truth to those who were astray. Boisil too had been accustomed to do this in his time.

It was indeed the custom among the English people at that time that, when a cleric or priest came to a village, everyone gathered at his command to hear the word. They willingly listened to what was said, and even more willingly followed by their actions whatever they could hear and understand.

Cuthbert possessed such skill in teaching, such love in persuading people to practice what he had begun to teach, and such light in his angelic countenance that none of those present dared conceal from him the hidden things of his heart. All openly confessed and declared what they had done, because they plainly thought that none of it could be hidden from him; and, according to his instruction, they wiped away the sins they had confessed with worthy fruits of repentance.

He especially used to travel through those places and preach to people who were shut away in steep and rugged mountains, far from others, so that they were frightening to visit and, through their poverty and rusticity alike, kept teachers from approaching them. Yet he willingly devoted himself to them in pious labor and cultivated them with such diligent teaching that, when he left the monastery, he often did not return home for an entire week, sometimes for two or three weeks, and occasionally for a full month. Remaining in the mountains, he called the rustic people toward heavenly things through both the word of preaching and the example of virtue.

## CHAPTER X. How the creatures of the sea, in which he had prayed through the night, offered him service when he returned, and how the brother who witnessed this, growing faint from fear, was restored by his prayer.

As the holy man increased in virtues and signs in that same monastery, and the fame of his deeds spread everywhere, there was a religious woman and mother of the servants of Christ named Abbe, who governed the monastery situated in the place called the city of Coludi.

[Note: Abbess. On her and the city of Coludi, see IV, 19.]

[Note: Which is situated in the place.]

[Note: Coludi. Turgot, in Book II, chapter 17, calls it the city of Coldingham. It is a city in modern Scotland, in the March or Merse. “In that place, however, in separate dwellings, there were communities of monks and nuns. Gradually falling away from the state of regular discipline, they gave the enemy an opportunity to deceive them through improper familiarity with one another … Cuthbert, raised to the episcopal chair, separated all association with women from them, lest those present or future should at any time provoke God’s anger against themselves by such an example.” See the preliminary observations. On Saint Abbe, abbess of Coludi, see the Life of Saint Ethildrita under the year 679. Ethildrita lived for some time in the same monastery and is said to have given Saint Cuthbert a stole and a maniple in chapter 9 of his Life.]

She was honored by all for both her religion and her nobility, for she was the uterine sister of King Osvin.

[Note: Osvin.]

She sent to the man of God and asked him to visit her and her monastery for the sake of exhortation. He could not refuse what charity, proceeding from the heart of the servant of God, requested of him. He therefore came to the place and, remaining there for several days, made the way of righteousness that he preached manifest to everyone alike by his conduct and his speech.

[Note: The way that he preached.]

When, according to his customary practice, he went out alone at night to pray while the others slept, and after long vigils deep into the night finally returned home as the hour of the common assembly approached, one night a brother of that monastery silently watched him as he went out. Secretly following his footsteps, he tried to discover where he was going and what he intended to do.

After leaving the monastery, Cuthbert descended to the sea, above whose shore the monastery stood. He entered the sea until the swelling water rose to his neck and arms, and spent the night awake amid the sounding waves, praising God. As dawn approached, he came up onto the land and again began to pray on the shore with his knees bent.

While he was doing this, two four-footed creatures immediately came from the depths of the sea. They are commonly called otters. Lying down before him on the sand, they began to warm his feet with their breath and took pains to wipe them dry with their fur. When their service was complete, they received his blessing and slipped back beneath the native waves.

[Note: He himself soon returned home.]

Cuthbert himself returned home and completed the canonical hymns with the brothers at the appointed hour. But the brother who had been watching from his hiding place, overcome by immense fear, scarcely made his way home under the pressure of his distress, walking with unsteady steps. Early the next morning he approached Cuthbert, threw himself on the ground, and with tears dared to ask pardon for his offense, having no doubt that Cuthbert knew what he himself had done and endured during the night.

Cuthbert said to him: “What is the matter, brother? What have you done? Did you try to investigate our nocturnal journey by spying on it? I forgive you this offense, but only on the condition that you promise to tell no one what you have seen before my death.”

In this command he plainly followed the example of the one who, showing his disciples the glory of his majesty on the mountain,

[Note: Of the Gentiles, who sometimes under a pretext …]

said: “Tell no one of the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”

[Note: And the rest of that passage.]

After the brother promised to do what he had commanded, Cuthbert blessed him and at the same time wiped away both the guilt and the distress that the rash man had incurred. The brother kept silent during Cuthbert’s lifetime about the power he had witnessed, but after his death took care to reveal it to many.

[Note: He took care to do so. The Anonymous author received the preceding account from the testimony of many people, among them the priest Pleculf. Book II.]

## CHAPTER XI. How he foretold a calm sea on a fixed day for sailors detained by a storm, and obtained food through prayer.

Meanwhile the man of God began also to possess the spirit of prophecy: to foretell future events and to announce to those present what was happening in their absence.

At one time, traveling by sea from his monastery on a matter of necessity, he reached the land of the Picts called Niduari, accompanied by two of the brothers. One of them afterward served as a priest and made known to many people the power of the miracle that the man of God displayed there.

[Note: The Niduari. A people living along the banks of the River Nid, which flows into the Solway Firth.]

[Note: Niduari.]

They arrived there after the day of the Lord’s Nativity, expecting to return quickly because the weather was favorable both on the water and in the air. For that reason they had not brought provisions with them, thinking that they would soon be back.

But events turned out very differently from what they expected. As soon as they touched land, a violent storm arose and blocked every route of return. While they wasted away there for several days amid the dangers of hunger and cold,

[Note: They were exposed to danger.]

the man of God nevertheless refused to spend his time in sluggish leisure or to devote himself to idle sleep; rather, he strove to remain awake in prayer through the night.

The most sacred day of the Lord’s Epiphany had arrived. Then he addressed his companions in gentle speech, as he was cheerful and affable:

[Note: Cheerful.]

“Why, I ask, are we so torpid in such great sluggishness, and do we not seek a way of salvation in every direction? Behold, the earth is dreadful with snow, the sky with mist, the air rages with opposing blasts, and the sea with waves. We ourselves are failing from want, and there is no human being here to refresh us. Let us therefore knock upon the Lord by our prayers, the Lord who once opened a way through the Red Sea for his own people and miraculously fed them in the wilderness. Let us pray that he may also have mercy on us in our dangers.

“I believe that, if our faith does not falter, he does not wish us to remain fasting on this day, which he himself has chosen to glorify through so many and such great miracles of his majesty. Let us go somewhere, then, seeking what food he may deign to provide for us in the joy of his festival.”

[Note: Wherever there was a route.]

Saying this, he led them beneath the bank where he himself was accustomed to keep vigil in prayer at night. When they arrived, they found three pieces of dolphin flesh, cut and prepared for cooking as though by human service. They bent their knees and gave thanks to God.

Cuthbert said: “You see, beloved ones, what grace God grants to the person who trusts and hopes in the Lord. Behold, he has prepared food for his servants, and by the number three he has also shown us how many days we are to remain here. Take, then, the gifts that Christ has sent us; let us go and refresh ourselves, and let us remain without fear, for after three days the promised calm of sky and sea will certainly come to us.”

[Note: The grace of trusting and hoping.]

It happened as he had said. The storm remained extremely violent for three days; only on the fourth day did the promised calm follow, carrying them back to their homeland on favorable winds.

[Note: Very strong.]

## CHAPTER XII. How, while traveling, he foretold that he would receive provisions from an eagle as a servant, and did receive them.

One day, as he went out from the monastery according to his custom to preach to the people, accompanied by a boy, and as they had already become quite tired from walking while a considerable part of the journey still remained before they reached the village toward which they were heading, he tested the boy by saying:

[Note: Of the journey. The Anonymous author, Book II: “The aforementioned priest Tydi reported another miracle, known to many: one day he was traveling beside the River Tesgeta, heading south, teaching and baptizing country people among the mountains. He also had a boy in his company, etc.”]

“Tell me, companion, where do you plan to refresh yourself today? Do you have anyone along the way whose hospitality you can seek?”

The boy replied: “I have been considering this very matter silently in my heart. We brought no provisions with us for the journey, nor do we know anyone along the road who would be willing to receive us as guests. A considerable part of the journey still remains, and we cannot complete it without distress while fasting.”

The man of God said to him: “Learn, my little son, always to have faith and hope in the Lord, for no one who faithfully serves God ever perishes from hunger.”

[Note: To him the man of God said.]

Looking upward and seeing an eagle flying high above, he said: “Do you see that eagle flying over there? Through its service, too, it is possible for the Lord to refresh us today.”

As they talked in this way, they continued their journey beside a certain river. Suddenly they saw an eagle sitting on the bank. The man of God said: “Do you see where the servant I foretold is sitting? Run, I ask you, and see what food she has brought us at the Lord’s command, and bring it back quickly.”

The boy ran up and brought back a sizable fish, which the eagle had recently caught from the river.

[Note: She had caught it from the river.]

The man of God said: “What have you done, my son? Why have you not given the servant her share? Quickly cut it in half and return to her the portion she deserves for serving us.”

The boy did as he was commanded and took the remaining portion with him.

[Note: After taking the remaining portion with him … and after taking it with him …]

When the time for refreshment arrived, they turned aside to the nearest village. They gave the little fish to be roasted and refreshed themselves and those to whose house they had come with a most welcome meal. Cuthbert preached the word of God and praised his benefits, for blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanities and false insanities.

Thus, having resumed their journey, they proceeded to teach those whom they had intended to visit.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, while preaching to the people, he foresaw the Devil’s illusory fire suddenly coming, and extinguished it when it came.

At that same time, while he was preaching the word of life to a great many people gathered in a certain little village, he suddenly foresaw in spirit that the ancient enemy was coming to impede the work of salvation. He therefore took care, through his teaching, to forestall the snares that he understood were about to come.

For, among the matters he had been discussing, he suddenly inserted an admonition of this kind:

“Dearest ones, whenever the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom are preached to you, you must always listen to them with attentive heart and the most vigilant understanding, lest perhaps the Devil, who possesses a thousand arts of doing harm, hinder you through needless cares from hearing about eternal salvation.”

Having said this, he resumed the order of the discourse he had interrupted. Immediately that most wicked enemy, bringing an illusory fire, set fire to a house nearby, so that firebrands seemed to fly throughout the entire village, while, with the wind’s assistance, the crash shook the air.

Then almost the whole crowd that he was teaching sprang up as though to extinguish the fire. He himself restrained a few with a gesture of his hand. The people eagerly threw water, but not even a drop of real water could extinguish the false flames. At last, as the man of God Cuthbert prayed, the author of the deception was driven away and carried the fictitious fires with him into the empty air.

Seeing this, the crowd was deeply and beneficially ashamed. They returned to the man of God, fell on their knees, and begged pardon for their unstable minds, confessing that they had understood that the Devil had not ceased, even for an hour, from trying to impede human salvation. But Cuthbert, strengthening the weakness of the frail, resumed the instructions about life that he had begun.

## CHAPTER XIV. How by prayer he extinguished the flames of a house burning with real fire.

He extinguished not only an illusory fire but also a real one, which many people were quite unable to put out with the cold waters of springs; he alone subdued it with the fervent streams of his tears.

For, traveling everywhere in the manner of the apostles for the sake of salutary instruction, he came one day to the house of a woman devoted to God whom he regularly visited, because he knew her to be intent upon good works and because she had nourished him from the earliest years of his childhood; for this reason he was accustomed to call her “mother.”

[Note: Woman. Her name was Kenspid. She was a widowed religious woman who had raised Saint Cuthbert from the age of eight until he reached maturity. See the Anonymous author of the Life of Saint Cuthbert, Book II, in Bollandus, 20 March. Smith. The Anonymous author’s words from Book II should not be omitted: “At that same time the holy man of God was invited by a certain woman named Kenspid, still living, a religious widow who had raised him from the age of eight until maturity, when he undertook the service of God; for this reason he called her mother and often visited her. One day he came to the village in which she lived, called Hruringaham, while a house at the far end of the village was burning, etc.” Mabillon.]

She had a house on the western side of the village. When the man of God Cuthbert entered it to sow the word, a house suddenly began to burn with extreme violence on the eastern side of the same village through someone’s negligence.

[Note: Very violently.]

A strong wind arose from that quarter, seized bundles of burning thatch,

[Note: Of the thatched roof.]

and scattered them widely throughout the village. Those present threw water, but the stronger flame drove them back and forced them farther away.

Then the aforementioned servant of God hurried to the house in which she had received the man of God, begging him to come to her aid through prayer before her house and the entire village perished.

But he said: “Do not be afraid, mother; be more composed. This voracious flame, however great it may be, will not harm you or yours.”

Immediately he went outside and prostrated himself on the ground before the door.

[Note: He prostrates himself.]

While he was still praying, the wind changed. Blowing from the west, it drove the entire danger of that great fire away from the village that the man of God had entered.

Thus, in two miracles, he imitated the virtues of two fathers: in the foreseen and dispelled illusory fires, the virtue of the most reverend and most holy Father Benedict, who by prayer drove from the eyes of his disciples a simulated fire resembling the burning of a kitchen;

[Note: Benedict. On this miracle of Saint Benedict, see Bollandus, 21 March.]

and in the real balls of fire, equally conquered and turned back, the virtue of the venerable Marcellinus, bishop of Ancona, who, when that city was burning, placed himself against the fire and by prayer restrained the flames, which so great a multitude of citizens had been unable to overcome by throwing water.

[Note: Marcellinus. Saint Marcellinus is commemorated on 9 January; see that date in Bollandus. Smith.]

Nor is it surprising that men who are perfect and faithfully serve God should receive such power over the force of flames, since by daily practice of virtue they know how to subdue the incitements of their flesh and extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one. The prophetic saying most aptly applies to them: “When you pass through fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not burn in you.”

But I and those like me, conscious of our own weakness and inactivity, are certainly confident that we dare not expect anything of this kind against material fire. Yet we are uncertain whether we will escape unharmed from that unquenchable fire of future punishment.

Nevertheless, powerful and abundant is the mercy of our Savior, which grants us, though unworthy, the grace of his protection both now, for extinguishing the fires of vices, and in the future, for escaping the flames of punishment.

## CHAPTER XV. How he cast out the demon from the prefect’s wife before he had even arrived.

[Col. 0753A]

But since a little earlier we explained how powerful that same venerable Cuthbert had been against the devil’s counterfeit deceptions, let us now also explain what power he possessed against his true and open fury.

There was a prefect of King Ecgfrith named Hildmaer, a man devoted, together with his entire household, to religious works. For this reason he was especially loved by blessed Cuthbert and, whenever the proximity of the journey made it convenient, was frequently visited by him. His wife, who was devoted to almsgiving and the other fruits of virtue, was suddenly seized by a demon and began to be tormented most violently. She gnashed her teeth, uttered pitiful cries [Note: [Col. 0753D] “By uttering (them).”], and jerked her arms and other limbs in different directions, causing no small horror to all who saw or heard her.

When she lay there thrown down and seemed about to die, her husband mounted his horse and hastened to the man of God. He entreated him, saying:

“I beg you: my wife is gravely ill and seems now close to death. Send a priest to visit her before she dies and administer to her the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood; and permit her body to be buried here in these holy places.”

For he was ashamed to admit that she was insane, since the man of God had always been accustomed to see her in her right mind. When Cuthbert had turned aside from him for a short while, intending to see which priest he should send with him, he suddenly learned in the spirit that the wife for whom the man was pleading was afflicted not by an ordinary illness but by a demon. [Note: [Col. 0753D] “By a demon.”] Returning to him, he said:

“I must not send another [Note: [Col. 0754D] “Another, but …”]; I myself must go with you to visit her.”

As they traveled, the man began to weep and reveal the grief of his heart through tears streaming down his cheeks. For he feared that, when Cuthbert found her possessed by a demon, he might begin to think that she had not served the Lord wholeheartedly, but with feigned faith. The man of God gently consoled him:

“Do not weep, as though I were going to find your wife in a condition displeasing to me. I know—as you are ashamed to say—that she is tormented by a demon. I also know that, before we reach her, the demon will be driven away and she will be freed. When we arrive, she will come joyfully to meet us in complete soundness of mind and will take these reins; then, begging us to enter quickly, she will diligently provide us with the service she was accustomed to render. For it is not only the wicked who are subjected to such torment; by the hidden judgment of God, even innocent people are sometimes held captive in this world by the devil, not only in body but also in mind.”

While Cuthbert continued speaking words such as these for the man’s consolation and instruction, they approached the house. Suddenly the evil spirit fled, unable to endure the arrival of the Holy Spirit, with whom the man of God was filled. The woman, released from her bonds as though awakened from a deep sleep, immediately rose and came joyfully to meet the man of God. She took hold of the bridle of the animal on which he was riding, and, as soon as the full strength of her mind and body had returned, she begged him to dismount quickly and enter to bless her house. Providing him with devoted service, she openly testified that, at the first touch of the bridle, she had felt herself freed from all the distress of her former affliction.

## CHAPTER XVI

### How he lived and taught in the monastery at Lindisfarne

When, therefore, the venerable servant of the Lord had spent many years in the monastery at Mailros, shining with many signs of spiritual virtue, its most reverend abbot, Eata, transferred him to the monastery situated on the island of the Lindisfarne people, so that there too he might, with the authority of a superior, teach the rule of monastic perfection and display it by the example of his virtue. [Note: [Col. 0753D] “He transferred him.” Simeon of Durham, I.6, asserts that this transfer took place in the year of Christ 664, when Saint Cuthbert was entering his fourteenth year in the perfection of monastic life. SMITH.] [Note: [Col. 0753D] “The rule.” The Anonymous author states this rule plainly in Book III: “Living there also according to Holy Scripture, conducting the contemplative life amid activity, and establishing for us a regular life, he set in order that life which we observe to this day together with the Rule of Benedict.” This is from a contemporary monk of Lindisfarne. MABILLON.] For the same most reverend father then governed that place by right of the abbacy. [Note: [Col. 0754D] “For he himself …” See this copied out in IV.27. SMITH.]

No one should be surprised that we have said that, on the same island of Lindisfarne, although it is very small, there was both the bishop’s residence and now also the residence of the abbot and monks. In truth, this is how it is. One and the same dwelling of the servants of God contains both groups together—or rather, it contains all the monks. Aidan, who was the first bishop of that place, was a monk and always practiced monastic life with all his companions. Therefore, from his time to the present, all the bishops of that place exercise their episcopal office in such a way that, while the monastery is governed by an abbot whom they themselves have chosen with the counsel of the brothers, all the priests, deacons, singers, readers, and the other ecclesiastical orders observe the monastic rule in every respect together with the bishop.

Blessed Pope Gregory showed that he greatly approved this manner of life when, in response to Augustine—whom he had sent as the first bishop to the English people—who had asked by letter how bishops ought to live with their clergy [Note: [Col. 0754D] “To one who inquired.”], he replied, among other things:

“But because your Fraternity, instructed in the rules of a monastery, ought not to be separated from your clergy in the Church of the English, which has only recently been brought to the faith by the grace of God, you should establish the manner of life that existed at the beginning of the newborn Church among our fathers. Among them no one said that anything of what he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common.”

Thus, when the man of God came to the church—or monastery—of Lindisfarne, he immediately imparted the monastic institutions to the brothers, both by living them and by teaching them. He also kindled the multitude of the common people living throughout the surrounding region, as was his custom, through frequent visits, urging them to seek and merit heavenly things. Moreover, having become even more renowned through signs, he restored many people afflicted by various illnesses and torments to their former health through the persistence of his prayers. Some he cured of the persecution of unclean spirits [Note: [Col. 0755C] “Not only while present by praying, or indeed …”], not only when present by touching, praying, commanding, and exorcising, but also when absent, either merely by praying or by foretelling their healing. Among these was the prefect’s wife, whom we mentioned above. [Note: [Col. 0755C] Above. In the preceding chapter. SMITH.]

There were, however, certain brothers in the monastery who preferred to obey their former custom rather than the discipline of the rule. Yet he overcame them by the modest virtue of his patience [Note: [Col. 0755C] “Moderation.”] and gradually converted them through daily practice to a better state of purpose. Indeed, when he was often discussing the rule in the assembly of the brothers and was wearied by the sharp insults of those who contradicted him, he would suddenly rise and, departing with a calm face and spirit, leave the gathering. Nevertheless, on the following day, as though he had suffered no objection the day before, he would give the same hearers the same admonitions as previously, until, as we have said, he gradually converted them to what he desired.

He was a man preeminent in the virtue of patience and utterly unconquerable in enduring bravely everything adverse that was inflicted upon either mind or body. Even amid the sorrows that occurred, he maintained a cheerful countenance, so that it was plainly understood that, through the inward consolation of the Holy Spirit, he despised outward afflictions. [Note: [Col. 0755C] Outwardly.]

He was also so devoted to vigils and prayer [Note: [Col. 0755C] “So diligent.”] that he is believed [Note: [Col. 0755C] “It was believed.”] on several occasions to have spent three or four consecutive nights without sleep. During all that time he neither went to his own bed [Note: [Col. 0755C] “His own, nor …”] nor had any place outside the brothers’ dormitory where he could rest. Whether he devoted himself alone to prayer in more secluded places, or worked with his hands while chanting psalms [Note: [Col. 0756C] “He worked with his hands.”], driving away drowsiness of sleep [Note: [Col. 0756C] “Of sleeping.”] by labor, or went around the island, investigating like a devout explorer how each thing stood, he likewise relieved the length of his psalmody and vigils by walking.

He was accustomed to rebuke the faintheartedness of the brothers who complained bitterly if someone roused them at an inconvenient hour during the time of night or midday rest:

“No one troubles me by waking me from sleep,” he would say, “but rather he makes me glad who wakes me. For, having shaken off the torpor of sleep, he makes me do or think something useful.”

He was so devoted to compunction and so ardent with heavenly desires that, when celebrating the solemn rites of Mass, he could never complete the service without shedding abundant tears. When he celebrated, in fitting order, the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, he himself imitated what he was doing, sacrificing himself to God in the contrition of his heart. To the people standing by he urged that they should lift up their hearts and give thanks to the Lord our God, raising his heart rather than his voice, and exhorting them more by groaning than by singing.

He was fervent in his zeal for justice when rebuking sinners, yet gentle and restrained in spirit when forgiving the penitent. Thus, when people confessed their sins to him, he would sometimes himself, out of compassion for the sick, shed tears and, though just, show by his own example what the sinner ought to do. [Note: [Col. 0755C] Bede makes mention of confession and the sacrament in several places, namely in *Ecclesiastical History* IV.25 and V.13–14, and in sayings of his reported in the *Council Rules*, chapter 36, section 6. See above, chapter 9. MABILLON.]

He wore ordinary clothing and lived so moderately that he was conspicuous neither for the cleanliness nor for the squalor of his garments. For this reason, to this day his example is observed in that monastery: no one may have clothing of varied or costly color, but they must be content especially with the kind of garment supplied by the natural wool of sheep.
