Through these and similar spiritual exercises, the venerable man both stirred the affection of all good people to imitate him and recalled the wicked and rebellious from their stubborn error to the discipline of the regular life. [Note: [Col. 0756C] Of the rule.]

## CHAPTER XVII

### How he made himself a dwelling on the island of Farne after driving out the demons

After he had completed many years in the same monastery [Note: [Col. 0755C] “He completed them.” Namely, twelve years; he therefore sought the solitude of seclusion in the year 676 (Florence of Worcester; Simeon of Durham, I.7; *Ecclesiastical History* IV.28). SMITH.—Namely, twelve years, for Turgot says in *History of Durham* I.7: “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 676, which was the seventh year of King Ecgfrith’s reign, when Cuthbert, the man of God, had spent twelve years and more in the priorship of the monastery at Lindisfarne, at last, with the favor both of the aforesaid abbot and of the brothers, he sought the secret silences of anchoritic contemplation.” Hence it is evident that this manner of speaking—“after long courses of years” and similar expressions—does not always denote, as some suppose, a considerable series of years among writers of the Middle Ages. Grimlaicus, in *Rule for Solitaries*, chapter 1, writes that blessed Arnulf died after spending many years in the desert, although Arnulf lived in solitude scarcely ten full years. We omit six hundred examples of this kind. MABILLON.] he at last, with the favor both of the aforesaid abbot and of the brothers, entered with great joy the long-desired, sought, and requested secrets of solitude.

He rejoiced because, after the long perfection of the active life, he was now deemed worthy to ascend to the repose of divine contemplation. He was glad to attain the lot of those of whom it is sung in the psalm:

“The saints shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.” [Note: [Col. 0757D] “They shall go from.”]

At first, in the beginnings of his solitary life, he withdrew to a certain place that appeared more secluded in the outer parts of his cell. But after battling there for some time with the invisible enemy through prayer and fasting, he eventually, presuming greater things, sought a more distant and remote place of combat, farther from human beings.

Farne is said to be an island situated in the midst of the sea. Unlike the region of the people of Lindisfarne, which becomes an island twice daily when the tide of the Ocean—which the Greeks call *rheuma* (“flow”)—comes in, and which, when the tide recedes and the shores are laid bare, is again joined to the mainland, Farne is separated from this peninsula by several thousand paces toward the east wind and is enclosed on one side by a very deep and on the other by an immeasurable ocean.

Before the servant of the Lord Cuthbert, no settler could easily live there alone, because of the phantasms of the demons dwelling there. [Note: [Col. 0757D] Before the servant.] But when the soldier of Christ entered, armed with the helmet of salvation, the shield of faith, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, every fiery dart of the wicked one was extinguished, and the wicked enemy himself, with the whole host of his followers, was driven far away.

When this soldier of Christ had defeated the tyrannical army and become ruler of the land to which he had come, he founded a city suited to his rule and erected houses appropriate to the city. The building was almost circular in shape, extending from wall to wall for roughly four or five rods. The wall itself was higher on the outside than the height of a standing man; on the inside, by cutting away the living rock, he made it much higher, so that, in order to restrain both the wantonness of the eyes and the wandering of the thoughts, and to raise the whole attention of his mind toward heavenly desires, the devout inhabitant could see nothing from his dwelling except the sky.

He constructed this wall not from hewn stone, brick, and mortar, but entirely from unworked stones and turf, which he had dug and removed from the middle of the site. Some of the stones were so large that they seemed scarcely capable of being lifted by four men; nevertheless, aided by angelic assistance, he was found to have brought them there from elsewhere and set them upon the wall. [Note: [Col. 0757D] Not from cut stone.]

Within his dwelling he had two houses: an oratory and another habitation suited to ordinary uses. He made their walls by digging and cutting deeply into the natural earth, both inside and out, and placed rough timber and hay above them as roofs. Near the island’s harbor there was a larger house in which the brothers who came to visit him could be received and rest; not far from it was a spring suitable for their needs. [Note: [Col. 0757D] At the gate.]

## CHAPTER XVIII

### How by his prayers he brought water from dry ground, and how he advanced in the anchoritic life [Note: [Col. 0757D] “He lived.”]

His dwelling itself was in need of water, since it had been established on an exceedingly hard and almost rocky crag. The man of God therefore summoned the brothers—for at that time he had not yet shut himself off from the sight of visitors—and said:

“You see that the dwelling I have entered lacks a spring. But let us ask him who turns solid rock into a pool of water and the crags into springs of water, that, giving glory not to us but to his name, he may deign to open for us a vein of water from this rocky crag as well. Let us dig in the middle of my little hut. I believe that he will give us drink from his stream of delight.”

They therefore dug a pit, which the next day they found filled with water flowing from within the earth. There could be no doubt that this water had been drawn forth by the prayers of the man of God from ground that had previously been utterly dry and hard. [Note: [Col. 0758D] Previously most arid.] In a wondrous way, the water remained within its original bounds: it neither boiled over and invaded the floor nor failed when drawn, so perfectly did the grace of the giver regulate it that it was neither excessive for the needs of those who received it nor insufficient for their support.

After the brothers had helped him complete the dwelling and the houses mentioned above, the man of God Cuthbert began to live alone. At first, when brothers came to him, he would leave his little cell [Note: [Col. 0758D] “His cell.”] and minister to them. While he devotedly washed their feet with warm water, however, he was sometimes compelled by them to remove his own shoes and offer them his feet to wash.

For he had so withdrawn his attention from the care of his body and transferred it to the care of the soul alone that, once shod in the skin *tribracae*—leg-coverings—which he habitually wore [Note: [Col. 0757] That is, stockings or leg-coverings, which the French of our country still call *des tricouses*.], he would remain so for entire months. It is even said that, having put on his shoes at Easter, he did not unshoe himself until Easter returned the following year, for the washing of feet customary at the Lord’s Supper. [Note: [Col. 0758D] “To have unshod himself.”]

Because he frequently prayed and bent his knees while wearing his shoes, he was found to have a long and substantial callus where his feet joined his shins. Then, as his zeal for perfection increased, he enclosed himself within his monastery and, removed from human sight, learned to lead a solitary life in fasting, prayer, and vigils. He rarely conversed with visitors from within, and then only through a window. At first, when the window was opened, he rejoiced both to be seen by the brothers and to see the brothers with whom he spoke. As time went on, he closed even that window and opened it only when some definite necessity required it, whether to give a blessing or for some other purpose. [Note: [Col. 0758D] “Except for giving.” He opened it for the sake of granting a blessing or for another definite necessity.]

## CHAPTER XIX

### How by his word he drove birds away from the crop he had sown with his own hand

At first he received from the brothers only a very small amount of bread for his food and drank from his own spring. Later, however, he considered it more fitting to live by the labor of his own hands, following the example of the fathers. He therefore asked that tools with which he could work the earth and wheat that he could sow be brought to him.

But although the earth was sown in spring, it produced no fruit until midsummer. When the brothers visited him according to their custom, the man of God said:

“Perhaps it is either the nature of this soil or the will of God that wheat should not grow for me in this place. Please bring barley, to see whether even that might be able to produce fruit. But if God does not wish to give it growth either, it is better for me to return to the monastery than to be supported here by another’s labor.”

When the barley was brought and he entrusted it to the earth far beyond the proper season for sowing and beyond all hope of bearing fruit, it quickly sprang up and yielded an abundant crop. As it began to ripen, birds came and eagerly set upon feeding upon it.

The most pious servant of Christ approached them and, as he later recounted—he often brought forward for the strengthening of his hearers’ faith things that he himself had obtained through faith, since he was cheerful in countenance and approachable—said:

“Why are you touching crops that you did not sow? Perhaps you need this more than I do. If you have received permission from God, do what he has permitted; but if not, depart and do not continue to damage what belongs to another.”

He had spoken, and at the first sound of his command the whole multitude of birds withdrew and thereafter entirely refrained from invading the same crop.

Here too the venerable servant of Christ followed, in two miracles, the example of two fathers. In the water drawn from the rock, he followed the deed of blessed Father Benedict, who is likewise said to have performed almost the same miracle in almost the same manner, but more abundantly, because more people were suffering from a lack of water. In the birds summoned away from the harvest, he followed the example of the most reverend and holy Father Antony, who restrained the wild asses from damaging the garden he himself had planted with a single word.

## CHAPTER XX

### How the ravens cleansed by prayers and a gift the injury they had inflicted upon the man of God

I wish to relate another miracle performed by blessed Cuthbert, following the example of the aforementioned Father Benedict. In it, the obedience and humility of birds openly condemn human obstinacy and pride.

There were ravens that had long been accustomed to the dwellings of that island. One day the man of God saw them tearing with their beaks at the brothers’ small guesthouse, which I mentioned earlier, and carrying in their mouths the stalks from which its roof had been made, in order to construct a nest. He restrained them with a slight extension of his right hand and ordered them to cease injuring the brothers.

When they despised his command [Note: [Col. 0759D] “But when they despised the command.”], he said:

“In the name of Jesus Christ, depart as quickly as possible, and do not presume to remain any longer in a place that you are damaging.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when they immediately departed in sadness. After three days, one of the two returned. Finding the servant of Christ digging, it spread its wings mournfully, lowered its head to his feet, and, with a humbled voice, begged forgiveness for the offense by every sign it could give. [Note: [Col. 0759D] “It was begging. That …”]

Understanding this, the venerable Father gave it permission to return. Having obtained permission, it immediately departed to bring back its companion. Without delay, both returned, carrying with them fitting gifts: namely, half a piece of pork fat [Note: [Col. 0759D] That is, pork fat, used to grease axles; hence the customary derivation of the word. MABILLON.]. [Note: [Col. 0759D] “Worthy gifts to him.”]

The man of God would later show it frequently to the brothers when they came to him and provide it for greasing their shoes. He testified to them how great a concern human beings ought to have for obedience and how great a concern for humility, since the most arrogant bird hastened [Note: [Col. 0760D] “Hastened”—variant: “was hastening.”] to wash away, through prayers, lamentations, and gifts, the injury it had inflicted upon a human being. [Note: [Col. 0759D] The injury it had inflicted upon the man of God.]

Finally, as an example of correction for human beings, they remained and nested on that island for many years thereafter, and did not dare to cause anyone any further annoyance. [Note: [Col. 0760D] “Any other annoyance.”]

No one should think it absurd to learn the pattern of virtue from birds, since Solomon says:

“Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider its ways, and learn wisdom.”

## CHAPTER XXI

### How even the sea served his needs

Not only the animals of the air [Note: [Col. 0760D] “But received …” (the apparatus reading is fragmentary).] but also the animals of the sea—and indeed the sea itself—served the venerable man, just as did the air and fire, as we explained above. [Note: [Col. 0760D] Above. Chapters 3, 10, 13, and 14. SMITH.]

For one who faithfully and wholeheartedly serves the author of all creatures should not be surprised if every creature serves his commands and desires. But we usually lose dominion over the creatures subject to us because we ourselves neglect to serve the Lord and Creator of all.

Even the sea itself, I say, readily rendered service to the servant of Christ whenever he needed it. [Note: [Col. 0760D] “Where [he needed] a house …”] He was planning to build in his monastery a small dwelling suited to his daily needs. On the side facing the sea, where the rock, hollowed out by the frequent surge of the waters, had formed a very deep and considerable gap, a foundation was to be placed; it had to be twelve feet long, corresponding to the width of the gap.

He therefore asked the brothers who had come to visit him to bring, when they returned, a piece of timber twelve feet long for the foundation of the little house. They promised to do gladly what he requested. But once they had received his blessing and returned home, the request of the Father slipped from their minds.

When they returned to him on the appointed day, they did not bring what they had been asked to bring. He received them most kindly and, after commending them to God with his customary prayer, said:

“Where is the timber that I asked you to bring?”

Then, recalling his request and confessing their forgetfulness, they begged forgiveness for their offense. The gentlest of men consoled them in kindly speech and ordered them to remain and rest on the island until morning, saying:

“I believe that God will not forget my desire and my need.” [Note: [Col. 0761D] “Will not forget.”]

They did as he had said. Rising in the morning, they saw that the nightly tide of the Ocean had brought a piece of timber of the aforesaid length and had set it down precisely in the place where it was to be laid upon the building.

When they saw this, the men immediately marveled at the holiness of the venerable man, for even the elements served him. They also condemned, with due shame, the slowness of their own minds, since even an insensible element had taught them how greatly the saints ought to be obeyed. [Note: [Col. 0761D] That is, it also taught them.]

## CHAPTER XXII

### How, by giving saving counsel to many who came to him, he exposed the frail snares of the ancient enemy

Many came to the man of God, not only from the nearby districts of the people of Lindisfarne but also from more distant parts of Britain, drawn by the fame of his virtues. They confessed either the faults they had committed, or the temptations of demons that they were suffering, or the ordinary adversities of mortals with which they were afflicted, hoping to receive consolation from so holy a man.

Nor was their hope disappointed. No one left him without the joy of consolation, and no sorrow of mind that anyone had brought to him accompanied that person on the return journey. He knew how to restore the sorrowful through devout exhortation; he knew how to recall to the minds of the distressed the joys of heavenly life; he had learned to show that both the prosperity and adversity of this world are fragile; and he had learned to reveal to those undergoing temptation the many wiles of the ancient enemy, by which the mind could easily be captured if it were left bare either of fraternal or of divine love. But one who proceeded strengthened by whole-hearted faith, with the Lord’s help, passed through the adversary’s snares as though they were spiders’ webs.

“How often,” he said, “did they cast me miserably headlong from a high cliff? How often did they hurl stones as though to kill me? They also tried to terrify me and drive me from the place of this combat by attacking me with various other trials of phantoms [Note: [Col. 0761D] “By trials of phantasms.”], yet they could in no way injure my body or stain my mind with fear.”

He also used to tell the brothers repeatedly not to marvel at his way of life as though it were uniquely exalted because, having rejected worldly concerns, he preferred to live in seclusion.

“But rightly,” he said, “the life of cenobites is to be admired. They submit in every respect to the commands of their abbot and, according to his judgment, regulate all the times of their keeping vigil, praying, fasting, and working. I know many of them who far surpass my littleness both in purity of mind and in the height of prophetic grace.

“Among them is Christ’s venerable servant Boisilus, whom everyone should name with the highest honor. When I was a young man in the monastery at Mailros, he was an old man who nurtured me; while he was instructing me, he foretold with prophetic truth everything that was going to happen to me. Only one thing remains among all that he foretold to me—may it never be fulfilled.”

He said this because the aforementioned servant of Christ had indicated that Cuthbert would serve in the rank of bishop, the acceptance of which office he greatly dreaded because of his desire for a more secluded life.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### How Abbess Aelfleda and one of her maidens were healed of illness through his belt [Note: [Col. 0762D] “May be healed.”]

Nor did the miracles of healing cease to occur through the man of God, although he was living far from human beings. The venerable handmaid of Christ, Aelfleda [Note: [Col. 0761] Aelfleda. See III.24. She is commemorated on 8 February. SMITH.], who amid the joys of virginity cared with motherly affection for no small number of companies of Christ’s handmaids and added the distinction of royal nobility to the greater nobility of supreme virtue, always honored the man of God with profound love.

At that time, as she later related to Herefrid, the most reverend priest of the church of Lindisfarne, and as he related to me, she was struck by a severe illness and tormented for a long time, so that she seemed almost to have reached death. When the physicians had been unable to apply any remedy [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Could provide no treatment.”], she was gradually snatched from death by the divine grace working inwardly, although she was not completely healed.

The pain in her internal organs indeed ceased and strength returned to her limbs, but the ability to stand or walk was entirely absent [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Completely failed.”]. She could neither raise herself to stand nor move except on all fours. She therefore began, in sadness, to fear permanent disability, for she had long since despaired of help from physicians. [Note: [Col. 0762D] “She had already lost faith in it.”]

One day, amid the distress of her sorrowful thoughts, the blessed and peaceful way of life of the most reverend Father Cuthbert came to her mind. She said:

“If only I had something belonging to my Cuthbert! I know—and I believe and trust in the Lord—that I would quickly be healed.” [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Certainly, I believe and trust.”]

Not long afterward, someone arrived carrying a linen belt sent to her by him. She rejoiced greatly at the gift, and, understanding that her desire had already been revealed to the holy man from heaven, she girded herself with it. The next morning she was able to stand upright, and on the third day her health was fully restored.

A few days later, one of the virgins of her monastery began to suffer from an unbearable headache. As the illness worsened day by day and she seemed close to death, her venerable abbess entered to visit her. Seeing her gravely afflicted, she took the aforementioned belt of the man of God and had it tied around the girl’s head. The pain immediately departed that same day, and she was healed [Note: [Col. 0763C] “She was healed of the pain.”]. The girl took off the belt and put it away in her own chest.

Several days later, when the abbess looked for it, she could find it neither in that chest nor anywhere else. This is understood to have happened by divine providence: through the two miracles of healing, the holiness of the Father beloved by God was to appear to believers, while the unbelievers were deprived thereafter of any opportunity for doubt concerning his holiness.

If the same belt had always remained available, the sick would always have wished to flock to it. Then, if one of them had perhaps not been worthy to be healed of his illness [Note: [Col. 0763C] “If one of these should not deserve …”], he would have disparaged the powerlessness of the one who did not save him, when in fact he himself would have been unworthy of healing. Thus, by the provident dispensation of heavenly mercy, after the faith of believers had been confirmed, the material for the envy and disparagement of the faithless was immediately removed altogether.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### What he foretold, when the same Aelfleda asked him, concerning the life of King Ecgfrith and his own episcopate
[Note: [Col. 0763C] At another time.] The same most reverend virgin and mother of Christ’s virgins, Aelfleda, sent for him and entreated the man of God, adjuring him in the Lord’s name, that she might be deemed worthy to see him and speak with him about matters of importance. [Note: [Col. 0763C] Which he boarded.] He boarded a ship with the brothers and came to the island lying before the mouth of the river Coquet; [Note: [Col. 0763C] Coquet. The river Coquet cuts through the present county of Northumbria, and where it joins the ocean there is a nearby island of the same name. SMITH.] [Note: [Col. 0763C] It received its name.] it received its name from that river, and was itself distinguished by communities of monks. For the aforesaid abbess had asked him to meet her there. Having obtained his conversation, and hearing from him many things about which she inquired, suddenly, in the middle of their discussion, she fell at his feet and adjured him by that dread and venerable name of the heavenly King and his angels to tell her how long her brother Ecgfrid would live and govern the kingdom of the English.

“For I know,” she said, “that by the spirit of prophecy with which you abound, you can also tell me this, if you wish.”

But he was alarmed by her oath, and yet did not wish openly to reveal the secret she was asking about. “It is strange,” he said, “that you, a wise woman and learned in the holy Scriptures, should wish to call the periods of human life long, since the Psalmist says, ‘Our years are meditated like a spider’; and since Solomon warns: ‘If a man lives many years and rejoices in them all, he ought to remember the dark time and the many days; when they come, the past is shown to have been vanity.’ How much more does one to whom only a single year of life remains seem to have lived for a short time, when death stands at the door?” [Note: [Col. 0763C] One. Thus this conversation of Aelfleda with Saint Cudberctus took place in the year 684. King Ecgfrid was slain in the following year, IV, 26. ID.]

Hearing this, she wept bitterly over the dreadful forewarning. Then, wiping her face, she again, with womanly boldness, adjured him by the majesty of the Most High Divinity to tell her whom he would have as heir to the kingdom, since he had neither sons nor brothers.

After remaining silent for a little while, he said: “Do not say that he lacks one; he will have a successor whom you must embrace with the same affection with which you love Ecgfrid himself.” [Note: [Col. 0763C] “He does not lack one; he will have one.”]  

But she said: “I beg you, tell me where he is.”

He replied: “Do you see how great and spacious this sea is, and how many islands it contains? It is easy for God to provide from one of these someone whom he may set over the kingdom of the English.”

She therefore understood that he was speaking of Aldfrid, who was said to have been a son of her father and who at that time was living in exile among the islands of the Scots for the sake of his studies. She knew, moreover, that Ecgfrid proposed to appoint him bishop; and, wishing to discover whether the proposal would be fulfilled, she began her inquiry in this way:

“O how variously are the hearts of mortals divided in their intentions! Some rejoice in having acquired riches; others, though loving riches, are always in want. You reject the glory of the world, even when it is offered to you, although you might attain the episcopate, beyond which there is nothing higher among mortals; you prefer the enclosure of your desert to this rank.” [Note: [Col. 0764C] Rejoicing in riches.] [Note: [Col. 0764C] There is nothing among mortals.] [Note: [Col. 0764C] Whose enclosure.] [Note: [Col. 0764C] You prefer.]

He replied: “I know that I am not worthy of so great a rank, yet I cannot anywhere escape the judgment of the heavenly Ruler. If he has determined to subject me to so great a burden, I believe that after a short time he will set me free and perhaps, when no more than two years have passed, restore me to the accustomed rest of my solitude.” [Note: [Col. 0764C] He will restore.] “But I charge you, in the name of our Lord and Savior, not to tell anyone before my death what you have heard from me.”

When he had explained to her these and many other matters about which she had asked, and had instructed her in whatever she needed to know, he returned to his island and monastery and continued diligently to lead the solitary life he had begun.

Not long afterward, when a considerable synod had been assembled, [Note: [Col. 0763C] A synod. Bede explains this passage in his *History*, book IV, chapter 28: “It happened that, when a fairly large synod had been assembled in the presence of King Egfrid beside the river Alne, at a place called Adtwiforda, meaning ‘at the double ford,’ and when the blessed Theodore of revered memory presided over it, [Col. 0764C] etc. Yet the ordination was not decreed immediately; it was completed at York during the Easter solemnity after the winter that was approaching had passed—namely, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, as Turgot correctly states in book I, chapter 9—when seven bishops gathered for his consecration in the presence of the aforesaid King Egfrid, among whom the blessed Theodore held primacy. He was first elected to the episcopate of the Church of Hagustald in place of Tumberct, who had been deposed from the episcopate. But since Cuthbert himself preferred to be placed over the Church of Lindisfarne, in which he had lived, it was agreed that, when Eata returned to the see of the Church of Hagustald, for whose governance he had originally been ordained, Cuthbert should assume the governance of the Church of Lindisfarne.” Moreover, Cuthbert was ordained in the very year in which King Egfrid ended his life, according to the same author, book IV, chapter 27—that is, in the year 685, as is noted below. MABILL.] in the presence of the most devout and God-beloved King Ecgfrid, over which Theodore, archbishop of blessed memory, presided, he was elected by the unanimous agreement of all to the episcopate of the Church of Lindisfarne.

Although many messengers and letters had been sent to him, he could not in any way be brought from his place. At last the aforesaid king himself, together with the most holy bishop Trumwine and many other religious and powerful men, sailed to the island. They all fell to their knees, adjured him by the Lord, shed tears, and pleaded until they drew him, himself also full of tears, from his beloved retreat and brought him to the synod. When he arrived there, although he resisted strongly, the unanimous will of all prevailed over him, and he was compelled to bow his neck to undertake the office of the episcopate. Yet the ordination did not take place immediately; it was completed after the approaching winter had passed.

And so, in every respect, the prophetic words he had spoken were fulfilled: after one year Ecgfrid was slain by the sword of the Picts, and his brother Aldfrid, his illegitimate brother, was installed in the kingdom. He had previously spent many years in the regions of the Scots devoted to reading, [Note: [Col. 0765D] There, because of his love of wisdom.] voluntarily enduring exile for the love of wisdom.

## CHAPTER XXV. How, with water blessed by himself, he healed a sick servant of a count

When, therefore, the man of God Cudberctus, elected to the episcopate, had returned to his island and had served the Lord for some time in seclusion with his customary devotion, his venerable bishop Eata summoned him and ordered him to come to Mailros for a conversation with him.

[Col. 0765C] When this conversation had ended and he had begun to return home, a certain count of King Ecgfrid met him and earnestly asked him to turn aside to his small estate and house in order to give a blessing. [Note: [Col. 0765D] A count. The Anonymous, in book IV, calls him Count Sibba, living beside the river Opide. ID.] When he arrived there and was received with the gracious service of all, the man told him about the illness of his servant:

“I give thanks to God,” he said, “most holy Father, that you have deigned to see us and enter our house; and we truly believe that your arrival will bring us the greatest gain both of mind and body. We have a servant who has long been afflicted by a terrible illness and has today been brought to such a state of suffering that he appears more like a dying man than a sick one. For the extremities of his body already seem dead, and he appears to draw only the slightest breath through his mouth and nostrils.”

The bishop immediately blessed some water and gave it to a servant of the count named Baldhelm, who survives to this day and, holding the office of the priestly rank in the Church of Lindisfarne, fulfills it by his conduct. He has a practice sweeter than honey of recounting the virtues of the man of God to all who wish to know them; he himself told me this very miracle that I am relating. [Note: [Col. 0765D] Priestly rank.]

Giving him the blessed water, the man of God said: “Go and give it to the sick man to drink.”

Obeying these words, he brought the water to the invalid. When he had poured it into his mouth for the third time, the man immediately, contrary to his usual condition, relaxed into sleep. It was already evening. He passed the night quietly, and in the morning, when his Lord visited him, appeared safe and sound. [Note: [Col. 0765D] Evening.]

## CHAPTER XXVI. How he lived in the episcopate

The venerable man of God Cudberctus adorned the episcopal office he had undertaken with works of virtue, in accordance with the commands and examples of the apostles. He protected the flock entrusted to him with constant prayers, called it to heavenly things by most salutary admonitions, and—in what is especially helpful for teachers—first demonstrated by his own actions what he taught ought to be done.

He rescued the needy from the hand of the stronger, and the poor and destitute from those who plundered them. He took care to console the sad and fainthearted, but to lead those who rejoiced in wrongdoing back to the sorrow that is according to God. He diligently practiced his accustomed frugality and gladly, with watchful care, preserved the strictness of monastic life amid the crowds that surrounded him. He supplied food to the hungry and clothing to those suffering from the cold; and, adorned as was proper with the other insignia of episcopal life, he went about his duties.

The signs of miracles by which he shone outwardly also bore witness to his inner virtues—that is, to the virtues of his soul. We have decided to commit some of them briefly to memory. [Note: [Col. 0766D] By which he shone outwardly.]

## CHAPTER XXVII. How, while absent, he saw in the spirit the death of King Ecgfrid and of his army, whose future he had foretold

When King Ecgfrid was leading his army against the Picts with reckless boldness [Note: [Col. 0765D] “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 684,” Bede says in book IV, chapter 26 of his *History*, “Egfrid, king of the Northumbrians, sent an army into Ireland under the commander Berctha and miserably devastated an innocent people. [Col. 0766D] In the year immediately following this, when he had rashly led an army to devastate the province of the Picts, despite the strong opposition of his friends, and especially of Cuthbert of blessed memory, who had recently been ordained bishop, he was slain, together with most of the forces he had brought, in the fortieth year of his age and the fifteenth of his reign, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June.” MABILL.] and was devastating their kingdoms with savage cruelty [Note: [Col. 0766D] Their kingdoms with savage and ferocious cruelty.], the man of God Cudberctus knew that the time had arrived concerning which, the previous year, he had foretold to the king’s sister, when she asked him, that he would live no more than one year. He came to the city of Lugubalia [Note: [Col. 0766D] Lugubalia. Capgrave writes that at this place St Cudbert founded a community of nuns, appointed an abbess, and established schools; whether this is true or not, let the reader judge. See more about this in IV, 29. SMITH.], which is corruptly called Luel by the English peoples, to speak with the queen [Note: [Col. 0767D] The queen, named Ermenburg. SMITH.], who had decided to await the outcome of the war there in her sister’s monastery.

The next day, while the citizens were escorting him so that he might see the walls of the city and a fountain in it [Note: [Col. 0767D] A fountain. The most learned Caerliol, bishop, suspects that this Roman work, beside the cathedral church, still remains to be seen; yet he admits that it is extraordinary that the fountain could have been preserved so intact, since the city itself was almost leveled to the ground by the Danes. ID.] constructed with a remarkable work of Roman engineering, he suddenly became troubled in spirit. As he stood leaning on his staff, he lowered his sorrowful face toward the ground; then, raising himself and lifting his eyes to heaven, he groaned deeply and said in a quiet voice:

“Perhaps at this moment the battle has been decided.”

But the priest who stood nearby, understanding what he meant, was carried away by careless haste and replied: “How do you know?”

Unwilling to reveal further what had been disclosed to him, he said: “Do you not see how wonderfully changed and disturbed the air is? And what mortal is capable of investigating the judgments of God?” [Col. 0767B]

Nevertheless, he immediately entered to the queen and spoke with her privately. It was a Saturday.

“See to it,” he said, “that at first light on Monday you mount a carriage—for it is not permitted to travel by carriage on the Lord’s Day—and go at once into the royal city, lest perhaps the king has been killed. As for me, since I have been asked to come tomorrow to a neighboring monastery to dedicate a church there, I shall follow you immediately after the dedication.”

When Sunday came, he preached the word of God to the brothers of that monastery. When the sermon had ended and all who were present had expressed their approval, he began again in this manner [Note: [Col. 0767D] As he did once more.]:

“I beseech you, dearest ones, according to the Apostle’s admonitions, keep watch, stand firm in the faith, act bravely, and be strengthened, lest some temptation suddenly overtaking you find you unprepared. Rather, always remember that command of the Lord: ‘Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation.’”

They thought that he was speaking of some plague of pestilence that had recently struck down them and many people round about with widespread slaughter, and that he was saying such a plague would soon return.

But he took up the discourse again:

“Once, when I was still living as a solitary on my island, some brothers came to me on the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity and asked me to leave my cell and dwelling and spend with them the solemn and joyful day of such great veneration. [Note: [Col. 0768D] Yielding to their prayers.] Yielding to their devout prayers, I came out, and we sat down to a meal.

“In the middle of the meal I said to them: ‘I beg you, brothers, let us act carefully and watchfully, lest through negligence and security we should be led into temptation.’

“But they replied: ‘We beg you, let us keep this a joyful day, because it is the birthday of our Lord Jesus Christ.’

“And I said: ‘Let us do so.’

“After we had indulged for some time in food, rejoicing, and conversation, I again began to admonish them to remain vigilant in prayers and vigils and to be prepared for every assault of temptation.

“And they said: ‘You teach well, and very well indeed. Yet because there are many days for fasting, prayer, and vigils, let us rejoice today in the Lord. For when the Lord was born, the angel also proclaimed to the shepherds a great joy that was to be celebrated by all the people.’

“And I said: ‘Let us do so.’

“But while we were eating and passing the joyful day, when I repeated the words of that admonition for the third time, they understood that I was not offering these suggestions so earnestly without reason. They became frightened and said: ‘Let us do as you teach, because a great necessity rests upon us, that we may always keep spiritual watch, girded against the devil’s snares and every temptation.’

“When I said this, I did not know—nor did they—that any new temptation was about to befall us. I had merely been warned by an inward prompting that the heart’s condition must always be fortified against sudden storms of temptation.

“But when they had returned from me and reached their own monastery—that is, Lindisfarne—in the morning, they found that one of their number had died of the pestilence. As the same plague increased and raged for days, indeed for months and nearly an entire year, almost the whole of that most noble community of fathers and brothers passed over to the Lord.

“And now, brothers, you too keep watch in prayers, so that if any tribulation overtakes you, it may find you already prepared.” [Note: [Col. 0768D] Also prepared.]

When the venerable bishop Cudberctus said this, they thought—as I have said—that he was speaking of the return of the pestilence. But one day later a man arrived who had fled from the battle, and in miserable words disclosed the hidden prophecies of the man of God. It was proved that on that very day and at that very hour when this had been revealed to the man of God as he stood beside the well, the king, his guards having been slaughtered, had been struck down by the enemy’s sword. [Note: [Col. 0768D] Struck down. In the year 685; IV, 26. ID.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How he foretold his death to the hermit Hereberctus and obtained from the Lord, without delay, by his prayers, that Hereberctus should share his fate

Not long afterward the same servant of God, Cudberctus, came by request to the same city of Lugubalia, in order there to consecrate priests and to bless the queen after giving her the habit of holy conduct.

There was a venerable priest named Hereberctus, already joined to the man of God Cudberctus by a bond of spiritual friendship. He lived a solitary life on an island in that great lake from which the sources of the river Diorwentionis burst forth [Note: [Col. 0768D] Diorwentionis. Otherwise Derwentionis or Dorventionis; this river flows through the province of Cumbria and empties into the Irish Sea. MABILL.]. Each year he was accustomed to come to Cudberctus, receive from him instructions for eternal salvation, and return.

When he heard that Cudberctus was staying in the city, he came, as usual, desiring to be inflamed more and more toward heavenly aspirations by his salutary exhortations. While the two were making themselves drunk with cups of heavenly wisdom, Cudberctus said, among other things:

“Remember, brother Hereberctus, to ask me now whatever you need and speak with me, because after we have parted from each other, we shall no longer see one another with bodily eyes in this world. For I am certain that the time of my release is near, and the laying down of my tent is at hand.”

Hearing this, Hereberctus fell at his feet and, shedding tears with groans, said:

“I beg you by the Lord, do not abandon me. Remember your companion, and ask heavenly mercy that, since we have served it together on earth, we may pass together into heaven to behold its glory. For you know that I have always striven to live at the command of your lips, and whatever I have done wrong through ignorance or weakness, I have likewise endeavored to correct according to your will.”

The bishop devoted himself to prayer and immediately learned in the spirit that he had obtained from the Lord what he had asked.

“Rise, my brother,” he said, “and do not weep, but rejoice with joy, because heavenly clemency has granted us what we asked of it.”

The subsequent outcome of events confirmed both the truth of this promise and of the prophecy [Note: [Col. 0769D] And also.]: when they departed from one another, they did not see each other again bodily; and at the same moment, as their spirits left their bodies, they were immediately joined to one another in a blessed vision and, by angelic ministry, were carried together into the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0769D] “On one and the same day,” Bede says in book IV, chapter 29, “that is, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, as they left their bodies, their spirits were immediately joined to one another in a blessed vision, and by angelic ministry, etc.” The priest Hereberctus is entered in the Benedictine calendars on the same day as St Cuthbertus. MABILL.]

But first Hereberctus was worn down by a prolonged illness, perhaps by that dispensation of the Lord’s mercy whereby, if he had anything lacking in merit compared with the blessed Cudberctus, the continual suffering of a long illness might supply it; so that, made equal in grace to his intercessor, just as he deserved to leave his body with him at one and the same time of day, he might also deserve to be received with him into one and the same, undivided dwelling of everlasting blessedness. [Note: [Col. 0769D] Of blessed merit.] [Note: [Col. 0769D] At one and the same time.]

## CHAPTER XXIX. How, through his priest, he healed a count’s wife with blessed water

One day, as he traveled through his parish distributing words of salvation to everyone in the countryside, in cottages, and in fortified settlements [Note: [Col. 0769D] In the countryside.], and also laid hands upon the newly baptized to confer the grace of the Holy Spirit, he came to the small estate of a certain count. The count’s wife was lying there seriously ill, apparently close to death.

The count himself met him as he arrived [Note: [Col. 0769D] The count, named Heunna, living in the region called Henitis. SMITH.], knelt, and gave thanks to the Lord for his arrival. He then led him inside and received him with kind hospitality.

When the bishop had washed his hands and feet, as hospitality customarily required, and had sat down, the man began to tell him about the illness of his despairing wife, asking him to bless water with which she could be sprinkled.

“I believe,” he said, “that by God’s gift she will soon either be restored to health or, if she is to die, pass from death to eternal life, and by dying more quickly receive relief from such wretched and prolonged suffering.”

The man of God agreed to his plea, blessed the water that had been brought, and gave it to a priest [Note: [Col. 0770D] A priest, who was called Beta. ID.], ordering him to sprinkle the sick woman.

The priest entered the bedroom, where she lay almost like a corpse, sprinkled her and her bed, and, opening her mouth, poured in a taste of the life-giving drink.

A wondrous and utterly astonishing thing! As soon as the blessed water touched the sick woman, who had been completely unaware of what was being done to her, she immediately recovered full health of mind and body. Coming to herself, she blessed the Lord and gave thanks to him who had deigned to send such great and distinguished guests to visit and heal her.

Without delay she rose and, now healed, performed service for the very ministers of her recovery. In a beautiful spectacle, she herself, the first of the entire household of so great a man, offered the bishop a drink for his refreshment. Through his blessing she had escaped the cup of death, following the example of the mother-in-law of the apostle Peter, who, healed by the Lord of her fever, immediately rose and ministered to him and his disciples.

## CHAPTER XXX. How he healed a girl, anointing her with oil, from pain in her head and side

Many who were present testified that a similar miracle of healing was performed by the venerable bishop Cudberctus. Among them was the devout priest Aedilvald, then a minister of the man of God and now abbot of the monastery of Mailros [Note: [Col. 0770D] Aedilvald. See V, 12. SMITH.—Others call him Ethelwold. Having been made bishop of Lindisfarne after Eadbertus and Eadfridus, the successors of St Cuthbertus, he deserved a place in the catalogue of the saints. MABILL.].

As he was traveling about, teaching everyone according to his custom, he came to a village [Note: [Col. 0770D] A village, namely Bedesfeld. SMITH.] in which there were not many religious women [Note: [Col. 0770D] They were nuns.]; the man of God had recently granted them a place to remain there after they had fled from their monastery through fear of the barbarian army.

One of them, who was a relative of the aforesaid priest Aedilvald, was weighed down by a very serious illness. For an entire year she had been tormented by unbearable pain in her head and throughout one side of her body, and the physicians had completely despaired of her.

When the man of God’s companions told him about her and pleaded for her healing, he took pity on the unfortunate woman and anointed her with blessed oil. From that very hour she began to improve, and after a few days she recovered completely.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How a sick man was healed by bread blessed by him

We do not think that we should pass over in silence a miracle that we learned was performed through the power of the same venerable man, although he himself was absent.

Above we mentioned Hildmer the prefect, whose wife the man of God had freed from an unclean spirit. [Note: [Col. 0771C] Above, chapter 15. SMITH.] The same prefect later fell into a very serious illness [Note: [Col. 0771C] He fell into bed, oppressed by a grave illness.], so that, as his suffering increased day by day, he was brought low on his bed and seemed every moment about to die. [Note: [Col. 0771C] His suffering increased day by day and he seemed on the point of death.]

Many friends were present, having come to console the sick man. As they sat beside the bed on which he lay, one of them suddenly said that he had with him some bread which the man of God Cudberctus had recently given him as a blessing.

“And I believe,” he said, “that by tasting this bread he may receive the remedy of health, provided that the slowness of our faith does not stand in the way.”

They were all laymen, but religious men. Turning to one another, they each confessed that they believed without any doubt that he could be healed through communion in that blessed bread.

They filled a cup with water, put a very small piece of that bread into it, and gave it to him to drink. As soon as that taste of water, sanctified through the bread, touched his entrails, all pain in his internal organs fled, and the wasting of his external limbs fled as well.

Without delay, health followed and strengthened the man, now freed from his illness. It rightly lifted both him and all who saw or heard of the speed of such an unexpected healing to praise the holiness of Christ’s servant and to marvel at the power of sincere faith.

## CHAPTER XXXII. How, by praying, he brought back to life a young man presented to him on the road who was dying

At another time, as the most holy shepherd of the Lord’s flock was traveling through his sheepfolds [Note: [Col. 0771C] He traveled through them. “Leaving Hagustald, he was heading toward the city called Vel; yet he made his lodging halfway, in the region called Alise.” See the *Anonymous Life of St Cudberctus*, book IV. ID.], he came to mountainous and rural places where many people from the surrounding villages had gathered. [Note: [Col. 0772A] For whom hands had to be laid on. The Anonymous mentions not only the laying on of hands but also anointing, or chrismation, customarily used in the sacrament of confirmation. Thus, in book IV: “At one time the holy bishop, leaving Hagustald, was heading toward the city called Vel; yet he lodged halfway, in the region called Alise. For when the people from the mountains had gathered, he laid his hand on each person’s head, anointing them with the consecrated oil that he had blessed, and preached the word of God, remaining there for two days. Meanwhile women came carrying a certain young man lying on a bier, etc.” Therefore, above, in chapter 29, where Bede mentions only the laying on of hands, understand chrismation as included. Certainly the ancient writers sometimes call this sacrament, namely confirmation, simply the laying on of hands. Although in former times it happened in some places that priests placed the sign or anointing of the forehead upon the baptized, while the laying on of hands alone was reserved to bishops—as is still practiced among the Greeks. See Gregory the Great, letters 9 and 10, book III. MABILL.]

Yet no church or suitable place could be found in the mountains to receive the bishop and his companions. They therefore pitched tents for him along the road; cutting small branches from the neighboring forest, each person fixed up for himself whatever kind of shelter he could make in which to stay.

While the man of God preached the word for two days to the crowds flocking to him and, by the laying on of hands, bestowed the grace of the Holy Spirit upon those newly reborn in Christ, suddenly women appeared carrying a young man on a bier. He had been wasted away by the severity of a long illness. They placed him at the edge of the forest and sent word to the bishop, asking that they might bring him to him to receive a blessing.

When the bishop saw him brought before him and suffering most grievously [Note: [Col. 0772C] Afflicted.], he ordered everyone to withdraw some distance. Then, taking refuge in his customary weapons of prayer, he gave a blessing and drove away the disease that the attentive hands of physicians had been unable to overcome by compounding medicines.

Finally, rising at that very hour and strengthened after taking food, the young man gave thanks to God and returned to the women who had carried him. Thus it came about that those who had brought him there sorrowfully and sick returned home with him, now restored and joyful.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How, during a time of pestilence, he restored a dying boy alive and well to his mother

At the same time, a pestilence suddenly arose in those regions and settled upon them with extremely deadly force, so that in villages and estates once filled with large numbers of inhabitants [Note: [Col. 0772C] Inhabited places.], scarcely a few scattered survivors remained, and sometimes none at all.

Therefore the most holy Father Cudberctus, diligently traveling through his parish, did not cease to offer the ministry of the word and the necessary help of consolation to those same very few survivors who remained. [Note: [Col. 0772C] To those very few.]

When he arrived at a certain village [Note: [Col. 0772C] A village called Medilpong. SMITH.] and had offered the help of exhortation to everyone he found there, he said to his priest [Note: [Col. 0772C] A priest named Tidi. ID.]:

“Do you think there is anyone remaining in these places who needs our visit and conversation, or may we now, having visited all who were ill, pass on to others?”

The priest looked around and saw a woman standing some distance away. A short time earlier her son had died, and she was holding his brother, already near death, in her arms. Tears streamed down her face, testifying equally to her past and present distress.

When he pointed her out to the man of God, Cudberctus immediately went to her, blessed the child, and kissed him. Then he said to the mother:

“Do not be afraid, and do not grieve; the infant will be healed and will live, and no one else from your household will ever again perish from this plague.”

The mother and her son, who lived for a long time afterward, bore witness to the truth of this prophecy.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How he saw the soul of a man who died by falling from a tree being carried to heaven
Meanwhile, since the man of God, Cuthbert, foreseeing the death of his neighbor [Col. 0773B], had already resolved in his mind to lay aside the care of pastoral office and return to the solitary life, so that, freed from outward anxiety, he might await the day of death—or rather, the entrance into heavenly life—amid the liberty of prayer and psalmody, he first wished not only to go throughout his own parish [Note: [Col. 0773D] To travel around his parish.], but also, after visiting the other dwellings of the faithful in the surrounding region, to strengthen them all with the necessary word of exhortation, and thus refresh himself with the joy of the solitude he desired.

While he was doing this, he was invited by the most noble and holy virgin of Christ, the abbess Ælfflæd, whose memory I mentioned above (Chapters 23 and 24), to come to the estate of her monastery [Note: [Col. 0773] Of the monastery. It was situated in her parish, which is called Osingadun. SMITH.], so that he might see and speak with her there and dedicate the church. For that estate also flourished with a considerable company of Christ’s servants [Col. 0773C].

While they were seated at table at the hour of the meal, Cuthbert suddenly lifted his mind, turned away from bodily food, to contemplate spiritual things [Note: [Col. 0773D] He directed it.]. Thereupon, his bodily limbs were wearied by their service; the color of his face changed; his eyes, as though stunned, stared unusually; and the small knife he was holding fell onto the table.

When his priest, who was standing nearby and serving him, saw this, he leaned toward the abbess and said quietly: “Ask the bishop what he has seen [Note: [Col. 0774D] What he has seen: I know.]. For I know that his hand did not release the knife without cause, nor did his face change without reason; rather, he has seen some spiritual thing that the rest of us could not see.”

She immediately turned to him and said: “I beg you, my lord bishop, tell us what you have just seen, for surely your right hand did not become weary and drop the knife it was holding without cause” [Col. 0773D].

He tried to conceal that he had seen some secret thing and replied jokingly: “Was I able to eat all day? I had to rest at some point.”

But when she pressed him more earnestly and begged him to explain the vision, he said: “I saw the soul of a certain holy man being carried by angelic hands to the joys of the heavenly kingdom.”

She asked again: “From what place was it taken?”

He replied: “From your monastery.”

She pressed him to tell her the man’s name. He said: “Tomorrow, when I celebrate Mass, you will tell me his name.”

When she heard this, she immediately sent to her larger monastery to find out who had recently been taken from the body. But the messenger found everyone there safe and unharmed. When, at daybreak, he began to return to the Lady, he met men carrying the body of a dead brother in a cart for burial.

On asking who the man was, he learned that a certain shepherd, a man of good conduct, had climbed a tree carelessly, fallen to the ground, and, his body crushed, had breathed out his spirit at the very hour when the man of God had seen him being led to heaven.

When the messenger returned and reported this to the abbess, she immediately entered the church to the bishop, who was then dedicating it, and, with the astonishment of a woman announcing something new and uncertain, said: “I beg you, my lord bishop, remember my Hadwald at the Masses—for that was the man’s name—who died yesterday by falling from a tree.”

Then it became clear to everyone that the spirit of manifold prophecy dwelt in the holy man’s inmost heart: he had been able to see the soul’s secret departure in the present and to foresee what would have to be reported to him by others in the future.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### How, by tasting water, he changed it into the flavor of wine

After he had visited the places mentioned above in order, he came to the monastery of virgins, which, as we explained above (Chapter 3), was situated not far from the mouth of the River Tyne [Col. 0774C]. There he was magnificently received by the religious and also, in worldly rank, most noble servant of Christ, the abbess Verca. After they had risen from their midday rest, he said that he was thirsty and asked for something to drink.

They asked what he wished to drink, requesting permission to bring wine or ale. “Give me water,” he said.

They offered him water drawn from a spring. After giving a blessing, he tasted a little of it, then handed it to his attending priest, who returned it to the servant. The servant, taking the cup, said: “May I drink from the beverage from which the bishop drank?”

He replied: “Of course. Why would you not be allowed?”

That man too was a priest of the same monastery. He drank, and the water seemed to him to have been changed into the taste of wine. Wishing to have as a witness to the miracle the brother who was standing nearby, he handed the cup to him [Col. 0774D]. When the brother also drank, the water likewise tasted like wine to his palate.

They looked at one another in amazement, and when they had found a suitable opportunity to speak [Note: [Col. 0774D] They took the opportunity.], they confessed to one another that they seemed never to have drunk better wine. One of them later testified this to me personally, after spending a considerable time in our monastery, which is at the mouth of the River Wear, and where he is now buried in peaceful rest.

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### How a storm at sea kept certain disobedient brothers confined for seven days [Note: [Col. 0775C] A storm of the sea confined them for seven days.]

Thus, after two years had passed in episcopal government [Note: [Col. 0775C] The two years must be counted from his election, not from his consecration. He was consecrated in 685, at the time of the Easter solemnity; therefore, if one counted from his consecration, the two years would have elapsed at Easter in 687. But Chapter 37 makes it clear that he returned to the island before Easter, immediately after the solemn day of the Lord’s Nativity. The years must therefore be counted from his election, which took place as winter was approaching in 684. On his return to the eremitical life, see Book IV, Chapter 28. SMITH.], the man of God Cuthbert, knowing in spirit that the day of his departure was approaching, cast off the burden of pastoral care and hastened to return to the beloved struggle of the eremitical life, so that the thickets of worldly anxiety, long rooted in him, might be more freely consumed by the ancient flame of compunction.

At that time he often went out from his dwelling to the brothers who visited him and spoke with them in person. It is worthwhile to recount a miracle he performed then, by which it may more clearly shine forth how obedient one ought to be to holy men, even in matters that seem to have been commanded somewhat casually.

One day, when certain men had arrived and he had come out and refreshed them with exhortatory speech [Col. 0775B] [Note: [Col. 0775C] With an exhortation for them.], after completing his admonition he added: “It is now time for me to return to my dwelling. But since you are preparing to leave, first take some food and cook and eat that goose [Note: [Col. 0775C] Goose. It is clearer than it needs to be proved by the examples cited that by *auca*—“goose”—the bird called *oie* by the French is meant. Nor is it surprising that those monks ate goose meat, since perhaps even then they counted birds among the fishes. Certainly, from the Acts of Saint Columbanus and likewise of Saint Bertulf, abbots of Bobbio, we understand that the disciples of Saint Columbanus were sometimes permitted to eat the flesh of quails and ducks, although in the Rule, Chapter 3, Columbanus allows his disciples only vegetables, legumes, and flour mixed with water, together with a little bread broken into pieces. See Ratramnus, Book IV, *Against the Objections of the Greeks*, Chapter 2, volume II of Acher’s *Spicilegium*. MABILL.]; the goose is hanging on the wall. Then, in the name of the Lord, board the ship and return home.”

He said this, and, after giving a prayer and blessing, entered his dwelling. They took the food as he had instructed, but because they had an abundance of provisions that they had brought with them, they did not trouble to touch the goose he had mentioned.

When, however, they wished to board their small boat after eating, a violent storm suddenly arose and took away all possibility of sailing. Thus, shut in for seven days by the raging waves, they remained sadly on the island [Col. 0775C]. Yet even then they did not recall the fault of disobedience for which they were suffering this imprisonment [Note: [Col. 0775C] Nor did they then recall their fault.].

When they had repeatedly returned to the Father to speak with him and complained about the delay in their return, they received from him admonitions concerning patience. At last, on the seventh day, he went out to them, wishing to lessen their sadness through the grace of his visit and a kind word of consolation.

Entering the house in which they were staying, he saw that the goose had not been eaten. With a peaceful face and rather cheerful speech, he reproved their disobedience: “Is the uneaten goose still hanging there? And what wonder is it that the sea has not allowed you to depart? So put it into the cauldron [Note: [Col. 0776C] Into the cooking pot.] at once; cook and eat it, so that the sea may become calm and allow you to return home.”

They immediately did as he had ordered. In a wondrous sequence of events, just as the food began to boil in the cauldron over the fire at the man of God’s command, at that same hour the waves of the sea, when the winds ceased, came to rest from their own turbulence [Col. 0776A].

When they had finished their meal and saw that the sea was calm, they boarded the ship and, with favorable winds, returned home in joy and shame alike. They were ashamed of their disobedience and dull understanding, by which they had been prevented, even amid the chastisements of their Creator, from recognizing and correcting their offense [Note: [Col. 0776C] By which they were restrained.]. They rejoiced because they understood that God had shown such care for his faithful servant that he avenged the contempt shown to him even through the elements. They rejoiced because they saw that their Creator had shown such care for them that, even by a manifest miracle, he corrected their errors.

I learned this miracle not from just any informant, but from one of those who had been present and had related it—namely, Cynemund, a monk and priest of that monastery, who was already widely known among the faithful for his great age and long life.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### How, while ill, he endured many trials, and what instructions he gave concerning his burial

The man of God Cuthbert returned to his island and dwelling immediately after the solemn day of the Lord’s Nativity. As a crowd of brothers surrounded him while he was about to board the ship, one of them, an old and venerable monk, strong in faith but already physically weakened by dysentery, asked: “Tell us, my lord bishop [Col. 0776C], when should we hope for your return?” [Note: [Col. 0776C] One of them. On how he was healed of his dysentery, see the next chapter. SMITH.]

He answered the question simply, revealing simply what he knew to be true: “When you bring my body back here.”

After spending nearly two months in great joy at his renewed solitude and binding body and mind with the much more severe rigor of his customary discipline, he was seized by a sudden illness. Through the fire of temporal suffering he began to be prepared for the joys of everlasting blessedness.

I wish to describe his death in the words of the man whose account I received—namely, Herefrith, a priest of devoted religion who at that time also presided over the monastery at Lindisfarne as its abbot.

“For three continuous weeks,” he said, “worn down by illness, he came to the end in this way. He began to fall ill on a Wednesday, and again, on a Wednesday, when his illness was finished, he departed to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0776C] He began to be ill. He died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, that is, on 20 March; therefore he began to be ill on 27 February. ID.].

“On the first morning of his illness, I came to him—for three days earlier I had gone to the island with the brothers, wishing to receive from him the comfort of his customary blessing and exhortation. When I gave the usual signal to show him that I had arrived, he came to the window and, in answer to my greeting, gave a sigh.

“I said to him: ‘What is wrong, my lord bishop? Has your illness perhaps attacked you during the night?’

“He replied: ‘Yes, this illness attacked me during the night.’

“I thought he was speaking of his old illness, from which he was accustomed to be almost daily worn down, not of a new and unfamiliar one. Without asking further, I said: ‘Give us your blessing, for now the time has come to sail and return home.’

“‘Do as you say,’ he replied. ‘Board the ship and return home safely. But when God has received my soul, bury me here in this dwelling beside my oratory, to the south, opposite the eastern side of the holy cross that I erected there’ [Note: [Col. 0777D] Beside the eastern side.].

“‘There is a sarcophagus hidden beneath a covering of earth on the northern side of the same oratory, which the venerable abbot Cudda once gave me. Place my body in it, wrapping me in the shroud that you will find there. I did not wish to be clothed in it while alive, but, out of love for the woman beloved of God who sent it to me—namely, the abbess Verca—I took care to reserve it for wrapping my body.’

[Note: [Col. 0777D] When I heard these things.]

“When I heard this, I said: ‘I beg you, Father: since I hear that you are ill and dying, permit some of the brothers to remain here to minister to you’ [Note: [Col. 0777D] Ill.].

“He replied: ‘Go now, but return at the proper time.’

“Since I could not prevail upon him, despite repeated entreaties, to accept their service, I finally asked when we should return.

“He said: ‘When God wills, and he himself shows you.’

“We did as he had ordered. We immediately summoned all the brothers into the church and ordered that prayer be made for him without interruption. ‘For it seems to me,’ I said, ‘from certain words of his, that the day on which he will depart to God is approaching.’

“I was anxious to return because of his illness, but for five days a storm prevented us from doing so. The outcome of events proved that this had been divinely arranged. For almighty God wished to purge his servant completely from every stain of worldly frailty and to show his adversaries how powerless they were against the strength of his faith. He therefore willed that Cuthbert should be separated from human beings for so long and tested both by the pain of his flesh and by the sharper struggle with the ancient enemy.

“When the calm returned and we went back to the island, we found him outside his monastery, sitting in the house where we usually stayed. Since necessity required the brothers who had come with me to sail back to the nearby shore, I remained on the island and immediately undertook to minister to the Father.

“I heated water and washed his foot, which, because of a long-standing swelling, already had an ulcer [Note: [Col. 0777D] Ulcer. On the origin of this ulcer, see above, Chapter 18. SMITH.] and needed care because pus was flowing from it. I also heated wine and brought it to him, asking him to drink some. I could see from his face that he was greatly exhausted by both fasting and illness.

“When the treatment was complete, he sat quietly on his bed [Note: [Col. 0778D] On his couch.], and I sat beside him. When he was silent, I said: ‘I see, my lord bishop, that you have suffered greatly from illness since we left you. It is surprising that you did not wish us to leave some of our number here to minister to you.’

“He replied: ‘It happened through God’s providence and will that, deprived of human presence and assistance, I should suffer some adversity. For as soon as you departed from me, the illness began to grow worse. Therefore, when I left my dwelling, I entered this place so that, whenever one of you came to minister to me, you could find me here and would not need to enter my dwelling. From the moment I entered and settled my limbs in this seat, I have not moved from here; for these five days and nights I have remained quietly here.’

“I said to him: ‘And how could you live in this way, my lord bishop? Did you remain so long without taking any food?’

“Then he uncovered the bedding on which he had been sitting and showed me five onions hidden there. He said: ‘This was my food during these days. Whenever my mouth became dry and burned with excessive thirst [Note: [Col. 0778D] Became dry and burned.], I refreshed and revived myself by tasting them.’

“One of the onions appeared to have been gnawed by less than half.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] He added: “And …”]

“He added: ‘Moreover, my adversaries have never, during all the time since I began to dwell on this island, inflicted as many persecutions upon me as they have during these five days.’

“I did not dare ask what temptations he meant, but merely requested that he accept attendants. He agreed and retained some of us with him. Among them was the senior presbyter Bede [Note: [Col. 0777D] Bede. This man is not to be confused with Bede the Venerable, who is also said to have had a disciple of the same name [Col. 0778D]. SMITH.], who had always been accustomed to be familiarly present in his service.

“Therefore Bede was undoubtedly aware of all his gifts and acceptances, and Cuthbert especially wished him to remain with him so that, if he had failed to make a fitting return for anyone’s gifts, Bede’s reminder might bring it back to his memory and he might restore to each person what was owed before he died.

“He also designated another of the brothers in particular to attend him among his ministers. This man had been seriously ill for a long time with a flux of the bowels and could not be cured by physicians. Yet by the merit of his religious devotion, prudence, and gravity he had proved worthy to be a witness of the words the man of God would speak at the end, and of the manner in which he would depart to the Lord.

“Meanwhile, when I returned home, I told the brothers that the venerable Father had ordered that he be buried on his island. ‘It seems to me,’ I said, ‘far more just and fitting to obtain from him permission for his body to be brought here and buried in the church with the honor it deserves.’

“They approved what I had said, and we came to the bishop and asked him: ‘We have not dared, my lord bishop, to disregard your order by which you commanded that you be buried there. Yet it seemed to us that we should ask whether we might bring you to us and have you remain with us.’

“He replied: ‘It was also my wish to rest in body there, where I fought even a small battle for the Lord, where I desire to complete my course, and from which I hope to be raised by the merciful Judge to the crown of righteousness.

“‘But I also think it would be more convenient for you if I rested there, because of incursions by fugitives or any other criminals. If such persons should perhaps take refuge with my body, then, whatever sort of man I may be, since it has nevertheless become known that I am a servant of Christ, you would often have to intercede for such people with the powerful of this world. Thus you would have to endure great trouble because of the presence of my body’ [Note: [Col. 0779D] Whatever sort of man I may be.].

“But after we had long entreated him and assured him that such trouble would be welcome and easy for us, the man of God at last spoke after deliberation: ‘If you wish to overcome my arrangement and bring my body back there, it seems best to me that you bury it in the inner part of your basilica, so that you yourselves may visit my tomb whenever you wish, and so that it may be in your power to decide whether any of those who come should approach it.’

“We gave thanks for his permission and advice, kneeling on the ground, and returned home. From that time onward we did not cease to visit him frequently.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### How, while ill, he healed his minister from a flux of the bowels [Note: [Col. 0779D] The blessed man, ill. Peace.]

“As his illness increased and he saw that the time of his dissolution was near, he ordered that he be carried back to his little dwelling and oratory. It was the third hour of the day. We carried him, since the distress of his illness prevented him from entering on his own.

“When we reached the door, we asked permission for one of us to enter with him and minister to him. For many years no one except himself had entered that place.

“He looked around and saw the brother whom I mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0779D] Above, in the previous chapter. SMITH.], who was suffering from a flux of the bowels, and said: ‘Let Walhstod enter with me’; for that was the brother’s name [Note: [Col. 0779D] Of the brother.].

“When he had remained inside with him until the ninth hour, he came out and called me: ‘The bishop orders you to enter to him.’

“‘I can tell you something new and extraordinary,’ he continued, ‘for as soon as I entered there and touched the bishop in order to lead him to the oratory, I immediately felt myself free from all the trouble of that long illness.’

“There can be no doubt that this was brought about by the dispensation of heavenly mercy: the man who, while still healthy and strong, had cured many others, also cured this man while dying. Thus this sign too made clear how powerful the holy man was in spirit even when weakened in body.

“In this healing he followed the example of the most holy and revered Father, Bishop Aurelius Augustine. When Augustine was lying in bed, weighed down by the illness from which he also died [Note: [Col. 0780D] From which he died, he was lying ill.], someone came with a sick person of his own and asked him to lay his hand upon the man so that he might be healed.

“Augustine replied: ‘If I had any power in these matters, I would surely have exercised it first on myself.’

“Again the visitor said [Note: [Col. 0780D] Commanded to visit.]: ‘I have been commanded to visit you, for in a dream I was told: “Go to Bishop Augustine, let him lay his hand upon you, and you will be saved.”’

“When Augustine heard this, he immediately blessed the sick man and laid his hand upon him. Without delay he sent him home healed.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### What final instructions he gave to the brothers, and how, after receiving the viaticum, he surrendered his spirit amid words of prayer

“I entered to him,” he said, “at about the ninth hour of the day and found him reclining in a corner of his oratory opposite the altar. I began to sit beside him. He did not speak much, because the severity of his illness had reduced his ability to speak.

“But when I questioned him more carefully about what hereditary teaching, what final farewell, he would leave to the brothers, he began to say a few but forceful things about peace and humility, and about avoiding those who preferred to oppose these virtues rather than delight in them.

“‘Always preserve peace among yourselves and divine charity,’ he said. ‘When necessity requires you to deliberate about your condition, take care above all that you be united in your counsels.

“‘Maintain mutual concord also with the other servants of Christ. Do not despise members of the household of faith who come to you for the sake of hospitality; receive, retain, and dismiss such people familiarly and kindly, never considering yourselves better than the other companions of the same faith and way of life [Note: [Col. 0780D] Servants of Christ.].

“‘But with those who have departed from the unity of Catholic peace, whether by celebrating Easter at the wrong time or by living perversely, let there be no communion for you [Col. 0780D].

“‘Know and remember this: if necessity should force you to choose one of two evils, I would much rather that you remove my bones from the tomb, take them with you, and depart from these places, remaining wherever God may provide a dwelling for you, than that you should in any way consent to iniquity and submit your necks to the yoke of schismatics.

“‘Strive diligently to learn and observe the Catholic decrees of the Fathers. Carefully practice also those principles of regular life which divine mercy has graciously established for you through my ministry.

“‘For I know that, although I lived contemptibly in the eyes of some, after my death you will see more clearly what sort of man I was and that my teaching is not to be despised’ [Note: [Col. 0781C] After my death, what sort of man I was, and how …].”

The man of God spoke these and similar words at intervals, since, as we have said, the force of his illness had taken away his ability to speak. He spent the quiet day awaiting future blessedness until evening, and continued the night in quiet prayer, keeping vigil [Note: [Col. 0781C] Of rest.].

[Note: [Col. 0781C] But there.]
