When the customary hour of nocturnal prayer arrived, after receiving from me the saving sacraments [Note: [Col. 0781D] The sacraments—namely, penance and anointing, for he speaks afterward of the viaticum. MABILL.], he fortified his departure, which he now knew had come, with communion in the Lord’s body and blood. Then, raising his eyes to heaven and stretching his hands upward, he sent forth his soul, intent upon heavenly praises, to the joys of the heavenly kingdom [Note: [Col. 0781D] He sent it forth. This occurred, evidently, in the year 687, as Turgottus expressly proves in Book I, Chapter 11. Indeed, Bede also indicates this sufficiently when he states that Cuthbert was raised to the episcopal dignity in 685—as we noted above, Chapter 27—and died after two years, in Chapters 24 and 36 above and elsewhere. Finally, he died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, and on a Wednesday, according to no. 56; therefore in the aforementioned year 687, in which Sunday had the letter F and Wednesday the letter B. Thus Cuthbert’s two years of episcopate—as the Bollandist associates noted—must be counted not from the day of his consecration, celebrated on Easter Day in 685, but from his election, which took place toward the end of the preceding year. ID.] [Col. 0781B].

## CHAPTER XL  
### How, in accordance with the prophecy of the psalm they were singing at his death, the people of Lindisfarne were attacked but, with the Lord’s help, protected again

“I immediately went out and announced his death to the brothers, who themselves had spent the night in vigil and prayer. At that moment they happened to be singing, in the regular order of the nocturnal praises, the fifty-ninth psalm, whose beginning is: ‘O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us; you have been angry, and you have shown us mercy.’

“Without delay, one of them ran and lit two candles. Holding one in each hand, he climbed to a higher place to show the brothers who were staying in the monastery at Lindisfarne [Col. 0781C] that the holy soul had now departed to the Lord. For they had agreed among themselves upon this sign of his most holy death.

“A brother who had been keeping watch in the lookout of Lindisfarne, far across from us [Note: [Col. 0781C] On the opposite side.], awaiting the hour of this event, saw it and quickly ran to the church, where the whole community of brothers had gathered to celebrate the solemnities of the nocturnal psalmody. It happened that, as he entered, they too were singing the aforementioned psalm [Col. 0782A].

“The outcome of events showed that this had been arranged by heavenly providence. For after the man of God had been buried, so violent a storm of trial shook that church that many of the brothers preferred to abandon the place rather than become involved in such dangers.

“Yet after a year, when Eadberht had been ordained bishop [Note: [Col. 0781D] A year. For Bede testifies in Book IV of the *History*, Chapter 29: ‘The venerable bishop Wilfrid governed that church for one year, until someone could be chosen and ordained bishop in Cuthbert’s place. Afterwards Eadberht was ordained, and so forth.’ At that time the Bollandist associates say that the disaster described here occurred, supposedly because ‘Saint Wilfrid wished to abolish the ancient statutes of the Fathers and those of Saint Cuthbert himself, which they had hitherto observed and which Saint Cuthbert had commended to them while dying, and wished either to introduce the rule of Saint Benedict or to have it observed alone.’ But this is entirely uncertain. ID.], a man of great virtue, nobly learned in the Scriptures, and especially devoted to works of almsgiving, the storms of disturbance were driven away. [Note: [Col. 0782C] To use the words.]

To use the words of Scripture, the Lord built Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, and gathered the dispersed of Israel. He healed the brokenhearted and bound up their wounds. Thus it was openly made clear what the psalm meant when it was sung after the blessed man’s death: namely, that after his death his fellow citizens would be rejected and destroyed, but that after the display of threatening anger they would immediately be restored by heavenly mercy.

“Anyone who considers the rest of the psalm understands that its succeeding words also agree with this same meaning [Note: [Col. 0782C] Its meaning.].

“We placed the venerable Father’s body on a ship and brought it back to the island of Lindisfarne. A great crowd of people coming to meet it and choirs singing received it [Note: [Col. 0782D] It was received. The Anonymous author adds certain details in Book IV: ‘Brought to our island by those who sailed, his entire body washed, his head wrapped in a cloth, offerings placed upon his holy breast, clothed in priestly garments, with his shoes prepared for meeting Christ, cared for in a waxed shroud, his soul rejoicing with Christ, his incorrupt body resting as if sleeping in a stone tomb—they honorably placed him in the basilica.’ By the offerings he perhaps means a chalice, and so forth. ID.], and they laid it in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter, on the right side of the altar [Note: [Col. 0782C] On the right of the altar.], in a stone sarcophagus.”

## CHAPTER XLI  
### How a demon-possessed boy was healed when earth from the place where the water used to wash his body had been poured into water

Nor, after the servant of Christ had died and been buried, could the signs of healing that he had performed while alive cease. It happened that a certain boy in the territory of Lindisfarne was tormented by a most savage demon. He had completely lost the use of reason, and screamed and wailed, trying to tear with his teeth both his own limbs and anything else he could reach.

A priest from the monastery was sent to the possessed boy [Note: [Col. 0782D] A priest. Named Tidi. SMITH.]. Although he had been accustomed to drive out unclean spirits by the grace of exorcism, he was completely unable to help this afflicted child.

Therefore he advised the boy’s father to place him on a cart and carry him to the monastery, and there to pray to the Lord on his behalf at the relics of the blessed martyrs kept there.

The father did as he had been advised, but the holy martyrs of God did not wish to grant the requested healing, in order to show how exalted a place Cuthbert held among them. While the mad boy shook everyone’s sight and hearing with the greatest horror by howling, groaning, and gnashing his teeth, and no one could devise any kind of remedy, suddenly one of the priests, instructed in spirit that the boy could be healed through the help of the blessed Father Cuthbert, secretly came to the place where he knew that the water with which the dead man’s body had been washed had been poured out.

He took a small piece of earth from that spot and put it into water. Carrying the water to the sufferer, he poured it into his mouth, which was hideously gaping as it uttered dreadful and mournful cries [Col. 0783B].

As soon as the water touched him, he stopped his cries [Note: [Col. 0783D] His shouting.], closed his mouth, and closed his eyes, which had been open, bloodshot, and furious. He reclined his head and entire body into repose.

He spent the night in peaceful sleep. In the morning, rising from sleep and madness alike, he realized that he had been freed from the demon that oppressed him through the merits and intercession of the blessed Cuthbert.

It was a wonderful and delightful sight for all good people: to see the son, now restored to health, walking around the holy places with his father and giving thanks with a completely sound mind for the help of the saints. The previous day, in the madness of his mind, he had been unable to recognize either himself, who he was, or where he was.

When, with the entire community of brothers standing by, witnessing the event, and rejoicing, he knelt before the relics of the martyrs and gave praise to God the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ [Col. 0783C], he returned home freed from the enemy’s blows and made firmer in faith than he had been before.

To this day the pit into which that memorable washing-water was poured is displayed. It is square in shape, enclosed on every side by wood, and filled inside with pebbles [Note: [Col. 0783D] Filled with small stones.]. It lies beside the church in which Cuthbert’s body rests, on the southern side.

From that time onward, many healings were performed, by the Lord’s gift, through those same stones or through that same earth.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### How, after eleven years, his body was found without corruption [Note: [Col. 0783D] Found.]

[Note: [Col. 0783D] Wishing. See this chapter almost copied out in Book IV, Chapter 30. SMITH.]

Divine providence wished to show more broadly how greatly the holy man lived in glory after death, since even before his death his exalted life had been revealed by frequent signs of miracles [Col. 0783D]. After eleven years had passed since his burial, it put into the minds of the brothers that they should lift his bones and place them in a light coffin, in the same place but above the pavement, as a fitting honor.

They supposed that, according to the custom of the dead, after the rest of the body had been consumed and reduced to dust, they would find only dry bones [Note: [Col. 0783D] Which, as is customary.]. When they reported to their bishop Eadberht, around the middle of Lent, that this plan pleased them, he agreed with their proposal and ordered them to remember to do it on the day of his deposition, which is the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.

They did so. When they opened the grave, they found the entire body intact, as though he were still alive [Note: [Col. 0783D] Whole. In 1284, William, bishop of Dunblane, granted forty days’ indulgence to those visiting the incorrupt body of Saint Cuthbert. See the document taken from the original charter preserved at Durham in Appendix no. XXVI. ID.], and the joints of his limbs flexible, so that he seemed much more like someone sleeping than someone dead [Col. 0784B].

All the garments in which he had been clothed also appeared not merely undefiled, but astonishing in their former freshness and brightness.

When the brothers saw this [Note: [Col. 0784D] When they saw it, with great …], they were immediately struck with such great fear and trembling that they could scarcely speak, scarcely dared to look at the miracle displayed before them, and scarcely knew themselves what they should do.

They removed the outermost part of his clothing in order to display the sign of his incorruption—for they were altogether afraid to touch the garments that had lain closest to his flesh—and hastened to report to the bishop what they had found. [Note: **When he.**] At that time he happened to be living as a solitary in a place farther removed from the monastery, surrounded on every side by the ebbing waves of the sea. For he always customarily spent the season of Lent there, and there he was accustomed to pass the forty days before the Lord’s Nativity in great devotion to abstinence, prayer, and tears. In that same place his venerable predecessor Cuthbert, before departing for Farne, had for some time served the Lord in solitude, as we have also explained above.

They also brought part of the clothing that had enveloped the holy body. When he received these gifts gratefully and gladly listened to the account of the miracle—for he kissed the garments themselves with wondrous affection, as though they were still wrapped around the Father’s body—he said:

“Put new garments upon the body in place of those which you have removed [Note: **Clothe it.**] and so return it to the chest which you have prepared. I know with complete certainty that the place consecrated by so great a power of heavenly miracle will not remain empty for long. Truly blessed is the man to whom the Lord, author and giver of true blessedness, deigns to grant a resting place there.”

And, adding to the marvel, he recited what he had once composed in verse, saying:

> Who could unfold in words the heavenly gifts of the Lord,  
> Or the riches of paradise that the ear receives?
>
> While the merciful One, when the burden of hostile death has been broken,  
> Grants him to live forever in the starry citadel;
>
> He who now adorns these dead limbs with such great honor,  
> And offers beautiful pledges of everlasting aid.
>
> How blessed you are, O house, and how you shine beneath so great a guest,  
> You who, ignorant of stain, sparkle joyfully in the light!
>
> Nor is it difficult for you, Almighty One, to command beneath the earth  
> That consuming corruption not devour the buried dead;
>
> You who preserve the prophet within the whale’s belly for three days,  
> Opening a path of light from the mouth of death;
>
> You who guard innocent limbs amid the fires,  
> So that the Chaldean flame may not harm the beauty of the Hebrew;
>
> You who renew four times ten, through the frosts, the covering of the people  
> Who, fleeing the changing world, preserve an uncharted land;
>
> You who reshape the light ashes into restored limbs,  
> When the world trembles beneath the angelic trumpets from heaven.

[Note: **Laid down.**]

[Note: **While the merciful One.**]

[Note: **So that it may not harm the Hebrew.**]

[Note: **May not harm.** Correctly so; for *noceo* is not rarely joined with the accusative by good authors. Others emend *noceat* to *laedat*. MABILL.]

[Note: ***Insonita* (“innocent”).**]

[Note: **Clothe it.** At the discovery of the sacred body in the year 1104, besides “a pallium, a dalmatic of purple, and linen cloths,” they found “an ivory comb, scissors, a silver altar, corporals with a paten, and also a chalice, small indeed but precious in material and workmanship; its lower part, bearing the figure of a lion made of the purest gold, carried on its back an onyx stone hollowed with the finest artistry,” as is related in the book *On the Translation*. The Anonymous author adds: “For when they unrolled the sudarium with which his head was bound, preserving the beauty of its former whiteness, and the new shoes with which he was shod, they kept them in our basilica among the relics as testimonies down to the present day.” Below, near the end of Book IV, he also testifies that Cuthbert’s footwear, or shoes, was used for the healing of a paralytic. MABILL.]

When the bishop had completed these and many similar verses with many tears and deep contrition, speaking in a trembling voice, the brothers did as he had ordered. They wrapped the body in a new garment, placed it in a light chest, and set it above the pavement of the sanctuary.

## CHAPTER XLIII. How they placed the body of Bishop Eadberht in the tomb of the man of God and set his sarcophagus above it

Meanwhile the bishop beloved by God, Eadberht [Note: **Eadberht.** See also IV.30 concerning his death. SMITH.], was seized by a grievous illness. As the fever of his sickness increased daily and grew steadily more severe, not long afterward—namely, on the day before the Nones of May [Note: **The day before the Nones of May.** On that very day the Benedictine Martyrology commemorates Saint Eadelberht, whose death occurred eleven years after the death of Saint Cuthbert, namely in the year of Christ 698, when Saint Cuthbert’s translation took place. Read Bede’s *History*, Book IV, chapter 30. MABILL.]—he too departed to the Lord. He had obtained from Him the gift he had earnestly requested: that he should not pass suddenly from the body, but should depart after being refined by a long illness.

They placed his body in the tomb of the blessed Father Cuthbert and set above it the chest in which they had laid the incorrupt limbs of that same Father. To this day, whenever the faith of those who ask requires it, signs of miracles do not cease to occur there. Nor are the garments that had clothed his most holy body, whether living or buried, without the power of healing.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How a sick man was healed by praying at his tomb

A cleric from overseas, belonging to the most reverend and holy Wilbrord Clement [Note: **Wilbrord.** See V.10–11 concerning Wilbrord. SMITH.], bishop of the Frisian people, came there. While he was staying as a guest for several days, he fell into a very serious illness, so that, as the affliction continued for a long time, he lay in despair. When, overcome by pain, he seemed unable either to die or to live, he found a salutary resolve and said to his servant:

“I beg you to take me today, after Mass has been celebrated [Col. 0786A]—for it was a Sunday—to worship at the body of the most sacred man of God. I hope that, through the grace of his intercession, I shall be delivered from these torments, so that I may either return healed to this present life or, if I die, reach eternal life.”

The servant did as he had asked. With considerable effort he led the sick man, leaning on a staff, into the church. When the man bent his knees at the tomb of the most holy and God-beloved Father, lowered his head to the ground, and prayed for his recovery, he immediately perceived that his body had received such strength from the incorrupt body of the saint that he rose from prayer without assistance and returned to the guesthouse without support from either the servant who led him or the staff that sustained him. A few days later, when his strength had been fully restored, he completed the journey he had planned.

## CHAPTER XLV. How a paralytic was healed through his footwear

In a certain monastery not far from there lived a young man afflicted with the disease that the Greeks call *paralysis*, deprived of the use of all his limbs. His abbot, knowing that the monastery of Lindisfarne possessed highly skilled physicians [Note: **At Lindisfarne.**], sent him there, asking them to provide whatever treatment they could for the sick man.

Although they carefully attended him at the command of their abbot and bishop and devoted to him whatever medical skill they possessed, they could accomplish nothing at all. Rather, the disease increased daily and gradually worsened, so that, except for his mouth, he could scarcely move any limb from its place.

When he lay abandoned and given up for lost by the fleshly physicians, who had labored in vain for a long time, he fled to the help of the heavenly Physician [Note: **To the help of the divine heavenly Physician.**], who, when truly invoked, is merciful toward all our iniquities and heals all our diseases. He asked his servant to bring him some portion [Note: **A small portion.**] of the relics of the incorrupt sacred body, because he believed that through its power, with the Lord’s generosity, he would return to the grace of health.

With the abbot’s permission, the servant brought the shoes that the man of God had worn on his feet in the tomb and wrapped them around the sick man’s powerless feet—for the paralysis had first seized him in the feet. He did this at the beginning of the night, when it was time for rest. Immediately the sick man, released into peaceful sleep, began, as the deep silence of the night advanced, to twitch his feet alternately. Thus the servants who were awake and watching plainly perceived that, by the healing power granted through the relics of the holy man, the desired health would pass from the soles of his feet through the rest of his limbs.

When the customary signal for the monastery’s nocturnal prayer sounded, he awoke at the noise and sat up. Without delay, his nerves strengthened by an inward power, all the joints of his limbs restored, and the pain driven away, he realized that he had been healed. He rose and spent the entire period of the night office and morning psalmody standing, in thanksgiving to the Lord.

When morning had come, he went to the church. In the sight of everyone, who rejoiced with him, he went around the holy places in prayer and offered a sacrifice of praise to his Savior. [Note: **He went around.**]

And it came to pass, through this most splendid reversal of circumstances, that the man who had been carried there in a vehicle, his whole body helpless, returned home by himself, all his limbs firm and strong, completely healed. Hence it is pleasing to remember that this is the changing of the right hand of the Most High, whose wondrous deeds, worthy of remembrance, have never ceased to shine upon the world from the beginning.

## CHAPTER XLVI. How the hermit Felgeldus [Note: *Felgidus*, *Felgildus*.] was cleansed of a swelling on his face by the covering of his wall

I think that we must not pass over a heavenly miracle that divine mercy displayed even then through the relics of the most holy oratory in which the venerable Father had been accustomed to serve the Lord as a solitary. Whether this should be attributed to the merits of that blessed Father Cuthbert or to those of his successor [Note: **Aedilwaldus.** The venerable Bede discusses Saint Edilwald, or Ethelwald, in Book V, chapter 1. He says that after Cuthbert he remained on the island of Farne for twelve years, died there—namely, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, the day on which he is commemorated in the Benedictine calendars—and was buried in the church of Saint Peter at Lindisfarne. MABILL.] Aedilwald, a man equally devoted to God, is known by the inner Judge. Nor does reason forbid us to believe that it happened through the merits of both, together with the faith of the most reverend Father Felgeldus, through whom and in whom the miracle of healing that I am relating was accomplished.

He was the third heir of that place and of its spiritual way of life. Now more than seventy years old, he awaits the end of his present life with a great longing for the life to come. After the man of God, Cuthbert, had been translated to the heavenly kingdom, Aedilwald began to dwell on that island and in that monastery. He too had previously been tested for many years in the monastic way of life and was rightly ascending the height of the eremitical calling [Note: **Had ascended.**].

He discovered that the walls of the aforementioned oratory [Note: **Oratory.** On the island of Farne there was a succession of monks who lived a solitary life. Besides those whom Bede mentions here, the *Life of Saint Bartholomew*, preserved in a manuscript in the Bodleian Library marked Fairfax 6, relates that Bartholomew, having obtained permission from Father Laurence, prior of Durham, came to Farne and found there a brother named Elwinus, who was displeased by his arrival. It also says that Thomas, prior of Durham, withdrew to Farne. By a charter still preserved in the church of Durham, Alexander II, king of the Scots, in the thirty-first year of his reign, namely in the year of Christ 1245, granted and confirmed to “Henry the monk and the monks who would succeed him in Farneland” eight sterling shillings to be received annually as a free alms from the rent of his mill at Berwick, in place of half a *celdra* of grain which he had been accustomed to receive from that mill by a charter of King William. SMITH.]—constructed of boards fitted together with insufficient care—had been loosened by long decay, and, with the boards separated from one another, would easily have given the winds entrance.

But the venerable man, who sought the beauty of a heavenly rather than an earthly building, took hay or clay, or whatever material of that kind he found, and stuffed the cracks, so that the daily violence of rain and wind would not hinder him from persevering in prayer.

When Aedilwald entered and saw this, he asked the brothers who frequented the place for a calfskin. He nailed it in the corner where both he and his predecessor Cuthbert had often stood or knelt in prayer, and set it against the violence of the storms.

After he too, having completed twelve uninterrupted years there, entered the joy of heavenly blessedness, it pleased the most reverend bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne, Eadfrith, to restore that oratory, loosened by age, from its foundations.

When the work had been completed, many people, with devout religious zeal, asked the blessed athlete of Christ, Felgeldus, to give them some particle of the relics of the holy and God-beloved Father Cuthbert or of his successor Aedilwald. It seemed good to him that the aforesaid calfskin should be divided into pieces and given to those who asked.

Before giving it to others, however, he first tested in himself what power it possessed. His face was covered with a disfiguring redness and swelling. Signs of the illness that was to come had previously appeared on his face while he was still living the common life among the brothers. But when, withdrawn into solitude, he devoted less care to his body and practiced greater abstinence, and, as though confined in a long imprisonment, more rarely enjoyed either the warmth of the sun or the breath of the air, the illness grew worse and filled his entire face with a swollen heat.

Fearing, therefore, that because of the severity of this illness he might have to abandon the solitary life and return to the common way of living, he acted with faithful confidence. He hoped to be healed by the help of those whose dwelling he rejoiced to occupy and whose life he rejoiced to imitate.

He placed a piece of the aforementioned calfskin in water and washed his face with that water. Immediately the entire swelling that had afflicted it, together with the foul scab, disappeared. A certain devout priest of this monastery at Girwy, who first told me this, said that he had known Felgeldus’s face when it was swollen and disfigured and had afterward touched it with his hand through a window when it had been cleansed.

Felgeldus himself later related the matter, affirming that it had happened just as the priest had said, and that from that time onward, although he remained enclosed for many years, his face always remained, as before, free from such an affliction. This was accomplished by the grace of almighty God, who is accustomed to heal in the present many, and in the future all, the illnesses of our hearts and bodies; who satisfies our desire with good things and crowns us forever with his mercy and compassion. Amen.

# THE LIFE OF BLESSED FELIX THE CONFESSOR (C)

The most glorious triumph of blessed Felix, which by the Lord’s help he merited in the city of Nola in Campania, was described most beautifully and fully in hexameter verse by Paulinus, bishop of that same city. Since these verses are more suitable for readers versed in meter than for ordinary readers, we have decided, for the benefit of many, to elucidate the same history of the holy confessor in plainer speech and to imitate the industry of the man who translated the martyrdom of blessed Cassian from the metrical work of Prudentius [Note: **Of Prudentius.** See his *On Crowns* (Περὶ Στεφάνων), hymn 9.]

Felix was born at Nola in Campania, but his father was a Syrian named Hermias [Note: **His father.** As Saint Paulinus writes in *Natales* 5, he had served in the army under Caesar and had completed his military service.]. Hermias came from the East to Nola and, living there as though a native, fathered Felix. When he died, he left him an inheritance of substantial wealth, but Felix placed above it the gifts of the inheritance promised in heaven.

He also had a brother bearing their father’s name, Hermias, with whom he divided his earthly patrimony. This brother’s character was far removed from Felix’s, and therefore he became unworthy of everlasting happiness. For he strove to love earthly goods alone and chose to be a soldier of Caesar rather than of Christ.

Felix, on the other hand, fulfilling by his deeds the mystery contained in his name, subjected himself from childhood to divine service. As the grace of his virtues increased, he first assumed the office of reader in the Church and afterward advanced to the rank of exorcist, beginning to drive unclean spirits from possessed bodies.

When he had also become renowned for his virtues in this ministry, he soon undertook the priestly rank appropriate to his merits. Nor did he remain inferior to his rank in mind and conduct, as the storm of persecution that followed also proved.

At that same time a persecution of the unbelieving arose and assailed the Church with a grievous struggle. Yet the gates of death could not turn the daughters of Zion away from proclaiming praise to their Creator.

When the leaders and teachers of unbelief first directed the assault of their madness against the teachers of truth and the Lord’s faith, and conspired either to put the foremost bishops and priests of the churches to death, as a terror to lesser men, or to compel them to deny the faith, it happened that the agents of error and hostile fury, arriving also at Nola, sought the city’s bishop, Maximus [Note: **Maximus.** Several days are assigned to his memory in the calendars of different churches. According to Ghinius of Siena and Galesinius, he is commemorated on 15 January; but the Church of Nola celebrates his feast on 7 February. The Church of Benevento, prevented on 7 February from celebrating the feast of Saint Hermolaus the martyr with a double office, celebrates Saint Maximus on the following day, 8 February, with a semidouble office, as Marius de Vipera reports in his *Catalogue of the Saints of the Church of Benevento*.], a man venerable for his learning, piety, and age, in order to subject him to torture.

When Maximus noticed this, remembering the Lord’s command, which says, “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another,” he sought for a time the refuge of a more remote place. He left Felix the priest to protect the city, embracing him as a son and desiring to receive him as heir to his see.

When the persecutors could not find the bishop, they lost no time in attempting to lay hands on Felix. They strove first to cast down, as the greatest stronghold of the city after the bishop, a man famous for the steadfastness of his virtue—either by flattering him with promises or by terrifying him with punishments.

Thus Felix was seized by his raging adversaries. Yet he relied greatly upon the inward consolation of the Holy Spirit. He was sent into a dark prison, where iron chains bound his hands and neck and his feet were confined in the stocks. Fragments of pottery were also scattered beneath him, so that, bound amid the horror and cold of the long night, he could not obtain either sleep or rest, continually pierced by their sharp edges.

Meanwhile the bishop, who had withdrawn while fleeing from the enemy to the hiding places of the mountains, endured a martyrdom no less painful than if he had been bound in iron, laid upon shards, or given over to be burned in flames.

The greatest anxiety for his flock burned in his mind, while hunger, together with the harshness of the cold winter, burned his body. Lying among thorn bushes without shelter or food, he continued the night together with the day in wakeful, anxious prayers. Nor was it difficult for such a force of evils, pressing upon limbs weakened by old age and long fasts, to drive him even to death.

But so that heavenly mercy might show most clearly how worthy that man was of God’s care, an angel was sent from heaven. The angel ordered blessed Felix the confessor, freed from his bonds, to come quickly to seek out, revive, and bring back home the bishop.

Several others were confined in the same prison. But when the angel arrived, he appeared only to Felix, who had been bound for the sake of piety. He shone with flashing light and filled the whole prison with the grace of that light. Moved at once by the angel’s voice and radiance, Felix trembled.

At first he thought that he was being deceived by a dream. But the angel ordered him to rise and follow him as he left. Astonished at the command of the one who spoke, Felix protested that he could not get out, because he was held by his chains, the prison’s confinement, and the vigilance of the guards.

Then the angel repeated in a loud voice that he should rise quickly, since the chains could offer no resistance. At once, faster than words can tell, the chains fell from his hands and neck, and the shackles dropped from his feet.

The angel led him outside by a wondrous ordering of events: the prison door was open for Felix but closed to the others. Thus they passed by the very guards who kept watch, unaware of what was happening. The angel, like the pillar of Moses, provided Felix with both guidance and light through the radiance of his presence until he had escaped the hands of the enemy.

When blessed Felix the confessor reached the deserted place where the bishop had withdrawn, he found him drawing faint sighs with a thin breath. He rejoiced that he had found him alive, but he was deeply saddened to see that the man he had found was near death.

He therefore embraced and kissed the Father and began to try whether, by the frequent breathing of his own mouth and the warmth of his body, he could bring some heat to the bishop’s frozen limbs.

After laboring for a long time, he could awaken no sign of vital awareness in either the bishop’s mind or body, whether by calling out or by touching him. Nor did he have fire or food nearby with which to revive him as he stiffened and wasted away.

At last, finding a salutary course, he bent his knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and humbly begged that He would help him from heaven, so that he might fulfill toward his father the ministry of compassion he had been commanded to perform.

Without delay, his prayer was heard. He saw a cluster of grapes hanging on a nearby thorn bush and recognized it as the gift of Him who is the creator and author of all natures—who brought water from dry rock and, when He willed, changed water itself into wine.

Greatly rejoicing in this gift of divine mercy, he took the cluster and brought it to the dying bishop’s mouth. But because the bishop’s teeth were clenched like those of a corpse, since he was deprived of all perception of heart and soul, he did not know how to receive the taste offered to him.

At last the holy priest Felix, struggling compassionately with his hands, opened his dry lips. He then crushed the grapes into the bishop’s mouth and poured in as much health-giving juice as he could. When the bishop had tasted it, he immediately recovered the awareness of his soul and body. His eyes opened, and his tongue, which had clung to his dry throat, was released for speech.

When he had fully revived and recognized that Felix had come to seek him, he embraced him with paternal affection and complained that he had come so late.

“Where have you been delayed so long, my son?” he said. “For the Lord promised me long ago that you would come to me. You see that although I yielded for a time, overcome by the weakness of the body, I nevertheless preserved the steadfastness of a faithful spirit, as the condition of this place to which I withdrew also shows.

“I could certainly have entered some village or another city where I would have been safe from my enemies, if faith had been cheap to me and this life dear. But now, avoiding every human refuge and fleeing to the deserts of the mountains, I entrusted myself solely to the protection of divine grace, so that He Himself might preserve me in this life or transfer me to the next, by whatever method or order He wished.

“Nor did the hope I had in God deceive me, as your arrival clearly proves. Through you I have been recalled, so to speak, from the very threshold of death to life. Therefore, my son, hasten to complete the work of compassion you have begun, and strive to carry me home upon your shoulders.”

After these words, Felix completed as quickly as possible what he had been ordered to do. He carried the bishop home on his shoulders to a house guarded by a single old woman. The venerable bishop had become so detached from the things of the world that, out of all the household and all its wealth, only one old woman remained to him.

Felix knocked at the door and awakened her. When she rose and opened it, he gave the bishop into her care and entrusted him to her. The bishop then offered blessed Felix the thanks due for the service of compassion he had rendered. Placing his right hand upon Felix’s head, he bestowed upon him a father’s blessing.

Felix left that place and hid for a few days in his own house until the storm of persecution had passed. When this had happened, he left his hiding place and presented himself to his fellow citizens, who rejoiced at his arrival and made him welcome.

Going about everywhere, he comforted and strengthened in words of exhortation the hearts of those who had been greatly disturbed by the bitterness of the preceding storm. He taught them not only by word but also by his own example to despise both the prosperity and adversity of the world, to seek only the joys of the eternal homeland, and to fear only the anger of the heavenly Judge.

[Note: **Again.** James of Voragine writes that Felix was promoted to the episcopate before this new persecution; most say that he was sought for it. But the authority of Paulinus is more reliable.]

When persecution broke out again, Felix was sought once more. The enemies came even to his dwelling, eager to seize him quickly and put him to death. At that time he happened to be away from his house, standing with friends in the middle of the city and, as was his custom, preaching the word of faith to the surrounding crowds.

When his adversaries heard that he was there, they immediately ran up with drawn swords. But when they reached him, divine providence changed either his appearance or their minds, and they were utterly unable to recognize the man they knew perfectly well.

When they asked Felix where he was, the most prudent man understood that God had acted so that they would not recognize him. Laughing, he said to those who were asking:

“I do not know the Felix you seek.”

He did not deceive them entirely, for no one knows himself by his own face.

They immediately left him and turned elsewhere, asking those whom they happened to meet where Felix was. One of them, entirely unaware of the situation and thinking that they had gone mad, began to rebuke them for their stupidity: they could not recognize the very man with whom they were speaking. At the same time he pointed out to them the direction in which the man they sought had gone.

They pursued the tracks of blessed Felix with even greater fury. As they approached, Felix was alerted by the uproar of the city ahead of him and by the shouts of the populace, stunned by the arrival of the enemies. He withdrew into a more secluded place that had no stronger fortification: it was enclosed only by the fragment of a half-ruined wall.

But as soon as it received the man of God, the hand of God protected him there by a wondrous act. For suddenly a mound of fallen rubble gathered together and blocked the place. At the same time, by divine command—for all creation serves God—a spider immediately stretched its wavering web across that very spot.

When the enemies arrived there, they were astonished. They spoke to one another in hushed voices, saying:

“Would it not be foolish for us to enter here searching for the man, when it is perfectly clear that no one has gone in? If anyone had entered, these spider threads could not possibly have remained intact. Even tiny flies sometimes tear them as they pass through. It is therefore certain that the man who said Felix had withdrawn here did so deceitfully, in order to draw us farther away from finding him. Let us leave and abandon the search of this man’s hiding place here, since the very appearance of the place shows that no one has entered.”

Thus their anxious search was deceived. They hurried away, raging no less against the man who had led them by his tricks into such places than against Felix himself. Here the great wisdom of our merciful Creator and Protector shone forth.

Certainly, the highest and strongest walls of cities sometimes betray their citizens to enemies who besiege them, rather than freeing them. But Christ hid His humble servant from armed persecutors beneath the trembling fabric of a spider’s web, so that he could neither be found nor captured, truly as the venerable Father Paulinus says of such things:

> Wherever  
> Christ is with us, a spider’s web becomes a wall;
>
> But for the one from whom Christ is absent, a wall becomes a spider’s web.

The enemies departed as evening was already approaching. When they had gone, Felix sought a more secluded hiding place, rejoicing in the help of divine protection and singing to himself:

> Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for you are with me.

When day came, he withdrew to a more secluded place among the roofs of the buildings. There he remained hidden for six continuous months, separated from the knowledge of all human beings but enjoying the grace of the divine presence, according to the Psalmist’s words: “In the hiding place of his face, away from the disturbance of men.”

During that entire period God fed him by a wondrous method unknown to human beings. In nearby houses lived a woman devoted to God, and the Lord, who is the fountain and source of all knowledge, used her service knowingly although she herself was unaware.

The woman baked loaves and prepared other foods for her household. Then, falling into an ecstasy of mind, she carried them to the place where Felix the confessor was hiding and set them there for him to eat. She never knew that she had entered or returned from that place. Believing that she had placed the prepared food somewhere in her own house, she would always leave, remembering that she had to set the food down but immediately forgetting that she had done so.

Thus, as I have said, they relate that blessed Felix remained for six months in the same dark and narrow hiding place, separated from human society but never deprived of the presence of the heavenly citizens. He lived a blessed life on sparse food, though food supplied from heaven.

During this period he is also said to have been repeatedly deemed worthy of the gift of divine conversation. In the same buildings where he lived there was an old cistern, from which he initially drew his scant drink. But when it dried up from the excessive heat of summer, the blessed confessor was not left without the means of sustaining life.

For the merciful Creator and provider of our salvation, who once drenched a single fleece with heavenly rain while the surrounding air remained dry, supplied His confessor, in an utterly silent and cloudless sky, with the gift of hidden dew as often as he needed it, by which the thirsty man might be refreshed.

When this period had been completed, Felix was warned by a divine oracle to come out of hiding, because the storm of persecution had now passed.

When he suddenly appeared in public, everyone received him with the greatest joy, as though he had come from paradise. He immediately began to strengthen the faith of all, which the violence of the storm had shaken severely.

Meanwhile the bishop beloved by God, Maximus, advanced in age, died. Without delay, by the judgment of all, Felix was chosen as bishop. He was an unconquerable confessor, a most gentle teacher, and had himself fulfilled in deed everything good that he taught with his mouth.

But Felix, wishing to show how great was the height of humility within his heart, excused himself in a modest voice from accepting this rank. He said that his fellow priest Quintus could undertake the honor of that office much more worthily, since he had been promoted to the priestly order seven days before Felix himself.

This was carried out as he requested. Quintus assumed the episcopal office and administered it in such a way that, humbly subject to the most blessed confessor, he ordered Felix to preach to the people on his behalf, while Quintus governed the people in office and Felix governed them by teaching.

Felix was outstanding in steadfast confession and virtue, but he was also a supreme lover of voluntary poverty. From his paternal inheritance he had possessed many estates, houses, and great wealth. But during the persecution, having been proscribed, he lost everything.

When peace was restored to the churches, he could have reclaimed his rights, but he had no desire to do so. His friends urged him to recover what was legally his and then distribute it to the poor, together with the great interest of heavenly reward. But he would not consent at all. With firm resolve he rejected their suggestions, saying:

“Everything is lawful for me, but not everything is beneficial. Far be it from me to reclaim the possessions I lost for the sake of my confession. Far be it from me to seek again, by any means, earthly riches which I once despised in contemplation of heavenly goods, as though these alone were insufficient.

“Rather, poor in spirit, I will follow Jesus, so that I may receive the gifts of the kingdom of heaven more abundantly. Nor should I doubt that He who rescued me from the chains and darkness of a dreadful prison, and who fed me in hiding from human beings for so long, will Himself nourish me for the remainder of my life, since I cast my care upon Him.”

Holding to this disposition, the blessed confessor possessed only three *iugera* of modest land, and even these he rented, together with a single garden of his own, from which he lived. He cultivated both with his own hands, without the help of even one servant. He always rejoiced to share with the poor the produce of his harvest and the growth of his garden.

The most blessed man also practiced the same frugality in his clothing. He was content with a single garment, which sometimes scarcely sufficed for him. Whatever remained over, he gave to the poor. If it happened that he obtained a second garment from elsewhere, he immediately warmed the naked man with the better one.

[Col. 0795C] Living in such devotion, the man Felix, blessed both in name and in merit, full of days and good works, died [Note: [Col. 0795D] Deceased. Paulinus does not state the age of Saint Felix. Christophorus Phreislebius absurdly writes that he lived around the time of Theodosius. Henricus Fabricius thinks that he died around the year 300, but what peace then existed for the Church? Haraeus places him around 310, and Michael the monk not long after the year 312, when peace was granted to the Church. This is also the probable opinion of others.]. Following the way of his fathers, he was received into eternal glory, as the many signs that have occurred in the church in which he was buried also testify [Note: [Col. 0795D] Buried. Many Martyrologies, and also the Roman Breviary, state that he was buried near Nola, in a place called Pincis or Pineis. Yet quite a few Martyrologies, under the name of Usuard, and others, remember that Saint Felix the Roman presbyter and martyr, who was buried on the Via Portuensis [Col. 0796D], was buried in this place. Certainly there is a district of the city of Rome, now the fourteenth, which took its name from Pinea; Octavius Pancirolus thinks that the name arose from some pine tree. Perhaps the body of the holy martyr was transferred to that district from the Via Portuensis, not far away, and a basilica was erected for him there—one that either no longer exists or has changed its name. Nevertheless, the people of Nola maintain that their Felix the confessor was buried at Pincis, and that at Nola, in the district called Coemeterium, there was an old episcopal residence and a place at Pincis. There is also a well there which is visited with great devotion, because it is said once to have been full of the blood of martyrs. In so obscure a matter it is difficult to determine the truth.].

For there was there a certain rustic, poor in possessions but upright in faith, who supported his narrow poverty by owning only two oxen—either using them himself or lending them to his neighbors for an agreed payment. Though very needy, he loved and tended them with great care; one night, however, they were stolen and he lost them. When morning came and he discovered with complete certainty that they had been stolen, having abandoned all hope of searching for or finding them, he hurried swiftly to the church of Saint Felix. [Col. 0795D] Arriving there, he prostrated himself before the doors of the holy house, fixed his face upon the ground, and implored and entreated Saint Felix to return the oxen he had lost. With many tears he declared that he would never leave the place [Col. 0796A] unless he recovered the oxen.

After he had done this throughout the entire day, with a rustic voice indeed but with utterly faithful devotion, evening came; he was forcibly expelled by the crowd and driven away from the sacred buildings. He returned home, but did not cease to spend the night awake in continual lamentation. Yet because everyone who asks receives, whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened, and because, as the Psalmist says, “the Lord has heard the desire of the poor,” at midnight, while all other people and things were at rest, he alone lay awake, roused by his grief and poverty. Suddenly, astonishing to relate, the oxen he was seeking came to his door: by divine prompting they had been rescued from the robbers and led back to their master’s house through trackless places amid the darkness and confusion of night. Knocking with their horns upon the doors [Col. 0796B] of the little hut in which he lived, they signaled that they had arrived.

But he, trembling greatly, now believing that the thieves, rather than his oxen, had come again, delayed opening the doors for some time. At last the same oxen, as though understanding the reason for their master’s delay, also lowed, thereby showing that they were the ones knocking at the household doors. Once the oxen had been recovered, the rustic acted not rustically but wisely and faithfully: early in the morning he hastened to render due thanks to his benefactor. Taking the oxen with him, he came to the church of Saint Felix, proceeding on foot with them and, upon arriving there, repeating and displaying with joyful voice the benefits he had received from the holy confessor.

Because he had wept so profusely, both while seeking his oxen and while receiving them in his joy, he had also suffered considerable damage to his eyesight; seeking consolation for this loss from blessed Felix, he received it. Thus he returned home filled with a double gift of heavenly grace.

When a smaller church was being built in honor of the same blessed confessor, two rustic buildings stood close beside it, inconveniently situated and ugly to behold; by their darkness they marred no small part of the church’s beauty. The venerable and God-beloved bishop Paulinus wished these buildings to be removed and the places on which they stood to be cleared. He therefore asked their owners to show this reverence to blessed Felix: that, for the sake of making his church’s site brighter and more beautiful, they should allow their private dwellings to be demolished. [Col. 0796D]

But they, despising his pleas with rustic obstinacy, said that they would sooner give up their lives than abandon their possessions. When the bishop grew weary of overcoming the rustics in argument [Col. 0797A], they were overcome by the hand of divine power. For one night, while everyone was asleep, a sudden fire broke out in one of these small buildings and gradually began to spread toward the neighboring structures. It grew larger and larger, so that it seemed likely to consume all the dwellings, both near and far.

Then, awakened by such great crashes and balls of flame, the citizens rushed together, intending either to extinguish the whole fire, if they could, by pouring water upon it, or each to rescue and carry away whatever he could from his own house. When they saw that they were powerless, they began to seek divine assistance where human help failed. Led by the bishop, they hastened to the church of Saint Felix, bent their knees, and implored the aid of heavenly protection. From there they turned to the church of the blessed [Col. 0797B] apostles, which adjoined the church of blessed Felix, and there they pleaded, through apostolic intercession, for the gifts of heavenly protection.

After prayer had been offered, the bishop returned home. Taking a small splinter from the wood of the Lord’s cross, he cast it into the midst of the raging fire. Immediately, the immense masses of flame that so many men had been unable to extinguish by throwing water upon them were put out when he added that piece of wood. Such was the power of the holy cross that nature itself yielded: the fire, which ordinarily devours every kind of wood, was consumed, as though burned up, by the wood of the Lord’s Passion. [Col. 0798A]

When so great a storm had been calmed and, with morning’s return, the citizens came to inspect the dreadful work of the night, they expected that the great fire had caused them considerable damage. Yet it was found that absolutely nothing had been burned except what ought to have burned. Of the two houses mentioned above, which the people had intended to destroy and remove, they saw that only one had been consumed by the flames.

At this the rustic was deeply ashamed—the man who, in foolish obstinacy, had defended his dwellings against the beauty of the sacred buildings. He saw that, against his will and without compensation, he had lost what he had refused to give up voluntarily for the sake of the saints. Immediately he himself began, with his own hands, to destroy what had survived the fire, so that the entire area around the church of the blessed confessor might as quickly as possible be made distinguished by a brightness and radiance suitable to the saints. Once all the ugliness of the ruins and filth of those buildings had been removed, the blessed bishop [Note: [Col. 0797C] Paulinus. Each year he celebrated the feast of Saint Felix with a festal poem. Ten of these poems survive complete. Dungalus, an ancient writer who lived before the year 800, while defending the veneration of the holy cross, relics, and images against the views of Claudius, bishop of Turin, lists fifteen feasts sung by Paulinus and produces fragments from those that have remained unknown until now. Paulinus is commemorated on the tenth day before the Kalends of July.] Paulinus continued bringing to completion the church he had begun. He finished the entire building in three years and completed its paintings and all its ornamentation with the proper conclusion. In it the most blessed life and passion of Felix, forever worthy of remembrance, are celebrated; on the fourteenth day of January, having completed the course of his glorious contest, he received the crown of life that God promised to those who love him.

## Historical Works of Bede the Venerable, Presbyter

### Second Section: Martyrologies, according to the Cologne and Bollandist Exemplars

[Col. 0797]

[Col. 0797]

## The Editor of the Patrologia to the Reader

No work of Bede the Venerable has so often appeared from the press as the Martyrology bearing his name, for it has been published no fewer than five times. It was first published in the edition of all Bede’s works completed at Cologne in the year of our Lord 1616; the second time, among the Bollandist Monuments, from which it passed into the London edition prepared by the most learned Smith in 1722.

Since those two editions, which are preferred to the others, complete one another, and since the later edition is enriched by Smith’s scholarly and extensive notes, we have decided to join both editions together in our pages, so that they may be viewed at a glance. We shall then append to them, as a supplement, three different epitomes of the same Martyrology.

In the following presentation of the Bollandist edition, we have distinguished by compressed line spacing those ADDITIONS which, as Smith himself says, are printed in the middle—that is, the smaller—type, except for the passages of the Supplement that bear the name of Florus himself and therefore require no distinction.

[Col. 0799]

## Smith’s Preface

The Martyrology that we have now presented was taken from volume II of the *Acts of the Saints* for March. For when Henschenius had formerly established that the Martyrology printed under Bede’s name was not genuinely his little work, on the ground that Ado and Usuard testify that he left very many days untouched, this sure indication prompted him, while examining the manuscripts of Queen Christina of Sweden at Rome, to discover a fragment of this Martyrology, formerly copied for the use of the Church of Bourges. To make the belief that what he had found belonged to Bede still more certain, the codex was sealed with the customary ancient formula: “Here ends the Martyrology of Bede the presbyter.”

Later he saw the work complete at Dijon, in the library of the most distinguished senator Bonherius. When he compared that codex with the royal fragment, he found that the two exemplars agreed throughout in precisely the same words, with scarcely any change even in the final letter, except that the complete manuscript contained certain additions written in very small letters, which were absent from the earlier, incomplete copy.

At first he suspected that these additions belonged to Florus. Later, however, he determined that Florus had no part in this supplement, since it was exceedingly brief and meager and therefore did not fit what Usuard reports in his prologue—namely, that Florus had followed Bede’s style in composing the eulogies.

Henschenius compared six other manuscripts with the Dijon codex: first, one from Saint Peter’s at the Vatican; second, one from the Monastery of Saint Cyriacus at the Baths; third, one from the library of the most eminent Cardinal Francesco Barberini; and finally three Belgian manuscripts. From all of them he collected additions and supplements. He distinguished this Supplement, which he published under the name of Florus, by middle-sized type.

Here I give, for the sake of brevity, the explanation of the letters he used in collecting the additions:

- A: Arras.
- B: Barberinian.
- C: Saint Cyriacus.
- D: Dijon.
- L: Liège.
- R: Queen of Sweden.
- T: Tournai.
- V: Vatican.

Finally, he wishes the reader to know for certain that in all these manuscripts everything printed in larger type under Bede’s name is found word for word, unless the margin notes the contrary in some cases; and that the Martyrology printed in Bede’s works is taken from Ado.

[Col. 0799]

## Martyrology

[Note: [Col. 0799] The Cologne edition and the Bollandist edition are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### Cologne Edition

The month of January has thirty-one days and thirty lunar days.

[Col. 0799A]

### A. Kalends of January

The Circumcision of Our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, and the eighth day of the Lord’s Nativity.

At Rome, the feast of Saint Almachius the martyr, who, when the prefect of the city, Alypius, ordered him to be killed because he said, “Today is the eighth day of the Lord’s Day; cease from the superstitions of idols and polluted sacrifices,” was seized for this reason and killed by gladiators.

Also at Rome, Saint Martina the virgin, who, under the emperor Alexander, was killed by the sword after many tortures.

On the same day, at the city of Spoleto in Tuscany, Saint Concordius the martyr, who was beheaded after very many tortures.

Also at Rome, on the Appian Way, the crown of thirty soldiers.

In Africa, the feast of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of the Church of Ruspe, whose life is regarded as full of virtues.

At Alexandria, Saint Euphrosyne the virgin.

On this day also, Saint Paragodus, the seventh bishop of Vienne.

Also Saint Basil the bishop and Saint Eugendus the abbot.

### B. Fourth Day before the Nones of January

The feast of blessed Macarius the abbot.

And at Thomis, a city in Pontus, the feast of three brothers—Argeus, Narcissus, and Marcellinus, a boy—who, having been seized under Licinius among the recruits and refusing to serve in the army, was beaten nearly to death, tormented for a long time in prison, and finally drowned in the sea, thus completing his martyrdom. His body was carried to the shore and buried by devout men, and it shines with great miracles.

And Saint Isidore the bishop and martyr.

### C. Third Day before the Nones of January

At Rome, the feast of Saint Antherus, pope and martyr, who was the twentieth after blessed Peter. After governing the Church for twelve years, one month, and twelve days, he suffered under Maximian and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

In the city of Paris, Saint Genevieve the virgin, who was dedicated to Christ by blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre. She became widely renowned for her wondrous virtues and grew old in Christ’s service until the age of eighty.

On the same day, Saint Florentius, bishop of Vienne and the eighth martyr of that city.

The feast of Saint Theogenes the martyr and Saint Peter the martyr.

At the city of Thomis, the feast of Saint Philo the bishop, who, after other tortures, was drowned in the sea.

### D. Day before the Nones of January

The feast of blessed Titus, a disciple of the apostles, who was ordained by the apostle Paul as bishop of the Cretans. The same apostle wrote him an epistle of the greatest usefulness to the whole Church. Finally, after faithfully completing the duty of preaching, he attained a blessed end and was buried in the church where blessed Paul the apostle had judged him worthy to be appointed a minister.

In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Aquilinus, Geminius, Eugenius, Marcianus, Quintus, Theodotus, and Tryphon, whose acts are extant.

On the same day at Rome, the holy martyrs Prisca the presbyter and Priscillianus the cleric, together with the blessed and most religious woman, during the reign of Julian, the most impious Augustus. They completed their martyrdom by the sword.

Also at Rome, blessed Daphrosa, wife of the blessed martyr Fabian. After her husband was condemned, she was first banished into exile; then the impious Julian ordered her to be put to death by beheading.

And Saint Ferrutius the martyr.

[Col. 0803B]

### E. Nones of January

At Rome, the feast of Saint Telesphorus, pope, who, ordained as the seventh pontiff after the apostle Peter, held office for eleven years, three months, and twenty-one days.

He established that a fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter, that Masses should be celebrated at night on the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, and that the angelic hymn—that is, “Glory to God in the highest”—should be sung at the hour of the Mass sacrifice. Finally, under the emperor Hadrian, he underwent a glorious martyrdom.

Also at Antioch, the deposition of blessed Symeon the monk, who in the thirteenth year of his age renounced this world and sought a monastery. There, allowing himself food only on the seventh day, he learned the Psalter within four months. Finally, he stood upon a column until the end of his life.

At Jerusalem, the deposition of Symeon the prophet, who carried the Lord Jesus in his arms.

[Col. 0804B]

### F. Eighth Day before the Ides of January

The Epiphany of the Lord.

On the same day, the passion of Saint Marca the virgin. When Riciovarus, being present, ordered her to be tortured and thrown into the fire, she remained unharmed. Then, after her breasts had been cut off and she had been afflicted by the squalor of prison, she was rolled over extremely sharp potsherds and burning coals; praying, she departed to the Lord.

### G. Seventh Day before the Ides of January

The return of the child Jesus from Egypt.

And the feast of Saint Lucian, presbyter and martyr of the Church of Antioch, a man of great learning and eloquence, who suffered at Nicomedia under the persecution of Maximinus and was buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia.

At Antioch, blessed Clerius the deacon and martyr, who was beheaded after very many tortures.

### A. Sixth Day before the Ides of January

At Naples in Campania, Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor, brother of the most blessed Victorinus, a man renowned for miracles. Following his brother’s example, he too, after performing many virtues, rested full of holiness. He was buried in the place where he had lived before being called to the episcopate.

At Beauvais, the holy martyrs Lucian and Messianus.

And in Greece, Saint Timothy.

### B. Fifth Day before the Ides of January

In Caesarean Mauretania, Saint Marciana the virgin and martyr.

On the same day at Antioch, Saint Julian the martyr and Basilissa his wife. These chaste spouses, bound by a most holy vow, lived together for several years, preserving their flesh as virginal for Christ. From their possessions they established monasteries, so that blessed Julian became the father of as many as ten thousand monks.

Basilissa, the mother of many virgins, after sending their victorious multitude ahead to the Lord, herself, proven most perfectly by the conduct of her life, departed to the Lord amid words of prayer.

Later Julian was ordered by the governor Marcianus to be beaten to death after innumerable tortures and sufferings, together with the presbyter Antonius, Marcionella, and Celsus, her son.

[Col. 0807B]

### C. Fourth Day before the Ides of January

In the Thebaid, the feast of blessed Paul, the first hermit, who from the sixteenth year of his age until his one hundred and thirteenth year remained alone in the desert. Antonius saw his soul carried by angels into heaven amid the choirs of apostles and prophets.

Saint Hyginus, pope, who sat at Rome for four years. He established the clergy and distributed its ranks. He was buried in the Vatican on the third day before the Ides of January.

In Cyprus, blessed Nicanor, who was one of the first seven deacons.

### D. Third Day before the Ides of January

At Alexandria, the feast of the holy confessors Peter, Severus, and Leucius, whose acts are extant.

In Africa, the feast of Saint Salvius. On his feast day, Saint Augustine preached a sermon to the people at Carthage.

The bringing of the Lord out of Egypt.

### E. Day before the Ides of January

In Achaea, the feast of Saint Satyrus the martyr, a citizen of Arabia. Passing by a certain idol and blowing upon it, he immediately caused it to collapse after signing his forehead with the cross; for this reason he was beheaded.

On the same day, Saint Arcadius the martyr, renowned in birth and miracles.

### F. Ides of January

At Rome, on the Lavican Way, the crown of forty soldiers under the emperor Gallienus.

At Poitiers, Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor, who was banished to Phrygia for four years on account of the Catholic faith. Among his other virtues, he is said to have raised a dead man.

At Vienne, Saint Verus the bishop, who presided over the Church after Saint Evantius.

At Trier, Saint Agritius the bishop.

And the octave of the Epiphany.

### G. Nineteenth Day before the Kalends of February

At Nola in Campania, blessed Felix the presbyter. He was elevated to the dignity of the priesthood by Maximianus, bishop of the city of Nola. Though he suffered many things from the faithless for the name of Christ, and although everyone in that city wished him to be raised to the episcopate, he did not consent. Instead, he chose another for the honor of the pontificate.

Twelve years later, when the persecution had ceased, after the mysteries had been celebrated on the Lord’s Day and peace had been granted to all, he threw himself upon the pavement to pray. Immediately the soul of the holy man departed from the prison of the flesh, and he who was truly Felix ascended into blessed realms.

He was buried near the city by the holy presbyter Helpidius, in a place called Pincis, where he shines with glorious miracles.

At Vienne, Saint Cadeoldus the bishop.

### A. Eighteenth Day before the Kalends of February

The prophets Habakkuk and Micah, whose bodies were discovered by divine revelation under the emperor Arcadius.

Also blessed Macarius the abbot, disciple of blessed Antonius, renowned for his life and miracles.

On the same day, blessed Isidore, illustrious in holiness of life, faith, and miracles.

At Bourges, the translation of Saint Sulpitius, bishop and confessor. Educated in the sacred writings from childhood and distinguished by the brightness of a holy way of life, he was also renowned for his virtues while still a layman. Later, after cutting his hair, he became the father of monks; then, promoted to the episcopal chair, he rested illustrious in life.

And Saint Maurus the abbot.

### B. Eighteenth Day before the Kalends of February

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, the feast of Saint Marcellus, pope. At the command of the emperor Maximian, he was first beaten with clubs and then expelled from the presence of the one whom he rebuked.

He established cemeteries on the Salarian Way and founded twenty-five titular churches in the city of Rome, for the baptism and penance of the many pagans who were converted, and for the burials of martyrs.

After many years, therefore, clothed in a hair shirt in the service of God, he died. He was embalmed by the presbyter John and the blessed Lucina and buried in the cemetery of Priscilla.

At Arles, Saint Honoratus the bishop, whose life shone forth illustrious in teaching and miracles.

And Saint Fursey the confessor.

[Col. 0813A]

### C. Sixteenth Day before the Kalends of February

In Egypt, in the Thebaid, blessed Antonius the monk. Although he had no knowledge of letters, he is said to have understood the divine Scriptures by hearing them repeatedly and to have retained them through wise reflection. He lived a most distinguished life as the father of many monks.

Under the emperor Justinian, his body was discovered by divine revelation, brought to Alexandria, and buried in the church of blessed John the Baptist.

At Langres, the feast of the holy twin brothers Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Melasippus. When they were twenty-five years old, they were crowned with martyrdom together with their grandmother Leonilla and Lonella and Neonilla, during the reign of the emperor Aurelian.

The twins were hung upon a single tree, their hands bound upward and their feet downward, their bodies stretched so that they were almost thought to be separated from the very structure of their limbs. After this they were thrown into the fire, yet were not harmed; amid words of prayer they departed together to the Lord.

### D. Fifteenth Day before the Kalends of February

The Chair of Saint Peter the apostle, on which he first sat at Rome.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Publius, bishop of Athens. He was the governor of the island of Malta and had hospitably received blessed Paul the apostle, who was sailing to Rome under guard, for three days, treating him kindly, as blessed Luke relates. At that time Publius’s father happened to lie ill with fever and dysentery. When blessed Paul entered to see him, laid his hands upon him, and prayed, he healed him.

Publius, who afterward clung to the blessed apostle, was ordained and sent by him to preach as bishop. Distinguished in virtues and eminent in teaching, he was gloriously crowned with martyrdom for Christ. For first Dionysius, and then this Publius, presided at Athens.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Prisca the virgin and martyr.

And in Pontus, the feast of the holy martyrs Moses and Ammonius. Though they were soldiers, they were first assigned to the mines and finally handed over to the fire.

[Col. 0816A]

### E. Fourteenth Day before the Kalends of February

At Smyrna, the feast of Saint Germanicus the martyr. Though he flourished in the beauty of early youth, by the grace of God’s power he cast out the fear of bodily frailty. Condemned by the judge, he voluntarily challenged the beast prepared for him. Torn to pieces by its teeth, he merited, by dying for the true bread—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—to be incorporated into him.

On the same day, Saint Pontianus the martyr.

On this day also, the feast of the holy Marius and Martha, with their sons Audifax and Abacuc, noble Persians who came to Rome to pray during the reign of the emperor Claudius. After enduring clubs, the rack, fire, claws, and the cutting off of hands, Martha was thrown into a well and killed; the others were beheaded, together with many others.

### F. Thirteenth Day before the Kalends of February

At Rome, Fabian the bishop. After presiding over the Church for fourteen years, eleven months, and twelve days, he suffered martyrdom under Decius and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

He divided the regions among deacons and appointed seven deacons to preside over seven notaries, so that they might collect the acts of the martyrs in full.

On the same day, Saint Sebastian the martyr, who was so dear to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian that they entrusted him with command of the first cohort. When Diocletian learned that he was a Christian, he ordered him to be bound in the middle of a field, like a target for arrows, and shot by soldiers.

When he stood full of arrows, like a hedgehog, they thought him dead and departed. But during the night a woman named Irene came to take away his body and found him alive. She brought him into her house and cared for him. When he recovered, he strengthened many in the faith. Soon afterward he appeared before the emperors themselves and rebuked them as they deserved.

Then Diocletian ordered him led to the palace hippodrome and beaten with clubs until he expired. Believing him dead, they threw him into the great sewer. But he appeared in a dream to the holy matron Lucina and said: “Near the Circus you will find my body hanging on a hook; the filth has not touched it. When you have lifted it down, carry it to the Catacombs and bury me in a crypt near the apostles’ remains.” She came that very night with servants and fulfilled everything accordingly.

### G. Twelfth Day before the Kalends of February

The feast of the most blessed Agnes, virgin and martyr, who suffered at Rome in the thirteenth year of her age. As she was returning from school, the prefect’s son fell in love with her. Since she was unwilling in any way to associate with him, she was stabbed in the throat with a sword after many tortures.

Blessed Agnes suffered under Simphorianus, prefect of the city, and Aspasius, his deputy.

In the Spanish city of Tarragona, the feast of the holy Fructuosus the bishop and the deacons Augurius and Eulogius. Under Gallienus, during the governorship of Aemilianus, they were first thrust into prison and then thrown into the flames. When their bonds had burned away and they had stretched out their hands in the form of a cross, they prayed that they might be consumed by the fire, and obtained their wish. Soon one of the brothers and the governor’s daughter, who was standing nearby, saw the souls of the saints ascend crowned into heaven.

At Troyes, Saint Patroclus the martyr.

### A. Eleventh Day before the Kalends of February

In Spain, the feast of Saint Vincent the deacon and martyr. Together with his bishop Valerius, he was taken from the city of Zaragoza to Valencia in heavy chains, at the command of Dacianus. There he was long tormented by hunger and the squalor of prison, tortured on the rack and by the dreadful tearing of hooks, and then roasted for a very long time on an iron bed, sprinkled with drops of fat and crackling salt.

After this he was thrust into a most dreadful prison, with his legs spread apart in a stock, and thrown upon extremely sharp fragments of pottery. There a great light appeared during the night, and the martyr, freed by God’s power, sang a hymn among the angels, by whom he deserved to be visited, so that the jailer himself believed.

When morning came, Dacianus ordered him laid upon a very soft bed, so that, having recovered somewhat, he might be tortured more harshly again. But he gave his unconquered spirit back to Christ.

Then Dacianus ordered his body exposed in a field to wild beasts and birds. But soon a raven, divinely assigned to guard it, not only kept away the other birds but also drove a savage wolf away from the holy body.

When this was reported to Dacianus, he ordered the body sewn into a sack and sunk into the depths of the sea with a very heavy stone attached to it. But before the rowers could touch the harbor, it floated by God’s power upon the waves, was carried to the shore, and buried in the sand.

After the holy martyr revealed himself to a certain faithful old woman named Jonica, when the fury of persecution had ceased, Christians reverently took up the body and buried it in a basilica.

In Gaul, at the city of Embrun, the holy martyrs Vincent, Orontius, and Victor.

At Rome, at the Salt Pools, the feast of Saint Anastasius, a monk and martyr from Persia. After enduring very many tortures of imprisonment, scourging, and chains in Caesarea of Palestine, he was finally subjected to much punishment by the Persians in Persia and at last beheaded by their king Chosroes, together with seventy others.

His bodily relics were first kept at Jerusalem in his monastery and then brought to Rome; they are venerated in the monastery of blessed Paul the apostle, called “at the Salt Pools.”

And Saint Vincent the presbyter and martyr.

### B. Tenth Day before the Kalends of February

At Rome, Saint Emerentiana, virgin and martyr, who was Saint Agnes’s foster-sister. While she was praying at Agnes’s tomb, asking that Agnes defend her from the violence of the pagans, they stoned her.

And in Mauretania, at the city of Caesarea, the feast of Saint Severianus and Aquila his wife, who were burned by fire.

At Philippi, blessed Parmenas the deacon, who was one of the seven deacons. Delivered by the brothers to the grace of God, he completed the ministry of preaching entrusted to him with complete faith, attained the glory of martyrdom, and rested at Philippi.

### C. Ninth Day before the Kalends of February

At Ephesus, the feast of Saint Timothy, disciple of blessed Paul. He was ordained bishop at Ephesus by the blessed apostle and, after many struggles for Christ, fell asleep. His body was transferred to Constantinople in the twentieth year of Constantius, together with the relics of blessed Andrew and Luke.

At Antioch, Saint Babylas the bishop, who, during the persecution of Decius, glorified the Lord frequently through his sufferings and tortures and finally attained the end of his glorious life in chains. A great miracle concerning him is related in the tenth book of Ecclesiastical History.

When the emperor Julian had turned to the worship of idols and, on a certain occasion, was sacrificing to Apollo at Daphne, a suburb of Antioch, near the Castalian spring, he received no response to any of his inquiries. When he asked the priests the reason for the silence, the demons replied that the tomb of the martyr Babylas stood nearby and that for this reason no answers were being given.

Then he ordered the “Galileans”—for he was accustomed to call our people by this name—to come and remove the martyr’s tomb. Immediately the Christians assembled, girded with great rejoicing, took up the martyr’s coffin, and, singing in the ears of the impious ruler, carried it for six thousand paces with loud voices and exultation, saying:

“Let all those who worship carved images be put to shame, and those who glory in their idols.”
