The scribes and Pharisees threw him from the pinnacle of the temple; he died when a fuller’s club struck him on the head. He governed the Church of Jerusalem for thirty years and was buried near the temple. [Col. 0898A]

In Gaul, Saint Andeolus the subdeacon, under Caesar Severus, whose head was split in the form of a cross with a piece of wood.

At Agaunum, the Passion of Saint Sigismund, king, son of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians. When he realized that he could not resist the Franks, he fled alone, laid aside his crown, and adopted the religious habit. Devoting himself day and night to fasts and vigils, he was captured by the Franks with his wife and children and died after being thrown into a well. He was afterward revealed to an abbot and honorably buried by him; he also became renowned for miracles.

And the feast of Saint Walburga, virgin.

And at Jerusalem, the Passion of Saint Judas, also called Quiriacus, bishop, to whom the wood of the Lord’s Cross was revealed.

### C. The sixth day before the Nones of May

The feast of our holy father Athanasius, bishop and confessor of the city of Alexandria. He endured many plots by the Arians and, in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, after many struggles and many crowns of patience, rested in peace. [Col. 0899B]

And the feast of Saints Saturninus and Neopolis, who rested in prison. [Col. 0900A]

### D. The fifth day before the Nones of May

At Jerusalem, the discovery of the Holy Cross by Queen Helena under the emperor Constantine, whose mother she also was.

At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, at the seventh milestone, Saints Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus, presbyters, under the emperor Trajan and the judge Aurelianus. Alexander held the episcopate of the Roman Church for ten years, two months, and ten days, fifth after Peter. He was incomparable in holiness and distinguished in faith. He converted the greater part of the city’s senators to the Lord. After imprisonment, the torture-horse, hooks, and fires, he was finally killed by repeated punctures throughout his body. The others, after a long confinement in prison, were tested by fire and were finally beheaded.

And the feast of Saint Juvenal, bishop, and the burial of Saint Philip the confessor. [Col. 0900B]

### E. The fourth day before the Nones of May

In Palestine, at the city of Gaza, the feast of Saint Silvanus, bishop of that city, who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian together with many of his clergy.

At Vienne, Saint Justus, bishop.

At Metallophanum, forty holy martyrs, who were beheaded together.

At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Antonia. After being tortured excessively and afflicted with various torments, she was suspended by one arm for three days and thrust into prison for two years. At last she was burned by the flames by the governor Priscillianus. [Col. 0902A]

On the same day, at Lauriacum, a place in Noricum Ripense, the feast of Saint Florian. At the command of the governor Aquilinus, he was thrown into the river Anisus with a stone tied around his neck. Immediately, before the eyes of all who were standing around, the eyes of the man who had thrown him burst.

On that same day, Blessed Quiriacus, glorious bishop and martyr, under the emperor Julian.

And Saint Bothehard, bishop and confessor.

### F. The third day before the Nones of May

At Alexandria, Saint Euthymius the deacon, resting in prison. [Col. 0903A]

At Thessalonica, the feast of Saints Irenaeus, Peregrinus, and Hyrenes, who were burned in the fire.

In Gaul, at the city of Arles, Saint Hilary, bishop, a most distinguished man. He loved poverty and was concerned for the provision of the needy not only through the compassion of his heart but also through the labor of his body. For the refreshment of the poor, although a man of noble birth, he even practiced farming beyond his strength. Nor was he negligent in spiritual matters: he possessed grace in teaching, imposed correction on everyone without respect of persons, and composed the life of his predecessor, Saint Honoratus.

He died under the emperors Valentinian and Marcian.

### C. The day before the Nones of May

At Rome, Saint John the apostle before the Latin Gate. From Ephesus, by order of Domitian, the brother of Titus, during the second persecution—which Domitian himself carried out after Nero—he was brought to the city of Rome and, in the presence of the senate, placed before the Latin Gate in a cauldron of boiling oil. But the blessed apostle emerged from it as free from punishment as he had been immune from the corruptions of the flesh.

He was then exiled to the island of Patmos, where he saw the Apocalypse. Therefore, to preserve a worthy memory of him and in recognition of the constancy of apostolic faith, Christians built at the aforementioned place, before the Latin Gate, a church bearing his ecclesiastical veneration, with splendid and marvelous workmanship. There they still hold a festive gathering on the day before the Nones of May.

On the same day, Blessed Evodius, bishop and martyr of Antioch, who was the first to be ordained there by the apostles. [Col. 0904A]

Also, Blessed Lucius, who, having been instituted by the apostles, was the first to govern the Church of Cyrene as bishop.

### A. The Nones of May

The dedication of the church of Saint Mary the Virgin.

And the feast of Saint Juvenal the martyr and Blessed Domitilla. She was the granddaughter through his sister of Flavius Clemens, the consul, and Saint Clement consecrated her with the sacred veil because of her perseverance in integrity. During the persecution of Domitian, because of the testimony she bore to Christ, she was deported into exile with many others to the island of Pontia, where she endured a long martyrdom. Later transferred to the city of Tarracina, she first converted Euphrosina and Theodora, then others, to the faith of Christ. Finally, she completed the course of her martyrdom together with the aforesaid virgins under the persecution of Trajan, where they had been confined in prison. For they departed after prostrating themselves on their faces and praying to the Lord. Saint Caesarius the deacon placed their bodies together in a new sarcophagus and buried them deep in the earth. [Col. 0906A]

At Nicomedia, the Passion of the holy martyrs Flavius, Augustus, and Augustinus, brothers.

At Rome, Benedict, pontiff, who held the episcopate for one month under the emperor Constantine and was buried at Blessed Peter’s.

### B. The eighth day before the Ides of May

At Milan, Saint Victor the martyr. He was a Moor by nationality and a Christian from his earliest youth. When he was a soldier in the imperial camp and already honored with gray hair, Maximian compelled him to sacrifice to idols. He persevered most bravely in confessing the Lord. First he was severely beaten; then liquid lead was poured over him, but he was not harmed at all. Finally, by the cutting off of his head, he won the course of glorious martyrdom.

When Saint Martin heard what had happened, he gathered his body and buried it honorably in the aforesaid city.

At Vienne, Saint Dionysius, the city’s sixth bishop.

### C. The seventh day before the Ides of May

The feast of Saint Hermes, whom the apostle Paul mentions in writing to the Romans: “Greet Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, and the brothers who are with them.”

In Persia, four hundred holy martyrs.

At the town of Nazianzus, Blessed Gregory, bishop, called the noble Theologian, educated at Athens and a companion of Blessed Basil, later bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. After he had devoted himself entirely to the service of God, he presumed so much upon his companion that he removed Basil, who was seated at the teacher’s right hand, and led him by the hand with him to the monastery. There, for thirteen years, they excluded all secular Greek books and devoted themselves solely to the volumes of Holy Scripture. [Col. 0907B–0908A]

At Constantinople, the feast of Saint Timothy, when his sacred bones were brought from Ephesus.

At Ariopolis, the feast of Quirillus, Hindeus, and Genon.

At Tarsus in Cilicia, Aphrodisius.

At Rome, Saint Beatus the confessor.

### D. The sixth day before the Ides of May

The feast of the prophet Joel.

At Rome, on the Latin Way, in his cemetery, the feast of Saints Gordianus and Epimachus.

The emperor Julian the Apostate, among the many Christians whom he had committed to public custody, arrested Blessed Januarius, an elderly presbyter, and handed him over to a certain deputy, Gordianus, for interrogation. Gordianus listened patiently to Blessed Januarius and, enlightened by the Spirit of God, began to believe. The blessed presbyter immediately baptized him, together with his wife, Marina by name, and fifty-three members of his household, of both sexes, and more.

When Julian heard this, he ordered the holy presbyter Januarius and Blessed Gordianus to be condemned in the official records. He ordered Gordianus’s wife to remain at the salt waters in the service of peasants.

Clementianus, however, seated on the tribunal, had Blessed Gordianus brought before him bound in chains. Firm in his confession of Christ, he was beaten for a long time with leaded scourges and finally beheaded. The wicked judge ordered his body to be thrown before the temple of Apollo to be gnawed by dogs. [Col. 0909B]

During the night, Christians seized it and placed it in a crypt a little more than one mile from the city of Rome, where the body of Blessed Epimachus the martyr had long before been buried.

This Epimachus went to Alexandria with his companion Alexander. After being tortured for a long time in chains and the torments of prison, he was later consumed by fire. His relics were afterward transferred to Rome.

At Rome, the feast of Cleopodius, an elderly presbyter, under the emperor Alexander. Alexander had him killed by Laodiceus, his body dragged through the city, and then thrown into the Tiber on the day of the Kalends of May. Fishermen found it, lifted it out, and reported it to Bishop Callistus. He received it, embalmed it with spices and linen cloths, and buried it in his cemetery, in a crypt at the third milestone from the city, on the sixth day before the Ides of May.

Then Palmatius the consul was beheaded by Alexander, together with his wife and children and forty-two other members of his household, both male and female. With them also were Simplicius the senator, his wife, children, and household, sixty-eight persons of both sexes; and likewise Blanda, with her husband. They had recently been baptized through the teaching of Pope Callistus and the presbyter Cleopodius.

Also at Rome, the feast of Saints Quartus and Quintus. [Col. 0910B]

### E. The fifth day before the Ides of May

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, at the twenty-second milestone, the feast of Saint Anthunus and the Passion of Saint Evellius. When Evellius saw the Passion of Saint Torpetes the martyr and the miracles he performed, he believed in Christ. Previously he had been a counsellor of the emperor Nero, concerning the manner in which Christians were martyred.

At Vienne, Saint Mamertus, bishop, who, because of an impending disaster, instituted the solemn litanies before the Ascension of the Lord. [Col. 0911A]

### F. The fourth day before the Ides of May

At Rome, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the feast of the holy martyrs Nereus and Achilleus, brothers. They were eunuchs of Blessed Flavia and, with her, endured a long exile for Christ on the island of Pontia. Later, by Aurelianus, the fiancé of Domitilla—whom she herself had rejected for the love of Christ—they were first confined under very severe beatings and then handed over to Memmius Rufus, the consul. When he compelled them with the torture-horse and flames to sacrifice, they said that they had been baptized by Blessed Peter the apostle and could in no way sacrifice to idols; they were beheaded. [Col. 0912A–0913A]

Auspicius, their disciple and the fosterer of Saint Domitilla the virgin, took away their bodies and buried them in a sandy crypt.

Also, on the Aurelia Way, at the second milestone, the feast of Saint Pancratius the martyr. When he was fourteen years old, he completed his martyrdom by beheading under Diocletian. Octavilla, a distinguished woman, secretly took up his revered body during the night, embalmed it with spices, and buried it.

On the same day, Blessed Dionysius, the uncle of the same Blessed Pancratius, through whose efforts Pancratius was both baptized and strengthened in the fear of God and encouraged to martyrdom.

On Cyprus, Saint Epiphanius, our holy father, bishop of Salamis.

### G. The third day before the Ides of May

The feast of Saint Mary of the Martyrs. Under the emperor Phocas, Blessed Boniface, pope, removed the defilements of idolatry from the ancient shrine called the Pantheon and dedicated it as a church of Blessed Mary ever-virgin and of all the martyrs. The most sacred day of this dedication is celebrated at Rome on the third day before the Ides of May.

On the same day, Saint Servatius, bishop of the Church of Tongeren. At the time when the Huns were laying waste to Germany, he was warned by a revelation of the Lord. So that he would not see the destruction of his city and Church, he crossed over to the village of the people of Maastricht. There he died and was buried in the middle of the public roadway.

To manifest his merit to the people, although in winter snow filled everything around it, snow and rain never covered his tomb until his successor, Saint Munulfus, bishop, built a great church in his honor.

And the feast of Saint Gangulf the martyr and Saint Onesimus the confessor. [Col. 0914B]

### A. The day before the Ides of May

Our holy father Pachomius, who was distinguished by works of apostolic grace and was the founder of the monasteries of Egypt. He wrote rules for monks, which he had learned through the dictation of an angel, as well as rules concerning the time of Easter. [Col. 0915A]

In Syria, the feast of Victor and Corona, under the emperor Antoninus and Sebastian, governor of Alexandria.

Victor was a soldier from Cilicia. Sebastian ordered that the fingers of his hands be broken and torn out because of his confession of faith. Then he ordered him to be thrown into a furnace, where he remained for three days without being harmed. Next he ordered him to drink poison, but he did not die; rather, he converted the poisoner to the faith.

Afterward, he ordered the sinews of his body to be removed. Then boiling oil was poured onto his private parts. After this, he ordered burning lamps to be applied to his sides while he was suspended. Next he ordered vinegar and lime to be mixed together and given to him. Then he ordered his eyes to be torn out. Then he was suspended by the head for three days [the reading is uncertain; F: “ordered”], and while he was still breathing, he ordered him to be flayed. [Col. 0915B]

Then Corona, who was the wife of a certain soldier, began to bless Saint Victor for the glory of his martyrdom. As she was doing this, she saw two crowns falling from heaven, one sent for Victor and the other for herself.

When she proclaimed this before all who were listening, she was seized by the governor. He ordered two palm trees to be bent toward one another and Corona to be tied by her hands and feet to each of them with hempen ropes, and then ordered the trees to be released. When this was done, Corona was torn into two parts. She was sixteen years old.

Then Victor too was beheaded, and he himself deserved the triumph of everlasting victory. [Col. 0916A]

### B. The Ides of May

The feast of the holy confessors Torquatus, Isefontus, Secundus, Indaletius, Caecilius, Esitius, and Euphrasius, who were ordained bishops at Rome by the holy apostles and sent to Spain to preach the word of God, which was still entangled in pagan error.

When they came to the city of Acci, they rested briefly because of the labor of their journey and sent their disciples into the city to purchase provisions. Soon a crowd of pagans, who happened at that time to be celebrating festivals for their gods, pursued them as far as a river. A bridge of remarkable size and strength had been built over it. As the saints crossed, by God’s will the bridge collapsed completely with the entire crowd of pursuers.

Terrified by this miracle, the others followed the example of a certain great senatress, Luparia, who, divinely inspired, received them kindly and believed. Abandoning their idols, they believed in Christ the Lord.

Afterward they preached in different cities and brought countless multitudes under the faith of Christ. Torquatus rested at Acci; Isefontus at Vergium; Secundus at Abula; Indaletius at Urci; Caecilius at Iliberis; Esitius at Carcesa; and Euphrasius at Iliturgi.

On the island of Chios, the feast of Saint Isidore the martyr.

At Damosacum, the Passion of Saints Peter and Andrew, Paul and Dionysia.

### C. The seventeenth day before the Kalends of May

At Isauria, the feast of Saints Aquilinus and Victorianus, whose acts are preserved.

At Auxerre, the Passion of Saint Peregrinus, the first bishop of that city; and of Saint Maxima, virgin, who, renowned for many virtues, rested in peace.

At Sirmium, the feast of Timothy and seven virgins.

In Sardinia, the feast of Simplicius the presbyter, Saint Rosula, and Saints Diocletian and Florentius.

Within the territory of Cassino, the burial of Fidolius, presbyter and confessor.

### D. The sixteenth day before the Kalends of June

In Tuscany, Saint Torpetes the martyr, under the emperor Nero. He held a high office in Nero’s service and was baptized by Blessed Antonius the presbyter and instructed in the faith of Christ.

When Nero learned that he was a Christian, he handed him over to a certain relative of his, Satellicus, to compel him to sacrifice. But when the blessed man, strengthened by the Spirit of God, remained immovable, Satellicus had him beaten with slaps [Col. 0917B] and tied to a column, where he was scourged until blood dripped from his body.

Suddenly, while he was being beaten, the column fell and crushed the judge and fifty men with him. Then Torpetes was seized by attendants and placed on a wheel. Afterward he was thrown to wild beasts by Satellicus’s son, named Silvius, but was not harmed by them at all.

After this, at Silvius’s command, he was led outside the city to Pisa and completed his martyrdom by beheading, on the third day before the Kalends of May.

The criminal attendants placed his body in a nearly broken and worm-eaten boat, throwing a dog and a rooster into the river’s current together with him.

An angel of the Lord appeared to a venerable woman named Celerina and instructed her to search for the holy martyr’s body and bury it. When she found it, she buried it with every mark of reverence and, after the persecution had ceased, built a church over it at her own expense.

The martyr’s festival and the citizens’ gathering are celebrated on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June. [Col. 0918A–0918B]

At Alexandria, the feast of Adrion, Victor, and Basilla.

### E. The fifteenth day before the Kalends of June

In Egypt, Saint Dioscorus the lector. The governor inflicted many and varied tortures upon him, even tearing out his fingernails and setting his sides ablaze with lamps. But the attendants fell down, terrified by the splendor of heavenly light. Finally, after being burned with red-hot plates, he completed his martyrdom.

And the feast of Saints Hortasius and Serapion, and of Mark, pope, and Potamion.

### F. The fourteenth day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, the feast of Saint Pudentiana, or Potentiana, virgin. She was of very distinguished lineage and was the daughter of Pudens, the disciple of Blessed Paul the apostle. Her mother was Sabinella, and her sister was Praxedis. Their father instructed them in every aspect of the Christian religion and left them as virgins to Christ. [Col. 0919A–0920A]

After the death of their holy father, they advanced so greatly in every exercise of piety that, night and day, they served the Lord unceasingly with hymns and prayers together with their household, while Blessed Pius, bishop of the city, joined them in the praises of God.

Thus, destined to receive a reward for their most devout labors, after innumerable struggles, after reverently providing burial for many martyrs, and after placing all their possessions in the bowels of the poor and commending them faithfully to Christ, they finally departed from earth to Christ.

Potentiana, worthy of veneration, was buried on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way. Praxedis, likewise a most holy virgin, was buried on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, also with her sister beside their holy father.

On the same day, Blessed Pudens, the father of these virgins.

Also at Rome, the feast of Saints Calocerus and Parthenius, eunuchs of the wife of the emperor Decius. One was chief chamberlain and the other chief secretary. Since they refused to sacrifice to idols, they were killed by Decius. Their bodies were placed beside the Appian Way.

The burial of Lord Alchuinus.

### G. The thirteenth day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the feast of Saint Basilla, virgin and martyr of Christ. She was of royal descent and had a very distinguished fiancé named Pompeius. Through Blessed Eugenia and Saints Protus and Hyacinthus of God, she was converted to the faith. Her aforesaid fiancé accused her of being a Christian. [Col. 0921A]

Immediately Gallienus Augustus, who was then persecuting the Church of Christ, decreed that she must either accept her fiancé or die by the sword. When questioned about this, she replied that she had as her fiancé the King of kings, who is Christ, the Son of God. After she had said this, she was pierced through with a sword.

In Gaul, at the city of Nîmes, the feast of Baudelius. He was seized by pagans who were celebrating the sacrifices of their gods. When he refused to sacrifice and remained steadfast in the faith of Christ amid beatings and tortures, he received the palm of martyrdom through a precious death.

### A. The twelfth day before the Kalends of June

In Caesarean Mauretania, the feast of Saints Timothy, Polius, and Eutychius the deacon. While spreading the word of the Lord in that region, they deserved to be crowned together.

Also at Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saints Polyvetus, Victorius, and Donatus.

In Africa, Castus and Aemilius, who completed their martyrdom through the suffering of fire. Cyprian writes about this in his book *On the Lapsed*.

On Corsica, the feast of Saint Julia, who was crowned with the punishment of the cross; and of Saint Valens, martyr and pontiff, with three boys. [Col. 0922B]

### B. The eleventh day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, the feast of Saints Faustinus, Timothy, and Venustus.

At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Helena, virgin; and at Ravenna, the feast of Saint Martyria.

In the city of Auxerre, Blessed Uvalis, presbyter and confessor.

### C. The tenth day before the Kalends of June

At Langres, the Passion of Saint Desiderius, bishop. When he saw his people being ravaged by the army of the Vandals, he went out to their king to plead for them. The king immediately ordered him to be killed. For the sake of the sheep entrusted to him, he willingly extended his neck and, struck by the sword, departed to Christ.

His executioner was soon seized by madness and died.

The blessed martyr was buried there in a basilica within the city walls. Many others from his flock also suffered with him and were buried in the same city. [Col. 0923A]

Also at Vienne, the feast of Saint Desiderius, bishop, who suffered in the territory of Lyon.

### D. The ninth day before the Kalends of June

The feast of Saint Manaen, foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch, teacher and prophet under the grace of the New Testament, resting in Christ at Antioch.

Also, the most blessed Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward, whom the Evangelists mention.

At the Roman harbor, the feast of Saint Vincent the martyr.

In Gaul, at the city of Nantes, the feast of the holy martyrs Donatianus and Rogatianus, brothers.

In Istria, the feast of Saints Zoellus, Servilius, Silvanus, and Diocles.

### E. The eighth day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the feast of Saint Urban, bishop and martyr. He held the episcopate for three years, ten months, and ten days. Through his teaching, many were crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Alexander.

At Milan, Saint Dionysius, bishop and confessor. The emperor Constantius condemned him for the Catholic faith in Cappadocia, where he rested in exile. Blessed Ambrose received the relics of his body from Saint Basil, bishop of the aforesaid city, and deposited them with fitting honor.

In Moesia, at the city of Dorostorus, the feast of the holy martyrs Passicrates, Valention, and others crowned together. [Col. 0926A]

Also at Rome, the feast of Eleutherius, pope, who held the episcopate for fifteen years. He received letters from Lucius, king of Britain, asking that he become a Christian through his command. He was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter the apostle.

### F. The seventh day before the Kalends of June

The feast of Blessed James the apostle, brother of John the Evangelist, who was beheaded by King Herod at Jerusalem, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles teaches.

His most blessed sacred bones were transferred from Spain and buried at its farthest limits, namely opposite the British Sea. [Col. 0927A]

At Athens, Blessed Quadratus, bishop and disciple of the apostles. He established that no food which is rational and human should be rejected by Christians.

Also, Quadratus the martyr, on whose solemnity sermons of Saint Augustine are found to have been delivered.

At Rome, the blessed martyrs Sinmitrius the presbyter and twenty-two others, whom the emperor Antoninus caused to be punished with the sword for Christ. Blessed Praxedis buried their bodies during the night.

At Todi in Tuscany, the feast of Saints Felicissimus, Heradius, and Paulinus.

In the territory of Auxerre, the Passion of Saint Priscus the martyr with a great multitude.

In Britain, Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor. Sent by Blessed Pope Gregory, he was the first to preach the Gospel of Christ to the English people, and there he rested, glorious in virtues [Col. 0927B] and miracles.

At Vienne, the Passion of Saint Zacharias, the second bishop of that city.

### G. The sixth day before the Kalends of June

In Moesia, at the city of Dorostorus, the feast of Saint Julius. During the persecution, when he was a veteran of completed military service, he was arrested by officials and brought before the governor Maximus. Since he refused to sacrifice to idols, he was condemned to death.

As he was being led to the place where the execution was to be carried out, a certain soldier named Esicius, who himself had been arrested and detained for the faith of Christ, begged him, saying: “Remember me, for I too will follow you. First, greet Passicrates and Valention, who have already gone before us to the Lord through a good confession.”

Julius kissed Esicius and said: “Brother, hasten to come; those whom you greeted have already heard your message.”

Then, taking his prayer-cloth, he bound it over his eyes and received the palm of martyrdom when the sword struck him.

In Gaul, at the city of Orange, Saint Eutropius, bishop and confessor. [Col. 0928A–0928B]

### A. The fifth day before the Kalends of June

The feast of Saint John, pope. During his time, King Theodoric killed two distinguished senators and consuls, Symmachus and Boethius. The king himself suddenly died on the ninety-eighth day after Pope John died.

Because John was orthodox and had been gloriously received by the orthodox emperor Justin when he came to Constantinople, the Arian king Theodoric detained him on his return to Ravenna and brought him to death together with other equally Catholic men.

Saint Gregory mentions him in the book of the *Dialogues*. His body was transferred and buried in the basilica of Saint Peter the apostle on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, during the consulship of Olybrius.

At Paris, Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor, who, after innumerable virtues, departed to the Lord at the age of eighty.

In Sardinia, Saints Aemilius, Felix, Priamus, and Lucianus.

### B. The fourth day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, on the Aurelia Way, Saint Restitutus. On the Tiburtine Way, the seven brothers.

At Trier, Blessed Maximinus, bishop and confessor, by whom Athanasius, fleeing the persecution of Constantius, was honorably received.

Also, the Passion of Saint Conon the martyr and his son under the emperor Aurelian, at the city of Iconium in the province of Isauria, before the judge Domitianus. Conon, distinguished in faith, was brought before the judge with his twelve-year-old son. In a true confession they revealed that the Holy Spirit dwelt within them.

They were then subjected to frying and afterward suspended while a strong fire was placed beneath them. Finally, their hands were crushed with a wooden mallet, and they gave up their spirits in praise of almighty God.

On the same day, the feast of Saints Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander, who, in the regions of Agaunum, while pagan men persecuted them, obtained the crown of martyrdom. [Col. 0930B]

### C. The third day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, on the Aurelia Way, the feast of Saint Felix, pope. He established that Masses should be celebrated over the memorials of the martyrs. After governing the Church for five years, he was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Claudius. [Col. 0931A]

At Turris in Sardinia, the feast of the holy martyrs Gabinius and Crispulus.

At Antioch, the holy martyrs Sitinus and Palatinus, who suffered many torments for the name of Christ.

### D. The day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, Saint Petronilla, virgin, who was the daughter of the most blessed apostle Peter. After many miracles of healing, when a certain Flaccus wished to take her as his wife, she requested a delay of three days. Together with Saint Felicula, her foster-sister, she devoted herself to continual fasting and prayers.

On the third day, after the mysteries of the Lord’s offering had been celebrated by the presbyter Saint Nicomedes, as soon as she received Christ’s sacraments, she reclined on her little bed and gave up her spirit.

At Aquileia, the feast of the holy martyrs Cantius, Cantianus, and Cancianilla, brothers.

At Turris in Sardinia, the feast of Saint Crescentianus.

### June

The month has thirty days; the moon, thirty-nine.

### E. The Kalends of June

At Rome, the dedication of Nicomedes the martyr and presbyter, whose martyrdom is celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

At Caesarea in Palestine, the feast of Saint Pamphilus the presbyter, a man of remarkable faith and holiness, who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Maximinus. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, set forth his life in three books.

At Vienne, Saint Claudius, the eleventh bishop.

On the same day, Saint Caprasius, abbot of the monastery of Lérins.

At Thessalonica, Octavius.

At Antioch, Zosimus.

At Trier, Saint Simeon the recluse.

F. Fourth day before the Nones of June.—At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Marcellinus, presbyter, and Peter, exorcist, who, while instructing many in the faith in prison, were beheaded under the judge Serenus after dreadful chains and very many tortures. The man who beheaded them saw their souls, splendidly adorned, carried by angels to heaven; thereafter, doing penance, he was baptized in his old age under Pope Julius, receiving the name Theodore.

At Lyons, Saint Blandina, with eleven other martyrs and eight more, whose tortures, renewed continually from first light until evening, finally caused the torturers to confess themselves defeated; and when she was struck a second time, she was tortured but not overcome. On the third day she was tied to a stake and stretched out in the form of a cross, being prepared as food for wild beasts. Since none of the beasts dared touch her, she was brought back again to prison. On the fourth day she was driven forward by scourging, burned on grates, and subjected to many other sufferings; finally she was slaughtered with the sword. Then the boy Ponticus, fifteen years old, was led through every kind of torture with her and, strengthened by her maternal exhortation, completed his martyrdom before her.

In Campania, the blessed martyr and bishop Erasmus, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. By order of the impious emperor Diocletian, he was first cruelly beaten with leaden clubs, then for a very long time beaten with rods. Afterwards, when resin, sulfur, lead, pitch, wax, and oil had been melted together, he was drenched with them, yet by a great miracle he appeared unharmed. When many saw this, they rejected their idols and accepted the faith of Christ. Then he was bound with an immense weight of iron and shut in prison under severe guard, from which he was freed and rescued by an angelic visitation. Later, when his most illustrious fame had spread, he was seized by the other emperor Maximian, by whom he was tortured with various punishments, until he was made to wear a tunic of heated bronze. Again he was thrown into a cauldron heated with lead, pitch, wax, resin, and oil; by the power of the Lord he overcame everything and emerged unharmed. Thus, at last, preserved by the Lord to strengthen the others, he reached Campania fortified by angelic assistance. There, after strengthening very many in the faith or converting them to the faith of Christ, he was called by the Lord and, illustrious in martyrdom, rested in a holy death.

G. Third day before the Nones of June.—At Arezzo, a city of Tuscany, the feast of the holy martyrs Pergentinus and Laurentius, brothers. While still boys, during the persecution of Decius and under the judge Turcius, after enduring harsh chains and displaying great miracles, they were struck down with the sword and buried near that same city.

[Col. 0935A]

A. The day before the Nones of June.—In Siscia, a city of Illyricum, the feast of Saint Quirinus, bishop. During the persecution of Maximinus, for the faith of Christ—as Prudentius writes—he was thrown into a river with a millstone tied to his hand. After speaking at length with those standing around, so that they would not be frightened by his example, he scarcely obtained by his prayers that he be submerged. His relics were transferred to Rome and placed in the Catacombs. In Tuscany, Saint Laurentius and four hundred others. At Orléans, the burial of Saint Lifard, presbyter. At Nineveh, the feast of Dinoscius, Attalus, Camarius, Tyrinus, Julia, Saracia, and Cyprinus.

[Col. 0936A]

B. The Nones of June.—Saint Boniface, archbishop, whose martyrdom was completed among the Frisians together with the other servants of God: Vuinthruga and Waltera, Scirpalda and Bosan, Hamonda and Adelhera, Wancara and Gundacara, Willehera and Athaliolfa.

In Egypt, the feast of the holy martyrs Martianus, Nicander, and Apollonius, whose acts are preserved. On the same day, the passion of Saint Boniface the martyr, who suffered at Tarsus under Diocletian and Maximian, but was buried at Rome on the road called the Latina. His mistress Aglaes sent him from Rome—although she had committed adultery with him—to places where the persecution of Christians was most severe, so that he might acquire for her at a price the body of some saint and bring it back. Obeying his mistress’s words, he went there among the Christians. Thus he was arrested and, by order of the ruler, was first drenched with boiling oil mixed with pitch; but he was harmed in no way, and finally was struck by the executioner.

Afterwards, following his martyr’s crown, he was brought back to his mistress by his companions who had traveled with him. Receiving him, she buried him at Rome on the Latina road. The blessed Aglaes renounced the world, distributing everything she possessed to the poor and to monasteries and releasing her entire household from the yoke of slavery. She earned such favor from the Lord that she became renowned through signs of miracles performed in his name. She lived thirteen years longer in the habit of a nun and was buried near the aforementioned martyr.

[Col. 0937B]

C. Eighth day before the Ides of June.—The feast of Saint Philip the deacon, who was one of the seven deacons whom the apostles ordained with blessed Stephen immediately after the Lord’s ascension. Concerning him, blessed Luke reports in the Acts of the Apostles that, by performing signs and wonders, he converted Samaria to the faith of Christ through his preaching and baptized the eunuch of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. He came to rest at Caesarea; near him lie buried his three daughters, virgins, while his fourth daughter, filled with the Holy Spirit, died at Ephesus.

At Rome, Saints Artemius, his wife Candida, and their daughter Paulina. Artemius was guardian of the prison and was holding Peter the exorcist in custody. Since his only daughter was tormented by a demon, she was immediately healed through the prayers of blessed Peter. Artemius himself, together with his wife and that same daughter, believed in Christ and was baptized by blessed Marcellinus the presbyter, along with his entire household and many others, so that the number of men, excluding the women, reached three hundred. When the judge Serenus heard of this, he ordered Artemius, Candida, and their daughter Paulina to be brought before him and buried beneath an enormous weight of rubble. Thus the saints of God were led to the place of their passion. Blessed Artemius was struck with the sword, while Saints Candida and Paulina were thrown down through the entrance of a crypt and buried beneath stones.

[Col. 0939A]

D. Seventh day before the Ides of June.—At Constantinople, the feast of Saint Paul, bishop of that city. During the time of the Arian perfidy, he was driven into exile by the emperor Constantine to a certain small town of Cappadocia called Cucusa because of the catholic faith; he was then cruelly strangled through the schemes of the Arians and departed to the heavenly kingdom.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Lucianus the martyr. In Africa, Saints Amantius and Lucius. At Alexandria, Andrew, Donatus, and Peregrinus, and the burial of the blessed bishop Claudius.

E. Sixth day before the Ides of June.—In the Gallic city of Soissons, the burial of Saint Medardus, bishop and confessor, whose life, full of miracles, has been written. He was generous in almsgiving, illustrious in virtue, and possessed the spirit of prophecy. For fifteen years he held the bishopric of the city of the Veromandui; at last, departing to the heavenly realms, his body was transferred to the city of Soissons and buried there, where it became renowned through many manifestations of virtue.

At Angers, Saint Licinius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Carileffus the confessor and Saint Nabor the confessor. At Tarsus in Cilicia, twenty martyrs under the judge Simplicius.

F. Fifth day before the Ides of June.—At Rome, on the Caelian Hill, the feast of the holy martyrs Primus and Felicianus, who suffered many tortures for the name of Christ under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. Those most wicked emperors handed them over to the governor Promotus for punishment. When he saw that they could in no way be turned away from confessing Christ, he separated them from one another. First he ordered Felicianus, who was eighty years old, to be beaten with leaden clubs; afterwards he sent him to prison and for three days would not allow food or water to be given him. Then he likewise ordered Primus to be beaten with rods; thereafter, in the amphitheater, he commanded that the holy martyrs be given to lions. Yet they were harmed by them in no way. When the crowds saw this, more than fifteen hundred believed in Christ.

[Col. 0942A]

Finally the holy martyrs were beheaded by the aforementioned count. Their bodies were secretly taken away at night by faithful Christians and buried at the Nomentan Arches, inside the sand-pit.

In the Gallic city of Agen, at a place called Pompeiacum, the passion of Saint Vincent, levite and martyr. In Scotland, Saint Columba the confessor.

G. Fourth day before the Ides of June.—At Rome, on the Aurelia road, at the thirteenth milestone, the feast of Saint Basilides the martyr. Saints Tripodes and Mandales, under the emperor Aurelian and the governor Plato, and twenty other martyrs.

On the same day, the blessed martyr Gethulius, in the time of the emperor Hadrian and under the judge Licinius. Since he was a most Christian man and had performed many good works, he was handed over to the deputy Cerealis for punishment. But Saint Gethulius converted him to the faith of Christ by sound preaching, just as he had converted his brother, the tribune Amantius. Saint Pope Sixtus baptized Cerealis and confirmed him in the faith.

When the aforementioned emperor later heard of this, he handed Saint Gethulius over to his prefect Licinius, ordering him, if Gethulius refused to sacrifice to idols, to cast him and his companions into a burning furnace. When this had been done, they were harmed by the fire in no way. Then, with their heads battered by clubs, they completed their martyrdom. The blessed Simphorosa, wife of the martyr Gethulius, gathered their bodies and buried them on her estate.

In Africa, Aresirogatus and fifteen others. In Spain, Saints Crispulus and Restitutus. At Nicomedia, Saint Zacharias. At Auxerre, the burial of Censurius, bishop.

A. Third day before the Ides of June.—The feast of Saint Barnabas the apostle, who, being a Cypriot, was ordained with Paul, the apostle to the gentiles. Afterwards, because of John, the disciple who was also called Mark, he separated from Paul; nevertheless, he carried out the work of evangelical preaching entrusted to him. His body was discovered during the reign of the emperor Zeno, through a revelation from the saint himself.

At Corinth, Saint Sosthenes, a disciple of Saint Paul the apostle. At Aquileia, the feast of the holy martyrs Felix and Fortunatus, under the persecution of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian and the governor Eusimius. Since they were brothers by birth and fervent in the faith of Christ, they were first suspended on the rack, with burning lamps placed beside their sides; but these were soon extinguished while the martyrs sang psalms. Afterwards they were drenched over the belly with boiling oil and finally beheaded.

B. The day before the Ides of June.—At Rome, on the Aurelia road, at the fifth milestone, the passion of the holy martyrs Basilides, Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius. Grodegandus, bishop of Metz, transferred Nabor and Nazarius, together with the martyr Gorgonius, from Rome to Gaul, with the permission of Pope Paul of Rome, in the year 765 of the Lord’s Incarnation. The aforementioned bishop placed Saint Gorgonius in the monastery called Gorze, Saint Nabor in the monastery called Nova Cella, and Saint Nazarius in the monastery called Lorsch, where signs and miracles frequently occur in the healing of the sick and weak.

At Milan, the feast of the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus the boy. Saint Nazarius was instructed and baptized by blessed Clement. Anolinus, after afflicting him for a long time in prison during the fury of Nero’s persecution, ordered him to be struck with the sword together with the boy Celsus, whom Nazarius himself had raised. Christians stole their bodies and buried them in their own gardens; blessed Ambrose discovered them through a revelation from the Lord.

And the burial of Saint Odolfus, presbyter.

[Col. 0945A]

C. The Ides of June.—At Rome, the feast of Saint Felicula, virgin. When the count Flaccus wanted to take her as his wife after Petronella’s death and sought to terrify her, saying, “Choose one of these two things: either be my wife or sacrifice to the gods,” he received this answer from her: “I shall neither be your wife, because I have been consecrated to Christ, nor shall I sacrifice to idols, because I am a Christian.”

Then Flaccus handed her over to the deputy, who had her shut in a dark room without food for seven days. Afterwards they brought her to the virgins of Vesta, where she remained another seven days without food, since she would in no way accept food from their hands. Then she was raised onto the rack and ordered to be tortured until she gave up her spirit. Her body was then thrown into a sewer; Saint Nicomedes the presbyter took it out and buried it seven miles from the city of Rome.

In Africa, Lucianus and Fortunatus.

D. Eighteenth day before the Kalends of July.—The prophet Elisha, who is buried near Samaria in Palestine, where Obadiah also rests, and where John the Baptist—than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women—is also buried, and where many miracles occur.

At Soissons, the passion of the holy martyrs Valerius and Rufinus. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Basil, bishop, brother of Gregory and Peter. At Vienne, Saint Etherius, bishop.

E. Seventeenth day before the Kalends of July.—In Sicily, the holy martyrs Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia. Blessed Vitus, mature in virtue even in childhood, was first tempted by his sacrilegious father Hylas to abandon the worship of God; then, beaten by the judge Valerian with rods, he remained steadfast in confessing Christ.

Afterwards he was returned to his father. When his father was planning to torment him, Vitus boarded a ship at an angel’s instruction, accompanied by his tutors Modestus and Crescentia, and reached the territory of Thani Agrigentinus. Because the daughter of the emperor Diocletian was tormented by a demon, he was sought out and brought to the emperor, and healed his daughter by prayer.

But when the impious emperor could not persuade him in any way to agree to the idols, he ordered him, together with Modestus and Crescentia, to be bound with iron chains and cast into a most loathsome prison. Afterwards Diocletian ordered them to be thrown into a cauldron heated with resin, pitch, and lead. When they emerged from the cauldron unharmed, a savage lion was released upon them; but it immediately began to lick their feet.

Finally, while they were resting beneath a tree beside the river called the Siler, they surrendered their souls to the Lord. The most illustrious woman Florentia gathered the saints’ bodies and buried them with spices in a place called Marianus.

In Moesia, Saint Hesychius, who was crowned with martyrdom under the governor Maximian.

F. Sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.—Near the city of Besançon, Saints Ferreolus, presbyter, and Ferrutio, deacon, who were sent by blessed Irenaeus, bishop and martyr of Lyons, to preach the word of God. Under the judge Claudius they were stretched on the rack and scourged; then shut in prison, they preached the word of God the next morning with their tongues cut out. Afterwards thirty awls were driven into the hands, feet, and breasts of both; finally they were struck with the sword.

In the city of Mainz, the passion of Saints Aureus and Justina, his sister, who were killed in a church by the Huns while they were devastating Germany.

Likewise at Antioch, Saints Cyricus and Julitta, his mother. The former, after dreadful scourging, also had lime with vinegar and mustard put into his mouth. Then they were fastened with nails, their eyes torn out, and thrust into prison. Afterwards, having their scalps removed and their skin flayed, they were roasted on burning coals upon a bronze bed. Finally, after being mangled with iron instruments and having their tongues cut out, they completed the course of their martyrdom by beheading. Four hundred and four others suffered with them.

On the same day, the burial of Saint Alexius the confessor.

[Col. 0949A]

G. Fifteenth day before the Kalends of July.—At Rome, two hundred and sixty-two holy martyrs, who were placed on the old Salaria road, at the Cucumber Hill.

On the same day, Saint Vultmarus the confessor, a man of admirable holiness and religious devotion. In the city of Nantes, Saint Similianus, bishop and confessor. At Lyons, the burial of Saint Aurelianus, bishop of Arles. Near Vienne, Saint Domnolus, bishop. In the city of Orléans, Saint Vitus, presbyter and monk, whose life shone with miracles. Among other deeds, while the other brothers were weighed down by sleep, he raised a dead monk in the church from death through prayer poured out to the Lord.

A. Fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.—At Rome, on the Ardeatine road, the feast of the holy brothers and martyrs Marcus and Marcellianus, of illustrious lineage, sons of Tranquillinus and Marcia. They first suffered imprisonment for the faith; afterwards, when seized by the judge Fabianus and tied to a stake, sharp nails were driven into their feet. When one day and one night had passed and they continued praising God, they were pierced through the sides with spears and departed in the glory of martyrdom to the starry realms.

At Antioch, the passion of Marina, virgin, who suffered many tortures for the name of Christ under the prefect Olibrius: chains, prisons, scourges, and the rack. The devil also tested her in the form of a dragon and likewise in the form of an Ethiopian, but he was overcome by the sign of the holy cross. Finally she was beheaded by the aforementioned prefect and completed her life in holy martyrdom.

B. Thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.—At Milan, the feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius. After being shut up together in one upper room for ten years, occupied with readings, prayers, and fasts, they reached the palm of martyrdom in the eleventh year, when they were seized by the count Astachius. He first ordered Gervasius to be beaten with leaden clubs for so long that he breathed out his spirit; then he ordered the other, namely Protasius, to be beaten with rods and beheaded.

Their bodies were secretly taken away by Philip, a religious man, together with his son, and buried in a marble sarcophagus in his house. Much later, under the emperor Theodosius, blessed Ambrose discovered their tombs through a revelation from the Lord and found their bodies so incorrupt that they seemed to have been killed that very day. When they were being carried into the city, a man who had long been blind received his sight by touching the bier.

At Ravenna, Saint Ursicinus the martyr, who, under the judge Paulinus, completed his martyrdom by being beheaded after excessive tortures.

C. Twelfth day before the Kalends of July.—Pope Sylverius, who sat in Rome for one year. With the consent of the emperor Justinian, he was deposed by the patrician Belisarius, became a monk, and died in exile as a confessor.

At Rome, Saint Novatus, brother of Timothy, presbyter, who was instructed by the blessed apostles. Concerning him, the Pastor writes in the Acts of the virgins Pudentiana and Praxedis.

And the translation of Saint Zeno the martyr and Saint Florentia the virgin.

D. Eleventh day before the Kalends of July.—At Mainz, the feast of Saint Albanus the martyr, who, under the emperor Diocletian, traveled from the island of Nansia with Saint Theonestus and Ursus and came to Milan. Leaving there, with the Lord’s help he reached Gaul, where he remained in God’s service, ready for martyrdom for the name of the Savior.

After blessed Ursus had received martyrdom in the city of Augsburg, Theonestus reached Mainz with Albanus. While preaching the word of God there, Albanus, his disciple, completed his martyrdom and was buried near the aforementioned city.

At Syracuse, the feast of the holy martyrs Rufus and Martia. At Rome, Saint Demetria, virgin, who was the daughter of the blessed Faustus. When she was being brought before the impious Julian on account of the faith of Christ, she gave up her spirit in confession. She was buried by the blessed presbyter John near her mother, Saint Daphrosa, and her sister Bibiana, near the Lucian Palace.

E. Tenth day before the Kalends of July.—In Britain, Saint Albanus the martyr, who, in the time of Diocletian, was beheaded in the city of Verulamium after scourging and cruel tortures. When he fell to the ground, the eyes of the man who struck him fell out as well. One of the soldiers also suffered with him because, although ordered to strike him, he refused, terrified by the divine miracle: he had seen the blessed martyr, as he hastened toward the crown of martyrdom, make the channel of the intervening river passable by prayer.

In the city of Nola in Campania, the feast of Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor, concerning whom blessed Gregory narrates in the Book of Dialogues.

And the burial of blessed Nicetas, bishop of the city of Remesiana, and of Consortia, virgin. And the passion of ten thousand martyrs.

F. Ninth day before the Kalends of July.—The feast of John the presbyter, whom the impious Julian ordered to be beheaded on the old Salaria road before an image of the sun, without a hearing. His body was gathered and buried by blessed Concordius the presbyter near the councils of the martyrs.

In Britain, Saint Etheldreda, virgin and queen, whose body, after being buried for eleven years, was found incorrupt.

And the vigil of Saint John the Baptist.

G. Eighth day before the Kalends of July.—The Nativity of the blessed John the Baptist, forerunner of the Lord, son of Zachariah and Elizabeth. Filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb, he was strengthened for Israel and was moved by the Spirit in the deserts. He was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his loins; his food was locusts, and he ate wild honey.

In the thirtieth year of his age, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pilate was governor in Judea and the kingdom of the Jews had already been divided into four principalities, he came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.

At Rome, Fiscus and Lucia, with twenty-two others. At Autun, the burial of Saint Simplicius.

A. Seventh day before the Kalends of July.—At Beroea, Saint Sosipater, a disciple of Saint Paul the apostle.

At Alexandria, Saint Gallicanus the martyr, who was converted to the faith of Christ through the preaching of John and Paul. After performing innumerable good deeds, he was struck with the sword by the count Raucianus and departed to Christ.

At Rome, Lucia the virgin, with twenty-two others, and Accia the king. At Thessalonica, the saints Bigatus and Lantanus, and the falling-asleep of Saint John the Evangelist.

B. Sixth day before the Kalends of July.—At Rome, John and Paul, brothers. The first was superintendent and the second chief secretary of Constantia the virgin, daughter of Constantine. Since they daily refreshed companies of Christians from the resources that the most holy virgin of Christ had left them, this became known to Julian. He sent the military commander Terentianus, and they were beheaded inside their own house; Terentianus, however, later became a Christian.

On the same day, Saint Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, who was appointed in place of blessed Publius as bishop of Athens and gathered together by faith and diligence the Church, which had been scattered in great terror.

[Col. 0957A]

C. Fifth day before the Kalends of July.—In Galatia, the blessed Crescent, bishop, a disciple of Saint Paul the apostle.

At Tibur, a city of Italy, the feast of Saint Simphorosa, wife of the blessed Gethulius, with her seven sons. Their mother suffered death with the greatest steadfastness for the Christian faith under the emperor Hadrian. He ordered her to be beaten with palms and then hanged by her hair. Since she could not be overcome in any way, he ordered her to be thrown into a river with a stone tied to her.

Her brother Eugenius, a leading member of the municipal council, gathered her body and buried it. The next morning the emperor ordered seven stakes to be fixed and the sons to be stretched upon racks there. Crescentius was pierced through the throat, Julianus through the breast, Nemesius through the heart, and Primitivus through the navel. Justinus, stretched out by his limbs, was cut apart through each joint and articulation of his body. Stacteus was pierced with innumerable spears until he died on the ground. Eugenius was split [the reading is uncertain] from the breast down to the lower parts.

On the following day Hadrian ordered their bodies to be thrown into a deep pit. The priests of the temples gave that place the name “At the Seven Violent Deaths.”

At Córdoba, Saints Zoilus and nineteen others.

At the city of Ephesus, the festival is celebrated of the seven sleeping brothers: Maximianus, Malchus, Marcianus, Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine.

D. Fourth day before the Kalends of July.—Pope Leo, who sat in the city of Rome after the apostle Peter, forty-seventh in succession, for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days. Explaining the catholic faith with many bishops, he condemned the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies and through his efforts caused the most holy Council of Chalcedon to be assembled.

He established that, during the celebration, one should say “the holy sacrifice,” and that a nun should not receive from a bishop the blessed veil for her head unless her virginity had first been tested and confirmed.

At Alexandria, the holy martyrs Plutarchus, Serenus, Heraclides, and Heron; likewise Serenus, Potamiena, Marcella, Catechumena, Hera, and Nomia, who attained the baptism of martyrdom. Among them Potamiena the virgin shone especially brightly. After countless struggles, she was consumed by the punishments of fire together with her venerable mother Marcella and departed from earth to heaven.

At Lyons in Gaul, Saint Irenaeus, bishop, who, together with almost the entire population of his city, was crowned with glorious martyrdom under the emperor Severus. He was buried by the presbyter Zacharias in the crypt of the basilica of blessed John the Baptist, beneath the altar.

And the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul.

E. Third day before the Kalends of July.—At Rome, the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, who suffered under the consuls Bassus and Tuscus.

In the second year of Claudius, after his episcopate of the Church of Antioch and his preaching to the dispersion of those of the circumcision who had believed in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, Peter was sent to Rome to overthrow Simon Magus. There he held the priestly chair for twenty-five years, until the final year of Nero, by whom he was fastened to a cross and crowned with martyrdom, with his head turned toward the earth and his feet raised upward, declaring himself unworthy to be crucified as his Lord had been.

He was buried in the same city at the Vatican, beside the Triumphal Way, where the whole world honors him in celebration. He ordained two bishops, Linus and Cletus, to provide all priestly ministry in the city of Rome for the people and for those arriving there; he himself devoted his attention to prayer and preaching.

[Col. 0962A]

F. The day before the Kalends of July.—It is certain that Paul came to the faith in the same year in which the Lord suffered. Twenty-five years after the Lord’s Passion, that is, in the second year of Nero, after he had filled the region from Jerusalem to Illyricum with the Gospel of Christ, Paul was sent to Rome in chains. As he himself writes in the Second Epistle to Timothy, he was rescued from the mouth of the lion—that is, from Nero, the most savage persecutor—and preached the Gospel of Christ also in the regions of the West.

In the fourteenth year of Nero, therefore, on the same day as Peter, he was beheaded at Rome for Christ and buried on the Ostian Way, thirty-seven years after the Lord’s Passion.

Likewise, the blessed Lucina, a disciple of the apostles; and at Limoges, Saint Martial, bishop and confessor. At Cologne, Saints Asclepius and Pamphilus.

**JULY.** It has thirty days; the moon, thirty.

[Col. 0961D]

G. Kalends of July.—On Mount Hor, the burial of Aaron the priest.

On the same day, at Tours, Saint Monegundis, virgin. At Vienne, blessed Martin, the third bishop of that city, sent to the aforementioned city by the apostles. In the territory of Lyons, the burial of the most blessed Domitianus, abbot, who first led an eremitical life there; and the feast of Areleffus the confessor.

And the octave of Saint John the Baptist.

A. Sixth day before the Nones of July.—At Rome, in the cemetery of Damasus, the feast of the holy Processus and Martinianus, who were baptized and instructed by the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, together with forty-seven persons of both sexes.

When the prefect Paulinus heard this, he sent soldiers and seized them, ordering them to be thrust into custody. The next day he commanded that their mouths be battered with stones, that they then be suspended on the rack, stretched out, and beaten with sinews and clubs, and that flames be placed around their sides.

After three days Paulinus, seized by a demon, expired. The prefect Caesarius reported these events to Nero, and Nero ordered him, saying: “Let them not be delayed, but let them be destroyed more quickly.” Then they were brought outside the walls of the city of Rome and struck down with the sword.

The blessed Lucina gathered their bodies and buried them with spices on her estate.

Likewise, the holy martyrs Aristio, Crescentianus, Eutychianus, Urbanus, Vitalis, Justus, Felicissimus, Felix, Marcia, and Simphorosa, all of whom were crowned with martyrdom in Campania.

B. Fifth day before the Nones of July.—Pope Leo, who sat in Rome for ten months. He was most eloquent and sufficiently instructed in the divine Scriptures, learned in both Greek and Latin. He held the sixth holy synod, which was celebrated in the imperial city, where Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter, Macarius, Stephen, Polychronius, and the new Simon were condemned for preaching one will and one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

At Edessa in Mesopotamia, the translation of the body of Saint Thomas the apostle. At Caesarea in Pontus, the feast of Saint Gregory, bishop and martyr, brother of the blessed Athenodorus, bishop, who by praying turned a certain pond into dry land.

C. Fourth day before the Nones of July.—The prophets Hosea and Haggai.

At Tours, the translation of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor, the establishment of his bishopric, and the dedication of his basilica.

In Africa, Saint Jucundianus the martyr, drowned in the sea. At Sirmium, the feast of Saints Innocentia and Sabbatia, with thirty others. At Bourges, the feast of Saint Laurianus the martyr and the burial of Saint Dalricus, bishop and confessor.

D. Third day before the Nones of July.—In Syria, Saint Domitius the martyr, who by his virtues grants many benefits to the inhabitants.

At Rome, the feast of Saint Zoa, wife of the blessed martyr Nicostratus. While she was praying at the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, she was seized by pagans and brought to the commander of the naval arena. He first thrust her into a very dark prison and for six days deprived her of every comfort of light and nourishment. On the seventh day she was suspended by the neck and hair, her body hanging below; smoke was applied beneath her, and she gave up her spirit in confessing the Lord.

In Sicily, Agatho and Tryphena. And at Tomis, Marinus, Theodotus, and Sodepha.

E. The day before the Nones of July.—The prophets Isaiah and Joel; the octave of the apostles; and the first entry of the blessed apostle Paul into the city of Rome, in the second year of Nero.

Likewise, the burial of the blessed Goar the confessor, who was born in Aquitaine and, in the time of Hildebert, king of the Franks, was a true worshiper of God from infancy. Afterwards consecrated a presbyter there, he abandoned his homeland and parents and chose to serve God freely in the province adjoining the banks of the Rhine, called Trigoria and belonging to the diocese of Trier, remaining there until the end of his life.

At Rome, the feast of Saint Tranquillinus the martyr, father of the saints Marcus and Marcellianus. Having believed in the Lord Jesus Christ through the preaching of blessed Sebastian, he was seized by pagans and stoned while praying at the confession of blessed Paul on the octave of the apostles, and so completed his martyrdom.

F. The Nones of July.—At Rome, the blessed martyrs Nicostratus, chief secretary, Claudius, registrar, Castorius, Victorinus, and Simphorianus, whom blessed Sebastian taught to believe in Christ and Saint Polycarpus the presbyter baptized.

While they were searching for the bodies of the saints at the mouths of the Tiber, they were seized and brought before the prefect of the city. The judge was Fabianus, who urged them to sacrifice, pressing them for ten days with threats and blandishments, but he could not move any of them in the least. He then made a report about them to the emperors, who ordered them to be tortured three times. Since they yielded under no compulsion, the emperors ordered them to be thrown into the sea. Bound with enormous weights, they were cast into the waves of the sea, so that in a pure place amid the waters they might celebrate the crown of martyrdom.

At Alexandria, Saint Pantaenus, an apostolic man. At Vienne, Eooldus, bishop. Likewise at Alexandria, Parnienus, Heraclas, Elias, Apollonius, Anobus, and nineteen others. On the same day, Saint Willibaldus the confessor.

G. Eighth day before the Ides of July.—In the district of Austria, at the fortress called Würzburg, situated beside the River Main, the feast of Saint Kilianus the martyr and his two companions. Coming from Ireland, the island of the Scots, they preached the name of Christ in the aforementioned places and were slaughtered there for confessing the truth under a certain judge named Gozbert. Afterwards, through many signs, they became manifest as true martyrs of Christ.

In Palestine, the feast of Saint Procopius. Brought from Nicopolis to Caesarea, he was beheaded by the enraged judge Fabianus after his first confident reply.

In Asia Minor, Saints Aquila and Priscilla, his wife, whom Luke mentions in the Acts of the Apostles.

[Col. 0969B]

A. Seventh day before the Ides of July.—At Rome, at the flowing Gutta, Saint Zeno the martyr and ten thousand two hundred and three others.

At the city of Tyre, the feast of the holy Anatholia and Audax, under the emperor Decius. When Anatholia had healed many sick, lunatics, and demoniacs in a town of Picenum, she was brought, by order of Faustinianus, to the city of Tyre and tormented with various kinds of blows. Afterwards she was shut up for the entire night with a serpent and was not harmed at all. Indeed, she rescued from being devoured the very Marsus who had released the serpent, a man named Audax, and converted him to Christ and to martyrdom.

After this, because he confessed the truth, he was placed in custody and soon crowned with a capital sentence. The virgin of Christ herself was pierced through while standing with her hands extended in prayer, so that the sword entered through her right side and came out through her left. She was buried in the morning by the citizens of Tyre. She suffered on the seventh day before the Ides of July; but Audax, because he was from the East, was transferred there by his wife and children.

B. SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF JULY. At Rome, the seven brothers, sons of Saint Felicity: namely Januarius, Felix, Philip, Silvanus, Alexander, Vitalis, and Martial, under Publius, prefect of the city, in the time of the emperor Antoninus. Of these, Januarius, after scourging with rods and imprisonment, was killed with leaded clubs; Felix and Philip were put to death with clubs; Silvanus was killed by being thrown over a precipice; Alexander, Vitalis, and Martial were punished by capital sentence. In Africa, the commemoration of Januarius, Marinus, Nabor [Col. 0972A] and Felix, who were beheaded; their bodies were transferred to Milan.

C. FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF JULY. The translation of Saint Benedict, abbot. For after his monastery had been ravaged by the pagans, as he himself had foretold while alive, his body was found through the Lord’s revelation and transferred to Gaul, and it was honorably buried in the monastery called Floriacum. The body of blessed Scholastica, his sister, was likewise transferred and buried through the devotion of the religious in the region of the Cenomani. In Lesser Armenia, in the city of Nicopolis, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Januarius and Pelagia, who [Col. 0973A] were tortured for four days on the rack with claws and fragments of pottery and completed their martyrdom. At Rome, Saint Pius, pope, who sat in the episcopate for nineteen years.

D. FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF JULY. At Aquileia, the commemoration of Saint Hermagoras, the first bishop of that city and a disciple of Saint Mark the Evangelist. In Cyprus, the commemoration of blessed Nason, an ancient disciple of Christ. In Caesarea [Col. 0974A], Saint Deus. At Rome, Saint Cletus, pope, who sat there for twelve years. At the command of blessed Peter, he ordained twenty-five priests in the city of Rome. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter. At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of Saint Juvenc the bishop.

E. THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF JULY. The commemoration of Saint Silas the apostle. Since he was one of the first brothers and had been sent by the apostles to the churches of the gentiles with Barnabas and [Col. 0975A] Judas, he was later taken up by the apostle Paul and, full of the Lord’s grace, diligently completed the ministry of preaching; afterward, glorifying Christ through his sufferings in Macedonia, he came to rest. At Antioch, the passion of Saint Margaret, virgin.

F. DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF JULY. In Pontus, the commemoration of Saint Phocas, bishop of the city of Sinope, who under the emperor Trajan and the prefect Africanus overcame imprisonment, chains, iron, and even fire for Christ. His relics are kept in the basilica of the apostles in the city of Vienne in Gaul. At Lyons in Gaul, the commemoration of Saint Justus, bishop and confessor.

G. THE IDES OF JULY. At Nisibis, the commemoration of Saint James, bishop, a man of great virtue, so that through his prayers the city was often delivered from danger [Col. 0976A]. At Rome, in the port, Eutropia, Zosima, and Bonosa, sisters. In Alexandria, Saints Philip, Zeno, Narseus, and ten infants. On the same day, the raising of the body of the holy emperor Henry. At Carthage, the commemoration of Saints Florentius, Catulinus the deacon, Januarius, Julia, and Justa, who are buried in the basilica of Faustus; and at Sirmium, Agrippinus, Secundinus, Maximinus, Martial, and James, bishop. On the same day, Saint Reginswinda, virgin, and the dispersion of the apostles.

A. SEVENTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. At Ostia, the commemoration of Saint Hilarinus, who, under the persecution of Julian, refused to sacrifice and suffered martyrdom, being beaten with clubs. At Antioch in Syria, the commemoration of Saint Eustachius, bishop [Col. 0977A] and confessor, who under the emperor Constantius, on account of the catholic faith, was driven into exile to the city of Trajanopolis in Thrace, where he came to rest.

B. SIXTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. At Carthage, the commemoration of the Scillitan saints, namely Speratus, Narthal, Cythinus, Bethurius, Felix, Aquilinus, Letacius, Januaria, Generosa, Beffia, Donata, and Secunda, under the prefect Saturninus. After their first confession of Christ, they were sent to prison and fastened to a stake; in the morning they were beheaded with a sword. Their relics, together with the bones of blessed Cyprian and the head of Saint Pantaleon the martyr, were transferred from Africa to Gaul and are venerated at Lyons in the basilica of blessed John the Baptist and of Saint Alexius the confessor.

[Col. 0978A]

C. FIFTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. At Carthage, the commemoration of Saint Gundenes, who, during the consulship of Plautianus and Zeta, was tortured four times at different periods by being stretched on the rack and tormented by the dreadful tearing of claws; she was also afflicted for a very long time by the squalor of prison, and finally was struck down with a sword. In the city of Metz, Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor, illustrious for holiness and the grace of miracles, who loved the eremitical life and came to rest in a blessed death. Also, at Milan, Saint Maternus, bishop and confessor.

D. FOURTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. In the Thebaid, our holy father Arsenius, of whom it is related in the Sayings of the Elders that, because of the abundance of his tears, he always kept a handkerchief [Col. 0979A] in his bosom or in his hand for wiping them. In Spain, in the city of Seville, the commemoration of Saints Justa and Rufina, who were seized by the governor Diogenianus and tortured by stretching on the rack and tearing with claws; afterward they were thrust into prison and afflicted by hunger and suffering. After this the governor ordered that, wherever he went, they should follow him barefoot. At last Justa breathed out her spirit in prison; her body was thrown into a well and recovered by Bishop Sabinus, then buried in the cemetery at Seville. Rufina’s neck was broken and her body was consigned to the fire; the faithful took care of her relics.

E. THIRTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. The commemoration of Saint Epaphras, who, ordained bishop of Colossae by blessed Paul, distinguished for his virtues, won the palm of martyrdom through manly combat for the sheep entrusted to him [Col. 0979B]; he was buried in that same city. Also the commemoration of blessed Joseph, who was called [Col. 0980A] Justus and who, together with blessed Matthias, was appointed by the apostles to complete the number twelve. But when Matthias filled the place of Judas the betrayer, blessed Joseph nevertheless continued to serve in preaching and holiness, enduring much persecution from the Jews for the faith of Christ; he came to rest in Judaea with a most victorious end. It is related of him that he drank poison and, because of the Lord’s faith, suffered no harm from it. In Damascus, Saints Sabinus, Maximinus, Julian, Macrobius, Cassia, Paula, and ten others. In Africa, the commemoration of Lucian, Peter, Amabilis, Nunna, and Victor of Thebaid.

F. TWELFTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. Saint Daniel the prophet. At Rome, Saint Praxedes, virgin. Together with her sister Potentiana, she had been instructed by blessed Pudens, their father, in all chastity and the divine law. After performing many acts of almsgiving and burying the saints, she came to rest in a blessed death [Col. 0980B] and was buried beside her sister at Rome on the Salarian Way. On the same day, the passion of Saint Victor, bishop of Marseille, who under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian was slaughtered for the faith of Christ by the governor Aterius, together with the soldiers Alexander, Felician, Longinus, and Deutherius.

[Col. 0982A]

G. ELEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. The commemoration of Saint Mary Magdalene, from whom, as the Gospel relates, the Lord cast out seven demons. Among her other outstanding gifts, she was also worthy to be the first to see Christ risen from the dead. And the falling-asleep of blessed Syntyche, who lies buried at Philippi, concerning whom the blessed Apostle writes to the Philippians [Col. 0983A]: “I urge Euodia, and I appeal to Syntyche, to be of the same mind in the Lord.” At Ancyra in Galatia, the commemoration of Saint Plato the martyr, whose acts are preserved. At Antioch, Cyril the bishop and Andrew.

A. TENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. At Ravenna, Saint Apollinaris, bishop. He was ordained at Rome by blessed Peter the apostle and sent to Ravenna. He also preached in Aemilia, in the regions of Corinth, in Mysia, along the bank of the Danube, and in the regions of Thrace. In these places he was sent into exile, and wherever he arrived he performed countless miracles and endured sufferings. For after he had been beaten excessively and again beaten with clubs for a long time, he was placed barefoot upon burning coals; again beaten, he was hung on the rack and tortured; his mouth was crushed with a stone; he was shut up under a very heavy weight of iron in a dreadful prison [Col. 0983B], and stretched upon a wooden frame. There he was neglected by men but publicly fed by an angel. Then he was chained and sent into exile. In exile he was again beaten for a long time with clubs and again bound by pagans; he was beaten and wounded, then sent back to prison and beaten, and so completed his martyrdom under Caesar Vespasian and the patrician Demosthenes. He governed the Church for twenty-eight years and four days.

B. NINTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Vincent [Col. 0984A]. At Emerita, a city of Spain, the commemoration of Saint Victor the soldier, who, together with his two brothers Tricinus and Antinogenes, underwent various examinations and punishments and completed his martyrdom. At Tyre in Italy, which is near Lake Bolsena, the commemoration of Saint Christina, virgin. Believing in Christ, she broke the golden and silver gods of her father Urbanus, the prefect, and distributed them to the poor. For this reason, at her father’s command, she was afflicted with slaps and torn by scourging; weighed down with iron, she was thrown into prison. After she had been mangled for a very long time and with extreme cruelty, she threw pieces of her flesh into her father’s face. When she was bound to a wheel, with fire placed beneath it and oil poured over her from above, the escaping flame killed a thousand pagans. Returned to prison, she was healed and restored by an angel’s visitation. Then, when she was thrown into the sea with a great weight of stone, she was delivered by angelic protection. After her father had been killed on account of his crimes, his successor Dion afflicted her with many punishments. Finally, the successor of the aforementioned man, named Julian, after the fiery furnace in which she remained unharmed for five days, and after serpents had been sent against her by a magician but overcome through the faith of Christ, ordered her to be pierced with arrows after her tongue had been cut out. Thus she completed the course of her martyrdom in the eleventh year of her age. On the same day, the vigil of Saint James the Apostle.

[Col. 0985A]

C. EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST. The commemoration of Saint James the apostle, son of Zebedee. In Cilicia, in the city of Samos, the commemoration of Saint Christopher the martyr, who under King Dagnus was crushed with iron rods and saved by the power of Christ from the flames of a raging fire; finally, pierced by the blows of arrows, he completed his martyrdom by decapitation. In Spain, in the city of Barcelona, the commemoration of Saint Cucuphas the martyr, who came from the city of Scillium and suffered at Barcelona under Galerius, Maximian, and Rufinus.
