Also the blessed martyrs Ptolemy and Lucius, who suffered under Antoninus Pius and his son, and Saint Aquilinus, bishop and confessor.

F. **Thirteenth day before the Kalends of November**.—In Gaul, at the city of Agaunum, Saint Caprasius, martyr. While he was hiding in a cave to avoid the fury of the persecution, he heard that the blessed virgin Faith was bravely struggling for Christ. [Col. 1077A] Encouraged to endure suffering, he prayed to the Lord that, if He truly judged him worthy of the glory of martyrdom, the clearest water might flow from the stone of that cave. When the Lord immediately granted this, he confidently hastened to the arena of combat and, fighting bravely, earned the palm of martyrdom. Also the feast of Simplicius.

G. **Twelfth day before the Kalends of November**.—At Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Dasius, Zoticus, and Gaius, with twelve soldiers. On the same day, our holy father Hilarion, whose life Jerome wrote as full of virtues. Also the feast of Saint Asterius, priest of [Col. 1078A] Pope Callistus. After he had lifted Callistus’s body from the well and buried it, Alexander the emperor, hearing of this six days later, ordered Asterius to be thrown from a bridge. His body was found and buried in the same city by certain Christians. This is written in the Passion of Saint Callistus, as is the departure of Saint Viator, lector. In Cologne, eleven thousand holy virgins.

A. **Eleventh day before the Kalends of November**.—At Jerusalem, the blessed Mark, who, being a most distinguished and learned man, was the first from the Gentiles at Jerusalem to receive the priestly office of that city after the bishops from the circumcision; not long afterward he completed his course by martyrdom. Also the blessed Salome, who is read of in the Gospel as caring, with the other holy women, for the Lord’s burial. At Adrianople in Thrace, the passion of Saints Philip, bishop, Severus, priest, Hermes, deacon, and Eusebius. During the savage persecution of Christians, they opposed the emperor Julian’s order, through wicked governors, to close and plunder the churches. For this reason they were afflicted by the governor Bassus and also by Justin with many tortures—that is, prisons, chains, scourges, and finally the burning of flames. But strengthened by the Lord’s power, they persevered to the end in confessing his name.

[Col. 1079A]

B. **Tenth day before the Kalends of November**.—At Antioch in Syria, the feast of Saint Theodore, priest. During the persecution of the [Col. 1079B] impious Julian, under the prefect Julian, his uncle, when the church of Antioch had been stripped and all religious people dispersed by fear of him, Theodore remained intrepid in the church. Ordered to be seized, after the punishment of the rack and many extremely severe tortures, burning lamps were also placed around his sides. But when these were extinguished by divine power, and the soldiers holding them fell [Col. 1080A] on their faces, terrified by the sight of angels, and, believing in Christ, refused their impious service, Julian ordered them to be drowned in the sea. To them the blessed Theodore said: “Go before me, brothers; I, overcoming the enemy, will follow the Lord.” Thus he completed his martyrdom by execution with the sword. In Spain, the feast of Saints Servandus and Germanus, who, after scourging, the squalor of prison, the hardship of hunger and thirst, and the toil of a very long journey—which, loaded with chains, they endured at the command of the governor Viator—finally completed the course of their martyrdom with their necks struck by the sword. At Cologne, Saint Severinus, archbishop and confessor. At Vienne, Saint Joditus, bishop. Also Saint Venantius, abbot.

C. **Ninth day before the Kalends of November**.—At Venusia, a city of Apulia, the feast of Saints Felix, bishop of the city of Tubrocis, Audactus and Januarius, priests, and Fortunatianus and Septimus, lectors. In the time of Diocletian, in their city of Tycus, they were long tormented by the procurator Magnellianus with many chains and imprisonments; then, in Africa and Sicily, they finally completed their course by execution with the sword. They were honorably committed to burial between Carthage and Utica. At Nicomedia, the feast of Severus and Dorotheus.

[Col. 1080B]

[Col. 1081A]

D. **Eighth day before the Kalends of November**.—Boniface, pope, who sat at Rome for three years. He was buried on the Salarian Way beside the body of Saint Felicitas. He decreed that a slave should not be made a cleric or be subject to the municipal council or to any other obligation. In Gaul, at the city of Soissons, the feast of Saints Crispinus and Crispinianus, who, during the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, were stretched on racks and beaten with clubs. After their fingers had been pierced with awls and strips of skin had been cut from their backs, they were finally slaughtered with the sword and obtained the crown of martyrdom. At Périgueux, the feast of Saint Fronto, who was ordained bishop at Rome by the blessed Peter and sent with the priest George to preach the Gospel. [Col. 1082A] When George died on the third day of the journey, the grieving Fronto returned to the Apostle. He took Peter’s staff and placed it upon the body of the deceased, restoring his companion from death. Then, coming to the aforementioned city, he converted a great multitude of that people to Christ and, distinguished by many virtues, rested in peace. At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the feast of forty-six soldiers who were baptized together by the blessed Pope Dionysius and immediately beheaded by order of the emperor Claudius.

E. **Seventh day before the Kalends of November**.—In Africa, the feast of Saints Rogatianus, priest, and Felicissimus, who were crowned with illustrious martyrdom during the persecution of Decius and Valerian. The blessed Cyprian writes to the confessors in a letter, in these words: “Follow,” he says, “in all things Rogatianus, the glorious old priest, who by religious virtue and divine favor is making for you a way to the glory of our time. Together with our brother Felicissimus, ever calm and sober, he received the attack of the raging crowd and first prepared lodging for you in prison; in a certain sense your guide, he now also goes before you.” At Nicomedia, the feast of Lucian and Filorus, Heraclides and Martial. On the same day, Saint Amandus, confessor.

F. **Sixth day before the Kalends of November**.—In Spain, at the city of Ávila, the feast of Saints Vincent, Sabina, and Cristetes. They were first stretched on the rack so violently that all the joints of their limbs were loosened; [Col. 1083B] then their heads were placed upon stones and crushed with powerful bars until their brains were dashed out, and thus they completed their martyrdom under the governor Datianus. At the fortress of Thyla, the feast of Saint Florentius, martyr. At Rome, Evaristus, pope, who sat for nine years, was crowned with martyrdom under Trajan and buried in the Vatican. He appointed two priests in the city [Col. 1084A] and ordained seven deacons to attend the preaching bishop. And the vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.

G. **Fifth day before the Kalends of November**.—The feast of the holy apostles Simon the Cananaean, who is also written as the Zealot, and Thaddeus, who is also read as Judas of James and elsewhere is called Lebbaeus, which is interpreted as *corcuculus* (“little heart”; the Latin form is retained here because the precise intended term is uncertain). Thaddeus is said to have preached in Mesopotamia, and Simon in Egypt. From there they entered Persia together; after subjecting an innumerable multitude of that nation to the faith and seeing the Church of God already widely established, they completed their martyrdom there in due course and finished their blessed contest. They were honorably buried by the Christian peoples whom they themselves had begotten for the Lord. At Rome, Saint Cyrilla, daughter [Col. 1084B] of Caesar Decius, who was slaughtered with the sword by the emperor Claudius and buried by the priest Justinus with her mother beside Saint Hippolytus. Also Saint Fidelis, martyr.

A. **Fourth day before the Kalends of November**.—The feast of Saint Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, a man praiseworthy for holiness, patience, and faith. Once, on the solemn day [Col. 1085A] of the Easter vigils, oil ran out for the lamps; then he suddenly commanded the nature of water to be changed into oil. He departed to the Lord at the age of one hundred and sixteen. At Sidon, Saint Zenobius, priest, who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian. At Vienne, the deposition of the blessed Theodorus, abbot. In Lucania, Saints Hyacinthus, Quintinus, Feliciana, and Lucinius. On the same day, Saint Felix, deacon and martyr.

B. **Third day before the Kalends of November**.—At Rome, the feast of Saint Pontianus, [Col. 1086A] pope and martyr, whom the emperor Alexander sent into exile with the priest Hippolytus on the island of Sardinia, where he died. At Tingis, the passion of Saint Marcellus, centurion, who completed his martyrdom by beheading under Agricola, acting in place of the prefects of the praetorium. In Africa, two hundred and twenty martyrs. At Antioch, the blessed Serapion, bishop.

C. **Day before the Kalends of November**.—At Rome, the blessed Nemesius, [Col. 1087A] deacon, and his daughter Lucilla, whom the holy pontiff Stephen baptized and whom he appointed deacon. Nemesius completed his martyrdom by beheading, together with his daughter, under Valerian and Gallienus, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. His body was buried in the same place by the blessed Pope Stephen; afterward it was lifted by the blessed pontiff Sixtus on the day before the Kalends of November [Col. 1088A] and reverently placed in a crypt. In Gaul, at the town of Vermand, the feast of Saint Quintinus, who suffered under the emperor Maximian. Fifty-five years later he was found, when an angel revealed his body, and he was buried on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. And the vigil of All Saints. On the same day, Saint Wolfgang, bishop and confessor.

**November has thirty days and the moon thirty.**

[Col. 1087C]

D. **Kalends of November**.—The Feast of All Saints. For when Pope Boniface made his request, the emperor Phocas ordered that the old sanctuary called the Pantheon, which had previously been built by Domitian, should, after the filth of idolatry had been removed, become a church of the blessed ever-virgin Mary and [Col. 1088C] of all the martyrs. Thus, where once the worship had been offered not to all gods but to demons, thereafter the memorial of all the saints would be celebrated. From that time it was observed in the city of Rome on the Kalends of November as a solemn and universal feast. In Gaul, however, at the urging of the bishop Gregory, of holy memory, the most devout emperor Louis, with the consent of all the bishops of his kingdom and empire, [Col. 1089A] decreed that the Feast of All Saints should solemnly be observed every year forever on the aforesaid day. The whole Church received this holy decree with reverent spirit.

At the fortress of Dijon, the feast of Saint Benignus, priest, who, together with Antiochus, his fellow priest, and Thyrsus, deacon, was sent from the East into Gaul by Saint Polycarp. When Count Terentius learned through his preaching of him, he ordered Benignus, bound and beaten, to be brought before him; and, after again hearing the steadfastness of his words, he ordered him to be beaten with extremely hard sinews. After this he was stretched on racks and beaten, then committed again to prison. In the morning he destroyed the idols by prayer and was led back to prison. Ten red-hot awls were driven into his hands, and with molten lead his feet were fixed into a perforated stone; twelve savage dogs were shut in with him [Col. 1089B] for six days. An angel brought him heavenly bread, removed the awls, and freed him from the lead and iron. After this, Terentius ordered his neck to be beaten with an iron bar and his body pierced with a lance. When this had been done, a snow-white dove ascended from the prison to heaven before the eyes of the Christians, and a very sweet fragrance, as though from paradise, followed. The blessed Leonilla came and, after embalming it with spices, buried the body not far from the prison.

Also Saints Caesarius, deacon, and Julianus, priest. Caesarius, coming from Africa to Terracina, a city of Campania, in the time of Claudius, was publicly seized by Firminus, the pontiff, while he was denouncing the idolaters, and confined in custody. After being tormented there for many days, he was handed over to Leontius, the consul of Campania. Since Leontius could not overcome him by words, he ordered him, bound, naked, and with his hands tied, to be dragged before his own chariot all the way to the temple of Apollo. When Caesarius arrived there, the temple collapsed at his prayer and killed the pontiff Firminus. After this, Luxurius shut him in the first prison of the city, where he remained for one year and one month. Then Luxurius brought him out into the forum. While Caesarius was praying, he was surrounded by heavenly light, so that Leontius himself believed, clothed the naked Caesarius in his own military cloak, was baptized, and received the body and blood of the Lord from the hand of the priest Julianus. Without delay, after a prayer had been spoken over him, Leontius gave up his spirit on the third day before the Kalends of November. Then Luxurius ordered Julianus and Caesarius to be placed in a sack and thrown into the sea. They were cast back onto the shore that same day and buried by Eusebius, a man of God, near the city of Terracina. That same Eusebius later suffered martyrdom with Felix, priest. Also the deposition of Saint Severinus, monk, from the city of Tibur, and of Saint Mary, martyr.

E. **Fourth day before the Nones of November**.—The feast of Saint Victorinus, bishop of Poitiers, who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian. At Laodicea, the blessed Theodotus, bishop, a man adorned not only in words but also in deeds and virtues. He had indeed been a physician by profession, but by the Lord he was transferred to the medicine of souls, truly incomparable. He excelled almost all men in faith, mercy, zeal, vigilance, and every excellent discipline. He also labored greatly in the divine Scriptures and then rested, buried in a good old age. Also Saint Ambrosius, abbot of the monastery of Agaunum. At Vienne, Saint George, bishop of that city. In Africa, Saints Publius, Victor, Hermes, Justus, and Papias.

F. **Third day before the Nones of November**.—The feast of Saint Quartus, a disciple of the apostles. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saints Germanus, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Vitalis, who nobly endured martyrdom during the persecution of Decius. At Vienne, Saint Domninus, glorious bishop. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Pirminius, bishop and [Col. 1093A] confessor, and of Saint Hubertus, bishop and confessor.

G. **Day before the Nones of November**.—At Alexandria, the blessed Hierius, priest, a man of keen intellect. In Gaul, at the city of Rennes, the feast of Saint Amantius, bishop and confessor, whose life was glorious in holiness and miracles. At Autun, the blessed Proculus, bishop. In Gaul, at Bourges, the deposition of the blessed Illusor, a child and confessor. In Africa, the feast of Primus, Caesar, Gregory, [Col. 1094A] Porphyrius, Amantius, Saturninus, and Victorina.

A. **Nones of November**.—Zechariah the prophet, father of John the Baptist. In the city of Terracina in Campania, the feast of Saints Felix, priest, and Eusebius, monk, in the time of the emperor Claudius. Eusebius had buried the holy martyrs Julianus and Caesarius, and while praying at their tombs had converted many to the faith; Felix the priest baptized them. [Col. 1095A] Both were seized by Leontius, the son of Leontius the consul, chiefly because Caesarius had made his father a Christian. They were brought before his tribunal but were not overcome. Then they were shut in prison, and that same night, when they refused to sacrifice, they were beheaded and thrown into the river. Their bodies reached the sea and were left on the shore. They were found by a certain priest named Quartus, from Capua, who immediately placed them on a vehicle and carried them to his hut. Carefully searching, he also found their heads, joined them to the bodies, and buried them beside Saint Caesarius.

[Col. 1096A]

B. **Eighth day before the Ides of November**.—At Tumissa in Africa, the feast of Saint Felix. On the occasion of his solemnity, the blessed Augustine appears to explain a certain psalm to the people, saying: “The martyr Felix is truly fortunate, both in name and in crown; today is the celebration of his feast.” In the East, at the city of Theopolis, ten holy martyrs, who are said to have suffered under the Saracens in the Acts of the Forty Saints. In the city of Limoges, in the province of Aquitaine, Saint Leonard, confessor, a disciple of Saint Remigius, bishop.

C. **Seventh day before the Ides of November**.—At Alexandria, the blessed [Col. 1097A] Achilleas, bishop, distinguished in learning, faith, manner of life, and conduct. Also at Perugia in Italy, Saint Herculanus, bishop, and Saint Amarantus, who was martyred at the city of Albi. The deposition of Willibrord, bishop, of the English people, a most holy man and exceptionally distinguished by the grace of miracles. He was ordained at Rome by Pope Sergius and sent to Germany to preach, and there he also rested. Also Saint Rufus, bishop and confessor of Metz, who was transferred from that city, with the consent of Bishop Drogo, into the district of Worms, to an estate called Oternheim, in the time of the emperor Lothair and King Louis. There, too, his holiness shone forth through many virtues. In Africa, the feast of Rogatus and Donatus.

[Col. 1097B] **D. 6th day before the Ides of November.**—At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, who suffered in the time of the emperor Diocletian for the name of Christ, because they refused to worship the gods of the pagans. For although they were distinguished craftsmen, and knew better than all the imperial artisans how to carve images in marble stones, and although the emperor was greatly pleased by their skill in the art, nevertheless, when philosophers accused them because they refused to adore false gods, Diocletian ordered that they all be enclosed in leaden coffins and thrown into the river. Simplicius also suffered with them; they had converted him from the practice of paganism [Col. 1098A] to the faith of Christ. After forty-two days, a certain Christian named Nicodemus came, raised the bodies of the martyrs together with the coffins, and honorably placed them in his own house. They suffered on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

On that same day, the feast of the holy Four Crowned Martyrs, namely Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus. When they were being compelled to sacrifice, they resisted and gave no assent whatsoever to the impious rites, remaining steadfast in the faith. This was reported to the emperor Diocletian, who immediately ordered that they be beaten to death with leaded scourges before the statue of Asclepius. He ordered their bodies to be thrown into the street to the dogs; they lay there unharmed for five days. Then Christians came, gathered the bodies, and buried them.

On the Via Labicana, at the third milestone from the city, in a sand-pit beside the bodies of the holy martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius. Nevertheless, two years after the passion of these five martyrs, since their names could not be found, the blessed bishop Melchiades decreed that the anniversary of the Four Crowned Martyrs should be commemorated under the names of the five holy martyrs. In the intervening years, however, their names were also revealed to a certain holy man. The feast therefore remained, as it had been established, celebrated together with the feast of the other martyrs, and the place continued to be distinguished by the name of the Four Crowned Martyrs. On the same day, a commemoration of All Saints.

[Col. 1099A] **E. 5th day before the Ides of November.**—The feast of the blessed martyr Theodore, in the time of the emperors Maximian and Maximinus. When he was a soldier under Brycha, commander of a legion, he was sent to prison; after the door had been sealed, he was there comforted by a divine visitation. After several days he was again brought before the governor, suspended on a tree, and his sides scraped with iron claws until his ribs were exposed. Then, with his hands bound behind his back, he was thrown into a furnace. Looking around, he saw Cleonicus weeping in the crowd; Cleonicus had been brought in with him as a recruit. He cried out: “Cleonicus, I am waiting for you; hurry and follow me.” When the blessed martyr was already surrounded on every side by balls of flame, he poured forth a prayer, praising the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and thus gave his holy soul back to Christ.

A certain woman named Eusebia gathered his body, wrapped it in a clean shroud, and transferred it to her estate, to a place called Euchata. At Bourges, Saint Ursicinus, who was ordained at Rome by the successors [Col. 1100A] of the apostles and sent as the first bishop to that city.

**F. 4th day before the Ides of November.**—In the territory of Agde, the feast of the holy martyrs Tiberius, Modestus, and Florentia, who, tortured by various torments in the time of Diocletian, completed their martyrdom. On the same day, Saint Martin, pope, who, on account of the Catholic faith, was seized from the church by order of the heretical emperor Constantius through the exarch Theodore, brought to Constantinople, and exiled to Cherson in the province of Lycia; there he ended his life, still shining forth to this day in that place through many signs of virtue. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Leo, bishop. At Antioch, the feast of Demetrius, bishop, Amnesius, Eustochius, and their companions. At Orléans, the deposition of the blessed Monitor, bishop.

[Col. 1100B] **G. 3rd day before the Ides of November.**—In Gaul, at the city of Tours, the feast of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor, whose life and teaching are made clear to nearly all the faithful through the miracles that the Lord performed through him. It is unnecessary for us to recall anything further here, because Sulpicius described his life, virtues, and signs plainly and in brilliant prose; likewise Gregory, bishop of that same city, discussed them most fully in his books of *Miracles*.

At Scythia, the metropolis of Phrygia, the passion of Saint Menas the martyr. During the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, although he was a soldier of noble birth from the province of Egypt, he renounced earthly military service and first served the heavenly King in secret devotion in the desert. Then, coming forth publicly during the birthday celebrations of the aforesaid emperors, he openly declared before them that he was a Christian. He was handed over to the commander Pyrrhus for torture, who ordered him confined in prison for as long as the emperors’ birthday festivities lasted.

When the celebration had ended, at the commander’s order, his hands were tied with ox sinews [Col. 1101B], and he was beaten by the soldiers with rods until the streets were filled with his blood. Then he was stretched on the rack, his flesh torn away; torches were applied to his sides, and his wounds were rubbed with haircloth, while burning coals were placed upon them. He was also dragged, with hands and feet bound, over thorns and iron stakes. He was severely beaten on the neck and jaws with leaded scourges, yet remained unmoved in the praise of almighty God. Finally, he was ordered to be executed by the sword [Col. 1102A], and his body burned. Christians secretly snatched it from the midst of the fire, embalmed it with clean linen cloths and spices, and cared for it with due veneration. At Lyon, the feast of Saint Veranus, bishop.

**A. The day before the Ides of November.**—In Africa, a commemoration of Saints Arcadius, Paschasius, Probus, and Eutychianus. Born in Spain, they were held dear and distinguished by Genseric, king of the Vandals, because of their deserved wisdom and faithful service. Since they would in no way permit the Arian perfidy [F. *in Arianam*—“into the Arian”], to which he himself was devoted, to be adopted, they provoked the barbarian to the most furious anger. First proscribed, then driven into exile, tortured with the most atrocious punishments, and finally killed by various deaths, they gloriously and wondrously fell in illustrious martyrdom. [Col. 1102B] Paulinus, a boy and the brother of Eutychianus and Paschasius, was beaten for a long time with clubs and condemned to the lowest form of slavery.

At Cologne, Saint Cunibert, bishop and confessor. Likewise Saint Melanius, bishop of the city of Rennes. At Vienne, Saint Hesychius, bishop. In Africa, the holy martyrs Aurulus and Publius. In Caesarea of Cappadocia, Saints Germanus, Theophilus, Caesar, and Eusebius.

[Col. 1103A] **B. The Ides of November.**—At Ravenna, the feast of the holy martyrs Valentinus, Solutor, and Victor. At Tours, the deposition of Saint Brictius, bishop and confessor. In the province, at the city called Aquis, the blessed Metrius, a most renowned martyr.

**C. 18th day before the Kalends of December.**—At Heraclea, a city of Thrace, the feast of the holy martyrs Clementinus, Theodotus, and Philominus. At Alexandria, the blessed Serapion, whom the persecutors under Decius subjected to the most cruel punishments in his own house. First they dislocated all the joints of his limbs; then they threw him down from the upper parts [Col. 1104A], and thus he became a martyr of Christ. Likewise Heraclius, Martialis, Donatus, and many others.

**D. 17th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of Saint Felix, bishop, who had been distinguished by the glory of miracles from the fifteenth year of his age, and who completed his martyrdom with thirty others under the governor Martianus. The priest Elypidius buried his body in the church at Nola. In Africa, the feast of the martyrs Secundus, Fidentianus, and Varicus.

[Col. 1105A] **E. 16th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, a man of admirable faith, life, and teaching. At Capua, the feast of Saint Augustine. In Africa, Vitalis and Januarius, and the deposition of the blessed abbot Othmar.

**F. 15th day before the Kalends of December.**—At Alexandria, the blessed Dionysius, bishop, often distinguished by many confessions and renowned for the variety of his sufferings and tortures, in the time of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. In Spain, at the city of Córdoba, the passion of the holy martyrs Acisclus and Victoria. At Orléans, a city of Gaul, the deposition of Saint Anianus, bishop and [Col. 1106A] confessor. At Vienne, Saint Mamatus, bishop and confessor. Saint Gregory, our father and wonder-worker, of Tours.

**G. 14th day before the Kalends of December.**—At Antioch, the feast of Saint Romanus. When, in the time of Diocletian, the prefect Asclepiades burst into a church, Romanus urged the other Christians to resist him. Therefore the prefect first had him stretched on the rack, then severely beaten with leaded scourges. After this he had his jaws scraped with a very sharp razor. Then, at Romanus’s request, he ordered a small boy to be brought in. Romanus invoked the name of Christ and asked him whether it was better to worship one god or several [Col. 1107A], so that the prefect might be confounded by the boy’s confession. When the boy said that one must believe in one God alone, Asclepiades, enraged, ordered him to be hanged from a stake, beaten, and finally beheaded. His name was Barulas.

Romanus, meanwhile, was again suspended on the rack and torn with claws. He was led to a blazing pyre into which he was to be thrown. But while he prayed, a sudden, flooding rain came and extinguished it. After this the prefect ordered his tongue to be cut out. When this had been done, Romanus praised Christ in a very clear voice. He was shut in prison and finally strangled with a noose; thus the holy martyr departed to Christ.

Likewise, in the same city, the feast of Saint Hesychius. Under the aforementioned emperor, when he was a soldier and had heard the order that anyone who did not sacrifice to idols should surrender his military belt, the emperor, for this reason, dressed him in a woman’s tunic and first assigned him to the women’s quarters. Then, after tying a huge stone to his right hand, he ordered him to be thrown into the river. The octave of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor.

[Col. 1108A] **A. 13th day before the Kalends of December.**—At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of Saint Maximus, priest and martyr, who suffered in the persecution of Maximinus and was placed at Saint Sixtus. The feast of Pope Gelasius, who sat in the episcopate for four years. He recalled Bishop Mesenum, whom his predecessor Felix had condemned, and restored him to communion and to his Church. He composed books against Eutyches and Nestorius.

At Vienne, the holy martyrs Severinus, Exuperius, and Felicianus. Likewise Saint Faustus, deacon, to whom God granted such grace that, when no one dared approach the saints who were being afflicted, he, together with his colleague Eusebius, was not denied entry to the confessors of Christ by any of the hostile parties. Thus the very old blessed Faustus was brought to completion by decapitation [Col. 1108B]. On the same day, at Marburg, the blessed Elisabeth, landgravine.

**B. 12th day before the Kalends of December.**—At Rome, Saint Pontianus, pope. When Maximinus was stirring up persecution against the priests of the Churches, Pontianus was deported to Sardinia with the priest Hippolytus. There he was beaten to death with clubs and completed his martyrdom. His body was brought back by Pope Fabian and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He sat in the episcopate for nine years, five months, and two days.

At Messina, a city of Sicily, Saints Ampelus and Gagus. At Chalon, Silvester, bishop. At Heraclea, Bassus, Dionysius, Agapitus, and forty others.

**C. 11th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of the blessed Rufus, concerning whom the blessed apostle Paul writes to the Romans: “Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.”

Likewise the feast of Saint Maurus the martyr, who had been a Christian from infancy and devoted himself to prayers and fasts. Under the emperor Numerianus and the prefect Celerinus, he was tortured by various punishments: first he was beaten with knotted clubs [Col. 1109B]; then his jaws were ordered to be crushed with leaded scourges; afterward he was suspended on the rack, scraped with claws, and burning lamps were applied to his sides; finally his head was cut off.

When African sailors recognized that his body had come from their homeland, they seized it. Wrapping it in clean cloths with spices, they placed it in a sarcophagus and wrote at his head: “Maurus, servant of God and of Christ Jesus, leaving this age for the faith of Christ, acquired eternal life.” The prefect Celerinus ordered the sailors to be arrested, but they all fled. Then he ordered the ship in which the martyr’s body lay to be filled with branches and burned in the middle of the sea after fire had been placed beneath it. But, with the Lord as pilot, the martyr was brought to the harbor of salvation wherever He willed.

[Col. 1110A] **D. 10th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of Saint Cecilia, virgin, in the time of the emperors Marcus, Aurelius, and Commodus. She thoroughly instructed her husband Valerian and his brother Tiburtius to believe in Christ, and then encouraged them to martyrdom.

After their martyrdom, Almachius, prefect of the city, had her seized and compelled to offer incense to demons. The attendants, observing her beauty and prudence, begged her not to abandon such dignity. But she sufficiently impressed upon them a pious counsel, and, seeing that they had been moved to believe in Christ, said to them: “Go and tell the wretched Almachius that I ask for a delay, and that I shall bring into my house one who will make you all participants in eternal life.”

Accordingly, Pope Urban came and baptized more than four hundred men and women. [Col. 1110B] Again Almachius ordered the blessed Cecilia to be brought before him. When he saw that she remained unconquered in her confession of faith, he ordered her to be taken to her house and burned there in the flames of the baths. Shut inside for an entire day and night, she remained unharmed and in perfect health as though in a cool place, while fires were continually fed with heaps of wood. When Almachius heard this, he sent someone to behead her. The executioner struck her three times but could not sever her head; she survived for three days. Then Saint Urban took away her body by night and buried her among his fellow bishops. Likewise Saint Mederasma, virgin.

**E. 9th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of Saint Clement. He was ordained the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter. [Col. 1111A] He divided the city into seven regions, assigning faithful notaries to investigate carefully the acts of the martyrs. At the command of the blessed Peter, he assumed the pontificate of the Church. Linus and Cletus are therefore written before him because they were ordained bishops for priestly ministry by the prince of the apostles himself.

At the command of Trajan, Clement was sent into exile across the Pontic Sea, into a desert. After calling many to the faith through his miracles and teaching, he was thrown into the sea with an anchor tied around his neck. But, when his disciples prayed, the sea withdrew for three miles, and they found his body in a stone coffin, in a marble temple, with the anchor beside it. In this martyrdom the disciple of Peter was crowned.

Likewise the feast of Saint Felicity, mother of seven sons who were martyrs; at the command of Antoninus she was beheaded for Christ. In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, the deposition of Saint Columbanus, abbot, founder of many monasteries and father of countless monks, who, renowned for many virtues, rested in a good old age. And Saint Drudo, confessor.

**F. 8th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of Saint Ignatius, bishop and martyr, who ruled the Church of Antioch as the third after the apostle Peter. Condemned to the beasts in the persecution of Trajan, he was sent to Rome in chains. There, in the presence of Trajan and with the senate seated around him, his shoulders were first crushed with leaden clubs; then his sides were torn with claws and rubbed with rough stones. Afterward his hands were stretched out and filled with fire, and his sides were burned with papyrus soaked in oil and set alight; then he was placed over coals scattered on the pavement, where his holy feet had stood. After the flaming bed, after his back had been torn and lacerated with claws, after vinegar and salt had been poured into his wounds, after his blessed body had been bound with iron chains and his feet enclosed in wood at the bottom of the prison, he remained there three days and nights without eating bread or drinking water.

While Trajan sat in judgment in the amphitheater and the entire Roman crowd gathered, Ignatius was bound and thrown before two lions. When he heard the roaring beasts already rushing toward him, he said in the ardor of suffering: “Roman men who watch this contest, I have not labored without cause, for I suffer these things not because of wickedness but because of piety. I am Christ’s grain; let me be ground by the teeth of the beasts, so that I may be found to be pure bread for God.” As he said this, the lions ran toward him and, falling upon him from both sides, suffocated him only; they did not touch his flesh.

Likewise at Rome, the feast of Saint Chrysogonus the martyr, who, by order of Diocletian, was thrown into chains for two years. There he endured much and was nourished by the alms of Saint Anastasia. Finally he was beheaded and thrown into the sea. The old priest Zoilus found his body, joined the severed head to it, and placed it in his chamber. And the feast of Saint Crescentianus the martyr, under the persecution of Maximian.

**G. 7th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of Saint Peter of Alexandria, [Col. 1114A] bishop, outstanding among the foremost. In the twelfth year of his episcopate, at the time of the emperor Maximian, he earned the crown of martyrdom by decapitation. At the same time, many other bishops from Egypt were slaughtered with him, together with almost six hundred and sixty clergy and laypeople.

While he was being held in prison and the entire population of Alexandria watched the prison doors out of love for their father, the wretched Arius—who was regarded as excommunicated and degraded by the blessed Peter because of his erroneous doctrine—learned of Maximian’s sentence against the blessed Peter. He hurried to the church, begging the clergy and people to intercede for him with the bishop, thinking that after Peter’s departure he himself would be made bishop.

Those who had come to make the request therefore began to plead with the blessed bishop for Arius. The holy bishop answered them with a great sigh: “Arius is already dead to God and cast away from the presence of God, because he has gravely blasphemed against the essence of the Godhead by teaching that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not of one essence and nature.”

Taking two priests, Alexander and Achillas, aside from the crowd, he said to them privately: “Although I am a sinner, I know that by a heavenly calling I have been summoned to this struggle of martyrdom. I therefore confess to you the mystery of God that has been revealed to me: after my martyrdom, you will succeed to my see and episcopate. You, Achillas, will be first, and Alexander after you.

“At this hour of the night, so that I may reveal everything to you about Arius: when I had completed the customary sacrifice of prayers to God, suddenly Christ my Lord appeared to me in the form of a boy. At his presence I was illuminated by an immense radiance and was unable to look upon his majestic face. He was dressed in a very white tunic, which, torn from top to bottom, he held together with both hands around his breast, in a manner covering his nakedness.

“When I saw him, I was seized with great fear, but at last, taking courage, I said to him: ‘What is this, Lord, that I see? Your tunic is torn from top to bottom.’ He answered me: ‘You deal with it every day and do not know how it was torn. Arius did this, for he separated from me the people of my inheritance, purchased with my blood.

“‘I now command and warn you: do not receive him into communion, and when those whom he has sent come to you to plead with you, do not grant him pardon. Make known to the two priests what I have revealed to you, so that after you they too may reject him by anathematizing him, lest the people be deceived by his error.’”

After addressing them with a word of exhortation and commending them to the Lord in whom they had believed, urging them to remain in the unity of the Catholic faith, he dismissed them in peace. On the same day, the passion of Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr of Christ, and of others.

**A. 6th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of Saint Linus, pope, who held the Roman Church after the apostle Peter for twelve years, three months, and twelve days. At the command of the blessed Peter, he decreed that a woman should enter the church with her head veiled. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried in the Vatican.

At Alexandria, the feast of the holy martyrs Faustus, priest, Didius, and Ammonius, who were slaughtered together with the blessed Peter, bishop of that city, at the command of Maximian. On the same day, the blessed bishop and martyr, under the emperor Antoninus, who, among other miracles, raised a dead man. At Rome, Syricius, bishop; and at Capua, Nicanor, Cassianus, and Felicissimus. At Autun, the deposition of Saint Amator, bishop. At Nicomedia, the blessed Marculus, priest and martyr, who endured the greatest persecutions in the time of the tyrant King Constans and was finally thrown down from a high cliff.

**B. 5th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of the holy martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, who, after other torments, were finally crucified and completed their martyrdom at Bologna in Italy. Their bodies had later been placed among the graves of the Jews and were wholly unknown to the Christian people. The blessed Ambrose, when the holy martyrs revealed themselves, found them at Bologna; after a church had been built, he placed them beneath the altar amid great joy among the faithful and the punishments of demons confessing the merits of the martyrs.

At Riez, a city of Gaul, the feast of Saint Maximus, bishop, who, endowed from his earliest age with the grace of every virtue, was first abbot of the monastery of Lérins and then bishop of the Church of Riez, renowned for signs and wonders. Finally, among his other magnificent deeds, while still alive he raised three dead men: one by touching the coffin in which he was being carried to the tomb. At Nicomedia, Marcellus, Peter, Numerius, Hierena, and Melosus. And the deposition of Bishop Optatus.

**C. 4th day before the Kalends of December.**—The feast of Saint Sosthenes, [Col. 1116C] a disciple of the apostles, and of Trophimus, concerning whom the Apostle writes [Col. 1117A] to Timothy: “But I left Trophimus sick at Meleti.” Ordained bishop at Rome by the apostles, he was the first sent to the city of Arles in Gaul to preach the gospel of Christ there. From his fountain, as the blessed Pope Zosimus writes, all Gaul received the streams of faith. He rested in peace at that same city.

The feast of Pope Gregory, who ruled the Church for ten years. He established that the priest should say in the canon: “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the presence of your Majesty, O Lord our God, throughout the whole world; among whose company [may we be numbered], and so forth.” He was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

On the same day, Saint Rufus the martyr, whom the Lord Jesus Christ, together with his entire household, won through the martyr Chrysogonus, and whom Diocletian, together with his entire household, punished and made a martyr of Christ.

In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Papius and Mansuetus, bishops, who during the Vandal persecution under the Arian king Genseric, in defense of the Catholic faith, were burned over their entire bodies with glowing iron plates and completed their glorious contest. At that time other holy bishops also—Quodvultdeus, Valerian of Carthage, Urbanus, Crescens, the man called Habetdeus, Eustachius, [Col. 1118A] Cresconius, Crescentianus, Felix, Hortulanus, and Florentianus—completed the course of their lives in exile after being condemned.

At Vienne, Saint Philip, bishop of that city. In Syria, Trophimus, Theodolus, Expicatus, Erucerus, Eusebius, and Julius.

**D. 3rd day before the Kalends of December.**—At Rome, the feast of Saint Saturninus the martyr and Sisinnius the deacon. Under Maximian, they were first condemned, together with other servants of God, to dig sand for the construction of Diocletian’s baths. Then they were tortured for a long time in prison, where they taught and baptized many pagans. Brought out again, bound in chains and barefoot, they were ordered by Laodicius, prefect of the city, to be raised on the rack, stretched with sinews, and beaten with clubs and scorpions. Later he ordered flames to be applied to their sides [Col. 1118B], and, after they had been taken down from the rack, their heads to be cut off. Traso gathered their bodies and, with the priest John, buried them on his estate on the Salarian Way.

At Toulouse, the feast of Saint Saturninus, bishop, who, in the time of Decius, was seized by pagans in the Capitol of that city. Because all their gods became speechless at his presence and could give no response to those offering sacrifice, they tied him with ropes to a bull prepared for sacrifice. When the animal was goaded more violently, Saturninus was thrown from the highest tower of the Capitol down all the steps, his skull crushed, his brains scattered, and his whole body torn apart; thus he breathed forth a soul worthy of Christ. His body is venerated with due honor in the church. And the vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

**E. The day before the Kalends of December.**—At the city of Patras in the province of Achaea, the feast of the blessed apostle Andrew, whose name is interpreted “manly” or “beautiful,” the brother of Peter. He preached in Scythia. Seized by the proconsul Aegeas, and remaining steadfast in the faith of Christ and in the gospel, he was first shut in prison, then severely beaten before the proconsul. Finally, with his hands and feet bound to a cross and his whole body stretched with ropes so that his torture might last longer, he survived there for two days, never ceasing to teach the people what belongs to God.

When those who had believed in Christ were earnestly entreating the Lord that he be taken down and were pressing Aegeas to accomplish it, the apostle of the Lord, with the people standing around and the proconsul Aegeas working for his release, after speaking a prayer was surrounded for nearly an hour by heavenly radiance from above. As the light withdrew, he gave up his spirit and went to the Lord. The powerful matron Maximilla reverently took down his body and buried it.

At Saintes, the feast of Saint Trophianus, bishop, a man of virtue. At Rome, Castulus and Euprepes.

**DECEMBER.** It has 31 days; the moon, 29.

[Col. 1119B]

**F. Kalends of December.**—The feast of the holy martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria, who suffered at Rome in the time of Numerianus, under the judge Celerinus. Chrysanthus’s father, Polemius, was a distinguished man. He joined his son to a certain virgin who is known to have been from the noblest Roman family. Chrysanthus converted her to the faith of Christ and had her baptized.

It came about that through Chrysanthus a multitude of men and through Daria innumerable women flocked to the grace of Christ. The prefect Celerinus handed them over to the tribune Claudius, who assigned seventy soldiers to torture Chrysanthus. They bound him with raw sinews, but soon all the bonds were loosened. Then they placed him in a stocks, tightening his leg in its third notch; immediately the wooden stocks dissolved into ashes. Then they drenched him with the most foul-smelling human urine [Col. 1120B], saying, “So that you may lose your magic”; but the stench was changed into a sweet odor.

Next they bound him naked in fresh calfskin and laid him under the blazing sun, but through the power of the Lord the skin remained as soft as it had been. Then they bound his neck, hands, and feet with iron chains and shut him in a very dark place. At once the chains were loosened and a great light shone forth.

Daria, meanwhile, was placed in a public brothel, but a lion came from its cage and, by the Lord’s power, was given to protect her. It entered the chamber where the holy woman of God lay prostrate in prayer and prostrated itself beside her, so that it might drive away those who came near.

When Celerinus reported all these things to the emperor, he ordered them to be taken to the sand-pit on the Salarian Way, lowered alive, and covered with earth and stones. It happened that on their feast day an immense crowd of people gathered. This was reported to the emperor, who ordered the wall at the entrance of the crypt to be removed. Thus it happened that, while all were receiving the sacraments of Christ, they celebrated the glory of martyrdom; among them were Diodorus the priest, Martinianus the deacon, and very many clergy.

On the same day, the blessed Egilius, bishop of Noyon. At Rome, Candida and Umbonus.

**G. 4th day before the Nones of December.**—The feast of Saint Viniana the martyr, daughter of the blessed martyrs Faustus and Daphrosa. At the command of the sacrilegious emperor Julian, she was beaten with leaded scourges until she gave up her spirit. By the emperor’s order, her body lay in the forum for two days. Finally, it was secretly taken away at night by the priest John and buried in a house where her mother and her sister Demetria had already been buried, beside the Licinian palace.

At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Primentius, Pontianus, Piminus, Demetrius, and Juvianus. In Mauretania, Severus, Securus, Januarius, and Victorinus.

**A. 3rd day before the Nones of December.**—At Tingis, the capital of Mauretania, the feast of Saint Cassianus, priest and glorious martyr.

Likewise the holy martyrs Claudius the tribune, his wife Hilaria, their sons Jason and Maurus, and sixty soldiers, who all believed in Christ through the preaching of the blessed Chrysanthus. When this was reported to the emperor Numerianus, he ordered the tribune Claudius to be bound to a huge stone and thrown headlong into the middle of the sea [Col. 1122B], while the seventy soldiers, together with Jason and Maurus, the sons of Claudius, were punished by capital sentence.

At the place where they were beheaded there was an ancient mound. Christians cleared it during the night and buried all the bodies together on the Salarian Way. The holy Hilaria, a widow and martyr, gathered the bodies of Jason and Maurus; while she devoted herself to constant prayers, she departed to the Lord.

In the East, Mecrobius, Claudius, and Felix. At Nicomedia, Ambicius, Victor, and Julius. In Africa, Claudius, Crispinus, Magina, John, and Stephen. In Pannonia, Saint Agricola.

[Col. 1123A] **B. The day before the Nones of December.**—At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Symphronius and Olympius, in the time of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.

Symphronius was handed over to the tribune Olympius, who was to demand from him, under examination by punishments, the property of Nemesius. When questioned by the prefect, he replied: “If you are seeking the property of Nemesius, my master, I have already given it to poor Christians, since it belonged to him. But if you compel me to offer sacrifice, I sacrifice to Christ Jesus, my God, the sacrifice of praise.”

Olympius, enraged, had him stretched out on a rack and beaten with clubs. Then a golden statue of Mars together with its tripod was brought in. At Symphronius’s words it immediately melted like mud. When Olympius saw this, he, his wife Exuperia, and their son Theodolus prostrated themselves at Symphronius’s feet and did penance.

The blessed Pope Stephen was summoned. He came by night to Olympius’s house, baptized him, and baptized all who had believed in the house of Olympius. When the emperors heard this, [Col. 1124A] they sent orders that they be brought before them.

Symphronius was brought in burdened with iron chains, naked and wearing a halter, together with Olympius, his wife, and his son. Gallienus said to Olympius: “I am still delaying the infliction of punishments upon you, because I am uncertain about your conscience.” Olympius replied: “I did not act as Olympius, but as an impious and cruel man. I repent of these crimes and shed tears in the sight of Him whom I believe to be living and true.”

Then the sentence was given that they should be consumed by fire. They were led before the statue of the Sun; stakes were driven into the ground, and they were bound fast with their hands tied. Fire was set beneath a heap of branches and thorns. At the very beginning of the fire, they sang thanks to Christ and gave up their spirits. Saint Stephen, the bishop, gathered their bodies [Col. 1124B] and buried them. Likewise Heraclius, Christianus, and Pudens.

**C. Nones of December.**—In Africa, at the city of Thebeste, the feast of Saint Crispina. When she refused to sacrifice in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, she was beheaded at the command of the proconsul Anolinus.

Likewise the feast of Saint Dalmatius the martyr, and of the holy martyrs Crispinus, Felix, Julius, Potamia, Gratus, and seven others, and of Zelotus, Fortunatus, and Gattus.

**D. 8th day before the Ides of December.**—The feast of Saint Nicholas, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Myra.

In Africa, Saints Dionysia, Dativa, Leontis, Aemilianus the physician, and a religious man named Tertius; Boniface, Servius, Victrix, and Majoricus the young man. During the Vandal persecution under the Arian king Huneric, for confessing the Catholic faith and refusing to be rebaptized by the Arians, they were tortured with the most severe and countless punishments and deserved to be numbered among the confessors of Christ. Among them, Majoricus completed his palm-bearing course in the contest.

**E. 7th day before the Ides of December.**—At Alexandria, the blessed martyr Agathon. Although he was a soldier, when he stood by while the blessed martyrs were being torn apart—including Julian and Eunus, who persevered in the confession of the Lord Jesus Christ—he prevented certain people from mocking even the dead bodies of the martyrs. A cry then arose against him from the entire populace. The powerful soldier, now the Lord’s, was brought before the judge and, never becoming inferior in his confession, remained steadfast; he was condemned to death by decapitation for his piety.

At Saintes, the blessed abbot Martin, disciple of Saint Martin, bishop of the city of Tours, who rests in peace in the monastery he built. At Antioch, the feast of Polycarp and Theodorus. On the same day, the octave of Saint Andrew.

F. VI IDES OF DECEMBER.—The Conception of holy Mary, perpetual virgin. At Rome, the feast of Saint Eutychianus, pope, who ruled the Church for one year and, crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian, was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He himself also buried with his own hand, in various places, three hundred and forty-two martyrs. He decreed that only beans and grapes should be blessed as produce upon the altar. At Alexandria, blessed Macarius, under Decius. He was by birth a Pibycus; although the judge tried with many words to persuade him to deny his faith, he professed it with even greater constancy and was finally ordered to be burned alive. At Verona, the feast of Saint Zeno the martyr.

G. V IDES OF DECEMBER.—The feast of Saint Leocadia, virgin, who in the time of Diocletian and Maximian was subjected to the dreadful confinement of prison by Dacianus, governor of Spain, at Toledo. When there she heard of the most grievous tortures of blessed Eulalia and the other martyrs being killed by Dacianus, she fell to her knees in prayer and gave back her undefiled spirit to Christ. On the same day, blessed Cyprian, abbot of Petragorica, a man of splendid holiness. In Africa, the feast of Peter, Successus, Primitivus, Publicinus, and twenty others. At Trier, the burial of Saint Eucharius, bishop and confessor.

A. IV IDES OF DECEMBER.—At Rome, Saint Melchiades, pope, who sat in the episcopate for three years and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He decreed that no one should fast on Sunday or Thursday, because the pagans celebrated those days as though with a sacred fast. He also decreed that, from the consecration of a bishop, offerings should be distributed through the churches on account of the heretics. At Mérida, a city of Spain, the feast of Saint Eulalia. When she was thirteen years old, by order of the governor Dacianus she endured many tortures. Finally she was hung upon the rack and torn with hooks, while burning torches were placed against both sides of her; having breathed in the fire, she gave up her spirit. In the sight of Christians, her soul rose to heaven in the form of a snow-white dove. Her body hung upon the wood for three days by order of the governor. But to one who had been denied human gifts, divine gifts were granted. Snow fell from above upon the girl’s body, so that what the fire placed on either side had consumed in its own burning heat was covered with snowy whiteness and made white by divine grace. Thus the Christians reverently took it away and, with due devotion, buried it beneath the sacred altar, where it became illustrious through the grace of miracles. In the aforementioned city, the passion of Saint Julia, who was the virgin-companion of blessed Eulalia and clung to her as an inseparable companion and associate when she hastened toward her passion. Likewise at Seville, the city, the holy martyrs Carcophores, presbyter, and Abundius, deacon. During the persecution of Diocletian, under the judge Martianus, they were first cruelly beaten with clubs in their confession of Christ; then they were shut up in prison, denied food and drink. From there they were led out by an angel, and while preaching the word of God they were seized again; their faces were battered with stones, they were tortured once more on the rack, and afterward were tormented for a long time in prison. Finally they were struck with the sword. At Vienne, Saint Sindulfus, bishop and confessor.

B. III IDES OF DECEMBER.—Daniel the prophet. At Rome, Damasus, pope, who ruled the Church for eighteen years, three months, and two days. He decreed that the Psalms should be sung day and night throughout all the churches. He searched for many bodies of saints and found them, and also commemorated them in verse. Likewise at Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Pontianus, Praetextatus, and Tarso. Tarsus, while a powerful and wealthy Christian, supplied food to the holy martyrs condemned to prison and the mines. Through the blessed Sisinius and Cyriacus, he himself too was soon arrested by Maximian and deserved to receive the palm of martyrdom with two others. At Amiens in Gaul, the holy martyrs Victoricus and Fuscianus. In Spain, Saint Eutychius, whose acts are preserved, and Saint Gentianus the martyr.

C. THE DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF DECEMBER.—The holy martyrs Hermogenes, Donatus, and twenty-two others. [Col. 1131A] At Alexandria, the blessed martyrs Epimachus and Alexander, who, after being tortured for a long time and with great sufferings by chains and imprisonment, were finally ordered to be consumed by fire. Likewise, four holy women: Ammonaria, Mercuria, Dionysia, and another Ammonaria. When they displayed extraordinary constancy before the judge, and he was ashamed to be defeated by women, they endured unheard-of forms of torture and received the end of all things by the sword that struck them down. They were buried gloriously at Alexandria.

D. THE IDES OF DECEMBER.—At Syracuse, a city of Sicily, Saint Lucia, virgin and martyr, who suffered in the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian under Paschasius, the consular governor. This most noble woman of Syracuse, after distributing to the poor, widows, orphans, pilgrims, and those serving God everything that had remained to her from her parents, was denounced by her betrothed to Paschasius as a Christian and was driven to sacrifice to demons. When she refused in every way, she was handed over to pimps, so that they might invite the people to violate her chastity and she might be abused until she was reported dead. The pimps could not move her in the least. Then Paschasius ordered a great fire to be lit around her and pitch, resin, and boiling oil to be thrown over her; but she stood immovable in the name of the Lord. At last she was struck with a sword thrust into her throat. As long as she wished, she addressed the crowd standing around her, and she did not die at all until priests arrived and she received communion of the Lord’s body and blood. She was buried at the place where she was struck, and afterward a basilica was built over her body.

E. XIX KALENDS OF JANUARY.—At Antioch, the holy martyrs Drusus, Zosimus, Arsenius, Isidore, and Theodore. At Alexandria, the blessed martyrs Heron and Dioscorus, who, under the persecution of Decius, were torn apart by various tortures and finally handed over to the flames. Likewise blessed Lupicinus, eighth bishop of the Church of Vienne. In Cyprus, the feast of Saint Spyridon, bishop, a man of extraordinary blessedness, who was one of those confessors whom Maximian had condemned to the mines after gouging out their right eyes and cutting through their left knees. He also led a prophetic life. At Lyon in Gaul, Saint Viator, bishop. At Reims, Nicasius, bishop, and Eutropia, Aspedia, and Theodulus.

F. XVIII KALENDS OF JANUARY.—In Africa, Saint Valerian, bishop and confessor. During the Vandal persecution, when all the priests of the Lord were being forced by order of the Arian king Geiseric to hand over the divine mysteries or books—so much so that those impious Arians made shirts and undergarments for themselves from the altar cloths—he fought manfully lest he surrender the divine sacraments. He was ordered to be expelled alone beyond the city, with the command that no one should allow him to live either in a house or on a farm. Though he was more than eighty years old, he lay naked for a long time on the public road under the open sky, and thus completed the course of his blessed life in confession of the Catholic truth. At Orléans, blessed Maximinus, presbyter. In Africa, the feast of Faustinus, Lucius, Candidus, Caelianus, Marcus, Januarius, and Fortunatus.

G. XVII KALENDS OF JANUARY.—The martyrdom of the three holy men Ananias, Azariah, and Misael. In Tuscany, Saint Barbara, virgin, who suffered for Christ in the time of the emperor Maximian. First she was long afflicted by her father Dioscorus under harsh confinement; then she was handed over to the governor Marcianus, stripped, and beaten and torn with bull-hide thongs. Her wounds were rubbed with rough haircloth. Next she was shut in prison, where she was consoled by divine light. Then lamps were applied to her sides, her head was beaten with hammers, and her breasts were cut off. Afterward she was led through the streets and tormented for a very long time with scourges; finally she completed her martyrdom by the sword. At Ravenna, Valentinus, Navalis, Agricola, and Concordius. At Vienne, blessed Ado, bishop. On the same day, the translation of the holy martyrs Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrice.

A. XVII KALENDS OF JANUARY.—The translation of Saint Ignatius the martyr, who ruled the Church of Antioch as its third bishop after the apostle Peter. He suffered at Rome but was afterward buried at Antioch. On the same day, blessed Lazarus, whom the Lord raised from the dead, and blessed Martha, his sister. A church built not far from Bethany, where their house was nearby, preserves their venerable memory. In the East, at Eleutheropolis, the city, the passion of fifty holy martyrs who suffered under the Saracens.

B. XV KALENDS OF JANUARY.—The blessed martyrs Rufus and Zosimus, who belonged to those first disciples through whom the primitive Church was founded among Jews and Greeks. They rest near the Macedonian city of Philippi. In Africa, the feast of Saint Moyses the martyr. At Tours, Saint Gratianus, bishop, who was sent to that city from Rome and, renowned for many virtues, rested there in peace. At Laodicea, Theotinus and Basilianus. In Africa, Quintus and Simplicius.

C. XIV KALENDS OF JANUARY.—In Egypt, blessed Nemesius the martyr, who was first brought before the judge Aemilianus by false accusation as a robber. Once that charge had been cleared, he was accused on the ground that he was a Christian. In this matter the judge showed no mercy, but, after torturing him with doubled punishments, ordered him to be burned with the robbers. He did not know that by his cruelty he had given the excellent martyr a likeness to the Savior, who, for the salvation of the human race, endured the cross together with robbers. At Orléans, Saint Vitus, abbot, who was illustrious in the spirit of prophecy. At Nicomedia, Cyriacus, Palilus, Secundus, Anastasius, and Syddimus, bishops, and Gregory the pope.

D. XIII KALENDS OF JANUARY.—The blessed martyrs Ammon, Zeno, Ptolemy, Ingenius, and Theophilus. While they were standing before the tribunals at Alexandria, a certain Christian was being tortured by the judge and was already almost persuaded to deny the faith. The martyrs were bursting inwardly with anguish and, by their faces, eyes, and gestures, tried as if to raise up the man who trembled under torture. At times they also stretched out their hands and, by movements and postures of their entire bodies inclined in various ways, seemed eager to lift up the spirit of one who was falling. Then, turning toward them, and recognizing from their movements what they were professing about themselves, before the crowd could almost begin to attack them with shouts, they themselves burst into the midst and declared that they were Christians. Through their victory, Christ triumphed most gloriously over the enemy. At Rome, Zefennus, bishop, and the saints Liberatus and Bajulus. And the vigil of the apostle Thomas.

[Col. 1137A] E. XII KALENDS OF JANUARY.—The feast of blessed Thomas the apostle, who preached the Gospel to the Parthians and Medes and suffered in India. His body was transferred to the city that the Syrians call Edessa and was buried there with due honor. At Châlons, Saint Maximus, bishop, the first sent to that city from Rome; among innumerable other miracles, he raised a dead man. In Tuscany, the feast of Saints John and Festus.

F. XI KALENDS OF JANUARY.—At Rome, on the Lavican Way between the two laurel trees, the feast of thirty martyrs, all crowned on one day in the persecution of Diocletian. At Alexandria, blessed Chiridon, martyr. While he was managing the affairs of a certain powerful man for payment, he was ordered by him to sacrifice to idols. When he refused, he was compelled by insults; when he persisted, he was again coaxed with flatteries. When he despised both, he was pierced through the middle of the entrails with a very strong sharpened stake and handed over to death. On the same day, many other martyrs who, wandering in the deserts and mountains of Egypt, were consumed by hunger, thirst, cold, sickness, robbers, and wild beasts. All of them, imitating God’s chosen prophets, were crowned with the glory of martyrdom. Among them was the venerable old man Cheremon. He was bishop of an Egyptian city called Nicopolis; when he withdrew to the Arabian mountain with his aged wife, he appeared to no one thereafter. At Rome, the burial of Saint Felix, bishop. At Antioch, the feast of Saint Basileus; elsewhere, the passion of Theodosia, virgin, and Didymus, monk.

G. X KALENDS OF JANUARY.—At Rome, the feast of Saint Victoria, virgin, during the persecution of the emperor Decius. She had been betrothed to the pagan Eugenius, but refused both to marry and to sacrifice. Because a destructive dragon had been driven from those places, because other miracles had occurred, and because she had gathered virgins to serve the Lord, she was struck in the heart with a sword by the executioner Thaliarchus. Her body was treated with every reverence. At Nicomedia, twenty holy martyrs whom the persecution of Diocletian made martyrs for Christ through the most grievous tortures. Likewise at Rome, blessed Servulus, whom blessed Gregory remembers in his homilies. Elsewhere, Evaristus, Victor, and eight hundred thirty-two others.

A. IX KALENDS OF JANUARY.—The vigil of our Lord Jesus Christ. At Antioch in Syria, forty holy virgins who completed their martyrdom through various tortures in the persecution of Decius. On the same day, Saint Gregory, presbyter and martyr, at Spoleto, in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, under the judge Flaccus. Because he persevered steadfastly in the faith, his back was beaten with knotted clubs until it was broken, and his belly was ripped open and torn apart. Then his hands and feet were bound and he was placed upon a grating with wood beneath it. Immediately an earthquake occurred, and one district of the city of Spoleto collapsed and crushed more than three hundred people serving idols. Afterward he was bound with iron and thrust into prison under the guard of soldiers, where he was consoled by an angelic visitation. When he was led from prison, his knees were struck with iron hooks; his sides were also burned with flaming lamps. The blessed martyr said to the wicked judge: “Even if you destroy my whole body, my Lord Jesus Christ is present, who heals and strengthens me.” Then Flaccus ordered a certain Tircanus to drag blessed Gregory into the amphitheater and behead him. When this had been done, Tircanus ordered terrifying wild beasts to be released so that they might devour the body of the holy martyr, but none of them touched the sacred body. A woman named Abundantia asked for the martyr’s body; since she could not obtain it otherwise, she gave Tircanus thirty-five gold pieces, received the body, and buried the martyr as was fitting beside the stone bridge. At the city of Thropoli, Saints Lucianus, Metrobius, Paulus, Zenotus, Theutinus, and Drusus.

B. VIII KALENDS OF JANUARY.—JESUS CHRIST, THE SON OF GOD, IS BORN IN BETHLEHEM OF JUDEA, IN THE FORTY-SECOND YEAR OF CAESAR AUGUSTUS OCTAVIAN, IN THE THIRD YEAR OF THE 193RD OLYMPIAD, AND IN THE 752ND YEAR FROM THE FOUNDING OF THE CITY. The disturbances of all the nations throughout the world having been quieted, and the firmest peace having been established by divine ordinance through Caesar Augustus Octavian, at the time when Quirinius, sent to Judea by decision of the senate, was recording the census of persons and possessions, he consecrated the sixth age of the world by his most holy coming.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Anastasia. In the time of Diocletian she first endured the harshest and most pitiless confinement from her husband Publius; yet in it she was greatly consoled and strengthened by Chrysogonus, the confessor of Christ. Then she was tormented by the governor of Illyricum in a most severe and prolonged imprisonment, in which she was nourished for two months by heavenly food through Saint Theodora, who had suffered martyrdom earlier. Then she was placed on a ship with two hundred men and five hundred women, to be drowned in the sea; but she was carried to the Palmaria Islands, where she was stretched out by her hands and feet, tied to stakes, and fixed there, while a fire was lit around her middle. In it she completed her martyrdom, and all who had come with her gloriously completed their martyrdom by various deaths.

Among them was one man of utterly innocent character named Eutychianus. Although he was rich, after all his possessions had been taken from him he remained silent, thinking of nothing and fearing nothing except that he might lose the resources and riches of faith. Whenever he was heard, whenever he was questioned, he said nothing else: “Even he who cuts off my head cannot take Christ from me.”

Then Apollonia, a Christian matron, took up the body of blessed Anastasia and kissed it. Wrapping it in spices and clean linen, she built a basilica in her own garden and buried the martyr there as was fitting. On the same day at Rome, in the cemetery of Apronianus, the passion of Saint Eugenia, virgin. In the time of the emperor Gallienus, after many notable deeds of virtue and the sacred choirs of virgins whom she had joined to the Lord Christ, she was bound to a stone by Nycetius, prefect of the city, and thrown into the Tiber, but could not be drowned. Then she was shut inside a heated bath and found unharmed. Finally, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, as the Savior himself had previously revealed to her, she was killed in prison by the sword of an executioner. Christians took up her body and placed it not far from the city, on the Latin Way, in her own estate, where she herself had buried the remains of many.

C. VII KALENDS OF JANUARY.—In the Jerusalemite village of Caphargamala, the passion of Saint Stephen, Christ’s protomartyr, who not long after the Lord’s ascension was ordained deacon by the apostles. Blessed Luke the evangelist writes of his passion in the Acts of the Apostles.

On the same day, Saints Ignatius and Rufus, and Zosimus, pope. He sat at Rome for one year. He decreed that the deacon should cover the left side with cloths, and ordered that no cleric should offer a cup in public except in the cells of the faithful and clergy. Of their blessed struggle, Saint Polycarp writes in his letter to the Philippians, saying:

“I beseech all of you to devote yourselves to obedience and to meditate upon the endurance that you saw in the blessed men Ignatius, Rufus, and Zosimus, knowing that they did not run in vain, but in faith and righteousness, until they came to the place prepared for them by the Lord, since they became participants in his sufferings. They did not love the present age, but Christ, who died for them and for all and rose again.”

[Col. 1143A] D. VI KALENDS OF JANUARY.—The feast of blessed John the evangelist, whom the Lord Jesus loved greatly. When Domitian stirred up the second persecution after Nero, John was plunged into boiling oil and suffered nothing; afterward he was exiled to the island of Patmos, where he saw the Apocalypse. After Domitian was killed and his acts, because of his excessive cruelty, were annulled by the senate, John returned to Ephesus under the emperor Pertinax. Since he saw that the faith of the Church had been shaken in his absence by heretics, he promptly established it by setting forth in his Gospel the eternity of the Word of God.

The bishops of Asia had asked him to write against Cerinthus and the other heretics, and especially against the doctrine of the Ebionites then arising, who asserted that Christ had not existed before Mary. For this reason he was compelled to undertake the sacred work of writing the Gospel. He persevered until the reign of Trajan, founded and governed all the churches of Asia, and, worn out by old age, died sixty-eight years after the Lord’s passion, at the age of ninety-nine. He was buried near that same city.

At Rome, Dionysius, pope, who sat in the episcopate for six years; he was buried on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus. He gave churches to presbyters, assigned and established the parishes of the diocese. And the episcopate of Saint James, the Lord’s brother, who was the first of the Jews to be ordained by the apostles at Jerusalem.

E. V KALENDS OF JANUARY.—At Bethlehem of Judea, the feast of the Holy Innocents. When Herod learned of Christ’s birth through the report of the Magi, he ordered them killed in the thirty-fifth year of his reign. In the thirty-sixth year he died miserably and deservedly from dropsy, with worms swarming throughout his body.

F. VI KALENDS OF JANUARY.—David the king. Likewise at Arles, the feast of Saint Trophimus, bishop and confessor, a disciple of the apostles Peter and Paul. On the same day, Saint Crescentius, a disciple of the apostle Paul and the first teacher of the Church of Vienne. In Africa, the feast of Domninus, Victor, Primianus, and Lybosus, bishop. At Rome, Callistus, Felix, and Boniface, bishops, in the cemetery of Callistus. On the same day, Saint Thomas, archbishop and martyr of Canterbury.

[Col. 1145A] G. III KALENDS OF JANUARY.—At Spoleto, the passion of Saint Sabinus, bishop; Exuperantius and Marcellus, deacons; and Venustianus with his wife and children, under Maximian Augustus.

Blessed Sabinus, being distinguished in all divine instruction, was arrested by Venustianus, governor of Tuscany, together with the two deacons Exuperantius and Marcellus and many clerics. Venustianus offered him his god Jupiter, which he kept in his bedroom, fashioned wonderfully from stone and clothed in golden garments, to be worshiped. Blessed Sabinus took it in his hands, prayed, and immediately dashed it upon the pavement and shattered it.

When Venustianus saw this, he angrily ordered Sabinus’s hands to be cut off, and Marcellus and Exuperantius to be hung upon the rack in his presence, beaten with clubs, their sides scraped with hooks, and fire placed beneath them. Having done this, they gave up their spirit in confession of the Lord. But he ordered Bishop Sabinus to be thrust into prison.

A fisherman and a presbyter, hearing of this, gathered the bodies of the saints and buried them beside the road on the day before the Kalends of January. Serena, a Christian widow caring for Saint Sabinus the bishop, brought to the prison her nephew Priscianus, who was blind. Saint Sabinus then placed his severed hands over the boy’s eyes and restored his sight.

Those who were in custody saw this, and eleven of them threw themselves at his feet and were baptized. When this was reported to the governor Venustianus, his eyes became painful, and from the pain he could take neither food nor drink nor sleep. He sent his wife and two sons to bring blessed Sabinus from prison to his house.

When Sabinus had been brought, Venustianus fell weeping at his feet, together with his wife and sons, who repented and asked to be baptized. As soon as he had been baptized and lifted from the font, Venustianus felt no pain in his eyes. This was reported to Maximian, who, angered, ordered Sabinus to be condemned and Venustianus himself to be beheaded.

The tribune Lucius came and, without a hearing, killed blessed Venustianus with his wife and children in the city of Assisi. He brought Bishop Sabinus to the city of Spoleto and ordered him beaten until he died. The venerable Serena gathered his body, having preserved his hands in a glass vessel with spices and placed them beneath her house; she buried him about a mile from the city of Spoleto on the seventh day before the Ides of December. Nevertheless, his feast and that of the martyrs named above are celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 1147A] A. THE DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JANUARY.—At Rome, the feast of Sylvester, pope and confessor, who, after blessed Peter, was the thirty-fifth to sit and ruled for twenty-four years, ten months, and eleven days. Through his efforts, the most illustrious synod of three hundred and eighteen Fathers was celebrated throughout the world at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, during the consulship of Constantine Augustus and Licinius, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July. It was completed, however, during the time of Pope Julius. Sylvester decreed that no cleric should enter the court for any reason or plead a case before a judge, and that the sacrifice of the Church and altar should be celebrated upon a linen cloth.

In December he carried out six ordinations: forty-two presbyters, twenty-five deacons, and sixty-five bishops in various places. He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way. He decreed that chrism should be prepared by the bishop and that the presbyter should anoint the baptized. He also decreed that no layperson should dare bring an accusation against a cleric, and that deacons should wear dalmatics in church so that their left side might be covered.

At Sens, Saint Columba, virgin, under the emperor Aurelian. After overcoming the fire, she was struck by the sword.
