Likewise at Sens, the blessed Sabinus and Potentianus, who were sent by the blessed apostles to preach and made the aforementioned city illustrious by the confession of their martyrdom.

## BOLLANDIST EDITION

[Col. 0799]

# JANUARY

[Col. 0799A]

## 1.—ON THE KALENDS

The Octave of the Lord and, according to the flesh, his Circumcision. Also the feast of Almachius, who, when he said, “Today is the octave of the Lord’s Day; cease from the superstitions of idols and polluted sacrifices,” was killed by gladiators at the command of Alypius, prefect of the City.

A. T. L. C. On the same day, the feast of Saint Basil, bishop.

[Note: Basil of Cappadocia, bishop. C.: archbishop. A.: At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the burial of Saint Basil, whose solemn celebration is chiefly observed on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July. Usuard.]

And [At Rome: passion. T.] the passion of Saint Martina, virgin.

[Note: Martina. Born when her father was consul for the third time, she was tortured by various kinds of torment under the emperor Alexander and at last crowned with martyrdom at Rome. In vengeance for her, the emperor ended his impious life by tearing himself apart. Bolland, Hrabanus, Notker.]

A. And the feast of Saint Euphrosyna.

[Note: Euphrosyna. At Alexandria: born from a barren mother through the prayers of her father Paphnutius, she secretly sought the monastic life when still a child, taking for herself the name Smaragdus. After twenty-eight years, when struck by illness and recognizing that death was near, she revealed herself to her father, who had been searching for her. Her burial is celebrated on the third day before the Ides of February. Ado.]

L. On the same day, at Ethiopia, Rutulus. At Jerusalem, the feast of Saint Stephen.

## 2.—THE FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE NONES

Baeda has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Rome, the feast of Saint Telesphorus, pope and martyr.

[Note: Telesphorus. See Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History IV.10, and Saint Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.3. Ado and Usuard celebrate him on the Nones of January; Zegerus Paulus, the author of his Life preserved among the Bollandists, likewise reports that he suffered on that day. See also below, under the Nones of January, in the Additions. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican. The Greeks celebrate him on 22 February, as is evident from the Menaea.]

From being a hermit, he presided over the Roman Church for twelve years. He instituted the seven weeks’ fast before Easter, the Mass at night on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, and, before the sacrifice, the singing of the Angelic Hymn, namely, “Glory to God in the highest.” He suffered martyrdom in the time of Antoninus and Marcus.

[Col. 0801B] D. At Antioch, the passion of blessed Isidore, bishop.

[Note: Isidore. The Martyrology of Jerome edited by D’Achery has: “At Antioch, of Siridon, bishop of that same place.” Baronius, however, in his notes on the Martyrology, says that Isidore, who seems to be the same person as Jerome’s Siridon, was by no means bishop of Antioch, although he is said to have suffered at Antioch. Eusebius, who lists all the bishops of Antioch, names no one of that name, nor does Nicephorus Callistus. Galesinius asserts that this man was killed by the impious Arians. On this day another Isidore, bishop of Nitria, is also celebrated.]

And in the Pontic city of Tomis, the three brothers, Argeus, Narcissus, and Marcellinus, boys. Marcellinus, who had been seized among the recruits under the emperor Licinius, was martyred by drowning in the sea.

C. V. At Jerusalem, Stephen, Macarius the abbot, and Isidore the bishop. T. On the same day, the burial of blessed Macarius the abbot.

[Note: Macarius of Alexandria. There was also another Macarius of Egypt, simply called “the Egyptian.” On the Macarii, see Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History II.4; Socrates IV.18; and Sozomen III.13.]

## 3.—THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE NONES

At Rome, the feast of Anterus, pope and martyr, who ruled the Church for twelve years and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

[Note: Anterus. He diligently investigated the acts of the martyrs through the notaries and deposited them in the church; for this reason he was crowned with martyrdom by the prefect Maximus, under the emperor Maximian. See Baeda’s Chronicle and all the martyrologies. Eusebius, however, in Ecclesiastical History IV.20, says that Anterus assumed the pontificate after Gordian had succeeded Maximian, and that he did not rule the Church for twelve years but held the priesthood for less than a month.]

On the same day, at Paris, Genovefa, virgin.

[Note: Genovefa. Dedicated to Christ by blessed Germanus, she became widely renowned for wondrous virtues and grew old in Christ’s service until the age of eighty. Ado, Usuard, Notker. See her Life among the Bollandists and in the Appendix to Chifflet’s Baeda.]

Florus in A. T. L. adds: “While still in the body, she was so powerful in virtue that she raised a dead person.”

Florus in A. T. L.: In the city of Auclara [rather, in the city of Aulona], the passion of Saint Peter, who was crucified under the emperor Maximian.

[Note: Peter. Apselamus, or Balsamus, born in the village of Anea in the territory of Eleutheropolis. By order of the governor Severus, he was hung up, torn with hooks, and finally crucified—or killed by the sword, according to Hrabanus—or consumed on a pyre, as Eusebius relates in his treatise on the Martyrs of Palestine, chapter 10. Hrabanus assigns him to the following day.]

On the same day, the passion of Saint Theogenes, who was thrown into the sea in the time of Licinius.

[Note: Theogenes. He was the son of a bishop and was brought before the tribune Zilicentius and the prefect Posidonius. First he was stretched between four stakes and beaten with clubs; then he was thrown into prison to die there from tortures and hunger. But there he was fed by the Holy Spirit. Finally he was drowned in the sea. Eutyches, Eustathius, Zoticus, and other brothers took him from the sea and buried him near the walls, in a village belonging to the very devout man Adamantius or Amandus, in an underground chamber. See his Acts among the Bollandists. Hrabanus and Notker assign him to the second day before the Nones of January.]

And the feast of Potitus.

[Note: Potitus. See his Acts among the Bollandists, on 13 January, the day on which he is celebrated according to Baronius’s Martyrology.]

Under the emperor Antoninus, he was first beaten with clubs; then he was shut in prison and condemned to bear a great weight of iron. From there he was brought out and hung upon the rack. When the soldiers, by order of the emperor, wished to cut him up and throw him to the dogs, they could not touch him. Next he was ordered to be fried in a pan, and after being fried, to be covered with molten lead. Later he was fixed upon an iron stake from head to foot. When an angel rescued him from this, the emperor ordered his tongue to be cut out and his eyes to be pierced. Since he still could not be overcome, he was ordered to be beheaded, although he was a boy of thirteen years.

A. In the district of Vermandois, the discovery of the body of blessed Quirinus, martyr, by Bishop Eligius, and its translation.

[Note: Quirinus. More correctly, Quintinus. This is the second discovery of this saint’s body. After suffering martyrdom under Maximian, he was submerged in the Somme River in lead and remained hidden for a long time. At last his body was found and placed by the matron Eusebia in a high location of the prominent town anciently called Augusta Veromanduorum; it was found again by Eligius, bishop of Noyon. Sigebert, History, under the year 904.]

For a time the body of this martyr had been placed in hidden locations, and there the people long venerated it, although it was not there. Thus Saint Eligius, stirred by divine prompting, searched for it and found it at night. When the tomb was pierced, such a light poured from it, accompanied by an immense fragrance, that it changed the darkness of night into the great brightness of day. He lifted the body from the earth and kissed it; when he took teeth from its jaw as relics, a drop of blood came out from their roots. This is written in his Acts.

## 4.—THE SECOND DAY BEFORE THE NONES

Baeda has nothing.

D. The feast of blessed Titus, who was ordained by the apostle Paul as bishop of the Cretans.

A. T. L. In Africa, the feast of Aquilinus, Geminus, Eugentius, Vinctus, and Tryphon [L lacks “Tryphon”]. In the East, at the city of Bononia, Hermes, Aggaeus, and Gagius.

C. V. In Africa, Aquilinus. At the city of Bononia, Hermes and Aggaeus.

[Note: Hermes. Cherubinus Ghirardaccius mentions these three martyrs in book II of his History of Bologna, where he reports that their relics were placed by Bishop Eusebius in the church of the Holy Cross.]

Both names are absent in C.

## 5.—THE NONES

Baeda has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Jerusalem, the burial of Simeon the prophet, who received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death until he had seen the Lord’s Christ.

In the church at Antioch called “Repentance,” the burial of Saint Simeon the confessor, who lived with the strictest asceticism standing upon a column and granted many healings to the inhabitants of that place.

[Note: Simeon. He was called Stylites; see his Acts among the Bollandists.]

After his conversion he never once looked attentively upon a woman. But after, burning with more exalted holiness, he had mounted the taller column, he did not permit himself to be seen not only by an unrelated woman but even by his own mother. This is written in his Acts.

D. At Rome, the commemoration of Telesphorus [Note: [Col. 0803C] Telesphorus. See above, on the fourth day before the Nones of January.] pope and martyr, who was ordained the seventh pontiff after Peter. V. C. At Jerusalem, Simeon the prophet, and Simeon the confessor, who stood upon a column. A. On the same day at Noviomum, the translation of the body of Blessed Eligius [Note: [Col. 0803D] Eligius. Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, states in his Life of Saint Eligius that his body was translated on the very day of the anniversary of his passing, which falls on the Kalends of December. Therefore the Nones of January were not the day of the translation. See below, on the Kalends of December.] the confessor and pontiff, who shone greatly through signs of miracles. T. On the same day, the commemoration of the saints Honorius, Lucianus, and Jocundus [Note: [Col. 0803D] Saints. These suffered in Africa. Jerome, Notker.].

### 6.—The eighth day before the Ides. The Epiphany of the Lord.

Florus adds in A. T. L.:

When the Magi came from the East to the Lord, guided by the star, and honored him with mystical gifts as God, man, and king.

The same Florus in the same place:

At Antioch, the passion of the holy Julian [Note: [Col. 0803D] Julian. Julian and Basilissa were joined in marriage in outward appearance only. From their possessions they founded monasteries so numerous that Julian became the father of ten thousand monks, and Basilissa the mother of many virgins. Having sent these before her in peace to the kingdom of heaven, she herself followed them; Julian, however, was afterward tortured by the governor. Most martyrologies state that he suffered at Antioch, but do not specify which Antioch; consequently, later writers commonly interpret it as Antioch in Syria. In his Notes on the Roman Martyrology, Baronius adds that near Antioch there was a very famous church named after Julian. But Chrysostom’s homily proves that this place had been consecrated to another Julian, namely Saint Julian of Cilicia, who is said to have been plunged into the sea at Cilicia, enclosed in a sack with serpents, after very lengthy tortures. The same things are related in the homily, which also mentions a temple dedicated to this saint outside Antioch. Moreover, these are the words of the Greek Menologion: “The contest of Julian in Egypt. He suffered under Diocletian, with Marcianus as governor, in Antinopolis, a city of Egypt.” The Greeks likewise state in the Menaia that he lived in Antinoüs, a city of Egypt. A very ancient manuscript Martyrology of the monastery of Saint Maximin near Trier, and Hrabanus Maurus in his Martyrology, name “Antioch of Egypt”; among the Greeks it is called Antinopolis, Ἀντινόου πόλις, “the city of Antinoüs,” in Egypt. Stephen writes it Ἀντινόεια, which differs from Ἀντιόχεια by only one character. For those unfamiliar with the places, it was easy to reject the less-known Ἀντινόεια and substitute Ἀντιόχεια. The Greeks celebrate their memory in the Menaia on 8 January. Baronius’s Martyrology, the edition published at Cologne under the name of Bede, and also Usuard, Notker, Ado, and Florus’s own Additions below, honor them on 9 January. Hrabanus and the Martyrology of Saint Maximin treat of them on 13 January, and Wandalbert on the Ides of February. Paulus Morigia writes that their feast is celebrated on 20 June. The Greeks celebrate them in the Menologion on 21 June. See more about them in Bollandus, 9 January. Julian is also commemorated below in Florus’s Additions on 11 January.]

and Basilissa his bride, whom God received in peace while she was praying, and of the boy Celsus, under the governor Martianus, in the time of Diocletian and Maximian. Thus far L. Julian, after scourging, bonds, and various tortures, converted the aforementioned boy, named Celsus, the governor’s son, and afterward the guards and the boy’s mother, the governor’s wife. Later they were sent to prison. After the others had been slaughtered—namely, twenty soldiers and seven brothers—Julian was reserved for trial, together with the boy Celsus and his mother, Antonius the priest, and the man whom Saint Julian had raised from the dead. Then the governor ordered that the scalp of Saint Julian and the boy Celsus be removed, and the eyes of Saint Antonius the priest and Anastasius, who had been raised from the dead. But the Lord protected the boy’s mother, Saint Marcianilla, so that she could not be touched. After such tortures, however, when they were found to be unharmed, they were put to the sword.

L. And the commemoration of Albert, bishop and confessor. D. In the territory of Reims, the passion of Saint Macra [Note: [Col. 0805C] Macra. She suffered in the persecution of Diocletian. When she had escaped unharmed from the flames, her breasts were cut off and she was weakened by the squalor of prison. After being rolled over exceedingly sharp potsherds and burning coals, she departed to the Lord in prayer. She was buried not far from the place where she suffered. Wandalbert celebrates her on 3 March. Her body was translated by a certain Lendulphus, a herdsman, to a church of Saint Martin. Later, the venerable man Dangulfus founded a splendid house and transferred Saint Macra’s body there on 30 May, under the reign of the supreme emperor Charles.] the virgin, who, when she had been thrown into the fire at the command of the governor Rictiovarus, remained unharmed.

At Rennes, Saint Melanius [Note: [Col. 0805C] Melanius. He belonged to the parish of Vannes and was raised on an estate called Placio. He succeeded Amando in the episcopate of Rennes and became counselor to Clovis, king of the Franks. When a synod had been assembled in the city of Orléans, he especially distinguished himself above the other bishops. By the remarkable resurrection of a dead man, he converted the people of Vannes to the faith. He died about the year 530. Although he is said to have died on 6 January, he is not celebrated on that day but on 6 November in the diocese of Rennes; indeed, the appendix to Ado, under 8 November, states: “In the city of Rennes, the commemoration of Saint Melanius, bishop and confessor.” Ado himself and the commonly circulated Bede assign him to 12 November. The Martyrology of the Charterhouse of Utrecht presents him on 11 October. Paschalis Robinius, who published his Life, states, among other things, that in the year 853, when the Normans had ravaged Nantes, the body of Saint Melanius was carried to Bourges. Argentraeus, History of Britain IV.16, states that in 1231 the body of Saint Melanius was transferred by the archbishop of Tours to the fortress of Prulliacum, commonly called Preuilly, in the diocese of Tours. BOLLAND.] bishop and confessor.

V. C. And the passion of Saints Julian, Basilissa, and Celsus.

### 7.—The seventh day before the Ides. Bede has no entry.

Florus in the manuscripts A. T. L.:

At Nicomedia, Saint Lucian [Note: [Col. 0805D] Lucian. He was a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, praised for the continence of his life and his knowledge of the sacred Scriptures. He was taken to Nicomedia, where the emperor was then staying, thrown into prison during the persecution of Maximinus, and killed. Eusebius, History IX.6. Suidas and Symeon Metaphrastes say that he suffered under Maximian, but this conflicts with the authority of Eusebius and Jerome, Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 77, as well as with the Martyrologies of Usuard and Ado. The manner of his death is variously reported: Metaphrastes says that he died of hunger and torture, or that he was thrown into the sea while still breathing and carried to land by a dolphin; Rufinus says that he was beheaded. Florus, Notker, and others write that he was cut into four pieces. In the Gallican Martyrology, Andreas Saussayus says that the relics of Saint Lucian were brought by Charlemagne to Arles, and that a church was built in his honor, where they were deposited by Turpinus, archbishop of Reims. The Greeks celebrate him on 15 October.] the presbyter, who was divided into four parts. Each part, tied to a separate stone, was sunk in the sea; but when God restored them, the body, made whole, was found at Elenopolis on the following day, together with the stones.

Likewise, the cleric and deacon [Note: [Col. 0806C] Cleric. There is an obvious error here. For all the martyrologies read as follows: “At Antioch, Saint Clerus the deacon, who, tortured seven times for the glory of his confession and long tormented in prison, was finally beheaded and completed his martyrdom.” The sentence should therefore be corrected as follows: “Likewise Saint Clerus, the Antiochene deacon, who, tortured seven times and brought out of prison, was beheaded.”] of Antioch, who, tortured seven times and brought out of prison, were beheaded.

D. The return of the boy Jesus from Egypt. D. V. C. At Nicomedia, Saint Lucian the presbyter. V. C. In the city of Militana, the commemoration of Polioctus and Januarius.

### 8.—The sixth day before the Ides. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.:

At the city of Beauvais, the commemoration of Saints Lucian [Note: [Col. 0806D] Lucian. A disciple of Saint Peter, he was afterward assigned by Pope Clement as companion to Dionysius the apostle of Paris. As they traveled together, Lucian was imprisoned near Parma while preaching; after being released by Christians, he preached at Ticinum and then among the people of Arles. Finally he came to Beauvais with his companions Maximianus—also called Massianus, Messianus, and Maxianus—and Julianus, and preached there. When news of them reached the pagan persecutors, Maximianus and Julianus were seized and beheaded first, followed by Saint Lucian himself. These events occurred under the emperor Domitian, when Julianus the prefect, not the emperor, harassed the Christians.] the presbyter, Maximianus, and Julianus, martyrs. Lucian, having departed from the city of Rome and reached the territory of the Beauvaisians in Gaul, acquired a great multitude for the Lord by the word of his preaching and the brilliance of his miracles. When Julian the emperor’s officers searched for him, they beat him with his hands bound and beheaded him. His lifeless body, as the story goes, rose up, seized the sacred head that had been severed with its own hand, and carried it with steady steps to the place that the holy man had chosen for his burial. This is recorded in his acts.

D. At Naples in Campania, the commemoration of Saint Severinus [Note: [Col. 0807D] Severinus. The name Naples is wrongly placed here in the martyrologies instead of Septempeda. For Severinus, who is honored at Naples and to whom the basilica where his body is kept is dedicated, was not a bishop but an abbot and apostle of Noricum; his body was transferred from Noricum to Naples. The Severinus mentioned here, likewise called a bishop and brother of Victorinus, was bishop of Septempeda in Picenum. Bollandus. He is celebrated in Baronius’s Martyrology on 8 June.] bishop and confessor, brother of Blessed Victorinus the martyr. V. C. In Greece, Rusticus the bishop, Timothy, Telesphorus, and Anastasia.

### 9.—The fifth day before the Ides. Bede has no entry.

D. Near Antioch, the holy martyrs who, under Diocletian and Maximian, together with many others, attained the glory of martyrdom. Their names were lacking or had been erased.

A. The commemoration of Julian [Note: [Col. 0807D] Julian. See under the eighth day before the Ides of January.] and Basilissa, martyrs; it is placed here incorrectly. In Africa.

A. T. L. In Africa, the commemoration of Epictetus, Jocundus, and Quintus. At Smyrna, Revocatus, Firminus, and Saturninus. In L., Epictetus is absent; and, with his companions omitted in the intervening place, Saturninus is joined to him: in V. and C. it read as follows: “In Africa, Epictetus, Jocundus, Secundus, Vitalis, and Felix.” C. adds, “and seven others.”

### 10.—The fourth day before the Ides. The commemoration of Paul [Note: [Col. 0807D] Paul. He was the first to inhabit the desert. A Theban by birth, at about sixteen years of age he sought the desert under the persecutors Decius and Valerian, in order to escape the persecution raging against Christians. He lived in the desert for ninety-eight years and, visited by the great Antony, met his final day. See his Life by Saint Jerome. Baronius’s Martyrology adds: “His feast is celebrated on 15 January. The relics of Saint Paul were transferred to Constantinople by the emperor Manuel; then, in the year 1240, to Venice; and finally to Hungary, under King Louis.” Bollandus gives the history of his translation.] the first hermit, who remained alone in the desert from his sixteenth year until his one hundred and thirteenth year. Antony saw his soul carried by angels into heaven amid the choirs of apostles and prophets.

On the same day at Rome, Melchiades [Note: [Col. 0808D] Melchiades. Also called Miltiades; he suffered much in the persecution of Maximian. Jerome’s Martyrology reads: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, the commemoration of Melchiades the bishop.” He is celebrated on 10 December.] the bishop and confessor.

Florus adds in A. T. L.:

He ruled the Church for four years, the thirty-second after Saint Peter.

C. adds: “and twelve others.”

### 11.—The third day before the Ides.

In Africa, Saint Salvius [Note: [Col. 0808D] Salvius. As Galesinius writes in his notes, his body was honorably and reverently deposited in the basilica at Carthage. Hrabanus calls him a confessor, but incorrectly; for the others, following Possidius, state that he was a martyr. He was distinct from Salvius the Donatist, the pseudo-bishop of Membressa in Africa, whom Saint Augustine mentions in Against Cresconius the Grammarian IV.48–49.], on whose anniversary Saint Augustine preached to the people at Carthage.

Florus in A. T.:

The passion of the holy Polyuctus, Candidianus, and Philotimus, who, persevering together in confessing Christ, were handed over to the fire.

A. T. L. In Achaea, the passion of Saint Julian [Note: [Col. 0808D] Julian. See under the eighth and fifth days before the Ides of January.] the martyr, who was killed by the sword in prison under the governor Martianus.

### 12.—The second day before the Ides.

In Achaea, the commemoration of Blessed Saturus [Note: [Col. 0808D] Saturus. In the manuscript author of the Florarium: “At Achaea, the commemoration of Saint Saturus the martyr, a citizen of Arabia, beheaded in the year of salvation 267, during the eighth persecution, in its ninth year.” Notker writes that he suffered in Arabia; others, near Antioch.] the martyr. Thus D. But V. has: “In Achaea, Cyriacus.”

C. and R. have the full and complete text:

In Achaea, Cyriacus, Mosantus, and Saturus, a citizen of Arabia, who, passing before a temple of an idol, blew upon it and, after making the sign upon his forehead, caused it to fall. Those who were watching him there seized him and led him to the governor. When they reported what had happened, he was beheaded. This, as we judge, is taken word for word from Bede’s source.

Florus in A. T. L. softened the barbarous diction as follows:

In Achaea, the commemoration of Saturus, a citizen of Arabia. It is reported that, while he was passing before a certain idol’s temple, he blew upon the same idol and made the sign on his forehead, whereupon it immediately fell. When the idol’s worshipers saw this, they told the governor, relating what he had done; for this reason he received the stroke of beheading.

V. In Achaea, Cyriacus. V. C. In Africa, Zoticus, Rogatus, and Modestus. C. adds Castulus, Corona, and eleven soldiers.

### 13.—On the Ides.

At Poitiers, the commemoration of Hilary [Note: [Col. 0809B] Hilary. He was a powerful bulwark of the Church against the Arians. On account of the Catholic faith, he was condemned by them at the synod of Béziers and exiled by the emperor to Phrygia. Most believe that his death occurred on 13 January in the year 367. On that day his commemoration is indeed found in Jerome, Bede, Florus, the Gellone codex given by Charlemagne to the monastery, and many sacramentaries, missals, and books of collects. Sulpicius supports the same opinion when he writes that Hilary died in his homeland six years after returning. Yet Hilary’s memory is not recorded in all the ancient ecclesiastical books as occurring on the Ides of January without also being commemorated elsewhere—for example, on another day of January, on 26 June, or on the Kalends of November. On the Kalends of November, five Masses are found in an ancient copy of the church of Saint Gatianus of Tours; the fifth is for Saint Hilary, with this inscription: “For on this same day is the solemnity of Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor.” One would readily grant that some solemn translation is indicated here, were it not that a codex of the king of France, written about nine hundred years ago, and a very ancient pontifical of the church of Évreux designate not merely a solemnity but the commemoration of Saint Hilary on those same Kalends. Moreover, this latter date agrees far better than the former with whatever the ancient records have handed down concerning Hilary’s death—unless perhaps Sulpicius is excepted. First, Gregory of Tours testifies that Saint Hilary departed to heaven in the fourth year of Valentinian and Valens. But the fourth year of Valentinian and Valens began on 27 February of the year 367. Thus, just as the Ides of January of 367 do not fall within that year, neither do they mark Hilary’s death. The same conclusion can be drawn precisely from Jerome’s chronicle, in which Hilary’s death is recorded under the year 367, with Gratian’s elevation to the imperial throne mentioned first; Gratian assumed the empire on 24 August 367. In Jerome, therefore, the sequence of events is properly ordered if Hilary died on the Kalends of November 367, but not if he died on the Ides of January. For these reasons, those who, moved by the testimony of nearly all the manuscripts, prefer the Ides of January believe that he lived until the year 368. Gregory of Tours agrees with this opinion, and Jerome’s Chronicle does not contradict it if the numerical note “368” is raised by a single line. See the new Life of this confessor published before the Benedictine edition of his works.] bishop and confessor of Poitiers; among his other virtues, it is said that he raised a dead person.

Florus in A. T. L.:

He was exiled to Phrygia by the emperor Constantius because of the truth of the faith. He shone greatly through his teachings and miracles.

The same Florus in the same place:

At Reims, the commemoration of Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 0810B] Remigius. Also called Remedius. After Bennadius died, he was taken into the episcopate of Reims at the age of twenty-two. King Clovis—called Louis during his baptism—summoned a synod at Orléans on the advice of Remigius. Remigius was also present at the synod of the bishops of Gaul and Belgium, where, when he entered, a certain Arian heretic became speechless. After administering the episcopate for seventy-four years, he died at the age of ninety-six and was buried in the little church of Blessed Christopher the martyr. Sigebert, in his Chronicle, writes that he was born in 449, made bishop in 471, and died in 545. He is especially celebrated in the martyrologies on the Kalends of October, because on that day his body was translated by angelic hands into a crypt constructed behind the altar. It was translated a second time into a larger and more beautiful crypt in 852. His Life appears in Surius’s January.] the bishop and confessor. He was the first to baptize the people of the Franks, together with their ruler Clovis. Shining through signs of many miracles, he raised a girl whom he had previously healed when she was afflicted by a demon, after she had died. This is recorded in his acts.

In the same place, the octave of the Epiphany, or Theophany, is placed before everything else.

### 14.—The nineteenth day before the Kalends of February.

In Campania, the commemoration of Felix [Note: [Col. 0810C] Felix. Bede wrote his Life, as is clear from the catalogue of his works at the end of the Ecclesiastical History, where one reads: “I converted into prose the Book of the Life and Passion of Saint Felix the confessor from the metrical work of Paulinus.” Felix was born at Nola, the son of Hermias the Syrian, and was ordained presbyter by Maximus, bishop of Nola. When Maximus, weakened by old age, fled the persecution, Felix was captured and tortured in various ways in prison. With the help of angels, however, he was led out of prison; he sought the bishop, found him almost lifeless, restored him, and carried him home. When the persecution broke out again and the enemies sought Felix himself, he hid in the ruins of a half-destroyed dwelling, which was suddenly enclosed by a spider’s web. Later, withdrawing elsewhere, he was fed for six months by a pious woman who did not know who he was. After Maximus died, he was elected but refused the episcopate, and finally rested in peace. Ado, Notker, and others confuse him with Felix the Roman presbyter. Some call him a martyr, but although he endured many tortures, he did not die from them. The commonly circulated Bede, Ado, and others state that he was buried by the presbyter Elpidius. The Turonian, Marcellus, Bede in the Life, and Paulinus do not mention this; indeed, Paulinus writes that his funeral was arranged by the whole people on his anniversary, 6 January.], the presbyter and confessor. Among other things, the bishop Paulinus writes of him that, when he was being sent to prison by persecutors and lay bound beneath a load of potsherds and pieces of earthenware, an angel released him and led him out during the night.

Florus in A. T. L.:

On the same day at Antioch, the commemoration of Clerus the deacon, who suffered many tortures and was thrown into the sea.

### 15.—The eighteenth day before the Kalends. Bede has no entry.

D. Abacuc and Micah [Note: [Col. 0811C] Prophets. The commonly circulated Bede, Ado, Usuard, Hrabanus, Notker, and others state that their relics were discovered under Arcadius and Honorius; Baronius’s Martyrology places the discovery under Theodosius the Elder. Sozomen, VII.28, writes that their bodies were revealed by a divine vision in a dream to Sabennus, then bishop of Eleutheropolis. Abacuc was found in the city of Cela, Micah in Barathsatia. The Greeks treat of them separately: Habacuc on 2 December and Micah on 14 August.] the prophets, and Blessed Macarius [Note: [Col. 0811D] Macarius. He is called the Egyptian, distinct from the Alexandrian who is celebrated on 2 January. He was a disciple of Saint Antony, not of Blessed John. He chiefly inhabited Scetis, or Scetin, or the Scetic desert in Libya.] the abbot, disciple of Blessed John.

V. In Egypt, Crisconius. C. Tyrsus. V. C. And the commemoration of Abacuc the prophet. C. And Saint Remedius [Note: [Col. 0811D] Remedius. See Remigius on the Ides of January.] the bishop.

A. T. In Egypt, the passion of the holy martyrs Crisconius and Tyrsus. And the commemoration of Abacuc and Micah the prophets. And the commemoration of Saint Maurus [Note: [Col. 0811D] Maurus. Abbot of Glanfeuil in Gaul. Maurus, born to Eutychius and Julia, was handed over by his parents at the age of twelve to Saint Benedict to be brought up under the discipline of the rule. When Bertigrannus, bishop of Le Mans, asked Benedict to send brothers to establish a monastery for him according to the order of regular observance, Maurus was sent to Gaul with four others. Meanwhile, when that bishop died, his successor Domnolus refused to receive them. They were nevertheless summoned into the territory of Anjou and honorably welcomed. When a powerful man named Florus donated a site, they founded the monastery of Glanfeuil and completed it in eight years. After governing it for thirty years, Maurus died before the altar of Blessed Martin. See more about him in Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictines, century I.] the abbot. And Saint Macarius. And Saint Isidore [Note: [Col. 0811D] Isidore. Rufinus lists him among Saint Antony’s disciples. He was both presbyter and keeper of a hospice of the Church of Alexandria. He traveled to Rome twice, first with Saint Athanasius and then with Saint Demetrius the bishop. Palladius, Lausiac History, chapters 1–2. He was appointed bishop to the people of Constantinople by Theophilus. Theophilus loved him for this reason: when Theodosius was fighting Maximus in battle, Theophilus sent certain gifts to the emperor through him and placed two letters in his hands, instructing him to give both the gifts and the letters to whichever man proved victorious. George of Alexandria, Life of Chrysostom. Isidore later incurred the hatred of Theophilus and was expelled from the Church of Alexandria. When he came to Constantinople with Dioscorus, Chrysostom received him with honor. Socrates VI.19.] the bishop.

T. S. Maurus the abbot.

On the same day in Egypt, the holy martyrs Crisconius and Tyrsus, and the commemoration of Abacuc the prophet.

L. The commemoration of Abacuc the prophet. And in Egypt, the holy Crisconius and Tyrsus. And on the same day Saint Maurus, disciple of Saint Benedict.

### 16.—The seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

The commemoration of Saint Marcellus [Note: [Col. 0812D] Marcellus. At the command of Maximianus—or rather Maxentius, not Maximinus.] pope, who, at the command of the emperor Maximinus, was beaten with clubs and driven away from the presence of the man whom he was reproving. Later, when the emperor heard that Marcellus had made the house of Saint Lucina—which he himself had condemned to confiscation because she had given her possessions to Christians—into a church and was celebrating Mass there in the middle of the city, he ordered boards to be laid in that church [D. has “straw to be spread”] for the animals of the public stable, and assigned the bishop to that stable for service to the animals under public guard. After serving there for many years, dressed in a hair shirt, he died; John the presbyter and Blessed Lucina embalmed him with spices and buried him in the cemetery of Priscilla.

Florus in A. T. L.:

On the same day at the monastery of Péronne in Gaul, the commemoration of Furseus [Note: [Col. 0812D] Furseus. See Bede’s Ecclesiastical History III.19.] the abbot, who, being taken up bodily, heard and saw many things concerning the heavenly realms; after his body had been restored to life, he later proclaimed these things for twelve years [L. has “sixteen years”]. This is recorded in his acts.

V. C. At Arles [“At Arles” is absent from V.], the commemoration of Saint Honoratus [Note: [Col. 0812D] Honoratus. He was born of a consular family. After the death of his brother Venantius, with whom he had traveled, he withdrew to the island of Lérins, where he led a solitary life. Later ordained to the priesthood, he built a monastery and instructed the monks admirably. Hilary, in his Life, apud Bollandus.], bishop.

The passion of Saint Martha.

### 17.—The sixteenth day before the Kalends.

In Egypt, the commemoration of Antony [Note: [Col. 0813C] Antony. Sozomen, I.13, says that he was born of a patrician family who inhabited Coma, a village near Heraclea, among the Egyptians of the Arcadian region. According to Eusebius in his Chronicle, he was born under the emperor Decius, in the year of Christ 250. At about twenty years of age he renounced the world, withdrawing a little from his homeland. When this exercise had strengthened his spirit, he chose a dwelling for himself in the tombs of the dead, somewhat farther away, and remained there until the thirty-fifth year of his life, A.D. 285. In that same year he withdrew into the desert near Aphroditon, where he lived alone for twenty years in a deserted fort, removed from human sight during the persecution, until A.D. 305; he also built monasteries on the desert mountain. When the tyrant raged against the Christians, he went to Alexandria and strengthened the martyrs. Antony also became renowned for miracles. Therefore, distressed by the multitude of visitors, he fled to a mountain divinely shown to him in the inner desert and lived there alone. Visitors came to him, and he himself also visited the earlier monasteries, soon returning to the mountain. About the year 330, brought to Alexandria by Athanasius, he openly professed his faith in order to refute heretics and schismatics. In 339 Antony was warned by a divine oracle of an impending new storm that would shatter the peace of the Church. Fifteen years before his death, when he was ninety years old, he accepted the service of two brothers, whom he allowed to live with him on the inner mountain from the year 340, when he visited Saint Paul. Finally, in the nineteenth year of Constantius, according to Saint Jerome in his Chronicle, Antony died in the desert in the year of Christ 356, at the age of 105. If you wish to read something about his miracles, consult his Life written by Athanasius. His body was discovered by divine revelation under the emperor Justinian, carried to Alexandria, and buried in the church of Blessed John the Baptist. ADO, USUARD.]

Antony the monk.

Florus adds in the manuscripts:

He, being of an exceedingly ascetic life, blossomed forth through many miracles; Blessed Athanasius composed his Life.

And at Langres, the commemoration of the twin brothers Pseusippus, Elasippus, and Melasippus [Note: [Col. 0813D] The Twins. If Benignus, the disciple of Saint Polycarp, baptized them, they are not correctly said to have suffered under Aurelian. For there is no chronological connection between Saint Polycarp and the emperor Aurelian: Saint Polycarp suffered martyrdom in 168, while Aurelian did not obtain the empire until 270. Baronius therefore restores “Aurelius” in place of “Aurelian,” since Saint Polycarp suffered martyrdom in the seventh year of Aurelius.]

When they were twenty-five years old, they were crowned with martyrdom, together with their grandmother Leonilla and with Ionilla and Neone, in the time of the emperor Aurelian. The twins were suspended from a single tree, their hands bound upward and their feet downward, stretched so that they seemed about to be separated at the very joints of their limbs. After this they were thrown into the fire, but were not harmed by the flames; amid their prayers they departed together to the Lord.

Here A. ends.

When Ionilla saw this, she confessed that she too was a Christian. Afterward she was seized by the crowds, hung by her hair, and afflicted with many tortures. Since she refused to deny Christ, she was killed by the sword together with Leonilla. Neon, the recorder of the acts, also confessed the name of Christ and was crowned with martyrdom. These twins were taught and baptized by Benignus the presbyter, whom Blessed Polycarp, the hearer of Blessed John the apostle, sent from the East into Gaul with Andochius the presbyter and Thyrsus the deacon.

The same twins were buried at the second milestone from the city of Langres.

The manuscripts of Tournai and Letiensis lack the material enclosed in the square brackets; in the Tournai manuscript Saint Antony is also placed at the very end.

Florus in A. T. L.:

At Bourges, Saint Sulpicius [Note: [Col. 0814C] Sulpicius. By surname Pius, he flourished under Chlothar II and Dagobert. There was another Sulpicius, surnamed Severus, under King Guntram; both were numbered among the saints: the former on 29 January, the latter on this day. Pius took up the clerical office under Theodoricus; in the camp of Chlothar he obtained the office of abbot, and at Chlothar’s command he was deemed worthy of the episcopal see. He died about the year 647. According to Ado, his translation took place on 15 January.] the bishop and confessor, through whom the Lord deigned to perform glorious miracles.

### 18.—The fifteenth day before the Kalends. The commemoration of Saint Prisca [Note: [Col. 0814C] Prisca. Baronius is uncertain whether Saint Prisca suffered under Claudius I or Claudius II. Her acts attest that she was crowned with martyrdom in the third year of Claudius and confirm that she died in that same year; this does not at all fit the earlier Claudius, but fits the second sufficiently. The elder Claudius ruled for fourteen years, so Prisca did not die in the very year in which he died. The second Claudius, although, as Eutropius IX and Bede himself in the Chronicle write, he died within two years of his reign, nevertheless reached a period of three years if these are reckoned from the Kalends of January: he became emperor in 268 and died in 270. Yet, as Baronius continues, several records of the church of Saint Prisca state that she suffered while the apostle Peter was alive, under the elder Claudius. It is therefore necessary to conclude that an error entered the other acts in the number of Claudius’s regnal years, and that she suffered in the thirteenth year of his reign, not the third. Some assign her ten years of age, others eleven, and most thirteen. On account of her faith she was first struck in the face and thrown into prison; then tortured by scourging and hideously smeared with boiling fat. Afterward she was exposed to a lion and escaped unharmed. Then, weakened by fasting for nearly three days, she was suspended on the rack; next her flesh was torn with iron claws; afterward she was thrown into the fire but preserved unharmed; finally she was beheaded outside the city. Galesinius, in the Martyrology.]

Prisca, virgin and martyr.

Florus in A. T. L.:

On the same day in Egypt, thirty-seven soldiers [Note: [Col. 0815C] Soldiers. In the eastern part of Egypt, Paul, Pansius, Dionysius, Thonius, Herpresius, Horus, Dionysius, Ammon, another Ammon, and Agatho preached; in the northern part, Recumbus, Bastamus, Sarmatas, Proteas, Orion, Collotus, Didymus, Plesius, and Aratus; in the southern part, Theonas, Hippias, Romanus, Saturninus, Pinutius, Serapio, Bastammo, Papa, and Pantherus; finally, in the western part, Papias, Dioscorus, Hero, Potamo, Pethecus, Oeconomus, Zoticus, Cyriacus, and Ammonius. See Bollandus.] who, divided into four groups, were ordered to be killed. Those who had been separated in the eastern group were handed over to the fire; those in the northern group were beheaded; those in the southern group were burned by fire; while those who belonged to the western group were delivered over to the Lord’s Passion.

C. And the commemoration of Saint Mary the Virgin, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0815C] Commemoration. In certain calendars, the election of Blessed Mary is assigned to this day.].

L. And the passion of Saint Thyrsus with his companions.

A. And the commemoration of Atta the abbot.

T. Before all these entries, it has:

At Rome, the Chair of Saint Peter the apostle [Note: [Col. 0815C] Chair. That is, the annual celebration of the day on which Peter assumed the episcopate at Rome. That solemnity had ceased at Rome, but was restored by Pope Paul IV, as is clear from his bull.]

### 19.—The fourteenth day before the Kalends. Bede has no entry.

[Col. 0816B] **D.** In Smyrna, the blessed martyr Germanicus, who under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius, through the grace of God’s power, banishing fear of bodily frailty, voluntarily provoked the beast prepared for him. [Note: On his endurance and greatness of spirit, see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, IV, 15.] At Spoletum, Saint Pontianus, martyr. [Note: Rabanus and Notker commemorate him on 14 January; the common recension of Bede and Baronius’s *Martyrology* commemorate him on this day. Molanus treats him in his *Usuard* on both days and, on 19 January, after reporting his eulogy, adds: “He completed his martyrdom on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February; but on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February his sacred body was moved, that is, transferred into another shrine.” The martyrologies report that he suffered in the time of Antoninus: the judge Fabianus first ordered him to be scourged and to walk barefoot over coals; when he was unharmed, he was ordered to be suspended on the rack and by iron hooks and then cast into prison. Afterward he was exposed to lions and drenched with boiling lead, and at last slain by the sword.] **V.** In Africa, Paul, Quintus, Germanus, and thirty-nine others. **A. T. L.** In Africa, Saints Paul, Hermes, Quintus, Januarius, Successus, Valens, Publius, Gagias, with six hundred others. **A.** Also the deposition of Martha and Maria. [Note: “Maria” is falsely written for Marius. See the following day.] Also the translation of Saint Hugo, archbishop of Rouen. [Note: Saint Hugo, son of Drogo, duke of Burgundy, by Adaltrude, was first primicerius of the Church of Metz. On the death of Bishop Ranilandus, he governed the churches of Paris and Bayeux together with that of Rouen, while at the same time serving as abbot of Fontenelle and Jumièges. He died at Jumièges about the year 730, on 9 April. Buried there in the basilica of Saint Mary, he was later transferred thence with Saint Aicradus, abbot, to Hasnon. The day of the translation is assigned as 29 March in the Martyrology of Jumièges. For what reason Saint Hugo is commemorated on 19 January is not established by any historical evidence. On this saint see Molanus’s *Index of the Saints of Belgium*.] **T.** On the same day, the deposition of Saint Launomarus, abbot and confessor. [Note: He was born among the Franks while Chlothar I reigned and received baptism from Blessed Remigius, bishop of Rheims. Some years after his ordination as priest, being impatient of the world, he fled to the wilderness. Many companions thereafter gathered to him and built a small monastery; but, leaving this cell and wishing to remain more hidden, he withdrew with his followers to another place. There, when Ragnosointhus, a very wealthy man, gave him the site, he built the monastery of Corbion in the second year of Chilperic—that is, in 564 if reckoned from his father’s death, or 572 if reckoned from the death of his brother Charibert. While visiting Malardus, bishop of Chartres, he fell ill and died, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin. See Surius under January.] **L.** Also at Jerusalem, Saints Maria and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus.

**20.—XIII Kalends.** At Rome, Saint Fabianus, bishop, who, after Anterus, was elected pope during the reign of Maximinus when a dove flew down from above and settled upon his head. [Col. 0816D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VI, 19. The acts of this saint, preserved under 14 May by Bollandus, relate that the two emperors named Philippus learned the mysteries of the Christian religion from Saint Pontius and were baptized by Pope Fabianus. It is related of the elder Philippus that, when he wished to attend the final Paschal vigil and participate in the sacred mysteries, Bishop Fabianus did not permit him to do so until he had confessed his sins and stood among the penitents. Eusebius, VI, 34. There is considerable disagreement among authors concerning the duration of this pontificate. One source says that he held the see for fourteen years, ten months, and eleven days; another, fifteen years and four days; another, fourteen years, eleven months, and twelve days; our author, twenty-five years; another, thirteen years. Yet, to discover the truth amid such confusion of numbers, let us determine how much time elapsed between the killing of Saint Anterus and the death of Saint Fabianus himself. We may therefore conclude that fourteen years and seventeen days truly intervened. Pagi consequently appears to have correctly calculated the period in his *Chronology*. Together with the celebrated Pearson, he held that the see was vacant for eight days and that Saint Fabianus occupied it for fourteen years and ten days. He died in the year 250, crowned with martyrdom under Decius, who, out of hatred for Philippus, began a persecution against the Church. The Greeks commemorate him on 5 August, as is clear from the *Menaea*.

Saint Fabianus was bishop; after presiding over the Church for twenty-five years, he suffered martyrdom under Decius and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

On the same day, Saint Sebastian of Milan, who was so dear to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian that they entrusted him with command of the first cohort. [Note: Those wishing to read of this saint’s relics and translations should consult Bollandus on this very day; the Greeks commemorate him on 18 December.] When Diocletian learned that he was a Christian and could not be recalled from the faith, he ordered him to be bound in the middle of the field like a target for arrows and shot by the soldiers. When he stood covered with arrows like a hedgehog, they supposed him dead and departed. During the night a certain woman named Irene came to remove the body, found him alive, brought him to her house, and cared for him. When he recovered, he strengthened many in the faith; [and, without delay, appearing before the emperors themselves, he reproached them as they deserved. [Note: Everything between “without delay” and “he completed” is absent from A and L.]] Then Diocletian ordered him brought to the hippodrome and beaten until he died. They threw his corpse into the great sewer; but he appeared in a dream to the holy matron Lucina, saying: “Near the Circus you will find my body hanging on a hook. It has not been touched by the filth. When you have washed it, take it to the Catacombs and bury me in a crypt near the apostles’ remains.” That very night she came with servants and carried out everything accordingly.

On the same day, the feast of Saints Marius and Martha, with their sons Audifax and Abacuc, noble Persians who had come to Rome to pray during the reign of the emperor Claudius. After enduring beatings, the rack, fires, claws, and the cutting off of their hands, Martha was killed at Nympha, while the others were beheaded; and everything else was burned. [Note: Their bodies were burned so that they might not receive burial. A certain matron named Felicitas, however, seized their half-burned bodies and buried them on her estate; she also lifted Martha from the well and joined her to the holy bodies on 20 January. See their acts in Bollandus. The Martyrologies of the common recension of Bede and of Baronius, as well as the additions of Florus, commemorated them on the preceding day. Saint Martha is likewise placed above, in the Additions of Florus, on 16 January.]

**L.** Their limbs were cut apart and burned.

**21.—XII Kalends.** At Rome, Saint Agnes, who, under the prefect of the city, Sempronius, because she refused to take his son as her husband out of love for Christ and for virginity, was taken naked to a brothel for the purpose of being dishonored. At first she was covered by her own hair; afterward she was clothed with a heavenly garment. When the prefect’s son, who pursued her with excessive shamelessness, was strangled by the devil for this reason, she restored him to life through the power of prayer. After this she was cast into the fire, and so forth. [Note: Notker says that she suffered under the emperor Gallienus. Molanus, in his *Index of the Saints of Belgium*, writes that Saint Agnes’s relics rest honorably in a tomb at Utrecht, in the cathedral church, and that Bishop Balderic transferred them there in 966, under Otto. The day of the translation is 2 September.]

Saint Agnes, who, after being thrown into the fire under the prefect of the city, Sempronius, had the flames extinguished through her prayer and was struck with the sword.

**Florus in A. T. L.** On this day, in the Spanish city of Tarragona, the passion of Saints Fructuosus, bishop, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons, who received the glory of their confession through fire under the prefect Aemilianus, during the reigns of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. [Note: At first they were thrust into prison, then thrown into the flames. When their bonds had burned away, they stretched out their hands in the form of a cross and obtained what they prayed for: to be burned. Immediately one of the brothers and the prefect’s daughter, who was standing nearby, saw the souls of the saints ascending crowned into heaven. Ado, Bede, common recension.]

**L.** And in the city of Valeria, Saint Valerius, bishop and martyr. [Note: He was bishop of the city of Caesaraugusta. Together with Saint Vincent, the deacon, he was brought as far as Valentia by order of the governor Dacianus and was then sent into exile. He did not suffer at Valeria but at Valentia. Jerome, Ado, Rabanus, Notker, and the common recension of Bede say that he suffered on the following day.]

**C.** Elsewhere, Felix, Fructuosus, Caecilianus, and Martialis.

**[Col. 0819C] 22.—XI Kalends.** In Spain, the feast of Vincent, deacon and martyr. [Note: He suffered together with Saint Valerius under the emperor Diocletian. Whoever wishes to read more about him should consult Bollandus.]

At Aquae Salviae, Saint Anastasius. [Note: He came with the army of Sais, prince of the Persians, to besiege Chalcedon; from there he returned to the East, left the army, and lived first at Hierapolis and afterward at Jerusalem with a goldsmith. Having embraced the faith of Christ and indeed the monastic life, he persevered in a monastery for seven years, beginning in the eighth indiction, the tenth year of Heraclius, A.D. 620. Then, inflamed with the desire for martyrdom, he left the monastery for Diospolis, Garizim, and Caesarea of Palestine, where he was imprisoned in A.D. 627, the seventeenth year of Heraclius. In September he celebrated the feast of the Exaltation of the Lord’s Cross under Constantine the Great. Finally he was taken to Persia and crowned with martyrdom in A.D. 628, the eighteenth year of Heraclius. Bollandus. He was strangled with a cord together with seventy others; afterward his head alone was cut off. His bodily relics were first taken from Jerusalem to his monastery and then brought to Rome, where they are venerated in the monastery of Blessed Paul the Apostle, called Aquae Salviae. Ado, Notker, common recension of Bede. In the *Menologion* edited by Canisius, Saint Anastasius is commemorated on 15 January.]

Saint Anastasius, monk and martyr from Persia, who, after enduring many tortures of imprisonment, beatings, and chains in Caesarea of Palestine at the hands of the Persians, was at last subjected to many punishments in Persia and finally beheaded by their king Chosroes.

**Florus in A. T. L.** In the city of Valentia in Spain, the passion of Saint Vincent, deacon, under the governor Dacianus. The governor first ordered him to be hung on the rack and tortured violently. Taken down from it, he was tortured, beaten, flogged, and burned; as his limbs were stretched apart, his body grew under the punishment. But the spirit that confessed Christ the Lord remained victorious. Thus far the Atrebatensis; from this point it turns to Anastasius. Two other manuscripts continue the eulogy in these words:

“Burning plates are pressed upon his breast, and the liquid, melted between the edges of the glowing iron, is sprinkled in drops amid crackling flames. Wounds are impressed upon wounds, and the tortures rage above them. Salts scattered upon the fires leap in tiny crackling fragments across his limbs; now the weapons of punishment are hurled not merely at his limbs but at his very entrails, with no part of his body remaining whole. Later he was shut in prison and thrown down to lie upon a heap of broken potsherds. Not long afterward, afflicted by such punishments, unconquered in faith, he gave out in body.”

**T.** On the same day, the feast of Victor and Orontius. [Note: Usuard, Notker, the common recension of Bede, and Baronius’s *Roman Martyrology* write of these saints as follows: “At Ebredunum in Gaul, Saints Vincent, Orontius, and Victor, who were crowned with martyrdom in the persecution of Diocletian.” In fact, however, they did not suffer at Ebredunum but at Gerunda in Spain, under the governor Rufinus, and were afterward carried by a certain Hactor in a cart to Ebredunum. All were beheaded.]

**23.—X Kalends.** At Rome, the feast of Saint Emerentiana, virgin of Christ and martyr, who was Saint Agnes’s foster-sister. While she was praying at Saint Agnes’s tomb and defending the assembled worshipers from the violence of the pagans, she was stoned by them.

**A.** Also the passion of Parmenas, deacon, and Macarius. [Note: Parmenas was from Philippi in Macedonia and was one of the first seven deacons. Entrusted to the grace of God, he completed with full faith the ministry of preaching assigned to him by the brethren and attained the glory of martyrdom under Trajan. Baronius’s *Martyrology*. In his notes on the *Martyrology*, Baronius says that the Greeks commemorate him on 11 March and again on 3 May, as appears from their *Menologion*. His name appears on neither date in the *Menologion* edited by Canisius or in the *Menaea*. In both, however, he appears on 2 May; again in the *Menaea* on 12 May, in the *Menologion* on 6 May, and once more on 28 July in the same *Menologion*.]

**C.** On the same day, Saint Sabina, virgin.

**T. L.** On the same day, the feast of Saint Macarius, martyr. [Note: Rabanus has: “On the same day the passion of Saints Macarius and Eugenius is celebrated. Under the judge Julian they endured many torments: a fiery grate, upon which pitch and oil had been poured, though the fire did not harm them; then they were handed over to poisonous serpents, yet were in no way injured by them. Afterward they extinguished a huge dragon by their prayers, and finally were crowned with martyrdom.” Their memory is celebrated in Baronius’s *Martyrology* on 20 December.]

**24.—IX Kalends.** The feast of Saint Timothy, apostle. [Note: When the enemies of the faith were celebrating at Ephesus, according to ancestral custom, a certain festival of idolatry called *katagōgion* (καταγώγιον), carrying idols in their hands, wearing masks, singing in them, and attacking men and women like brigands, Blessed Timothy could not bear to witness such an outrage and rebuked their folly. For this reason the impious beat him with clubs and removed him from their midst, while Nerva was governing the empire, as Polycrates, the most ancient writer of his life, says. The Greeks and some Latins speak of him on 22 January, the day on which he was killed. His body was transferred to Constantinople in the twentieth year of Constantius, together with the relics of Blessed Andrew and Luke. Notker, common recension of Bede.]

At Antioch, Saint Babylas and the three boys Urbanus, Prilidianus, and Epolonius. [Note: Eusebius, both in his *Ecclesiastical History* and in his *Chronicle*, and Jerome in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 54, write that Saint Babylas exchanged this life for immortality under Decius after his confession, while in prison. The writers of his acts and others, however, assert that he suffered under Numerianus, and that he did not die in prison but was beheaded after various tortures together with three boys. In view of this, some have reasonably thought that there were two bishops named Babylas. Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, V, 18, reports that Gallus, the brother of Julian, transferred the shrine of the martyr Babylas to Daphne, a suburb of Antioch where there was a temple of Apollo; from that time, it is said, the demon no longer uttered any oracle where it had been accustomed to do so. When Julian heard this, he ordered the sacred body to be removed from there; accordingly the Christians brought it back into the city of Antioch with psalmody.]

On the same day, Saint Sabina. [Note: She was the sister of Saint Sabinianus and was born to unbelieving parents. When her brother, instructed by an angel, fled from his father’s house, she was afflicted by longing for him and vainly sacrificed to her idols. Warned by an angelic vision, she too fled her homeland with her sole maidservant Maximiniola, seeking her brother. After traveling for a long time, she finally came to Rome, where she was baptized by Pope Eusebius. Then, again warned by an angel to go to her brother, she set out for Ravenna. When she had come within sight of the city of Troyes, she learned from a certain Lucerius of her brother’s death and burial. On learning this, she too asked the Lord for death and gave up her devout spirit at the age of forty-eight, on 29 January. Her acts are preserved by Bollandus under 20 January, on which day she and her brother are commemorated in certain martyrologies. Our author and others, however, commemorate them today. Some also commemorate her on 20 August and 5 September.]

Saint Sabina, virgin.

**Florus in A. T. L.** In Antioch, the passion of Saint Babylas, bishop, and the three boys Urbanus, Parilidanus [A., Prilidanus] and Epolonius, under the emperor Numerianus. The emperor ordered him to be bound with heavy chains by the hand of the commander Victorinus and dragged through the city. After this he ordered Babylas to be hung on the rack and the boys to be beaten. The first was twelve years old, the second nine, and the third seven. Then, since they persevered together in faith and courage, the emperor ordered them all struck with the sword.

On the same day, at Troyes, the passion of Saint Savinianus, martyr. [Note: He was also called Sabinianus, Sabianus, Fabianus, and Savinus. He left his homeland and came into the territory of Troyes, converting many through the miracle of a flowering staff. For this reason the emperor Aurelianus sent him to prison, where the forty-eight soldiers ordered to guard him were converted by him and beheaded for the faith. Saint Sabinianus himself was beaten, tortured with a heated helmet, and placed upon a red-hot bench. By divine power he was rescued from prison, but eventually he was found and beheaded on 24 January. He is commemorated not only on 29 February but also on 8 June, according to Saussay.]

And the deposition of Saint Sabina [T., Sabiana; L., Savina], virgin, his sister.

**A.** At Ephesus, the feast of Saint Timothy, bishop and martyr, disciple of Blessed Paul the Apostle. On the same day, the elevation of the body of Saint Autbertus. [Note: He flourished in the time of Dagobert, the illustrious king of the Franks, under whom Hainaut began to flourish in the faith of Christ. His disciples there were Landelinus, abbot of Crespin; Vincent Madelgarius, count; and his wife Waldetrudis. Many preachers from Scotland and Gaul joined them, as did the most holy Gislenus from Greece. Through them Hainaut was imbued with the beginnings of the faith. He was buried at Cambrai outside the walls, in the church of Saint Peter, which, after the walls were enlarged, is now within the city and is the abbey of Saint Autbertus. His feast is on the Ides of December. Molanus, *Index of the Saints of Belgium*.]

Saint Autbertus, bishop of Cambrai.

**[Col. 0823B] 25.—VIII Kalends.** Saint Gregory the Theologian and the feast of Saint Projectus. [Note: Gregory was born at Arianzus. He was the great friend of Basil the Great; first he became bishop of Sasima, then of Nazianzus, and finally of Constantinople. When the Constantinopolitan synod appointed Nectarius bishop of the imperial city, he voluntarily resigned the governance of the Church. Although he was earnestly entreated to become bishop of his homeland, he could not be persuaded to accept the episcopate; instead, he appointed a certain Eulalius, his friend, bishop of Nazianzus. He himself practiced the monastic life at Arianzus until, having reached the age of ninety and beyond, he exchanged life for death while Theodosius was in the thirteenth year of his reign. See the Life written by Gregory the presbyter, Jerome’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Suidas. On 9 May Bede, Usuard, Ado, and finally the other Latins commemorate him; the Greeks, however, do so in the *Menologion* on 19 January, the day on which they celebrate the elevation of the body of Gregory the Theologian. Again, on this day, 25 January, they observe a more solemn feast of him.]

Saint Projectus. [Note: A manuscript martyrology of Saint Gudula at Brussels has: “At Clermont, Saint Projectus, bishop and martyr, who was crowned with martyrdom by the nobles of his city in revenge for Hector, the patrician of Massilia, whom Childeric, king of the Franks, had killed because of the injustices he had inflicted upon the Church of Clermont. And Amarinus, a man of God, who was slaughtered by the nobles of the said city of Clermont together with the aforementioned bishop Projectus.”]

**Florus in A. and T.** In the city of Miletus, the passion of Saint Thyrsus. [Note: Saint Thyrsus suffered during the reign of the emperor Decius. Ado, common recension of Bede, Notker. The Latins commemorate him together with Saints Leucius and Callinicus on 18 and 28 January, and the Greeks on 14 December. Thyrsus himself is commemorated separately on 25 January.]

He suffered under the proconsuls Cumbricius, Sylvanus, and Plautus in the city of Caesarea. First he was ordered to be stretched out in chains as a punishment, so that his limbs might be torn apart. When the chains broke, a vessel was ordered to be filled with water, and the martyr was suspended upside down and scourged with his head submerged in it. When the vessel was shattered by the Lord’s power, he was confined in prison twice and held for trial. Later he was scourged with cords and handed over to beasts. Emerging unharmed, he was ordered to have a small chamber made, into which he was placed so that he might be cut in two. But when those who were to cut him became exhausted, and Blessed Thyrsus was coming out of the chamber, by divine providence his heel adhered to it. Recognizing this, he placed himself in the chamber again and thus brought his passion to its conclusion.

In the same manuscripts, and likewise in L.: On the same day, in the district of Auvergne, the feast of Projectus, bishop and martyr, who, chosen in prophetic fashion from the womb, preserved his purple robe in triumph.

**C. A. T. L.** The Conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle.

**26.—VII Kalends.** The feast of Saint Polycarp. [Note: “He was a disciple of the apostle John and was ordained bishop of Smyrna by him; he was the foremost man of all Asia. Because of certain questions concerning Easter, under the emperor Antoninus Pius, while Anicetus governed the Church in the city, he came to Rome, where he brought back to the faith many believers who had been deceived by the persuasion of Marcion and Valentinus. Later, while Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus were reigning, when the proconsul was seated at Smyrna and the whole people were shouting against him in the amphitheater, he was handed over to the fire.” Jerome. The proconsul was Tatius Quadratus.]

Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, who, under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, while the proconsul was seated at Smyrna and the whole people conspired against him (*conjurante*; variant *conjurgante*, “railing”), was handed over to the fire.

**Florus adds in manuscripts A. T. L.** When he was eighty-six years old.

**L.** It is written in the *Ecclesiastical History*.

**T.** “When they therefore wished to bind him with chains, observing custom and law, he said: ‘Permit me to remain thus; for he who gave me the will will grant me also the ability, and will make even the heat of the violent fire bearable.’ Accordingly no one bound him with iron; but with his hands tied behind his back, like a devoted ram, he entered upon the threshold of his passion. When his prayer had been completed, they set fire to him; but the flame did not touch the martyr’s little body with any embrace. Thus, made wholly radiant in the fire, he gave forth from himself a marvelous odor instead of a stench. Then it was ordered that a small sword be thrust into the holy breast. When this was done, behold, a great stream of blood suddenly flowed from the body, a dove emerged, and the fire, immediately stilled by the blood, ceased.”

**T.** On the same day, at Bethlehem, the passing of Saint Paula, dedicated to God. [Note: This most noble Roman woman, daughter of Rogatus and Blaesilla and wife of Toxotius, bore four daughters—Blaesilla, Paulina, Eustochium or Julia, and Rufina—and a son, Toxotius. After becoming a widow, she lived five years at Rome; then, having traveled through Judaea and Egypt, she settled at Bethlehem. There she founded four monasteries, one for men and three for virgins, and, after living there twenty years, was buried there. She is renowned on the testimony of Saint Jerome, who wrote her Life. The whole span of her life amounted to fifty-six years, eight months, and twenty-one days. Saint Paula died during the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the sixth time and Aristaenetus, on the third day of the week; the year was A.D. 404, with the Sunday letter C in January. She was therefore born on 5 May 347, while Constans ruled in Italy and Constantius in the East. The common recension of Bede, Usuard, Ado, and others assign her to the following day.]

Saint Paula, dedicated to God.

**27.—VI Kalends.** Bede has no entry.

**[Col. 0826B] D.** The feast of Blessed John, surnamed Chrysostom, who greatly benefited the Christian religion by his words and example. [Note: He has several days made famous by the veneration attached to his name for various reasons. The first is 15 December, the day of his election to the episcopate, according to the Greek *Menaea*. The second is 26 February, the day of his consecration, as George of Alexandria relates in his Life. In the manuscript *Florarium*, under 5 May: “At Constantinople, the deposition from the episcopate of Blessed John, bishop.” Then his first exile is recorded on 19 March. Metaphrastes assigns his recall to 13 November. According to the manuscript *Florarium*, his second exile fell on 20 January. According to the *Menaea*, he died on 14 September. The most celebrated of all his days is 27 January, when his sacred body was brought back to Constantinople and placed in the church of the Holy Apostles, in the time of the patriarch Proclus and Theodosius the Younger; so the Greeks state in the *Menologion*. On the following day, 28 January, these sacred relics are said by Theodore the Reader, book II of the *Collection*, at the end, to have been deposited at the Holy Apostles—that is, after the solemn transfer performed on the preceding day. Finally, the Greeks commemorate him again in the *Menaea* on 30 January together with Saints Basil and Gregory Nazianzen.]

**V. C.** In Africa, Dativus [V., Davitus] and Julianus, Vincentia, Secundus, Aemilianus, and thirty-five others.

**A. T. L.** In Africa, the passion of Saints Secundus and Fortunatus. And the feast of Saint Processus. And Saint John Chrysostom. Processus is absent from L. In T., Chrysostom is placed first, but incorrectly in Burgundy.

**28.—V Kalends.** The feast of Saint Agnes, virgin, concerning her birth. [Note: See also 21 January. This is the ancient inscription for this day, and for this reason: it is not the octave of the first day, so that it should be called an octave; rather, the heavenly vision that was shown on the eighth day is celebrated. On this day the memory is recalled of the time when, while her parents were keeping vigil at her tomb, she appeared to them amid a choir of holy virgins and, testifying that God had granted her everlasting glory, consoled them, as is contained in her acts preserved by Saint Ambrose. Baronius in the *Martyrology*.]

**T. otherwise:** At Rome, the nativity of Saint Agnes, virgin.

**V. C.** Perpetua, Julianus, and forty-four others. [Note: She is commemorated together with Dativus, Julianus, Publianus, Quintillus, and Festus also on the preceding day.]

**A.** In Africa, the feast of Dativus and Julianus.

**L.** It has the same names, but without the place of their contest.

**T.** On the same day, the feast of Publianus, Quintillus, Festus, Dativus, and Julianus.

And in Burgundy, Saint John, abbot. [Note: He was abbot of the monastery of Reomay in the diocese of Langres, within the jurisdiction of Tonnerre, a town of Celtic Gaul on the boundary of Burgundy and Brie. He was born in the territory of the city of Langres, of noble parents, his father Hilary and his mother Quieta. At about twenty years of age he built a cell in a remote part of the estate and devoted himself to God. Seeking an even more secluded retreat, he built a monastery at the deserted place called Reomay. Resigning authority over the monks for the sake of humility, he withdrew to the island of Lérins in his desire to remain hidden; there, however, he was recognized and recalled to his own people. At last he died at about the age of 120. The author of his Life expressed Saint John’s age as follows: “From the time of the emperor Valentinian and the emperor Marcian, who after Theodosius the Younger obtained the dignity of sole rule, until the time of the emperor Justinian, he endured. It was also during this period that the Franks, together with King Clovis, setting aside civil government and invading the Roman boundaries with military force, invaded Gaul. He thus endured until the time of King Theodoric, who was the son of the aforementioned Clovis, and of his son Theudebert.” From this it follows that Saint John was born no earlier than 425, when Valentinian III assumed the empire, and died no later than 548, when Theudebert died. Perhaps he died in 545, adding 120 years to the year 425.]

**[Col. 0827B] 29.—IV Kalends.** At Rome, the feast of Saints Papias and Maurus, soldiers, during the time of Diocletian. When they saw the steadfastness of the martyrs Saturninus and Sisinnius, they were converted to the faith. Immediately the prefect Laudicius ordered that the mouths of the saints, with which they confessed Christ, be crushed with stones and that they be thrust back into prison. There they were baptized by Blessed Marcellus. Twelve days later he ordered them brought out, laid upon the ground, and beaten with clubs; then, lifted from the ground, they were beaten with leaded scourges until they expired. The priest John gathered their bodies by night and buried them on the Nomentan Way, at the place of the Nymphae of Blessed Peter, where he baptized. Written in the acts of Blessed Pope Marcellus.

**30.—III Kalends.** Bede has no entry.

**Florus in A. T. L.** At the monastery of Malbodium, the deposition of Saint Aldegundis, virgin, who was born of royal stock, her father being Walbertus and her mother Bertilia; she was also the sister of the most blessed Waldetrudis. She founded the monastery of Malbodium, which is now a town of Hainaut and contains the famous college of noble canonesses, or ladies. Thus Molanus in his *Index of the Saints of Belgium*. She was buried at Curtissolra, where she died. Later, by King Sigebert the illustrious—or rather by Theodoric, son of Clovis II—and by the blessed virgin Aldetrudis, abbess, her body was transferred to the town of Malbodium, as may be seen in her Life preserved by Bollandus. She flourished in the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks.

She was born of royal lineage and, rejecting her mother’s persuasion concerning marriage, chose Christ as her bridegroom. Thus she was worthy both to enjoy his conversation and often to experience angelic visitations.

**D.** At Antioch, the passion of Saint Hippolytus. [Note: Near Antioch, the passion of Blessed Hippolytus, martyr, who, having been somewhat deceived by the schism of Novatian, was corrected through the working of Christ’s grace and returned to the charity of the Church, for which and within which he afterward completed a glorious martyrdom. Common recension of Bede, Ado, Usuard, Notker.]

At Jerusalem, Saint Matthias, bishop. [Note: At Jerusalem, the most holy Matthias, bishop, concerning whom marvelous deeds full of faith are related. After enduring many things for Christ, he finally ended his life in peace. He governed the Church as the eighth bishop after James. Common recension of Bede, Ado, and others.]

**V. C.** In Africa, Felicianus, Philippus, and others.

**C.** One hundred and twenty-three.

**A. T. L.** At Antioch, the passion of Saint Hippolytus. In Africa, the feast of Saints Celerus [L., Celeris], Pellianus, Philippianus, and one hundred and twenty-three others.

**31.—II Kalends.** Bede has no entry.

D., Alexandria: the martyr Mytrani [Note: [Col. 0827D] He was also called Metras. The Decian beasts dragged him away with extreme cruelty and compelled him to say things that left nothing undone for the utmost injury, insult, and blasphemy against Christ. Since he obeyed them less than they wished, they scourged his entire body most savagely with clubs, cut his face to pieces with a sharp reed, pierced his eyes, and tore his inner organs and the hidden parts of his body. Finally, as though renouncing their own brutality, they buried him beneath a great mass of stones. Nicephorus Callistus, Ecclesiastical History, V, 30.] Mytrani.

At Tridentum, Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr. [Note: [Col. 0828D] This bishop of Tridentum flourished in the year 390. While attempting to eradicate the remnants of idolatry completely, he was, according to the Roman Martyrology, June 26, struck by a shower of stones by wild and barbarous men and completed his martyrdom for the name of Christ under the consulship of Stilicho, that is, in the year 400, or at least 405. A small work by him, On the Martyrdom of Sisinnius and His Companions, still exists among his writings in Surius under May 29. Meanwhile, it should be noted that there were several Vigiliuses in this and the following century, and that our Vigilius is often confused especially with Vigilius of Tapsus, who wrote against Eutyches. Cave, *Literary History*. Usuard and Baronius’s *Martyrology*, however, celebrate him on June 26.]
