V., In Alexandria, the feast of Saints Abbaciri and John, Cyriacus, Tarsus, Galericus, and fifteen other priests.

A. T. L., In Alexandria, Saints Tyrsicus, Zoticus, and Ammon. In Africa, Saints Victor and Publius. L., and Polycarp. And [Note: [Col. 0828D] “Burial.” More properly, translation, for the day of his departure is commemorated on March 30. Veronus was the brother of Saint Verona; he was buried at Lembeca, formerly a town on the border of Hainaut and Brabant. But his body was transferred from there to a safer place, namely, to the hills of Hainaut. Molanus, *Catalogue of the Saints of Belgium*. Also in his additions to Usuard, January 31. At Gastrilocus, the translation of Saint Veron, confessor.] the burial [Col. 0829A] of Saint Veron, confessor.

A. T., And the Passion of Saints Callinicus and fifteen other priests.

C., In Alexandria, Tarsacius, Zoticus, Cyriacus, Tyrsus, Galenus, and others, and [Note: [Col. 0829A] “Ciri.” He was an Alexandrian by birth and cultivated the medical art; John, however, was from Edessa and served in the army. When the Church was afflicted by Diocletian’s persecution, Cyrus fled to Arabia and lived a monastic life. When John heard of Cyrus’s fame, which had spread everywhere, he abandoned military service and, longing for Cyrus, went to Arabia. As the persecution grew harsher, these inseparable companions went to Canopus, where Athanasius and her three daughters—Theodosia, Theoctista, and Eudoxia—were being held captive, in order to strengthen them for the truth. They were brought before the Syrian prefect and cruelly tortured while the virgins looked on; the virgins themselves, together with their mother, were first tortured and then beheaded, followed by Cyrus and John. All were honorably buried in the temple of the apostle Saint Mark. See the Acts in Bollandus. [Col. 0830B] Their bodies were later transferred to Rome.] Cyrus and John.

## [FEBRUARY.]

[Col. 0829C]

### 1.—KALENDS. The feast of Saint Brigid, virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0829C] Born in Scotland—that is, in Ireland, which is ancient Scotland—in the village of Fochart in Muirthemne, in the province of the Ulaid, specifically in the district called Conaille Muirthemne. When she had grown up, she set out with three girls to the two bishops Mel and Melchu, disciples of Saint Patrick who lived in the towns of Meath, and received the veil from Saint Macaille, their disciple. The principal monastery built by Saint Brigid was Kildare, which later grew into a large city. She also founded other monasteries in the regions of Meath, Connacht, and Munster. After performing many astonishing miracles, she died in 523, on Wednesday, February 1, thirty years after Saint Patrick’s death, in the eightieth year of her age, and was buried at Kildare. If you wish to know more about this holy virgin, read what is written about her in her Acts in Bollandus.]

Florus, in A. T. L., places her in Scotland and then adds: “She was joined to Christ by love from her earliest age. Living most holily according to a chaste purpose, she shone forth through many miracles.”

[Col. 0830C] V. C., In Greece, Saints Polycarp [Note: [Col. 0829D] See January 26 concerning Saint Polycarp.], Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0829D] He was a companion of Saint Pionius, who suffered at Smyrna either under Antoninus Verus, as Ado, Notker, the Vulgate recension of Bede, and others hold, following Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, where under the seventh year of Marcus Aurelius—corresponding to A.D. 167—the Latin manuscripts read: “When persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom”; or under Decius, as the Acts indicate. See Jerome’s Martyrology, where Saint Dionysius is listed with Paeni, who is the same as Paeonius or Pionius.] martyrs.

C., On the same day, the feast of Saints Apronianus, Fortunatus, and Felicianus.

A. T. L., On the same day, the Passion of Saints Vindemialis [Note: [Col. 0830C] Bishop of Tapsus and martyr in Africa, who, together with Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, contending against the Arians by doctrine and miracles, was ordered by King Huneric to be beheaded. Thus Baronius under May 2. Galesinius and Saint Jerome’s Martyrology, however, commemorate him today with our author. Concerning this Arian persecution, see the history of Victor of Vita, bishop.] and Eugenius.

At Augusta, Saint Ursus, bishop and confessor. [Note: [Col. 0830D] Apparently he was not a bishop but only a priest and disciple of Bishop Theonestus. When Theonestus was driven from his see by the Arians, he traveled toward Rome with his disciples Alban, Ursus, Tabra, and Tabrata. Passing through Etruria into Liguria, he reached Augusta, the praetorium of the Salassi, on the river Dora, among the Alpine mountains. Because Ursus zealously defended Catholic doctrine against the Arians, he was killed around the year 560. See Bollandus for more about him.]

L., And the feast of Saint Praecordius. [Note: [Col. 0830D] A priest of Scottish origin who came to Valliacum in the district of Soissons and lived there until his death. He became so distinguished for perfection that he was made a familiar companion of Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims. After he had lain buried at Valliacum for ninety years, the priest who guarded his tomb secretly carried him to England. The priest Tihard, however, pursued the thief, secretly recovered the relics, and happily brought them back to Gaul. He continued until he reached Folliacum, an estate of the church of Corbie, where a heavenly light revealed the relics. The matter was reported to Abbot Berengarius, and the relics were brought to Corbie. His feast is celebrated at Valliacum on February 1; the translation to Corbie took place on June 5. It is clear that he lived in the sixth century, since he was a companion of Saint Remigius, who died in 532.]

L. A., And the Passion of Saint Ignatius, martyr. [Note: [Col. 0831B] He succeeded Evodius as the third bishop of the Church of Antioch after the apostle Peter. For the faith of Christ he was brought from Syria to Rome, exposed to wild beasts, and won the palm of martyrdom in the eleventh year of Trajan, according to Jerome’s *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. There is considerable variation concerning the day on which Saint Ignatius’s feast is celebrated. The Antiochenes, according to John Chrysostom, Homily 42, *On Saint Ignatius*, commemorate him on the day after Saint Pelagia the virgin, whose memory is celebrated on June 9 and 10. Some assign his feast to November 24 or December 14; more commonly, to December 17. Nevertheless, his principal solemnity in the Roman Church is held on the Kalends of February, as Ado, Notker, Usuard, Baronius, and other more recent writers attest.]

T., And at Ravenna, the feast of Saint Severinus, bishop. [Note: [Col. 0831C] More properly Severus. While earning a living for himself and his household through wool-working, at the time when, after Marcellinus’s death, the people of Ravenna were deliberating over the election of a bishop, he was divinely designated as bishop when a dove settled upon his head. From a wool-worker he miraculously became a great theologian and fought bravely for Saint Athanasius against the Arians at the Council of Sardica. At last, worn down by old age, he was divinely informed of the day on which he would die. After celebrating Mass in the presence of the entire people, still wearing his sacred vestments, he went to the tomb. There, having bent his knees and raised his hands and eyes toward heaven as though devoutly pouring out prayers, he fell asleep in the Lord. Galesinius. Saint Vincentia was his wife, and Saint Innocentia, a virgin, was his daughter. He died around A.D. 390.]

### 2.—IV NONES. The Hypapante of the Lord.

On the same day, the feast of Saint Apronianus. [Note: [Col. 0831D] A *commentariensis* who, while still a pagan, was escorting Saint Sisinnius from prison to present him to the prefect Laodicius during Maximian’s persecution. He was converted by a heavenly light and voice. When the prefect learned of this, he ordered him to undergo the death sentence. He was therefore led along the Salarian Way to the second milestone and beheaded; he died a martyr and victor, and was buried on the very spot by the priest John. Ado, Usuard, the Vulgate recension of Bede, Rabanus, Notker, Peter de Natalibus, and Baronius. His feast is also celebrated above on the Kalends of February together with Fortunatus and Felicianus, who are also commemorated today.]

Apronianus.

V. adds: “And Felicianus.” C. referred him to the preceding day.

L., And in Jerusalem, the burial of Blessed Simeon, prophet. [Note: [Col. 0832B] The *Menaea* place him on the third day before the Nones, and Ferrarius likewise writes that he was honored at Jadera in Illyricum on that day. Peter de Natalibus says that he was buried in Jerusalem on the second day before the Nones of February. The Roman Church, however, according to Baronius, commemorates him on October 8.] He received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death until he had first seen the Christ of the Lord.

### 3.—III NONES. Bede has no entry.

D., The blessed Celerinus. [Note: [Col. 0832B] Saint Cyprian ordained him lector during his retreat, or, as the Martyrologies maintain, deacon. At the beginning of the Decian persecution, according to Cyprian’s Letter 34, “for nineteen days he was surrounded by prison custody and was kept in the stocks and in irons.” Later he writes: “His grandmother Celerina had long ago been crowned by martyrdom, as likewise his uncles Laurentinus and Ignatius”; they seem to have suffered martyrdom before the Decian catastrophe, for Cyprian calls Celerinus “the first in the battle of our time.” If he was the first to endure the torments of this catastrophe, then those in whose footsteps he walks must have suffered in some earlier persecution.]

Celerinus the deacon and Celerina his grandmother.

V. C. S., Blasius. [Note: [Col. 0832C] Whether this was Blasius of Oretum or Blasius of Sebaste, the bishop, is uncertain. Saint Blasius of Oretum was made bishop in Spain by Saint Anastasius, a disciple of Saint James the apostle, son of Zebedee. He suffered martyrdom during Nero’s persecution at a town called Centumfontes in Celtiberia.]

Blasius the bishop.

In Africa, Felix, Simpronius, Laurentius, Hippolytus, and Felicitas.

A. T., In Africa, Felix and Felicitas.

At Sebaste in Cappadocia [This is absent from T.], the Passion of Saint Blasius. [Note: [Col. 0832C] He suffered at Sebaste, a city of Cappadocia, or, according to others, of Armenia. The Greeks celebrate him on February 11; Ado and Notker on February 15, though Notker also commemorates him today. When persecution raged at Sebaste, Saint Blasius hid on Mount Argeus, where he healed sick animals that came to him. One day the persecutors saw a multitude of animals standing before him and reported this to the governor Agricolaus, who ordered him to be brought before him. When Blessed Blasius entered the city, Agricolaus sent him to prison and ordered him to be severely beaten with clubs. Later, the holy man was suspended and scraped with iron combs.

As the saint was being taken back to prison, seven holy women followed him and collected drops of his blood on linen cloths. For this they were brought before the governor, who ordered them to sit on fiery seats. They remained unharmed, however, were raised onto the rack, and had their flesh torn with iron combs. Then the two boys, sons of one of them, approached their mother and asked to become Christians. The governor imprisoned them together with Saint Blasius.

The next day he ordered the holy women to be thrown into a furnace. Though they remained unharmed amid the flames, they were finally beheaded. Saint Blasius was brought out of prison and thrown into a lake; an angel drew him out, but at last he was beheaded. Peter de Natalibus.

Not everyone agrees concerning the date of Saint Blasius’s martyrdom. Constantius Felicius says that he was crowned under Diocletian in A.D. 287, although others refer him to the time of Julian the Apostate. The author of the *Florarius* assigns the same year; Canisius, 288. Galesinius and Peter de Natalibus assert that he was killed under Diocletian. The Greek Menologion places him under Maximian. The *Menaea*, however, the second and third Acts published by Bollandus, and Baronius, *Annals*, vol. III, under A.D. 316, no. 45, place him under Licinius. There was also another Saint Blasius besides this one and Blasius of Oretum; he was a shepherd or herdsman and a martyr at Caesarea in Cappadocia.]

Blasius, bishop and martyr.

At Lyon, the burial of Lupicinus, bishop and confessor.

L., At Monte Castriloco, the translation of Saint Waldetrudis. [Note: [Col. 0833C] Molanus writes the following about her: Saint Waldetrudis’s parents were Walbert and Bertilia; her sister was Aldegund; her husband was Saint Vincent, count of Hainaut; her children were Saint Landric; Saint Aldetrudis and Madelberta, who presided over the monastery of Maubeuge; and the boy Dentelin, who died in the white garment of baptism. All are invoked in the litanies of the Church of Mons.

When Vincent, wholly intent on heavenly things, had taken the monastic habit at Hautmont, his wife Waldetrudis, at the urging of Saint Gislenus, obtained the sacred veil from Blessed Aubert, bishop, and built a cell on the mountain called Castrilocus. That cell is now in the principal city of Hainaut, namely Mons. The church of Saint Waldetrudis, converted into a collegiate chapter of noble canonesses, has the count of Hainaut as its perpetual abbot. Her passing is celebrated on April 9; the translation, today. The separation of her head from the rest of her body is celebrated on August 12, and her canonization on November 2. This saint is also commemorated on March 28 by Molanus, Canisius, and Ferrarius. She is also honored on February 2 in the additions to the *Floraria*.]

Waldetrudis.

And in Africa, the feast of Felix and Felicitas, and of Saint Blasius, bishop and martyr.

### 4.—II NONES. Bede has no entry.

D., In the Egyptian city of Thmuis, Blessed Phileas, bishop of that same city, and Philoromus the tribune, and innumerable martyrs. [Note: [Col. 0833D] Concerning Phileas and Philoromus, Eusebius writes in *Ecclesiastical History*, VIII, 9: “Philoromus held no ordinary office but the high office of procurator of the imperial treasury at Alexandria; and, surrounded daily by soldiers in accordance with the dignity and privilege of his Roman rank, he administered justice. Phileas was also bishop of the Church of Thmuis, a man who had discharged every civic honor and office in his homeland with the highest distinction and was highly renowned in philosophical studies.

When innumerable relatives and friends, some of them magistrates and men of rank, begged them to yield, and when the judge himself urged them to take pity on themselves and provide for their wives and children, they could never be induced by any of these considerations to disregard, for the sake of preserving their lives, the divine laws concerning confession and denial of the name of Christ. Instead, with manly and philosophical courage—or rather, with a religious mind consecrated to God—they stood firm against all the judge’s threats and insults, and both were struck with the sword. They suffered under the emperor Diocletian and the governor Culcianus.”]

V. C., The feast of Geminus, Gelasius, Mannia, Donatus, and Aquilina.

A. T. L., The feast of Gemini, Gelasius, and Magnus. [Note: [Col. 0834B] They suffered at Forum Sempronii, as the Vulgate recension of Bede, Usuard, Notker, and others hold. Some have written that they suffered at Rome, in the Forum of Sempronius. Since none of the nineteen places situated outside Rome called *Fora* was called Sempronium, it is more likely that they suffered at Forum Sempronii, a city of the highest standing in Umbria. Ferrarius, in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, writes that they completed their martyrdom by beheading.]

A., perhaps from Florus: “On the same day, the burial of Saint Waldetrudis; placed in great honor, she left the world after receiving the sacred veil from the hands of Blessed Aubert, bishop, and was often deemed worthy to see her heavenly bridegroom.”

On the same day, the Passion of Saint Liphardus, martyr and archbishop of Canterbury. [Note: [Col. 0834C] He is said to have been bishop of Canterbury, but this seems scarcely possible. For in Bede’s history, in the seventh century, during the time of King Dagobert, no bishop of Canterbury of this name is found. Perhaps he was a bishop among the Britons who ruled over the Britons of Dover, who had been driven from their homeland by the Saxons, as Bollandus holds.

Saint Lietphardus traveled to Rome together with Cadruele, son of the king of Britain. While returning, Cadruele was killed in the woods of Aridae Gamantiae, and his body was buried in a garden beneath a tree at Trescaltium. It was later transferred to the village of Honnecourt, or Hunonis Curia, four miles from Cambrai, turning away from the road to Péronne. Molanus, *Catalogue of the Saints of Belgium*.]

### 5.—NONES. Saint Agatha, virgin in Sicily, under Quintianus the consul in the time of Diocletian. [Note: [Col. 0834D] There is great controversy between the people of Palermo and those of Catania concerning Saint Agatha’s birthplace, and each side insists that she was its own citizen. The question nevertheless remains undecided. This, however, can be asserted with certainty: she suffered in the province of Sicily, in the city of Catania, under the emperor Decius, when Decius was consul for the third time—that is, in A.D. 252—under the proconsul Quintianus. Bede wrongly writes that she completed her martyrdom under Diocletian: her Acts were written by those who witnessed the virgin’s contest at Catania, and many Martyrologies testify with the greatest authority that she suffered under Decius.]

After slaps and imprisonment, after the rack and tortures, after the cutting off of her breasts—though the Lord healed her—and after being rolled over potsherds and coals, she finally completed her course in prison.

L., At Ghent, the burial of Saint Bertulf, confessor. [Note: [Col. 0834D] A native of Alemannia, who, during the reign of the younger King Sigebert, left his pagan parents and came to Renty, a place in Artois, in the diocese of Thérouanne or Boulogne. There he received baptism and the clerical office.

At that time Count Wambert and his wife Hamburga had built a monastery in honor of Saint Dionysius and three churches. Bertulf entered their service, and, after they had recognized his goodness, they placed him over their entire household. When they later went to Rome, they made him heir of Renty and its churches, where he died in peace.

When pirates were ravaging the coast of Gaul, Count Erkengarius transferred the saint’s body from Renty to Boulogne. Later, when a certain Breton had secretly carried the body away, Count Arnulf of Flanders intercepted him and ordered the body to be transferred to Harelbeke, intending soon to move it to Blandinium, the monastery of Saint Peter at Ghent. His Acts are in Bollandus. Molanus, *The Saints of Belgium*; Ferrarius; Ghinius of Siena.]

### 6.—VIII IDES. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L., but with the order altered in A. because of Saint Vedast.

At Elnone, the burial of Saint Amandus, bishop. [Note: [Col. 0835C] He was born around A.D. 594, on May 7, to Serenus, duke of Aquitaine, and Amantia. After living for some time on the island of Ogie, he came to Bourges, where he was kindly received by Austregisilus around A.D. 612. He was enclosed there in a cell for fifteen years and finally went to Rome in A.D. 627. Later, warned by a vision, he returned to Gaul and was ordained bishop around A.D. 628.

He went to Rome a second time in A.D. 630. Returning, he preached at Ghent in A.D. 631, where he suffered many injuries. After raising a dead man at Fornaci in A.D. 632, he began to build monasteries throughout the surrounding region. Meanwhile, because he had reproved King Dagobert’s immorality, he was banished in A.D. 634. The same king later recalled him from exile, and in A.D. 635 he baptized the king’s son Sigebert.

From A.D. 636 he governed the monasteries begun at Ghent for eight years. In A.D. 638 he obtained from the king a suitable place for building the monastery of Elnone, and in A.D. 646 he built the monastery of Marchiennes. When Bishop John Agnus of Utrecht died in A.D. 646, Saint Amandus was substituted for him and governed that church for three years; he also consecrated the monastery of Nivelles.

In A.D. 649, because of the clergy’s disobedience, he left Utrecht and appointed Jonatus over the people of Elnone. In A.D. 650 he went to Rome for the third time, returning in A.D. 651. Around A.D. 653 he consecrated the oratory of Saint Gislain. He dedicated the church of Antwerp around A.D. 660.

From A.D. 665 he instructed the Basques, built a monastery in the territory of Bourbon, another at Nanto among the Rutenes, and another at Barisis in A.D. 666. In A.D. 667 he was present at the translation of Saint Vedast. Finally, he died in the monastery of Elnone in A.D. 684. This is proved at length by Bollandus against Molanus, Ghinius of Siena, and all who wish him to have died in A.D. 661.]

He was distinguished by the power of many miracles. Among other things, it is said that a man condemned by a cruel judge, from whom he could not obtain life before his death, obtained life and salvation after death from Christ the merciful judge.

On the same day, at the city of Arras, the burial of Saint Vedast, bishop and confessor. [Note: [Col. 0836C] He encouraged King Clovis to accept the faith after opening the eyes of a blind man by the power of Christ. When Saint Remigius had baptized that same king, he consecrated Saint Vedast bishop of Arras. There he preached the Gospel under favorable auspices and built a church in honor of God and the Blessed Virgin Mary. After administering the bishopric for forty years, he died around A.D. 570, according to Molanus and Ghinius of Siena; Bollandus prefers A.D. 540.]

Vedast, bishop [Col. 0836B] and confessor. While shining with the signs of many miracles and imparting various healings to various people, he gradually converted the barbarous Frankish people to the Catholic faith.

D., At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Dorothea, virgin, and Theophilus the scholastic. [Note: [Col. 0836C] Dorothea was entrusted to two sisters, Christa and Callista, who had apostatized from the faith, so that they might turn her away from Christ. Instead, she converted them again to Christ, and the prefect Apricius had them put into a barrel and burned. Dorothea was then led to the place of punishment, where she also suffered. When a certain scholastic named Theophilus mocked her because she said that Christ would send her apples and blooming roses, she obtained these things quickly. When Theophilus saw them, he immediately confessed Christ as the true God and suffered martyrdom under the same prefect, being beheaded. Rabanus. Dorothea was stretched upon the rack, burned with lamps, and beheaded. They all suffered under Diocletian.]

V. C. A. T., At Rome, on the Appian Way, the Passion of Saint Soter, virgin. [Note: [Col. 0836D] After being severely and at length beaten with slaps, and after overcoming every other kind of punishment, she finally completed her martyrdom by the sword. Some more recent writers say that she suffered in the East; but since the older writers say that she was crowned with martyrdom at Rome, and Saint Ambrose, in Book III *On Virgins*, where he explains her Acts, calls her a martyr relative—that is, a kinswoman—it is established that she was Italian. She is also celebrated on February 10. She suffered under Diocletian in A.D. 304.]

Soter, virgin.

And Saint Dorothea, virgin. [Note: [Col. 0836D] Born of a noble family in Alexandria, she was accused of adultery by Maximian Galerius. Having obtained a delay and fearing the loss of her virginity, she secretly fled by night and sought a cave, where she devoted herself to God for a long time and died peacefully. Eusebius, *History*, VIII, 14.]

### 7.—VII IDES. In Britain, at Augusta, the feast of August, bishop and martyr. [Note: [Col. 0837C] They did not suffer under Decius, as Ghinius of Siena holds, but rather under Diocletian. For if this martyrdom is referred to the Decian catastrophe, it is necessary to depart from the common agreement of British writers, who hold that Alban was the first of all in Britain to shed blood for Christ.]

V. and C. add, with a comma inserted: “And the martyr Anatolius.”

A. T. L., “And Saints Statianus and Saturninus.”

### 8.—VI IDES. Bede has no entry.

D., Dionysius, Aemilianus, and Sebastianus. [Note: [Col. 0837C] Saints Dionysius, [Col. 0837D] Sebastianus, and Aemilianus suffered in Lesser Armenia.]

In Alexandria, Saint Coynta, martyr. [Note: [Col. 0837D] Concerning Coynta, or Quinta, Eusebius writes in *Ecclesiastical History*, VI, 41: “After this they seized a faithful woman named Quinta and led her to the temple of an idol, compelling her to worship it. When she rejected and cursed it, they bound her feet and dragged her through all the streets of the city, paved with rough stones. After crushing her with millstones and beating her with whips, they took her likewise to the outskirts of the city, where they killed her with stones.”]

V. C., The feast of Saint Inventius [C., Venantius], bishop and confessor. [Note: [Col. 0837D] More properly Juventius, bishop at Ticinum in Italy. He was sent to that city together with Saint Syrus by Hermagoras, a disciple of Saint Mark the evangelist. Preaching the Gospel of Christ there and shining with great virtues, they also enlightened the neighboring cities by divine works and rested in peace after a glorious end. Usuard commemorates him on September 12.]

V. C. A. T. L., At Rome, the burial of Saint Paul, bishop.

Lucius.

C., “And elsewhere, Lucius, and the burial of Thomas.”

A. T. L., “And Pope Julius.”

In Armenia, Saints Dionysius and Sebastianus.

### 9.—V IDES. Bede has no entry.

D., At Alexandria, Saint Apollonia, virgin. [Note: [Col. 0837D] Concerning her, Dionysius writes in Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, VI, 41: “They also seized that remarkable virgin Apollonia, already advanced in age. [Col. 0838C] They struck her jaws and knocked out all her teeth. Then they kindled a pyre outside the city and threatened to burn her alive unless she uttered impious words with them. She appeared for a short while to ask permission, but, having meanwhile been released, she quickly leaped into the fire and was consumed,” under Decius.]

V. C., The feast at Alexandria of Alexander [C., Alexandrius] and thirty-eight others.

V., The burial of Thomas. [Note: [Col. 0838C] The burial of Thomas is also celebrated on the preceding day.]

A. T. L., At Sueno in Cyprus, the feast of Alexander, Ammon, and Didymus.

L., At the monastery of Fontanella, the burial of Saint Ansbert, archbishop of Rouen. [Note: [Col. 0838D] Born to his father Siwinus in the district of Vexin. From the monastery of Fontanella, situated in the territory of Rouen on the Seine, he was taken after Saint Ouen and made bishop of Rouen. Brought before Prince Pepin, he humbly endured the hardships of exile at the monastery of Hautmont in Hainaut. There he also slept in the repose of death. After his death he requested to be taken back to Fontanella. Accordingly, Halidulf, abbot of Hautmont, transported his body there with great honor. This took place in the year 695.]

C., On the same day, the construction of Blessed Benedict the abbot, and of Saint Sena, virgin. [Note: [Col. 0838D] Bollandus doubts whether this is Saint Xena, or Eusebia, a Roman virgin who died at Mylasa in Caria, or Serena, whose relics were brought to Metz.]

### 10.—IV IDES. At Rome, Saints Zoticus, Irenaeus, Hyacinthus, and Amantius. [Note: [Col. 0838D] Galesinius indicates the time of their martyrdom by writing that they were killed for Christ during the Decian persecution.]

[Col. 0839B] C. adds: “And ninety others.”

A. T. L., On the same day, in Campania, the feast of Saint Silvanus, bishop and confessor. [Note: [Col. 0839C] He was a bishop at the city of Terracina, in the Pomptine Marshes.]

V. C. A. T. L., “And Saint Scholastica, virgin and nun, whose brother Benedict saw her soul ascend to heaven in the form of a dove,” Rabanus. Her body was buried in Saint Benedict’s own tomb.

A. T., On the same day, at Bethlehem in Judea, under King Herod, the Passion of Saints Andrew and Aporus. [Note: [Col. 0839C] The persecution in which these martyrs were killed seems to have been the one in which the apostle James was killed and Saint Peter cast into prison, when Herod Agrippa, having been made king of all Judea in A.D. 41, began to attack the Church in order to please the Jews. Bollandus.]

A. L., “And Saint Soter.” [Note: [Col. 0839C] See February 6.]

L., And the elevation of Saint Gertrude, virgin. [Note: [Col. 0839C] This virgin was especially famous throughout Belgium. She was born at Landen, a town in Brabant. She was the daughter of Pepin, the first duke of Brabant, who was also mayor of the palace in the kingdom of Austrasia. She is said to have been mistress of Bergen op Zoom, Bergen Saint Gertrude, Nivelles, and Vorst, or Forest, in the Campine. After her father’s death, she changed her own house at Nivelles into a monastery together with her mother Iduberga, at the urging of Saint Amandus, bishop, who veiled mother and daughter.

She held Foillanus, Ultanus, and other preachers of the word of God from Ireland in the highest honor. She died as the first abbess of Nivelles on the feast of Patrick, apostle of the Irish, in A.D. 664. Saint Gertrude’s feast is celebrated on March 17; the translation, February 10; the consecration and veiling, December 2. Molanus, *Catalogue of the Saints of Belgium*.]

Gertrude, virgin.

### 11.—III IDES. At Rome, Callocerus and Parthenius. [Note: [Col. 0839D] They suffered under the emperor Decius. They were eunuchs of Decius’s wife, Triphonia: one was superintendent of the bedchamber, the other chief chamberlain. When the emperor discovered that they were Christians and that they refused to sacrifice to idols, he killed them with the sword. Peter de Natalibus. Their feast is also celebrated on May 19. See below, May 10.]

On the same day, at Lyon, Desiderius, bishop. [Note: [Col. 0840C] See below, May 23.]

A. T. L., In Campania, the feast of Basilianus and Amantius.

### 12.—II IDES. Bede has no entry.

D., At Barcelona, Eulalia, virgin and martyr. [Note: [Col. 0840C] During Diocletian’s reign, under the governor Dacianus, after scourging and the rack, and after her sides had been burned with torches, she gave up her spirit, which appeared to fly away in the form of a dove. Her Acts are in Bollandus.]

At Alexandria, Modestus and Ammonius.

V. C., In Africa, the Passion of Damianus, soldier.

At Carthage, Modestus and Julianus.

[Col. 0840B] A. T. L., In Africa, the Passion of Saint Damianus, martyr. In Italy, the burial of Simplicius, bishop. On the island of Ratensis, the feast of Saint Basil, monk.

T., In the city of Carthage, the feast of Saints Saturninus, Dativus, and Felix. [Note: [Col. 0840C] While these men, together with other Christians, were celebrating the Lord’s Day at the city of Abitina, they were arrested and taken to Carthage. They suffered under the proconsul Anolinus during Diocletian’s persecution. Baronius states in his notes on the Roman Martyrology that the African Church commemorates them today; the Roman Martyrology places them on the preceding day.]

### 13.—IDES. Bede has no entry.

D., Agabus the prophet in the New Testament, at Antioch.

Saint Polyoctus, martyr of Melitene in Armenia. [Note: [Col. 0840C] Under the emperor Decius, although he himself was a pagan and a friend of the Christian Nearchus, Polyoctus learned that an edict had been issued against Christians. Having been encouraged by Christ in a dream, he became a Christian. After his arrest and scourging, he was not moved by his wife’s tears but completed his martyrdom by a glorious death. He is also commemorated above on January 7 in the additions to the *Floraria*, and by the Greeks on January 9; some Latins also celebrate him on January 10. His most celebrated veneration, however, falls on the Ides of February.]

V. C., At Nicomedia, the Passion of Saint Julianus. [Note: [Col. 0840D] Perhaps he is the same as Juliana; see below, February 16.]

And elsewhere, Saint Dicentius.

And the burial of Stephen, bishop. [Note: [Col. 0840D] Galesinius and Canisius celebrate his memory on February 12.]

A. T. L., At Nicomedia, the Passion of Saint Julianus, martyr. In Alexandria, the feast of Saints Tullianus [L. Tullius] and Ammonius.

At Lyon, the burial of Blessed Stephen, bishop.

## 14 February — XVI Kalends of March

Memorial of Saint Valentine [Col. 0841B], priest of Rome [Note: [Col. 0841C] When he was presented to the emperor Claudius II in the amphitheater and asked why he did not worship the gods, he demonstrated the Christian faith by many arguments, to such an extent that the emperor praised him for his wisdom. But when the prefect Calpurnius said that the emperor had been led astray, he handed him over to the official Asterius, so that, after being brought to his house, he might persuade him to sacrifice to the gods. When the saint entered the official’s house, he restored sight to his adopted daughter, who was blind, and immediately converted and baptized him with his household. When Claudius learned this, he ordered Asterius and his entire family to be killed at the city of Ostia; but he ordered Saint Valentine to be beaten with clubs and beheaded on the Via Flaminia. His body was buried in that same place by a certain matron, Savinella. Peter de Natalibus. — Claudius began to reign in the year 268, around 24 March, and reigned until the beginning of 270; therefore Saint Valentine’s death must necessarily be assigned to the year 269, since Claudius was not alive in February of the following year.] who, after many notable deeds of healing and teaching, was beaten with clubs and thus beheaded under Caesar Claudius.

On the same day, the memorial of Saint Valentine of Terni [Note: [Col. 0841D] Bishop. He was ordained bishop by Saint Felician, bishop of Foligno, with the permission of Pope Victor; he suffered either under Aurelian or Claudius. Bollandus.] the bishop, who was seized by pagans, beaten with rods, and, after a prolonged beating, committed to prison. When he could not be overcome, he was taken from prison in the silence of midnight and beheaded by order of the furious Placidus, prefect of the city.

Thus far A. Then Proculus, Efybus [D. T. L.: Esibus], and Apollonius, his disciples, carried the body to their church in the city of Terni and buried it at night. While they remained there in daily vigils, they were seized by the Gentiles and handed over to the custody of the governor Leontius. He ordered them to be brought before his tribunal in the middle of the night; and when they could be recalled from the faith neither by entreaties nor by threats, he ordered them to be beheaded. They were buried not far from the body of Saint Valentine.

A. T. L., On the same day, the memorial of Saints [Note: [Col. 0841D] Vitalis. Usuard and Ado write that these suffered at Rome. Notker also adds the Via Ardeatina. Ghinius, in his Catalogue of the Saints, calls Vitalis a priest, and Wandelbert celebrates Saint Felicula, a virgin.] Vitalis, Felicula, and Zeno.

L., In Alexandria, of Bassianus [Note: [Col. 0841D] Bassianus was a lector; Orion, or Cyrion, a priest; Agatho, an exorcist.], Orion, and Agatho, who were burned by fire.

## 15 February — XV Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L., At Bourges, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0841D] Austregisilus. He was born near Bourges to his father Gundinus. As a young man he lived at the court of King Guntram; afterward he was ordained subdeacon by Blessed Aunarius, bishop of Auxerre, and priest and abbot by Aetherius, bishop of Lyon, of Blessed Nicetius. Then, after Bishop Apollinaris of Bourges died, he succeeded him and governed that Church for twelve years. He finally died in 627. His Acts are in Surius, vol. III. Ghinius of Siena. — Usuard, Notker, Baronius, Peter de Natalibus, and most Martyrologies commemorate his burial on 20 May. Saussaius, in his Martyrology, celebrates not his burial but his ordination today.] Austregisilus, bishop and confessor, who was magnificent and distinguished in the things of God.

D., At Rome, Saint [Note: [Col. 0842C] Craton. An Athenian, an orator at Rome, distinguished in the Latin and Greek languages. When he had a son named Chaeremon who had fallen ill, and he had summoned Blessed Valentine of Terni to heal him, he offered the boy to him on the condition that, if the child were healed, he himself and his whole household would become Christians. When the child was healed, he fulfilled what he had promised; and, after being baptized with his wife and entire household, he completed his life by martyrdom. Baeda Vulgata, Ado, Notker.] Craton, martyr.

At Sebaste, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 0842C] Blaise. Perhaps this is the same as Saint Blaise who is commemorated on 3 February.] Blaise, bishop.

V. C., At Terni, the memorial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0842D] Agape. Ferrarius explains her Acts as follows in his Catalogue of the Saints of Italy: Agape was a noble virgin born at Terni. She flourished under Valentine, bishop of Terni, and was one of the number of those who, instructed by that same Saint Valentine, lived as nuns. When the worshipers of idols raged against the Christians and persecuted them especially at Terni after the death of their teacher, she too was seized at Terni. Since she remained steadfast in confessing Christ, she was punished with the sword and joined the palm of martyrdom to her virginity on 15 February. Her body was buried in the place called Interturres.] Agape the virgin, Saturninus, Castulus, and Magnus.

V., In Antioch, Joseph the deacon, and Romanus, Lucius, and Rogatus. C. associates Lucius with those of Terni.

A. T. add thirty martyrs, companions of Saint Agape.

T., And the burial of Saint Silvinus, bishop and confessor.

On the same day, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 0842D] Desiderius. The bishop of Vienne seems to be indicated here; he is commemorated above on 11 February. His memorial is also celebrated below on 23 May.] Desiderius, bishop and martyr.

On the same day in Antioch, the memorial of Saints Josippus and Rufinus.

L., On the same day, of Saints [Note: [Col. 0843C] John. Saints John and Magnus were killed together with Saints Lucius and Rogatus, who are mentioned above in this same entry, together with Saint Agape the virgin at Terni. They are also commemorated on 17 February. Ferrarius, Catalogue of the Saints of Italy.] John, Magnus, and Joseph the deacon.

A. On the same day, at the city of Thérouanne, the burial of Blessed [Note: [Col. 0843C] Silvinus. Called by some a bishop of Toulouse and by others of Thérouanne. He shone among the Morini for his admirable religion and was distinguished by noble ancestry. He also flourished during the time of the earlier King Charles and of Childeric, his prince, remaining alive until the battle of Vinciacum, which was fought between Charles and Ragenfrid, king of the Franks. His Acts are in Bollandus. Some assign him to 17 February. Because he is said to have survived until the battle of Vinciacum, some think that he died in 715, when the war began, and others in 717, when the battle was fought at Vinciacum. But he died in neither of those years if, as his Acts record, he died in the evening of Holy Saturday. For if he died today, namely 15 February, it must be said that he died in 716, when 15 February was a Saturday; if on 17 February, as some write, it must be said that he died in 720, when Childeric died and 17 February was a Saturday. He died at Alciacum and was buried there.] Silvinus, bishop of that same city.

While he lived in the body, he shone with many signs of miracles; and, as the book of his Life clearly reveals, he was greatly abstinent, wishing to return to his Creator without fraud the talents entrusted to him, with interest. Later, called from Egypt to the promised land, he lives with God, possessing the joys of everlasting blessedness.

These words bear the stamp of Florus’s style.

## 16 February — XIV Kalends

Saint [Note: [Col. 0843D] Onesimus. For him Blessed Paul sends a personal letter to Philemon. The same blessed apostle ordained him bishop and entrusted him with the word of preaching, leaving him in the city of Ephesus; after Blessed Timothy, he himself presided there as bishop. Brought to Rome, he was stoned there for the faith of Christ and buried as Christ’s first martyr there; afterward his body was carried to the places where he had been ordained bishop. Baeda Vulgata, Usuard, Notker. — Saint Ignatius mentions Onesimus, bishop of Ephesus, in his Letter to the Ephesians.] Onesimus, apostle.

At Cumae, the memorial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0844C] Juliana. A short time after Saint Juliana had been beheaded, a certain senatorial woman named Sephonia, passing through the city of Nicomedia and coming to the city of Rome, took the body of Blessed Juliana. But when a violent storm arose, the ship went as far as the shores of Campania. Blessed Juliana was placed near the territory of Puteoli. She was later transferred to Cumae and placed in the church of Blessed Maximus. Her Acts are in Bollandus.] Juliana the virgin, who, under the emperor Maximian, was first beaten by her own father Africanus and severely tortured by the prefect Eolesius [L.: Eleusius; Rab.: Eulesius], whom she had had as her betrothed, she was beaten naked with rods, hung by her hair, and had molten lead poured over her head (thus far A.); then she was again taken into prison, where she openly contended with the devil; afterward summoned again, she overcame torments involving wheels, flames, and a boiling cauldron, and completed her martyrdom by beheading. She suffered at Nicomedia, but after a short time, by God’s providence, was transferred to Campania.

V. C., Elsewhere, Maxima, Junella, and fifty-four others [Note: [Col. 0844D] These suffered in Africa with many others, whose names may be read in the Martyrology of Saint Jerome.].

L., And the burial of [Note: [Col. 0844D] Tetrardus. Called Tetradius by Jerome. Bollandus conjectures that Tetradius of Bourges is meant here. There was an illustrious family of Tetradii in Gaul.] Tetrardus, bishop.

## 17 February — XIII Kalends

In Babylonia, the memorial of [Note: [Col. 0844D] Polychronius. According to Ado and Notker, bishop of both Babylon and Ctesiphon. His body was buried before the walls of the Babylonian gate; he suffered around the year 251.] Polychronius, bishop of that same city, who, while the persecutor Decius was present, had his mouth beaten with stones. Raising his hands and lifting his eyes to heaven, he gave up his spirit. Written in the Passion of Saint Laurence. [T. adds: “his.”]

L., On the same day, Saints [Note: [Col. 0844D] Donatus. He and Secundianus are not the same as Donatus and Secundianus of Concordia, who are also commemorated today. For the time, place, and manner of martyrdom in which these men suffered are entirely unknown.] Donatus, Secundianus, Castus, and Marcellus.

V. C., On the same day, Saint [Note: [Col. 0844D] Faustinus. Baronius writes in his Martyrology that he suffered at Rome with his companions.] Faustinus, martyr, and forty-four others, whose names God knows.

## 18 February — XII Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Jerusalem, [Note: [Col. 0845C] Simeon. All the Latins commemorate him today; the Greeks on 27 April. After the martyrdom of Saint James, he was made bishop of Jerusalem. He was the son of Clopas, the brother of Joseph, and according to the flesh a cousin of Christ. Finally accused by heretics of being a Christian and of belonging to the stock of David, he was crucified at the age of 120, during the reign of Trajan, while Atticus, the consular legate, governed Syria. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History III, 11, 32. He suffered in the year 107.] Simeon, bishop and martyr.

V., In Africa, Saints Rutulus [V.: Retulus], Silvanus, Classicus [C.: Casticus], Secundinus, and Fructulus.

A. T., In Africa, Rutulus, Damasus, Silvanus, and Casicius.

And the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0845C] Martial. It is uncertain whether this is one of the African martyrs. He seems rather to be Saint Martial of Limoges, who is commemorated on 30 June.] Martial, bishop.

L., In Africa, the memorial of Saints Rutulus and Damasus. On the same day, of Silvinus and Paulinus.

## 19 February — XI Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Rome, [Note: [Col. 0845C] Gabinus. Brother of Blessed Pope Caius, from the family of the emperor Diocletian. When Diocletian wished to give Gabinus’s daughter Susanna in marriage to Maximian, and she refused, while Gabinus would not persuade her to accept, Saint Gabinus died after suffering imprisonment. The Acts of Susanna are in Surius, vol. IV.] Gabinus, priest and martyr.

V., In Africa, Publius, Julianus, Marcellus, Lampasius, Maiulus, and others. These same names, except Lampasius, occur in A. T. L.; but Marcellus is listed last, and in L. he is Marcellinus.

C., In Africa, Marubius, Publius, Julianus, Marcellus, Tullius, Jamnasius, Julius, Victor, and Corona.

## 20 February — X Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Tyre [Note: [Col. 0845C] These martyrs were killed by Veturius, master of the soldiers, at the command of Diocletian, by various successive kinds of torture. First they were torn by scourges; afterward they were handed over to beasts. When none of the wild animals harmed them, the beasts’ fury passed into human beings, and what the beasts could not accomplish was done by swords. Ado, Usuard, Notker. — The most distinguished of all the martyrs in Phoenicia were Tyrannio, bishop of the Church of Tyre, and Zenobius, a priest at Sidon; Silvanus too was bishop of the Church of Emesa. The latter was thrown to wild beasts in the city of Emesa itself and killed together with certain others. The former suffered at Antioch: Tyrannio was thrown into the depths of the sea, while Zenobius died amid his torments as his sides were furrowed with hooks. Silvanus, bishop of Gaza, was beheaded with thirty-nine others near the metal mines at Phaeno. Certain Egyptian priests, Peleus and Nilus, were also consumed by flames. Compare Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VIII, 13, with Ado and Usuard. See also the same author VIII, 7, and the final chapter concerning the martyrs of Palestine.] of martyrs whose number only God’s knowledge can calculate.

V. C., At Cyprus, the memorial of Potamina.

At Rome, on the Via Appia, the burial of [Note: [Col. 0846C] Caius. Brother of Gabinus, discussed above on 28 February. He succeeded Pope Eutychianus in the Roman episcopate. Fleeing the persecution of Diocletian, he was crowned with martyrdom while living in the crypts.] Caius, bishop.

A. T. L., At Rome, on the Via Appia, in the cemetery of Callistus, the burial of Caius, bishop. At Cyprus, the memorial of the saints Potamia and Didymus.

A. T., And elsewhere, of Victor, martyr.

T., first place: In the city of Tournai, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0846C] Eleutherius. At first he was an eminent preacher at Tournai. Then the Christians, seeing his outstanding holiness, sent him to Rome, and, when he returned with authority, had him consecrated bishop. He suffered many hardships from pagans and Arian heretics, but was visited by an angel in prison. Consecrated bishop in 484, or, according to Bollandus, in 487, he was soon afterward expelled from Tournai with the Christians. He then settled at Blandinium in the suburb for about eight years, after which he lived for thirty-seven years in his native place, Tournai. Finally he rested at Blandinium, where Bishop Heidilo elevated him in 881; from there he was transferred to the cathedral church of Tournai. This church celebrates his memorial on 20 February, his translation on 22 August, and his elevation on 9 July. Molanus, Index of the Saints of Belgium.] Eleutherius, bishop and confessor of that same city.

## 21 February — IX Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., In Sicily, seventy-nine martyrs [Note: [Col. 0846D] They received the crown of their confession through various tortures. Ado, Usuard, Notker.].

V. C., In Africa [Note: [Col. 0846D] In the city of Hadrumetum, according to Usuard and Baronius, under the Vandal persecution, according to Baronius.] the memorial of Saints [Col. 0847B] Verolus, Secundinus, Servulus, Siricius, and Felix.

C., Saturninus.

A. T. L., In Africa, the memorial of Saints Secundus, Servulus, Julianus, Saturninus, Felix, and seventeen others. The first is absent from L.

A., first place: At the monastery of Nobiliacum, the dedication of the church of Saint [Note: [Col. 0847C] Vedastus. Saint Aubertus, warned by an angelic vision, transferred the relics of Saint Vedastus to the city of Nobiliacum; for this reason a church was dedicated there in honor of Saint Vedastus. See Bollandus in the Life of Saint Vedastus.] Vedastus, bishop and confessor, which was revealed through an angelic revelation to Blessed Aubertus, bishop.

## 22 February — VIII Kalends

At Antioch, the Chair of Saint [Note: [Col. 0847C] Peter. He sat there for seven years. His chair at Rome is celebrated on 16 January. See above.] Peter.

[Col. 0847C] V. and C. add: And Saint Thecla.

A. T., At Nicomedia, the memorial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0847C] Thecla. She is commemorated below on 23 September. Today, however, she is said to have suffered at Nicomedia; on that other day, at Iconium in Lycaonia.] Thecla the virgin, disciple of Saint Paul the apostle.

At Rome, on the Via Tiburtina, at Saint Laurence’s, the memorial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0847D] Concordia. The persecution of Decius slew her. Baeda Vulgata, Rabanus, Notker; concerning her, see below, 13 August.] Concordia.

At Sirmium, the memorial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0847D] Serena. This seems to be the same as Sinerius or Sirenus, who is commemorated on the following day.] Serena, who received martyrdom by decapitation in the time of Maximinus.

The same entries occur in L., but Concordia is absent.

## 23 February — VII Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0847D] Sinerius. While he cultivated his own garden and was an intimate friend of one of the household of the emperor Maximian, he one day found that man’s wife walking in his garden at an unsuitable hour. He sharply rebuked her for her immodesty and drove her away indignantly. She complained to her husband about Serenus; angered by his wife’s words, he accused Saint Serenus to the emperor as a Christian. Thus Serenus was seized at the emperor’s command, confessed himself a Christian, and was beheaded. Peter de Natalibus.] Sinerius the monk and sixty-two martyrs.

V. C., In Asia, [Note: [Col. 0847D] Polycarp, bishop. He is said to have been crowned with martyrdom on this day and is commemorated by the Greeks, as is clear from the Menaea and Menologion. He is also entered in the Martyrologies of Saint Jerome, [Col. 0848C] Rabanus, Galesinius, and others; but concerning him see above, 26 January.] Polycarp, bishop, with twelve others, and Saint Herotus [V.: Eloritus].

A. T. L., The nativity of Saint [Note: [Col. 0848C] John. His nativity must be discussed on 27 December.] John the Evangelist.

A. T., At Smyrna, the memorial of the ancient saints Herotus and Garphorus.

T. inserts: On the same day, the memorial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0848C] Polycarp. Notker has: At Rome, Saint Polycarp the priest. Baeda Vulgata, Ado, Usuard, and our author call him a confessor; it is therefore probable that he died a natural death. This much is certain: when, by order of Diocletian, the prefect Chromatius was sent into exile in Campania with many Christians, Polycarp voluntarily shared his exile. What happened to him afterward, however, is entirely unknown. The Martyrologies agree that he converted very many people to the faith of Christ together with Sebastian and led them to the glory of martyrdom.] Polycarp, priest and confessor.

L., And in [Note: [Col. 0848D] Pannonia. The very ancient Roman Martyrology, or that of Saint Jerome, indicates that these men suffered at Sirmium. Bollandus.] Pannonia, Saints Antigonus, Rutulus, Libius, Ominander, and Zeno.

## 24 February — VI Kalends

[Note: [Col. 0848D] Finding. According to Baronius, the first discovery of the head of Saint John is said to have taken place today. Baeda, in his Chronicle under the emperor Marcian, writes: “John the Baptist revealed his head to two eastern monks who had come to Jerusalem for prayer, near the former dwelling of King Herod; it was afterward carried to Emesa, a city of Phoenicia, and honored with due veneration.” The discovery must be discussed again on 29 August.] The Finding of the head of John the Forerunner [Col. 0848C], and the memorial of Saint Matthias the apostle.

Florus adds in A. T. L.: He was chosen by lot from among the seventy disciples and substituted as the twelfth apostle in place of Judas Iscariot.

V. has similar material and adds: Alone without a surname, to whom the preaching of the Gospel in Judaea is entrusted.

A. T., At Nicomedia, the memorial of Lucian the priest.

L., And at Rome, Saint Primitivus.

V., Primitiva.

C., At Rome, the memorial of Saint Primitiva.

## 25 February — V Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., In Egypt, [Note: [Col. 0849C] According to the Menaea and Galesinius, all these men were Greeks, or citizens of Corinth. They were brought before Tertius, the proconsul who governed Greece from Corinth with consular authority under Decius, and were expelled from Corinth, perhaps under Decius. When they were exiles in Egypt, they survived there until the time of Numerian. Under the command of Sabinus, one of them, Victor, was placed in a ball pierced all around and for a very long time stabbed through each opening. Taken out of the ball, he was beheaded. Another, Victorinus, after his hands and feet had been cut off, was placed in the same ball, endured the torture of the former, and was finally killed by the sword. Nicephorus, when he had voluntarily entered the ball, angered the judge, who ordered him to be brought out, roasted and turned over a grating covered with burning coals, and finally cut to pieces with a sword. Four others—Claudianus, Dioscorus, Serapion, and Papias—were killed: Claudianus and Dioscorus by fire, Serapion and Papias by the sword. Baeda Vulgata, Usuard, Notker. The Greeks commemorate them in the Menaea on 31 January.] Victorinus, Victor, Nicephorus, and other martyrs.

V. C., In Africa, Donatus, Justus, Hereneus, Ingenuus [C.: Ingenua], and forty-five others.

A. T. L., In Africa, the memorial of Saints Donatus and Justus.

In Pamphylia, the memorial of Nestor and [Note: [Col. 0849D] Casta. Saints Casta and Nestor have been added in the Martyrology published under Baeda’s name to the African martyrs who are commemorated on this day. But Nestor is also treated separately on the following day.] Casta.

And the burial of Saint Eugenia. She is absent from L., where Castus is read in place of Casta.

## 26 February — IV Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Perge in Pamphylia, Blessed [Note: [Col. 0849D] Nestor. Bishop among the Mandenses, or rather, according to Bollandus’s correction, bishop of Magydus. During the persecution of Decius, while he devoted himself continually, day and night, to prayer, asking that Christ’s flock be guarded, he was arrested by the Irenarch and sent to the governor Pollio. He was tortured most cruelly on the rack. Thereafter he departed victorious through suspension on a cross. Baeda Vulgata, Usuard, [Col. 0850D] Notker. He is also commemorated by the Latins on the preceding day and by the Greeks in the Menaea on 28 February.] Nestor, bishop.

V. C., The memorial of Saints [Note: [Col. 0850D] Alexander. In certain Martyrologies the following men are said to have suffered at Alexandria.] Alexander and Nestor.

V., Fortunatus.

V. C., And twenty-six others.

A. T. L., In Alexandria, the memorial of Saints Felix, Alexander, and Nestor. The last is absent from L.

## 27 February — III Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Alexandria, [Note: [Col. 0850D] Juliana. Rather Julianus, a man afflicted with the pains of gout, who was brought together with two others who carried him. One of them immediately denied Christ. The other, named Cronion and called Eunus, and Julianus himself, having confessed Christ, were carried through the whole city seated on camels and scourged with raised whips; finally they were consumed by a very fierce fire while a crowd stood around them. Letter of Dionysius in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI, 41.] Juliana, martyr.

V. C., [Note: [Col. 0850D] Alexander. Galesinius, Baronius, and Ferrarius in the Catalogue of the Saints of Italy assigned Rome as the place of their contest. But the Martyrology of Saint Jerome, Baeda Vulgata, and Rabanus Maurus more correctly report that they suffered at Thessalonica.] Alexander, Abundantius, Januarius, Dionysius, and twenty-four others.

A. T. L., At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the memorial [Col. 0851A] of Saint [Note: [Col. 0851B] Felix. A pope. If he is Felix I, he is commemorated below on 30 May; if Felix II, on 29 July.] Felix, bishop and martyr.

At Smyrna in Asia, the memorial of Saints Servilianus, Dacianus, and Leander.

T., And the translation of Saint [Note: [Col. 0851B] Ragnulfus, or Ranulfus, father of Saint Hadulfus, bishop of Arras. Usuard records him on 27 May, but the Breviary of Arras places him on 9 November. Molanus, Index of the Saints of Belgium.] Ragnulfus, martyr.

## 28 February — II Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Alexandria, [Note: [Col. 0852B] Metranus. See above, 31 January.] Metranus, martyr, and others.

V. C., The memorial of Saints Celerus, Pupillus, Serapion, and Justus.

V., Candidus.

C., Claudianus.

A., In Alexandria, the memorial of Saints Dionysius, Claudianus, and Theophilus.

T. L., In Alexandria, the memorial of Saints Serapion, Celerus, and Claudius.

T. adds Victorinus, Saturninus, Alexander, and Victor.

# March

[Col. 0851C]

## 1 March — Kalends

Baeda has nothing.

D., [Note: [Col. 0851D] Saints. They had been condemned to dig sand in the name of Christ. Claudius ordered them to be shut up in a pottery outside the walls near the Salarian Gate and killed by arrows in the amphitheater of the city. They were buried by Marius, Martha, and Saint John the priest in a crypt on the Via Salaria near the Clivus Cucumeris. Ado, Usuard, Notker. Their Acts are in Bollandus.] Two hundred and sixty saints who suffered in the time of Claudius.

V. C., The memorial of Saints [Note: [Col. 0851D] Leo. Certain Martyrologies cited by Bollandus note that they suffered in Africa, at Carthage.] Leo, Donatus, Habundantius, Nicephorus, and nine others.

A. T. L., In Africa, the passion of Saint Leo and Donatus.

And at the city of Angers, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0851D] Albinus. He was nobly born in the region of Vannes, near the Ocean and the British frontier. At the monastery of Cincillacum he was a canon; afterward he became abbot, and then was made bishop of Angers. Finally, after he had holy administered the episcopal dignity for more than twenty years and had attended the Third Council of Orléans, he departed to heaven at more than eighty years of age, around the year 550. Ghinius of Siena.] Albinus, bishop, whose Life was composed by Fortunatus the priest and adorned with miracles.

This last entry is absent from L., which places first: The burial of [Note: [Col. 0852D] Moses. He is commemorated again on 4 September.] Moses, the man of God.

## 2 March — VI Nones

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Rome, [Note: [Col. 0852D] Jovinianus. These men suffered on the Via Latina under the emperors Gallienus and Valerian. Baeda Vulgata, Ado, Usuard. — Galesinius adds that they were struck with an axe; Peter de Natalibus says with a sword.] Jovinianus and Basileus and very many martyrs.

V. C., In Caesarea of Cappadocia, Luke, bishop, and Primitivus.

At Rome, Paul and Januarius.

V., Marinus.

C., Antigonus and Januarius.

A. T. L., In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the memorial of Luke [A.: Lucius], bishop, Januarius, and Primitivus.

T., On the same day, at the Roman port, in the cemetery of Paul, the memorial of Secundola and Januaria, virgins.

## 3 March — V Nones

Baeda has nothing.

D., Saints [Note: [Col. 0853C] Emeterius. This sentence should be corrected as follows: At Calahorra, an ancient city of the Vascones, Saints Emeterius and Celedonius, martyrs. They were first soldiers at the city of Legio in Galatia. When persecution was raging, they were harassed with fire and hooks for confessing the name of Christ, brought as far as Calahorra, and crowned with martyrdom. Baeda Vulgata and others.] Emeterius and Celedonius and the martyrs of Calahorra.

V. C. A. T. L., Felix, Justus, and Fortunatus.

V., Marcia, Antigonus, and Januarius.

T. places the site of the contest first: In Africa, the memorial of Saints, etc.

## 4 March — IV Nones

Baeda has nothing.

D., [Note: [Col. 0853D] Lucius. He is commemorated today by Ado, Baeda Vulgata, Usuard, and Notker. He is also commemorated below on 25 August.] Lucius, pope and martyr, and eight hundred [Note: [Col. 0853D] Some count eight hundred and ten, others nine hundred, or nine hundred and ten. They suffered at Rome on the Via Appia and were placed in the cemetery at Saint Cecilia. Ado, Notker, Baronius, and many others.] martyrs.

V. C., The memorial of eight hundred and ten martyrs [C.: DCCCX].

At Rome, the burial of Julius [C.: Julianus], bishop, and twenty-seven others.

A. T. L., At Rome, the burial of Julius, bishop, Sisinnius, and Caius.

And on the Via Appia, the memorial of eight hundred holy martyrs. L., however, joins these with the preceding group and places all of them together in the cemetery on the Via Appia.

A. T., At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 0853D] Adrian. His solemnity is also celebrated below on 8 September.] Adrian, with twenty-three others, and Natalia, his wife.

## 5 March — III Nones

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Antioch, Saint [Note: [Col. 0853D] Phocas. Usuard’s words are: “After suffering many injuries for the name of the Redeemer, how he triumphed over that ancient serpent is declared to the peoples even today.”] Phocas, martyr, and Saint [Note: [Col. 0854C] Eusebius. These martyrs suffered in Africa.] Eusebius Palatinus, and eight other martyrs.

V. C., In Africa, Adrianus.

At Antioch, the passion of Saint Phocas.

C., And twelve others [Col. 0854B].

A. T. L., The memorial of Saints Adrianus, Rusticus, Victor, and Eusebius. L. puts the place first: At Antioch. A. omits Victor.

A. T., At Antioch, the passion of Saint Phocas [Note: [Col. 0854C] A virgin. This arose through an error caused by the ending of the word in the genitive case [Col. 0854D].] the virgin.

T., On the same day, in Gaul, at the city of Soissons, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0854D] Drausius, or Drautius. He was born to noble parents, namely Leudomarus, his father, and Rachilde, his mother. He was entrusted for instruction to Saint Ansericus, bishop of Soissons. Under Ansericus’s successor, Bettolenus, he became archdeacon. When Bettolenus voluntarily resigned the episcopate, Drausius was chosen bishop in his place. At the place called Rotundum he built a monastery for men; afterward he arranged for another to be built for virgins by Ebroinus the nobleman, with the assistance of Leutrude, his wife. Finally he died around the year 680 and was buried in the basilica of the nuns.] Drausius, bishop.

## 6 March — II Nones

Baeda has nothing.

D. A. T. L., At Nicomedia, Victor and Victorinus.

D. adds: who died in prison.

A. T., And the burial of Saint Claudianus.

T., And [Note: [Col. 0854D] Diodorus. Notker writes that these were martyrs at Nicopolis.] Diodorus and Mercurius.

L. joins Claudianus and Mercurius to the first two.

V. C. gives a fuller and more distinct account of them: At Nicomedia, Victurus and Victorinus, who, after being presented for three years during the persecution at the city of Apamea in Bithynia, together with Claudianus and Bassa his wife, were seized as laypeople, afflicted with many tortures, and shut up in prison, where they completed the course of their lives.

What if perhaps these words of Baeda were rashly omitted in other manuscripts? So Ado seems to have found them, and Notker copied them.

## 7 March — Nones

At Carthage, [Note: [Col. 0854D] Perpetua. According to Bollandus, she suffered with her companions in the year 203, when Geta Caesar and Septimius Plautianus were consuls. Baeda Vulgata, Ado, Usuard, Notker, and others write that they suffered martyrdom in the Mauritanian city of Thuburbo. But this very fact proves that the Martyrology commonly marked with Baeda’s name is not genuinely Baeda’s work, because in his Chronicle he writes that they suffered at Carthage under Severus. Very many ancient manuscript Martyrologies, as well as the printed Martyrology of Rabanus Maurus, support Carthage; and Victor of Vita, in Book I of The Vandal Persecution, speaks of the great basilica where the bodies of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas are. Saturus, Saturninus, Revocatus, and Secundulus suffered with them. The last died in prison; all the others were handed over to beasts. Their Acts are in Bollandus.] Perpetua and Felicitas, who were condemned to the beasts under the emperor Severus. When Felicitas was giving birth in prison, the prayers of all the soldiers who were suffering together with them obtained that she should give birth in the eighth month.

Among other things, Perpetua was granted that her mind was, in a certain sense, turned away from the body. Thus, when she endured the assault of a heifer, she awaited as something still future what she did not know had already happened to her.

L., And Saint Cassianus, bishop.

## 8 March — VIII Ides

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Carthage, [Note: [Col. 0855D] Pontianus. Or Pontius, deacon of Blessed Cyprian, bishop. He endured exile with him until the day of his own passion and left an excellent volume on his Life and Passion. Always glorifying the Lord in his sufferings, he merited the crown of life. Baeda Vulgata, Usuard, Ado.] Pontianus, deacon, and Blessed [Note: [Col. 0856D] Cyprian. He is entered in some Martyrologies perhaps because of Saint Pontius, his deacon, who is commemorated today. But he must be treated below on 14 September.] Cyprian, martyr.

V. C., At Nicomedia, Quintillus, bishop.

In Africa, Rogatus, Felix, and Felicitas.

A. T. L., In Africa, the memorial of the saints Rogatus, Felix, Urbanus, and Cyril, bishop.

T. L., At Nicomedia, Quintillus, bishop, and Capitulinus.

## 9 March — VII Ides

At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, [Note: [Col. 0856D] Forty. According to the additions of Florus placed below, they are commemorated by Ado, Rabanus, and Notker on 11 March. Bollandus also says, under 10 March: “Now, because of the double feast of Saint Frances of Rome, the solemnity of these martyrs has been transferred from 9 March to the following day.”] forty soldiers, in the time of King Licinius, under the governor Agricolaus. After very frequent imprisonment and chains, and after their faces had been beaten with stones, they were sent into a lake. There the ice-bound bodies were broken by the cold during the night, and in the morning they completed their martyrdom by the breaking of their legs.

Afterward their bodies were burned and thrown into the river; but by divine providence their relics were found intact and buried with due honor. The more distinguished among them were Quirion and Candidus.

## 10 March — VI Ides

Baeda has nothing.

D., At Apamea, Alexander and [Note: [Col. 0856D] Caius. Eusebius speaks of these martyrs in Ecclesiastical History V, 16. According to the Latin Martyrologies, they were crowned with martyrdom at Apamea during the persecution of Antoninus Verus.] Caius of Eumenia.

In Persia, forty-two martyrs.

V. C., At Nicaea, Gorgonius [V.: Golgonius], Palatinus, and Firmus.

V. C. A. T. L., In Antioch, Agape the virgin.

T. L., And Mariana.

A. T., In [Note: [Col. 0856D] Antioch, the memorial. More correctly, Nicaea.] Antioch, the memorial of Saints Firmianus and Palatinus.

T. L., And in Alexandria, the memorial of Saints [Note: [Col. 0856D] Candidus. These men are treated on the following day.] Candidus and Valerius.

## 11 March — V Ides

Baeda has nothing.

D., [Note: Sebaste. For these soldiers, see above, 9 March.] the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste in Lesser Armenia [Col. 0857B] under Licinius. V. C., At Carthage, Heraclius and Zosimus. In [Note: Alexandria. All of these, up to the last, Quirillus, except Gorgonius, are said to have suffered at Carthage according to the printed Martyrology of Jerome and very many ancient manuscript Martyrologies.] Alexandria, Gagus and Candidus. C., And fifteen others. A. T. L., At Nicomedia, the holy martyrs Gorgonius, Heraclius, and Alexander; but L. lacks the place of their contest. T., At Carthage, Zosimus. At Alexandria, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Candidus, Marcianus, and Quirillus. L., At Carthage, Zosimus, Candidus, Marcianus, and Quirillus. A., In the district of Arras, the deposition of Saint Vindicianus. [Note: Born at Bellecourt around the year 620 and instructed by Saints Eligius and Autbertus; after the latter’s death, he was appointed to the episcopal see, namely that of Arras. Together with King Theodoricus, he enlarged the church of the Mother of God at Arras with villages, churches, lands, mills, and other endowments from his own resources. At the village of Hunolcourt in the diocese of Cambrai, he built a monastery with the most precious martyr Lambert, to the praise of God and the veneration of Saint Peter, and established clerics and nuns there. He migrated to Christ at Brussels, in the territory of his diocese; and he chose to be buried on Mount Saint Eligius, because Blessed Eligius, to whom he had been closely attached in familiar affection, had made his dwelling there. It is an abbey, an hour’s distance from Arras, in which he was raised up by Fulbert, the fifteenth successor to the episcopate. Molanus, *On the Saints of Belgium*. Colvenerius states that he occupied the see for thirty-six years and departed this life in 712, in his notes on chapter 28 of book I of Baldericus’s *Chronicle of the Bishops of Cambrai and Arras*.] Vindicianus.

### 12.—IV IDES

The deposition of Saint Gregory, pope of blessed memory. [Note: Gregory. Bede gives a fuller account of him in *Ecclesiastical History* II.1; there one may also see for what reason, after being admonished, he took such diligent care for the salvation of the Anglo-Saxon people. From chapter 23 of book I of the *Ecclesiastical History* through the final chapter, one may read with what zeal and by what methods Augustine, sent to us as an apostle by Saint Gregory, converted our people to the faith. His ordination is commemorated below, on 29 March.]

Florus, in A. T. L.: And at Nicomedia, the passion of the presbyter Pionius. [Note: Pionius. He did not suffer at Nicomedia but at Smyrna. Almost all Martyrologies celebrate his commemoration on 1 February, with Saint Dionysius, who is mentioned above on that very day. The Greeks, however, celebrate him on 11 March. During the persecution of Antoninus Verus, or at least of Decius, after his unshakable constancy in answering and the squalor of imprisonment, where by his exhortations he strengthened many of the brethren for martyrdom, he was finally subjected to many tortures, nailed to a cross, and placed upon a blazing pyre; thus he obtained a blessed end for Christ. Fifteen others suffered with him. Bede in the common recension, Ado, Notker.] He suffered under the proconsuls of Asia, Julius Proclus and Quintilianus; after imprisonment and the laceration of his body, he was fastened to a wooden stake and handed over to the fire with the presbyter Metrodorus.

V. C., At Nicomedia, Egdonus [C., Agdonus], presbyter, and seven others strangled on successive days. C., So that fear might be instilled in those who saw it. At Rome, the deposition of Innocentius, bishop, who is also named in A. T. L. [Note: Innocentius. According to Jerome’s Martyrology, Rasus the bishop and Julianus were his companions. Bollandus writes of them as follows: “Here a difficulty now arises concerning these saints: where they were bishops, and by what kind of death they were taken away. We know that later writers believed Saint Innocentius to have been the Roman pontiff, and that Saint Rasus was erased. Innocentius I died in 417, on 28 July. His body was transferred by Pope Sergius II, who was created in 844. We can conclude nothing certain; nevertheless, we are led to the opinion that these two bishops, Innocentius and Rasus, lived during a time of persecution and came to Rome from elsewhere, where they either rested there in holy peace, or were crowned by martyrdom, or at least, if they had suffered elsewhere, their bodies were then brought to Rome and buried there.”]

### 13.—III IDES

At Nicomedia, the commemoration of Macedonius the presbyter, and of Patricia his wife and their daughter Modesta.

A. T. L., and Saint Euphrasia, virgin. [Note: The daughter of Antigonus, a senator, and Eupraxia, under the emperor Theodosius, whose relative she was. After Antigonus died, her mother Eupraxia commended her to Theodosius, who betrothed her to a certain senator. She nevertheless departed with her mother and went to the Thebaid of Egypt, entering a monastery in which there were virgins; she was then sixteen years old. Because of her outstanding virtue, blessed Euphrasia received the grace of miracles, by which she freed many people from various illnesses, and she herself attained a blessed end at the age of thirty. Her Acts are found in Bollandus. The Greeks celebrate her on 25 July.]

### 14.—II IDES

Bede has no entry.

D., At Rome, forty-seven soldiers baptized by the blessed apostle Peter. [Note: Baptized. Namely, while Saint Peter was being held in the Mamertine prison with his fellow apostle Paul, where they were detained in chains for nine months. All of these were slain by Nero’s sword while making a most devout confession of the faith. Bede in the common recension, Ado, and others.] V. C., At Nicomedia, Felicissimus, Dativus, Frontina [B., Frontiana], and Pionius. But C. connects the last two with Modesta on the preceding day. A. T., At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Peter the martyr. A., Euphrosius and Frunimius. [Note: Euphrosius. They were crowned by martyrdom at Thessalonica, not at Alexandria, where they are later mentioned in this entry as having suffered.] And Saint Leo, pope. [Note: For Pope Leo, see below, 11 April.] T., At Thessalonica, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Alexander and Euphrosius, and Saint Frunimius. L., At Alexandria, Saints Alexander and Euphrasius. B., which up to this point is acephalous: In Africa, Alexander and Peter. At Antioch, Nimedia, Pionius. [Note: Nimedia. In Saint Jerome’s Martyrology, “at Nicomedia.” With this appended word we remain uncertain whether the name of either a male or female martyr at Antioch should be accepted—which seems quite probable—or rejected as inserted elsewhere by error; for on 12 March a certain Pionius is reported to have suffered at Nicomedia.]

### 15.—IDES

Bede has no entry.

D., At Thessalonica, Matrona, servant and martyr. [Note: Matrona. She was the maidservant of a certain Jewish woman, Plautilla; secretly worshiping Christ and attending church daily by stealth, she was discovered by her mistress, afflicted in many ways, and finally beaten to death with heavy clubs. Roman Martyrology of Baronius, Ado, and others.] B. C., In Cappadocia, Saint Longinus. [Note: When, during the Lord’s Passion, he pierced his side with a spear, he believed in Christ after seeing the earthquake and the signs that occurred; and after serving Christ for thirty-eight years and converting many to the faith of Christ, he finally completed his martyrdom in Cappadocia under the governor Octavius. Bede in the common recension, Notker.] B. C. V., At Nicomedia, Lucius the bishop. V. C., At Carthage, Saint James, the brother of the Lord. B., At Carthage, Paul, Salvator, Alexander, Theophilus, Octavius, and Theodolus. A. T. L., At Jerusalem, the commemoration of the holy apostles James and Luke the evangelist. [Note: James. He is celebrated below, on 1 May.] [Note: Luke. His commemoration is celebrated on 18 October. Today, however, his ordination is recorded according to the Tamlact manuscript cited by Bollandus.] At Nicomedia, the commemoration of Saint Lucius, bishop and martyr. In A., corrected by a later hand: Lucianus. C., And the vigil of Saint Cyriacus. [Note: His memory is celebrated again on 8 August.]

### 16.—XVII KALENDS OF APRIL

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Cyriacus, who, after the long mortification of imprisonment that he endured under Maximian, together with his deacon Sisinnius and Smaragdus and Largus, after performing many miracles—including, at her request, curing and baptizing Artemia, the daughter of Diocletian, who was possessed by a demon—[up to this point A.] and, having been sent for this purpose by Diocletian, likewise freeing from a demon and baptizing Jobia, the daughter of Sapor, king of the Persians, together with the king himself and four hundred and thirty others [up to this point, S. Cyriacus; thereafter the text is lacking until 18 July]—returned to Rome after Diocletian’s death. He was arrested among other Christians by his son Maximian and sent into custody because he had made his sister a Christian. Then Maximian ordered that, on the day of his procession, he should be dragged naked, bound in chains, before his chariot. After this he was brought out of prison with his companions Largus, Smaragdus, and Crescentianus by the deputy Carpasias, and his head was drenched with melted pitch. Again, brought out of prison, he was stretched out on a rack, pulled with cords, and beaten with clubs; afterward, at Maximian’s command, he was beheaded with Largus, Smaragdus, and twenty others. This is written in the Acts of Pope Marcellus. At the same time Maximian killed his sister Artemia.

B., At Nicomedia, Castor, Dionysius, Nonnus, Serenus, and Quiriaca.

### 17.—XVI KALENDS

In Scotia, Saint Patrick, confessor. [Note: In Scotia, that is, Ireland. Captured by pirates from Britain together with others and sold, but later ransomed, he eventually came to Rome. Living canonically and educated in letters, he was sent by Pope Celestine and, after Palladius, first preached Christ to the Scots and Irish, bringing the whole island of Ireland back to the faith. After administering the episcopate there most excellently for forty years, and for sixty years from the beginning of his mission, he migrated to Christ at the age of 122, renowned for miracles and virtues, in the year 491.]

On the same day, the death of Saint Gertrude, virgin.

Gertrude is absent from Rabanus. [Note: At Nivelles in Brabant. See 10 February.] In B. she is placed at Niviala. Then at Rome, Alexander the bishop and Theodolus the deacon.
