[Note: For these, see 3 May.] B., At Jerusalem, Quiriacus the bishop. [Note: Concerning him, see Bede in the common recension, Usuard, Ado, and Notker on 4 May. He was surnamed Judas and found the Lord’s cross with Helena; afterward he was baptized and named Quiriacus and ordained bishop of Jerusalem. When the emperor Julian was proceeding against the Persians, he came to Jerusalem and invited Quiriacus to sacrifice to the gods. When Quiriacus refused, Julian had his right hand cut off. Then he ordered molten lead to be poured into his mouth. Next he ordered him to be stretched face down upon an iron bed, coals to be placed beneath him, salt and fat to be sprinkled over him, his back to be beaten with rods, and then him to be thrown into a pit full of serpents. Yet all the serpents were suddenly killed. Later Quiriacus was placed in boiling oil and finally pierced through with a sword. Peter de Natalibus. Baronius, in the Martyrology, writes that this man was not bishop of Jerusalem, for at that time Saint Cyril was seated there and survived into the time of Theodosius; rather, the man in question was bishop of Ancona.]

### 18.—XV KALENDS

Bede has no entry.

D., Saint Alexander, bishop. [Note: According to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, in the twelfth year of the emperor Severus, A.D. 205, he was renowned for his confession of the Lord’s name. In the second year of Caracalla, A.D. 213, while Narcissus was still alive but advanced in age, he was ordained bishop of Jerusalem. For Alexander, divinely admonished, had gone from Cappadocia, where he had first been ordained bishop, to Jerusalem; and the brethren of that church, receiving him most kindly, did not allow him afterward to return to his homeland, and so forth. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.11. Together with Theoctistus, bishop of Caesarea, he ordained Origen a presbyter. Jerome, in his account of Origen among his ecclesiastical writers. Eusebius also says, VI.20, that Alexander established a library at Jerusalem. At Caesarea in Palestine, under Decius, he was thrown into prison; after a second confession he won great glory, and finally breathed out his soul in custody. Eusebius, VI.39.] who assumed the governance of the church of Jerusalem with Narcissus. V. B. T., At Alexandria, Collegi the deacon. [Note: Collegi. In certain Martyrologies cited by Bollandus these men are celebrated on the preceding day.] V. B., Rogatus and Saturus. At Rome, Pigmenius the presbyter. [Note: For Saint Pigmenius, see 24 March.] A. T. L., In Campania, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Rogatus and Victor. A. T. and S., Lucianus. T. L., And Maurus. L., And Saturninus. B., At Nicomedia, Apurilis and Servulus. In Campania, Quintus, Lucianus, Victor, and Maurus. In Mauritania, Currentius and Timotheus. [Note: He is celebrated on the following day in Bede’s common recension.]

### 19.—XIV KALENDS

Bede has no entry.

D., At the city of Parara, Saint John, a man of great holiness. [Note: A man of great holiness who came from Syria [Col. 0863C] to Italy and, after establishing a monastery near the city of Penara, served as father of many servants of God for forty years and, renowned for many virtues, rested in peace. Usuard. Bernardinus Campellus, in a letter written to Bollandus: John, abbot of Panaca, is the same as the man whom others call Pinnensis. He was called Panacensis from the village of Panaca near Spoleto, where he was father of many monks. Pinnensis, Pennariensis, Pinarensis, and Pararensis were names given by foreign martyrologists through ignorance of the aforementioned village.] B. V. L., At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Theodorus the presbyter. B., In Africa, Lucilla, Basilius, Apollonius, and Ammonius. A. T., In Africa, the deposition of Saint Leo, bishop and confessor. [Note: He seems to be the same as Leontius of Saint Jerome.] And Saint Quintus. On the same day, the commemoration of Theodorus the bishop. And Saint Landualdus, archpresbyter and confessor. [Note: At Ghent, Saints Landoaldus, a Roman presbyter, and Amantius, a deacon, who were sent by Pope Martin to preach the Gospel and were afterward glorified by many miracles. This Saint Landoaldus nurtured Saint Lambert the bishop in childhood and instructed him in sacred letters; while Saint Amandus was engaged in converting the pagans, Landoaldus administered the bishopric of Tongeren in his place for a full nine years, with the highest praise. The father of Saint Lambert gave him the village of Wintershoven, where he built a church in honor of Saint Peter. He flourished around the year 670. He died in that village and was buried in Christian fashion. His relics were transferred in 980 to the monastery of Saint Bavo at Ghent. Ghinius of Siena and Molanus, *On the Saints of Belgium*.]

### 20.—XIII KALENDS

Saint Gutbertus the bishop. [Note: Or Cudbertus; consult above for his Life, described both in plain prose and in heroic verse.]

A. and T. incorrectly add: In Africa. V. B., At Antioch, Saint Joseph. [Note: Bollandus writes of him as follows: “We might readily suspect that this is the very foster-father of the Lord whom the Martyrologies occupying the place immediately after the ancient Hieronymian Martyrologies present on the preceding day, and who was transferred here by Eusebius of Caesarea because of the special veneration at Antioch; but, lacking proofs, we do not dare assert it. Therefore we prefer to count him separately among the martyrs of Antioch.”] V. B., In Syria, Paul. B., Cyril and Exuperius. D., Archippus, Paul the apostle’s fellow soldier. [Note: Saint Ambrose, writing on the Epistle to the Colossians, regards Archippus as bishop of the Colossians.] A. T., And the deposition of Wulfrannus, bishop, and Saint Valentinus. [Note: Bishop of Sens, who assisted Saint Wilbrord in the conversion of the Frisians. In the year 700, with the permission of King Childebert and Prince Pepin, he turned his attention to preaching to the Frisian people. He carried out this work tirelessly for five years, and many nobles were baptized, among them Radbod, son of the king. In advanced old age, and frequently troubled by pain in his feet, he resigned the episcopate and withdrew to the monastery of Fontenelle, where he died in the year of the Lord 720. Ghinius of Siena, Molanus, *On the Saints of Belgium*.] T., At Rome, on the Appian Way, the commemoration of Fabianus, bishop and martyr. [Note: This certainly refers to Saint Fabianus the pope, buried on the Appian Way; see 20 January.]

### 21.—XII KALENDS

Saint Benedict, abbot. [Note: He is celebrated at Cassino in Italy. The Greeks celebrate him on 14 March. Pope Saint Gregory included his deeds in the second book of the *Dialogues*. According to some, he fell asleep in the Lord in 542; according to Leo of Ostia, in 543. Martyrology of Baronius.]

Perhaps Florus adds in L.: “Shining with the greatest virtues, he composed the rule and order of the monks. Blessed Pope Gregory elucidated his Life in a lucid style.”

A. T. L. B., At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saints Serapion the monk [B. adds Polycarpus] and Amator. [Note: This does not appear to be the same as Serapion of Arsinoe, father of ten thousand monks. For why should an Arsinoite be assigned to Alexandria, when the Arsinoite region lies far from that city?] D., And Serapion the hermit.

### 22.—XI KALENDS

Bede has no entry.

Florus, in A. T. L.: At the city of Narbonne, the commemoration of Saint Paul, bishop. [Note: The blessed apostles ordained him first bishop of Béziers in Gaul, then of Narbonne. His Acts are found in Bollandus. They say that he was the very Sergius Paulus, the prudent man and proconsul from whom the apostle Paul received his name, and whom he had subdued to the faith of Christ. After diligently fulfilling the ministry of preaching in that region, renowned for miracles, he was crowned by his confession of Christ and buried. Bede in the common recension, Notker.] whom domestic labor and tribulation so disciplined that they proved him to be a true servant of the Lord.

D., At Narbonne, Saint Paul, bishop and disciple of the apostles. V. B., In the city of Narbonne, Saint Paul the confessor. V., In Africa, Saturninus.

### 23.—X KALENDS

Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Antioch, Theodericus the presbyter. [Note: Because, as their custodian, he could point out the records of the church of Antioch, Julian the Apostate’s uncle first arrested him; then he beat him severely with blows; finally, after interrogating him with every kind of torture and receiving courageous answers, he ordered him to be struck with an axe. But when Julian’s uncle had seized the sacred vessels, he began insolently to mock Christ. At once, however, his genitals became gangrenous, and the flesh surrounding those parts of his body turned into worms. Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* V.7.] who, in the time of the emperor Julian, was struck down by the sword and died.

D., In Africa, the martyrs Victorianus, Frumentius, and two brothers. [Note: Citizens of Hadrumetum: Victorianus, proconsul of Carthage; two brothers from Aix; and two merchants named Frumentius. During the Vandal persecution, under the Arian king Hunneric, they were tortured with the most savage punishments for the Catholic faith and gloriously crowned. Victor of Utica, *History of the Vandal Persecution in Africa*.] V. B., In Africa, Fidelis. At Antioch, Theodorus the presbyter. V., Julianus. B., In Provence, Carmilla, Paulus, and in Caesarea, Julianus. L., And Saints Paulus and Julianus.

### 24.—IX KALENDS

D., At Rome, Pigmenius the presbyter and martyr. [Note: Pigmenius. Under Julian the Apostate he was thrown into the Tiber and killed for the faith of Christ. Baronius, in the Martyrology. The accounts concerning Julian’s education at Rome under Pigmenius together with Donatus, found in the Martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, Notker, and others, are unsatisfactory. For it is sufficiently established from the ancient Greek and Latin records, especially from Julian’s own letters, that Julian lived as a boy with his brother Gallus in Cappadocia, was educated as a young man at Athens, and later served in the armies in Gaul. The body of Saint Pigmenius was collected by a matron named Candida and buried in a crypt in the cemetery of Pontianus at the Bear with the Cap on 20 April, as is read in his Acts. Nevertheless, Pigmenius is mentioned above, under 18 March.] B., In Syria, Seleucus. In Africa, Agapitus and Romulus. V., Rogatus. A. T. L., In Syria, the commemoration of Saints Seleucus, Agapitus, and Romulus. T. L. B., And in Mauritania, Verulus, Felix, and Saturninus. B., And sixteen others. There, before the other three, Secundulus.

### 25.—VIII KALENDS

The Annunciation of the Lord.

The commemoration of Dula, a soldier’s maidservant, who was killed for her chastity. And at Rome, Cyrinus, who was killed by Claudius and thrown into the Tiber, found on the island of Lycaonia, and buried in the cemetery of Pontianus. [Note: He was buried by Marius and Martha and their sons Audifax and Abacuc.] Written in the Passion of Saint Valentinus [elsewhere, Laurentius].

V., first: In Jerusalem, Our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified; last: And the Forty Martyrs and Saint Theodola. A., second: And the crucifixion of Christ; last: And the deposition of Monas, confessor of Christ and bishop. [Note: Monas, bishop of Milan in the third century of Christ, died on this 25 March. But because this day is occupied by the sacred mysteries of Christ incarnate and crucified, the Church of Milan devoted 12 October to his cult; on that day his sacred body was transferred in 1030, and on that same day he was entered in the Roman Martyrology. Bollandus.] T., At Nazareth, a city of Galilee, as the faith of the faithful adores, venerates, and proclaims, the angel Gabriel reverently greets the Virgin who is to give birth to the Lord. On the same day, Our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified according to the flesh. And the victory of Michael the archangel. B., At Nicaea, Victorinus, Alexander, Euphrates, Cassula, Nicostratus, Lucilla, and four hundred martyrs. Elsewhere, Saint Theodola.

### 26.—VII KALENDS

At Sirmium, Montanus the presbyter, his wife Maxima, and forty others. [Note: These martyrs were thrown into a river, and their bodies were found and buried nine miles from the city. Ado, Usuard, Notker.]

Florus in A. T. L.: On the same day at Rome, Saint Castulus the martyr. [Note: He was a palace notary and a host of the saints. Arrested by the governor Fabianus, after Carinus had been killed at Margum, during the consulship of Maximus and Aquilinus—that is, in the year 285—he was killed and buried on the Via Labicana. The Greeks celebrate Saint Sebastian with many of the martyrs related in his Acts, including Saint Castulus, on 18 December.] When he had been restrained in the time of Diocletian, he was hung up three times and interrogated three times; persevering in his confession of the Lord, he was thrown into a pit, and a mass of sand was poured over him. By such a martyrdom he migrated to Christ. Written in the Acts of Saint Sebastian.

B., At Antioch, Timotheus and Diogenes. [Note: Baronius’s Martyrology and others celebrate Saints Timotheus and Diogenes on 6 April, but say that they suffered in Macedonia. Nevertheless, there seem to be other and different saints of the same names, celebrated below on 7 April, who suffered at Antioch with their companions Macaria and Maxima. Hence they perhaps appear to have been wrongly transferred from 7 April to 26 March.] In Africa, Victor, Saturninus, Salvator, and twelve others.

### 27.—VI KALENDS

Bede has no entry.

D., In Egypt, John the hermit. [Note: Born at Lycopolis, and when he was about thirty years old he withdrew to the Mountain of Wolves, where, completing forty years, he foretold the victories of Theodosius over the tyrants Maximus and Eugenius. Bollandus writes of the day of his death as follows: “Although it is certain that 27 March was not the day of his deposition, as Usuard writes, it seems very likely to us that the actual day of his death is still honored among the Copts, namely the twentieth of the month Baba, which corresponds to 17 October.”] V., The commemoration of Saint Marcianus. [Note: The first bishop of the church of Tortona. He was converted to the faith by Blessed Barnabas; under the emperor Hadrian and Sapricius, governor of the province of Milan, after a burning plate had first been pressed unsuccessfully against his breast, he was beheaded in the year of Christ 120. He held the episcopate around the year 44. His Acts are found in Bollandus. His commemoration was once observed on 27 March, but is now celebrated on 6 March, as it is proclaimed in the Roman Martyrology.] In Africa, Romulus and Donatus. And the Resurrection of Our Lord Jesus Christ. A. T., The Resurrection of the Lord. A. T. L., At Nicomedia, the commemoration of Saints Pastor and Victorinus. [Note: For these, see below, 29 March.] A. T., In Africa, the commemoration of Romulus. B., In Africa, Romulus, Marolus, and Successus. In Pannonia, the passion of Saint Alexander the martyr. [Note: Baronius writes of him in the Martyrology: “At Drizipara in Pannonia, Saint Alexander the soldier, who, after overcoming many contests for Christ under the emperor Maximian and performing many miracles, completed his martyrdom by beheading.” But he does not seem to be the same Alexander mentioned here by our author: for Drizipara is in Thrace, far from Pannonia, and the man who suffered there was martyred not on 27 March but on 13 May.]

### 28.—V KALENDS

Bede has no entry.

D., At Caesarea in Palestine, the martyrs Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander. [Note: Eusebius mentions them as follows in *Ecclesiastical History* VII.12: “Moreover, during this persecution of Valerian, three men, after an illustrious confession of Christ, were condemned to the beasts at Caesarea in Palestine and crowned by a divine martyrdom.”] V., At Caesarea, Rogatus, Alexander, and Dorotheus. L. omits Dorotheus. A. and T., Alexander; with him also omitted, B. has Audacta. T. adds: “and ten others.” B., At Tarsus in Cilicia, Castor. B. T. L., In the city of Cabillonum, the deposition of Guntrannus, king. [Note: He devoted himself so completely to spiritual works that, abandoning the pomp of the world, he distributed his treasures to churches and the poor. Bede in the common recension, Usuard. After the death of King Chlothar in 561, Guntrannus divided the kingdom with his brothers; he died in 593 and was buried in the church of Saint Marcellus, in the monastery he himself had built.]

### 29.—IV KALENDS

Bede has no entry.

D., In Africa, the confessors Armogastes, Archinimus, and Satyrus. [Note: Under the Arian king Geiseric they confessed the orthodox faith. Saint Armogastes was condemned to dig trenches and guard cattle; Saint Archinimus, while a sword threatened to kill him, remained a steadfast confessor; Saint Saturus, steward of Hunneric’s household, lost all his possessions through his Catholic confession. Victor of Vitas, Book I of the History.]

V. B., At Nicomedia, Pastor, Victorinus, and Saturninus. [Note: These are celebrated above, on 27 March.] B., And three others. A. T., At Nicomedia, the commemoration of Saints Pastor and Victor. And the deposition of Saint Saturninus. A., And the ordination of Saint Gregory the pope. [Note: His deposition is celebrated above, on 12 March.] B. T. L., At Antioch, the commemoration of Saint Theodorus the presbyter and Julianus. L., And at Nicomedia, Saint Victor.

### 30.—III KALENDS

Bede calls this day.

D., At Rome, Quirinus the tribune. [Note: He was baptized with his entire household by Pope Alexander, whom he held in custody, and under the emperor Hadrian was handed over to the judge Aurelianus. Because he persisted in the confession of the faith, after the cutting out of his tongue, suspension on the rack, and amputation of his hands and feet, he completed his martyrdom by the sword. Baronius, in the Martyrology. Some wrongly say that he suffered under Trajan.] V., In the city of Thessalonica, Domninus and Palatinus. B. inserts Philophilus. B., And elsewhere, Victor, Marcellinus, Saturninus, and Eulalia the virgin. A. T., The commemoration of Saint Eulalia the virgin and Palatinus. A. T. L., At [“At Silvanectis” is absent from A.] Silvanectum, the deposition of Saint Regulus, bishop and confessor. [Note: He is said to have been a disciple of Saint John the apostle. Sent from Rome by Pope Clement, he was ordained bishop of Arles and succeeded Saint Trophimus. There he destroyed idols, expelled demons, converted many to the faith, and built temples in honor of God and the saints. From there, going to the town of Silvanectum, he likewise introduced the faith; for this reason he is also called its first bishop. There he fell asleep in the Lord in the sixtieth year of his age. Ghinius of Siena.] 

### 31.—II KALENDS

Bede has no entry.

D., At Rome, Saint Balbina, virgin. [Note: Daughter of Saint Quirinus, celebrated on the preceding day. She was disfigured by a glandular swelling; but, after being touched with the chains of Pope Saint Alexander and invited by an angel to virginity, she was healed. Bede in the common recension, Notker. Arrested by the judge Aurelianus, and after explaining the reason for her conversion, she was subjected to various tortures and then condemned to death. She was buried by the faithful beside her father on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus. Ado. Her Acts are found in Bollandus.] V. B., In Africa, Anesius, Felix, Diodolus, Cornelia, and Valeria. A. T., At Antioch, the commemoration of Saint Romanus the monk. A. T. L., And Saint Cornelia, virgin. T. L., In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Felix, Anesius [L., Onesi], and Diodolus.

## APRIL

### 1.—KALENDS

At Thessalonica, the commemoration of Agape and Chionia under Diocletian. [Note: These martyrs are said in Jerome’s Martyrology to have suffered at Heraclea. For the Thessalonian martyrs of the same names, see below, 3 March.] They were first tormented in prison and afterward thrown into the fire; but, untouched by the flames, they gave up their souls after pouring out a prayer to God.

V., The commemoration of Paternus, Quintianus, and Victuris. B., In Egypt, the passion of Saints Victor and Stephanus. In Armenia, the commemoration of Saints Partinus, Quintianus, and Secundus.

### 2.—IV NONES

Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Lyons, the commemoration of Saint Nicetius, bishop and confessor. [Note: Born of noble stock, he was educated in letters as a cleric and became a presbyter. When Saint Sacerdos, bishop of Lyons, was near death, he asked King Childebert that Nicetius be appointed in his place. Thus, after Saint Sacerdos, Nicetius became the twenty-fifth bishop of Lyons. He shone with miracles both in life and after death. He died around the year 570. Ghinius of Siena.] He completed a life of complete holiness, most chaste conduct, and outstanding charity.

D., At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Theodosia, virgin. [Note: When the fifth year of the Diocletian persecution was already passing, Theodosia, a virgin from the city of Tyre and not yet eighteen years old, approached certain prisoners who were sitting before the praetorium. For doing this she was seized by the soldiers and led before the governor. He immediately tortured her with cruel punishments and tore her sides and breasts down to the very bones with iron claws; then, while she was still breathing and enduring everything with a joyful face, he ordered her to be drowned in the sea. Eusebius, *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 7.] V., In Africa, Amsanus, Victuris, and ten others. And Marcellus. B., In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Amphianus, Victor, and fourteen others. And elsewhere, Marcellinus and Quiriacus with six others. At Lyons in Gaul, the deposition of Saint Nicetius, bishop. T., On the same day, at Luxeuil, the deposition of Eusebius, abbot. A., On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Mary of Egypt. [Note: At the age of twelve she abandoned her parents and lived for seventeen years as a public prostitute in Alexandria. When she sailed to Jerusalem with several young men and behaved shamefully both on the journey and in the holy city, so much so that, when Mary attempted to enter the temple at the hour of the Exaltation of the Cross, she was repeatedly repelled, she finally grew weary, recognized her disgrace, and, after promising amendment before an image of the Blessed Virgin, obtained entrance. Then, having given thanks to the Mother of God and being instructed to cross the Jordan, she took three loaves as provisions and, strengthened by the sacraments, went into the wilderness, where she lived for forty-seven years. Finally, after her death, she was buried by the monk Saint Zosimus, who wrote her Life. She died around the year 321. Her Acts are found in Bollandus.] 

### 3.—III NONES

Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Rome, Saint Sixtus, pope and martyr. [Note: Or Xystus; see below, 6 April.] While he presided over the chair of Saint Peter at Rome for ten years, he established that, during the service, the priest beginning should chant the hymn to the people, namely: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” and so forth. He was crowned by martyrdom in the time of Verus and Anniculus. [Note: In L. the whole passage beginning “of the chair” and including “Sabaoth,” etc., is sometimes absent.]

[Col. 0872C] D., at Thessalonica, the virgins [Agape. See the Kalends of April. These sisters were first brought before the governor Dulcitius, who was divinely driven mad; afterward they were crowned under the governor Sisinnius.] Agape and Chionia. V. B., in Caesarea of Palestine, [Theodosia. She is also commemorated on the preceding day, but is incorrectly assigned to Caesarea in Cappadocia.] Theodosia the virgin; at Nicomedia, Donatus. T. A. L., in Caesarea of Palestine, the feast of St. Theodosia the virgin. And in Sicily, the feast of Saints Evagrius and Benignus. B. C., in [Sicily. — Cilicia. Ado, Usuard, Notker, and the printed Bede have “in Scythia, in the city of Tomis.”] Cilicia [C, Sicily], the feast of Saints Thomas and Evagrius. B., Benigna, Rufus, and Patricius. And the passion of St. [Amprianus. Perhaps this is the same as Amphianus, the African martyr commemorated on the preceding day.] Amprianus the martyr.

[Col. 0873B] 4.—The second day before the Nones. At Milan, the deposition of St. [Ambrose. See below, 7 December. He is commemorated in the ancient missal and Breviary of the Church of Milan on 5 April; but he is commonly commemorated on this 4 April in martyrologies and the breviaries of various churches, as though he had died on the day before Easter in the year 397, when Easter was celebrated on 5 April. Some, however, think that his death should be assigned to the following year, 397, which was still reckoned as 397 by later generations who began the year from Easter. But if Easter was then celebrated on 18 April, his death would have to be assigned to the 17th. His feast is chiefly celebrated in the Roman and Milanese Churches on 7 December. Bolland.] Ambrose the confessor.

Florus adds in A., T., and L.: “who shone with immense learning and virtues.”

B. At Thessalonica, the feast of Saints [Agathon. Under the emperor Maximian and the governor Faustinus, these men, because of their confession of the Christian faith, were thrown into the sea with a stone tied around the neck. Baron, Martyrology. The time of their martyrdom is not merely noted as having been under Maximian Caesar, that is, Galerius, and therefore after the year 293, when he was named Caesar together with Constantius [Col. 0873D] Chlorus by the emperors Diocletian and Maximian; it is also understood that it must be placed after the year 302, when the first edict was issued ordering the sacred books of the Christians to be burned. For we read in their Acts that Faustinus tried to obtain the sacred books from Theodulus.] Agathon the deacon and Theodulus. Elsewhere, Paul, Matutinus, and Orbanus.

5.—The Nones. At Thessalonica, the feast of [Irene. After being struck by an arrow, she was burned with fire, as Baronius writes in the Martyrology. Her sisters are said above to have suffered either on the Kalends or on the third day before the Nones of April.] Irene, who, after enduring imprisonment and interrogation, was struck with an arrow by the count Sisinnius, under whom her sisters Agape and Chionia also suffered martyrdom.

V., in [Sicily. Rather Cilicia, where Taracus suffered with Probus and Andronicus on 11 October, the day on which he is commemorated below], Sicily, Taracus. C., at Nicomedia, the feast of Claudianus and Taracus. B., at Nicomedia, the feast of Saints [Martianus. They are incorrectly said to have suffered at Nicomedia; in the martyrologies of St. Jerome, Ado, Usuard, Notker, and in the additions of Florus they are reported in Egypt on 5 June.] Martianus, Nicander, and Apollonius. At Alexandria, the feast of Saints [Col. 0873C] Didymus the presbyter, Quiricus, Pancratius, and Successus.

6.—The eighth day before the Ides. Bede has no entry.

[Col. 0874B] Florus in A. T.: “In the city of Sirmium, the passion of St. [Irenaeus. After being pierced with a sword under the governor Probus, he was thrown into the river now called the Sava.] Irenaeus the bishop,” who was struck with a sword during the reign of the emperor Diocletian.

D. [Xystus. According to Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book III, chapter 3, he succeeded Alexander and was the sixth bishop appointed from the apostles. He sat from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus, that is, from the year 117, to the year 127—ten years, three months, and twenty-one days. He was therefore crowned with martyrdom in the tenth year of the emperor Hadrian. He was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter in the Vatican. The Acts of St. Sixtus are in the catalogue of the popes. See also the third day before the Nones.] Xystus, pope and martyr, who suffered during the reign of Hadrian. V., at Nicomedia, [Firmus. Galesinius has: “At Nicaea in Bithynia, Saints Firmus, etc., who received the crown of martyrdom under the emperor Julian.” Jacobillus writes that the head of this Firmus is preserved at Terni in Umbria, in the cathedral church.] Firmus and Irenaeus the bishop. And elsewhere, the feast of St. Marina. A. T. L., in Upper Libya, the feast of Saints [Theodorus. Usuard, Ado, and other martyrologies commemorate these men on 26 March and state that they suffered in Pentapolis of Libya.] Theodorus the bishop, Erenaeus the deacon, and Serapion.

T. L. B., in Africa, the feast of St. [Epiphanius. Usuard and Baronius celebrate their memory on the following day.] Epiphanius the bishop, Donatus, Rufinus [Rufinus is added in B.], Modestus, and eleven others [B. omits “eleven”]. C., in Africa, the feast of Epiphanius and Rufinus. B., at Nicomedia, Firmus and Benereus the bishop. At Sirmium, Rufina, Moderata, Romana, Secundus, with seven others. In Macedonia, [Timothy. See another Timothy and Diogenes on the seventh day before the Kalends and the seventh day before the Ides of April.] Timothy and Diogenes.

[Col. 0874C] 7.—The seventh day before the Ides. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T.: “At Chalcedon, the passion of St. [Euphemia. These matters will be treated on 13 April.] Euphemia [Col. 0875B] and Eucapia,” who, enduring many torments for the name of Christ, fell asleep in Christ.

D. [Hegesippus. He lived near the apostolic age and composed five books in which he wove together the histories of ecclesiastical events from the Passion of the Lord to his own time, collecting here and there much material useful to readers. He states that he came to Rome under Bishop Anicetus and remained until Eleutherius, bishop of the same city. St. Jerome, Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers; and Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History IV, 22.] Hegesippus, who lived near the apostles. V. C. B. L. T., at Antioch in Syria, [Timothy. See the seventh day before the Kalends of April.] Timothy, Diogenes, and Macaria. The final name is absent in L. and T.; B. adds Maxima. And elsewhere, [Eleusius. Perhaps this is the same as Peleusius, who is said by Baronius, the printed Bede, Usuard, and our author to have suffered at Alexandria.] Eleusius the presbyter. In Upper Libya, Coprica and Victor. At Alexandria, the feast of St. Peleusius the presbyter.

8.—The sixth day before the Ides. Bede has no entry.

D., at Tours, [Perpetuus. A man of admirable holiness, born of senatorial stock and educated in letters and excellent morals, who was consecrated the sixth bishop of the see of Tours after St. Eustochius and governed it for thirty years. He dedicated a church to St. Martin, where he also placed the saint’s sacred body with greater honor. He took part in the first Council of Tours and in the Council of Vannes, and finally passed to glory around the year 490. Ghinius of Siena.] Perpetuus the bishop. C., in Africa, Timor and Macharius. V., in Africa, Macarius, Conexus, [Col. 0875C] Maxima, and Concessus. B., in Africa, Timor, Macharius, Conexus, and Maxima. And elsewhere: Concessus, Ammonius, and Successus. L., in Africa, Saints Macarius, Conexus, and Maximus. A. T. L., and the deposition of the Savior and of St. [Maria. See 2 April. She is also commemorated on the following day.] Mary of Egypt. A. T., in Africa, the feast of St. Macarius and St. Frontinus the monk.

[Col. 0876B] 9.—The fifth day before the Ides. At Sirmium, the feast of seven virgins, who deserved to be crowned together.

A. T. L. B., and the feast of St. Demetrius the deacon. B., Hilary and Concessus. And elsewhere, Fortunatus and Donatus. A., and the deposition of St. [Hugh. He was noble by birth but nobler in virtues. Inflamed by divine inspiration, he relinquished the reins of his episcopate and received from St. Aichardus at Jumièges the monastic discipline and habit. When the Normans burned the churches, the bodies of both men were transferred to the village of Haspram, between Cambrai and Valenciennes. Molanus, Catalogue of the Saints of Belgium.] Hugh, bishop of Rouen. T., on the same day, the feast of St. Mary of Egypt. L., and the translation of St. [Waldetrudis. Her feast falls on 3 February.] Waldetrudis.

10.—The fourth day before the Ides. Ezekiel the prophet.

B., at Alexandria, [Apollonius. Maurolycus and Peter de Natalibus write that this man was drowned at sea together with his attendant Philemon, whom he converted to the faith. But the man subjected to this punishment was a deacon, not a presbyter, as can be seen in Lives of the Fathers, part I, chapter 19. He is therefore not the same as our Apollonius.] Apollonius the presbyter, Saturninus, and Concessus. In Thrace, the feast of [Gaianus. In some martyrologies he is said to have suffered in Dacia.] Gaianus. A. T., [Col. 0876C] the feast of St. Saturninus. A. T. L., in Africa, the feast of Saints Successus and Marcellus. [The place is missing in L.]

11.—The third day before the Ides. At Rome, [Leo. He was Tuscan by nationality and was born to Quintianus. According to Prosper in his Chronicle, after Sixtus, the Roman pontiff, died in the consulship of Valentinian V and Anatolius—that is, in the year of Christ 440—Leo was made pope. He exposed two heresies, and after sending a legation to the emperor Marcian, the synod assembled at Chalcedon condemned Eutyches and Nestorius. He is commemorated in the martyrologies on 11 April, 14 March, 15 March, 10 November, and 28 June; by the Greeks, on 18 February.] Leo, pope and confessor.

B. At [Salmona. More correctly, Salona: Domnio was born at Antioch to Theodosius, a tenant farmer; he was converted with his parents by St. Peter and followed St. Peter as far as Rome. He was sent as bishop to Salona, where he converted many. Captured by the faithless, he confessed the faith before the governor Maurelius, who ordered him to be beaten with clubs and then beheaded. He suffered on the Nones of May. The Acts are in Bolland.] Salona in Dalmatia, Domnio the bishop, and eight soldiers; and [Dalmatus. We commemorate on this day several martyrs who suffered in Dalmatia. Regarding their Acts, we are uncertain whether “Dalmatus” or “Dalmata” should be understood appellatively; and in the title we would prefer that it be removed.] Dalmatus. In Africa, Fortunatus and 240 others. A. T., and Domninus the bishop, and St. Dalmatius. V., [Donatus. In Africa, that is, with Fortunatus. Notker.] Donatus and 241 others. A., on the same day, at Noviomagus, the deposition of St. [Godeberta. She was born of noble lineage in the district of Amiens. Blessed Eligius, already elevated to the episcopate, betrothed her sacred virginity eternally to Christ with his ring in the presence of King Chlothar III. Eligius was ordained bishop in 640. Since Godeberta became a religious woman in the flower of her early youth, it will not be unreasonable to think that her death occurred toward the end of the seventh century or even later. She was buried in the oratory of St. George at Noviomagus, in the church now called that of the Holy Apostles. The Acts are in Bolland.] Godeberta, an outstanding virgin, who was born of noble lineage in the district of Amiens. T., on the same day, at Lyon, the deposition of [Fiagrus. Better, Siagrius: in certain manuscript martyrologies cited by Bollandus he is called a confessor; Molanus, in his Usuard, changed the name and wrote: “At Lyon, Sicharius the bishop.”] Fiagrus and Patricius.

12.—The second day before the Ides. At Rome, the deposition of [Julius. The Roman pontiff, who was ordained on 6 February in the year 337. He lived chiefly during the time of Constans, son of Constantine the Great and ruler in Italy, not during the time of the heretic Constantius; nor was he driven into exile by the latter and returned in glory after Constantius’s death, as is foolishly related in the Liber Pontificalis and by Anastasius. Nor, to preserve those claims, can the name Constans be substituted for Constantius: Constans’s Catholic faith always remained most highly praised, and in the final year of his reign St. Athanasius was at Rome with St. Julius, who wrote to the Alexandrians on his behalf. Nothing about his exile is found either in the manuscript catalogues of the popes compiled in the sixth or eighth century or in the manuscript Deeds of the Popes brought down to Martin V. He died in 352. Bollandus. [Col. 0878B] He was buried on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone, in the cemetery of Calepodius. Ado. Notker.] Julius [B., Julianus], bishop and confessor, who under the Arian Constantius, son of Constantine, endured tribulations and exiles for ten months and, after Constantius’s death, returned with great glory to his see.

[Col. 0878B] V. adds: [Placed. That is, transferred by Innocent II to the Church of Blessed Mary across the Tiber.] placed at St. Mary’s across the Tiber. C., at Capua, Cypriana. B., at Capua, the feast of Saints Cyprian, Novella, and Silvanus. In the city of Cepingus, the deposition of Blessed [Constantine. Not in the city of Cepingus but of Vapincum. He was the first bishop of Vapincum and, according to Saussay in his Gallican Martyrology, flourished under Pope Symmachus and Clovis, the first Christian king of the Franks. But Sainte-Marthe, in Gallia Christiana, does not regard Constantine as the first bishop of Vapincum; from the ancient records of that church he places a certain St. Demetrius first. Constantine subscribed the Council of Epaon in 517, under Sigismund, king of the Burgundians. Baronius writes in the Martyrology that he attended the Council of Orange in 441; but since no place is added in the council, this is entirely uncertain.] Constantine the bishop. And elsewhere, Euphemia, Macharius, and nine others.

13.—The Ides. Bede has no entry.

D., at Pergamum in Asia, [Carpus. Eusebius mentions these martyrs in Ecclesiastical History IV, 15. They did not suffer during the reign of Marcus Antoninus, as Baronius writes in the Martyrology, misled by the fact that their Acts follow in Eusebius the letter of the Smyrnaeans concerning the martyrdom of Polycarp, who was indeed crowned during the reign of Marcus Antoninus; rather, they suffered under the emperor Decius, as their Acts still testify. After many illustrious confessions, they were brought to completion by a glorious death. Their Acts are found in Bollandus; the Greeks celebrate them on 13 October.] Carpus the presbyter, Papyrus, Agathonice, and many other women. B. V. A. T. L., at Chalcedon, the feast of St. [Euphemia. Euphemia of Chalcedon is also recorded on 16 September and on 17 August; and on the preceding day another Euphemia is discussed. Given this, why should not the honorable name Euphemia have been common to several women at Chalcedon, some of whom may have been killed out of hatred for the Christian faith?] Euphemia, virgin and martyr. L. T. B. add: “and Eucapia,” B. adding, “who, after many torments, rest.” V., Secutor, Carolus, [Januarius. The Martyrology of Rabanus gives the following: “At Rome, in the cemetery across the Tiber, the translation of St. Januarius the martyr.”] Januarius. A. T., on the same day, the feast of St. Secutor. B., and elsewhere, Januarius and Paul.

[Col. 0879B] 14.—The eighteenth day before the Kalends of May. At Rome, [Tiburtius. Tiburtius and Valerian, his brother and the betrothed of St. Cecilia, were converted by Cecilia herself to the faith. When they had been led by their torturers to the house of Maximus for custody, Maximus too was converted by an angelic vision. All suffered martyrdom under the emperor Alexander, around the year 229. They were buried on the Appian Way in the cemetery of Praetextatus. Ado, the printed Bede, Notker.] Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, under Almachius, prefect of the City. The first two were beaten with clubs and then struck with the sword; the last was beaten with leaded scourges until he gave up his spirit.

B., Valerian, Quiriacus, and Optatus. At Terni, Proculus and [Valentinus. Perhaps this is the bishop of Terni discussed on 14 February.] Valentinus. At Alexandria, [Fronton. More correctly, Fronton, the monk who lived in the Nitrian desert and took seventy monks with him into the desert. Read in Notker and Rabanus how, by divine command, camels sent to Fronton by a wealthy head of household came by a straight route, without a guide, to the cell of the starving saints. He lived under the emperor Antoninus, but it is uncertain which Antoninus.] Fronton the monk.

[Col. 0879C] 15.—The seventeenth day before the Kalends. In the city of Cordula, the feast of [Olympias. After these martyrs had died, they were left to be eaten by dogs. But the dogs did not touch their bodies; on the fifth day certain Christians gathered the bodies and buried them in their house, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. The Acts are in Bollandus. They were martyred in the year 251.] Olympias and Maximus, nobles, who, at the command of Decius, were beaten with clubs and then with leaded scourges; finally their heads were battered with axes until they gave up the spirit.

B., in Mesopotamia, Archelaus, Cyprian, [Diogenes. He is called a deacon in the Hieronymian Martyrology.] Diogenes, with two brothers. In [Spain. In the city of Zaragoza, Lupercus and [Col. 0880C] Apodemus, who were killed under the governor Dacian during the persecution of Diocletian, together with sixteen others. Usuard and Baronius commemorate them on the following day.] Spain, at Caesarea, the passion of Saints Lubertus and Apomedes, with two brothers.

16.—The sixteenth day before the Kalends. Bede has no entry.

D., at Corinth, Calixtus and Carisius, with seven others, drowned in the sea. V., in Achaia, at the city of Corinth, Calixtus and Leonidas. And the passion of all the holy martyrs at sea. B., in Achaia, at the city of Corinth, the feast of Saints Callistus, Carissus, Leonidas, Lota, Tertia, Christina, Galla, and Theodora; all these were drowned in the sea. In Mauritania, the feast of Basilia. And elsewhere, the feast of [Mauritanus. Otherwise Marcianus, who suffered with Faustinus and Lucianus, together with others, in Pontus, a region of Asia. St. Jerome’s Martyrology.] Mauritanus, Faustinus, and Lucianus. A. T. L., in Achaia, the passion of St. Callistus the martyr. L., and Faustus. A. T., on the same day, the feast of Saints Faustus and Leonidas. T. L., in the district of Coutances, the deposition of St. [Paternus. He became a monk in childhood; when he had advanced in age, however, he went with St. Scubilion to the district of Coutances and taught the idolaters at Sesciacus the faith of Christ. Thereafter, he was ordained deacon and priest by St. Leontianus, bishop of Coutances, who flourished around the year 510. Through the cities of Coutances, Bayeux, Le Mans, Avranches, and Rennes he founded many monasteries. At the age of seventy he was made bishop of Avranches. His predecessor was Aegidius, who subscribed the Council of Orléans in 547; Paternus seems to have succeeded him around 552 and afterward to have attended the Third Council of Paris around 556. Finally, he died in 565 at Sesciacus, where he was buried. The Acts are in Bollandus.] Paternus, bishop and confessor.

17.—The fifteenth day before the Kalends. Bede has no entry.

D., in Africa, St. [Mappalicus. Cyprian writes about him in a letter, p. 21 of the Oxford edition. Peter de Natalibus asserts that their martyrdom took place in the city of Thagaste. Baronius places the time of their martyrdom during the persecution of Decius, continued after his death.] Mappalicus. D. V. A. T. L., [Col. 0881B] at Antioch, Peter the deacon and Hermogenes his minister. B., [Fortunatus. Rabanus writes that these men suffered in Africa.] Fortunatus and Marcianus. In Africa, [Julianus. In the Hieronymian Martyrology these men are joined with Mappalicus.] Julianus the presbyter, Banicus, Theodora, and Meconius. And elsewhere, St. [Domninus. Or Domnio, whom we discussed on 11 February.] Domninus the martyr. A. T. L., at Rome, the feast of St. [Eleutherius. He is discussed on the following day.] Eleutherius the bishop and St. [Fortunatus. Perhaps this is the same man who suffered in Africa with Marcianus.] Fortunatus. L., and at Tours, the deposition of [Cogitosus. Since there was no bishop named Cogitosus among the people of Tours, it is scarcely possible to determine whom this entry indicates.] Cogitosus the bishop.

18.—The fourteenth day before the Kalends. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T.: “In Africa, the feast of Saints Victor and Donatus.” On the same day at Rome, the passion of St. [Eleutherius. So many fables seem to have been fabricated about this man that it is scarcely possible to extract anything true from his Acts. For they claim that he was ordained bishop when he was only twenty years old and that lions and leopards lived in the Roman forests and obeyed him. They further say that Eleutherius’s mother Anthia saw St. Paul while he was still alive in the body; and Eleutherius, at the age of twenty, is made to have suffered under Hadrian in the twenty-fifth year of that emperor’s reign. But the martyrdom of Saints Peter and Paul occurred in the year 65, while Hadrian began to reign in 117. Let us suppose, then, not that Eleutherius was twenty-five years old—for Hadrian did not reign so many years—but that in at least the fifteenth year of his reign the emperor, returning from the East, heard of Eleutherius; that year would have been 131. If Eleutherius was then twenty years old, one would have to imagine a very aged mother who bore him around the year 110 and had seen St. Paul before the year 65. In the manuscript of Dijon he is assigned to Nessay in Apulia; Ado, Usuard, Notker, and others write Mescena, Misana, or Messana instead of Hecana in Apulia, whose bishop the Acts make him. Hecana was the same city that is now called Troia. Rabanus, Notker, and the author of the spurious Bede write that he was ordained bishop of Aquileia.] Eleutherius and his mother Anthia (up to this point A.); they suffered under the emperor Hadrian. Eleutherius was placed on a gridiron over burning coals; afterward he was thrown into a blazing furnace and was not consumed; he was then tied to four untamed horses, yet was not torn limb from limb but was released by an angel; finally, at the emperor’s command, he was struck with the sword. His mother Anthia, however, after throwing herself upon her son’s body and confessing herself a Christian, was immediately beheaded.

D., at Nessay in Apulia, Eleutherius the bishop and Antia his mother. V. B., at Rome, Eleutherius the bishop and Antia his mother. V., Proculus and Apollonius. A. T. L., on the same day at Lobbes, the feast of St. [Ursmarus. He was born in the district of Thour, in the village of Fléon, where his house is still shown, in the territory of Hainaut near Avesnes. Summoned by Duke Pippin, he undertook the government of the monastery of Lobbes. Consecrated bishop for the conversion of a barbarian people, he converted many to Christ in parts of Gaul, namely Fania and Thour, and built many churches. From there he went to preach in Flanders, toward the territory of the Menapians. Those converted to the faith by his constant preaching made him heir to a large part of their estates and gave to Christ the church at Lobbes. He also, as lord of the region, gave Aldo a village named Aldenburg after him, in which he consecrated a church in honor of Blessed Peter. He died in 713 and was honorably buried at Lobbes, not far from the monastery, in the oratory of St. Mary on the hill. Molanus, On the Saints of Belgium. Ghinius of Siena.] Ursmarus the bishop. B., in the city of Salona, the feast of Saints Septimius the deacon and Victoricus. In Africa, Victor, Pamphilus, and Priscianus. T., at Tours, the deposition of [Cogitosus. Colganus thinks that Cogitosus, the writer of the Life of St. Brigid, is commemorated on this day, and that “Cogitosus the wise” is mentioned in the Martyrology of Tallaght. We know nothing further.] Cogitosus the bishop.

19.—The thirteenth day before the Kalends. Bede has no entry.

D., at Corinth, [Timon. He first sat as a teacher at Beroea; afterward, spreading the word of the Lord, he came to Corinth. There he was first thrown into the flames by Jews and Greeks but was unharmed; then he was fastened to a cross and completed his martyrdom. Usuard, the printed Bede, Baronius.] Timon, one of the seven, the deacon. At Melitene, Hermogenes with five others. V. T., in Armenia, Hermogenes, Gagius, Expeditus, and Rufus. The last is omitted here in T.; L., however, places Rufus before Expeditus and inserts Vincentius, adding with T. “who were likewise crowned.” A. T. B., in the city of Militana, the passion of St. Rufus the martyr. A. T., and [Vincentius. He did not suffer in the city of Militana but rather at Caucoliberis in Nearer Spain, as Rabanus, Ado, Notker, and others write.] Vincentius. B., Antonicus. A. T., at Rome, the feast of [Hadrian. This refers to Eleutherius, who is commemorated with his mother Anthia on the preceding day.] Hadrian the bishop and Anthia his mother, who were struck with the sword under the emperor Hadrian. B., in Africa, Sericianus, [Col. 0883B] Heladius, and Hermogenes. A., on the same day, the deposition of Leo the pope, resting in the church of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. L., and the deposition of [Leo. The ninth, a German by nationality, named Bruno, made bishop of Toul in 1026 and elected pope at Rome in 1049, during the reign of Henry III. He held councils at Rome, Pavia, Mainz, Reims, and Vercelli to condemn Berengar and others, to provide for the condition of the Church, and to recall the Greeks to unity. He kindly urged the emperor of Constantinople to restore the Lord’s tomb and the church there, destroyed by the barbarians. He died after sitting for five years, two months, and eight days, in the year of salvation 1054, and was buried at St. Peter’s.] Leo, pope of blessed memory, who was named Bruno.

20.—The twelfth day before the Kalends. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L., at Rome, the deposition of St. [Anicetus. He held the pontificate from the year 150 to the year 151 and suffered during the reigns of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, not Severus, as the martyrologies falsely write. Baronius commemorates him in the Martyrology on 17 April, and the author of the spurious Bede on 16 April.] Anicetus, pope and martyr, who governed the Roman Church for eleven years and suffered during the time of Severus and Marcus.

D. At Rome, the deposition of [Victor. Ado, Notker, and the spurious Bede judged this man to have been a Roman pontiff; having found Victor, a bishop and martyr at Rome, they thought no further. But the cult of Victor the Roman pontiff continues to this day on 28 July; and from the comparison of the martyrologies cited by Bollandus, it seems not unlikely that this Victor was a bishop brought from elsewhere to suffer at Rome.] Victor the bishop and martyr, [Sulpitius. These were not Victor’s companions; they were converted to the faith of Christ by the preaching and miracles of Flavia Domitilla, who had also won their betrothed women, Theodora and Euphrosina, to the hope of eternal life. When they refused to sacrifice to idols, they were beheaded by Anianus, prefect of the City. Christians seized their bodies and placed them on their estate on the Latin Way, at the second milestone. Ado, etc.] Sulpitius and Servilianus. V. B., at Rome, the deposition of St. Victor the bishop, Felix, and Alexander. And in the cemetery beside the Nomentan Way, Salvianus, Aragacus, or beside [Col. 0883C] Silvanus, Aiaracus. B., Donata. A. T., on the same day, the deposition [Col. 0884B] of St. Victor the bishop and the passion of Donatus the martyr. In the city of Auxerre, the deposition of St. [Martin. He is called Marcus in the manuscript Martyrology of the monastery of St. Sabinus of Levitania in the Pyrenees. But since no bishop of Auxerre of this name is recorded, we think that either Mamertinus the abbot or, rather, Marianus the monk is intended; both lived at Auxerre and are commemorated on this day. Bolland.] Martin, bishop and confessor. B., in Africa, the feast of Servanus, Silvanus, and John. In the city of Auxerre, the deposition of St. [Marcianus. A monk who came from the region of Bourges to Auxerre and, out of love for religion, while St. Mamertinus governed the monastery of St. Germanus, asked to be admitted into the fellowship of the ascetics. Received there with the greatest charity, he produced abundant fruits of outstanding holiness. Saussay, Gallican Martyrology, 29 April. When he was asked to celebrate Easter at the monastery of Fontenay, he was seized by a fever and died; he was brought back to Auxerre, received with solemn ceremony, and buried in the church of St. Germanus. The Acts are in Bollandus.] Marcianus the presbyter. C., the deposition of Victor the bishop and Servianus.

21.—The eleventh day before the Kalends. Bede has no entry.

D., in Persia, St. [Simeon. Bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon. At the command of Sapor, king of the Persians, he was seized, loaded with chains, and brought before unjust tribunals. Because he refused to worship the sun, he was first confined for a long time in prison with a hundred others, some of whom were bishops, some presbyters, and some clerics of various orders. Then Eusthazanes, the king’s foster-son, who had previously fallen away from the faith but had been recalled to repentance through Simeon, steadfastly underwent martyrdom. On the following day, which was Easter, all the others were slaughtered with the sword before Simeon’s eyes, and finally he himself was beheaded. He suffered in the year 349.] Simeon the bishop, with a hundred others. V. B., at Rome, in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, [Valerian. These men are commemorated above on 14 April.] Valerian, Tiburtius, and Maximus. A. T., at Rome, the deposition of St. Valerian. In Alexandria, the feast of St. Victor [L., Amator] the presbyter and Vitalis. T. B., at Terracina in Campania, the passion of St. [Caesarius. His memory is chiefly celebrated on 1 November.] Caesarius the deacon. B., in Alexandria, the feast of Saints Fortunatus, Arator the presbyter, [Col. 0884C] Felix, Silvius, and Vitalis, who rest in prison.

[Col. 0885B] 22.—The tenth day before the Kalends. At Rome, the deposition of St. [Gaius. He is also commemorated above on 20 February; he sat at Rome from the year 283 to the year 296.] Gaius, pope, who, after governing the Church for twelve [A. T. L., eleven] years, four months, and twelve days [Four months and eleven days are absent in A. and T.], was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian, together with his brother Gabinius. On the same day, in the city of Corduba, the feast of [Parmenas. At Cordula near Babylon, these martyrs were presbyters and deacons at Babylon under Polychronius the bishop, as the account of the passion of St. Laurence indicates. Polychronius is commemorated on 17 February.] Parmenas, Elymas, and Chrysotelus, presbyters [A., “the presbyters,” omitting Chrysotelus], and Lucius and Musa, deacons (up to this point A.), from Babylonia, whose severed tongues continued to speak. They were all suspended on the rack and bound tightly with cords; then burning plates were applied around their sides and they were scorched, and their flesh was torn with claws. Finally they were beheaded with the sword, in the presence of the persecutor Decius. (Up to this point T.) This is written in the Passion of St. Laurence.

L., and St. [Eutropius. It is unclear who he was, unless he is the man who, according to the martyrologies, was consecrated bishop by Blessed Clement, the successor of the apostles, and sent to Gaul to preach. Having fulfilled this office, when pagans rose up—whom the author of the account did not permit to believe because of envy—he died victoriously after his head was struck by an axe. He is said to have been the first bishop of Saintes.] Eutropius the martyr.

[Col. 0886B] 23.—The ninth day before the Kalends. The feast of St. [George. In the Persian city of Diospolis, under the emperor Diocletian. His Acts are so full of fables that nothing certain can be narrated about this saint. It must nevertheless be said that under this martyr’s patronage the celebrated Order of the Garter of England serves throughout the world, and that the English people especially entrusted themselves to the protection of St. George—not only in more recent times but from the very beginnings of Anglo-Saxon rule. We think this can be proved from this very passage of the genuine Martyrology of Bede, which indicated the feast of St. George with the same simplicity with which it indicated the feasts of Christ and the apostles.] George the martyr.

Florus in A. T. L., and in Egypt, the passion of Saints [Victor. These men are also commemorated on the following day, but chiefly on 14 May.] Victor and Corona under the emperor Antoninus. After Victor’s sinews had been torn out, boiling oil poured upon his private parts, and his eyes gouged out, he was hung upside down, flayed, and then beheaded. Corona, however, was tied to two trees and torn apart.

V. B., at Rome, Nabor. V., Vitalis, [Note: [Col. 0886D] Felix, priest; Fortunatus and Achilleus, deacons. They were sent by the blessed Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, to preach at Valence. After converting a very large part of that city to the faith, they were thrust into prison by the governor Cornelius and then beaten for a very long time with an exceedingly harsh scourging of the sinews. Afterwards, with their hands bound behind their backs, their loins and legs broken, they were fastened around the revolving wheels; bitter smoke was also placed beneath them and continued day and night; they were suspended on the rack by stretching, and at last were beheaded with the sword. Usuard, Ado, Peter de Natalibus, and others following them wrote that Valence was a city of Spain, but falsely, for these apostles were sent by Irenaeus not to Spain but to Valence in Gaul. Bollandus appears to have established that they suffered around the year 212.] Felix. L., The Passion of Saints Felix, Fortunatus, and Achilleus. T., The feast of Saints Felix the priest, Fortunatus and Achilleus, and Saint Nabor the martyr. A., The feast of Saint Nabor. On the same day, Saint [Note: [Col. 0886D] Regulus. Concerning this bishop of Senlis, see 30 March.] Regulus, bishop and confessor. B., In Africa, Catulinus, Felix, Theodore, Venustus, Vitalis, and Faustinus.

[Col. 0887B] 24.—VIII Kalends. Burial of [Note: [Col. 0887D] Mellitus. Concerning how he was sent to Britain by Saint Gregory to assist Saint Augustine in preaching the word of God, see Ecclesiastical History I.29–30; and concerning how he later became a bishop, and his deeds during his episcopate until his death, see Ecclesiastical History II.3–7.] Mellitus, bishop in Britain.

Florus in A. T. L., In Gaul, at the city of Lyons, the passion of Saints [Note: [Col. 0887D] Alexander. In the seventeenth year of the reign of Antoninus Verus, A.D. 177. Eusebius writes in the preface to the fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History: “A violent persecution broke out.” In this same persecution, but in the following year, Saints Epipodius and Alexander suffered at Lyons—the former on 22 April, the latter today. Alexander was Greek by nation, while Epipodius was a native of the city of Lyons. Their Acts are found in Bollandus.] Alexander and Epipodius, with thirty-four others; [Col. 0887C] Alexander was stretched upon a cross and so mangled by the cruelty of his executioners that, when the framework of his ribs was broken and his viscera exposed, the secrets of his soul were laid open; thus, having been deprived of life, he gave up his spirit. Epipodius, however, with his entire mouth shattered by leaden blows, was suspended on the rack and afterwards struck with the sword.

V., On this day also, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who are also called Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael: they were delivered from the furnace of blazing fire in the great city of Babylon. In the city of Lyons in Gaul, the passion of Saint Alexander with thirty-four others, and the dedication of the crypt where their bodies rest. And elsewhere, a commemoration of Saint George. B., In Alexandria, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 0888D] Corona. Concerning Saints Corona and Victor, see the preceding day.] Corona the virgin, Victor, and Zotichus. In Africa, the feast of Saints Faustinus, Victorinus, and Valerius. And the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 0888D] Hecheractus. He is also called Hecberactus and Herberactus. This incorrect spelling of the name makes it difficult to discover who he really was. Nevertheless, it is clear from very many Martyrologies that he was an English saint; but it is not equally clear whether he was Hereberctus the hermit, Huetberctus the abbot of Wearmouth, Ecgberctus the priest of Iona, or Ecgberctus, bishop of York.] Hecheractus and [Note: [Col. 0888D] Ulfredus. Namely, Wilfridus, bishop of York, concerning whom see Ecclesiastical History V.19.] Ulfredus. The same Alexander with his companions is mentioned in B.

[Col. 0887D] 25.—VII Kalends. The feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist in Alexandria: after he had established and confirmed Churches [Col. 0888B] throughout Libya, Marmarica, Ammoniaca, Pentapolis, Alexandria, and all Egypt, he was finally seized by the pagans who remained in Alexandria. (Thus far A.) When they saw him celebrating Mass on the holy day of [Col. 0888C] Easter, they put a rope around his neck and dragged him to the places called Bucoli, which were beside the sea beneath the cliffs, where a church had been built. His flesh fell away onto the ground, and the rocks were stained with blood. When evening came, they threw him into prison. There, around midnight, he was first strengthened by an angelic visitation; then, when the Lord himself appeared to him, he was called to the heavenly kingdoms. In the morning, while he was being dragged again to the places called Bucoli, he gave thanks and said, “Lord, into your hands I commend my spirit.” He died in the eighth year of Nero and was buried by religious men of Alexandria, with glory, in a place hewn from the rock. He had appointed Annianus bishop of Alexandria in his place; and he had also provided bishops, priests, and deacons for the Churches far and wide.

V. L., On the same day, the Greater Litany. B., In the city of Syracuse [Col. 0889A] in Sicily, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 0889B] Evadus. According to the Greek menologia, these were holy brothers of German origin who, condemned to the sword, completed their course after their necks had been cut off. Nothing certain is known concerning the time when they suffered martyrdom. Rocchus Pirrus, in volume II of *Sacred Sicily*, in his account of the Church of Syracuse, says that they suffered in the year 309; Ferrarius writes that it was during the savage persecution of Diocletian. Why should they not have suffered earlier, since the Martyrology of Saint Jerome lists them first? The city of Syracuse had the first fruits of its martyrs under Nero. BOLLAND.] Evadus, Hermogenes, and Callista. At Lyons, Saint Rusticus, bishop.

[Col. 0889B] 26.—VI Kalends. The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0889C] Cletus. On this same day Usuard, Ado, and others commemorate him; the spurious Bede, however, places Anacletus here and Cletus on 3 May. Because of the similarity of the names, great confusion arose among both Latins and Greeks concerning Cletus and Anacletus. Unless the fault lies in the manuscript, the carelessness of copyists seems to have caused not merely lesser but even very eminent writers to err in these names. Saint Irenaeus appears to have done so in *Against Heresies*, book III, chapter 3; Eusebius likewise in the *Chronicle* and *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 12; and Nicephorus in *History*, book III, chapter 2. Among the Latins also, Optatus of Milevis, book II *Against Parmenianus*, and Augustine, letter 165, apparently believing that Cletus was the same as Anacletus, passed over the former. Conversely, many who knew Cletus did not know Anacletus, including Saint Epiphanius, who in *Panarion*, heresy 27, mentions Cletus and omits Anacletus. Later, however, after his book on the Roman pontiffs, Saint Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men*, under Clement, lists Cletus after Linus. The name Cletus is found in the anciently written Canon of the Mass. The Vatican indexes likewise mention him. BARONIUS, in his notes on the Martyrology.] Cletus, pope and martyr.

Florus adds in A. T. L., He governed the Church for twelve years, third after Peter, and suffered martyrdom in the time of Vespasian and Titus.

On the same day, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0889D] Marcellus—more properly Marcellinus; the Greeks do not distinguish them because of the similarity of their names. Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*, after giving the consuls Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius Caesar for the second time—that is, A.D. 296—writes as follows: “Marcellinus assumed the episcopate of the Roman Church and held it for nine years. Then, omitting Saint Marcellus, Eusebius records that Marcellinus was succeeded under the consulship of Constantius Augustus for the sixth time and Maximian Caesar for the sixth time, A.D. 396.” Other Greeks, following Eusebius, likewise omitted Marcellus; George Syncellus also passed over Eutychianus together with him. Marcellinus did not hold the pontificate for nine years and four months, but only eight years and four months. For, according to the ancient list of pontiffs, in the year 296 Marcellinus was appointed pope in succession to Saint Caius; he died a martyr under the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth, that is, in the year 304, when those emperors laid down the purple. Another ancient list of pontiffs states that he was led to sacrifice in order to offer incense, and that he did so; but a few days later, moved to repentance, he was beheaded by the same Diocletian for the faith of Christ, together with Claudius, Quirinus, and Antoninus. Their holy bodies lay in the street for twenty-five days, or, as it is written elsewhere, thirty-five or thirty-six. Since their bodies are said here to have lain in the street for so long before burial, it may reasonably be doubted whether Saint Marcellinus was buried only on 26 April, and whether he was crowned with martyrdom earlier, at the beginning of this month or rather in the preceding March. Saint Marcellus, pope, is commemorated on 16 January. According to the list of pontiffs, he governed the Roman Church for one year, seven months, and twenty days. He lived in the time of Maxentius, from the consulship of Maxentius for the tenth time and Maximian for the seventh, until after the consulship of Maxentius for the tenth time and Maximian for the seventh. The years indicated here are 308, when Saint Marcellus appears to have been made pope near the end of May, and the following year, 309, beyond which he scarcely lived as pope, since he died on 16 January.] Marcellus, pope: after he had governed the Church for nine years and four months, [Col. 0890A] in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, he was beheaded by that same Diocletian and buried thirty-four days later [Col. 0890B] on the Salarian Way, in a chamber, by the priest Marcellus and the deacons, with hymns.

V. adds: 6 Kalends of May.

A. T., on the same day, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0890C] Richarius. He was born at Centula, a village in the province of Ponthieu. Having been admonished by two Irish priests, Caidocus and Frichorius, whom he had received as guests, he was made a priest and preacher from a peasant; and he shone forth as a distinguished man not only in his own regions but also among the Britons across the sea, whom he visited and cultivated. He was also a friend of Saint Rictrudis and baptized her son, Saint Maurontus, whom he likewise saved from the immediate danger of death. Afterwards, seeking the monastic life, he entrusted to another the governance of the Church he had founded at Centula and withdrew into the forest of Crécy, which Gislemarus and Maurontus gave him. After his death, at the end of five months and twelve days, the brothers of Centula carried his body to their monastery. His life was written by Alcuin.] Richarius, confessor. T., Priest of Christ. B., In Africa, Honoratus, Paulus, Maximus, and Apollonius.

27.—V Kalends. Bede has nothing.

D., Saint [Note: [Col. 0890D] Anastasius. When Siricius, Roman pontiff, died, Saint Anastasius, a Roman by birth and the son of Maximus, was appointed in his place. The year was then 398, during the second indiction, in the consulship of Honorius for the fourth time and Eutychianus, as Marcellinus Comes records in his *Chronicle*. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Pammachius and Marcella, indicates that Saint Anastasius condemned the Origenist heresy. He also urged the Africans not at all to conceal the plots and wickedness of the heretical and schismatic Donatists. On the Mamurtine Way in the city of Rome he built a basilica called Crescentiana in the second district, as Anastasius the librarian writes in his *Lives of the Pontiffs*. He died in 402 and was buried in his own cemetery at Ursus Pileatus.] Anastasius, pope. At Nicomedia, Saint [Note: [Col. 0890D] Anthimus. Concerning him and the innumerable multitude of martyrs who suffered in the persecution of Diocletian at that time, Eusebius writes in *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.6 as follows: “At that time also Anthimus, bishop of the Church of Nicomedia, was beheaded in the same city because of his confession of Christ. An immense multitude of martyrs was added to him. For, during those same days, a fire was accidentally kindled in the palace. When public rumor falsely alleged, on the basis of a suspicion, that our people had caused it, by imperial order all the worshipers of God who were there, together with their families, were destroyed in heaps—some by the sword, others by fire. Then men and women, stirred by a kind of divine eagerness, are said to have leapt together into the blazing pyre. The executioners also threw countless others, bound and placed in boats, into the depths of the sea.”] Anthimus, [Col. 0891B] bishop, with an innumerable multitude of martyrs. V., In the city of Tarsus in Cilicia, the feast of Saint Castorius. At Nicomedia, Anthimus, bishop. And [Note: [Col. 0891D] Stephen. It is uncertain where he and Antoninus suffered, for in the Martyrologies they are now joined to Anthimus of Nicomedia, now to Castor of Tarsus. According to Ferrarius, in his catalogue of the saints, Saint Antoninus suffered at Lucca in Tuscany.] Stephen, bishop. A. T. L. B., At Nicomedia, Saint Anthimus, bishop. B., Stephen, bishop; Antoninus, priest. A. T. L. B., And in Egypt, the burial of Victor, Maximus, Martianus, [Note: [Col. 0891D] B., Paulinus, Germanus, with six others.] Paulinus, and Germanus [and Germanus]. L., Castor and Stephen, bishops. A., On the same day, at Noviomagus, the translation of the blessed [Note: [Col. 0891D] Mummolenus. His burial is celebrated on 16 October.] Mummolenus and Huno, and of Saint [Note: [Col. 0892C] Godeberta. See 1 April concerning her.] Godeberta, virgin. T., On the same day, in the city of Tarsus in Cilicia, the feast of Saint Castor. T. L., And in the city of Milan, the soldiers Hermes and Eppeius. T., Priests. B., In Lydia, Genesius, Sodocles, and Marinus.

28.—IV Kalends. [Note: [Col. 0892C] D. and V. incorrectly read: “The passion at Rome.”] The passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 0892C] Vitalis. “The time of his passion is uncertain. The Warmian Breviary, printed in 1516, records that Saint Vitalis suffered in the time of Nero; and the Bodecense manuscript refers the martyrdom of Saint Ursicinus to the same period. All the manuscripts say that he was crowned under the consul Paulinus. If this was C. Suetonius Paulinus, as Rubeus thinks—he was consul in the year 66 and in Nero’s twelfth year—and if, as is clear from Tacitus, during the war waged by Otho against Vitellius after the deaths of Nero and Galba he was commander of many troops, then Saint Vitalis’s martyrdom would not have been far removed from the reign of Nero. [Col. 0892D] But if that letter which stands first among the seventh book of Saint Ambrose’s letters really is by Saint Ambrose—namely, the letter in which he reports to the bishops and Christians of Italy that he had discovered, by divine prompting, the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius—his martyrdom must be referred to the year 161. For in the booklet found at their tomb it is said that they survived their parents by ten years and were slain for Christ in the Marcomannic War. This war was waged in the year 171 under the emperors Aurelius and Verus; no mention anywhere exists of another war of this name before that time.” BOLLAND.] Vitalis, martyr.

Florus adds in A. T. L., While he had entered Ravenna with his judge Paulinus and saw before him a certain Christian named Ursicinus, who, after excessive tortures and the sentence of beheading, was afraid, he exclaimed, saying: “Do not, do not, physician Ursicinus, who are accustomed to cure others, wound yourself with the eternal dart of death” (thus far A.); “and you who through excessive sufferings have come to the palm, do not lose the crown prepared for you by the Lord.” Hearing this, Ursicinus knelt and urged the executioner to come, repenting that he had been afraid in Christ’s martyrdom. Immediately Vitalis had the martyr’s body carried away and buried with the greatest honor within the city of Ravenna. For this reason Paulinus ordered that Vitalis himself be arrested; and because he refused to sacrifice to idols, Paulinus had him plunged on his back into a pit as far as the water and covered with earth and stones.

On the same day, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0892D] Christopher. He is also mentioned by Rabanus and in certain manuscript Martyrologies. In a document of the Carthusian house at Brussels, a translation of Saint Christopher is mentioned. His feast, however, is considered to be 25 July; see below under that date.] Christopher, martyr.

Florus in A. and L., On the same day, at the city of Bourges, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0892D] Eusicius. He was not a bishop but only a priest and confessor, and is said to have died in the Lord on 27 November. Ferrarius, in his catalogue.] Eusicius, bishop and confessor (thus far [Col. 0893C] L.), who despised all the gold and riches of this world as dung.

A., On the same day, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0893C] Winwaloeus. Around the year 455. He was born in Armorican Britain and derived his nobility from royal stock. He is said to have been entrusted for instruction to a certain Budocus. After Saint Patrick appeared to him at night and instructed him, he withdrew with eleven companions to the island of Topepigia, where he remained for three years. At the end of that time, crossing the sea, he built the monastery of Landevennec, where he received and instructed Gradlon, king of western Cornwall. At last, after a life full of miracles, he died on 3 March and was buried in the wooden church he had ordered to be built. Later, however, he was transferred to the larger church on 28 April, on which day his solemnity is celebrated, so that the season of Lent might not interfere. His Acts are in Bollandus.] Winwaloeus, confessor. L., And a commemoration of the translation of the relics of Saint [Note: [Col. 0893C] Lambert, bishop of Maastricht, who was first buried at Maastricht in the church of Saint Peter. Twelve years later he was transferred, together with the cathedral see, by Blessed Hubert to the town of Liège, then an obscure village of Lorraine but ennobled by Lambert’s martyrdom and miracles. Later, through the merits of his patronage, it was transformed into the very famous city now called Liège and made the capital of the entire territory of Liège. The feast of Saint Lambert is 17 September; see that date. Molanus, *On the Saints of Belgium*.] Lambert, bishop and martyr. B., In Alexandria, the feast of Saint Victurinus. At Tarsus in Cilicia, Marina with 170 others. In Africa, the feast of Saints Malinius, Maurillus, and Lucanus, with 270 others. In Pannonia, [Note: [Col. 0893C] Eusebius. They suffered under Diocletian in the city of Cibala in Pannonia.] Eusebius, bishop. In Cornwall, the feast of Saint Guingualoeus, confessor.

29.—III Kalends. Bede has nothing.

[Col. 0894C] D., At Paphos, [Note: [Col. 0894C] Tychicus. He is frequently mentioned in Holy Scripture. In the catalogue of Hippolytus the martyr he is designated bishop of Colophon. The Greeks, in the *Menologion* of the emperor Basil Porphyrogenitus, write under 2 December that Sosthenes was the first bishop of Colophon and that Tychicus succeeded him. In a synopsis bearing the name of Dorotheus the bishop, Tychicus is said to have been the first bishop of Chalcedon in Bithynia. In a Greek manuscript of the King of France, Tychicus is said to have been appointed bishop of Neapolis in Cyprus. Nevertheless, Usuard, Bellinus, Maurolycus, and others call him a deacon at Paphus. BOLLAND.] Tychicus, a disciple of the apostles. V. T. B., In Alexandria, the feast of Saint Germanus, priest. B., And [Note: [Col. 0894C] Prostochus. In some Martyrologies he is said to have suffered at Nicomedia.] Prostochus, deacon. V. L. B., At Nicomedia, Prudentius and Martialis [B., Martianus]. B., And Theodora, virgin. A. T. L., At Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Urban and Valentinus [L., Valentinianus]. T., And Martialis. And the burial of Saint Prudentius. A., And the burial of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor.

30.—II Kalends. Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L., At Rome, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0894C] Quirinus. The place of burial is indicated in this way in the Roman manuscript of Duke Altemps: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the burial of Quirinus, bishop”; the Appian Way is added in the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden. It is not stated of what place Quirinus was bishop, and no bishop of that name appears among the Roman bishops. Indeed, he may perhaps have been crowned with martyrdom elsewhere, and his body brought to Rome and buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way. Below it reads: “At Rome, Praetextatus, Quirinus.” This seems to be corrected as follows: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, Quirinus.”] Quirinus [Col. 0895B] [B., Quiricus], bishop and martyr. On the same day, in Asia, the passion of Maximus the martyr. In the time of the emperor Decius and the proconsul Optimus, after being beaten with clubs and suspended on the rack, he was taken down and then buried beneath stones.

[Col. 0896B] D., The holy martyrs [Note: [Col. 0895B] Marianus and James. The former was a lector, the latter a deacon. Although Marianus had already overcome the attacks of the Decian persecution some time before, he was again seized with his beloved companion at the city of Cirta in Numidia. There, after terrible tortures—Marianus was suspended by the tips of his thumbs and cruelly tormented with a heavy weight attached to his feet—they were worn down for a long time in prison. Then they were sent to the city of Lambesis to the governor, again confined for a long time in the prison workhouse, and finally put to death by the sword with many others. Ado, Usuard.
