These martyrs suffered after Saint Cyprian, who, as their Acts make clear, appeared in a vision to Saint Marianus, having already become a martyr in the year 258, on 14 September. Their martyrdom therefore appears referable to the following year, 259.] Marianus and James. V. B., In Alexandria, the feast of Saint Dorotheus, priest. V., And elsewhere, Podonianus, deacon. At Rome, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, Quirinus. B., Rodocianus, deacon; Clement, Honoratus, Reductus, and Secundinus, bishop.

## MAY

[Col. 0895C] 1.—On the Kalends. Jeremiah the prophet. And at Hierapolis, Philip the apostle and James, the apostle and brother of the Lord.

Florus adds in A. T. L., [Note: [Col. 0895D] The words from “of whom” to “rests” are missing in A.] The first of these suffered in Asia, in the city of Hierapolis in the province of Phrygia, and rests there with his daughters. The second was holy from his mother’s womb. After Christ’s Ascension, the apostles conferred upon him the episcopal see at Jerusalem. But when he preached Christ, the Son of God, to the Jews, they threw him from the pinnacle of the Temple and stoned him. (Thus far A.) [Col. 0896C] While they were stoning him, he prayed for those same persecutors, saying: “I beseech you, Lord God the Father, forgive them this sin, for they do not know what they are doing.” And behold, one of them, a fuller, seized a club of the kind used to wring out wet clothing, struck his skull, and thus brought him to completion in martyrdom. He was buried in the same [Col. 0896D] place, near the Temple. This is written in the *Ecclesiastical History*, book II.

The same Florus in A. T. L., On the same day, the passion of Saint Judas, bishop of Jerusalem, surnamed [Note: [Col. 0896D] Quiriacus. Until these latest centuries no one doubted that he was a bishop of Jerusalem; nor would there yet be reason for doubt, unless so many writings were read concerning the discovery of the cross through his indication, his ordination as bishop arranged by Helena, and his martyrdom suffered in the presence of the apostate Julian. Learned men observed that from Saint Macarius, under whom the cross was discovered, to Julian, under whom Cyriacus was believed to have suffered, there was no place for any other bishop, whether Catholic or heretical, except those whom we find named in the episcopal catalogues of Eusebius, Epiphanius, Nicephorus, and Theophanes, and who are known from reliable contemporary writers and public records. They therefore thought it sufficient to seek another episcopate for him; and there was none toward which conjecture could incline more closely than Auxerre, where he had long been venerated as patron. Baronius accordingly adopted this view, followed by Ughellus and others. Whenever a bishop-martyr is recorded in the Martyrologies as having suffered in a particular episcopal city, he is generally believed to have been bishop of that same city in which he suffered, unless something else prevents it, especially when his name is found in ancient catalogues. Now, among the bishops of Jerusalem a Judas is found as the fifteenth. We may presume that he either himself assumed the surname Cyriacus or received it from Christians, because of the memory of the betrayer and their hatred of that accursed nation, so that they were unwilling to use his proper name. Theodoricus Pauli writes of him as follows: “The holy Judas, however, the patriarch, cruelly tortured by the Jews and repeatedly harassed by various punishments, finally, for the faith of Christ, under the emperor Hadrian, earned the crown of martyrdom by beheading.” This martyrdom will seem sufficiently certain if one considers the end of the Judaizing Church at Jerusalem, as it is described by Eusebius. According to his *Chronicle*, Judas, the last bishop from the circumcision, presided until the destruction that Jerusalem suffered under Hadrian—that is, until about the year 134. Usuard and Ado transferred the name and eulogy of Judas Quiriacus from 1 May to the fourth day. The practice of the Roman Church follows them.] Quiriacus, who suffered at Jerusalem under the emperor Julian, and the passion of his mother Anna, as well as of Ammon the magician. (Thus far A.) For when Julian, setting out for the Persian war, came to Jerusalem, he immediately ordered the bishop of that city to be brought before him. When he found him steadfast in the confession of the faith, he ordered his right hand to be cut off; then, with iron tongs, his mouth to be opened and molten lead poured in, so that his inner organs might burst forth. When he still did not keep silent, he ordered a bronze bed to be brought and the holy man to be stretched upon it; burning coals were placed beneath him, salt and fat were scattered over him, and he was beaten with rods, so that his belly and internal organs might be loosened by the fire. When, by the power of the Lord, he was still not consumed in this way, he was afterwards kept in confinement. His mother Anna came to him, comforting and strengthening him. When she was recognized as a Christian, the emperor ordered her, suspended by her hair because of her confession of Christ’s name, to be torn with hooks; large lamps were applied to her sides until she died. Afterwards Quiriacus was summoned and thrown into a pit full of serpents, but emerged unharmed. When Ammon the magician saw this, he confessed the power of Christ and was immediately ordered to be beheaded. Saint Quiriacus was then placed in a cauldron of boiling oil; when he did not perish, Julian ordered him to be struck in the chest with a great wedge and thus killed. L., Written in his Passion.

C., And Saint [Note: [Col. 0897C] Sigismund. He was the son of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, and the first of his people to embrace the Christian religion. At Agaunum he established choirs of singers. When the Franks were devastating almost the whole of Gaul, a very large number [Col. 0897D] of Burgundians joined the Franks. Then Sigismund, seeing himself pressed on every side, sought Mount Versalis and assumed the habit of a monk. Betrayed by his own people, however, he was captured and brought with his wife and sons, Gistaldus and Gundebaldus, to a place called Belsa; there they were all thrown into a well. After three years had passed, their sacred bodies were carried to the monastery of Agaunum. Ado. He suffered around the year 524, when his brother Gondemar is recorded in the *Chronicle of Marius* as having been established king of the Burgundians.] Sigismund, king. B., At Toulouse, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0897D] Orientius. Bishop of Auch in Novempopulania. He became famous among the people of Toulouse because, when the Roman emperor sent the generals Aetius and Litorius against Theodoric, king of the Goths, the king, terrified by their arrival, sought protection from Saint Orientius and sent him as an envoy to the enemy. Aetius received him kindly, but Litorius malevolently, threatening to bring destruction upon the city of Toulouse. Nevertheless, while Saint Orientius prayed for the city, the people of Toulouse captured and killed Litorius, and the city was liberated around the year 439. A chapel was erected in this city in his memory and later entrusted to the Crosier monks. To establish his ancient veneration more firmly, some of his relics were carried from Auch to Toulouse and, on 12 July 1354, presented to the religious of the Holy Cross and deposited in the church of Saint Orientius. His Acts are in Bollandus.] Orientius, bishop. At Auxerre in Gaul, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0898C] Amator. Bishop and confessor. Learned in letters from his earliest years and devoted to God, he unwillingly—indeed, under compulsion—married a noble virgin. But when God granted his desire, he found that she shared his purpose; he did not have intercourse with her, and both vowed virginity. The angel of God placed two crowns upon their heads. Therefore the virgin bride entered a monastery of women, while Amator became a cleric. After the death of Eladius, bishop of Auxerre, he was appointed in his place and held that see for thirty years. When he realized that his death was near, he went to the church and celebrated Mass; then, blessing the people and sitting on his throne, he breathed forth his soul. The holy man died in the year 421. GHINIUS OF SIENA.] Amator, bishop. At Agaunum, the passion of Sigismund, king. In Cornwall, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0898C] Corentinus. Also Corentinus, bishop of Quimper in Armorican Britain. His translation is celebrated on this day in the Church of Quimper; concerning the apostles, however, it is celebrated on the next unimpeded day. Throughout the diocese, the feast of Saint Corentinus is likewise held on the next unimpeded day. He is also mentioned on this day in the Barberinian manuscript preserved at Cologne among the Carmelites, as well as by Bellinus of Paris in his enlarged Martyrology, Grevenus, Molanus, Canisius, Saussayus, and others. His feast is 12 December. BOLLAND.] Corentinus, confessor and bishop. And [Note: [Col. 0898D] Briocus. Also Briocius, bishop in Armorican Britain. His Acts were published in French by Albert le Grand in his treatise on the Lives of the Saints of Armorican Britain, with several additions here and there. He also cites the Breviary of the diocese of Léon in the same Armorican Britain, in which he asserts that Briocus’s feast is celebrated on 29 April. Perhaps for this reason Saussayus transferred his feast to 30 April. Albert likewise cites the Breviary of Quimper, in which he states that the feast is celebrated on 2 May. The feast of the translation of his relics to his own church is held on 18 October. According to the Breviary of Saint-Brieuc, the period of his life must be inferred from the time of the see and the death of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, by whom he is said to have been instructed in learning [Col. 0899B] and virtue and presented by his parents while not yet ten years old; afterwards he was ordained priest by the same Germanus, not long before Germanus’s death, which occurred in the year 576. If these facts are accepted, Saint Briocus may be placed as having been born around the year 550 or somewhat later; and because he reached the age of ninety, he may be considered to have died around the year 640 or even somewhat later. He was descended from the Coretic people of greater Britain. Saussayus and others substitute Germanus of Auxerre for Germanus of Paris. Bollandus conjectures that he may perhaps have been commended to some Saint Germanus of Ireland.] Briocus, bishop.

[Col. 0899B] 2.—VI Nones. Our holy father [Note: [Col. 0899C] Athanasius. “After suffering many plots by the Arians, he fled to Constans, prince of Gaul. Returning from there with letters, and again driven into exile after Constans’s death, he remained hidden until the reign of Jovian, by whom the Church was restored to him; under Valens he died.” Whoever wishes to examine all the Acts of Saint Athanasius has available the Life of him copied before the Paris edition, as well as another Life among the Bollandist brothers, and Saint Gregory of Nazianzus’s Oration in his praise.] Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Florus adds in A. T. L., Orthodox, who endured many sufferings for the faith of Christ.

The V. manuscript adds: “And his ordination is believed to have occurred on 6 Kalends of January.” N., At Alexandria, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0899D] Saturninus. In the older Martyrologies, the arena of combat of these two martyrs is either assigned to Alexandria or left unmentioned. Galesinius, however, assigned them another arena, namely Rome; but he did not write how he knew that they suffered at Rome. Baronio, trusting Galesinius, consequently went astray. Bucelinus, in the *Benedictine Sacrarium*, asserts that their bodies rest in the monastery of Antecum in Bavaria.] Saturninus, resting in prison with his companion Neapolis. B., And Saturninus with Neapolis. And the feast of Saints Caelestinus, Urbanus, and Privata. At Auxerre, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 0899D] Optatus. The translation of these saints is commemorated at Auxerre today. The more famous of them is the bishop Optatus, whose feast is 31 August. The others are said to be commemorated on 6 and 7 September.] Optatus, bishop, Memorius, and Santianus, priests.

[Col. 0900B] 3.—The fifth day before the Nones. At Rome, the holy martyrs [Note: [Col. 0899D] Alexander. He succeeded St. Evaristus in the pontificate. The catalog of the supreme pontiffs records that Alexander reigned for eight years, two months, and one day, and that he lived in the time of Trajan, from the consulship of Palma and Tullus—that is, from the year 109—until the consulship of Aelianus and Vetus, the year 117. The Acts of St. Alexander [Col. 0900B] indicate that, by God’s will, the emperor Trajan died in that same year, [Col. 0900C] three months and seven days having elapsed after the martyrdom of St. Alexander. For this reason Ado observes that Hadrian had not yet become emperor when St. Alexander and his companions suffered martyrdom. Therefore Usuard and Baronius wrongly inserted the name of the emperor Hadrian. He baptized Quirinus, who is commemorated on 30 March, and his daughter Balbina, who is commemorated on 31 March.] Alexander, pope, and Eventius and Theodulus, priests. (Thus far A.) The first of these, after chains and prisons, the rack, iron claws, and fires, was killed by being pierced with countless punctures throughout his body; the others, after likewise enduring a long imprisonment, were tested by fire and finally beheaded, under the judge Aurelian, in the time of the emperor Trajan. On the same day, the finding of the holy [Note: [Col. 0900C] Cross. Helena, the mother of Constantine, went to Jerusalem and there asked the inhabitants about the place where the most holy body had hung, fastened to the gallows. It had been difficult to discover because the ancient persecutors had fixed an image of Venus there, so that if any Christian wished to worship Christ in that place, he would appear to be worshiping Venus. Consequently, the place had become deserted and almost forgotten. When the devout woman hastened to the spot indicated to her by a heavenly sign, removing all profane and polluted objects from it, she cleared away the rubble and found three crosses in confused disorder. But [Col. 0900D] the joy of this discovery was disturbed by the inability to distinguish the particular identity of each cross. The title, written by Pilate in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters, was indeed present separately; but even it did not clearly reveal which was the Lord’s cross. Blessed Macarius, bishop of that city, resolved the doubt in the following manner. A noblewoman suffering from a prolonged illness was brought forward, and each cross was applied to her in turn with fervent prayers. Thus the hidden power became known. For as soon as this cross touched the woman’s body, it immediately drove away the severe illness and restored her to her former health. Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History I, 7; Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History I, 18; Sozomen II, 1. On the construction of the magnificent church at the place where the crosses were found, see the letter that the emperor Constantine wrote to Bishop Macarius, in Eusebius, Life of Constantine III, 3, and in Theodoret I, 17. This discovery of the cross occurred in the year 326.] of the Cross.

Florus adds in A., T., and L.: “By Helena, two hundred and thirty-three years after the Passion of the Lord, during the reign of the emperor Constantine.”

L.: On the same day, St. [Note: [Col. 0901B] Juvenal. Bishop and confessor of Narni. Coming from Africa to Rome, he was ordained bishop by the supreme pontiff and sent to Narni to preach. Once, when idolaters compelled him to eat of the things sacrificed, and he resisted, one of them tried to strike the saint in the chest with a sword. But by divine power the blow was turned back upon the attacker’s throat, and he died. At the sight of this sign nearly seven thousand pagans embraced the faith. Ghinius the Elder. Gregory the Great, Book IV, chapter 12, calls him a martyr. From the alteration of the titles “confessor” and “martyr” arose the dispute whether two bishops of Narni named Juvenal should be posited, one a confessor and the other a martyr. Baronius maintained this, among others, in his notes on 3 and 7 May; on the latter day the martyr Juvenal is also commemorated below.] Juvenal, bishop. B.: [Note: [Col. 0901C] At Auxerre. In the Lucense and Blumian Martyrologies it is read as follows: “At Auxerre, the deposition and translation of the bodies of the holy confessors Eusebius the priest and Avitus the deacon.” Bolland.] At Auxerre, the deposition of St. Eusebius the priest and Avitus the deacon. Elsewhere, St. [Note: [Col. 0901C] Juvenal. Perhaps this is the same as the earlier Juvenal, bishop of Narni. There is, however, another Juvenal who is commemorated at Fossano; hence arose a great controversy between the people of Narni and Fossano, each claiming St. Juvenal wholly and indivisibly for itself.] Juvenal, martyr.

[Col. 0901B] 4.—The fourth day before the Nones. Absent from Bede.

Florus in A., T., and L. seems to have copied from the same author from whom V. took the following: At Nicomedia, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 0901C] Antonia. In the ancient Epternacensis codex, it is read that St. Antonina suffered today in the city of Nicaea. She is also commemorated on the Kalends of March, and is said to have suffered martyrdom under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian and the governor Priscillianus. Although she is said to have suffered at Nicaea in Bithynia, she may nevertheless be the same woman who is here said to have been crowned at Nicomedia in Bithynia, although the latter is called Antonina and this one Antonia.] Antonia, who, after being tortured excessively and afflicted with various torments, suspended by one arm for three days and confined in prison for two years, died after being burned by flames by the governor Priscillianus.

[Col. 0902A] B.: In Africa, the holy martyrs Callistus, Felix, and Urban. At Caesarea, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 0901D] Silvanus. Eusebius writes of St. Silvanus: “Among the martyrs of Palestine, Silvanus, bishop of the city of Gaza, was beheaded at the metal mines in Phaeno, together with forty-nine others.” Ecclesiastical History VIII, 13. In the treatise that follows on the martyrs of Palestine, he describes in greater detail the matters concerning St. Silvanus, and in chapter 7 says: “When the fifth year of the persecution was already passing” (that is, the year 308 of Christ), “on the fifth day of the month Dios, which according to the Romans is the Nones of November, in the city of Caesarea, Silvanus, who was still at that time a priest and confessor, . . . and certain other companions of his were condemned to work in the mines at Phaeno, and it was decreed [Col. 0902B] that the joints of their feet should first be weakened with red-hot iron.” Again, in chapter 13, he states: “The seventh year of the persecution was already drawing to a close . . . when in the mines of Palestine a very great multitude of confessors, gathered together in one place, enjoyed incredible freedom, so much so that they even built churches. When the governor of the province heard of their manner of life, he immediately reported the matter to the emperor. Then the superintendent of the mines divided the confessors into various groups. Their leader was Silvanus, born at Gaza, who, having been distinguished from the first day of the persecution onward by various struggles of confession, was preserved until that time so that he might be the last to close that contest in Palestine . . . Forty-nine men, by order of the wicked Maximinus, were beheaded on one and the same day.” Thus far Eusebius, whose seventh year of the persecution fell in the year 310 of Christ. Alexandria is improperly inserted between him and the Forty Martyrs. Whether this was because some of them were Egyptians and had received some cult there, or for another reason, I do not care to conjecture.] Silvanus. In Alexandria, the forty martyrs. At Auxerre, the deposition of St. [Note: [Col. 0902C] Concordinus. In Ado’s manuscript of the Church of the Morini and in that of the monastery of St. Lawrence at Liège, this saint is given the following eulogy: “At Auxerre, the deposition and translation of the body of St. Corcodomus, a name that means the same as Concordinus, deacon and confessor. When he was arch-subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, he was ordained deacon by Pope St. Sixtus and sent with St. Peregrinus to Gaul to preach the word of God. Having therefore completed his ministry with complete faithfulness, after the martyrdom of the most blessed Bishop Peregrinus he rested in peace in the third century.” Bolland.] Concordinus, deacon. D.: At Gaza, Silvanus the bishop, crowned together with several of his clergy. A. T.: The Passion of Antoninus the Martyr. A.: In the suburbs of Verdun, the translation of the holy [Col. 0902B] confessors and bishops [Note: [Col. 0902D] Pulchronius. Pulchronius or Polochronius was discussed under 17 February. The feast day of the others is assigned to 3 December.] Pulchronius, Bossessor, and Firminus.

5.—The third day before the Nones. Absent from Bede.

D. B.: At Alexandria, [Note: [Col. 0902D] Euthymius. Galesinius describes the time and other circumstances as follows: “During the persecution of Diocletian, he was thrown into prison for Christ. There, exhausted by filth, hunger, and the severity of his confinement, and strengthened more fervently for the confession of the faith, he gave his soul back to God.” In his notes he assigns the year 305 of Christ, when Constantius V and Maximian V were consuls.] Euthymius [B., Petinius], deacon, resting in prison. B. V.: At Arles, the deposition of St. [Note: [Col. 0902D] Hilary. He was born around the year 403. As a young man, St. Honoratus brought him to the island of Lérins, where he remained. St. Honoratus became bishop of Arles in 426, in the consulship of Theodosius the Younger XII and Valentinian II, as Prosper noted in his Chronicle. After completing two years in his episcopate, Honoratus died in 429, on 16 January. St. Hilary was appointed in his place in that year and presided over the Council of Riez held in 439, when the case of Armentarius, bishop of Embrun, was discussed because he had been ordained bishop by two men contrary to the canons. He then attended the First Council of Orange in 441, where thirty canons were issued and he signed first. He survived until this fifth day of May in the year 449, when he died, having scarcely completed a full cycle of forty-eight years of life, during the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes. His deposition is also celebrated below on 7 May. Ado, the common recension of Bede, Peter de Natalibus, and other later writers adorned him with an honorable eulogy. His body was first deposited in the church of St. Stephen and then buried in the church of St. Genesius. Later, however, it was translated and committed to burial in the Elysian Fields, in the church now called that of St. Honoratus.] Hilary, bishop. V. T. L.: At Vienne, the deposition of [Col. 0903B] [Note: [Col. 0903C] Nectarius. When Ado was treating the year 337, concerning Constantius and his brothers, the emperors Constantine and Constans, he added: “At that time Nectarius, bishop of Vienne, was flourishing, outstanding in the teaching of the faith. He was the first to attend the venerable synod at Vaison and preached in the Church that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one nature, power, and might.” After describing the times of Valentinian and Valens, he adds: “Nectarius of Vienne and Hilary of Poitiers, bishops, died.” We have said that Hilary died either in the year 367 or the following year, under 13 January.] Nectarius. V.: And [Note: [Col. 0903D] Nicetas. In the ancient ecclesiastical calendars he is joined with Nectarius. In his Chronicle, Ado places him under the reign of Gratian and his brother Valentinian, saying that at the same time Nicetas, a most distinguished bishop in the doctrine of the faith, governed the Church of Vienne. In the manuscript Martyrology of Vienne, renewed through the study and labor of Jean le Lièvre, it is written that he attended the Council of Valence in Dauphiné, held in 375, and that he was buried in the church of St. Martin, the fourth bishop of Vienne, which he himself had built in that bishop’s honor. John Chenu, in his Chronological History of the Bishops of Gaul, says that St. Nicetas had formerly been educated by SS. Paschasius [Col. 0904B] and Claudius, bishops of Vienne, so that he even became a deacon of Blessed Claudius.] Nicetas. T.: And Nicetius. B. A. T.: The Ascension of the Lord. At Thessalonica, the feast of the holy [Note: [Col. 0904B] Herenaeus. If any confidence can be placed in Galesinius, he suffered with Peregrinus and Irene in the time of Diocletian, around the year 300 of Christ.] Herenaeus. B.: strangers; A. T.: and Peregrinus; who were burned in the fire. A. T. L.: At Auxerre, the passion of St. [Note: [Col. 0904C] Juvinianus. He came to Auxerre with Blessed Peregrinus, bishop and martyr, during the pontificate of Pope Sixtus II. Because he vigorously resisted the superstitions of the pagans, he was arrested; and, persevering in his confession of Christ, he was killed by them. Molanus in his Additions to Usuard.] Juvinianus [A., Vivianus], lector and martyr. A.: On the same day, at Douai, the deposition of St. [Note: [Col. 0904C] Maurontus. He was prominent at the court of King Theuderic I. But at his mother’s urging, despising the world and also the woman whom he had decided to marry, he was tonsured as a cleric by St. Amandus. He built a church on his estate at Liège, which was then called Broylus but is now called Meuriville, as though “the town of Maurontus.” There he exercised the office of abbot with the greatest vigilance above all the other brothers. After fulfilling this administration for twelve years, he departed to the Lord in the monastery of Marchiennes in the year 701 and was buried in that monastery’s crypt. Molanus, On the Saints of Belgium. John Buzelinus, in Book V of his Annals, records that in 1139 the sacred bones of St. Maurontus were transferred by Bishop Alvisus of Arras into a new reliquary at Douai.] Maurontus, confessor and levite. T. L.: In Gaul, on the same day, the feast of St. Maurontus, abbot.

6.—The second day before the Nones. Absent from Bede.

V.: In Persia, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 0904D] Matthew. This day is incorrectly called the feast of Matthew the apostle, for his day is 21 September. In Baronius’s Martyrology, however, the following is celebrated: “At Salerno, the translation of St. Matthew the Apostle, whose sacred body, formerly brought from Ethiopia to various regions and finally conveyed to that city, was there honorably buried in a church dedicated in his name.” This translation took place around the year 1080, when Pope Gregory VII wrote a letter to Alfano, bishop of Salerno, congratulating him on the discovery of the apostle’s sacred body and admonishing him to honor the holy relics worthily, and together with Prince Robert and his wife to venerate the sacred pledges with pious devotion.] Matthew, apostle and evangelist, [Col. 0904B] who, called by Christ from being a tax collector, preached first in Judaea and afterward in Macedonia; he suffered in Persia and came to rest in the Mountains. His feast is celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. On the same day, St. [Note: [Col. 0904D] John. Tertullian mentions this miracle in his book On the Prescription Against Heretics. His feast is 27 December.] John the apostle and evangelist before the Latin Gate. This last entry is also found in all the other manuscripts, and alone in the Divionese manuscript, though everywhere with varying wording, so that from this alone it appears not to belong to Bede. L. continues: when he was thrown before the senate into a cauldron of boiling oil by order of Domitian Caesar, and emerged unharmed through the protection of the Lord, he was deported into exile to the island called Patmos. B.: In Africa, St. Secundianus, bishop and martyr. [Note: [Col. 0905B] From Ab. A. T. onward, the damaged folio of B. is lacking from Milan until the day before the Ides.] A. T.: At Milan, the feast of the holy [Note: [Col. 0905B] Victor. And Felix, who had many companions in martyrdom; see them in the Hieronymian Martyrology. We judge that these champions suffered when the emperor Maximian had his imperial residence at Milan. For, as is stated in the Acts of St. Maurus, “when the impious emperor Maximian was reigning, a great persecution of Christians was raging in the city of Milan.” St. Ambrose also asserted in his sermon for the feast of the martyrs SS. Nazarius and Celsus that the city of Milan possessed multitudes of martyrs—those given today, or at least some notable number of them.] Victor and Felix. A. T. L.: In Gaul, at the village of Julio, the deposition of St. Gerontius, confessor, and Edentius. V.: On the same day, St. [Note: [Col. 0905C] Florian. We know nothing certain about him, unless he is the same man of whom Rabanus writes under 4 May: “The passion of St. Florian the martyr in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, while the most wicked governor Aquilinus was raging, in Noricum Ripense. When Aquilinus saw himself overcome by Florian, he ordered him to undergo the death sentence and to be led to the river Enns and thrown from the bridge.”] Florian and St. [Note: [Col. 0905C] Valerius. Philip Labbe published in volume I of his New Library of Manuscripts a History of the Bishops of Auxerre, where the following eulogy of Valerius is found: [Col. 0905D] “Valerius sat for seventeen years. He lived in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, when Carus and Carinus were consuls and when Gaius, Marcellinus, and Marcellus held the priestly office at Rome; they too were martyred by those same tyrants. Departing to Christ, he was buried near Mount Autricus, beside his predecessor St. Marcellianus, bishop.”] Valerius, bishop.

7.—The Nones. Absent from Bede.

D.: [Note: [Col. 0905D] Juvenal. The name of this saint, assigned to this 7 May and to several other days, is well known; but his deeds are hidden, so that nothing certain can even be stated about the place and time in which he flourished. We discussed Juvenal, bishop of Narni, under 3 May; Baronius believes that he is commemorated on this day. Ferrarius, however, does not approve this, preferring in his Catalogue of the Saints of Italy Juvenal, deacon of Pope Alexander, whom Galesinius treats in his Martyrology under 3 May. Ferrarius also assigns to this day, in both of his saints’ catalogues, St. Juvenal, bishop of Interamna, for whom St. Proculus, the second bishop of Interamna of that name, built a church on the hill named after the holy bishop, in the territory of Interamna.] Juvenal, martyr. And [Note: [Col. 0906B] Flavia Domitilla. Bede writes of her in his Chronicle under Domitian: “And Flavia Domitilla, granddaughter through his sister of Flavius Clemens the consul, was exiled to the island of Pontia on account of her testimony to the faith.” Ado continues in this manner: “Finally, when she had been transferred to Terracina, a city of Campania, by Aurelian her betrothed, whom, after being consecrated by St. Clement with the sacred veil, she had rejected for Christ; and when she had first converted Euphrosyna and Theodora, her foster-sisters, and then others to the faith, she completed her martyrdom when Luxorius, Aurelian’s brother, set fire to the chamber in which she was staying together with the aforementioned virgins, during the persecution of Trajan. St. Caesarius the deacon placed their bodies together in a new sarcophagus and buried them by putting it into the ground.” Baronius in the Martyrology says that she was commemorated together with the holy martyrs Nereus and Achilleus on 12 May.] Flavia Domitilla. [Note: [Col. 0906C] Nicomedes. See below, under 25 September.] Nicomedes and others. V.: In Nicomedia, Flavius the bishop, Augustine, Marcellinus, and Maximus. A. T.: The feast of St. Augustine, bishop of Nicomedia. A. T. L.: At Arles, the deposition of [Note: [Col. 0906C] Hilary. We discussed St. Hilary under 5 May.] Hilary, bishop and confessor. At Augustodunum, the deposition of Blessed [Note: [Col. 0906C] Placidus. Whether St. Placidus should rightly be counted among the bishops of Augustodunum is doubtful. For Antonius Monchiacenus, Demochares, John Chenu, Claudius Robertus, and the Sammarthani recognize no Placidus who was bishop of Augustodunum; and it seems that the older manuscript Martyrologies should be trusted, since they call him a priest. Bolland.] Placidus, bishop. T.: In the district of Aquitaine called Herbatilicus, the nativity of St. [Note: [Col. 0906D] Amandus. He is said to have been born today. We discussed his nativity under 6 February.] Amandus. On the same day, the translation of St. [Note: [Col. 0906D] Nicholas. His feast is 6 December.] Nicholas to the city of Bari.

8.—The eighth day before the Ides. Absent from Bede.

D.: At Milan, St. [Note: [Col. 0906D] Victor. A Moor by birth and a Christian from his earliest years, he was a soldier in the imperial camps. When Maximian compelled him to sacrifice to idols, he persevered most steadfastly in confessing the Lord. First he was severely beaten with clubs, but under God’s protection felt no pain; then he was covered with molten lead, yet was not harmed at all; finally he was beheaded. Baronius, Ado, Usuard, and others.] Victor, martyr. V. A. T. add: beheaded. A. T.: At Saintes, the deposition of St. [Note: [Col. 0906D] Martin. Priest and abbot of the monastery of Vertou, or, according to Gregory of Tours, abbot of the city of Saintes; a disciple of Martin, bishop of Tours. He rests in peace at a village of that city, in the monastery of Salignac, which he built after receiving his master’s teaching. Our author wrongly calls him a bishop. He is commemorated today by Notker and very many manuscripts; but Usuard and Baronius celebrate his feast on 24 October, when he is said to have died in the year 589.] Martin, bishop. A. T. L.: On the same day, the feast of St. [Col. 0907B] [Note: [Col. 0907C] Elladius. Elladius sat for twenty-three years. He lived during the time of Constantius and Constantine, the sons of Constantine, under the Roman pontiffs Mark, Julius, and Liberius. He made St. Amator a cleric and St. Martha a nun, and died full of holiness and virtues. He was buried beside his predecessors on Mount Autricus. Philip Labbe, volume I of the Library of Manuscripts. The period of his episcopate seems to be calculated most accurately from the Acts of his successor St. Amator, who died in 418 after sitting for thirty years, one month, and five days; he had therefore been ordained in 388, when, after the unhappy popular uprising following St. Elladius’s death, the people unanimously demanded St. Amator as bishop. Elladius may accordingly be considered to have died in 387. Twenty-three years are assigned to him as ruler of the Church of Auxerre, so that he appears to have been consecrated bishop around the year 364.] Elladius, bishop. On the same day, the apparition of St. [Note: [Col. 0907C] Michael. More about this apparition is given under 29 September, when a church was dedicated in his name on Mount Gargano.] Michael the archangel on Mount Gargano.

9.—The seventh day before the Ides. Absent from Bede.

V. D. A. T. L.: In [Note: [Col. 0907D] Persia. No one records the time or manner of death by which they completed their contest; and since many persecutions against Christians were raised among the Persians, it is difficult to distinguish them. Florentinus fixes his attention on Sapor, king of the Persians, because many were crowned with martyrdom under him for the faith of Christ.] Persia, the feast of three hundred and ten martyrs. D. T. L. (though everywhere with varying wording): At the town of Nazianzus, Blessed [Note: [Col. 0907D] Gregory. We discussed him under 25 January, on which day his principal feast is celebrated among the Greeks.] Gregory, bishop, who is called the Theologian. A. T.: At Anziopolis, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 0907D] Quirillus. Galesinius and Ferrarius, following Galesinius, falsely write that he suffered at Rome.] Quirillus. [Col. 0908B] At Rome, the feast of the holy [Note: [Col. 0907D] Beatus. Rabanus, the pseudo-Bede, and Galesinius assert that he died at Rome; but the place is more correctly indicated in the oldest Martyrology, the Queen of Sweden manuscript numbered 313, in this manner: “In the territory of the city of Chartres, at the fortress of Vendôme, the feast of St. Beatus the confessor.” Usuard likewise describes the place: “At the fortress of Vendôme, the deposition of St. Beatus the confessor.” Bellinus, Grevenus, Molanus, Maurolycus, and others have the same. It is especially uncertain when this man flourished. “His Acts say that he was chosen by St. Peter, together with other apostolic men, and sent into Gaul. Meanwhile, when Pommeratus sent the Acts to Henschenius, he indicated in the accompanying letter that he thought Beatus flourished in the fourth [Col. 0908C] or fifth century of Christ. Indeed, some doubt is raised by the readings of the Breviary of Chartres, since they contain no mention either of the city of Rome or of St. Peter, whereas from this mission of St. Beatus by St. Peter the high dignity of that diocese might derive its origin.” Acts of the Saints.] Beatus, confessor, and St. [Note: [Col. 0908C] Primolus. Beatus and St. Primolus are wrongly joined here. We showed above that Beatus did not die at Rome, whereas Primolus did suffer there, on the Latin Way. He and Gordianus are also commemorated on the following day.] Primolus. L.: At Rome, on the Latin Way, the passion of St. Primolus. V.: At Rome, the feast of the confessors [Note: [Col. 0908C] Gordianus. All the Martyrologies report that both of these suffered at Rome. But Rabanus, Ado, Notker, and the author of the pseudo-Bede seem to imply that they did not suffer together, saying that St. Gordianus was placed in the crypt where St. Epimachus had long before been buried. In the Martyrology of Ado published by Rosweyde and in various manuscripts the following is added: “This Epimachus at Alexandria, together with his companion Alexander, was tortured for a long time both in chains and in prison torments; and after being worn out by frequent and various punishments, he persevered in the faith and was finally consumed by fire. But this Alexandrian Epimachus does not appear to be the same as the Roman Epimachus under discussion here, who, according to the menologion of the emperor Basil, was not consumed by fire but was killed by beheading. Gordianus, in the time of Julian the Apostate, was beaten for a long time with leaden clubs and finally beheaded. Baronius in the Martyrology.] Gordianus and Primolus. T.: On the same day, at Constantinople, [Note: [Col. 0908D] the feast. So read four copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology and others, which would suggest that this was one of the ancient Byzantine martyrs, of whom many are given on the preceding day, unless Ado, together with various manuscripts, added: “When his sacred bones were brought from Ephesus”; and unless Notker called it not a feast day but a translation, concerning which we spoke under his feast day, 24 January.] the feast of St. Timothy.

10.—The sixth day before the Ides. The feast of SS. Gordianus and Epimachus, and at Rome the feast of [Note: [Col. 0908D] Calepodius. They suffered around the year 222.] Calepodius, an elderly priest, [Col. 0909B] under the emperor Alexander. He had him killed by Laodicius, and ordered his body to be dragged through the city and thrown into the Tiber on the day of the Kalends of May. Fishermen recovered it and reported the matter to Bishop Callistus. He took the body, embalmed it with spices and linen cloths, and buried it in the cemetery on the same Aurelian Way, at the third milestone from the city, on 6 May. Then the consul Palmatius was beheaded by Alexander, together with his wife and children and forty-two others of both sexes, including the senator Simplicius, who had recently been baptized through the teaching of Pope Callistus and the priest Calepodius. Written in the Passion of Pope Callistus.

[Col. 0910B] V.: And the deposition of [Note: [Col. 0909C] Job. The year or day of his death is not sufficiently certain. The Greeks, together with the other Eastern peoples, celebrate his feast on 6 May, but the Latins today. Philip Labbe assigns the death of the patriarch Joseph to the year 2399 of the world and to the year 1655 before the common era of Christ; and he adds that it seems that St. Job was then tempted by the devil at the age of seventy. If the 140 years that followed are added, the total is 210 years, and thus he was also given double the years of his life, as is deduced from the final chapter of Job. Accordingly, Labbe assigns his death to the year 2539 of the world and to the year 1515 before the common era of Christ. But since the Greeks, together with the Seventy translators, assert that he lived altogether 248 years, according to this calculation his death would have to be moved to the year 2577 of the world and to the year 1477 before the common era of Christ.] Job, the prophet.

11.—The fifth day before the Ides. Absent from Bede.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Vienne, the deposition of St. [Note: [Col. 0909D] Mamertus. The first record of St. Mamertus is found in two letters of Pope St. Hilary. The earlier is dated on the sixth day before the Ides of October, during the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus—that is, in the year 463. In it, Leontius, bishop of Arles, is charged to examine at a synod the case of Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, who had improperly ordained a bishop for the people of Die outside his own boundaries. The second letter was given the following year, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, to twenty bishops, so that Mamertus might be admonished through Bishop Veranus to abstain from improper ordinations and so that the man whom Mamertus had consecrated for the people of Die might be confirmed at the discretion of Leontius, bishop of Arles, by whom he ought to have been consecrated. Mamertus is also mentioned among the thirty bishops to whom the priest Lucidus sent a written statement correcting his error, in which he sets out his profession of faith according to the decrees of the Council of Arles and the letter of Faustus, bishop of Riez, sent to him. Sirmondus presents these matters in volume I of the Councils of Gaul and considers them to have taken place around the year 475. St. Mamertus had as his successor St. Isichius, who lived until about the year 490. Bolland. Concerning his burial and translation, John Chenu writes: “His body first lay in the basilica of the Apostles outside the walls of Vienne, on the right side of the altar . . . Afterwards it was translated to the Constantinian basilica of the Holy Cross.”] Mamertus, bishop and confessor. During his episcopate, there was a very great earthquake in the city of Vienne, and wild beasts were also rushing upon and devouring human beings. Therefore this same bishop, after consulting many people, instituted the three-day fast that the people of Gaul observe before the Ascension of the Lord, and thereby earned the conversion of God’s anger into mercy.

V.: At Rome, on the Salarian Way, at the twelfth milestone, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 0909D] Anthimus. According to Usuard, after distinguished deeds of virtue and preaching, he was thrown into the Tiber; an angel rescued him from there and restored him to his own oratory. Then, having been sentenced to death by beheading, he departed victoriously to heaven. Baronius’s Martyrology adds the persecution of Diocletian. According to Ado and Notker, he suffered at the twenty-second milestone of the Salarian Way. When the emperor Diocletian had appointed Pinianus proconsul of Asia, Pinianus was already raging against Christians even before he departed for that province. But he was struck by a severe illness that no art could cure. At the urging of his wife Lucina, he summoned Christians, among whom was Anthimus. Anthimus announced Christ to Pinianus, converted him to the faith, baptized him together with Lucina and his entire household, and freed him from his illness. Ghinius the Elder.] Anthimus. D.: At Rome, St. Anthimus. At Vienne, Mamertus, bishop, who, because disaster was imminent, instituted the solemn Litanies before the Ascension of the Lord. T. L.: On the same day, at Rome on the Salarian Way, the passion of SS. Achilles, Serapion, and Januarius. A. L.: And St. [Note: [Col. 0911B] Gengulphus. An exceptionally devout man, St. Gengulphus flourished in the eighth century of Christ under Pippin, king of the Franks and father of the emperor Charlemagne. He was treacherously killed through the plotting of his wife by her adulterous lover and was counted among the martyrs. Soon, in that same century and the following one, he attracted not only Burgundy but also the neighboring regions along the Meuse, Moselle, and Rhine to his cult and veneration; he is especially honored at Varennes. He was entered under the name of Bede in the Martyrology printed on 12 May, but since St. Gengulphus lived after Bede, that Martyrology too was composed later. Moreover, it is clear from the ancient Breviary of the Church of Utrecht that the Church of Utrecht was accustomed to celebrate him on 9 May. Finally, other churches celebrate him on 12 October, as the Breviaries of Brussels and Bruges and the Missal of Tournai indicate. Molanus in his Notes on Usuard. Bolland.] Gengulphus, martyr. A. T.: On the same day, the deposition of St. [Note: [Col. 0911C] Maiolus. St. Maiolus was a native of Provence. Coming to Mâcon, a city of Burgundy, he was first made a cleric there and then archdeacon. He humbly refused the archbishopric of Besançon when it was offered to him. Entering the monastery of Cluny, he lived as a monk under Abbot Aymardus. Meanwhile, since Aymardus, worn out by old age, could no longer bear the burden of governing the monastery, he proposed Maiolus as his successor; Maiolus accepted the abbatial office unwillingly. Religious life flourished so greatly under the rule of so great a man that the emperor Otto sent a mission concerning the matter and invited him to undertake the reform of monasteries. When he was returning to his own people, after crossing the Alps and traveling along the slopes of Mount Jovinus, he was captured by the Saracens and forcibly taken to a village called Pons Ursariae. At last he was ransomed by his people and returned home. Around the same time, while the Roman see was vacant, he rejected the Roman pontificate with every effort. This man also shone through the spirit of prophecy: he foretold the deaths of both Otto I and Otto II. Coming to a village called Silviniacus, he fell ill; and after living a life full of miracles, he died and was buried in the church of Blessed Peter at Silviniacus, behind the altar of the cross, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, a Friday, which followed the Ascension of the Lord, in the year 994 of Christ and the forty-first year of his ordination. A feast of the translation of St. Maiolus the abbot is celebrated on 4 May in the manuscript of St. Lambert at Liège. See the Acts of St. Maiolus in the Acts of the Saints.] Maiolus, abbot.

### 12 — IV Ides

At Rome, the commemoration of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.

[Note: These were brothers, eunuchs of Blessed Flavia Domitilla, whom we discussed above on the Nones of May; with her they endured a long exile on the island of Pontia. Later, by Aurelianus, Domitilla’s fiancé—whom she herself had rejected out of love for Christ—they were first subjected to extremely severe beatings and then handed over to the consul Memmius Rufus. When he compelled them with the rack and flames to sacrifice, and they declared that they had been baptized by Blessed Peter the Apostle and would in no way sacrifice to idols, they were beheaded. Their disciple Auspicius, Domitilla’s foster-father, seized their bodies, placed them in a small boat, and brought them to Domitilla’s estate; there he buried them in a sandy crypt on the Via Ardeatina, one and a half miles from the city wall. Ado, Notker.]

Nereus and Achilleus. And Saint Epiphanius, our holy father.

[Note: Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus. Sozomen explains his homeland and youthful education (Ecclesiastical History VI, 32): “Epiphanius studied philosophy near the village of Benanducus, situated in the territory of Eleutheropolis, from which he originated. Since from his earliest age he had been instructed by eminent monks, and for this reason had spent a long time in Egypt, he became especially renowned in monastic philosophy.” How hostile he was toward John of Constantinople, and how he supported Theophilus’s party, may be seen in Sozomen (VIII, 13). Socrates also mentions him (VI, 10–11), as do Sozomen (VII, 26), Nicephorus (XIII, 12), and Jerome, Letter 61 to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem. He died near the end of 402, or at least at the beginning of the following year, in extreme old age—almost one hundred years old—and in the thirty-sixth year of his episcopate. Indeed, if Polybius is to be believed, when Epiphanius withdrew from Constantinople he told the emperor Arcadius that he was 115 years and three months old. But this is of doubtful and uncertain credibility.]

Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus.

And at Rome, Saint Pancratius.

[Note: He was born in Phrygia, in the city of Synnada. After the death of his parents, Cleonius and Cyriada, he was entrusted to the guardianship of his paternal uncle Dionysius. They went to Rome and lived on the Caelian Hill. At a certain time they approached Caius, the Roman pontiff, were instructed by him in the faith, and were baptized. After Dionysius’s death, Pancratius was arrested and brought before Diocletian. Unshaken by the emperor’s promises and threats, he was beheaded on the Via Aurelia. Octavilla then secretly took up his body by night and buried it. The Acts are found in the Bollandists.]

Pancratius, who, when he was fourteen years old, completed his martyrdom under Diocletian by decapitation.

**T.** On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Rictrudis.

[Note: Born in Gascony of noble parents, she made great progress in piety under the holy bishop Amandus. At that time Saint Amandus was living there in exile because he had rebuked Dagobert. She married Adalbald, a man distinguished by his noble birth, who possessed many estates in the Flemish, Liège, Adartian, Arras, and Pabulian districts. While traveling to Vasconia, he was killed by wicked men. By him Saint Rictrudis had four holy children: Saint Maurontus, deacon and abbot; Saint Clotsend, who after her mother’s death became abbess of Marcianus; Saint Eusebia, who governed Hamaticus; and Saint Adalsend, who was taken away by a premature death. When Rictrudis was being pressed into a second marriage, she received the veil from Saint Amandus and chose a monastery at Marcianus for herself and her daughters. There she governed with great distinction until the age of seventy-four. Molanus, On the Saints of Belgium. According to Ghinius of Siena, she flourished around 710. Henschenius, however, in the Acts of the Saints, asserts that she was born around 614. She therefore died around 688. In the Acts published by Mabillon, the year 687, with the statement that she was seventy-four and had governed for forty years, has been inserted.]

Rictrudis.

### 13 — III Ides

Dedication of Saint Mary.

[Note: Baronius explains the matter in the Martyrology as follows: “At Rome, the dedication of the church of Saint Mary of the Martyrs, which Blessed Pope Boniface IV, after cleansing the ancient temple of all the gods called the Pantheon, dedicated in honor of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin and all the Martyrs, during the reign of the emperor Phocas.”]

Saint Mary of the Martyrs.

On the same day, Saint Servatius.

Florus in A. T. L.: the commemoration of Saint Servatius at Trajectum by the Port.

[Note: Servatius, bishop of Tongeren and confessor. He pronounced his judgment against Euphrates the pseudo-bishop at the Council of Cologne, held in 346. Our Servatius is greatly praised among the bishops of Gaul by Sulpicius Severus: at Rimini he did not yield to the threats and terrors of the Arians, but issued professions of faith against them. Athanasius also mentions him splendidly. Magnentius was sent as envoy by Constantius to his brother Constans. That tyrant killed Constans and seized the empire of the West at Autun in 350. Athanasius was immediately accused of having conspired with Magnentius to kill Constans. He therefore wrote an apology to Constantius, in which, among the witnesses to his innocence, he first names Servatius, the bishop who had once been sent by Maxentius as an envoy to Constans. The feast of Servatius is celebrated today; the day of his translation is 7 June. The feast of the vision he had at Rome concerning the destruction of Gaul falls on the Annunciation of the Lord, but it is transferred to the Sunday after the octave of Easter. Finally, the triumph of Saint Servatius is commemorated on the first Sunday of July. Molanus, On the Saints of Belgium.]

Servatius, bishop. While he was praying to the Lord at the tomb of Blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, for the deliverance of the people of Gaul, that they might not be ravaged by the Huns, he is said to have received from the Apostle, in a vision, the answer that he himself would soon depart this life and that no city of Gaul would be spared except Metz, because the relics of Blessed Stephen the Martyr were preserved there.

In Palestine: Taracus, Probus, and Andronicus.

[Note: See below, 1 October.]

Up to this point, A. They were thrown into the amphitheater under the governor Maximus after enduring many tortures. Since the wild beasts did not harm them, they were condemned to the sword.

[Col. 0913C] The same, apparently, but in T. alone: On that day, the passion of Saint Mucius.

[Note: He was a presbyter of the Church of Amphipolis. His parents were Euphratius and Eustathia, originally from Old Rome. At Amphipolis he was afflicted with many punishments. When the entire people cried out that he should be released, he was sent to Philippesius at Perinthus, a city of Thrace now called Heraclea, and from there to Byzantium, where he was beheaded. Later, Constantine the Great built a most splendid church for him, and he was translated into it. He suffered under Diocletian. The Greeks celebrate him on 11 May. Bollandus, 11 May.]

Mucius, presbyter, who suffered at the city of Amphipolis under the proconsuls Laodicius and Maximus. He was first ordered to be hung up and clawed almost to the bones; then he was thrown into a furnace of blazing fire. Emerging unharmed by the Lord’s power, he was placed beneath two wheels so that, as they turned, they might divide his limbs. When these had been removed, he was finally handed over to the sword.

### 14 — II Ides

Saint Pachomius, our holy father.

[Note: Sozomen, in his Ecclesiastical History (III, 13), writes that Pachomius was the founder and organizer of the monks of Tabennisi in the Thebaid. At first he practiced the philosophical life alone in a cave, but afterward an angel appeared to him and instructed him to gather younger monks; the angel also gave him a tablet, which the monks still preserve. His Acts state that he died when Saint Athanasius returned to his Church, namely in 349.]

Pachomius, who was distinguished by deeds of apostolic grace and was the founder of the Egyptian coenobia, wrote rules for monasteries, which he had learned at an angel’s dictation; he also wrote concerning the time of Easter.

On the same day in Syria, the commemoration of Victor and Corona under the emperor Antoninus, with Sebastian as governor of Alexandria. Up to this point, A.

[Note: These martyrs are celebrated above on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.]

Victor was a soldier from Cilicia. Sebastian ordered that, because of his confession of faith, his fingers be crushed and his skin torn away. Then he ordered him to be thrown into a furnace of fire, where he remained for three days without being harmed. Next he was ordered to drink poison, but he did not die; rather, he converted the poisoner to the faith. Then it was ordered that the sinews of his body be removed; afterward boiling oil was poured onto his private parts.

[Note: L omits the words from “After this” up to “hung by the head.”]

After this, he ordered burning lamps to be fastened against the sides of the man hanging there. Next he ordered vinegar and lime to be mixed together and given to him in the mouth; then his eyes were torn out; then he ordered him to be hung by the head for three days, and while he was still breathing, he ordered him to be flayed. At that point Corona, who was the wife of a soldier, began to praise Saint Victor for the glory of his martyrdom. While she was doing this, she saw two crowns fall from heaven, one sent to Victor and the other to herself. When she proclaimed this before all who were listening, she was seized by the judge. It was ordered that two palm trees be bent toward each other and tied with hempen ropes to Corona’s two hands and two feet, and then that the trees be released. As this was done, Corona was torn into two parts. She was sixteen years old. At that time Victor too was beheaded, and he likewise earned the triumph of everlasting victory.

**V.** On the same day, Saint Boniface in the Apennines.

[Note: Boniface, bishop of Ferento in Tuscany. As Blessed Gregory relates in the first book of the Dialogues, he was renowned for holiness and miracles from childhood. Baronius teaches that Saint Boniface flourished around the time of the emperor Justin; Ferrarius says that he lived approximately in the time of Pope Saint Gregory.]

**B.** In Milan, Victor, Felix, and Rusticus.

[Note: In this and most manuscripts, 304 additional martyrs are appended, who suffered with Saint Cyricus, as though they had been companions of the martyrs named above. In the most ancient manuscript of Echternach, however, after the Milanese martyrs have been listed, 304 martyrs are said to have suffered elsewhere with Cyricus. These are the martyrs who suffered at Tarsus in Cilicia—or, according to others, at Antioch—with Saint Cyricus, or Quiricus, and his mother Julitta, on 16 June. Saint Cyricus is celebrated below on that date.]

Rusticus. And the commemoration of the 304 holy martyrs who suffered with Saint Cyrius.

### 15 — Ides

Beda has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Lampsacus, the passion of Saints Peter, Paul, Andrew, and the virgin Dionysia. Peter was struck with the sword after various tortures; Andrew and Paul were buried beneath stones; Dionysia was condemned to the sword. B. has only the place and names.

**D.** The commemoration of the holy confessors Torquatus, Ctesiphon, Secundus, Indaletius, Caecilius, Esicius, and Euphrasius.

[Note: They were ordained bishops at Rome by the holy Apostles and sent to preach the word of God in Spain, then entangled in pagan error. After evangelizing various cities and bringing countless multitudes under the faith of Christ, Torquatus came to Acci, Ctesiphon to Vergium, Secundus to Abula, Indaletius to Urci, Caecilius to Eliberi, Esicius to Corcesus, and Euphrasius to Eliturgi, where they rest. Usuard. The arrival of these bishops in Spain is celebrated on 1 and 5 May.]

Euphrasius.

**B.** In Sirmium, Timothy, and elsewhere, seven virgins.

In Sardinia, Simplicius.

[Note: On the following day, 16 May, the Pseudo-Beda calls him a presbyter. Ferrarius, in the Catalogue of the Saints of Italy, gives this summary of his Acts: “Simplicius, bishop of Phausania, a city now called Terranova in the province of Gallura in Sardinia, was arrested for the Christian faith by order of the governor Barbarus after the passion of Saints Gavinus, Protus, and Januarius. The governor’s threats could not deter him. When he declared that the gods were demons and mute images, the governor pierced him with a spear, and he fell half-dead; after three days he gave up his soul to God, around the year 304. His body was buried there, where a church was later built in his name. The people of Civita especially venerate him as their patron.”]

Simplicius.

B. V. A. T. L.: At the Roman Port, the commemoration of Saints Praestabilis, Felix, Victor, Cyricus, Januarius, and Gerulus. Of these, Victor appears only in V; Gerulus only in B; Cyricus in V and L. In L, however, he is the last; in B he is called Cyrinus.

### 16 — XVII Kalends of June

Beda has no entry.

**D.** At Isauria, Aquilinus and Victorianus. T. and L. add: whose Acts are found in the aforesaid place, though they may perhaps belong elsewhere.

[Note: These Acts, cited here by Usuard, have nowhere yet been found. Bollandus.]

**V.** In the city of Auximum in Picenum, Florentius and Diocletianus.

And Saint Peregrinus, bishop.

[Note: Vincent of Beauvais, Antoninus in his Chronicle, and Baronius, following both, assert that Saint Peregrinus was sent to Gaul by Sixtus I. But his most ancient Acts state that he was sent during the reigns of Valerian and Gallienus, under whom Saint Sixtus II was pope from 256 to 258. In the same way, the History of the Bishops of Auxerre, toward the end of its account, adds that these events occurred under the emperors Gallienus and Valerian, when Aemilianus and Bassus were consuls—that is, in 259. We believe, however, that Saint Peregrinus did not suffer martyrdom in that year, but began to announce Christ at Auxerre and survived until the time of Aurelian. After various tortures he was beheaded under Alexander, the protector of Aurelian’s flank—not under the emperor Alexander, as John Chenu conjectures in his catalogues of the bishops of Auxerre.]

Peregrinus, bishop.

A. T. L.: In a city of Picenum, the commemoration of Saint Florentius. At Auxerre, the passion of Saint Peregrinus, the city’s first bishop.

**B.** In Caesarea, the commemoration of Saints Aquilinus, Victorinus, and Paulinus.

[Note: Isauria is more correct; see the first part of this entry.]

In the city of Ephesus, Mangenis, Gaianus, and Jovinus. At Auxerre, the passion of Bishop Peregrinus. And the burial of Fidolus.

[Note: Fidolus, abbot at Troyes in the Gallic Campania. He was carried away captive under King Theodoric; we believe this occurred in 507, during Chlodovech’s war against Alaric, king of the Visigoths. At that time, as Gregory of Tours writes (II, 37), after Alaric was killed, the chief men of the Arverni and the leading senators fell, and Chlodovech sent his son Theodoric to the Arverni. The latter, departing, brought those cities under his father’s dominion from the Gothic frontier to the boundary of Burgundy. At that time, therefore, Saint Fidolus, a noble youth who had been ordained a cleric, was carried away from his homeland among the Arverni and ransomed by Saint Aventinus, abbot at Troyes. In his monastery he was first a monk, then provost; afterward, when Aventinus withdrew into solitude, Fidolus lived as abbot until his death. How long he survived is unknown.]

Fidolus, presbyter.

### 17 — XVI Kalends

Beda has no entry.

**D.** In Tuscany, the martyr Torpes under Nero.

[Note: “At first he held a high office in the service of Nero Caesar, but afterward, for the faith of Christ and by Nero’s order, he was struck on the face, subjected to prolonged scourging, and handed over to the beasts to be devoured; but they did not harm him at all. Finally, by decapitation, he completed his martyrdom on the third day before the Kalends of May, although his feast is celebrated more solemnly here.” Usuard. He suffered at the city of Pisa. Notker.]

**V.** The commemoration of Saint Syrus, confessor.

[Note: The first bishop of Pavia. His translation is indicated for today by Galesinius, Ferrarius, and others; his day of death is 9 December.]

And the burial of Liberius, bishop.

B. A. T. L.: At Rome, on the old Via Salaria, Saints Paternus and Primus, and Liberius, bishop.

[Note: Only L has the words “on the Via Salaria … and Primus.”]

**B.** Bishop Gallicorus.

In Alexandria, Victor and Basil.

B. A. T. L.: At Nividunum, the commemoration of Heraclius and Paulinus [B.: Paulus], and of Minerius, Aquilinus, and Artemius.

[Note: The place of their martyrdom, Nivedunum, is Noviodunum according to Baronius. Saussay follows him in the supplement to the Gallican Martyrology, where he lists all the martyrs indicated by Galesinius. I have no doubt that he understands Noviodunum, later called Noviomum, an episcopal city under the archbishop of Rheims, not far from Soissons. Philippe Labbe, in the French translation of the Roman Martyrology, places Nivedunum, popularly Nyon, at Lake Geneva. Philippe Ferrarius, in his Topography for the Roman Martyrology, seeks it in Lower Moesia on the Danube, where Ptolemy, Geography III, 10, has the Greek name Νουιόδουνον (Noviodunum). We present these possibilities to the reader because, from the bare names, we cannot choose one place over the other.]

### 18 — XV Kalends

Beda has no entry.

**D.** In Egypt, Dioscorus the lector.

[Note: The governor inflicted many and varied tortures upon him while he was detained: he tore his flesh with claws and set fire to his sides with lamps. Finally, he completed his martyrdom by being burned with red-hot plates. Ado, Usuard, Notker, Baronius.]

L. and T. add: who endured many tortures for the name of Christ.

**L.** At Rome, the passion of John, bishop.

[Note: His day of death is celebrated below by Beda on 28 May.]

**V.** In Alexandria, Patamon the presbyter, Ortasius the presbyter, and Serapion.

A. T.: In Alexandria, the commemoration of Saint Hortasius the presbyter and Maximus, otherwise Maxima.

**B.** In Alexandria, Partomus the presbyter and Serapion the presbyter.

And Saint Martin, pope.

[Note: Pope Martin is celebrated below on 12 November.]

In Egypt, Dioscorus the lector, who suffered much.

At Constantinople, Dativus, Lucius, and Marcianus.

And elsewhere, the commemoration of Saints Cassius and Victor.

### 19 — XIV Kalends

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Pudentiana.

[Note: Daughter of Pudens and Savinella, and sister of Praxedis. After her father’s death, she devoted herself to every exercise of piety with the household. The most blessed Pius, bishop of the city of Rome, consecrated the entire household with the water of baptism. She died at the age of sixteen. Pope Pius died in 161.]

Potentiana [sic], virgin.

Florus adds in A. T. L.: At Rome, the commemoration of Calocerus and Parthenius, eunuchs.

[Note: Beda, Rabanus, Notker, Wandalbert, and Galesinius celebrate them on the third day before the Ides of February. Bollandus thinks that their translation to Gaul took place on that day. They suffered under Decius Augustus, when Gratus was consul—that is, in the year 250.]

Up to this point, V. They were killed under the emperor Decius because they refused to sacrifice to idols. Rabanus and B. give a somewhat fuller account.

**A.** At Arras, the burial of Saint Hadulf, bishop.

[Note: He became abbot of the monastery of Saint Vedastus in 710. In 717, by order of King Chilperic, he was appointed to the bishopric of Cambrai, or Arras, the eleventh after Blessed Vedastus. Molanus, On the Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium. He died in 728. Labbe, volume II of the New Library, p. 753. He was buried at Arras in the church of Saint Peter and was later translated to the more distinguished church of Saint Vedastus. Ghinius of Siena.]

Hadulf, bishop.

And the burial of Saint Dunstan, archbishop.

[Note: During the reign of King Athelstan, who was raised to the kingship in 924, Dunstan was born in the territory of Wessex. He was the nephew, through his brother, of Archbishop Athelmus, and a relative of Alphege, bishop of Winchester, from whom he later received both the monastic habit and the priesthood. At Glastonbury, where he was educated, he was appointed abbot by the favor of King Edmund in 942. The following year, when Alfgiva bore King Edmund a son, Edgar, Dunstan heard voices singing and saying: “Peace of the angels to the Church, now raised up in the time of this boy and of our Dunstan.” When King Edmund was killed in 946, Saint Dunstan buried him at Glastonbury.

In 955 King Eadred fell ill and, sending a swift embassy, summoned Blessed Dunstan, the father of his confession. As Dunstan hastened toward the palace and had already completed half the journey, a voice sounded clearly from above, heard by him: “King Eadred now rests in peace.” The king’s body was carried to Winchester and buried by Dunstan in the old monastery.

In 956 Dunstan was proscribed by King Eadwig for the sake of justice and crossed the sea. Arnulf, a man of royal lineage, received him honorably and gave him a residence at Blandinium during his exile. In the following year, King Edgar of Mercia recalled Blessed Dunstan with honor. When Ceonwalch died, Dunstan was elected to the bishopric of Worcester and, in the following year, to that of London.

In 959, after Brithelm, bishop of Dorset, had been elected to the Church of Canterbury but was afterward judged unfit for so great an office, Dunstan succeeded Alfinus of Canterbury. Instructed by Dunstan, King Edgar expelled the clergy from the monasteries, gathered groups of monks and nuns, and ordered more than forty monasteries to be established.

In 960 Dunstan went to Rome and received the pallium from Pope John. When he had returned to his homeland, King Edgar, moved by his prayer, promoted Blessed Oswald to the bishopric of Worcester.

In 969 King Edgar ordered Dunstan and the other bishops to expel the clergy and place monks in the larger monasteries built throughout Mercia.

In 973 the same king was anointed king at the city of Acamann by Dunstan and Oswald. In 975, after Edgar’s death, those bishops anointed his son Edward king. After Edward was treacherously killed, they consecrated his brother Aethelred to the kingship. Finally, Dunstan died in 988. Florus, the Worcester tradition.]

Dunstan, archbishop.

**L.** On the same day, in the basilica of Saint Quentin, the arrival of the relics of Saints Firminus, Fuscianus, Victoricus, Gentianus, Accius, Aciolus, Honoratus, Walericus, and another Firminus.

**B.** In Alexandria, the commemoration of Saint Arenus, deacon.

[Note: Notker writes: “In Alexandria, Saint Irenaeus, deacon.” In the Prague manuscript he is called Herenius the deacon. The Greek name Irenaeus seems more suitable for an Alexandrian martyr than the name Arenus. Nothing could more easily have happened than for the initial name, pronounced by Latins with aspiration, to have acquired an A instead of an H in the course of writing. Bollandus.]

**D.** And Pudens, disciple of the Apostles.

[Note: It is impossible, on chronological grounds, for this Saint Pudens to be the same as the one mentioned by Saint Paul in the Second Epistle to Timothy. Nevertheless, he is called Saint Paul’s disciple in most Martyrologies. Antonius Gallonius indeed thinks that another Pudens descended from the elder Pudens mentioned by Saint Paul, and that the younger is therefore said to have been taught by Saint Paul and to have been a friend of the Apostles only because he was especially devoted to their memory; he preserved by family tradition the teaching that the other Saint Pudens, his grandfather or uncle, had received from Paul. Whatever may be thought of this explanation, which appears sufficiently forced, this Saint Pudens, the father of Saints Pudentiana and Praxedis, flourished in the second century, in the time of Saint Pius, bishop of Rome. Pius was Hyginus’s vicar from 146 and later became supreme pontiff himself, succeeding Anicetus in 154; he lived until 161. He consecrated Pudens’s house under the title of Pastor and, after Pudens’s death, established a baptistery there at the request of his daughters.]

### 20 — XIII Kalends

Beda has no entry.

**V.** In Africa, Victus, Maurella, Quintus, Primolus, Salustius, and Fortunatus.

**B.** In Africa, the commemoration of the holy women Victoria, Marcellosa, and Falsa.

And elsewhere, the burial of Vallesus and Faustulus, bishops.

[Note: Or Faustinus, as others have it. It is difficult to determine anything about these saints, since neither a place nor an episcopal see nor the time in which they lived is indicated. Florentinius considered Faustinus, about whom Saint Cyprian wrote in his letter to Stephen, praising him for standing against Marcianus, bishop of Arles, who had joined himself to Novatian. Even so, he did not dare to assert the identification with certainty.]

**D.** At Rome, on the Via Salaria, Saint Basilla, virgin and martyr.

B. A. T. L.: At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Basilissa.

[Note: Also called Basilissa. Since she was of royal descent and had a highly distinguished fiancé, she was accused by him of being a Christian. The emperor Gallienus decreed that she must either take him back or die by the sword. Summoned on this matter and refusing to consent, she was pierced through with the sword. Ado, Usuard, who follow the authority of the Acts of Saint Eugenia. Papebrochius, however, proves in the Acts of the Saints that those Acts of Saint Eugenia should be rejected as fables, so that nothing certain can be learned from them about Basilissa. Observing that there had been a cemetery of Basilla on the Via Salaria, he believes that the following reading of the ancient Hieronymian Martyrology may be derived from this: “At Rome, on the Via Salaria, in Basilla’s [sc. cemetery], Basilissa and Aureus.”]

Basilissa and Aureus. [L omits “and Aureus.”]

**B.** At the city of Nîmes in Gaul, Blandius.

[Note: Or Baudelus, “who, when he was arrested because he refused to sacrifice, and remained steadfast in the faith amid beatings and tortures, received the crown of martyrdom by a precious death.” Usuard, Ado.]

T., Bautlius. B., Bauddus. L., Bautlius the martyr.

A. T. L.: With his companions.

### 21 — XII Kalends

Beda has no entry.

Florus in T. and L.: In the territory of Évora, the passion of Saint Mantius.

[Note: Molanus, in his additions to Usuard, writes that Saint Mantius suffered in the Lusitanian village of Miliana. He noted, however, that what was said about him was marked with the letter Q, indicating that it had been taken confusedly from some Church Martyrology, since it could not be stated to which particular church it belonged. The Church of Évora, in whose district the event occurred, used to celebrate, and still celebrates, the solemn feast of Saint Mantius on 21 May. Bollandus.]

Mantius, who suffered at the hands of the Jews. Because of his confession of the Son of God, they stretched him out, bound him with ropes, and beat him with blows. Later they tied his entire body with the tightest bonds and inflicted so many wounds upon it that his limbs became food for worms.

[Note: L lacks the words “They add that, from sunrise to sunset, for the purpose of further torturing him, the tally of punishments was to be increased again by a harsher treatment.”]

They add that, from sunrise to sunset, for the purpose of further torturing him, the tally of punishments was to be increased again by a harsher treatment; but undefeated by all these things, he gave his spirit back to God.

**V.** At Rome, Basilissa and Aureus.

[Note: Basilissa is celebrated with Aureus on the preceding day.]

Gervasius and Protasius.

[Note: See 10 June.]

**D.** In Mauritania, Timothy, presbyter, and Eutychius, deacon.

[Note: They suffered in Caesarean Mauritania, according to Ado.]

**B.** In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Victus, Marcella, Quintus, Primolus, Salustius, and Fortunatus.

In Britain, the commemoration of Timothy, deacon.

[Note: One might reasonably wonder whether “Britain” has not been produced from “Mauritania.”]

At Auxerre, the burial of Blessed Vatis, presbyter.

A. T. L.: In Mauritania, the commemoration of Saints Polientius, deacon, Timothy, and Victus, who were worthy to be crowned on one day.

[Note: This is written by a hurried copyist for Pollius and Eutychius the deacon.]

### 22 — XI Kalends

In Africa, Castus and Aemilius.

[Note: Saint Cyprian writes of these men as follows: “Thus the Lord at one time forgave Castus and Aemilius; thus, defeated in the first contest, he made them victors in the second battle, so that those who had previously yielded to the fire might become stronger than fire, and might conquer in the very thing by which they had been overcome.” In the Pseudo-Beda they are celebrated on the preceding day. They suffered around the year 250.]

They completed their martyrdom through the fire of their passion.

[Note: V omits the words “Cyprian wrote this, and so forth.”]

Cyprian wrote this in his book On the Fallen.

**B.** At Rome, the commemoration of Saints Faustinus, Timothy, and Venustus.

On the island of Corsica, the passion of Saint Julia.

[Note: The first place mentioned in the Acts is Carthage. After it was conquered by barbarian enemies, Julia was carried away from there. Baronius, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology and in his Annals under the year 440, refers to the time of the Vandals, when Carthage was captured by them and remained in their possession until 533. Shortly before they were expelled from Africa, Julia may still have been a small child when they sold her into slavery; after twenty or more years had passed, she may have arrived in Corsica with her master. This seems to have been the view of the authors of the lessons at Brescia, since they say that approximately two hundred years elapsed between the burial of her body at Gorgona and its translation to Brescia around 763. Henschenius, however, thinks that Saint Julia was more likely carried into slavery when the Persians, after passing through Syria, Egypt, and Libya, occupied Carthage in 616. This holy woman was crucified.]

At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Helena, virgin.

[Note: She was present when Saint Amator, bishop of Auxerre, was dying in his cathedral, as is related in the Acts of Saint Amator. She shone with many virtues and miracles. Not only her burial but also her translation is celebrated today, although Saussay places the latter on 20 June. It is not known how long she lived after the death of Saint Amator, who died around 418.]

Helena, virgin.

### 23 — X Kalends

Beda has no entry.

Florus in T. L.: In Africa, the passion of Julian the martyr.

And at Vienne, the burial of Saint Desiderius, bishop.

[Note: Born of noble lineage in the city of Autun, Desiderius lived at Vienne under four bishops and there received the office of deacon. When the last of these bishops, Saint Verus, died, Desiderius was raised to his place in 596. Acts of the Saints, 603. A synod was assembled at Chalon; they deposed Bishop Desiderius, and, at the instigation of Aridius, bishop of Lyons, and Brunhilda, whom Desiderius had accused of an incestuous marriage, a man named Domnolus was substituted for him in the priestly office. Desiderius, however, was driven into exile on a certain island.
