In 607, Theodoric, following the counsel of the same Aridius and persuaded by his grandmother Brunhilda, ordered Saint Desiderius, who had returned from exile, to be stoned. It must therefore be believed that, on account of this wicked deed, the kingdom of Theodoric and his sons was destroyed. Chronicle of Fredegar the Scholastic.]

Desiderius, bishop. By order of King Theodoric and Queen Brunhilda, he was first stoned; and when he was already breathing out his life, he was struck on the neck with a club and thus killed.

**D.** At Rome, Pope Caius and 250 others.

[Note: Caius is celebrated above on 22 April and 20 February. We read nothing elsewhere about his companions.]

At Lyons, Epipodius.

[Note: See 24 April, when he is mentioned with Saint Alexander.]

**V.** At Vienne, the passion of Saint Desiderius the martyr, Quintus, Lucius, and Januarius.

**A.** The commemoration of Saint Julius the martyr and Desiderius, bishop.

**B.** In Africa, Quintus and Lucius.

[Note: They suffered with Julian in Africa, and, according to Galesinius, during the Vandal persecution.]

At Bienna, the passion of Saint Desiderius, bishop and martyr.

In Spain, the commemoration of Saints Epictetus, Aptonius, and Basil, bishop.

### 24 — IX Kalends

Beda has no entry.

**D.** Manahen, Herod’s foster-brother, resting at Antioch.

[Note: According to Luke in the Acts of the Apostles, at the beginning of chapter 13, he is said to have set apart Saul and Barnabas for the work of the ministry together with Simon called Niger and Lucius of Cyrene.]

**B. V.** At the Roman Port, the commemoration of Saint Vincent.

In Syria, Zoilus and Saturus.

**B.** Timius and Saturninus.

B. A. T. L.: In Gaul, at the city of Nantes, the passion of Saints Rogatianus and Donatianus, brothers and martyrs.

[Note: During the reign of Diocletian and Maximian, they were sent to prison for their steadfastness in the faith. They were hung on the rack and torn, then pierced with a military spear, and finally beheaded. Usuard, Notker.]

**B.** In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Fortunatus and three others.

25.—VIII Kalends. At Rome, the feast of Saint Urban, pope and confessor, whose teaching led many to be crowned with martyrdom. [Col. 0924D]

[Note: Urban. After Callistus died in 222, Urban succeeded him in the same year. Baronius therefore was not mistaken when he wrote that Urban began his pontificate in 227. For in the Chronicle of Damasus one reads: “Callistus: five years, two months, ten days. He lived in the times of Macrinus and Heliogabalus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Adventus until that of Antoninus IV and Alexander.” Cuspinian has the same words in his Fasti. Pope Urban completed his mortal course in the year 230, in the consulship of Agricola and Clementinus. For again the Chronicle of Damasus reads: “Urban: eight years, eleven months, twelve days.” Cuspinian also has these words. It is nevertheless clear that an error entered the Chronicle of Damasus, and that Urban could not have sat for eight years and so forth, since he died on 25 May 230 and assumed the pontificate in October 222. He therefore held it for only seven years and some months and days. Papebrochius, in his *Chronological-Historical Essay on the Catalogue of the Popes*, in order to attribute to Urban as many years as are mistakenly read in the Chronicle of Damasus, writes that Callistus, while he was in prison, appointed Urban his vicar; but if this were so, Urban would no more have escaped death at that time than Callistus, and some trace of so important a matter would remain.] [Col. 0925B–C]

V. and S. add: Maro.

[Note: Maro. While she was exiled on the island of Pontia, Flavia Domitilla had great affection for this man, Eutyches, and Victorinus. When Aurelian learned of it, after first obtaining permission from the emperor Nerva, he sent them separately, as though they were slaves, to his own estates, Maro indeed to the hundred-and-thirtieth milestone from the City on the Salarian Way, and ordered them to dig the ground. After killing two of Maro’s companions by various tortures, he ordered Maro to be crushed beneath the weight of a huge stone. But when they placed upon his shoulders an enormous rock which seventy men could scarcely weigh at a pulley, Maro carried it unharmed for two miles. Later, after receiving an order from Aurelian, the provincial governor killed him. The people hollowed out the stone which he had carried on his shoulders and buried him there. Maro and his companions are commemorated in the Martyrologies on 15 April. The revised Acts of their passion are found in the *Lives of the Holy Martyrs Nereus and Achilleus* in the Bollandists, 12 May.] [Col. 0925C–D]

B. has, at Milan, the deposition of Dionysius the bishop, Polegratus, and four other crowned martyrs. Elsewhere, at Troyes, Saint Marcellinus the bishop; at Troyes, Leo the martyr.

[Note: Dionysius. He was bishop of Alba, the chief city of Italy. When the bishops of the East were vigorously pressing, at the Council of Milan held around the year 3[.....]9, for a decree to be made against Saint Athanasius, Dionysius rose with Eusebius of Vercelli and loudly protested that the Christian religion would be overthrown by their deceitful efforts. He declared that the accusation brought against Saint Athanasius was manifestly false. When the emperor understood this, he ordered them to go into exile. Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* II, 29. Dionysius had initially been intimate with King Constantius, while he did not yet know that Constantius supported the heretics; but once he learned that the king defended heretics, he rejected the king’s impious familiarity. Faustinus, *Book of Petitions*. He died in Cappadocia, where he had lived in exile; and when the relics of his body had been received at Milan by Saint Basil, bishop of that city, Blessed Ambrose buried them with fitting honor. Ado, Usuard. Notker adds: “Although others maintain that he was exiled to Armenia, to the city of Reditium, and died there, and that he was transferred to Milan by Saint Aurelius, bishop of that city; and that Aurelius himself, having fallen ill there and died, was buried in the same monument as Saint Dionysius.”] [Col. 0925C–0926B]

26.—VII Kalends. In Britain, the deposition of Saint Augustine, the first bishop of the English. [Col. 0926B]

[Note: Augustine. Bede discusses the mission of Augustine and his companions, their preaching, miracles, and the conversion of the English in *Ecclesiastical History* I, 23–24 and following, and II, 2–3, in the *Epitome*, and in the *Chronicle*.]

[Note: D. omits “the first of the English.”] [Col. 0926C]

B. A. T. L.: At Auxerre, the passion of Saint Priscus the martyr with his companions, an innumerable multitude.

[Note: Priscus. Philip Labbe, in the *New Library*, in the first chapter of his *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, writes concerning Saint Priscus and his companions: “When Alexander, the protector of the emperor Aurelian’s person, had arrived at a place called Totiacus in the county of Auxerre, he found Priscus, a Christian man of the highest nobility and distinguished there above many cohorts. He had come from the city of Besançon with many others, against whose ranks Alexander rushed with most savage speed. … But when he saw that they were unconquerable in faith, he ordered them all to be killed by the sword.” And in chapter 7: “God revealed the head of the most blessed martyr Priscus to Saint Germanus, who built and consecrated a basilica four miles from the city for its burial and then handed it over to the people for veneration.”] [Col. 0926C–D]

B. omits “an innumerable multitude.” V. has also Saint Priscus. B.: In Africa, Rufinus and Valeria.

D.: And at Athens, Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles.

[Note: Quadratus. After Publius, bishop of Athens, had been crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, Quadratus was appointed in his place. By his faith and diligence he gathered together the Church, which had been scattered in great terror. When Hadrian had spent the winter at Athens, visiting Eleusis and being initiated into nearly all the sacred rites of Greece, he gave occasion to those who hated Christians to harass believers without an imperial order. Quadratus presented him with a book composed in defense of our religion. Demonstrating its antiquity, he said that he had seen many people who had been healed after being afflicted by various calamities in Judaea, and others who had risen from the dead. Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV, 3. The same Eusebius, III, 34, also declares that Quadratus was distinguished by the prophetic gift.] [Col. 0926C–D]

At Rome, Symmitrius and twenty-two other martyrs.

[Note: Symmitrius. They suffered under the emperor Antoninus. When this holy presbyter, mentioned above, was hiding with other Christians at the house of the virgin Praxedes and celebrating the divine mysteries in the title-church of Saint Pastor, which Saint Pope Pius had built in her house, Antoninus sent and seized Symmitrius and his companions. He ordered them to be punished by the sword, without any hearing, in that same title-church. The virgin Praxedes buried their bodies in the cemetery of Priscilla. Peter de Natalibus.] [Col. 0926D–0927C]

27.—VI Kalends. Bede has no entry. [Col. 0927B]

Florus in A. T. L.: The passion of Saint Julius, who completed his martyrdom by beheading under the governor Maximus.

[Note: Julius. In the city of Dorostorum in Moesia. In the time of the emperor Alexander, although he was a veteran who had completed his military service, he was arrested by officials and brought before the governor Maximus. In his presence he cursed the idols and steadfastly confessed the name of Christ; he was condemned to death. Baronius.] [Col. 0927C]

V. T. L.: At Alexandria, Aquilinus [B.: Aquili], priest, of the Gospel, and fourteen others.

[Note: A. V. and B. read only “of the Gospel.”]

A. T. L.: In Africa, Saints Martialis and Litianus [L.: Lucianus]. A. T.: At Rome, the feast of Saint Castulus.

[Note: Castulus. He is commemorated above, on 26 March.]

A.: In the county of Arras, the translation of the body of Saint Ragnulf the martyr.

[Note: Ragnulf. Father of Saint Hadulf, bishop of Arras. His translation is recorded today, but his passion is placed on 9 November. He rests at Arras in the monastery of Saint Vedast. Molanus, *On the Saints of Belgium*.]

B.: At Tomi, Helias, Lucianus, and Eutychius the bishop. D.: In the Moesian city of Dorostorum, Julius the martyr.

28.—V Kalends. At Paris, Germanus the confessor.

[Note: Germanus. A native of the territory of Autun, born to Eleutherius and Eusebia. He was trained in honorable conduct by the teacher Scopilio. Saint Agrippinus, bishop of Autun, first ordained him deacon, then, after three years, priest; and Bishop Nectarius deservedly appointed him abbot at Saint Symphorianus. He foretold the death of King Theodebert. When Eusebius, bishop of Paris, died, Germanus succeeded him before the Third Council of Paris, held in 557, to which Saint Germanus subscribed. He ordained Felix bishop of Bourges and Syagrius bishop of Autun. He excommunicated King Charibert because he had married Marcovefa, the sister of Merofledis, who had been his wife. He died around 576, almost eighty years old, and was buried in the church of Saint Vincent, which is called Saint-Germain-des-Prés after him. Ghinius of Siena; and his Life written by Fortunatus, which is found in Surius and Bollandus on 28 May, and in volume I of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*.] [Col. 0927C–0928C]

Florus adds in T. and L.: “He was a man of such great virtue that, as is read in his Acts, it was as easy for this holy man to cure cases of illness as to touch them.” Or, as A. has it: “This blessed bishop of the same city, and the extent of his holiness and merit, as well as the miracles by which he became renowned, were set forth by Bishop Fortunatus in truthful style.” [Col. 0928B–C]

On the same day, the deposition of Saint John, pope.

[Note: John. A Tuscan by nationality, son of Constantius, he sat for two years, eight months, and fifteen days, from the consulship of Maximus—that is, the year 523—until the consulship of Olybrius—that is, the year 526. King Theodoric summoned him to Ravenna and, at the king’s request, sent him on an embassy to Constantinople to the emperor Justin, who ardently desired to remove the heretics from the Christian religion. For he dedicated the churches of the Arians as Catholic churches with the greatest zeal. Thereupon Theodoric, enraged, wished to lay waste all Italy with the sword. Then the venerable Pope John went out and walked in tears, while the distinguished ex-consuls Theodorus, Importunus, Agapitus, and another Agapitus received a mandate of embassy: that the churches in the Greek territories should be restored to the heretics; and if this were not done, he would destroy all Italy with the sword. But when Justin, together with the senators and such great men of the city of Rome, met him, he granted the entire request and, for the sake of Roman blood, restored the churches to the heretics according to Theodoric’s will, so that Christians, especially priests, would not be put to the sword. Then, while John and the distinguished men remained in Constantinople, Theodoric seized two senators, Boethius and Symmachus, and killed them with the sword. When the aforementioned men came with John the bishop, King Theodoric received them with deceit and great hatred. He wished to punish them with the sword, but, fearing Justin’s indignation, he did not do so; nevertheless, he tortured them all in custody. Forty days after John’s death, Theodoric suddenly died, struck by God. Catalogues of the Roman pontiffs in Papebrochius, April, volume I.] [Col. 0928C–D]

Because he was orthodox and had been gloriously received by the orthodox emperor Justin when he came to Constantinople, King Theodoric, an Arian, on John’s return to Ravenna, kept him in custody and brought him to death together with other equally Catholic men. Saint Gregory mentions him in the *Book of Dialogues*. His body was transferred from Ravenna and buried in the basilica of Saint Peter on V Kalends of July, in the consulship of Olybrius.

The indication of the time is lacking in V. and L.; in T. only the day is lacking; A. omits the entire eulogy and the very commemoration of Pope John.

B.: In Sardinia, Emilius, Felix, Priamus, and Lucianus.

29.—IV Kalends. At Trier, Maximinus the bishop and confessor.

[Note: Maximinus. He attended the Council of Cologne, held after the consulship of Amantius and Albinus, in the year 346. Jerome speaks of him in the *Chronicle* and says that he received Saint Athanasius as a guest when Athanasius was exiled at Trier; Athanasius remained there for a full two years and four months, as Theodoret writes, *Ecclesiastical History* II, 1. The same Maximinus was present at the Council of Sardica. When Saint Athanasius lists the bishops of Gaul who assembled there, he places Maximinus first, in *Apology* II, col. 423. He died in the time of the same emperor Constantius, as is clear from Athanasius’s *Apology to Constantius*. He himself suffered severely under that emperor because he favored the Catholics and opposed the heretics, as Nicephorus writes at length, *Ecclesiastical History* IX, 12. In the lists of the bishops of Trier, Maximinus is recorded by Democh as the twenty-sixth bishop.] [Col. 0929C–D]

Florus adds in A. T. L.: “He demonstrated himself to his people as a great advocate by great virtues.” And, first: “At Caesarea, the passion of Saint Cyril” (up to this point L.), “who freely accepted the dangers of death for the faith of Christ.” [Col. 0929D–0930B]

B. T.: At Rome, the feast of Saint Restitutus.

[Note: Restitutus. He is said to have suffered under Diocletian and to have been condemned by the prefect of the praetorium Hermogenianus; concerning him, consult volume II of Baronius’s *Annals*, under the year 301.] [Col. 0929D]

B.: And the feast of seven brothers.

[Note: The brothers. Their martyrdom on the Tiburtine Way is celebrated below, on 27 June.]

V.: At Rome, on the Aurelia Way, Restituta; the seven brothers; and the dedication of Saint Clement.

B.: In Africa, the feast of Saints Primus, Accidia, Passimus, and fifty-three others.

[Note: Fifty-three. Jerome’s *Martyrology*, edited by D’Achery, has one hundred and fifty-three.] [Col. 0929D]

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Cyril, Primolus, and Venustus.

30.—III Kalends. Bede has no entry.

D.: On the Aurelia Way, in the cemetery of Felix, the pope.

[Note: Felix. A Roman by nationality, son of Constantius, who sat for five years, eleven months, and twenty-five days. He lived in the times of Claudius and Aurelian, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus until that of Aurelian and Capitolinus. The emperors Aurelius Claudius II and Ovinius Paternus were consuls in the year 269; but the predecessor Dionysius occupied almost the whole of that year, except its last five days. From this we might perhaps infer that Saint Felix was his vicar; and thus the five years, eleven months, and twenty-five days could be reckoned up to 30 May, the day on which he is entered in the ancient Martyrologies. The last consuls, the emperor Aurelian II and Gaius Julius Capitolinus, were consuls in 276. Saint Felix lived beyond that year until the aforementioned 30 May of the following year. Catalogues of the Popes in Papebrochius.] [Col. 0929D–0930C]

At Turris in Sardinia, Gabinus and Crispulus.

B.: In Sardinia, the feast of Saints Gabinus and Crispulus.

[Note: Gabinus. They suffered under Hadrian. This is thought to be the day of their translation, for their feast day is observed on 25 October; hence the Sardinians also call the month of October “Gabinus.” Among them the day of the dedication of his church, celebrated on 4 May 517, is also famous. Gregory, *Register* VII, letter 7, mentions a monastery in Sardinia named for Saints Gabinus and Luxorius.] [Col. 0930C]

V.: At Antioch, Palatinus, who suffered many tortures.

[Note: Gavisus and Scrispulus. More correctly, Gabinus and Crispulus.]

Gavisus and Scrispulus.

A. T.: At Rome, Saints Processus and Martinianus.

[Note: Processus. They are especially commemorated below, on 2 July, and also on the following day.] [Col. 0930C–D]

A. T. L.: In Aquileia, the feast of Saints Cantius, Cantianus [L. omits “Cantianus”], Protus, and Chrysogonus.

[Note: Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla, brother and sister martyrs, suffered near Aquileia under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, with Dulcitius as governor and Sisinnius as count. They were citizens of Rome, descended from the emperor Carinus. Fleeing the persecution, they came to Aquileia, where they joined Protus, a teacher of sacred Scripture. When it became known that they were publicly proclaiming Christ there, the emperors gave the count and governor authority to execute them if they refused to sacrifice. When the blessed martyrs heard this, they left Aquileia with Protus in a vehicle and fled. Nevertheless, Sisinnius and Dulcitius pursued and captured them at Aquae Gradatae, and beheaded them in that same place. Their bodies were collected by the presbyter Zeno and buried near the city. Peter de Natalibus. Usuard, Ado, and others commemorate them on the following day.] [Col. 0930D–0931A]

[Note: Chrysogonus. He seems to be the same person who is commemorated on 24 November, where he is mistakenly said to have suffered at Rome, although he actually suffered martyrdom at Aquileia.] [Col. 0931B]

B. T. L.: At Antioch, the passion of Saints Sicius, Palatinus, and Eutychius [E. omits Eutychius]. T.: “who were also afflicted with many tortures.” B.: “who suffered many tortures.”

31.—II Kalends. At Rome [V. omits “at Rome”], the feast of Petronilla the virgin.

[Note: Petronilla. Her father, Saint Peter, caused her to suffer from paralysis and afterward healed her. She rejected the marriage of Flaccus, a nobleman. After receiving a three-day interval for deliberation, she devoted herself meanwhile to fasting and prayer with Felicula, her milk-sister. On the third day, as soon as she had received the sacrament of Christ from Nicomedes the presbyter, she gave up her spirit. Her death is discussed in the *Acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus*.] [Col. 0931B–0932B]

T. and L. add: “daughter of Blessed Peter the apostle.”

V. D.: At Rome, on the Aurelia Way, Processus and Martinianus.

A. T.: In Antioch, the feast of Paulinus, Isicius, and Justus. B.: In Antioch, Paulinus and Isicius.

In the city of Gerunda, the feast of Saints Germanus, Victurus, and Silvanus.

[Note: Germanus. From the Martyrology of Canisius, who says that they suffered at Emporiae. Emporiae is a town in Spain on the coast between Gerunda and Rhoda. In the *History of the Saints of Catalonia*, Germanus, Justus, Paulinus, and Sereius are mentioned, with no mention of Victurus and Silvanus. So also in the Tables and the Ecclesiastical Calendar of Gerunda, where their feast is celebrated on the second day after the feast of the Trinity. Ferrarius, *General Catalogue*.] [Col. 0932B]

In the city of Sista, Donatianus.

## June

[Col. 0931C]

1.—On the Kalends. The feast of Nicomedes the martyr.

B.: At Rome, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Nicomedes.

[Note: Nicomedes. There was at Rome a noble title-church of Saint Nicomedes, whose annual dedication is observed on this day, as appears from the Martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, and Bede. His martyrdom is celebrated on 17 September.] [Col. 0931D]

M. T.: And of the martyrs Reverianus.

[Note: Reverianus. Reverianus, bishop of Autun, and the priest Paulus, with ten others, were crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian. Usuard.] [Col. 0931D]

V.: At Thessalonica, Lucia the virgin and Aucega, queen of the barbarians.

[Note: Aucega. A queen. In Jerome’s Martyrology she is called a king.] [Col. 0931D]

A. T. B.: At Vienne, the deposition of Saint Claudius the bishop.

[Note: Claudius. “In the year 322 a council of six hundred bishops was assembled at Arles, Martinus then being bishop of that city; at Vienne, Claudius was the eleventh bishop.” Ado, in his *Chronicle* and *Martyrology*.] [Col. 0931D]

A. T.: At Rome, the feast of Saint Exuperantius.

L.: In Vienne, Saints Helladius and Claudius, bishops.

B.: In Africa, Crispinus, Juventius, and Cyriacus.

2.—IV Nones. At Rome, Marcellinus the presbyter and Peter the exorcist, who, after instructing many in the faith in prison, were beheaded after terrible chains and many tortures under the judge Serenus. The man who beheaded them saw their souls, splendidly adorned, carried to heaven by angels. He repented and was baptized in his old age under Pope Julius, receiving the name Dorotheus. [Col. 0932C–D]

On the same day at Lyons, Saint Blandina, with forty-seven martyrs. From first light until evening, the torturers continually renewed the tortures against her; at last they confessed themselves defeated by her. On the second day, beaten again with tortures, she was not overcome.

[Note: L. omits the words from “and on the second day” through “on the fourth.”]

[Note: Forty-seven. Among them were Vettius; Epagathus, of noble birth; Sanctus the deacon; Maturus; Attalus; Pothinus, bishop of Lyons; Biblis; and Alexander, a Phrygian. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 12. They suffered in the seventeenth year of Antoninus Verus. Spartianus, in his *Life of Severus*, testifies that the province of Lyons was administered by imperial legates under Marcus Antoninus. For he writes of Severus: “Then he received the province of Lyons as legate.” Perhaps Severus was appointed governor over this Lyons catastrophe, for he was legate of the province of Lyons under Marcus. Valesius, *Notes*. In Ado’s *Martyrology*, forty-eight martyrs are counted in this order: Photinus the bishop, Zacharias the presbyter, Epagathus, Macarius, Alcibiades, Silvius, Primus, Ulpius, Vitalis, Cominus, Octuber, Philuminus, Geminus, Julia, Albina, Grata, Rogata, Aemilia, Potamia, Pompeia, Rhodana, Biblis, Quartia, Materna, Helpes, also called Amnas. These were handed over to the beasts: Sanctus, Maturus, Attalus, Alexander, Ponticus, and Blandina. The following died in prison: Aristaeus, Cornelius, Zosimus, Titus, Julius, Zoticus, Apollonius, Germinianus, Julia, Ausonia, Aemilia, Jamnica, Pompeia, Domna, Justa, Trophima, and Antonia. Their remains were burned by the persecutors and scattered in the river Rhône. But at the place where they had been burned, the ashes were collected and placed beneath an altar. The place where they suffered is called Athanacum; hence they are called the Athanacian martyrs.] [Col. 0932D–0933D]

On the third day she was also tied to a stake, stretched out in the form of a cross, and prepared as food for the beasts. [Note: A. omits the words from “On the third day also” through “under Antoninus Verus.”] Since none of the beasts dared touch her, she was taken back to prison. On the fourth day she was beaten, burned on grates, and subjected to many other sufferings; finally she was slaughtered by the sword. Then Ponticus also, a boy of fifteen years, was led through every kind of torture with her and, strengthened by her motherly exhortation, completed his martyrdom before her under Antoninus Verus. Written in the fifth book of *Ecclesiastical History*. [Col. 0933B–0934B]

V.: On the same day, Saint Erasmus the bishop and confessor.

[Note: Erasmus. He suffered in Campania. He lived for seven years on Mount Lebanon; afterward, by order of the impious Diocletian, he was first cruelly beaten with leaded clubs, then tormented for a very long time with rods. Later, after resin, sulfur, lead, pitch, wax, and oil had been melted together, he was drenched with them and, by a great miracle, appeared unharmed. When many saw this, they embraced the faith of Christ. He was then bound with an enormous weight of iron and confined in prison under harsh guard, from which he was freed by an angelic visitation. Later, when his most famous reputation had spread, he was seized by another emperor, Maximian, who tortured him with various punishments. He was clothed in a tunic of heated bronze and again thrown into a cauldron in which lead, pitch, wax, resin, and oil had been boiled; by the power of the Lord he overcame everything and emerged unharmed. Thus he eventually reached Campania, where he strengthened many in the faith or converted them to the faith of Christ. Called by the Lord, he rested in a holy death, renowned for his martyrdom. Usuard; the pseudo-Bede; Peter de Natalibus. Notker, Ado, and the manuscript of Dijon commemorate him below, on the following day.] [Col. 0933D–0934D]

3.—III Nones. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Magdunum, a village of Orléans, the deposition of Saint Liphard the presbyter, who possessed such great abstinence that he used only an ounce of barley bread, prepared with his own hands, and drank water very sparingly, even until the third day.

[Note: Liphard. Born at Orléans of illustrious ancestry. He was the brother of Saint Leonard. Having abandoned the world, he attached himself to Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, who ordained him deacon. Later, at Mount Magdunum, he lived an eremitical life with Urbicius, where by his prayers he killed a huge dragon. Marcus of Orléans, residing at the village of Clariacum for certain reasons, ordained him priest. Many, venerating his piety, joined him so that they might be instructed in his discipline. As he was dying, he designated his companion Urbicius as his successor. He died around the year 490. Surius, June; Ghinius of Siena.] [Col. 0934D–0935C]

T.: “This man, rich in the greatest merits, saw the soul of Theodemir, formerly abbot of Miciacum, come to meet the choir of the heavenly hosts, and saw it carried joyfully to heaven with singing.” Written in his Acts. [Col. 0935A]

D.: At Arezzo in Tuscany, the martyrs Pergentinus and Laurentinus.

[Note: Pergentinus and Laurentinus. Noble by birth, they suffered in the persecution of Decius under the judge Tiburtius while they were still boys. After enduring terrible punishments and displaying many miracles, they were struck with the sword and buried near the same city. Usuard, Ado. Notker adds: “and four hundred other men.” The Martyrologies of Ado and the pseudo-Bede call the judge Turtius; Notker also calls him Tertius; Surius, Tiburtius.] [Col. 0935A–C]

In Campania, Erasmus the bishop and martyr.

V.: At Rome, the feast of Saints Marcellus, Donatus, Gaius, Januarius, and Victoria. [Col. 0935B]

[T. omitting Gaius, gives the name Urbanus instead of Victoria.]

A. T. L.: In Africa, the feast of Saint Quirinus.

[Note: Quirinus. Under the governor Galerius, for the faith of Christ he was thrown into a river with a millstone tied around his neck. But when the stone floated, he spent a long time exhorting the Christians standing around not to be terrified by his punishment or waver in the faith. Finally, in order to attain the glory of martyrdom, he obtained from God by his prayers that he be submerged. Ado, Usuard. In the Acts published by Mombritius, volume II, he is said to have suffered in the persecution of Diocletian under Maximus, elsewhere Maximianus, the governor, whom Prudentius calls Galerius. There is no discrepancy, for Galerius himself was called Maximinus and was later named Caesar by the same emperor. There was also another Galerius Maximinus, who, while serving as proconsul in Africa under the emperor Valerian, pronounced the sentence of ultimate punishment against Saint Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. Baronius, *Notes*. His body was found in the Danube and buried by the faithful in a basilica near the principal gate of the city of Scarabantis. When the barbarians invaded those regions, the Christians fled and carried away the martyr’s body; bringing it to Rome, they placed it on the Appian Way, three miles from the city, in the church at the Catacombs. Peter de Natalibus.] [Col. 0935C–0936C]

B.: At Rome, Marcellus, Saturninus, Urbanus, Felix, and Veneria. Elsewhere, Silvanus with eighty-two others. At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Liphard the presbyter.

4.—II Nones. Bede has no entry.

D.: In the Illyrian city of Sissia, Quirinus the bishop and martyr.

B. V. T. L.: At Rome, in the cemetery at the Catacombs on the Appian Way, at the fourth milestone, the feast of Saints Pictus, Aretius, and Datianus.

[V. omits “in the cemetery at the Catacombs”; T. and L. omit “at the fourth milestone”; B. omits everything except the names.] [Col. 0936C]

A. T. L.: At Nividunum, the feast of Saint Saturnina, Zoticus, and Eutychius. Lacks the place of their contest.

B.: In Cilicia, the feast of Saints Expergentius, Philippus, Julia, and Saturninus. At Salaria, Rustilus with two others.

[Note: Rustilus. Ferrarius corrects the passage as follows: “At Sabaria in Pannonia, Saint Rutulus.” Concerning them, see Antonius Bonfinis, *History of Hungary*.]

5.—Nones. Bede has no entry.

Twenty years after the death of this Bede, the passion of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, was completed in the martyrdom of the Frisians. He had come from England to Rome and had been sent by Gregory II into Germany to preach the faith of Christ to those peoples. After bringing a very great multitude, especially of Frisians, Bavarians, and Saxons, under the Christian religion, he deserved to be called the apostle of the Germans. After preaching in Frisia for sixteen years, he was attacked by unbelievers and killed with the sword, completing his martyrdom together with Eobanus the chorepiscopus; the priests Wenturgius, Walterus, and Adhale; the deacons Stricbaldus, Hamuntius, and Boso; the monks Waccarus, Gundetherus, Willerus, and Adolphus; and nearly fifty other servants of God. The people of Utrecht gave their bodies honorable burial in the church of Saint Boniface, now called Saint Saviour’s, although Boniface was carried back to Mainz.

[Note: Boniface. Archbishop of Mainz. Ghinius of Siena. He suffered, as is written in the Continuation of Bede’s *Epitome*, in the year 754. Trithemius, however, in *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, writes that he died in 755.] [Col. 0936C–D]

So D. and V. have it: “The passion of Saint Boniface, archbishop, was completed in the martyrdom of the Frisians, together with Eobanus, his fellow bishop, and their other companions, the servants of God.” B. has nearly the same: “In Frisia, the passion of Saints Boniface, archbishop, and Eobanus, his priest, with twelve other servants of God.” Then it adds: At Rome, Felicula and Felicitas.

[Note: Felicula. At the seventh milestone, with many others. Notker.]

In Egypt, Marcianus, Nicander, and Apollonius.

[Note: Marcianus. They completed their martyrdom in the persecution of Galerius Maximianus. Baronius. See also 5 April. The citizens of Venafrum placed the body of Saint Nicander in their city, while the citizens of Atina placed the body of Marcianus in their town. They suffered in the territory between the two cities. Peter de Natalibus.] [Col. 0936D]

A.: At Pulda—rather, at Fulda—the monastery of Saint Boniface, archbishop, who, while announcing the word of God to the Frisians, was crowned with martyrdom.

T., omitting the place, adds: “On the same day, Eobanus the bishop with other servants of God.”

L.: In Frisia, the feast of Saint Boniface, archbishop, who, while announcing the word of God to the Frisians, was crowned with martyrdom. On the same day, the passion of Eobanus, his fellow bishop, with their other companion servants of God.

The Martyrology of Rabanus: “On the Nones of June, Boniface, archbishop, whose martyrdom was completed in Frisia; and Eobanus, his fellow bishop, with the servants of God Wintrungus and Walthere, Scirbaldus and Boso, Hamundus and Aethelhere, Waccarus and Gundacarus, Willerus and Hadovolfus.”

Moreover, just as Rabanus inserted this account into his Martyrology because of the burial of the sacred body in the church at Fulda and the fame of its miracles, so the memory of the same holy martyr, most honored throughout Gaul, seems to have been entered immediately in all the most ancient calendars of the Gallican churches—and even in copies of Bede not yet expanded—with the diversity of wording displayed by the manuscripts noted above. This explains why the same formula is found in V. and D., which otherwise have nothing in common except Bede’s text; and why in D. it is written as though it had been Bede’s. We do not presume to guess whether any of these formulas belongs to Florus, or which one. [Col. 0936D–0937B]

6.—VIII Ides. Bede has no entry. [Col. 0937C]

D.: Philip, one of the seven deacons.

[Note: Philip. He preached the Gospel in Samaria and baptized Simon Magus; afterward, he baptized one of the officials of the queen of Ethiopia. Eusebius II, 1. He died at Hierapolis, having grown old in virginity together with his two daughters. Ibid. III, 31. In the time of Saint Jerome, the memory of Saint Philip the deacon and his daughters was still recent at Caesarea Maritima in Palestine: the little church of Philip and the cells of his daughters were still intact. Saint Paula visited all of them on her journey to Jerusalem, as Saint Jerome writes in Letter 27 to Eustochium.] [Col. 0937C–D]

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Licinianus.

[Note: Licinianus. Perhaps he is the same as Lucianus, who is commemorated on the following day.] [Col. 0937D]

B. V.: In Africa, the feast of Italus and Zoticus. B.: And Talus. V.: And at Terni, the translation of the body of Proculus the martyr.

[Note: Proculus. Saint Proculus, bishop of Terni, is also commemorated on 14 April.]

B.: And the deposition of Caeratus.

[Note: Caeratus. Wandelbertus writes of him as follows:

“The octave of the Ides is adorned by Caeratus the bishop,”]

[The supplied source ends here, with the quotation incomplete.]

“[The city] which supports the town named under the rule of Gratian.”] Of Caeratus, bishop. B. A. T. L.: At Nividunum, the feast of Saints Amantius, Lucius, [Note: [Col. 0937D] Gratianopolis. This word must be referred to Caeratus.] Gratianopolis [A. T. L. omit Gratianopolis], and Alexander. T. L.: At Ghent, the deposition of Saint Gudualus, bishop and confessor.

[Note: Gudualus. A bishop in Britain who, having abandoned his episcopate, withdrew to a monastery in his diocese, where he gathered 188 disciples. Since the place was scarcely sufficient for them, he built another monastery on the estate of Mevoti. He flourished around the year 340. After his death he was buried on an island called Plet or Plecit. Later, when barbarians invaded Britain, the monastery’s brothers carried away the sacred body, crossed the sea separating Britain from Gaul, and reached Francia. Arnulf, margrave of Flanders, by authority of the bishop, arranged through the reverend abbot Gerard for its translation to Ghent, to the monastery called Blandinium. His feast is on the eighth day before the Ides of June. This translation, however, took place on the third day before the Nones of December, while Chlothar governed the kingdom among the Franks, namely in the year 956. Surius, volume III; Molanus, On the Saints of Belgium.]

T.: On the same day in Alexandria, the passion of Philip and the deposition of Claudius.

[Note: Claudius. Saint Claudius, bishop of Besançon in Gaul, who was descended from the distinguished Palatine family. Well educated and trained in letters, he became a cleric of the Church of Besançon. Devoting himself to pious works, when the bishop of Besançon died he was sought by all and consecrated in his place. But since he longed for solitude, after seven years, with his affairs well arranged, he withdrew to the monastery of Lérins. Having served there most devoutly as abbot for many years, he passed into heaven at about ninety-five years of age, in the fourth year of the reign of Childebert III—that is, in the year 698. His body was buried in the church of Saint Eugendus and remains incorrupt. Ghinius the Elder. He is found to have attended and subscribed the Council of Epaon, as the acts of that synod demonstrate. The author of the spurious Bede assigns him to the following day.]

Of Claudius, bishop. L.: The passion of Philip, bishop of Alexandria.

T.: First, the translation of the holy virgins and martyrs of Christ, Honorata and Florina, together with many relics, from Cologne to the city of Tournai. Among them were relics from the most sacred body of the eminent virgin and martyr Ursula.

[Note: Ursula. See below, October 21.]

She held first place in that most renowned company of eleven thousand virgins and shone forth as the leader of the entire company toward Christ. They were translated and deposited in the church of Saint Martin of Tournai, in the suburb of the city; this is known to have been done through the clemency of divine mercy in the year 1170 of the Incarnation of the Word.

[Col. 0939A] 7.—VII IDES. Bede has no entry.

D.: At Constantinople, of Paul.

[Note: Paul. When Saint Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, died in the year 340, Paul succeeded him during the reign of the emperor Constantius. The populace was divided into two parties. The Arians were eager for Macedonius to be ordained, while the Homoousians worked for Paul to be made bishop, and in the end their effort prevailed.

Not long afterward Paul was expelled from his see by the emperor Constantius, after a council of Arian bishops had assembled for that purpose. Eusebius was transferred from Nicomedia and designated bishop of Constantinople. When he died shortly afterward, in the year 342, the people of Constantinople again brought Paul into the Church; the Arians, however, ordained Macedonius bishop. This caused a great disturbance in the imperial city, so that the house of Hermogenes, the master of the soldiers sent by the emperor to expel Paul, was burned, and Hermogenes himself was dragged by the feet, horribly mutilated, and thrown into the sea by the people.

Socrates writes that, after Paul had again been expelled from his see because of these disturbances, he came to Rome. Valesius, however, in his Ecclesiastical Observations on Socrates and Sozomen, book II, chapter 6, rightly suspects that Paul was exiled by Constantius to Singara and shortly afterward transferred from there to Emesa, evidently because of fear of a Persian invasion. For after Athanasius had first mentioned Paul’s exile, while he was still a presbyter, which occurred under Constantine, he says: “Again, however, he was bound in iron chains by Constantius, deported to Singara of Mesopotamia, and from there transferred to Emesa.” Since Athanasius expressly asserts this in his Letter to the Solitaries, it cannot be assigned to any other time than the present.

Baronius indeed writes that Paul, driven from his church, went to Julius at Rome, and that after receiving from him letters by which he was restored to his see, those letters proved ineffective, since Paul recovered his church only after the Council of Sardica. But since there is no mention of him in the letter of the Council of Sardica, he does not seem to have been restored by that council. Indeed, Theodoret, book II, chapter 5, expressly states that Paul was not present at the Sardican synod. Valesius thinks this happened because the citizens of Constantinople did not want Paul to travel there, fearing that the Arians would kill him by treachery on the journey.

Paul therefore had already recovered his episcopal seat before the Sardican synod, either through Constantius’s favor toward the people of Constantinople, who were devoted to him with a particular affection, or because of fear of the emperor Constans, who, by frequent letters to Constantius, had demanded that Paul, Athanasius, and others be restored to their sees.

After the death of the emperor Constans, which occurred in the year 350, the Arians, now entirely free from fear, rose against the Catholic bishops much more violently than before. They attacked Paul first and persuaded Constantius to send him into exile. The Arian emperor therefore ordered Philip, the prefect of the praetorium, to remove Paul from his see immediately.

Philip entered the bath of Zeuxippus and summoned Paul to him, as though he wished to consult him. When Paul arrived, the prefect secretly lowered him through a window and ordered him to be carried to the palace. From there he put him on a ship and sent him into exile at Cucusus, a town of Cappadocia. There the Eusebians shut him in a very confined and dark place and completely withheld food from him, intending to kill him by starvation. On the sixth day, when they entered and found him still breathing, they strangled him with twisted strips of his cloak, as Athanasius writes to the Solitaries.

Valesius, Second Ecclesiastical Observation on Socrates and Sozomen; Pagi, years 340, 342, and 348.]

Of Paul, bishop. V. A. T. L.: In Byzantium, which is Constantinople, the feast of Saints Paul and Fortunatus. L.: Of Primus. A. T. L.: And of Achaicus, monk. V.: And of Lucian, martyrs.

[Note: Lucian. He is also commemorated on the preceding day.]

Ast. A. T. B.: In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Julian, martyr. B.: And elsewhere, of Paul, Fortunatus, and Macarius, monk. L.: And the passion of Lucian of Caesarea. B.: In Africa, of Victurus, Evasus, and Privata.

[Note: Evasus and Privatus are also commemorated on June 5.]

[Col. 0940A] 8.—VI IDES. At Soissons, Saint Medard, confessor.

[Note: Medard. Born at Salency of Nectardus and Protagia. After passing through the ranks of the lower orders with great distinction, he was compelled to undertake the priestly office. It happened that, not long afterward, the bishop of Vermand died, and Saint Medard, although unwilling, was appointed in his place.

Before the most blessed pontiff had been elevated to the episcopal chair, the city of Vermand was destroyed, along with other cities of Gaul, by the frequent invasions of the barbarians. He therefore established his episcopal see at Noyon, which was defended by walls. After Eleutherius, bishop of Tournai, had died, Medard was also compelled to assume the governance of the Church of Tournai.

Finally, having completed the course of his good work, he died—according to Cointius, in 545; according to the Chronicle of Sigebert, in 556; and according to Valesius, in 560. King Chlothar I buried him with the highest honors at Soissons and began to build a basilica over him, which his son Sigebert later completed. Surius, June; Gregory of Tours, History IV, 19.]

Florus adds in A. T. L.: And a bishop from whose mouth a dove, whiter than snow, was seen to emerge when he ended his present life.

B.: And Licinius, bishop and confessor.

[Note: Licinius. In the city of Angers. Ado; Notker.]

V. B.: At Rome, the feast of Saints Nabor and Nazarius. T.: On the same day, Saint Gildardus, bishop and confessor.

[Note: Gildardus. Brother of Saint Medard; both were twins, born on the same day, namely the sixth day before the Ides of June; consecrated bishops on the same day; and finally they died on the same day, as stated above. Peter de Natalibus. Gildardus is found to have attended the First Council of Orléans, held during the reign of Chlodovech, king of the Franks, as appears from its acts. The tables of Democharis number him as the fifteenth bishop of the see of Rouen.]

L.: And Saint Gildardus, archbishop of Rouen. T.: And the second translation of Saint Audomar, bishop.

[Note: Audomar. Molanus writes the following concerning this translation in his additions to Usuard: “The return to the monastery of Sithiu of Saint Audomar, bishop, when Saint Folquinus, after driving out Hugh, abbot of Lisbourg, brought back his body in the year 843 and buried it beneath the earth at Sithiu beside the body of Blessed Bertinus. There it remained hidden from human beings for many years; but it was revealed when the Lord willed.”]

B.: In Sardinia, the feast of Salustianus.

[Note: Salustianus. Ferrarius counts him among the bishops of Cagliari.]

9.—V IDES OF JUNE. The feast of Saints Primus and Felicianus, martyrs.

[Note: Felicianus. Under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. These glorious martyrs, sometimes enduring equal tortures together and sometimes different and elaborate tortures separately, were finally executed by the sword by Promotus, governor of Nomentum. Usuard; Ado. Pope Theodore raised the bodies of these martyrs, which were in the cemetery on the Nomentan Way, transferred them into the city, and deposited them in the basilica of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, offering many gifts. Baronius, in his notes.]

The following was later added to manuscript D.: On Mount Cilinius; but in A.: On Mount Caelius at Rome. B. adds: And Vincentius, martyr.

[Note: Vincentius. Martyred at Aginnum, a place in the territory of Pompeius. Ado. Gregory of Tours discusses the miracles performed at his tomb in On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 105, and History VII, 35. The Fathers gathered at the Council of Chalon offered prayers to this holy martyr for the life of King Chlodovech, as is clear from chapter 1 of the acts of that synod.]

L., however, has: At Rome, on the Nomentan Way.

Florus in A. T.: At Aginnum, the passion of Saint Vincentius, martyr, who, shining with the whiteness of the levitical robe, attained martyrdom for the love of Christ and very often shines forth through great miracles.

[Col. 0942B] V.: Elsewhere, of Januarius and Alexander.

[Note: Januarius. They suffered martyrdom in Alexandria together with Maximus and Amandus. Martyrology of Jerome.]

B.: At Rome, the passion of fifteen holy soldiers. In Alexandria, of Maximus, presbyter, Amandus, and Januarius.

10.—IV IDES. Bede has no entry.

D.: At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, of Basilides, Tripodis, and others.

[Note: Basilides. Tripodis and he flourished in the city of Orléans in the time of the emperor Aurelian. When Basilides was an official of the prefect Plato in the eastern regions, Christ appeared to him and commanded him to abandon pagan service. Basilides therefore sailed with his companions to Italy, to the harbor of the city of Aurelia. When they heard how Aurelian was persecuting Christians, they were afraid to go into the city. Christ appeared to them again and refreshed them with food; after they had eaten, they fell asleep. In the morning, when they awoke, they found themselves at the very place where they had disembarked from the ship. They then prayed Christ to receive their souls in peace, and at that moment they gave up their spirits. Peter de Natalibus.]

B.: At Rome, the soldiers Basilides, Rogatus, Martianus, and twenty others. V.: At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, at the thirteenth milestone, Basilius, Aurisius, Rogatus, and Januarius.

[Note: Aurisius. He is also called Aresius and Rogatus, according to Jerome, the common text of Bede, and Baronius; they suffered in Africa.]

L.: At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, the passion of Saints Rogatus and Januarius with thirteen companions. A. T.: At Rome, the feast of Basilides, Rogatus, and Victor. T. B.: In Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Zacharias. B.: At Auxerre, the deposition of Censurius, bishop.

[Note: Censurius. He sat for thirty-eight years, three months, and six days. During his time, Constantius, the orator, at the request of Saint Patient, bishop of Lyons, composed the Life of Blessed Germanus, worked on it with every diligence, and afterward sent it to that same bishop Censurius to possess. He was buried in the church of Saint Germanus the bishop. He lived during the pontificates of Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, and Hormisdas, and during the reigns of Anastasius and Justin the Elder. History of the Bishops of Auxerre, in Philip Labbe’s New Library.]

[Col. 0943B] 11.—III IDES. Barnabas the apostle.

[Note: Barnabas. He was one of the seventy disciples, as Eusebius writes in History II, 1. His body was discovered during the reign of the emperor Zeno, through his own revelation, together with a copy of the Gospel of Saint Matthew written by his hand. Ado; Baronius.]

Florus in A. marks “In India,” and in both that manuscript and T. and L. adds: He brought the price of his field and laid it at the feet of the apostles, and afterward was appointed, together with Paul, apostle of the Gentiles. [Thus far L.] But afterward, because of John, the disciple who was also called Mark, he separated from Paul; nevertheless, he carried out the work of evangelical preaching entrusted to him.

D.: And Sosthenes, Paul’s disciple.

[Note: Sosthenes. He is also commemorated on November 28.]

V.: At Rome, the feast of Saint Basilla. And the feast of Saint Crispillus and Onuphrius. B.: At Aquileia, of Emeritus, Heretius, and Victurianus. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Babilla. And of Saints Crispillus and Restitutus. Elsewhere, the feast of Saints Nabor and Felix.

[Note: Nabor and Felix. They suffered at Milan and are commemorated below on July 12.]

And Saint Onuphrius.

[Note: Onuphrius. The Greeks and Baronius commemorate him on the following day. The Greeks discuss him in the Menologion in these words: “Our holy father Onuphrius of Egypt, who, while he was in a coenobium in the city of Hermopolis of the Thebaid and heard of the life of the prophet Elijah, left the coenobium and lived in the desert for sixty years, seeing no human being.” After he died, the great Paphnutius buried him.]

12.—II IDES. The feast of Saints Basilides, Cirinus, Nabor, and Nazarius.

[Note: Basilides, etc. They suffered at Rome during the persecution of Diocletian. Born in the city itself, they came to the city of Aurelia and distributed all their possessions to the poor. Returning to Rome, they were brought before the emperor Maximian. Because they were not afraid to confess Christ, they were first beaten severely with scorpions, then thrown into prison and tormented there for seven days. Afterward they were brought out and beheaded by order of the same emperor, and their bodies were exposed to wild beasts for devouring. But by God’s grace, when their bodies were found unharmed, Christians buried them three miles from the City, in a place called the Catacombs. Peter de Natalibus. Baronius, however, says that they suffered under the prefect Aurelius. Concerning the translation to Gaul of Nabor and Nazarius, together with Saint Gorgonius, carried out by Grodegandus, bishop of Metz, in the year 765, see Notker, Molanus’s Additions to Usuard, and the Chronicle of Sigebert, year 764.]

V. and C. add: Tripodis and Magdalis.

[Note: Tripodis and Magdalis. They are commemorated together with the Basilides celebrated on June 9, who is different from the Basilides now under discussion.]

L. marks “At Rome.” D., in first place and in the same type as the other entries of Bede, had: At Milan, the discovery of Nazarius and Celsus the boy. We do not dare to accept this from a single manuscript as Bede’s. A.: And the translation of Saint Leodegarius, bishop, and Saint Odulfus, confessor.

[Note: Leodegarius. If Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, is intended here, his feast is October 2.]

[Note: Odulfus. He was born at Oorschot in Brabant during the time of Louis Augustus. After the priesthood he wished to go to Utrecht, but, overcome by his parents’ entreaties, he served for some time as pastor of the Church and people of Oorschot. Not long afterward, however, being deeply devoted to the monastic life, he moved to Utrecht, where he was kindly received by Bishop Frederick.

When Saint Frederick could not recall the fierce Frisians either personally or through his archdeacons, he summoned Odulfus. Odulfus converted many more than had been hoped and instructed them for several years. Returning from there to Utrecht, full of years, he fell asleep in a slight fever. His relics are kept at Saint Savior’s in Utrecht. Surius, volume III.]

B.: Elsewhere, of Zabinus, Aurelius, and Secunda.

[Note: Elsewhere. According to Jerome, at Rome.]

[Col. 0945B] 13.—THE IDES. In Africa, the feast of Saints Lucianus, Fortunatus, and Crescentianus; at Rome, of Saint Felicula.

[Note: Felicula. She was the foster-sister of Petronilla, whose feast is celebrated on the second day before the Kalends of June. After Saint Petronilla’s death, Flaccus, a count who had previously loved her, handed Felicula over to a judge because she refused to marry him or sacrifice to idols. Since she persevered in confessing Christ, the judge, after a dark imprisonment and starvation, had her tortured on the rack for so long that she gave up her spirit. She was then thrown into a sewer, and Saint Nicomedes buried her on the Ardeatine Way, seven miles from the city. See the Acts of the Holy Martyrs Nereus and Achilleus in the Acta Sanctorum, May 12.]

V. B. C. add the name Thecla at the end. D. omits them all and instead has, from the following day, the prophet Elisha. T.: At the fortress of Ghent, the raising of the body of Saint Landualdus, confessor.

[Note: Landualdus. His feast is celebrated above, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.]

14.—XVIII KALENDS OF JULY. The translation at Orléans of the body of Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor.

[Note: Elisha. He prophesied and flourished under the kings of Israel, Joram, Jehu, and Jehoahaz. He was buried in Samaria of Palestine, which Herod later called Sebaste in honor of Augustus. The prophet Obadiah and John the Baptist also rest there. Various miracles occur at their tombs, as Jerome says in his book On the Life of Paula.]

In D. “the feast” is written; in V. B. C. “And Felicula” is inserted, wrongly repeated from the preceding day.

Florus in A. T. L.: In the district of Soissons, the passion of Saints Valerius and Rufus, martyrs.

[Note: Rufus. Otherwise Rufinus. When Christians wished to carry their bodies to the city of Reims, they were entirely unable to move them from the place where they had been beheaded. They buried them there.]

[The following continues in L. alone, though the eulogy is nevertheless attributable to Florus:] They left Rome during the time of Diocletian and Maximian and entered Gaul. They were arrested by the prefect Rictiovarus, handed over to chains and prison, suspended on racks, and beaten with leaden balls. They were afflicted with such severe punishments that the entire appearance of their bodies was covered by a single wound, and as the flesh fell away the hidden entrails were exposed. Thus they were again sent to prison and there strengthened by an angel of the Lord; finally they were killed by the sword.

T. adds: And the liberation of that city from the Vandals.

[Note: Liberation. When Attila, king of the Huns, was pressing the city of Orléans under siege, Saint Anianus, bishop of that place, obtained God’s aid by his prayers. Aetius, Theodoric, king of the Goths, and his son Thorismund hastened to the city and drove back the enemy. Gregory of Tours, History II, 7; Fredegar, Fragments of the History of the Franks, chapter 3. The History of the Patriarchs of Bourges, chapter 13, in Philip Labbe’s New Library, says that Saint Anianus liberated the city in the sixth year of Palladius, the thirteenth archbishop of Bourges—that is, in the year 454.]

A. T. B.: At Aquileia, the feast of Saint Protus.

[Note: Protus. He is commemorated above with Cantius and Cantianus on May 30. Ferrarius nevertheless lists all of them today in his General Catalogue.]

B.: In the city of Soissons in Gaul, the passion of Saints Rufinus and Valerius, martyrs.

15.—XVII KALENDS. The feast of Saint Vitus, martyr.

[Note: Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia. Blessed Vitus, mature in virtue despite his childhood, was first tested by his sacrilegious father Hylas, who tried to make him abandon the faith. Then, beaten with clubs by the judge Valerianus, he remained steadfast in confessing Christ.

Returned to his father, when his father planned to afflict him with punishments, he boarded a ship at an angel’s command, accompanied by his tutors Modestus and Crescentia, and came to the place called Alectorius. Because the daughter of Diocletian was tormented by a demon, he was sought out and brought to her, and healed her by prayer.

When the emperor could in no way persuade him to agree to idolatry, he ordered him, bound with iron chains, to be thrown into prison with Modestus and Crescentia. Later Diocletian ordered them cast into a cauldron heated with resin, pitch, and lead. They emerged from the cauldron unharmed, and a fierce lion was released upon them; it immediately began to lick their feet.

Finally, when the boy prayed that they might be freed, an angel instantly placed them beside the river called the Silarus in Lucania. There, resting beneath a tree, they gave their souls to God. Florentia, a noblewoman, gathered the saints’ bodies and buried them, embalmed with spices, in a place called Marianus.

Ado; Surius, volume III. Sigebert writes in his Chronicle, under the year 755, that the body of Saint Vitus was translated from Rome to Paris. From there, he says, it was carried to Saxony in the year 836. He is especially celebrated in Sicily, as is clear from the martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, the spurious Bede, and our Florus.]

[Col. 0946C] V. and C. add Modestus and Crescentia.

[Col. 0947B] Florus more fully in A. T. L.: In Sicily, the feast of the holy martyrs Vitus the boy, Modestus the old man, and Crescentia [A. and L. omit Crescentia], who under Diocletian and Maximian were afflicted with various punishments for the name of Christ and crowned through their sufferings.

T. and L. (though L. omits this passage): At Crispinus, the feast of Saint Landolinus, confessor and priest.

[Note: Landolinus. Born at Cambrai of a noble Frankish family during the reign of King Dagobert, and instructed in letters and pious morals by Blessed Autbert, bishop of Cambrai. Seduced by certain relatives, however, he fled and became a wicked robber. To conceal his name, he called himself Maurentius. But, brought back through the prayers of the holy bishop Autbert, he was tonsured by him and purified through prolonged penance; he was also ordained a priest.

After making three journeys to the threshold of the apostles, by authority of Pope Martin he built four monasteries: Lobbes, Aulne, Wasler, and a fourth on the River Hon near Valenciennes, which he called Crispin. He finally died there around the year 660. Ghinius the Elder.]

B.: At Aquileia, of Cantianus and Clement. In Lucania, of Candidus, Protus, and Chrysogonus.

[Note: Aquileia Lucania. Are these not the same as those commemorated above on May 30 and the preceding day?]

16.—XVI KALENDS. Of Ferreolus, presbyter, and Ferrutio, deacon.

[Note: Ferreolus. In Gaul, near the city of Besançon. Learned men judge that their martyrdom occurred at the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Caracalla. They were sent to Besançon, where they suffered, to preach the faith by Saint Irenaeus. Gregory of Tours discusses miracles performed at their tomb in On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 71.]

Under the judge Claudius they were stretched on pulleys and scourged, then shut in prison. In the morning, with their tongues cut out, they preached the word of God. After this, thirty awls were driven into the hands and feet of both, and finally they were struck in the chest with a sword.

A. T. L. mark: In the city of Visoncium. C.: At Ubesoncium. B.: At Vendôme.

Florus in A. and T.: In the city of Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Adrian and his companions, who suffered under the emperor Maximian. When they were recognized as Christians, the emperor ordered them stretched out and severely beaten with clubs. Then, after they had been taken to prison, he ordered a bronze anvil placed beneath their feet and their legs cut off and broken until they died.

The same in T., in first place: Near Antioch, the passion of Saint Cyricus and his mother Julitta. After dreadful beatings, the former also had lime with vinegar and mustard poured into his mouth. Then they were nailed together, their eyes torn out, and they were thrown into prison. Afterward, their heads were shaved and their skin flayed, and they were roasted on coals upon a bronze bed. Under the reign of Alexander and before the governor Alexander, they completed the course of their martyrdom by beheading. Four hundred and forty-four others suffered martyrdom with them.

A. has this briefly and at the end: And the feast of Cyricus and Julitta, his mother, with four hundred and four martyrs. In V. there is simply mention of Quiricus and Julitta, his mother.

[Note: Quiricus. All Latins commemorate them today, but the Greeks do so in the Menologion on the Ides of July, where they say that they suffered martyrdom at Tarsus in Cilicia. Their acts, published in Surius, volume III, confirm this. Many Latin writers who report that they suffered at Antioch should be corrected on this point.]

L. and B. mark them: At Antioch. B.: In the city of Nantes, the feast of Saint Similinus.

[Note: Similinus. More correctly Similianus.]

In Africa, the feast of Saints Diogenes, Valerius, and Martia.

17.—XV KALENDS. At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Avitus, priest and confessor.

[Note: Avitus. He was abbot of Micy. It is highly probable that two Avituses flourished at the same time in the monastery of Micy. Bede, who celebrates one of them today, and Ado’s Martyrology, which celebrates the other on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, provide evidence for this view.

Gregory of Tours adds considerable support. In History III, chapter 6, he reports the prophecy of Saint Avitus, abbot of Micy, against King Chlodomer. In his book On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 99, however, he presents another Avitus, abbot of Perthe. But why, I ask, would Gregory call this abbot of Perthe the abbot of Micy if he did not believe that there were two Avituses?

In the Lives of Saint Carilefus and Saint Maximinus, abbot of Micy—the former written by Bertoldus and the latter by Siviardus, both published by Mabillon in the first volume of the Benedictine century—it is stated that Avitus withdrew from the monastery of Micy into the wilderness of Perthe, where he built a monastery with the aid of the king’s generosity and never returned to Micy. It therefore seems entirely probable that he is the same person whom Gregory of Tours calls the abbot of Perthe, and certainly distinct from Avitus, abbot of Micy.]

[Col. 0949B] Florus in A. T. L. adds: The account of whose life, among the other miracles of his virtues, attests that he raised a dead man.

It is not sufficiently certain, however, that this first entry belongs to Bede. For V. and C. read: At Rome, Cyriacus, Blasius, Nicander, Diogenes, and Avitus the presbyter. In A. T. L., the entries concerning Avitus occupy the final place, as is usually the case with material that truly belongs to Bede.

T. and L. begin: At Rome, near the Seven Columns, the passion of Saints Quiriacus, Blasius, and Diogenes; A. has: At Rome, the feast of Saint Quiriacus. Then all three manuscripts proceed in the same way: In Alexandria, the passion of Saints Dioscorus and Marinus, martyrs. At Orléans, etc.

B.: At Rome, the feast of Saints Nicander, Alexander, Dorostolus, Alexander, Dioscorus, and Marinus, martyrs. And of Saint Bartholomew, apostle.

[Note: Bartholomew. See below, August 25.]

And of Saint Elijah, prophet.

[Col. 0950B] 18.—XIV KALENDS. At Rome, of the holy martyrs Mark and Marcellianus.

[Note: Mark. They were noble by birth, namely sons of Tranquillinus and Marcia. After completing their martyrdom through various torments, they were buried at night on the Ardeatine Way. Peter de Natalibus. Saint Sebastian, in whose Acts they are mentioned, is commemorated on January 20.]

Florus adds in A. T. L.: Strengthened in the faith of Christ by the exhortations of Blessed Sebastian, they were bound to a stake under the prefect Fabianus and received spikes in their feet. There they remained for one day and one night in psalms and hymns, and both were struck through the sides with spears; by such a martyrdom they passed to the heavenly kingdoms. [Thus far A.] Written in the Acts of Blessed Sebastian.

V. and C. add: Cyriacus, Thomas the apostle [C. omits “apostle”], and Paul.

[Note: Cyriacus and Paul, or, according to Usuard, Paula. They suffered in the city of Málaga in Spain. After many torments had been inflicted upon them, they were buried beneath stones among the rocks and expired. Usuard; Peter de Natalibus.]

[Note: Thomas. The apostle. He will be treated on December 21.]

B.: At Ravenna, the feast of Saints Felix, Aemilius, and Crispinus. In Alexandria, the feast of Saint Marina.

[Note: Marina. She was her father’s only daughter. When he entered a monastery, he entrusted her to a relative. As he grieved for his daughter, the abbot asked him why he was sad. He replied that he had left an only son in the world, for he did not wish to reveal that the child was a daughter. Since the abbot loved the man, he allowed him to have his son received into the monastery.

When the father approached death, he called his daughter and confirmed her in her holy purpose. Once, when Marina had gone outside the monastery to obtain necessities and night prevented her from returning, she lodged in the house of a certain nobleman named Pandochius. When his daughter conceived a child by a soldier, she asserted that her brother Marinus had violated her.

Thus Marina, as though she had committed this crime, received undeserved punishment. When she died, her abbot ordered her body to be buried far from the monastery. But when the brothers were washing the body and saw that it was a woman, the abbot, confessing that he had sinned gravely, ordered her to be buried honorably inside the monastery.

Saint Marina is also commemorated on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, and perhaps she is the same as Marinus, who is commemorated on the preceding day. Hrabanus also mentions today a certain Marina who, after various torments, was beheaded by the prefect Olibrius.]

19.—XIII KALENDS. Of Saints Gervasius and Protasius at Milan.

[Note: Gervasius and Protasius. Florus, Peter de Natalibus, and others write that they suffered at this place under Nero, together with Nazarius and Celsus. But in the Acts of Gervasius and Protasius, said to have been written by Saint Ambrose from a booklet by Philip and published in Surius, volume III, there is no mention of Nazarius and Celsus; they are also said to have suffered under a different governor. For Nazarius and Celsus are reported to have suffered under Anulinus, Gervasius and Protasius under Astasius.

What especially leaves me uncertain is that the aforementioned Acts contain no mention of Nero or of any other individual emperor, but speak of several Augusti reigning together at that time, so that their martyrdom seems to belong to a period other than Nero’s. Moreover, since those Acts mention the Marcomannic War, it is clear that no such war was waged under Nero.

Since it is established from those Acts that several Augusti ruled together at that time and that the Marcomannic War had also broken out, we are compelled to adopt the view that they suffered during the reigns of the Augusti Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Verus, in the ninth year of whose rule the Marcomannic War began.

Indeed, neither Bede, nor Usuard, nor Ado, nor any other ancient writer, when discussing these martyrs or their father Vitalis, mentions Nero at all. Their bodies were discovered in the year 386, when the Ambrosian basilica was being dedicated by Saint Ambrose, and two days later—that is, on Friday—they were carried into that church. In the year mentioned, June 19 coincided with Friday. Therefore their feast is none other than the day of their translation. Pagi, year 387. See above, the feast of Saint Vitalis, namely April 28.]

[Col. 0951B] A. T. L. adds, perhaps from Florus: “Whom the emperor Nero, after various tortures, ordered the prefect Amilius to kill. Ambrose, when the Lord revealed it, found their tombs, and their bodies were so incorrupt that they seemed to have been killed that very day. When they were being brought into the city, a man who had long been blind received his sight by touching the bier.”

V. and C. add: “of the holy [Note: [Col. 0951D] Nazarius. See above, on the twelfth day of this month.] Nazarius and Celsus the boy”; but in manuscripts A. and T., the name “Celsus the boy” is joined to the preceding two. B.: “At Rome, Hippolytus, Honorius, Peter, [Note: [Col. 0951D] Valeria. She is perhaps the same Valeria who was the mother, and Vitalis the father, of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.] Valeria, Marcellinus, Vitalis.”

## 20.—XII Kalends

Bede has no entry.

D.: “At Rome, [Note: [Col. 0951D] Novatus. He was instructed not by the apostles, but rather, together with his father Saint Pudens, by Blessed Pius, Roman pontiff. See 19 May concerning Saint Pudens.] Novatus, brother of Timothy the presbyter; they were instructed by the apostles.”

B.: “At the city of Tomis, the feast of Saints Paul, Cyriacus, Feliciana, Felix, and Aemilius. On the same day, the passion of Saints Crispinus and Vitalis, martyrs.”

V. C.: “At the city of Tomis, Paul, Cyriacus, Paula, Felicia, Vitalis, and Crispinus.”

A. T.: “At the city of Tomis, the passion of Saint Crispinus the martyr, of Aemilius, and of Saint Felix.”

## 21.—XI Kalends

Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: “At Caesarea in Palestine, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0951D] Eusebius. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea and a most learned writer of ecclesiastical history, died in the year 340. Bernard de Montfaucon, in the Prolegomena to the Paris edition of Eusebius’s Commentaries on the Psalms, openly condemned him for Arian heresy. Because he favored the Arian party, Baronius, in his Notes, thinks that an error entered the Martyrologies, which improperly display Eusebius of Caesarea in place of Eusebius of Samosata, whom the Greeks also commemorate in the Menologion on the following day. But, as Florentinius says in his Notes on the Hieronymian Martyrology for 21 June, since Eusebius of Samosata earned the martyr’s crown not at Caesarea but at Doliche, a city of Syria on the Euphrates, according to Theodoret, book V, chapter 4, or received veneration in the church of Samosata itself, a city situated on the Euphrates, and since the name Caesarea is very different from the names Doliche or Samosata, another cause of this error seems likely. Since there are several Caesareas, the Eusebius commemorated in the Martyrologies today is none other than Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia and the immediate predecessor of Saint Basil. For in the ancient manuscript Martyrology of Saint Jerome, commonly called by learned men the Corbeiensis, one reads on this day: ‘At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Eusebius the bishop.’ Florentinius, cited above, proves this Eusebius’s holiness at length, and observes that Usuard was the first to number Eusebius of Palestine among the saints. Hence this error arose in the eighth or ninth century of the Church, when, for the sake of pious emperors, shorter accounts of the saints’ deeds began to be added to Martyrologies or catalogues of sacred names, even in the manuscripts of the martyrs. Since those pious martyrologists knew no Caesarean Eusebius of this name besides Eusebius of Palestine, who was famous through many editions of his books, many of them agreed in identifying the name with him and added his praises. Pagi, year 340, section 24.] Eusebius the confessor, who was exceedingly devoted to the divine Scriptures and, together with the martyr Pamphilus, a most diligent investigator of the divine library.”

D.: “At Syracuse, Rufinus. At Rome, [Note: [Col. 0952D] Demetria. She was the daughter of Blessed Faustus. When she was brought before the impious Julian on account of her faith in Christ, she gave up her spirit while confessing it. She was buried by Blessed John the presbyter beside her mother Dafrosa and her sister Bibiana, near the Licinian palace. Ado, Usuard, Notker.] Demetria the virgin.”

V. C.: “Saturninus, Quiriacus, Apollinaris, Januaria, Rufinus, and Marcia.” [V. omits Apollinaris and Januaria.]

A. T.: “In Africa, the feast of Saints Saturninus and Quiriacus.”

B.: “In Africa, Saturninus. At Caesarea, the burial of Eusebius the bishop. On that same day, at Mainz, Saint [Note: [Col. 0952D] Albinus. Also Albanus. Under the emperor Theodosius, he came from the island of Namsia to Milan with Saints Theonestus and Ursus. Departing from there, with the Lord’s help he reached Gaul and, remaining in God’s service, was ready for martyrdom in Christ’s name. After Blessed Ursus received martyrdom at the city of Augusta, Theonestus and Albanus reached Mainz. While Albanus was preaching the word of God there, he completed his martyrdom and was buried near the city. Rabanus, Notker. There is great disagreement among writers about the date of this martyrdom. Some, mistakenly judging that he was the same as Albanus, the British protomartyr, report that he suffered under Diocletian. Others, however, such as Peter de Natalibus, X, 97, and Galesinius, when discussing Theonestus, his companion in martyrdom, on 30 October, assert that he was killed by the Arians in the time of Damasus. Sigebert differs from all of these in his Chronicle, reporting that the martyrdom of Albanus and his companions occurred in the year 425.] Albanus the martyr. In Sicily, Rufinus and Martia. Likewise in Africa, Quiriacus and Apollinaris.”

[Col. 0953B]

## 22.—X Kalends

“At Verulamium in Britain, Saint [Note: [Col. 0953D] Albanus. Concerning his martyrdom and that of his companions, see Bede’s Ecclesiastical History I, 7.] Albanus the martyr.”

A. adds: “with eight hundred and eighty-eight others. He was beheaded in the city of Verulamium during the reign of the emperor Diocletian, after scourging and cruel tortures; but when he fell to the ground, the eyes of the man who struck him also fell out.” (Thus far A.) “One of the soldiers also suffered with him because he refused to strike him when ordered to do so. He had been terrified by the divine miracle, for he had seen the blessed martyr, while hastening toward the crown of martyrdom, make the channel of the intervening river passable by prayer.”

V. and C. add: “And with him eight hundred and eighty-nine others were placed at Cathalacum, whose names are written in the book of life.”

B. prefaces this: “At the city of Alexandria, the feast of Saint Rufus; and the feast of Saint James the apostle; and the feast of one thousand four hundred and eighty saints.” (Thus far L.)

B.: “At the city of Nola, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0953D] Paulinus. He was originally from Bordeaux, a town of Gaul. He took Therasia as a wife, who was like him in character. When Italy, especially the regions of Campania, had been ravaged during the time of the Vandals’ attacks, and many people from that land had been taken to Africa, Paulinus gave all his possessions to the captives and the poor. When he had nothing more to give, a certain widow asked him to redeem her son with money; he gave himself into servitude in order to redeem the boy and worked in cultivating a garden until he was freed, together with many others, and returned to his flock. Saint Paulinus, bishop, died under the consuls Basso and Antiochus, that is, about the year 431. Surius, volume III. Paulinus remained captive under Guntharic, king of the Vandals, not under Alaric, as Balduinus conjectured in his notes on Optatus.] Paulinus the bishop.”

Florus in A. T. L.: “On the same day, at Nola” (the place is missing in A.), “the burial of Saint Paulinus the bishop and confessor, who, being very rich and wealthy, sold everything he had for the word of the Lord and gave it to the poor. Afterwards, when he became a bishop, he shone with such multiplied virtue and gifts of grace that, at his death, he saw with bodily eyes Saint Martin and Saint Januarius, the Italian bishop, before he gave up his spirit; for they had departed from this world before him.”

## 23.—IX Kalends

“Saint [Note: [Col. 0954D] Æthelthryth. See Bede’s Ecclesiastical History IV, 19–20.] Æthelthryth” [V. and C.: “Etheldryth”], “virgin and queen in Britain, whose body, after having been buried for eleven years, was found incorrupt. And the vigil of Saint John the Baptist.”

B.: “At [Note: [Col. 0954D] Nicomedia. Pistis, Elpis, and Agape, and their mother Sophia. Notker.] Nicomedia, the passion of the holy virgins Pistis, Elpis, and Agape, their mother Sophia, Capito, and seventy-eight others.”

## 24.—VIII Kalends

“The Nativity of the Lord’s Forerunner.”

Florus in A. T. L.: “On the same day, at Augusta of the Veromandui, on the river Somme, the discovery by Eusebia of the body of Blessed [Note: [Col. 0954D] Quintinus. See 31 October concerning his passion. His body was discovered about the year 342.] Quintinus the martyr, outstanding in holiness.”

[T. continues:] “For the same noblewoman, having received a revelation from an angel, came to the district and to the place on the river where the body had lain for fifty-five years. After proclaiming a prayer, she received it, coming toward her with extraordinary brightness and fragrance, without any stain of corruption. When she wished to bury it in the town of Vermand, it became so heavy that it could not be moved farther from the place which it had consecrated with its blood. In return for the benefits she had rendered, the finder herself received back the sight she had lost; and all who happened to come there at that same hour recovered their former health.”
