B. C. V.: “At Rome, Saints Sixtus and Lucius.”

B. C.: “with twenty-two others.”

A. T. L. B.: “At Autun, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 0955C] Simplicius.—He succeeded Egmonius in the bishopric of Autun. He flourished under the emperor Constantius and, together with Saint Servatius, attended the Council of Cologne, held in 346 against Euphrates, bishop of that city. See more about him in Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapters 76–78.] Simplicius the bishop and confessor.”

## 25.—VII Kalends

Bede has no entry.

D.: “At Beroea in Pyrrhus,” [Note: [Col. 0955C] Sosipater. At Beroea of Pyrrhus. Origen says in his Letter to the Romans that he was ordained bishop of Thessalonica, although Dorotheus asserts in his Synopsis that he occupied the see of Iconium and was one of the seventy-two disciples.] “Sosipater, disciple of the apostle Paul.”

C. V.: “Lamptas, Salunica” [C.: “Lalunica”], [Note: [Col. 0955D] Luceia. Luceia, a virgin, and Anceias, her temporal lord, suffered martyrdom at Rome in the time of Diocletian. Of Roman origin, she was captured by Anceias, king of the barbarians, and brought to his homeland. When the barbarian wished to violate her, he heard from her that she had God as her bridegroom and that he would avenge her defilement; he was afraid and treated her reverently. Through her prayers the same king also triumphed several times over his enemies, and for this reason he was converted to Christ and set the virgin free. When she wished to return to her homeland, Anceias abandoned his kingdom and followed the virgin all the way to Rome, where both were struck down with the sword. Peter de Natalibus. It is wrongly said here that Lucia suffered at Thessalonica.] “Luceia the virgin and Accegas the king” [V.: “Accegas Rina”].

L.: “The feast of Saint Lucia the virgin and King Auceus, with nine others.”

A. and T.: “At the city of Thessalonica, the feast of Saint [Col. 0956B] Lucia the virgin. And the feast of Saint Agapitus.”

A.: “And of Saint Amantius the bishop. The translation of [Note: [Col. 0955D] Eligius and Vindicianus. Eligius’s burial is celebrated on 1 December; Vindicianus’s on 11 March.] Eligius and Vindicianus in the first place.”

T.: “On the same day, Saint [Note: [Col. 0956C] Lietbuin. If this is the same person as Lebuinus the presbyter, he was of English origin. Leaving his homeland, he went to Utrecht and was sent by Saint Gregory the bishop, together with Saint Marcellinus, to the river IJssel and the regions beyond it, where he preached. After the conversion of many and many labors, he died at Deventer and was buried in the cathedral church. His burial is celebrated on 12 November; his translation on 25 June. Molanus, On the Saints of Belgium; Ghinius the Elder.] Lietbuin the bishop and confessor, and King Auceus with eight others.”

B.: “At Thessalonica, Lamptas and Bigitta. At Genelaicum, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0956D] Amandus. At Gemelaicum, with Domnolenus. Molanus, in Usuard, remembers them on the preceding day, and Ferrarius says that they suffered at Limoges.] Amandus the confessor.”

## 26.—VI Kalends

“At Rome, Saints [Note: [Col. 0956D] John and Paul. See more about them in Ado, Notker, and Peter de Natalibus.] John and Paul, of whom the first was superintendent and the second chief secretary of Constantina, the virgin daughter of Constantine. Later, under Julian, they earned martyrdom by beheading at the hands of Terentianus, the commander of the troops; he afterwards became a Christian.”

T. and L. add, as we think from Florus: “When he had destroyed a certain idol in a certain place and was sitting on the base of that idol preaching the divine word, the inhabitants of that place overwhelmed him with a rain of stones, and thus he was crowned with the glory of martyrdom.”

The same source in A. T. L.: “On that day, at Valenciennes, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 0956D] Salvius. Bishop of Engolism, who, scattering the seeds of God’s word throughout Aquitaine, came with a companion named Superius to the city of Valenciennes. He wished to go to Condat, to the monastery of Blessed Mary. On the journey itself, in a village called Beviticum, he was struck on the head with an axe by order of a certain tyrant, Winegarius, acting on the command of his master Winegardus, and suffered martyrdom with the companion mentioned above. Both bodies were placed in a stable and, after three years, were discovered by the emperor Charlemagne through divine revelation. They were buried at the place where the priory of Saint Salvius now stands. The monastery is outside Valenciennes, in the diocese of Cambrai. His martyrdom is commemorated on 26 June, his translation on 7 September, and his elevation on 15 October. Molanus, On the Saints of Belgium. His martyrdom occurred in the year 801, according to Sigebert in his Chronicle.] Salvius the bishop and martyr.”

T.: “who, leaving his own people for Christ’s name and entering Gaul, attained the martyr’s crown.”

T. A.: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Nicholas.”

B.: “At Alexandria, Agatho and Diogenes.”

C.: “In Africa, Gaudentius, Felix, Agapitus, Agatho, and Diogenes.”

## 27.—V Kalends

Bede has no entry.

D.: “In Galatia, Blessed [Note: [Col. 0957C] Crescentius. Passing into Gaul, he converted many to the faith by the word of preaching. He occupied the see of Vienne in Gaul for several years and there ordained Zacharias as bishop in his place, as Ado declares both in his Martyrology and in his Chronicle. He likewise remained at Mainz as its first bishop, as the complete lists of the bishops of Mainz recited by Demochares indicate. Returning to the people to whom he had been specially given as bishop—the Galatians—he strengthened them in the faith of Christ until the end of his life and finally completed his martyrdom under Trajan, about the year 100. Ghinius the Elder.] Crescentius, disciple of the apostle Paul.”

V. C.: “At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, at the ninth milestone, Crispus, Crispinianus, and Felix. [Note: [Col. 0957C] Seven brothers. These were the seven sons of Saints Symphorosa and Getulius, martyrs. They all suffered various tortures under the emperor Hadrian at the city of Tibur and, after their passion, were thrown into a deep pit. Their bodies rest at the ninth milestone on the Tiburtine Way. Ado. They are also commemorated above, on 29 May.] Seven brothers.”

B. adds the fourth name, Spinella.

A. T. L.: “[Col. 0958B] At Rome, Crispinus” [L.: “Crispus”] “and Crispinianus. On the same day, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 0957D] Vigilius. While trying completely to eradicate the remnants of idolatry, he was struck by wild and barbarous men with a rain of stones and completed his martyrdom for Christ, during the consulship of Stilicho. Baronius, Usuard. Stilicho’s first consulship is placed in the year 400. Saint Vigilius lived in the time of Saints Ambrose and Simplicianus and died a martyr either during that first consulship of Stilicho or at least during the second, which fell in the year 405. The authorities mentioned above commemorate him on the preceding day.] Vigilius, bishop of the city of Trent. And at Ephesus” (the place is absent from A.), “the seven [Note: [Col. 0957D] Sleepers. At Ephesus. Fleeing the persecution of Decius, they hid in a cave on Mount Caelius, where they slept until the thirtieth year of the emperor Theodosius, son of Arcadius. Baronius commemorates them on 27 July.] sleeping brothers,” whose names T. lists as “Maximian, Malchus, Martinian, Constantine, Dionysius, John, and Serapion.”

T. L.: “On the same day, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 0957D] Irenaeus. He will be discussed on the following day.] Irenaeus and his companions.”

B.: “In Spain, Crescentius, Julian, Eugenius, and Novatian. On the island of [Note: [Col. 0957D] Via. According to the Additions to the Martyrology, this word is called Oia; according to Molanus in his additions to Usuard, Hoia.] Via, the translation of Saint Florentius.”

## 28.—IV Kalends

“The vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul. On that day, Saint [Note: [Col. 0957D] Leo. After Agatho had died and been buried on 10 January 681, Leo II succeeded him. But this did not happen, as Anastasius writes, after an interregnum of one year, seven months, and five days; for since Agatho administered the Roman Church for three years and several months, as seems certain, the see could not have remained vacant for so long after his death. Therefore Onuphrius, in his Chronicle, reduced the interregnum to seven months. That interregnum was either incorrectly copied by scribes or was unknown even to Anastasius. Since Saint Leo was ordained on 17 August 682, the see was vacant for only seven months and seven days, excluding the day of death. Anastasius also writes that Leo sat for ten months and seventeen days and was buried on 3 July; Ordericus, book II, and Marianus Scotus likewise state in their Chronicles that he died on that day, and no one in all antiquity assigned him a longer pontificate. Since he was ordained on 17 August 682, he died the following year, on 3 July. That date cannot be referred to one of his translations. Nor is it an objection that this Leo is commemorated on 28 June, for in ancient records of the Church that date had previously been sacred to Leo I, as Quesnellus demonstrates at length in volume II of his Works of Saint Leo, dissertation 1, on his life and deeds down to the year 461. He adduces numerous proofs of this from ancient historians, Martyrologies, and similar books. Nevertheless, he wrongly argues there that Leo II died on that day. He says that scarcely any other reason can be imagined why this feast was attached particularly to that day, even after Leo I’s feast had been removed from it, than that it was known in the Roman Church that Leo II had died on that date. But 28 June was assigned to the feast of Leo II because, when it pleased the apostolic see to honor him with a liturgical office, that date was preferred to the others because Leo the Great had been honored on it for many centuries; at that time his memory had been transferred to 11 April, the day on which his first translation had occurred. Pagi, years 682 and 684.] Leo the pope.”

[Col. 0959A]

A. T. L.: “At Alexandria, Saints [Note: [Col. 0959B] Serenus. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI, 3, mentions two Sereni: one completed his martyrdom by fire, the other by beheading.] Serenus and Theodore.”

B.: “In Africa, Fabianus, Felix, Venustus, and Crescentius. At Alexandria, the feast of Saints Serenus and Theodore.”

“At Lyons in Gaul, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0959B] Irenaeus. He was Greek by birth. The holy man relates in his letter to Florinus, a fragment of which Eusebius quotes, that while he was still a boy—or, as he says in his work Against Heresies, in the earliest part of his life—he heard Polycarp, already very old, and was instructed by him in the first principles of the Christian religion. Since Polycarp suffered martyrdom about the year 166, we shall not be far from the truth if we say that Irenaeus was born about the year 140. How long he had lived in the East cannot be determined, since the ancients are silent about it. This is certain: Irenaeus went to Gaul and came to Lyons, but exactly when, by whom, and for what reason he was sent is entirely uncertain. From Jerome’s words it may be inferred that he was ordained a presbyter by Saint Pothinus, bishop of Lyons, for Jerome calls him the presbyter of Bishop Pothinus. How admirably he conducted himself as a presbyter is sufficiently shown by the words with which the martyrs of Lyons commend his piety in Eusebius V, 4, in the letters they wrote to Pope Eleutherus and entrusted to Irenaeus for delivery. Around the beginning of the persecution under Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, after Bishop Pothinus had died, about the year 177, Saint Irenaeus was appointed in his place and consecrated at Rome by Blessed Eleutherus. To adorn the province he had received more worthily, he spared no labor: he refuted heretics by word and writing and labored greatly to restore unity among the Churches, especially in settling the controversy over Easter. For this reason he peacefully admonished Victor, Roman pontiff, by letter, when Victor was preparing to anathematize the Churches of Asia. He was beheaded during the persecution of Severus in the year 202. In Gregory of Tours’s time his body rested buried in the crypt of the basilica of Blessed John, beneath the altar, with Epipodius on one side and Alexander on the other. But when Lyons was captured in 1562, the Calvinists, driven by insane fury, shamefully violated the holy martyr’s tomb. After the bones were scattered, the skull was disgracefully thrown into the middle of the street and lay there until it was rescued; it is now piously preserved at Lyons. René Massuet, second preliminary dissertation to the books of Irenaeus.] Irenaeus, with six others.”

## 29.—III Kalends

“At Rome, the feast of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0959D] Peter. They suffered in the year of Christ 65, under the consuls Nerva and Vestinus, as is read in the Catalogue of the ancient pontiffs—not in the year 67, or, which is the same thing according to Baronius, in the year 69. For, according to the common tradition, they suffered in Nero’s presence, on 29 June; yet it is completely certain that Nero was absent from Rome on that date in the year 67. In the second place, they were killed not after Nero’s return from the East, but before Nero departed for the East. Some also thought that the martyrdom of these apostles occurred on 22 February, because the following is read under that date in the Laterculus of Silvius: ‘The burial of Saints Peter and Paul.’ From these words they inferred that Peter and Paul did not suffer on 29 June, or 20 June, as some have it, but on 22 February. This inference is futile. In ancient times, as now, the Chair of Saint Peter at Antioch was celebrated on 22 February. In the Index of the burial of the martyrs apud Bucherium, one reads on that day: ‘The feast of Peter of the Chair.’ The relics of the saints, however, were often translated on the same days as their feasts. Therefore, where the Laterculus of Silvius reads under 22 February the burial of Saints Peter and Paul, we understand that their relics were translated on the day when Peter was already being celebrated at Antioch. The ancients often expressed the translation of saints by the term ‘burial,’ as numerous examples show. Thus, in the year 258, when Saint Sixtus, Roman pontiff, wished to transfer the bodies of these apostles to the Catacombs, he chose no other day than 29 June, dedicated to their feast, as we learn from the Index cited above: ‘29 June: Peter at the Catacombs and Paul at the Ostian Way, under the consuls Tuscus and Bassus.’ Not understanding these words, Bucherius says in the margin that the consuls’ names must have been corrupted, convinced that the passage concerned the martyrdom of the holy apostles, although it concerns a translation performed on their feast day. The distinguished Pearson, in his Annals of Cyprian under the year 258, when Tuscus and Bassus were consuls, thinks that the martyrdom of the apostles occurred on one day and their translation on another, and that the solemnity and feast followed the translation. He also thinks that, before the time of Pseudo-Isidore and the publication of the Pontifical Acts, another day was assigned to their feast, and that this is clear from the Laterculus of Silvius. But the learned man is mistaken. During Sixtus’s pontificate, the relics of Peter and Paul, previously kept at the Vatican and on the Ostian Way, were transferred to the Catacombs on 29 June, the day on which their solemnity was customarily celebrated. See more in Pagi, year 67, sections 3–4.] Peter and Paul.”

Florus adds in T. and L.: “Peter was crowned with martyrdom by crucifixion at the command of the emperor Nero, and Paul by beheading.”

The manuscript V. contains longer encomia of each, beginning with the etymology of their names, which we omit, as well as similar encomia of the other apostles, inscribed under the days assigned or to be assigned to each. They contribute nothing to distinguishing the texts of Bede or Florus and are found elsewhere.

B.: “And the feast of Saint Novatian the martyr, with nine hundred and seventy-eight other martyrs.”

C.: “And of [Note: [Col. 0960D] Others. They suffered at Rome.] nine hundred and seventy-eight other martyrs.”

[Col. 0961B]

## 30.—II Kalends

Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: “At the city of Limoges, the burial of [Note: [Col. 0961B] Martial. He is said to have been present when Christ fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish and when he washed the disciples’ feet at the supper. After the Passion, he remained with Blessed Peter, accompanying him to Galilee, Antioch, and Rome. Peter ordained him bishop and sent him to preach in Gaul with two presbyters, Alpinianus and Austriclinianus. On this journey, passing through Etruria and Tuscany, he is said to have converted some at Siena and in the Val di Chiana. After entering Gaul, he preached the word especially at Limoges and was its first bishop. It is also said that he established the episcopal Churches of Le Puy, Rodez, Clermont, Mende, Bourges, Toulouse, and others. In these places he built various basilicas in honor of God, Blessed Mary, Saint Stephen, and Saint Peter, and confirmed his preaching with miracles. Finally, worn out by old age, he died in peace in the year of the Lord 74, during the reign of Vespasian Augustus, after twenty-eight years as bishop, and was buried at Limoges. Ghinius the Elder, Peter de Natalibus. Gregory of Tours is notably mistaken in book I, chapter 30, when he says that Martial came to Gaul with the others whom he lists there during the reign of the emperor Decius.] Martial the bishop, who was one of the seventy-two.”

T. L.: “who was sent from Rome by Blessed Peter into Gaul and began to preach in the city of Limoges; after overthrowing the rites of the idols and filling the city with belief in God, he departed from this age.”

A. T.: “At the city of Angers, the translation of the body of [Note: [Col. 0962B] Albinus. His body was buried and for some time lay in the basilica of Saint Peter at Angers. Not long afterwards it was transferred by Eutropius, his successor, and Saint Germanus of Paris, together with other bishops of the province, to the basilica then dedicated to Saint Germanus of Auxerre. From that time it became especially famous under the name and title of this holy bishop, and his body was placed in the part of the basilica called the confession. From the monastic breviary of Saint Albinus of Angers, published by Mabillon. In volume I of the Acts of the Benedictine Saints, Mabillon writes in his notes that this translation took place in 556 or 555, when Germanus assumed the see of Paris, six years after Albinus’s death. Another translation of this saint took place in 1128 on 1 March, the very day on which his burial is celebrated.] Albinus the bishop and confessor.”

V.: “[Note: [Col. 0962C] Commemoration. It is celebrated today because the feast of both apostles could not be celebrated on the same day in the liturgy, and one of them would otherwise lack a separate office. Pope Gregory therefore ordered that on the day on which they had suffered the solemnity of Peter should be held, and on the following day the commemoration of Paul.] Commemoration.”

C.: “The feast of Saint Paul the apostle.”

C.: “And the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 0962C] Timothy. They suffered in Africa. Notker.] Timothy, Zotichus, and Pamphilus.”

B.: “At Limoges, the burial of Saint Martial the bishop and confessor. At the city of Angers, the translation of the body of Saint Albinus the bishop.”

# [JULY]

[Col. 0961D]

## 1.—Kalends

Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: “At Rome, the feast of the holy virgins [Note: [Col. 0961] Faith. They are said to have suffered at Nicomedia above, on 23 June.] Faith, Hope, and Charity, and their mother Sophia. The first, when she was twelve years old, was slaughtered by order of Hadrian with excessive bloodshed, torn by the cutting off of her breasts, placed upon a grating, laid in a frying pan, and finally killed by the sword. The second, after being long beaten with sinews, was thrown into the fire, cruelly tortured and beaten, and boiled in a bronze vessel filled with pitch and resin; since she was not consumed, she died by the sword. The third was hung upon the rack and thrown into a furnace, but was protected by angels; afterwards she received the sentence of beheading. Their mother, thrown down at their tomb, was overcome by sleep and rested in peace. It is written in their Acts.”

The entry is absent—an extremely rare occurrence—from the supplement D., unless it was written in by a later hand: “Ecolesma [Note: [Col. 0963B] Esparsi. Eparchius is better. He came from the city of Périgueux; his father was named Felix and his mother Principia. He was first appointed secretary of his grandfather Felicissimus, the count. After spending fifteen years with him, he went to the monastery of Sedaciacum and became a monk. Finally, coming to Angoulême, he built himself a cell in which, after gathering a few monks, he remained constantly in prayer. If Gregory of Tours VI, 8, is interpreted correctly, Eparchius died in the sixth year of Childebert the Younger, corresponding to the year 581, not after forty-four years of enclosure, as it reads there, but after thirty-nine, as it correctly reads here, since Aptonius, under whom Eparchius withdrew, obtained the see of Angoulême after the year 541.] Esparsi the presbyter and confessor.”

V. C.: “At Rome, [Note: [Col. 0963C] Gaius. See 22 April concerning him.] Gaius the pope. And the holy [Note: [Col. 0963C] Lucius. Their celebration was mentioned on 25 June.] Lucius the virgin and Accegas the king, with eight others.”

V. C. B.: “And on Mount Hor, the burial of Aaron, the first priest.”

A.: “The feast of Saint Gaius the pope, [Col. 0964A] [Note: [Col. 0963C] Carilefus. A native of Auvergne, he was educated in letters at the monastery of Menat in the diocese of Clermont. Desiring the eremitical life, he embarked with Avitus, a monk of the same monastery, and reached the outskirts of Orléans. Having heard of the reputation of Saint Maximin, abbot of Micy, they both approached him, stayed for some time in his monastery, and were ordained priests. Desiring a more remote dwelling, they left the monastery and wandered through the vast solitudes of the Perthe forest. They settled in a fertile place called Piciacus. Blessed Carilefus, however, leaving Avitus in those regions and taking with him two companions, Daumerus and Gallus, finally reached a place then called Casa Gaiani, situated in the parish of Labrocinium. Near this place flowed the river Anisola, where he built a cell. He died about the year 540. He flourished during the reigns of the Frankish kings Childebert and Chlotar.] Carilefus the confessor, and the octave of Saint John.”

T.: “On the same day, Saint Kerlefus, who shone through good works and signs of miracles. At Rome, the burial of Gaius the pope. And the passion of Saints Esicius, Serenus, and Victor.”

L.: “On that day, at Rheims, Saint [Note: [Col. 0963D] Theodoricus. His father, Marchardus, came from the district of Rheims and the village called the Court of the Alamanni. He was a disciple of Blessed Remigius the bishop. To obey his parents, he took a bride, but did not have relations with her and persuaded her to preserve virginity. Sent by Blessed Remigius to Mount Hor, three miles from the city of Rheims, he built a monastery. Among his other signs of virtue, he restored the daughter of King Theodoricus to life by prayers and anointing with oil. To establish the date of Saint Theodoricus’s death, we have two chronological indications: one derived from King Theodoricus, who carried the holy man’s body to the tomb on his own shoulders; the other from Romanus, bishop of Rheims, who, according to Adalgisus in the Book of the Miracles of Saint Theodoricus, arranged the funeral. Romanus succeeded Saint Remigius in the see of Rheims not in 545, as Sigebert thought, but about the year 532, since Flavius, Romanus’s successor, signed the Council of Auvergne in 532. King Theodoricus died, Gregory of Tours says in III, 5, in the twenty-third year of his reign, that is, in the year 534. Therefore the year of Saint Theodoricus’s death must be assigned to the year of Christ 533.] Theodoricus the confessor.”

B.: “At the monastery of Anisola, the burial of Saint Carilefus the presbyter. In Mesopotamia, Zelius with six others; Orion with eight others; and two hundred and seventy-four others. At Autun, the burial of Leontius the bishop and Quintianus the confessor.”

## 2.—VI Nones

“At Rome, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 0964C] Processus. They suffered during the reign of the emperor Nero. While Blessed Peter and Paul were being held in custody by the prefect Paulinus, these two men, seeing the miracles performed by the apostles, were converted to the faith and baptized by Blessed Peter. When Paulinus tried to turn them away from the true faith and could not do so, although he subjected them to many tortures, he finally ordered their heads to be cut off with the sword. Rabanus.] Processus and Martinianus.”

These are read as follows in A, B, and T:

At Rome, the feast of Saints Damasus, Processus, and Martinianus, soldiers. [Note: Damasus. Ado corrects this passage as follows, and the supposed Bede likewise: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Damasus, the feast of Saints Processus and Maximianus.”] V, C, and B add: “And the deposition of Pope Melchiades.” [Note: His day of death is 10 January; see that date. In the Chronicle of Damasus we read: “Melchiades, for three years, six months, and nine days, from the sixth day before the Nones of July, in the consulship of Maximianus for the eighth time alone”—which was in September, under Volusianus and Rufinus—“until the third day before the Ides of January, under the consuls Volusianus and Annianus.” Melchiades, therefore, who was ordained on 2 July 310, departed to God on 10 January 314, while Volusianus and Annianus were consuls, after having held office for three years, six months, and nine days if the day of his death is included, or eight days if it is excluded. What Anastasius relates—that Melchiades was buried on the third day before the Ides of December, the day on which he is now also commemorated, and on which Baronius believed him to have died—must be understood only of some translation of his remains, which is designated by the term “burial,” as often happens. His ordination is celebrated today.]

A: “The body of Saint Vedastus was discovered.” [Note: Under the abbot Adelard of Vedastinum, by authority of Saint Theodoricus, bishop of Cambrai, the body of Saint Vedastus was raised because of the Norman persecution, in the year and on the day mentioned here; and in the following year it was restored to its place on 4 June. Bollandists, 6 February, on which day he is also commemorated above.] This occurred in the year 852 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

B: At Tours, the deposition of Saint Monegunda, virgin. [Note: She was a widow, but a religious woman, and for that reason is honored under the title of virgin. She was a native of the city of Chartres. After leaving her cell, in which, once deprived of her daughters, she had led a solitary life, she went to Tours. There, in a small cell belonging to the church of Saint Martin, she gathered a few nuns and established a rigorous way of life. Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 19. She was buried in the church of Saint Peter the Maiden, where her relics were preserved in a precious shrine until 1562, when the enraged Calvinists plundered it.]

L: The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. [Note: This solemnity was instituted by Urban VI and confirmed and promulgated by Boniface IX.]

Florus, in A, T, and L: At Tours, Saint Monegunda, who, deprived of her two daughters and rejecting the companionship of her husband, hastened to Christ; out of love for him she shut herself up in a small cell, where she shone through great abstinence, both before and after her passing, by the multitude of her miracles.

### 3.—The third day before the Nones

The translation of Saint Thomas the Apostle at Edessa from India. [Note: Edessa. In that city there is an outstanding church dedicated to Saint Thomas, and a great multitude of people frequently gathered there because of the sanctity of the place. Socrates IV.14; Sozomen VI.18. See below, on his feast day.]

B adds: “He suffered in India on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.”

A, T, and L: At Alexandria, the feast of Saints Menelaus, Ammonius [L: Ammon], and Cyril.

B: At Alexandria, Tryphon, Menelaus, Cyril, and Julian; at Constantinople, Euphemia, Acacius, and Demetrius.

### 4.—The fourth day before the Nones

At Tours, the translation of Saint Martin the Confessor, or his episcopal ordination, or the dedication of his basilica. [Note: According to Gregory of Tours, *History* X.31, Martin held office for twenty-six years, four months, and twenty-seven days. Since Saint Martin gave up his spirit to God on 11 November 400, it is clear that his ordination fell in the year 374, on 15 June, which was a Sunday. His ordination is indeed celebrated on the fourth day before the Nones of July, as various martyrologies teach, besides *History of the Franks* II.14. But just as the ordination of Saint Basil, which is paired with 14 June in the church calendars, did not take place on that day, so Saint Martin’s ordination did not take place on 4 July. The Tours historian, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin* I.6, testifies that in the sixty-fourth year after Saint Martin’s passing—that is, in the year 461 according to Gregory’s reckoning, which counts this epoch from 397—the episcopal chair of Tours came to Perpetuus, and that he wished Saint Martin’s relics to be honored in a larger church than the one Bricius had built. He therefore built a basilica in Saint Martin’s honor and summoned neighboring bishops and abbots to dedicate it on the Kalends of July and transfer Saint Martin’s relics into it. But when the earth “which was above the holy tomb could not be dug up,” one of the clergy said to him: “Know that after three days it was accustomed to be the feast of his episcopate; perhaps he is warning you that he ought to be transferred on this day,” as the Tours historian relates in the passage cited, adding that this indeed happened. This translation took place in the year 473, which was the hundredth year after his ordination. Pagi, on the year 374, book VI, and elsewhere.]

Florus, in A, T, and L: At Rome, the feast of Zoe. [Note: Usuardus, Ado, the supposed Bede, Baronius, and all the others treat her on the following day.] She was the wife of Nicostratus (thus far L), and had been mute for six years because of the severity of an illness. She was cured by Saint Sebastian and became a most devoted Christian. While she was praying at the tomb of Saint Peter on the feast of the apostles, she was seized by lurking pagans and taken to the patron of the district, Naumachius. [Note: More correctly, *Naumachia*, as it is written in the Acts of Saint Sebastian edited by Bollandus under 20 January. There were several naumachiae in the city: one in Region 9, Domitian’s district; others in Regions 13 and 14; and two across the Tiber. Baronius, under the year 286, no. 13, believes that this occurred across the Tiber, and that at that time new assignments were made to particular places and people for the purpose of seeking out Christians, so that several patron-officials were assigned to one district of the city, each seeking Christians in the area entrusted to him.]

She was compelled to burn a drop of incense before a little statue of Mars that stood there. (Thus far A.) Laughing at this, she was thrown into a very dark prison, where for five days she saw neither light nor received food or drink, while the jailer threatened her. When six days had passed, she was ordered to be hung by the neck and hair from a tall tree, with smoke from a dung heap applied beneath her. Suspended there, she gave up her spirit in confession of the Lord. Her persecutors took her body, tied it to a stone, and submerged it in the bed of the Tiber, saying: “Let Christians not take it and make her their goddess.” This is written in the Acts of Saint Sebastian.

C, V: And the feast of Saint Laurianus. [Note: John Vasaeus, in his *Chronicle of Spain* under the year 544, writes: “At this time those who wrote about the saints of Spain commit to memory Saint Laureanus, archbishop of Seville, a Pannonian by birth. When Torila, then ruling the Ostrogoths in Italy as an Arian, sent men to kill him, he went into voluntary exile at the admonition of an angel; and seven years later, by the command of that same Totila, he was beheaded in Gaul. His head was carried to Seville and restored to the city, which had suffered many calamities during that entire seven-year period. His body was piously buried by Saint Eusebius, bishop of Arles, at Bituricum—read *Bituricensis* and understand not the metropolis itself, but another city called Vastinum or Vatan. His passion is described by Philippe Labbe, *Bibliotheca Nova*, vol. II, p. 411, who says that Laurianus’s persecutor should rather be called Agila, who at that time ruled the Visigoths in Spain, than Totila.”]

Laurianus the martyr, whose head was carried to Spain [C: was carried to Seville]. But A, T, and L read: “At Bituricas, the passion of Saint Laurianus the martyr, whose head was carried to Spain.”

B: In Sirmium, Sabbatia and Innocent with thirty others. At Bituricum, the feast of Saint Laurianus, bishop and martyr.

### 5.—The third day before the Nones

Bede is silent.

D: In Syria, Saint Donatus the martyr. [Note: More correctly, Domitius, as Usuardus, Ado, and Baronius testify; Gregory of Tours discusses him in *On the Glory of the Martyrs* I.100. For some reason Baronius distinguishes him from the man praised by Gregory.]

At Rome, Zoe, the wife of Nicostratus. [Note: The same Zoe was treated on the preceding day.]

C, V: In Sicily, Agatho, Tryphon, Ferator [Ferator appears only in C], Theodosius, and Secundinus.

A, T, and L: At Tomis, the feast of Saints Theodotus and Secundinus.

A, T: At Alexandria, Saint Arpotas.

T, L, and B: In Sicily, the passion of Saints Agatho and Tryphon.

B: At Tomis, Strator, Theodorus, Rodophia, and Secundinus. At Alexandria, Erpotas.

### 6.—The second day before the Nones

[Note: Isaiah. He was cut in two under King Manasseh and died; he was buried beneath the oak of Rogel, near the crossing of the waters. Baronius.]

The prophet Isaiah and the octave of the apostles.

Florus, in A, T, and L: At Rome, the passion of Saint Tranquillinus. [Note: See the Acts of Sebastian in Bollandus under 20 January.] He was the father of Mark and Marcellianus [A: Petris], and through the teaching of Saint Sebastian became a most devoted Christian. When he had gone to the shrine of Saint Paul, he was ambushed, seized, and stoned by the people; he died, and his body was committed to the waters of the Tiber. This is written in the Acts of Saint Sebastian.

B: In Syria, Zotices, Amandus, and Arteris. At Autun, the deposition of Saint Leontius, bishop. At Alexandria, Arthotas and Zetes.

B and L: And at Binga, the feast of Saint Goar, the Confessor. [Note: In the district of Trier. He was born in the province of Aquitaine. In the time of Hildebert, king of the Franks, he abandoned his homeland and parents and resolved to serve God in the province adjoining the Rhine, called Trigoria, which belongs to the diocese of Trier. When the episcopate of Trier was offered to him with great insistence, he not only refused it, but obtained from God, lest he be dragged there unwillingly, the release of his body within twenty days. His body was buried by two companion priests and others in the same church that he himself had built, in the year of the Lord 600. Peter de Natalibus; Ghinius of Siena.]

### 7.—The Nones

Bede is silent.

C, B, and V: At Alexandria, Parthenius, Heraclius [B: Apollonius], and Publius with eighteen others [V: seventeen].

A, T, and L: At Alexandria, the feast of Saints Apollonius [L: Heracleus], Heleus, and Parmenus, thus far A, with nineteen others.

B: And elsewhere, Alexander and Parthiminius.

D: At Alexandria, Saint Pantaenus. [Note: A philosopher of the Stoic school. In accordance with an old custom at Alexandria, where ecclesiastical teachers had always existed from the time of Mark the Evangelist, he possessed such wisdom and learning in both the divine Scriptures and secular literature that, when representatives of the Indian people requested him, Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, sent him there. He found that Bartholomew, one of the twelve apostles, had preached the coming of the Lord Jesus according to Matthew’s Gospel, which had been written in Hebrew; on his return he brought it with him to Alexandria. He taught under the emperor Severus and Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla. He was also the teacher of Clement of Alexandria. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*; Eusebius, *History* V.10–11.]

At Rome, the martyrs Nicostratus, Primitivus, Sesinius, Claudius the registrar, Castorius, Victorinus, and Symphorianus, whom Saint Sebastian taught to believe in Christ and whom the priest Saint Polycarp baptized. [Note: Nicostratus was the husband of Saint Zoe, who is commemorated above on the fourth day before the Nones of July. He too was chief secretary; for this reason *Primi, Sesinii* is incorrectly written. Claudius and all the others are discussed in the Acts of Saint Sebastian edited by Bollandus under 20 January. They are entirely different from the martyrs who bore the same names and whose feast is treated below on the sixth day before the Ides of November, as their different Acts make clear.]

### 8.—The eighth day before the Ides

The feast of Procopius in Palestine. [Note: Procopius was from Aelia, but lived at Scythopolis, where he was a lector and exorcist. He interpreted for the people in their native language, namely Syriac, the sacred Scriptures that were read in the church in Greek. Eusebius, in his *Little Book on the Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 1, calls him the first of the martyrs of Palestine and teaches that he was beheaded on the eighth day of the month Desius—that is, in Roman reckoning, on the seventh day before the Ides of June. The heading of his Acts assigns his feast to the fourth day before the Nones of August; the Acts themselves to the Nones of July. Nevertheless, in all martyrologies the feast of Saint Procopius is celebrated on the eighth day before the Ides of July. The Greeks also celebrate on this very day the commemoration of the great martyr Procopius, as may be seen in their *Menologion*. But this Procopius is entirely different from ours, although he too was from Aelia and suffered at approximately the same time and in the same city as our Procopius. For our Procopius was a lector and exorcist, as Eusebius testifies; the other was a military commander in Egypt. The former was a Christian from childhood; the latter was initially a worshiper of demons. Our Procopius lost his life by the sword without suffering any torments and earned the crown of martyrdom by the briefest kind of death. The other underwent a long and extremely difficult martyrdom and endured severe torments under the two governors of Palestine, Justus and Flavianus. Finally, our Procopius was captured at Scythopolis, taken from there to Caesarea of Palestine, and beheaded there. The other was apprehended in Egypt and completed his martyrdom in the Phoenician city of Caesarea, also called Paneas, if we believe Symeon Metaphrastes. Valesius, in his notes on the foregoing chapter of Eusebius.]

He was led from Scythopolis to Caesarea and, because of his confidence in his first answer, was beheaded by the enraged judge Flavianus.

B: At Augusta of the Viromandui, the discovery of the body of Saint Quintinus the martyr. [Note: Peter de Natalibus writes of this discovery: “After 320 years had passed, when the body of the holy martyr had again become unknown, it was revealed to Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon. After a three-day fast, while he was excavating the place shown to him where it lay hidden, such a great light from heaven surrounded him at night that many believed day had dawned; a very sweet fragrance also burst forth. Having found the body of the saint and raised it, he placed it in an honorable reliquary and built a church and monastery there in the year 657.”]

And elsewhere, Agrestus and Primulus. At Nicaea, Sostratus and Eradius.

### 9.—The seventh day before the Ides

At the city of Tyre [V: Tora; T: Thyra; L: Tiria], the feast of Saints Anatolia and Audax under the emperor Decius. [Note: More probably Thora, which Dionysius of Halicarnassus says lies forty stadia from Reate on the Latin road.]

When Anatolia had cured many sick, epileptic, and demon-possessed people in Picenum, she was taken at the command of Festinianus to the city of Tyre and subjected to various kinds of torture. Then she was shut up for the whole night with a serpent and remained unharmed. Indeed, she rescued from being devoured by his own serpent the very servant who had introduced it, a man named Audax, and converted him to Christ’s martyrdom. (Thus far A.) After this, for his confession of the truth, he himself was placed in custody and, without delay, crowned by a capital sentence. The virgin of Christ was also pierced through with a sword while standing with her hands extended in prayer, so that the sword, entering through her right side, came out through her left. She suffered on the seventh day before the Ides of July and was buried in the morning by the citizens of Tyre. Audax, who was from the East, was transferred there by his wife and children.

On the same day, the deposition of Saint Ephrem, our holy father. [Note: A deacon of the church of Edessa. The Latins celebrate his feast on 1 February, the Greeks on 28 January. Yet he does not seem to have died on either day. Palladius, who was his contemporary, writes in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 101, that after spending a full year in Edessa caring for the sick, and after an abundant harvest had arrived, he returned to his cell and died a month later. He should therefore be regarded as having died rather at the beginning of autumn, or at least in summer, perhaps on this very day, 11 July, than in midwinter.]

Florus, in T and L: In Egypt, the passion of Cyril, bishop. [Note: The place of this saint’s combat is highly uncertain. Peter de Natalibus places him at Rome; Baronius at Cortyna in Crete; but Rabanus and Notker, together with our author, place him in Egypt. The Greeks, in their *Menologion*, describe his martyrdom as having been completed under Diocletian; but his Acts, which Surius prints in volume IV, show that he suffered under Decius.] At the time of the emperor Decius, at the command of the duke Lucius, he was first thrown into a fire; when he emerged unharmed, he was afterward condemned to death.

A: At Sens, Saint Heraclius, bishop and confessor. [Note: This was a bishop of Sens; he is commemorated in Philippe Labbe, *Bibliotheca Nova*, p. 700, on the sixth day before the Ides of June. Today, however, the general catalogue of Ferrarius celebrates Heraclius, bishop of Troyes.]

B: At Rome, the feast of the virgins Floriana and Faustina.

### 10.—The sixth day before the Ides

At Rome, the seven brothers, sons of Saint Felicitas—that is, Felix, Philip, Vitalis, Martial, Alexander, Silvanus, and Januarius—under Publius, prefect of the city, in the time of the emperor Antoninus. Of these, Januarius was killed after being beaten with rods, imprisoned, and scourged with leaded whips. Felix and Philip were beaten to death with clubs; Silvanus was killed by being thrown from a height; Alexander, Vitalis, and Martial were punished by capital sentence.

L: On the same day, the feast of Saint Ettho, bishop and confessor. [Note: A companion of Saint Fursey. He came from Ireland with others to preach the word of God in Gaul. After producing much fruit for God, he rested at Fisciacum, near Avesnes in Hainaut, in a priory dependent on the abbey of Laetium. A few years ago he was transferred to Laetium, where his feast is celebrated today. Molanus, *The Saints of Belgium*.]

C and V: On the same day, the feast of the holy virgins Rufina, Secunda, and Fortunata [“and Fortunata” is absent in C]. [Note: These were noble Roman women, born of distinguished parents, Asterius their father and Aurelia their mother. They were given in marriage to the pagans Armentarius and Verinus. When their husbands discovered that they were Christians, they accused them to the count Archesilaus, who pursued them with his soldiers and captured them fourteen miles from the city on the Flaminian Way. He brought them back to the city and presented them to the prefect Junius Donatus. During the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus, after subjecting them to other tortures, he finally ordered one to be beheaded and the other’s neck to be cut. Their bodies are honorably preserved in the Lateran basilica near the baptistery. Surius; Baronius, *Martyrology*, volume IV.]

### 11.—The Ides

The deposition of Saint Benedict, abbot. [Note: A very serious dispute arose between the Gauls and the Italians, and between the monks of Monte Cassino and those of Fleury, over the translation of the body of their common father Benedict. The Gauls, with the support of the great agreement of their own people and almost all outsiders, assert that after the monastery of Cassino had been destroyed by the Lombards, Aigulf, at God’s command and by order of Mummolus, abbot of Fleury, during the reign of Chlodoveus II, king of the Franks, went to Italy and carried the sacred relics of Saints Benedict and Scholastica from the solitude of Cassino to the Gallic monastery in the territory of Orléans called Fleury. The people of Fleury received the relics of Saint Benedict, while the townspeople of Le Mans, who had accompanied Aigulf on his journey, were enriched with those of Saint Scholastica.

The Cassinenses, lacking the support of outsiders and divided among themselves in their opinions, accept the translation mentioned above in some cases, but attempt to establish a return to the monastery of Cassino; others, by far the majority, follow as their guide Cardinal Leo of Marsi, bishop of Ostia, who entirely denies the translation.

For those who defend the claim that the relics of Saint Benedict truly were transferred to Gaul, the testimony of the Venerable Bede supports them. He deserves even greater credence because that most learned man flourished at approximately the time when this translation occurred. Yet he calls this translation a deposition. Those even slightly acquainted with ecclesiastical writers know what the day of a deposition is: it is the day on which the body of a saint is placed either in its primary tomb or, after some translation, in another place. Florus clearly explains precisely this meaning of “deposition” here.

It is certain that the translation took place while Chlodoveus, son of Dagobert, was reigning, not in the earlier years of his reign, when the foundations of the monastery of Fleury were laid, but in the later years. According to the chronology of the reigns of Dagobert and Chlothar established by Hadrian Valesius, the distinguished historian of Frankish affairs, Chlodoveus held the reins of government from 638 to 654. The beginnings of the monastery of Fleury should therefore be assigned to approximately 641 and the translation to approximately 653.]

Florus, in A, T, and L: The translation of the body.

T: On this day he was brought from the aforesaid regions of Rome to Fleury.

A and T: He who, shining with the greatest virtues, set down the rule and order for monks. Blessed Pope Gregory clarified his life in lucid prose.

At Nicopolis, a city in Armenia, the passion of Saints Januarius and Pelagia. [Note: Peter de Natalibus, in his *Catalogue* V.85, reports that they suffered under Licinius.] They endured such great tortures that their bodies were torn not only with hooks but even with potsherds until the fourth day.

B: In the district of Orléans, the bringing in of the body of Saint Benedict, abbot, and the deposition of the same.

L: And in the district of Poitiers, Saint Savinus the martyr. [Note: More correctly, Sabinus. In the year 458, Sabinus and Cyprian, brothers born in the city of Brescia and soldiers, had denounced both the people of Brescia and their neighbors of Amphipolis for worshiping idols, especially Dionysus. They were summoned and questioned by Ladicius, the proconsul; afterward they were released from prison and, coming from Italy, traveled as far as Lyon and Auxerre, where they visited Saint Germanus on his return from Britain. Finally they reached the territory of Tours and then the vicinity of Poitiers, near a place called Confluentium, where the river Wartimpa flows into the river Creuse.

There they saw the proconsul Maximus, stirred up by Ladicius’s kinsman, pursuing them with 200 Italian soldiers. After crossing the river they were captured above the Wartimpa at a place called Cercheus, one mile from the village of Antiniacum. They were then taken to an island in the same river opposite an estate called Psellis, where Saint Savinus was beheaded together with ten men whom he had intended to baptize.

Saint Cyprian and the two priests Asclepius and Valerius were taken to Antiniacum. Asclepius and Valerius, however, having been rescued from their hands, carried Saint Savinus’s body to a mountain called the Three Cypresses, where there had once been a church of Saint Vincent the martyr, later abandoned during the Vandal persecution. Saint Savinus’s body is buried there today. From the ancient legends of Limoges, in Philippe Labbe, *Bibliotheca Nova*, vol. II, p. 665.

Henri-Louis Castaneus Rupipozaeus, in his notes on the Litanies of Poitiers, testifies that Saint Savinus suffered under the emperor Marcianus, who ruled from 451 to 457.]

C, V, and B: At Rome, the feast of Saints Leontius, Stephen, and Maurice. B adds Melito.

### 12.—The fourth day before the Ides

Bede is silent.

D: At Aquileia, the feast of Saint Hermagoras. [Note: The first bishop of Aquileia, ordained by the apostle Saint Peter. While converting the people, he was accused by the priests of the idols of destroying their worship. He was arrested, beaten with sinews, suspended on the rack, and torn with hooks. When burning plates were applied to his sides, he confessed Christ with still greater zeal and was thrown into prison. But when the place was illuminated by heavenly light, unbelievers were converted in even greater numbers, and all the sick who were brought to him were healed and baptized. The governor, enraged still further by this, inflicted capital punishment on him and his deacon Fortunatus. Ghinius of Siena.]

Hermagoras, the first bishop of that city and a disciple of Saint Mark the Evangelist.

C and V: At Aquileia, Fortunatus. [Note: He was the deacon of Saint Hermagoras.] Agatha the virgin. Nabor and Felix. [Note: Their translation is celebrated today. They were beheaded in Africa on the sixth day before the Ides of July, together with Januarius and Marinus, but on this day their bodies were carried to Milan. Notker. Paulinus discusses their bodies, placed at Milan and frequently visited, in his *Life of Saint Ambrose*. Saint Ambrose also speaks of these martyrs in book VII, chapter 13 of his commentary on Luke, and mentions their basilica in his letter to Marcellina concerning the discovery of the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius. See also 11 June.]

A and T: In Sicily, the feast of Saint Nabor and Saint Felix.

At Lyon in Gaul, the deposition of Saint Vincent, bishop. [Note: More correctly, as is also written below, Viventiolus. He succeeded Lupicinus and, according to the lists of the bishops of Lyon preserved by Demochare, was the twenty-ninth bishop of Lyon. He was also present at the Council of Epaon during the pontificate of Pope Gelasius.]

A: Hermagoras, bishop, and Fortunatus, deacon.

T and L: At Aquileia, the passion of Fortunatus.

L and B: At Milan, the feast of Nabor, Felix, and Primitive.

B: At Aquileia, the feast of Saints Fortunatus and Armogenes; at Lyon in Gaul, the deposition of Saint Viventiolus, bishop.

### 13.—The third day before the Ides

Bede is silent.

D: Ezra and Joel, prophets. And in Africa, the feast of the holy confessors Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, glorious in faith, virtues, and miracles, and the entire clergy of that same church. [Note: They suffered in the Vandal persecution under Hunneric, the Arian king. Victor of Vita gives a full account of that persecution. Saint Eugenius is also commemorated above on 1 February.]

B, C, V, A, T, and L: At Alexandria, Saints Serapion, Meleus [in B alone: “Meleus … Nasius”], Attalus, Zeno, Nasius, Trophimus, and Menaeus the priest. The last is absent in V and C, where not *Trophimus* but *Trophima* is read; in A, T, and L, Attalus is absent; Zeno is also omitted by A.

L adds: And at Rome, the deposition of Anacletus, bishop. [Note: Of him the Chronicle of Damasus reads as follows: “Anacletus, twelve years, ten months, and three days.” He lived in the time of Domitian, from the consulship of Domitian for the tenth time and Sabinus until that of Domitian for the seventeenth time and Clemens. He therefore succeeded Cletus in the year 83, when Domitian was consul for the ninth time and Rufus for the second. In the Chronicle of Damasus, the pontificate of a successor begins with the consuls who opened the year after the predecessor’s death. Anacletus died in the year 95, when Domitian and Clemens held the consulship for the seventeenth time.

Anacletus is commemorated today, but this day should rather be referred to some translation of his relics, as must be thought of the other ancient pontiffs. There are very learned men who do not distinguish Cletus and Anacletus and affirm that they were one and the same person. But in an uncertain matter one should not depart from the common opinion. See Saint Cletus on 26 April.]

### 14.—The second day before the Ides

Saint Phocas, bishop of Pontus [A, T, and L: Phocatus]. [Note: It should be known that there were two martyr Phocases: one, the subject of this day; the other, commemorated on the third day before the Nones of March. The one commemorated today was originally a sailor and later became bishop of Sinope in Pontus, where he suffered and, after many torments, departed to heaven without the sword. The other is said to have been a gardener and completed his martyrdom by being beheaded at Antioch.]

Under the emperor Trajan and the governor Africanus, he overcame prison, hooks, iron, and even fire for Christ. His relics are preserved in the Basilica of the Apostles in the Gallic city of Vienne.

A: On the same day, at a village called Somnias, the deposition of Blessed Vincent. [Note: Count of Hainaut, formerly called Madelgarius, and by no means the least among the palatines of Dagobert, king of the Franks. He also had as his wife the blessed Waldetrudis, and the king appointed him governor of Ireland for several years. Returning from there to Gaul, he brought with him Saints Foillan, Fursey, and other preachers of the faith. At the advice of Autbertus, he abandoned his military belt, built a monastery on the Sambre in a district called Monsaltus, and lived there according to the rule for many years. Others followed his example, namely Ansbertus, bishop of Rouen, who had been condemned to exile, and other servants of God. He also built the monastery of Sonegias, where he spent and ended the remainder of his holy life in the Lord. He received his deposition and became famous for miracles around the year 640. Ghinius of Siena; Molanus, *The Saints of Belgium*.]

He abandoned the world at the exhortation of Blessed Autbertus, bishop, and exercised himself in deeds of good conduct.

L: At the monastery called Sonegias, the feast of Saint Vincent, abbot, who built the place of Altimontis through an angel of the Lord.

C and V: In Gaul, the feast of Saint Justus, bishop and confessor. [Note: He is commemorated on 2 September, the day on which he died in Egypt, where he led an eremitical life; today he was gloriously translated to Lyon. Notker.]

B: At Lyon in Gaul, the deposition of Saints Justus and Amatus, bishops. [Note: Amatus is called Amicus by Notker and in the Hieronymian Martyrology. It is not sufficiently certain who this man was.]

### 15.—The Ides

Bede is silent.

D and B: Cyricus and his mother. [Note: The Latins commemorate them on 16 June; see that date above. The Greeks commemorate them today.]

B: Julitta, whose name is written in D as a rubric; this occurs only twice in the entire little book. Their feast is also recorded in the first place in T.

C, V, and S: Cyricus, Philip, Secundinus, Martial, and Saint James, bishop of Nisibis. [Note: These did not suffer in the same place. Saint Cyricus and Julitta are especially venerated at Tarsus; Philip at Alexandria; Secundinus and Martial at Sirmium; and James at Nisibis. Hieronymus, *Martyrology*.]

Saint James, bishop of Nisibis, performed many miracles in the body and alone saw Noah’s ark on the mountain; none of the others who had gone with him was permitted to see it. [Note: Bishop of Nisibis, or of Antioch in Mygdonia. He was one of the confessors under the persecutor Maximianus and one of those who condemned the Arian perversity at the Council of Nicaea. He also attended the Council of Antioch on behalf of the Catholics against the Arians. He died in the time of Constantius and was buried within the walls of the city of Nisibis. Gennadius, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 1. How this man preserved the city of Nisibis unharmed by his prayers when King Shapur of Persia was besieging it may be read in Theodoret, *History* II.30. The Greeks commemorate him on the day before the Kalends of November in their *Menologion*.]

T: On the same day, Saint Florentius. [Note: He suffered with the deacon Catholinus at Carthage during the Vandal persecution. This is the Catholinus, or Catulinus, in whose praise Saint Augustine is said by Possidius, in his *Index*, chapter 9, to have written a treatise. They were placed in the basilica of Faustus, which is mentioned at the beginning of the Council of Carthage and in chapter 74 of the African Council. Victor also mentions it in book II of his account of the Vandal persecution.]

And Saint James, bishop.

L: He designates him first in Armenia and likewise continues: “through whom the Lord performed many miracles.”

B: At Alexandria, the feast of Saints Philip, Zeno, Nasius, and the ten sisters. At Carthage, Saint Catholinus the deacon.

The first division of the twelve apostles. [“First” appears only in A.] T adds: “to preach.” A continues as follows: “when the Lord Jesus himself, before his passion, sent them to preach and proclaim the kingdom of God, commanding them and saying: ‘Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans,’ and so forth.”

On the same day, the translation of Saint Vedastus from Beauvais in the year 893 of the Lord’s Incarnation. [Note: For another translation, see the sixth day before the Nones of July.] He had remained in the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr in the aforesaid city for twelve years, nine months, and twenty-three days. On the day mentioned above, Jerusalem was captured by the army of the Christians and freed from the hands of the pagans.

### 16.—The seventeenth day before the Kalends of August

At Ostia, the feast of Saint Hilarinus, a monk. [Note: A native of the city of Arezzo, he had formerly associated with the blessed Donatus, bishop and martyr, and performed many miracles with him. Later, while living in the city of Ostia, he received Gallicanus the martyr when he came there and strengthened him in the faith of Christ. Finally, he was captured and killed at Ostia by the governor Quadratianus. Peter de Natalibus. Baronius, however, says in the *Martyrology* that this man suffered martyrdom at Arezzo in Tuscany and that his body was transferred to Ostia on the Tiber.]

He suffered martyrdom under the persecution of Julian because he refused to sacrifice, and was beaten to death with clubs.

C. V., In Antioch, Theodosius. Eustasius [Eustasii is absent in V.], Dionysius. L., On this same day, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 0977C] Monulphus and Gondulphus. Of these, Monulphus was the son of King Dionatus. At Liège he founded an oratory of Saints Cosmas and Damian; and at Maastricht he built a magnificent church in honor of Saint Servatius, where he established clergy. After he had presided at Maastricht for about thirty-nine years, he surrendered his soul to God in that same church and was buried there, around the year 600. Saint Gondulphus was the son of the duke of Lorraine and was brought up at Maastricht on the Meuse. After Saint Monulphus, he governed the Churches of Maastricht and Tongeren for seven years, and departed this world around the year 607, on the same day of the year as his predecessor; equal to him in merits, he was also buried in the middle of the church of Saint Servatius. GHINIUS OF SIENA.] Monulphus and Gondulphus, bishops. T., On this same day, the arrival of the body of Saint Cassianus, bishop, at the basilica of the martyr Quintinus, gloriously radiant with signs and miraculous powers. And the body of Saint [Note: [Col. 0977D] Bertinus. These are the words of Molanus in his additions to Usuard: “In the monastery of Sithiu, the body of Saint Father Bertinus is transferred by Blessed Folcwinus and deposited in the year 846.” For another translation of this saint, see above, 2 May.] Bertinus is transferred and deposited. B., In Caesarea, the feast of Saints Paul and [Note: [Col. 0977D] Mammetis. His passion, explained as more marvelous than true, may be seen in Notker.] Mammetis. And the feast of Saints Valentina, Theon, and Diocletis.

### 17.—16 Kalends [of August]

In Carthage, the Scillitan martyrs—that is, Martialis, Cithius [D. Urius], Vesturius, Felix, Aquilinus, Lactantius, Januarius, Generosus [A. Generosa], Vesta [B. Vasta], Donata, and Secunda—under Saturninus the prefect. After their first confession of Christ, they were sent to prison and crucified on a wooden stake; at sea they were beheaded with the sword.

[Col. 0978B] C. V., At Auxerre, [Note: [Col. 0977D] Theodosius. Concerning him it is written as follows in Philippe Labbe’s *Bibliotheca Nova*, vol. I, p. 418: “Theodosius occupied the see for eight years and twenty-three days, and today died, having completed seventy-five years of life; on account of the merit of his holiness he received a distinguished burial in the church of Blessed Germanus. He lived in the times of Boniface and Mercury, who was also called John, until Agapitus, while Justinian Augustus was emperor and Lampadius consul. [Col. 0978C] We also find that this holy man took part in the council of bishops held by order of Clovis the Great, king of the Franks, at Orléans, a city of Gaul.”] Theodosius, bishop. V., And Saint Alexius in Ap . . . and Marina. A. T. L., At Rome, Saint [Note: [Col. 0978C] Alexis. The son of the senator Euphemianus and Aglaia. On the first night of his marriage, leaving his bride untouched, he departed from his home. After a long pilgrimage, he returned to the City and, for seventeen years, remained unknown, received as a beggar into his father’s house as a guest. After his death, however, he was recognized both by a voice heard throughout the city’s churches and by his written account, and, under Pope Innocent I, was carried with great honor to the church of Saint Boniface. He flourished around the year 388. PETER DE NATALIBUS.] Alexis, confessor. B., At Milan, the feast of Saint Marcellus.

### 18.—15 Kalends

The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0978C] Arnulfus. At Metz in Gaul, Saint Arnulfus, bishop, who was prominent at the royal court, was dear to Pepin, duke of Brabant, and was employed by him as secretary; Pepin took the greatest pleasure in his counsel. When Pappo, bishop of Metz, died, Arnulfus was appointed against his will; but after fifteen years he led the life of a hermit and died in the year 640. His body was then brought to Metz. SURIUS, vol. IV.] Arnulfus, confessor.

Florus adds in A. T. L.: “whose life was of the greatest holiness.”

In A. it is noted: “In Gaul, at Silva Aquilina, the passion of Saint Arnulfus, bishop”; in T.: “On this same day, at Metz, a city of Gaul, the deposition of Saint Arnulfus, bishop and confessor”; but in L., at the place not previously marked, he is given only the title of martyr. C. V., At Rome, [Note: [Col. 0978D] Symphorosa. For these matters, see below, the 21st of this month.] Symphorosa, mother of seven brothers. B. adds the names and eulogy given below, on the 12th day before the Kalends. A., “Saint Symphorosa with her seven sons.” B., In Pontus, at the city of Amanthea, Pontinus, Philantius, Heliana the virgin, and Maria the virgin.

### 19.—14 Kalends

Our Holy Father [Note: [Col. 0978D] Arsenius. Born at Rome, he advanced to the innermost reaches of philosophical and sacred learning and was ordained deacon by the Roman Church. After Theodosius had assumed the empire following Valens, and at the urging of the emperor Gratian and the Roman bishop, Arsenius reluctantly went to Constantinople and undertook the education of Theodosius’ sons, Arcadius and Honorius. When he chastised Arcadius with blows for some offense, Arcadius’ sword-bearer warned him that Arcadius was plotting to put him to death. Arsenius therefore [Col. 0979C] secretly boarded a ship prepared to sail for Alexandria. On arriving there, he went directly to Mount Scetis and joined the number of the monks who practiced there. Thus Arsenius remained hidden throughout Theodosius’ lifetime. After Arcadius succeeded to the empire, he sent Arsenius a letter confessing his plots and offering him the revenues of all Egypt, to be distributed by him among the poor and to the monasteries for their necessities. Arsenius nevertheless humbly refused what was offered. He lived piously as a monk and died in that state. SURIUS, vol. IV.] Arsenius, of whom it is reported in the *Sayings of the Elders* that, because of the abundance of his tears, he always kept a handkerchief either in his bosom or in his hand.

C. V., And elsewhere, [Note: [Col. 0979C] Rusticus. He appears to be the same as the one commemorated on 25 April.] Rusticus. V., “Priest and confessor.” B., At Lyon in Gaul, the deposition of Rusticus, bishop and confessor. In Alexandria, Sisinnius. In Spain, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0979C] Justus. Justa is preferable, according to what is written among the other martyrologists. She suffered martyrdom with Rufina in the city of Seville under the prefect Diogenianus. Justa’s body was thrown into a well and then raised and buried by Sabinus, the bishop. Since Rufina’s body was burned, however, her bones were collected by the same bishop and, together with Justa’s body, transferred to the city of Seville. ADO, USUARD, PETER DE NATALIBUS.] Justus.

### 20.—13 Kalends

Bede has nothing.

D. The feast of Blessed Joseph, who was surnamed Justus and who, together with Blessed Matthias, was appointed by the apostles to complete the number of the Twelve. [Col. 0980B] C. V., At Rome, the passion of Saints Stria, Magrinus, Nestica [C. Nestita], Satyrus, Amarinus, and Secundus. B., At Rome, the feast of Saints Passeria, Macrinus, and Saturus. In Africa, Sabinus, Lucianus, and Amabilis. In the Thebaid, the feast of Victor. A. T. L., In Africa, the feast of Saints Lucianus, Sabinus, and Sandi [Sandi is absent from A.]. On this same day, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 0979D] Margaret. She was from the city of Antioch in Pisidia and was the daughter of Aedesius, a highly distinguished priest of idols, who hated her because she had embraced the Christian faith. When the prefect Olybrius was traveling from Asia toward Antioch, he saw Margaret, also called Marina, and burned intensely with love for her. When she rejected him, he cruelly tortured her with chains, imprisonment, scourges, and the rack. The devil also tested her in the form of a dragon and likewise in the form of an Ethiopian, but he was overcome by the sign of the cross. Finally, she was beheaded by the aforesaid prefect and completed her martyrdom. Usuard. Surius, vol. IV. —This Marina is commemorated by Notker and Hrabanus on 18 June. There is also another Marina, likewise celebrated above on 18 June, whose contest took place at Alexandria. In their readings for 18 June, the Spaniards say that Marina was from Antioch in Galicia.] Margaret [Margaret is absent from T., but is found in C.], virgin and martyr. T., In the district of Gaul, at the monastery of Silmaco. T. A., The deposition of Saint [Note: [Col. 0980C] Wulmarus. He came from Boulogne of the Morini to the monastery of Hautmont, situated in Hainaut on the Sambre. There he first attended the school of letters and was occupied with tending oxen and carrying wood to the brothers’ workshops. Released from this service, he was enrolled among the clergy and entered the priesthood. To avoid human praise, he entered the wilderness of Flanders. From there he went to the district of Boulogne, where he had been born; there, in a forest, he built a monastery in honor of Blessed Mary and Saint Peter. He rests in that monastery, not far from our Belgium, in the diocese of the Morini. He lived around the year of the Lord 688. For, according to the epitome of his Life in Surius, King Ceadwalla of the West Saxons visited him while traveling to Rome—that is, in the year 688, according to Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 7. The manuscript from which Surius copied this epitome states that the man of God was translated on 17 June. GHINIUS OF SIENA, MOLANUS, *The Saints of Belgium*, SURIUS, June 17.] Wulmarus, abbot. B., In Damascus, the feast of Lucianus and Macrobius, with ten others.

### 21.—12 Kalends

The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0980D] Praxedis. She was the sister of Saint Potentiana and the daughter of Saint Pudens, concerning whom an account was given on 10 May. After her father’s death, she devoted herself continually to vigils and prayers and, together with her blessed sister, spent the entire patrimony on the support of the poor. After her sister’s death, Saint Novatus came to console her; when he died not long afterward, the virgin of the Lord, Praxedis, asked Bishop Pius to consecrate Novatus’ baths as a church. Saint Pius agreed, and Novatus’ baths were dedicated in honor of Blessed Potentiana in the district called the Patrician. Another church was also dedicated under the name of Saint Praxedis within the city of Rome, in the district called Lateran. When the emperor Antoninus learned that assemblies were being held at the title of Praxedis, he arrested many of them, including Simetrius, and ordered them to be executed by the sword without trial. Blessed Praxedis buried their bodies at night [Col. 0981B] on the seventh day before the Kalends of June in the cemetery of Priscilla. Fifty-four days after the passion of those saints, she herself died and was buried beside her father Pudens by Blessed Pastor the priest, on the Salarian Way in the cemetery of Priscilla. According to the reckoning of the Bollandist brothers in their preliminary commentary [Col. 0981C] on the Acts of Pudentiana, and so forth, Praxedis is thought to have died around the year 159.] Praxedis, virgin, and Saint [Note: [Col. 0981C] Daniel. The Greeks discuss him together with the three youths on the 16th day before the Kalends of January in the *Menologion*. Epiphanius, *On the Life and Death of the Prophets*, chapter 10, has the following at the end: “He was buried in a narrow cave with great honors, and his monument still stands, well known to all in Babylon, down to our own age.” Their relics were transferred from Babylon to Alexandria and placed in the church of Saints John and Cyrus, as their Acts indicate; these same relics are said to have been transferred to Venice. It is also reported that a leg of Saint Daniel is preserved at Vercelli. BARONIUS in his notes to the Martyrology.] Daniel, prophet.

And at the city of Tibur in Italy, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0981C] Symphorosa. These martyrs are also celebrated above on the 18th day of this month.] Symphorosa with her seven sons—Crescent, Julian, Nemesius, Primitivus, Justinus, Stacteus, and Eugenius. She suffered together with them under the emperor Hadrian, who ordered Symphorosa herself first to be beaten with palms and then hung by her hair; but when she could not be overcome by any means, he ordered her to be thrown into the river with a stone tied to her. Her brother Eugenius, a leading member of the Tiburtine curia, gathered her body and buried it. The next morning the emperor ordered seven stakes to be fixed in place and her sons to be stretched upon racks there. Crescent was pierced through the throat, Lucianus through the chest, Nemesius through the heart, Primitivus through the navel, Justinus was stretched out and cut apart through each joint and articulation of his body, Stacteus was pierced with innumerable lances until he died on the ground, and Eugenius was split from the chest down to the lower parts. (Thus far A.) On the following day Hadrian ordered their bodies to be removed and thrown into a deep pit; and the priests gave that place the name “Ad septem Biothanatos.”

This last section is absent from T. and L., and in its place appears: “and that Christians did not have them.” It is also absent from B. at the 15th day before the Kalends. L., On this same day, Victor and his companions. B., On this same day, Saint Daniel the prophet. At Marseille, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 0981C] Victor. Under the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, when he was a soldier and refused either to serve in the army or to sacrifice to idols, he was first thrust into prison by his tribune, Austerius; but every night an angel led him out to visit the sick. Then, by order of the prefect Eutychius, his arms were twisted behind him and bound with fine cords, and his feet were tied with a rope; he was dragged through the middle of the city. After this he was beaten with clubs, hung up, and tortured with thongs. An altar was also brought before him; since he could not bear even to look at it and kicked it from the priest’s hand, the governor ordered his foot to be cut off. Finally, remaining steadfast in his confession of Christ, he was thrown into a baker’s mill and there completed his martyrdom. Alexander, Felicianus, and Longinus suffered with him; and the boy Deuterius also gave up his spirit while praying at his tomb. Peter de Natalibus. —There was also another Victor of Marseille, renowned for his learning, who lived in the times of the emperors Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian; Gennadius discusses him in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 6.] Victor, Alexander, Felicianus, and Longinus.

### 22.—11 Kalends

The feast of [Note: [Col. 0981D] Mary. When persecution broke out after the stoning of Stephen the protomartyr, Maximinus, one of the seventy-two disciples, crossed into Gaul, taking Mary Magdalene with him, and buried her after her death at the city of Aix, over which he presided. When the city of Aix was devastated by the Saracens, her body was transferred by Count Gerard of Burgundy to the monastery of Vézelay, which he had founded. Although some write that it rests at Ephesus, without any covering over it. SIGEBERT, writing about its translation in the year 754.] Mary Magdalene.

T. prefaces this: “At Marseille.” B. C. V., In Antioch, [Note: [Col. 0982C] Cyril. He was the nineteenth bishop of Antioch. Eusebius discusses him in the *Chronicle* and *Ecclesiastical History* VII, 32. He began to occupy the see in the fourth year of the emperor Probus and remained there until the seventeenth year of Diocletian.] Cyril [C. Arillus], Andrew. B., Tabellus. T., At Marseille, the feast of Saint Adrianus. A. T. L., And Saint Cyril. And at the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint [Note: [Col. 0982C] Wandregisilus. He was first a count of the palace under Dagobert. His grandfather was Saint Arnulfus, prince of Lorraine and bishop of Metz. Abandoning the royal court of Dagobert and the bride with whom he had lived chastely and who had likewise taken the religious habit by mutual consent, he built a house in the region of Verdun, on his own estate, where he devoted himself to God through fasts and prayers. Then he went to the monastery of Bobbio, Saint Columbanus’ foundation, and visited the apostles’ thresholds at Rome. Returning to his homeland, he crossed the Alps and was received at the monastery called Romans, where he lived as a monk. Finally, summoned to Rouen by the fame and holiness of Bishop Audoenus, he was ordained priest by Saint Audomarus at Audoenus’ command. He built the monastery of Fontenelle in the year 645, where he remained until the age of ninety-two and where, after his death, he was buried in the year 665. On account of the Norman persecution, however, he was transferred to Boulogne, and from there to Ghent with Ansbertus and Wulframnus. SURIUS, vol. IV; MOLANUS, *The Saints of Belgium*; GHINIUS OF SIENA.] Wandregisilus, abbot. A., And the [Note: [Col. 0982D] octave. The translation of this saint took place on the 15th day of this month.] octave of Saint Vedastus, our Father. B., And elsewhere, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0982D] Plato. He suffered at the city of Ancyra in the province of Galatia during the reign of the emperor Maximian, under the prefect Agrippinus. When he refused to sacrifice to the gods, he was first severely beaten by twelve men who succeeded one another; but, remaining steadfast, he was thrown into prison. Then, after being roasted over coals, after the rack and burning torches had been applied to his sides, and after other unheard-of tortures, he was finally beheaded with the sword. Peter de Natalibus. —The emperor Justinian erected a magnificent monument in honor of Saint Plato, as Procopius writes.] Plato.

### 23.—10 Kalends

The feast of Saint Apollinaris, bishop, at Ravenna. He was ordained at Rome by the Apostle Peter and sent there. He also preached in Emilia, in the regions of the Corinthians [D., Thoritians, [Col. 0983C] perhaps Carinthians], in Mysia, on the bank of the Danube, and in the regions of Thrace [T. L., Thracia]. In these places he was sent into exile. Wherever he could, he performed innumerable miracles and endured sufferings. He was first struck with very severe blows, then beaten for a long time with clubs, placed barefoot upon burning coals, hung and stretched upon the rack, and had his mouth crushed with a stone. He was shut in a dreadful prison under a very heavy weight of iron and stretched upon a wooden stake, [Note: [Col. 0983D] The words beginning “where he was neglected by men” and ending “beaten” are omitted by L.] where, neglected by men, he was openly fed by an angel. [Note: [Col. 0983D] The words “Then . . . he was sent” are omitted by A.] Then he was chained and sent into exile.
