There he was again beaten for a long time with clubs; again, after being bound at Ravenna, he was beaten and wounded by pagans; and again he was thrown into prison and beaten. Thus he completed his martyrdom under Caesar Vespasian, with Demosthenes as patrician. He governed the Church for twenty years and eight days.

Thus D. But B. C. A. T.: twenty-eight years and four days. V.: thirty-eight years. L.: eighteen years and four days.

C. V., At Rome, [Note: [Col. 0983D] Vincentius. At Rome on the Tiburtine Way. Bede in the common recension, Usuard, Ado, Baronius, and others discuss him on the following day.] Vincentius. The feast of Primitivus. B., [Note: [Col. 0983D] Primitiva. According to Notker, she suffered on the Via Accula; others mention only her at Rome.] Primitiva.

### 24.—9 Kalends

The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0983D] Christina. She suffered in Tuscany, at the city of Tyre, which is near Lake Bolsena. Confirmed in the faith of Christ at a tender age, she smashed the golden gods of her father Urbanus, the prefect, and distributed them to the poor. At her father’s command she was struck in the face, torn by scourging, loaded with iron, and thrown into prison. After she had been torn for a very long time and with extreme cruelty, she threw pieces of her flesh into her father’s face. When she was tied to a wheel, fire was placed beneath it, and molten oil was poured over her, the erupting flame killed a thousand pagans. She was again handed over to prison, but was healed and restored by an angel. Then, after she was thrown into the sea with a great stone tied to her, she was rescued by angelic protection. After her father suddenly died, his successor Dion again afflicted her with many tortures; but when she prayed, the statue of Apollo, whom she had been ordered to worship, was suddenly reduced to ashes. Through this miracle three thousand people were converted to the faith of Christ. Finally, after Dion also died, the new prefect Julian, following a blazing furnace, serpents sent by a magician, and the cutting out of her tongue, ordered her to be pierced with arrows. Thus the blessed virgin completed the course of her martyrdom in the tenth year of her age. ADO, NOTKER; around the year 287. Her body was brought by the inhabitants of the place to Venice, to the monastery of Saint Mark, where it is said to rest today. PETER DE NATALIBUS. The body of Saint Christina is said to be preserved at Palermo in Sicily; they say that this is not another Christina but the same one. BARONIUS, in his notes to the Martyrology.] Christina [sic], virgin.

A. T. L. preface: “At the city of Tyre.” C. V., In Am . . . . . Saint [Note: [Col. 0984D] Victorinus. At the city of Amiternum, eighty-three miles from the city of Rome, on the Salarian Way. Jerome’s Martyrology says that he suffered at Rome; Notker writes that he suffered there.] Victorinus. B. A. T. L., In Armenia, the passion of Saints Theozonus, Victor, and Militaris [B., Militonius], who endured many tortures. The first of these is absent from manuscript L. B. gives only the region and the names of the martyrs.

### 25.—8 Kalends

The feast of Saint James the Apostle, son of Zebedee.

Florus adds in T. and L.: “brother of John the Evangelist,” concerning whose passion Clement of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0985C] Clement. What is excerpted here from the seventh book of Clement of Alexandria’s *Institutions* is also cited by Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History* II, 9.] writes: [Note: [Col. 0985C] James. The Greeks discuss him in the *Menologion* on the day before the Kalends of May, when Herod ordered him to be killed. The Latins celebrate him on this day, when his body was transferred from Ilia Flavia to Compostela, where he has continued to be honored with the most celebrated offices.] about it, says: “And the one who had brought him”—that is, James—“to the judge for execution, being himself moved, also confessed that he was a Christian.” Both were led together to execution. As they were being led away, the man asked James to grant him forgiveness. After reflecting for a little while, James said, “Peace be with you,” and kissed him; and so both were beheaded together.

The same Florus in A. and T.: “On this same day, at the city of Samos in Lycia, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 0985C] Christopher. Baronius believes that he suffered not under Dagnus but under the emperor Decius. In Peter de Natalibus there is an unheard-of fable in which it is said that he carried Christ across a river on his shoulders, along with other tales of the same kind, [Col. 0985D] which surpass even the Jews’ belief in Apella.] Christopher.” The same appears in B., and T. alone continues:

“Who, by order of King Dagnus, was confined in prison. He converted Nicaea and Aquilina, whom the tyrant himself had sent to seduce him, so completely that, fervent in the faith of Christ, they tied the idols of Jupiter and Apollo, which they had previously worshiped, to their belts and threw them to the ground. Therefore, by Dagnus’ command, one was torn limb from limb, while the other was hung from a stake, exposed to fire, and then slaughtered with the sword. Saint Christopher, however, with his hands and feet bound, was beaten with iron rods; then he was placed on an iron bench and covered with burning oil; afterward he was hung from a stake and struck by the soldiers’ arrows. But when the arrows hung to his right and left, one of them, twisted back as if by a gust of wind, entered Dagnus’ eye. Thus sentence was pronounced, and that athlete of Christ was beheaded. After his beheading, Dagnus himself came to his tomb the next day and, in accordance with the martyr’s promise, received healing for his eye and glorified the God of Saint Christopher magnificently.”

L. C. V. have simply the name Christopher on this day. V. adds: “At the port, Saint Acontius.”

The following also appears to belong to Florus in T. and L.: “At the city of Barcelona, Saint [Note: [Col. 0985D] Cucuphas. He was born in the city of Scillium. He traveled with a certain Felix to Caesarea; when they learned that persecution under Maximian and Diocletian was raging with great force in the East, they sailed westward and landed at Barcelona, where Cucuphas became famous for his miracles. When their fame reached the ears of Galerius the proconsul, he sent soldiers to drag him before the tribunal. Because he would not offer incense to the gods, he was beaten most severely until his body was torn open and his entrails were visible. Then, while the man of God poured out prayers to the Lord, Galerius suddenly fell dead. Later, by order of the prefect Maximian, he was stretched upon a grating, and, remaining unharmed, was cruelly beaten with iron hooks and thongs. While he was being scourged, God again heard the holy man’s prayers, and the judge Maximian was suddenly carried off by death. By order of the impious Rufinus, Cucuphas was finally beheaded. He was buried at Barcelona; later he was transferred by Fulcadius, abbot of the monastery of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, to a cell belonging to the same monastery. SURIUS, vol. IV.] Cucuphas, martyr. And Saint [Note: [Col. 0986C] Eutychianus. His day of death is 8 December. Papebrochius, in his *Chronological-Historical Essay on the Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, concludes that some elevation or translation took place today in the fifth century under Innocent I, when he built the notable basilica of Saint Sebastian at the Catacombs in the cemetery of Callistus, above the Platonia, beneath which the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul had long lain.] Eutychianus, pope and martyr. After governing the Roman Church for twenty-eight years after Peter [L. omits “twenty-eight”], he buried 342 martyrs with his own hands and suffered martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian.

[Col. 0986C] A., On this same day, the deposition of Blessed [Note: [Col. 0986D] Judocus. His feast is celebrated on 13 December, as will be seen below. Perhaps his elevation is commemorated today; it took place sixty years after his burial.] Judocus, an outstanding confessor, who, among his other virtues—which cannot be counted because of their multitude—is also said to have raised two dead persons. B., At Paris, the translation of the body of Saint [Note: [Col. 0986D] Germanus. This translation was made from the chapel of Saint Symphorianus to the basilica of the Holy Cross and Saint Vincent adjoining it, in the very year in which Pepin, anointed king by Pope Stephen, became king—that is, in the year 754. The author of the translation was Lantfredus, abbot; King Pepin was its approver and witness. This was the Lantfredus whom Charles, the prince, sent as envoy to Hunaldus, duke of Aquitaine. The history of this translation may be read in the second part of volume III of the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictines.] Germanus, bishop and confessor.

### 26.—7 Kalends

Bede has nothing.

[Col. 0987A] Florus in A. T. L.: In Laodicea of Phrygia, the feast of Saint Saturninus and Saints Julianus and Felix. In the Italian city of Arezzo, the passion of Saints [Note: [Col. 0987B] Donatus. See below, 7 August.] Donatus, bishop, and Elarinus, monk. They completed their martyrdom by beheading during the reign of the emperor Julian, under the prefect Quadratinius [A., Adrianus; L., Quadritonus].

D., At Rome, at the port, Saint [Note: [Col. 0987B] Hyacinthus. He was first thrown into the fire and then cast into a running stream, from which he emerged unharmed. After this, struck by the sword by the consular Leontius under the emperor Trajan, he ended his life. Julia, a matron, buried his body on her estate near Rome. ADO, BARONIUS, SURIUS, vol. IV.] Hyacinthus, martyr, who suffered under the consular Leontius, Luxurius, a leading citizen, handing him over. B. C. V., In Laodicea of Phrygia, Jobianus, Julianus, Felix, Marcianus, and [Note: [Col. 0987C] Pastor. We do not immediately accept the statement found in Anastasius the Librarian and others that he was the brother of Saint Pius, Roman pontiff; we fear that it was inserted by those who judged him to be the same as Hermes, to whom an angel appeared in the form of a shepherd and whom many call the brother of Pope Saint Pius. It may also be questioned in what sense Saint Pastor, writing the Acts of Pudentiana and Praxedis to Timothy the priest, says immediately at the beginning of his letter, “Pudens, our brother.” It seems sufficiently clear, however, that brotherhood of religion, not of blood, is meant. Saint Pudens, the father of Pudentiana, dedicated a title in his name. Onuphrius Panvinus, in his work on the principal churches of the City, writes that this title and that of Pudentiana were the same; but although they were indeed in the same district, the Patrician, they were different churches. When Pastor’s church had either fallen into ruin or become deserted, its title was united with the other, though it is uncertain when and by whose authority—perhaps under Innocent I, or at least under Innocent II, as Henschenius conjectures in his commentary preceding the Acts of Pudentiana, and so forth, on 19 May.] Pastor, priest [“Pastor, priest” appears only in V.]. B., And elsewhere, Marciana and Laudaia, holy women.

### 27.—6 Kalends

Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: On this same day, at Rome, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 0987D] Symphronius. He was the servant of the tribune Nemesius. When, during an inquiry by the tribune Olympius, he confessed that he was a Christian, an idol of Mars was brought before him. When Sempronius saw it, he said, “May the Lord Jesus Christ crush you.” At these words the idol suddenly melted. Olympius went to his wife Exuperia and related what Sempronius had done by invoking Christ’s name. Immediately he believed in Christ, smashed all his gods, and was baptized with his wife and son Theodulus by Blessed Stephen, the pope. When Sempronius had been burned by order of the emperor Valerian, Blessed Stephen came with clergy and religious men, gathered Saint Sempronius’ relics, and placed them with the most holy relics of Olympius and his companions, who had previously been killed for Christ. SURIUS, vol. IV, in the Life of Pope Stephen. He is commemorated on the preceding day in the martyrologies of Usuard and Baronius.] Symphronius, together with Olympius, his wife Exuperia, and his son Theodulus; by order of Valerian and Gallienus, they were burned in the fire.

B. C. D. V. A. T., In [Note: [Col. 0988C] Syria. According to Ado and Usuard, in Sicily.] Syria [D., Rigia; B., Sicily], Simeon the monk. A. T., At Rome, Saints Agontius and Emeritus. T. B., At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint [Note: [Col. 0988C] Aetherius. He was the eighteenth bishop of Auxerre after Romanus and held the see for nine years and six months. After his death he was buried in the basilica of Blessed Germanus. He lived in the time of Pope Benedict, while Tiberius Constantine was emperor. LABBE, *Bibliotheca Nova*, vol. I, p. 419.] Aetherius, bishop and confessor. B., In Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Julia, Secundus, and Januaria.

### 28.—5 Kalends

Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Milan, the passion of Saints [Note: [Col. 0988C] Nazarius. They did not suffer under Julian, but under the prefect Anulinus. After various tortures, they were struck with the sword, as is clear from their Acts, published in Surius, vol. III, p. 396. Their translation took place on 12 June; they are also commemorated on the 19th of that month.] Nazarius and Celsus, boys, who, by order of Nero under the prefect Julianus, were sacrificed to Christ after their heads had been cut off. Blessed Ambrose, by divine revelation, found their bodies preserved in a marvelous manner.

At Lyon [L., in Nicomedia], the feast of [Note: [Col. 0988C] Pantaleon. He was the son of Eustorgius. While, by order of Maximian, he was studying medicine, he was converted to the faith of Christ by the priest Hermolaus, performed many miracles, and brought his father Eustorgius, a senator, under the Christian faith. For this reason he was hung upon a wooden stake and torn with iron claws; torches were then applied to his sides. Afterward he was thrown into molten lead, then into the sea and to the beasts. When he had escaped all these punishments unharmed, he was finally executed by beheading. SURIUS, vol. IV. He is commemorated on the preceding day by Baronius, by Bede in the common recension, and by the Greeks in the *Menologion*. He suffered not at Lyon but at Nicomedia.] Pantaleon, who was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Maximian. (Thus far L.)

In Britain, at the monastery of Dol, the deposition of Saint [Note: [Col. 0988D] Samson. He was born in Demetia, in the western parts of Wales, to parents named Ammon and Anna. He was entrusted for education to Eltutus, a disciple of Saint Germanus, and sufficiently instructed in the sacred Scriptures. He was ordained deacon by Dubricius and, after a year, priest. When he was applying himself to stricter fasts, he considered leaving Eltutus’ monastery and, with Eltutus’ permission, went to Piron on a certain island. After Piron’s death, he was chosen abbot of that monastery. Having governed it for no more than a year and a half, he withdrew into solitude with his father, who had by then become a monk, and two others. From his anchoritic life he was summoned to a certain synod and placed in charge of the monastery built by Saint Germanus; not long afterward he was ordained bishop. Warned by God, he crossed into Armorica and built the monastery of Dol, where, after a life full of miracles, he peacefully breathed out his soul. See the Life of this saint written by an anonymous contemporary author, published by Mabillon in the first century of the *Acta Benedictina*. John Boscius published his Life in the *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, as did Baldric, bishop of Dol, in the twelfth century. Matthew of Westminster and others after him call Samson archbishop of York. Since Saint Samson signed the acts of the Second Council of Paris, held in 556, and did not attend the likewise Second Council of Tours, held in 566, he seems to have died around the year 565. Yet he did not reach 120 years, as the author of the Life published by John Boscius writes; otherwise Saint Maglorius, who succeeded him and long outlived him, could not have been his fellow student in Eltutus’ school.] Samson, bishop and confessor.

[Col. 0989A] V. C.: In Nicomedia, the feast of Julian, Jocundus, and Saint Pantaleon the martyr. At Milan, of Nazarius and Celsus. In Britain, of Saint Samson, bishop and confessor. The Nicomedia entry, however, is found in C. on the preceding day. B.: In Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Nazarius and Celsus. In Laodicea, a city of Phrygia, the feast of Saints Theophilus, Prudentius, Philip, and Alexander. And elsewhere, the feast of Saint Augusta, virgin, in the western regions. V.: At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Pantaleon: while, at the command of Maximian, he was studying the art of medicine, he was converted to the faith of Christ by the presbyter Hermolaus and performed many miracles. T.: At Rome, of Saint Victor.

[Note: [Col. 0989B] Victor. When Eleutherus, Roman pontiff, died in the year 185, Victor succeeded him and began to occupy the see on 12 June. He excommunicated—or rather threatened to excommunicate—the Asians who insisted that Easter should be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon; but after Irenaeus’ admonitions, Polycrates and the other Asians immediately returned to communion. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 24; Sozomen VII, 19.

[Col. 0989C] In Baronius’ *Annals*, under the year 198, no. 17, Victor’s third letter to Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, and another to Bishop Paracodus concerning the Easter controversy are regarded by Labbe as of doubtful authenticity in volume I of the *Councils*. In the latter it is said that the Eastern Church was separated from the Western on account of the celebration of Easter, and in the former that presbyters who had seen the apostles had governed the Church of Vienne down to that time; in fact, they bear the mark of a more recent style. Two decretal letters of his are likewise regarded with suspicion by learned men. He died in the year 197, after occupying the see for twelve years, one month, and sixteen days, if one counts from 12 June 185, when he began to occupy it, to the day on which he was buried. The *Book of Apostolic Names* states that Saint Victor’s day of death was 20 April, but this is contrary to the testimony of nearly all the Martyrologies. That Victor was a martyr, as Baronius relates, was stated by none of the ancients.]

Victor, bishop.

[Col. 0989B] 29.—Fourth day before the Kalends. The feast of Saints Felix,

[Note: [Col. 0989D] Felix. When Liberius was deported into exile on account of the Catholic faith, Felix was ordained by the Arians in the year 355, as Socrates II, 37, and Sozomen IV, 2, relate. So too Athanasius, in his letter to those leading the solitary life, and Jerome in the *Chronicle* under the year 352.

Nevertheless, in the ancient catalogue of the pontiffs it is said that the priests assembled and, with their counsel, Liberius appointed Felix in his place. In the year 358, when Liberius had subscribed to the formula of heretical faith at the third synod of Sirmium, he returned to Rome on this very day by the permission of Constantius and at the desire of the people, and expelled Felix. Sozomen IV, 15; Jerome in the *Chronicle*; and Faustinus and Marcellinus in the preface to the *Book of Petitions*.

The same Marcellinus and Faustinus, after recounting Felix’s two expulsions from the city, say: “After eight years, when Valentinian and Valens were consuls—that is, in the year 365—Felix died on the tenth day before the Kalends of December.” Thus it is the day of his deposition from the episcopate, not the day of his death, that is celebrated here. Since the accounts of Felix’s martyrdom given by Anastasius, and after him by Ado and other martyrologists, appear fabulous, while Marcellinus and Faustinus—although schismatics, they may safely be trusted in this matter—relate, on the basis of events witnessed by the whole city, that he died a natural death, I believe that this Felix was called a martyr because he endured much for Christ, not because he was killed on Christ’s account. No one should say that Felix the First, who suffered martyrdom under Aurelian, is meant here. Felix the First departed to God shortly before the persecution of Aurelian, and he is mentioned in the Bucherian Catalogue of the depositions of bishops, but not in the Catalogue of the depositions of martyrs.]

of Simplicius,

[Note: [Col. 0990C] Simplicius. The first two, during the reigns of Diocletian and Maximian, after many tortures, had a stone tied around their necks and were thrown from the Ponte Lepidi into the Tiber. Their bodies were recovered by their sister Beatrice and by the presbyters Crispus and John, and were buried at a place called Sextum Philippi on the Via Portuensis. When Lucretius learned this, he had Saint Beatrice suffocated by night; Blessed Lucina buried her beside her holy brothers. Surius, in the Acts of Saint Anthimus, volume III, 11 May; Ado.]

of Faustinus and Beatrice. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Lupus,

[Note: [Col. 0990C] Lupus. Having become bishop of Troyes from a monk of Lérins, he sailed to Britain with Saint Germanus of Auxerre to combat the Pelagians, and there took part in the synod of Verulamium. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* I, 17, and elsewhere. Sidonius wrote several letters to him, repeatedly calling him “bishop of bishops,” “easily the foremost of the bishops of Gaul,” “a holy man,” and so forth. After serving for fifty-two years in the priesthood at Troyes, he died and was buried in the suburban church of Saint Mary, later called Saint Lupus because of the frequent miracles occurring at his tomb. When this church was destroyed by the Northmen toward the end of the ninth century, a new one was soon built within the city under the same name of Saint Lupus, and the relics of the blessed pontiff were placed there. Surius gives his Life for today.]

bishop of Troyes, who came to Britain with Germanus and served fifty-two years in the priesthood; when Attila was devastating Gaul, he fortified Troyes by his prayers, as is sung in his hymn, “while all battles were destroying.”

The number of years of his priesthood is only six in D.; in A. and B., fifty; in C., none is given. V. adds to the names of the martyrs, “And of Saint Seraphia,”

[Note: [Col. 0990D] Seraphia, or Seraphina, in the city of Mammes. Baronius; Molanus, additions to Usuard.]

a virgin; and after the commemoration of Saint Lupus the following is found there:

The deposition of Blessed Prosper,

[Note: [Col. 0990D] Prosper. He succeeded Saint Arrianus. A letter of Sidonius Apollinaris to him is extant, book IX, letter 15. He lived in the time of Leo the Great, Roman pontiff, and was a contemporary of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine. Baronius’ notes.]

bishop. C. has the same entry.

[Col. 0991B] [Note: [Col. 0991D] [The following note is printed at the foot of column 991, but its callout letter, d, does not appear in the text.] Germanus. By nationality a native of Auxerre, born of his father Rusticus and his mother Germanilla, he received a wife named Eustachia and was sent to Gaul to hold the office of military governor. When Saint Amator, bishop of Auxerre, made known that the end of his life was at hand, Saint Germanus entered the church surrounded by his clergy; Amator had Germanus’ head tonsured, foreseeing that he would succeed him in the episcopate. When Amator died not long afterward, Germanus was unanimously demanded as bishop and, compelled, accepted the priesthood.

For his two voyages to Britain to refute the heresy of Pelagius, see *Ecclesiastical History* I, 17 and following, and the *Chronicle* under Marcian. Prosper’s chronology, according to which he was first sent to Britain by a Gallic synod in 429 with Lupus of Troyes, appears more probable than the chronology of Sigebert, who states that Germanus undertook this journey in 446. The reason is that the anonymous author of the Life of Saint Lupus writes: “After a period of two years had elapsed”—namely, from the episcopate of Lupus in 428 until the following event—“he set out for Britain with Saint Germanus against the Pelagian heresy, which attacked the sound faith.” The same anonymous author also indicates that the Gallic synod took place in the autumn of 429, when he says that they departed during the winter season, that is, toward the end of that year.

Moreover, in the chronology of English affairs during this century, other leaders should be followed rather than Sigebert, since he frequently falls into great anachronisms. Nor does Sirmond’s argument in the Appendix to volume III of Labbe’s edition of the *Councils* seem especially compelling: he thinks that Germanus’ first embassy to Britain belongs to the year 446 because Bede writes in *Ecclesiastical History* I, 10, that the Britons fought with the Picts and Saxons in Germanus’ presence. For Saxons frequently used to invade Britain long before Hengist and his Saxons landed there.

Baronius assigns Saint Germanus’ second voyage to the year 435 and asserts that he died afterward. But Germanus’ death cannot be removed from the year 448. Constantius says in his Life: “Germanus occupied the episcopal chair for thirty years and twenty-five days; he died, however, on the day before the Kalends of August, while Valentinian was still reigning as a young man with his mother Placidia.” The same Constantius had already written in I, 5, that Saint Amator, his predecessor, departed to God on the Wednesday before the Kalends of May, and therefore in a year marked by the Sunday letter F, such as the year of Christ 418, when Amator accordingly gave up his spirit to God on the first day of May, which fell on a Wednesday. Thus Saint Germanus was likewise consecrated bishop in that year, on 7 July, which had the Sunday letter F; after occupying the see for thirty years and twenty-five days, he died on the last day of July in the year 448.

Since, shortly before his death, as is clear from book II of Constantius, Saint Germanus crossed to Britain with Saint Severus, bishop of Trier, as his colleague, this embassy belongs approximately to the year 447.

[Col. 0993A] Whether Bede himself devised this chronological scheme for Saint Germanus’ two journeys to Britain may reasonably be doubted, if one compares the passage from his *Chronicle* cited above, where the first embassy of Saint Germanus appears to be placed after the year 446, with *Ecclesiastical History* I, 21, where little time is said to have intervened between the two embassies. But if the chronology explained above seems to possess the greatest likelihood of truth, special thanks are owed to the distinguished Antonio Pagi, whose chronology should be consulted under the years 429 and 435.]

30.—Third day before the Kalends. At Rome, Abdon and Sennes, sub-kings,

[Note: [Col. 0991C] Abdon. When their bodies had lain for three days where they were killed, a certain Quirinus, a subdeacon, gathered them and secretly buried them in his house, where they remained hidden until the time of Constantine. Their bodies were then taken from there and transferred to the cemetery of Pontianus. Peter de Natalibus; Notker; Ado.]

who, while suffering imprisonment in the Persian city of Cerduba under Decius,

[D.: Credula; B.: Cordula; C.: Corduba]

were finally brought to Rome by him, bound in chains and tormented by various punishments. There they were first beaten with leaded clubs and then killed by the sword.

Florus in A. and T. altered the wording and sense as follows: At Rome, the passion of Saints Abdon and Sennes, who came from Persia to Rome and, under the emperor Decius, after being tormented by various punishments, were finally killed by the sword.

The same Florus in T. and L.: On the same day, at Rome, the passion of Saint Tertullinus,

[Note: [Col. 0991C] Tertullinus. He will be treated below, on 4 August.]

who, when he refused to sacrifice to the gods at Valerian’s command, was first beaten with clubs and afflicted with fire; then he was handed over to the prefect Sapricius, after which he was ordered to have his mouth beaten with stones, to be afflicted again with fire, and to be suspended on the rack. When he could not be overcome, and his steadfastness was reported to Valerian, sentence was given that he should be punished by beheading. But the abridged version in L. concludes: “Who, by Valerian’s order, was commanded to be punished by beheading after dreadful tortures.”

B.: At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Ursus, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0991C] Ursus. He lived as a recluse and anchorite beside the basilica of Saint Amator; when a fire broke out in the city, he extinguished it by his prayers. On that occasion, once the holy man’s merit had been made manifest, when Censurius, the tenth bishop, had died, he was forcibly taken and installed in the episcopate; his cell was converted into a church. He completed the course of his life at the age of eighty-one and, dying on this day, was buried in the basilica of Saint Germanus. He lived in the time of Popes John and Felix. Labbe, *Bibliotheca Nova*, volume I, p. 418.]

31.—Second day before the Kalends. Bede has no entry.

The Dijon Supplement likewise has no entry.

V. C.: At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Germanus. And the feast of Saints Secundinus and Maxima. C.: On the same day, the reconciliation of Saint Nicholas. B.: In the African city of Sindana, the feast of Saints Democritus,

[Col. 0993A] [Note: [Col. 0994A] Democritus. Baronius states that these martyrs suffered at Synnada in Phrygia Pacatiana.]

Secundus, Dionysius, and Thyrsus. A. T.: In Africa, of Saints Dionysius, Secundus, and Thyrsus. A. T. L. likewise have on this day what is found everywhere else on 1 August concerning Saint Germanus from Bede.

[AUGUST.]

[Col. 0993C]

1.—On the Kalends. At Saint Peter’s,

[Note: [Col. 0993C] Peter. The dedication of the basilica of Saint Peter *ad Vincula* is celebrated here. The Greeks also customarily celebrate the feast of Saint Peter’s chains on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February. The Acts of the Apostles, chapter XII, report that Saint Peter was bound with two chains in Jerusalem. One of these was carried by the empress Eudocia to Constantinople; the other was sent by her to Rome to the empress Eudoxia, her daughter and the wife of the emperor Valentinian. A feast day was established in both places. Surius has an encomium concerning them in volume IV. Just as a basilica was built at Constantinople in honor of one of the chains, so at Rome a titular church was erected by Eudoxia, the daughter of Eudocia; in ancient records it is found called both by Eudoxia’s name and by the name of Saint Peter’s Chains. Sigebert records the history of the event, among other places, in his *Chronicle* under the year 408, although through the error of copyists Eudoxia is written instead of Eudocia as the founder, since it was Eudoxia who erected the church. Baronius, Notes on the Martyrology. This church is also said to have been the first built and dedicated by Peter himself in Europe.]

of Saint Peter *ad Vincula*. And of the Holy Maccabees.

B.: The dedication of the first basilica built by Blessed Peter, which is called Saint Peter *ad Vincula*. Concerning the Maccabees, A. T. L. B. read as follows: At Antioch, the passion of the Holy Maccabees, who suffered under King Antiochus with their mother.

And at Auxerre

[C.: Calciodorum]

of Germanus, bishop,

[Note: [Col. 0993D] Germanus. We said enough about him yesterday, when he is celebrated by all the martyrologists.]

who, distinguished by many virtues, learning, and continence, defended the faith of the Britons against the Pelagian heresy on two occasions. And at Vercelli, of Eusebius, bishop,

[Note: [Col. 0994C] Eusebius. Because he refused to depose Athanasius with the Arians at the synod of Milan, he was sent into exile by the emperor Constantius. Socrates II, 36; Sozomen IV, 9. Under the emperor Julian he returned from exile from the Upper Thebaid; when he reached Alexandria, he convened a synod together with Athanasius, at which they explicitly declared the Trinity to be consubstantial. The same, III, 7, and V, 12. Finally, when the Arians persecuted him, he endured martyrdom by being dragged over steps, but nevertheless escaped unharmed and at last rested in peace. Notker.]

who, when the Arians had stirred up persecution, suffered martyrdom under the emperor Constantius.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Rome, the passion of Saints Boni,

[Note: [Col. 0994D] Boni. These men were beheaded on the road called the Aqueduct. Tertullinus took care of their bodies and placed their relics near the bodies of Saints Juvinus and Basileus on the Via Latina. Surius IV, p. 467.]

Faustus, Maurus, Primitivus, Calumniosus, John, Exuperantius, Cyrillus, and Honoratus, who, although they were clerics of Blessed Stephen, bishop, were all beheaded by Valerian and Gallienus without any trial for the name of Christ. In T. and L.: On the same day, at Rome, of Saint Victor, pope,

[Note: [Col. 0994D] Victor. See above, under 28 July.]

who, when the priests had asked about the cycle of Easter, after conferring with the bishops and presbyters, summoned Theophilus,

[Note: [Col. 0994D] Theophilus. He was not bishop of Alexandria, but of Palestine, as Eusebius writes, V, 25; indeed, he was bishop of Caesarea, as is clear from Bede’s book on the vernal equinox, where the acts of this Caesarean synod are quoted.]

bishop of Alexandria, and established that from the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month through the twenty-first, holy Easter should always be celebrated on a Sunday; and he suffered martyrdom in the time of Commodus and Granianus.

[Note: [Col. 0995C] Commodus. And Glabrio, not Granianus. He did not suffer martyrdom during their consulship but began his pontificate. For in the *Chronicle of the Ancient Pontiffs* one reads: “He was [pope] from the fifth consulship of Commodus and Glabrio—that is, from the year 186—until Lateranus and Rufinus—that is, until the year 191.”]

Written in the book of the bishops. In Spain, in the city of Gerunda, the passion of Saint Felix:

[Note: [Col. 0995C] Felix. A native of Scillitanum, he came west by ship together with Cucuphas, mentioned above on 25 July. After preaching for some time at Barcelona, Emporiae, and Gerunda, he was arrested by the official Rufinus on the orders of Dacianus during the reign of Diocletian. After various tortures he was killed and buried at Gerunda in a tomb that he himself had prepared. Ado; Surius, volume IV, in the Acts of Saint Cucuphas and under 1 August, where he is treated.]

for after many tortures he was tied to mules and dragged through the city; then he was suspended and thrown into the sea. When he reached the shore with the Lord’s help, he was so torn apart by iron claws that he died from the mutilation.

V.: The feast of Hope, Faith, Charity, and their mother Wisdom.

T.: On the same day, the translation of Saint Jonatus,

[Note: [Col. 0995D] Jonatus. He was the first abbot of Marcianus, or Marcenus, and rests there after being elevated. His feast falls on the Kalends of August; his translation on 8 April. Molanus, *On the Saints of Belgium*.]

a disciple of Saint Amandus. B.: In Spain, at Gerunda, the feast of Saint Felix.

2.—Fourth day before the Nones. At Rome, of Saint Stephen,

[Note: [Col. 0995D] Stephen. He succeeded Pope Lucius in the year 253 and lived during the time of Valerian and Gallienus, from the consulship of Volusianus and Maximus until the fourth consulship of Valerian and the third of Gallienus—that is, from 253 to 257. He threatened excommunication against Cyprian and the African Church, and against Firmilian and his Eastern party, because they held that heretics and schismatics should be rebaptized. See Saint Firmilian’s letter to Cyprian, extant among the works of Saint Cyprian. He suffered martyrdom today and, according to the expanded *Chronicle of the Ancient Pontiffs*, was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Via Appia on the third day before the Nones of August.]

pope, who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of the emperor Valerian. On the same day, the feast of Saint Theodota with her three sons in the province of Bithynia, in the city of Nicaea, during the reign of Diocletian, under the count Leocadius,

[Note: [Col. 0995D] Leocadius. He tried for many days to compel Theodota to marry him; but when she would in no way consent, he sent her, bound in chains together with her sons, to Nicetius. Ado; Peter de Natalibus.]

who sent her, bound in chains with her sons, to Nicetius, the governor of Bithynia. He first had her firstborn son Evodius, who confidently confessed Christ, beaten with clubs; then he had her and all her sons consumed by fire. (Thus far A.) Written in the Passion of Saint Anastasia.

[Note: [Col. 0996C] Anastasia. She is commemorated below, on 25 December.]

B.: In Italy, in the city of Verona, the feast of Saints Felix and Niceus.

[Note: [Col. 0996C] Niceus. In Notker he is called Nicetius.]

3.—On the Nones. Bede has no entry.

V.: At Rome, of Saints Diogenes and Stephen. And the deposition of Saint Eufronius, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0996C] Eufronius. Gregory of Tours II, 15, writes of him as follows: “At that time, that is, in the time of King Childeric, the basilica of Blessed Symphorianus, martyr of Autun, was built by the presbyter Eufronius. Thereafter Eufronius himself received the episcopate of this city. He sent with great devotion the marble that is placed above the holy tomb of Blessed Martin.” He governed the church of Autun toward the end of the fifth century. He attended the ordination of John, bishop of Chalon, as Apollinaris Sidonius testifies, book IV, letter 25; the same author wrote to him in book VII, letter 8, and book IX, letter 2. A distinguished letter of his and of Lupus, bishop of Troyes, on ecclesiastical discipline is extant in Sirmond, volume I of the *Councils*. Idatius praises another letter of his to Count Agrippinus in his *Chronicle*. He also attended the Council of Lyons and subscribed, with others, the letter of Faustus condemning the errors of the Pelagians. In the *Hagiology of France*, in volume II of Labbe’s *New Library*, his feast is celebrated at Autun on the fourth day before the Nones of August.]

C.: At Rome, the feast of Saint Drogentius. Of the protomartyr Stephen at Ancona,

[Note: [Col. 0996D] Ancona. In Bede, “Antioch” is erroneously written instead of “Ancona.” Saint Augustine writes in volume V, sermon 323, about the very ancient memorial of the protomartyr Stephen established at Ancona, and about the stone with which he was struck on the elbow, which was taken up by one who witnessed his stoning, brought to Italy, and left at Ancona; from that time a memorial of Saint Stephen existed there.]

where one of the stones with which he was struck is said to be preserved. B. D. A. T. L.: At Jerusalem, the discovery

[Note: [Col. 0997C] Discovery. Gamaliel revealed the relics of these saints to Saint Lucian in a dream, in the consulship of Honorius for the tenth time and Theodosius for the sixth, that is, in the year 415, on 3 December. They were transferred to Jerusalem during the episcopate of John, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January. Since neither their discovery nor any translation occurred today, why was their commemoration assigned to this day rather than to another? This difficulty is resolved in the Notes on Baronius’ Martyrology by Don Antonio Geronio of Tarragona, whose opinion is that long before the discovery of Saint Stephen, this very day had been dedicated in his honor as protomartyr, and afterward became more solemn through the commemoration of the discovery mentioned above; for it is established above that Stephen was celebrated at Ancona on this day. Avitus’ and Lucian’s letters concerning this discovery may be read in Surius, volume IV, under 3 August, and in Baronius’ *Annals* under the year 415.]

of the body of the protomartyr Stephen (thus far A.), and of Saints Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibon. A. T.: At Autun, the deposition of Eufronius, bishop. B.: At Rome, the feast of Saints Diogenes and Stephen. At Constantinople, the feast of Saint Acella.

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Acella. Rather, Achilla or Achilleus.]

4.—Second day before the Nones. Bede has no entry.

[Note: [Col. 0997D] B.: At Rome, on the Via Tiburtina, the feast of Saints Laurentius.]

D.: Of Blessed Aristarchus,

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Aristarchus. The inseparable companion of the apostle Paul and his fellow captive in chains at Rome. After Paul’s passion, because Paul had appointed him bishop of the Thessalonians—or, as the abbot Dorotheus writes, bishop of Apamea—he was crowned by Christ after long struggles. Peter de Natalibus.]

a disciple of Saint Paul the apostle. At Rome, of the martyr Tertullinus.

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Tertullinus. See above, under 30 July.]

B. C. V.: At Rome, in the cemetery of Saint Lawrence, of Crescentianus and Justus. L.: The feast of Saints Crescentianus, Justus, and Hyacinth, martyrs. A.: At Rome, of Saint Justin the presbyter and Saint Crescentiana. T.: At Rome, the feast of Saint Justus and Saint Crescentiana. And the passion of Saint Justin,

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Justin. During the persecution of Decius, Gallus, and Volusianus, he was especially distinguished by the glory of his confession. Blessed Sixtus ordained him. After he had committed to burial the bodies of Blessed Sixtus the pope and Lawrence the archdeacon, Hippolytus and his entire household, and many other martyrs, a year having passed, he too earned martyrdom by beheading during the same persecution. He was buried at Rome on the Via Tiburtina beside the body of Lawrence in the Veran field. Usuard; Peter de Natalibus. In Baronius’ *Martyrology* he is commemorated on 17 September.]

the presbyter, who gathered and buried many bodies of the saints. B.: In Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Saga and Bartholomew.

5.—On the Nones. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: On this day, the feast of Saint Cassian,

[Note: [Col. 0998C] Cassian. He was made bishop of the city of Orte in the time of the emperor Jovian.]

bishop and confessor, who, instructed in heavenly disciplines by the martyr Theon

[A.: Zone; L.: Azone]

in the city of the Egyptians called Orte, was ordained bishop. While he was building a church there, Blessed Lawrence the martyr appeared to him and urged him to dedicate it to his own name. (Thus far L.) Then, entering Gaul by divine revelation, he came with his companions to the city of Autun and was honorably received by Saint Simplicius, bishop of that city.

[Note: [Col. 0998C] Simplicius. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 25, therefore seems to require correction, since he places Cassian before Egemon and Simplicius. Indeed, Simplicius is listed among the bishops said to have attended the Council of Cologne in 346 against Euphratas, bishop of that city; he was therefore already occupying the see before Cassian’s arrival, for Cassian became bishop in the time of Jovian, that is, in 368.]

When Saint Simplicius had administered the priesthood and died, Saint Cassian was appointed bishop in his place.

[Col. 0998B] There he shone with many miracles and rested in peace. When Bishop Germanus of Auxerre came to his tomb and, as was customary, offered prayers to Christ, he is said to have addressed him: “What are you doing, glorious brother Cassian?” Blessed Cassian replied: “I enjoy sweet rest in peace and await the coming of the Redeemer.”

Afterward, his body, made renowned by the multitude of its miracles, was transferred to the town now called Augusta Viromanduorum

[Note: [Col. 0998D] Transferred. This translation took place around the year 840.]

and buried inside the basilica of the martyr Blessed Quintinus.

D.: In the province of Raetia, in the city of Augusta, the feast of Saint Afra,

[Note: [Col. 0998D] Afra. For Afra, Afer should be restored according to Notker, who writes: “At Augusta Euphratensis, the birth of Saint Afer the martyr. Because of the similarity of these names—namely, Augusta and Afer—our countrymen were led to believe that on this day the passion of Saint Afra was completed at Augusta Raetia, or Vindelica.” Concerning Afra, see below, under the seventh day of this month.]

who, though a pagan and prostitute, was converted to Christ through the teaching of Saint Narcissus, bishop, and baptized with her entire household; for confessing the Lord, she was handed over to the fire. B. V.: At Autun, of Saint Cassian, bishop. B.: In the city of Augusta, the passion of Saint Afer the martyr. C. V.: At Châlons, of Saint Memmius, bishop. V.: And elsewhere, of Florianus and Philistina. C.: And of Agapitus. A. T.: In the city of Anxiopolis, the feast of Saints Heraclius and Ereutius. And at Châlons, of Saint Memmius,

[Note: [Col. 0998D] Memmius. Frodoard is the authority for the claim that Memmius was sent by Saint Peter into Gaul together with Saint Sixtus, the first bishop of Reims. An ancient author of his Life, said to have flourished in the seventh century, likewise attributes this mission to Saint Peter; but Almannus, a monk of Hautvillers in the diocese of Reims, who flourished in the ninth century, thought it sufficient to attribute it to Saint Clement. See Mabillon, *Analecta*, volume II, p. 86 and following, where his discovery under Charles the Bald in 868 is also discussed. “At Châlons” is written as “of Châlons.”]

bishop.

[Col. 0999B] 6.—Eighth day before the Ides of August. At Rome, of Saint Xystus,

[Note: [Col. 0999C] Xystus. When Pope Stephen suffered martyrdom in the year 257, Xystus was appointed in his place in the same year, on or about 24 August. Baronius correctly reproduces his martyrdom under the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus; he errs only in connecting their consulship, which fell in the year of Christ 258, incorrectly with the year 261 of the same era, and thus makes a chronological error of three years. He therefore occupied the see for only eleven months and six days. Eusebius assigns eleven years to his pontificate, whereas the same number of months should have been assigned to him.]

bishop, and of Felicissimus and Agapitus, deacons,

[Note: [Col. 0999D] Felicissimus. These men were not deacons; nor were Januarius and the others subdeacons; nor did they suffer on the same day as Xystus, as is clear from the distinguished Pearson’s *Cyprianic Annals*.]

who were beheaded under Decius.

[Note: [Col. 0999D] Decius. Rather, during the time of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.]

(Thus far A.) Four other subdeacons—Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius, and Stephen—were beheaded with him, as is read in the *Acts of the Pontiffs*.

V., in first place, as also in L., but on the following day: The Transfiguration of Our Lord Jesus Christ on Mount Tabor.

Florus in A. T. L.: In the city of Complutum, the passion of Saints Justus and Pastor, who, while boys studying at school, heard of the search for Christians, threw down their writing tablets at school, and voluntarily presented themselves to the prefect Dacianus. After he had ordered them to be severely scourged, he had them both beheaded (sic).

B.: In the province of Raetia, in the city of Augusta, the passion of Saint Afra, virgin, and 166 others.

[Col. 0999C] [Note: [Col. 0999D] Afra. See the following day.]

C.: On the same day, the passion of Saint Afra.

7.—Seventh day before the Ides. At Arezzo, of Saint Donatus,

[Note: [Col. 0999D] Donatus. The accounts given in the Acts of Saint Donatus concerning Julian’s upbringing at Rome with Donatus appear false. “It is also wholly contrary to reason that during the persecution of Julian, who did not reign for even two complete years, Saint Donatus should still be said to have been a lector, then consecrated a deacon, ordained a presbyter after many years, and finally, while Julian was still reigning, appointed in the place of Bishop Saturus when he died; and, moreover, that while Julian was still alive he should have been crowned with martyrdom. How also is he said to have still been a lector in Julian’s time when he is said to have been ordained bishop by Julius, the Roman pontiff? What I think about this matter I shall gladly and freely state, without prejudice to the truth. I believe that Donatus’ boyhood and upbringing at Rome, and the death of his parents, occurred not under Julian but under Diocletian, around the end of that persecution. From that time until Julian there intervened a period of fifty-two years, during which Donatus, having escaped by flight, withdrew to Arezzo. There he was admitted to the sacred orders by Bishop Saturus; after Saturus’ death, he was appointed in his place by Saint Pope Julius; and finally, under the emperor Julian, he was crowned with martyrdom.” Baronius, Notes on the Martyrology.]

bishop and martyr, who, as Gregory relates in book I of the *Dialogues*, restored by prayer during Mass a sacred chalice broken by pagans.

[Note: [Col. 1000D] Chalice. See Saint Gregory, *Dialogues* I, 7.]

Florus in T. and L.: In the city of Augusta, the passion of Saint Afra,

[Note: [Col. 1000D] Afra. Since they relate that she was converted to the faith by Narcissus, bishop, some—including Peter de Natalibus VII, 28—think that this was the famous Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem. Others have said that this was Narcissus the martyr of Gerunda; her Acts testify to this.]

who was at first a gentile, but afterward converted and baptized by Narcissus, bishop, and, under Diocletian and the judge Gaius, because she refused to sacrifice to idols, was condemned to the fire. When her body was found intact on the same day and her mother Hilaria was committing it to burial with her three daughters, namely Digna, Eumenia, and Euprepia, the daughters too were burned in the same place because they opposed the worship of the gods, and were likewise adorned with the glory of martyrdom. On the same day, at Caesarea in Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Mammes,

[L.: Mammae]

the martyr, who, after the rack, fire, and various tortures, was handed over to the beasts; and when even then, by the power of the Lord, he remained unharmed, he died by stoning under the presiding judge Hadrian.

D.: At Rome, the passion of twenty-five holy martyrs. At Antioch, the feast of Saints Suffroneus, Veneria, and six others. At Milan, the feast of Saint Faustinus.

[Note: [Col. 1001C] Faustinus. After many contests, he obtained the palm of martyrdom under Aurelius Commodus. Notker; Ado; Baronius.]

8.—Sixth day before the Ides. The feast of Saint Cyriacus.

[Note: [Col. 1001C] Cyriacus. The feast of him, Largus, and Smaragdus is celebrated above, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April. Their bodies were buried by the presbyter John on the Via Salaria; on this day Pope Marcellus transferred them to the estate of Lucina on the Via Ostiensis. They were afterward brought into the city and placed in the deaconry of Saint Mary on the Via Lata.]

T. adds Largus and Smaragdus; V. further joins the names of Crescentianus, Memmia, and Julianus; C., omitting Smaragdus, has the names Crescentianus and Theodorus. Florus reworked the account in A. and T. as follows: The emperor Diocletian, greatly honoring him because he had cured his daughter of demonic affliction, sent him for this reason to the king of the Persians. When he had also freed the king’s daughter from the demon, he baptized her together with her father and 430 others. On his return, Maximinus ordered him to be bound in chains and dragged naked before his chariot, and to be afflicted with various punishments by his deputy Carpasius; then he ordered him and twenty others to be put to death by beheading.

L. gives a shorter version: At Rome, the translation of the body of Saint Cyriacus with his companions, whom Maximinus, son of Diocletian, after afflicting them with various punishments, ordered to be beheaded together with twenty others. B.: At Rome, of Saint Cyriacus the martyr and his companions. At Nicomedia,

[Note: [Col. 1001C] Nicomedia. In Notker, the sentence reads as follows: At Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Nazarius, Julianus, and Agape the virgin, Eutychianus, Philadelphia, and Leonidas.]

the feast of Saints Nazarius, Julianus, and Agape the virgin. At Philadelphia, the feast of Saint Leo.

### 9 — The Fifth Day before the Ides

[Note: Vigil. Why vigils are held for Saint Lawrence more than for other martyrs was due to no other cause than that ancient practice of the faithful, who began to keep watch over the body of so great a martyr with particular devotion, as his Acts testify. For they read as follows: “When they had committed Saint Lawrence to burial, they fasted and kept night vigils for three days, with a great gathering of Christians, nor did they cease from mourning and tears.” Baronius, in the notes.]

Vigil of Saint Lawrence. On the same day at Rome, Saint Romanus, a soldier who, moved by the confession of Saint Lawrence, asked to be baptized by him; and presently, by order of Decius, he was brought forth, beaten with clubs, and beheaded.

Florus, in A. and T.: At Cologne, the commemoration of Saints Faustinus, Marcellinus, and Secundianus.

[Note: Marcellinus and Secundianus, who, having become Christians from among the persecutors, were first beaten under Decius, during the tenure of the consular governor Promotus; then they were suspended on the rack, scraped with hooks, and roasted with fire applied to their sides. Finally, having been beheaded, they earned the triumphant palm of martyrdom. Surius, vol. IV; Usuard.]

On the same day at Verona, the passion of Saints Firmus and Rusticus, who, after fire and other tortures, were beheaded under Maximian, by Anulinus [T. Aemilius], his counselor.

[Note: Firmus. While Caucarius, deputy of the city of Verona, was keeping watch near the bodies, seven men, claiming to be merchants, removed the bodies; after loading them on a ship, they were seen no more. The bodies themselves were conveyed to the Carthaginian province, to the city called Praedones. Later they were transferred to Capras, a city of Histria, where they remained until Saint Mary of Verona, called the Consolatrix, brought them back to Verona. Peter de Natalibus.]

L. has only their names and the place of their contest.

[Col. 1002C] B.: At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saints Antoninus, Tiburtius, and Valerian. C. V.: In the East, Firmus, Rusticus, Crescentianus, Theodorus, or Theodolus.

### 10 — The Fourth Day before the Ides

[Note: Lawrence. His martyrdom belongs to the year 258. For in the letter of Saint Cyprian to Successus, written in that year, Pope Sixtus is said to have been executed in the cemetery on the eighth day before the Ides of August—that is, on the sixth day of the month. Since only three days intervened between the death of Sixtus, Roman pontiff, and the martyrdom of Lawrence, as is clear from the Acts preserved by Surius, the latter must therefore be assigned to the tenth day of the same month. Saint Augustine praises Lawrence in many places, and the distinguished scholar Ruinart, in *The Sincere and Selected Acts of the Earliest Martyrs*, p. 180, supplies much concerning Saint Lawrence, excerpted from brief works of other holy Fathers and ancient writers. Since Saint Sixtus suffered martyrdom under Valerian, Saint Lawrence must likewise have suffered under the same emperor. The Acts of Saint Lawrence, therefore, and nearly all the Martyrologies, except Baronius’s Martyrology, must be corrected, since they falsely report that he suffered under Decius. His body was buried by Blessed Hippolytus and the presbyter Justin in the cemetery of Cyriaca in the Veran field.]

Commemoration of Saint Lawrence under Decius. After very numerous tortures—imprisonment, various scourging, and burning plates—he finally completed his martyrdom by being roasted upon an iron gridiron.

V. C.: And the life of the seven Sleeping Brothers.

[Note: On these, see 27 June.]

B.: And elsewhere, of Crescention, Januarius, and Exuperatus.

### 11 — The Third Day before the Ides

At Rome, Saint Tiburtius, martyr, and Saint Susanna.

[Note: Tiburtius, son of Chromatius. In the time of Diocletian, he was betrayed by Torquatus, who falsely claimed to be a Christian and deceitfully arranged for the unbelievers to seize Saint Tiburtius while he was praying; Tiburtius suffered beheading. See the Acts of Saint Sebastian in the Bollandists, 20 January.]

[Note: Susanna was the daughter of Gabinius, the presbyter commemorated above on 18 February, and the niece of Pope Caius, commemorated above on 20 February. Since she was exceptionally beautiful, Diocletian sent his cousin Claudius to Gabinius to ask Maximian Caesar for her as a wife. Her father requested a delay and disclosed the matter to his daughter in the presence of Pope Caius. She nevertheless refused, having embraced virginity at her father’s urging. When Claudius asked for her again, she rejected his kiss and urged him toward baptism. Not long afterward he was baptized by Pope Caius, together with his wife, children, and brother Maximus. When she refused to comply with Diocletian’s wishes, Diocletian ordered that she be punished with the sword within her own house. After this had been done, Serena Augusta gathered the holy martyr’s body by night and placed it beside the bodies of the saints in the cemetery of Alexander, in a sand-pit and crypt near Saint Alexander. Surius, vol. IV.]

This entry is absent from A. T. L., although Florus describes his deeds as follows:

“He was received from the sacred font by Blessed Sebastian and strengthened in the faith of Christ. When he detested the idols’ images, he was arrested by the prefect Fabianus. (Up to this point, A.) Before his feet the same prefect scattered burning coals, saying: ‘Either place incense upon these coals, or walk barefoot over them.’ But he made the sign of the cross and steadfastly walked over them with bare feet. From there he was led along the Lavican Way, pouring forth prayers to the Lord; struck with a sword, he departed to Christ. Written in the Acts of Blessed Sebastian.”

Florus likewise says there:

“On the same day, in Gaul, in the city of Cambrai, the burial of Saint Gaugericus bishop (up to this point, A.), who was a man of great abstinence and great religious devotion, generous in almsgiving and a worker of miracles; and of Saint Taurinus, his brother.”

[Note: Gaugericus was born in Evosio, a town of Gaul now called Yvois. Saint Magnericus, bishop of Trier, ordained him cleric and deacon. Meanwhile Vedulphus, bishop of Cambrai, died, and by common consent Gaugericus was installed in the see of Cambrai by Bishop Aegidius of Reims. Full of good works and years, he died peacefully in the year of the Lord 594, after thirty-nine years as bishop. He was buried near Cambrai in the basilica that he himself had built in the name of Saint Medard. From there, together with the college of canons, he was transferred to the church of Saint Vedast, which was also called Saint Gaugericus after him. Molanus, *On the Saints of Belgium*; Ghinus of Siena; Surius, vol. IV.]

V. B. C.: And the passion of Saint Cassian.

[Note: Perhaps this is the same person who is commemorated on the fifth or thirteenth day of this month.]

### 12 — The Second Day before the Ides

In Sicily, in the city of Catania, the commemoration of Euplius the deacon, who, after being tortured for a very long time, was beheaded by Calvisianus [C. Lusius; B. Claudianus], the consular governor, during the reign of Diocletian and Maximian.

B.: At Rome, the commemoration of Chrysantus and Daria. In Syria, the commemoration of Saints Macarius and Julian.

### 13 — On the Ides

At Rome, Saint Hippolytus.

[Note: Hippolytus was converted to the faith and baptized by Blessed Lawrence, commemorated above on the tenth day of August. He did not suffer under Decius, as the Martyrologies and the Acts of Saint Lawrence falsely assert, but under Valerian, three days after Saint Lawrence, together with his entire household. Saint Justin buried their bodies in a field beside the Veran estate.]

He was bound by the feet to the necks of untamed horses and thus dragged through thistles and thorns until he gave up his spirit, in the time of Decius. And Concordia, his nurse, was beaten with leaded scourges before him and suffered martyrdom. And nineteen others from his household were beheaded at the same time. (Up to this point, A.)

On the same day, at Rome, the commemoration of Saint Cassian.

(C. continues only this far.) When he refused to worship idols, the persecutor asked him what profession he practiced. He replied that he taught children their letters. Immediately, after his clothes had been stripped off and his hands bound behind his back, he was placed in the midst of them. The children were summoned, and because he had become hateful to them through teaching, they were given permission to kill him. But just as deeply as they had grieved while learning, so gladly did they take revenge: some struck him with tablets or boxwood writing-slips [D. box-tree branches], while others wounded him with their styluses. The weaker their age, the more grievous the punishment of his martyrdom became through its prolonged death. The poet Prudentius wrote this.

[“The poet Prudentius wrote” is absent from B.]

Florus, in T.:

“In Gaul, in the city of Poitiers, the burial of Saint Radegundis the queen.”

[Note: She was from the region of Thuringia: her grandfather was King Bessinus, her paternal uncle Hermenfrid, and her father King Beretharius. She was taken captive by Chlothar, king of the Franks, around the year 530, and was placed under guard in the royal villa at Athies, in the Vermandois region, for the purpose of being raised there. Married to King Chlothar, she lived in such a way that she seemed joined in marriage not to the king but to Christ. After her brother had apparently been killed, she was veiled by Blessed Medard at Noyon and withdrew to the monastery she had built at Poitiers. When King Chlothar, her husband, sought to reclaim her, he desisted at the urging of Saint Germanus. After living a life full of miracles, Radegundis died in the year of Christ 587, according to Gregory of Tours, who in book IX, chapter 2, assigns her death to the twelfth year of King Childebert. She was buried by Gregory of Tours in the Basilica of Saint Mary. See her Life in Surius, vol. IV, and in Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, vol. I.]

She reclined on the marriage-bed of Lothar, king of the Franks, but was called a nun rather than a wife. Rejecting his companionship, she embraced Christ, whom she loved, and earned such great power that she even raised the dead.

L.: On the same day, Saint Radegundis the queen.

### 14 — The Nineteenth Day before the Kalends of September

Commemoration of Saint Eusebius the presbyter.

[Note: Eusebius, while steadfastly defending the Catholic faith in the presence of the Arian emperor Constantius and grieving that Pope Liberius had consented to Arian perfidy, was confined by order of that same Constantius in a certain room of his house, four feet in width. There he persevered steadfastly in prayer for many days and, after seven months, died while still confined. The presbyters Gregory and Orosius gathered his body and buried it in a crypt beside the body of Blessed Sixtus, bishop and martyr, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus. Ado; Notker.]

T. L. add: Of the Titulus of the Founder. A. has:

[Note: The Titulus. This is the ancient Titulus of Saint Eusebius, mentioned in the first council held at Rome under Pope Symmachus. The venerable bodies of Saints Eusebius, Orosius, and Paulinus, together with many relics of other martyrs, are preserved there, as the ancient records of that church make clear. Pope Zacharias arranged for the same church, which had collapsed through age, to be restored. Both inscriptions carved in marble and the *Book of the Roman Pontiffs* testify to this. Baronius, in the notes.]

The Titulus and Saint Conditor. V. and C. add: And Peregrinus. B. prefixes Viridena of Syria.

A. T. L.: Vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary, Mother of God.

B.: In Africa, the commemoration of Saint Demetrius. In Africa, the commemoration of Saint Strato. Likewise, in Africa, of Paul, Heraclius, and Possessor. In Aquileia, the commemoration of Saints Felix, Fortunata, and Vincentia.

### 15 — The Eighteenth Day before the Kalends

The Dormition of Saint Mary.

[Col. 1007B] The rubric is noted in D., A., T., L., B., and C. In D. it is called the Assumption. V. C. add: And elsewhere, of Tration [Stration], Philip, and Anticianus. A. T. L.: In Nicomedia, the commemoration of Saints Philip and Eutychianus [Eutychius]. In Carthage, the commemoration of Saints Isaac and Maximianus. B.: In Nicomedia, the commemoration of Saints Strato, Philip, and Eutychianus, with their companions.

### 16 — The Seventeenth Day before the Kalends

Bede has no entry.

D.: In Nicaea of Bithynia, the commemoration of Saint Ursacius the confessor.

[Note: More properly Arsacius. He was Persian by nationality. While serving in the army as one appointed to care for the emperor’s lions, he became a man of no little distinction among the confessors during the reign of Licinius. He foretold the earthquake by which Nicomedia was destroyed, in the consulship of Datianus and Cerealis, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, as Ammianus Marcellinus and Hydatius record in their chronicles; this was the year of Christ 358. Before the disaster occurred, Arsacius prayed to God that he might die before seeing the city’s ruin with his own eyes. Sozomen, IV, 16.]

V. C.: The commemoration of Simplicianus and Saint Thyrsus, Orion, and Emilius.

A. T. L. B.: In Persia, the commemoration of Thyrsus with his companions. In Alexandria, the passion of Saints Orion and Agnatius. In Gaul, in the city of Metz (this phrase is absent from B.), the commemoration of Saint Arnulf the bishop and confessor.

[Note: Arnulf was born of noble parents. He married a woman named Doda and had two sons by her. After having flourished in various honors at the royal palace, he planned, together with the distinguished man Romaricus, to go to Lérins, but some obstacle prevented the fulfillment of both their vows. After Pappolus, Arnulf obtained the see of Metz in the year 614. After governing the Church excellently for several years, he withdrew to the wilderness, namely to the Holy Mountain, where Romaricus lived; there coenobites and anchorites dwelt, besides consecrated virgins. On what day and in what year Saint Arnulf died seems uncertain. Bede above, Ado in his Martyrology, and the Roman Martyrology assign his feast to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August. But the testimony of the reliable Usuard and Wandelbert seems entirely preferable: they record Arnulf’s death on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, since the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August was the day of his translation. The author of the Life of Saint Goericus says: “After offerings had been given, they carried the same body of Saint Arnulf on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August to the church then called that of the Holy Apostles.” The author of the Life of Saint Arnulf agrees, saying that the translation occurred almost a year after his death. For if Arnulf’s death had occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, and his translation on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, one would say that the translation took place not after almost a full year but after the year had elapsed. The year is more difficult to determine. Sigebert assigns the year 640, and we have decided to follow him until more certain evidence appears. Yet Jonas, writing in the third year after the death of Saint Bertulf, abbot of Bobbio—that is, in the year 643—praises Arnulf as bishop of Metz at the beginning of his Life but does not yet call him a saint. See the Life of Saint Arnulf in section II of the *Benedictine Acts*.]

In A., with Orion omitted, only this is read: And the burial of Saint Agnatius. In B. it is written Ignatius, and the name Emilius is inserted.

### 17 — The Sixteenth Day before the Kalends

The Octave of Saint Lawrence.

V. C.: And Saint Mametes [C. Numetes] the monk.

T.: The passion of Saint Mammes.

[Note: He came from Paphlagonia; his parents were Theodotus and Rufina, and he was born while his parents were imprisoned for the faith. When his parents died in prison, a woman distinguished by birth, wealth, and finally piety, named Ammia, took up the infant and raised him as her son. When he was fifteen years old, he was brought before the tribunal of Democritus, governor of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Shortly afterward, before Aurelian himself, he professed the faith. After scourging, fire, and stoning, he was ordered to be thrown into the sea. But an angel immediately came down from heaven, struck terror into those who were leading him and put them to flight, while commanding the martyr to go to the mountain near Caesarea and live there. On that mountain he was nourished on the milk of wild beasts. Finally he was brought before the governor Alexander, under whom he successfully completed his martyrdom. Surius, vol. IV.]

L. B.: In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the commemoration of Saint Mammes the monk and martyr.

A. B. T.: In Chalcedon of Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Euphemia the virgin.

[Note: She is commemorated below on 16 September.]

T.: On the same day, the passion of seven martyrs who suffered under King Huneric.

[Note: Septem. In Carthage in Africa, the holy martyrs Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Servus and Rusticus the subdeacons, Rogatus and Septimus the monks, and Maximus the boy. During the Vandal persecution, for confessing the Catholic faith and defending the one baptism, they were tormented with various unheard-of punishments. Finally they were nailed to the wood on which they were to be burned. Although the fire was repeatedly kindled, it was always extinguished by divine intervention. By order of Huneric they were beaten with the bars of oars, and, their skulls having been crushed, they were killed, completing the course of their contest. Victor of Vita wrote their deeds in book III of *On the Vandal Persecution* and in a separate booklet placed in the appendix to that work. Although they are recorded as having suffered there on the sixth day before the Nones of July, all the Martyrologists nevertheless commemorate them on this day, perhaps because their translation took place then.]

B.: In the district of Le Mans, at the monastery of Anisola, the translation of the body and the dedication of the basilica of Saint Carilephus, abbot and confessor.

[Note: Translation. The relics of Saint Carilephus were transferred, after the devastation caused by the Normans, to the fortress of Blois—commonly called Blois—located on the Loire in the diocese of Chartres. They are still preserved in the oratory called that of Saint Carilephus within the fortress enclosure, except for the upper part of the skull, which, together with two vertebrae, is kept in the saint’s own monastery at Anisola. The feast of Saint Carilephus is celebrated above on the Kalends of July.]

### 18 — The Fifteenth Day before the Kalends

The commemoration of Saint Agapitus the martyr.

[Note: When he was fifteen years old, Agapitus was arrested by order of the emperor Aurelian. He was first beaten for a long time with raw sinews and imprisoned for four days. Then, when he had been brought before the governor Antiochus, the latter ordered burning coals to be placed upon his head. But while the martyr was giving thanks to God, he was beaten with scourges and suspended naked, head downward, over a sharp smoke made beneath him. He was then beaten again with scourges, and boiling water was poured over his belly. When Antiochus suddenly died, Saint Agapitus was thrown to the lions by the emperor’s order, but was not harmed. He was then struck with a sword by the servants, so that he might be crowned. Ado; Notker. His memory is especially celebrated at Praeneste, where his sacred relics are preserved. Baronius, in the notes.]

D. adds: Under the emperor Aurelius, with Antiochus as governor.

B. A. prefix: In the city of Praeneste.

C. V.: Silantia [C. Philantiae], Heliana the virgin, and Marciana the virgin.

[Note: Silantias. In the city of Amea in Pontus, the commemoration of Saints Pontinus, Philantias, and others. Jerome’s Martyrology.]

L.: And in the city of Praeneste, the commemoration of Eziachus with his companions. And the commemoration of Helena.

[Note: Helena. Concerning Saint Helena’s piety, greatness of spirit, beneficence, and the devout manner in which she conducted herself in the churches, see Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* III, 42–46. For how she discovered at Jerusalem the cross of the Lord, which had long been sought, see Socrates I, 17, and Sozomen II, 1. Her death occurred in the year 326, as is shown by the consulship held in the following year by Flavius Valerius Constantius, brother of Constantine the Great. Since Helena cherished the grandchildren of Constantine the Great, his children, with the greatest affection, she took every precaution to prevent any of the sons of Constantius, the brothers of Constantine, from taking the empire away from them. Therefore, as long as she lived, she kept them as exiles, now at Toulouse in Gaul, as Ausonius writes, now at Corinth, as Julian reports in his Letter to the Corinthians, a fragment of which survives in Libanius’s speech for Aristophanes of Corinth. There Libanius states that, through Helena’s counsel and the hatred of a stepmother, Constantius, Julian’s father, was moved from place to place. Since Constantine, brother of Constantine the Great, served as consul in the following year, as Zonaras reports, there is no doubt that after his mother’s death Constantine the Great bestowed this honor upon his brother. The body of Helena Augusta was brought to Rome, as Eusebius testifies in *Life of Constantine* III, 44, and after two years was transported to Constantinople, as Nicephorus reports, VIII, 30. But Socrates I, 17, while transcribing Eusebius’s words, interprets τὴν βασιλεύουσαν πόλιν—“the imperial city”—as New Rome, although Eusebius ordinarily designates Rome by the term “royal city.” Moreover, Constantinople had not yet been dedicated and therefore could not have been called the imperial city, since at that time it was only old Byzantium.]

Helena the queen.

A.: And Saint Martin the pope.

[Note: See below, 12 November, concerning Pope Martin.]

A. T. B.: And the commemoration of Saint Candidus.

P.: In the city of Amantia, the commemoration of Saints Pontimus, Philantias, and Heliana, virgins.

### 19 — The Fourteenth Day before the Kalends

The commemoration of Saint Magnus.

[Note: Ado, Usuard, and Rabanus wrongly identify him with Saint Andrew. Saint Magnus was killed at Anagni during the persecution of Decius. Such is attested by the records and ancient monuments of the Church of Anagni, as Baronius writes in the notes. Others on this day commemorate another martyr Magnus at Caesarea in Cappadocia, during the reign of the emperor Aurelian and under the governor Alexander; see Peter de Natalibus VII, 76. There was also another Saint Magnus, bishop of Altinum, concerning whom see the same author in the appendix, chapter 17.]

B.: Magnus. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Andrew.

Or Saint Andrew.

[Note: Andrew was a tribune under Antiochus in the regions of Syria. When he had gained, by divine favor, a notable victory over the Persians, many of his soldiers, sharing in that victory, embraced the Christian faith. When Antiochus learned this, he became angry and ordered Saint Andrew to be placed upon a burning bronze bed; then he threw him into prison. By order of Maximian, he was released from prison with his companions and went to Tarsus in Cilicia, where he received baptism from Peter, bishop of Tarsus. Fleeing from Tarsus with his companions across the entire Taurus range, he stopped when they reached the mountain passes, going no farther while awaiting martyrdom. There all of them were slaughtered by the soldiers of Seleucus, who was in command of Cilicia. Surius, vol. IV. It is wrongly said below that Andrew and Magnus suffered in Alexandria.]

Andrew, with his 2,597 companions.

[B.: 2,597 soldiers. V.: 2,598.]

A. T. L. prefix: In Alexandria. But A. and T. distinguish the entry as follows:

“In Alexandria, the commemoration of Saints Magnus and Andrew, martyrs. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Marianus.”

[Note: Marianus. The feast of his burial is also celebrated below on 10 September. Labbe published his Life from a very ancient breviary in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Nova*, p. 342. It says that he lived for six years in the princely monastery under Saint Faterius the abbot, then withdrew to the village of Spinolaium, where he spent forty-four years living as a hermit. Tetradius, bishop of Bourges, who is said to have dedicated his church, took part in the Council of Agde in 506 and in the Council of Orléans I in 511. From this we infer that Marianus flourished during the reign of Clovis I. The village of Evaunus is a village in the diocese of Limoges, commonly called Evaux. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, 81, says that Marianus was buried there; he had been found dead in a nearby forest, the forest of Antreaignes in Combraille. His sacred body had been deposited in the wall of the church now occupied by Augustinian canons, but was later transferred into a silver shrine by Reginald de la Porte, bishop of Limoges, in the year 1300, as Bernard Guy reports in Labbe, vol. I of the *Bibliotheca Nova*, p. 635. The words “with 2,597” are wrongly added here, since they seem rather to belong to Saint Andrew.]

They then add: At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Magnus the martyr.

### 20 — The Thirteenth Day before the Kalends

[Note: Samuel. As Blessed Jerome writes in his book against Vigilantius, the emperor Arcadius transferred Samuel’s bones from Judaea to Thrace, carried by bishops. Theodore the Lector writes in *Collection*, book II, that they were brought to Constantinople under Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, and placed in a church situated at the Seventh.]

Samuel the prophet.

Florus, in A. T. L.:

“At the fortress of Caino, the burial of Saint Maximus the confessor.”

[Note: Maximus, wishing to conceal what he was, sought to live as a stranger at the monastery of the Island-Barbara belonging to Lyon. When he was recognized there as well, he decided to return to his homeland. While crossing the river Saône, he suffered shipwreck. He then came to the fortress of Caino, in the territory of the city of Tours, and founded a monastery there around the year 463. There he died full of days and was buried. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, 22.]

He shone with the greatest virtues and, as the book of his Life teaches—a Life written in verse—he was a disciple of the most blessed Martin.

And Saint Philibert.

[Note: Philibert was born in the territory of Élissane, the son of Filibaldus, bishop of Vicojulius. Raised at the court of King Dagobert, he later placed himself under the discipline of Agilus, abbot of Rebais.
