When Agilus died, Philibert himself was elected abbot by the unanimous consent of all the brothers. Then, from Chlodoveus, king of the Franks, and his queen, named Balthild, he received a place in the district of Rouen called Jumièges. Around the year 654, after spending several years governing Rebais after Agilus and undertaking various journeys, he built a monastery there. After performing many works of piety, Ebroin, because Philibert had rebuked him for his pride, incited certain clerics of Rouen against the blessed man. They falsely accused him before Audoenus and succeeded in having the bishop order him thrown into prison. Released from prison, he withdrew to Ansoald, bishop of Poitiers, and, with his assistance, founded a monastery on the island of Herio in the sea. After living there for eight years, he was recalled by Saint Audoenus after his enemy Ebroin had died. In the territory of Caltivus, Waratto, master of the palace, gave him the town of Villare, where he built a monastery for virgins. Then, after appointing Aicadrus abbot of Jumièges, he returned to Herio, where he died. Blessed Philibert, recalled from exile after Ebroin’s death, survived him only a short time. Sigebert says that Ebroin was killed in the ninth year of King Theuderic, that is, in the year of Christ 681 or the following year. Saint Philibert’s death therefore seems to belong approximately to the year 684. Surius, vol. IV; Mabillon, *Benedictine Acts*, second age.

His translation, occasioned by the Normans, was carried out by Hilbodus, abbot of Herio, in the year 836, on 7 June, first from the monastery of Herio to Deas, by Ampennus, Varinnas, and Palus. After the monastery at Deas was burned—the conflagration occurred in the year 847—the sacred body nevertheless remained there until the year 857, when it was transferred to the small monastery of Conaldus in the territory of Angers. From there, in the year 862, it was carried to Masciacum among the Poitevins in order to recover certain estates. It remained there until the year 875, when it was transferred to the abbey of Tournus. Mabillon, *Benedictine Acts*, part I, fourth age.]

Philibert was an abbot who healed various human illnesses through the Holy Spirit and foresaw future events. In T. he is placed first.

C. V.: And Saint Valentine the martyr.

[Note: Valentine is commemorated together with Leontius also on the following day in Jerome’s Martyrology.]

T.: In Lucania, the commemoration of Valentine.

B.: In Lucania, the commemoration of Saints Valentinianus and Leontius. In Alexandria, the commemoration of Saint Dioscorus.

### 21 — The Twelfth Day before the Kalends

Bede has no entry.

Florus, in A. T. L.: And the passion of Saint Privatus.

[Note: When the Alamanni invaded Gaul under their leader Chroco, Saint Privatus, bishop of the city of Javols, was found in a crypt of Mount Memmat, where he was occupied with fasting and prayer, while the people of the fortress of Grèzes were shut up in its defenses. But since the good shepherd would not consent to hand over his sheep to wolves, he was compelled to sacrifice to demons. Abominating and rejecting this defilement, he was beaten with clubs until he was thought to be dead. Yet from the beating itself, after a few days had passed, he breathed out his spirit. Gregory of Tours I, 32; Surius, vol. IV.]

He ended his life during the reigns of Valerian and Gallienus, when he was bishop of the Minatienses, having been afflicted by the barbarians with scourging and burning because of his confession of the holy faith.

B. C. V. L.: In Spain, Julius and Julian.

C. V.: Vincentius, Augurius, and Fructuosus.

B.: In Sardinia, the commemoration of Saints Luxurius, Trajanus, and Quadratus the bishop.

[Note: Luxurius, who was beheaded with Cisellus and Camerinus during the persecution of Diocletian, under the governor Delphius. Baronius in the Martyrology. Trajanus also suffered with Luxurius, if one trusts our author, Notker, and Jerome’s Martyrology; and Quadratus, according to our author and Jerome. Baronius writes in the notes that this man is found, without the title of the place of his bishopric, both in the ancient Roman Martyrology and in ancient manuscripts up to the present day, and that no one teaches to which church he was appointed. Peter de Natalibus considers him the same person as the one commemorated on 26 May.]

In Syndofaga, the commemoration of Saints Artosius, Diomedes, and Zoticus. And elsewhere, of Privatus the martyr.

D.: In the territory of the city of Javols, Privatus, bishop and martyr.

A. T.: In Spain, the commemoration of Saint Vincent. On the same day, of Julian.

T.: Colodi.

### 22 — The Eleventh Day before the Kalends

The commemoration of Saint Timothy.

[Note: Timothy suffered neither after the year 312 nor before the year 310. For before 310, Miltiades had not yet held the pontificate at Rome, and in the year 312, after the death of Maxentius, Constantine, who ruled in the West, restored peace to the Church. Peter de Natalibus is therefore clearly mistaken when, in discussing Timothy, he says that he suffered under the emperor Valerian, since Valerian has nothing in common with Pope Miltiades, during whose time Peter himself states that Timothy suffered. His martyrdom is also wrongly placed by Cuspinianus under the sixth consulship of Constantius. Since Timothy suffered while Pope Miltiades occupied the see, it cannot possibly be assigned to the period when, after the pontificate of Marcellinus, the Roman see was vacant.]

Timothy came from Antioch to Rome and, under Pope Miltiades, was received as a guest by Saint Sylvester, who later became bishop. (Up to this point, A.) After preaching there for a full year and several months and converting many to Christ, he was arrested by Tarquinius, prefect of the city. After being worn down by a long imprisonment, and refusing to sacrifice to idols, he was beaten a third time and subjected to the most severe tortures. Finally he was beheaded and buried beside the blessed apostle Paul. This is written in the history of Saint Sylvester.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Symphorianus the martyr.

Florus, in A. T. L., adds, after prefacing the city of Autun:

“He was arrested under the emperor Aurelian by Heraclius the consular governor. Because he refused to worship the statue of Berecynthia, he was beaten and committed to prison; then he was led outside the walls and struck down by the persecutor.”

V.: And Saint Hippolytus at Portus.

[Note: Concerning him, see the following day.]

And elsewhere, Martialis and Aurea in the city of Ostia.

L.: On the same day, Saint Maurus the martyr with his companions.

[Note: They suffered in Reims, a city of Gaul. Maurus came from Rome to Reims with Blessed Timothy. After spreading the word of God there and baptizing Apollinaris with many others, he was beheaded by the prefect Lampadius together with the holy companions whom he had baptized.]

B.: In Antioch, the commemoration of Marinus. In Gaul, in the city of Autun, the commemoration of Saints Medardus and Emilianus with their eight sons.

### 23 — The Tenth Day before the Kalends

Bede has no entry.

Florus, in A. T. L.:

“In Aquileia, the commemoration of Saints Fortunatus, Hermogenes, and Martialis. And in the city of Aegeae, the passion of Saints Claudius, Asterius, and Neon, who were crucified under the governor Lysias.”

[Note: Claudius. The governor first ordered him to be beaten with rods, then suspended on the rack and flames applied to his feet. Pieces cut from his heels were also brought before him; he was tormented with hooks, his sides scraped with the sharpest shards, and burning candles were applied. Asterius was tortured on the rack, his feet burned, and his body savagely scourged. Neon’s neck was broken, burning coals were thrown upon him, and his back was torn with sinews. Finally, all three brothers were affixed to a cross. Donvina and Theonilla suffered with them, in the consulship of Diocletian II and Aristobulus. According to the more accurate reckoning, this was the year 285 after Christ.]

On the same day, in the city of Reims, the passion of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris [A. Apollonius]. They were sent from Rome to Gaul and, having completed their martyrdom near the city of Reims, earned the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: Timothy. The Acts of these martyrs state that they suffered, together with the presbyter Maurus and many others, under the emperor Nero and the governor Lampadius. This opinion is not accepted by those who admit no martyrs in Gaul before the time of Marcus Aurelius. They nevertheless seem to be older than the time of Maximian, for they are nowhere said to have suffered under the governor Rictius Varus, like the other martyrs of Belgic Gaul from that period. Concerning them, see Marlot, *Metropolis of Reims*, book I, chapter 21. Frodoardus provides the Acts almost in full but does not state the time of their passion. He writes that Timothy came to Reims from the East and praises Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs* I, 55.]

D. The commemoration of the holy martyrs Donatus, Restitutus, Valerian, Fructuosa, and twelve others, who were crowned at Antioch with the most glorious honor of confession. V. S., at Cyriaca’s, near Saint Lawrence. At Nepe, Saint Tholomaeus, bishop and martyr. C., At Aquileia, Saint Fortunatus.

[Note: According to the records of the Church of Aquileia, which possesses their relics, they suffered at Singidunum in Moesia under the governor Victorianus, during the reign of the emperor Diocletian. The former was a lector, the latter a deacon; they suffered at the time when Saint Donatus and his companions, concerning whom Ferrarius treats in his General Catalogue on the twenty-first day of this month, suffered.]

Hermogenes. And at the port of the city of Rome, the commemoration of Saint Hippolytus.

[Note: He is also commemorated on the preceding day, in Usuard and others. Saint Jerome writes about Hippolytus of Portus in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 61, and in the preface to his commentary on Matthew, where he calls him a martyr. He flourished during the reign of the emperor Alexander, as Eusebius writes, IV, 16. Nicephorus, treating of the same man, calls him bishop of Portus. We are astonished that Jerome, when writing about him, should testify that he was unable to know of which church he had been bishop. Gelasius, however, in his book *Against Eutyches on the Two Natures*, when citing Hippolytus, says that he was bishop of Menopolis in Arabia; I think this was true before he came to Italy. Concerning this Hippolytus, it is plainly evident that Prudentius was mistaken in his eleventh hymn, attributing to him what belonged to another Hippolytus, a presbyter of Antioch and formerly a Novatian. Again, we think that what Peter Damian says of Hippolytus of Portus in his letter to Nicholas II, Roman pontiff—where he also attests that this man was called Nonnus, namely the one who converted that prostitute of Antioch to a better way of life—is wholly inconsistent with the truth. That Nonnus was bishop of Edessa and lived during the reign of the emperor Theodosius the Younger, as Nicephorus writes, XIV, 30; he is also mentioned in the Council of Chalcedon. The commemoration of Nonnus, moreover, is recorded in Baronius’s Martyrology on 2 December. The memory of Saint Hippolytus, bishop, still flourishes at the Roman port, and there one sees a deep pit filled with water, into which he was thrown and completed his martyrdom. Baronius in the notes. On this same Hippolytus, see also Bede’s *Chronicle* under Marcus Aurelius.]

Hippolytus, who is called Nonnus.

B. At Rome, the commemoration of the holy Laurence, Abundius, and Innocentius. In Gaul, at the city of Rheims, the commemoration of the holy Timothy and Apollinaris. At Autun, the burial of Saint Flavian.

[Note: The records of the Church of Autun, ancient manuscripts, and more recent sources likewise mention him on this day.]

Flavian.

### 24.—Ninth day before the Kalends

In India, the commemoration of Bartholomew the apostle.

[Note: Baronius treats this saint’s commemoration on the following day. It seems clear from Eusebius, V, 10; Rufinus, III, 1; and Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, that he announced the faith among the Indians. It is not, however, altogether certain which region those authors intended by the name “India.” See Tillemont, volume I of his *Ecclesiastical History*. As for his relics, the city of Dara, on the borders of Persia, was especially distinguished by them, as Theodore the Reader writes in book II of his *Collection*, and Nicephorus, XVI, 37. Procopius, book II of *The Buildings of the Emperor Justinian*, mentions the magnificent church erected there by the emperor Justinian. The tomb of Saint Bartholomew at Lipari was violated by the Saracens in the year 808, and his sacred relics were transferred to Benevento in the following year. From there they were brought to Rome by Otto III and deposited on the Tiber Island, where they are still preserved. There are differing opinions concerning the manner of his death. In Hippolytus’s brief commentary on the twelve apostles, it is stated that Saint Bartholomew was crucified with his head hanging downward. Josephus, cited by Metaphrastes, likewise testifies that he was crucified, and Nicephorus affirms this in book II, chapter 39. Others report that he was flayed, as in Isidore’s *On the Life and Deaths of the Saints*, §177. Our source, finally, says that he was beheaded.]

[Col. 1016A] Florus adds in A. and T.: “He was beheaded in Further India for Christ by order of King Astyages.” This is absent on this day in V. and is reported on the following day.

The same Florus in A., T., and L.: At Rome, the martyrdom of Saint Genesius.

[Note: See the following day, on which he is commemorated by almost all martyrologies.]

Genesius, who, while he was a soldier, submitted himself to the Christian faith. (Thus far A.) When, by order of the emperor Diocletian, he had long been placed upon the rack, tortured with claws, and scorched with lamps, yet persisted in his holy confession and said to the judge: “Even if you multiply the tortures inflicted upon me a hundredfold, you will not be able to take Christ from my mouth or Christ from my heart,” he was ordered to be killed with the sword.

On the same day, at Rouen, the burial of Saint Audoenus, bishop and confessor.

[Note: He was born at Soissons of noble family and served as a chamberlain at the court of King Chlothar, where he conducted himself very well together with Saint Eligius. According to Pagi, he was ordained bishop of Rouen in the year 640. Famous for every virtue, he founded monasteries, churches, and hospices, and governed that church for many years. After his death he was buried in the monastery of Saint Peter in the suburb of Rouen, now celebrated under the name of Saint Audoenus. The true day of this saint’s death seems to be unknown to everyone. Fridegodus, an Englishman by birth, nevertheless supposed that Audoenus died on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, a Sunday. But he did not die on that day, since Fridegodus himself states that he died in the year 677—or, according to a manuscript, 678. Since 24 August is a Sunday, the letter E would have to be in the calendar, but it falls in neither year before 682, although Audoenus was still alive in August of that year. See Pagi, year 684, §20.]

Audoenus, bishop and confessor, who, shining with many signs of miracles, obtained rain from heaven by holy prayer, after the manner of Elijah.

D. At Carthage, the martyrs of the White Mass.

[Note: They suffered during the reigns of Valerian and Gallienus. Among other tortures, it is said that the governor then caused a lime kiln to be heated and burning coals mixed with incense to be brought before the Christians. The governor said to them: “Choose one of these two alternatives: either offer incense to Jupiter upon these coals, or be plunged into the lime.” Then three hundred men, armed with faith, swiftly cast themselves into the fire while confessing Christ, and were buried amid the clouds of powdered lime. From this the group of blessed soldiers also deserved to be called the White Mass. Ado; Baronius.]

V. C. At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Genesius the martyr. And at Ostia, Saint Aurea, virgin.

[Note: She is said to have suffered during the reign of the emperor Alexander, under the prefect Ulpian. Her memory still flourishes at the mouths of the Tiber, where her sacred relics are also preserved.]

Aurea.

B. At Antioch, the commemoration of Jebonius, Capitulanus, and Italia. At the city of Redon.

[Note: “Rhedon” is preferable to “Rotomagus.”]

The burial of Saint Audoenus, bishop and confessor. At the city of Nevers, the burial of Saint Patrianus, abbot and confessor. At the city of Le Mans, the commemoration of Rigomerus, priest and confessor.

### 25.—Eighth day before the Kalends

Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. and T.: At Arles, the martyrdom of Saint Genesius.

[Note: There are four saints bearing this name who are honored in the regions of Aquitaine. The first is the famous man of Arles, who is under discussion here. The second is Saint Thiernius, patron of Tulle, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 77; his feast is celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of November. The third is the bishop of Clermont, concerning whom see the order for the third day before the Nones of July and the catalogue of bishops. The last is the Count of Clermont, concerning whom see the catalogue of counts, the histories of Saints Praejectus and Bonitus, and Labbe’s *New Bibliotheca*, II, 719. See his Acts in Surius, written by Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and the remarkable miracle concerning him written by Blessed Hilary, bishop of Arles.]

Genesius the martyr, who by the severing of his head preserved his contest for Christ’s name with powerful fervor.

L. “Who, as tradition says, was baptized with no baptism other than his own blood.”

Florus continues in T. and L.: And at Rome, the commemoration of Saint Lucius.

[Note: He did not die today but on 4 March; see above. There is great difficulty in assigning the year of his death. Nevertheless, from the sound portions of the Chronicle of Damasus, where it treats of Cornelius and Stephen, Pearson gathers with sufficient certainty in his *Cyprianic Annals* the period during which Lucius sat between the two. According to that Chronicle, Cornelius died during the consulship of Gallus II and Volusianus, that is, in the year 252. Stephen was ordained, according to the same Chronicle, during the second consulship of Volusianus and Maximus, that is, in the year 253. No other consuls are recorded in the fasti between Volusianus’s first and second consulships. Therefore Lucius, ordained one year after Cornelius’s death, died before Stephen’s pontificate in 253. Nicephorus, VI, 7, accurately records the duration of Lucius’s pontificate: “After the Church had been governed for less than seven complete months, it received Stephen as his successor.” Some today celebrate a translation of Saint Lucius. Thus the author of the manuscript Florarium has: “The translation of the holy pontiffs, Pope Lucius, etc.” The Martyrology under the name of Usuard, printed at Cologne, and another printed at Lübeck together with a handbook for clergy in 1490, have the following: “In Dacia, in the church of Roskilde, the translation of Saint Lucius, pope and martyr.” Hermann Greven, in his additions to Usuard, restricts this as follows: “The translation of the head of Saint Lucius, pope and martyr, from the city of Rome to Dacia, to the church of Roskilde.” Saint Cyprian wrote two letters from Africa to Saint Lucius: the first, when he had been raised to the pontificate, which we regret has perished; the second, when he had returned to Rome from exile, to congratulate him, together with his African colleagues, on his return.]

Lucius, bishop and martyr, who was the twenty-first after Peter. After governing the Church for three years and three months, he was driven into exile during the reigns of Gallienus and Valerian [L.: Gallus and Volusianus], but afterward, by God’s will, returned unharmed to his own church; then he endured martyrdom in the confession of Christ.

V. Saint Bartholomew the apostle.

[Note: Concerning him and Saint Aurea, see the preceding day.]

He preached in Lycaonia and finally, while still alive, was flayed by barbarians in the city of Albanum in Greater Armenia. By order of King Astyages he was beheaded, and thus was committed to the earth and buried there. His commemoration is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.

C. In the city of Ostia, Saint Aurea. At Rome, Saint Genesius the martyr.

[Note: He is also commemorated on the preceding day, where he is said to have been a soldier. But from his Acts, published in Surius, volume IV, it is clear that he was an actor. While in the theater, in order to please the emperor Diocletian, he was presenting Christian rites in mockery and was sprinkled with water as though in a fictitious baptism, he immediately confessed Christ truly and was therefore crowned with martyrdom. Mombrizio and Peter de Natalibus confuse him with Genesius of Arles. His memory is illustrious at Rome; Pope Gregory III restored his church and adorned it with gifts, as is clear from the book on the Roman pontiffs under Gregory III. He suffered under the prefect Plutianus.]

Genesius the martyr.

D. The commemoration of Saint Genesius the martyr, who had previously been a teacher of the art of mime in the city.

B. In Syria, the commemoration of Saint Julian the martyr.

[Note: Peter de Natalibus, XI, final section, 224, calls him a martyr and priest.]

In the city of Capua in Campania, the commemoration of the holy Rufinus and Julius. Hermetes.

B. A. T. In Spain, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor.

T. In the district of the Viromandui, the commemoration of Saint Hunegundis.

[Note: She was born in the district of the Viromandui of noble parents and was lifted from the baptismal font by Blessed Eligius, bishop of Noyon. When she reached adulthood, she was betrothed to a man named Eudaldus. Since she wished to become a nun, however, she urged her fiancé to undertake a pious pilgrimage. She therefore traveled with him to Rome and asked the pope for the veil; from him she received the veil with a blessing. The Church of Saint-Quentin identifies Pope Martin I in the fourth lesson of its breviary. This could stand only if Eligius had lifted Hunegundis from the font before he became bishop. Eligius occupied the see of Noyon before Martin occupied the Roman see. Hunegundis, abandoned by her angry fiancé because he had been rejected after she had become a nun, returned to her homeland and gave herself and all her property to the monastery of Humolaris, where she finally died about the year 690. Hunegundis was indeed lifted from the baptismal font by Blessed Eligius, who passed to heaven around the year 660. Hunegundis is mentioned in the additions to Usuard, in the Benedictine and Gallican Martyrologies, and in ours on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, although, because of the feast of Saint Louis, her office is transferred by the canons of Vermandois to the following day. Her body was raised from the tomb in the year of Christ 946, on the day before the Nones of October. Bernerus, abbot, described the history of this event in the fifth Benedictine century; afterward, in 1051, it was transferred by Macarius, abbot of the monastery of Humolaris, to a more precious shrine.]

Hunegundis the virgin. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Aredius, abbot.

[Note: Aredius was a native of the city of Limoges. His father was named Jocundus and his mother Pelagia. According to Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, II, 39, ed. Benedictine, he had a brother named Renosindus; in the common editions his father is mistakenly given this name. Aredius was presented to King Theudebert and attached to the royal courtiers. But finally abandoning the king’s palace, he adopted a holier way of life at the advice of Saint Nicetius, bishop of Trier. After a life filled with miracles, when he was more than eighty years old, he drew up his will, appointed the holy bishops Martin and Hilary his heirs, fell ill, and died after several days—namely, in the sixteenth year of King Childebert, as Gregory of Tours writes, that is, in the year 591. He was buried by Saint Ferreolus, bishop of Limoges, in the church of Blessed Julian the martyr. Gregory of Tours wrote about Aredius in book II of *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 39, and in book II of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 40. The learned Ruinart published his Life in his edition of Gregory, distinct from the one published among the Acts of the Saints in the first Benedictine century, p. 349.]

A. The burial at Tumularia of Saint Hunegundis the virgin. L. omits the place.

### 26.—Seventh day before the Kalends

At Rome, the commemoration of the holy Erenaeus and Abundius. During the persecution of Decius, Valerian ordered them to be thrown into a sewer because they had retrieved the body of Blessed Concordia after it had been cast into a sewer.

[Note: They did not suffer under Decius but under the emperor Valerian, approximately in the year 258. See above, concerning Saint Lawrence, on the tenth day of this month.]

The priest Justin also retrieved their bodies and buried them in a crypt near Blessed Lawrence.

Florus in A. and T.: On the same day, in the city of Thessalonica, the commemoration of Saint Anastasius.

[Note: He did not suffer at Thessalonica but at Salona, a city of Dalmatia, during the persecution of the emperor Diocletian. Born at Aquileia, he practiced the trade of a fuller. Because he confessed Christ, however, a great stone was fastened around his neck and he was hurled headlong into the sea. A certain Christian matron named Asclepia, wishing to possess the martyr’s body, sent some of her servants to find it. Certain Africans discovered the corpse and carried its head to their homeland, where they built a church in his name. The matron devoutly received the body, which had been brought to her without the head. She concealed it on her estate until the persecution had subsided; then she built a church and placed the martyr’s body in the territory of Salona. Peter de Natalibus commemorates him on the following day, as does Baronius on the twenty-first day of this month.]

Anastasius: He was a fuller, but because of the merit of his faith he was numbered among the martyrs.

L. And in the city of Salona, the commemoration of Saint Anastasius the martyr. V. Elsewhere. C. In the city of Salona. V. C. The commemoration of Saint Anastasius, who was a fuller and a martyr.

Quintinus the martyr.

[Note: If this is the same as Quintus in Jerome’s Martyrology, he suffered at Rome together with Basilla and Maximilian.]

B. In the city of Salona, the commemoration of Saint Anastasius the martyr.

At the city of Auxerre, the burial of Saint Eleutherius, bishop.

[Note: He occupied the see for twenty-eight years, eight months, and nine days. His episcopate began before the year 533, for in that year he subscribed to the Second Council of Orléans. Therefore he did not depart to heaven after the year 561, since from 533 to 561 there are twenty-eight years. Thus he did not reach, as is stated in the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre* in Labbe’s *New Bibliotheca*, I, 419, the reign of Justin the Younger, who did not succeed Justinian before 565. Saint Eleutherius took part in the councils held at Orléans: the Second in 533, the Third in 538, the Fourth in 541, and the Fifth in 549. He died full of days and was buried with his holy predecessors in the basilica of Saint Germanus the bishop. In Baronius’s Martyrology his feast is observed on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September. In the cited passage of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca* it is observed on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of the same month. Perhaps, therefore, a translation is being celebrated today.]

Eleutherius the bishop.

### 27.—Sixth day before the Kalends

Bede has nothing.

[Col. 1021A] Florus in A., T., and L.: At the city of Arles, the burial of Saint Caesarius the martyr.

[Note: He was born in the territory of Chalon. The bishop of Chalon, Silvester, made him a cleric. He then transferred himself to the monastery of Lérins, where he lived for some time in the greatest abstinence and holiness. Ordained priest by Eonus, bishop of Arles, he was later unwillingly appointed in his place. He patiently endured many injuries from his enemies, exiles, and a sentence of death; and, being delivered by the Lord, he also saved his persecutors from death. He went to Rome to Pope Symmachus. He took part in various councils, especially that of Vaison in 529. He founded monasteries, particularly for women, placing his sister Saint Caesaria over them. The following chronological indications must be observed in determining Saint Caesarius’s death. Thirty years had already passed since the monastery for nuns was founded when Saint Caesarius departed this life, as we read in his Life, II, 36. This monastery was begun before the death of Alaric, king of the Goths, and was destroyed when Theodoric, king of Italy, attacked Arles—an event which Valesius proves in book VI of *The History of the Franks* to have occurred in 508—as is stated in the Life of Caesarius, I, 15. In the following year, or the year after, Caesarius began restoring the monastery, which he could not complete for two or three years. Therefore the year of his death, which occurred thirty years after the monastery had been built, must be assigned to 542. See his Life, written in two books, in the first Benedictine century.]

Caesarius the martyr.

And in Egypt, at the city of Oxyrhynchus [the words “at the city of Oxyrhynchus” are absent in L.], sixteen martyrs, whose acts are preserved. After overcoming beasts and fire, they fell by the sword.

On the same day, at Rome, the martyrdom of Nemesius the deacon and his daughter Lucilla, who were killed by beheading, on the orders of Valerian and Gallienus, for confessing Christ, without a hearing.

[Note: Pope Stephen baptized this man together with his daughter and ordained Nemesius a deacon. These martyrs were beheaded on the day before Symphronius gave up his spirit in the fire, as is written in the Acts of Stephen in Surius, volume IV. The commemoration of Symphronius is celebrated either on 26 or 27 July in the Martyrologies; Nemesius, therefore, seems to belong on the preceding day. Why they are referred to this day is uncertain. Baronius’s Martyrology states on 1 October that they were beheaded on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. If he had assigned the eighth day before the Kalends of August, he would, in my opinion, have been much more correct. They are commemorated, however, on 31 October because, after their bodies had previously been buried by Blessed Stephen, they were more honorably entombed on the Appian Way on that day by Blessed Sixtus, and transferred by Gregory V to the diaconia of Saint Mary the New, together with Saint Symphronius, Olympius, Exuperia, and Theodulus. These saints’ bodies, discovered there under Pope Gregory XIII, were placed more honorably beneath the altar of the same church on the sixth day before the Ides of December.]

[Col. 1022A] The supplement of D. is blank, except that the name of Syagrius the bishop may have been written by a more recent hand.

V. C. In Lucania, the commemoration of Felix, Savinianus [V. Sabanianus], Honoratus, and Saint Rufinus.

[Note: Jerome’s Martyrology has “in the city of Potentia.”]

T. And the martyrdom of the holy martyrs Felix, George the monk, Liliosa, Aurelius, and Natalia.

[Note: All these suffered at Córdoba in Spain. Liliosa was the daughter of Felix, and Natalia the wife of Aurelius. George was born in the land of Bethlehem and spent twenty-five years living under the regular discipline at the monastery of Saint Sabas. Sent to Africa by the abbot David to obtain provisions for the monks, he went from there to Spain at the urging of the bishop of Carthage. There he suffered martyrdom with these companions. After George himself had been torn by various instruments and cruelly wounded by the kicks and blows of the soldiers; after the hair had been torn from Natalia’s severed head and she too had been savagely beaten; they first killed Felix, then George, afterward Liliosa, and finally Aurelius and Natalia with the sword. Surius, volume IV. Baronius treats of them on 27 July, as do the records of the Church of Córdoba.]

On the same day, the translation of Saint Sulpitius the bishop.

[Note: Bollandus writes as follows concerning this translation in his treatment of Sulpitius the Pious, bishop of Bourges, on 17 January: “But again, on 27 August, the Carthusians of Cologne in their supplement to Usuard, Bellinus of Padua in the Paris edition of 1521, and the German Martyrology have the following: ‘At the city of Bourges, the translation of Saint Sulpitius, bishop and confessor.’” Certain manuscripts and Saussay also remember him on that day.]

B. At Arles, the burial of Saint Caesarius the bishop.

[Note: See the preceding entry.]

At Constantinople, the holy Ollius and Stephen the deacon. At Autun, the commemoration of Saint Agrius the bishop.

[Note: Siagrius is preferable. Gregory of Tours writes about him in *On the Deeds of the Franks*, V, 5; IX, 23 and 41; and X, 28, as well as in his *Epitome of Frankish History*, chapter 89. Ado of Vienne, in his *Chronicle* under the year 575, calls him a man of the highest holiness and testifies that he took part in the First Council of Mâcon. He also lived into the time of Pope Gregory, several of whose letters to him survive. Siagrius himself came to Rome and subscribed to the privilege granted to the Church of Saint Medard in the eleventh indiction, in the year 593; he seems to have died around that time.]

Agrius the bishop.

B. A. T. L. At Capua, the commemoration of Saint Rufus the martyr.

[Note: When Rufus held the rank of patrician, Apollinaris, a disciple of Saint Peter and bishop, raised his daughter from the dead and instructed him in the faith and baptized him, together with his daughter, his wife, and his household—324 persons of both sexes—as is written in the Passion of Apollinaris in Surius, volume IV. When Nero Caesar heard this, he relieved him of the command at Ravenna. When Rufus came to Capua, he was arrested by Messalinus, the prefect’s deputy. He refused to sacrifice and was beheaded. Peter de Natalibus.]

### 28.—Fifth day before the Kalends

The commemoration of Saint Hermes the martyr.

[Note: Saint Alexander, the Roman pontiff, baptized Hermes, who had been prefect of the city, together with his wife, sister, and sons. When this became known, Aurelianus, a subordinate officer sent by the emperor Trajan to destroy all the Christians, entered Rome at once and confined Saint Hermes and Alexander in prison. Not long afterward he beheaded Hermes. His sister Theodora gathered his body and buried it on the old Salarian Way, where it remains today. See the Acts of Saint Alexander in Bollandus on 3 May. Ado is mistaken in saying that he suffered under the emperor Aurelian. That Aurelianus was a judge, not the emperor, as the aforementioned Acts demonstrate. Baronius is no less mistaken in his notes when he says that Hermes suffered under the emperor Hadrian; for the same Acts testify that he was crowned with martyrdom before Alexander, during the reign of Trajan. See above, concerning Saint Alexander, on 3 May.]

In Africa, Saint Augustine the bishop.

[Note: He was from the African province, from the city of Thagaste. First he taught grammar in his own city and afterward rhetoric at Carthage. Later he crossed the sea to Rome and to Milan, where the retinue of the emperor Valentinian the Younger had then been established. As a young man he had been seduced at Carthage by the heresy of the Manichaeans, but he was instructed in the Catholic faith and confirmed by Saint Ambrose, who also baptized him. After he had passed his thirtieth year, he returned to Africa and was chosen by Valerius, bishop of Hippo, for the rank of priest. Having become a priest, he immediately established a monastery within the church and received authority to preach the word of God before the bishop. He composed many books against the African heresies, especially against the Donatists, Manichaeans, and pagans. Valerius, fearing that another church might seek Augustine for the episcopate and knowing that he himself was extremely weak in body and advanced in age, obtained—although Augustine was unwilling—that Augustine be ordained his co-bishop by Megalius, primate of Numidia and bishop of Calama. Through Augustine’s authority the Catholic Church vigorously flourished, despite the futile resistance of the Donatist fury. This happened especially after the conference held at Carthage between all the Catholic bishops and the bishops of the Donatists. He labored no less energetically against the Pelagians than against the Donatists, composing books for nearly ten years and arguing very frequently with the people in church against that error. Finally, tireless in undertaking labors for the good of the Church, vigorous in defending the Catholic faith, and diligent in refuting the deceits of heretics, while the Vandals and Goths were pressing the city of Hippo in a close siege during the thirteenth month, he was seized by a fever and died in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the fortieth of his episcopate, in the year of Christ 430, during the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian II. See his Life by Possidius, published in the final volume of the Benedictine edition. Concerning this translation from Sardinia to Ticinum, see the final entry of Bede’s *Chronicle*.]

Augustine, who was first transferred from his own city to Sardinia because of the barbarians, and recently brought from there to Ticinum and honorably buried by Luitprand, king of the Lombards.

[Note: From the word “recently” it should be observed that this Martyrology was composed not long after this translation. Since the translation occurred in the fourth year of Leo the Isaurian, that is, in the year of Christ 721, and Bede died in 734, this seems to me a highly probable argument that this Martyrology was in fact compiled by Bede, since it is clear that it was composed shortly after the translation.]

Florus in A., T., and L.: At the city of Sconis [T.: Comis; L.: Scottiis], the commemoration of Bibianus, bishop and confessor, who granted healing to many sick people.

And in Gaul, at Arverni, in a village called Brioude, the martyrdom of Saint Julian.

[Note: While he was the companion of Blessed Ferreolus the tribune and secretly served Christ in military dress, he was seized by soldiers during the persecution of Diocletian and killed by the horrible death of having his throat cut. Baronius. No one denies that Julian the martyr suffered and was buried at Brioude. But since there are two villages bearing this name—ancient Brioude and new Brioude—there is a dispute about where Saint Julian was first buried. Savaro, Sirmond, and others think that he was buried at ancient Brioude; they believe Gregory of Tours, Fortunatus, Apollinaris Sidonius in his *Propempticon*, or poem 24, and other ancient writers spoke of that place. Others, however, understand these references to concern new Brioude, where Saint Julian’s body is still preserved in a very famous basilica. See Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book II.]

Julian the martyr, who, when pagans under the governor Crispinus were seeking him for punishment, voluntarily offered himself for love of Christ’s name and was killed by the sword.

C. And the burial of Saint Faustinus the bishop. Saint Balbina.

B. At the city of Saintes, the burial of Saint Vivianus, bishop and confessor. Likewise at Rome, Basileus and Elias. At Constantinople, the burial of Saint Alexander.

[Note: He succeeded Metrophanes in the episcopate of Constantinople. He refused to receive Arius the transgressor and his associates into communion, although Eusebius of Nicomedia made grave threats. He asked God that, if Arius’s position were correct, he himself might not live to see the day appointed for the dispute; but if the faith which he professed were true, that Arius might suffer the punishment of his impiety, since he was the author of every evil. Nor did Alexander pray in vain, as the astonishing and sudden death of Arius abundantly demonstrates. Socrates, I, 37–38; Sozomen, II, 29. After spending twenty-three years in the episcopate and living ninety-eight years, he departed this life. Beforehand he had instructed those who possessed the right of election to choose one of two men whom he would name; he therefore proposed Paul and Macedonius. Socrates, II, 6.]

At Arverni, the commemoration of Saint Julian the martyr.

### 29.—Fourth day before the Kalends

At Rome, Saint Sabina, virgin and martyr.

[Note: She suffered during the reign of the emperor Hadrian, under Elpidius, prefect of the city. She was the wife of a certain distinguished man named Valentinus and the daughter of Herod the metallurgist. Saint Seraphia converted her to the Lord; Sabina afterward buried Seraphia’s body. After Seraphia’s martyrdom, Blessed Sabina devoted herself for nearly a full year to works of charity. Finally, arrested by Elpidius, prefect of the city, she was compelled to deny Christ. When she refused to offer incense to idols, she was beheaded. Christians buried her body in the town of Vindium, near the Arch of Faustinus. Peter de Natalibus.]

[Note: D. has this material concerning the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist at the end of the following day.]

On the same day, the beheading of Saint John the Baptist, who was first buried in Samaria and then in Alexandria; moreover,

[Note: In Alexandria. The translation of the relics of Saint John the Baptist from Sebaste, a city of Palestine, to Alexandria is treated fully in Bede’s *Chronicle* under Julian and in Rufinus, *History*, II, 28.]

[Note: According to Sozomen, VII, 21, his head was brought to Constantinople in the time of the emperor Theodosius. The second discovery of this head in the city of Emesa is also treated today according to Usuard’s Martyrology, although the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle says that it occurred under Valentinian and Marcian on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, and Marcellinus in his *Chronicle* says that the Baptist’s head was discovered again on 24 February. See above, 24 February.]

his head was brought from Jerusalem to Emesa, a city of Phoenicia.

[Col. 1025C] T. adds: The evangelists declare that he was beheaded as the feast of Easter was approaching and that, when the Paschal season returned again in the following year, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion was completed.

C. And the repose of Saint Elisha the prophet, disciple of Saint Elijah the prophet.

B. C. V. And of nine hundred other martyrs who suffered on the same day.

[Note: Jerome’s Martyrology treats of them on the following day.]

T. At Peronne, Saint Fursa, abbot.

[Note: Peter de Natalibus, VIII, 126, writes that he commendably completed his life today. All the martyrologists, however, agree that he died on 16 January.]

B. In Antioch of Syria, the commemoration of the holy Basileus and Paul. In Sirmium, the commemoration of Saint Basilla the virgin.

### 30.—III Kalends

In the city of Venusia in Apulia, the feast of Saints Felix, bishop of the city of Tubzoca, Audactus and Januarius, priests, and Fortunatianus and Septiminus, readers: they were arrested in their own city in the time of Diocletian by Magnelianus the governor, then for a long time tormented with many chains and imprisonments; and in Africa and Sicily they were finally brought to completion by the sword. Felix died a virgin at the age of fifty-six. (Thus far L.)

[Note: Felix. These saints will be discussed below on 24 October, when Usuard, Ado, Baronius, and others celebrate their feast. They seem to have been assigned to this day through an error, because in the other martyrologies a certain Felix the presbyter and Adauctus, who suffered at Rome on the Ostian Way under Diocletian, are commemorated today. There is variation concerning the African city of which Felix was bishop. Our text reads “of the city of Tubzoca”; Ado has “Tibrurensis,” as is also read in the Acts of these martyrs preserved in Surius, volume V. From the ancient manuscripts, however, I prefer the more accurate reading “Tibirensis.” The city of Tibiris or Tibiritana is mentioned in the Council of Carthage in the time of Saint Cyprian. Baronius, in his notes.—Felix. On the Ostian Way under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. After the sentence had been pronounced and he was being led to execution after the rack, a certain Christian met him. When this man willingly professed himself a Christian, he was immediately beheaded together with Felix. Since the Christians did not know his name, they called him Adauctus, because he had been added to Saint Felix for the crown. Usuard, etc.]

The distance between Carthage and Tibzoca [manuscripts: Tibiuca] is thirty-five miles.

C. V.: At Rome, the feast of Saints Felix and Audactus.

B.: On the same day, Saint Severa.

### 31.—II Kalends

Baeda is silent, as is manuscript D in its supplement.

[Col. 1027A] C. V.: At Trier, the burial of Saint Paulinus.

[Note: Paulinus. He succeeded Maximinus in the Church of Trier. Socrates II.36 and Sozomen IV.9 write that he attended the Council of Milan in 355, where, it is said, he vigorously opposed the Eastern bishops, insofar as he could, when they were striving to obtain a common judgment against Saint Athanasius, and that for this reason he was sent into exile. Baronius, however, in the year 353 of his Annals, states that he was not present at the Council of Milan but rather at that of Arles, which had been convened two years earlier. Saint Jerome records in his Chronicle that he died in exile in Phrygia in the twenty-first year of Constantius. Saint Athanasius discusses him in his book On His Flight, Hilary in his pamphlet Against Constantius, Pope Liberius in his letter to Lucifer of Cagliari, and Severus in book II of his History. His body was brought back to Trier and buried in a crypt together with the holy martyrs; at last it was discovered in 1071, as Sigebert writes in his Chronicle.]

C.: And Saint Paul, apostle and confessor.

[Note: Paul the apostle. More correctly, “Paulinus, bishop and confessor.”]

V. C.: Elsewhere, Gayanus, Julianus, Rufinus, and Vincentius.

B. A. T. L.: At Trier, the burial of Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor, who, having been exiled for the Catholic faith by the emperor Constantius, son of the emperor Constantine, rested there.

B.: Elsewhere, the burial of Saint Elladius, bishop.

A.: On the same day, at Arras, the burial of Saint Hadulfus, bishop and confessor.

[Note: Hadulfus. He is celebrated today in the Church and diocese of Arras on account of a translation. In the supplement to Usuard, Molanus reports it and calls it a translation. Galesinius and the continuator of Canisius follow Molanus. Saussay, however, calls it an elevation of the body, as he does also on 20 May, with a fairly lengthy encomium. See above, 19 May.]

T. B.: At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Optatus, bishop.

[Note: Optatus. Labbe, in New Library, volume I, page 418, writes as follows: “Optatus occupied the see for one year, eight months, and five days. He built a basilica in honor of the martyr Saint Christopher beside the basilica of Saint Germanus on the eastern side, with the assistance of his two priests, Sanctinus and Memorius. He was buried together with them in the same basilica that he had built. Later, after the passage of years, their bodies were transferred to the church of Saint Germanus with such solemnity that the day of the translation is recorded in all the Martyrologies as 2 May, while the burial is marked on 31 August.” Peter errs in his Catalogue when he supposes that this was the same Optatus who was bishop of Milevis. He is counted as the fourteenth bishop of Auxerre, successor of Saint Gregory, and lived in the time of the emperor Justinian.]

### September

#### 1.—Kalends

Baeda is silent.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Le Mans, the burial of Saint Victor, bishop and confessor, who, while the city itself was being consumed by fire and powerful balls of flame were driven here and there by the wind, like a good shepherd who could not endure the ecclesiastical folds to be ravaged by Satan’s assaults, offered himself against the whirlwind; and, raising his hand and making the sign of the cross against it, immediately caused the entire fire to cease.

[Note: Victor. More accurately, Victorius, bishop of Le Mans, who succeeded his father Victurus and was ordained by Saint Martin, whose disciple he had been. He held the see for forty-one years, six months, and ten days, and was renowned for miracles both before and after his death, as the author of the Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans testifies in chapter 6, published in volume III of Mabillon’s Old Analecta; that author praises a Life of the same holy man written by himself. He attended the Council of Angers concerning the ordination of Thalassius in 453, and the First Council of Tours in 461; he is also recorded, together with Thalassius of Angers, as having attended the Council of Vannes in 465. He died on the Kalends of September during the consulship of Faustus the Younger and Longinus II, that is, in 490. See also Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 56.]

D.: Joshua son of Nun and Gideon, prophets.

B. C. V. D. L.: At Capua [B.: at Aquaria], the feast of Saint Priscus.

[Note: Priscus. According to Peter de Natalibus, this was the householder in whose house Christ ordered the Passover to be prepared for him. After the Lord’s ascension, he came to Rome with the apostle Peter and preached the Gospel in the region of Campania. He was buried near Capua on the Aquarian Way, as Ado says.]

(Thus far V. C. and B.) He was one of Christ’s ancient disciples. Alternatively, he is said to have been one of the seventy-two disciples.

C. V. A. T. L.: In the territory of Todi [C.: “Tude Terentiani,” at Todi, of Terentianus], the feast of Saints Felix and Donatus.

A. L.: At Sens, the burial of Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor.

[Note: Lupus. He was born in the territory of Orléans, to a father named Betto and a mother named Austregildis, whose surname was Agia. His uncles Austrenus and Aunarius, respectively bishops of Orléans and Auxerre, enrolled him among the clergy. Accordingly, as soon as Arthenius, bishop of Sens, died, Saint Lupus was appointed his successor. When Chlothar, son of Theodoric, was besieging Sens, Lupus freed the city through prayer and the ringing of a bell. Falsely accused and sent into exile at the estate called Andesagina beside the river Aucia, he came to the pagan duke Bason Landegisilus, whom he converted to the faith by preaching and by restoring sight to a blind man. Recalled to his homeland, while traveling toward Paris, he freed many captives from prison by his power. He died after being seized by illness at the estate of Briennon, according to Sigebert, in 616. Surius, volume V; Ghinius of Siena.]

T.: At Rome, the burial of Saint Columba, virgin.

B.: At Carthage, the feast of the twelve holy brothers.

[Note: Carthage. According to Baronius, Ghinius of Siena, and Molanus on Usuard, they suffered at Benevento. Their names are Donatus, Felix, Acontius, Honoratus, Fortunatus, Savinianus, Septiminius, Januarius, Felix, Vitalis, Satyrus, and Repositus. Born in Africa of noble families, some of them clerics, they brought a multitude of people to Christ through their preaching. Consequently they were handed over to prison, where they encouraged others to martyrdom; they themselves were tortured, nailed, thrown into a fire and half-burned, beaten with blows, and finally struck with an axe, completing their martyrdom under the emperor Maximian. Their bodies are preserved in the church of Saint Sophia of the Canons Regular. Ghinius of Siena. Bishop Alfanus of Salerno wrote their Acts in heroic verse; they are printed in volume VII of the supplement to Surius.]

A.: On the same day, Saints Sixtus, Sinicius [or Sisinius], and Juvandus, bishops, and Firminus, bishop, and Saint Aegidius, abbot.

[Note: Sixtus and Sinicius. Or Sisinius. They were bishops at Reims in Gaul and disciples of the apostle Saint Peter; they were crowned with martyrdom under Nero. Ghinius of Siena.—Firminus. Jerome’s Martyrology reads: “At the city of Amiens, the burial of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor.”—Aegidius. Abbot of Nîmes. In his Acts he is said to have been of royal stock and to have come from Greece to the province of Gaul to Caesarius, bishop of Arles. After crossing the Rhône, he joined the hermit Veredemius and then entered a more secluded place, where he was fed, it is said, with the milk of a hind. He was also reportedly discovered by the hunters of Flavius, king of the Goths, and became the adviser who induced Flavius to establish a monastery, later called Saint-Gilles, which was subsequently converted to secular use. It is also read that he was summoned to Orléans by order of Charles, king of France. The chronology of Caesarius, however, does not agree with the rule of Charles Martel, the first Frankish ruler to bear that name. Moreover, the construction of a monastery by Amalaric, the most savage of the Visigothic kings, or by his Arian successors, is historically impossible. If one says that there was another Caesarius, bishop of Arles, contemporary with Charles Martel, the difficulty is still not explained, since after Amalaric all the Visigothic kings lived in Spain, except Liuva, who, content with the kingdom of Narbonese Gaul, ruled at Narbonne for three years, as Hadrian Valesius noted in On Frankish Affairs, book VII, page 357. Since the time of the Albigensians, the relics of Saint Aegidius have been preserved at Toulouse in the church of Saint Saturninus.]

B.: In Provence, the burial of Saint Aegidius, confessor.

L.: In the place called Vallis Flaviana, overlooking the sea, the feast of Saint Aegidius, abbot, born at Athens to his father Theodore and mother Pelagia.

B.: At Bectantia Prima, the feast of Saints Marcianus, bishop, Sisinius, and Amausius.

At Le Mans, the burial of Saint Victor, bishop and confessor.

#### 2.—IV Nones

Baeda is silent.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Lyons, the burial of Saint Justus, bishop and confessor, who, after a fugitive of that same Church had, at the request of the leading man of the city, been surrendered and put to death, taking that punishment upon himself, abandoned the flock entrusted to him, which he had governed for many years with great purity, moderation, and patience; he gave himself to the desert, cleaving to the Lord and to His servants, namely Saint Macarius and Saint Paphnutius, in whose life and death he shared. He withdrew to Egypt, where he died; the people of Lyons, however, went as far as Egypt and brought his body back to Lyons.

[Note: Justus. He withdrew to Egypt, where he died; the people of Lyons went as far as Egypt and brought his body back to Lyons. Surius, volume V. Ado of Vienne discusses him in his Chronicle under the year of the Lord 379. This is the Justus who served as legate for all the Gallican bishops at the Council of Aquileia in the time of the emperor Gratian. In the lists of the bishops of Lyons he is placed thirteenth in order. Baronius, in his notes.]

T.: And in Sicily, the feast of Felix and Secundus.

V. C.: In Alexandria, Theodore. In Antioch, Timothy.

Elsewhere, the burial of Saint Justus.

[Note: Justus. He withdrew to Egypt, where he died; the people of Lyons went as far as Egypt and brought his body back to Lyons. Surius, volume V. Ado of Vienne discusses him in his Chronicle under the year of the Lord 379. This is the Justus who served as legate for all the Gallican bishops at the Council of Aquileia in the time of the emperor Gratian. In the lists of the bishops of Lyons he is placed thirteenth in order. Baronius, in his notes.]

C.: Bishop.

D.: The feast of Saint Justus, bishop of Lyons, of extraordinary holiness and prophecy.

But all these entries occur later in the manuscripts mentioned; at the beginning the following are prefixed.

In A. T. L.: The Passion of Saints Anicetus and Photinus, his brother.

[Note: Anicetus. They suffered at Nicomedia with many others under the emperor Diocletian. See Baronius’s Martyrology, 12 August, on which day the Greeks commemorate them in the Menologion.]

T.: Who, after numerous and savage tortures, were handed over to the fire.

At Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Gorgonius and Theodota.

A. T. L. B.: On the same day, Saint Antoninus, martyr.

[Note: Antoninus. He suffered near Apamea, a town of Syria. Since he was born in that same town and had risen to the order of presbyter, he went forth from there spreading the word of the Lord. Returning to Apamea and attacking the pagans, he foretold his martyrdom to the faithful. While he was visiting sacred places with some Christians and had moved a little distance away from them, he was seized by pagans and beheaded beside the river that runs at the foot of Mount Apamea. Peter de Natalibus. He seems not to be different from the one reported in the Roman Martyrology as having suffered on this day at Pamiers in Aquitaine. Ferrarius, in his notes to the General Catalogue.]

A. B.: At Autun, the burial of Saint Syagrius, bishop and confessor.

[Note: Syagrius. He is discussed above on 27 August.]

B.: At Alexandria, the feast of Saint Theodore.

At Lyons, the burial of Saint Justus, bishop.

At Nicomedia, Saints Zeno, Gorgonius, Monolappus, and Theodota with her sons.

#### 3.—III Nones

Baeda is silent.

C. V.: Saints Leo and Marinus, confessors.

[Note: Leo and Marinus. They flourished in the city of Rimini in the time of Diocletian and Maximian. While these emperors were gathering from every region masters and laborers of various crafts to rebuild Rimini, two Christian stonecutters from Dalmatia, namely Leo and Marinus, happened to arrive. At the order of the prefects, they saw Christians burdened with unjust weights and began to assist them in their labor. Marinus also bought a little donkey to help the brothers carry the stones. After three years Leo established a cell for himself on Mount Felicianus and led an eremitical life; Marinus, after the city’s building was completed, likewise hid himself in a cell at the foot of Mount Titanus. When Gaudentius, bishop of Rimini, heard the fame of Saints Leo and Marinus, he summoned them to himself and ordained Leo priest and Marinus deacon. Marinus remained in his cell until he died in 257; he was buried there on Mount Titanus, which is called Poena Marini. Peter de Natalibus, who, together with Baronius, celebrates them in the Martyrology on the following day.]

At Aquileia, Syricius, Euphemia [V. omits Euphemia], and Aristo.

D.: At Rome, the blessed Seraphia, virgin, under the emperor Hadrian and the judge Beryllus.

[Note: Seraphia. When she had been handed over to two lustful young men and they had been wholly unable to deceive her, nor afterward to set her on fire with blazing torches, she was beaten with clubs at the order of the judge Beryllus and then beheaded with a sword. She suffered on 29 July and was buried by Saint Sabina in her tomb beside the estate of Vindicianus. Her martyrdom, however, is more solemnly commemorated on this day, when the sarcophagi of the two women were placed and decorated there and a suitable place of prayer was dedicated. Surius, volume V; Peter de Natalibus. See 29 July.]

L.: In Sicily, the feast of Saint Felix.

[Note: Felix. He also seems to have been commemorated on the preceding day.]

And at Stavelot, Saint Remaclus, bishop of Tongeren.

[Note: Remaclus. Born of noble family in Aquitaine, he was educated under Saint Sulpitius, bishop of Bourges; he was then entrusted to Saint Eligius, who appointed him superior of the monastery of Solignac. He excelled so greatly in virtues that after Saint Amand’s resignation, in 652, he was consecrated bishop of Maastricht and Tongeren. He governed the people excellently, dedicated churches in the diocese of Liège under the name of Saint Sulpitius, and, at his urging, King Sigebert built two monasteries in the same diocese, Stavelot and Malmedy. Finally, he obtained from the king permission to leave a successor in the episcopal see and withdraw to the monastery of Stavelot, where he died, though the year is uncertain. Henschenius, in his Commentary on the Life of King Sigebert, section 10, 1 February, assigns Remaclus a ten-year episcopate on substantial evidence. He survived at least two years as a solitary at Stavelot; accordingly, we place his death around 664. His body was buried in the church or oratory of Saint Martin, as Notger and Hariger testify. His Life is to be read both in Surius, volume V, and in Mabillon, second century of the Benedictine Acts.]

B.: At Alexandria, the feast of Saint Aristo, bishop.

[Note: Aristo. In Jerome’s Martyrology he is written Aristonippus.]

And the feast of Saints Euphemia, Siricius, and Aristo with their companions.

T.: The feast of Saint Justus, bishop.

[Note: Justus. Perhaps this is the same person celebrated on the preceding day, the bishop of Lyons.]

T. A. B.: In the province of Syria, the feast of Saint Antoninus, a boy of twelve years.

[Note: The age of twelve years appears only in B.]

And Saint Aristaeus, bishop.

[Note: Aristaeus. Ado and Usuard, who discuss them on this day, testify that their Acts existed, but we think they have perished, since they are not found even in their own Church. There, omitting Aristaeus, we find only Antoninus mentioned in the Breviary. Hence we conjecture that, through the innumerable disasters of war, the records of that Church were destroyed. Baronius, in his notes.]

T.: And confessor.

T. A.: And the burial of Saint Euphemia.

[Note: Euphemia. There was a certain Euphemia who, at Aquileia, was beheaded with Dorothea, Thecla, and Erasma under Nero after many tortures and was buried by Saint Hermagoras. But whether the woman mentioned here is the same as this one, or as the woman who suffered together with Siricius and Aristo, seems uncertain.]

And Saint Remaclus, bishop.

A.: At the monastery of Stavelot, the burial of Saint Remaclus, bishop and confessor.

#### 4.—II Nones

Baeda is silent.

Florus in A. T. L.: In Gaul, in the city of Chalon, the feast of Saint Marcellus, martyr, who, shining with miracles and steadfastly persevering in his confession of the Lord, completed his martyrdom under Antoninus, with Priscus as governor, after being buried halfway in the earth.

B. V. T. L. C.: At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the burial of Saint Boniface, bishop.

[Note: Boniface. Buried in the cemetery of Maximus, according to Jerome’s Martyrology.]

B.: Likewise at Rome.

B. C. V.: At Saint Felicitas, Magnus, Castus, and Saturninus.

D.: Moses, prophet.

At Ancyra in Galatia, the feast of the three holy boy-martyrs Rufinus, Silvanus, and Vitalica.

B.: At Chalon, the Passion of Saint Marcellus, bishop.

At Trier, the feast of Saint Paulinus, bishop.

[Note: Paulinus. See above, 31 August.]

#### 5.—Nones

Baeda is silent.

Florus in A. and T.: At Vienne, the Passion of Saint Ferreolus, martyr.

[Note: Feriolus, or Ferreolus. Although he held tribunician authority, he was arrested at the order of Crispinus, the most impious governor, first cruelly beaten, then burdened with the heavy weight of chains and thrust into a dreadful prison. When, by God’s will, his bonds were loosed and the prison doors opened, he came out, but was again seized by his pursuers and received the palm of martyrdom by decapitation. Baeda in the common recension, Usuard, and Ado discuss him on the eighteenth day of this month. Surius published his deeds in volume V. Sidonius Apollinaris’s letter to Saint Mamertus, book VII, letter 1, concerns a translation of his relics. Ado writes in his Chronicle, under the year 719, about another translation carried out by Bishop Wilicardus. Gregory of Tours discusses the body of Saint Ferreolus, placed at Vienne, in On the Miracles of Saint Julian, chapter 2.]

who received the sentence of the sword under the governor Crispinus.

On the same day, the burial of Saint Bertinus, confessor and monk, who, wise in divine matters and innocent in evil, shone through divine virtues.

[Note: Bertinus. He was born in the territory of Constance and professed the monastic life at the monastery of Luxeuil under Eustasius. Leaving it together with two companions, Mummolinus and Ebertramnus, he preached the word throughout Gaul. After a long interval he approached Saint Audomar, bishop of Thérouanne, to become his companion in preaching, and received from Adroald a place at Sithiu where he could build a monastery. This occurred in the eleventh year of Chlothar, son of Dagobert, that is, in 648 or the following year. There he died in old age in 698, in the fifteenth year of Childebert, king of the Franks. See his Life published in Mabillon’s third century of the Benedictine Acts. The fifteenth year of King Childebert more correctly corresponds to the year 709. The concealment of Saint Bertinus’s body, carried out by Folquinus in the ninth century, is entered on 16 July; its elevation, celebrated in the eleventh century by Wido, archbishop of Reims, on 8 May; and its translation into a more precious shrine, carried out in the thirteenth century by Peter, bishop of Thérouanne, on 16 July.]

V. C.: At the Roman harbor, Quintus, Taurinus, Arestosius, Donatus, Saturninus, and Ingenuus.

B.: At Rome, the feast of Saints Taurinus and Saturninus.

D.: At Rome.

B.: Victorinus, martyr.

[Note: Victorinus. This Victorinus, whose brother is said to have been Severinus of Naples, is celebrated in all the Martyrologies on 15 April at the Baths of Cutilia, where he was crowned with martyrdom because he was believed to have strengthened Saint Flavia Domitilla, together with Saints Maro and Eutyches, in her resolve to preserve her virginity. They think he was their bishop at Amiternum. Again, on 5 September, the same person is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology and elsewhere, but as though he were a different man, killed at the Baths of Cutilia under the emperor Nerva while he was bishop of Amiternum. On that day Ado calls him the brother of Severinus, but clearly assigns to him the details belonging to Victorinus the confessor, although he then wishes to make him bishop of Amiternum. We suspect that on 5 September Saint Victorinus the confessor, bishop of Amiternum, was formerly celebrated; because he was said to have died a martyr and to have had Severinus as a brother, this gave rise to the belief that he was different both from Victorinus, companion of Saints Nereus, Achilleus, Maro, and Eutyches, and from Victorinus the confessor. The name of Victorinus the confessor was entered in the Roman Martyrology on 8 June in these words: “At Camerinum, Saint Victorinus, confessor.” This entry cannot be found in Baronius’s older Martyrologies. Bollandus, on Severinus of Septempeda, 8 January.]

They were two brothers, Victorinus and Severinus.

A.: At Rome, the burial of Boniface, bishop.

[Note: Boniface. He is also celebrated on the preceding day.]

L.: At Vienne, the Passion of Saint Ingenuus, bishop.

A. T. L. B.: In Capua of Campania, the feast of the holy Quintus and Donatus.

B. inserts Arcontius.

#### 6.—VIII Ides

Zachariah, prophet.

This is placed last in T. and L., second in A., and elsewhere first.

D.: And the feast of Saint Onesiphorus, disciple of the apostles.

[Note: Onesiphorus. Together with Saint Porphyrius, he was severely beaten at the order of the proconsul Hadrian for preaching the faith and was dragged by wild horses; thus he gave his spirit back to God. The Latins discuss him today, while the Greeks commemorate him in the Menologion on 29 April. They report that he was made bishop of Colophon; Dorotheus, however, says of Coroneia. They also commemorate him together with Evodius on 10 October.]

B. C. V. A. T. L.: At Rome, Saint Eleutherius, bishop.

[Note: Eleutherius. He was an abbot; the title “bishop” has been added incorrectly. Pope Saint Gregory, in Dialogues III.33, writes that Eleutherius raised a dead man through prayer and tears.]

A. T. L.: And the burial of Saint Humbertus, confessor of Christ.

[Note: Humbertus. Founder of the monastery of Maroilles in Hainaut. His feast is celebrated on 25 March, but the feast of his translation is today. On this day his body was found, after the hundred and fiftieth year from his death, so intact and incorrupt as if he had died that very day. See Bollandus, 25 March, for more about Saint Humbertus and this translation.]

Alternatively, “priest.”

B.: In the territory of Cappadocia, in the city of Reate, the feast of Saint Cartidius with his companions.

[Note: Cartidius. More correctly Cottidius, who, according to Baronius, was a deacon and had Eugenius as his companion.]

#### 7.—VII Ides

Saint Clodoaldus, confessor.

Florus expanded this in A. T. L. as follows: On the same day, in the territory of Paris, at the village of Novigentum, Saint Clodoaldus, confessor and king.

[Note: Clodoaldus. The youngest son of Chlodomir, king of the Franks. He had two brothers whom their uncles slaughtered; and, if they could have found Clodoaldus himself, they would have killed him too had brave men not rescued him from death. After the death of his two brothers, Clodoaldus alone was appointed heir to his father’s kingdom, but immediately rejected royal pomp, devoted himself to reading, prayer, and mercy, desired perfection, submitted himself to the discipline of Saint Severinus, and adopted the monastic habit. At Paris he was ordained priest by Eusebius, bishop of that city. He later founded a monastery in a village called Novientum, now commonly called Saint-Cloud. Although the monastery was destroyed long ago, its collegiate church is still seen there, and his sacred body is preserved in it. His Life is found in the first century of the Acts of the Benedictine Saints. Gregory of Tours writes about him in On the History of the Franks III.6 and 18.]

A similar account is read in B.

The same Florus places first the following: At Orléans, the burial of Saint Evurtius, bishop and confessor, who, in the time of the emperor Constantine, having set out to seek his brothers, entered the city of Orléans. At that time the clergy and people were observing a three-day fast for the future bishop. The church doorkeeper received Evurtius as a guest, and by God’s will he was kept there until the third day of the appointed fast. When all the bishops and the entire people had been summoned and gathered at the church, he entered together with his doorkeeper. As they prayed and awaited the Lord’s mercy, behold, at God’s prompting, a dove entered through an open window. Shining like immense light, it began to fly about almost the whole church, as though searching for a person. When it saw Saint Evurtius clinging to the doorway, it immediately settled upon his head. Astonished at this sign, the people poured out still more prayers to God, asking that the miracle be repeated and tripled. While they continued praying, the dove came a third time and settled a third time upon the head of the aforesaid man. By this heavenly sign he was made bishop for the people of Orléans. The Lord granted him such great grace that he provided medicinal remedy for the sick and boundless help for those exhausted by various calamities. For even at the hour of the breaking of the bread from heaven, when, according to priestly custom, he raised the host in his hands and offered it to God for blessing after presenting it three times, something like a shining cloud appeared over his head, and a hand extended from the cloud blessed the offering with outstretched fingers. Only he, his subdeacon, one penitent, and one consecrated woman were permitted to see this miracle. After forty years he received his captive brothers back unharmed. It is written in his Deeds.

B. T.: At Benevento, the Passion of Saints Januarius, Ferreolus, and Desiderius.

V. C.: At Capua, Januarius and Desiderius. And the Passion of Anastasius.

[Note: Anastasius. He suffered at Aquileia and is said by Molanus, in his additions to Usuard, and by Baronius, who follows him, to have been a fuller. Perhaps this Anastasius is no other than the one celebrated above on 26 August, who was both a fuller and a citizen of Aquileia.]

D. and B.: John, deacon and martyr, at Nicomedia.

[Note: John. He does not seem to have been a deacon, for no other martyrologist designates him by that title; and Eusebius appears to oppose this opinion in Ecclesiastical History XIII.5. He writes as follows: “Immediately, therefore, one of those men, who were not obscure but, according to the distinctions of this age, as they were thought, most illustrious, as soon as the edict against the Churches had been posted at Nicomedia, moved by zeal for God and impelled by fervent faith, openly and publicly tore down the document that had been posted as profane and most impious. Two emperors were present in the same city, as well as the man who was the most honored among the others and held the fourth rank of imperial authority after the emperor. But the one who first performed this noble deed in such a manner also endured the sufferings that were inflicted upon him as though he had dared so great a deed.” That these words refer to John may be confirmed by consulting nearly all the Martyrologies, which unanimously attribute this event to him.]

B.: In Gaul, at Arles, the burial of Saint Augustalis.

[Note: Augustalis. Although he is placed at Arles, since the same bishop is found subscribed to the First Council of Orange in the time of Pope Leo, when Saint Hilary presided over the see of Arles and attended that synod, he seems rather to have been bishop of another city. For in the lists of the bishops of Arles copied by Demochares, there is no mention of a bishop Augustalis. Baronius, in his notes.]

On the same day, the feast of Saint Regina, virgin.

[Note: Regina. She suffered at Alise under the prefect Olybrius, enduring imprisonment, the rack, and torches, and was finally condemned to death. Peter de Natalibus.]

#### 8.—VI Ides

The feast of holy Mary, Mother of God.

On the same day, at Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Hadrian, martyr, with twenty-three others.

[Note: Hadrian. His feast is more correctly celebrated on 2 March. Together with others, after many tortures under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, he completed his martyrdom by having his legs broken. The relics of these martyrs were rescued by Natalia, Saint Hadrian’s wife, and other faithful Christians from the fires into which their bodies had been thrown so that Christians could not recover them; they were brought to Byzantium and received there with reverence. Later Saint Hadrian’s body was transferred to Rome on this day. Surius, volume V, should be consulted concerning these martyrs. From this passage of Baeda it seems possible to establish that the Passion of Saint Hadrian and his companions, although his Passion may have been recorded on 2 March, was formerly celebrated today. Since on the day of his translation the anniversary of his death was also commemorated at Rome, it came about that the place of combat, Nicomedia, rather than the place of translation, was entered in the Martyrologies. The fact that the Greeks commemorate Saint Hadrian neither on this day nor on 2 March, but on 26 August, probably means that they observe the day on which the first translation took place, when his body was brought from Nicomedia to Constantinople.]

A. and T. insert Saint Nemesius.

[Note: Nemesius. According to Jerome’s Martyrology, he suffered at Alexandria together with Demetrius and Severus.]

V. and C. add: Demetrius and Severus with eleven others.

L., changing the wording: On this day, at Nicomedia, the Passion of Saint Hadrian and his companions, twenty-three in number, who suffered under Maximian.

B.: At Antioch, the feast of Saints Timothy and Faustinus.

[Note: Faustinus. Baronius and Usuard call him Faustus; Jerome calls him Faustinianus.]

#### 9.—V Ides

The feast of Saint Gregory.

[Note: Gregory. At Alcalá in Spain, near Seville, he confessed Christ. Ferrarius, today, in the General Catalogue.]

L. adds: “And of Dorotheus among the martyrs.” V., C., and D.: “In the [Note: [Col. 1038C] Sabines. These martyrs, that is, suffered thirty miles from Rome. Usuard, Ado.] Sabines: Hyacinthus, Alexander, and Tiburtius.” A.: “The feast of Saint Gorgonius the martyr and Tiburtius. And the burial of Saint Alexander.” T.: “The passion of the blessed martyrs [Note: [Col. 1038D] Dorotheus. Both he and Gorgonius attained the highest honors under Diocletian Augustus. Because they detested the persecution that he was inflicting upon the Christians at Nicomedia, they were ordered, in his presence, first to be hung up and their entire bodies torn with whips; then, with their entrails laid bare by stripping away the skin, to be drenched with vinegar and salt, and thus roasted on a gridiron; finally, they were killed by the noose. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VIII, 1, etc., through chapter 7. They suffered martyrdom in the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, that is, in the year of Christ 302. After some time, however, the body of Saint Gorgonius was brought to Rome and placed on the Via Latina, and thence translated to Saint Peter’s basilica. Sigebert also bears witness that relics were transferred from Rome to Gaul, in his Chronicle under the year 764.] Dorotheus and Gorgonius.” T.: “And the burial of Saint Alexander.” B.: “In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the feast of Saints Fortunatus and Ammon.”

Florus in A., T., and L.: “On this day, at Tarvenna, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1038D] Audomarus. He was born not far from the city of Constantia, in a place called Aurea Vallis, to his father Friulfus and his mother Domitta. His father brought him to the monastery of Luxovium, where he led a religious life. After many years had passed, he was summoned by King Dagobert and by the entire Frankish people, about the year 647, and, with the assistance of Saint Acharus, bishop of Noviomagus, was ordained bishop of Tarvenna. He restored to the faith many of the people of Tarvenna who had relapsed into the worship of idols. He received three helpers from the region of Constantia—Mummolinus, Ebertramnus, and Bertinus—who, with his support, built the monastery of Sithiu. After Saint Audomarus had governed the Church of Tarvenna for thirty years, he died about the year 677 and was buried by Saint Bertinus, the abbot, in the monastery of Sithiu. His body is still kept there, except for his head and certain bones, which are preserved in the church of Blessed Mary in Audomaropolis. It is said in the proper Acts of these saints that Audomarus consecrated Wandregisil to the priesthood, and Austreberta and Waldetrude to the veil.
