Surius published his Life in volume V, and Mabillon in the second century of the Acts of the Benedictines.] Audomarus, bishop and confessor,” (up to this point L.), “who, dead to the world and living for God, and distinguished by signs of very many virtues, converted the people of the city of Tarvenna to divine worship.”

### 10.—IV IDES

Baeda has no entry.

B., C., V., A., T., and L.: “At Rome, the burial of Blessed [Note: [Col. 1039C] Hilarius, or Hilary. He succeeded Leo the Great in 461 and was ordained on 12 November. He died in 468. Marcellinus in his Chronicle consequently misled Baronius, Papebrochius, and others down to the present, when, under the consuls of the year 467, he related the beginning of the administration of Simplicius, Hilary’s successor. Saint Hilary’s death occurred in the following year, and he governed the Roman Church not for five years and several months, as all more recent writers have assigned to him, but for six years, three months, and ten days, as is clear from Anastasius, Ordericus, Book II, Luitprand, Abbo of Fleury, and Honorius of Autun, as well as from the Vatican-Palatine Catalogue, six other catalogues, Regino, Hermannus Contractus, and others. Marianus Scotus also correctly recorded the day of his death in his Chronicle. For he writes: ‘Pope Hilary died on the ninth day before the Kalends of March,’ that is, on 21 February. On that date Bollandus says that he is entered in the Florarium Sanctorum, the martyrologies of Maurolycus, Galesinius, and Canisius, various calendars, and Greven’s additions to Usuard. Hilary therefore was not buried on this day; rather, his body was probably translated, since the six years, three months, and ten days during which he governed the Roman Church ended on 21 February 468. Pagi, in his Historical and Chronological Criticism of Baronius’s Annals, under the year 467.] Hilary, pope” (up to this point B.), “through whom [Note: [Col. 1039D] Victorinus, or Victorius. Baeda writes in his Chronicle under the emperor Leo: ‘Victorius, at the command of Pope Hilary, wrote a paschal cycle of 352 years.’ But it can more truly be said that Victorius composed his Cycle in the year 457, when Hilary was still archdeacon of the city of Rome, as is clear from the preface, in which Victorius says that Constantine and Rufus were then consuls, who gave their names to the year 457. Bucherius published that paschal canon of Victorius in his work On the Doctrine of the Times.] Victorinus wrote the Paschal Order.” T. and A.: “In Alexandria, the feast of the holy Nemesius, Ammon, and eight hundred and six others” (A.: “and five”). B.: “In Alexandria, Ammon, Orion, Orosius, and eighty-six others.” D.: “In Africa, the feast of the holy bishops [Note: [Col. 1040B] Nemesianus. All these bishops stood with Cyprian at the council concerning the baptism of heretics; for all their names appear in the Carthaginian synod. Nemesianus of Thubunis is called suffragan 5; Felix of Bagai is listed as suffragan 12, and Felix of Amaccura as suffragan 33. There are indeed other Felixes there, but they belonged to Byzacena. Lucius is mentioned as suffragan 8 and also 31; both were Numidians, while others of that name belonged to Leugitania. Litteus occurs as suffragan 82; we have Polianus as suffragan 13, who is said to be from Mileum. Suffragan 78 presents Victor of Octava in Numidia; the other Victor of Gor does not appear to belong here. Jader of Midila occurs as suffragan 45. Finally, Dativus of Badis is mentioned as suffragan 15. Only concerning Nemesianus may it be questioned whether he was a Numidian or a Moor, except that Tubuna occurs in Numidia no less than in Mauretania, as appears from the Carthaginian collation. See concerning these matters Saint Cyprian’s letters 76, 77, and 79. They were first beaten with clubs and then condemned to the mines, under the consuls Valerian II and Gallienus III, in the year 257.] Nemesianus, Felix, and Lucius. Also Felix, Litteus, Polianus, Jader, and Dativus.” B.: “In Africa, the feast of Saints Doletatulus, Tuscus, and Valentinus.” L.: “And of Saint [Note: [Col. 1040C] Theodardus, the twenty-eighth bishop of Traiectum, a disciple of Saint Remaclus and his successor in that see. When he approached King Childeric to recover the property of his church, which certain men had seized, he was killed by them in Alsace, in the forest of Bewalt near Nemetum, his body being cut into pieces. It is read in his Acts, preserved by Surius under 10 September, that two lights miraculously shone forth there and that sight was restored to a blind woman. These are the only matters in his Acts worthy of note. It is added that his members were carried by Saint Lambert to the city of the Tungri. He suffered about the year 655.] Theodardus, bishop and martyr. At Santanacum, Saint [Note: [Col. 1040C] Dagobertus. He was the son of Sigibert, king of Austrasia. After his father’s death, Dagobert was exiled to Ireland about the year 660. About the year 614, however, he was admitted to a share in his father’s kingdom, and at that time Wilfrid, archbishop of York, gave him assistance in horses and men. In 679 or 680 a war occurred among the Lingones between the kings Theodoric and Dagobert; Dagobert was defeated there together with the sub-king Vulfoaldus. Mabillon discusses his return to Gaul at length in the preface to the fourth century of the Acts of the Benedictines, part I, section 9, no. 198 and following. He is the same king and martyr who is venerated at Satanacum. He is mentioned in the calendar of Queen Emma, preserved at Reims in the Remigian Library, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, on which an ancient author says that he suffered martyrdom; Mabillon proves that this occurred in 679. If Dagobert was killed on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, then a translation is celebrated today.] Dagobert, martyr.” B., entered by a later hand: “The translation of the body of Saint [Note: [Col. 1040D] Benedict. In the territory of Bergomum, Blessed Benedict, a certain hermit of the Order of Vallombrosa, is venerated on 20 January; he died in 1107. Another Benedict, also a hermit, is venerated at Nitria in Hungary on 16 July. Ferrari, in the General Catalogue.] Benedict, hermit.”

### [Col. 1041B] 11.—III IDES

At Rome, Saints [Note: [Col. 1041C] Protus. These men were buried at Rome on the Via Salaria, in the cemetery of Basilla. Under the emperor Gallienus they were arrested because they were Christians. Their deeds survive in the Acts of Saint Eugenia, concerning whom see Surius, volume VI, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.] Protus and Hyacinthus, who were eunuchs of Saint Eugenia.

Florus in A., T., and L. adds: “But through the fervor of faith they became teachers of Christian law, and therefore received the sentence of death.”

A., T., L., and B.: “At Lyon, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1041C] Patiens, the twenty-fourth bishop of Lyon, who was a most vigorous defender against the Pelagians. He took part in the council of Gallican bishops at which the Catholic faith of Faustus of Lerins, condemning the teachings of Pelagius, was examined and approved. During a time of extreme want and famine, he generously sent grain not only to his own people but also to the people of Arles, Auvergne, and others, and thus came to their aid. He died about the year 480. Gregory of Tours mentions him in History II, 24, and Sidonius Apollinaris praises him for the church he built at Lyon, Book II, Letter 10.] Patiens, bishop.” B.: “In Alexandria, the feast of Saints Syrus and Serapion. In Apuria, the feast of Saints Felix and Donatus.” C.: “And at the port of the city of Rome, [Note: [Col. 1041C] Ingenui. Jerome’s Martyrology gives him Hippolytus as a companion.] Ingenui.”

### 12.—II IDES

C. and V.: “In Pamphylia, Saint Syrus; elsewhere, Saint Euplus.” V.: “And Serapion.” D.: “At the city of Ticinum, also called Pavia, the holy confessors Syrus and [Note: [Col. 1041D] Hyventius, or Inventius, or Eventius, or Juventius; concerning him, see again above, on the sixth day before the Ides of February. Usuard and Ado commemorate the bishops Hyventius and Syrus today. In the records of the Church of Ticinum, however, each is treated separately: Hyventius on the eighth day before the Ides of February, and Syrus on the fifth day before the Ides of December; they celebrate his translation on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.] Hyventius.” B.: “In the city of Catana, Saints [Note: [Col. 1041D] Euplus, or Euplius, who suffered at Catana in Sicily together with Serapion. Ferrari, in the General Catalogue, thinks that they lived under Constantine and Irene, and commemorates them on the preceding day.] Euplus and Serapion, bishop.” [Col. 1042B] “At Lyon in Gaul, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1041D] Sacerdos, the thirtieth bishop of Lyon. He built and endowed the church of Saint Paul and the church of Saint Eulalia, now called Saint George. He took part in the Fifth Council of Orléans, celebrated in 549. He died near Paris after that synod which expelled Saffaracus, when Saint Nicetius was elected his successor. Saffaracus was deposed at the Second Synod of Paris, dated by Sirmondus to 555 and by Cointius to 551. Ghinius; Saint Gregory of Tours, History IV, 36, and the same author’s Lives of the Fathers VIII, 3.] Sacerdos, bishop. In Pamphylia, the feast of Saint Cyricus, bishop and confessor. A. and T.: At Rome, the feast of Saint Hippolytus. A., T., and L.: At Autun, the burial of Blessed [Note: [Col. 1042C] Evantius. He is not found in the lists of the bishops of the Aedui preserved by Demochares, unless he is the one called Eunuthius, the tenth bishop of Autun, although no indication of sanctity is attached to him.] Evantius, bishop.” T. and L.: “In Sicily, the passion of Serapion, bishop, and thirteen others.”

### 13.—IDES

Baeda has no entry.

D.: “In Egypt, in the city of Alexandria.” B.: [Note: [Col. 1042C] “Philip. Baronius writes concerning him in his Notes: ‘Ado and the other recent writers must be corrected when, on the basis of the Acts of Saint Eugenia, they say that he was bishop of Alexandria; for his office was secular, not priestly. Eusebius, both in his Chronicle and in his History, when he gives the succession of the bishops of Alexandria, and Nicephorus Callistus and others who did the same, do not number Philip among the Alexandrian bishops. Others again were mistaken concerning this same Philip, the father of Saint Eugenia, when they thought him to be the emperor Philip, as Cedrenus does under Maximinus; Zonaras rightly refutes them concerning Philip the emperor.’ He was beheaded with a sword at the command of Terentius, the prefect and his successor, while Severus and Antoninus his son were reigning, as the Acts of Eugenia testify.] Philip, bishop and martyr.” C., V., L., A., and T.: “At Augustodunum, the burial of Blessed [Note: [Col. 1042D] Nectarius. He was the eighteenth bishop of Augustodunum, as appears in the Tables of Demochares. He is mentioned in the Life of Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, whose contemporary he was.] Nectarius, bishop.” L.: “And at Tours, [Note: [Col. 1042D] Litorius, or Lictorius, the second bishop of Tours. He was ordained in the first year of the reign of Constans, in the year of Christ 337. He was a citizen of Tours. He built the first church within the city of Tours, and the first basilica was made from the house of a certain senator. He sat for thirty-three years, died, and was buried in the aforementioned basilica. Gregory of Tours, History X, 31.] Lictorius, bishop.” B. and A., T.: “In Gaul, in the city of Tours, the burial of Saint Lictorius [B.: Lidonius], bishop. At Rome, the feast of Saint Dionysius, bishop. On the same day, at Douai [T. and B. omit ‘at Douai’], the burial (elsewhere, the passing) of Saint [Note: [Col. 1042D] Amatus. When Senecio, bishop of the Senones, died, he was elected by the common consent of all. Accused through the envy of wicked men, he was driven into exile by King Theodoric and taken to the village of Péronne in the territory of Vermandois, where he was placed under the custody of the holy abbots Ultan and Fursa. Afterwards he was placed under Saint Maurontus, whom Saint Amandus had appointed abbot of the clergy at a place called Broilus. He died at Broilus in the year 690. The monastery of Broilus was destroyed in 870, when, as the Danish persecution threatened, the brothers serving God and Saint Amatus carried the saint’s body to Douai and placed it in the church of Blessed Mary, which belonged to them. That church of the Mother of God is now called the collegiate church of Saint Amatus. Mabillon, second century of the Acts of the Benedictines, p. 947.] Amatus, bishop.” B.: “In Apulia, the feast of Saints Felicissimus and Secundinus. In Alexandria, the feast of Saint Theophilus, bishop. At the city of Angers, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1043C] Aurilius. Rather, Maurilius. He was an illustrious citizen of Milan and a disciple of Saint Martin. At Martin’s urging, he was elected bishop of Angers. For his miracles, the reason why he left the bishopric and crossed the sea, his return to his people, and how he restored to life a boy who had been dead for eight years, see his Acts in Surius, volume V.] Aurilius, bishop.”

### 14.—XVIII KALENDS OF OCTOBER

At Rome, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1043C] Cornelius. He was Roman bishop from 4 June 251, when the two Decii were consuls, until 14 September of the following year, when Gallus and Volusianus were consuls. Baeda here relates from the Acts of Saint Cornelius that Saint Cornelius was beaten with leaded scourges under Decius and afterward beheaded. This is certainly plainly false, and Baronius attempted in vain to defend it by arguing that the name Decius had entered the text and replacing it with Volusianus. For all the other sources consistently give the name Decius, which is also recited in the readings of the Roman Breviary. The Acts of his martyrdom are therefore spurious. Gallus did exile Cornelius to Centumcellae, a most pleasant place, as Pliny testifies, and we must agree with the author of the most ancient Catalogue, who says that he received his repose at Centumcellae. Concerning the infamous schism whose leader was Novatianus, unlawfully ordained bishop at Rome although Cornelius had previously been lawfully elected, see the letters of Saint Cyprian.] Cornelius, bishop: his mouth was first beaten with leaded scourges, and thus he was beheaded with twenty-one others of both sexes [R.: twenty-two]; and the soldier Cerealis and his wife Salustia, whom Cornelius had cured of an illness, suffered under Decius. [Note: [Col. 1043D] The words ‘On the same day,’ etc., are omitted by T. and B.] On the same day, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1043D] Cyprian, a Carthaginian, distinguished by his profession of oratory. He spent the greater part of his life among the pagans as a defender of idolatry, until, through Caecilius, a Carthaginian presbyter, he passed over to the faith of Christ in the year 246. At the end of 247 he became a Carthaginian presbyter, and in the following year, when he was already a mature man, at the urging and almost the seizure of the people, although he himself humbly resisted, he was raised to the episcopal throne after the death of Donatus. He had held that office for scarcely more than a year when, upon the persecution arising under Decius and being repeatedly summoned before the lion in the Circus, he sought refuge. When the persecution subsided in 251, he emerged from hiding and was restored to his Church, and he held a synod at Carthage concerning those who had lapsed. When controversy arose in 255 concerning the baptism of heretics, Cyprian attempted to settle it by a decree of the Carthaginian council, declaring the baptism of heretics invalid and wholly null. A synod of seventy-one bishops held the following year confirmed that judgment. Since, however, not a few—and especially Stephen, bishop of Rome—vigorously resisted, Cyprian summoned a larger and more frequent council on the Kalends of September of that same year, at which eighty-seven bishops confirmed the earlier decree by their votes. In 257 the emperor Valerian began a persecution against the Christians. Cyprian, after making a confession before the proconsul Aspasius, was sent into exile at Curubis in the province of Leugitana; the following year he was recalled from exile and condemned to behead­ing. He was a truly remarkable man, a supreme cultivator of Christian piety and a most vigorous defender of ecclesiastical discipline and episcopal authority.] Cyprian [C.: Cyriacus], bishop, who under the emperor Valerian, after a long exile, completed his martyrdom by decapitation six miles from Carthage.” On the same day, the Exaltation of the Holy [Note: [Col. 1044D] Cross, when the emperor Heraclius, after defeating King Chosroes, brought it back from Persia to Jerusalem.] Cross.

B.: “And the burial of Ebarcus, bishop.”

### 15.—XVII KALENDS

The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1044D] Nicomedes. At Rome, on the Via Nomentana, Blessed Nicomedes, presbyter, who, when those compelling him to sacrifice said so, replied: ‘I sacrifice to no one except almighty God.’ After being beaten for a very long time with leaded scourges, he departed to the Lord. Acts of the Saints, in the Acts of Nereus and Achilleus, 12 May.] Nicomedes, martyr (D.: bishop). L. adds “and [Note: [Col. 1044D] Valerianus. In the territory of the people of Chalon, at the fortress of Trenortius. He was one of the fifty saints who, in the time of Antoninus Verus, were thrown into prison at Lyon and who, together with Blessed Marcellus, escaped when the doors of their confinement were miraculously opened. When he reached the aforementioned fortress and, preaching the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, converted many to his faith through divine inspiration, he was denounced to the governor Priscus upon returning from the city of Chalon, where Priscus had killed Blessed Marcellus the martyr for the name of Christ. Priscus first attempted to break him by threats; then he had him hung up, tortured by the tearing of hooks, and finally put to death with the sword. Ado.] Valerianus.” On the same day, Saint [Note: [Col. 1045C] Aper. He is listed seventh in order in the Tables of the Bishops of Toul, copied by Demochares. From a legal advocate he became a monk, and from a monk he became bishop. Concerning him, see Paulinus of Nola, Letters 30–32, in the Library of the Fathers.] Aper, bishop. A. and T. preface: “In the city of Toul.” B., however: “In the territory of Chalon, at the fortress of Trinor­tium.” And [Note: [Col. 1045C] Leobinus. He first lived as a monk in the monastery of Micy. After leaving it eight years later, he went to the city of Gavalum, where he was received into clerical orders by its bishop Hilary. Departing from there, he went to Blessed Lupus and remained with him for a full five years in the same monastery. Meanwhile, while the Franks were stirring up wars against the Burgundians and the monks of that monastery were fleeing, he alone was left with one aged brother, and the barbarians cruelly tortured him because he refused to disclose the monastery’s property. Escaping these tortures, he went with Eufronius and Rusticus to Blessed Avitus, who was living in the wilderness of Pertica. Avitus received them and appointed Leobinus cellarer. Later Saint Aetherius advanced him to the diaconate, and afterward he was placed over the brothers of the monastery of Brajacum. When Blessed Aetherius of Chartres died, Leobinus was elected his successor. After performing many miracles, he died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin. See his Life published by Philippe Labbe in volume II of the New Library, p. 582. He flourished in the time of Childebert, king of the Franks, and died in 537. The priory of La Veyre and the parish church of Poligny in the diocese of Poitiers have him as their patron. Ibid., p. 730.] Leobinus, confessor.” Aper and Leobinus are absent from L.

A. and T.: “At Beauvais, the translation of the body of Saint [Note: [Col. 1046C] Lucianus. His feast is celebrated above on 28 January.] Lucianus.” On the same day, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1046C] Aicadrus. He died in the year 687 of the Christian era. Saint Aicadrus survived Blessed Filibertus by three years, as is clear from the beginning of the final chapter of the Life of Saint Aicadrus in Mabillon’s second century of the Acts of the Benedictines; Filibertus certainly died in 684. Since Aicadrus therefore lived sixty-three years, he must be said to have been born in 624. At the age of twelve he withdrew to the monastery of Ansion in 636; later, at the age of thirty, he founded the church of Quin­tiacus in 654. After governing it for several years, he was sent by Blessed Filibertus about the year 670 to the monastery of Jumièges, which he ruled until his death. Balderic says in his Chronicle of Cambrai and Arras, Book II, chapter 29, that the body of Saint Aicadrus, together with the relics of Blessed Hugh of Rouen, was transferred to the village of Hasprum because of the attacks of the Normans.] Aicadrus, abbot, who is also found in L. B.: “In Alexandria, the feast of the three brothers Cyrinus, Leontius, and Serapion.”

### 16.—XVI KALENDS

The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1046D] Euphemia. Surius published her Acts from ancient records in volume V.] Euphemia, virgin, who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian and the proconsul Priscus in the city of Chalcedon. She overcame for Christ tortures and prisons, beatings and devices of wheels, fires and the weights of cornerstones, wild beasts and clubs, sharp saws and flaming pans, and again the bite of a beast; and she was buried one thousand paces from the city of Chalcedon by her father, the senator Philosophron [D.: Philophron].

On the same day, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 1046D] Lucia. After serving God in praiseworthy virginity for thirty-six years, she was accused by her son Euprepius and compelled to offer sacrifice to idols under the emperor Diocletian, with Apofrasius and Megasius as judges. Refusing to do so, after imprisonment and savage beatings she was thrown into a cauldron boiling with pitch and lead. Emerging unharmed, she was dragged through the streets of the city, loaded with iron and lead. When she passed the house of Geminianus, that man, moved by a heavenly miracle, came to the place where the holy woman was being tortured, asked for baptism, and was beheaded at Rome together with her. ] Lucia [D.: Lucius] and Geminianus.

[Col. 1046C] C. and B., V.: “And elsewhere, Saint [Note: [Col. 1046D] Emerentiana, or Emerentianis, or Emerentianitis. On the Via Nomentana, at the Caput, in the cemetery of Martha. Jerome’s Martyrology.] Emerentiana.”

### [Col. 1047B] 17.—XV KALENDS

The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1047C] Lambertus. He succeeded Theodardus in the bishopric of Traiectum, with the approval of King Childeric. When King Childeric was killed in 673, Lambertus was exiled to Stavelot, and a certain Faramundus was placed in his chair. After seven years Faramundus was deposed, and Lambertus was restored to his see. At one point he entered Toxandria and brought its people to the faith. Finally, because of the killing of certain men who were plundering the goods of the Church, Lambertus, while staying at Liège, was attacked by Dodon with an armed band and killed with his companions in 708; his body was carried to Traiectum. On the cause of his death and the year of his martyrdom, see Mabillon, first part of the third century of the Acts of the Benedictines, p. 76 and following.] Lambertus [R. and C. and B.: Landebertus], bishop and martyr. In Britain, Socrates and Stephen.

Florus in A., T., and L. prefaces: “In Gaul, in a village called Leudegus”; and adds concerning Saint Lambertus: “By pursuing justice, he attained the palm of martyrdom.”

A. and T.: “At Milan, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1047D] Eustorgius. See the following day concerning him.] Eustorgius.” B.: “At Evidunum, the feast of Saints Valerianus, Macrinus, and Gurdianus.” L.: “On this day, the Elevation of Saint [Note: [Col. 1047D] Hyltrudis. She was buried in the church of Saint Lambert, which her parents had built at Laetiacum; Bishop Eluinus of Cambrai elevated her. Her feast is on the twenty-seventh day of this month.] Hyltrudis, virgin.”

### 18.—XIV KALENDS

Baeda has no entry.

Florus in A., T., and L.: “In the territory of the city of Langres, at the monastery of Segestrum, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1047D] Sigo. Ado, Notker, and others treat him on the following day. When he was a boy, without his parents’ knowledge or consent, he withdrew into solitude. As a young man he received the tonsure from the presbyter Eustadius. After he had first been promoted to the diaconate and then to the priesthood, he went to Saint John, abbot of Réomay, to learn the monastic life from him. Trained in monastic discipline, he sought out a very secluded forest and founded a monastery, in which he was buried. It is uncertain in what year Saint Sigo, or Sequanus, went to heaven. He submitted to the discipline of Abbot John of Réomay while still young and, full of days, rested in peace. Since Saint John lived somewhat beyond the year 540, we infer that Sequanus survived him by about forty years. See his Life in Mabillon, first century of the Acts of the Benedictines.] Sigo, presbyter and confessor. And the passion of Saints Felix [Col. 1048B] and [Note: [Col. 1048D] Constantius. See below, on the twentieth day of this month, concerning them.] Constantius, who suffered under the emperor Nero.”

B., C., and V.: “In Alexandria, Saint Trophimus. In Nicomedia, Saints Oceanus, Sixtus, and Medeteus.” B.: “At Milan, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1048D] Eustorgius. Saint Ambrose mentions him in his work Against Auxentius, concerning the handing over of the basilica, in these words: ‘Far be it from me to hand over the inheritance of Dionysius, who died in exile for the sake of the faith; the inheritance of Eustorgius the confessor, etc.’ Mombritius published his deeds from ancient records in volume I of the Lives of the Saints. He was called ‘the first’ in relation to the younger Eustorgius, who flourished in the time of Theodoric, king of Italy, and concerning whom the Martyrologies speak on 6 June.] Eustorgius, bishop.”

### 19.—XIII KALENDS

At Naples in Campania, the feast of the holy [Note: [Col. 1048D] Januarius. According to Baronius’s notes, these men suffered under the consuls Constantius V and Maximianus, that is, in the year 305.] Januarius, bishop of Beneventum, together with Sosius, deacon of Misenum, his own deacon Festus, and his lector Desiderius. After imprisonment and chains, they were beheaded in the city of Pozzuoli under the emperor Diocletian and the judge Dracontius. As they were being led to death, they saw among the others Proculus, deacon of Pozzuoli, and two laymen, Eutyches and Acutius, and asked why just men were ordered to be killed. When the judge saw that they were Christians, he ordered them to be beheaded with the others. Thus all seven were beheaded together. Christians carried away their bodies by night. The Neapolitans placed Januarius near the city in a basilica; the people of Misenum likewise placed Sosius in a basilica; the people of Pozzuoli placed Proculus, Eutyches, and Acutius in the basilica of Saint Stephen; and the people of Beneventum gathered Festus and Desiderius.

The Laetian manuscript agrees as far as Desiderius; afterward it adds the names of the other three.

[Col. 1049C] V. and B. and D.: “And the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1049D] Eustochius, the fifth bishop of Tours. He is said to have established churches in the villages of Brixis, Iciodorum, Luccas, and Dolus. He also built a church within the city walls, in which he deposited the relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, which were brought from Italy to Saint Martin. He took part in the Council of Angers in 453 and, together with Leo and Victorius, wrote a letter against clerics who had recourse to secular tribunals. He sat for seventeen years and was succeeded by Briccius. He was buried in the basilica that Briccius built over Saint Martin. Gregory of Tours, X, 31.] Eustochius.” V. and C.: “Elsewhere, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1049D] Marianus. See above, on 10 August, concerning him.] Marianus.” B.: “At the city of Trier, the burial of Saint Miletus, bishop.”

### 20.—XII KALENDS

At Cyzicus, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 1049D] Fausta. The Greeks venerate them in the Menologion on the day before the Nones of January. Surius published their Acts in volume I, on 6 February.] Fausta, virgin, and Evilasius under the emperor Maximianus. Evilasius, who was chief of the palace, ordered her head to be shaved and her hair cut off as a disgrace; then he ordered her to be hung up and tortured. At that time lightning from heaven struck many of the servants. Next he ordered small boxes to be brought and, after she had been put into one and fastened in place like a piece of wood, commanded her to be sawn in half. But the executioners could not injure her with the saws. Evilasius, astonished by this, began to believe in Christ. When this was reported to the emperor, he sent a prefect to have Evilasius hung up and severely tortured. He also ordered Fausta, naked and without a cloak [A., B., V.: maforte], to be brought out of prison, her head pierced and fixed with nails. Later not only her head and face, but also her breast and her entire body down to the shins, were filled with nails. After this he ordered a frying pan to be heated, but while she was singing psalms it cooled. Then a voice from heaven called them, and they gave up their spirits. Fausta was thirteen years old [D.: sixteen; B.: twelve], and Evilasius was eighty [V. and C.: seventy].

C., B., V., D., T., and A.: “The vigil of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist.” B.: “At Nocera, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 1049D] Felix. They completed their martyrdom by being beheaded with a sword at the city of Nocera. Peter de Natalibus, VIII, 86.] Felix and Constantius, who suffered under the most impious emperor Nero.”

### 21.—XI KALENDS

The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1050D] Matthew. He wrote his Gospel account in Hebrew, as is clear from Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History III, 24. Socrates, in History I, 19, states that he was sent to Ethiopia. We omit as fictitious what Nicephorus writes about him in II, 41. On his passion, see Peter de Natalibus, VIII, 10.] Matthew, apostle and evangelist.

Florus places before this in A., T., and L.: “In Persia”; and adds: “While he was praying, he was struck from behind with a sword. And he died.” B.: “He suffered in the city of Tharim.”

V. and C.: “Elsewhere, Saint [Note: [Col. 1050D] Vincentius. Molanus notes the translation of this saint on this day in his Additions to Usuard. His feast is 14 July; see above, together with the second century of Mabillon’s Acts of the Benedictines, where his Life is described.] Vincentius, martyr.” A.: “And the passion of Saint Alexander, bishop.” B.: “At Milan, the feast of Saint Victor, martyr.”

### 22.—X KALENDS

The holy martyrs, the [Note: [Col. 1050D] Thebans. Concerning them, see the Life written by Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, and published by Surius in volume V. The opponents of monarchy labor in vain when, with all their force and utmost zeal, they endeavor to prove this notable testimony to Christian endurance under tyrannical rulers fictitious and worthless.] Thebans Maurice, Candidus, Exuperius (up to this point R.), Victor. R. adds: “With six thousand six hundred and eighty-five other martyrs.”

Florus explains these words in A., T., and L. as follows: “With their companions, whose total number is said to have been six thousand six hundred and sixty-six, all of whom were killed together by the sword at the command of Maximian Caesar for the name of Christ.” He prefaces them with: “At Agaunum, the passion, etc.”

V., after Victor, adds: “Innocentius and Vitalis with seven companions” [C.: six]. Innocentius and Vitalis are also named in A. and C.

B. gives a fuller account, so that one might consequently believe that this Martyrology was written for the use of the monastery of Agaunum, or of another monastery following the same rule:

“In Gaul, at Sedunum, in the city of Senoctum Dorovallense, at the place called Agaunum, the passion of the holy Theban martyrs Maurice, Exuperius, Candidus, Innocentius, Victor, and Vitalis, with their companions, six thousand six hundred and sixty-six, under Diocletian and Maximian. These men came armed to the aid of Maximian when he was assigned to the persecution of the Christians. When they refused not only to sacrifice to idols but also to persecute Christians, they were decimated a second and a third time. But a dispute arose among them, in which each man, presenting himself, desired to be the tenth. At last, for the sake of justice, but after laying down their arms, they offered their necks to their persecutors, or exposed their uncovered bodies, remembering only to confess him who was led to slaughter like a lamb and did not open his mouth; they too, like the Lord’s flock, allowed themselves to be torn apart and suffered like sheep attacked by wolves. Victor, an old man who had not belonged to that legion, became exhausted on the journey and was taken to the place polluted by slaughter. While he was being invited to the banquet out of respect for his age, he learned the reason for the bodies that had been killed. He detested both the banqueters and the banquet, and immediately the crowd of profane men surrounded him. They threateningly ordered him to say whether he was a Christian. As soon as he confessed Christ, he was joined to the martyrs.”

V., At Rome, Saints Digna and Merita. B., At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Babilla [perhaps Basilla]. According to Jerome’s Martyrology, she was buried at Rome on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery bearing the same name. Of Saint Babilla, and of Saints Digna and Merita. They suffered in the persecution of the emperor Valerian under the judge Gaius and were buried in the cemetery of Commodilla on the Ostian Way, at the church of Felix and Adauctus. Baronius, in his Notes. Digna and Merita.

### 23.—The ninth day before the Kalends

The commemoration of Saint Sosius, deacon of the city of Misenum in Campania. When he was thirty years old, he received martyrdom by decapitation together with Blessed Januarius, bishop of Benevento, during the reign of the emperor Diocletian. (Thus far L.) Once, while he was reading the Gospel in the church of Misenum, with Bishop Januarius present—for the bishop frequently used to visit him because of his holiness and prudence—the same bishop suddenly saw a flame rising from his head, which no one else saw, and foretold that he would become a martyr. After not many days the same deacon was arrested and thrown into prison. When the bishop came to visit him, together with his deacon Festus and his lector Desiderius, he too was arrested, and all of them, along with three others, were killed together.

On the same day, the commemoration in the East, in the city of Iconium, of Saint Thecla, virgin. Instructed by the apostle Paul in the confession of Christ, she conquered fire and wild beasts; and after many struggles, having come to Seleucia to teach many, she rested in peace.

Florus in A. T. L.: On the same day, at Rome, Saint Linus. Saint Linus the pope did not depart to the heavenly homeland in the year 80, as Baronius believed, but in the year 67, as is clear from the Chronicle of Damasus, in which it is written: “Linus: twelve years, four months, and ten days. He lived in the time of Nero, from the consulship of Saturninus and Scipio until that of Capito and Rufus,” who entered their names in the official lists in the year 67. Yet it seems that, together with the fuller Chronicle of the ancient pontiffs, one should read: “Linus: eleven years.” For twelve years and several months did not elapse from the year 56 to 67. From this it appears that Linus was Peter’s vicar. In the fuller Chronicle of the ancient pontiffs it is said: “He was buried beside the body of Blessed Peter in the Vatican, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October,” on which day he is commemorated in this Martyrology. Yet one should not think that Linus passed to heaven on that day, since the days on which the ancient pontiffs are commemorated in Martyrologies, and on which the fuller Chronicle says they were buried, generally refer to some translation of their relics.

Linus, pope and martyr: he governed the Roman Church for nine years as Peter’s successor and was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Nero.

V. C., At Rome, the burial of Saint Liberius. There was dissension between him and Felix over the episcopate of the city of Rome. Marcellinus and Faustinus, Luciferian priests who lived at that time, state in the preface to their *Book of Petitions* addressed to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius that Liberius was taken from this life on the following day, during the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaiphus—that is, in the year 366. Since, however, both this Martyrology and others record his name on this day, we understand from this discrepancy that Liberius died on 23 September and was buried on the following day, unless 24 September is to be referred to some translation of his relics. See 29 July concerning Saint Felix.

### 24.—The eighth day before the Kalends

The Conception of Saint John the Baptist.

And at Augustodunum, the commemoration of Saints Andochius, priest, Thyrsus, deacon, and Felix. Sent from the East by Saint Polycarp to teach Gaul, they were gloriously crowned under the emperor Aurelian. They were beaten with scourges, finally hung all day with their hands bound behind them, and thrown into the fire, but were not burned; at last their necks were struck with bars.

[Note: Symphorianus. Faustus, together with his son Symphorianus, buried their bodies. But not under Aurelian, who did not reign before the year 270, but rather under the emperor Aurelius, who in the year 177 celebrated his seventh Quinquennalia, while he was in the seventeenth year of his reign; at that time a violent persecution against Christians broke out. And how can priests and deacons sent into Gaul by Saint Polycarp be said to have suffered martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian? Symphorianus, as is clear from this passage, suffered at Augustodunum.]

Symphorianus, then twenty years old, who later suffered martyrdom, was always keeping vigils and offering prayers.

B. V. C., Elsewhere, the burial of Rusticus. After the death of Bishop Venerandus among the Arverni, Rusticus succeeded him and is counted as the seventh bishop in order of the see of Clermont. He lived during the reign of the emperor Honorius and that of his successor Valentinian. See Gregory of Tours, *History* II, 13, 16.

T. L., On the same day at Lyon, the burial of Saint Lupus, bishop. Bede in the common recension, Usuard, Ado, and other more recent writers place him on the following day. Since the martyrologists say that he became bishop from being a hermit, we think he is the one who lived the monastic life on the island of Lérins after Lupus of Troyes.

B., And the return of the holy cross.

### 25.—The seventh day before the Kalends

Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: In the city of Amiens, the burial of Saint Firminus, bishop and martyr. He was the first bishop of the see of Amiens. Peter de Natalibus is mistaken in calling him a priest, VIII, 119. Usuard and Baronius say that he suffered under the governor Rictiovarus; our author, together with Peter de Natalibus, says that he suffered under Sebastian.

During the reigns of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, he left his homeland and parents and entered the regions of Gaul. Shining through the abundance of his preaching and miracles, he converted the peoples of the Arverni, the Angevins, the Beauvaisians, and the Amiens region. There he also suffered for Christ and endured many plots laid by his persecutors. Then he was seized by the prefect Sebastian, and after imprisonment and dreadful scourging was handed over to custody. In the silence of the night he was secretly beheaded in prison.

B. V. C., In Asia, Saints Eucarpius and Bardonianus, and twenty-six others. They suffered with twenty-six other martyrs. Baronius.

B., And elsewhere, the burial of Saint Firminus, bishop.

D. L., The commemoration of Saint Cleophas, to whom the Lord appeared third at the Resurrection.

### 26.—The sixth day before the Kalends

Saints Cyprian, bishop, and Justina. These martyrs suffered at Nicomedia under the governor Eutholmius. The Acts of these martyrs, in Surius, volume V, wrongly confuse this Cyprian of Antioch with Cyprian of Carthage, although they are distinguished from one another by very many differences. Those same Acts, and our Bede at this point, are no less mistaken in saying that this Cyprian suffered in the time of the emperor Claudius. Their bodies were thrown to wild beasts, but certain Christian sailors secretly carried them away and brought them to Rome. They were later transferred to the Constantinian basilica and buried near the baptistery.

Justina suffered much for Christ under Diocletian. She also converted Cyprian to Christ, although he was a magician and was trying to drive her mad by his magic. Later, when he had become a bishop and renowned teacher, she suffered martyrdom with him under the emperor Claudius.

B. V. C., At Rome, the burial of Saint Eusebius. He both assumed the see and departed to God in the year 310. In the Chronicle of Damasus it is written: “Eusebius: four months and sixteen days, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May until the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.” But these statements are plainly corrupt, as becomes certain and indisputable from that same Chronicle of Damasus when it speaks of Melchiades, his successor. For if Melchiades was consecrated on 2 July in the year 310 and held the Roman see until the beginning of the year 314, how could Eusebius have been ordained on 18 April and administer the Roman see until 16 August, having held it for four months and sixteen days, according to the same Chronicle? Since Marcellus died on 16 January of the year 310 and was buried on the following day, and since the pontificate remained vacant for twenty days, it is clear that Eusebius was consecrated on 5 February and died on 21 June, not on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, as the Chronicle of Damasus has it, nor on this day, on which he is commemorated in many Martyrologies.

Eusebius, bishop and confessor.

B., At Clermont, the burial of Saint Apollinaris, bishop. In the table preserved by Demochus he is listed as the twenty-first bishop of Clermont.

### 27.—The fifth day before the Kalends

The commemoration of Saints Cosmas and Damian under the persecution of Diocletian, with Lysias as governor, in the city of Aegea. After enduring many tortures, imprisonment, and chains, and after divinely overcoming the sea and fire, the cross, stoning, and arrows, they were finally beheaded.

Acts of them are said to have been written by a certain Nicetas; see Surius, volume V. If anyone wishes to defend those Acts, he must assert that they were different men from those under discussion here, since those Acts establish that the two rested in peace without martyrdom. There are also other Acts of these men and of their three brothers, Anthimus, Leontius, and Euprepius. They were published from ancient manuscripts in Surius, volume VII, and seem more reliable than the others. They are discussed in the Seventh Ecumenical Council, session 4. A Mass for their feast is found in the Gregorian sacramentary. They are called by the Greeks Ἀνάργυροι, “the Unmercenary Ones,” because they are said to have practiced medicine without payment.

L. adds: With their brothers Antinous, Leontius, and Euprepius.

Florus in A. T. L.: On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Timothy, Paul’s disciple. The same “Vessel of Election” took him up as a child, taught him the whole discipline of the Church, and, through the laying on of hands, made him suitable for the Churches. Remaining chaste and a virgin, he rests buried with great honor at Ephesus, on the mountain called Pion.

L., In the first place: The commemoration of Saint Hyltrudis, who, born of Count Wibert and his wife Ado, flourished in the time of King Pippin beside the river Helpram, in a place called Laetia. Fleeing, for love of Christ, from Hugh, prince of Burgundy, her earthly bridegroom, she courageously adhered to the one she had chosen and brought her good purpose to an honorable conclusion. She received the sacred veil from Theodoric, bishop of Cambrai. She died about the year 790 and was buried in the church of Saint Lambert, which her parents had built at Laetia. She had as a brother Blessed Gontard, the first abbot of Laetia. Concerning the elevation of her body, which occurred about the year 1000, see above, on the seventeenth day of this month. See her Life in Mabillon, part II, third century, *Acts of the Benedictines*.

V. C., And at Ephesus, Saint Timothy, to whom the apostle Paul wrote Epistles.

B., At Tarsus in Cilicia, the passion of Saints Tarachus, Probus, and Andronicus.

### 28.—The fourth day before the Kalends

Bede has nothing.

D., In Spain, at Córdoba, Saints Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis. They were first tortured on the rack; then their eyebrows were shaved, their ears and noses cut off, and their upper teeth knocked out. After being disfigured, they finally completed their martyrdom by suffering in the fire. Baronius commemorates them on 13 October.

V. C., In Africa, Saints Martialis and Laurus—or Laurentius. Lucian mentions Martialis and his companions in a letter preserved as number 22 among the letters of Saint Cyprian. Concerning Laurentius, or Laurentinus, who may perhaps be the same person, Cyprian himself writes in Letter 30.

At Rome, Saint Stacteus [V., Stracteus].

And in the monastery of the Lord Savior, the dedication of the basilica of Blessed Peter the Apostle.

A. T. L., In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Martialis, Laurentius, Faustinus, and Candidus.

T. L., On the same day, Saint Exuperius, bishop. Saint Jerome praises him in his letter to the monk Rusticus and elsewhere. Pope Innocent I also wrote to him. Concerning a certain Exuperius who was counted among distinguished orators, there is an epigram by Ausonius the Gaul. Baronius therefore thinks that he was first a rhetorician before becoming a bishop, although Joseph Scaliger holds another opinion.

A. T., In Gaul, in the city of Genua, the burial of Saint Salonius, bishop and confessor.

T., On the same day at Rome, the passion of Saint Stacteus.

At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Alodius, bishop. While Blessed Germanus was still alive, he presided over his monastery as abbot; after Germanus died about the year 488, he succeeded him as the eighth bishop of Auxerre. He died about the year 518, after having held the see for thirty years, one month, and twelve days, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Germanus.

B., At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Justin, priest.

In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Martialis, Marius, and Faustinus.

At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Fraternus, bishop. The following day is his feast; see there.

### 29.—The third day before the Kalends

The dedication of the church of the holy angel Michael. This church was built in a humble form but endowed with heavenly power. When the Roman pontiff and the bishop of Sipontum were inquiring about the consecration of that place, and were therefore observing a three-day fast with the citizens, on the final night of the fast Saint Michael appeared in a vision to the bishop of Sipontum and instructed him to enter the church, which he himself had dedicated, and celebrate Masses there according to custom. Usuard and Ado. The apparition is discussed above, on 8 May.

More fully in V. and C. [C omits the words “At Rome, on the Salarian Way … at the seventh milestone”]: At Rome, on the Salarian Way at the seventh milestone, the dedication of the basilica of the holy archangel Michael; or, on the mountain called Garganus, where God displayed many wonders.

A. T. L., At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Fraternus, bishop. He succeeded Allodius and, as the ninth to receive that see, held it for only one day: on the very day he was ordained bishop, he was crowned with martyrdom by the barbarians. See Philip Labbe, *Bibliotheca Nova*, volume I, *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*.

B., Elsewhere, the commemoration of Saints Sosius and Januarius.

### 30.—The second day before the Kalends

At Bethlehem in Judea, the burial of Saint Jerome, priest, who died in the ninety-first year [B. omits “first”].

Jerome was by birth a Dalmatian and had Stridon, a town formerly situated on the border of Pannonia and Dalmatia, as his native place. He was born to his father Eusebius in the year 329. From childhood he was educated in the better disciplines. In grammar he had Donatus; in rhetoric, Victorinus; in Hebrew, Barhanina and other Jews; and in sacred letters, Gregory the Theologian, Apollinaris of Laodicea, Paulinus of Antioch, and, when already middle-aged, Didymus of Alexandria as his teachers.

He was baptized at Rome in adulthood. After leaving Rome, he began to travel through foreign regions. He traversed all Gaul, then went to Aquileia, and from there, through Dalmatia, Thrace, and various provinces of Asia, proceeded to Antioch. Afterward he embraced the monastic way of life and, at the age of thirty, settled for four years in a dreadful wilderness among Syrians and Saracens. In the year 378 he was raised to the priesthood by Paulinus of Antioch.

In the year 382 Paulinus and Epiphanius were summoned to Rome and took Jerome with them from the East as their traveling companion. While staying in Rome, he lodged for three years with the devout noblewoman Paula and acquired the highest reputation among everyone, so that Pope Damasus chose him to compose his letters.

After the death of Damasus, in the year 385, harassed by the slanders of the Origenists, Jerome left Rome. He boarded a ship and was carried to Cyprus, where Epiphanius received him. From there he went to Antioch, and, escorted by Paulinus, entered Jerusalem in midwinter.

In the following year he set out for Egypt, visited the monasteries of Nitria, and remained for some time at Alexandria. But offended by the excessive zeal for Origenism that he discovered among the monks, he returned to Palestine and chose for himself a dwelling in the countryside of Bethlehem. There he devoted himself diligently to study and produced innumerable writings.

In the year 410, after the Goths had conquered Rome, he assisted as many refugees from the city as he could with the greatest possible generosity. Finally, in the year of Christ 420, satisfied with fame and with his days, he was taken from human affairs in his retreat at Bethlehem, at the age of ninety-one.

Florus in A. T. L.: He contributed much to the holy Church through his labor; for the world was crucified to him and he to the world. He died in his ninety-first year.

V. C., In the city of Piacenza, Saint Antoninus. Although Usuard and Ado call him a confessor, it is nevertheless clear from his Acts that he died a martyr. Peter de Natalibus recounts them in VIII, 133, where he also discusses the discovery of his body, made in the time of Saint Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza; that discovery is commemorated annually on this day. Baronius, in his Notes.

V. C. A., At Milan, the translation of the body of Saint Victor, martyr. A certain Victor is commemorated above at Milan on 8 May.

L. and T., On the same day, the commemoration of Saints Victor and Ursus, martyrs. They too belonged to the glorious Theban Legion. At first they were tortured with dreadful punishments under the emperor Maximian; but when a heavenly light flashed over them, the executioners fell to the ground and they were rescued. Then they were thrown into the fire, but were not harmed at all; finally they were put to death by the sword. Saint Eucherius discusses them in the Acts of Saints Maurice and his companions.

C., At Rome, the passion of Saint Sophia with her three daughters, Pistis, Elpis, and Agape.

B., And Saints Pistis, Elpis, Agape, and Sophia. Concerning them see also 1 July.

## October

### 1.—On the Kalends

The feast of Saint Remigius in the city of Reims. Concerning him see above, 13 January, which is his feast day. Today, however, his translation is celebrated; Hincmar writes about it in volume IV. Surius, p. 300 and following.

Florus in A. T. L.: In the city of Elissipona, the passion of Saints Verissimus, Maximus, and Julia [A., Julius], who suffered under the governor Datianus. When Datianus learned of their confession, he ordered a tribunal chamber to be prepared and lictors admitted; the martyrs were stretched out, scourges brought near, claws fastened, racks displayed, and cords tightened. Since none of these things either frightened the servants of God by the threat or overcame them when applied, they were finally put to death by the sword.

A. T., On the same day, in the district of Medratum, the commemoration of Saint Piato, martyr. He is said to have been born within the territory of Benevento. Together with Blessed Quintinus, Lucius, Lucianus, Albinus, Crispinus, and Crispinianus, his companions, he went from Rome to Gaul for the sake of preaching. After converting many people at Tournai to the faith of Christ, during the persecution of Maximian he was attacked by the pursuing soldiers. His companions were slaughtered by the sword; he himself was pierced with keys and beheaded, thus completing his martyrdom about the year 300. His body rests at Siclinium in the territory of Melantes, where, in honor of the martyr and first apostle of the people of Tournai, a college of canons was established. Ghinius the Elder. Peter de Natalibus says that he went to Gaul not with Quintinus but with Dionysius; but the records of the Church of Tournai testify concerning Quintinus, as Molanus explains in his *Index of the Saints of Belgium*.

A. T. L., In the city of Trier, the burial of Saint Nicetius, bishop. He was present at the First Council of Clermont in 535, the Second Council of Orléans in 549, and the Second Council of Clermont in the same year. In 555 he attended the Second Council of Paris. The Council of Toul was convened on his account in 550, but Mapinius, bishop of Reims, refused to attend because it had been summoned without consulting him, as is clear from his letter to Nicetius. Fortunatus praises him in Book III, poem 9, and in the following poem his castle above the Moselle. In poem 11, Magnericus, his successor and disciple, calls him his teacher.

He wrote to the emperor Justinian to recall him from heresy, and to Chlothsind to promote the conversion of the Lombards. Some learned men have written, on the basis of a manuscript, that Bishop Nicetius was the author of the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, but they were uncertain whether he was Nicetius of Lyon or Nicetius of Trier. Yet this hymn is older than both Nicetii, since it is praised in chapter 11 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.

V. C., At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor. Germanus died at Ravenna on 31 July; see that day above. This, however, is the day of his burial. Constantius writes in the final chapter of the Life of Saint Germanus: “His most sacred body, carried with an honorable procession and accompanied by the works of his virtues, was brought to his own city; and there, on the day before the Kalends of October, it was fittingly committed to burial with the most celebrated devotion of his fellow citizens.”

B., And elsewhere, Saint Vedastus, Saint Bavo, and Saint Pieton. His proper name was Allowinus. His father was Eilolfus and his mother Adeltrudis. Born in the duchy of Hasbaye, he married the daughter of Count Adilo, by whom he fathered Agletrudis. After his wife died, at the urging of Saint Amandus, bishop, he distributed his possessions among holy places and gave them to the poor. In the monastery at Ghent, which Saint Amandus had built, he received the tonsure and, at the hands of that bishop, attained clerical rank.

After obtaining permission from the blessed bishop, he visited various monasteries. Then he returned to Ghent and shut himself up in a cell, where he lived until his death, which seems to have occurred in the year 653. Various translations of Saint Bavo are recorded. In the Bavonian Chronicle preserved by Sanderus, it is said that his body was raised from the earth by Blessed Eligius. His relics and those of others, when the Normans invaded, were first taken by Abbot Eynkeric to the fortress of Saint-Omer and then to the city of Laon. From Laon the monks carried them about from place to place for nearly a hundred years; they remained for some time in the monastery of Nigella, commonly called Nelle, and then in Picardy. From there they were brought back to Ghent in the year 939. See his Life in Mabillon, second century, *Acts of the Benedictines*.

In the city of Tumis, the commemoration of Saints Priscus, Crescentius, and Evagrius. And of Saint Melor.

### 2.—The sixth day before the Nones

Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: In Gaul, the passion of Saint Leodegarius, bishop. He was educated by the efforts of Dido, bishop of Poitiers, in letters and in both branches of law; he was ordained and placed in charge of the Churches of his diocese, and appointed abbot of Saint Maxentius. He conducted himself so holily and nobly that, summoned by Chlotar, king of the Franks, and honored at the palace, he was also consecrated bishop of Augustodunum. He carried out this office vigorously for ten years.

After Chlotar died, Childeric succeeded him, and Leodegarius was declared mayor of the palace, while Theuderic, Childeric’s brother, was excluded from the kingdom. Ebroin, who under Chlotar had been mayor of the palace because of his tyranny, was tonsured and confined in the monastery of Luxeuil in Burgundy.

After Childeric later died, Theuderic recovered the kingdom, and Ebroin, having fled, again became mayor of the palace. Thinking that he had been expelled through the faction of the aforementioned bishop, Ebroin inflicted the cruelest tortures on him. After hunger and the filth of prison, after the tearing out of his eyes, after the cutting off of the soles of his feet, and after the cutting of his tongue and lips, he shut him up in the monastery of Fécamp. Although his tongue had been cut out, he nevertheless spoke words of salvation correctly to everyone. Therefore the ashamed and cruel Ebroin had him beheaded near Arras.

From this it is possible to determine the year in which Saint Leodegarius died. Ebroin was killed in the ninth year of Theuderic’s reign—if we believe Sigebert—in the year of Christ 681 or the following year, nearly three years after Leodegarius had suffered martyrdom, as is established by Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictines*, second century, p. 705. Accordingly, Leodegarius was killed in the year 678, as Charles Le Cointe also believes. His body was first buried at the village of Sarcinum; it was then transferred to the diocese of Poitiers and buried in the monastery of Blessed Maxentius. See more in the work of Mabillon cited above.

Leodegarius, bishop and martyr, who by order of Ebroin—formerly a monk and then mayor of the palace—was deprived of his eyes and tongue, but was not destroyed by hunger; afterward, reduced to extreme want, he was killed and finally received punishment by the sword.

The supplement is lacking in D.; a later hand, however, has written: “The commemoration of Saint Leudegarius, martyr.”

B. V. C., At Antioch, Primus, Quirillus, and Secundianus; at Rome, Saint Eusebius. Concerning him see above, 26 September.

Elsewhere, Saints Felix and Castus. [The words “In the district of Poitiers” are omitted by V. C.] The burial of Leodegarius, bishop and confessor.

T., At Rome, on the Appian Way, the burial of Eusebius, bishop, and Beatus, bishop.

B., At Nicomedia, Saint Eleutherius. When Diocletian’s palace had been burned, Eleutherius and countless others, falsely accused of this crime, were killed in heaps by order of the same emperor. Some were cut down with swords, others burned in fires. Their first martyr, Eleutherius, after being tortured for a long time and growing stronger through each torment, completed his martyrdom in the fires as the victory of his faith. Eusebius writes about those who suffered martyrdom for this reason in *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, 6.

### 3.—The fifth day before the Nones

Among the ancient Saxons, the commemoration of the two Ewalds, priests. Concerning them see above, Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History* V, 10. They came into Germany with Bishop Willibrord and proceeded among the Saxons. When they began preaching Christ there, they were seized by the pagans and killed. For a long time a great light appeared over their bodies, revealing where they were and what their merits were.

C. V., In Africa, Victor and Urbanus.

V. C. B., Elsewhere, Felix [C., Elicius] and Castus.

A., In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Victor and Castus.

T., In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Victor, Felix, and Castus.

And Saint Dionysius. He was an Athenian by birth. At first he devoted himself to humane studies at Athens, then at Heliopolis in Egypt. Returning home, he was admitted to the council of the Areopagus, from which he also took the name “Areopagite.” About the year 50 of Christ, while Paul was preaching at Athens, he embraced the Christian faith. Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, even states that he was appointed the first bishop of Athens. Indeed, if Suidas, Nicephorus, Syncellus, and others are to be believed, he was ordained by Paul himself.

Finally, after a most illustrious confession of faith and the gravest kinds of torture, the Athenian philosopher Aristides reports in his *Apology* that he was crowned with glorious martyrdom—provided that Usuard and Ado really cite that work in their Martyrologies. At what time he died—under Trajan, Hadrian, or, as seems more probable, Domitian—is uncertain. In his Martyrology Baronius places here another Dionysius, who suffered with companions under Valerian and Gallienus.

This is placed first in both sources concerning the Africans; in A. it is added at the end: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Dionysius, bishop.”

B., At Antioch, the commemoration of Saint Theogenes.

In the district of Poitiers, the passion of Saint Leodegarius, martyr. Concerning him see the preceding day.

### 4.—The fourth day before the Nones

Bede has nothing.

B. V. C., In Egypt, Saints Marcus and Marcian. Together with them countless others of both sexes and every age suffered. Some, after scourging; others, after horrible tortures of various kinds, were handed over to the flames; others were thrown into the sea; some were beheaded; very many were consumed by hunger; others were fastened to crosses; and some, with their heads turned downward and their feet raised on high, earned the most blessed crown of martyrdom. Eusebius writes of their martyrdom in *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, 8, although he passes over their names in silence.

V. C., Elsewhere, Marcellus, bishop.

V., And the burial of Marsus. He was not a bishop but a priest of Auxerre. He was ordained priest by Pope Sixtus of Rome at the same time that Peregrinus was ordained the first bishop of Auxerre. Philip Labbe, *Bibliotheca Nova*, in the Passion of Saint Peregrinus, p. 526.

B. C., At Auxerre [C. omits “at Auxerre”], the burial of Marcus, priest.

In Africa, Maurusius and Restitutus.

D., At Corinth, Crispus and Gaius, whom the Apostle mentions when writing to the Corinthians. In the First Epistle, chapter 1. They are also mentioned in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 16, and in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 18.

B., At Anxiopolis, the commemoration of Saint Clasius. He is called Dasius in Jerome’s Martyrology.

A. T. L., In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Restitutus and Marcellus, bishop.

At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Marcus, priest.

L., And the commemoration of Saint Francis, confessor. He died at Assisi in Umbria. He was the founder of the Order of Friars Minor, whose Life, full of holiness and miracles, was written by Saint Bonaventure and published by Surius, volume V. He departed this life in the year 1226. He was enrolled among the saints by Pope Gregory IX in the year 1228. His body was translated in the year 1230.

### 5.—The third day before the Nones

Bede has nothing.

V. C., In Sicily, Saints Placidus, Eutychius, and thirty others. Placidus, of the family of the Anicii, was offered to Saint Benedict at the age of seven. Later, he is said to have been rescued from a shipwreck by Blessed Maurus and to have assisted Saint Benedict when he asked for a spring on the mountain. He founded the monastery of Saint Erasmus.

Sent to Sicily, he performed many miracles. Received at Messina, he avoided the houses of secular people, built a monastery, healed all the sick of Sicily, and constructed a church. Finally, together with his companions Eutychius, Victorinus, and their sister Flavia, Donatus, Faustinus, Firmatus, and thirty others, he was beheaded by the pirate Mamucha, whom Abdallah, the barbarian king of Spain, had sent, after various tortures, in the year 541.

All these were buried by Gordianus, who had followed Blessed Placidus from the monastery of Cassinum. Placidus is called the first martyr of the Benedictines. See the Life of Saint Placidus in Mabillon, first century, *Acts of the Benedictines*.

Elsewhere, Victorinus and Faustus.

D., In Sicily, Saints Placidus, Eutychius, and thirty others.

B. A. T. L., In Gaul [B., Africa], in the city of Valence, the burial of Saint Apollinaris, bishop. Born at Vienne of noble parents, he cared for the flock entrusted to him with paternal concern and labored especially to abolish vices. Thus, when a certain Stephen, a member of King Sigismund’s household, after the death of his wife had contracted an unlawful marriage with her sister and had not corrected himself when admonished, Apollinaris, after consultation with Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne and his own brother, excluded him from communion with the faithful.

After governing that see most worthily for thirty-four years, he intended to visit his relatives and arrived at Marseilles. He was kindly received but fell ill with fever; when he obtained the opportunity to return, he departed from the world. He attended the Council of Epaon, held in Gaul in the time of Pope Gelasius, in the year 595. Ghinius the Elder.

The words “At Auxerre,” and so forth, through “deacon,” are omitted by L.

At Auxerre, the burial of the saints Firmatus, deacon, and Saint Flavina, or Flavia, or Flaviana, virgin. The word “brothers” occurs only in B. They suffered with Saint Placidus.

### 6.—The second day before the Nones

Bede has nothing.

V. C., At Rome, the burial of Marcus, bishop. Concerning him see the following day. A certain translation of his relics occurred today.

And in Africa, Rogatus, Saturninus, Januarius, Faustinus, and Martialis [Al., Faustus and Marcus].

B., On the same day, the passion of Saints Faustus, Januarius, and Mercialis.

B. D., At Capua, Saints Marcellus, Castus, Aemilius, and Saturninus. As for Castus and Aemilius, since these names are known to belong to African martyrs whose feast is celebrated on 22 May, we are readily led to suppose that these are the same men; but their feast may also be celebrated at Capua because African bishops, driven from Africa during the Vandal persecution, landed on the Campanian coast and deposited there the relics they had brought with them.

As for the martyr Marcellus, there was a martyr of that name in Africa, commemorated on 19 February. Moreover, many Saturnini of the same name are found to have suffered in that province, as is easily gathered from the Martyrologies. Baronius, in his Notes.

It should also be observed that it has often happened that where the Vatican and Saint Cyriacus manuscripts read “in Africa,” the Dijon manuscript reads “at Capua,” so that perhaps “Carthage” was written somewhere.

A. T., At Rome, the burial of Saint Marcus, bishop.

At Capua, the commemoration of Saints Castus and Saturninus.

A. T. B., At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Romanus, bishop.

At Agen, Saint Faith, martyr.

T., And her companions Caprasius, Primus, and Felicianus.

B., At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Balbina.

L., At Capua, the commemoration of Saints Castus and Saturninus.

And at Agen, Saint Faith, virgin.

### 7.—NONES

Feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1065D] Mark. In the Chronicle of Damasus we read: “Mark: eight months, twenty days. He lived in the time of the consuls Constantine, Nepotianus, and Facundus, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February until the Nones of October, the aforesaid consuls being in office.” Mark was therefore ordained Roman pontiff in the year 336, after the death of Sylvester, on the eighteenth day of January, a Sunday, which was also distinguished at Rome as the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter. He died on this very day, notwithstanding that the author of the Longer Chronicle of the ancient pontiffs, and after him Anastasius and others, say of Saint Mark that “he was buried in the cemetery of Balbina on the Via Ardeatina, on the day before the Nones of October”; for they must be understood to refer to one of his translations. Saint Mark, while still a Roman presbyter, attended with Pope Miltiades the Roman synod held in 313 concerning the Donatists. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History X, 8.] of Pope Mark. On the same day, the feast of Saint Linus, pope.

The final entry is absent from manuscripts A, T, and L.

V. C. B., and of Saints [Note: [Col. 1065D] Sergius. They suffered in the province called Augusta Euphratensis, under the emperor Maximian and the governor Antiochus. Bacchus was beaten with raw sinews until, torn apart throughout his body, he gave up his spirit in confession of Christ. Afterwards Sergius, with his feet shod in boots studded with nails, remaining steadfast in the faith, was sentenced and ordered to be beheaded. The place where he rests was called Sergiopolis after him. See Surius, vol. V. For the miracle that occurred at Sergiopolis, and for the gifts that Chosroes, king of the Persians, sent to the holy martyr Sergius, see Evagrius Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History IV, 28, and VI, 21.] Sergius and Bacchus. At Capua, Quartus and Marcellinus. L., and Saints Marcellus [Note: [Col. 1066D] Marcellus. They abandoned Simon Magus through the apostle Peter and devoted themselves to apostolic teaching; afterwards, under the consul Aurelian, they won the crown of martyrdom and were buried not far from the city of Rome. Usuard, Ado. For Marcellus, see the Acta Sanctorum, May 12, in the Acts of Nereus and Achilleus.] and Apuleius, martyrs.

A. T., At Rome, the burial of Saint Mark, pope. On the same day, the feast of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, martyrs. A. T. B., At the city of Bourges, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1066D] Augustine. More correctly, Augustus. He was not a bishop but a presbyter and confessor, of the household of Saint Desideratus, bishop of that city, whose hands and feet were so contracted that he could support himself only on his knees and elbows. Assisted by alms at Brioude, he built an oratory in honor of Saint Martin. When he had brought that saint’s relics there, he was immediately healed; living there regularly with several companions, he was appointed abbot by the bishop in the basilica of Saint Symphorianus. In both places he instructed disciples in a proper manner of life. Saint Ursinus, once the first bishop of Bourges, appeared to him once and twice in a vision; and with Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, to whom he had likewise appeared, and with the aforesaid Saint Desideratus, Augustine took part in the discovery and translation of Saint Ursinus. He died finally around the year 580. Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 80.] Augustine [B., Augustalis], bishop and confessor. A. T., On the same day, the feast of Saints Marcellus and Apuleius.

[Col. 1066C] 8.—EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES. Absent from Bede and the supplement (Diu.).

[Col. 1067B] B. V. C., At Antioch, Dionysius, bishop, [B. omits “bishop”], Januarius, and Faustinus, martyrs; Martial [C. omits “martyrs: Martial”], Privatus [B. omits Privatus]. A. T., At the city of Antioch, the feast of Saints Januarius, Privatus, and Faustinus, martyrs. A. L., At Auriniacum, Saint [Note: [Col. 1067C] Benedicta. She suffered in the territory of the city of Lyons. Born in the city to Roman senators, she heard of the contest of Saint Quentin and the others and set out for Gaul with twelve other virgins. When the others separated from her, she came to Lyons with Scoberia alone and settled at the estate of Myriniacum beside a grove. The judge Macrobius detained her, tortured her with intolerable torments, and ordered her to be struck with an axe. Peter de Natalibus.] Benedicta, martyr. In Caesarea of Palestine, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 1067C] Reparata. She suffered under the emperor Decius. Since she refused to sacrifice to idols, she was tortured by various kinds of torment and finally struck with the sword. In the course of time her body was translated and now rests in Florence. Peter de Natalibus.] Reparata, virgin. A., At Hunulficurtum, the burial of Saint Valeria, virgin. On the same day, at Donninus, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1067D] Ragenfreda. Her father was Aldebert, count of Austrasia; her mother was Saint Regina, granddaughter of Pippin, king of the Franks. At Donon, two miles from Valenciennes, her parents founded for her, from their own property, a cell or monastery, over which she presided first and in which she died peacefully. Molanus, On the Saints of Belgium.] Ragenfreda, virgin. T., On the same day, the feast of the holy virgins Ranghenfleda and Benedicta, martyr. B., On the same day, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 1067D] Marcellus. See the preceding day concerning them.] Marcellus and Apuleius.

### 9.—SEVENTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES

At Paris, the feast of the holy martyrs [Note: [Col. 1067D] Dionysius. This, it seems, was not that Dionysius the Areopagite, but rather Dionysius, the first bishop of Paris. Some hold that the two were the same; but Sirmond, in his Dissertation on the Two Dionysiuses, and Launoy, in his book On the Two Dionysiuses, together with others, deny that Dionysius, bishop of Paris, was the same as Dionysius the Areopagite. Schelstratius briefly summarizes the arguments of both sides in the second part of his Illustrated Antiquities, dissertation III, chapter 3, article 3. Rusticus is said to have been a presbyter and Eleutherius a deacon; they were sent into Gaul with Saint Dionysius by Blessed Clement, Roman pontiff, and at last were put to death by the prefect Fescenninus Sisinnius, together with him, by the sword.] Dionysius, bishop, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.

A. and T. add: “Who, confessing the Trinity, gloriously deserved to be crowned with a threefold martyrdom.” But L. has: “Who, after excessive torments, submitted their necks to axes in the reign of Domitian.”

[Col. 1067C] On the same day, at Cologne, [Note: [Col. 1068C] Gereon. Nearly all the other Martyrologies discuss him and his companions on the following day. They are said to have been Thebans and, together with that legion of Blessed Maurice, to have crossed into Gaul from there by order of the emperor Maximian and settled along the banks of the Rhine. Rejecting the tyrant’s wicked command, they patiently submitted their necks to the sword for true piety. See their Acts in Surius, vol. V.] Gereon, martyr, with three hundred and fifteen others.

As it appears in R.; but in [lacuna], seventeen; in the Barberinian manuscript and that of Saint Cyriacus, 318; in V., eighteen. They are all absent from A., T., and L.; therefore we are uncertain.

C. and V., On the same day, Saint [Note: [Col. 1068C] Domninus. Domninus suffered in the territory of the city of Chrysopolis, under the emperor Maximian, whose first chamberlain he had been. In the sixth year of his reign, when the emperor in question had come from Rome to Milan, he issued an edict imposing capital punishment on Christians. After this, Domninus and about five hundred others remained in hiding; but when the emperor had returned to Rome, they openly professed themselves Christians with the greatest steadfastness. The emperor ordered all of them to be beheaded. After some of them had been killed, several fled, among them Saint Domninus. Nevertheless, messengers of Maximian captured him on the Claudian Way in the territory of the city of Chrysopolis; without delay they beheaded him. Peter de Natalibus. Baronius writes that he was beheaded at Julia, in the territory of Parma.] Domninus, martyr. B., At Rome, the feast of Saints Marcellinus, Genuinus, and Nivius. And between the two laurel trees, the feast of Saint Primina.

### 10.—SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES

The passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 1068D] Victor. He was part of the Theban legion with his companions. Reaching a Frankish town called Troy or Xanthus, he was killed there with three hundred and thirty other soldiers. Their deeds are recounted in the Acts of Saint Gereon, in Surius, vol. V.] Victor, martyr. And in Britain, [Note: [Col. 1068D] Paulinus. Concerning this first bishop of York, see above, Bede, Ecclesiastical History II, 9 and following, and III, 14.] Paulinus [B. C., Paul], bishop of York.

But Victor is absent from the manuscripts A. and T., and Paulinus is placed last. For A. and T. prefixed the following: “In Africa, the feast of Saints Venustus and Crescentius, and Saint Victor, martyr. At Cologne, called Agrippina, the feast of Gereon, martyr, with three hundred and [Col. 1068C] eighteen others.” The latter entry appears to belong to Florus; it is also found in L., where Victor alone is placed last.

V., Malosius with three hundred and thirty others. B., In Africa, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 1069C] Eusebius, Heraclius, and Dionysius. They suffered with Venustus, Crescentius, and Victor, as is clear from Jerome’s Martyrology.] Eusebius, Heraclius, and Dionysius. And elsewhere, [Note: [Col. 1069C] Malusius. He suffered at Xanthus together with Saint Victor [Col. 1069D] and his companions.] Malusius with three hundred and thirty others.

### 11.—FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES

Bede is absent.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Tours, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1069D] Venantius. His burial is more correctly celebrated by all the Martyrologies on the thirteenth day of this month. Perhaps, therefore, he died today and was buried on that day; or perhaps some translation took place on this day. His sacred relics were later, as we conjecture, during the time when the Northmen were devastating everything, transferred from there and deposited at the village of Cuvinium in the district of Lomacum near Namur.
