There the monks of Saint Germanus of the Meadows, at the beginning of the tenth century, were, according to the author of the Life of Saint Gerard of Brogne, “keeping watch over Saint Abbot Venantius.” At the end of that same century, however, the Germanus monks, compelled to leave Cuvinium, returned to Paris, carrying with them the relics of the blessed abbot; these are still preserved in the basilica of Saint Germanus. See below, on the thirteenth of this month, for more concerning him.] Venantius, abbot and confessor, a man of extraordinary holiness, who, while still alive in the body, brought aid to many sick persons.

C. V., Saints Tanas(ius), presbyter, Ampodius, Faustus, [Col. 1069C] Januarius. V., Marcellus. C., Martial. D., At Tarsus, the metropolis, the martyrs [Note: [Col. 1069D] Tarachus. During the persecution of Diocletian, under the governor Maximus, they were punished with imprisonment, beaten with sinews, their flesh scraped with hooks, burned with blazing papyrus, subjected to the breaking of their jaws and the tormenting of their legs, and tortured by vinegar and mustard being poured into their nostrils. After burning stakes had been applied, after their fingers had been pierced with nails, after the light of their eyes had been extinguished and their tongues cut out, they were thrown to bears and lions. But when none of the beasts harmed them, they were slaughtered with the sword. Ado, Notker, Surius, vol. V.] Tarachus, Probus, and Andronicus, who were martyred in the persecution of Diocletian. A. T., first: At Antioch, the feast of Saint Athanasius, bishop, Heraclius, and Placidus. T., At Cologne, called Agrippina, on the Rhine, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1070D] Malusius. See the preceding day concerning him.] Malusius with three hundred and thirty others. L., last: And at Antioch, the passion of Heraclius and Placidus. [Col. 1070B] B., At Acerbus in Sicily, the feast of Saints Thasius, presbyter, Placidus, and Martial. At Antioch, the feast of Saint Heraclius.

### 12.—FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES

Bede is absent.

B. V. C., In the province of Syria, the saints. V. B., Evagrius, Proseria [B., Prosyria]. At Rome, Caelestinus [B., Caelestis], Saturus. C., Evagrius and Seria. At Rome, Caelestis. B., In Egypt, Saint Eustasius, presbyter. D., In Africa [Note: [Col. 1070D] These suffered in the Vandal persecution under Hunneric, the Arian king. Some were bishops, others presbyters and deacons; having joined themselves to crowds of faithful people, they were driven into exile in the desert in defense of Catholic truth. Of them, many, while being cruelly led by the Moors, were driven forward to run by the points of spears and beaten with stones; others, their feet tied, were dragged like corpses over rough and rugged places and torn limb from limb; finally, after suffering various tortures, they completed their martyrdom. Victor of Vita gives a fuller account of their sufferings in his book On the Vandal Persecution.] Africa, four thousand nine hundred and seventy-six holy confessors and martyrs. A. T. B., In Campania, the feast of Saints Eucharistus and Fortunatus. B., Priscianus. A. T., At Rome, the burial of Saints [Col. 1070C] Saturus and Callistus. T., At Ravenna, the feast of Saint Edistus. L., At Ravenna, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 1070D] Edistus. Hieronymus Rubeus, in book II of his History of Ravenna, writes that he suffered in the persecution of Diocletian.] Edistus. And at Rome, the passion of Saint Saturus. B., At Bourges, Saint [Note: [Col. 1070D] Opinion. More correctly, Opion.] Opion, presbyter.

### 13.—THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES

Bede is absent.

V. C., In Spain, [Note: [Col. 1070D] Faustus. First tortured on the horse, then, after their eyebrows had been shaved, their teeth pulled out, and their ears and nostrils cut off, they completed their martyrdom by the torment of fire. Peter de Natalibus.] Faustus and Marcia. Elsewhere, Adrian. At Alexandria, Athanasius, bishop. B., In the Spanish city of Córdoba, Faustus and Marcia. At Tours, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1071C] Venantius. He was a native of the territory of Bourges and, in his youth, was bound by his parents in a betrothal. Coming to the city of Tours and seeing the miracles of Saint Martin, he abandoned his fiancée and went to Silvinus, abbot of the monastery near the basilica of Saint Martin. Silvinus tonsured him and admitted him to the monastic community. When the abbot died, the brothers chose Venantius as his successor. Gregory of Tours, Life of the Fathers, chapter 16. He died near Ghigny in the territory of Sens around the year 425. According to Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors XV, he rests not far from the basilica of Blessed Martin.] Venantius, abbot and confessor. D., Saint [Note: [Col. 1071C] Polycarp. More correctly, Carp. He is said to have been one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ and bishop of Beroea in Macedonia. This city seems to have been fifty miles from Thessalonica, where Saint Paul preached, and he also visited Troas, leaving his cloak with the same Saint Carp.] Polycarp, Paul’s disciple, at Troas. B. A. T. L., At Chalcedon, the feast of the holy men Adrian, Januarius [B. omits Januarius], and Marcellus. T. L., In Spain, the passion of Saints Faustus and Rusticus. T., first: The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1071D] Gerald. Ferrarius writes of him in his General Catalogue: “At Aurillac in Gaul, Saint Gerald, confessor.” He was the most distinguished of the nobles of Auvergne and baron of Aurillac, born in the same year in which Charles the Bald was anointed king at Limoges, namely, in 838. At Aurillac he also built a monastery dedicated to God and Saint Peter, giving it all his possessions. After traveling to Rome seven times for religious reasons, he finally, famous for miracles, departed this life around the year 882 and was buried in the monastery of Saint Peter that he had built. Labbe, New Bibliotheca, vol. II, pp. 271–272.] Gerald, confessor.

### 14.—SECOND DAY BEFORE THE IDES

The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1071D] Callistus. He departed to God in the year 222. In the Chronicle of Damasus we read: “Callistus: five years, two months, ten days. He lived in the time of Macrinus and Heliogabalus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Adventus until that of Antoninus III and Alexander.” He had begun his pontificate on July 18, 217, the year marked by the consulship of Praesens and Extricatus. Papebrochius, in his Chronological-Historical Essay, argues that October 14 is the day of his death, not the day of his burial, and cites Jerome’s Martyrology, in which, although these words are written, “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, in the cemetery of Callistus, bishop,” Papebrochius adds: “But for this reason we should not fear that the days recorded in that Martyrology for other persons whose Acts do not survive are not truly the days of their deaths.” But this is incorrect. If Callistus’s day of death were recorded in Jerome’s Martyrology, the burial of Saint Callistus would be commemorated not on October 14 but on September 28, since on that day he was crowned with the glory of martyrdom and on October 14 was committed to the earth. From this and from other passages to be cited in various places, it is clear that the Hieronymian Martyrology does not always record the day of death, although Papebrochius believes that the days entered in it concerning pontiffs’ feasts must always be interpreted in that way. [Col. 1072D] The Acts of this saint are found in Surius, vol. VII.] Callistus, pope, who during the persecution under the emperor Alexander was tormented for a long time by hunger and beaten daily with clubs. He was strengthened and consoled in a vision by his presbyter Calepodius, who had previously completed his martyrdom. While confined in the same prison, Callistus healed a soldier named Privatus both from the pain and foulness of his ulcers and from unbelief. When Alexander heard of this, he had the soldier beaten to death with lead-weighted scourges; but he ordered blessed Callistus to be thrown from the window of a house, and, after a stone had been tied around his neck, to be plunged into a well and buried beneath a heap of rubble. After seventeen days his presbyter Asterius came at night with clergy, lifted the body, and buried it in the cemetery of Calepodius. The day before the Ides of October [D. and R. omit “the day before the Ides,” etc.].

V. C. adds: “Thus he died.”

A., On the same day, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1072D] Donatianus. He is especially venerated at Bruges. He was the seventh archbishop of Rheims; his body was transferred from Rheims to Bruges. His translations are commemorated on August 30 and on the feast of the Epiphany. His relics were first brought from Gaul in the year 863 to the monastery of Torhout, and then, with great solemnity, to the port of Bruges by order of Baldwin Iron-Arm, margrave of Flanders. Afterwards his sacred remains were transferred at Bruges from an old shrine to another, and a letter of Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, concerning this saint was found in the former shrine with the body. Some saw that very letter during the third translation, carried out by Peter Curtius, the first prelate of Bruges, in 1562. Molanus, Index of the Saints of Belgium.] Donatianus, bishop. B., In the city of Córdoba, the feast of Saints Lupus and Aurelia.

### 15.—IDES

Bede is absent.

V., The holy Moors who were soldiers [Note: [Col. 1072D] Soldiers. Namely, of the Theban legion. The Martyrologies disagree about their number: some testify that there were only fifty, others 360.] and Saint Legadia. But C., “The soldiers and Saint Gaida, virgin.” D., The passing of Saint [Note: [Col. 1072D] Justus. See above, September 2. This is the day of his translation from Egypt to Lyons; other Martyrologies celebrate it on the preceding day.] Justus, bishop of Lyons, in the desert. [Col. 1073B] B., At Rome, the feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1073B] Fortunata. On the Via Aurelia, in her cemetery. [Col. 1073C] Jerome’s Martyrology.] Fortunata. A. T. L., At Rome, the passion of Saint Silvanus, martyr, and Saint Fortunatus. At Cologne Agrippina, the feast of the holy Moorish soldiers, or, as L. has it, of countless Moorish martyrs. B., In Gaul, at Cologne Agrippina, the feast of the holy Moorish soldiers. On the same day, the feast of [Note: [Col. 1073C] Savina. Perhaps Sabinus, bishop, who presided over the Church of Catania under Constantine Copronymus.] Savina.

### 16.—SEVENTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER

Bede is absent.

V. C., The burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1073C] Gallus. He came from Ireland to Gaul and afterwards withdrew with Columbanus into Alemannia. He settled at Brigantium and restored an oratory there. Because he was ill, he could not accompany Columbanus into Italy. He sought a solitary place and humbly refused the bishopric of Constance. Though absent, he saw Columbanus’s passing; he declined to become abbot of Luxeuil; he died at Arbon around the year 646, more than ninety years old. It should be noted that Saint Gall is commemorated in the genuine Martyrologies of Usuard and Ado not on October 16, the day on which our author celebrates him, but on February 20. Perhaps February 20 commemorates his elevation, when the body of Saint Gall was transferred by Boso, bishop of Constance, to a more suitable place, as is related in book 2 of the Miracles of Saint Gall [Col. 1073D]. See the Life of Saint Gall in Mabillon’s Benedictine Acts, century II.] Gallus, confessor. And likewise of two hundred and seventy others [C., eighty]. D., The holy martyrs [Note: [Col. 1073D] Marcianus. During the Vandal persecution under Geiseric, the Arian king, they were slaves of a certain Vandal and were converted to faith in Christ by Saint Maxima, a virgin and fellow slave. For the steadfastness of their Catholic faith they were first beaten with knotted clubs and torn to the bone. After enduring such things for a long time and nevertheless being restored unharmed each following day, they were finally sent into exile. There they converted many barbarians to the faith of Christ. Finally, with their feet bound behind the backs of running chariots, they were ordered to be dragged to death among thorny woodland. Maxima, after overcoming many agonies, was freed by divine intervention and peacefully died a holy death in a monastery as mother of many virgins. Victor, book I On the Vandal Persecution.] Marcianus and Satyr(i)anus, with their two brothers and two hundred and seventy others. A. T. L., In Africa, the passion of seven hundred and sixty holy martyrs [Col. 1074B]. A. T., And the feast of Saint Saturninus and Nereus. T. and L., At the city of Noviomagus, the burial of Saint [Note: [Col. 1073D] Mummolinus. He was born in the region of Constance and came with Ebertramnus and Bertinus to Audomar, bishop of Tarvanna, assisting him in preaching the Gospel. After the monastery of Sithiu had been built, Audomar appointed Mummolinus its first abbot. Some, however, hold that Saint Bertinus was the first abbot of the monastery of Sithiu. John of Ypres completely removes Mummolinus from the list of abbots of Sithiu; the San-Marthans in Gallia Christiana place him after Bertinus, but certainly without justification, since Mummolinus succeeded Blessed Eligius in the see of Noviomagus in 659 and governed it for twenty-six years, as the author of the Life of Saint Audomar testifies, and therefore ceased to live long before Saint Bertinus. It is plausible that Mummolinus had been abbot of the old monastery for fourteen years before assuming the episcopal see and had supervised the construction of the new monastery of Sithiu, though he may not have governed the monks there except perhaps for a short time, since he was called to the episcopate when the monastery had scarcely been completed; Bertinus then presumably put the finishing hand to the building and was placed over the colony of monks. Mummolinus died in 684. His body is preserved in the major church of Noviomagus, and part of his head in the monastery of Sithiu. See the Life of Saint Audomar in Mabillon’s Benedictine Acts, century II.] Mummolinus, confessor. But T. places first: The feast of Saint [Note: [Col. 1074C] Julianus. More correctly, perhaps, Junianus, confessor, in the territory of Limoges, whose feast is celebrated today. Molanus, in The Feasts of the Saints of Belgium, testifies that he was born at Cambrai and lived for forty years in solitude near Limoges. We learn the location of his hermitage from the Chronicle of Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, chapter 15, On the More Distinguished Saints near Limoges, where he writes: “The people of Comodoliacum celebrate Junianus with Amadus, his teacher; for that monastery, together with the church of Saint Peter of Quadrivium, Geoffrey, once treasurer, fraudulently took from the jurisdiction of Saint Martial.” The church in which he was buried had been built by Ruricius the Younger, bishop of Limoges, whom the holy man had freed from a demon. He flourished with the hermit Saint Amadus under Clovis I and his sons.] Julianus, confessor. B., In Africa, the passion of Saints Ceiera and two hundred and seventy others. And elsewhere, Saturninus and Nereus. And the burial of Saint Gallus, confessor, and Berarius, confessor. At Nicomedia, the feast of Saints [Note: [Col. 1074D] Alexander. He seems to be the same as the one celebrated at Nicomedia on the following day.] Alexander and Victorius. And the passion of [Note: [Col. 1074D] Silvanus. Perhaps the same as the one called Sylvarius in Ferrarius’s General Catalogue. The Calendary of Limoges and the Monuments of Agedunum, a town in the diocese of Limoges, where he is said to have suffered, make clear that he underwent martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian and the governor Heraclius.] Silvanus.

### 17.—SIXTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS

C. V., At Nicomedia, Alexander. Elsewhere, Maurianus, Crescentianus, Turinus [C., Crescentius, Ruffinianus], Donatus. D., Martha, sister of Lazarus, and Aristion, who [Col. 1075B] was one of the seventy disciples of Christ. A. T. L., In Mauritania, the feast of the holy men Donatus, Nobilitanus, Crescentianus, Defensor, and Rusticianus. But Nobilitanus is absent from L. and A.; Crescentianus is likewise absent from the latter. B., In Mauritania, Saints Nenilucius, Socrates, Venerius, Prima, Donata, Victoria, and Basilla.

### 18.—FIFTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS

The feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist. He was a Syrian from Antioch, a physician by profession, and a disciple of the apostles; afterwards he followed Paul, serving the Lord blamelessly until Paul’s confession. For he never had a wife or children and died in Bithynia at the age of seventy-four, full of the Holy Spirit. At Rome, Saint [Note: [Col. 1075D] Tryphonia. Saint Tryphonia was buried today; inquire whether she also died today. For her conversion, see the Acts of Saint Lawrence in Surius, vol. IV, August 10.] Tryphonia, wife of Caesar Decius. After her husband had been divinely punished following the killing of the blessed Sixtus and Lawrence, she asked to be baptized with Cyrilla by the presbyter Justinus; on the following day she died and was buried near Saint Hippolytus in a crypt.

[Col. 1076B] B., At Anxiopolis, the feast of Saints Hermes and Taxius. In Campania, at the city of Puteoli, Januarius and Eutychus. And elsewhere, [Note: [Col. 1075D] Elsewhere. For they suffered in Africa.] Victrix and Martial.

### 19.—FOURTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS

B. V. C., At Ostia, Asterius [B. C., Austerius]. At Naples, the holy men Januarius [B. omits Januarius], Festus, and Desiderius. [Col. 1076C] D., [Note: [Col. 1075D] Luke … Asclepiades. In nearly all the Martyrologies these are celebrated on the preceding day. After Serapion’s death at Antioch, Asclepiades became the ninth bishop of that Church. Alexander of Jerusalem mentions his ordination in his letter to the Antiochenes; from this it follows that Eusebius’s Chronicle is wrong to place Asclepiades’ ordination in the first year of Antoninus Caracalla. Asclepiades was ordained at the same time that Alexander was thrown into prison for confessing the Christian name. Eusebius himself testifies in the Chronicle that this occurred under the reign of Severus. See Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History II, 11. Saint Asclepiades died under the emperor Alexander. Ibid., chapter 21. Hence Usuard, Ado, and the others who followed them are clearly in error when they say that he suffered in the persecution of Decius.] Luke the Evangelist and Asclepiades, bishop of Antioch. A. T., At Ostia, the feast of the holy men [Note: [Col. 1076D] Januarius. They did not suffer at Ostia but at Naples, as is clear somewhat earlier.] Januarius, Festus, and Desiderius. T., On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs [Note: [Col. 1076D] Sabinianus. Their festival, which had been celebrated from ancient times on the day before the Kalends of January, was transferred to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November because their bodies were translated on that very day and angelic voices were heard. They were the first bishops of Sens and suffered death for the faith of Christ. See Peter de Natalibus concerning them.] Sabinianus and Potentianus and their companions. A., On the same day, [Note: [Col. 1076D] At Douai. For Saint Amatus, who was transferred from the monastery of Brogne to Douai, see above, September 13.] at Douai, Saint Amatus, archbishop of Sens. T. L., And the burial of Saint Amatus, bishop and confessor. At Tours, the burial of Saint Columbanus, abbot. T. B., And at Antioch in Syria [T. omits “in Syria”], the passion of the saints [Note: [Col. 1076D] Pelagius. More correctly, Pelagia and Beronicus. According to other Martyrologies, they suffered with forty-nine others.] Pelagius and Berenice [B., Beronicus]. B., In the city of Puteoli, Proculus and Nicea, his mother.

### 20.—THIRTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS

B. V. C., At Puteoli, Sozimus, Januarius, Dorothea [Col. 1077B] [V., Dorotheus]. V. C., Elsewhere, Euticius [C., Eutychus], Marcellinus. A. T. L., The feast of Saints Eutychus, Lucius, and Marcellianus. B., At Nicomedia, Eutychius, Promatus, Lucius, and Marcellinus. D., At Antioch, at Beroea, [Note: [Col. 1077B] Pelagia. She is commemorated on the preceding day.] Pelagia and forty-nine others. B., At Rome, the feast of [Note: [Col. 1077B] Asterius. See concerning him on the following day.] Asterius, presbyter. A. T. L., At Agen, the passion of Saint [Note: [Col. 1077B] Caprasius. He suffered with Primus and Felicianus, brothers, in Gaul, at the city of Agen, under the governor Dacianus. While hiding in a cave to escape the fury of the persecution, he finally heard how the blessed virgin Faith was suffering for Christ. Encouraged to endure suffering, he prayed to the Lord that, if he judged him worthy of the glory of martyrdom, clear water might flow from the rock of the cave. When the Lord granted this, he went confidently to the arena of combat and, suffering bravely under Maximian, won the palm of martyrdom. Peter de Natalibus.] Caprasius, martyr. B. prefaces: “In Gaul.”

### 21.—TWELVE DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS

Our holy Father [Note: [Col. 1077C] Hilarion. He was born in the village of Thabatha in Palestine and was entrusted at Alexandria to a grammarian. Thereafter, hearing of the celebrated name of Antony, he went to him and, as soon as he saw him, changed his former clothing and remained with him for nearly two months, observing the order of his life and the gravity of his conduct. Returning to his homeland with certain monks, and his parents already dead, he distributed part of his property to his brothers and part to the poor. At the age of fifteen he entered the solitude that lies seven miles from the market-town of Gaza, Majuma, where travelers turn left along the coast toward Egypt. There, after living for many years in holiness and austerity, he became the founder and teacher of this way of life in Palestine. When a great monastery had grown up and a multitude of brothers lived with him, he formed the intention of returning to his former manner of life, namely, the eremitical life. He therefore went to Blessed Antony; but because Antony had died before Hilarion arrived, he returned to Aphroditon and, keeping only two brothers with him, remained in a neighboring desert. Seeing that even there he was being honored with extraordinary honors, he went to Alexandria, intending from there to cross into the desert of the farther Oasis. He did not remain there long, because the people of Gaza had obtained from the emperor Julian an order for Hilarion’s death. He entered the Oasis through an impassable wilderness; after spending approximately a year there, and after the emperor Julian had been killed, he sailed to Sicily, where he thought he could remain concealed. But he was betrayed by a demoniac whom he had healed, and the beginning of his miracles in Sicily brought an innumerable multitude to him thereafter. For this reason Hesychius, his disciple, who had traced Hilarion by the fame of his virtues, led him to the city of Epidaurus in Dalmatia, where he burned a dragon of extraordinary size. Then he sailed to Paphos, remaining there for two years and seeking a solitude among secluded and rugged mountains. He lived in that place for five years and died. When Hesychius heard this in Palestine, he sailed to Cyprus and after nearly ten months secretly took away Hilarion’s body. Bringing it to Majuma, he buried it in the old monastery. See more in his Life written by Jerome. Sozomen also speaks of him in Ecclesiastical History V, 10. Saint Hilarion was born in 290 and died at the age of eighty, as Saint Jerome writes in his Life; he was sixty-five years old when the great Anthony died, according to that same Jerome. Antony died in 356. Saint Hilarion therefore also died in 370.] Hilarion, whose Life Jerome wrote, full of accounts of his virtues. On the same day, the feast of Saint Asterius, presbyter [Note: [Col. 1078C] of Callistus. See above, on the day before the Ides of this month, concerning him.] of Callistus, who, after he had buried Callistus’s body when it was lifted from the well, was, six days later, ordered by the emperor Alexander, upon hearing of this, to be thrown from a bridge. His body was found and buried by certain Christians in the same city. Recorded in the Passion of Saint Callistus, pope.

A. T. L., At Cologne Agrippina, the passion of eleven thousand [Note: [Col. 1078C] virgins. Among them the most prominent was Ursula. Having undertaken a pilgrimage to Rome with her companions and encountered the Huns on the journey, she was murdered by them together with her companions in the year 453, as Sigebert testifies in his Chronicle. The history of these virgins, disseminated among writers, is highly doubtful and uncertain.] virgins. This appears first, with some variation; at the end L. adds: And Saint [Note: [Col. 1078D] Cilinia. Mother of Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims, at the castle of Laon. For more concerning her, see the Life of Saint Remigius in Surius, January. Remigius is celebrated on January 13 and October 1.] Cilinia. B., At Nicaea in Bithynia, the feast of Macarius, Proculus, Modestus, with two hundred and seventy others. At Lyons in Gaul, the feast of Blessed [Note: [Col. 1078D] Viator. He held the office of lector and was the companion of Saint Justus, bishop of Lyons. When Justus abandoned the episcopate, Viator boarded a ship with him and sailed to Egypt, where he diligently served him in the desert. After Justus died, Viator himself followed him to heaven seven days later, as Saint Justus had foretold. Justus died on the Ides of October, and Viator rested in peace twelve days before the Kalends of November. The citizens of Lyons later took the bodies of both and brought them back to their city, placing them with due honor in the church of the Seven Maccabees on the fourth day before the Nones of September. Peter de Natalibus.] Viator, a boy and disciple of Saint Justus, bishop. In Africa, Modestus and Eutychus.

### 22.—ELEVEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS

Bede is absent.

[Col. 1079C] V. C.: At Adrianople [C., Trajanopolis], the feast of Severus, [Note: [Col. 1079C] Philip. They prevented the churches from being closed and plundered by wicked governors at Julian’s command, and for this reason were subjected to many tortures: namely, imprisonment, chains, scourges, and finally the burning of flames. But strengthened by the Lord’s power, they persevered to the end in confessing his name. St. Athanasius, *Apology concerning his flight to Constantius*.] Bishop Philip, Eusebius, and Hermes. B.: In Thrace, the feast of St. Severus. At Adrianople, Philip the bishop, Eusebius, and Hermes. T.: In Thrace, the feast of Saints Hermes, Eusebius, and Philip the bishop. L.: In Thrace, the feast of Philip the bishop, Severus the presbyter, and Hermes the deacon. A.: In Thrace, the feast of Saints Hermes, Eusebius, and Philippianus.

On the same day, the passion of St. [Note: [Col. 1079D] Gratian. Ferrarius, in the *General Catalogue*, says that he suffered in the territory of Halbia, and doubts whether he should be called Gatianus.] Gratian the martyr, and the burial of St. Autbodus the bishop. B.: Elsewhere, the passion of St. Leugatus the martyr. D.: At Antioch, [Note: [Col. 1079D] Theodoritus. Rather, Theodore. Julian the emperor had him, as guardian of the sacred vessels of the Church of Antioch and therefore one able to disclose their whereabouts, arrested and most severely tortured. When, however, he answered courageously amid the torments and distinguished himself in confessing the Christian faith, Julian finally ordered him to be beheaded. Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 8. There was also another Theodore who was tortured by the pagans under Julian so severely that, when released, he was thought unlikely to live any longer. But God preserved the young man; after this confession he lived for a very long time. Socrates III, 19. Usuard, Ado, and other later writers commemorate this man on the following day.] Theodoritus the presbyter.

23.—The tenth day before the Kalends. Bede has nothing.

C. V. B.: At Adrianople, Severus and Dorotheus. C., on the preceding day: At Trajanopolis, Severus the bishop, Dorotheus, and St. Orestes. D.: At Venusia, [Note: [Col. 1079D] Felix. See above, August 30, concerning these men.] Felix the bishop of Tubzoca, and Audactus and Januarius the presbyters. A. T.: The feast of Saints Severinus, Dorotheus, and Victor.

In the territory of Cadiz, the passion of Saints [Note: [Col. 1080C] Servandus. During the persecution of Diocletian, under Viator the vicar, after scourging, the squalor of prison, the hardship of hunger and thirst, and the labor of a very long journey—which they endured laden with chains—they finally completed the course of their martyrdom by having their necks cut. Of these, Germanus was buried at Mérida and Servandus at Seville. Ado.] Servandus and Germanus, who, for confessing the Lord, were ordered by Viator the prefect to be beheaded.

A.: On the same day, the burial of St. [Note: [Col. 1080D] Romanus. He was the twentieth bishop of that see in succession and occupied it in the year 622, as the records of his church preserved by Demochare indicate.] Romanus, archbishop of Rouen. T. B.: On that day, at Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Longinus. B.: At Caesarea in Cappadocia, St. Serenus, and elsewhere St. Longinus. L.: At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the passion of Saints Longinus, Severus, Victor, and Dorotheus.

And St. [Note: [Col. 1080D] Severinus. He is thought to be the same Severinus who presided over the Church of Cologne in the time of St. Martin; although absent, he is said to have learned by divine revelation of Martin’s death, as related in Book I, chapter 4, of *The Miracles of St. Martin*. All this is recounted in a sermon by an ancient author published by Surius on October 23, where further details are given concerning his death and tomb, which the people of Bordeaux venerate greatly. Some maintain that the Severinus mentioned here passed from the episcopal see of Trier to that of Bordeaux; Cointius refutes them under the year 597, no. 9. See the history of Lopes and Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, XLV. His relics were also honorably brought to Cologne, with part of them left in Aquitaine. Guinius Sen.] Severinus, archbishop of Cologne.

24.—The ninth day before the Kalends. Bede has nothing.

The Dijon manuscript also has nothing, except that the account of the forty-six soldiers placed here from the following day is subsequently repeated in its proper place in Bede’s text.

B. V. C.: At Nicomedia, Vitalis, Felix, Rogatus, Victoria, Flavianus, and Victor [B. omits “Victoria … Victor”]. A. T. L.: At Nicomedia, the feast of Rogatus, Flavianus, and Vitalis. T. L. add Felix and Papperius. B.: At Hierapolis in Phrygia, the feast of Saints Claudianus, Eleutherius, Justus, and Victor.

[Col. 1081B] 25.—The eighth day before the Kalends. At Soissons, the feast of the holy martyrs Crispinus and Crispinianus.

Florus adds in A. T. L.:

“Whom the prefect Rictiovarus, acting on the order of the emperor Maximian, arrested because they refused to sacrifice to idols. He had them stretched on the rack and beaten with clubs; then stakes were driven beneath their nails. After strips had been taken from the back of each one, their necks were submerged in the river with millstones hung upon them; and they were burned with molten lead, boiling pitch, and oil. Protected in all things by the right hand of Christ, and after the prefect Rictiovarus had been slain in these events by divine vengeance, they were cut down with the sword at the command of the emperor Maximian. An angel gave warning, and an old man, carrying their bodies secretly by night in a little boat against the current of the river, buried them.”

[Col. 1081C] On the same day at Rome, on the Via Salaria, the feast of forty-six soldiers who were baptized together by Pope Dionysius and soon afterward beheaded by order of the emperor [Note: [Col. 1081C] Claudius. Baronius writes that the emperor Claudius promulgated an edict against Christians, relying on two foundations. The first consists of the Acts of the holy martyrs Marius and Martha his wife, and their sons Audifax and Abachum, which Bollandus recites in full from various manuscripts on January 19. The second is taken from the Acts of St. Laurence recited by Surius on August 10; at their conclusion the martyrdom of St. Cyrilla, daughter of St. Tryphonia, once the wife of Caesar Decius, is mentioned. But none of the ancients mentions a persecution initiated by Claudius; and the Acts of St. Laurence recited by Surius are plainly adulterated and spurious. The Acts of Saints Marius, Martha, and their sons appear no less spurious.] Claudius. There were also placed there another one hundred and twenty-one martyrs, among whom were four soldiers of Christ: Theodotius, Lucius, Marcus, and Peter. This is written in the *Passion of St. Xystus*.

A. T.: On the same day, in the district of Vermandois, the dedication of the church of St. [Note: [Col. 1081D] Quintinus. See August 8 and January 3 concerning two other translations.] Quintinus and the translation of his body. C.: At Rome, Saints [Note: [Col. 1081D] Chrysanthus. He was born to an Alexandrian man named Polemius, who went to Rome with his son. The boy was entrusted to the study of philosophy, but came upon the books of the Gospels and learned the sacred writings from the presbyter Carpophorus, and was baptized. His father Polemius, angered, ordered him shut up in prison. Then he ordered him dressed in silk clothing and confined with his son the most beautiful maidservants, among whom was a virgin named Daria, to entice him toward luxury and lust. But the holy man remained so firm in his resolve that he despised the girls’ blandishments and converted the very beautiful Daria to Christ. After they had together endured many punishments under the emperor Numerianus, he was buried beneath earth and stones and found death and burial at the same time.] Chrysanthus and Daria. B.: The translation of St. [Note: [Col. 1081D] Bartholomew. Concerning this translation, see above, August 24.] Bartholomew from the island of Lipari to Benevento.

On the same day, Grisanti and Daria. In Italy, in the city of Florence, the passion of St. [Note: [Col. 1082C] Miniatus. The Acts of St. Miniatus published by Surius in volume V are of the same reliability and authority as the Acts of St. Laurence. For they report that St. Miniatus, after Pope St. Xystus and St. Laurence the archdeacon—who suffered under Valerian and Gallienus—completed his martyrdom under Decius, which plainly cannot have happened. Sigebert mentions the translation of his relics into Gaul in the time of the emperor Otto, in his *Chronicle* under the year 969.] Miniatus the martyr, with his companions. On the same day, the passion of Saints Lucianus and Marcianus.

26.—The seventh day before the Kalends. Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Nicomedia, the feast of the holy martyrs Martianus, Florus, and Lucianus, who in the time of the emperor Decius were delivered to the fire under Sabinus the proconsul.

B. V. C.: At Nicomedia, Lucianus, Marcianus, Florus [V., Flora], and Heraclius [C., Herodius]. B.: Tutti and Florinus. D.: At the city of Alehela, Vincentius, Sabinus, and Christeta. [Note: [Col. 1082C] Alehela. Rather, Abula. At first they were stretched so severely on the rack that all the joints of their limbs were loosened. Then, with their heads placed upon stones, they were beaten with powerful bars until their brains were shaken out, and thus they completed their martyrdom, while the governor Dacianus was acting under the emperor Diocletian. Usuard, Ado, and the other later writers treat of them on the following day.]

A. T. L.: On the same day, at the monastery of Elnone, the translation of the body of St. Amandus and the dedication of his church. B.: And [Note: [Col. 1082D] Amandus. The translation of his body from the church of St. Peter, where he had first rested, into the new basilica dedicated on this very day is described in a sermon by a certain Milo, a monk of Elnone, in Bollandus, February 6. That account nevertheless falsely asserts that the church was dedicated and the relics of St. Amandus translated by St. Eligius the bishop. Eligius died in 665, nearly twenty years before the death of St. Amandus, who died in 684. Since his body was raised sixteen years later, it is more accurate to say that this translation was carried out by Guido, the successor of Mummolinus, or by Gerulphus, Guido’s successor. The ordination of St. Amandus is also celebrated at Maastricht. Molanus, *Additions to Usuard*.] Amandus the bishop and confessor.

[Col. 1083B] 27.—The sixth day before the Kalends. Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Rome, St. [Note: [Col. 1083C] Evaristus. He was Greek by nationality, from Antioch, the son of a Jewish father from the city of Bethlehem. He lived not only during the times of Domitian and Nerva but also of Trajan, and governed the Roman Church for twelve years and some months from the year of Christ 95, marked by the seventeenth year of Domitian and the consulship of Clemens. He died in 108, though the month and day are uncertain. According to Baronius, he is commemorated on October 26, and the more extensive *Chronicle of the Ancient Pontiffs* reads: “He was buried beside the body of St. Peter in the Vatican, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.” But the dates assigned to the early pontiffs seem to refer rather to certain translations of their bodies than to their feasts.] Evaristus, who, governing the Roman Church for nine years and eleven months, sixth after Peter, was crowned with martyrdom in the times of Domitian and Nerva.

B. C. D. V. A. T. L.: The vigil of the apostles Simon and Thaddeus. C. V.: In Africa, Polycarpus. V.: At Rome, Marcianus, Lucianus, Marcianus, Florianus, and Lucius. Elsewhere, St. Florentius. C.: At Rome, Martianus, Lucius, and Florentius. A. T. L.: In Sardinia, Saints Victus, Protus, and Florentius.

[Col. 1083C] T.: At the monastery of Maslinas, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 1083D] Romaldus. Archbishop of Ireland, who, abandoning his homeland and the archbishopric of Dublin, went to Rome and, after receiving the pontiff’s blessing there, arrived—following an angelic apparition—at the place where the River Scheldt empties into the sea, namely Mechelen. There he instructed the people so thoroughly in the rudiments of the faith that he is rightly regarded as the apostle of the people of Mechelen. In the year 775, on the feast of the Baptist, two assassins killed him with axes. His feast is celebrated at Mechelen on the Kalends of July. Some translation seems to have taken place today; his body, however, was raised five years after his death, as is clear from the Acts of St. Romaldus published by Surius in June.] Romaldus the martyr. L.: On the same day, St. [Note: [Col. 1084C] Rictrudis. Her feast is celebrated on May 12.] Rictrudis. B.: The feast of Saints Marinianus, Lucius, and Victus. In Sardinia, the feast of St. Florinus. In Phrygia, Saints Tarcus, [Note: [Col. 1084C] Polycarpus. He is said above to have suffered in Africa.] Polycarpus, Gagius, Metrobius, and Eumenia.

28.—The fifth day before the Kalends. The feast of the holy apostles Simon and Thaddeus.

A. T. L. adds: “Who were killed by the priests of the temples in the great city of Suanis in Persia.” B.: In the great city of Silantis in Persia.

[Col. 1084B] And at Rome, St. Cyrilla, daughter of Caesar Decius, who was slaughtered and killed with the sword under the emperor [Note: [Col. 1084D] Claudius. Rather, under Valerian and Gallienus. For she suffered martyrdom in the same year as St. Laurence, who is commemorated above on August 10, while St. Justin, who buried her, suffered martyrdom the following year, on the fourth day before the Ides of the same month. Therefore, reader, correct the note we gave above concerning St. Justin, and in place of Decius, Gallus, and Volusianus, put the emperors Gallienus and Valerian.] Claudius, and was buried by the presbyter Justin with her mother near St. Hippolytus.

Florus in A. T. L.: On the same day, the passion of Saints [Note: [Col. 1084D] Vincentius. These saints are also commemorated above on the twenty-sixth day of this month.] Vincentius, Sabina, and Christeta, who suffered in the city of Ávila. They were stretched one by one on the rack, upward and downward, with the joints of their limbs spread apart and dislocated by scourging. When they still did not give way, their necks were placed upon stones and their brains crushed with a club struck from above; thus completing their martyrdom, they surrendered their souls together.

B.: At Carthage, St. Suffratianus and St. Ritus the confessor.

29.—The fourth day before the Kalends. Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: On the same day, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 1084D] Pontianus. The martyrdom of St. Pontianus must be assigned to the year 235. For in the *Chronicle of Damasus* it is written: “Pontianus, five years, two months, seven days, from the consulship of Pompeianus and Pelignianus . . . . On that same island, namely Sardinia, he was divested of his office on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, and Anterus was ordained in his place on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, during the consulship of the holy pair.” Anastasius, or the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, who had read the Chronicle of Damasus, has *died* in place of these words, *was divested of his office*, but incorrectly, since the fuller *Chronicle of the Ancient Pontiffs* says that Pontianus died on the third day before the Kalends of November, and Florus celebrates Pontianus’s feast today. Cuspinianus also gives the passage of Damasus in full in his *Fasti*, except that he has “three months” instead of “two,” and rightly so, since Pontianus occupied the see for five years, three months, and seven days: namely, from June 22 of the year 230, when he was ordained, to September 28 of the year 235, when he abdicated in exile on the island of Sardinia. This abdication is expressed by the words “he was divested of his office” on the fourth day before the Kalends of October. He died on the fourth or third day before the Kalends of November, and was brought by ship from Sardinia to Rome by Fabianus and buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, at least on the thirteenth, twelfth, or eleventh day before the Kalends of December. He was banished under Alexander and suffered under the emperor Maximinus.] Pontianus, pope and martyr, who, under the consuls Severus and Quintianus, was deported by the emperor Alexander, together with the presbyter Hippolytus, to the island of Bucina in Sardinia, where he completed his martyrdom. This is written in the *Book of the Bishops*.

B. V. C.: In Lucania, St. [Note: [Col. 1085C] Saccintus. Also called Jacinthus and Hyacinthus. St. Gregory mentions his relics in *Registrum*, Book VII, indiction 2, letter 15.] Saccintus, Quintus [B., [Col. 1085B] Quintinus], Felicianus, and Lucius. C.: And the feast of St. Euphrosyna. A. T. L.: In Lucania, Saints Lucianus and Quintus, and St. Felicianus the martyr. T., first place: The feast of St. [Note: [Col. 1085D] Theuderius. He was born in the province of Vienne. While still a boy, he began to aspire to pious studies. Eventually, after distributing his possessions, he planned to go to Lérins. Having therefore left his parents, he went to the city of Arles, where he was detained by Caesarius, the bishop of that city. Made a presbyter by him, he returned to his homeland, built various cells, and became abbot of many monks. By Philip, the twenty-first bishop of Vienne, he was chosen as the people’s spokesman before God, an office he held for twelve years. He died around the year 575. His life, written by Ado of Vienne, may be read in Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, first century, p. 678.] Theuderius the confessor. D.: [Note: [Col. 1085D] Narcissus. The thirtieth patriarch of Jerusalem, who presided over his church in the time of Caracalla Antoninus. [Col. 1086C] He was ordained in the year 197. Having been most unjustly defamed, he withdrew from the multitude of the Church and hid for many years in desert places and more secluded fields. When he had concealed himself so completely that no one knew where he lived, it seemed necessary to the bishops of the neighboring churches to ordain another in his place. St. Pius was therefore elected, then Germanion or Germanus, and after him Gordius. After Gordius’s death, when the surrounding bishops had assembled at Jerusalem to ordain someone worthy of so great a priesthood, St. Narcissus suddenly appeared, as though returned from the dead. His arrival produced immense joy throughout the holy city, among both clergy and people, and the brethren immediately asked him again to preside over the Church. He therefore governed his church once more. At length, because of his great age, Alexander was associated with him in the year 212. He departed to eternal joy in the year 214. Concerning him, see Eusebius, *Chronicle* and *Ecclesiastical History* V, 12, and VI, 9–11. Narcissus is commemorated by the Greeks on August 7.] Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem.

30.—The third day before the Kalends. Bede has nothing.

V. C.: At Nicomedia, Januarius and Marcialis. B. V. C. D.: And in Africa, the passion of two hundred and twenty holy martyrs [C., thirty]. B.: At Nicomedia, Saints Calendion, Marcialis, and Theophilus. D.: In the city of Tingis, the passion of St. [Note: [Col. 1086D] Marcellus. In the *Chronicle of Spain*, Vasaeus, discussing Marcellus the centurion, says that he suffered under the second consulship of Faustus and Gallus, that is, in the year 298; Prosper rightly noted in his *Chronicle* that the persecution against the soldiers began in that year.] Marcellus the centurion. B.: And elsewhere, the passion of St. Felicianus with his companions. On the same day, the passion of St. Marcellus the martyr.

A. T. L.: The passion of St. Marcellus, who completed his martyrdom by decapitation at the command of the ruler Agricolanus. (And this perhaps belongs to Florus.) In Africa [L. omits “in Africa”], the feast of Saints Theophilus and Eusebius. At Toulouse, the translation of St. [Note: [Col. 1086D] Saturninus. It is established from Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, 48, that his relics were translated into the territory of Auvergne. His relics were also in Burgundy, ibid., 31. Later they were also translated to Tours, ibid., 31, and *On the Glory of the Confessors*, 20. Concerning him, see below on his feast day, November 29.] Saturninus, bishop and martyr. T. L.: [Col. 1086A] At Nicomedia, the passion of Calendion, Marcialis, and Germanus.

31.—The second day before the Kalends. In Gaul, St. Quintinus, who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Maximian; and after fifty-five years his body was discovered through an angel’s revelation and buried on the eighth day before the Kalends of July [D. omits “on the eighth day before the Kalends of July”].

[Col. 1086B] Florus in A. T. L. gives a fuller account in this form:

“In Gaul, at Augusta of the Vermandois, the passion of St. [Note: [Col. 1086D] Quintinus. Concerning his various translations, see the eighth day before the Kalends of July, the eighth day before the Ides of July, and the eighth day before the Kalends of November. Surius published his Acts, volume V.] Quintinus the martyr, who, born at Rome of senatorial rank, but moved by love of Christ, entered Gaul in the time of the emperor Maximian and shone gloriously through the greatest preaching, signs, and miracles. When the prefect Rictiovarus heard of his fame, he ordered him sought out, arrested, bound in chains, and committed to prison. Finally, after questioning him concerning his religion in the official hearing, because he despised sacrificing to idols, he ordered him beaten with the most savage scourges. During this beating, with the eyes of his mind and body directed toward heaven and giving thanks to the Lord, while his torturers fell to the ground and a voice descended from heaven, he deserved to hear this divine address: ‘Quintinus,’ it said, [Col. 1087A] ‘stand firm; act manfully. I shall be with you.’ He was again chained and shut in prison. There, after experiencing an angelic vision and passing through all the prison’s guards under the angel’s guidance, he came to the place shown to him. After delivering a long sermon to the people, he converted nearly six hundred men.

“Enraged by this, Rictiovarus ordered him tortured on the rack [Col. 1087B] so violently that his limbs were forced to come apart by the extreme force. He also ordered him beaten with iron cords; burning oil, pitch, and boiling-hot fat applied to his back; lime, vinegar, and mustard poured into his mouth; his neck bound again with heavy chains; two iron stakes driven from his neck to his legs; and ten nails driven between his fingernails and flesh. Having overcome these torments through divine protection, he finally ordered him put to death by decapitation, and his body weighted with lead and submerged in the river at night. When his head had been cut off, a white dove, like snow, was immediately seen to emerge from his neck and penetrate heaven in the freest flight. [Col. 1087C]

“His body, which had been submerged with weights in the River Somme, was revealed fifty-five years later by an angel to a Roman matron. She found it in the town now called Augusta of the Vermandois and buried it on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. This is written in his Acts.”

At Nicomedia, the passion of St. Eusebius, who in the time of the emperor Maximian, under the governor Maxentius, completed his martyrdom by beheading. [Col. 1088B]

In the Laetiensian manuscript, the words enclosed in the first brackets are abbreviated in this manner: “When the prefect Rictiovarus learned of this, he ordered the bound man brought before him; and after many prison tortures, chains, and various scourges, finally burning oil, etc.” The rest concerning the discovery of the body, likewise marked with brackets, is absent from the Atrebatian manuscript.

V. C.: The feast of St. Quintinus [C., Quintus] the martyr, Felix, Donatus, and twenty-nine others. B.: In Macedonia, Saints Vitalis, Peter, Crescentius, and Alternus.

## [November]

[Col. 1087C]

[Col. 1087D] 1.—On the Kalends. The feast of All Saints. And at the castle of Dijon, the feast of St. Benignus the presbyter, who was sent from the East to Gaul by St. Polycarpus the bishop, together with Andochius his fellow presbyter and Thyrsus the deacon, in the time of the emperor [Note: [Col. 1087D] Aurelian. They rather suffered under Marcus Aurelius. For how could a disciple of Polycarpus have survived until the time of Aurelian?] Aurelian. When the emperor learned of his preaching, he ordered him bound and beaten and brought before him. [Note: [Col. 1087D] The words “bound,” etc., through “After this” are omitted by the Atrebatian manuscript.] Then, after hearing the steadfastness of his speech, he had him beaten with very hard sinews and handed him over to Count Terentius to be overcome. Terentius had him stretched on the rack and beaten, then confined again in prison. In the morning he destroyed the idols by prayer and was led back to prison. There they drove ten heated awls into his hands and fixed his feet with molten lead in a perforated stone. [Col. 1088D] They shut twelve savage dogs in with him for six days. An angel fed him with heavenly bread, removed the awls, and rescued him from the lead and iron. After this, he was ordered to have his neck beaten with an iron bar and pierced with a lance. When this had been done, a snow-white dove ascended from the prison to heaven before the eyes of the Christians, and a most fragrant odor, as though from Paradise, followed. When Aurelian had departed from the place, Blessed Leonilla arrived and buried the body, embalmed with spices, far from the prison itself.

On the same day, the feast of St. Caesarius the deacon and Julianus the presbyter (thus far A.); Caesarius, coming from Africa to Terracina, a city of Campania, in the time of [Note: [Col. 1088D] Claudius. Caesarius did not suffer under Claudius. For it is clear from the Acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus that he committed the bodies of Domitilla and her companions to burial in the time of Trajan. How, then, could he have been crowned one hundred and seventy years later under Claudius? If Claudius Nero is intended, an equally obvious error is found, since Nero died long before the emperor Trajan. [Col. 1089D] Baronius, in the Notes.] Claudius, was publicly seized by Firminus the pontiff while proclaiming against idolaters and was confined in custody. After being worn down there for many days, he was handed over to Leontius, the consular governor of Campania. Since Leontius could not overcome him by words, he ordered him bound, naked, with his hands tied, and led before a cart all the way to the temple of Apollo. When they arrived there, the temple collapsed at his prayer and killed the pontiff [Col. 1089C] Firminus.

After this, Caesarius was confined in prison by Luxurius, the city’s chief magistrate, and remained there for one year and one month. Then he was brought out into the forum, where, as he prayed, he was surrounded by heavenly light from God. Leontius himself believed, covered the naked Caesarius with his own military cloak, was baptized, and received the body and blood of the Lord from the hand of Julianus the presbyter. Without delay, after a prayer had been spoken over him, Leontius gave up his spirit on the third day before the Kalends of November.

Then Luxurius ordered Julianus and Caesarius [Col. 1090B] placed in a sack and thrown into the sea. On the same day they were cast back onto the shore and buried by [Note: [Col. 1089D] Eusebius. Concerning him and St. Felix, see below, November 5.] Eusebius, the servant of God, near the city of Terracina. The same Eusebius later suffered martyrdom with Felix the presbyter.

On the same day [L. omits “on the same day,” etc.], the burial of [Note: [Col. 1089D] Severinus. His body is said to be buried at Tivoli, at St. Laurence, as the ancient monuments of that church indicate. Baronius, in the Notes.] Severinus, a monk from the city of Tivoli.

Florus in A. and T.: On the same day, the passion of the holy [Col. 1090C] martyrs Eustachius and his wife Theospis, and their sons Agapitus and Theospis, who, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, because they refused to sacrifice to the gods, were all sent into a bronze bull and burned in the fire. In the Laetiensian manuscript this is placed on the following day.

A. T.: On the same day, the translation of the body of St. [Note: [Col. 1089D] Audomarus. Concerning the translation, or rather return, of St. Audomarus, see Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, third century, part I, p. 123: “This translation, or restoration, took place in the year 843. When Hugo, abbot of Sithiu, attempted by force to carry the body of St. Audomarus from Vermandois to the monastery of St. Quintinus, he carried his entire company as far as a village called Lisburg. But when he wished to proceed farther, the whole multitude was unable to lift the body from the ground. Then Folquinus, bishop of Sithiu, came with his people, recovered that treasure, and, taking precautions lest the holy body should be carried away in the same manner, buried it on the island of Sithiu beside the body of Blessed Bertinus.”] Audomarus the bishop and confessor.

T.: On the same day, the feast of St. Remedius the bishop and confessor.

V. C.: At Poitiers, the dedication of the basilica of St. [Note: [Col. 1090C] Hilary. Today this translation was carried out by the ministry of angels, from the old suburban monastery church to the new urban basilica that the abbot Tredelinus had built. The bishop looked on in wonder. After the solemn rites of the church’s dedication had been completed, and after the nightly prayers in which he persevered with the abbot and monks, he decided to transfer the body from its old place to the appointed shrine. This same translation is celebrated on June 26.] Hilary the bishop and confessor.

B.: And elsewhere, the burial of [Note: [Col. 1090D] Eustachius. Eustachius was a commander of the army; while still a pagan, he was called Placidus. When he went out hunting, the image of the Crucified appeared to him between the antlers of a stag, and a voice sounded, ordering him to approach a Christian priest and be baptized. His wife also, warned in a dream, was told to become a Christian together with her husband. They therefore went with their two sons to the priest John, and all were baptized. Thereafter a severe plague struck Eustachius’s household and deprived him of everything over which he had authority, namely human beings and animals. Unable to bear the disaster, he decided to go into exile and secretly depart with his family for Egypt. When he had disembarked from the ship, the barbarian boatman laid hands on Theospis and took her from Eustachius as payment for the voyage. While Eustachius continued directly toward Egypt, he also lost his two sons, one carried off by a lion and the other by a wolf. Some farmers nevertheless rescued them unharmed from the beasts’ mouths and raised them among themselves. After these many calamities, Eustachius was reduced to poverty and forced to live by his labor. After he had endured servitude for a long time, he was recognized by those whom the emperor Trajan had sent to search for him. He was found by the searchers with no less joy than that with which the emperor himself received him. Since the emperor needed the commander of his army, Eustachius was restored to his former dignity.

To complete his happiness, he recognized his wife, who had not been violated by the barbarian, since divine justice had pursued him, and also his sons, who were serving in the same army over which he himself commanded. One day the young men spoke among themselves about their parents and about what had happened to them in infancy; one recognized the other, and when they had disclosed this to Eustachius, he embraced them with all the joy a father could possess.

After this, he returned victorious to Rome. Trajan had died, and Hadrian had assumed the empire. But because Eustachius refused to accompany the emperor in sacrificing to idols for the victory, the emperor first took away his command of the army, then ordered him brought with his sons and wife before the tribunal, and afterward sent them to the beasts, which left them unharmed. Finally, he cast them into a heated bronze bull. Surius, volume VI, November 2.] Eustachius the soldier, with his wife [Col. 1091A] and two sons.

At Paris, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 1091D] Marcellus. Surius gives the Life of St. Marcellus, written by the presbyter Fortunatus, on November 1. He was buried in a suburban church, which Launoius maintains was at that time the cathedral, though Valesius and others object. The body of the holy bishop was subsequently transferred to the larger church, where it is preserved in a very rich reliquary. He is listed as the ninth bishop of Paris in Demochare’s tables.] Marcellus the bishop and confessor.

On the same day, at the city of Le Mans, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 1091D] Domnolus. He is commemorated on May 16, but died on the Kalends of December, as is clear from his Acts published in the *Acta Sanctorum* on May 16. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* VI, 7, assigns Domnolus only a little more than twenty-two years as bishop and writes that, in the time of King Chlothar, he presided over the monastic community at the basilica of St. Laurence in Paris. In 567 Domnolus is found at the Second Synod of Tours. According to Henschenius’s calculation in his preliminary commentary on the Acts of St. Domnolus, he died around the year 581.] Domnolus the bishop and confessor.

On the same day, the feast of St. [Note: [Col. 1092C] Vigor. In the time of Childebert, king of the Franks, he had parents distinguished by nobility and faith. He was educated in letters at the monastery of St. Vedastus. Abandoning his wealth and parents, he reached the village of Reviers in the region of Bayeux, where by preaching, expelling a serpent, and raising a dead man, he converted nearly everyone to Christ. When St. Patricius, bishop of Bayeux, died, Vigor was chosen by all and appointed in his place. Once, as he went to preach on Mount Phaenus, one mile from the city, he was driven away by the inhabitants, who were still pagans and worshiped a statue of a woman. When he reported this to Childebert, the king immediately granted the mountain to the bishop as his possession. The holy bishop purified it, built a church there, and called the mountain Chrismatus; he was buried there after his death. Surius, volume VI. Vigor was the tenth bishop of Bayeux.] Vigor.

[Col. 1091B] 2.—The fourth day before the Nones. Bede has nothing.

B. V. C.: The dedication of the basilica of Saints [Note: [Col. 1092D] Sixtus. Sixtus is treated on August 6, Hippolytus on August 13, and Laurence on August 10.] Sixtus, Hippolytus, and Laurence. D.: At Laodicea, [Note: [Col. 1092D] Theodotus. Theodotus succeeded Stephanus at Laodicea. He was highly skilled in medicine, a man of exceptional humanity and integrity of character. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII, 32.] Theodotus the bishop, who was a physician by profession. A. L.: In Africa, the feast of the saints Victor, Hermes, and Justus. A.: On the same day, the elevation of the body of St. Bertinus the abbot.

On that day the commemoration of all the faithful departed is celebrated, devoutly instituted by Blessed Odilo, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, in the year of Christ 1002. T.: The solemn commemoration of all the faithful departed.

T. B.: In Africa, the passion of Saints Poplianus, Victor, Hermes, Justus, [Col. 1092B] Vitalis, and Papias [T. omits “and Papias”].

On the same day, [Note: [Col. 1092D] Lautenus. Abbot of Autun, who is said to have been trained under Abbot Laurence and then to have withdrawn into the wilderness, where he built a monastery of seventy monks called Siestum. Later, as the number of disciples increased, he built another monastery of forty monks in a place called Maximiacum. When he was more than fifty years old, he was ordained a presbyter by Bishop Amandus. His disciple Pharadaeus is said, in obedience, to have thrown himself into a burning pyre. St. Lautenus is commemorated in the old Breviary of Valladolid and in the Cluniac Breviary on September 25. Ferrarius, in his *General Catalogue*, commemorates him today and says that his body rests at Poligny in Burgundy.] St. Lautenus the abbot.

And [Note: [Col. 1092D] Elevation. Concerning St. Bertinus, see above, September 5.] the elevation and translation of St. Bertinus the abbot and confessor.

3.—The third day before the Nones. Bede has nothing.

B. V. C.: In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the commemoration of Germanus, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Vitalis [B.: in Africa]. Elsewhere, the passion of Saint Agricola. B.: And the passion of Saint Pabulus, who suffered under King Herod [Col. 1093A]. D.: [Note: Quartus, concerning whom Paul writes in Romans 16. Dorotheus states in his *Synopsis* that he was appointed bishop of the Church of Berytus, deriving this from the booklet of Hippolytus on the seventy-two disciples.] Of Quartus, a disciple of the apostles.

The martyrs Germanus, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Vitalis of Cappadocia, who were martyred during the persecution under Decius. A. T. L.: In Africa, the commemoration of the saints Germanus, Theophilus, and Vitalis.

On the same day, Saint [Note: Hubertus. Son of Bertrand, duke of Aquitaine. Because of the tyranny of Ebroin, he moved to Austrasia, to Pepin. While he was still a pagan in the parish of Tongeren and was hunting, Christ appeared to him between the antlers of a stag and sent him to Bishop Lambert. Lambert received him kindly, instructed him in the faith, and baptized him. Hubert then went to Rome, where he remained for some time; meanwhile Lambert was killed by impious men, and Pope Sergius, despite Hubert’s reluctance, consecrated him as Lambert’s successor. This occurred in 698. In 710 he transferred the body of Saint Lambert and the episcopal see from Maastricht to the Meuse, to Liège. He died at Furae, between Leuven and Brussels, in 730, but was buried at Liège in the church of Saint Peter, beside the altar of Saint Albinus. Surius records him for this day.] Hubert, bishop and confessor.

L. inserts among these: And the passion of Saint Agricola, virgin.

T., in first place, has this: The passion of the holy martyrs [Note: Valentine. During the persecution under Maximian, they were thrown into the Tiber with a heavy stone because of their faith in Christ; divinely rescued from it by an angel, they finally received the crown of martyrdom when their heads were cut off. Baronius, in the *Martyrologium*.] Valentine and Hilary.

On the same day, the passion of [Note: Innumerable martyrs. These are also called the Massa Candida; they are discussed above, 24 August.] innumerable martyrs who suffered under the governor Datianus.

### 4 — 4 November. Baeda has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: [Note: Bituricas. In a village of the territory of Dol near Bourges, the blessed Lusor, son of Leucadius the senator, is buried; he is said to have departed this life in white garments. Even now, in the underground crypt of the church of Saints Stephen and Saturninus at Dol, two very ancient tombs decorated with various figures can be seen. Saint Lusor is said to have been buried in the marble one, and Leocadius, his father, in the stone one. In his edition of the Breviary of Bourges, D. Roland Hebert removed the name of Saint Lusor and the three lessons inserted about him, but unjustly. On Saint Lusor, see Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors* 97, and Labbe, *Bibliotheca Nova*, vol. II, pp. 426–427. In the same volume of Labbe, p. 705, Saint Lusor is commemorated in the *Hagiologium Franco-Galliae* on 1 November.] At Bourges, the burial of Saint Lusor, a boy who is said to have died in Gaul as the son of a certain senator.

At his tomb, Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, was once celebrating vigils. His clerics, wearied by the long standing, leaned upon the saint’s tomb with their arms locked together, as though seeking some relief. Immediately the tomb of the holy confessor trembled. The bishop, terrified by the shaking, ordered the sleepy men to be removed from above it, saying: “Withdraw far from the tomb, you sluggish men, lest annoyance be caused to God’s saint.” After they had been removed, they felt no further trembling. This is written in the *Book of the Miracles* of Gregory, bishop of Tours.

B. V. T. C.: In Africa, Primus [T. omits Primus], Caesarius [V. T. C. omit Caesarius], Gregory, Porphyrius [C.: Gerius, Porphyrius]; and at Nicaea, Domninus.

D.: The presbyter Hierius of Alexandria [Note: Hierius—or rather, Pierius. Jerome writes of him in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Pierius, a presbyter of the Church of Alexandria, under the emperors Carus and Diocletian, when Theonas governed that same Church as bishop, taught the people with the greatest distinction. He attained such elegance in speech and in the treatment of various subjects, works that still exist today, that he was called the younger Origen. It is agreed that he was a man of remarkable asceticism, an advocate of voluntary poverty, and highly learned in dialectical and rhetorical skill; after the persecution he spent the remainder of his life at Rome. His is a very lengthy treatise on the prophet Hosea, which, as the discourse itself shows, was delivered during the vigil of Easter.” Eusebius praises him in *Ecclesiastical History* VII, 32, among the ecclesiastical men who flourished in his own age.]—a man of most pure life and nobly learned in the Scriptures.

A. T., in first place: At Lyon, the burial of Saint [Note: Genesius. He was abbot of the Palatine or court monastery, chief chaplain of King Clovis II, and almoner of the pious Queen Saint Balthild. Later he was appointed archbishop of Lyon. Before the queen’s death, he appeared to her at the very moment of her death in great light with angels and led her to the dwelling of eternal peace. He was succeeded by Landebertus, abbot of the Church of Fontenelle, in 678. See the Life of Saint Balthild in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, second century, and the *Chronicle of Verdun* in Labbe, *Bibliotheca Nova*, vol. I, p. 102.] Genesius, bishop and confessor, and of Saint [Note: Quartus. He was discussed on the preceding day.] Quartus.

At Autun, Saint Proculus, bishop, who alone and in first place is recorded in L. B.

At Redon, the burial of Saint Amandus, bishop.

T., after the African martyrs, also has [Note: Amantius. Read his Life in Surius, vol. VI; Labbe published it more fully in *Bibliotheca Nova*, vol. II. Gregory of Tours, in *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 4, relates that his body was transferred by Saint Quintianus, who succeeded him in the bishopric of Rodez.] Amantius.

### 5 — 5 November

At Terracina, a city of Campania, the commemoration of the holy Felix, presbyter, and Eusebius, monk, in the time of the emperor Claudius (up to this point, the manuscript of Atr.).

When Eusebius had buried the holy martyrs [Note: Julian and Caesarius. See above, under the Kalends of this month.] Julian and Caesarius, and by praying and fasting at their tombs had converted many to the faith, whom Felix the presbyter baptized, both men were seized by Leontius, son of Leontius the consul—especially because Caesarius had made his father a Christian. They were brought before his tribunal, and since they could not be overcome, they were shut up in prison. On that same night, because they refused to sacrifice, they were beheaded and thrown into the river. Their bodies came as far as the sea and, cast upon the shore, were found by a certain presbyter from Capua named Quartus. He immediately placed them on a cart and took them to his house; searching carefully, he also found their heads, joined them to the bodies, and buried them beside Saint Caesarius.

B.: In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the commemoration of the holy Domninus, Epiphanius, and Antoninus.

In Capua, a city of Campania, the commemoration of the holy Marcia, Secunda, and Quartus.

### 6 — 6 November. Baeda has no entry.

D.: At Toniza in Africa, Felix the martyr and forty other martyrs [Note: Toniza, or Thinissa. Saint Felix, a confessor who had been reserved for torture, was found dead in prison on another day, as Saint Augustine relates when explaining Psalm 127 to the people on his feast.]

V. B. C.: In Nicomedia, Adrianus, Julia [V. C. omits Julia], and Eusebius.

V. B. A. T.: In Africa, the commemoration of the saints Donatus, Paul, and Balsam.

C.: In Africa, Donatus and Paulinus.

The commemoration of Saint Leonard, in first place.

A. T. L.: In Gaul, at Redon, the burial of Saint [Note: Melanius. See above, 6 January.] Melanius, bishop and confessor; and the burial of Saint Winnoc, abbot. The latter is read in T. as follows:

And at the cell of Wormholtvoorta, the death of [Note: Winnoc. He originated in Armorica from royal stock. Accompanied by Quadonocus, Ingenocus, and Madocus, men distinguished both by birth and by life, he came to Saint Bertinus, abbot of Sithiu, and submitted himself with his companions to his governance. When they had attained the height of monastic perfection, a nobleman named Heremarus gave Saint Winnoc an estate called Weromholt, where he built a monastery in 695. After the departure of the three companions, Winnoc was appointed abbot there. John of Ypres places Saint Winnoc’s death in the very year in which Duke Charles fought against Chilperic at Vinciacum in the district of Cambrai. According to the continuation of Fredegar’s Chronicle, chapter 106, they fought on a Sunday in Lent, 21 March. These indications correspond to the year 717. This Winnoc is different from the one of whom Gregory of Tours writes in *History* XV, 21, and VIII, 34. Winnoc was not, as most think, the brother of Saint Judoc, but his nephew. See Mabillon’s third century, part I, where the Life of Saint Winnoc is published.] Winnoc, confessor of Christ.

B.: In Gaul, at the city of [Note: Redon. More correctly, Limoges. Leonard was the spiritual son of Clovis I and a disciple and monk of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims. He preached in Aquitaine and the region of Bourges. By his prayers he restored a queen, nearly dead from the difficulty of childbirth, to health. For this reason the grateful king gave him royal gifts and part of a forest, where he built a monastery and called it Nobiliacum, now the town of Saint-Léonard. He became famous for liberating captives. He died in 559. He must be distinguished from Leonard, abbot of Vendœuvre in the diocese of Le Mans, and from Leonard, abbot of Celle in the diocese of Bourges; both flourished in the same century. Read his Life in Surius, vol. VI.] Redon, the burial of Saint Leonard, confessor.

### 7 — 7 November. Baeda has no entry.

V. C.: In Nicomedia, Eusebius, Eustasius, Marius, Primus, Julian, and Januarius.

B.: In Nicomedia, the commemoration of the holy Polysius and Euthasius, Primus, and Rogatianus. In Africa, the commemoration of the holy Rogatus, Donatus, Prima, and Juliana [C.: Julia].

D.: At Alexandria, Saint [Note: Achillas. The Alexandrian bishop Theonas enrolled him among the presbyters. Eusebius, VII, 37. After Peter, he himself became bishop of Alexandria. Arius obtained pardon from him and was again permitted to serve the dragon; afterward he was also admitted to the presbyteral order, according to Nicephorus, VIII, 5. Achillas did not succeed Saint Peter before the year 312. Gelasius of Cyzicus testifies in book XI of his *History of the Council of Nicaea*, chapter 11, that after Peter’s martyrdom the Church of Alexandria remained widowed for one year, and after that year had passed Achillas was ordained in the see of this martyr. Since he survived only five months, Alexander succeeded him. Therefore, since Saint Peter died for the faith on 25 November 311, Achillas did not assume leadership of the Church of Alexandria before the end of the following year, and Alexander did not succeed him before 313. Certainly Theodoret, book I, chapter 11, writes that Achillas governed the Church for only a short time, and Eusebius in his *Chronicle* places Alexander’s accession in the year mentioned above. Nicephorus of Constantinople and Theophanes assign one year to Achillas; they seem to have come closer to the truth than Gelasius, since Peter died in November 311, Achillas was ordained around November 312, and did not die before 7 November of the following year, if his feast is correctly celebrated today.] Achillas, bishop.

At Perugia, Saint [Note: Herculanus. He became bishop after being a monk. When Perugia was conquered by the forces of Totila, Herculanus was first beheaded by Totila’s order and then his entire body was flayed. Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* III, 13. Procopius writes that Perugia was conquered in book III, in the fourteenth year of the Gothic War, corresponding to A.D. 549.] Herculanus, bishop and martyr.

A. T. L.: In Nicomedia, the commemoration of the saints Castor, Gaudius, and Victor.

T. L.: In Africa, the passion of the saints Donatus and Rogatus.

T. adds [Col. 1097C] Balsam.

A.: On the same day, the commemoration of Saint [Note: Willibrord. See above, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 10–11.] Willibrord, confessor.

### 8 — 8 November

At Rome, the holy Four Crowned Martyrs: Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius.

Florus inserts the earlier names in T. as follows: Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, Carpophorus, and five others—Claudius, etc.—and then adds this account in A. T. L.:

While they were searching along the banks of the Tiber for the bodies of Saints Tranquillinus, father of Marcus and Marcellianus, and of Zoe, wife of Nicostratus, they were seized by the persecutors and brought before the prefect of the city.

[The judge was Fabianus, who urged them to sacrifice. For ten days he sent for them, but despite dealing with them by entreaties, he could not move them in the least. Then he reported them to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. They ordered them to be tortured a third time; and when they could not be compelled by any means to yield to the tortures, they were ordered to be thrown into the sea.]

Thus, bound with immense weights, they were cast into the waves of the sea. In a pure place among the waters they celebrated the crown of martyrdom.

Written in the Acts of Saint [Note: Sebastian. These men are different from those whose martyrdom is narrated in the Acts of Sebastian published by Bollandus on 20 January, and who are commemorated above on 7 July. Simplicius is found nowhere in the Acts of Sebastian, and different Acts are read in all the Martyrologies. These men were all skilled craftsmen in carving marble; Symphorianus was their master. Because they refused to fashion and worship the god Aesculapius and the false gods, they were first imprisoned, then beaten with scorpions, and finally thrown into the sea. But Claudius and Nicostratus, who are commemorated on 7 July, were *primiscrinii*. Castorius was Nicostratus’s brother, and Symphorianus was Claudius’s son; Simplicius did not suffer with them, but Victorinus did. Peter de Natalibus writes that these craftsmen suffered in Pannonia, whereas all the others testify that they completed their martyrdom at Rome.] Sebastian.

Nevertheless, A. gives a shorter version at the beginning: “They were tortured under the judge Fabianus, by order of the emperors Maximian and Diocletian, and drowned in the sea.”

L., more briefly, in the middle of the passage enclosed in brackets: “They were tortured a third time; and when they could not be overcome, they were bound with immense weights, etc.”

A. adds:

The names of the Four Crowned Martyrs are these: [Note: Severus. When they refused to sacrifice, Diocletian immediately ordered that they be beaten to death with leaded clubs before the statue of Aesculapius. Their bodies were collected and buried on the Lavican Way in a sandpit, beside Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius. Ado.] Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, and Carpophorus.

Because the day of their commemoration had been neglected through carelessness and could not be found at all, it was therefore decreed that in their church the feast of the five saints whose names are recited in the Mass should be celebrated, so that their memory might likewise be commemorated together with these. But this passage is mutilated and confused, as is evident, and on the authority of a single manuscript we do not dare attribute it to Florus.

B.: In Africa, the commemoration of the holy Primus, Macharius, Justus, and Amandus.

### 9 — 9 November

The commemoration of Saint Theodore, martyr.

Florus prefaces this in T.: At Amasea, a city; and adds the account:

Under the emperors Maximian and Maximus, he was bravely beaten and cast into prison for confessing the Christian faith. Then, when the Lord and Savior appeared to him and urged him to act steadfastly and courageously, he was granted a revelation.
