Finally, after he had been hung and scraped with hooks until his inner organs were exposed, he was handed over to the flames.

The following is added there:

On the same day, at Bourges, Saint [Note: Ursicinus, or Ursinus. Gregory of Tours, *History* I, 29, relates that the man who first entered the city of Bourges and announced Christ to its people was one of those disciples who were sent into Gaul under the consulship of Decius and Gratus. Yet the tradition seems more credible and more widespread which teaches that they were sent from Rome into Gaul in the apostolic age, since the other tradition rests solely on the authority of Gregory of Tours, who is not entirely consistent with himself. For in his book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 48, he wrote that Saturninus had been ordained by the disciples of the apostles, and he said the same of Saint Ursinus, bishop of Bourges, in his book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 80.] Ursicinus, confessor, who was ordained at Rome by the successors of the apostles and sent as the first bishop to that city.

Florus in A. T. L.:

On the same day, in Spain, at Córdoba, the passion of the saints Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis, who were all thrown into the fire by order of the governor Eugenius.

B. V.: The dedication [Note: Of the basilica. It was also called the Lateran basilica; it was established by the blessed Pope Sylvester in Constantine’s palace at the Lateran. Molanus, *Additions to Usuard*.] of the basilica of the Savior.

V. A. T. B. C.: At Rome.

L.: Of Saints Clement and Symphronius [B.: Symphorianus].

B.: In Nicomedia, the commemoration of [Note: Damianus. Restitutus, Donatus, Victorinus, Salutaris, Crescens, Demetrius, Nemesius, Exuorgius, and Eusebius suffered with him. Jerome’s *Martyrology*.] Damianus.

In Spain, Saints Faustus and Martialis.

A.: On the same day, the passion of Saint [Note: Ragnulfus. See above, 6 June.] Ragnulfus, martyr.

T.: On the same day, the commemoration of Saint [Note: Vitonus. At Verdun, the commemoration of Saint Vitonus, the eighth bishop of that city. Elected in the time of Clovis at the Council of Orléans in 502, he diligently taught and governed the Church entrusted to him for nearly twenty-seven years. He died in 529. Democh.] Vitonus, bishop and confessor.

### 10 — 10 November. Baeda has no entry.

V. C.: In Antioch, Eustochius and his companions.

At Rome, the burial of [Note: Leo. See above, 13 April and 28 June.] Leo, bishop.

D.: At Chersonesus in Lycia, [Note: Martin. See below, on the twelfth day of this month.] Martin, pope, who was exiled there for the Catholic faith.

B. A. T. L.: At Rome, the burial of Saint Leo, pope.

In Antioch, the commemoration of the holy Demetrius, bishop [Note: The words “bishop, etc.,” as far as “his,” are omitted by B.], and Amonesius, deacon, Eustochius and his companions.

A. T. L.: On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Martin, pope.

B.: At Orléans, the burial of [Note: Amonitorus, or Monitorus, the eleventh bishop of that city according to Democh’s tables.] Amonitorus, bishop.

### 11 — 11 November

The commemoration of Saint [Note: Martin. In the eighth year of Valens and Valentinian—that is, A.D. 371—he was ordained bishop. He was from the region of Pannonia, from the city of Sabaria. At Milan he first established a monastery, but because he fearlessly preached the Holy Trinity, he was beaten with rods by the heretics and expelled from Italy. He came to Gaul, converted many pagans, destroyed their temples and idols, and performed many signs among the people. He transferred the body of the blessed Gatianus and buried him beside the tomb of Saint Litorius. He restrained the tyrant Maximus from sending a sword into Spain to kill the heretics, declaring that it was sufficient for them to be excluded from the churches and communion of Catholics. Having completed the course of this present life, he died at the village of Condat, in his own city, at the age of eighty-one, in A.D. 397. Gregory of Tours, X, 31. See also his deeds, written by Sulpicius Severus in three books of dialogues, and Gregory of Tours’ four books on the miracles of Saint Martin.] Martin, bishop, at the city of Tours.

Florus adds in A. T. L.:

He shone more abundantly in virtues after the apostles.

L.: And he became a glorious raiser of three dead persons.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint [Note: Mennas. He suffered at Cotyaeum in Phrygia. He abandoned military service because the emperor Diocletian was forcing Christians to worship idols and withdrew into the desert. Later, when the emperor’s birthday was being celebrated, he came into the city and rebuked the idolaters. For this reason he was tortured by the governor Pyrrhus. The governor ordered him stretched upon a stake and beaten with bull’s sinews; afterward he ordered iron spikes to be made, Saint Mennas to be tied and dragged over them; then he ordered burning torches to be placed beneath him; finally, he ordered him beheaded. Surius, vol. VI.] Mennas, martyr.

A. and L. add: And Saint [Note: Bertuinus. He was educated in England in a monastery called Othbellum and was appointed bishop of that parish. He came to Rome and stayed there for two years; then he moved to Gaul, to the river Sambre. His virtues were admired not only by the prince Odoarius, who commended him to Pepin; Pepin granted the holy man five estates. Bertuinus founded an oratory in the village of Malonne on the Sambre, in honor of Mary ever-virgin, where he was buried after his death. Molanus, *On the Saints of Belgium*. Sigibert mentions him under the year 651.] Bertuinus, bishop.

T.: On the same day, at Alexandria, the burial of Saint [Note: John. He was born at Amathus in Cyprus and succeeded Theodore Scribonius in the Alexandrian see in 606. When Alexandria was about to be surrendered to the Persians, John fled to Cyprus and not long afterward died at Amathus on 11 November. See his Life by Leontius in Bollandus, 23 January. Theophanes, book XVIII, chapter 5, and Cedrenus state that Alexandria was captured in the sixth year of Heraclius’ reign, that is, A.D. 616.] John, patriarch.

B.: At Ravenna, the commemoration of the holy [Note: Valentine. They were crowned during the persecution under Diocletian. Baronius’s *Martyrology*.] Valentine, Felicianus, and Victorinus.

### 12 — 12 November. Baeda has no entry.

B. C. V.: At Rome, Saint [Note: Martin. Saint Martin became Roman pontiff in 649, after the death of Theodore, and summoned the Lateran Synod to condemn the Monothelites. Because Martin condemned that heresy, the emperor Constans, inflamed with rage, exiled him to the island of Naxos in 653. After he had remained there for a full year, he was taken to Byzantium and in 655 sent into exile at Chersonesus. He died there that same year, on 16 September, and was brought back to Constantinople and buried at Blachernae on 20 September. His burial at Rome, where his body was later transferred, is commemorated on 12 November.] Martin, pope.

B. C. A. T. L.: In Africa, [Note: Maurulus. Baronius in his notes thinks these were the same as Aurelius and Publius, Asian bishops whom Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 19, reports as having subscribed Serapion’s letter against the Cataphrygians.] Maurulus and Publius.

In Caesarea of Cappadocia, Germanus, Caesarius [C. and V. omit Theophilus], and Eusebius [A. T. L. omit Eusebius].

In C., through the error of the scribes, the African and Caesarean martyrs are assigned to the preceding day. The Africans, however, are written again on this day.

D.: In Africa, [Note: Arcadius. Prosper writes about them in his *Chronicle* under the year 438 as follows: “At about this time, four Spanish men—Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius, and Eutychius—had long been held in high regard by Geiseric for their wisdom and faithful service. The king ordered them to pass over to the Arian sect, in order to bind them more closely to himself. But they steadfastly rejected this crime. The barbarian, driven into a most violent rage, first proscribed them, then sent them into exile, and afterward tortured them with the most savage punishments. Finally, killed by various deaths, they gloriously and wondrously met their end in martyrdom.” Usuard discusses them on the following day.] Arcadius, Paschasius, Probus, and Eutychius, five Vandal martyrs in the persecution.

T.: At Ravenna, the burial of Saints [Note: Victor. Usuard, Ado, and other more recent writers discuss them on the following day.] Victor and Solutor.

### 13 — 13 November

At Tours, the commemoration of Saint [Note: Bricius. He was ordained in the second year of Arcadius and Honorius, that is, A.D. 397. He was a citizen of Tours. In the thirty-third year of his episcopate, the citizens of Tours accused him of adultery. After expelling him, they appointed Justinianus, and after Justinianus’s death Armentius succeeded him. Bricius, however, lived for seven years at Rome with the pope, where he was found innocent and ordered to return to the city. He built a basilica over the body of the blessed Martin, and he himself was buried there. He died around 443, after having held the episcopate for forty-seven years. Gregory of Tours, *History* X, 31; Ghinius, *Sanctorale*.] Bricius, bishop.

Florus adds in T. and L.:

When accused by the people of Tours, he brought before them the thirty-day-old infant about whom the charge was made and adjured it to declare before everyone whether he was its father. The infant said to him: “You are not my father.”

When the people again raged, he placed burning coals upon his cloak and carried them as far as the tomb of Saint Martin, saying: “Just as you see this garment unburned by these fires, so know that my body has remained undefiled by the touch of a woman.” [Note: Written in his Acts. See also Gregory, *History* II, 1.]

B.: In Thrace, the commemoration of the holy Secundus, Fidentianus, and Martialis.

In Antioch, the commemoration of the holy Donatus, Restitutus, Valerianus, and Fructuosus, with twelve others.

C. V.: And Saint [Note: Antonius. Joined with him were Zebinas, a native of Eleutheropolis, and Germanus. They were arrested under the emperor Maximinus at Caesarea of Cappadocia and beheaded by order of the governor Firmilianus. Eusebius, *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 9.] Antonius, and the burial of Saint James.

L.: At Malbodium, the translation of Saint [Note: Aldegundis. See above, 30 January. We find three translations of Saint Aldegundis’s relics: the first arranged by Saint Aldetrudis, daughter of Waldetrudis, who was Aldegundis’s sister; the second in 1161, by Abbess Fressendis; the third in 1439. We believe the first occurred today. The Life of Saint Aldegundis wrongly says that this translation was carried out by the illustrious King Sigebert and Aldetrudis. King Sigebert died in 654, nearly twenty years before Aldegundis herself, and therefore could not have attended her translation. Whether another distinguished man named Sigebert was present, whom later writers, without sufficient attention to chronology, called a king; or whether King Theuderic of the Franks, or one of his sons, or Pepin of Herstal, mayor of the palace—sometimes called king because he ruled the kings—was present, cannot be determined with certainty. This translation occurred toward the end of the seventh century.] Aldegundis, virgin.

A. T.: At the city of Roten, the commemoration of Saint Amandus, bishop.

A.: In the district of Cambrai, in a village called Calderiacus, the commemoration of Saint [Note: Maxellendis. She was born to Humlinus and Ameltrudis. When a certain Harduinus, born of noble stock among the people of Cambrai, unsuccessfully sought her hand in marriage, he killed her in a fit of madness around 683, as is clear from the Life of Saint Vindicianus published by Bollandus, chapter 2. Her parents first buried her body in the church at Pomerellum; afterward they transferred it to Calderiacus, where she had been killed.] Maxellendis, virgin and martyr.

On the same day, the burial of Saint [Note: Kilianus. Born in Ireland, and flourishing in many virtues, he became a bishop. Moved by a desire for pilgrimage, he departed with Saints Livinus, bishop, Elias, and Foillanus and reached Rome, where he served God in the Church of Saint Peter for more than eleven years. From Rome he went to Gaul and visited Saint Fiacrius. Sent by Faro, bishop of Meaux, to the people of Arras, he settled in the village of Albiniacum and died around 640. Molanus, *On the Feasts of the Saints of Belgium*.] Kilianus, bishop and confessor.

T.: On the same day, in Thrace, the passion of Saints Eudictus, Eutychus, and Agestus.

### 14 — 14 November. Baeda has no entry.

V. C.: In Heraclea, the commemoration of Clement, Theodota, Philomenus, and many others whose names God knows. They are read in L. B. as follows:

In the city of Heraclea in Thrace [L. omits “in Thrace”], the commemoration of Saints Clement, Clementinus [B. omits Clement], Philomenus, Theodotus, and Heraclius.

For these, A. and T. have only: Clementinus, Philomonus, and Heraclius.

At the end, B. adds: And the commemoration of Saint Eradius.

A.: On the same day, the reinterment of the holy bodies of Quintinus, martyr, and Cassianus, bishop, in the midst of the greatest sorrow.

D.: At Alexandria, [Note: Serapion. When they found him with his household, they tortured him with the most bitter punishments and, after breaking all his limbs, threw him headlong from an upper room. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI, 41.] Serapion, who, having been thrown down under Decius, became a martyr.

### 15 — 15 November. Baeda has no entry.

V. C.: In Africa, Secundinus, Martialis, Calendion, Valerius, and Fructuosus, with twelve others [C. omits “twelve others”].

D.: [Note: Felix. He is wrongly confused in the Martyrologies with Saint Felix of Nola, the presbyter, since he too is said to have suffered at Nola.] Felix, bishop, who was distinguished by the glory of miracles.

B. A. T. L.: In Africa, the commemoration of Saints Secundus, Fidentianus [B.: Saints Martialis and Fidentianus], and Demetrius [L.: and Secundinus].

In Antioch, Donatus and Restitutus, with thirty others.

B. adds two, concluding as follows: Valerianus and Fructuosus, with twelve others.

A.: On the same day, Saint [Note: Machatus, more correctly Machutus, also called Maclovius. Born to British parents, he was piously educated by Saint Brendan. As a young man he became a monk; later, when the bishop of that region died, he was unwillingly consecrated bishop of the city of Gummi-Castrum. Desiring to lay down the burden of the episcopate, he fled to Armorica to Abbot Aaron. He converted the Aietans to the faith and, willingly or unwillingly, was made bishop by the people who had already been converted. He established seventy canons and an equal number of monks. Harassed by his own people, he withdrew to Aquitaine, where he was received with great devotion by the blessed Leontius, bishop of the see of Saintes. Meanwhile Britain mourned its exile and sent men to bring him back to his parish as quickly as possible, but he did not remain long with the Britons. Loving solitude, he returned to Aquitaine and died weakened by age around 565. The body of Saint Maclovius was brought to Paris in 975 under King Lothair, who placed it in his chapel, now called Saint Michael at the Palace. From there it was transferred to the basilica of Saint Maglorius. See his Life in Mabillon’s first century of the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti* and in Surius, vol. VI.] Machatus.

L.: And the passion of Saint [Note: Eugenius. He completed his martyrdom in the territory of Paris. Gerard, abbot, placed part of his body in his monastery at Braine; another portion was carried from the church of Saint Denis out of Gaul to Toledo in 1565 with magnificent ceremony, during which the Catholic king Philip II carried the relics on his own shoulders back to their ancient home. Molanus, *Additions to Usuard*, and his *Index*.] Eugenius, bishop of the see of Toledo, the precious disciple of Dionysius the archbishop.

### 16 — 16 November. Baeda has no entry.

B. C. V.: In Africa, Rufinianus, Marcus, Valerius, Victor [B. omits Victor], and Honoratus.

C. V.: Marina, Secundinus, and Fronto.

In Antioch, Augustinus, Justa, Matrona, and Fructa.

D.: In Africa, Rufinus, Fidentianus, Augustinus, and Felix.

B.: And elsewhere, the commemoration of Secundianus, Aurelianus, and Marcellus.

A. T. L.: In Capua, the commemoration of the saints Vitalis and Justus.

A. T. L. B.: At Lyon in Gaul [“in Gaul” only in B.], the burial of Saint [Note: Eucherius. Having turned from the noble senatorial order to a religious life, he long shut himself voluntarily within the confines of a cave. Later, at the city of Lyon, when the bishop had died, the entire Church, following the ancient custom, sought from the Lord through three days of fasting and prayer a revelation of whom it should receive as its governor. When an angel revealed the choice, Eucherius was solemnly placed in the episcopal chair. Ado, Usuard. He is listed as the twentieth bishop of that see and is known to have attended the third Council of Arles, held in 453, as well as the councils of Orange and Carpentras.] Eucherius, bishop.

17.—FIFTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. At Orléans, the feast of Saint Anianus [Note: How he delivered the city of Orléans from the fury of the Huns by prayer may be read in Gregory of Tours, *History* V, 7. Anianus was the seventh bishop of that see.] the confessor. And of our holy father Gregory, worker of miracles [Note: Born of noble stock, his father was Florentius and his mother Armentaria, niece of Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres. He was born in 544 and educated in the liberal arts by Gallus, bishop of Clermont. In 566 he withdrew to Tours; in 569 he was ordained deacon; and finally, in 573, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, he was designated by Bishop Euphronius as his successor before Euphronius’s death and became archbishop of Tours. In the following year he dedicated an oratory in the city of Tours, in which he deposited relics of many saints. In 577 he attended the Council of Paris and vigorously defended Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, who had been accused by King Chilperic. In 580 he was falsely denounced before Chilperic for allegedly saying that Queen Fredegund had an illicit relationship with Bertram, bishop of Bordeaux. He was summoned to the Synod of Berny-Rivière and, after clearing himself by oath, was acquitted. At that same synod he restored King Chilperic, who was tending toward Sabellianism, to sound doctrine. In 585 he steadfastly defended in the city of Orléans Bishop Theodore of Marseille, who had been reproached by Guntram for the murder inflicted upon Chilperic. In 588 King Childebert sent him to Guntram at Metz to conduct business with him, both civil and ecclesiastical. In 590 he debated one of his priests who denied the resurrection and freed the poor man from a most pernicious error. In 594 he went to Rome to visit Pope Gregory and the thresholds of the apostles. After returning home, he died in 595. See his Life written by Abbot Odo and published by Surius, vol. VI, and by Ruinart in his edition of Saint Gregory’s works.]

Florus weaves the following eulogy for the preceding saint in A.T.L.: “When he was chosen as the future successor of Saint Evurtius, his predecessor, and of the people of Orléans, so that the harmony of divine election might shine forth in him, after a three-day fast, while the child—still unable to speak—was brought in and touched the *Brevi* placed upon the altar, through the power of Christ he cried out three times: ‘Anianus has been appointed bishop of this city by God.’ Thus made bishop, he later shone forth through many miracles.”

V., and Victor, Theodeta, Alpha, and Zachaeus. C., Factor, Theodora, Alphaeus [Note: Alphaeus and Zachaeus underwent capital punishment after many tortures in the first year of Diocletian’s persecution. Baronius, in the *Martyrology*.], Alpheus, and Zachaeus. A.T., at Carthage, the feast of Dubitatus and Valentinus. B. inserts Tuscius. At the same place, in Rome across the Tiber, the feast of Saint Cecilia. At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Ammon. And the feast of Saint Thecla, virgin.

18.—FOURTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A.T.L.: “At Córdoba, the passion of Saints Acisclus [Note: Baronius writes in the *Annals* CCCIII, 142, that these men suffered while Hosius was bishop of Córdoba. They are commemorated on the preceding day by Usuard, Ado, and others.] and Victoria, who, after imprisonment and tortures, were thrown into a river with their feet bound to their necks. But when they emerged from the water by the power of the Lord, they were bound to wheels and rolled over a fire, so that their limbs were shattered. Afterwards Victoria, with her breasts cut off and her tongue amputated, breathed forth a spirit worthy of God; Acisclus, meanwhile, completed his martyrdom by decapitation under the governor Sidonius.

“At Caesarea, the feast of Saints Maximus, Lucian, and Marcial. At Antioch, the passion of Romanus the monk and the boy Baralus, as well as of Ysicius, a Palatine soldier, who were killed for the name of Christ in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. Romanus, after many scourging blows and the cutting out of his tongue, was killed in prison; the boy Baralus was beheaded; Ysicius was tied to a stone and drowned in a river.”

C.V., at Antioch, of Romanus the monk [Note: The Greeks distinguish two martyrs named Romanus in the *Menaion*: one who was condemned at Antioch by the prefect Asclepiades under Galerius, and another, a Caesarean deacon, about whom Eusebius speaks in *The Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 2, whom they say suffered under Diocletian. But since they acknowledge that both suffered on the same day and underwent the same kind of martyrdom, who does not see that they are needlessly distinguished as two Romans? I am nevertheless surprised that this opinion pleased Baronius in his notes on the *Martyrology*. Certainly, if there were two martyrs named Romanus, and if both suffered martyrdom at Antioch on the same day, why did Eusebius in this passage mention only one? Eusebius also mentions this martyr elsewhere, namely in the second book *On the Resurrection and Ascension of Christ*, where he describes Romanus’s martyrdom in a detailed and rhetorical manner, and where likewise he recognizes only one Romanus who suffered martyrdom at Antioch.], and at Caesarea of Victor and Maxima, and the dedication of the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle. B., in the city of Antioch, the feast of Saints Romanus and Ysicius, martyrs. D., at Antioch, of Romanus the monk and martyr, and of Hesychius the Palatine and martyr. A.T.B., on the same day in Spain, at Córdoba, the passion of Saint Ascla [B., Aciscla], virgin and martyr. T. adds: “On this day roses are gathered there.” A., on the same day at Cambrai, the elevation of the body of Saint Gaugericus [Note: He died on 11 August; see above under that date.], bishop. A.L., and the deposition of Saint Eusebia [Note: Ferrarius, in his *General Catalogue*, conjectures that this is the same Eusebia as the abbess of Hamay, commemorated on 16 March.], virgin.

19.—THIRTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. Bede has no entry.

D. At Rome, of Maximinus [Note: Or Maximus. During the persecution of Maximian, he was subjected to various tortures and insults, and, after being beheaded, completed his martyrdom. He was placed at Saint Sixtus. Usuard says that he suffered under Maximinus; Baronius, under Valerian.], priest and martyr, and of Faustinus [Note: Or Faustus. He possessed such confidence that, when no one dared approach the Christians detained in prison, permission was nevertheless granted to him and to his colleague Eusebius to enter the confessors’ presence. Saint Faustus, full of days, was beheaded under Diocletian. *Peter de Natalibus*. This Faustus, however, seems to be confused here with that Faustus, the Alexandrian deacon, whom Eusebius mentions in *History* VIII, 11.], deacon, and Eusebius, martyrs. B., at Autun, the deposition of Saint Simplicius [Note: He is also commemorated above, on 24 June.], bishop. B.V.C., at Caesarea in Cappadocia, of Maximus, Mucianus, Neopherus, Januarius, and Vitalis [B. omits Vitalis]. A.T., at Caesarea, the feast of Saints Januarius, Neopherus, and Vitalis. T., of Castorius, Marcian, and Zephyrus. L., at Caesarea, the feast of Januarius, Castorius, Zephyrus, and Vitalis. And the deposition of Saint Elizabeth [Note: She was born of the noblest parents in Hungary, her father being King Andrew and her mother Queen Gertrude. She married Louis, son of Herman, prince of Thuringia. She died in 1231 and was buried in the castle of Marburg in Germany. Surius published a sufficiently lengthy Life of this saint in vol. VI.], widow.

20.—TWELVE DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. Bede has no entry.

D. At Rome, of Pontian [Note: See above, under the fourth day before the Kalends of October, when he died. Today the burial of Saint Pontian is celebrated; Usuard and Baronius, however, celebrate it on the preceding day. Pontian is said to have been buried on the ninth day before the Kalends of December in the old catalogue published by Papebroch in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I of April.], pope and martyr. At Messana, of Ampelius and Gaius. B.V.C., at Heraclea, of Bassus, Dionysius, and Orion. V.C., in Spain, of Maximus the priest. A.T., at Heraclea, the feast of Saints Gagius and Dionysius. T., of Bassus and Classius. A.L., in Spain, the deposition of Saint Crispinus [Note: He and Maximus suffered at the same time, according to Jerome’s *Martyrology*.]. T., in Sicily, the passion of Saint Ampelius. B., at Antioch, the feast of Saints Basil and Dionysius. At Turin, the feast of Saints Octavius [Note: Ambrose, or Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, has a sermon on Octavius and his companions.], Solutor, and Adventor.

21.—ELEVEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. Bede calls this day.

D.: Rufus, whom the Apostle greets in his Letter to the Romans [Note: In chapter 16 of Romans. Dorotheus, in his *Synopsis*, says that he was made bishop of Thebes.]. C.V., at Antioch, of Basil and Auxilius, Saturninus, Caralus, and Eutychius. B., at Antioch, the feast of Saints Basil, Auxilius [V., Auxius], and Matron. And elsewhere, the feast of Saints Demetrius, Quintianus, and Sisinnius. A.T.L., at Antioch, the feast of Saints Basil and Saturninus. In the city of Histria, the feast of Saint Maurus [Note: He was born in the city of Castellum in the province of Africa. When he was eight years old, he went to Rome, where, by order of the prefect Celerinus under the emperor Numerian, he was beaten with rods, crushed with leaden balls, hung on the rack, torn with iron claws, and finally beheaded with a sword. Certain sailors, his fellow citizens, brought his body to the shore of the city of Parentium in the province of Histria, where he is honored with great solemnity as patron and protector of the church on this very day. *Peter de Natalibus*.], martyr. L., and of Saint Columban [Note: Of Irish nation and born in Leinster, he was a disciple of Congall, abbot of the monastery of Bangor in eastern Ireland. After crossing into Britain and remaining there for some time, he went in 589 to Burgundy, where he founded and governed the monastery of Luxeuil. After presiding over it for about twenty years, he was driven into exile by Theuderic, king of the Austrasians, because he censured the king’s immoral conduct with his customary freedom. After traversing all Gaul, he withdrew into Italy, where, having found a suitable place from Agilulf, king of the Lombards, he built the monastery of Bobbio near Naples. Jonas, a monk of Bobbio, wrote his Life, which is found in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century II. See also above, *Ecclesiastical History* II, 4.], abbot. T. records his feast first. L. adds: “Also, the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.”

22.—TEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. The feast of Saint Cecilia [Note: She suffered under the emperor Alexander, not under Commodus, as Usuard and Ado assert; for she was crowned with martyrdom during the pontificate of Urban.], virgin, who instructed her own husband Valerian and his brother Tiburtius in belief in Christ and in martyrdom; she herself afterward suffered martyrdom, overcoming fire but being killed by the sword under Almachius, prefect of Rome.

A.T., at Alexandria, the feast of Saints Demetrius and Felix. At Soissons, the deposition of Saint Medresina, virgin. B., in Cappadocia, of Saints Longinus, Leontius, and Faustus. C.V., of Maximus. S., of Longinus [Note: He is also commemorated above, on 15 March.], who opened the Lord’s side with a lance. The Laetian manuscript has here a longer eulogy from Florus; see below, under the fourth day before the Nones of December.

23.—NINE DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. At Rome, the feast of Saint Clement [Note: The chronology of the succession of the first Roman pontiffs is highly doubtful and uncertain. We cannot determine with certainty either whom Saint Clement succeeded or when he succeeded him. Irenaeus, book III, chapter 3, says that he succeeded Anacletus; Eusebius agrees with him both in the *Chronicle* and in the *History*, and all the Greeks follow Eusebius. Among the Latins, some place him after Cletus, some after Cletus and Anacletus, and others assign him as successor to Linus. It is inevitable that this variation in the order in which Saint Clement is placed should create uncertainty about the time of his succession. In a matter so ambiguous, it seems best not to depart from the Catalogue of Damasus. Accordingly, according to that catalogue, Clement succeeded Saint Linus in the year 67 and governed the Church until 77, when he resigned the pontificate, as may be gathered from Epiphanius, *Heresy* 27. He is said to have been drowned in exile in the third year of Trajan, in the hundredth year of Christ. Yet the distinguished Dodwell, in his notes on Pearson’s *Dissertations on the Series and Succession of the First Roman Bishops*, attempted to prove that Saint Clement did not suffer martyrdom and that what is said in the martyrologies about his exile and martyrdom is rather the invention of storytellers than something resting on historical testimony.], bishop, who, by Trajan’s order, was sent into exile beyond the Pontus Sea. After many had been called to the faith through his miracles and teaching, he was thrown into the sea with an anchor fastened around his neck. But when his disciples prayed, the sea withdrew for three miles, and they found his body in a stone coffin in a marble temple, with the anchor beside it. On the same day, Saint Felicity, mother of seven martyr sons, who was beheaded for Christ by order of Antoninus.

Florus in A.T.L.: “On the same day, at the village of Hasbania, the deposition of Saint Trudo [Note: He was born in Hasbania of noble parents. After his parents died, he went, on the advice of Remaclus, to Saint Clodulphus, bishop of Metz. There he surrendered to the church of Metz, in honor of Saint Stephen, whatever patrimony he possessed in Hasbania. When Clodulphus had ordained him priest and saw him to be suitable in character, learning, and piety for sowing the word of the Lord, he sent him back to his homeland. There he built a church on pagan land in honor of Saint Quintinus and Bishop Remigius, at the Rivulus Cisindria, in a place called Sarcinium. Since many young men sought to be received into his fellowship, he built a magnificent monastery for them. He also founded another monastery commonly called Saint Trudo, half a mile from the Flemish city of Bruges. The date of Saint Trudo’s death can be inferred both from the pontificate of Clodulphus, bishop of Metz, and from the death of Pepin, father of Charles Martel, who donated two estates to the tomb of Saint Trudo. Clodulphus did not assume the see of Metz before 654; Trudo approached him around 660, at the age of fifteen or perhaps twenty, and therefore survived until the end of the seventh century. His death cannot be placed later, since some time must be allowed for his memory to be celebrated before Pepin’s death; Pepin died in 714. See Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century II.], confessor, who, despising the world, shone forth through the greatest virtues.”

L., and Saint Severinus [Note: Ferrarius, in his *General Catalogue*, and Labbe in his *Hagiologium* mention today a Parisian monk of this name.]. V.C., on the same day, the feast of Saint Columban [Note: See above, under the eleventh day before the Kalends of this month], at Bobbio. B., in Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, the deposition of Saint Columban. In the city of Bourges, Saint Faterius [Note: In Labbe’s *Hagiologium*, Saint Faretrius, a priest of the city of Bourges, is said to be commemorated today in the village of Carebrivas. In the same volume of his *New Bibliotheca*, p. 432, Saint Marianus is said to have been a monk under Fraterius in the monastery of Princay.], priest. And elsewhere, Saint Trudo the confessor.

24.—EIGHT DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. At Rome, the feast of Saint Chrysogonus [Note: He instructed Saint Anastasia in the faith and endured many tortures for Christ for two full years. Anastasia often ministered to him in prison. When Saint Chrysogonus was beheaded, his body was thrown into the sea; it was later found by a certain Zoilus, a priest. See the Life of Saint Anastasia in Surius, vol. VI.], who, beheaded under Diocletian, completed his martyrdom. It is written in the Passion of Saint Anastasia [Note: She is commemorated below, on 25 December.].

On the same day, the feast of Saint Crescentianus, who was in prison under the persecution of Maximian, son of Maximin, with Caesarius [Note: Rather Cyriacus. See about him, and about Largus and Smaragdus, under 16 March and 8 August.], the deacon, and Largus and Smaragdus. He was brought out of prison by order of Carpasianus, the vicar, suspended on the rack, beaten with clubs, and scraped with claws; then, after being burned for a long time with flames applied around his sides, he gave up his spirit and was buried by John the priest in the cemetery of Priscilla.

On the same day, Maximus [Note: More correctly Maximianus, who had married the daughter of Diocletian, Artemia’s sister.] killed his sister Artemia [Note: Ferrarius writes in his *General Catalogue of the Saints* that on 12 August Saint Artemia, virgin and martyr, is commemorated at Rome in the church of Saint Sylvester, while the rest is unknown; in the index of the *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, he says that she was the daughter of Diocletian, that she is commemorated on 8 August, and that her body is preserved in the church of Saint Sylvester. Other martyrologies list her with her mother Serena on 16 August.]. This is written in the Acts of Marcellus [Note: See his Acts in Bollandus and above, under 16 August], pope.

V.C., on the same day, of Saint Eleutherius and Maximus. And of Saint Flavian, bishop and confessor. And of Saint Romanus [Note: Bishop Martin of Tours committed him to burial. His tomb is adjacent to the castle of Blaye, on the bank of the Garonne. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 46. The abbey of Saint Romanus, possessed by the Augustinian regular canons, can still be seen there. Sigebert, under the year 385—which he calls the penultimate year of the emperor Gratian and therefore the year 382—has this: “In Gaul, Saint Romanus of Blaye died.”], priest.

25.—SEVEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. The feast of Saint Peter [Note: He was first promoted to the diaconate and soon afterward to the priesthood by Theonas, bishop of Alexandria. When Theonas died around the year 300, Peter succeeded him as bishop. He had governed the Church for three years when, in 303, the most savage persecution of Diocletian broke out. Among countless others, Peter was arrested; and when this was reported to the emperor, he ordered that Peter’s head be cut off. After designating Achillas as his successor, he completed his martyrdom in the ninth year of the persecution, that is, in the year of Christ 311. When he learned that Arius was everywhere stirring up disturbances through his impiety, he deposed him and expelled him from the Church, and never restored him to ecclesial communion. He suffered on the twenty-ninth day of the month Athyr, corresponding to 25 November, although his memory is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 26 November. The Greeks celebrate it on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, namely 24 November. The Copts place it on the second day of Athyr in their calendar, and on the twenty-fifth in the Seldenian calendar. Eusebius Renaudot, *History of the Jacobite Patriarchs of Alexandria*. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII, 32; IX, 6.], bishop of Alexandria. Although adorned with every virtue and inferior to none of his predecessors in divine Scripture, truly a priest and an offering to God, he was suddenly seized and, by order of Maximinus, beheaded; many others from Egypt were slaughtered with him. This is written in the *Ecclesiastical History*, book nine.

B.V.C., and Saint Catherine [Note: The words of Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 14, concerning a noble Alexandrian woman whom Maximinus loved—words which Baronius, under the year 307, interprets of the contest of Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr—cannot refer to her; otherwise she would not have completed her martyrdom under Maximinus, which Baronius nevertheless endeavors to establish. The Acts of Saint Catherine in Surius under 25 November state that she was subjected to martyrdom by order of Maximinus; but the woman whom Eusebius discusses was punished only with exile. Nor are either the Acts preserved in Metaphrastes or those reported by Leo Allatius in his *Dissertation on the Simeons* genuine, since the former say: “In the thirty-fifth year, while the impious and wicked Maxentius was reigning,” which is entirely fabulous. Papebroch, in the *Greek-Muscovite Ephemerides* prefixed to the first volume of the *Saints of May*, under 25 November, says: “The Greeks call her Hekaterina; the Latins, Catharina. The Acts among both peoples, however much they possess of the marvelous, suffer equally from even greater difficulty in obtaining credence. No lighter difficulty concerns the translation of her sacred body to Mount Sinai: it is indisputable in substance, but exceedingly obscure with respect to its authors and date. This is certain: there is no saint whose fame and cult were more obscure in the first centuries after the persecution and more celebrated in later ages, not only in the Eastern but also in the Western Church. In our Belgium it would be difficult to find any city, or even town or borough, where this saint does not have either an altar or a church, and so forth.”], virgin. A.T.L., on the same day, the passion of Saint Catherine. B., elsewhere, of Lucian, Marcian, and Claudian.

26.—SIX DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. Bede has no entry.

D. At Rome, of Linus [Note: See above, under 23 September.], pope, and of Alexander, bishop and martyr, who suffered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October and was transferred on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, when his feast was dedicated. B.C.V.A.T.L., at Rome, of Saints Siricius [Note: Siricius was made bishop in the year 383, during the consulship of Merobaudes II and Saturninus. Thus reports Marcellinus, who also assigns fifteen years to his episcopate. We find the death of Saint Siricius recorded on this very day in many martyrologies; in some, however, cited by Florentinius in his notes on Saint Jerome’s *Martyrology* under 26 November, his deposition is entered under the eighth day before the Kalends of March; and in the old catalogue published by Bollandus, volume I of April, he is said to have been buried on the seventh day before the Kalends of March. In truth, both dates should rather be referred to some translation of Saint Siricius.], bishop, and Saturninus. At Aquileia, of Valerian [Note: He took part in the synod of 370 held at Rome by 113 bishops. You may read their synodal letter in Greek in Theodoret, II, 17, and in Sozomen, VII, 27. He also took part in the Council of Aquileia held in 381 against the heretics Palladius and Secundianus. He very quickly cleansed the church of Aquileia, which had been weakened by his predecessor Fortunatianus, from every stain, and made it renowned throughout the world by a new growth of excellent clergy. Thus Jerome, on his way to the East, remained there for some time to enjoy their companionship, and rightly said of them in his *Chronicle*: “The clergy of Aquileia are regarded as a choir of the blessed.” He was succeeded by the equally holy Chromatius. The same Valerian is mentioned by Rufinus, priest of Aquileia, in book I of the *Invectives*. Baronius commemorates him on the following day in the *Martyrology*.], bishop and confessor. B.A.T.L., at Autun, the deposition of Saint Amator, bishop.

27.—FIVE DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. Bede has no entry.

V.C., at Nicomedia, of Marcellus, Peter, Serena, and Victorinus [C., Luctorinus]. V.C.D., in the city of Bologna, of Agricola and Vitalis, martyrs. A.L., at Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Peter, Marcellus [L. omits Marcellus], and Serinus; one of whom was crucified for the faith of Christ, while the other was beheaded. More correctly and fully, T.B., at Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Marcellus, Peter, and Serenus. In the Italian city of Bologna, the passion of Saints Agricola and Vitalis; T. alone continues: “One of whom was crucified for Christ, the other beheaded.” At Milan, the feast of John, Severus, and Andrew. The same names occur in L. But it incorrectly prefixes: “In the city of Bologna, the passion of Agricola the virgin.”

28.—FOUR DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. Bede has no entry.

D. [Note: Sosthenes. He was one of the Seventy disciples and wrote a letter to the Corinthians together with Paul. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* I, 12. Dorotheus, in his *Synopsis*, reports that he was ordained bishop of Colophon; this is taken from a little work by Hippolytus on the Seventy disciples.] Sosthenes, a disciple of the apostles. And Rufus the martyr, together with his entire household, won over through Chrysogonus [Note: Peter de Natalibus reports that he was converted to the faith of Christ by the example of the blessed martyr Sebastian and baptized together with his entire household by Saint Polycarp the priest. In the old manuscripts, however, Baronius writes that he and his household were converted by Saint Chrysogonus.]. In Africa, of Papirius [Note: Rather Papinianus, bishop of Utica, who, according to Victor of Vita, book I *On the Vandal Persecution*, was burned over his whole body on plates of glowing iron. Likewise Mansuetus of Urci was burned at the Porta Fornitana under Geiseric, the Arian king.], and Mansuetus, bishops. B.C.V., in Syria, of Trophimus, Theodulus, and Eucerius. And elsewhere [B.C. omits “and elsewhere”], of Eusebius and Julius. A.L., in Syria. T., in Africa, the feast of Saints Trophimus, Eusebius, and Julius. T.L., and of Theodulus, martyrs.

29.—THREE DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. At Rome, of Saint Saturninus the martyr and the old man [Note: More correctly, “the old man” (*senis*), rather than “Sennis.” Saint Saturninus was elderly.] and Sisinnius the deacon, under Maximian. They were first condemned, along with others, to dig sand for the construction of Diocletian’s baths; afterward they were kept in prison for a long time. There they instructed many pagans and baptized them. Then they were brought out again, bound with chains, and, barefoot, ordered by Laodicius, prefect of the city, to be raised onto and stretched upon the rack. They were beaten with sinews, clubs, and scourges; afterward he ordered flames to be applied to their sides. When they had been taken down from the rack, he ordered that they be beheaded [Note: Namely, on the Nomentan Way at the first milestone. They were buried on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, although they are commemorated today. See the Acts of Saint Marcellus in Bollandus, 16 January.].

The very Christian Thrason, who had supplied the martyrs with much from his own resources, gathered their bodies together with John the priest and buried them on his estate on the Salarian Way. While these men were thus placed in the midst of their contest, two soldiers, Papias and Maurus [Note: See above, under 29 January.], believed. They were immediately arrested by Laodicius and, not long afterward, crowned with martyrdom. This is written in the Acts of Pope Marcellus.

L. gives a shorter account: “After imprisonment, they were raised onto the rack, stretched with sinews, and finally beheaded; their bodies, and so forth.”

Florus in A. and T.: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Chrysogonus [Note: See above, under 25 October.], and of Daria, together with eighty soldiers who, through Saint Chrysogonus, had been converted to the faith and were likewise killed by order of the emperor Numerian. Chrysogonus and Daria, after many tortures, imprisonment, wild beasts, and the rack, were thrown together into a pit and buried under stones.”

The same Florus in A.T.L.: “At Toulouse, the passion of Saint Saturninus [Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs* I, 48, asserts that Saint Saturninus was ordained by disciples of the apostles, contradicting himself in *History* I, 30, where, drawing on the Acts of Saturninus himself, he dates the beginning of his episcopate at Toulouse to the consulship of Decius, Germanicus, and Gratus, that is, the year 250.], bishop, who, in the time of Decius, Germanicus, and Gratus, was seized by pagans, tied to a bull, and thrown down from the Capitol. Immediately, at the first descent of the steps, his head was dashed, his brain scattered, and every part of his body torn apart; Christ received his soul, worthy of God.”

B.V.C., on the same day, the vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle. B., and the feast of Saints Chrysogonus, Daria, and Maurus. C., of Maurus and seventy-two others.

30.—TWO DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS. The feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

Florus more fully in A.T.L.: “In Achaea, in the city of Patras, the passion of Saint Andrew the Apostle, who, crucified for the name of Christ, completed his martyrdom.”

B., at Rome, the feast of Saint Maurilius, Consulus, and Theodulus. C., and at Milan [Note: Namely, in the city of Milan.], of Saint Amator, bishop.

## DECEMBER

[Col. 1119C]

1.—ON THE KALENDS. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A.T.L.: “At Noyon, the deposition of Saint Eligius [Note: He was a Gaul by nation, born in the village of Chaptelat near the city of Limoges, to Eucherius and Terrigia. In the city of Limoges he practiced the art of goldsmithing for some time. In 635 he was sent by King Dagobert as ambassador to Brittany, where he concluded a truce with Duke Clippius. While still a layman, he founded many monasteries and basilicas; finally, he was ordained bishop of Noyon in 640, not, as is commonly reckoned, in 646, as Charles le Cointe demonstrates in *Annals of France*, vol. II, under the year 640, no. 20, and elsewhere. Once bishop, he devoted himself to building churches and instructing the Flemings, Frisians, and Suevi in the Christian faith. In 644 he took part in the third Council of Chalon. In 650 he founded a monastery for men at Tournai and one for women at Noyon, and dedicated the church of Kortrijk to the memory of Saint Martin. He died on the Kalends of December in 658, according to Pagi in his *Historical-Critical Chronology* under the year 665; according to the common calculation, in 665, and according to others, in 963. His Acts, written by Saint Ouen, are reproduced by Surius in volume VI. See also Molanus, in the *Index of the Saints of Belgium*.], bishop and confessor, who, shining with great prudence and holiness in the palace of Lothair, king of the Franks, became a bishop and, removing many bodies of saints, buried them with the greatest propriety; he blossomed forth in the greatest virtues and signs of miracles.”

D. At Rome, of Chrysogonus and Daria, martyrs [Note: See above, under 25 October and 29 November.], who suffered at Rome in the time of Numerian, under the judge Celerinus. V.C., at Interamna, or Narni, of Saint Proculus [Note: Concerning Proculus, Ephebus, and Apollonius, who buried Saint Valentine, see above, under 14 February. Galesinius and Ferrarius list Saint Proculus, bishop of Interamna, under the Kalends of January; he is also commemorated at Bologna on 1 June with another Proculus, a soldier; at Interamna on 1 December, because the translation of his body took place on that day. See the account of Saint Proculus among the martyrs of Interamna on 14 April in the *Acta Sanctorum*. Baronius, in his notes on this day, conjectures that he was a different person from Saint Proculus of Interamna, and Usuard calls him a priest.], bishop and martyr. At Torrente [C., Thure], of Saint Marina. V., at Ursus Pileatus, of Saint Candida. A.T.L.B., at Rome, the feast of Saint Candida. B., of Lucius and Marina, Ambon, and Filatus. In the city of Noyon, the deposition of Saint Eligius, bishop and confessor. The feast of Saint Constantia.

The Laetian manuscript has here the eulogy of Saints Chrysogonus and Daria given above, and then adds: “On the same day, the arrival of the holy relics from the city of Constantinople.”

2.—ON THE NONES. Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. and T., in first place, and in L., but under the tenth day before the Kalends of December: “In the city of Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Longinus the soldier, who is said to have opened the Lord’s side with a lance. After converting to the faith and preaching Christ, he was arrested by the prefect Octavius. After his teeth had been shattered with iron and his tongue cut out, he underwent capital punishment.”

V., at Rome, the feast of Primitivus, Pontianus, and Pimenius. Elsewhere, of Verus, Severus, and Januarius. At Rome, of Saint Bibiana [Note: Daughter of Faustus and Dafrosa. By order of the emperor Julian, she was beaten with leaden scourges until she gave up her spirit. Her body lay in the forum for two days by order of the emperor; finally, it was taken away by John the priest and buried in a house where her mother and her sister Demetria had already been buried, near the Licinian Palace at Rome. Ado. Concerning her, see the Life of Saint Pigmenius, 24 March.]. A.T., at Rome, the feast of Saints Victorinus, Demetrius, and Donatus. T., and the passion of Saints Primentius, Pontianus, Dafrosa, and Julian. L., at Rome, the feast of Saints Victorinus, Primentius, Pontianus, Dafrosus, Demetrius, and Urbanus. D., at Rome, of Juvinianus and Faustus, martyrs. And of Dafrosa the daughter. B., of Agnes the second. C., at Rome, the feast of Pimentius, Pontianus, and Pisinnus. Elsewhere, of Securus, Januarius, Bibiana, and Dafrosa. B., at Rome, the feast of Saints Primitus, Pontianus, and Vinianus. In the city of Le Mans, the deposition of Saint Domnolus [Note: Saint Domnolus died on the preceding day, and the people of Le Mans commemorate his feast annually on that date. I do not know why he is mentioned today, unless the saint commemorated on the preceding day was transferred to the following day through a simple error.], bishop and confessor. In Mauretania, of Securus, Victorinus, and Fortunatus.

3.—THREE DAYS BEFORE THE NONES. Bede has no entry.

D., At Rome, the feast of Claudius [Note: Claudius, who was converted from persecution to Christianity when he saw Chrysanthus endure every torture and heard him refute the gods of the nations by clear arguments. Not only was he himself converted to the faith, but also his wife Hilaria, and their sons Jason and Maurus, together with seventy soldiers. Of these, the emperor Numerian ordered Claudius to be bound to a huge stone and thrown headlong into a river, while the soldiers and Claudius’s sons were punished by capital sentence. After blessed Hilaria had buried her sons’ bodies, she was shortly afterward assailed by pagans while praying at their tomb and departed to the Lord. Their deeds are joined to the Acts of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria in Surius, volume V, October 25, and in Petrus de Natalibus.], of Claudius the tribune, and of Hilaria his wife, and of Jason and Maurus. B. C. V., In the East, of Meronius, Claudicus, and Felix. In Africa, of Crispina, Magna, and John. B. A. T. L., In Africa, the feast of Saints Crispinus, Magnus, and John. T. L., And of the martyrs Stephen. B., Stephen, Victor, and Martin. In Bologna, of Saints Agricola and Cassian [Note: Cassian did not suffer at Bologna, but at Tingis, the metropolis of Mauretania Tingitana. He had long performed the office of court recorder; at last, inspired from heaven, he regarded it as detestable to serve in the killing of Christians. Therefore, renouncing that office, he merited to obtain the triumph of martyrdom under Christian confession. His body was buried in the aforementioned city and, in the course of time, was transferred from there to the city of Imola. Petrus de Natalibus.].

[Col. 1123B] **4.—The second day before the Nones.** Bede has no entry.

D., At Rome, of Symphronius and Olympius [Note: Concerning these, see July 26.], Exuperius [Note: More correctly, Exuperia.], and Theodolus, martyrs translated by Blessed Sixtus on the second day before the Nones of December, when their feast is celebrated. C. V., Saint Barbara [Note: She suffered for Christ in the time of Maximian. Her father, named Dioscorus, afflicted his only daughter with many tortures because she did not wish to marry or worship false gods. Finally, by order of the governor, she was beheaded by her own father, and her martyrdom was completed in a good confession together with Saint Juliana. The sources greatly disagree about the place of her martyrdom: some place it in Tuscany, others at Nicomedia, while most report that she suffered at Heliopolis. Baronius considers Nicomedia to have been the place of her contest, and assigns her not to the time of Maximian but rather to the time of Maximinus, who succeeded Alexander.], virgin, of Heraclius [Note: Perhaps more correctly, with the Hieronymian Martyrology, Heraclea, which is the name of a place rather than of a martyr.], Christianus, Pudens, and Victor. And at Laodicea, of Felix. A. T. L., In Laodicea, the feast of Saints Felix, Heraclius, and Prudentius [T., Pudens]. On the same day at Orléans, in the place called Floriacum [Col. 1124B], the bringing of the body of Saint Benedict [Note: The first translation to Floriacum is discussed above, on July 11. After Saint Benedict’s body had been deposited at Floriacum, it changed locations several times. When the Norman disaster broke out, it was carried here and there through Burgundy, wherever the storm drove it, and it remained for some time at Orléans in the church of Saint Aignan, until, when affairs had been restored to peace, it was brought back to Floriacum. The ancient authors give two possible origins for this feast, one of which may be called primary and the other secondary. The primary explanation is given by Adelbertus, Adrevaldus, Saint Odo the abbot, and others: namely, that on this day Saint Benedict was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary. For when Saint Benedict’s body had been transferred from Monte Cassino and deposited in the Floriacum monastery in the oratory of Saint Peter, it remained there until a suitable place was prepared for it in the church of Saint Mary. Adelbertus the monk, and Aimoinus after him, in the little book On the Translation of Saint Benedict, relate that it was finally placed there on the day before the Nones of December. From that time the day of the burial was celebrated both at Floriacum [Col. 1124C] and in most monasteries of Gaul. The secondary explanation is the return, or bringing, of Saint Benedict’s body from the city of Orléans to the monastery of Floriacum, which took place around the beginning of Carloman’s rule, about the year 883. This feast, celebrated under the name of burial, later acquired the name of bringing, and obscured the memory of the older celebration of the burial. See concerning this bringing in Mabillon’s fourth century, part II.], abbot and monk. T. adds: “At his arrival, it is said that the trees there blossomed.” A., Near Antioch, the passion of Saint Barbara, virgin. L. and T. have the same entry, omitting the place. B., At Rome, Barbara, virgin, and Pudens. In Laodicea, the metropolis, Felix and Merobius.

**5.—The Nones.** Bede has no entry.

B., The feast of Saint Dalmatius [Note: He was born in Italy to a senatorial father and preached first at Alba, then at Ticinum, where he was appointed bishop. Later, crossing into Gaul, he converted many to the faith. Afterward, while returning to his own church, he was captured by unbelievers near the river Ticinum and completed his martyrdom by being struck in the head with swords. Petrus de Natalibus. Baronius, in the Martyrology, writes that he suffered at Pavia.], martyr. V. S., of Saba [Note: Born at Mutalasca, an obscure village among the Cappadocians, to parents of distinguished rank, John and Sophia. He was born in the year 439. While still a boy, he embraced the monastic way of life in his homeland, and at eighteen years of age came to Palestine. He remained in a coenobium for seventeen years. In 484, at the age of forty-five, he undertook the priestly order and the governance of the Great Laura. In 501, the dedication of the new church of the Mother of God, built by Saint Saba the abbot, was performed by Elias, bishop of Jerusalem, on July 1, in the ninth indiction, while the great Saba was sixty-three years old. In 511, Saint Saba was sent by Bishop Elias as an envoy to the emperor Anastasius, and obtained from the emperor that Elias should not be removed from his see. Baronius correctly records in this year the death of Saint Saba the abbot, which Cyril the monk notes in his Life as having occurred on December 5, in the tenth indiction. Cotelerius published this Life of Cyril in Greek and Latin in the Monuments of the Greek Church. Baronius states in his Notes to the Martyrology that Saba’s body was transferred to Venice.], monk. C. V., In Africa, Humilis, Felix [Note: These suffered at Thagura in Numidia.], Julius, Potamia, and Victor. C. S., Saba and twenty others. V., And eight others. A. T., In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Felix, Julius, Potamia, Privatus, Fulgentius, and Crispinus. L., In Africa, the feast of Saints Felix [Col. 1125B], Privatus, Fulgentius, and seven others. And of Saint Crispina [Note: During the time of Diocletian and Maximian, because she refused to sacrifice, she was beheaded by order of the proconsul Anulinus. She suffered at Thebeste in the colony. Thebeste was in Numidia. Antoninus, Itinerary. At the solemnity of Saint Crispina, Augustine expounded Psalm 137 and mentioned her in Sermon 53 On the Words of the Lord.], virgin. B., In Africa, the feast of Saints Humilis, Felix, Julius, Potamia, Crispinus, Trophimus, and Eucarpiona. And elsewhere, of Saint Saba the confessor.

**6.—The eighth day before the Ides.** Bede has no entry.

D. S., of Nicholas [Note: He was born at Patara in Lycia and educated in liberal studies. His uncle Nicholas appointed him superior of the monastery he had built under the name of holy Zion. Burning with a desire to see Palestine, he undertook a pilgrimage to the holy places. After remaining there for an appropriate period, he returned to his homeland. Not long afterward, as the story goes, warned from heaven, he moved to Myra and was commended to the people of Myra, whose bishop had recently died; they anointed him bishop. When the fiercest persecution of Diocletian was raging, he was taken into custody, but when Constantine restored the Christian cause, he was set free. He attended the Council of Nicaea. Among his many celebrated miracles, this is said to be especially notable: although far away, he turned the emperor Constantine toward mercy by appearing to him in a vision, warning and threatening him concerning the execution of certain men. He was buried at Myra. See Surius, volume VI.], bishop of Myra in Lycia. B. C. V., Saint Nicholas, bishop. In Africa, Zetulus [B., Zelotus], Fortunatus, Gaithus [B. omits Gaithus], Hermogenes, and Rogatus. A., In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Rogatus, Hermogenes [Col. 1126A], and Fortunatus. On the same day, the burial of Saint Nicholas the confessor, through whom the Lord deigned to perform illustrious miracles. T., The burial of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor. In Africa, the feast of Saints Rogatus, Hermogenes, and Fortunatus. In Greater Asia, the feast of Saints Zelotus [Col. 1126B], Zecula, Agathius, and Fortunatus. L., In Greater Asia, the feast of Saints Zelotus and Fortunatus. And in the city of the Myreans, Saint Nicholas, bishop.

**7.—The seventh day before the Ides.** Bede has no entry.

C. V., The feast of Saint Ambrose [Note: Roman by origin, Gaul by birth; his father was Ambrose, at that time prefect of the praetorian prefecture of Gaul. Trained in every branch of learning, he pleaded cases in the court of the praetorian prefecture with such eloquence that Probus, prefect of the prefecture, took him as his adviser and soon bestowed on him the consular insignia, entrusting to his administration the provinces of Liguria and Aemilia. Saint Ambrose entered the province and established his residence at Milan. When Auxentius, bishop of that city, died in 374, and Catholics on one side and Arians on the other were fiercely disputing over the election of a new bishop, a voice like that of a child was suddenly heard among the people: “Ambrose, bishop!” Everyone acclaimed the voice. Ambrose recoiled and sought safety in flight, but at length, worn down by their entreaties, he yielded. Once made bishop, he sold his possessions and devoted himself entirely to theological studies. Around the year 374, when barbarian peoples were invading the Roman Empire, he fled into Illyricum and, taking the opportunity, also went to Rome. In 380, while the Arians were vainly raging, he appointed Anemmius bishop of Sirmium. The following year he presided over the synod of Aquileia. In 383, sent by Valentinian to Maximus the Briton, he used his authority to make the tyrant confine himself within the transalpine provinces. When Symmachus advocated the pagan cause in the dispute over restoring the altar of Victory, Saint Ambrose so surpassed him in eloquence and the truth of his case that Symmachus not only lost the case but was shortly afterward expelled from the city. The Arians, although supported by the patronage of the empress Justina and her son Valentinian, and although in 386 they demanded that the basilicas be handed over to them, were likewise defeated when Ambrose courageously opposed them. Three years later, the barbarous massacre of the Thessalonians was carried out by order of Theodosius; Ambrose therefore refused to admit him to the church until he had performed a long penance. In 392, after Valentinian was killed by the intrigues of Arbogast and Eugenius seized the tyranny, Ambrose left Milan and withdrew to Bologna, then went to Faenza and finally to Florence; after Eugenius was soon defeated, he returned home. Four years later, he died in 397, or in the following year, as Bollandus writes in his special investigation concerning the year and day of Saint Ambrose’s death.], confessor. At Spoleto, Saint Sabinus [Note: Baronius writes in his Annals that Saint Sabinus suffered in the year 301; but no edict concerning the persecution of Christians was promulgated in that year, only persecution against soldiers. Therefore the martyrs whom Baronius places before the year 303 did not suffer then. Certainly, in the Passion of Saint Sabinus, a fragment of which Baronius published and which Baluzius published in full from the Colbert manuscript, there is no chronological indication from which a certain knowledge of the year of the event can be drawn. Baluzius therefore correctly associated that martyrdom with the year 303, when persecution was in fact decreed. In his Notes he adds that Sabinus suffered martyrdom at Spoleto, but was not bishop of Assisi, since his Acts merely say that he was captured in the city of Assisi and “committed to custody in that same place together with two deacons and many clerics with them, and beaten without trial for so long until he expired.” Saint Sabinus is commemorated in various places and on various days, as Ferrarius relates in his Notes to the General Catalogue.], C., bishop and martyr. The same entry, but without the place, appears in B. D., At Alexandria, Saint Agathomus [Note: Or Agatho. When certain people were being led to execution under Decius, he stood by and drove away those who were insulting them. The people then shouted against him, and he was brought to court. After he had conducted himself bravely in that contest of piety, he was struck with an axe. ADO.], martyr and soldier. B. A. T. L., At Antioch, the city, the feast of Saints Polycarp and Theodore. At Rome [Col. 1127B], the burial of Saint Eutychianus [B., “Curationi”], bishop. In the Laetiensian [manuscript], the place is lacking in this final entry. C., At Rome, Eutychius.

**8.—The sixth day before the Ides.** Bede has no entry.

D., At Rome, of Eutychianus [Note: In the Chronicle of Damasus one reads: “Eutychianus, eight years, eleven months, and three days. He lived in the time of Aurelian, from the consulship of Aurelian III and Marcellinus until the seventh day before the Ides of December, when Carus II and Carinus were consuls. Aurelian III and Marcellinus held office in the year 275; Carus and Carinus in the year 283.” Therefore, since Eutychianus died on December 7 of the year 283, it is correctly said that he held office for eight years, eleven months, and three days, and his beginning fell exactly on January 5 of the year 275. In the Hieronymian Martyrology, on December 8, one reads: “At Rome, of Eutychianus.” Perhaps, therefore, that Martyrology records not his day of death but his day of burial. Papebrochius correctly concludes from the fact that in the longer Chronicle of the ancient pontiffs, in Anastasius, and elsewhere, Eutychianus is said to have been deposited or buried on the sixth or eighth day before the Kalends of August, that the feast day of the Roman pontiffs must be sought somewhere other than in the aforementioned authors. This may have prompted them to write of some elevation or translation performed on that day in the fifth century, under Innocent I, when he built in the cemetery of Callistus the notable basilica of Saint Sebastian at the Catacombs, over the Platonia, beneath which the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul had long lain [Col. 1128C]. In the Roman Martyrology Eutychianus is said to have suffered under Numerian. Since Baronius gives no witness to this martyrdom either in the Annals or in the Notes to that Martyrology, and since Eutychianus is placed not in the List of the Burial of Martyrs apud Bucherium but in the List of the Burial of Bishops, this holy pontiff seems to be numbered among the confessors. Certainly both lists, written under Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, are older than all the Martyrologies, and therefore great credence must be given to them. The decretal letters circulated under Eutychianus’s name are spurious.], pope and martyr, who personally buried 342 martyrs. C. B. V. A. T. L., At Rome, Saint Eusebius, bishop, and Uranius, priest, and Successus, bishop. In L., Eusebius is absent; in T. and A., the place is absent. T. adds: “And the feast of Saint Sabinus.” In V., The burial of Eutychianus, bishop. A. T. L., The Conception of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord.

**9.—The fifth day before the Ides.** Bede has no entry.

[Col. 1128B] C. V., The feast [Note: They say that this Saint was a disciple of Hermagoras, ordained by him as bishop and sent to Pavia, and that he finally died after spending fifty-eight years in the episcopate, when he was in his 112th year. Surius, volume VII; Petrus de Natalibus.] of the translation of Syrus [C., Saint Sisinnius], confessor. In Africa, Peter and Successus [C. omits Successus]. D. and L., Saint Leocadia, virgin, who in the time of Diocletian and Maximian was cruelly weakened by imprisonment under the custody of Dacianus, prefect of Spain, at Toledo [Note: Prison. When, during the persecution of Diocletian, she saw the very severe tortures of blessed Eulalia and the other martyrs whom Dacianus was killing, she knelt in prayer and gave up her spirit. Usuardus, ADO. More about her is found in the Toledan Breviary, where her deeds are sung in a sacred hymn.]. A., At Antioch, the feast of Saints Gerontius [Col. 1128C], Valentinus, and Hermogenes. T. L., At Antioch, the feast of Saints Gerontius, Valentinus, Silvana, Donata, and Agnilla. T., And Hermogenes. And the passion of Saint Leocadia, virgin. On the same day, Saint Siricius, bishop. B., In Africa, Saints Peter, Successus, Basinus, Porphyrius, and Urbanus. In Africa, Saints Generatus, Polentia, Silvana, Valentina, Felix, and Eutychianus.

**10.—The fourth day before the Ides.** The feast of Saint Eulalia [Note: The priest Donatus carefully instructed her mind at Barcelona in the first elements of the Christian faith. She suffered and was buried at Mérida in the year 303. Prudentius, hymn 3, *On the Crowns* (περὶ Στεφάνων).], virgin, in the city of Barcelona in Spain, under the governor Dacianus. When she was thirteen years old, after many tortures she was beheaded; and when her head sprang back from her, a dove was seen to emerge from her body.

T., On the same day, Saint Valeria [Note: She is venerated at Limoges in Gaul. According to the calendars and the monuments of the Church of Limoges, Ferrarius writes in the General Catalogue that she was a disciple of Saint Martial, the first bishop, converted by him to the faith, and finally beheaded because she rejected the marriage of Duke Stephen. Her body is now said to be preserved in the Cambon monastery in the diocese of Limoges. Her memory is celebrated on this day, on which she suffered martyrdom under the emperor Claudius. In the Roman Martyrology she is commemorated on the preceding day.], virgin and martyr. B., In the city of the Arverni, the feast of Saint Agricola.

[Col. 1129C] **11.—The third day before the Ides.** The feast of Saint Damasus [Note: He was the son of a certain Antonius, Spanish by nation and from Mantua Carpetana by homeland; others, however, wish him to have been from Tarragona, or from the Lusitanians at Idanha. A deacon of the Roman Church under Liberius, then a priest, and finally appointed bishop in 366, while another faction ordained the deacon Ursinus, or Ursicinus, bishop at Rome. The matter was conducted with great contention and much bloodshed on both sides, so that, as Ammianus records, 137 citizens were killed in a single day. Moreover, Damasus long raged against Ursicinus’s party with savage cruelty, if Faustinus and Marcellinus tell the truth in the preface they placed before the *Book of Petitions*. At last Ursinus was defeated, and Damasus held the see in peace. Around 369, at a synod held at Rome, he condemned Auxentius of Milan and the acts of the Council of Rimini, and confirmed the Nicene faith. In 373, he held another synod at Rome, attended by Peter, bishop of Alexandria, at which Apollinaris and his disciple Timothy were deposed for heresy. In 381, he invited the fathers of the Council of Constantinople to assemble at a synod in Rome. Damasus died in 384, as Prosper testifies in his Chronicle and the epitaph of his successor Siricius proves. Papebrochius nevertheless calls this into question in his chronological-historical investigation of the Catalogue of Pontiffs, because Marcellinus in his Chronicle places the beginning of Siricius under the consuls of the preceding year [Col. 1130D]. But Marcellinus errs so frequently in chronology when relating the affairs of this century that it is not surprising that he made a mistake in determining the beginning of Siricius’s pontificate. Jerome, in his Martyrology, assigns Damasus’s burial to December 10; but the longer Chronicle of the ancient pontiffs and the Catalogue published by Papebrochius, whose title is “Names of the Apostles,” as well as our Bede, say that it occurred on December 11. From this difference it appears that Damasus departed to God on December 10 and was buried the following day on the Via Ardeatina, in the basilica he himself had built.], pope.

Florus in A. T. L.: In Gaul, in the city of Amiens, the passion of Saints Gentianus, Victoricus, and Fuscianus. Victoricus and Fuscianus, having departed from Rome and proclaimed the word of life to many, were captured near Amiens by the governor Rictiovarus during the time of Maximian. First they were confined in prison with their hands bound behind their backs with iron; then stakes were driven into their nostrils and ears, and their heads were pierced with nails; finally they were beheaded. When the Spirit came upon them, they carried their own heads in their hands as far as the lodging of blessed Gentianus the martyr, and there they rested.

[Col. 1130C] B., At Alexandria, Sammonus and Emeritus. At Antioch, Saints Zosimus, Paul, and Cyriacus. In Gaul, in the city of Amiens, the feast of Saints Victricius and Fuscianus, martyrs. A. and T., And Praetextatus [Note: Together with Thrason, Pontianus, and many others without number, he was ordered to undergo capital punishment at Rome under Maximian. Petrus de Natalibus; Hieronymus Martyrologium.].

**12.—The second day before the Ides.** Bede has no entry.

V. B. D. A. T. C., The feast of Saints Hermogenes [Note: It is recorded in the *Treasury of Sermons*, volume II, that they were cast into a certain marsh and thus completed their martyrdom.] and Donatus. V. B. C. D., And twenty-two others. D., At Alexandria, Epimachus and Alexander [Note: Concerning these, see Eusebius, VI, 41. The Greeks celebrate the feast of Epimachus on the day before the Kalends of November, while they commemorate his translation to Constantinople on the fifth day before the Ides of March.], who, after enduring for a long time the torments and exhaustion of imprisonment in chains, steadfast in the faith, were finally ordered to be consumed by fire. L., In the district of Vimmo. T. A., The burial of Saint Walericus [Note: He was from Auvergne. He lived as a monk in the monastery of Autun and Auxerre, then at Luxeuil. King Chlothar, with the consent of the bishop of Amiens, granted him the place called Leuconaus in the district of Witmacum for habitation, and there he built a monastery. He died today, on a Sunday, while King Chlothar was alive, in the year of Christ 622. The same saint is celebrated in his monastery on two other occasions: namely, on the Kalends of April, when his translation by Bercundus, bishop of Amiens, is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology—the translation from the chapel in which his body had been buried into the monastery’s principal church; and on June 2, when his body was brought back from the monastery of Bertin by Hugh Capet in the year 981. See his Life in Mabillon’s second century of the Benedictine Acts. He is incorrectly called a bishop.], who was from Auvergne. L., Bishop. T., Confessor. A. T., In Spain, Saint Eulalia [Note: See above, the fourth day before the Ides of this month.] and another virgin, cruelly tortured.

[Col. 1131C] **13.—The Ides.** The feast of Saint Lucy, virgin, of Syracuse, under the consul-governor Paschasius. When, by Paschasius’s order, pimps wished to corrupt her, they could not move her at all, not even with ropes added and many teams of oxen harnessed to her. She received pitch, resin, and boiling oil without being harmed. Finally, struck after a sword had been thrust into her entrails, she nevertheless did not die until priests arrived and she received Communion of the Lord’s body and blood. She suffered during the time of Diocletian and Maximian.

This final entry is absent from the Laetiensian manuscript. The Atrebatian manuscript has it in a more abbreviated form at the beginning: “When, under Paschasius, she received pitch, resin, and boiling oil without harm.”

A. T. L., On the same day, in Gaul, at the city of Cambrai, the burial of Saint Autbertus [Note: Saint Autbertus flourished in the time of King Dagobert. Under him, Hainaut began wonderfully to flourish in the Christian religion, for he had as disciples there Landelinus, abbot of Crespin, Vincent Madelgarius, count, and his wife Saint Waldetrudis. He died at Cambrai around the year 668 and was buried outside the walls in the church of Saint Peter, which, after the walls were enlarged, is now inside the walls and is the abbey of Saint Autbertus. See his Life in Surius, volume VI.], bishop and confessor. A., Through whom the Lord deigned to perform illustrious miracles. T., On the same day, the burial of Saint Judocus [Note: The year in which Saint Judocus died is uncertain. Judicael, king of Lesser Brittany, wished to resign the Armorican territory to his brother Judocus in the fifteenth year of Dagobert, A.D. 636. Judocus, having obtained an eight-day delay, fled to Ponthieu, where he was the guest of Duke Haymo for seven years. In 643 he withdrew into the desert of Brachium. After spending eight years there, he moved to a place called Runiacus, where he was to remain for thirteen years—or, as it appears in Surius, fourteen. Finally, he settled at the site of his monastery; how long he remained there is uncertain. Certainly, after constructing two oratories with little difficulty and completing a journey to Rome, he soon died, as Florentius in Surius, volume VI, and an anonymous author in Mabillon’s second century relate. Judocus went to Rome before the year 665; therefore his death seems to belong to the year 668.], confessor. L., And the feast of Saint Odilia [Note: She flourished around the year 700, as is clear from the *Chronicle of Germany*.], virgin, who was born blind but healed by God and received from the sacred font by three bishops. V. C., Elsewhere, Leocandidus [C., Locandus], confessor, and Valentinus. B., At Ravenna, the feast of Saints Valentinus and Leuchadius, confessors. At Milan, the passion of the holy martyrs Gervasius [Note: Concerning these, see above, June 19.] and Protasius.

**14.—The nineteenth day before the Kalends of January.** Bede has no entry.

[Col. 1133B] Florus in A. T. L.: At Jerusalem, the passion of Saints Justus and Abundius, who, after slaps, prisons, and wheels, were handed over to the fire under the emperor Numerian and the governor Olybrius. At Lyon [L. omits “At Lyon,” etc.], the burial of Saint Viator, bishop. At Reims, the passion of Saint Nicasius [Note: These suffered in the year 453, as is clear from the Chronicle of Reims in Labbe’s *New Bibliotheca*, volume I.], bishop [and martyr, and of his sister Eutropia, virgin, together with other citizens of the same city [Note: “And martyr” through “citizens” is absent in T.]], who, after the solemn celebration of Mass had been completed, suffered martyrdom inside the church of Reims at the hands of the Vandals.

B. C. V., At Lyon, Saint Victor [V., Viator]. At Vienne, Saint Lupicinus [Note: Maurolycus and Galesinius celebrate his feast on this day, and the calendars of the Church of Vienne in Gaul agree with them.].
