At Reims, the feast of Saint Nicasius, bishop. B. adds to the first two the title “bishop” and calls it a burial. D., Saints Drusus, Zosimus, and Theodore, martyrs. B., At Antioch, the feast of Saints Drusus and his companions.

**15.—The eighteenth day before the Kalends.** Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Orléans, the burial of Saint Maximianus, priest and confessor (up to this point also B. V.), who lived in the highest devotion, and through whose merits the Lord deigned to perform many miracles.

D., Valerianus [Note: Bishop of the city of Abba in Africa. When he had fought courageously lest he surrender the divine sacraments, he was ordered to be expelled from the city alone. It was further commanded that no one should allow him to live either in a house or in the countryside. For a long time he lay naked in the public road, exposed to the air. He was more than seventy years old. Victor of Vita, *On the African Persecution*.], bishop and confessor. C. V., In Africa, Saint Faustus, Lucius, and Candidus, martyrs. A. T. L. B., In Africa, the feast of Saints Candidus [B., Candi], Caecilianus, and Faustus.

**16.—The seventeenth day before the Kalends.** Bede has no entry.

D., Three martyrs, Ananias, Azarias, and Misael. B. V., At Ravenna, the feast of Saints [Note: Valentinus was master of the soldiers; Concordius was his son; and Navalis and Agricola suffered for Christ during the persecution of Maximian. Their martyrdom is narrated by Hieronymus Ruberus in *History of Ravenna*, book II.], Valentinus, Navalis, Agricola, and Concordia. A. T. L., At Ravenna, the feast of Saints Valentinus, Navalis, and Concordius [R., and Concordius]. A., In Tuscany, the passion of Saint Barbara [Note: She was first afflicted for a long time by her father Dioscorus under harsh confinement; then handed over to the governor Martianus, stripped, beaten severely with sinews and leather thongs, and torn apart, while her wounds were rubbed with sackcloth. Then she was shut in prison. Soon burning lamps were applied to her sides, her head was battered with hammers, and her breasts were cut off. Next she was led naked through the streets and tormented for a very long time with whips. At last she completed her martyrdom by the sword. ADO.], virgin, under the emperor Maximian. T., And the passing of Saint Everardus [Note: He rests at Cisoing in the monastery of Saint Callistus, which belongs to the canons of the order of Saint Augustine between the Isles and Tournai. He was duke of Friuli, but distinguished for the holiness of his life, and gave the Cisoing monastery its beginning. Meierus dates this to the year 838. The feast of his burial is December 16; that of his translation is December 10. Molanus, in the *List of the Saints of Belgium*.], confessor. B., At Arles, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Genesius [Note: His feast is celebrated on August 25.], martyr.

[Col. 1134C] **17.—** [Note: C. reverses this day with the following one.] **The sixteenth day before the Kalends.** The feast of Saint Ignatius [Note: Saint Ignatius’s sacred bones, initially deposited at Rome in a distinguished place, were later brought back to Antioch. The Greeks celebrate this solemnity on January 29, but the Latins on December 17. Among the Latins, only Galesinius celebrates this translation in January—not, however, on the 29th, following the Greek custom, but on the 18th. Chrysostom describes this translation in a homily. Galesinius writes that the translation took place in the year immediately following the martyrdom.], bishop and martyr, who was the third bishop of Antioch after the apostle Peter and, in the twelfth year of Trajan, was sent bound to Rome for the beasts. His bodily remains nevertheless lie at Antioch [up to this point A. and T.], outside the Daphne Gate [Note: The remains were later transferred under Theodosius the Younger to the temple of Tyche.], in the cemetery of the church.

[Col. 1135B] T., On the same day, Saints Lazarus and Martha, his sister. C. V., In Africa, Victurus, Victor, and thirty-three others, and [Col. 1135C] Victorinus, Adiutor, and Quartus. B., In Africa, the feast of Saints Victonus, Victorianus, Adiutor, Honoratus, Vincentius, Felix, and twenty-four others.

**18.—The fifteenth day before the Kalends.** Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Jerusalem, the passion of Saints Alexander [Note: This is another Alexander, distinct from that Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, who assisted Narcissus when he was already advanced in age.], bishop, and Theodolus. Alexander was suspended on the torture frame and afterward handed over to the fire together with Theodolus under the emperor Aurelian.

D., Blessed martyrs Rufus [Note: They rest in the city of Philippi in Macedonia.] and Zosimus, who were among the first disciples, through whom the Church was first founded among Jews and Greeks. C. V. T., At Laodicea, Saints Theotenus and Basilianus. V. C., In Africa, Saint Quintus [Note: Quintus was bishop in Mauretania during the time of the emperor Decius; Saint Cyprian’s Letter 71 to him is extant. He is also addressed in other letters of Cyprian. He suffered with Saint Simplicius and others, whose names are found in Jerome’s Martyrology, during the time of the emperor Valerian.]. V. T. C., Elsewhere, the passion of Saint Afra. A. T., In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Vincentius and Rogatianus. A., And the passion of Saint Luke, virgin. T., At Rome, the feast of Saints Antonius, Erenaeus, and Theodore. B., At Laodicea, the city, the feast of Saints Quintus, Simplicius, Paulus, Victoria, and Privatus. And elsewhere, the feast of Saints Dignus and Badegisilus, and Honoratus with thirty others.

[Col. 1136C] **19.—The fourteenth day before the Kalends.** Bede has no entry.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Auxerre, the burial of Blessed Gregory [Note: Concerning him, the history of the bishops of Auxerre in Labbe’s *New Bibliotheca*, volume I, says: “Gregory sat for twelve years and six months; and when the term of his office had been completed, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, laying aside his human condition, he received his final honor in the church of blessed Germanus. He spent eighty-four years in all of his life. He lived in the time of the Roman pontiffs Silverius and Vigilius, while Justinian was emperor.”], bishop and confessor, who, as his book of deeds reveals, possessed such great sobriety that, placed in the midst of the world, he shone forth as a new hermit and often manifested himself through many miracles.

D., In Egypt, blessed Nemesius, martyr, who was first denounced to the judge Aemilianus on a false accusation, as though he were a thief [Note: Later, after he had disproved this accusation before the centurion, he was denounced as a Christian and brought in chains before the prefect. That most wicked judge, after afflicting him with tortures and beatings twice as severe as those inflicted on the other thieves, ordered him to be burned among the thieves. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VI, 41.]. B. C. V., At Nicaea [Note: A city of Bithynia, in B.’s text.], a city of Bithynia, Saints Zosimus, Paul, Secundinus, and Quintus. At Auxerre, the burial of Blessed Gregory, bishop. A., And the feast of Saint Cyricus. L., Zosimus and Cyricus. T., And Paul in the city of Nicaea in Bithynia.

**20.—The thirteenth day before the Kalends.** Bede has no entry.

D. The blessed martyrs Ammon, [Note: [Col. 1136D] Ammon. While they were standing before the tribunals, and a certain Christian undergoing torture was trembling and already almost inclined to deny the faith, they tried to encourage him by their expression, eyes, and gestures. When, for this reason, the whole crowd’s outcry burst against them, they came forward into the midst and declared that they were Christians. Through their victory Christ, who had given them such steadfastness of soul, triumphed most gloriously. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI, 41.] Zeno, Ptolemy, Ingenus, and Theophilus. B. C. V. In Thrace, in the city of Gildoba, [Note: [Col. 1137B] In the city of Gildoba, in B alone.] the feast of St. Julius. [Note: [Col. 1137B] Gildoba. Pliny, book XIX, chapter 5, says that Gelduba is a fortress situated on the Rhine; we find no other Gelduba. Baronius, in the Notes.] At Rome, St. Zephyrinus, bishop. [Note: [Col. 1137B] Zephyrinus. Zephyrinus died in the year 217, during the consulship of Praesens and Extricatus, on 10 July; he began his pontificate in 197, on 10 August. In both this and the Hieronymian Martyrology his feast is recorded today; in the other Martyrologies followed by Baronius, on 26 August. Both dates, however, should be referred to his translations. Papebrochius, in his *Chronological-Historical Attempt toward the Chronology of the Ancient Pontiffs*, believing that the feast-days of Roman pontiffs are recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrology, connected Zephyrinus’s death with 20 December 217. Since it is certain that Callistus, his successor, was already seated before that date, he says that Zephyrinus had appointed him as his vicar; but such vicariates are plainly spurious. The letters of Zephyrinus that circulate are fictitious.] In the East, St. Thecla. [Note: [Col. 1137C] “In the East, St. Thecla” is absent in B.] The feast of St. Liberatus. [Note: [Col. 1137C] Liberatus. According to Bede, the Vulgate Martyrology, and Baronius, he suffered at Rome together with Bajulus; Usuard, however, treats Liberatus alone, as though he had suffered at Amphitrea.] A. T., The feast of St. Anastasius. [Note: [Col. 1137C] Anastasius. At Antioch, St. Anastasius, bishop, who was most savagely killed by the Jews under the emperor Phocas. The author of the Alexandrian Chronicle says that in the sixth year after the consulship of Phocas Augustus: “The prefect of the poorhouses reported, in the month of September, in the fourteenth indiction, that Anastasius of Antioch had been killed by soldiers.” He was therefore killed in the year of Christ 610. Baronius celebrates Anastasius on the following day.] A. T. L., At Rome, the deposition of St. Zephyrinus. In the East, the feast of St. Liberatus. T., At the Bear with the Cap, the feast of St. Pontianus.

### 21.—XII Kalends of January

The feast of St. Thomas the Apostle. [Note: [Col. 1137D] Thomas. He preached the Gospel to the Parthians, as Eusebius attests, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 1; Socrates I, 19; and Clement in book IX of the *Recognitions*. It also seems certain that he spread the faith of Christ among the Indians, as Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 25; Jerome, Letter 148; Ambrose, on Psalm XLV; Paulinus; and other holy Fathers testify. Among them, Gaudentius and others, together with the older Martyrologies, say that he ended his life there, indeed by martyrdom. Concerning his translation to Edessa, see above, 5 July.]

Florus adds in A. T. L.: “He suffered in India, for he died pierced through with a lance; his body was then translated to the city of Edessa.” T., 5 July.

B. C. V. A. T. L., At Rome, St. Innocent, bishop. [Note: [Col. 1137D] Innocent. An Italian by nation and Alban by birth, he became Roman bishop toward the end of the year 401. After assuming the episcopate, he began to wage serious disputes with the Eastern bishops concerning St. John Chrysostom, whose cause he had vigorously defended. While Chrysostom was alive, he strengthened him by his authority and consoling letters, and after his death he did not abandon his cause; rather, he stubbornly refused communion with the Eastern bishops until Chrysostom’s name was restored to the sacred diptychs. In 409, Honorius sent him as an envoy to Alaric, king of the Goths, who was bringing an army against Rome, so that he might turn the barbarians away from the siege. The embassy failed, but Innocent was removed from the city in this way and remained at Ravenna, seeing from afar the miserable ruin of his see. He spent the remainder of his life opposing the Novatians and Pelagians. Zosimus, book V, falsely accused Innocent of permitting the pagans, when Alaric was already threatening Rome, secretly to perform their ancient rites and sacrifices. Against Zosimus, a pagan writer, one may set Socrates IX, 7, and Sozomen VII, 9. In recounting the siege of Rome and the machinations of the pagans, they are entirely silent on this matter—something they certainly would not have done had Innocent committed such a crime, since their hatred of the Novatian sect had made him hateful to them. He died in 417, not on 28 July, as Baronius maintains. For from a rescript of Zosimus, Innocent’s successor, it is certain that Zosimus was already governing the Roman Church on 25 March of that year; rather, Innocent died on 12 March, as is clear from very many Martyrologies. Nor did he die on 21 December of the preceding year, as Papebrochius argues in his *Chronological-Historical Attempt*. Besides the fact that it is established that he lived into the beginning of this year, since he condemned the Pelagians in January, on that reckoning he would have occupied the see only fourteen years, eleven months, and twenty-one days—something the catalogues of pontiffs do not permit, since they agree that Innocent exceeded fifteen years, although Papebrochius believes this without the authority of any Anastasian Codex or catalogue of pontiffs. Perhaps, therefore, his ordination is celebrated today, for Innocent was ordained on this day; or at least some translation occurred on the day of his ordination. See above, 12 March.] A. T., And the passion of St. Honoratus, bishop. C., And the passion of St. Phocas. B., At Heraclea, the feast of St. Passus. And elsewhere, the passion of Saints Phocas, Florius, Honoratus, bishop and confessor.

D., At Châlons, St. Memmius, [Note: [Col. 1138D] Memmius. See concerning him 5 August.] the first bishop of that city, sent from Rome, who, among countless other miracles, raised a dead man. His tomb is now made illustrious by very frequent miracles. And in Tuscany, John and Festus; but perhaps these belong to the following day, on which St. Thomas is incorrectly recorded in this manuscript.

### 22.—XI Kalends

Bede has nothing.

C. V., At the Two Laurels, the feast of the thirty martyrs, [Note: [Col. 1138D] Thirty. They suffered during the persecution of Diocletian.] all of whom were crowned on one day. A. T. L. B., At Rome, on the Lavican Way, the feast of the thirty holy martyrs, who were crowned on one day. A. T., At Rome, the deposition of St. Felix, bishop. L. adds: “of Porto.” A. T. B., And the passion of St. Theodosia, virgin. And of Didymus the monk, B. At the Roman harbor, the feast of St. Aristus and St. Felix, bishop. On the same day, the passion of St. Gregory the martyr. [Note: [Col. 1139D] Under Diocletian, he was first beaten with knotted clubs, then, after the rack and prison, struck on the knees with iron thorns; he was also burned at the sides with blazing lamps, and finally beheaded.]

### 23.—X Kalends

The deposition of St. Victoria at Rome under Decius. [Note: [Col. 1139D] Victoria. According to Usuard and Ado, she suffered at Rome; according to Peter de Natalibus, near the city of Tibur.] She had been betrothed to the pagan Eugenius, but when she would neither marry nor sacrifice, after performing many miracles—including bringing many virgins into the service of the Lord—she was struck with a sword by the executioner Taliarchus, an attendant of the temples, at the request of her fiancé. She was buried on the tenth day before the Kalends, that is, on this day.

C. V., On the same day, St. Gregory, martyr of Spoleto, and another nine hundred and thirty. [Note: [Col. 1139D] Thirty. The persecution of Diocletian made them martyrs of Christ through the most grievous torments. Usuard, Ado. Concerning the Nicomedian martyrs who suffered in this persecution, Eusebius writes, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, 5–6.] A. T., At Rome, the feast of Saints Eleutherius and Cornelius. B., At Rome, the feast of Saints Eugenius, Eleutherius, Urbanus, Cornelius, Trajan, Victor, Castula, and eight hundred and thirty others. At Nicomedia, the feast of thirty-five martyrs. And elsewhere, the feast of Saints John and Felix. L., On the same day, the arrival of the relics of St. Lambert, martyr and pontiff. [Note: [Col. 1139D] Lambert. In 1143, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, according to Jacques Chapeaville in the notes to Bishop Stephen’s prologue to the *Life of St. Landebert*, the relics of the blessed Lambert were solemnly transferred at Liège from the vessel in which St. Hubert, bishop, had placed them after the martyr’s passion into another vessel, splendidly made in his honor, in the presence of Bishop Albero and a large gathering of nobles and clergy. Among others, Unedericus, the third abbot of Laetia, attended this re-entombment and carried back to Laetia great gifts: namely, a bone from the martyr’s body and some of the ashes both of his flesh and of the garments and bed on which he was first buried, and so forth. The feast of St. Lambert is celebrated on 17 September.] The revered lord Unedricus, third abbot of this place, had devoutly obtained these relics from Albero II, bishop of Liège, and on 23 December solemnly brought them into the Church of Laetia, instituting that the memory of that day should thereafter be solemnly celebrated each year.

### 24.—IX Kalends

The vigil of the Lord’s Nativity.

D., Near Antioch in Syria, the feast of forty holy virgins, who completed their martyrdom through various torments during the persecution of Decius. V., The feast of forty holy virgins. A. T. L., At Rome, the feast of Saints Metrobius, Paul, and Lucian. [Note: [Col. 1140D] At Rome. According to Usuard, Rabanus, and Baronius, these suffered at Tripoli.]

### 25.—VIII Kalends

The Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ.

Florus adds in A. and L.: “He foresaw in the power of his divinity the time of his birth and chose the mother through whom he would be born.”

And St. Eugenia, virgin. [Note: [Col. 1141D] Eugenia. The daughter of Philip, prefect of Alexandria under the emperor Gallienus, she assumed male clothing and entered a monastery with her companions Pratus and Hyacinthus, later becoming its abbess. After many distinguished deeds, she endured a long struggle under Nicetius, prefect of the city, and was finally beheaded. Her Acts, written by Metaphrastes, are found in Surius, volume VI. They nevertheless contain some details requiring criticism, such as the statement that Philip, Eugenia’s father, became bishop of Alexandria. The catalogues of the bishops of Alexandria, described by Eusebius in the *Chronicle* and *Ecclesiastical History*, clearly show that this is entirely fictitious.]

On the same day, the feast of St. Anastasia. At the time of Diocletian she first endured a harsh and cruel confinement imposed by her husband Publius; yet during it she was greatly consoled and strengthened by Chrysogonus, confessor of Christ. [Note: [Col. 1142D] Chrysogonus. Concerning him, who converted Anastasia to the faith, see 24 November.] Then she was tormented by the prefect of Illyricum in an equally severe and prolonged imprisonment (up to this point A.), during which she was nourished for two months with heavenly food by St. Theodota, who had previously suffered martyrdom. She was then placed on a ship with two hundred men and seven hundred women and taken to the Palmaria Islands to be drowned. There she was stretched out by her hands and feet, tied to fixed stakes, and a fire was kindled around her. In it she completed her martyrdom, while all who had come with her likewise glorified martyrdom through various forms of execution.

Florus in A. T. L. prefixed: “At Sirmium.”

B., At Constantinople, St. Anastasius.

### 26.—VII Kalends

The feast of St. Stephen, protomartyr.

Florus in A. T. L.: “In the Jerusalem district, in the village of Caphargamala, the passion of St. Stephen, who, ordained a Levite by the apostles, was the first after the Lord’s ascension to complete his martyrdom when the Jews stoned him” (up to this point A.). He saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of the power of God; commending his spirit to him and praying for his persecutors, he fell asleep beneath a shower of stones.

B. C. V., At Rome, St. Dionysius, bishop. [Note: [Col. 1143C] Dionysius. According to the Chronicle of Pope Damasus, he became pontiff in 259, during the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, and died in 269, during the consulship of Claudius and Paternus. Some discuss him on the following day; but when writers differ by only one day concerning the death of a pontiff, one should understand one as referring to the day of death and the other to the day of burial. In the Hieronymian Martyrology, under 14 September, we read: “The deposition of St. Dionysius, bishop.” It is certain, however, that this records not his day of death but some translation or elevation.] T., On the same day at Rome, the passion of St. Marinus. [Note: [Col. 1143D] Of senatorial rank, he was arrested under the emperor Numerian and the prefect Marcianus on account of the Christian religion. He was punished in the servile manner with the rack and hooks, then thrown into a frying pan; but when the fire was changed into dew, he was freed. He was also thrown to wild beasts, which left him unharmed. Finally he was led again to an altar, and when the idols fell at his prayer, he obtained martyrdom by the sword. Peter de Natalibus.] B., At Antioch, Julian and Marcian.

### 27.—VI Kalends

The feast of St. John, apostle and evangelist, the beloved of the Lord.

Florus in A. T. L. begins: “At Ephesus,” and then continues: “The one whom the Lord loved not only above the others but also more familiarly than the others. He reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the supper; later, when the Lord had been lifted upon the cross, he entrusted the Virgin Mother to the virgin.” (Up to this point A.) Compared among the four living creatures with the eagle, he perceived the divinity of Christ more clearly than all the others and proclaimed it in writing at the beginning of his Gospel.

T. L. B., On the same day, the ordination to the episcopate of St. James, the brother of the Lord, who was the first of the Jews to be ordained bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles. [Note: [Col. 1143D] Ordination. “James was ordained bishop of the Church established at Jerusalem,” says Eusebius in the *Chronicle*—certainly in the same year in which Christ was crucified, rose, and ascended into heaven, a year marked by the consulship of the two Gemini and corresponding to A.D. 29. Jerome confirms this in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he concludes his notice of James with these words: “He governed the Church at Jerusalem for thirty years, until the seventh year of Nero,” which is A.D. 66. His ordination is therefore celebrated today. This also relates to what Eusebius says, *Ecclesiastical History* VII, 19: “The chair of that James . . . preserved down to our own times, the brothers of that Church have continued from their ancestors to honor with great reverence.” His feast is celebrated on 1 May. The Church of Milan celebrates his ordination on 29 December. Ferrari, in the *General Catalogue*.] B., And in the middle of Easter he was crowned with martyrdom. V. C., And St. James, the brother of the Lord.

### 28.—V Kalends

The feast of the holy Innocents.

Florus in A. T. L. adds: “They bore witness to Christ not by speaking but by dying, and through a blessed death were brought to completion by Herod’s impiety.”

V., The feast of Eutychius, presbyter, Domitian, deacon, and Castorius. [Note: [Col. 1144D] Eutychius. They suffered at Ancyra in Galatia; Castorius, however, in Africa. Jerome, *Martyrology*.]

### 29.—IV Kalends

Bede has nothing.

D., David, king. At Arles, St. Trophimus, bishop and confessor, disciple of the apostles Peter and Paul. [Note: [Col. 1144D] Trophimus. Gregory of Tours I, 28, wishes Trophimus to have been made bishop by the Roman pontiff and sent to Arles in the consulship of Decius and Gratus, that is, in 250, as the first bishop of that see. But another tradition is much more celebrated: it teaches that Trophimus was sent from Rome to Arles in the age of the apostles. The authority of Gregory of Tours is completely overturned by the letter in Cyprian’s works concerning Marcianus, who was bishop of Arles under Decius, Gallus, and Valerian.]

V. C., In Africa, Crescentius, Primianus, Secundus, Saturninus, and Honoratus. At Rome, Felix and Boniface, bishops—the latter also appearing first in A. T. L. In Africa, Saints Domitius, Victurus, Primianus, Honoratus, Saturus, and Felix. L., And the passion of St. Thomas, archbishop and martyr of Canterbury. [Note: [Col. 1145C] Thomas. By nationality an Englishman and by civic origin a Londoner, he was instructed in the first elements of learning by the prior of Merton. He studied first at Oxford and then at Paris. Returning to England, he was admitted among the household of Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury. The archbishop soon sent him to Bologna to learn canon law. On his return he was endowed with the archdeaconry of Canterbury, the provostship of Beverley, the rectories of Bromfield and Mount St. Mary, and two prebends, one at Paul’s and the other at Lincoln. He was soon summoned to court and made lord chancellor of England. After Theobald’s death, he was raised to the see of Canterbury in 1162 and consecrated on Pentecost. After he had opposed the royal right to punish the English clergy according to the ancient customs of the kingdom for several years, and had become burdensome to the king and kingdom, he was killed at Canterbury by four royal retainers, though without royal authorization, at the end of 1170. Six books of his letters survive, collected and arranged long ago by John of Salisbury, together with many letters by others to Thomas and concerning him. Christian Lupus brought this collection to light at Brussels and saw it published along with the *Quadrilogue*, or Life of Thomas, once composed from four authors.]

B., At Rome, Felix and Boniface, bishops, concerning the ordination. In the district of Oximus, at Oticus Monastery, the deposition of St. Ebrulfus, confessor. [Note: [Col. 1145D] Ebrulfus. Born of noble stock and originating from the city of Bayeux, he was born in 517. At the urging of friends he married; after his wife had taken the veil, he withdrew to a monastery, and from there to the hermitage of Oximus or Uticus with three companions, where he built cells around the year 560. He regularly established fifteen other monasteries for men and women, whose names have been lost. In the two manuscript Chronicles of the monastery of Uticus, now called that of St. Ebrulfus, St. Ebrulfus is said to have been born in 517 and to have died in 596. William of Jumièges agrees, book VII, chapter 23, in these words: “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 596, in the eightieth year of his age, while Gregory, supreme teacher and apostle of the English, occupied the apostolic see, the blessed Ebrulfus departed this life on 29 December.” See Mabillon, *Benedictine Acts*, first century.]

### 30.—III Kalends

Bede has nothing.

Florus in A. T. L.: At Tours, the deposition of Bishop Perpetuus and confessor, [Note: [Col. 1146D] Perpetuus. See concerning him above, 8 April. It is uncertain which day was St. Perpetuus’s feast. In the older Martyrologies, however, it is recorded on 30 December.] who, when he removed the body of the blessed Martin with a great and religious vow, obtained an angelic visitation.

D., Near Spoleto, the passion of St. Sabinus, bishop, and of Exuperantius and Marcellus, deacons, and of Venustianus with his wife and children under the emperor Maximian Augustus. [Note: [Col. 1146D] Sabinus. The governor Venustianus ordered Sabinus’s hands to be cut off; Marcellus and Exuperantius were hung on the rack, severely beaten with clubs, scraped with hooks, roasted at the sides until they gave up their spirit, and their bodies thrown into the river. Sabinus, however, was cast into a filthy prison. When the governor Venustianus was afflicted with pain in his eyes and could find no remedy, Sabinus baptized him with his wife and children, and all the eye pain immediately disappeared. When Maximian heard this, he ordered Lucius the tribune to behead Venustianus with his wife and children, but to beat the holy Sabinus to death with leaded clubs. Serena buried his body near Spoleto. Ado.]

V. T., In Alexandria, Mansuetus (up to this point T. and B.), Severus, Appianus [Securi, Apanis], Donatus, Honorius, B., Poledisius. On the island, [Note: [Col. 1146D] “On the island,” namely Oia.] Saints Florentius, Serenus, Paul, Stephen, Papianus, and Cleteogenes. At Tours, Perpetuus, bishop and confessor.

### 31.—II Kalends

The deposition of St. Silvester, bishop. [Note: [Col. 1147B] Silvester. In the catalogue of Damasus we read: “Silvester, twenty-one years and eleven months. He lived in the time of Constantius, from the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, beginning on the day before the Kalends of February, until the Kalends of January, when Constantine and Albinus were consuls,” that is, in the year 335. Papebrochius, in his *Chronological-Historical Attempt*, thinks that the catalogue of Damasus should read “until the day before the Kalends of January.” Nevertheless, nothing seems to require alteration: the author of the aforementioned catalogue excludes the Kalends of January but does not include them. His Acts are spurious.]

Florus places before this in A. T. L.: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Priscilla, on the Salarian Way.” He then adds: “He was the thirty-third ruler of the Roman Church after the blessed Peter, and governed it for twenty-two years, made wondrous by miracles of virtue and by the teachings of his preaching.”

And the passion of St. Columba, virgin, at Sens, under the emperor Aurelian: after overcoming the fire, she was slain.

C. V., At Rome, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of the Jordans, Donata, Paulina, Rusticiana, Nominanda, Serotina, Saturninus, Hilariana [C., Hilaria], Retiaria, Hermes, and the Exorcist. In the province of Sicily, in the city of Catania, Stephen, Pontianus, Attalus, Flavianus, Cornelius, Sextus, Floridus, Quintianus, Menerbinus, and Symphorianus. B., Donatus and Paulus.

# Appendices to Bede’s Martyrology

## First Appendix: The Anglican Calendar, or Annual Booklet of the Venerable Bede the Priest

[Martène, *Amplissima Collectio Veterum Scriptorum*.]

## January

The month of January has thirty-one days and thirty lunar days.

On the Kalends of January: the Circumcision of Our Lord Jesus Christ; the feast of St. Basil, confessor; and of Almachius, martyr.

On the fourth day before the Nones: at Jerusalem, the octave of St. Stephen; at Antioch, Sindonius, bishop; and elsewhere, Macarius, abbot.

On the third day before the Nones: the feast of St. Genevieve, virgin, and of St. Antherus, pope and martyr.

On the second day before the Nones: in Africa, Aquilinus, Martianus, and Quintus.

On the Nones of January: the vigil of the Epiphany and the deposition of St. Simeon, who stood on a pillar.

On the eighth day before the Ides: the Epiphany of Our Lord Jesus Christ and St. Melanius, bishop.

On the seventh day before the Ides: at Nicomedia, Lucian, presbyter of the Church of Antioch.

On the sixth day before the Ides: the feast of the holy martyrs Lucian, Maximian, and Julian.

On the fifth day before the Ides: in Africa, Epictetus, Jocundus, Quintus, and Saturninus.

On the fourth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Paul, first hermit.

On the third day before the Ides: the Lord’s departure from Egypt, and the feast of St. Salvius.

On the second day before the Ides: the feast of St. Quiriacus, Moscentius, and Saturus.

On the Ides of January: the octave of the Epiphany and the deposition of the holy confessors and bishops Hilary, Remigius, and Agricola of Trier.

On the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February: the feast of St. Felix, bishop and martyr, on the Pincian Hill.

On the eighteenth day before the Kalends: at Antioch, Licerius, deacon, and the deposition of the prophet Habakkuk.

On the seventeenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Marcellus, pope, and the deposition of Honoratus, bishop.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Antony, monk, and St. Sulpicius, bishop. The sun enters Aquarius.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Prisca, virgin.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Marius and Martha, martyrs.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Fabian and Sebastian, martyrs.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Agnes, virgin.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Vincent, martyr.

On the tenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Emerentiana, virgin, and St. Macarius, martyr.

On the ninth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Babylas, bishop, and of the Three Children.

On the eighth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Praejectus, martyr, and the conversion of St. Paul the Apostle.

On the seventh day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Polycarp, bishop.

On the sixth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. John Chrysostom.

On the fifth day before the Kalends: the Nativity of St. Agnes, virgin and martyr.

On the fourth day before the Kalends: at Trier, the deposition of St. Valerius, bishop and confessor.

On the third day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Flavianus, martyr, and the deposition of Aldegundis, virgin.

On the second day before the Kalends: the feast of Tarsicius, Zotikus, Ammonius, and St. Concordius, martyrs.

In this month the night has sixteen hours and the day eight.

## February

The month of February has twenty-eight days and twenty-nine lunar days.

On the Kalends of February: the feast of Saints Publius and Saturninus and St. Brigid, virgin.

On the fourth day before the Nones: the Purification of St. Mary. In Africa, the feast of St. Victor.

On the third day before the Nones: in Africa, Felix, Celerina, and Felicitas, and the deposition of St. Lupicinus, bishop.

On the second day before the Nones: the feast of St. Gelasius and the passion of St. Eulalia, virgin.

On the Nones of February: the feast of St. Agatha, virgin.

On the eighth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Vedast, bishop and confessor. At Elnone, St. Amandus, bishop and confessor.

On the seventh day before the Ides: the feast of St. Augulus, bishop and martyr. Spring begins and has ninety-one days.

On the sixth day before the Ides: the deposition of St. Paul, bishop, Dionysius, and Lucius.

On the fifth day before the Ides: the feast of Alexander and Ammonius.

On the fourth day before the Ides: the feast of Soteris and Saints Zotikus, Erenaeus, and Hyacinthus, and of St. Scholastica, virgin.

On the third day before the Ides: the feast of Desiderius, bishop, and St. Euphrasia, virgin.

On the second day before the Ides: the feast of St. Eulalia, virgin, and the passion of Damian.

On the Ides of February: the feast of St. Polyuctus, martyr.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March: the feast of Saints Valentine, Vitalis, Felicula, and Zeno, martyrs.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Castula, Magnus, and Saturninus.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Onesimus and St. Juliana. The sun enters Pisces.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Polychronius, bishop.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Rutulus, Silvanus, and Secundinus.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Publius, Julian, and Marcellus.

On the tenth day before the Kalends: the deposition of St. Gagius, bishop, and Victor.

On the ninth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Hilary, pope, and the deposition of St. Felix, bishop.

On the eighth day before the Kalends: at Antioch, the Chair of St. Peter, and the feast of St. Thecla, virgin.

On the seventh day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Polycarp, presbyter, and St. Serenus, monk.

On the sixth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Matthias, apostle; the finding of the head of the Lord’s Forerunner; and the feast of St. Sergius, martyr.

On the fifth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Justus and Erenaeus.

On the fourth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Felix with his companions; likewise the feast of St. Nestor and Fortunatus.

On the third day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Leander and Dionysius.

On the second day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Publius, Justus, Theophilus, and Felix.

In this month the night has fourteen hours and the day ten.

## March

The month of March has thirty-one days and thirty lunar days.

On the Kalends of March: the feast of St. Donatus, martyr, and St. Albinus, confessor.

On the sixth day before the Nones of March: the feast of St. Luke, bishop, Primitiva, and Secundilla.

On the fifth day before the Nones: the feast of Fortunatus, Felix, and Claudianus.

On the fourth day before the Nones: the feast of St. Lucius, pope, and Hadrian, martyr.

On the third day before the Nones: the feast of St. Phocas, martyr. (The death of Hrotgangus, bishop, in another hand.) Seventh embolism.

On the second day before the Nones: the feast of Saints Victor and Victorinus. Third embolism.

On the Nones of March: the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicitas.

On the eighth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Quintolus, bishop, and Pontius, deacon.

The first incension of the Paschal moon.

On the seventh day before the Ides: the feast of Saints Felix, Rogatus, and Philip.

On the sixth day before the Ides: the feast of Saints Alexander and Caius.

On the fifth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Heraclius and Zosimus.

On the sixth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Gregory, pope.

On the third day before the Ides: the feast of St. Machedonius, presbyter.

On the second day before the Ides: the feast of St. Leo, pope and martyr, and of Felix and Davitus.

On the Ides of March: the feast of the holy martyrs Longinus and Lucius.

On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April: the feast of Saints Cyriacus and Castor, martyr.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Patrick, bishop, and St. Gertrude, virgin.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Alexander, bishop, and Collegus, deacon. The sun enters Aries.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Theodore, bishop, Bassus, and Apollonius.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Cuthbert, bishop and confessor.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Benedict, abbot. The spring equinox.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Paul, confessor. First Easter and the seat of the epacts.

On the tenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Fidelis and Theodore.

On the ninth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Seleucus and Agapitus. The place of the concurrents.

On the eighth day before the Kalends: the Annunciation of the archangel to St. Mary, and the Lord was crucified.

On the seventh day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Castulus and the deposition of Chilianus, bishop.

On the sixth day before the Kalends: the Resurrection of Our Lord Jesus Christ and the passion of Alexander, martyr.

On the fifth day before the Kalends: at Caesarea, Saints Rogatus and Dorotheus.

On the fourth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Gregory Nazianzen and St. Eustasius, abbot.

On the third day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Domninus, Paulinus, and Eulalia, virgin.

On the second day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Felix and Diodolus and St. Balbina, virgin.

In this month the night has twelve hours and the day twelve.

## April

The month of April has thirty days and twenty-nine lunar days.

On the Kalends of April: the feast of Saints Venantius, Anastasius, and St. Walericus.

On the fourth day before the Nones: the deposition of Nicetius, bishop, and St. Theodosia, virgin.

On the third day before the Nones: the feast of Saints Evagrius and Pancratius.

On the second day before the Nones: the feast of St. Agatho, deacon, and St. Ambrose.

On the Nones of April: the feast of Claudianus and Andronicus. The final incension of the Paschal moon.

On the eighth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Xystus, pope and martyr.

On the seventh day before the Ides: the feast of St. Celestine, pope, and Saints Timothy and Diogenes.

On the sixth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Macarius and Perpetuus.

On the fifth day before the Ides: the feast of the seven holy virgins and the blessed Demetrius, deacon.

On the fourth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Apollonius, presbyter.

On the third day before the Ides: the feast of St. Siagrius and St. Leo, pope.

On the second day before the Ides: the feast of St. Carpus, bishop, and Julius and Cyprian, bishops.

On the Ides of April: the feast of St. Euphemia, virgin.

On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May: the feast of Saints Tiburtius and Valerian.

On the seventeenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Olympias and Maximus.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Callistus and Charisius.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Peter, deacon, and Hermogenes. The sun enters Taurus.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Eleutherius, bishop, and Apollonius, senator.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Rufus and Antoninus.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Victor, bishop.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Valerian, Tiburtius, and Maximus.

On the tenth day before the Kalends: the deposition of St. Caius, pope.

On the ninth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, and the passion of St. George, martyr.

On the eighth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Mellitus, bishop, and St. Alexander.

On the seventh day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Mark the Evangelist and the greater litany. The last Easter.

On the sixth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Cletus and Marcellinus.

On the fifth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Anastasius, pope, Victor, and Maximus.

On the fourth day before the Kalends: in the city of Misitania, St. Hermogenes. At Rome, the feast of St. Vitalis, martyr.

On the third day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Germanus, presbyter.

On the second day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Dorotheus, presbyter, Viator, and Terentius.

In this month the night has ten hours and the day twelve.

## May

The month of May has thirty-one days and thirty lunar days.

On the Kalends of May: the feast of the apostles Philip and James.

On the sixth day before the Nones of June: the feast of St. Germanus and St. Anastasius.

On the fifth day before the Nones: the feast of Saints Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus, presbyter. The finding of the Holy Cross.

On the fourth day before the Nones: the feast of Saints Silvanus and Florianus, martyrs.

On the third day before the Nones: the feast of Saints Hilary and Nicetius, bishops.

On the second day before the Nones: the feast of St. John the Apostle before the Latin Gate.

On the Nones of May: the feast of St. Juvenal, martyr.

On the eighth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Victor, martyr, and St. Martin, presbyter.

On the seventh day before the Ides: the feast of Saints Quirillus, Zeno, and Macarius, abbot. Summer begins and has ninety days.

On the sixth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Gordianus, martyr, and Epimachus. And at Rome, Calepodius, presbyter.

On the fifth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Antimus and St. Mamertus, bishop.

On the fourth day before the Ides: the feast of Saints Nereus, Achilleus, and Pancratius, martyrs.

On the third day before the Ides: at Auxerre, the deposition of Marcellianus, and the feast of St. Servatius, confessor.

On the second day before the Ides: the feast of St. Victor, martyr, and St. Pachomius, monk.

On the Ides of May: the feast of the holy martyrs Isidore and Timothy.

On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June: the feast of Saints Aquilinus, Victorinus, and Peregrinus.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Heraclius and Paul, and St. Torpes, martyr.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Dioscorus. The sun enters Gemini.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Potentiana, virgin and martyr.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Basilla, virgin and martyr.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Timothy, deacon.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Faustinus and Timothy, and St. Julia, who was crowned on the cross.

On the tenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Quintus and Lucius, and St. Desiderius, bishop.

On the ninth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Donatianus and Rogatianus.

On the eighth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Urbanus.

On the seventh day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Augustine, bishop, in Kent.

On the sixth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Julius and Esinus, martyrs.

On the fifth day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Germanus, bishop and confessor, and St. John, pope.

On the fourth day before the Kalends: at Trier, St. Maximinus, bishop and confessor.

On the third day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Felix, pope.

On the second day before the Kalends: the feast of St. Petronilla, virgin.

In this month the night has eight hours and the day sixteen.

## June

The month of June has thirty days and twenty-nine lunar days.

On the Kalends of June: the feast of Saints Claudius and Pamphilus, bishops.

On the fourth day before the Nones of June: the feast of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs.

On the third day before the Nones: the feast of St. Marcellus, martyr, and St. Gudualus, confessor.

On the second day before the Nones: the feast of St. Quirinus, bishop, Pictus, and Datianus.

On the Nones of June: the feast of St. Boniface, bishop, and St. Apollinaris, martyr.

On the eighth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Saturninus, bishop, Amantius, and Lucius.

On the seventh day before the Ides: the feast of St. Lucian, martyr, and St. Macarius, monk.

On the sixth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Medardus, bishop, and Saints Nabor and Nazarius.

On the fifth day before the Ides: the feast of the holy martyrs Primus and Felicianus and St. Columba.

On the fourth day before the Ides: the feast of St. Zacharias and Barnabas, who was a companion of the apostles.

On the third day before the Ides: the feast of St. Babylas and Saints Crispulus and Restitutus.

On the second day before the Ides: the feast of the holy martyrs Basilides, Cyriacus, Nabor, and Nazarius.

On the Ides of June: the feast of Saints Lucius and Fortunatus.

On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July: the feast of Saints Rufinus and Valerius, and the translation of the body of St. Anianus.

On the seventeenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Vitus and Modestus, martyrs.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends: the feast of Saints Diogenes, Ferreolus, presbyter, and Ferrutio, deacon.

XV days before the Kalends of July. Feast of Saint Quiriacus and Avitus the presbyter. The sun enters Cancer.

XIV days before the Kalends. Feast of Saints Mark and Marcellian.

XIII days before the Kalends. Feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs.

XII days before the Kalends. Feast of Saints Paul and Cyriacus. Summer solstice.

XI days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Albinus the martyr and Saint Eusebius.

X days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint James in Persia, and of Saint Alban the martyr.

[Col. 1152C] IX days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Avitus the confessor, and vigil of Saint John the Baptist.

VIII days before the Kalends. Nativity of Saint John the Baptist.

VII days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Sosipater, disciple of Saint Paul.

VI days before the Kalends. Feast of Saints John and Paul, martyrs.

V days before the Kalends. Feast of Saints Crispinus and Crispinianus, martyrs.

IV days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Irenaeus the bishop, and vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul.

III days before the Kalends. Feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.

II days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Paul the apostle, and Saint Martial the bishop.

In this month the night has six hours, and the day eighteen.

## JULY

The month of July has thirty-one days and the moon thirty.

[Col. 1152D] On the Kalends of July. Feast of Saint Gaius the bishop; and on Mount Hor, the deposition of Aaron the priest.

VI days before the Nones of July. Feast of Saints Processus and Martinianus, martyrs, and Saint Monegundis the virgin.

V days before the Nones. In Alexandria, [the feast of] Tryphon, Menelaus, Cyril, and Julian, and of Saint Gregory the bishop and martyr.

IV days before the Nones. Feast of Saint Laurianus the bishop and martyr, and Saint Innocent.

III days before the Nones. Feast of Saints Maximus and Secundus, martyrs, and Agatho and Tryphon.

II days before the Nones. Octave of the apostles Peter and Paul, and feast of Saint Goar the confessor.

On the Nones of July. Feast of Heraclius, Parthenius, and Apollonius.

VIII days before the Ides of July. Feast of Saint Kilianus the bishop and martyr, and Saint Procopius the martyr.

VII days before the Ides. At Rome, feast of the holy virgins Floriana, Faustina, and Felicitas, and of Saint Cyril the martyr.

VI days before the Ides. Feast of the seven sons of Saint Felicitas.

[Col. 1153A] V days before the Ides. Feast of Saint Papius the confessor. At Floriacum, the arrival of Saint Benedict the abbot.

IV days before the Ides. Feast of Saints Nabor, Felix, and Primitivus, and Saint Margaret the virgin.

III days before the Ides. Feast of Saint Serapion, Zeno, and Naseus.

II days before the Ides. Deposition of Saints Justus and Amacius, bishops.

On the Ides of July. Feast of Saints Cyricus, Cassianus, and Julia.

XVII days before the Kalends of August. Feast of Saints Aquilinus, Hilarinus, Paul, and Mammeus.

XVI days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Speratus the bishop and martyr. At Milan, Saint Marcellus.

XV days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Symphorosa with her seven sons. The sun enters Leo.

XIV days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Rusticus the bishop and confessor, and Saint Arsenius the confessor.

XIII days before the Kalends. Feast of Saints Lucianus and Peter.

XII days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Praxedis the virgin, and Saint Victor the [Col. 1153B] martyr.

XI days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, and Saint Cyril at Antioch.

X days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Apollinaris the bishop and martyr.

IX days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Victorinus, Saint Christina, and Saint Glodesinda the virgin.

VIII days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint James, brother of John, and Saint Segolena the virgin.

VII days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Hyacinthus the martyr and Saints Jovianus and Martianus.

VI days before the Kalends. Feast of Saint Simeon the monk, and Saint Aetherius the bishop and martyr.
