# APPENDIX II. NECROLOGY INSERTED INTO THE VENERABLE BEDE’S MARTYROLOGY

[(Eckhart, Commentary on the Affairs of Eastern Francia.)] (C)*

[Col. 1157C] On the second day before the Nones of January: deposition of Adalramus the archbishop and Baturicus the bishop. On the second day before the Ides of January: deposition of Baturicus the bishop. Fourteen days before the Kalends of February: Walah died. Twelve days before the Kalends of February: Helmgaudus the bishop died. Eight days before the Kalends of February: Madalgarius died. Five days before the Kalends of February: [lacuna]. On the same day died the lord Charles, of most noble memory, emperor, who most sacredly adorned the kingdom of the Franks with the Catholic religion. On the Nones of March: [lacuna]. On the same day died Humbertus the bishop. On the fourth day before the Ides of March, on that same day, Kunapertus the bishop died. Twelve days before the Kalends of April: [lacuna]. On the same day Einhardus died. On the second day before the Kalends of April, Drahof died. Fifteen days before the Kalends of May, Bliddrudis died. Twelve days before the Kalends of May, Otgarius the archbishop died. Three days before the Kalends of May, death of Fonaschah. Three days before the Kalends of May, death of Adalbert the count, brother of Bauzleib and Count Hatto. Seventeen days before the Kalends of June, Brantohc.

[Col. 1157D] Twelve days before the Kalends of June, Walgerus. Ten days before the Kalends of June, Wolfehere. Seven days before the Kalends of June, Walcoum. Six days before the Kalends of June, Engilfridus. Four days before the Kalends of June: at Trier, Maximinus the bishop and Clement the presbyter, palace tutors. Two days before the Kalends of June, death of Theatmarus. On the Kalends of June, Heriuvic died. Eighteen days before the Kalends: death of Ratleicus the abbot. Eight days before the Kalends of June: death of Amolrichus the abbot. Eight days before the Ides of July: [lacuna]. On that same day Saint Kilianus the bishop was martyred at the fortress of Würzburg with his companions, Totmannus the presbyter and Colmannus the deacon, under Duke Gozbert. Nine days before the Kalends of September, Richni died. Eighteen days before the Kalends of October, Scencho the presbyter died.

[Col. 1158C] Fifteen days before the Kalends of October, Blessed Albinus the presbyter died, and Count Ebarachar. Eight days before the Kalends of October, Francho the bishop died. Four days before the Kalends of October, death of Hadeward the bishop. Six days before the Nones of October, Swab died; on the same day Wolfhardus died. Five days before the Nones of October, Blidgoz the monk died. Three days before the Nones of October, Berahtgoz the cleric. Two days before the Nones of October, death of the empress Irmingard, and of Erfrmannus the monk and Deotger the monk. Eight days before the Ides of October, death of Frechulf the bishop. Six days before the Ides of October, death of Anno the monk. Four days before the Ides of October, death of Tagulfus. On the Ides of October, death of Christiana the holy woman. Twelve days before the Kalends of November: nothing concerning the eleven thousand virgins is found recorded; but only this is added after the mention of Saints Hilarion and Asterius: “Death of Saint Christiana, holy nun.” Three days before the Kalends of November, Count Adalhelm died.

[Col. 1158D] Four days before the Nones of November: dedication of Gozbald’s church at Ochsenfurt, in honor of the holy martyrs Cyprian and Sebastian, reverently celebrated by Humbertus the bishop. Two days before the Ides of November, deposition of Wolfgarius, bishop of Würzburg. On the Ides of November, death of Hunnanus. Eleven days before the Kalends of December, a commemoration for Wolfbirin. Six days before the Ides of December, Hatto the bishop died. On the fifth of December, Christianus died. Four days before the Ides of December, deposition of Imma. Twelve days before the Kalends of January, deposition of King Pippin, son of the emperor Louis. Three days before the Kalends of January, Megina died.

THE NECROLOGY ENDS. (What follows comes after the Martyrology.)

# ON THE PLACES OF THE HOLY MARTYRS THAT ARE OUTSIDE THE CITY OF ROME

[Col. 1159A]

First, Peter rests in his body in the western part of the city, beside the Cornelian Way at the first milestone; and the pontifical order, except for a small number, rests in the same place in its own tombs. There also, beside the same road, is the seat of the apostles; and their table and couch, made of marble, are visible to this day. The table as well—which now serves as an altar and which Peter made with his own hands—is there. Beside the same road lie Saint Rufina, Saint Secunda, Saint Mary, Saint Marius, Saint Ambacus, Saint Audifax, and very many other saints.

Not far from there, on the left, beside the Aurelian Way, lie buried Saints Processus, Martianus, Pancratius, Paulinus, Arthemius, Felix, Callistus, and Calopus, together with many others. Beside the Portuensian Way, which is also in the western part of the city, Saints Abdon and Sennen, Milex and Vincentius, Polio, Julius, Pymeon, Felix, Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix sleep.

In the southern part of the city, beside the Ostian Way, the apostle Paul rests bodily, and Timothy the bishop and martyr—of whom the book of Sylvester makes mention—also sleeps there. In front of the same basilica is an oratory of Stephen the martyr. The stone with which Stephen was stoned has been placed there upon the altar. Not far from there, toward the south, is the monastery of Aqua Salviae, where the head of Saint Anastasius is kept, and the place where Paul was beheaded. Near the basilica of Paul is also the church of Saint Thecla, where she herself lies bodily. Not far from there is the church of Saint Felix, where he sleeps; when he departed to heaven, Adauctus was hastening there together with him, and both rest in one place. There too lies the martyr Nemesius with very many others.

Beside the Ardeatine Way is the church of Saint Petronilla; Saints Nereus and Achilleus are there, together with Petronilla herself, buried. Near the same road Saint Damasus the pope was laid to rest, together with his sister Martha. In another basilica not far away, Mark and Marcellian are honored; and in yet another church another Mark, together with Marcellinus, is held in honor.

Beside the Appian Way, in the eastern part of the city, is the church of Saint Soteris the martyr, where she lies with many martyrs. Beside the same road is the church of Saint Sixtus the pope, where he sleeps. There also rests Cecilia the virgin; Saint Tarsicius and Saint Gerefinus lie in one tomb. Saint Eusebius, Saint Colocerus, and Saint Parthenius lie there separately, and eight hundred martyrs rest there.

Not far from there, in the cemetery of Callistus, Cornelius and Cyprian sleep in the church. Beside the same road is a church of many saints, namely Januarius, who was the eldest of Felicitas’s seven sons; Urbanus, Agapitus, Felicissimus, Cyrinus, Zeno the brother of Valentinus, Tiburtius, and Valerianus; and many martyrs rest there.

Beside the same road is the church of Saint Sebastian the martyr, where he sleeps. There are the burial places of the apostles, in which they rested for forty years. There too the martyr Cyrinus is buried. Along the same road one reaches the city of Alba, and through that city the church of Saint Senator, where Perpetua also lies bodily, and where innumerable saints are found and great marvels take place.

Beside the Latin Way is the church of Saint Gordianus, where he rests with his brother Epimachus in one burial place. There also are Quartus and Quintus; Sulpicius and Servilianus, Saint Sophia, and Trophimus sleep buried there with many martyrs. Beside the same road: Tertullianus, and the basilica where he lies with many martyrs. The church of Saint Eugenia is also beside that road, where she lies with her mother in one tomb. There are Saint Stephen the pope with his entire clergy, thirty-eight martyrs; Saint Nemesius, Saint Olympius, Saint Symphronius, Saint Theodulus, Saint Superius, Saint Obloteris, and Saint Tiburtianus are buried there as martyrs.

Beside the Lavican Way is the church of Saint Helena, where she lies bodily. These saints sleep there: [Col. 1160A] Peter, Marcellinus, Tiburtius, the thirty holy soldiers, Gorgonius, Genuinus, Maximus, and the four crowned saints—namely Claudius, Nicostratus, Simpronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius. In crypts beneath the earth an innumerable multitude of martyrs lies buried there.

Beside the Tiburtine Way is the church of Saint Agapitus, greatly honored for the bodies of martyrs. Near the same road is the greater church of Saint Lawrence, in which his body had first been buried; and there is a new basilica of extraordinary beauty, where he now rests. Abundus is also buried beneath the same altar, and outside, in the portico, is the stone that once hung around Abundus’s neck when he was thrown into the well. There lie buried Hereneus, Julianus, Primitivus, Tacteus, Nemesius, Eugenius, Justinus, Crescentianus, and Romanus; and Saint Cyriaca, Saint Symphorosa, and Justina are buried there with many martyrs.

From there, going upward toward the north, is the basilica of Saint Hippolytus, where he lies with his entire household, nineteen martyrs. There is also the prison in which Lawrence was held. Here are Trifonia, wife of Caesar Decius, and Cyrilla, his daughter; between the two are Concordia and Saint Genesius, and many martyrs are there.

Beside the Nomentan Way is Saint Nicomedes, and beside the same road is the basilica of Saint Agnes, of extraordinary beauty, where she lies bodily; nearby is her sister Emerentiana, although she sleeps in another basilica. There also, in a separate church, rests Constantia, daughter of Constantine; and Saint Alexander, Saint Felix, Saint Papia, Saint Victor, and many others sleep there.

Beside the Salarian Way is the church of Saint Felicitas, where she lies bodily. There also her son Silvanus, one of the seven, is buried, and Boniface sleeps there with many saints. Beside the same road Saint Saturninus sleeps with many martyrs. Nearby are Saint Alexander, Saint Vitalis, and Saint Martialis, who are three of Felicitas’s seven sons; they lie there with many martyrs. There also rest seven virgins, namely Saint Saturnina, Saint Hilaria, Saint Dominanda, Saint Serotina, Saint Paulina, Saint Donata, and Saint Rogatina.

Beside the same Salarian Way Saint Sylvester rests, together with very many others, namely Saint [Col. 1160C] Caelestinus, Saint Potentiana, Saint Praxedis, Saint Marcellus, Saint Crescentianus, Saint Maurus, Saint Marcellinus, Saint Prisca, Saint Paul, one of the seven, Saint Philip, one of the seven, Saint Semetrius, and three hundred and sixty-two in one burial place.

Along the same road one comes to the church of Saint Michael, seven miles from the City. Not far from there, toward the west, beside the road, in underground crypts reached by eighty steps, lie Saint Pamphilus, Candidus, and Saint Cyprian, with many martyrs. Proceeding westward from there, the basilica of Saint Hermes appears, where the martyr himself lies. There are buried Saint Crispus, Saint Herculanus, Saint Maximilianus, Saint Basilissa, Saint Hyacinthus, Saint Protus, and Saint Leopardus, with many martyrs.

Not far from there, to the west, is the church of Saint John the martyr, where his head is placed beneath the altar in one place and his body in another. There are buried Saint Diogenes, Saint Sixtus, Saint Liberatus, Saint Blasius, Saint Maurus, and Saint Longina, John’s mother. From there, nearby, beside the Flaminian Way, appears the splendidly adorned church of Saint Valentinus the martyr, where he lies bodily and where many saints are buried.

## THESE CHURCHES, HOWEVER, ARE LOCATED WITHIN ROME

The Constantinian Basilica, also called that of the Savior; it is also called Saint John’s.

The basilica called Saint Mary Major.

The basilica called Saint Anastasia, where the crosses carried through the station churches are kept.

The basilica called Saint Mary Antiqua.

The basilica called Saint Mary Rotunda.

The basilica called Saint Mary across the Tiber; there is an image of Saint Mary that was made by itself.

The basilica called that of the apostles James and Philip.

The basilica called that of John and Paul, where both lie in one tomb.

The basilica called that of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

[Col. 1161A] The basilica called that of Saint Lawrence, where his gridiron is kept.

The basilica called Saint Peter ad Vincula, where the chain with which Peter was bound is kept.

The basilica called Saint Adrian.

The basilica called Saint Chrysogonus.

The basilica called Saint Clement.

The basilica called Saint Agatha.

[Col. 1162A] The basilica called Saint Stephen.

The basilica called Saint Mark.

The basilica called Saint Marcellinus.

The basilica called Saint Michael the archangel.

The basilica of Saint Boniface the martyr, where he sleeps.

In all these basilicas a public station is held at designated times.

# APPENDIX III

[Col. 1161]

Mai’s notice on the following chronicle.

[Col. 1161B] For a long time I had seen in the Vatican Palatine manuscript a certain Latin Chronicle; nevertheless, I had not turned my attention to preparing an edition of it, because, although the manuscript, written in Roman square script, should be assigned to approximately the eighth century, its Latinity is nevertheless extremely rough—or rather, as it now reads in the manuscript, it is afflicted by countless solecisms and astonishing corruptions. The historical yield also rarely seems to be new, since much of the work is occupied with expounding passages of the Gospel text tropologically. Finally, its catalogue of emperors is especially filled with intolerable errors.

Nevertheless, the exceptional antiquity of the manuscript, as suggested, I have said, by its kind of script; and, moreover, the conclusion of the Chronicle in the ninth year of Justin the Younger—that is, A.D. 574—which seems to indicate the age of the chronicler and the time of the work itself, since it does not even extend through the whole reign of Justin, which lasted thirteen years—these considerations, I say, were of such weight with me that I have now judged that this brief Chronicle should be transmitted in these pages of my volume, merely correcting here and there the most serious solecisms of its diction, especially since rough antiquity sometimes pleases more than polished novelty.

At the very beginning, and soon afterward in chapter 4, our chronicler sharpens his pen against the systems and chronological canons of the Scots. This leads me to suspect that he is an Englishman, or a Celt, or a Frank, who, as happens, rails against his neighbors or those closest to him. Certainly, one can see what the Latinity of the English or Franks was like in those times in the Grammarian Virgilius, in the Hesperian Sayings [Note: For the *Hesperian Sayings*, see Patrologia, vol. XC, col. 1185. EDITOR], and in the prefaces to the new lexicon, writings that we published elsewhere.

But does our chronicler oppose Bede’s then-recent book on the six ages of the world? I would not be greatly surprised if a Frank called Bede a Scot, since in former times the designation “Scots” extended more widely throughout [Col. 1162B] Britain than it does now. As for the matter itself, Bede certainly says that Christ was born in the sixth age of the world, but according to his system he denies that the sixth age had then been completed; indeed, he holds that it was still proceeding while he was alive. Our author expressly and emphatically contradicts this in chapter 24. But I am troubled to spend time on these minor questions, which I hope someone will examine more carefully at leisure.

What finally stirred my greatest astonishment was that, in the first ten chapters and in the catalogue of emperors, I found this chronicler agreeing with no one more closely than with the Greek John Malalas—whose very words he sometimes translates and reproduces—or at least with the authors whom Malalas cites: Clement, Theophilus, Timothy, and Eusebius. What follows from this? Did this Latin Englishman or Frank see the Greek work of Malalas of Antioch?

I set aside for the moment the controversy debated between Hody and Cave concerning Malalas’s date. Even leaving that aside, it seemed to me scarcely probable that an author from Antioch, and not one of great renown, had already reached the shores or islands of the Ocean, although it certainly reached them later; for Malalas’s work was found among the Bodleian manuscripts in England, from which an edition also proceeded.

Nor are we unaware that in the Middle Ages marvelous narrators, such as Malalas, or authors of new and unusual matters, were more commonly read than severe and sound historians. In any case, that Greek books were certainly well known in Gaul during the reign of Charles the Bald is demonstrated by the various labors of John Scotus and his mastery of the Greek language. We discussed this man in the fifth volume of the classical authors, where we published his poems, which breathe—or rather boast of—their Hellenism.

I therefore do not wish to indulge in conjectures any longer, since our Scholia will soon demonstrate the agreement of the Latin chronicler with the Greek Malalas.

[Col. 1161]

# THE MOST ANCIENT CHRONICLE DRAWN FROM THE PALATINE MANUSCRIPTS

*(Mai’s Roman Spicilegium.)* (C, S)

## HERE BEGINS THE AUTHORITY OF THE PRESENT WORK. CHRIST, FAVOR GOOD PETITIONS.

[Col. 1161D] 1. Now the time has come for truth, with the shining eyes of reason, to look upon everyone and reveal itself to them face to face; now, with a wiser effort, as though through the hidden channels of caverns, let truth disclose itself anew and whole from the womb. Now let not the scholars of the Scots deceive us with their long-winded speech, but let truth itself present itself to us through the clearest lips, dripping with nectar, so that it may remove from us all the bitterness of alien teaching; so that, while falsehood darkens the caves of gloom, its own truth may illuminate us from above with its light like the radiance of the sun; so that, fleeing falsehood, truth may embrace us; and so that, while the gloom of a dark night obstructs the true light of causes, the most joyful day may shine forth for all upon the face.

Now, therefore, if it pleases you, let us investigate the certain purposes of the world itself: at what time, in what age of the world, Christ the Savior appeared in the flesh, and under whose consulship and imperial rule this world was then being governed on earth, while the Son of God from heaven sat like a king in the womb of the Virgin.

The prologue ends.

## HERE BEGINS THE CHRONICLE-HISTORY, WHICH WAS ALSO EXPOUNDED IN LIKE MANNER BY CLEMENT, THEOPHILUS, AND TIMOTHY, MOST BELOVED BISHOPS OF GOD AND CHRONOGRAPHERS, AND BY EUSEBIUS PAMPHILUS, THE BELOVED CHRONOGRAPHER OF GOD

[Note: These very words are said in Greek by John Malalas, *Chronography*, part I, Venetian edition, p. 96; at this point our author is a mere translator. Further, concerning the authorities cited by Malalas from Clement, Theophilus, Timothy, and Eusebius, see Hody’s *Prolegomena*, nos. XXII, XXIII, and XXIV, which should nevertheless be compared with the contradictions in G. Cave’s article on Malalas.]

[Col. 1163A] **2.** In the forty-second year of Octavian Augustus Caesar, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was born. [Note: [Col. 1163D] The manuscript has “Eusebius” above instead.] For Eusebius says that, after the forty-first year and the sixth month of the reign of that Caesar had passed [Note: [Col. 1163D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* I.5.], in the month of Dystros—that is, according to the Latins, March—on the twenty-fifth day of the month, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, which according to the Greeks is called Xanthicus, at the second hour of the day, as the third day, Sunday, was beginning, the archangel Gabriel was sent to announce the good news to blessed Mary, in the Galilean city called Nazareth, during the consulship of [Note: [Col. 1163D] Malalas, or the historians cited by him, p. 95, have “Quintus and Longinus.” They likewise agree concerning the procurator Vitellius.] Quirinus and Longinus, when she had been betrothed to a man named Joseph, while Vitellius was governing Syria, who at that time was serving as a young man under that same Augustus Caesar. Therefore, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April—that is, at the spring equinox—the Lord was conceived in the Virgin’s womb.

For on that same day he also ascended the cross’s gallows and was afterward placed in the tomb. Other great deeds of the Lord also took place on that day: on that day this world itself received its beginning from God; then the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea as though on dry land; then the devil was conquered and cast down from heaven with his angels; and on that same day the Jews threw James, the Lord’s brother, down headlong from the pinnacle of the temple.

The Lord, then, was conceived in the Virgin’s womb on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, that is, on the twenty-fifth day of March. This was the forty-first year of the empire of Augustus Caesar, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the month Apellaeus, which is December, on the twenty-fifth day of the month, at the seventh hour of the day, in the Judaean city called Bethlehem, under Quirinus, former consul and governor of Syria; while the consulship belonged to that same Octavian Augustus and Silvanus [Note: [Col. 1163D] The historians cited by Malalas, p. 96, say the same.], and Herod the elder, son of Archelaus, was toparch of Judaea, as the evangelist testifies.

**3.** From Adam to Phaleg, son of Eber, three thousand years are reckoned. From Phaleg to the forty-second year of the reign of Augustus Caesar, 2,967 years are reckoned. Thus, from Adam, the first man, to the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and the forty-second year of the reign of Augustus Caesar, 5,967 years are reckoned. From that point our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ lived among human beings on earth for approximately thirty-three years, lacking a little.

Thus, from Adam to the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, to his passion on the cross, and to his assumption into heaven to the Father, a full six thousand years are completed. For Phaleg, according to the prophetic utterance of Moses, is said to have stood at the midpoint of time before the future coming of Christ in the incarnation. Just as God formed the human being from the earth on the sixth day, as Moses, that great recorder of times, set out in his writings, so he determined this: “One day of the Lord,” he says, “will be like a thousand years.”

Therefore, on the sixth day God fashioned the human being, and the human being fell under sin. This too becomes clearer in the following way: just as on the sixth day the human being was formed in paradise and fell into sin, so in the sixth millennium of the world Christ appeared upon earth and saved humanity, restoring it through the sign of the cross’s wood and through the resurrection from the dead [Note: [Col. 1164D] It is entirely apparent that this whole passage, and partly the following one as well, was taken from Malalas, pp. 96–97, or from the historians whom he cites.]

**4.** Clement, Theophilus, and Timothy, the most beloved bishops and chroniclers of God, likewise explained this, agreeing with one another here. But Eusebius Pamphili, the beloved chronicler of God, also says that Christ the Savior appeared in the sixth millennium of years, corresponding to the number of the six days of Adam’s formation, though before six thousand years had been completed.

“For,” he said, “the Lord God Jesus Christ, our Savior, appeared to rescue the human race; and,” he says, “having been born from a Virgin and made human, our Lord Jesus Christ suffered and rose again in the five-thousand-five-hundred-and-second year, and was taken up into heaven in the year of the world’s age from Adam, 5,533.” [Note: [Col. 1164D] Compare Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, Roman edition, book I, chapter 18, p. 92.]

All agree that the Lord appeared in the sixth millennium of years, although the *Scotti* do not wish to agree—those who think they possess wisdom but have lost knowledge—or else they have said that one year more and another less. In the sixth millennium of years, according to the prophetic utterance, all expressions agree, even though those who explained the number of years grow sluggish. Nevertheless, all have testified that the Savior appeared in the last times, as divine Scripture indicates.

For in the holy Gospels also you will find this event: one says that Christ was crucified at the third hour—namely, Mark—while the others assert that he was crucified upon the wood at the sixth hour. Thus, among the unlearned these statements may seem contradictory, but they are not contradictory to true reason, when divine Scripture thus coheres purely with itself [perhaps “equally”], provided that it is pondered and carefully interpreted by those who rely not on their own wisdom but on God’s.

**5.** When, then, the Lord Jesus had been born in Bethlehem, in the forty-second year of the reign of Augustus Caesar, under Herod king of the Jews and Quirinus governor of the province of Syria, the Son of God spent two years among human beings at the Virgin’s breast. Magi came from Persia, with a star providing them guidance. Then Herod the king [Note: [Col. 1164D] Again, our author takes much of what follows from Malalas.]—or toparch of the Jews—learned that scouts had come to the city of Jerusalem. Ordering them to be brought in, he began to question them.

They had come because they had learned, through the mysterious star that had appeared to them in the East, about the humanity of our Savior Jesus Christ. They brought him gifts as truly a great king and triumphant ruler, in accordance with what the heavenly star had announced to them. They, who had come from the eastern regions, also asked, saying: “Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews?” And the Jews were troubled.

Moreover, when the magi became known, they were seized and brought before Herod the king [Note: [Col. 1164D] Literally from Malalas: “These magi, once recognized, were seized and brought before King Herod.”]: and he asked them why they had come into Judaea as spies. The magi explained the miracle of the star, that a great king had been born into this world, and that they had come bringing gifts for him, intending to offer gifts to him as to a great king [Note: [Col. 1164D] In other manuscripts I have occasionally found *offertum* and *offerta* instead of *munera offerturi*.]. They said: “We are presenting to God the gifts that we have brought; for we saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him.”

When Herod heard this, he remained astonished, reflecting: “After Augustus Caesar, what sort of power belongs to this king who has been born?” [Note: [Col. 1164D] Everything is taken directly from Malalas, p. 97.]

**6.** The magi therefore came to Jerusalem during the consulship of [Col. 1164D] Vindicius and Varius [Note: [Col. 1164D] Malalas, p. 93, has “Valerius.”], in the forty-fourth year of the empire of Augustus Caesar, because the Savior had been born in the forty-second year of that same Augustus Caesar, and in the second year after his birth the magi came to Jerusalem.

Herod therefore asked them about the time when the star had appeared. When he had learned this, [Col. 1165A] he said to them: “Go and investigate this child carefully; and when you have found him, return and report to me, so that I too may come and worship him.”

The magi departed, and the star—which had withdrawn from them for a short while—again provided them guidance as before, the star they had seen in the East. They found Jesus and his mother Mary in a house; and, falling upon the floor, they worshiped Christ the Savior and offered him the gifts they had brought with them in their treasures: gold, frankincense, and myrrh, as to God and king.

After receiving an answer from an angel in a dream, they returned to their own region in the lands of the Persians by another route, disregarding King Herod. When King Herod saw that he had been mocked by the magi, he became exceedingly angry. He inquired of the leaders of the Jews where Christ was to be born, according to what the prophet had foretold; then, sending out an armed force, he killed all the boys in the city of Bethlehem of Judaea and throughout its surrounding territory, from two years old and younger, according to the time that he had ascertained from the magi, [Col. 1165B] as divine Scripture says.

Immediately after Herod had completed this crime, he was struck by God, swarming with worms, and gave up his soul [Note: [Col. 1165D] Malalas, p. 97.]

**7.** Archelaus, that same Herod’s son, became toparch—or king—in the tetrarchy of the Jews for eight years, during the consulship of [Note: [Col. 1165D] Malalas, in the passage cited, has “Lamias and Servilianus.”] Lamias and Servilianus. Under him the Savior and his virgin mother Mary entered Egypt with Joseph, in accordance with God’s command, communicated through an angel appearing to Joseph, as it is written: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a swift cloud; he will come into Egypt and shatter all the idols and carved images of the Egyptians together.”

At the Savior’s arrival, seated upon the lap of his virgin mother, as he entered Egypt, there was a temple of idols there. In Christ’s presence all their images leapt from their places and pedestals, were shattered, and were reduced to dust. Blessed Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, also records this.

When four years had been completed in Egypt, an angel again appeared to Joseph and commanded him to [Col. 1165C] return to the land of Judaea with the child and his mother. Because of fear of Archelaus, Herod’s son, he lived in the city of Nazareth in Galilee, as though in concealment. Everything happened according to what had previously been foretold by the holy prophets, as testimonies from the prophetic books are also brought forward in the Gospel.

**8.** When the child Jesus was already twelve years old, Joseph and Mary went up with the child Jesus to the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem, as the evangelist Luke relates. After this he no longer mentions Joseph, because, being an old man and full of days, a righteous man in all things, he rested in peace with his fathers. He lived until the Savior was twelve years old and thereafter rested, as the authority handed down by our fathers commends to us.

In the fifty-sixth year of his reign, in the month of October, which according to the Athenians is called Hyperberetaeus [Note: [Col. 1165D] Rather, according to the Macedonians.], Augustus Caesar went to the Capitol, which is in the middle of the city of Rome, to learn through divination who would reign after him in the Roman state. The prophetess told him that a Hebrew infant, descending from the heaven of the blessed at God’s command, would soon come into this dwelling; that he would be born without stain and would be a stranger to their altars.

Therefore, after leaving the divination, Augustus Caesar built a great altar in the Capitol, in a higher place, and wrote on it in Latin letters: “THIS IS THE ALTAR OF THE SON OF GOD.” On that site, after so many years, there was established the dwelling and basilica of blessed and ever-virgin Mary, which remains to the present day, as the chronicler Timothy also records [Note: [Col. 1165D] Timothy, in Malalas, p. 98, mentions only the altar erected by Augustus. Our author, therefore, was reading more in the Timothy whom he cites.]

[Col. 1166A] After this Augustus himself died in old age, when he was seventy-five years old.

**9.** After the reign of Augustus Caesar, during the consulship of [Note: [Col. 1165D] So also in Malalas, p. 98.] Sextus and Sexticianus, Tiberius Caesar began to reign, while the Lord Jesus Christ was among human beings and was fifteen years old.

In the fifteenth year of the reign of that same Tiberius Caesar, during the consulship of Silvanus and Nero [Note: [Col. 1165D] Malalas, p. 99, has “Albanus and Nerva.”], the holy John the Forerunner began to preach the baptism of repentance, and all Judaea was being baptized, according to the prophetic utterance.

Then the Lord Jesus Christ came to him from Galilee at the Jordan, beginning his thirtieth year—that is, twelve days beyond twenty-nine years—for he was born of the Virgin on the eighth day before the Kalends of January and was baptized with water on the eighth day before the Ides of January, after which he also began to perform miracles.

He was baptized in the Jordan River of Palestine, in the month Audinaeus, which is January, on the sixth day of the month, the eighth day before the Ides of January, at night, at the tenth hour of the night—that is, at dawn—during the consulship of Rufus and Rubellio.

From this point John the Baptist also became famous among human beings. Herod later beheaded him in prison, in the city of Sebastia, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, during the consulship of Falco and Rufinus, because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, since he had unlawfully taken her, as it is written [Note: [Col. 1166D] These things too are found in Malalas, p. 100.]

**10.** In the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar [Note: [Col. 1166D] Again from Malalas, p. 101.], in the seventh month of the eighteenth year of his reign, Jesus Christ our Lord, being about thirty-three years old, was betrayed by his disciple Judas Iscariot. It was the month of Dystros, which is March, the twenty-fourth day of the month, that is, the ninth day before the Kalends of April; the moon was thirteen days old, and it was the fifth day of the week, at the sixth hour of the night.

He was led to Caiaphas, the chief priest, and from there handed over to Pontius Pilate, the governor, early in the morning. Immediately Pilate’s wife, whose name was Procla, sent word to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for today I have suffered greatly in a dream because of him.”

When the Jews learned this, they stirred up a rebellion, saying: “Take him away, take him away; crucify him!” It was therefore the third hour when the Jews cried out aloud: “Crucify the Son of God!”

[Col. 1166C] After receiving the sentence, our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified specifically on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the month of March [Note: [Col. 1166D] Malalas has “the twenty-fourth.”], on the twenty-fifth day of the month, when the moon was thirteen days old. It was the sixth day, the day of Preparation, at the sixth hour of the day. The sun was darkened, and there was darkness throughout the whole world.

These things occurred in the eighteenth year of the empire of Tiberius Caesar, so that there was an exceedingly great eclipse of the sun, greater than those previously known to have occurred, and night came at the sixth hour of the day, so that the stars appeared in heaven. The Savior Jesus Christ gave up his spirit at the ninth hour.

Immediately there was [Note: [Col. 1166D] The manuscript reads, erroneously, “light.”] night over the whole earth, a great earthquake, the tombs were opened, and the rocks were split, and the dead rose, as is truthfully proclaimed in the divine Gospels. The Jews said: “Truly this was the Son of God whom we crucified.”

Jesus Christ was buried at the tenth hour, on that same day of Preparation, during the consulship of Sulpicius and [Note: [Col. 1166D] Malalas, p. 101, has *Sōla*; our author has *Solatius*. Both are corrupt readings for *Sulla*.] Solatius, while Cassius was governing Syria as governor.

**11.** Our Lord and God Jesus [Col. 1166D] Christ rose again in the month of Dystros, which is March, [Note: [Col. 1166D] Malalas has “the twenty-fifth.”] on the twenty-seventh day of the month, that is, the sixth day before the Kalends of April, at the tenth hour of the night, near dawn, as the day of Sunday was beginning, in that month of March, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, when the moon was sixteen days old.

He first appeared early in the morning to Mary Magdalene, and afterward to his apostolic disciples and to many other saints. After he had risen from the dead, he remained with them on earth for forty days.

Our Lord and God Jesus Christ was taken up into heaven in the month of Artemisius, which is [Col. 1167A] May, on the fifth day of the month, that is, the third day before the Nones of May, on the fifth day of the week, at the second hour, while the holy apostles and another crowd of disciples were watching how he was taken up by the clouds, with the holy angels saying:

“Why do you look into heaven, men of Galilee? This Jesus who has been taken up from you will come again in the same way as you see him going into heaven.”

According to the Lord’s promise, the holy life-giving Spirit descended upon the apostles in the month of Artemisius, which is May, [Note: [Col. 1167] Malalas has “the fourteenth.”] on the fifteenth day of the month, on Sunday, at the third hour, while Pontius Pilate—who had been appointed to rule the Jewish people by that same Tiberius Caesar—was governing Judaea. Tiberius dissolved the kingdom of the Jews and appointed over them as ruler whomever he wished, during the high priesthood of the Jewish priests Annas and Caiaphas [Note: [Col. 1167] Up to this point our chronicler has for the most part followed Malalas.]

**12.** At this point one may observe that everything Christ, our salvation and redemption, endured was accomplished in a human being complete with God. The fact that Christ was announced to the Virgin through an angel was intended to nullify the serpent’s plan against Eve in paradise.

The fact that he was born from a Virgin was on account of the first-created Adam, whom God made in his own image from virgin and undefiled earth. When Adam, persuaded by the devil, had incurred the destruction of death, his dwelling—both body and soul—was to be restored by the Lord Christ alone, the renewer and creator of all things, through Christ’s immortality.

The fact that he reached the limit of the tenth month in the Virgin’s womb—that is, completing six days beyond the ninth month—concerns the measure that none of the children of human beings reaches in birth through the seed, except Christ alone, the true Son of God and of humanity, born from a virgin without seed. Thus, when the days are gathered together into one total, they amount to 276.

This number is understood allegorically or through a typological inquiry, as he himself said in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” But the Jews, not understanding the key to the reasoning, brought forth a testimony to the truth, and replied to the Lord: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?”

But, says the evangelist, he was speaking about the temple of his body. The Jews could not grasp its dispensation, and therefore they brought before the Lord the number of years required to build the temple, which bore the form of the true temple. This number is read as having elapsed not under Solomon, the founder of that temple, but under Zerubbabel, who is also Ezra, its restorer, because the nations that surrounded it hindered the work. For Solomon completed the construction of the Lord’s temple in seven years.

**13.** Indeed, our Jesus, the peaceful Solomon, built for himself, through wisdom, in the most holy Virgin, the temple of his body according to this sacred number: nine months and six days. For every male birth reaches the beginning of the tenth month and thus emerges into the openness of this life.

According to the authority of our elders and predecessors, the conception of the human race is said or read to occur in the following order: for six days the seed lies in the womb, resembling milk; afterward it changes into blood until the eighth day; then it increases until the twelfth; afterward eighteen more days are added, and it is immediately coagulated and stretches toward the outlines of the limbs. Six and eight, twelve and eighteen together make forty-five. Add one, and they make forty-six. From there one proceeds by parts: six times forty makes 240; and again, the same number through six times six makes thirty-six, thirty-six times six, which together in one total make 276.

Therefore, in the Lord alone one day falls beyond the forty-five, because of his unique incarnation from a virgin, without corruption or the coagulation of seed. Just as, according to the type of the historical temple, built over forty-six years, so Christ, restoring the wall of his human body by this progression in himself—the wall that the cunning serpent, the devil, had overthrown in Adam through his deceptions—would restore that saving structure; and, after suffering, would raise it up on the third day, never again to die; and thus would free every human being from subjection [Col. 1168A] to the devil.

For forty-six signifies the sixth age that the world was undergoing when the restorer of his own work came; and through the number of perfection, forty, he demonstrated perfect repentance to penitents by the fast. Hence the Savior himself, tempted by the devil as a human being, emerged victorious. Thus, as God, through the number forty and six and the doubled third, he fermented and coagulated the entire mass of the human race into one kneaded mixture of faith.

**14.** The fact that he was brought forth from a woman’s womb, placed in a manger, and wrapped in swaddling clothes was on account of the verse in which God had promised David by an oath, saying: “From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne.”

The manger is said to be the whole world, in which the Lord of majesty supplies food to his rational animals. He is wrapped in swaddling clothes because he endured our miseries; applying poultices to us in them, he provided medicine for our wounds.

The fact that Christ wished to be born in Bethlehem, the city of Judaea—so the manuscript reads [Col. 1168B]—was on account of what had earlier been proclaimed to Jacob as he fled, when, having fallen asleep, he saw a ladder there reaching to heaven, saw the angels of God ascending and descending, and saw God resting at the top. He said: “This is truly the house of God and the gate of heaven”; hence it is called Bethel.

And the stone that Jacob had placed beneath his head, in the likeness of that cornerstone [“he raised it as a monument”], to which he joined two walls coming from opposite directions, he united in himself: namely, the joining together of the peoples, Jews and Gentiles, bringing peace to both.

The fact that he was wonderfully found by shepherds, or watchmen, and that he was worshiped in the cradle, bore the type of the excellent shepherds whom Christ, the master of the household, appointed over male and female servants, commanding them anxiously and carefully to distribute the measure of wheat justly.

Or it signified the one to whom he said three times, entrusting him with the command: “Feed my sheep,” lest, disturbed by the assault of wolves, they lose their pastures—that is, my pleasing will.

**15.** The fact that he was worshiped by the magi, the first of all the nations [Col. 1168C] and peoples, signifies that the creator and ruler of all was to come; that he would be believed in by the nations; and that in the offering of gifts he would be worshiped as God and king.

Myrrh is also said to have been apportioned for his burial, so that through the three kinds of gifts—gold for the king, frankincense for God, and myrrh for the one who was to die—the holy and undivided Trinity, one deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, might be worshiped in Christ, believed in throughout the world, and proclaimed among the nations.

The fact that the star provided the magi with guidance was on account of what is written: “A star,” he says, “will arise from Jacob, and a man will rise in Israel, and he will shatter all the leaders of foreign peoples.” And also: “All will come from Sheba, bringing gold, frankincense, and myrrh, proclaiming the salvation of the Lord.”

The fact that he was persecuted by Herod, the treacherous and bloodthirsty king, was so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: “A voice was heard on high”—that is, in Rama—“weeping and great mourning; Rachel weeping for her children, and she did not wish to be comforted because they are not.”

For Herod, deceived by the magi, raged against Christ. As though he could slaughter the one whom the wretched man feared would succeed him, by killing one infant, he impiously and cruelly slaughtered thousands of little children. But, warned in a dream by a holy angel, Joseph took the child and his mother into Egypt. Herod, meanwhile, burdened by the guilt of the innocent children and condemned by his own judgment, put an army of infants to death.

**16.** The fact that Christ endured circumcision in the flesh was on account of what the Apostle says: “For Christ,” he says, “must be believed to have been a minister of circumcision”; and also the passage from Exodus:

“When Moses was departing for Egypt at the Lord’s command, and his wife accompanied him with their children, an angel met him, intending to kill him. Then Zipporah, struck with fear, took a stone and circumcised the child; and because of the child’s circumcision blood, the angel spared him and did not kill him.”

Therefore, through Christ’s circumcision all the wrath of the law ceased, and his blood bore the harsh burdens, since Christ is the end of the law, who released us from the curse of antiquity and freed us from the yoke of slavery.

The fact that he is said to have increased in wisdom also, before God and human beings, means that he possessed the full and perfect completeness of a human being in the course of life. Thus, when he began his thirtieth year, he voluntarily sought baptism from John in the Jordan, on account of what the Apostle says: “Until we all,” he says, “arrive at the perfect man, at the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.”

**17.** God also formed the first human being from the earth with a perfect age, endowed with understanding and reason, so that he might be the governor of his own will and free choice. He likewise brought forth his wife from the side of the sleeping man, fully marriageable in years, a virgin in breast, beautiful in every limb, and already mature—not as an infant.

For it is not to be believed that God first made them from the clay of the earth with the movements of little children, or with the tender minds of boys shaking within small bodies, impeded in their feet, hands, tongues, speech, and actions. Rather, he made them full in age, reason, solidity of limbs, and wisdom, so that offspring might be generated from their substance—just as branches or fruits from a tree appear at first delicate and afterward gradually mature and become firm.

Thus every sound and solid nature displays whatever it produces, while God the creator restores it as he generates. It must likewise be believed that the human being, made by the Lord at the beginning, was of proper age, full in mind, and capable of reason—so that he might have gained victory if he had commanded the author of death.

For this reason he incurred the penalty of death: not as a child, with childish movement and weak understanding, but as a human being full of reason he sinned in paradise, because sin was imputed to him who knew how to do good and did not do it.

He is renewed by the grace of the Creator, who not only crowned little ones when he was born but also subdued the devil when he suffered, granting us what he himself accomplished in the flesh: so that, likewise through Christ’s resurrection, every soul may rise at the age of thirty in this same flesh in which it lived while in the body, so that each person may receive according to what he did in the body, whether good or evil.

**18.** The fact that Christ willingly received baptism from John was so that you would not disdain to receive it from a fellow servant. Though he was not indebted, but Lord, he wished to receive baptism without sin from a servant, so that amid the very waters of the Jordan the authority of the holy Trinity might be revealed concerning the one mediator between God and human beings: God the Father in the voice, the Son in the human being, and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove—one divinity, a constant and undivided deity and majesty.

The fact that he was driven by the Spirit into the desert signifies that he had become a human being in the flesh, which he had assumed on account of the old Adam. The devil had conquered the old Adam amid the delights of paradise; here Christ, wishing to engage the enemy in the desert, gained victory over him through the gift of fasting, so that he might hand him over to be trampled underfoot by all his faithful.

The prophet Zechariah had sung beforehand of this victory, saying: “I saw,” he says, “Jesus the great priest, and the devil stood at his right hand”—that is, on the side of justice—“preparing his deceits. And I said to him: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, devil, the one who redeems Israel and has chosen Jerusalem.’”

Thus he conquered for us, because he alone was able to gain victory over the devil.

The fact that he made disciples from fishermen was so that he might establish the twelve pillars of the Church as its leaders, not from the nobility of applauding bloodlines, but humbly from the flock of the poor who possessed understanding—just as the twelve patriarchs of that assembly came from Jacob.

For in the New Testament each tribe of Israel produced one apostle, as though twelve living stones from the bed of the Jordan. Thus they traversed the whole world like the months of the year, containing within themselves the sun of righteousness; and they enclosed souls wandering amid the waves of exile with the luminous commandments of God, as though in fishing nets [the manuscript reads *lina*], into the midst of the Church by their hands.

For he says: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of human beings.”

**19.** The fact that he willingly bore our weaknesses and illnesses, as I think Isaiah had foretold, running through everything as a giant through the road, requires us to consider how, by consecrating the Church in himself, he commended each of its degrees—that is, how he sanctioned its being entrusted to the altar through seven grades of ministry [Col. 1170B]. They are: doorkeeper, gravedigger [Note: [Col. 1169D] This passage is highly significant for assessing the antiquity of this *Chronicle*. The ancient author of the letter on the orders of the Church (*St. Jerome, Works*, final volume, p. 115) says: “The first order among clerics is that of the gravediggers,” whereas our author places it second. Aringhi observes (*Roman Subterranean Antiquities* I, p. 60) that these gravediggers, ministers of the Church, are called κοπῶντας (*kopōntas*, “toilers”) by St. Ignatius in his letter to the Antiochenes, and κοπιατὰς (*kopiatas*, “laborers”) by St. Epiphanius in *The Exposition of the Faith* [Col. 1170D]. Boldetti discusses these Christian gravediggers, or fossors, learnedly in *On the Cemeteries* I.15, and presents an image found in the sacred crypts with the inscription: “DIOGENES, GRAVEDIGGER, LAID TO REST IN PEACE,” and so forth. Concerning the variety and number of the minor orders in different Churches, it will also be useful to read what Joseph Assemani writes in his dissertation *On Coptic Ecclesiastical Matters*, *Ancient Writers*, vol. V, part II, p. 187.], reader, subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, and bishop.

Christ fulfilled these seven grades in the flesh. He was a doorkeeper when he opened and again closed the door of the ark. He was a gravedigger when he called Lazarus out of the tomb, already foul-smelling on the fourth day. He was a reader when he opened the book of the prophet Isaiah in the middle of the synagogue before the ears of the people, read it, and, when he had rolled it up again, handed it to the attendant.

He was a subdeacon when he poured water into a basin and humbly, of his own accord, washed the feet of the disciples. He was a deacon when he blessed the cup and offered it to his apostles to drink. He was a presbyter when he blessed the bread and likewise handed it to them. He was a bishop when, in the temple, he taught the people the kingdom of God as one possessing authority.

Saint Ephraem also commemorates these things in a similar manner.

**20.** The fact that he was sold to the Jews by his own disciple for thirty pieces of silver was prefigured earlier in Joseph, who was sold by his brothers to the Ishmaelites.

The fact that he is described as bound by the Hebrew attendants was so that he might release those who were held captive in fetters by the devil and break the bonds of sins.

The fact that he was struck in the face with open hands gave us true freedom. The fact that his head was beaten with blows restored our head to health. The fact that he was smeared with filthy spittle wiped disgrace from our face. The fact that his back was struck with whips removed from us the wounds of death and the devil’s scourges.

The fact that he stood before the tribunal of Pontius Pilate took away from us the terror and fear of the judges and rulers of this world. The fact that he endured many false witnesses confirmed the testimony of his saints against the impious.

The fact that he was reckoned among the wicked was so that he might show adoptive sons to be participants in the angels through faith. The fact that he received one and rejected another was so that he might demonstrate the difference between humility and pride, and how far despair is from the hope of salvation, or clemency from malice.

The fact that he was fastened with nails signified that the sting of death, which had been exceedingly burdensome to us, had been destroyed. The fact that his garments fell by lot was so that the lot of the saints might be made firm in heaven.

**21.** The fact that, by his own power, he brought his death to completion, saying, “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, gave up his spirit, was on account of the statement: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again.” He offered himself voluntarily to the Father as a sacrifice for us.

The fact that he alone, one and the same, was free among the dead was so that our mortality might be given life through his immortality.

The fact that the legs of the others were broken, while his were not broken at all, was on account of what had been foretold: “You shall not break a bone of him” [the manuscript reads *ossum*]. For he is the paschal lamb to be slaughtered for the people. By his holy blood he led the fathers with their children from Egypt to the promised land, through the midst of the sea reddened by his own blood, after striking Pharaoh and drowning him with his attendants in the depths of the waters.

The fact that he was taken down from the cross and placed in a tomb was so that he might consecrate the burial of all the saints and remove the fear of death.

The fact that he descended into the lower regions of the earth, while he did not withdraw from the heavenly seat or from the Father’s bosom, was so that he might lead his own out from the prison’s bondage, destroy the devil’s power, crush the dominion of death, abolish the power of hell, and grant his kingdom not only to the righteous but also to the thief.

The fact that he rose from the dead after three days [Col. 1171B] gave life to the dead, displayed the first fruits of the resurrection, and strengthened the hearts of all the faithful for the resurrection to come.

The fact that he remained with his disciples for forty days after his resurrection was so that he might subdue the hearts of unbelievers and bestow upon his Church the gifts of the law fourfold.

22. Now, the fact that he is recorded as having ascended into heaven on the fortieth day was so that to the one to whom it had been said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return,” it might afterward be said, once victory had been won over the devil in Christ: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” Thus, ascending, Christ led captivity captive, and in accordance with his promise he gave gifts to human beings on the day of Pentecost. Christ ascended to the Father, and the Holy Spirit descended to the people. The one who descended also ascended above the heavens, in order to fulfill all things. But when the Paraclete descended to the apostles, through him all things in heaven and on earth are confirmed. For through the Holy Spirit gifts are bestowed upon all the faithful, as the Apostle says: “To one, indeed, is given the utterance of wisdom according to the same Spirit; to another, the utterance of knowledge; to another, the grace of healings; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of tongues, by the one same Spirit,” and so forth.

[Col. 1171C] God and Christ perform all these gifts in the same Holy Spirit, who is the fullness of the one divinity and substance; for it is recognized that the three persons and three subsistences are one divinity and essence. For who could adequately set forth, in due order, how many gifts are bestowed upon the Church by the one and same Lord Christ? Whatever, therefore, was accomplished in Christ’s birth, whatever in his age, whatever in his preaching, whatever in his passion, whatever in Christ’s resurrection, whatever in the Lord’s ascension, whatever in the utterance of all languages by the divine Spirit, was done as a sacrament or ministry of the holy catholic Church and was carried out for the increase of the children of God.

[Col. 1171D] 23. But now let me return to the point from which I digressed (thus the manuscript), so that I may prove that Christ came at the end of the ages as mediator between God and human beings in the flesh, just as we explained above, with the Apostle preaching after he said: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman,” and so forth. The evangelist John also says in his Epistle: “Little children, it is the last hour.” And blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, says the same in his Epistle: “Let this not be hidden from you,” he says, “that with God one thousand years are like one day, and one day like one thousand years.”

For this world is said to have been perfected by God in six days, together with everything that is in it; and God is proclaimed to have rested from his work on the seventh day—that is, when the course of the world had been completed, God rests in the human being. For after the work of the sixth day, we do not read that this or that was made; rather, it says: “God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” Therefore every human being rests from his work, or this world from its occupations, as on the seventh day, after its sixth age, just as God rested from all his work. It is therefore now the Sabbath, so that no worker in God’s vineyard may be found, until the one who promised suddenly comes, after the end of the world, to rest in all his saints. For the first day, on which the beginnings of the world were made, he has made an eighth day for us through the resurrection, on which God granted rest to the saints.

24. Therefore the sixth millennium of this world’s age has been completed, although those who do not wish to understand this contradict it, and the seventh is now in progress [Note: [Col. 1171D] Recall what we said in the preceding warning.]. This age does not know the day of its festivity and its duration, nor the hour and day of its end; for, as is announced in the Apocalypse, at the seventh trumpet, or in the seventh bowl of God’s wrath, the words of God will be fulfilled.

[Col. 1172B] But lest anyone think that the world will complete seven millennia in the course of its duration, he will in no way find this stated beforehand, since this world will have rest on the Sabbath day; rather, the hour and day are declared by the Lord to be unknown to angels and human beings. For he says: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone.”

And lest anyone, thinking in a carnal manner, suppose that the Father knows something of which the Son is ignorant, and thereby fall entangled in heresy, the Lord wished rather to signify this: because the Son, remaining in the Father, knows all things together with him. For whatever the Father does is one with the Son and the Holy Spirit, without whom he does nothing. And whatever the Holy Spirit does is one with the Father and the Son, without whom he does nothing. Therefore whatever the Father knows, the Son and the Holy Spirit likewise know everything together with him. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and inseparable divinity, ineffably abiding in itself, and it knows and comprehends all things.

But since the seventh day is already hastening toward rest, [Col. 1172C] this world—that is, the elements themselves—must necessarily rest from servitude, so that the Lord may rest in his saints, and they may rest perpetually in him from all agitation. Then the righteous will truly keep Sabbath with the Lord, and the first day will become an eighth in the resurrection of the saints, when the threshing floor has been winnowed and the grain has been separated from the chaff, when what is now hidden will no longer be hidden. For what, I ask, is the world seen to be, while it appears worthless? Thus it is now completing its perfection beyond 6,000 years [Note: [Col. 1171D] That is, beyond the sixth millennium of years.] in the number of the Gospel, so that it may be present for the salvation of those who are to come, to the extent that the Divinity itself has granted—he alone knows how much may be expedient for us.

25. Let us therefore begin the years of those Caesars or emperors during which they reigned.

Let it be permitted to explain matters from the Savior’s coming in the flesh according to the chronological sequence.

Augustus, who was also Caesar or emperor Octavian, reigned for 55 years; but in the 42nd year of his reign [Col. 1172D] Christ was born in the flesh from the Virgin.

Tiberius reigned for 22 and a half years. In the fifteenth year of his reign, however, the Lord Jesus was baptized in the Jordan River by John the Forerunner. In the eighteenth year of the reign of that same Tiberius Caesar, the same Lord Jesus Christ suffered; and he revealed to us the saving and precious wood of the cross, on which he joined the Church to himself through blood and water from his own side. After Tiberius,

Gaius reigned for 4 years and 7 months.

Claudius reigned for 14 years and 9 months.

Nero reigned for 13 years and 2 months.

Galba reigned for 1 year and 7 months.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] Malalas calls him Lucius Otho, p. 109. In both places this is erroneous in place of Salvius.] Lucius reigned for 3 months.

Vitellius reigned [Note: [Col. 1172D] Our author takes this major error from the historians whom he follows, Malalas, p. 110. Therefore delete the years and retain the months.] for 9 years, 8 months, and a half.

[Col. 1173A] Vespasian reigned for 9 years and 10 months.

Titus reigned for 2 years. These men conquered Judaea and Jerusalem after the Lord’s passion, killing to the last those who remained unbelieving. For the faithful, divinely protected in the place called Pella, were saved.

Domitian reigned for 15 years and 2 months. Under him the blessed John, the apostle and evangelist, eloquent in divine speech, was brought into the city of Rome; he remained in this world until then, and Domitian released him, and he went to Ephesus. After Domitian,

Nerva reigned for 1 year and 1 month.

Trajan reigned for 19 years and 6 months.

Hadrian reigned for 22 years.

Antoninus Pius reigned for 23 years.

Marcus reigned for 18 years and 9 months.

Antoninus Verus reigned [Note: [Col. 1173C] A serious error concerning the reign of Lucius Verus, who reigned for nine years together with Marcus and died before him. Malalas also goes badly astray here.] for 1 year.

Commodus reigned [Note: [Col. 1173C] So too Malalas, whom Chilmealdus has already corrected, arguing for 12 rather than 22.] for 22 years and 8 months.

Pertinax reigned for 1 year, 2 months, and 18 days.

[Col. 1173B] Didius Julianus, who was also Salvius, reigned for 7 months.

Septimius Severus Afrus (thus the manuscript) reigned for 17 years, 8 months, and a half.

Antoninus Geta reigned for 1 year.

Antoninus Caracalla, son of Severus, reigned for 6 years and 22 days.

Valerian reigned [Note: [Col. 1173C] A most egregious error, into which Malalas himself also falls, p. 126.] for 6 years.

Macrinus Gallus (thus the manuscript) reigned for 1 year and 7 months.

Another Antoninus reigned for 3 years and 2 months.

Alexander (thus the manuscript), Mammaea’s son, reigned [Note: [Col. 1173C] Rather, 14 years.] for 8 years and 4 months.

[Note: [Col. 1173C] That is, Maximinus.] Maximus reigned for 4 years and 10 months.

Balbinus reigned for 1 year and 3 months.

Pupienus reigned for 3 and a half months.

Gordian reigned for 22 days.

Another Gordian reigned [Note: [Col. 1173C] This is a fiction.] for 20 years (thus the manuscript).

Gordian III reigned for 6 years.

[Note: [Col. 1173C] Marcus is fabricated here as well.] Marcus reigned for 6 years.

[Col. 1173C] Philip reigned for 6 and a half years.

[Col. 1174A] Valerian reigned for 2 and a half years.

Gallus the Younger reigned for 5 months.

Decius reigned for 1 year and 8 months.

Aemilianus reigned for 4 months.

Valerian reigned for 6 years.

Gallienus, who was also Licinius, reigned for 14 years.

Claudius, who was also [Note: [Col. 1174C] Malalas has Ἀπολλιανός, “Apollianus.”] Pullianus, reigned for 9 years.

Quintilianus reigned for 17 days.

Amelianus reigned for 6 years.

Tacitus reigned for 7 months.

Florianus reigned for 2 months.

Aelius Robus reigned for 3 years and 3 months.

Carus reigned for 2 years.

Numerianus reigned for 2 years.

Carinus reigned for 2 years.

[Note: [Col. 1174C] Licinius is to be understood.] Licinianus reigned for 7 years (thus the manuscript).

Diocletian and Maximian reigned for 19 years.

Constantine the Great reigned for 32 years.

Constantius reigned for 1 year [Note: [Col. 1174C] This too is monstrous.].

[Col. 1174B] Julian the Apostate reigned for 7 years [Note: [Col. 1174C] Correct to 2, as in Malalas.].

Jovian reigned for 7 and a half months.

Valentinian reigned for 17 years.

Valens reigned for 13 years [Note: [Col. 1174C] Malalas likewise has this.].

Gratian reigned for 7 years and 10 months.

Theodosius the Great reigned for 17 years.

Arcadius reigned for 23 years.

Honorius reigned for 31 years.

Theodosius the Younger reigned for 48 years.

Marcian reigned for 6 years and 5 months.

Leo the Great reigned for 16 years and 11 months.

Leo the Younger reigned for 1 year and 22 days.

Zeno reigned for 15 years and 2 months.

Anastasius reigned for 27 years, 9 months, and 9 days.

Justin reigned for 9 years and 22 days.

Justinian reigned for 39 and a half years.

Justin reigned for 9 years.

[Col. 1174C] THE CHRONICLE ENDS. THANKS BE TO GOD. AMEN [Note: [Col. 1174C] This is the conclusion of the Chronicle, lest anyone should think that the work in the manuscript is mutilated. It therefore ends in the ninth year of Justin the Younger, whom we know to have reigned for thirteen years. Thus our chronographer was completing his writing while Justin was still emperor.].

[Col. 1173]

APPENDIX IV. A BRIEF CHRONICLE FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE WORLD TO THE YEAR OF CHRIST 810. From an ancient manuscript codex of Bede’s *On the Reckoning of Time*, which belonged to the church or monastery of Saint-Denis in France.

(Duchesne, *Writers of the History of the Franks*, vol. III.)

THE FIRST AGE.

[Col. 1173D]

When Adam was 130 years old, he begot Seth. Seth, being 105 years old, begot Enos, while Adam was alive and 235 years old. Enos, being 90 years old, begot Cainan, while Adam was alive and 325 years old. Cainan, being 70 years old, begot Mahalaleel, while Adam was alive and 395 years old. Mahalaleel, being 65 years old, begot Jared, while Adam was alive and [Col. 1174D] 460 years old. Jared, being 162 years old, begot Enoch, while Adam was alive and 622 years old. Enoch, being 65 years old, begot Methuselah, while Adam was alive and 687 years old. Methuselah, being 187 years old, begot Lamech, while Adam was alive and 874 years old. Lamech, being 172 years old, begot Noah. Noah, being 500 years old, begot Shem. When Shem was 100 years old, the Flood took place. [Col. 1175A] Here the total of 1,666 years is completed.

THE SECOND AGE.

In the second year after the Flood, Shem, being 102 years old, begot Arphaxad. Arphaxad, being 35 years old, begot Shelah. Shelah, being 30 years old, begot Eber. Eber, being 34 years old, begot Peleg. Peleg, being 30 years old, begot Reu. Reu, being 32 years old, begot Serug. Serug, being 30 years old, begot Nahor. Nahor, being 29 years old, begot Terah. Terah, being 70 years old, begot Abraham. Here the total of the second age ends at 292 years, and the years of the two ages together amount to 1,948.

THE THIRD AGE.

Abraham, when he was 100 years old, begot Isaac. Isaac, being 60 years old, begot Jacob. Jacob, being 90 years old, begot Joseph, who lived 110 years. From him until the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt under Moses as leader, there were [Col. 1175B] 165 years. From Israel’s departure until Joshua, 40 years. From Joshua, therefore, until Othniel, there are 26 years. From Othniel until Ehud, 40 years. From Ehud until Deborah, 80 years. From Deborah until Gideon, 40 years. From Gideon until Abimelech, 40 years. From Abimelech until Tola, 3 years. From Tola until Jair, 23 years. From Jair until Jephthah, 22 years. From Jephthah until Ibzan, 6 years. From Ibzan until Elon, 7 years. From Elon until Abdon, 10 years. From Abdon until Samson, 8 years. From Samson until Eli, 20 years. From Eli until Samuel, 40 years. From Samuel until Saul, 12 years. From Saul until David, 30 years. Here the total of the third age is completed at 942 years, and the years of the three ages together amount to 2,890.

THE FOURTH AGE.

[Col. 1175C]

From David until Solomon, 40 years. From Solomon until Rehoboam, 40 years are reckoned. From Rehoboam until Abijah, 22 years. From Abijah until Asa, 3 years. From Asa until Jehoshaphat, 41 years. From Jehoshaphat until Jehoram, 25 years. From Jehoram until Azariah, 8 years. From Azariah until Athaliah, 1 year. From Athaliah until Joash, 6 years. From Joash until Amaziah, 40 years. From Amaziah until Uzziah, 29 years. From Uzziah until Jotham, 52 years. From Jotham until Ahaz, 16 years. From Ahaz until Hezekiah, 16 years. From Hezekiah until Manasseh, 29 years. From Manasseh until Amon, 55 years. From Amon until Josiah, 2 years. From Josiah until Jehoiakim, 31 years. From Jehoiakim until Zedekiah, 11 years. From Zedekiah until Nebuchadnezzar, 11 years. Here the total of the fourth age ends, containing 483 years, and the years of the four ages amount to 3,363.

THE FIFTH AGE.

The years of the fifth age up to Cyrus amount to 30. From Cyrus until Cambyses, 30 years. From Cambyses until Darius, 9 years. From Darius until Xerxes, 35 years. From Xerxes until Artaxerxes, 21 years. From Artaxerxes until Darius, 40 years. From Darius until another Artaxerxes, 18 years. From Artaxerxes until another Artaxerxes, 40 years. From Artaxerxes until Arses, 26 years. From Ars(es) until Darius, 4 years. From Darius until Alexander, 6 years. From Alexander until Ptolemy, 5 years. From Ptolemy until Philadelphus, 40 years. From Philadelphus until Euergetes, 38 years. From Euergetes until Philopator, 26 years. From Philopator until Epiphanes, [Col. 1176A] 17 years. From Epiphanes until Philometor, 24 years. From Philometor until another Euergetes, 35 years. From Euergetes until Soter, 29 years. From Soter until Alexander, 17 years. From Alexander until Ptolemy, 10 years. From Ptolemy until Dionysius, 13 years. From Dionysius until Cleopatra, 30 years. From Cleopatra until Julius Caesar, 2 years. From Julius until Octavian Augustus, 5 years. From Octavian until Christ, 42 years. Here the fifth age ends, containing 580 years, and the years of the five ages together amount to 3,952.

THE SIXTH AGE.

From the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ until Tiberius, 14 years are counted. From Tiberius until Christ’s Passion, 19 years. From Christ’s Passion until Gaius, 5 years. From Gaius until Claudius, 4 years. From Claudius until Nero, [Col. 1176B] 14 years. From Nero until Vespasian, 14 years. From Vespasian until Titus, 14 years. From Titus until Domitian, 2 years. From Domitian until Nerva, 16 years. From Nerva until Trajan, 1 year. From Trajan until Hadrian, 14 years. From Hadrian until Antoninus, 21 years. From Antoninus until another Antoninus, 23 years. From Antoninus until Commodus, 19 years. From Commodus until Helvius Pertinax, 13 years. From Helvius until Severus, 1 year. From Severus until Antoninus Caracalla, 18 years. From Antoninus Caracalla until Macrinus, 7 years. From Macrinus until Aurelius, 1 year. From Aurelius until Alexander, 4 years. From Alexander until Maximinus, 13 years. From Maximinus until Gordian, 3 years. From Gordian until Philip, 7 years. From Philip until Decius, 7 years. From Decius until Valerian, 3 years. From Valerian until Claudius, 15 years. From Claudius [Col. 1176C] until Aurelian, 2 years. From Aurelian until Probus, 6 years. From Probus until Carus, 5 years. From Carus until Diocletian, 2 years. From Diocletian until Constantine, 20 years. From Constantine until Constantius, 21 years. From Constantius until Julian, 24 years. From Julian until Jovian, 2 years. From Jovian until Valentinian, 1 year. From Valentinian until Valens, 11 years. From Valens until Theodosius, 4 years. From Theodosius until Arcadius, 27 years. From Arcadius until Honorius, 13 years. From Honorius until Theodosius, 15 years. From Theodosius until Marcian, 26 years. From Marcian until Leo, 6 years. From Leo until another Leo, 17 years. Again, from Leo until Zeno, 1 year. From Zeno until Anastasius, 16 years. From Anastasius until Justin, 27 years. From Justin until Justinian, 9 years. Again, from Justinian until Justin, [Col. 1176D] 39 years. Again, from Justin until Tiberius, 13 years. From Tiberius until Maurice, 4 years. From Maurice until Phocas, 20 years. From Phocas until Heraclius, 8 years. From Heraclius until Constantine, 30 years. From Constantine the father until Constantine the son, 1 year. Again, from Constantine until Constantine, 27 years. From Constantine until Justinian, 17 years. From Justinian until Pippin the Elder, 2 years. From Pippin the Elder until Charles, 27 years. From Charles until Pippin and Carloman, 27 years. From Pippin and Carloman until Pippin was made king, 10 years. From Pippin until Charles and Carloman, 17 years. From Charles and Carloman until Charles, 4 years. From that time lord Charles alone assumed the kingdom and, with God protecting him, governs it prosperously up to the present year, which is the 42nd year of his reign but the 9th of his empire. The total number of years from the origin of the world to the present year is [Col. 1177A] 4,761.

691. Pippin’s battle at Tertry, where he defeated the Franks.

702. The death of King Childebert.

708. When Drogo died in the springtime.

709. When Pippin marched into Swabia against Wilarius.

713. Afterward, under Bishop Dubertus, in the month of March.

714. Afterward, under Grimoald in the month of April, and under Pippin in the month of December.

715. When the Saxons ravaged the land of the Chattuarii.

[Col. 1177B] 716. When Radbod came to Cologne in the month of March.

717. There was a battle between Charles and Ragenfred at Vinchy, in the month of March, in mid-Lent, on Sunday.

718. Charles was in Saxony for the first time.

719. Radbod died.

720. Charles fought against the Saxons.

721.

722.

723.

724.

726.
